Since <s>saṃskāra</s> too has some connection with the object — either as an indicator or as an effect — the same [consequence] applies, and thus validity would attach even to it, the cause of apprehension in the form of memory. This is not so, because it is excluded by the word <s>pramāṇa</s>. For <s>pramāṇa</s> is the instrument of <s>pramā</s> (veridical cognition), and memory is not <s>pramā</s>. For the connection between word and meaning is determined by common usage (<s>loka</s>). And common usage designates as <s>pramā</s> an apprehension other than memory — one born from <s>saṃskāra</s> alone — that is non-deviating with respect to the object. Therefore, that which is the cause of that [pramā] is <s>pramāṇa</s>, and there is no unwanted consequence regarding the cause of memory. And the property of apprehending what has not been previously apprehended — we do not regard this as negating the <s>pramāṇa</s>-status of streaming cognitions (<s>dhārāvāhikavijñāna</s>) that have previously apprehended objects as their domain, whose <s>pramāṇa</s>-status is well-established in common usage. Nor is it proper to say that streaming cognitions have objects not previously apprehended due to temporal difference, since we, with our fleshy eyes, cannot discern the most subtle distinctions of temporal moments. Nor should one say that because the object has been displayed by the very first cognition, and because the person has been prompted to act, and because of the attainment [of the object] — therefore these subsequent cognitions are not <s>pramāṇas</s>. For the leading of cognition to an object is nothing other than prompting, and prompting too is nothing other than displaying the object. Therefore, cognition whose sole function is the mere display of the object is both the prompter and the one that leads [to the object]. And the display is the same — undifferentiated — for subsequent cognitions as for the prior one; so how is only the first cognition a <s>pramāṇa</s> and not the subsequent ones also? If validity depends on the person's [need], then there would be the unwanted consequence that cognition of the moon, stars, and the like — which is not needed by a person — would not be a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And it is not the case that even cognition of such objects is needed by the person due to the great distance or the avoidability of its objects, since it has objects that are to be disregarded. And that what is to be disregarded, though not to be adopted, is [still] to be avoided — this will be explained. And by saying that <s>pramāṇa</s> is the cause of apprehension, the [views that] apprehension of previously unapprehended objects, correspondence with the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>), and the self-luminous or other-luminous power constitute <s>pramāṇa</s> — these are all rejected. Because by the non-deviating apprehension that is other than memory, and by calling it the cause of that — by the word 'cause' (<s>hetu</s>), correspondence and power, being non-different from the result, are eliminated; and because the relation of cause and caused is untenable in identity.

tat kasya hetorapacatyapi pākasaṃbandhaṃ pratyasti svarūpśaktirdevadattādāviti? dvayī hi śaktiḥ kārakāṇāṃ kāryopajananaṃ prati svarūpaṃ ca sahakārigrāmasamavadhānaṃ ca /
children.translated_text: For what reason, then, does there exist an inherent capacity for connection with cooking even in <s>Devadatta</s> and the like who are not [currently] cooking? For the capacity of <s>kārakas</s> (agent-factors) for producing their effects is twofold: the inherent nature and the co-presence of the assemblage of cooperative factors.

children.text: tatrāsatyapi sahakārigrāmasamavadhāne kārakaśabdānāṃ pravṛtteḥ, satyapi ca svarūpe trekālyavyāpini trekālyayogikāryāsaṃbhave 'pravṛtteḥ traikālyayogikāryopahitamaryādameva svarūpaṃ kārakaśabdānāṃ pravṛtau nimittamiti /
children.translated_text: There, since <s>kāraka</s>-words apply even when the assemblage of cooperative factors is not present, and since they do not apply when the inherent nature exists but is pervaded by all three times yet the effect appropriate to all three times cannot occur — therefore, the inherent nature delimited by the effect appropriate to all three times alone is the ground for the application of <s>kāraka</s>-words.

children.text: asatyapi pratyutpannapramāhetupramāṇasaṃbandhe pramātṛprameyaśabdayoḥ pravṛttiriti upapannaṃ pramātṛprameyābhyāṃ pramāṇa janyata iti /
children.translated_text: Even when the connection with the <s>pramāṇa</s> as the present cause of <s>pramā</s> does not exist, the application of the words 'knower' and 'knowable' is justified — thus it is established that the <s>pramāṇa</s> is produced from the knower and the knowable.

children.text: tat pramāṇamupalabdhisādhanaṃ sākṣāt, na pramātṛprameye iti siddham //
children.translated_text: That <s>pramāṇa</s> is the direct instrument of apprehension, not the knower and the knowable — this is established.

Now, he raises an objection to this on the grounds of over-extension — 'because of being the same.' He reconciles — 'this is the distinction.' The meaning is as follows: every agent acts through the operation of instrument and object-domain, but does not directly operate upon the result. And the instrument is of two kinds: established (<s>siddha</s>) and unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>). There, an established [instrument] like an axe, being lifted again and again, striking the pieces of wood so as to split them, is said to 'cut the wood.' But the splitting of the wood into two is not directly the domain of the agent's operation; rather, the agent's operation — characterized by lifting and striking — is directed only at the axe, which has become the instrument through possessing contact and velocity. Similarly, one who desires heaven (<s>svarga</s>) as agent does not directly operate upon heaven, but rather accomplishes the sacrifice (<s>yāga</s>) — which is the unestablished instrument — by establishing it. Heaven, however, arises directly from the operation of the sacrifice, through the factor called <s>apūrva</s>, which is based on consciousness and which, through the specific transformation produced by differences of place, time, and condition, [produces its result]. In the same way here too, the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) is fulfilled by operating upon — or producing — only the instrument: the established sense organs and the like, and the unestablished sense-object contact and the like. But the instrument — the sense organ and the like, or the sense-object contact and the like — is not fulfilled elsewhere; it operates directly upon apprehension, which is the result. As for the knowable object (<s>prameya</s>), there is no property of being a cause of apprehension anywhere other than in perception; and even there, the knowable object is useful only for mere contact with the sense organ. It is the sense organ itself, or the sense-object contact and the like, that is the direct cause of <s>pramā</s> (veridical cognition). From this it is established that the knower is not the direct cause of <s>pramā</s>, because of being an agent. Whoever is an agent is never the direct cause of the result — like a woodcutter or a sacrificer. And so is this [knower]. Therefore, it is so. Similarly, the perceptible knowable object (<s>prameya</s>) is not the direct cause of <s>pramā</s>, because of being a <s>prameya</s>. Whatever is a <s>prameya</s>, all of that is not the cause of <s>pramā</s> — like an inferential object and the like. And so is this. Therefore, it is so. Thus, the knower and the knowable object are fulfilled in the <s>pramāṇa</s>, but the <s>pramāṇa</s> itself is not [merely] fulfilled [by them]; therefore it alone is the cause of the result. The knower and the knowable object, however, engage for the purpose of the result, and thus are causes [only] in some manner. He objects — 'non-instrument.' The meaning is: a non-instrument agent cannot encompass even the <s>pramāṇa</s>. He resolves — 'no, because of sense organ and object.' When cognition is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the sense organ and object are its instruments — this is the meaning. He again objects — 'if then.' He resolves — 'even in that.' He objects — 'if the <s>pramāṇa</s> [arises] from the knower and the knowable, both being existent.' The meaning is: without the <s>pramāṇa</s>, <s>pramā</s> would be absent, and hence the knower and the knowable would be unestablished. He asks — 'how?' The answer — '<s>pramāṇa</s>.' [One might ask:] why should not the mere essential nature of the substance be the <s>kāraka</s> (agent-factor)? And that [essential nature] exists even before being connected with the action — therefore he says — 'not mere substance.' Let there be, then, its subsidiary operation that is the <s>kāraka</s> in the principal action to be accomplished, since that too is the cause of the principal action — therefore he says — 'not mere action either.' For <s>Devadatta</s> is not a cutter by his mere essential nature, nor is his operation of lifting and striking applicable to a clod of earth and the like. Where then does the word <s>kāraka</s> apply? — therefore he says — 'for the word <s>kāraka</s>.' The word <s>kāraka</s> applies to a cause of accomplishing the principal action that is endowed with a specific subsidiary operation. For in the result of splitting, which is the principal operation: the agent's subsidiary operation directed at the instrument is lifting and striking; and the object's — the wood's — subsidiary operation is the contact with a sharp, heavy, velocity-possessing axe. For it is through that [contact] that the wood, by the separation of its parts arising from the vibration of its own parts, undergoes splitting. Therefore, having established in general that a <s>kāraka</s> is endowed with both subsidiary and principal operations, he applies it to the case at hand — 'the words knower and knowable.' 'Without action' means without principal action — this is the meaning. He resolves — 'no, like the words cook (<s>pācaka</s>) and the like.' For the connection between word and meaning is determined by common usage. And common usage employs <s>kāraka</s>-words with the mere intention of connection with past, future, or present action: 'bring the cook' [future], 'this one cooked' [past], and 'this cook is cooking' [present] — the usage across all three times is seen equally.

lakṣyalakṣaṇayorabhedavivakṣayā sāmānadhikaraṇyam, na tu pramātṛprameyānvayavyatirekānuvidhānamapyasti pramāyā anvayavyatirekayorityata āha--na pramātarīti /
pramātṛprameyābhyāṃ saha pramotpādasyānyayogavyavacchedena saṃbandhaḥ /

pramimīta iti svatantraṃ kartāraṃ daśayati pratipādyāt karaṇād vyavacchettum /

sa ceti /
co 'vadhāraṇe /

pramāyā asamavāyikāraṇa khalvātmamanaḥsaṃyogaḥ /
sa ca sarvapramāsodhāraṇaḥ /
nāsau pramātrā prameyeṇa vā śakyo viśeṣṭum, tayorapi tadvadeva sādhāraṇyāt /

children.translated_text: But the <s>pramāṇa</s>, being uncommon, differentiates the conjunction of self and mind as appropriate.

children.text: eve sukhādiprameyāṇāmapi mana evāsādhāraṇaṃ vyavacchedaṅka draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: Similarly, for the knowable objects such as pleasure and the like too, the mind alone should be seen as the uncommon differentiating [factor].
This is its superiority.
It has been said that by the intention of non-difference between the superiority and that which possesses the superiority, [the superiority] is expressed by the word 'superiority.' //

Even when there is the property of being a means of apprehension for both the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) and the knowable (<s>prameya</s>), the charge that they are causes of apprehension does not apply here, because among the most effective and least effective [causes], the most effective one is distinguished by its superiority, since it has emerged with the effect-cognition [directly following it] — thus he says — 'because of being the most effective.' / He asks the meaning of 'most effective' — 'what then?' / The answer — the meaning of 'most effective' is that the presence and absence of valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), which is the effect, corresponds to the presence and absence of the <s>pramāṇa</s>. / The co-referentiality [of the terms 'most effective' and 'pramāṇa'] is due to the intention of non-difference between the defined and the definition. But the valid cognition does not follow the positive and negative concomitance of the knower and the knowable — therefore he says — 'not the knower.' / The relation of the production of valid cognition with the knower and the knowable is one of exclusion of disconnection (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>). / But the relation of the production of valid cognition with the <s>pramāṇa</s> is through both exclusion of non-connection and exclusion of disconnection — this is the superiority of <s>pramāṇa</s>. / For the knower and the knowable, whose functioning is exhausted by the <s>pramāṇa</s>, do not operate in [producing] valid cognition [independently]. / Therefore, since an obstacle is possible, valid cognition does not necessarily arise when the operations of the knower and the knowable are present. / But when the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> is present, valid cognition necessarily arises — thus he states an alternative — 'or, that which possesses [the pramāṇa] measures — that is the superiority.' / 'Measures' (<s>pramimīte</s>) indicates an independent agent, in order to distinguish it from the object to be known and from the instrument. / And the word 'that which possesses' (<s>yadvān</s>) is used with a restrictive sense. / Therein, 'that which possesses' excludes another agent [i.e., the knower]. / For the agent is not 'one who possesses an agent,' but rather 'one who possesses a <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / For the independent substrate is depended upon by the dependent one. / For it has been stated that the instrument is dependent on the agent. / The knower may sometimes possess the knowable too, since the knowable is under its own control. / But [the knower] does not always possess the knowable, since in inference and the like, the knowable being past and the like precludes possessing it. / But [the knower] is never without knowledge of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the like — this is the result of the restriction. / This is the distinction of <s>pramāṇa</s> from the knower and the knowable. / And he shows the superiority of this very distinction through positive and negative concomitance — 'when the <s>pramāṇa</s> is present.' / He states an alternative — 'when there is an excess.' / By the former [alternative], the superiority characterized by the predominance of positive [concomitance] was shown for something of a certain type; here, for something of that very same type, the superiority characterized by the predominance of negative [concomitance] is the distinction. / The meaning is: [the pramāṇa has] the property of not being an agent and not being a [mere] cause. / He states an alternative — 'or, like conjunction, being the final [condition].' / For the instrument that operates with its requisite accessories — that is the instrument, not the mere intrinsic nature of the eye and the like. / But it was previously stated that the intrinsic nature would be merely the ground for the application of the word 'instrument' and the like. / And that [final condition] is either established or not established — [if not established,] the operation of the knower and the knowable comes to fulfillment as such only afterwards — hence it is called 'the final [condition].' / This is its superiority of being the final condition — similarly, in the threads' production of cloth, the final conjunctions of the threads are that immediately after which the cloth is produced. / He states an alternative — 'or, immediacy to apprehension.' / Because the <s>pramāṇa</s> is the final condition, immediately after it the apprehension, i.e., the valid cognition, arises. / The immediacy to apprehension is itself the superiority of the <s>pramāṇa</s>. / 'And that' — the particle 'ca' is in the sense of restriction. / This too is stated with the intention of non-difference between the defined and the definition. / He states an alternative — 'or, being the uncommon cause.' / Indeed, these four valid cognitions — perception and the like — are experienced as having distinct cognitive designations. / And the knower is not the cause of their distinction, because of being common [to all]. / Nor is the knowable, because even when one knowable occurs [simultaneously in different cognitions], it would be common to all apprehensions. / But the <s>pramāṇas</s> are respectively uncommon in each of the four valid cognitions — hence they are the grounds of distinct cognitive designation. / This uncommonness is the superiority. / Every person as knower is intended here. / He states an alternative — 'being the cause of valid cognition.' / The non-inherent cause of valid cognition is indeed the conjunction of self and mind. / And that is common to all valid cognitions. / It cannot be differentiated by the knower or the knowable, because of their being common in the same way.
