ayamabhisandhiḥ, pravṛttisāmarthyena hi kāryeṇa pramāṇasyārthavattvamanumātavyam /
na caitat sākṣāt pramāṇasya kāryam, kiṃ tvarthapratipatteḥ /
tadanantaraṃ hi samarthā pratipattirūpajāyate /
arthapratipattistu pramāṇakāryeti samarthā pravṛttiḥ pramāṇakāryā satī pramāṇasyārthavattvamanumāpayati /
tasmādarthagamyamapi pramāṇamarthapratipattikaraṇatvena dyotanīyam /
anyathā pramāṇamarthavadarthapratipatteḥ masarthapravṛttijanakatvāditi kiṃ kena saṃgatam? pramāṇasya viśeṣaḥ pramāṇabhāsād vyāvṛttiḥ, tasya jñāpanam /
sa evārtho yasya pramāṇagrahaṇasya tat tathoktam /
tasya bhāvastattvam /
tasmādetaduktaṃ bhavati--pramāṇakāryāyā arthaprapitteḥ pravṛttisāmarthyaṃ na tadābhāsakāryāyāḥ /
tasmāt pramāṇasyārthavattvaṃ gamyata iti /
tadidamuktam--tad yeha pramāṇena pratipattiḥ sā pravṛttisāmarthyaṃ pratipādayati pramāṇam /
ayamarthaḥ /
pramāṇa kartṛ, pravṛttisamārthyaṃ pratipadyamānaṃ prāpnuvattat pratipādayati prāpayati pramāṇakāryārthapratipattiriti /
idamapi pramāṇagrahaṇasya prayojanamityāha-- na ca pramāṇagrahaṇamiti /
ekadeśivyākhyānamupanyasyati--sukheti /
na kevalaṃ sukhaduḥkhahetutvādarthyamānatvāt jñāyamānatvācca /
dūṣayati--neti /
sarvasya sukhaduḥkhataddhetutvena heyapakṣanikṣepāt upādeyānāṃ pramāṇaśāstrāpavargāṇānāmabhāvaprasaṅgād vyāghātaḥ /
avivakṣitatvācceti /
caśabdasamuccitamaśakyahānatvaṃ hetvantaramādarśayati-- na ca pramāṇādihānamiti /
sukhadaḥkhataddhetavo hi heyāḥ sane hānopāyamapekṣante /
na ca pramāṇāderanyaḥ tadupāyaḥ saṃbhavati /
na ca pramāṇādiḥ svocchedāya paryāptaḥ /
na cāsmādapavargo nādhigamyate /
tasmānna śakyaṃ pramāṇādinā pramāṇadihānamiti /
na caitanniḥśreyasahetuṃ śāstraṃ praṇayataḥ sūtrakārasya tadanuvartino vā bhāṣyakārasya vivikṣitamityāha--na ca pramāṇādihānaṃ vivakṣitam /
tasmādasmadvacākhyānameva śobhanamityāha--kiṃ tviti /
pravṛttisāmarthyādhānayogyavamamadhikāraḥ /
tasmāt sukhaduḥkhataddheturūpārthapratipattireva hi samarthāṃ pravṛttimādhatte, na tvarthamātrāpratipattirityarthaḥ /
na kevalaṃ vyāghātāśakyahānāvivakṣitatvairarthapadena na sarvasaṃgraho 'śakyatvādapi na sarvasaṃgraha ityāha--na saṃvida iti /
sukhaduḥkhataddhetutayā na saṃvido grahaṇaṃ saṃgrahaḥ sarvamadhyapatitāyā api /
kutaḥ? anadhikārāt, sukhaduḥkhataddhetuyogyatāvirahāt /
nāpyarthyamānatvena saṃgraha ityāha--akarmatvācca /
na tāvat sarvā eva saṃvidaḥ saṃvidgocarā manoyonayaḥ, saṃvedyā bhavitumarhanti /
ekanīlaviṣayasaṃvitparamparāmātra eva puruṣāyuṣasahasraparyavasānāt, viṣayāntarasaṃcārābhāvaprasaṅgācca /
tasmādanavasthābhayādante kasyāścit saṃvido 'saṃvedyatayā phalamātratvamabhyupeyam /
tathā ca sā nārthyate /
na ca sukhaduḥkhe tatreturiti na sarvasaṃgrahaḥ saṃvido 'saṃgrahādityarthaḥ /
tadevamādivākya vyākhyāya bhāṣyavākyāntaramavatārya tatraikaderśivyākhyānaṃ dūṣayitumupanyasyati--so 'yaṃ pramāṇārtha iti /
dūṣayati--nobhayasyāpi parisaṃkhyātatvāt, arthastu sukhamityādinā bhāṣyagranthena /

children.translated_text: The duality is through cause and effect.

children.text: prāṇabhṛdbhedasyāparisaṃkhyeyatvāditi ca hetuḥ śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ kākasya kārṣṇyāditivanna pratijñārthena saṅgacchate ityāha--prāṇabhṛdbhedasya ceti /
children.translated_text: And the reason 'because of the innumerability of the distinctions among living beings' does not agree with the thesis, like [the statement] 'the palace is white because of the blackness of the crow' — thus he says — 'and of the distinctions among living beings.'
He says that this fault of the partial interpretation does not exist in this [present] interpretation — 'not of the word artha (object).'

children.text: candranādiviṣayaṃ pramāṇaṃ sukhaprayojanameva, kaṇṭakādiviṣayaṃ ca pramāṇaṃ duḥkhotpādaprayojanamevetyetadubhayaṃ parisaṃkhyātuṃ niyantumaśakyamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: it is impossible to exhaustively enumerate, to restrict, both of these — that the <s>pramāṇa</s> directed toward objects such as the moon and the like has only the purpose of pleasure, and that the <s>pramāṇa</s> directed toward objects such as thorns and the like has only the purpose of producing pain. //

He explains the [term] 'apprehension of the object' (<s>arthagrahaṇa</s>), which comes next in order, according to its purport — 'apprehension of the object.' / Why is the apprehension that has <s>pramāṇa</s> as its object prohibited? — therefore he says — 'because it is not the apprehension of the object of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / The requisite action (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) is the performance; in that [context], / 'it is sought' means the object — things like water, thorns, and the like. / Its being of such a nature is its being sought-after. / And that is being a means to pleasure and pain. / What is a means to pleasure is sought after as something to be accepted, and what is a means to pain is sought after as something to be avoided. / He states another purport — 'what is to be disregarded.' / The <s>pramāṇa</s> directed toward what is to be disregarded does not have the capacity [to generate] activity — so that is negated. / And that is not a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>. / Because even of that, validity is inferred through the inferential mark of similarity with observed <s>pramāṇas</s>. / He raises an objection — 'non-apprehension of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / The meaning is: since the apprehension that generates effective activity does not arise from a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>, it is understood ipso facto that it arises from a <s>pramāṇa</s>. / He resolves — 'because it is for the purpose of making known the specific <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / This is the intention: the possession of an object by the <s>pramāṇa</s> is to be inferred through the effect, namely the capacity for activity. / And this is not directly the effect of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, but rather of the apprehension of the object. / For the effective apprehension arises immediately after that [pramāṇa]. / And the apprehension of the object is the effect of the <s>pramāṇa</s> — so the effective activity, being the effect of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, allows the inference of the <s>pramāṇa</s>'s possession of an object. / Therefore, although the <s>pramāṇa</s> is understood from the meaning [implicitly], it should be illuminated by specifying it as the instrument of apprehending the object. / Otherwise, 'the <s>pramāṇa</s> possesses an object, [and it is known] from the apprehension of the object, because of its capacity to generate effective activity' — what would be connected with what? The specific nature of the <s>pramāṇa</s> is its distinction from the semblance of <s>pramāṇa</s>; making that known [is the purpose]. / That alone is the purpose of the mention of <s>pramāṇa</s> — so it is said. / Its being is its reality. / Therefore this is what has been stated: the apprehension of the object, which is the effect of <s>pramāṇa</s>, has the capacity for activity, not that which is the effect of its semblance. / Therefore the possession of an object by the <s>pramāṇa</s> is understood. / This is what was stated — 'that apprehension here which is from the <s>pramāṇa</s> demonstrates the capacity for activity of the <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / The meaning is: the <s>pramāṇa</s> is the agent; the apprehension of the object, which is the effect of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, makes [the person] attain the capacity for activity that is being attained — that is, it causes [the person] to reach it. / He states this too as the purpose of the mention of <s>pramāṇa</s> — 'and the mention of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / He presents a partial interpretation — 'pleasure' and so on. / Not only because of being a cause of pleasure and pain is [something] sought after, but also because of being known. / He refutes — 'no.' / Because everything, being a cause of pleasure, pain, and their causes, falls into the category of what is to be avoided, the non-existence of what is to be accepted — <s>pramāṇa</s>, <s>śāstra</s>, and <s>apavarga</s> — would follow, and there would be contradiction. / 'Because of not being intended' — the particle 'ca' connects an additional reason showing the impossibility of abandoning: 'and the <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like cannot be abandoned.' / For the things to be avoided — pleasure, pain, and their causes — require a means of avoidance when they exist. / And no other means of that is possible besides the <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like. / And the <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like are not sufficient for their own annihilation. / And from these, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) is indeed attained. / Therefore, the avoidance of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like is not possible through <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like. / And this is not intended by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, who composed the <s>śāstra</s> as a cause of <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, nor by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> who follows him — thus he says — 'and the avoidance of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like is not intended.' / Therefore, our interpretation alone is excellent — thus he says — 'but rather.' / The most worthy object [of knowledge] is the subject matter — that which is fit for bestowing the capacity for activity. / Therefore, the apprehension of the object in the form of being a cause of pleasure, pain, and their causes alone bestows effective activity, not the apprehension of just any object — this is the meaning. / Not only because of contradiction, impossibility of abandonment, and not being intended is there no inclusion of everything by the word 'object,' but also because of impossibility — thus he says — 'not of awareness.' / There is no inclusion of awareness as [being a cause of] pleasure, pain, and their causes, even though [awareness] falls within everything. / Why? Because of non-qualification — because of the absence of fitness to be a cause of pleasure, pain, and their causes. / Nor is there inclusion because of being sought after — thus he says — 'and because of being actionless.' / Not all awarenesses can be the objects of awareness, the mental products of awareness, and the objects of experience. / Because [otherwise] even a thousand human lifetimes would be exhausted in merely a succession of awarenesses having a single blue [object], and there would follow the non-occurrence of any experience of another object. / Therefore, because of the fear of infinite regress, the experiential character — i.e., being merely a result — of some final awareness must be accepted as not being an object of experience. / And thus that is not sought after. / And [awareness] is not a cause of pleasure or pain — therefore there is no complete inclusion; because awareness is not included — this is the meaning. / Having thus explained the opening statement and so on, he introduces another statement of the <s>bhāṣya</s> and presents a partial interpretation in order to refute it — 'this meaning of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' / He refutes — 'no, because neither of the two [options] is exhaustively enumerated' — by the <s>bhāṣya</s> passage 'but the object is pleasure' and so on.

children.text:
evaṃ kilātra śaṅkyate, sukhaduḥkhahetubhāvo vastūnāṃ svābhāviko bhavenna vā? svābhāvikatve nīla iva sarvān pratyarthaḥ sukha iti karabhavanmanuṣyāṇāmapi kaṇṭakaḥ sukhaḥ syāt /
evaṃ nidādhe 'pi kuṅkumaṃ sukhaṃ syāt /
candanaṃ ca hemantate 'pi sukhaṃ bhavet /
evaṃ tṛṣṇaja ivāpāṃ suhitasyāpaḥ sukhāḥ prasajyeran /

children.translated_text: But if not intrinsic, then pleasures, pains, and the like — which arise from the variety of beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) and follow the constructs of individual dispositions — cannot serve as the purpose of <s>pramāṇa</s>.
To this the following presents itself — 'this meaning of <s>pramāṇa</s>.'

children.text: nivedayiṣye hi kṣaṇabhaṅgādhikāre tathā sthemabhājāmapi vastunāmakramāṇāmapi kramavatsahakārikāraṇasamavadhānavaśādupajanāpāyadharmāṇaḥ kramavanto dharmā bhavantīti, tadihāpi /
children.translated_text: For I shall demonstrate in the section on momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>) that even for things that possess stability, even for those that are non-sequential, sequential properties of arising and perishing come into being through the concurrence of cooperative causal conditions — and the same [applies] here too.

children.text: yadyapi na jātyā sukhaduḥkhahetubhāvo bhāvanāṃ bhavati, tathāpi jātideśakālāvasthāpuruṣabhedasahakārisamavadhānādupapatsyatesukhaduḥkhahetubhāvo 'vyavasthayeti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: Although the property of being a cause of pleasure and pain does not belong to things by their universal nature (<s>jāti</s>), nevertheless it will be accounted for through the concurrence of cooperative [conditions] differentiated by universal nature, place, time, circumstance, and person — so there is no disorder — this is the purport. //

Here the following objection may be raised: is the property of being a cause of pleasure and pain intrinsic to things, or not? If intrinsic, then just as blue [appears] as an object to all, a thorn should be pleasurable even for humans, as it is for camels. / Likewise, saffron would be pleasurable even in winter. / And sandalwood would be pleasurable even in the cold season. / Similarly, like [water for] one born of thirst, water should be pleasurable even for one who is fully satiated.

children.text:
tat siddhametat, pramāṇārtho 'niyataḥ, aniyataprāṇabhṛdbhedahetukatvāt /
yadyadaniyatakāraṇakaṃ kāryaṃ tatvasarvamaniyatameva, yathā aniyatakālameghodayanibandhanaṃ varṣam /
tathā cāyam /
tasmādaniyata iti /
kasmāt punaḥ pramātrādicaturvarge pramāṇasyaivārthavattvamucceta na pramātrādīnāmapītyāśaṅkānirākaraṇārthaṃ bhāṣyamanuvadanneva vyācaṣṭe-- arthavati ca samarthe samyagarthe 'rthāvyabhicāriṇīti yāvat /
pramāṇe 'rthavanti bhavan simarthāni samyagarthāni pramātrādīni /
arthasya tu samyaktvamidameva yad yādṛśaḥ pramāṇenopadarśistasya tathātvaṃ na punaranyathābhāva iti /
yadā tvādibhāṣyavākye 'rthaśabdaḥ prayojanavacanaḥ, tadaivaṃ vyākhyānam-- arthavati ca prayojanavati ca yataḥ samarthaṃ śaktaṃ pramāṇa pratipattyādikrameṇa pūrvoktena prayojanaṃ prati, ataḥ samarthe pramāṇe pramātrādīnyarthavanti prayojanavanti bhavanti, yatastānyapi pramāṇavadeva samarthāni śaktāni prayojanaṃ pratīti, atra hetaḥ anyatamāpāya iti /
tasyārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe--anyatamatvārtha iti /
nanvanyatamaśabdo bahuṣvanirdhānitaviśeṣamekamāha, na tu sādhakatamamityata āha--pramāraṇāditi /
sādhāraṇaśabdo hi pramaraṇād viśeṣe vartate /
tad yathā śivikāvahanapakrame puruṣamānayeti puruṣaśabdo viṣṭau /
tadvadihāpi pramātrādiparihāṇyā pramāṇasyārthavattvābhidhānaniyamaprakrama iti pramātrādibhyaḥ pramāṇasya viśeṣo vācya iti tatraivānyatamaśabdo vartate /
yadyapyarthapratipattyarthāvyabhicāradvāreṇa pramāṇasyāvyabhicāro gamyate dṛṣṭe viṣaye, tathāpyadṛṣṭe viṣaye na tajjanitaprapittayavyabhicāreṇāvyabhicāraḥ śabdasya pramāṇasya śakyo vijñātum, pratīyavyabhicārasya pramāṇāvyabhicāragrahaṇamanreṇāśakyajñānavat /
tasmād dṛṣṭārthasya mantrāyurvedasya pravṛttisāmarthyāvadhṛtārthāvyabhicārasya sādharmyādāptapraṇītvādagnihotrādivākyānāṃ pramāṇānāmavyabhicāragrahaṇapuraḥsarameva trivargasyāvyabhicāragrahaṇam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, by analogy with <s>mantra</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s> which have visible results and whose non-deviation from the object is ascertained through their capacity to produce activity, and because they are composed by trustworthy persons (<s>āpta</s>), the grasping of the non-deviation of the three aims of life (<s>trivarga</s>) is preceded by grasping the non-deviation of the <s>pramāṇas</s> such as statements about <s>Agnihotra</s> and the like.
The non-deviation of the <s>trivarga</s> (three aims of life) cannot be ascertained from any other source in this regard.

children.text: adṛṣṭārthaviṣayasya ca caturvargasyehārthavattvena prayojanaṃ dṛṣṭārthe sandehādapi vyavahāra siddheḥ /
children.translated_text: And for the fourfold group (<s>caturvarga</s>) whose objects are unperceived, the purpose here lies in its meaningfulness, since practical activity is established even from doubt regarding perceived objects.
This, then, is the primacy of <s>pramāṇa</s> among the fourfold group.

That is thus established: the object of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is indeterminate, because it is caused by indeterminate distinctions among living beings. Whatever effect has indeterminate causes, all of that is itself indeterminate, just as rain depends on the indeterminate timing of cloud formation. And so it is with this case. Therefore it is indeterminate. Now, why is it that among the fourfold group of the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) and the rest, only the purposefulness of <s>pramāṇa</s> is stated and not that of the knower and the rest? To remove this doubt, he explains while restating the <s>bhāṣya</s>— 'meaningful' means capable, correctly oriented toward the object, not deviating from the object. When the <s>pramāṇa</s> is meaningful, the knower and the rest become capable and correctly oriented toward the object. And the correctness of the object is precisely this: that the thing as revealed by the <s>pramāṇa</s> is truly so and not otherwise. But when in the original <s>bhāṣya</s> sentence the word 'artha' means 'purpose,' then the explanation is as follows— 'meaningful' means 'having purpose,' since the <s>pramāṇa</s> is capable, i.e., powerful, with respect to the purpose through the previously stated sequence of apprehension, therefore when the <s>pramāṇa</s> is capable, the knower and the rest become purposeful, because they too, like the <s>pramāṇa</s>, are capable with respect to the purpose; here the reason is 'the absence of any one of them.' He explains its meaning— 'for the sake of the sense of anyatama (any one).' Now, the word 'anyatama' designates one among many without specifying which, not the most efficacious; therefore he says 'from the common.' For the word 'common' (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>) operates in the sense of distinction by common usage. Just as in the procedure of palanquin-bearing, the command 'bring a man' uses the word 'man' in the sense of a servant; similarly here too, in the context of the rule stating the purposefulness of <s>pramāṇa</s> to the exclusion of the knower and the rest, the distinction of <s>pramāṇa</s> from the knower and the rest is to be expressed, and so the word 'anyatama' operates in that very sense. Although the non-deviation of <s>pramāṇa</s> is understood through non-deviation in apprehending the object in the case of perceived objects, nevertheless in the case of unperceived objects, the non-deviation of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) as a <s>pramāṇa</s> cannot be known through the non-deviation of the cognition produced by it, just as the non-deviation of the cognition cannot be known without grasping the non-deviation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text:
caturvargavibhāgapare bhāṣye pramātā prathamaṃ darśitaḥ /
tatastasya lakṣaṇamāha--pramātā svatantra iti /
svātantryaṃ pṛcchati--kiṃ punaḥ svātantryam, yasyābhisaṃbandhāt svantra iti? bhāṣyakṛtā pramātopalakṣito na lakṣitaḥ /
na khalvīpsājihāsayorvā pravṛttau vā svāntryaṃ pramātṛtvam, api tu pramāyārm /
ipsādisvātantryeṇa tu taduttarakālabhāvinā pramāyāṃ svātantryaṃ parvakālābhāvyupalakṣim /
tena taccarimanuvartamāno vārtikakṛt upalakṣaṇāntaraṃ kartṛtvottarakālabhāvyāha--kārakaphalopabhoktṛtvam /
na hi sarvaḥ kartā samastakārakajanyaṃ svargādi vaudanādi vā bhuṅkte ṛtvikpācakādiṣu ca vyabhicāradarśanāt /
kārakasya tu sataḥ kartṛtvottarakālabhāvinī phalopabhoktṛtā kartṛvanāntarīyakatayā dupalakṣayati, yajamānasya rājñaśca praiṣādinā tattadvayāpāre kartṛtvāt /
yathāhuratrabhavantaḥ,
tadabhisandhipūrvakaṃ preṣaṇamadhyeṣaṇaṃ va yuktaṃ tasarvaṃ pacyarthaḥ /
iti /
svātantryalakṣaṇamāha--tatsamavāyo vā /
kārakābhidhānena sannidhāpitāṃ kriyaṃ taditi sarvānāmnā parāmṛśati /
yasya hi vyāpāraṃ prādhānyena dhāturākhyātapratyayo vābhidhatte sa svatantraḥ kartā /
tathā hi viklidyantīyatra taṇḍulādayaḥ kartāraḥ, pacantītyatra devadattādayaḥ /
tat kasya hetoḥ? ekatra taṇḍulādervyāpāra upātto 'paratra devadattāderiti /
prādhānyena cāśeṣakārakanivarttyatvaṃ pradhānakriyāyāḥ, avāntaravyāpārabhede 'pi pradhānakriyoddeśena samastakārakapravṛtteriti /
puruṣa iti prakṛtakriyāpekṣam, pramāyāḥ puruṣāśrayatvāditi /
lakṣaṇāntaramāha--tatprayoktṛtvamitarāprayojyatā vā /
tasya cetanasya sarvakārakāṇi prati prayoktṛtvam, taiśca kārakairaprayojyatā vā /
acetanasya tu bhāktava kartṛtvaṃ na svābhāvikamiti bhāvaḥ parisamāptipadārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe--tattvaparisamāptiriti /
tattvaṃ hi pramāṇavyāpyatvaṃ pramāṇavyāpāraviṣayatvam /

children.translated_text: And that culminates in rejection (<s>hāna</s>), acceptance (<s>upādāna</s>), and indifference (<s>upekṣā</s>).

children.text: paryavasānaṃ parisamāptiḥ viniyojyeti vaktavye yogyatāgrahaṇamīpsite 'pi dṛṣṭe vastuni kutaścit pratibandhāt puruṣeṇānupātte mā bhūt tattvāparisamāptiriti /
children.translated_text: The use of the word 'fitness' (<s>yogyatā</s>) instead of saying 'to be employed' is so that there be no incompleteness of reality even when a perceived desirable object is not taken up by a person due to some obstruction.

children.text: yadyapi hi tat puruṣeṇānupāttaṃ tathāpyupādānayogyatāpradarśanādasti tattvaparisamāptiriti /
children.translated_text: For even though that is not taken up by the person, there is still completion of reality because of demonstrating the fitness for taking up.

children.text: tatpratiṣedhaśca ityatra tacchabdena hānopādānalakṣaṇaṃ viniyogaṃ parāmṛśati //
children.translated_text: And 'the negation of that'— here by the word 'that' he refers to the employment characterized by rejection and acceptance.

In the <s>bhāṣya</s> dealing with the division of the fourfold group, the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) is shown first. Then he states its definition— 'the knower is independent.' He asks about the independence— 'What then is this independence, by association with which one is called independent?' The <s>bhāṣya</s>-author has indicated, not defined, the knower. Independence does not consist in desire (<s>īpsā</s>) or aversion (<s>jihāsā</s>) or in activity, but rather in the act of knowing (<s>pramā</s>). But through independence in desire and the rest, which arises at a subsequent time, the independence in knowing is indicated as existing at a prior time. Therefore, following that characterization, the <s>vārttika</s>-author states another indication that arises subsequent to agency— 'being the experiencer of the fruit of action (<s>kāraka</s>).' For not every agent enjoys the result produced by all the <s>kārakas</s>, as deviation is observed in the case of priests (<s>ṛtvij</s>), cooks, and the like. But the status of being an experiencer of the fruit, which follows agency when <s>kāraka</s> is present, indicates as inseparable from the agent, because of the agency of the sacrificer (<s>yajamāna</s>) and the king in directing the respective activities through commands and the like. As the learned ones say: 'The command or request preceded by that intention— all that is for the purpose of the one who has it cooked.' He states the definition of independence— 'or the inherence in that.' By the general pronoun 'that' he refers back to the action brought near by the mention of <s>kāraka</s>. For he whose activity is primarily denoted by the verbal root, the verb, or the verbal suffix, is the independent agent. Thus, in 'the rice grains soften,' the rice grains and the like are the agents; in 'Devadatta cooks,' <s>Devadatta</s> and the like are. For what reason? Because in one case the activity of rice and the like is taken up, in the other that of <s>Devadatta</s> and the like. And the principal action has the character of being dependent on all <s>kārakas</s> for its cessation, because even though subsidiary activities differ, all <s>kārakas</s> operate for the sake of the principal action. 'Person' (<s>puruṣa</s>) is said with reference to the action under discussion, because <s>pramā</s> (valid cognition) rests in a person. He states another definition— 'being the instigator of that, or not being instigated by the others.' Of that conscious being, the instigator-ship with respect to all <s>kārakas</s>, or not being directed by those <s>kārakas</s>. But for the non-conscious, agency is figurative, not intrinsic— this is the meaning. He explains the meaning of 'completion of reality' (<s>tattvaparisamāpti</s>)— 'completion of reality.' For 'reality' (<s>tattva</s>) means being pervaded by <s>pramāṇa</s>, being the object of the operation of <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text:
kiṃ punastattvamityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācikhyāsustattvpratyayaprakṛtestado 'rthaṃ pṛcchati--kiṃpunariti /
uttaram--sadasatī tat /
praśnaṃ vibhajate--tasya bhāvastattvamityatreti /
uttaraṃ vibhajate--sadasatītat /

atha kasmāt prakṛtipuruṣau vā, pañcaskandhā vā, paraṃ brahmādvaitaṃ vā, jīvajīvastravādayo vā sapta, pṛthivyāpastejovayuriti vā catvāri bhūtānītyādīti na tado vācyāni bhavantītyata āha-- pramāṇaviṣayatvenādhikārāt /
children.translated_text: Now why are <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, or the five <s>skandhas</s>, or the non-dual supreme <s>Brahman</s>, or the seven categories beginning with <s>jīva</s> and <s>ajīva</s>, or the four elements earth, water, fire, and air, and the like, not to be stated as 'that'? To this he says— because of being treated under the topic of <s>pramāṇa</s>-objects.

children.text: sūtrabhāṣyavākyatadvivaraṇeṣu pramāṇa pramāṇaviṣayaścādhikṛtaḥ na ca saṃkhyādisiddhāntabhedānupātino 'rthāḥ pramāṇaviṣayāḥ /
children.translated_text: In the <s>sūtra</s>, <s>bhāṣya</s>, their statements, and their elucidations, <s>pramāṇa</s> and the objects of <s>pramāṇa</s> are the subject matter, and the objects that follow the different doctrines of <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and others are not objects of <s>pramāṇa</s> [in this context].
And how this is so will be explained in this very work later on.
He concludes— 'therefore.'

Wishing to explain the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'What then is reality?', he asks about the meaning of 'tat' which is the base of the derivative 'tattva'— 'What then?' The answer— 'that (tat) is the existent and the non-existent.' He analyzes the question— 'The state of being that is tattva, in this context.' He analyzes the answer— 'The existent and the non-existent— that is tat.'

children.text:
prakṛtyarthaṃ vyākhyāya pratyārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe-tadbhāva iti, sadasatoryathāsaṃkhyaṃ vidhāyakaprakāṇaviṣayatā sato bhāvaḥ, tatpratiṣedhaścāsato bhāvaḥ /
taditi vidhāyakapramāṇaviṣayatāṃ parāmṛśati /
tatpratiṣadhena ca pratiṣadhakaṃ pramāṇamupasthāpitam /
tena pratiṣedhakapramāṇaviṣayatvameva tatpratiṣedha ityanenoktaṃ bhavati /
etad vibhajate-tayoḥ khalviti /
śaṅkate-pramāṇaviṣayatvāditi /
sarvasāmarthyaviraheṇa tvasat sato vyāvartate /
yadi cāsadapi pramāṇaviṣayaḥ, tarhi nāsamartham /
tathā ca sadasatorabheda ityarthaḥ /
nirākarotina, anaikāntāt /
na vayamasāmarthyenāsato bhedamācakṣmahe yenaivamupālabhyemahīti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkā vibhajate--tatra bhavediti /
nirākaraṇaṃ vibhajate--tacca neti /
gavādi cetanam, acetanaṃ ghaṭādīti /
yadi sadasatī samarthe kutastarhi tayormeda ityata āha--svatantreti /
asadupalabdhireva sadupalabdheranyānupalabdhiḥ /
nanu saṃyogavibhāgādiṣu satsvapi taratantropalabdhikaraṇatvamatista, teṣāṃ saṃyujyamānavibhajyamānādyadhīnanirūpaṇatvāditya āha--pratiṣedhamukhena pratipadyate pratīyate /
satāṃ keṣāñcit pāratantrye 'pi na niṣedhyaniṣedhādhikāraṇapāratantryamityarthaḥ /
saṃprati sadupalambhakasya pramāṇasyāsadūpalambhakatvaṃ pratipipādayiṣatā bhāṣyakāreṇa pradīpo dṛṣṭānta upanyastaḥ /
satu sādhyasamaḥ, tasyāpi pramāṇasāmagrīniveśaditi śaṅkyamāno 'tyantalokaprasiddhatayāsya dṛṣṭāntatvaṃ samarthayate--pradīpavaditi /
gopālāṅganā api hi kimatrāsti steno 'smaddhanaṃ vā apavarake na veti sandihānā pradīpamupādāya samantādavalokyāpavarakamastīhāsmaddhanaṃ nāsti stena iti samameva niścinvanti, na tu stenābhāvaniścayāyopāyantaramupādadate /
tenāgāpālāḍnamā ca paṇḍitarūpebhyaḥ siddhaḥ pradīpo dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
tadidamuktam-na hyasatpratipattāvupāyāntaramāsthīyate lokena /
anāśrayaṇe hetumāha pradīpena dṛśyamāne hi ghaṭādike 'rthe svatantre nānena samānajātīyaṃ tulyopalambhayogyataṃ dṛśyāntaramasti /
nīlapītau hi parasparābhāvavantau, tena nalīniṣedhe nāvaśyaṃ pītavidhiḥ /
bhāvābhāvau tu parasparābhāvātmānau, no khalvabhāvābhāvo nāma kaścidanyo bhāvarūpāt /
nāpi bhāvābhāvo 'nyo 'bhāvāt /
tadevaṃ pradīpopāyasya pratipattuḥ pratītikramamuktvā parīkṣakāṇāmupapattikramamāha--yadyabhaviṣyaditi /
yadi kaścidāśaṅketa dṛśyatāmabhāvaḥ /
pradīpena bhāvo 'pi bhaviṣyatīti, tatraiṣa parīkṣakāṇāṃ tarka upatiṣṭhate--yadyabhaviṣayaditi /
tadevaṃ laukikaparīkṣakasaṃmataṃ dṛṣṭāntamupapādya dārṣṭāntike yojayati--eve pramāṇenāpi indriyādinā sati pramīyamāṇe iti /
pūrvavad vyākhyeyam /
upasaṃharati--tadevamiti /
sarvaṃ caitadupariṣṭādupapādayiṣyate /
nanu yadi sadasatī pramāṇaviṣayau, kasmāt sadbhedā ivāsadbhedā api sūtrakṛtā nocyanta ityata āha--tatra teṣu sadasadbhedeṣu madhye svātantryeṇāsadbhedā na prakāśanta iti nocyante /
niṣedhyaniṣedhādhikāraṇādhīnanirūpaṇatvādasadbhedānāṃ bhāvabhedatantraṃ pramāśanamiti bhāvabhedakathanenaivābhāvabhedā api gamyanta iti noktā ityarthaḥ /
atha vā kathitā eva yeṣāṃ tattvajñānaṃ niḥśreyasopayogi, yaṃ tu na tathā na teṣāṃ prapañcaḥ anupayuktabhāvaprapañca iva vaktavya ityāha--caturvargānantarbhāvād vā bhāvaprapañcavad abhāvaprapañca iti /
niḥśreyasānupayogini bhāvaprapañce yathā caturvargānantarbhāvaḥ, evamabhāvaprapañce 'pīti /
atha niḥśreyasopayogābhāvaḥ kuto 'vagantavya ityata āha--bhāvopadeśādevābhāva upadiṣṭo bhavatīti /
dvividhaṃ pramāṇaṃ bhāvo 'bhāvaśca, yathā kāraṇābhāvena kāryābhāvajñānaṃ yato dvitīyasūtrasamutyānam /
children.translated_text: <s>Pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is twofold: existence and non-existence, just as the knowledge of the non-existence of an effect arises from the non-existence of the cause— from which the second <s>sūtra</s> originates.
And among the <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge), <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) alone is the supreme one.
This same [principle] applies to <s>prayojana</s> (purpose) and the rest as well—thus it should be understood in each respective context.
He concludes—'therefore' (<s>ataḥ</s>).

Having explained the meaning of the base (<s>prakṛti</s>), he explains the meaning of the suffix— 'the state of that' (<s>tadbhāva</s>); according to the respective correspondence of the existent and the non-existent: being the object of a positive <s>pramāṇa</s> is the state of the existent, and the negation of that is the state of the non-existent. By 'that' he refers to being the object of a positive <s>pramāṇa</s>. And by 'negation of that,' a negative <s>pramāṇa</s> is brought to mind. Thus, being the object of a negative <s>pramāṇa</s> is what is meant by 'the negation of that.' He analyzes this— 'of these two, indeed.' He raises an objection— 'because of being objects of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' But the non-existent differs from the existent only by the complete absence of all capacity. And if the non-existent is also an object of <s>pramāṇa</s>, then it is not without capacity. And thus there would be no difference between the existent and the non-existent— this is the meaning. He refutes— 'because it is not invariable.' We do not assert the difference of the non-existent by means of incapacity, such that we could be criticized thus— this is the purport. He analyzes the objection— 'there it may be.' He analyzes the refutation— 'and that is not so.' The conscious is cattle and the like; the non-conscious is pots and the like. If both the existent and the non-existent are capable, then whence their difference? To this he says— 'independent.' The apprehension of the non-existent is itself the non-apprehension that is other than the apprehension of the existent. Now, even among existents there is dependence on other things for their apprehension, as in the case of conjunction, disjunction, and the like, since their determination depends on the things being conjoined or separated; to this he says— 'it is apprehended through the mode of negation.' Even though some existents are dependent, the dependence of the locus of what is to be negated and the negation is not [of the same kind]— this is the meaning. Now, wishing to demonstrate that the <s>pramāṇa</s> which apprehends the existent also apprehends the non-existent, the <s>bhāṣya</s>-author has adduced the lamp as an illustration. Regarding the objection that this is equal to the thesis to be proved, since even the lamp requires the assemblage of <s>pramāṇa</s> conditions, he justifies its being an illustration through its extreme familiarity in common experience— 'like a lamp.' For even cowherd women, when doubting whether there is a thief here or whether our belongings are in the inner chamber, take a lamp, look around on all sides, and determine equally 'our belongings are here in the chamber, there is no thief'— they do not resort to any other means for ascertaining the absence of a thief. Therefore the lamp is an established illustration even for cowherd women, not only for those learned in form. This is what is stated— 'for people do not resort to any other means for apprehending the non-existent.' He gives the reason for not resorting [to another means]: when a pot and the like, which are independent objects, are seen by a lamp, there is no other visible thing of the same kind having equal apprehensibility. For blue and yellow are mutually absent from each other; therefore, in negating blue, there is not necessarily an affirmation of yellow. But existence and non-existence are of the nature of mutual absence; there is no such thing as 'absence of non-existence' that is different from existence. Nor is 'absence of existence' different from non-existence. Thus, having stated the mode of apprehension of the lamp as a means, he states the mode of reasoning for the logicians— 'if it were to be.' If someone should doubt 'let the non-existent be seen; by a lamp, the existent too will be,' then this reasoning presents itself to the logicians— 'if it were to be.' Having thus established the illustration accepted by both common people and logicians, he applies it to the subject— 'thus, even by a <s>pramāṇa</s> such as the senses, when an existent thing is being ascertained.' This should be explained as before. He concludes— 'thus indeed.' And all this will be established later on. Now, if both the existent and the non-existent are objects of <s>pramāṇa</s>, why does the <s>sūtra</s>-author not state the varieties of the non-existent just as he does the varieties of the existent? To this he says— 'among those, the varieties of the existent and the non-existent, the varieties of the non-existent do not manifest independently,' and so they are not stated. Because the determination of the varieties of the non-existent depends on what is to be negated and the locus of negation, the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the varieties of non-existence is dependent on the varieties of existence; therefore, by stating the varieties of existence, the varieties of non-existence are also understood— hence they are not stated. Alternatively, they are indeed stated for those whose knowledge of reality (<s>tattva</s>) is conducive to the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>); but for those [topics] where this is not the case, there is no elaboration, just as the elaboration of existence that is not useful is not to be stated— thus he says— 'or because of not being included in the four aims (<s>caturvarga</s>), the elaboration of non-existence is like the elaboration of existence.' Just as there is no inclusion in the four aims for the elaboration of existence that is not conducive to the highest good, so too for the elaboration of non-existence. Now, how is the absence of conduciveness to the highest good to be known? To this he says— 'by the very teaching of existence, non-existence is taught.'

children.text:
tadevaṃ tātparyaṃ vyākhyāya avayavārthaṃ vyākhyātuṃ bhāṣyaṃ paṭhati--sacca khalu ṣoḍaśadhāvyūḍhamupadekṣyata iti /
atra prathame kalpe caśabdo 'vadhāraṇe, khalu śabdaḥ spaṣṭārthe /
tadeva ṣoḍaśadhā vyūḍhamupadekhyate nāsat, tasya sadadhīnaprakāśatvāditi /
dvitīye tu kalpe pāramārthike caḥ samucce, khaluḥ avadhāraṇe, sati ṣoḍaśādhaivopadekṣyamāṇe 'sadapyupadekṣyata ityarthaḥ /
prakṛtyarthaṃ vyācaṣṭe--vyūha iti /

sūtrasya saprapañca tātparyaṃ vyākhyāya avayavārthaṃ vyācikhyāsunā bhāṣyakāreṇa tāsāṃ khalvāsāṃ sadvidhānāmiti bhāṣyeṇa sūtramavatārya paṭhitaṃ tadasya vārtikakṛt tātparyamāha--ta ete sadbhedā iti sūtram /
children.translated_text: Having explained the purport of the <s>sūtra</s> in detail, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator), wishing to explain the meaning of the component parts, introduced and read the <s>sūtra</s> with the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'of these indeed six kinds' (<s>tāsāṃ khalvāsāṃ sadvidhānām</s>); the <s>vārtikakāra</s> (sub-commentator) states the purport of that—'these are the six divisions' (<s>ta ete sadbhedāḥ</s>), this is the <s>sūtra</s>.

children.text: ta ete pramāṇādayaḥ sadbhedā niḥśreyasopayogino na gaṅgāvālukādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: These—<s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) and the rest—are the six divisions useful for <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good), not things like grains of sand of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.
Therefore, among existing things, only these sixteen beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> are intended to be enumerated, defined, and examined,
not the grains of sand of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and such, even though they exist, because they are not useful for <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good)—this is the purport.

Having thus explained the purport, in order to explain the meaning of the component parts, he reads the <s>bhāṣya</s>: 'And indeed (<s>sacca khalu</s>), it will be taught as arranged in sixteen categories.' Here, in the first interpretation, the word 'ca' is used in the sense of emphasis, and the word '<s>khalu</s>' in the sense of making clear. That very [reality], arranged in sixteen ways, will be taught—not what is unreal, because its manifestation depends on what is real. In the second interpretation, however, 'ca' is used in the conjunctive sense according to the ultimate standpoint, and '<s>khalu</s>' in the sense of emphasis; the meaning is that when what is real is being taught under sixteen divisions, what is unreal will also be taught. He explains the meaning of the base word—'<s>vyūha</s>' (arrangement).

children.text:
dvandvasvarūpamāha--sarvapadeti /
dvandvaparigrahe tātparyamanvayavyatirekābhyāmādarśayati--sarva eva iti /
bahuvrīhikarmadhārayayorasaṃbhāvāt ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaparigrahe nigrahasthānasyāntyapadārthasya prādhānye vivakṣitārthahānaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ /
nirdeśe yayāvacanaṃ vigrahaityasta bhāṣyasya tātparyamāha--yathāvacanamiti /
anyonyanirapekṣāṇāṃ pratyekaṃ pramāhetubhāvaḥ pramāṇānāmiti hi bahuvacanaprayojanam /
prameyeṣu tu yadyapi prameyatā vāstavī pratyekamasti tathāpyapavargahetubhāvena prameyatā samudāye samāpyate, na tu pratyekam /
ātmādīnāmanyamatasyāpyatattvajñāne saṃsārānanivṛtteriti yadeva hi nirdeśa vacanabhedasya prayojanam, tadeva coddeśe 'pi, tayorekavākyatvāditi bhāvaḥ /
pramāṇādīnāmiti vibhaktyarthavyākhyānaparaṃ bhāṣyaṃ paṭhitvā pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
uttaram--kārakāṇāmiti /
tadvibhajate--yatreti /
kārakārthaḥ pradhānakriyā, yaduddeśena sarvakārakapravṛttiḥ /
kārakagrahaṇena ca tannāntarīyakatayā pradhānakriyāpyānīteti vivaraṇe sāpi darśitā /
yadyapi svasvāmibhāvādāvapi saṃbandhe 'ntargataḥ kriyākārakasaṃbandho 'sti saṃbandhamātrasya kriyāgarbhatvāt tannāntarīyakatvācca kārakasya, tathāpyasau na vivakṣyate /
saṃbandhamātrameva tu vivakṣyata ityarthaḥ /
tatra codayati--tattvasyeti /
ṣaṣṭhī cānarthikā avyatireke tadanupapatterityapi draṣṭavyam, tatrāniyamavādyekadeśī pariharati--na, ubhayathāpīti /
bhāvasya bhavitradhīnanirūpaṇatvād, bhāvanirūpaṇameva bhavitṛnirūpaṇamākṣipati /
abhede 'pīti /
iṣusthityā yathā tadbhāvapratiṣedha iṣobhāvo dharmo gatiḥ, tasya pratiṣadhaḥ sthitiḥ, tiṣṭhategratinivṛttyarthatvāt /
evamatrāpi na pramāṇaprameyādimātramacyate tattvagrahaṇenāpi tvarthāntaraṃ teṣveva yat yat samāropitaṃ rūpamanyathātvamiti yāvat tat pratiṣidhyate /
gatimaditi bhāvapradhāno nirdeśaḥ /
yathā dvekayordvivacanaikavacane /
iti dvitvaikatvayoriti /
saṃkhyevavikṣāyāṃ tu dvyekeṣviti syāt /
tena gati mattvamarthāntaramiṣornabhavatītyasminnarthe iṣoḥ sthitiriti prayujyata ityarthaḥ /
tadetad ekadeśimatamarthāntaratvaniyamavādī dūṣayati--tanneti /
pramāṇadibhyo 'narthāntarasya tattvasya ca iṣoranarthāntarasya gatyabhāvasya cāsiddheḥ / yathā ca bhāvātirikto 'bhāvastathā kṣaṇabhaṅgādhikāre nivedayiṣyate /
pramāṇādyatiriktaṃ ca tattvamanantarameva darśayiṣyatīti /
tattvasyajñānamityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyāpaṣṭe--tattvaṃ jñāyamānamiti /
ubhayaṃ pṛcchati-kiṃ punariti /

children.translated_text: The answer to the question about <s>tattva</s> (reality)—'<s>tattva</s>' means:
The causality, that is, the capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest.

children.text: sā ca dvayī svrūpalakṣaṇā sahakārisākalyalakṣaṇā ca, atīndriyasya sāmarthyasya naiyānikairanabhyupetatvāt /
children.translated_text: And that [capacity] is of two kinds: one characterized by its own essential nature, and one characterized by the totality of auxiliary conditions—because the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> (logicians) do not accept a supersensory capacity.

children.text: śakteśca bhāvatvena bhavitṛnirūpaṇādhīnanirūpaṇatvād bhaviturapi nirūpaṇaṃ bhavatītyuktam //
children.translated_text: And because the capacity, being of the nature of an effect, depends for its determination on the agent, it has been said that the determination of the agent also follows—this has been stated.

He states the nature of the <s>dvandva</s> (copulative compound)—'<s>sarvapadeti</s>.' He demonstrates the purport of adopting the <s>dvandva</s> interpretation through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>)—'all indeed.' Because <s>bahuvrīhi</s> and <s>karmadhāraya</s> [compounds] are impossible, if a <s>ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa</s> (genitive compound) were adopted, there would be the fault of abandoning the intended meaning, since the last member's referent would become primary—this is the meaning. Regarding the enumeration, the word-by-word analysis being 'as stated,' he explains the purport of the <s>bhāṣya</s>—'according to the statement' (<s>yathāvacanam</s>). The purpose of the plural number for <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of knowledge) is that each independently has the nature of being a means of valid cognition. But regarding <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge), although each individually possesses the real nature of being knowable, the status of being a <s>prameya</s> in terms of being a cause of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) is completed only in the aggregate, not individually, because even according to other schools, without knowledge of the true nature of <s>ātman</s> (self) and the rest, <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) does not cease—therefore whatever is the purpose of the difference in wording in the enumeration is also the purpose in the definition, since they form a single sentence—this is the purport. Having read the <s>bhāṣya</s> concerning the explanation of the case-ending meaning of '<s>pramāṇādīnām</s>' (of the means of knowledge etc.), he asks—'what then?' The answer—'of the <s>kārakas</s> (factors of action).' He analyzes that—'where.' The purpose of the <s>kāraka</s> is the principal action, for whose sake all <s>kārakas</s> operate. And by the mention of <s>kāraka</s>, the principal action too is brought in as inseparable from it, and thus is shown in the explanation. Although in the relation of property and proprietor and such, the relation of action and <s>kāraka</s> is included, since mere relation is pregnant with action and <s>kāraka</s> is inseparable from it, nevertheless that is not what is intended; only the mere relation is intended—this is the meaning. He raises an objection regarding that—'of the reality.' It should also be observed that the genitive is meaningless if there is no distinction, because without distinction it cannot be justified. There the partial advocate of the non-restriction view responds—'no, in either case.' Because the nature of an effect depends for its determination on the agent, the determination of the effect itself implies the determination of the agent. 'Even if there is no difference'—just as in the case of an arrow's rest, the negation of its nature means: the arrow's nature, its property, is motion; its negation is rest, since 'standing' means the cessation of motion. Similarly here too, by the word '<s>tattva</s>' (reality), it is not merely <s>pramāṇa</s>, <s>prameya</s>, etc. that are taught, but rather whatever superimposed form exists in them—that is, their being otherwise—is negated. '<s>Gatimat</s>' (possessing motion)—this is a statement with the abstract quality as primary, just as dual and singular numbers are used for 'two' and 'one' respectively. Thus in '[the nature of] duality and unity'—when number itself is intended, it would be 'in two and one.' Therefore, the possession of motion is not something different from the arrow—in this sense, 'the rest of the arrow' is used—this is the meaning. This partial view is refuted by the advocate of the 'different nature' position—'not so.' Because the reality (<s>tattva</s>), which is not different from <s>pramāṇa</s> etc., is unestablished, and because the absence of motion, which is not different from the arrow, is unestablished. And just as non-existence is different from existence, so will be explained in the chapter on momentariness. And that reality different from <s>pramāṇa</s> etc. will be shown immediately after. He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'ignorance of reality'—'reality being known.' He asks both [questions]—'what then?'

children.text:
abhimataṃ niḥśreyasaṃ grahītuṃ niḥśreyasadvaividhyamāha--niḥśreyasaṃ purariti /
takrijñadṛṣṭaṃ niḥśreyasaṃ grahītuṃ dṛṣṭamatiprasaṅgāpādanena dūṣayati--eve ca kṛtveti /
sūtrakārābhimataṃ niḥśreyasamāha--paraṃ tviti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, yadyapi niḥśreyasapadamabhimatamātravāci pramāṇāditattvajñānasya ca dṛṣṭamapi niḥśreyasaṃ saṃbhavati, tasyaiva tataḥ sākṣādutpatteḥ /
tathāpyātmādivācakaprameyapadasamabhivyāhārādadṛṣṭameva niḥśreyasamabhipreta sūtrakārasya /
tatra ca pramāṇamāditattvajñānasyāpi pārarmyeṇa hetubhāvo 'styeveti /
codayati--dṛṣṭamiti /
dṛṣṭe darśanameva pramāṇam /
adṛṣṭaṃ tu niḥśreyasamaprāmāṇikaṃ darśanābhāvādityarthaḥ /
pariharati--na, nāsti arthasya tathābhāvāt /
artha ātmādiḥ /
tasya āgamānumānasahakāriṇā kāraṇābhāvena kāryābhāvānumānamevātrārthe pramāṇamiti bhāvaḥ /
ye tu vaiyātyāt manyeran padārthatattvajñānamātrameva paraniḥśreyasaheturiti, yathāhuḥ---
eko bhāvastattvato yena dṛṣṭāḥ, sarve bhāvāstattvatastena dṛṣṭāḥ /
iti, tān pratyāha-- yadi punariti /
na hi bhāvānāṃ tattvamanyadataḥ pratyakṣaviṣayīkṛtād rūpāditi bhāvaḥ /
mokṣamāṇā iti, sani muco 'karmakasya guṇo vā iti guṇābhyāsalopau /
na kevalaṃ vastuvṛttiḥ, sūtrakārasyāpi saṃmatamedityata āha--pṛthagupadeśācca prameyasya pramāṇādibhyaḥ /

yadi ca yatkiñcitprameyatattvajñānānniḥśreyasasya parasya prāptiḥ, kimarthamātmādasūtreṇa dvādaśaiva prameyāṇi nādhikāni na nyūnāni cetyavadhāryate sūtrakārerṇa? tasmāt tadeva sākṣādupayoti niḥśreyase na padārthamātramityāha--prameyāvadhāraṇārthāyāṃ cotrarasūtraprikriyāyāmakuśalaḥ sūtrakāraḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: And if the attainment of the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s> were from the knowledge of the reality of any <s>prameya</s> whatsoever, for what purpose would the <s>sūtrakāra</s> determine by the <s>sūtra</s> beginning with '<s>ātman</s>' that the <s>prameyas</s> are exactly twelve—neither more nor less? Therefore, it is exactly that [specific knowledge of the twelve <s>prameyas</s>] which directly leads to <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, not mere knowledge of any category—he says: 'the <s>sūtrakāra</s> would be unskillful in the procedure of the subsequent <s>sūtras</s> aimed at determining the <s>prameyas</s>.'
Why? Because <s>prameya</s> would have been exhaustively treated by the first <s>sūtra</s> itself.

children.text: tasmād yadyupapattiḥ yadi ca sūtrakārabhimatasubhayathāpi prameyatattvaparijñānaṃ parasya niḥśreyasasya hetuḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, whether by reasoning or by the intention of the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, in either case, the complete knowledge of the reality of the <s>prameyas</s> is the cause of the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s>.
By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with '<s>ātmādi</s>' (the self and the rest) has been explained.

In order to grasp the intended <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (highest good), he states the twofold nature of <s>niḥśreyasa</s>—'<s>niḥśreyasa</s>, first.' He refutes the <s>niḥśreyasa</s> as conceived by the <s>Tārkikas</s> (logicians) by showing it leads to an undesirable over-extension—'having done thus.' He states the <s>niḥśreyasa</s> intended by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras)—'but the supreme.' This is what is meant: although the word <s>niḥśreyasa</s> merely denotes what is desired, and although a visible <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is possible from the knowledge of the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest, since it directly arises from that [knowledge], nevertheless, because of the co-occurrence with the word <s>prameya</s> which denotes <s>ātman</s> (self) and the rest, only an invisible <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is intended by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>. And therein, knowledge of the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest also has a causal role indirectly. He objects—'the visible.' For what is visible, direct perception alone is the means of knowledge. But invisible <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is without valid authority, due to the absence of perception—this is the meaning. He responds—'no, because the object is not thus non-existent.' The object is <s>ātman</s> (self) and the rest. The purport is that inference from the absence of effect due to the absence of cause, aided by scripture and inference, is the means of valid knowledge here. Those who, due to misinterpretation, think that mere knowledge of the reality of any category is the cause of the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, as they say—'One entity seen in its true nature means all entities are seen in their true nature'—to them he responds—'but if.' For the true nature of entities is nothing other than the form such as color which is the object of direct perception—this is the purport. '<s>Mokṣamāṇāḥ</s>' (those being liberated)—the <s>guṇa</s> vowel grade and loss of reduplication [apply] by the rule '<s>sani muco 'karmakasya guṇo vā</s>.' Not only is this the state of affairs, but it is also the view of the <s>sūtrakāra</s> himself—therefore he says: 'and because of the separate teaching of <s>prameya</s> from <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest.'

children.text:
atha kiṃ tattvajñānasyātmādiviṣayasyādṛṣṭa eva ko 'pi sāmarthyātiśayo yataḥ paraniḥśreyasotpādaḥ, maivam /
kiṃ tarhi? dṛṣṭayaiva dvāretyāha bhāṣyakāraḥ-- taccaitaditi niḥśreyasahetubhāvābhidhānasya anu paścāt udyate anūdyate /
tattvajñānotpāde hi sākṣāt tadviṣayamithyājñānādinivṛttikrameṇāpavargotpāda iti dvitīyasūtreṇānadyate /
tadetad bhāṣyaṃ taccaitadityādyadhigacchatītyantamanūdya vyācaṣṭe-heyamiti /
mithyājñānamātmādiṣu prameyeṣu avidyā tanmūlaṃ tṛṣṇā /
upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat, dveṣo 'pi draṣṭavyaḥ /
tanmūlau ca dharmādharmau, tadetaddheyam /
hānaṃ tattvajñānaṃ hīyate hyanenaitat sarvam /
tasya pramāṇasya /
upāyaḥ śāstram /
adhigantavyo mokṣaḥ /
evaṃmavayavān vibhajya tātparyamāha--etānīti /
etāni catvāryarthapadāni puruṣārthasthānāni, na kevalaṃ heyādhigantavyabhedena dvādaśavidra prameyaṃ darśayataḥ tadviṣayatattvajñānāya ca sopakaraṇanyāyābhidhānapramāṇavyutpādakaṃ śāstraṃ praṇayataḥ sūtrakārasya saṃmatam, api tu sarveṣāmevādhyātmavidāmācāryāṇāmiti bhāṣyatātparyamityarthaḥ /
tatra saṃśayādīnāṃ pṛthagvacanamanarthakam ityādi codyabhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭesaṃśayādyagrahaṇamiti /
satyamiti parihārabhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭai--na vidyeti /
codyaṃ vivṛṇoti--saṃśayādaya iti /
parihāraṃ vivṛṇoti--na vidyeti /
prasthānaṃ vyāpāraḥ /
teṣāṃ pṛthagvacanamityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭa--tasyāḥ saṃśayādīti /
na ca vācayamastu vidyātrayameva, kṛtamānvīkṣikyā vidyayeti, tasyā eva samastavidyāvadātīkaraṇahetutvāt /
yathā vakṣyati--pradīpaḥ sarvavidyānāmiti /
sa cāyaṃ kiṃsviditi vastuvimarśamātramanavadhāraṇajñānaṃ saṃśaya iti bhāṣyam /
tad vyācaṣṭe-tatra saṃśayādiṣu,
saṃśayastāvaditi jñānamavadhāraṇaṃ pratyaya iti paryāyā iti manvānaścādayati--anavadhāraṇātmaka iti /
na jñānamātraparyāyo 'vadhāraṇaśabdaḥ /
api tu tidvaśeṣaviścayavacanaḥ kiṃsviditi dolāyamānasyobhayakoṭispṛśaḥ pratyayasyārthe 'navadhāraṇātmakasyāpi pratyātmaṃ mānasena pratyakṣeṇāvadhāryamāṇatvāditi /
pariharati--na vyāghāta iti /
tat tasmāt abhayamiti /
tatra nānapalabdhe ityādi bhāṣyamavatārayituṃ pṛcchati-- sa kathaṃ nyāyasyeti /
yadi nyāyasyāṅga saṃśayo bhavet, so 'pi vyutpādyeteti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--yasmāditi /
etadākṣipati--upalabdha iti /
pañcarūpaścatūrūpo vā heturnyāyaḥ /
pratijñādyavayavasamūho vā nyāyaḥ /
nīyate prāpyate vivakṣitārthasiddhiraneneti /
tasyāśrayo viṣaya upalabdha ucyamāno nirṇota eva vaktavyaḥ /
sandigdhe hi tasmin hetuḥ sandigdhāśrayatayā asiddhaḥ syāt /
yatheha naganiku/je mayūraḥ kekāyitāpātāditi /
tadāpātasandehe ato na nirṇītaścennopalabdhaḥ /
tataścopalabdhaścānirṇotaśceti vyāhatamityarthaḥ /
pariharati--nāsti vyāghāta iti /
samāmanyataḥ parvatamātramupalabdhaṃ nirṇotam, tadviśeṣastu vahnimattvādiranirṇīta iti /
punaścodayati--evamapīti /
upalabdho nirṇota iti hi sāmānādhikaraṇyāt samānaviṣayatvaṃ darśayati /
tathā ca vyāghātaḥ /
sāmānyaviśeṣabhedena tu vyāghātaṃ pariharan sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na samarthayasa iti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati-na, yathā tatheti vyāpadeśāditi /

children.translated_text: because of the co-referentiality of the universal and the particular.

children.text: ya eva sāmānyo nirṇotaḥ, sa eva viśeṣato 'nirṇoto 'pi saṃbhavatīti na vyāghāta ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The very same thing that is determined as a universal can also be undetermined with respect to its particular—thus there is no contradiction, such is the meaning.
Thus, for the purpose of the operation of <s>nyāya</s>—because the operation of <s>nyāya</s> is impossible when there is no doubt.

children.text: na hi kariṇi dṛṣṭe cītkāreṇa tamanumīme pekṣāvanta iti //
children.translated_text: For when an elephant is seen, those who are curious do not infer it by its trumpeting.

Now, is there some unseen special power of <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality) directed at the self and other objects, from which the production of the highest good for others arises? It is not so. Then what? Through a visible means alone—the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) states this with 'taccaitad' etc.—after the statement of being the cause of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (liberation), it is restated. For upon the arising of <s>tattvajñāna</s>, liberation arises directly through the sequential cessation of false knowledge regarding its object—this is indicated by the second <s>sūtra</s>. Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s> passage from 'taccaitad' up to 'adhigacchati,' he explains—'<s>heya</s>' (what is to be abandoned): false knowledge regarding the self and other <s>prameyas</s> (objects of valid cognition) is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); rooted in that is <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving). And this is illustrative—<s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) should also be understood. Rooted in those are <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>—this is what is to be abandoned. The abandonment is <s>tattvajñāna</s>, for by this all of that is abandoned. Of that, <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) is the means—the <s>śāstra</s> (scripture). What is to be attained is <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). Having thus divided into components, he states the purport with 'etāni' etc. These four categories of meaning are the seats of human purpose; not only does the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (aphorist) show the twelve-fold <s>prameya</s> divided into what is to be abandoned and what is to be attained, and compose a <s>śāstra</s> that teaches <s>pramāṇa</s> along with the systematic exposition of <s>nyāya</s> (logic) with its instruments for the knowledge of reality regarding those—but this is the view of all the teachers of spiritual knowledge—such is the purport of the <s>bhāṣya</s>. There, regarding the objection beginning with 'the separate mention of <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) etc. is purposeless'—he explains the commentary objection with 'saṃśayādyagrahaṇam.' He explains the reply-commentary with 'satyam'—'na vidyā.' He elaborates the objection—'saṃśayādayaḥ.' He elaborates the reply—'na vidyā.' <s>Prasthāna</s> means activity. He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'their separate mention'—'of that, <s>saṃśaya</s> etc.' And let there not be said that there are only three sciences, that the science of <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic) is unnecessary, since it alone is the cause of purifying all sciences. As will be stated—'a lamp for all sciences.' And this <s>bhāṣya</s> states that doubt is merely a deliberation of 'what is this?'—a cognition without determination. He explains that with 'there, among <s>saṃśaya</s> etc., first <s>saṃśaya</s>'—considering that <s>jñāna</s> (cognition), <s>avadhāraṇa</s> (determination), and <s>pratyaya</s> (cognition) are synonyms, he begins with 'having the nature of non-determination.' The word <s>avadhāraṇa</s> is not merely a synonym for <s>jñāna</s>; rather, it denotes a particular ascertainment—because even a cognition touching both alternatives, wavering like a swing in the form of 'what is this?', though having the nature of non-determination, is determinable by mental direct perception individually. He resolves this—'there is no contradiction.' Therefore it is without fear. There, in order to introduce the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'not when unapprehended,' he asks—'how is that an ancillary of <s>nyāya</s>?' The sense is: if doubt were an ancillary of <s>nyāya</s>, it too should be explained. The answer—'because.' He raises an objection to this—'apprehended.' The five-membered or four-membered reason is <s>nyāya</s>. Or <s>nyāya</s> is the collection of members beginning with the proposition. That by which the desired conclusion is reached. Its substrate, the object called 'apprehended,' must be stated as already determined. For if that were doubtful, the reason would be unestablished due to having a doubtful substrate. Just as here: 'there is a peacock in the mountain grove, because of the sound of its cry'—if there is doubt about that appearance, then it is not determined, and hence not apprehended. And thus 'apprehended yet undetermined' would be contradictory—such is the meaning. He resolves—'there is no contradiction.' What is apprehended as determined is the mere mountain in general; but its particular feature, such as possessing fire, is undetermined. He raises another objection—'even so.' 'Apprehended' and 'determined,' being in grammatical co-reference, show identity of object. And thus there is contradiction. But in resolving the contradiction through the distinction of universal and particular, you do not justify the co-reference—such is the sense. He resolves—'no, because of the designation as such,'

children.text:
prayojanasvarūpapratipādanapūrvakaṃ prayojanapadaprayojanapradaśanārthaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣe--atha prayojanam /
vyākhyātuṃ pṛcchati--kiṃ punariti /
uttaṃraṃ-- yeneti /
sphuṭataramavaitat ityarthaḥ /
punaḥ pṛcchati--keneti /
ekadeśimatenottaramāha--dharmeti /
tatra kāma itīcchāmātraṃ vocyate, kāminīviṣayo vā rāgaḥ? pūrvasmina kalpe kāma ityevāstu kṛtaṃ dharmādibhaḥ, sarveṣāmeva kāmyamānatvāt /
uttarasminnavyāptiḥ, sarakamṛgayādīnāṃ kāmyānāmasaṃgrahāt /
dharmamokṣayorapi nāstikān pratyapravartakatvam /
tasmādayuktamediti manvāna āha-- vayaṃ tu paśyāma iti /
sukhasyāptyā duḥkhasya hānyā viṣayeṇa viṣayiṇaṃ pratyayamupalakṣamati /
asatyorakāraṇavāt, satyorvā anarthakatpavāt pravṛtteriti /
tathāpi sukhaduḥkhāptitahānyoreva kartuḥ pravṛttiprasaṅgo na tatsādhane, na hyanyadvijānāti icchati ca karoti cānyaditi ghaṭate, atiprasaṅgāt /
na ca phalaṃ puruṣapravṛttigocaraḥ, tatsādhanaṃ tu tadgocaraḥ /
tatsādhanatvavijñānāt tatsādhana eva pravartate /
tannātipasaṅga iti cet? hanta tarhi tatsādhanatvajñānameva pravartayati, na phalajñānam, jñānecchāpravṛttīnāṃ kāryakāraṇabhūtānāṃ sāmānādhikāraṇyena saṃpratipattaṃrityabhiprāyeṇāha--sukhaduḥkhasādhanabhāvat sarve 'rthāścetanaṃ prayojayantīti /
tuśabdaḥ phalād vyavacchinatti /
atrāpi viṣayeṇa viṣayiṇaṃ pratyayamupalakṣayati /
etaduktu bhavati, toyamupalabhya tajjātīyasyāpekṣisādhanāṃ dṛṣṭacarīmanusmarati /
atha tajjātīyatā liṅgena dṛśyamānasyāpekṣisāṇanabhāvamanumimīte /
anumāya ca pipāsuḥ pravartate /
tenopāyajñānasya sākṣāt puruṣapravṛttihetuvam, phalasya tvīpsitamasyodyeśatayeti sarvaṃ sundaram /
tadāśrayaśca nyāyaḥ pravartate iti bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe--tadidaṃ prayojanaṃ nyāyasyeti /
ākṣipati--ka iti /
samādhatte--upakārakatvamiti /
yathā rājāśritaḥ paṇḍita iti /
upakārakatvameva darśayatitanmūlatvāditi /
vidhiḥ pravṛttiḥ /
na jātu niṣprayojanā kākadantādau parīkṣāmārabhante prekṣāvanta ityarthaḥ /
ākṣipati--kā punariyamiti /
nyāyāśrayatvaṃ prayojanasya pratijñāya parīkṣāśrayatvasamarthanamasaṅgatamiti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--nyāyaḥ /
tasmānnāsaṃgatamityarthaḥ /
nanvevamapi nīyate prāpyate vivakṣitārthasiddhiraneneti vyupattyā pratyakṣādi pratyekaṃ nyāyaḥ /
na caitat pratyekaṃ prayojanamāśrayate /
ajihāsitānupāditsitānāmapyavijñāsitānāmarthānāṃ pratyakṣādigocaratvadarśanādittyākṣipati--kaḥ punarayaṃ nyāyaḥ? samādhatte--pramāṇairiti /
pratyakṣādipramāṇamūlāḥ pratijñādayaḥ pañcāvayavāḥ pramāṇāni /
tairarthasya liṅgasya parīkṣaṇa parīkṣā /
parīkṣitu tu liṅga pancāvayavopapannamanumeyapratyayaphalaṃ bhāvayatyeva, na tvatumeyārthaparīkṣā /
tasya sandigdhatve 'pi svarūpeṇa parīkṣānāspadatvāditi /
nanvavayavaiścedarthaparīkṣaṇa na tarhi pramāṇaiḥ, kāryakāraṇayorabhedābhāvādityata āha--kimuktaṃ bhavatīti /
na sākṣat pratijñādayo 'vayavā arthaparīkṣāyāmupayujyante /
api tu svakāraṇatatpramāṇasūcanena /
tasmāt pramāṇānāmavāntaravyāpāraḥ pratijñādaya ityupapannaṃ pramāṇairarthaparīkṣaṇam /
tadidamuktam--pramāṇavyāpārāditīti /
tasmāt naikaikaṃ pramāṇamiti /
samastapramāṇopakaraṇatvādeva cāsya paramatvamityāha--so 'yamiti /
pañcāvayavopapannatayā ca pratyakṣāgāmāśritatvam, na tadvirodha iti pradarśanārthaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣya tātparyāṃ vyācaṣṭe--prayakṣāgameti /
kathaṃ punaranena bhāṣyeṇa taducyata ityata āha--yadihānumāneneti /
yat punaranumānamityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭa--catra punariti /
yatra hi virodhastatra pramāṇamūlānāmavayavānāṃ pratijñādīnāmitaretarapratisandhānamekavākyatā nāsti /
pramāṇavirodhena cogyatāvirahiṇāṃ tatpadārthānāṃ pāramārthikānvayābhāvāditi /
tīrthaṃ darśanaṃ tasya pratirūpakaḥ /
adarśanamiva darśayatīti yāvat /
sa khalu tādṛśaḥ pañcāvayavaprayogo lābhapūjākhyātikāmaiḥ paṇḍitavya/janairūpavarṇyamānaḥ pratyavāyāya, prāgava tvapavargāyetyarthaḥ /
tadevaṃ samudāyato bhaṣyaṃ vyākhyāyavayavavibhāgāya paṭhati-yat punaranumānamiti /
pratyakṣaviruddhodāharaṇamāha--anuṣṇo 'giravayavī kṛtakatvād ghaṭavaditi /
atra codayati--kaḥ punariti /
idamātrākūtam--rūpatrayasaṃpannametat kṛtakatvaṃ na vā? na cet, tata eve tarhi tadanumānābhāsamiti kṛtaṃ pratyakṣavirodhena /
athānvayavyatirekapakṣadharmatatāsaṃpannamapi bādhitaviṣayatayaitatadapramāṇam? tadayuktam,
rūpatrayasaṃpattyāṃ khalvetat svāsādhyenāvinābhūtaṃ bhavati /
na ca bādhāvinābhāvayoḥ saha saṃbhavaḥ /
bādhāyāmapakṣadharmo bhavet, anaikāntikaśca hetaḥ /
vijñāsitadharmaṇo dharmiṇaḥ pacyamānatvena pakṣatvam, na punaḥ pratyakṣāvadhṛtasādhyaviruddhadharmasya /
tasyājijñāsitatvenāpakṣatayā taddharmasyāpakṣadharmatvānna caikāntikaḥ /
sādhyadharmiṇyeva pratyakṣopasthāpitasādhyadharmavati darśanena vyabhicārāt /
na ca sapakṣāsapakṣāvevānvayavyatirekāgamyāvinābhāvadarśanaviṣayau na pakṣa iti sāmpratam /
yadi hi pakṣaṃ vihāya bahireva sapakṣāsapakṣayoravinābhāvo gamyeta, tadā bahirvyāptimātrabalena pakṣadharmo 'pi heturna pakṣe sādhyaṃ sādhayet /
asiddhā hi tatrāsya svasādhyena vyāptiḥ /
tadetat paṇḍakamudvāhya mugdhāyāḥ putraprārthanamiva /
tasmādantarbahirvā sarvopasaṃhāreṇāvinābhāvo 'vagantavyaḥ /
evaṃ ca siddhaḥ pakṣe 'pi vyabhicāraḥ sādhanadharmasyetyanaikāntikatvam /
tathā ca rūpatrayasampanno heturbādhitaviṣayaścetyasaṃbhavaḥ /
tasmāt suṣṭhūkm--kaḥ punarasyānumānasya rūpatrayasamnnasya virodhaḥ? na hyasti saṃbhavo rūpatrayasaṃpannaṃ viruddhaṃ cetyarthaḥ /
atra samādhimāha--anumānāviṣaye prayogaḥ /
vakṣyati hyanumānādhikāre yathānaupadhikaḥ saṃbandho hetusādhyayoranumānāṅgam, na tu kāryakāraṇabhāvādiravyāpakatvādatiprasaṅgacceti /
sa caivaṃ pravartate--yo yaḥ kṛtakaḥ sa sarvo 'nuṣṇo yathā ghaṭadiriti /
na ca vahneriva dhūmasaṃbandhe ārdrendhanasaṃyogo gurvantavāsinoḥ sāhacarye iva svādhyāyādhyayanamupādhiḥ kṛtakatvānuṣṇatvayoḥ saṃbandhe upalabhyate /
so 'yaṃ śaṅkitaḥ samāropito vā prayatnena punaḥpunaranviṣyamāṇo 'nupalabhyamānastatra tatra ghaṭādāvupādhirnāstīti pratyakṣeṇa, yadyabhaviṣyad ghaṭādivadeva vyajñāsyatra, vijñānābhāvānnāstyeveti tarkasahāyena niśvīyate /
so 'yaṃ rūpeṇeva rasasya, śvastaneneva saviturūdayenādyanasya tadudayasya, samudravṛddhaceva candrodayasya samānakālasya, kṛtakatvasyānuṣṇatvena svābhāvika autsārgikaḥ saṃbandhaḥ sāmānyena yo yaḥ kṛkaḥ sa sarvo 'nuṣṇa ityavadhāritaḥ, na tu nirvibhajya tejo 'vayavini /
na hi sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptirekadeśaviṣayā bhavitumarhati /
ekadeśaviṣayatve yatraiva na darśitā tenaivānaikāntikatvamāśaṅkyeta /
tathā ca tatra tatraikadeśe pratyekaṃ vyāptipradarśanamaśakyam, ānanyāt /
tasmāt sarvopasaṃhāreṇaiva tadupadarśanam, tadiha kṛtakatvamautsargikasāmānyaviṣayavyāptismaraṇasadhrīcīnaṃ pakṣadharmatāvaśāt viśeṣe tejovayavini sādhayitumanuṣṇatonmukhaṃ yanna sādhayet tat kiṃ pratyakṣeṇāpahṛtaviṣayatvāt, āhosvidanaikāntikatvāt? na tāvadanaikānkitvam, prāgevasāmānyato 'naupādhikasaṃbandhasyāvadhāraṇāt /
uṣṇe tejovayavini kṛtakatvasya darśanād anaikāntikamapakṣadharmo vā kṛtakatvamiti cet-na, anumānena sāmānyato 'vadhṛtavyāptinā tasyānauṣṇyāsādhanāt /
pratyakṣeṇa tejo 'vayavina auṣṇyagraheṇa tatra kṛtakatvasya hetorvṛttāvutpannamapi vyāptivijñānaṃ bādhyate /
tataścānaikānkitvādapravṛttiranumānasyeti cet-na, anumānapravṛttiviṣaye sādhyadharmiṇi hetorvyabhicārānudbhāvanāt /
anyathā tadgatasādhyadharmasandehe tatropalabhyamānaḥ sādhanadharmaḥ sandigdhabyatirekivādanaikāntikaḥ syāt /
sandigdhasādhyadharme dṛṣṭānta iva sādhanadharmaḥ /

children.translated_text: And thus all inference would be destroyed, because of perception showing the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s>-property.
The fire-composite's not being established as not-hot, and thus inconclusiveness.

children.text: tadidamuktam--yasmina viṣaye tejaso 'nuṣṇatve etat prayuktam, sa pratyakṣeṇāpahṛta iti /
children.translated_text: This is what is stated—'the subject in which this is applied to prove that fire is not hot, that subject is removed by perception.'

children.text: evaṃ cānumāne dūṣite kṛtamapakṣadharmatvavyabhicārābhyāṃ tadupajīvibhyāmiti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: And thus, when the inference is refuted, there is no need for the charges of not-being-a-property-of-the-subject and deviation, which depend on it—this is the purport.

In order to present the nature of purpose (<s>prayojana</s>), he comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> to show the purpose of the word 'purpose'—now, purpose.
He asks for an explanation—'what then?'
The answer—'by which.'
The meaning is: 'this is more clearly stated.'
He asks again—'by what?'
He gives an answer according to one partial view—'<s>dharma</s>...'
There, does '<s>kāma</s>' refer merely to desire, or to passion directed toward women? In the first interpretation, let '<s>kāma</s>' stand as it is, since it is already included within <s>dharma</s> and the others, because everything is desired.
In the second interpretation, there is non-pervasion (<s>avyāpti</s>), since desired things like hunting deer and the like are not included.
Moreover, <s>dharma</s> and <s>mokṣa</s> do not motivate the <s>nāstika</s> (materialist).
Therefore, thinking 'this is improper,' he says—'but we see.'
By 'attainment of pleasure' and 'removal of pain,' the content is indicated through the relation of object to subject.
Because in the absence of both there is no cause, or in their presence there is no purposelessness of action.
Even so, the objection arises that action pertains only to the attainment and avoidance of pleasure and pain themselves, not to their means—for it does not work that one knows one thing, desires another, and acts upon yet another, due to over-extension.
And the result is not within the scope of human action; rather, the means to the result is within that scope.
From the knowledge of something being a means to that, one engages in that very means.
'Therefore there is no over-extension'—if so objected, well then, it is the knowledge of being-a-means that motivates, not the knowledge of the result, and since cognition, desire, and action, which stand in cause-effect relation, are to be understood through co-referentiality—with this intent he says: 'Because of being the means to pleasure and pain, all objects motivate the conscious being.'
The word 'tu' (but) distinguishes from the result.
Here too, the content indicates the subject through the relation of object to subject.
What is stated amounts to this: having perceived water, one recalls the observed capacity of that type to satisfy one's need.
Then, through an inferential mark, one infers the capacity of the perceived thing of that type to satisfy the need.
And having inferred, the thirsty one acts.
Thus, knowledge of the means is the direct cause of human activity, while the result is the intended goal to be aimed at—and all is well.
He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> that reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>) operates based on that—'this purpose of <s>nyāya</s>.'
He raises an objection—'who?'
He resolves it—'being helpful.'
Just as 'a scholar dependent on a king.'
He shows the helpfulness itself—'because it is the root of that.'
<s>Vidhi</s> means activity.
The meaning is: discerning people never undertake examination of purposeless things like crow's teeth.
He raises an objection—'but what is this?'
The sense is: having claimed that purpose depends on <s>nyāya</s>, supporting its dependence on examination is inconsistent.
The answer—'<s>nyāya</s>.'
Therefore it is not inconsistent—this is the meaning.
But even so, by the etymology 'that by which the intended meaning is led to, attained,' perception and the like individually constitute <s>nyāya</s>.
And each of these individually does not depend on purpose.
Since even things neither to be abandoned, nor to be acquired, nor to be investigated are seen to fall within the scope of perception and the like—thus he objects: 'what then is this <s>nyāya</s>?' He resolves—'by the <s>pramāṇas</s>.'
The five members (<s>pañcāvayava</s>) beginning with <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis), rooted in <s>pramāṇas</s> such as perception, are the means of knowledge.
Examination through them is the examination of the object through the inferential mark.
But the inferential mark, equipped with five members, produces the cognition of the inferable—it does not examine the object to be inferred itself,
since even when its own nature is in doubt, it is not a basis for examination.
But if the examination of objects is through the members, then it is not through the <s>pramāṇas</s>—since there is no difference between cause and effect—therefore he says: 'what has been said?'
The members beginning with <s>pratijñā</s> are not directly employed in the examination of objects.
Rather, they function by indicating their own cause, namely the <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Therefore, the members beginning with <s>pratijñā</s> are the intermediate operation of the <s>pramāṇas</s>, and thus examination of objects through <s>pramāṇas</s> is established.
This is what is stated—'through the operation of <s>pramāṇas</s>.'
Therefore, it is not any single <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And because it is the instrument of all <s>pramāṇas</s> combined, its supremacy is stated—'this is that.'
And by being equipped with five members and being based on perception and scripture, there is no contradiction with them—to show this, he comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> and explains its purport: 'perception and scripture.'
How does this <s>bhāṣya</s> say that? Therefore he says—'what is here by inference.'
He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'but what about inference'—'where moreover.'
For where there is contradiction, there is no unity of sentence—no mutual connection—among the members beginning with <s>pratijñā</s>, which are rooted in <s>pramāṇas</s>.
And because there is no real connection among those terms that are devoid of logical cogency due to contradiction with <s>pramāṇas</s>.
<s>Tīrtha</s> means a philosophical system; its <s>pratirūpaka</s> (counterfeit)
is one that appears to show but does not truly show—this is the meaning.
Indeed, such a five-membered argument (<s>pañcāvayavaprayoga</s>), when displayed by those appearing learned who are motivated by gain, honor, and fame, leads to harm, far from leading to liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)—this is the meaning.
Thus, having explained the <s>bhāṣya</s> as a whole, he reads for the purpose of distinguishing the members—'but what about inference.'
He gives an example contradicted by perception—'fire is not hot, is composite, because of being produced, like a pot.'
Here he objects—'what then?'
The underlying idea is this: does this 'being produced' (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) possess the triple character or not? If not, then it is a semblance of inference precisely for that reason, and there is no need to invoke contradiction with perception.
But if it possesses the triple character of positive concomitance, negative concomitance, and being a property of the subject, yet is invalid because its subject-matter is contradicted? That is improper,
for when it has the triple character, it is invariably concomitant with its <s>sādhya</s> (probandum).
And contradiction and invariable concomitance cannot co-exist.
In the case of contradiction, the <s>hetu</s> (reason) would not be a property of the subject, and would be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).
The status of the subject (<s>pakṣa</s>) belongs to the property-bearer whose property is to be investigated, by virtue of being under consideration—not to one whose property contradicting the <s>sādhya</s> is established by perception.
Since the latter is not a subject due to not being under investigation, its property is not a property-of-the-subject, and so the <s>hetu</s> is not inconclusive.
Rather, because there is deviation in the very subject where the property contradicting the <s>sādhya</s> is presented by perception.
And it is not proper to say that the homologous and heterologous instances alone—not the subject—are the domain for apprehending invariable concomitance through positive and negative agreement.
For if invariable concomitance were grasped only externally, apart from the subject, in homologous and heterologous instances, then by the mere force of external pervasion, the <s>hetu</s>, though a property of the subject, would not establish the <s>sādhya</s> in the subject.
For its pervasion with its own <s>sādhya</s> would be unestablished there.
This would be like marrying a eunuch and then hoping for a son from the deluded bride.
Therefore, invariable concomitance must be understood through universal inclusion, whether internal or external.
And thus deviation of the proving property in the subject too is established—hence its inconclusiveness.
And so, a <s>hetu</s> possessing the triple character and also having a contradicted subject-matter is impossible.
Therefore it is well said—'what contradiction is there for this inference possessing the triple character? For there is no possibility that something possesses the triple character and is also contradicted'—this is the meaning.
Here he states the resolution—'application in a domain not of inference.'
For it will be stated in the section on inference that just as an unconditional relation between <s>hetu</s> and <s>sādhya</s> is a component of inference, but not a causal relation and the like, because of non-pervasion and over-extension.
And that operates thus—'whatever is produced is entirely not-hot, like a pot and such.'
And unlike the connection of smoke with fire where moisture in the fuel is a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>), or unlike the accompaniment of a teacher and student where study is the condition, no <s>upādhi</s> is found in the connection between being-produced and being-not-hot.
This suspected or superimposed <s>upādhi</s>, when diligently sought again and again and not found in pots and such, is determined by perception to not exist there; and since if it had existed it would have been known just as in the case of pots and such, from the absence of such knowledge it is ascertained through <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) that it simply does not exist.
This natural, primary connection of being-produced with being-not-hot—like taste with form, like the rising of the sun with tomorrow's rising of the same, like the rising of the moon with the swelling of the ocean occurring at the same time—has been ascertained generally: 'whatever is produced is entirely not-hot'—but not specifically with respect to the fire-composite.
For a pervasion that encompasses all instances cannot be restricted to a particular domain.
If it were restricted to a particular domain, inconclusiveness would be suspected precisely where it was not shown.
And thus showing the pervasion in each particular domain individually is impossible, due to infinity.
Therefore, it should be shown only through universal inclusion. Thus here, being-produced, in accordance with the recollection of pervasion concerning the general primary scope, by the force of being a property of the subject, when directed toward establishing not-hotness in the specific case of the fire-composite—what prevents it from establishing that? Is it because perception has removed its subject-matter, or because of inconclusiveness?
It is not inconclusiveness, for the unconditional relation has already been ascertained generally beforehand.
If one objects that because being-produced is seen in the hot fire-composite, being-produced is inconclusive or not a property of the subject—no, because inference, having ascertained pervasion generally, establishes its non-hotness.
The pervasion-cognition that arose even when the <s>hetu</s> of being-produced occurred in the fire-composite—where hotness was grasped by perception—is overridden.
And therefore, due to inconclusiveness, inference does not operate—if so objected—no, because in the domain where inference operates, i.e., in the subject possessing the <s>sādhya</s>-property, no deviation of the <s>hetu</s> is apprehended.
Otherwise, when there is doubt about the <s>sādhya</s>-property in that subject, the proving property observed there would be inconclusive as one of doubtful negative concomitance,
like a proving property in an example where the <s>sādhya</s>-property is doubtful.
