children.translated_text: The relation is perceptible.
Therefore, audibility is imperceptible, and hence there is no contradiction with perception here.
This has been stated — 'because the operations of the sense organs are not themselves sense organs.'
The word <s>vṛtti</s> (operation) in its own meaning signifies relation — this is the meaning.

Now, he presents what <s>Dignāga</s> has cited as an inference contradicted by perception — 'others however' and so on. One who says 'sound is non-audible, because it is produced, like a pot and so on' denies the very nature of sound itself. For there is no cause of apprehending sound other than the organ of hearing. For there is no cause of apprehending sound other than the organ of hearing. And sound that is not apprehended cannot be an object of valid usage as existent. Therefore, for one who speaks thus, the non-existence of sound pervades his intention. And thus the meaning is that there is contradiction with perception. He refutes — 'by them' and so on. For the general rule is that in a qualified statement, both injunction and prohibition attach to the qualifier. But sometimes even qualified injunction occurs, due to there being no other possibility. For example: 'The priests move about wearing red turbans.' 'When possessing wealth, one should not be a renunciant wearing old and dirty garments.' Thus. Similarly here too, in the statement 'sound is non-audible,' by the force of the scriptural sentences, the negation attaches to the qualifier 'audibility' and is not connected with the qualified subject 'sound.' Nor does the negation of sound follow from the negation of audibility, as pervading the speaker's intention. Since a meaning that does not contradict the verbal meaning is understood through implication, and since the negation of audibility has sound as its substrate, the negation of that does not obtain in the absence of sound. And that absence is not void — this will be established in the third section. Nor is audibility an object of perception. For that is the relation between sound and the organ of hearing, since according to <s>Kātyāyana</s>'s statement: 'In <s>kṛt</s>, <s>taddhita</s>, and compound formations, relation is denoted by the suffixes <s>tva</s> and <s>tal</s>.' And perception does not operate on both the perceptible and the imperceptible.

tatra sopahāsam uttaramāha-tadāgamānuṣṭhānatātparyāvasthānāt kāpālikasyaivametat /
śrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇalakṣaṇāgamavihitamarthamācaratāṃ tannisiddhaṃ ca pariharatāṃ dākṣiṇātyānāmāhnenaivukādyanuṣṭhānamanādi adya yāvadanuvartamānamavigītamāmnāyamūlatāmanumāpayati ātmānaḥ śreyohetubhāvena, na khalvāgamānapekṣaḥ sahasreṇāpyanumānairimamarthamavagantumarhati /
kāpalikānāṃ tvāgamavihitamakurvatāṃ kurvatāṃ ca tanniṣiddhamarthaṃ prayatnenānādirapi vyavahāraḥ śākyamallakādīnāmiva na vedānumānamūlamiti bhāvaḥ /
atha trayīvidāṃ naraśiraḥkapālamapratyavāyaheturiti brūyāt, tadā trayyā vakṣyamāṇena nyāyena prāmāṇyopagamādāgamavirodhaḥ, tadīyasparśasya trayyāṃ niṣedhena pratyavāyahetuvaniścayāt /
api cāgamānapekṣo 'numānena śaucaṃ naraśiraḥkapālaṃvyavasthāpayan praṣṭavyo jāyate-- śuci naraśiraḥkapālamiti ko 'rthaḥ? nanu ca eva vākyāt pratīyate sa evārthaḥ, tat kiṃ pṛcchacata ityata āha--viśeṣavidhānaṃ ca śeṣapratiṣedhaparaṃ loke dṛṣṭam, yathā dakṣiṇena cakṣuṣā paśyatīti ukte na vāmeneti gamyate /
tadiha yadi śuci naraśiraḥkapālam, kimanyadaśucīti vaktavyam /
na hi naroccārādīnāmaśucitve pramāṇamanyadastyāgamāt /
āgamapramāṇyaṃ ca na manyasa iti bhāvaḥ /
atha trayīvidveṣād anumānapakṣāpātinā tvayā sarvameva naraviṭkapālādi śaucapakṣe nikṣipyata ityāha--atha sarvameva śuci /
pariharati--dṛṣṭānto nāsti /
kṛtaḥ? sarvasya pakṣīkṛtatvāt /
codayati--athānumānaviruddhra kasmādanumānaṃ na bhavatīti /
na khalu pramāṇatvena pratyakṣāgamābhyāmanumānasya kaścid viśeṣo yena tau bādhakāvanumānasya nānumānamiti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati--ekasminnanumānadvayasamāveśābhāvāt /
ayamabhisandhiḥ---yat tāvadanumānaṃ pūrvapravṛttaṃ tena bādhitaviṣayaṃ tabdalabhāvi paścattanamanumāna na svakāryāya paryāptam, yathoktamaśrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvād ghaṭādivadiyasyānumānasyānumānavirodha iti /
labdhasvarūpaṃ hi vastu kvacit kiścinniṣidhye, na tu jñānākārālīke bahiriti tṛtīye nivradayiṣyate /
tadiha śrāvaṇatvaṃ śabdasya niṣedhatāpūrvaṃ śravaṇamindriyamatīndriya tadgrāhrātvaṃ ca vastunī anumātavye śabdopalambhalakṣaṇena kāryeṇa /
tathā caitenaivānumānenāpahṛtaviṣayamaśrāvaṇatvānumānaṃ caramamanvayavyatirekasaṃpannamapi na svocitaṃ kāryā janayati /
eve tanubhuvanādīnāṃ na karteśvaro 'śarīritvānmuktasatmavat prayojanābhāvādityādyāpīśvaradharmigrāhimūlānamānenāpahṛtaviṣayatayā nyāyābhāsaṃ veditavyam /
tasmāt parasparānapekṣasamānakālapravṛttisamarthānumānadvayasamāveśābhāvābhiprāyametaduktam /
na hyanayoranyatarad bādhyaṃ bādhaka vā saṃbhavati, kiṃ tu mithaḥ satpratipakṣatayā na pramāṃ kurutaḥ /
kasmāt punarna samāveśo 'numānayoḥ? asamāveśe vā kutaḥ satpratipakṣatetyata āha--na hyanvayavyatirekasampanne iti /
ihānvayavyatirekagrahaṇena samānabalayoranvayavyatirekapakṣadharmatvāsatpratipakṣatvānyupalakṣitāni /
etaiḥ sampannayoryadi samāveśa ekasmin viṣaye bhavet, tata ekatarasya bādhyatvaṃ bādhakatvaṃ vā gamyetāpi /
na tvetadasti, asaprapipakṣatāsampatterabhāvāditi /
upasaṃharati- -tasmānnānumānavirudvam anumānaṃ tulyabalam, api tu satpratipakṣamityarthaḥ /
pratyakṣamapyanumeyaviruddhasādhanādanumānasya pratipakṣa iti satpratipakṣatayānvayavyatirekādisampannasyānumānasya na pratyakṣeṇa tadviruddhārthopasaṃhāriṇā samāveśa iti na bādhyabādhakabhāva iyabhiprāyeṇa codayati--pratyakṣavirodhyapīti /
pariharati na neti /
tulyabalau hi mithaḥ pratipakṣau bhavataḥ na tu durbalottamabalau /
children.translated_text: For mutual counter-arguments must be of equal strength, not one weak and the other strong.

children.text: na hi bhavati tarakṣuḥ prapikṣo hariṇaśāvakasya, kiṃ tu samarakaṇḍūnighnaviṣāṇakoṭisamullikhitagaṇḍaśailasya vipinamāhiṣasya /
children.translated_text: For a hyena is not a counter-argument to a fawn, but rather to a wild buffalo whose cheeks are scratched by the tips of horns itching for battle on a rocky mountain.
Therefore,

children.text: pūrvabhāvi pratyakṣamananyathāsiddhaṃ sadasatpratipakṣamanumānaṃ samānaviṣayasamāveśād bādhata iti yuktamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: perception, which arises first and is not otherwise established, overrides inference — whether it has a counter-argument or not — through co-application in the same domain. This is proper — such is the meaning.

He illustrates what contradicts scripture — 'pure' and so on. Since <s>Manu</s> and other lawmakers prohibit touching human bones, and since there is instruction of expiation upon touching them, the skull and other parts of a human are impure. The <s>Kāpālika</s> objects — 'how so?' The intention is: the <s>Vedas</s> and the <s>smṛtis</s> based on them are not authoritative for us. The reply — by saying 'the human skull is pure,' one who disregards <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, <s>Itihāsa</s>, and <s>Purāṇa</s>, relying solely on inference, must state the nature of purity in this matter. What does it mean to say 'pure'? If one says it means the absence of sin for the one who touches it, the <s>Siddhāntin</s> asks — whose sin is to be stated? If the <s>Kāpālika</s> were to say 'of the self,' then the uncontested customary practice of us <s>Kāpālikas</s> — characterized by touching human skulls and consuming food and drink placed in them — is conducive to welfare, just as the practice of <s>āhvāna</s> and <s>īkā</s> and the like is for southerners. Therefore the meaning is: the human skull is pure because it produces no sin for us. To this he replies with derision — 'by firm adherence to the practice of that scripture, this is so only for the <s>Kāpālika</s>.' The practice of southerners in performing <s>āhvāna</s> and <s>īkā</s> rituals, continuing from beginningless time to the present day without dispute, following the meaning enjoined by scripture in the form of <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, <s>Itihāsa</s>, and <s>Purāṇa</s>, and avoiding what is forbidden by them, leads one to infer its scriptural basis as a cause of one's own welfare. Without reference to scripture, even a thousand inferences cannot establish this meaning. But the practice of <s>Kāpālikas</s>, who do not perform what is enjoined by scripture and who perform what is forbidden by it — even though beginningless — is not based on Vedic inference, like that of the <s>Śākyas</s>, <s>Mallas</s>, and others. This is the import. If one were to say that the human skull is a cause of non-sin for followers of the three <s>Vedas</s>, then since the authority of the three <s>Vedas</s> is accepted by the reasoning to be stated, there is contradiction with scripture, because the prohibition of touching such things in the three <s>Vedas</s> establishes it as a cause of sin. Moreover, one who establishes the purity of the human skull by inference without reference to scripture is to be questioned — what does it mean that 'the human skull is pure'? The meaning understood from the sentence itself is the meaning, so why ask? Therefore he says — 'and a specific injunction is seen in the world to be intended for prohibiting the remainder,' just as when it is said 'he sees with the right eye,' one understands 'not with the left.' Similarly here, if the human skull is pure, then is everything else impure? For there is no authority other than scripture for the impurity of human excrement and the like. And you do not accept the authority of scripture — this is the import. Or if, out of hostility to the three <s>Vedas</s>, you who resort to inference place everything — human excrement, skulls, and the like — in the category of purity, then he says — 'then everything is pure.' He refutes — 'there is no example.' Why? Because everything has been included in the thesis. He objects — 'then why is there no inference contradicted by inference?' It is not the case that inference has any special distinction from perception and scripture as a means of valid knowledge, such that those two would override inference but not inference itself — this is the import. He replies — 'because two inferences cannot apply to a single subject.' The intention is this: whatever inference has arisen first, a subsequent inference whose domain has been overridden by it is not capable of producing its own effect, as stated in 'sound is non-audible, because it is produced, like a pot' — of which inference it is said that there is contradiction by inference. For a thing that has obtained its own nature may be negated somewhere in some respect, but not externally to the form of cognition — this will be explained in the third section. Here, prior to the negation of audibility, the audibility of sound, the sense organ of hearing being beyond the senses, and its capacity to apprehend — these things are to be inferred through the effect characterized by the apprehension of sound. And thus by this very inference, the inference of non-audibility, though possessing the final concomitance and exclusion, does not produce its proper effect, its domain having been taken away. Similarly, the inferences based on attributes ascribed to God — such as 'there is no creator God of this body, universe, and so on, because of being bodiless, like a liberated soul, because of absence of purpose' — are also to be understood as pseudo-reasoning, their domain having been taken away by this principle. Therefore this has been stated with the intention that two inferences of equal force, operating independently at the same time, cannot co-apply. For neither of these two can be the overridden or the overrider; rather, by being mutual counter-arguments, they do not establish valid knowledge. Why then is there no co-application of the two inferences? Or, if there is no co-application, how is there mutual counter-argument status? Therefore he says — 'for of what possesses concomitance and exclusion' and so on. Here, by the mention of concomitance and exclusion, the equal strength of the two, their status as properties of the thesis, concomitance and exclusion, and mutual counter-argument status are indicated. If there were co-application of these two possessing these qualities in a single subject, then one could determine one as overridden and the other as overrider. But this is not the case, because the condition for mutual counter-argument status is not fulfilled. He concludes — therefore there is no inference contradicted by inference; rather, they are of equal strength — that is, they are mutual counter-arguments. Even perception, being a counter-argument to inference that establishes something contradicting what is to be inferred, functions as a mutual counter-argument, so that an inference possessing concomitance and exclusion cannot co-apply with perception that leads to a contradictory conclusion — there is no overridden-overrider relationship. With this intention he objects — 'even what contradicts perception' and so on. He replies — 'no, no.'

children.text:
codayati--athopamānaviruddhamanumānaṃ kasmānna bhavati? gosadṛśo gavaya ityāraṇyakasya vākyaṃ śrutvā yadā nāgarako vanaṃ gato gosadṛśaṃ piṇḍamupalabhe, tadāsya vākyārthānubhavāhitasaṃskāraprabodhajanitasmṛtyapekṣa gosādṛśyajñānamupamānaṃ puro 'vasthitasya piṇḍasya gavayaśabdavācyatvajñāne pramāṇam /
tatra yadi kaścit /
pramāṇayet naiṣa piṇḍo gavayaśabdavācyo gopiṇḍasādṛśyād gopiṇḍāntaravaditi, tadidamanamānamupamānena bādhitaviṣayamastvityarthaḥ /
saṃpratipattiruttaram--nopamānaviruddhaṃ na bhavatīti anuṣajyate /
asti cet kasmānnoktamityata
āha--pūrvapramāṇavirodhānuvidhānānnoktamiti śeṣaḥ /
tad darśayati--upamānavirodha iti /

children.translated_text: He shows <s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) as a means of valid knowledge through its own result — 'contradiction with analogy' and so on.
He shows scriptural testimony as a means of valid knowledge through its own result — 'scripture' and so on.
He shows perception as a means of valid knowledge through its own result — 'knowledge of resemblance' and so on.
He concludes — because of contradiction with perception and scripture, the statement of contradiction implies what is said about inference contradicted by analogy.

He objects — then why is there no inference contradicted by analogy? When a townsman, having heard the statement of a forest-dweller that 'the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) resembles a cow,' goes to the forest and perceives an object resembling a cow, his knowledge of the resemblance to a cow, which depends on the memory generated by the awakening of the impression deposited by the experience of the meaning of that statement, is analogy — a means of valid knowledge for knowing that the object present before him is denoted by the word <s>gavaya</s>. Now if someone were to prove: 'this object is not denoted by the word <s>gavaya</s>, because of resemblance to a cow-object, like another cow-object' — let this inference, whose domain has been overridden by analogy, stand. The agreement is the reply — it is not the case that inference contradicted by analogy does not exist — this is to be connected. If it exists, why was it not stated? Therefore he says — because it was not stated, following the pattern of contradiction with the prior means of valid knowledge — this is the completion. He shows that — 'contradiction with analogy' and so on.

children.text:
bhāṣyamanubhāṣyākṣipati--tatra vādajalpāviti /
prayojanasvarūpopayogābhidhānānantaraṃ dṛṣṭāntapade vyākhyātavye tadullaṅghanena vādajalpayoḥ ko 'vasara ityarthaḥ /
avasaramāha--tenāneneti /
prayojanavyākhyānāṅgamevedaṃ na vādajalpavyākhyāṅgamityastyavasara iti bhāvaḥ /
tatraśabdārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe--tasminnyāyābhāse iti /
vādajalpakathayorhi na dvayorvādiprativādinoḥ sādhane samīcīne saṃbhavataḥ, vastuni viruddhadharmadvayasamāveśāmāvāt /
tasmād dvayorekasya nyāyaḥ, ekasya tu nyāyābhāsa iti vādajalpābhyāṃ vivicyate /
nyāyābhāsa iti tu sannidhānāduktam, sannihitārthatvāt sarvanāmna iti /
vitaṇḍā tu parīkṣyataṃ, saprayojanā niṣprayojanā veti /
tuśabdaḥ prasiddhaprayojanābhyāṃ vādajalpābhyāṃ vyavacchinatti /
pratipakṣasthāpanāhīnā hi vitaṇḍocyate /
tatra sthāpanāhīnatvāt pratipakṣahīneti pratīyate /
na khalu sthāpanābhāve sthāpyasaṃbhavaḥ /
tathā vitaṇḍacate vyāhanyate 'nayā pratipakṣasādhanamiti vyutpattyā parapakṣopaghātena pāriśeṣyāt svapakṣasiddhirasyāḥ prayojanaṃ pratīyate /
tadevaṃ sandigdhaprayojanā satī vitaṇḍā parīkṣyate, prayojanavatī na veti /
tatra yadi niṣprayojanā tato na sarvā vidyāḥ, sarvāṇi karmāṇi, tanmukhena ca sarve prāṇinaḥ prayojanena vyāptāḥ, vitaṇḍāyā eva karmarūpāyā vidyārūpāyā vā niṣprayojanātvāt /
atha prayojanavatī, tata upapannā prayojanavyāptiḥ /
kiṃ tāvat prāptam? tatra kecid bruvate niṣprayojanā vitaṇḍeti /
sthāpanāhīnatayā tāvat sthāpayaḥ pakṣo nāsti /
avayavavyutpattyāpi parasādhanāvidhātaḥ pratīyate /
na ca tāvanmātreṇa svapakṣasiddhirasti /
na hi parvatanitambavartiti dhūme asiddhatvādinā dūṣite vahnestatrābhāvo niścīyate /
tadidamuktam--dūṣaṇamātratvāditi /
tamimaṃ niṣprayojanavitaṇḍāvādinaṃ pratyāhatacca naivamiti /
parasādhanadūṣaṇenāsya pāriśeṣyāt svapakṣaḥ sidhyatu, mā vā saitsīt, sa tu svapakṣaseddhacaiva prayojanena pratipakṣasādhanamāhantīti bhāvaḥ /
tadaneva (sa) yadi prayojanamanuyukta ityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
atha na pratipadyata ityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭa--atha pakṣamapīti /
athāpītyādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe--atha parapakṣeti /
nāstiko hi sadasadubhayānubhayarūpatayā na vicāraṃ sahanta iti prameyāṇi sarvathā dūṣayati /
tadayaṃ parapakṣapratiṣedhamātraprayuktaḥ pravartate /
na tvasyāsti pakṣo na ca sthāpanā /
tayorapi prameyapakṣapātitayā dūṣyatvādityarthaḥ /
etadapītyādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭa-- tādṛgevaitat /
edadvibhajate--etasminnapi pakṣe caturvarga cet pratīpadyate so 'sya pakṣaḥ /
pratipattirabhyupagamaḥ /
yadyapi sthāpya eva pakṣaḥ, tathāpi tannāntarīyakatayā abhyupagamamātreṇa caturvargo 'pi pakṣa uktaḥ /
kaścaturvarga ityata āha--caturvarga iti /
eṣa sādhanavādī jñāpayati--ahaṃ vaitaṇḍiko jāne anena pañcāvayavena sādhānāvākyenedaṃ sādhyaṃ jñāpyata iti caturvargaḥ /
tatpratītyā khalvasya vaitaṇḍikasya parapakṣaniṣedhaḥ prayojanaṃ sidhyati /
tathā ca na viṣprayojano 'yaṃ vaitaṇḍika ityarthaḥ /
dvitīyaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati--atha na pratipadyata iti /
caturvarganāntarīyakatvāt dūṣaṇamapi na pratipadyate ityunmattavadupakṣaṇīya ityarthaḥ /
aparamapi nāstikavaitaṇḍikaṃ prati doṣamāha--pratipakṣeti /
asiddhaviruddhādidoṣo vākyasya vaitaṇḍikaprayuktasyārthaḥ /
taṃ yadi pratipadyate so 'sya pakṣaḥ /
athāsiddhaviruddhādīnāṃ sadbhāvābhyupagame prameyamadhyapātināṃ prameyamātravicārāsahatvābhyupagamo vighaṭata iti svavākyābhihitamevāddhiviruddhādi na pratipadyate, pūrvavaddoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if, while accepting the existence of unestablished, contradictory, etc. [faults], which fall within <s>prameya</s>, his acknowledgment of inability to tolerate any examination of <s>prameya</s> whatsoever is contradicted—and if he does not accept even the unestablished and contradictory etc. stated in his own words, the same fault applies as before.
He is neither a worldly person nor an examiner.

children.text: tasmād vitaṇḍāpi prayojanavatīti nāvyāpakaṃ prayojanamiti siddham /
children.translated_text: Therefore <s>vitaṇḍā</s> too has purpose—thus it is established that <s>prayojana</s> (purpose) is not non-pervasive.
This discussion arising incidentally is ancillary to the explanation of <s>prayojana</s>—he says 'purpose has been stated.'

He restates the <s>bhāṣya</s> and raises an objection—'there, <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s>.' The meaning is: after stating the nature and utility of <s>prayojana</s> (purpose), when the term <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) ought to be explained, what occasion is there for <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s> by skipping over it? He states the occasion—'by this.' This is indeed ancillary to the explanation of <s>prayojana</s>, not to the explanation of <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s>—so there is occasion, such is the sense. He explains the meaning of 'tatra'—'in that <s>nyāyābhāsa</s> (semblance of reasoning).' For in <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s> discussions, it is not possible that both the proponent and opponent have correct proofs, since contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single entity. Therefore, of the two, one has <s>nyāya</s> and one has <s>nyāyābhāsa</s>—this is distinguished through <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s>. '<s>Nyāyābhāsa</s>' is said due to proximity, since pronouns have proximate reference. But <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil) should be examined—whether it has purpose or is purposeless. The word 'tu' distinguishes it from <s>vāda</s> and <s>jalpa</s>, which have well-known purposes. For <s>vitaṇḍā</s> is said to lack counter-thesis establishment. There, due to lacking establishment, it is understood as lacking a counter-thesis. Indeed, the absence of establishment does not mean the impossibility of what is to be established. Also, from the etymology 'vitaṇḍā'—'that by which an opposing position is struck down'—through the elimination of the opponent's position, the establishment of one's own position is understood as its purpose. Thus, being of doubtful purpose, <s>vitaṇḍā</s> is examined—whether it has purpose or not. If it is purposeless, then not all sciences, all actions, and through them all beings are pervaded by purpose—since <s>vitaṇḍā</s> itself, being in the form of action or science, would be purposeless. But if it has purpose, then the pervasion by purpose is established. What then is accepted? Regarding this, some say <s>vitaṇḍā</s> is purposeless. Due to lacking establishment, there is no thesis to be established. From etymology too, only the destruction of the opponent's proof is understood. And by that alone, one's own thesis is not established. For when smoke on the mountainside is refuted as unestablished etc., the absence of fire there is not ascertained. This is what is meant by 'because it is mere refutation.' Against this advocate of purposeless <s>vitaṇḍā</s>, it is countered—'it is not so.' Whether his own thesis is established by elimination through refuting the opponent's proof or not—he who wishes to establish his own thesis attacks the opponent's proof with purpose, such is the sense. With that very point the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'if asked about purpose' etc. is explained. He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'but if he does not accept' etc.—'but even a thesis.' He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'but if' etc.—'but the opponent's thesis.' For the nihilist (<s>nāstika</s>), not tolerating examination in the forms of existent, non-existent, both, and neither, refutes all <s>prameyas</s> entirely. Thus this one engages solely in the negation of the opponent's thesis. But he has no thesis nor establishment. Because those too, falling within <s>prameya</s>, are subject to refutation—such is the meaning. He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'even this' etc.—'it is just so.' He divides this—'even in this thesis, if he accepts the four-fold scheme, that is his thesis.' Acceptance means acknowledgment. Although only what is established is a thesis, nevertheless, due to its being inseparable from that, even the four-fold scheme is called a thesis by mere acknowledgment. What is the four-fold scheme? He says—'the four-fold scheme.' This proponent of proof indicates: 'I, the <s>vaitaṇḍika</s> (cavilist), know that by this five-membered proof-statement this is proved'—that is the four-fold scheme. By accepting that, the <s>vaitaṇḍika</s>'s purpose of negating the opponent's thesis succeeds. And thus this <s>vaitaṇḍika</s> is not without purpose—such is the meaning. He refutes the second alternative—'but if he does not accept.' Because refutation too is inseparable from the four-fold scheme, he does not accept even refutation—so he should be disregarded as a madman, such is the meaning. He states yet another fault against the nihilist <s>vaitaṇḍika</s>—'<s>pratipakṣa</s>.' The meaning of the statement employed by the <s>vaitaṇḍika</s> having faults such as being unestablished or contradictory—if he accepts that, it is his thesis.

children.text:
dṛṣṭāntapadavyākhyānaparaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣate--pratyakṣaviṣaya iti /
ākṣipati--kimuktaṃ bhavatīti /
na tāvad yo yaḥ pratyakṣaviṣayaḥ, sa sarvo dṛṣṭāntaḥ, adṛṣṭāntasyāpi pratyakṣaviṣayatvāt /
nāpi yo dṛṣṭāntaḥ sa sarvaḥ pratyakṣa viṣayaḥ, āgamādiviṣayasyāpi dṛṣṭāntatvāt /
tasmādayuktametadityākṣepa iti /
tatsamādhānabhāṣyam--yatreti /
tadvacācaṣṭe--laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ darśanavighātaheturiti /
etacca kvacillaukikaparīkṣakāṇām, kvacit parīkṣakāṇāmiti mantavyam /
anyathā yadaprasiddhaṃ laukikānāṃ kevalaṃ paṇḍitarūpavedanīyaṃ paramāṇvādi tasyādṛṣṭāntatā syāt /
atra ca yo dṛṣṭāntaḥ sa evam, ta tu ya eve sa dṛṣṭānta iti draṣṭavyam /
evaṃbhūtavyākhyānasya prayojanaṃ darśayati--evaṃ ceti /
tad vibhajate--darśanāvidhāteti /
na kevalaṃ prameyavirodhaḥ sūtravirodhaścetyata āha--tataścodāharaṇasūtraṃ vyāhanyate /
yat teṣu teṣu śāstrapradeśeṣvatīndriyodāharaṇasūtraṃ siddhānte pūrvapakṣe vā yathā,
mantrāyurvedaprāmāṇyavat (2.1.68),
aṇuśyāmatānityatvavat (5.1.67)
ityevamādi, tad vyāhanyate /
na tūdāharaṇalakṣaṇasūtram /
taddhi pratyakṣaviṣayadṛṣṭāntatve 'pyupapadyata eva /
tasmād bhāṣye pratyakṣavacanaṃ dṛṣṭāntaviṣayapramāṇadāḍhrayaṃ lakṣayati /
pratyakṣamūlatvād vā pratyakṣo dṛṣṭāntaḥ, anyathānavasthāprasaṅgāditi /
so 'yaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ prameye 'ntarbhavannevamarthaṃ pṛthagukta ityāha--so 'yamiti /
nyāyasya pañcāvayavātmakasya vacanasamūhasya dṛṣṭānto mūlam, atastasya pṛthagupadeśaḥ /
ataścāsya pṛthagupadeśo yat--sati tasminniti /
anumānanimittatvamāha-- pūrva pratyakṣeti /
dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi dṛḍhatarapramāṇāvadhāritamityarthaḥ /
śābdamūlatāṃ drṛṣṭāntasya darśayati--pūrva jñātaṃ cārthamiti /
saṃbandhagrahaṇaviṣayo 'rtho dṛṣṭāntaḥ, saṃbandhagrahaṇaṃ ca śābdasyāpi jñānasya nimittaṃ prathamaśrāviṇaḥ śabdādarthajñānābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: <s>Dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) is the object in which the relation is grasped, and the grasping of the relation is the basis even of verbal knowledge, since one who hears a word for the first time has no knowledge of the meaning from the word alone.
Therefore <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> has utility even in verbal [testimony].
He states yet another purpose for its separate mention—'for the <s>nāstika</s> (nihilist).'
He states the reason for not elaborating—'that has been stated in the <s>bhāṣya</s>.'

He restates the <s>bhāṣya</s> devoted to explaining the term <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example)—'an object of perception.' He raises an objection—'what is being said?' It is not the case that whatever is an object of perception is an example, since even a non-example can be an object of perception. Nor is every example an object of perception, since even what is known through scripture etc. can be an example. Therefore this is improper—such is the objection. The <s>bhāṣya</s> resolving this—'where.' He explains that—'that which obstructs the vision of worldly people and examiners.' And this should be understood as referring sometimes to worldly people and examiners, sometimes to examiners alone. Otherwise, what is unfamiliar to worldly people and knowable only by scholars—like atoms etc.—would not be an example. And here, 'whatever is an example is such' should be understood, not 'whatever is such is an example.' He shows the purpose of such an explanation—'and thus.' He divides that—'obstruction of vision.' Not only is there contradiction with <s>prameya</s> but also with the <s>sūtra</s>—therefore he says 'and thus the illustration <s>sūtra</s> is contradicted.' Those illustration <s>sūtras</s> in various passages of the <s>śāstra</s>—supersensory illustrations in <s>siddhānta</s> or <s>pūrvapakṣa</s>—such as 'like the validity of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>' (2.1.68), 'like atomicity, darkness, and impermanence' (5.1.67), and so on—those are contradicted. But not the <s>sūtra</s> defining illustration. For that is appropriate even if <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> has perception as its object. Therefore the word 'perception' in the <s>bhāṣya</s> indicates the firmness of the means of knowledge regarding the object of the example. Or the example is called 'perceptual' because it is rooted in perception; otherwise there would be an infinite regress. This <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, though included within <s>prameya</s>, is separately mentioned for this purpose—he says 'this.' The example is the foundation of <s>nyāya</s>, the verbal aggregate consisting of five members—therefore its separate instruction. And the reason for its separate instruction is—'when that exists.' He states its being the basis of inference—'previously perceived.' The meaning is: firmly ascertained by a stronger means of knowledge in the example-locus. He shows that <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> is also rooted in verbal testimony—'and a previously known object.'

children.text:
siddhānpadavivaraṇabhaṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe--abhyupagameti /
tadvibhajate- -abhyupagama idimitthambhūtaṃ ceti /
tadvibhajate--idamitīti /
idamiti hi dharmiviṣayaṃ siddhāntaṃ darśayati, dharmo sarvatantrasiddhāntaviṣayaḥ /
itthamiti pratitantrādhikāraṇābhyupagamasiddhāntaviṣayaṃ darśayati /
vyavasthāyāmupalakṣaṇatayā pratitantrasiddhāntamātramudāharati--idaṃ sāṃkhyeṣveveti /
upalakṣaṇatāmudāharaṇasyājānānaścodayati--sarvatantreti /
pariharati--yo 'yamiti /
abhyupagamavyavasthitiranabhyupagamād vyavacchinatti /
na tu puruṣaviśeṣe vyavasthāpayatīti bhāvaḥ /
asyāpi prameyāntargratasyāpi sataḥ pṛthagupādānaprayojanamāha--tasya prameya iti /
children.translated_text: He states the purpose of its separate mention even though it is included within <s>prameya</s>—'of that, within <s>prameya</s>.'

children.text: tatra sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddhastāvad vipratipannānāmapi vādināṃ dharmo, tasya sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddhasya viśeṣeṣu pratitantrasiddhāntāḥ pravartanta /
children.translated_text: There, what is established as <s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s> is a property accepted even by disputants who disagree, and particular <s>pratitantrasiddhāntas</s> operate regarding the specifics of that which is established by <s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s>.

children.text: tathā hi yadi ghaṭo nāma na sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddhaḥ kimāśrayā avayavī vā paramāṇusamūho vā jñānākāro vā pradhānapariṇāmo vā brahmapariṇāmo vā tadvivarto veti pratitantrasiddhāntāḥ pravartante? kathaṃ ca pratitantrasiddhāntāśrayo vādajalpavitaṇḍāḥ pravartante? kimāśrayaśca nyāyaḥ syāt? tathā yadyadhikāraṇasiddhānto na bhavet, kathaṃ sādhyasāmānyavyāptaṃ sādhanasāmānyamiti sāṇanaviśeṣat sādhyaviśeṣo gamyeta? tasmādasti prameyasyāpi siddhāntasya pṛthagupādanaprayojanam /
children.translated_text: For instance, if the pot were not established by <s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s>, on what basis would the <s>pratitantrasiddhāntas</s> operate—whether it is a composite whole, an aggregate of atoms, a form of cognition, a transformation of <s>Pradhāna</s>, a transformation of <s>Brahman</s>, or an apparent modification thereof? And how would <s>vāda</s>, <s>jalpa</s>, and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> based on <s>pratitantrasiddhānta</s> operate? And what would be the basis of <s>nyāya</s>? Likewise, if there were no <s>adhikaraṇasiddhānta</s> (contextually established doctrine), how could a particular property to be proved be inferred from a particular proof that is pervaded by the general class of what is to be proved? Therefore there is purpose in the separate mention of <s>siddhānta</s> even though it is within <s>prameya</s>.

children.text: abhyupagamasiddhāntaṃ copariṣṭād vicārayiṣyati vāttikakṛt iti tatprayojanamihāsmābhinogktamiti //
children.translated_text: And the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> (author of the <s>Vārttika</s>) will examine <s>abhyupagamasiddhānta</s> (doctrine established by agreement) later—therefore its purpose is not stated here by us.

He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> expounding the term <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine)—'acknowledgment.' He divides that—'acknowledgment is this, of such a nature.' He divides that—'this.' For 'this' indicates a <s>siddhānta</s> concerning the property-bearer, while the property is the subject of <s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s> (a doctrine established in all systems). 'Of such a nature' indicates a <s>siddhānta</s> concerning acknowledgment in a particular system. By way of illustration, he cites only <s>pratitantrasiddhānta</s> (a doctrine peculiar to a system) in regard to arrangement—'this is in <s>Sāṃkhya</s> alone.' Not knowing that the example is illustrative, one objects—'<s>sarvatantra</s>.' He resolves—'that which.' The arrangement based on acknowledgment excludes [only] non-acknowledgment. But it does not restrict to a particular person—such is the sense.

children.text:
kramaprāptānavayavānāha--athāvayavāḥ /
nanu yathā tantavaḥ paṭasya samavācikāraṇaṃ kiṃ tathaivaite pratijñādayo vākyasya? no khalu rāganaguṇā varṇāḥ samavāyikāraṇatāṃ pratipadyanta ityāha-- vākyaikadeśā iti /
avayavā ivāvayavāḥ, na punaḥ samavāyikāraṇam, yathā hyavayavāḥ samudāyina ekasminnavayavini kārye dhārayitavye ca, evamekasmin vivakṣitārthapratipādane pratijñādayo 'vayavā vākyasya samudāyasya samudāyina iti /
nanu varṇānāmāśutaravināśināṃ kramavatāmekakālatvābhāve samudāyābhāvāt kutastatsamudāyo vākyam, kutaścaikadeśatetyāśayavānākṣipati--kiṃ punarvākyam? uttaram--pūrvapadasmṛtyapekṣo 'ntyapadapratyayaḥ smṛtyanugraheṇa pratisandhīyamāno viśeṣapratipattiheturvākyam /
viśiṣyata iti viśeṣaḥ padārtha ekaḥ, kriyā vā kārakaṃ vā prātipadikārtho vā padārthāntaraviśiṣṭo vākyārthaḥ /
yathā somena yajeta godohanena paśukāmasya yasya pitā pitāmaho vā somaṃ na pibet sa vrātya iti /
tasya viśeṣasyaikasya pratipattihetuḥ /
tadevaṃ samūhanibandhanaṃ padānāmekakāryatvaṃ sūcayati /
ko viśeṣapratipattiheturityata uktam--antyapadapratyayaḥ /
antyaṃ viśeṣyaṃ viroṣaṇapūrvakatvāt /
tasya padam /
na ca tadaviditaṃ sattāmātreṇa cakṣurādivad viśeṣyaṃ pratipādayatītyata uktam--pratyaya iti /
pratīyamānaṃ viśeṣyavāci padaṃ viśeṣyaṃ bodhayati /
pratītiśca nānubhavaḥ, api tu smṛti /
na hi kramavadvarṇasamudāyaḥ padaṃ śravaṇendriyānubhavagocaraḥ saṃbhavati, saṃbhavanti tu pratyekaṃ varṇāḥ /
na caite pratyekaṃ padam /
na ca pūrvavarṇasmṛtinicayasāhito 'ntyavarṇānubhavaḥ śrotraja
iti yuktam, smṛtīnāṃ svakāryasaṃskāravirodhinīnāmasahabhāvāt /
vinaśyadavinaśyadavasthayostūpāntyāntyavarṇasmṛtyanubhavayoḥ syāt /
na caitāvatārthapratyayaḥ pūrvavarṇasmṛtīnāṃ nirobhāvāt /
na ca pūrvavarṇānubhavanitasaṃskārasahakāriṇaḥ śravaṇādeva labdhajanmanaḥ pratyayasyaikasyādhyastatatsmṛtyanubhavarūpavaicitryasya sadasadvarṇāvagāhino viṣayabhāvamāpannā varṇā arthadhiyamādadhatīti sāmpratam, saṃbandhasaṃvedanāhitasaṃskārobdodhasamayajanmanā svajanitena saṃskāreṇa saṃbandhasmṛtyutpattisamaye vināśāt padārthāvabodhakatvānupapatteḥ /
tasmāt smṛtireva pratyayaḥ /
ata evādhyayanasamaye gurumukhād gṛhīto vedarāśirvedāṅgopāṅgajñānasaṃskṛtena smaryamāṇa eva tasyārthaṃ bodhayati /
evaṃ ca yadā padārthapratyāyana eva padānubhavo na kāraṇam, tadā vākyārthajñāne nānāpadārthasmaraṇākāṅkṣāyogyatāsannidhānāvadhāraṇādivyavahite kaiva katheti /
yadi tarhi viśeṣyapadameva smaryamāṇaṃ viśiṣṭamarthamavagamayati kṛtaṃ padāntaraiḥ, tata eva vākyārthapratipatterityata uktam--pūrvapadasmṛtyapekṣaḥ /

children.translated_text: The preceding [word] is the qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>), because the cognition of the qualificand is preceded by it.
Its word—dependent on the preceding words being remembered.

children.text: yadyapi smaraṇāni na saha saṃbhavanti tathāpyekasmṛtisamārūḍhāni vā padāni nirantarasmṛtisaṃtānasamārūsani vā parasparāpekṣāṇi /
children.translated_text: Although memories cannot co-exist, nevertheless the words are either mounted upon a single memory, or mounted upon an uninterrupted continuity of memories, and are mutually dependent.

children.text: tathā ca smaryamāṇaṃ viśeṣyapadaṃ viśeṣaṇapadāpekṣaṃ viśiṣṭamarthamavagamayatīti //
children.translated_text: And thus the qualificand word, when being remembered, being dependent on the qualifier words, conveys the qualified meaning.

He states the components (avayavas) that come in sequence—'now, the components.' Objection: just as threads are the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of cloth, are these components such as the thesis (pratijñā) likewise the inherent cause of the sentence? No indeed—colored qualities (varṇas, phonemes) do not assume the status of inherent cause—therefore he says 'parts of a sentence.' They are components as if components, but not inherent causes; just as parts sustain a single composite product, similarly the thesis and the rest are components of the sentence as a composite whole, serving a single intended meaning. Objection: since phonemes perish rapidly in sequence and cannot exist simultaneously, there is no composite, so how can the sentence be their composite, and how can there be a part-whole relation?—with this intent he objects: 'what then is a sentence?' The answer: a sentence is the cognition of the final word (antyapadapratyaya), dependent on the memory of preceding words, which, being connected through the aid of memory, is the cause of apprehending a qualified meaning (viśeṣa). That which is qualified is the <s>viśeṣa</s>—a single word-meaning, whether an action, a <s>kāraka</s> (factor of action), a nominal stem meaning, or a word-meaning qualified by another word-meaning—this is the sentence-meaning. As in: 'one should sacrifice with <s>Soma</s>,' 'by cow-milking for one desiring cattle,' 'whose father or grandfather did not drink <s>Soma</s>, he is a <s>vrātya</s>.' It is the cause of apprehending that single qualified meaning. Thus he indicates that the unity of function of words is based on their aggregate. What is the cause of apprehending the qualified meaning?—to this it is said: the cognition of the final word. The final word is the qualificand (<s>viśeṣya</s>), because it is preceded by qualifiers. Its word [is the final word]. And it does not convey the qualificand merely through its bare existence like the eye and such, without being cognized—therefore he said 'cognition' (pratyaya). The word denoting the qualificand, when cognized, conveys the qualificand. And this cognition is not experience (anubhava), but rather memory (smṛti). For a word as a sequential aggregate of phonemes cannot be an object of auditory experience—individual phonemes can be experienced, but they individually are not a word. Nor is it proper that the experience of the final phoneme accompanied by the accumulated memory of prior phonemes is born from the ear, since memories, being opposed to the impressions that produce their own effects, cannot co-exist. But in the two states of the perishing and the non-perishing, there could be the memory and experience of the penultimate and final phonemes. Yet even this much does not yield the cognition of meaning, due to the absence of the memories of prior phonemes. Nor is it proper that the phonemes—having become objects of a single cognition born solely from hearing, aided by the impressions deposited by the experience of prior phonemes, superimposed with the variety of memory and experience, and encompassing both existent and non-existent phonemes—produce the cognition of meaning; because the impression deposited by the cognition of the relation, at the time of the arising of the memory of that relation, would have perished due to its own generated impression, and thus could not produce the cognition of word-meaning. Therefore, the cognition is memory alone. For this very reason, the corpus of <s>Vedas</s> received from the teacher's mouth during study, when remembered with the refinement of knowledge of <s>Vedāṅgas</s> (auxiliary sciences) and their sub-branches, conveys its meaning precisely through being remembered. And thus, when the experience of a word is not the cause of conveying word-meaning, how can there be any issue regarding the mediation of memory of multiple word-meanings, expectancy, fitness, proximity, and determination in the knowledge of sentence-meaning? If, then, it is the qualificand word alone that, when remembered, conveys the qualified meaning, what need is there for other words—since the sentence-meaning would be understood from that alone?—to this he said: 'dependent on the memory of preceding words.'

children.text:
syādetat /
padamālā cet smaryamāṇā vākyārthavodhanī, kṛtaṃ tarhi padārthavodhanena, kṛtaṃ ca padatadarthasaṃbandhabodhanenetyata uktam--smṛtyanugraheṇeti /
pratyekaṃ padebhyo yāḥ padārthasmṛtayastadanugraheṇa /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, yadyapi vākyārthavodhanāya padamālā pravṛttā, tathāpi padārthasmṛtiravāntaravyāpārabhūtā apekṣate kāṣṭhānīva pākapravṛttāni jvalanamavāntaravyāpāram /
na ca padānyagṛhītasaṅketāti padārthān smārayantīti upapannā padārthasmṛtisaṃbandhasaṃvedanayorapekṣeti /
yadi hi padārthasmṛtyapekṣā padamālā vākyārthavodhanarī, hanta daśadāḍimāni ṣaḍapūpā bhavantītyevamādīnāmapi vākyārthabodhakatvaṃ syādityata āha--pratisandhīyamānaḥ /
pratipadaṃ sandhānaṃ ghaṭanaṃ pratisandhānam /
tacca svārthadvāreṇākāṅkṣāyogyatāsattyadhīnam /
na ca daśadāḍimādivākyādiṣu tadastīti na tato vākyārthāvabodha ityarthaḥ /
tadevamekasmṛtisamāroheṇa emārthāvacchedena ca padānāṃ samūho vākyam /
tasya bhāgā ekadeśā iti /
yāvatītyādi bhāṣyamavatārayati--te kiyantaḥ? bhāṣyavyākhyānenottaram--yāvabhdiriti /
pṛcchati--keti /
na hi samāpterniṣpatteranyā siddhirastītyabhiprāyaḥ /
uttaram--padārthasyeti /
dharmiṇaḥ siṣādhāyiṣitadharmaviśiṣṭatvaṃ vāstavamityarthaḥ /
samāpti pṛcchati--keti /
uttaram--viśeṣeti /
vāstavo dharmaḥ siddhiḥ, tadgocarastu viniścayaḥ puruṣadharmo niṣpattiriti viśeṣa ityarthaḥ /
kiyadbhiḥ kimabhidhānaiśca vibhāgaiḥ siddhiḥ parisamāpyata ityāśaṅkya bhāṣyakṛtoktam--tasya pañceti /
tad vyācaṣṭe--samākhyeti /
bhāṣyam anubhāṣyākṣipati--tatrāgama iti /
na hyagamavat pratijñāvacanaṃ niścāyakam, hetuvacanādivaiyarthyāt /
niṣpāditakriye karmaṇi sādhanasya sādhananyāyātipātāditi /
samādhatte--āgamādhigatasyeti /
ātmādiprameyapratipādanoddeśena hi śāstrametat pravṛttam /
tannāntarīyakatayā nyāyaṃ vyutpādayat tameva vyutpādayet, ya ātmādeḥ prameyasya sākṣāt niścāyakaḥ, tatpratipādakāgamapramāṇyaniścāyako vā /
tasya ca nyāyaviśeṣasyādyo 'vayavaḥ pratijñā, āgamārthaviṣayā sākṣāt, tadviṣayāgamapramāṇyapratipādakasya ca paramparayā /
tasmāt āgamaḥ pratijñā /
āgamopacārasya ca prayojanamidaṃ yadarthasaṃvādenāgamenānugṛhyate nyāyaḥ saprayojanaśca bhavati, āgamārthajñānasya niḥśreyasahetubhāvena nirūḍhatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the purpose of this figurative use of 'scripture' is that <s>nyāya</s> (logic), being supported by scripture through agreement of content, becomes purposeful, since the knowledge of scriptural meaning is firmly established as a cause of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good).

children.text: tasmād yadyapi na nyāyamātravartinī pratijñā āgamaḥ, tathāpi prakṛtanyāyābhiprāyeṇaitad draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, although the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), which pertains solely to <s>nyāya</s>, is not literally scripture, this should be understood with reference to the intention of the <s>nyāya</s> under discussion.

children.text: tathā cāgamārthasaṃbandhena pratijñāyāḥ kalpitaviṣayatvamapi parākṛtaṃ veditavyam /
children.translated_text: And thus it should be understood that the thesis's having a merely imagined subject-matter is also rejected through its connection with the subject-matter of scripture.

children.text: yadāhuḥ eke--sarvo 'yamanumānānumeyavyavahāro buddhyārūḍhenaiva dharmadharmibhāvena, na bahiḥsadasattvamapekṣate iti //
children.translated_text: As some say—'all this discourse of inference and the inferable operates only with the relation of property and property-bearer as mounted upon cognition; it does not depend on external existence or non-existence.'

There might be this [objection]: if a string of words when remembered produces the cognition of sentence-meaning, then what need is there for conveying word-meanings, and what need for conveying the relation between words and their meanings?—to this he said: 'by the aid of memory.' By the aid of the memories of word-meanings arising from each individual word. This is what is meant: although the string of words is operative for conveying sentence-meaning, nevertheless the memory of word-meanings, being an intermediate operation, is required—just as firewood, though operative for cooking, requires flame as an intermediate operation. And it is not the case that words whose conventional relation has not been grasped can produce memories of word-meanings—therefore the requirement of word-meaning memory and the cognition of the conventional relation is established. If the string of words, dependent on word-meaning memory, produces the cognition of sentence-meaning, then even strings like 'ten pomegranates, six cakes' should produce sentence-meaning cognition—to this he says: 'being connected' (pratisandhīyamānaḥ). Connection means the joining, the fitting together of each successive word. And that depends on expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), fitness (yogyatā), and proximity (sannidhi) through the medium of their own meanings. And since these do not exist in sentences like 'ten pomegranates' etc., there is no cognition of sentence-meaning from them—this is the meaning. Thus, a sentence is the aggregate of words based on the ascent into a single memory and the delimitation by a single meaning. Its divisions are its parts. He introduces the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'how many'—'how many are they?' The answer through the commentary explanation—'as many as.' He asks—'what?' The intention is: there is no accomplishment (siddhi) other than completion (samāpti) or establishment (niṣpatti). The answer—'of the object.' The meaning is: the real qualification of the property-bearer (dharmin) by the property to be established is [the accomplishment]. He asks about completion—'what?' The answer—'the particular determination' (viśeṣa). The meaning is: the real property is accomplishment (siddhi); the determination regarding it is a personal quality called establishment (niṣpatti)—this is the distinction. Anticipating the question 'by how many and by what named divisions is accomplishment completed?', he reads what the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> said—'of that, five.' He explains that—'by designation' (samākhyā). Having read the <s>bhāṣya</s>, he echoes and objects—'there, scripture' (āgama). For a mere thesis-statement, like scripture, is not determinative, because of the purposelessness of the reason-statement and the rest, and because of the transgression of the principle that an instrument should not be applied when the action has already been accomplished. He resolves—'of what is known through scripture.' For this <s>śāstra</s> was composed with the purpose of establishing <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) such as <s>ātman</s> and the rest. By virtue of being inseparable from that, while teaching <s>nyāya</s> (logic), it should teach precisely that <s>nyāya</s> which is the direct determinant of <s>prameyas</s> such as <s>ātman</s>, or which determines the validity of the scriptural <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes them. And the first component of that particular <s>nyāya</s> is the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>)—directly concerning the subject-matter of scripture, and indirectly concerning the establishment of the validity of the scripture that deals with that subject-matter. Therefore, the thesis is scripture (<s>āgama</s>).

children.text:
tathānumānasya nyāyānugrahākatvaṃ hetuvacanasyānumānatvopacāreṇa bhāṣyakāreṇoktam--heturanumānamiti /
tat khalvanumānapratipādakaṃ vacanaṃ viṣayatayānumānenānugrahītavyam /
na ca liṅgadarśanamātramanumeyapratipattihetuḥ, api tu saṃbandhasmṛtisahakāri /
na ca hetuvacanamātrāt sahakāritāvagamyate /

tadeva vibhajateyattu dvitīyaṃ liṅgadaśanam /
saṃbandhagrahaṇasamaye liṅgadarśanaṃ prathamam, tadapekṣayā sādhyadharmiṇi liṅgadarśanaṃ dvitīyam, tatsaṃbandhasmṛtivyaktihetubhāvāt smaryate 'nayeti smṛtiḥ saṃskāraḥ /
tasya vyaktiḥ kāryābhimukhīkaraṇam, tatra hetubhāvāt /
kvacit pāṭhaḥ--- saṃbandhasmṛtihetuvyaktihetubhāvāditi /
sa tu sugama eva /
ato heturityucyate /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, yat tad dvitīyaṃ liṅgadarśanaṃ śuddhamapyāpātataḥ saṃbandhasmṛtihetubhāvāt saṃbandhasmṛti sahakāryeva /
tathā cānumānam /
evaṃ ca tatpratipādakasya vacasa upapanno 'numānatvopacāra iti siddham /
evaṃ ca vāstavena liṅgena saṃbandhāt tadvacanasya buddhivikālpitaliṅgaviṣayatvaṃ parāstaṃ veditavyam /

children.translated_text: The same purpose should be applied to the other components yet to be discussed.
The <s>bhāṣya</s> states: 'the example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>) is perception.'
He explains that—'of the object of memory.'

children.text: yatra pratyakṣaviṣaye pūrvaṃ vyāptirgṛhītā tasya smṛtiriti smṛtiviṣayasya pratyakṣataḥ punarūpadarśanāt avipratipattyā punaḥ smaraṇāt tatsmārakaṃ vacanamudāharaṇaṃ pratyakṣam, mūlabhūtapratyakṣapramāṇasamutthatvādita //
children.translated_text: Where the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) was previously grasped in a perceptible domain, the memory of that is the memory-object; through the re-seeing of the perceptible from perception, through the re-remembering without error, the statement that triggers that memory is the example, which is perception—because it arises from perception as its foundational means of valid knowledge.

Similarly, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> has stated, through figurative attribution of the term 'inference' to the reason-statement, that inference supports <s>nyāya</s>—'the reason is inference.' That statement which establishes inference must be supported by inference as its subject-matter. And the mere seeing of the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is not the cause of apprehending the inferable—rather, it requires the aid of the memory of the relation. And the awareness of the auxiliary condition is not obtained from the reason-statement alone. Therefore, since the statement of the mark is not what establishes inference, how can there be a figurative attribution of 'inference' to it?—to this he says: 'thus, when only the mere seeing of the inferential mark is perceived, in the visible form of the mark devoid of the memory of the relation, the figurative use of cause constitutes the figurative use of inference—thus the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> has said the reason is inference.' He analyzes that very point—'but what is the second seeing of the mark.' The seeing of the mark at the time of grasping the relation is the first; relative to that, the seeing of the mark in the subject possessing the property to be proved is the second, because it serves as the cause of the manifestation of the memory of the relation—'it is remembered by this' means the memory, i.e., the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>). Its manifestation means making it face its effect. Because it serves as a cause therein. In some readings: 'because of being the cause of the manifestation of the cause of the memory of the relation.' But that is easily understood. Therefore it is called 'cause' (<s>hetu</s>). This is what is meant: that second seeing of the inferential mark, though pure in itself at first glance, by virtue of being the cause of the memory of the relation, is invariably accompanied by the memory of the relation. And thus it constitutes inference. And thus the figurative attribution of 'inference' to the statement that conveys it is established. And thus it should be understood that the real inferential mark's connection with its statement rejects the view that the statement has a merely imagined inferential mark as its subject-matter.

children.text:
kaḥ punarūpamānārtha iti /
pratyakṣamiva pratyakṣamityatrevakāre tatropamārthaḥ ka ityarthaḥ /
etadeva vibhajate--yasmāditi /
upamānamupanaya iti bhāṣyam /
tadvyācaṣṭe--yathā tathetyupamānaikadeśa iti /
upanayo hi tathā caitaditi pravartamāna udāharaṇasthaṃ yathāśabdārthamapekṣata iti yathā tatheti pravartata iti /
kiṃ punarūpamānaṃ yasyāyamekadeśa ityata āha--upamānaṃ khalu tathā gaustathā gavaya ityupadeśopayoge /
upayogastadarthaviṣayo 'nubhavaḥ /
tasmin sati paśvād vanaṃ gato nāgarakaḥ pratyekṣeṇādṛṣṭapūrvaṃ piṇḍaṃ paśyati /
smarati copadeśārtham /
piṇḍasya ca purovartinaḥ smaryamāṇena gavā sādṛśyaṃ pratyakṣeṇaiva paśyati /
tadevaṃbhūtaṃ sārūpyajñānaṃ gavayaśabdavācyo 'yaṃ piṇḍa iti pratītiheturūpamānam /
tadetasyopamānasyopadeśārthasmaraṇagavayapiṇḍagosārūpyāpratyakṣarūpasyaikadeśe sarūpye yo yathātathābhāvaḥ sa upanaye 'pyastītyetāvatopamānatvopacāra upanaya ityarthaḥ /
so 'yaṃ sarvapramāṇaviniveśena paramo nyāyaḥ stūyate /

na khalvavayavānāṃ pramāṇānāṃ vā vākye samavāyaḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--ekavākyeti /
adhyāropo buddhacā pratisandhānam /
sāmarthyaṃ pṛcchati--kiṃ punatiti /
uttaram--itaretareti /

iha tu vibhajyamānānāmavayavānāṃ nanmūlānāṃ ca pramāṇānāṃ sākāṅkṣatvameva dharmaḥ samārthyam /
tadatra samastarūpasampannaliṅgapratipādanamekaṃ prayojanaṃ vibhajyamānasākāṅkṣatvaṃ cāstīti siddhamekavākyatvamavayavānāmiti /
