yadyapi loke pratyakṣādīnāmekaikaśo 'pi vipratipannapuruṣapratipādakatvaṃ tatra tatropalabhyate, tathāpi yadetad vedaprāmāṇyamātmādipratipādanaṃ ca niḥśreyasopayoti, na tat pañcāvayavākyodatacchāstropadiṣṭopakaraṇād vinā sidhyatītyanenābhiprāyeṇa draṣṭavyam /
avayavānāṃ pṛthagabhidhānamākṣeptuṃ vikalpayati--kiṃ punaravayavā iti /
vikalpaprayojanaṃ pṛcchati--kiṃ cātaḥ? uttaram--yadi pramāṇāntaramiti /
samādhatte--napramāṇāntaramiti /
prayojanāntaramāha--ta eta iti /
yata eva vādādipravṛttihetavo 'ta eva tattvavyavasthāyāścāśrayā bhavantīti /
pṛcchati--ka iti /

children.translated_text: The meaning is: the establishment of reality does not rest on the members as a pot rests on jujube fruits.
The answer — their ability to establish the particular.
The particular is the property qualified by the property-bearer.
By the etymology 'that which is distinguished,' the ability of the members to establish that is their being the basis for the establishment of reality — this is the meaning.

What then is the meaning of analogy? In the expression 'like perception,' the particle 'iva' at 'perception' — what is the meaning of analogy there? — this is the meaning. He analyzes this very point — 'because' and so on. The <s>bhāṣya</s> states: 'analogy is application (<s>upanaya</s>).' He explains that — 'the expression "just as... so too" is a part of analogy.' For the application (<s>upanaya</s>), proceeding as 'so too this,' depends on the meaning of the word 'just as' found in the example, and thus proceeds as 'just as... so too.' What then is the analogy of which this is a part? Therefore he says — 'analogy indeed is the instruction "the cow is thus, the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is thus" when it is put to use.' The use is the experience whose object is the meaning of that [instruction]. When that has occurred, the townsman who has subsequently gone to the forest sees by direct perception an object never seen before. And he remembers the meaning of the instruction. And he perceives by direct perception itself the resemblance of the object present before him with the remembered cow. Such knowledge of resemblance, of this kind, is analogy — the cause of the cognition 'this object is denoted by the word <s>gavaya</s>.' Of this analogy — which has the form of recollection of the instruction's meaning, the <s>gavaya</s> object, the cow, resemblance, and perception — the 'just as... so too' relation that exists in one part, namely resemblance, also exists in the application — and to that extent the designation 'analogy' is extended to the application by courtesy — this is the meaning. This supreme <s>nyāya</s> (logical method), employing all means of valid knowledge, is praised. He comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> explaining the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>) and objects — 'what then?' The sense is: there cannot be a relation of inherence or connection among the members or the means of valid knowledge in a sentence. The answer — 'forming a single sentence.' Superimposition and its resolution by the intellect. He asks about the capacity — 'what then?' The answer — 'mutual.' For capacity is a property of words. But here, the property of the members being analyzed and the means of valid knowledge that are their roots is precisely their mutual expectancy — that is their capacity. Therefore, here, the establishment of the inferential mark endowed with a complete form is one purpose, and the mutual expectancy of the parts being analyzed also exists — thus the single-sentence nature of the members is established. He etymologizes the word 'conclusion' (<s>nigamana</s>) — 'they are concluded.' Having commented on the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'this is that,' he asks — 'what then is the meaning of the word "supreme"?' The answer — 'the supremacy of the subsequent-member sentence lies in its ability to convince a person in dispute.' He demonstrates this same point through negative concomitance — 'individually.' Although in the world the ability of perception and the like individually to convince a person in dispute is found here and there, nevertheless, the authority of the <s>Vedas</s>, the establishment of the self and the like, and what is conducive to <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good) — that cannot be accomplished without the instruments taught in the <s>śāstra</s> and expressed through the five-membered argument. With this intent it should be understood. He proposes alternatives to object to the separate statement of the members — 'what then, are the members?' He asks the purpose of the alternatives — 'and what follows from this?' The answer — 'if they are separate means of valid knowledge.' He resolves — 'they are not separate means of valid knowledge.' He states another purpose — 'these very.' Since they are the causes of engagement in debate and the like, they are also the basis for the establishment of reality. He asks — 'who?'

children.text:
kramaprāptatarkapadavyākhyānārthaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣate--tarko na pramāṇasaṃgṛhītaḥ /
pramāṇapadena hi catvāri pramāṇāni saṃgṛhītātina /
na caiteṣvanyatamastarka ityarthaḥ /
astu tarhi pramāṇapadasaṃgṛhītebhyaḥ pramāṇebhyaḥ pramāṇāntaramasaṃgṛhītaṃ pramāṇapadena prameyapadenevāsaṃgṛhītāḥ saṃśayādayaḥ prameyā ityata āha--na pramāṇāntaram /
bhāṣyamanubhāṣya hetumāha--aparicchedakatvāt aniścāyakatvāt /
tadeva vyatirekamukhena darśayati--pramāṇamiti /
syādetat /
aparicchedakatvamasiddhaṃ tarkajñānasya saṃśayādivad guṇatvenātmaliṅgatvāt /
anyathā tvakiñcitkaravādupādānavaiyarthyamityata āha--pramāṇaviṣayavibhāgāt tviti /
na hi vayaṃ guṇatvenotpattimattvena vā rūpeṇāniścāyakatvaṃ tarkasyācakṣmahe, kiṃ tu pramāṇaviṣayavibhāgahetutayā /
na caivamasyākiñcitkaratvamityarthaḥ /
pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
uttaram--yuktāyukteti /
idaṃ yuktamidamayuktamiti /
itikāreṇa yuktāyuktaviṣayaṃ tarkajñānaṃ parāmṛśati /
tadanena tarkasya svarūpaṃ darśitam /
tasya vyāpāramāha--yat tatra yuktaṃ bhavati, saṃbhavati tadanujānāti na tvavadhārayati tarkaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati pramāṇaṃ tattvāvadhāraṇāya pravṛttaṃ karaṇatayā itikartavyatāmapekṣate /
tarkaśca pramāṇaviṣayayuktāyuktavicārātmā pramāṇaṃ yukte tattve pravartamānamanujānan pramāṇamanugṛhṇarati /
tadanugṛhītaṃ pramāṇaṃ tattvanirṇayāya paryāptam /
na ca pramāṇaviṣaye cet tarkaḥ pravartate kṛtamasya pramāṇānujñayā, nanvayameva niścāyakaḥ kasmānna bhavatīti sāmpratam, tasya prasaṅgatayā pāratantryeṇa svayamasādhanatvāt /
asti hi prasaṅgo na prasaṅgo hetuḥ /
tathā hi pratyakṣameva tāvad bhūtale pravartamānaṃ tadviśeṣaṇatayā ghaṭābhāve 'pi pravartamānaṃ yadyatrābhaviṣyad ghaṭo bhūtalamivādrakṣyata, tena saha tulyadarśanayogyatvāt /
na ca dṛśyate /
tasmānnāstīti tarkeṇānujñāyamānaṃ ghaṭābhāviśiṣṭe bhūtale pravartate kevalamevedaṃ bhūtalaṃ neha ghaṭa iti /
evaṃ svargakāmo yajeta iti śabdo 'pi pravartamānaḥ paramāptasya bhagavatar iśvarasya niyogo nāsvargaphalāyāṃ yāgabhāvanāyāmavakalpata iti samānapadenopatto 'pi duḥkhatayā dhātvarthaḥ sādhya iti na yuktam /
bhinnapadopatto 'pi puruṣaviśeṣaṇamapi svarga eva bhāvanāphalaṃ yukta iti tarkeṇānujñāyamānaḥ pravartate /
na ca yadyabhaviṣyad ghaṭa iti vā yadyabhaviṣyad dhātvarthaḥ sāghya iti vā kriyātipattirasti, yadāśrayāniṣṭaprasaṅgenāyuktatvamitarathā tu yuktatvam, tat tarkeṇa niśvīyate /
tasmānna pramāṇam /
niśvayāya tu pravṛttaṃ pramāṇaṃ tadviṣayavivecanenānugṛhṇan itikartavyātvenopayujyate /

children.translated_text: As has been said —
<s>Tarka</s> (reasoning), designated as <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> (investigation), arises from all the <s>Vedas</s>.
Therefore it is [part of] the <s>Veda</s>, like salt that pervades [food] without being separately apprehended, like firewood and such.

In order to explain the word <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) which comes next in sequence, he comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> — '<s>tarka</s> is not included under <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).' For the word <s>pramāṇa</s> includes the four means of valid knowledge and nothing else. And <s>tarka</s> is not any one of these — this is the meaning. Let <s>tarka</s> then be a separate means of valid knowledge not included by the word <s>pramāṇa</s>, just as doubt and the rest are objects of knowledge not included by the words <s>pramāṇa</s> or <s>prameya</s>. Therefore he says — 'it is not a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>.' Having commented on the <s>bhāṣya</s>, he states the reason — 'because it does not determine,' because it does not ascertain. He shows this same point through negative concomitance — '<s>pramāṇa</s>.' One might object: the non-determining nature of <s>tarka</s>-knowledge is unestablished, since like doubt and the like, it is a quality and hence a mark of the self. Otherwise, if it were entirely ineffective, there would be purposelessness in employing it. Therefore he says — 'but because of the distinction of the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s>.' We do not say that <s>tarka</s> is non-determining in the sense of being a quality or of being produced; rather, it is so in the sense of being the cause of distinguishing the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s>. And thus it is not entirely ineffective — this is the meaning. He asks — 'what then?' The answer — 'what is proper and what is improper.' 'This is proper, this is improper' — by the quotative particle, he refers to <s>tarka</s>-knowledge as having the proper and improper as its objects. By this, the essential nature of <s>tarka</s> has been shown. He states its operation — 'what is proper therein, what is possible — that <s>tarka</s> approves but does not determine.' This is what is stated: a <s>pramāṇa</s>, having engaged in the determination of reality as an instrument, requires an ancillary procedure. And <s>tarka</s>, whose nature is the examination of what is proper and improper in the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s>, by approving when the <s>pramāṇa</s> operates regarding what is proper, assists the <s>pramāṇa</s>. A <s>pramāṇa</s> thus assisted is sufficient for determining reality. And if <s>tarka</s> operates in the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s>, and its task is done by approving the <s>pramāṇa</s>, then why is it not itself a determiner? — this is not appropriate, because it functions dependently, as an ancillary, and is not itself a means of establishing. For the <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) is a reason; the <s>prasaṅga</s> itself is not the reason. Thus: perception, operating on a ground surface, also operates with respect to its qualifier — even with respect to the absence of a pot — 'if a pot had been here, it would have been seen just like the ground surface, because of being equally fit to be seen.' And it is not seen. Therefore it does not exist — being thus approved by <s>tarka</s>, [perception] operates regarding the ground surface qualified by the absence of a pot: 'this is merely ground surface; there is no pot here.' Similarly, the verbal testimony 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice' also operates — the injunction of the supreme, trustworthy Lord is not applicable to the <s>yāga</s>-activity (<s>bhāvanā</s>) that does not have heaven as its fruit. Even though obtained from the same word-stem, the verbal root meaning as something to be accomplished in terms of suffering is not proper. Even though obtained from a different word, and even though a qualifier of a person, heaven alone being the fruit of the activity is proper — being thus approved by <s>tarka</s>, [verbal testimony] operates. And there is no unrealized past action (<s>kriyātipatti</s>) in 'if there had been a pot' or 'if the verbal root meaning were to be accomplished' — where by the undesirable consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>) based on the substrate, impropriety is determined, and otherwise propriety is determined — that is determined by <s>tarka</s>. Therefore [<s>tarka</s>] is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. But a <s>pramāṇa</s> that has engaged in determination is assisted by <s>tarka</s>'s examination of its domain, and thus [<s>tarka</s>] serves as an ancillary procedure.

children.text:
pūjitavicāravacano hi mīmāṃsāśabdaḥ /
ayuktapratiṣedhena yuktābhyanujñānaṃ tarkaḥ /
pramāṇetikartavyatātvena ca pramāṇād vedādbheda uktaḥ /

children.translated_text: 'Therefore it is [part of] the <s>Veda</s>' — by the intention of non-difference between the part and the whole.
And its nature as an ancillary procedure has been directly shown.
For when <s>dharma</s> is being ascertained by the <s>Veda</s> as an instrument,
<s>Mīmāṃsā</s> (investigation) will fulfill the ancillary procedural portion.

For the word <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> denotes honored deliberation. <s>Tarka</s> is the approval of what is proper by the rejection of what is improper. And its distinction from the <s>Veda</s>, which is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, has been stated by its being an ancillary procedure of the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text:
iti sarvamavadātam /
tasyodāharaṇaṃ bhāṣye karmeti /
karmakāraṇakamapūrvaṃ dharmādharmāviti yāvat, kārye kāraṇatvopacārāt /
etadupapādanāya pṛcchati--kathaṃ punatiti /
nikāyaviśiṣṭābhirapūrvābhiḥ śarīrendriyabuddhivedanābhirabhisaṃbandho janma, tasya kathaṃ karmanimittatetyarthaḥ /
atra pramāṇamanumānamāha--bhadavattvāt, vicitratvādityarthaḥ /
pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
bhedamāha--sugatiriti /
pramāṇamuktvā tasyetikartavyatābhūtaṃ tarkamavatārayati--so 'yaṃ bheda iti /
yadyekaṃ nimittaṃ syād vaicitryaṃ na bhavet /
na hyabhinnāt kāryavaicitryamupapadyate, tasyākasmikatvaprasaṅgāt /
ata uktam--anekamiti /
nanvanekaṃ yāgādibrahmahatyādikriyārūpaṃ kāraṇamastaṃ kṛtamapūrvairityata uktam--avasthitam /
yāgādikā tu kriyā āśutaravināśinī na cirabhāvine svargāya kalpata ityarthaḥ /
avasthitaṃ ced yāgādyāhitamapūrvaṃ dharmo 'stīti sadaiva sukhinā bhavitavyam /
evamadharmo 'stīti sadaiva duḥkhī syāditi sukhaduḥkhayoḥ kādācitkatvaṃ vyāhanyeta /
na hyavasthitāt kāraṇādanavasthitaṃ kāryamityata uktam--anityam /
na hyavasthānaṃ nityatāṃ brūmaḥ, kiṃ tu tāvadanena sthātavyaṃ na yāvadantyasukhaduḥkhasaṃvijñānaṃ janayati,
atha naśyatīti /
nanu bhinnāni santvapūrvāṇi, tathāpi sarvāṇi sarvātmasamavetāti, yathāvayavī svāvayaveṣu /
tathā ca sarvasādhāraṇyānnoktavaicitryotpāda ityata uktam--ekadravyam /
ekadravyaṃ cedastu tarhi sarvasādhāraṇe pṛthivyādau yatra kvacit /
tathāpi vaivitryānupapattirityata uktam--pratyātmaniyatam /
atha pṛthivyādyeva kāraṇa janmavaicitrye kasmānna bhavatītyāśayavān pṛcchati--kiṃ kāraṇamiti kasmāt kāraṇādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, with the thought 'why cannot earth and the like themselves be the cause of the variety of births?', he asks — 'what is the cause?' — meaning 'from what cause?'
The answer — 'of earth and the like.'

children.text: mā bhūt pṛthivyādi, pṛthivyādigataṃ kiñcid bhaviṣyatītyata āha-- pṛthivyādigatasyeti /
children.translated_text: Lest earth and the like themselves be the cause, he says — 'of what belongs to earth and the like.'
He states the reason for <s>tarka</s> being a <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) as stated in the <s>bhāṣya</s> — 'because of being an object of apprehension.'

Thus everything is clear. The example in the <s>bhāṣya</s> is '<s>karma</s>' (action). <s>Karma</s> as cause means <s>apūrva</s> (the unseen potency), that is, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — by the figurative transfer of causality from effect to cause. To establish this, he asks — 'how then?' Birth is the connection with a particular class of body, sense organs, intellect, and sensations that are unprecedented; how is that caused by <s>karma</s> — this is the meaning. Here he states inference as the <s>pramāṇa</s> — 'because of variety,' meaning because of diversity. He asks — 'what then?' He states the distinction — 'good destiny.' Having stated the <s>pramāṇa</s>, he introduces <s>tarka</s> as the ancillary procedure of that — 'this distinction.' If there were a single cause, there would be no variety. For variety of effects from an undifferentiated cause is untenable, since it would be random. Therefore it is said — 'multiple.' But are not the multiple ritual actions and the like, in the form of activities such as sacrifice and mortal sins, the cause? Those have ceased and are [preserved] by <s>apūrvas</s> — therefore it is said — 'persisting.' For ritual activity such as sacrifice, being quickly perishable, is not adequate for the long-enduring heaven — this is the meaning. If what persists — the <s>apūrva</s> deposited by sacrifice and the like — is <s>dharma</s>, then one should always be happy. Similarly, if <s>adharma</s> exists, one should always be unhappy — and thus the occasional nature of happiness and suffering would be contradicted. For an enduring effect does not come from an enduring cause — therefore it is said — 'impermanent.' For we do not say that endurance means permanence; rather, it must endure until it produces the final experience of happiness or suffering, and then it perishes. But let the <s>apūrvas</s> be different; even so, all of them inhere in all selves, just as a whole inheres in its parts. And thus, due to being common to all, the stated variety would not be produced — therefore it is said — 'inhering in a single substance.' If inhering in a single substance, then let it be in some common element like earth and the like. Even then, the variety would be unexplained — therefore it is said — 'restricted to each self.'

children.text:
tarkānantaraṃ nirṇaya uddiṣṭastarkahetukatvāt /
tasya svarūpamāha--nirṇayastattvajñānamiti /
yadyevamindriyāpātajanmapratyakṣajñānamapi tattvajñānamiti nirṇayaḥ syādityata āha--pramāṇanāmiti /
anena pañcāvayavavākyamupalakṣayati /
tatra satarkāṇāṃ pramāṇānāṃ samāvāyāt /
paramārthatastu tarkapūrvakastattvaviniścayo nirṇaya iti pratyakṣādīnāmapi tarkasahāyānāṃ nirṇayaphalatvamiti /
syādetat /
dhūmādigocareṇa nirṇayena vahnyādāvanumīyamāne pramāṇabheva nirṇayo na phalamityāśayavān pṛcchati--kadā punatiti /
viditābhiprāyasyottaram--yadeti /

children.translated_text: Having summarized, he states the purpose of the exposition of <s>tarka</s> and <s>nirṇaya</s> — 'these two.'
The examiner — here the world is referred to by the word 'world,' since <s>tarka</s> is impossible for one who is other than that.
'Having understood' means having examined and made a determination — this is the meaning.
The rest is explained by simple paraphrase.

After <s>tarka</s>, <s>nirṇaya</s> (determination) is enumerated, because it is caused by <s>tarka</s>. He states its essential nature — '<s>nirṇaya</s> is knowledge of reality.' If so, then perceptual knowledge born from the contact of the senses would also be knowledge of reality and thus <s>nirṇaya</s> — therefore he says — 'of the <s>pramāṇas</s>.' By this he indicates the five-membered argument. For therein, there is the combination of <s>pramāṇas</s> accompanied by <s>tarka</s>. But in the ultimate sense, <s>nirṇaya</s> is the determination of reality preceded by <s>tarka</s>, and thus even perception and the like, when accompanied by <s>tarka</s>, have <s>nirṇaya</s> as their result. One might object: when something like fire is inferred from smoke and the like through <s>nirṇaya</s>, then <s>nirṇaya</s> is itself the <s>pramāṇa</s>, not its result — with this thought he asks — 'when then?' The answer to one whose intention is understood — 'when.'

children.text:
nirṇayānantaraṃ vādavyākhyānārthaṃ bhāṣyam--vādaḥ khalviti /
tadanubhāṣyopapattimāhavāda iti /
nānā pravaktāro yasmin sa tathā /
ekasyāpi śāstrakartuḥ pūrvapakṣottarapakṣasādhanadūṣaṇapratipādako vacanasamūho vādaḥ syāditi nānāpravaktṛka ityuktam /
siddhāntabhedānavidhānena hi dvāvapi svasiddhāntānurūpaṃ sādhanaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ cāhaturityarthaḥ /
pratyadhikaraṇetyādi bhāṣyamanubhāṣyācaṣṭe--pratyadhikaraṇamasya sādhanam /
adhikriyata ityadhikaraṇaṃ sādhyam, tadadhikṛtya sādhanapravṛtteḥ /
pratyadhikāraṇa sādhanaṃ yasmin vāde sa tathoktaḥ /
asyaivārthaṃ niṣkarṣṭuṃ pṛcchati--kimuktaṃ bhavati? niṣkarṣati--ubhābhyāṃ vādiprativādibhyāṃ svasvasādhye sādhanaṃ vaktavyam /
tathā ca nānāpravaktṛkatvena tulyatve 'pi vādasya vitaṇḍāyāḥ pratyadhikaraṇasādhanatvena bhadeḥ siddho bhavati /
vitaṇḍāyāḥ pratipakṣasthāpanāhīnatayā pratyadhikāraṇasādhanatvābhāvāt /
tathāpi jalpādabhedo vādasya, asti hi jalpasya pratyadhikaraṇasādhanavatvaṃ ca nānāpravaktṛkatvaṃ ceti /
ata āha--anyatarasminnadhikaraṇe nirṇaya iti /
vāde hi tāvad brūte, na yāvadanyatarasmin pakṣe nirṇayo jātaḥ, tattvabubhutsorvādinorvāde 'dhikārāt /
jalpe tu puruṣaśaktiparīkṣālakṣaṇe 'pratibhādināpi parājyopapatternāvaśyaṃ tattvanirṇayaḥ /
tasmādanyataranirṇayāvasānatvena jalpād bhedo vādasyeti siddham /
yathā caitat, tathopariṣṭād upapādayiṣyate ityāha--tacceti /
tasya svarūpaṃ pṛcchati/--so 'yamiti /
uttaram--vākyeti /

children.translated_text: He raises an objection—'but is it not the case that...'
The meaning is: 'a collection of statements' and 'knowledge'—this is contradictory.
He resolves—'no.'
The meaning is: because the apprehension of proof and criticism has words as its object, there is no contradiction.

After determination (<s>nirṇaya</s>), the <s>bhāṣya</s> for explaining debate (<s>vāda</s>)—'debate indeed.'
Having commented on that <s>bhāṣya</s>, he states the justification—'debate.'
That in which there are multiple speakers is so called.
Even a single author of a <s>śāstra</s>'s collection of statements presenting the prior position, the reply, proof, and refutation constitutes a debate—hence it is called 'having multiple speakers.'
For without prescribing a difference in established doctrine, both parties present proof and refutation in accordance with their own established positions—this is the meaning.
He comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'for each subject'—'the proof for each subject.'
What is taken up for discussion (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>) is the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved), since the activity of proof proceeds with reference to it.
A debate in which there is proof for each counter-subject is so called.
To extract the meaning of this very point, he asks—'what has been said?' He extracts—'by both the proponent and the opponent, proof must be stated regarding their respective theses.'
And thus, even though <s>vāda</s> (debate) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil) are equal in having multiple speakers, their difference is established through having proof for each counter-subject.
Because <s>vitaṇḍā</s>, lacking the establishment of a counter-position, does not have proof for each counter-subject.
Even so, <s>vāda</s> is not different from <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling), for <s>jalpa</s> too has proof for each counter-subject and multiple speakers.
Therefore he says—'determination in one of the subjects.'
Regarding <s>vāda</s>, he states: the debate continues until determination has arisen in one of the positions, because the debaters in <s>vāda</s> have authority insofar as they seek truth.
But in <s>jalpa</s>, which is characterized by testing personal skill, defeat can occur even through lack of ready wit and the like, so determination of truth is not necessary.
Therefore, the difference of <s>vāda</s> from <s>jalpa</s> through culminating in determination of one position is established.
And as this is so, it will be demonstrated later—he says 'that.'
He asks about its nature—'this then.'
The answer—'statement (<s>vākya</s>).'

children.text:
yugapadeva jalpavitaṇḍe vyācaṣṭe--tadviśeṣāviti /
viśiṣyete bhidyate iti viśeṣau /
tasmād vādād viśeṣau bhinnau /
bhāṣyamanubhāṣya pṛcchati--kaḥ punarviśeṣaḥ? yadyogād viśiṣṭe vādāt jalpavitaṇḍe ityarthaḥ /
uttaram--aṅgādhikyamaṅgahāniśca yathāsaṃkhyam /
tadeva darśayati--chaleti /
tat kimidānī saṃśayādibhirivātyantavairūpyaṃ vādena jalpavitaṇḍayoḥ? netyāha--etāvatā viśeṣeṇa kathāmārgabheda iti etāvāneva viśeṣo na sarvathā, kathātvena saṃśayādivyāvṛttenasāmānyaviśeṣeṇa trayāṇāmapyabhedādityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He states yet another cause of difference—'and because of difference in subject matter.'
He analyzes that—'a pupil and so on.'
A '<s>śiṣya</s>' (pupil) here means one who is utterly mistaken, puffed up with false learning, pretending to be skilled—this is the meaning.
But one who is not of this kind—a pupil or the like who, though mistaken, is not arrogant—this is the purport.

He explains <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil) simultaneously—'the two distinctions of that.'
'They are distinguished, they differ'—thus '<s>viśeṣau</s>' (distinctions).
From that <s>vāda</s>, the two are distinguished, i.e., different.
Having commented on the <s>bhāṣya</s>, he asks—'what then is the distinction? By what conjunction are <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> distinguished from <s>vāda</s>?'—this is the meaning.
The answer—'excess of components and deficiency of components, respectively.'
He shows that very thing—'<s>chala</s> (equivocation)...'
Then is the dissimilarity of <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> from <s>vāda</s> as complete as that of doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) and the like? No—he says: 'by this much distinction alone is there a difference in the course of discourse'—the meaning is: there is only this much distinction, not in every respect, since all three share the common feature of being discourse (<s>kathā</s>), distinguished from doubt and the like.

children.text:
kramaprāptānāṃ hetvābhāsānāṃ svarūpamāha--anyatameti /
pañcasu caturṣu vā liṅgarūpeṣvanyatamaṃ liṅgaṃ dharmamekaṃ dvayaṃ trayaṃ vānuvidadhānā ahetavo hetuvadābhāsānta iti hetvābhāsā uktāḥ /
nigrahasthānebhya iti bhāṣyamavatārayitumāha--te ca nigrahasthānamiti /
avatārayati--nigrahasthāneti /
avatārya dūṣayitumekadeśimatena vyācaṣṭe--yasmāt kilaita iti /
kilaśabdo 'yamarucau /
tadetadekadeśivyākhyānaṃ dūṣayati--na, ubhayathāpyasaṃbandhāt /
kiṃ ye ye nigrahasthānebhyaḥ pṛthagupadiśyante, te sarve vāde codyante? atha ye ye vāde codyante te sarve pṛthugupadiśyante iti? ubhayathāpyanaikāntikatvāt nāvinābhāvalakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandha ityarthaḥ /
tadetad vibhajate--na vāde codanīyatvamiti /
kasmād ubhayathāpyavinābhāvābhāva ityata āha--yadi tāvaditi /
tasmāt nāyamavinābhūto heturvāde codanīyatvaṃ vā pṛthagupadeśo vā bhāṣyakāreṇokta ityupasaṃharati--tasmāditi /
vāde codanīyatvādityupalakṣaṇam, pṛthagupadeśāditi ca draṣṭavyam /
tadevamekadeśimataṃ dūṣayitvā svamatena bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe--etadeva tu nyāyyāmiti /
nigrahasthānebhyo hetvābhāsānāṃ pṛthagupadeśe prayojanaṃ yad bhāṣyākṣarebhyaḥ sākṣāt pratīyate /
sāmānyopadeśena viśeṣa upadiṣṭe viśeṣopadeśaḥ prayojanādhikyaṃ sūcayati /
yathā brāhmaṇān bhojaya kaṭha ceti kaṭhabhojane viśeṣo gamyate, tadvadihāpi nigrahasthānopadeśenaiva hetvābhāseṣu labdheṣu teṣāṃ viśeṣeṇābhidhānaṃ prayojanādhikyaṃ sūcayati /
etāvāneva sūtrakṛto vyāpāro yat sūtraṇaṃ nāma /
tatra nigrahasthānaviśeṣāṇāṃ hetvābhāsānāṃ svarūpaṃ vādasya ca tattvanirṇayāvasānatvamālocya vāde codanīyā bhaviṣyanti nigrahasthānatvena hetvābhāsā nāpratibhādaya iti prayojanaṃ varṇayāñcakāra bhāṣyakāraḥ /
syādetat /
bhavantu vāde codanīyā hetvābhāsāḥ, mā ca bhuvannapratibhādayaḥ /
kimevamapītyāha--vidyāprasthānapramedajñāpanārthatvāt /
vādajalpavitaṇḍā vidyāḥ paramparayā niḥśreyasopayogāt /
tāsāṃ prasthānaṃ vyāpāraḥ, tasya bhedaḥ, tajjñāpanārthatvāt /
ata eva jalpavitaṇḍayostu ityāha /
codayati--atha kasmāditi /
yadi vāde hetvābhāsāḥ prayujyeran tato nigrahasthānatvena codyeran, na tu teṣāmasti prayogo 'pramāṇatvāt pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambhatvācca vādasya /
tasmāt nigrahasthānamātratvaṃ hetvābhāsānām /
tathā ca na pṛthagupadeśaḥ, nigrahasthānopadeśenaiva labdhatvādityarthaḥ /
pariharati--pramāṇasāmānyāditi /
na khaluhetvābhāsan tabduddhyā prayu/jāte vādiprativādinau, api tu hetubuddhyā /
tathā cāsti teṣāṃ vāde prayoga iti vāde nigrahasthānatvena hevābhāsāścādyantām,
nāpratibhādīnītyarthavān pṛthagupadeśaḥ /
tadetad vikalpyākṣipati--vāde kāniciditi /
samādhatte--na, lakṣaṇaparatantratvādarthatathābhāvasyeti brūmaḥ /
lakṣyata iti lakṣaṇam, samānāsamānajātīyavyāvṛttaṃ rūpaṃ vādasya ca nigrahasthānānāṃ ca /
tadadhīno hi teṣāṃ tathābhāvo vyavasthā /
kānicideva nigrahasthānāni vāde na tu sarvāṇīti sāmānyato 'bhidhāya tadeva lakṣaṇaparatantratvamabhimate viśeṣe yojayati--vādasyeti /
uktamākṣipati--pramāṇapratirūpakatvāditi /
niścitau hi vādaṃ kurūtaḥ /
niścayaśca pramāṇaphalamiti kuto 'pramāṇasyāvakāśa ityarthaḥ /
uttaram--bhrānteriti /
na niścayaḥ sarvaḥ pramāṇamūlo 'pramāṇamūlasyāpi tasya darśanāt, anyathā viparyāsādapravṛttiprasaṅgāt /
vādinoścābhrāntatve vastuno viruddhadharmadvayasamāliṅgitatvamekadā syāditi bhāvaḥ /
pṛcchati--kaḥ punaḥ śiṣyeti /
upāsyopāsakayoḥ parasparaṃ na dhvaṃsanaṃ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--vivakṣitārthāpratipādakatvam eva na khalīkāra iti /
hetvābhāsānāṃ ca pṛthakkaraṇaṃ na vāde tanmātrāvadhāraṇārtham, api tu yasminnanuddhāvite 'pi nigrahasthāne tattvapratipattivyāghāto bhavati, tasya sarvasya saṃgrahārtham /
evaṃ ca nyūnādhikāpasiddhāntā api saṃgṛjītā bhavanti /

children.translated_text: Regarding that, he asks—'<s>nyūna</s> (deficient) and <s>adhika</s> (excessive)...'
The answer—'by the <s>pramāṇas</s>...'
He comments on and establishes the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'but in <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s>'—'but in <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s>.'

children.text: sāhaṅkāro vijigīṣurapratibhādibhirapi nigrahasthānaistiraskṛto galitāhaṅkārastattvabubhutsutāṃ nītaḥ paścād vādena vyutpādyata ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: one who is proud and desirous of victory, when humiliated by <s>nigrahasthānas</s> such as lack of ready wit (<s>apratibhā</s>) and the like, has his pride removed and is led to the desire to know the truth, after which he is educated through <s>vāda</s> (proper debate).

He states the nature of the fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) that come next in order—'any one of them.'
Among the five or four forms of the inferential mark, fallacious reasons are those that imitate a valid reason while exhibiting one, two, or three of the mark-properties—thus the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are stated.
To introduce the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'from the points of defeat,' he says—'and those are points of defeat.'
He introduces—'points of defeat.'
Having introduced, in order to refute, he explains according to a partial view—'because, reportedly.'
The word '<s>kila</s>' (reportedly) expresses disapproval.
He refutes this partial interpretation—'no, because of lack of connection in both cases.'
Is it that all those taught separately from the points of defeat are challenged in debate? Or that all those challenged in debate are taught separately? In both cases, because of inconclusiveness—there is no connection characterized by invariable concomitance—this is the meaning.
He analyzes this—'being challengeable in debate is not...'
Why is there absence of invariable concomitance in both cases? Therefore he says—'if indeed...'
Therefore this reason—challengeability in debate or separate instruction—is not invariably concomitant, as stated by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>—he concludes: 'therefore.'
'Because of challengeability in debate' is illustrative; 'and because of separate instruction' should also be understood.
Having thus refuted the partial view, he explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> according to his own view—'but this is proper.'
The purpose of teaching <s>hetvābhāsas</s> separately from <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) is directly understood from the words of the <s>bhāṣya</s>.
When the particular is taught through a general instruction, a separate particular instruction signals an additional purpose.
Just as when it is said 'feed the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, and the <s>Kaṭhas</s>' a special status for the <s>Kaṭhas</s>' feeding is understood, similarly here too, when <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are already obtained through the teaching of <s>nigrahasthānas</s>, their specific mention signals an additional purpose.
The activity of the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of aphorisms) is precisely this: composing <s>sūtras</s>.
Therein, having considered the nature of the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> as particular <s>nigrahasthānas</s> and the culmination of <s>vāda</s> in truth-determination, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> has explained the purpose: <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are to be challenged in <s>vāda</s> as <s>nigrahasthānas</s>, but not lack of ready wit (<s>apratibhā</s>) and the like.
This may be [objected]:
Let <s>hetvābhāsas</s> be challengeable in <s>vāda</s>, and let lack of ready wit and the like not be so.
What is the point even so?—he says: 'because of making known the distinction in the procedure of the sciences.'
<s>Vāda</s>, <s>jalpa</s>, and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> are sciences (<s>vidyā</s>), since they are ultimately useful for the highest good.
Their procedure (<s>prasthāna</s>) is their operation; its distinction; because of making that known.
For this very reason, regarding <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s>—he says.
He raises an objection—'but why then?'
If <s>hetvābhāsas</s> were employed in <s>vāda</s>, then they would be challenged as <s>nigrahasthānas</s>; but they cannot be employed because they are not valid means of knowledge, and because <s>vāda</s> is characterized by valid means of knowledge, <s>tarka</s>, proof, and criticism.
Therefore <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are merely <s>nigrahasthānas</s>.
And thus there is no separate instruction, since they are already obtained through the instruction of <s>nigrahasthānas</s>—this is the meaning.
He resolves—'because of the semblance of being <s>pramāṇas</s>.'
Surely the proponent and opponent do not employ <s>hetvābhāsas</s> with the understanding that they are <s>hetvābhāsas</s>, but rather with the understanding that they are valid reasons.
And thus they are employed in <s>vāda</s>—so let <s>hetvābhāsas</s> be challenged in <s>vāda</s> as <s>nigrahasthānas</s>,
but not lack of ready wit and the like—thus the separate instruction is meaningful.
He raises an objection through alternatives—'in debate, some...'
He resolves—'no, we say: because the actual state of things depends on definition.'
What is characterized (<s>lakṣya</s>) is the definition (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>)—the distinguishing form of <s>vāda</s> and of the <s>nigrahasthānas</s>, differentiated from similar and dissimilar kinds.
Their state of being such—their arrangement—depends on that.
Having stated generally that only some <s>nigrahasthānas</s> apply in <s>vāda</s>, not all, he applies that very dependence on definition to the specific case in question—'of <s>vāda</s>...'
He raises an objection to what was said—'because of being a semblance of a <s>pramāṇa</s>.'
For those who debate are certain. And certainty is the result of a <s>pramāṇa</s>—so how is there room for what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>?—this is the meaning.
The answer—'because of error.'
Not all certainty is rooted in a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since certainty rooted in what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> is also observed; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of no action from error.
And the purport is that if both debaters were unerring, a single thing would sometimes be invested with two contradictory properties.
He asks—'who then is a pupil?'
The purport is: between teacher and student, mutual destruction is not possible.
The answer—'the very failure to convey the intended meaning, not disparagement.'
And the separate treatment of <s>hetvābhāsas</s> is not merely for the purpose of determining that only those apply in <s>vāda</s>, but rather for the purpose of including everything whose non-identification would obstruct the apprehension of truth as a <s>nigrahasthāna</s>.
And thus <s>nyūna</s> (deficient), <s>adhika</s> (excessive), and <s>apasiddhānta</s> (false established doctrine) are also included.

children.text:
chalajātinigrahasthānānāṃ pṛthagupadeśaprayojanaparaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣate--chaleti /
upalakṣaṇārthamiti bhāṣyāvayavaṃ vyācaṣṭe /
parijñānārthameva kevalam, pirajñānasya phalamuktam--svavākye parivarjanam aprayogaḥ, paravākye codbhāvanamiti /
codayati--chalajātinigrahasthānānīti /
atra hi jāteḥ svavākye parivarjanamuktvā punaḥ svayaṃ prayogo na yuktaḥ /
kasmāt? vyāghātāt /
etad vibhajate--svākya iti /
pariharati--na vyāghātaḥ /
kutaḥ? praśnāpākaraṇārthatvāt /
tad vibhajate--svayaṃ ca sukaraḥ prayoga iti anena bhāṣyeṇa kimuktaṃ bhavati? pareṇa prativādinā jātau prayuktāyāṃ vādī prāśnikān sabhyān bravīti jātiranena prativādinā prayukteti /
te prāśnikā enaṃ paryanuyu/jīran he vādin kathaṃ kena prakāreṇa jātiḥ catuviṃśatyāṃ jātiṣu katamā jātiriti? so 'yaṃ prāśnikānāṃ praśnaḥ /

children.translated_text: For the purpose of answering that, one's own employment is easy—this is the meaning.
He concludes the topic at hand—'therefore these...'

He comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> concerning the purpose of separately teaching <s>chala</s> (equivocation), <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder), and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat)—'<s>chala</s>...'
He explains the component of the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'for the purpose of illustration'.
Merely for the purpose of complete knowledge; the fruit of complete knowledge has been stated—'avoidance in one's own statement means non-employment, and identification in the opponent's statement.'
He objects—'<s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>...'
For here, having stated that <s>jāti</s> should be avoided in one's own statement, it is not proper to then employ it oneself.
Why? Because of contradiction.
He analyzes this—'in one's own statement...'
He resolves—'there is no contradiction.'
Why? 'Because of serving to answer the question.'
He analyzes that—'and one's own employment is easy'—by this <s>bhāṣya</s> what is said? When the opponent has employed a <s>jāti</s>, the proponent tells the examiners and assessors: 'a <s>jāti</s> has been employed by this opponent.'
Those examiners would question him: 'O proponent, how so? In what manner? Among the twenty-four <s>jātis</s>, which <s>jāti</s>?' This is the question of the examiners.

children.text:
sūtrakāreṇa śāstrasyātyantikaduḥkhoparamarūpaniḥśreyasādhigamaḥ prayojanamuktam /
bhāṣyakārastu nāstyeva tat prekṣāvatāṃ prayojanam, catrānvīkṣikī na nimittaṃ bhavatītyāha--seyamānvīkṣikīti /
tadetad bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe--seyamānvīkṣikī nyāyavidyati /
yadyapītarā vidyāḥ pramāṇikamevārthamabhiniviśante tathāpyetadvidyāpratipādyameva pramāṇādyupajīvya sve sve vyutpādye tattve pravartantra, na tu pramāṇādyapi vyutpādayanti /
yathā pratyakṣādyupajīvya pravartamānamanumānaṃ na pratyakṣādiviṣayamapi tadānīmeva gocarayati /

na hi vidyāpadebhyo yāvanmātrāgatiḥ, tāvanmātreṇa prekṣavatāṃ paritoṣaḥ /
mā bhūt
ādityo vai yūpaḥ
ityādibhya ādityādīnā yūpāditā /
tasmāt saṃśayaparīkṣāpramāṇaviniveśa dvāreṇa tadarthatattvamavadhāryā tatra trayī viniveśanīyā /
evaṃ daṇḍanītivārtayoranugantavyam /
tasmādānvīkṣikīpariśodhitapramāṇapramāśitaṃ sāmādi itarā vidyāḥ kurvanti viṣayamiti śeṣaḥ /
api ca dravyaguṇakarmaṇāmabhimatānabhimatopāyatāprajñāpanena yathāyatha sarvā vidyāḥ prekṣāvataḥ pravartayanti nirvayanti vā /
tatra kimaviśeṣeṇa sādhyasādhanetikartavyatāsu pravartayantu, āhosvit sādhanetikartavyatāmātre? tatra yadi sādhyāṃśo 'pi pravartanāgocaraḥ, tadā śyenādisādhyāyā hiṃsāyā vihitatvena nānarthavatvam /
atha sādhyāṃśaṃ rāgataḥ prāptamanūdya sādhanetikartavyate eva vidharayete, tataḥ śyenādisādhyāyā hiṃsāyā avihitatvena na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni iti pratiṣadhādanarthatvam /
tadiha sādhyāṃśe 'pravartanamānvīkṣikīgamyam /
evamanuṣṭhānagatāḥ prayojakatvāprayojakatvādaya ānvīkṣikīgamyāḥ /

children.translated_text: And so it is also in the case of <s>Vārtā</s> (economics) and the rest.

children.text: tadevamānvīkṣikīmāśrayante sarvavidyā ityāha--āśrayaḥ sarvadharmāṇām sarvāsāṃ vidyānāṃ puruṣapravartanā dharmāḥ, teṣāmāśrayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, since all sciences depend on <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>, he says— 'the support of all <s>dharmas</s> (duties),' meaning the motivations for human activity belonging to all the sciences, of which it is the support.

children.text: vārtikakārastu dharmadvāreṇa vidyānāmevaśraya iti vyācaṣṭe--sarvavidyopakārakatvādāśrayaḥ, sarvāsāṃ vidyānāmiyamupakaroti /
children.translated_text: But the <s>vārttikakāra</s> (sub-commentator) explains through the door of <s>dharma</s> that this is the support of the sciences— 'because of being helpful to all sciences, it is the support'; it assists all the sciences.
The meaning is that it assists as an auxiliary when the activity to be performed through a science is being carried out.

The <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the aphorisms) has stated that the purpose of the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) is the attainment of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) in the form of the complete cessation of suffering. But the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) says that this is not indeed the purpose for discerning people, and that <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic) is not the cause of that— thus he says 'this <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>.' He explains this <s>bhāṣya</s>— 'this <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> is the science of logic (<s>Nyāyavidyā</s>).' Although other sciences deal only with objects established by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), nevertheless they rely on what is to be taught by this science, namely <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest, and proceed in their respective domains of reality to be elucidated, but they do not also elucidate <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest. Just as inference, which proceeds by relying on perception and the rest, does not at that same time bring within its scope the objects of perception and the like. Thus, by this mention of the instrument of knowledge, the function of <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> has been shown. Now, regarding the actions that are to be taught by the sciences— such as <s>Sāma</s> chanting, <s>Agnihotra</s> (fire ritual), agriculture, and the like— even in those, <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> is the means; thus he says— 'it is the means for all actions taught by the sciences, but not for the actions of ploughmen, hunters, and the like.' For from the words of a science, whatever extent of understanding is gained, to that extent alone discerning people are not satisfied. Let it not be that from passages like 'the sun indeed is the sacrificial post,' the sun and the like are identified with the sacrificial post and the like. Therefore, having ascertained the true meaning of those passages through the gateway of doubt, examination, and the application of <s>pramāṇa</s>, the three <s>Vedas</s> should be applied there. The same should be followed for <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> (political science) and <s>Vārtā</s> (economics). Therefore, the other sciences make as their subject-matter what is ascertained by <s>pramāṇa</s> purified through <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>— this is the completion. Moreover, by making known the status of substances, qualities, and actions as means to what is desired and what is not desired, all the sciences respectively either engage or disengage discerning people. There, do they engage indiscriminately in the end to be achieved, the means, and the procedure, or only in the means and the procedure? If the end to be achieved is also within the scope of engagement, then since violence accomplished through the <s>Śyena</s> sacrifice and the like is enjoined, it would not be harmful. But if the end to be achieved, already obtained through desire, is merely restated, and only the means and procedure are enjoined, then since violence accomplished through the <s>Śyena</s> and the like is not enjoined, it is harmful because of the prohibition 'one should not harm any being.' Here, the non-engagement in the end to be achieved is knowable through <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>. Similarly, matters pertaining to practice such as being a motivating factor or not being a motivating factor are knowable through <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>.

syādetat /
vyutpādyāścet pramāṇādayaḥ sarvavidyopayoginaḥ, tarhrātyantikī dukhaḥ- nivṛttirānvīkṣikyāḥ phalaṃ niḥśreyasapadādavagamyate /
vyutpādyasvabhāvālocanayā hi tad gamyate, sa ca vidyāntarasādhāraṇa iti vidyāntarādhigamyena niḥśreyasena saṅkaraprasaṅga ityata āha--tadidaṃ tattvajñānaṃ niḥśreyasādhigamaśca yathāvidyaṃ veditavyam /
vidyāntarāṇi tāvad yat tattvajñānaṃ kurvanti tatsvabhāvālocanayā hi tadvidyāsādhye eva niḥśreyasabhade upayujyante nānyatra /
iha tu pramāṇādi yadyapi sādhāraṇam, tathāpyasādhāraṇātmādirūpapramayasamabhivyāhṛtaṃ sadabhimata eva niḥśreyaseḥvatiṣṭhata iti /
viśuddhenārjanena homasādhanasya dravyasya prāptiḥ svāgatam /
ādigrahaṇena kramaparyantāṅgagrāmasākalyaṃ gṛhyate /
śvamārjārādibhiranupaghātaḥ anupahatatvam /
ādigrahaṇād viśuddhābhisandhiriti /
śeṣamatirohitam /
vādādīnāṃ nigrahasthānāntānāmupadeśaḥ parābhibhavopāyatayā madamānādihetutvena niḥśreyasaparipanthīti manvānaścodayati--madamānādīti /
pariharati--na, sūtrārthāparijñānāt /
nāyaṃ sūtrārthaḥ, sarveṣāṃ tattvajñānaṃ sākṣānniḥśreyasopayogīti, kiṃ tvātmāditattvajñānam /

tatra jalpādīnā parāhaṅkārapraśamanamavāntaravyāpāra iti na niḥśreyasaparipanthitā, kiṃ tvānukūlyamityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He says that the claim of their being the cause of pride, vanity, and the like is an unestablished reason— 'that which is said.'
He concludes— 'therefore, the understanding of debate and the rest is not a cause of attachment and the like.'
Thus.
At the conclusion of the <s>sūtra</s>. // 1 //

An objection may arise: if <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest that are to be elucidated are useful for all sciences, then the complete cessation of suffering is the fruit of <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s>, understood from the word <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (highest good). For that is understood through examination of the nature of what is to be elucidated, and since that nature is common to other sciences, there would be the unwanted consequence of confusion with the <s>niḥśreyasa</s> achievable through other sciences. Therefore he says— 'this knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>) and the attainment of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> should be understood according to each science.' The other sciences, whatever knowledge of reality they produce— through examination of the nature of their respective objects— that is useful only for the specific form of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> that is the goal of that particular science, and not elsewhere. But here, although <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest are common, being conjoined with the uncommon knowledge of <s>ātman</s> (self) and the rest, they serve only the intended form of <s>niḥśreyasa</s>. The acquisition of the material for the <s>homa</s> (fire offering) through pure earning is welcome. By the word 'and so on,' the completeness of all subsidiary limbs up to the final step is grasped. Non-destruction by dogs, cats, and the like means the state of being unharmed. By the word 'and so on,' pure intention is also included. The rest is clear. One objects that the teaching of debate (<s>vāda</s>) and the rest, ending with the points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>), being a means of defeating others, becomes a cause of pride, vanity, and the like, and thus an obstacle to <s>niḥśreyasa</s>— thus he objects with 'pride, vanity, and the like.' He resolves— 'no, because of incomplete understanding of the meaning of the <s>sūtras</s>.' This is not the meaning of the <s>sūtras</s>, that the knowledge of the reality of every category is directly conducive to <s>niḥśreyasa</s>; rather, it is the knowledge of the reality of <s>ātman</s> and the rest. The rest serves indirectly. In that context, debate and the like have as their subsidiary function the calming of another's ego, and so they are not an obstacle to <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, but rather favorable— this is the meaning.

<s>NyS</s> 1.1.2: From the successive cessation of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, and the absence of each upon the cessation of the one following it, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) [results].

children.text:
tadevaṃ prathamasūtreṇa śāstrasyābhidheyaprayojanasaṃbandhān darśayatā padārthāḥ pramāṇādaya uddhiṣṭāḥ /
teṣāṃ ca lakṣaṇamuktvā tatparīkṣā vartayiṣyate, aparīkṣya tattvajñānanirṇayāyogāt /
na cānirṇotaprayojanasaṃbandhānāṃ pramāṇādīnāṃ lakṣaṇaparīkṣayoravasaraḥ /
na ca prayojanasaṃbandhanirṇayaḥ parīkṣāṃ vineti tatparīkṣārthaṃ dvitīyaṃ sūtram /
tatra prayojanābhidhānasya dvaividhyāt saṃśayaḥ /
dvividhaṃ hi prayojanābhidhānaṃ granthakṛtāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ samīcīnamasamīcīnaṃ ca, yathā vātikādiprayojanābhidhānam āyurvedādiprayojanābhidhānaṃ ca /
tasmādabhidhānasāmānyād ubhayathādarśanācca saṃśayaḥ /
tatrotsūtreṇa prayojanābhisaṃbandhapratipādanaparaṃ pūrvapakṣabhāṣyam--tat khalu vai niḥśreyasamityādi /
tad vibhajate--na tattvaparijñānādapavargaḥ /
kutaḥ? ubhayathādoṣāt /
tadatyantavimokṣalakṣaṇo 'pavargo niḥśreyasam /
taccet tattvajñānānantaram, sampradāyocchedo vātaputrīyatā ca śāstrasya syātām /

children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good) does not follow immediately upon the knowledge of reality.
If that were the case, then <s>niḥśreyasa</s> would result from the knowledge of the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest.
This is false.
And the view of the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (prima facie advocate) is that there is no other <s>niḥśreyasa</s>.

Thus, having shown through the first <s>sūtra</s> the subject-matter, purpose, and connection of the <s>śāstra</s>, the categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been enumerated. Having stated their definitions, their examination will be conducted, because without examination there can be no determination of the knowledge of reality. And there is no occasion for the definition and examination of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest whose purpose and connection have not been determined. And the determination of purpose and connection cannot be made without examination— therefore the second <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of that examination. There, doubt arises because of the twofold nature of the statement of purpose. For a twofold statement of purpose by authors of treatises is observed— proper and improper— just as the statement of purpose in quack medicine versus the statement of purpose in <s>Āyurveda</s> (medical science). Therefore, from the commonality of the statement and from the observation of both kinds, doubt arises. In that context, the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie) <s>bhāṣya</s>, which aims to present the purpose and connection, is 'indeed that <s>niḥśreyasa</s>' and so on. He analyzes that— '<s>apavarga</s> (liberation) does not arise from the complete knowledge of reality.' Why? 'Because of the defect in either case.' That <s>apavarga</s> characterized by absolute release is <s>niḥśreyasa</s>. If that were to follow immediately upon the knowledge of reality, there would be the breaking of the tradition and the treatise would be rendered useless like the teaching of <s>Vātaputra</s> (a nihilist).

na ca prāyaśvittenevātmajñānenādattaphalānyeva karmāṇi kṣīyanta iti yuktam,
nābhuktaṃ kṣīyate karma /
