children.translated_text: Here this <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine) <s>sūtra</s> presents itself— 'suffering, birth...' and so on. Having stated its purport, he introduces it— 'the purpose and connection are not absent.' Why? 'Because of the distinction between proximate and remote forms of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good).' For there are four kinds of cognition regarding the <s>prameya</s> (knowable object) such as <s>ātman</s> (self) and the rest. The first is from scripture, which they call <s>śravaṇa</s> (hearing). The second is the establishment through examination by reasoning of what has been heard, which they call <s>manana</s> (reflection). And that pertains to <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic). And <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> employs the knowledge of the reality of doubt and the rest for the purpose of knowing the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s>. And the knowledge of the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s> serves for the complete knowledge of the reality of <s>prameya</s> as established in the division of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. And therein, the knowledge of the ten categories excluding the first and last serves the knowledge of the first and last alone, namely <s>ātman</s> (self) and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), which are to be accepted. But even one who has understood the reality of <s>prameya</s> through <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> is not satisfied, because the impressions of false knowledge regarding <s>ātman</s> and the rest continue just as before. Indeed, a person confused about directions does not remove the impression of false knowledge even by a thousand inferences. But the direct realization of reality (<s>tattvāsākṣātkāra</s>) does remove the impressions of false knowledge. And the impression born from that counteracts the impression of false knowledge— this is established in the world. Therefore, for one who seeks the fourth cognition— endowed with the direct realization of <s>ātman</s> and the rest, capable of calming the perversion of impressions regarding all objects of that cognition— the third cognition, designated by the words meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>), contemplation (<s>cintā</s>), and the like, having direct realization as its fruit, must be practiced for a long time with dedication and continuity. Then, when the means of meditation has been perfected, having attained the fourth cognition endowed with direct realization, freed from the entire net of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), no longer engaging in the means of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), with the production of future <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> ceased, having conquered the elements and senses, radiant with the light of wisdom, one is said to be liberated while still living (<s>jīvanmukta</s>). But even one in such a state, though free from attachment, does not immediately separate from the body and the rest, because the previously accumulated stock of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> that has not yet been experienced, and that which is currently being experienced, has not been exhausted. And it is not proper that actions whose fruits have not been given are exhausted merely by self-knowledge, like a <s>prāyaścitta</s> (expiation), because of the <s>smṛti</s> (tradition): 'unexperienced <s>karma</s> does not perish,' because actions that conflict with the experience of extreme pleasure and pain have been ascertained, because of the exception to the general rule made by the specific statement regarding expiation in certain cases, and because of the <s>śruti</s> (Vedic text): 'his actions are destroyed' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.8), and because it is also possible through the power of yogic accomplishment (<s>yogarddhi</s>) to experience simultaneously through multiple bodies produced at once.

children.text:
tāvadevāsya ciraṃ yāvanna vimākṣye 'tha supatsye /
# chāndogya 3/14/2 # iti cābhuktopabhajyamānaphalakarmaprakṣayāvaghitvadarśanam /
yogārddhivaśāccāniyatavipākakālānyapi dīrghakālaphalānyapi karmāṇi piṇḍīkṛtya bhūtendriyadavijayitayā yugapadeva bhuṅkte /
acintyo hi samādhiprabhāva ityuktam /
na cācintyatvād vinaivopabhogena karmāśayān prakṣayiṣyatīti yuktam, dṛṣṭānusāreṇa kathañcidupapattau atyantādṛṣṭakalpanāyā ayogāt /

children.translated_text: Therefore, for one in whom the direct realization of reality has arisen, since the cessation of activity occurs due to the absence of defects, the non-production of future new <s>karma</s> (action-residue)— that is the proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (highest good).
And that occurs immediately after the direct realization of reality.

children.text: tādṛśaśca munistattvajñānavān śāstrasya praṇeteti na vātaputrīyaṃ śāstramiti /
children.translated_text: And such a sage, possessed of the knowledge of reality, is the author of the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise)— therefore the treatise is not rendered futile like the teaching of <s>Vātaputra</s>.

children.text: paraṃ tu riḥśreyasaṃ yogarddhiprabhavasampadā yugapadupabhogenopāttakarmāśayasya kṣayāt sarvaduḥkhoparama ityupapannaṃ niḥśreyasadvaividhyamiti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: But the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (highest good) is the complete cessation of all suffering, resulting from the exhaustion of the accumulated repositories of <s>karma</s> through simultaneous experience by means of the accomplishment born of yogic power (<s>yogarddhi</s>)— thus the twofold nature of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is established. This is the purport.

'So long only shall I wait until I am freed, then I shall arrive' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 3.14.2)— this shows that the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> whose fruits are yet to be and are being experienced is what sets the boundary. And through the power of yogic accomplishment (<s>yogarddhi</s>), even actions of indeterminate ripening period and those with long-term fruits are consolidated and experienced all at once through mastery over the elements and senses. For the power of <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption) is said to be inconceivable. And it is not proper that simply because it is inconceivable, one would exhaust the repositories of <s>karma</s> without experience at all, since when some form of explanation is possible following what is observed, it is inappropriate to resort to a completely unobserved hypothesis.

children.text:
tadetad darśayati--yattāvaditi /
tattvasākṣātkāraḥ tattvajñānam /
saṃharṣaḥ sukham /
āyāso duḥkham /
tatrānāgatābhyāṃ tāvat pravṛttyabhāvādanutpādādevamucyate /
vidyamānakāraṇe api sukhaduḥkhe 'śakto 'dviṣaśca bhu/jano na sukhaduḥkhatayā manute /
na hyasti saṃbhavo na tatra tṛpyati tacca tasya sukham, na ca tad dveṣṭi tacca tasya duḥkhamiti /
syādetat bhavatvetadaparaṃ niḥśreyasam /
prakṛte tu kimāyātamityata āha--ayaṃ śāstrārthaḥ /
arthaśabdo nimitte /
aparaṃ niḥśreyasaṃ śāstrasya nimittam /
atha aparaniḥśreyasotpādasamaya eva paraniḥśreyasotpādo 'pi kasmānna bhavatītyāha--paraṃ tu niḥśreyasaṃ tattvajñānāt krameṇa bhavati /
no khalūtpannatattvasākṣātkāraḥ samucchinnavāsanāviparyāsajñānastatkāryadoṣatatkāryapravṛttīnaṃ nivṛttyai prayatate, kāraṇanivṛttyaivāyatnalabhyatvāt kāryanivṛtteḥ /
na hi kaphodbhāvajvarapraśamanāya kaphanivṛttau satyāṃ yatnāntaramātiṣṭhate, tata eva tatsiddheḥ /
paraṃ tu niḥśreyasaṃ na tāvad bhavati, yāvadupabhogādupāttakarmāśayapracayo na kṣīyate /
children.translated_text: But the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s> does not arise so long as the accumulated mass of <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic residues) that have been taken up is not exhausted through experience.
Therefore, after the effort for the attainment of direct realization of reality, one must resort to the effort of experiencing that [accumulated karma].

children.text: tathā ca na tulyakāla utpādaḥ parāparayorniḥśreyasayoḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus the arising of the supreme and the proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is not simultaneous.
This is what was said—'gradually.'

He shows this—'first, that.' Direct realization of reality is <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality). Delight is pleasure. Exhaustion is pain. There, regarding the two that have not yet arrived, it is said thus because of non-arising due to the absence of activity. Even when the causes of pleasure and pain exist, one who is neither attached nor averse, the experiencer, does not regard them as pleasure and pain. For there is no possibility that one is not satisfied there and yet that is his pleasure, nor that one does not hate it and yet that is his pain. It might be said: let this be the proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (liberation). But what has been achieved regarding the present subject?—therefore he says: 'this is the purpose of the <s>śāstra</s>.' The word 'artha' means cause. The proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s> is the cause of the <s>śāstra</s>. Now, why does the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s> not also arise at the very time of the arising of the proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s>?—he says: 'but the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s> arises gradually from <s>tattvajñāna</s>.' Indeed, one in whom direct realization of reality has arisen and in whom the latent impressions and erroneous knowledge have been completely severed does not strive for the cessation of the defects that are effects thereof and the activities that are effects of those, since the cessation of effects is obtained without effort by the very cessation of causes. For one does not make additional effort to quell a fever arising from phlegm when the phlegm has been removed, since that [cure] is accomplished by that alone.

children.text:
tadevamarthagati pariśodhya sūtramavatārayati--krimeti /
yadyapyaparasminnapi niḥśreyase mithyājñānadoṣapravṛttīnāmapi samucchedakramo 'sti, tathāpi janmaduḥkhocchedakramo nāsti, pūrvopāttasya karmāśayapracayasya tādavasthyāt /
tasmāt janmaduḥkhocchedakramasamabhivyāhṛto mithyājñānādyucchedakramaḥ parasyaiva niḥśreyasasya śāstraprayojanasya /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the sequence of destruction of false knowledge etc., expressed in conjunction with the sequence of destruction of birth-suffering, pertains only to the supreme <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, which is the purpose of the <s>śāstra</s>.
That whose purpose is the exposition of that is thus called '<s>tatpratipādanārtha</s>' (having exposition as its purpose).
And this is the subordinate purpose.
The principal purpose will be stated later.

Having thus purified the course of meaning, he introduces the <s>sūtra</s>—'how.' Although even in the proximate <s>niḥśreyasa</s> there is a sequence of complete destruction of false knowledge, defects, and activity, nevertheless there is no sequence of the destruction of birth-suffering, because the previously accumulated mass of <s>karmāśaya</s> remains as it is.

children.text:
atra kecit yogavibhāgamicchanti /
kāraṇocchedāt kāryocchedo 'bhimataḥ /
na cāsau duḥkhādīnāṃ mithyājñānāntānāmapradarśite kāryakāraṇabhāve sidhyati /
tasmād duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānāmityako yogaḥ /
atra kila samāsādeteṣāmitaretarayogaḥ avagamyate /
sa ca yogyatayā kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ /
kāryeṇa kāraṇaṃ yuktam, kāraṇena ca kāryamiti /
ataḥ siddhe kāryakāraṇabhāve uttarottarāpāye tadanantarābhāvādapavarga ityanena yogena kāraṇocchedakrameṇa kāryocchedakramapratipādanenāpavargaḥ pratipādyate /
atra cottaratvaṃ pāṭhāpekṣayā kāraṇasya /
tadanantaratvaṃ ca kāryasyāvyavahitādipāṭhāpekṣayā /
mithyājñāne kāraṇe tatkāryāḥ doṣāḥ /
eve śeṣeṣvapi yojyam /
tamimaṃ sūtravibhāgamamṛṣyamāṇo vārttikakṛd āha--idaṃ sūtram /
ekavacanena bhedaṃ vyāvartayati /
na hi samucchedakramapratipādanenāpavargaparatayaikavākyatve saṃbhavati vākyabhedo nyāyyaḥ /
evanivṛttyā anyanivṛttyaiva kāryakāraṇabhāva ākṣipta iti nāsau sūtre darśanīyaḥ /
na hyarthākṣiptaṃ sūtrakārā darśayanti /
tadidaṃ sūtragrahaṇaprayojanam /

children.translated_text: For thus—
Of few syllables, unambiguous, essential, universal,
without padding, and faultless—the knowers of <s>sūtra</s> know [such to be] a <s>sūtra</s>.

Here some desire a division of <s>yoga</s> (connection). The destruction of the effect through the destruction of the cause is accepted. And that does not succeed without demonstrating the cause-effect relationship among false knowledge and the rest. Therefore, 'of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge'—this is one <s>yoga</s> (construction). Here, from the compound, the mutual connection of these is understood. And that connection by fitness is cause-effect relationship. The effect is connected with the cause, and the cause with the effect. Thus, having established the cause-effect relationship, liberation is taught by the next <s>yoga</s>—through the sequential cessation of causes, the sequential cessation of effects is taught, and that is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). And here 'subsequent' is relative to the order of recitation of the cause. And 'immediately following' is relative to the order of recitation of the effect without gap. False knowledge being the cause, its effects are the defects. Similarly with the rest. The <s>Vārtikakāra</s>, not accepting this division of the <s>sūtra</s>, says—'this <s>sūtra</s>.' By the singular number he rules out division. For when the teaching of the sequential cessation of causes constitutes a single sentence aimed at liberation, division into sentences is not proper. By the cessation of one, the cessation of another—the cause-effect relationship is implied by this alone, so it need not be shown in the <s>sūtra</s>. For <s>sūtra</s>-authors do not show what is implied by the meaning. This is the purpose of the word '<s>sūtra</s>' [i.e., using singular].

children.text:
# viṣṇudharmottare 3.5.1 # iti /
astobhamanadhikam, arthalabhyapradarśane tvadhikaṃ bhavediti /
tat sūcanāt sūtraṃ syāt /

children.translated_text: For thus they say,
Light, of indicated meaning, of few syllables and words,
essential throughout—the wise call these <s>sūtras</s>.

Thus in the <s>Viṣṇudharmottara</s> (3.5.1). 'Without padding' means without excess; but showing what is obtainable from the meaning would be excess. It would be a <s>sūtra</s> because it indicates (<s>sūcanāt</s>).

children.text:
# # iti /
itaretarayogenāpi kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ sūcanīya eva /
sa varamekanivṛttyānyanivṛttyaiva sūcyatāmekavākyatānurodhāyeti /
paramatātparyamasyāha--etatsaṃbandhenaiva /
śāstrasya niḥśreyasādhigamalakṣaṇena prayojanena yaḥ saṃbandhaḥ pūrvamākṣiptaḥ, tatsamādhānenārthena arthavadetat sūtram /
saṃbandhapadena viṣayavācinā viṣacisamādhānaṃ lakṣayati /
tadevaṃ sūtratātparyaṃ vyākhyāyāvayavavyākhyānamavatārayati--padārthasviti /
yadyapi sāmabhedādau halaśakaṭadau ca mithyājñānamanekaprakāraṃ saṃbhavati, tathāpi na tat saṃsāraheturapi tvātmādidvādaśavidhaprameyaviśeṣaviṣayamiti sūtrasthaṃ mithyājñānaṃ viśeṣṭumāha--tatreti /
tadetena ātmādyapavargaparyanta ityādi bhāṣyamavatāritam /
tadetadākṣipati--ko vṛttyartha
iti /
na khalu yathā kuṇḍe vadaraṃ paṭe vā śauklyam, evaṃ prameye mithyājñānaṃ pravartate, tasya jñātṛsamavetatvādityarthaḥ /
uttaram--viṣayārthaḥ /
yāvaduktaṃ bhavati pramayaviṣayaṃ mithyājñānamiti, tāvaduktaṃ bhavati prameye vartata iti /
viṣayatvaṃ cāgre nivedayiṣyate /
anekaprakāram ityuktam /
tadāha--tatrāyaṃ bhedaḥ tatrātmani tāvat pradhāne prameye nāstīti /
kathaṃ punaretanmithyājñānamityata āha--ātmā tāvaditi /
atra śaṅgate--tasyānupapattiḥ /
kutaḥ? sadasatoḥ sārūpyābhāvāditi cet? sarvatra hi rajatodakādivibhrameṣu śuktirajatayorvā marūmarīcisalilayorvā sārūpyameva nimittaṃ pratīmaḥ na hi jātu rūpaṃ rasādiṣu hastinaṃ vā maśakādiṣu āropayanti /
asadṛśe 'pi śvete pītabhramaḥ, madhure ca tiktabhramaḥ, pītaḥ śaṅkhastikto guḍa iti ca dṛśyata iti cet--na, tatrāpi sārūpyasaṃbhavāt /
tathā hi bahinirgacchadatyacchanayanaraśmisaṃpṛktapittagataṃ pītimānamāśrayarahitam, śaṅkhaṃ ca doṣācchāditasitimānamanubhavan pītagaṇasya ca tadasaṃbandhamananubhavaṃstadasaṃbandhāgraheṇa pītacīravilvādisāmānādhikaraṇyena sārūpyāt śaṅkha pīta iti viparyasyati /
evaṃ tvagindriyopanītaṃ guḍadravyamananubhūyamānamādhuryamanubhavan rasanāgravartinaśca pittasyāsvabhāvajātatiktasya tiktatvamanubhavan tadāśrayaṃ ca pittamananubhavannasaṃbandhāgrahasārūpyāt tiktanimbasāmānādhikaraṇyena tikto guḍa iti vapiryasyati /
atiśīghratayā caiṣa kramo na lakṣyate /
na ca brūmo yatra sārūpyaṃ tatra bhrama iti, yenātiprasaktiścodyeta, api tu yatra bhramastatrāvaśyaṃ kathañcit sārūpyamiti /
children.translated_text: And we do not say 'wherever there is resemblance, there is error'—which would invite the charge of over-extension—but rather 'wherever there is error, there is necessarily some resemblance of some kind.'
Thus, even in cases of double moon, directional confusion, the firebrand-circle, and the like, some resemblance of some kind should be inferred.
And there is no resemblance whatsoever between the existent and the non-existent, which are utterly dissimilar.
Therefore, how can there be superimposition of non-existence upon <s>ātman</s>?—this is the objection.

Thus. Even by the <s>yoga</s> (connection) of mutual relationship, the cause-effect relationship is merely to be indicated. Let it rather be indicated by the cessation of one entailing the cessation of the other—as a single sentence—for the sake of maintaining unity of sentence. He states the ultimate purport of this—'by this very connection.' This <s>sūtra</s> is meaningful by the resolution of the connection—the relation with the purpose characterized as the attainment of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> by the <s>śāstra</s>—which was previously raised. By the word 'connection,' which denotes the subject-matter, he indicates the resolution of the subject. Having thus explained the purport of the <s>sūtra</s>, he introduces the word-by-word explanation—'of the terms.' Although false knowledge of many kinds is possible regarding differences in <s>sāman</s> melodies and the like, and regarding plows and carts and such, nevertheless that is not the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>; rather, only that which concerns the twelve specific <s>prameyas</s> beginning with <s>ātman</s> (self) is. Therefore, to qualify the false knowledge stated in the <s>sūtra</s>, he says—'there.' By this the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with '<s>ātmādi</s> up to <s>apavarga</s>' etc. has been introduced. He raises an objection to this—'what is the meaning of the locative?' Surely false knowledge does not operate in <s>prameya</s> as a plum in a bowl or whiteness in cloth—since it [false knowledge] inheres in the knower, such is the meaning. The answer—'in the sense of object.' What is said amounts to saying 'false knowledge having <s>prameya</s> as its object,' and that amounts to saying 'it operates regarding <s>prameya</s>.' And the nature of objecthood will be explained later. It was said 'of many kinds'—therefore he says: 'there, this is the division: regarding <s>ātman</s> first, the primary <s>prameya</s>—it does not exist.' How then is this false knowledge?—therefore he says: '<s>ātman</s> first.' Here one objects—'the impossibility of that.' Why? 'Because of the absence of resemblance between the existent and the non-existent'—if so? For in all cases of error—silver, water, etc.—we observe that resemblance alone between shell and silver, or between desert-mirage and water, is the cause. Never do they superimpose form upon taste etc., or an elephant upon a gnat etc. 'But even in the dissimilar—error of yellow in white, error of bitter in sweet—one sees a yellow conch, bitter jaggery'—if so—no, because resemblance is possible even there. For thus: the yellowness, devoid of substrate, present in the bile mixed with the transparent visual ray going outward, and experiencing the conch whose whiteness is concealed by the defect, and not experiencing the non-connection of that [yellowness] with that [conch], through non-apprehension of its disconnection, by co-referentiality with yellow garments, <s>bilva</s> fruits etc., through resemblance, one erroneously cognizes 'the conch is yellow.' Similarly, experiencing the jaggery substance brought by the tactile organ without experiencing its sweetness, and experiencing the bitterness of the bile resting on the tip of the tongue—which is naturally bitter—and not experiencing the bile as its substrate, through non-apprehension of disconnection and through resemblance by co-referentiality with bitter <s>nimba</s> etc., one erroneously cognizes 'the jaggery is bitter.' And this sequence is not noticed due to extreme rapidity.

children.text:
samādhatte--na, pramāṇagamyatopapatte /
ākṣepaṃ vibhajate--na hi sadasatī iti /
samādhānaṃ vibhajata--tacca naivamiti /
yadi sadasatoḥ samānatvaṃ nāsti, tarhi bhedaḥ /
tathā ca kasya kutrāropa ityata āha--kriyāguṇeti /
so 'yamasaddharmān kriyāguṇarahitatvādīn satyātmani samāropya asattayā viparyasyati--nāstyātmeti, natvātmānaṃ sarvato 'bhyarhitatamaṃ paśyan tatrāsau snihyati, snehācca tadupakārāya ghaṭate /
evaṃ tatparipanthinaṃ dveṣṭi /
dveṣācca tadapakārāya dyaṭate /
tataśca karmāśayam ācinoti /
tato janma /
tataśca duḥkhamiti /
evamātmanastādṛśasya mā bhūt tattvājñānam /
astu nāstitāsamāropa eva tāvad yato na pravartate /

children.translated_text: As they say,

children.text: sukhī bhaveyaṃ duḥkhī vā mā bhūvamiti tṛṣyataḥ /
children.translated_text: 'May I be happy, may I not be miserable'—for one who craves thus,
the very cognition 'I am' is itself the innate perception of being.

He resolves—'no, because accessibility to <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is established.' He divides the objection—'for the existent and non-existent.' He divides the resolution—'and that is not so.' If there is no sameness between the existent and non-existent, then there is difference. And if so, of what upon what is superimposition?—therefore he says: 'action and quality.' This person superimposes the properties of the non-existent—such as being devoid of action and quality—upon the real <s>ātman</s>, and erroneously cognizes it as non-existent—'the self does not exist.' But one who sees the self as supremely worthy does not become attached to it, and from attachment does not exert for its benefit. Similarly, one hates what obstructs it. And from hatred exerts for its harm. And from that accumulates <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic residue). From that, birth. And from that, suffering. Thus, let there not be ignorance of that kind of <s>ātman</s>. Let there be merely the superimposition of non-existence, from which no activity proceeds.

children.text:
# pra.vā. 1.202.3 # atrocyate /
yadyapi rāgādinivṛttiheturnairātmyadarśanam, tathāpi nāsti karma, nāsti karmaphalamiti dṛṣṭeḥ paramaṃ nidānam /
evaṃ pretyabhāvābhāvajñānasya ca /
tathā ca duḥkhahetorheyavargasyābhāvānna taddhānāyānena ghaṭitavyam /
na cāvaṅghaṭamāno heyaṃ hātumarhati /
so 'yaṃ vṛścikabhiyā palāyamānaḥ āśīviṣamukhenipatitaḥ /
secamāstikatvāyātmāstitopāsanīyā /

children.translated_text: And the supreme worthiness of <s>ātman</s> is established in the absolute cessation of suffering.

children.text: ayameva cāsyopakāro yadātyantikaduḥkhaśamanam, sūkhādhāne tvasya tadanuṣaṅgiduḥkhādhānādapakāraprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: And this alone is its benefit—namely, the quelling of absolute suffering; for in bestowing pleasure, since incidental suffering is also bestowed thereby, there would be the undesirable consequence of harm.

children.text: na hi jātu kaściccetanaḥ sukhamāpsyāmīti madhuviṣasampṛktamannamupabhuṅkte /
children.translated_text: For no conscious being ever consumes food mixed with honey and poison thinking 'I shall obtain pleasure.'
Therefore, the view of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) should be diligently uprooted by the discerning person—this is established.

Thus in <s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> (1.202.3), here it is said: although the perception of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) is the cause of the cessation of attachment etc., nevertheless the view 'there is no <s>karma</s>, there is no fruit of <s>karma</s>' is the supreme root cause [of saṃsāra]. Similarly for the knowledge of non-existence of afterlife. And thus, since the category of what is to be abandoned, being the cause of suffering, does not exist [for such a person], he need not strive for its abandonment. And one who does not strive cannot abandon what is to be abandoned. This person, fleeing from the fear of a scorpion, has fallen into the mouth of a viper. Therefore, for the sake of the doctrine of the self's existence, the existence of <s>ātman</s> should be cultivated.

children.text:
aparamapi saṃsārahetu mithyādarśanamāha--evamanātmanīti /
pṛcchati--ki punariti /
uttaram--ahaṅkāreti /
viśeṣamāha--icchādīti /
punaḥ pṛcchati--kathaṃ punariti /
uttaram--śarīreti /

children.translated_text: He concludes—'thus.'
The general property is being the locus of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense).
The specific property is being the substrate of desire etc.

children.text: tāṃ khalvayaṃ śarīrādiṣvāropya eta evāhamiti śarīrādiṣvātmabhāvamāropayati //
children.translated_text: Having superimposed that upon the body etc., one superimposes selfhood upon the body etc. as 'I am this.'

He states yet another form of false view that is a cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>—'thus, in the non-self.' He asks—'what then?' The answer—'<s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense).' He states the specific form—'desire etc.' He asks again—'but how?' The answer—'the body.'

children.text:
evaṃ siddhaṃ kṛtvā viparyayaṃ sarvamuktam /
saṃprati sandihāno viparyayasvarūpaṃ pṛcchati--kaḥ punarayaṃ viparyayaḥ? parīkṣakāṇāṃ vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ /
kecit svākārabāhyatvaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ viparyaya ityācakṣate /
anye 'sādviṣayaṃ jñānam /

children.translated_text: Yet others, an indefinable cognition.
Still others, merely non-apprehension.
But the elders [hold] <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (cognition of the otherwise).
The answer—'a cognition of that in what is not that.'

Having thus established [this], all regarding <s>viparyaya</s> (error) has been stated. Now, having doubts, he asks about the nature of <s>viparyaya</s>—'what then is this <s>viparyaya</s>?' Because of the disagreement among examiners, there is doubt. Some call <s>viparyaya</s> a cognition whose content is the externality of its own form. Others, a cognition of a non-existent object.

children.text:
idamatrākūtam--na tāvat svākāraṃ rajatādi bāhyatayā ālambante vibhramāḥ /
tathā hi jñānākāratvaṃ rajatāderanubhavād vyavasthāpyet, anumānād vā? anubhavo 'pi rajatapratyayo vā svād, bādhakapatyayo vā? na tāvad rajatapratyayaḥ /
sa hīdamanahaṅkārākārāspadaṃ rajatamādarśayati, na cāntaram /
ahamiti hi tadā syāt, pratipattuḥ pratyayādavyatirekāt /
bhrāntaṃ hi jñānaṃ svākārameva bāhyatā ālambate /
children.translated_text: For erroneous cognition apprehends only its own form as external.

children.text: tathā cānahaṅkārāspadamasya viṣayo jñānākāro 'pi, jñānākāratā punarasya bādhakajñānapravedanīyeti cet? hanta cakṣuṣī nimīlya vaitālikapakṣapātaṃ parityajyālocayatvāyuṣmān ki purovartidravyākāratāmātraṃ pratiṣedhati rajatasya, āhosvit jñānākāratāmapyasyādarśayati bādhakapratyayaḥ? tatra jñānākāratopadarśanavyāpāraṃ bādhakapratyayasya brūvāṇaḥ ślāghanīyaprajño devānāṃpriyaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus, its object, which is the form of cognition, is not a basis for ego-sense; but its being a form of cognition is to be made known by the sublating cognition—if so objected? Well then, let the venerable one close his eyes, abandon partisan bias, and consider: does the sublating cognition negate merely the form of being the object present before one as silver, or does it also show the form of being a cognition-form? One who attributes to the sublating cognition the function of showing its cognition-form is a praiseworthy intellect, a 'beloved of the gods' [said ironically].

children.text: purovartitvaniṣedhādarthāt jñānākāratāsiddhiriti cet? tanniṣedho vaṇigvīthyādāvupalabdhasya rajatasya vyāvasthāpane hetuḥ /
children.translated_text: If one objects that from the negation of being-present-before-one, the cognition-form is established by implication? That negation is the reason for determining that the silver perceived was in the marketplace and such places.

children.text: āntaratvaṃ tvasyānupalabdhacaraṃ kutastyam? na cānumānamatra prabhavatīti caturthenivedayiṣyate //
children.translated_text: But its internality, being beyond apprehension, whence does it come? And that inference has no force here—this will be explained in the fourth [section].

Here the underlying idea is this: errors do not apprehend their own form, such as silver, as external. For thus: should the cognition-form-nature of silver etc. be established from experience or from inference? Is the experience the silver-cognition itself, or the sublating cognition? Not the silver-cognition first. For that shows silver as a substrate of desire and ego-form that is 'this'—not as internal. For then [the cognition] would be 'I,' since the cognizer is not different from cognition.

children.text:
santu tarhi bādhakapratyayānurodhād asatprakāśanaśīlā eva mithyāpratyayāḥ /
tathā hi bādhakaṃ vijñānaṃ nedaṃ rajatamiti rajatajñānagocarasyāsattvaṃ gṛhṇāti /
na cāsato viṣayabhāvo nopapadyate /
na hi viṣayatvaṃ nāma kāraṇatvaṃ yenāsati na syāt, kiṃ tu svakāraṇadhīnaḥ sāmarthyātiśayaḥ /
sa tādṛśo jñānasya, yena santamivāsantamapi gocarayati/na ca viṣayasāmarthyamatropayujyate, jñānasya sāmarthyādeva tadbhāvasiddheḥ /
ata evāsatprakāśanasāmarthyameva mithyājñānānāmavidyātvamanirvacanīyaṃ kecidāsthiṣata /
atredamālocanīyam--kimetat mithyājñānamasat sadātmanā gṛhṇātītyasadviṣayamupeyate? āhosvit sadeva sadantarātmanā gahṇāti sataśca sadantarātmatvena asattvādasadviṣayamucyate? na tāvat pūrvaḥ kalpaḥ, rajatātmanā cet asadālambeta na satī śuktikām, kathaṃ punarasau rajātartho śuktau pravartate na punā rajatābhāve /
kaskāccedamiti purovarti dravyamaṅgulyā nirdiśya tasya rajatatvaṃ niṣedhati nedaṃ rajatamiti, yadi tatra na prasañjitaṃ rajatatvaṃ pūrvavijñānena? atha śuktireva rajatātmanā asatīti tadākāratayā tāmālambamānaṃ mithyājñānamasadālambanamucyate? tatrānujñayā vartāmahe /
na khalvanyathākhyātivādino 'pi sadantaraṃ sadantarātmanā sadabhyupagacchanti /
tathā satyanyathetyeva na syāt /

children.translated_text: As the proponents of <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (cognition-of-the-other) say:
Therefore, that which cognizes what exists in one way as existing in another way—
that cognition is without a real basis, and it has a non-existent basis.

Let erroneous cognitions then be, in accordance with the sublating cognition, of the nature of manifesting the non-existent.
For the sublating cognition apprehends 'this is not silver,' grasping the non-existence of what was the object of the silver-cognition.
And it cannot be maintained that the non-existent cannot be an object.
For objecthood is not causality, such that it would not apply to the non-existent; rather, it is a special capacity dependent on its own cause.
Such is this capacity of cognition, by which it makes even the non-existent an object as if it were existent. And the capacity of the object is not employed here, since the status of being such is established by the capacity of cognition alone.
For this very reason, some have maintained that the very capacity of erroneous cognitions to manifest the non-existent is their <s>avidyā</s>-nature (nature as ignorance), which is indescribable.
Here this should be considered: does this erroneous cognition apprehend the non-existent with the nature of the existent, and is thus taken as having a non-existent object? Or does it apprehend what is actually existent with the nature of something else that is existent, and because of the existent's having the nature of something else that is existent—which constitutes non-existence—is it called having a non-existent object? The first alternative does not hold: if it cognized the non-existent with the nature of silver without [cognizing] the existent shell, how would that person directed toward silver act upon the shell and not upon the absence of silver?
And why does he point with his finger at the object present before him saying 'what is this?' and negate its being silver with 'this is not silver,' if the nature of being silver had not been attributed to that by the prior cognition? Or is it that the shell itself, being non-existent as silver, is the basis of erroneous cognition that apprehends it in that form, and thus erroneous cognition is called having a non-existent basis? To that we assent.
Indeed, even the proponents of <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (cognition-of-the-other) do not accept that one existent is cognized as another existent with the nature of that other existent.
If they did, then 'otherwise' (anyathā) would not be applicable.

children.text:
# ślo. vā. nirālambanavāde 117-8 # iti /
na ca rajatātmanā purovartino dravyasyānirvacanīyatā, mithyājñānasamaye sattvena bādhakasamaye cāsattvena nirvacanīyatvāt /
na caivaṃbhūtasyāsataḥ prathā nopapadyate, tasya sadasadbhyāmupākhyeyatvāt /
yaḥpunaḥ advaitavādinā prapajco vaināśikānāṃ vā sāmānyādirno bahiḥ ki tvalīkam /
tadviṣayaṃ ca jñānaṃ mithyājñānamityapi na saṃbhavati, tasya sarvopākhyārahitasya kenacit sārūpyābhāvāt, tatkāraṇakatvācca bhrānteḥ, kāraṇābhāve kāryābhāvasya sulabhatvāt /
children.translated_text: that the cognition directed toward that is erroneous cognition is also not possible, since that which is devoid of all description has no similarity with anything; and since error is caused by that [similarity], in the absence of the cause the absence of the effect is readily obtained.

children.text: tasmāt prapañcaśca sāmānyādi ca vastusatī nāmamīcīnavijñānagocarau /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the phenomenal world and universals and the like are truly real things, objects of correct cognition.
And the sublation of that will be refuted later on.
Therefore, the <s>anirvacanīyakhyāti</s> (indescribable-error theory) is also not tenable.

[<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Nirālambanavāda</s> 117-8.]
And the object present before one is not indescribable in its silver-nature, because at the time of erroneous cognition it is describable as existent, and at the time of the sublating cognition it is describable as non-existent.
Nor is the manifestation of such a non-existent impossible, since it can be described through both the existent and the non-existent.
But what the <s>Advaitin</s> (non-dualist) considers as the phenomenal world, or what the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (Buddhists) consider as universals and the like—not as external but as unreal—

children.text:
syādetata /
anyadanyathā prakāśata iti saṃvidviruddham/na tāvat sadbhāvamātreṇālambanatvam /
tanmātrasya sarvapratyayasādhāraṇyena sarve 'rthāḥ savarpratyayaviṣayā iti savarsarvajñatāpattiḥ /
na ca kāraṇatvenālambanatvam, rūpādivijñānānāṃ rūpādivaccakṣurādyapi kāraṇamiti cakṣurādyālambanatvaprasaṅgāt /
atītānāgataviṣayatvaṃ ca vijñānasya na syāt, atītānāgatayorasattvenākāraṇatvāt /
tasmāt pratibhāsamānamālambanam /
tathā ca rajatapratibhāsaḥ śuktikālambanamiti durghaṭam /
api ca cakṣurādīnāṃ samīcīnajñānopajananasāmarthyamiti kathamebhyo mithyājñānaṃ bhavitumarhati? na hi śyāmākabījaṃ parikarmasahasreṇāpi kalamāṅkurāya kalpate /
doṣasahāyā locanādayo mithyāpratyayamādadhata iti cet--na doṣā hi kāraṇānāṃ sāmarthya nighnanti, na punaḥ kāryāntaropajananasāmarthyamādadhati, na khalu bhṛṣṭaṃ kuṭajabījaṃ nyagrodhadhānāyai kalpate, kiṃ tu na karoti kuṭajadhānām /
api ca svagocare vyabhicāre vijñānānāṃ sarvatrānāśvāsaprasaṅgaḥ /
tasmāt sarvameva vijñānaṃ samīcīnamāstheyam /
tathā hi rajatamidamiti dve jñāne smṛtyanubhavarūpe /
tatredamiti purovartidravyamātragrahaṇam, doṣavaśāt tadgatasya śuktikātvasāmānyaviśeṣasyāgrahaṇāt /
tāvanmātraṃ ca gṛhītaṃ sadṛśatayā saṃskārodbodhakrameṇa rajate smṛti janayati /
sā ca gṛhītagrahaṇasvabhāvāpi doṣavaśāt gṛhītatāṃśapramoṣeṇa grahaṇamātramavatiṣṭhate /
tathā ca rajatasmṛteḥ purovartimātragrahaṇasya va mithaḥ svarūpataśca viṣayataśca bhedāgrahaṇāt sannihitarajataviṣayavijñānasārūpyeṇedaṃ rajatamiti bhinne api grahaṇasmaraṇe abhedavyavahāraṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaṃ ca pravartayataḥ /
kvacit punargrahaṇe eva mitho 'gṛhītaprabhede, yathā pītaḥ śaṅkha iti /
atra hi viniryannayanaraśmivartinaḥ pittadravyasya kāyasyevātisvacchasya pītattvaṃ ca gṛhyate /
pittaṃ tu gṛhyate /

children.translated_text: The conch too, due to defects, is apprehended merely in its own form without qualities.

children.text: tadanayorguṇaguṇinorasaṃsargāgrahāt sārūpyāt pītacirabilvaphalapratyayāviśeṣeṇābhedavyavahāraḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaśca, bhedāgrahaprasañjitābhedavyavahārabādhānācca nedaṃ rajatamiti vivekapratyayasya bādhakattvamapyupapadyate /
children.translated_text: And due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between these two—quality and quality-bearer—because of similarity, the behavior of non-difference and usage of co-referentiality arise, as with the cognition of a yellow <s>cirabilvaphala</s> (wood-apple fruit); and the validity of the discriminating cognition 'this is not silver' as a sublating cognition is also explained by the non-apprehension of difference having given rise to the behavior of non-difference which is then sublated.

children.text: tadupapattau ca bhrāntatvamapi lokaprasiddhaṃ siddhra bhavati /
children.translated_text: And when that is established, the well-known status of being erroneous is also established.

children.text: tasmād yathārthāḥ sarve 'pi bhramāḥ pratyayatvāt paṭapratyayatvayavaditi prāptam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, even all errors are veridical, because of being cognitions, like the cognition of a cloth—this is the conclusion reached.

It may be objected:
'One thing manifests as another'—this contradicts experience. First, being an object is not merely by existing.
If mere existence were sufficient for objecthood, then since that is common to all cognitions, all objects would be objects of all cognitions, and omniscience would follow for everyone.
Nor is objecthood constituted by being a cause, since for cognitions of form and the like, the eye and such are also causes just as form and the like are, and the absurd consequence would follow that the eye and such are objects.
And cognition could not have past and future objects, since the past and future, being non-existent, are not causes.
Therefore, what appears is the object.
And thus it is difficult to maintain that the appearance of silver has the shell as its object.
Moreover, since the eye and the other senses have the capacity to produce correct cognition, how can erroneous cognition arise from them? For a <s>śyāmāka</s> (millet) seed, even with a thousand cultivations, is not fit to produce a rice sprout.
If one objects that the senses, aided by defects (<s>doṣa</s>), produce erroneous cognition—no, for defects destroy the capacity of causes; they do not bestow the capacity to produce a different effect. Indeed, a roasted <s>kuṭaja</s> (wrightia) seed is not fit to produce a banyan tree; rather, it simply does not produce a <s>kuṭaja</s> plant.
Moreover, if cognitions deviate in their own domain, the consequence would be distrust in them everywhere.
Therefore, all cognition should be accepted as correct.
For 'this is silver'—there are two cognitions of the form of memory and experience.
Therein, 'this' is the apprehension of merely the object present before one, because due to defects, the universal and particular nature of being-a-shell in that object is not apprehended.
And just that much apprehended, by virtue of similarity, through the sequence of awakening latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), generates memory of silver.
And that memory, though by nature apprehending what has been apprehended, due to defects, by the loss of the apprehended portion, remains as mere apprehension.
And thus, because of the non-apprehension of the difference—both intrinsically and in terms of object—between the silver-memory and the mere apprehension of what is present before one, due to similarity with a cognition having actually present silver as its object, the two—apprehension and memory—though different, produce the behavior of non-difference and the usage of co-referentiality in 'this is silver.'
Sometimes, however, there is non-apprehension of mutual difference within apprehension itself, as in 'the conch is yellow.'
For there, the yellowness of the bile-substance present in the rays going forth from the eye, and even of the body itself being extremely transparent, is apprehended.
But the bile is [also] apprehended.

children.text:
evaṃ prāpte 'bhidhīyate--asti tāvad rajatārthino rajatamiti jñāne sati purovartidravyapravṛttiḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaśceti sarvajanīnam /
tat kiṃ grahaṇasmaraṇayostadgocarayośca bhedāgrahād bhavatu, āhosvidabhedagrahāt? na tāvaccetano 'jñānāt pravartate, api tu jñānāt /
purovartivastugrahaṇarajatajñānādagṛhītabhedaṃ svarūpato viṣayato vā rajatārthinaṃ purovartidravye pravartayatīti cet? hanta bhoḥ kimetāvatā purovartivastugocaraṃ jñānaṃ rajatagocaraṃ bhavati, āhosvit tanmātragocarameva? yadi rajatagocaraṃ purovartirajatatayāgṛhṇāt, kathaṃ nānyathākhyātiḥ? atha tanmātragocaram, ko bhedāgrahasyopayogaḥ? na hi vṛkṣamātradarśanaṃ niścayena śiṃśapārthinaṃ pravartayati, na hi tatra śiṃśapājñānamasti /
asti tviha rajatavijñānam, agṛhītabhedamidamiti jñāneneti cet? nanu rajatavijñānaṃ purovartini dravye na vartate, purovartijñānaṃ ca na rajata iti tatra purovartidravyamātrārtho purovartini pravarteta na rajatārtho /
evaṃ rajatārtho yatra kvacana pravarteta na niyamena purovartina dravye /
children.translated_text: Similarly, the one desiring silver would act anywhere whatsoever, not necessarily upon the object present before one.
For it is not the case that the nature of being silver has been apprehended there by that [cognition].

children.text: athedaṃ rajatamiti dve jñāne, bhedāgrahādidaṃ rajatamityekajñānasadṛśe, tena taducitaṃ vyavahāraṃ pravartayataḥ? yadyevaṃ tadrajatam, iyaṃ śuktiriti bhedāvabhāsivijñānavyavahāramapi kasmānna pravartayataḥ? yathaiva hi bhedāgrahādabhinnavijñānasādṛśyam, evamabhedāgrahād bhinnavijñānasādṛśyamapi /
children.translated_text: But if there are two cognitions—'this' and 'silver'—and due to non-apprehension of difference they are similar to a single cognition 'this is silver,' and thereby produce the appropriate behavior? If so, [they should also produce] the behavior of the discriminating cognition 'that is silver, this is a shell'—why do they not produce that too? For just as there is similarity to a cognition of non-difference due to non-apprehension of difference, so too there is similarity to a cognition of difference due to non-apprehension of non-difference.

children.text: so 'yamubhayato bhedābhedagrahasārūpyāt pravṛttinivṛttibhyāṃ yugapadākṛṣyamāṇaḥ pratipattā kaṣṭāṃ daśāmāveśitaḥ prajñāśālibhirativyākhyayā //
children.translated_text: Thus, this cognizer, pulled simultaneously in both directions—toward action and inaction—by the similarity of apprehension of both difference and non-difference, is placed in a pitiable state by the over-explanation of those who consider themselves wise.

When this conclusion is reached, the response is given: It is universally acknowledged that when one who desires silver has the cognition 'this is silver,' there is activity toward the object present before one, and the usage of co-referentiality. Now, does this occur from non-apprehension of the difference between apprehension and memory, and between their respective objects, or from apprehension of non-difference? The conscious being does not act from ignorance, but from knowledge.
If one objects that the apprehension of the object present before one and the silver-cognition, with their difference unapprehended either intrinsically or in terms of object, cause one who desires silver to act upon the present object? Well then, does the cognition directed at the object present before one thereby become directed at silver, or does it remain directed at just that [present object]? If it becomes directed at silver, then it apprehends the present object as silver—so how is this not <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (cognition-of-the-other)? But if it remains directed at just that, what use is the non-apprehension of difference? For the mere seeing of a tree does not with certainty cause one who desires a <s>śiṃśapā</s> (rosewood) to act, since there is no cognition of <s>śiṃśapā</s> there.
But there is silver-cognition here, [together with] the cognition that 'this' [is unascertained]—if so objected? But the silver-cognition does not bear upon the object present before one, and the cognition of what is present does not bear on silver—so the mere desire for what is present before one would cause the one desiring what is present to act, not the one desiring silver.

children.text:
syādetat /
viparyayajñānotpāde 'pi śuktirajatayorbhedāgrahe 'sya vyāpāra āstheyaḥ, anyathā gṛhītabhedānāmapi viparyayotpādaprasaṅgāt /
tathā ca śakyaṃ tatrāpi vaktum--yathā bhedagrahād viparyayajñānotpāda evamabhedāgrahāt kasmānna samīcīnajñānotpāda iti /
tatra yastava parihāraḥ so 'smākaṃ vyavahāravyapadeśayorbhaviṣyatīti /
yathāhurakhyātivādinaḥ---
yeṣāmapi viparītakhyātisteṣāmapyajñānavāsananibandhano bhrama iti /
maivam, jñānahetūnām ajñātarūpakāryasaṃbandhānā cukṣurādīnāṃ darśanāt, cetanavyavahārāṇāṃ tvabuddhipūrvakāṇāmapratīteḥ buddhipūrvakatve tu vivekāgraha upayujyate, na vyavahāravyapadeśayoriti yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ /
yadyavivekagraho 'pi tatparipanthī vidyata iti kuto 'nyataranibandhano vyavahāraḥ? tasmāt samāropa eva bhedāgraha iti /
tat siddham etadvivādādhyāsitaṃ rajatādivajñānaṃ purovartivastuviṣayam, rajatārthinastatra niyamena pravartakatvāt /
yad yadarthina niyamena yatra pravarpayati tadvijñānaṃ tadviṣayam, yathobhayasiddhaṃ samīcīnarajatavijñānam /
tathā caitat, tasmāt yathā, yaccoktam--anavabhāsamāmā śuktiranālambanamiti, tatra kiṃ śuktikātvasya rajatamiti jñānaṃ pratyanālambanatvaṃ sādhyate, āhosvid dravyamātrasya sitabhāsvarasya purovartinaḥ? tatra pūrvasmin kalpe siddhasādhanam /
uttarasminnanavabhāsanamasiddham, idamiti purovartino dravyasyāṅgulyā nirdeśāt /
dṛṣṭaṃ ca duṣṭānāmapi kāraṇānāmautsargikakāryapratibandhena kāryāntarotpādakatvam /
tad yathā, vetrabījānāṃ dāvāgnidagdhānāṃ kadalīprakāṇḍajanakatvam, bhasmakaduṣṭasya caudaryasya tejaso bahutarānnapānapācakatvam /
nedaṃ rajatamiti ca pratyakṣabādhakapratyayādapahṛtaviṣayam, pratyayatvena vibhramāṇāṃ yathārthatvānumānaṃ nodetumarhati /
children.translated_text: And the sublating perception 'this is not silver' having removed its domain, the inference that errors are veridical because of being cognitions is not capable of being propounded.

children.text: yathā ca pramāṇābhāsavyabhicāre 'pi pramāṇe āśvāsaḥ, tathā pramāṇato 'rthapratipattau ityatropapāditam /
children.translated_text: And just as there is confidence in valid means of knowledge despite the deviation of pseudo-means, so too regarding the apprehension of objects through valid means—this has been established here.
Only a brief indication has been shown here.
But the elaboration has been made by us in the <s>Tattvasamīkṣā</s> — thus he desists.

It may be objected:
Even when erroneous cognition arises, the non-apprehension of the difference between shell and silver should be accepted as its operative factor; otherwise, error would arise even for those who have apprehended the difference.
And thus it could also be said there: just as from the apprehension of difference error does not arise, why should correct cognition not arise from the non-apprehension of non-difference?
Whatever resolution you have for that will be our resolution for the behavior and the usage.
As the proponents of <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension) say: 'Even for those who hold the view of erroneous cognition (viparītakhyāti), error is based on ignorance and latent impressions.'
This is not so, because it is observed that causes of cognition such as the eye and the like have connections with effects whose nature is unknown, while on the other hand, deliberate behavior of conscious beings that is not preceded by understanding is not observed. But when preceded by understanding, it is the non-apprehension of distinction that is useful, not for behavior and designation—this we see as proper.
If even the non-apprehension of distinction has its own adversary present, then on what basis is behavior grounded in one and not the other? Therefore, the non-apprehension of difference is itself a superimposition.
Thus it is established: the disputed cognition of silver and the like has the object present before one as its object, because it necessarily causes one who desires silver to act upon that present object.
Whatever cognition necessarily causes one who desires a certain thing to act upon a certain object, that cognition has that object as its object—just as the mutually accepted correct cognition of silver.
And this being so—therefore, regarding what was said, 'the shell, not appearing, is without basis'—there, is it the shell-nature that is being proved as not being the basis of the cognition 'silver,' or the mere substance that is luminous and present before one? In the first alternative, it is the proving of what is already proved.
In the second alternative, non-appearance is unestablished, since the present object is indicated by pointing with a finger saying 'this.'
And it is observed that even defective causes produce a different effect by obstructing their natural effect.
For example, bamboo seeds burnt by a forest fire generate banana stalks, and the gastric fire afflicted by <s>bhasmaka</s> disease digests a greater amount of food and drink.

children.text:
tadevamātmani mithyājñānaṃ vyākhyāya śarīrādiṣvekādaśasu mithyājñānaṃ bhāṣya eva darśitam /
tattu spaṣṭatvāt asmābhirna vyutpāditamityāśayavānāha--śeṣamiti /
tatra śarīrādiṣu manaḥparyanteṣu yathāyogaṃ mithyājñānaṃ duḥkhe sukham ityādinā apratihātavyam ityantena bhāṣyeṇoktam /
pravṛttyādiṣu śṛṅgagrāhikayoktaṃ pravṛttau ityādinā rocayet ityantena bhāṣyeṇa /
evaṃ mithyājñānasya svarūpaṃ darśayitvā mithyājñānadoṣapravṛttitajanmaduḥkhānāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvo doṣādīnāṃ svarūpaṃ coktam etasmāt ityādinā tāpa ityantena bhāṣyeṇa /
saṃprati mithyājñānādyucchedādapavarga iti vakṣyati /
taccāyuktam, satyapi taducchede saṃsāratādavasthyāt /
na hyānyocchede 'nyasyocchedaḥ /
tathā ca nāpavarga iti vakṣyamāṇamarthamupapādayitumaktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā, ta hame mithyājñānādaya ityādi /
tad vārttikakāro vyācaṣṭa--ta hame duḥkhādaya iti bhāṣyakāroktakramād viparītakramābhidhānaṃ vārttikakṛtaḥ evaṃ sūtrakāroktakramād viparītakramābhidhānaṃ bhāṣyakṛtaḥ /
tad duḥkhādīnāṃ mithyājñānapūrvakatvena mithyājñānasya duḥkhādipūrvakatvenānāditvaṃ darśayitum /

yadyeta eva saṃsārastarhi sūtrakāraḥ prameyasūtre kasmād duḥkhādibhyaḥ pṛthak pretyabhāvaṃ saṃsārāparanāmānamupādatte? tasmādebhyo 'nya eva saṃsāra iti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--duḥkhādīnāmiti /
naiṣāṃ svarūpamapi tu kāryakāraṇabhāva ityarthaḥ /
kramavyatikramatātparyamāha--sa cānādiriti /
atra hetumāha--pūrvāpareti /
duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣāḥ viṣayatvena tāvanmithyājñānasya kāraṇam /
evamasati janmani mithyājñānasyānutpattaraviṣayo 'pi janma mithyājñānasya kāraṇam /
evaṃ vinā pravṛttiṃ janmābhāvāt janmadvādeṇa pravṛtterapi mithyājñānakāraṇatvam /
pravṛttidvāreṇa ca doṣāṇām, tathā mithyājñānād deṣāḥ, doṣebhyaḥ pravṛttiḥ, pravṛtterjanma, janmano duḥkham /
yadyapi pravṛttireva sākṣāduḥkhahetuḥ, tathāpyanāyatanasya tasyānutpatterantarā janma karoti /
atha saiva duḥkhamiti? anāditvācca nānyonyāśrayaṃ cakrakaṃ vā bījāṅkurasantānayoriveti /
saṃpratibījāpāya iva tajjānyāṅkurapravāhanivṛttiḥ mithyājñānāpāye tajjanyadoṣapravṛttijanmaduḥkhamithyājñānādipravāhanivṛttiḥ, kāraṇanivṛttau kāryanivṛtteriti kathanaparaṃ bhāṣyam anubhāṣyākṣipati--yadā tu tattvajñānāditi /
apāyo 'pi tattvajñānānmithyājñānasya svarūpato vā, viṣayato, vā phalato vā syāt, na tāvat svarūpataḥ, tasyāśutaravināśinaḥ saṃskārād vā jñānāntarād vā apāyasya tattvajñānasādhāraṇyena tasyāpi bādhyatvaprasaṅgāt /
nāpi viṣayataḥ, na hi śuktikājñānaṃ rajatajñānasya rajataviṣayatāmapahartumutsahate jātaṃ hi tad rajataṃ viṣayīkṛtya /
yathāhuḥ
gṛhītvārthaṃ gatāścaurāḥ kastānācchettumarhati /
iti /
nāpi phalamapaharati, upadarśito hi tenārthaḥ, pravartitaśca tatra puyaṣaḥ /
tadidamuktam--kathamapāya iti /
uttaram--samānaviṣaya iti /
yasminneva hi purovartini dravye pūrveṇa rajatatvamāsañjitaṃ tatraivottaraṃ tadviruddhaṃ śuktikātvaṃ dharmamupanayati /
tathā ca pūrvasya vijñānasya mithyātvamādarśayattajjanitāṃ pravṛttiṃ vighaṭayat phalamasyāpaharatīti bhāvaḥ /
na tu samānaviṣayatāmātreṇa virodhaḥ, mā bhūdekasminnātmani nityatvavibhutvajñānayorvirodha ityata āha--yasmāditi /
tatvamithyātvakathanena mitho viruddhadharmaprasa/janaṃ sūcayati /

children.translated_text: But in the case of the cognitions of eternality and all-pervasiveness, although they have the same object, because they present non-contradictory properties, they are knowledge of reality — this is the meaning.
Why is there contradiction? Therefore he says — 'of the real thing.'

children.text: parasparābhāvadharmiṇorekatra samavāye nedaṃ svābhāvikaṃ nānātvaṃ kvacidapītyadvaitaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: If the two, whose properties are mutual absence, were to co-inhere in one thing, this natural diversity would not exist anywhere — and thus there would be the undesirable consequence of non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) — this is the sense.
He concludes — 'therefore.'

Having thus explained false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>) regarding the self (<s>ātman</s>), false knowledge regarding the body and the other eleven [categories] has been shown in the <s>bhāṣya</s> itself. Since that is clear, the intention being that it has not been expounded by us, he says — 'the rest.' Therein, regarding the body and the rest up to the mind, false knowledge as appropriate has been stated by the <s>bhāṣya</s> from 'pleasure in suffering' up to 'should not be resisted.' Regarding activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) and the rest, it is stated pointedly (<s>śṛṅgagrāhikayā</s>) by the <s>bhāṣya</s> from 'in activity' up to 'should please.' Having thus shown the essential nature of false knowledge, the cause-effect relation among false knowledge, defects (<s>doṣa</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), birth (<s>janma</s>), and suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), as well as the essential nature of defects and the rest, has been stated by the <s>bhāṣya</s> from 'from this' up to 'affliction.' Now he will say that liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) results from the cessation of false knowledge and the rest. But that is improper, because even when that ceases, <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) would remain as before. For the cessation of one thing does not entail the cessation of another. And thus, to establish the forthcoming meaning that there is no liberation, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> has stated: 'these false knowledge and the rest.' The <s>Vārtikakāra</s> explains that — 'these suffering and the rest' — the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> states them in reverse order from the order stated by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>; similarly, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> states them in reverse order from the order stated by the <s>Sūtrakāra</s>. That is, to show the beginninglessness [of the cycle] — suffering and the rest being preceded by false knowledge, and false knowledge being preceded by suffering and the rest. He asks — 'what then?' If these alone constitute <s>saṃsāra</s>, then why does the <s>Sūtrakāra</s> in the <s>prameya-sūtra</s> adopt <s>pretyabhāva</s> (afterlife existence), which is another name for <s>saṃsāra</s>, separately from suffering and the rest? Therefore <s>saṃsāra</s> is indeed something other than these — this is the sense. The answer — 'of suffering and the rest.' Not their essential nature, but rather their cause-effect relation — this is the meaning. He states the purport of the reversed order — 'and that is beginningless.' Here he states the reason — 'prior and subsequent.' Suffering, birth, activity, and defects — as objects, they are the cause of false knowledge. Similarly, even without birth, the non-arising of false knowledge being impossible, birth too, even as an object, is the cause of false knowledge. Similarly, without activity there is no birth, so through birth, activity too is a cause of false knowledge. And through activity, defects too [are causes]. Thus: from false knowledge arise defects, from defects activity, from activity birth, from birth suffering. Although activity alone is the direct cause of suffering, nevertheless, without a locus it cannot arise, and birth supplies that intermediary. If so — the cycle — then is activity itself suffering? And because of beginninglessness, there is no mutual dependence or circular reasoning, just as in the continuity of seed and sprout. Now, just as upon the destruction of the seed the flow of sprouts born from it ceases, so upon the destruction of false knowledge, the flow of defects, activity, birth, suffering, false knowledge, and so on born from it ceases — the cessation of the effect follows upon the cessation of the cause. With this intention, he comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s> and objects — 'but when through knowledge of reality.' The destruction of false knowledge through knowledge of reality may be either in its essential nature, or in its object, or in its result. Not first in its essential nature, because false knowledge, being quickly perishable, perishes either through its impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) or through another cognition, and since such destruction is common [to all cognitions], even knowledge of reality would be subject to cancellation. Nor in its object, for the cognition of a nacre-shell cannot remove the silver-objecthood of the cognition of silver — for that cognition has already arisen having taken silver as its object. As they say: 'Thieves who have seized the goods and gone — who can take back from them?' Nor does it remove the result, for the object has already been shown by it, and the person has already been impelled toward it. This has been stated — 'how can there be destruction?' The answer — 'having the same object.' For the very object in which the prior cognition superimposed silver-hood, in that very same object the subsequent cognition presents the contradictory property of nacre-shell-hood. And thus, by showing the falsity of the prior cognition and disrupting the activity generated by it, it removes its result — this is the sense. But not merely by having the same object is there contradiction, lest there be contradiction between the cognitions of eternality and all-pervasiveness regarding a single self — therefore he says — 'because.' By stating truth and falsity, he indicates the attribution of mutually contradictory properties.

children.text:
atra deśayati--kathaṃ punariti /
prathamamutpannaṃ mithyājñānamanupajātavirodhi, tenāpahṛtaviṣayaṃ paśrvāttanaṃ tattvajñānamudetumeva notsahate, prāgeva tu mithyājñānaṃ bādhitumiti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--mithyājñānasyeti /
tatra hi prathamamupajātenānupajātavirodhinā jñānenottaraṃ bādhyate, yatra pūrvāpekṣamuttaramupajāyate /
tat khalu pūrvavirodhe na jāyeta /
ajātaṃ sat kathaṃ pūrvaṃ bādheta, yathā pratyakṣādiviruddhamanumānam? iha tu dve api jñānedoṣopahatānupahatendriyārthasannikarṣajanmanī parasparānapekṣe /
tatra pūrvamanupajātavirodhitvāt ki bādhatām, anāgatasyāprāptatvena bādhitumaśakyatvāt, svakāraṇabalādāsādyamānajanmanaścotpattivirodhasya cāśakyātvāt? tadevamutpannamuttaramupajātavirodhitayā pūrvabādhātmakaṃ sannānupakṛdya pūrvamutpattumarhatīti bādhate /
tattu na pūrveṇa nāpyanyena kenaciditi bhāvatyarthasahāyam /
arthāsahāyaṃ ca mithyājñānam /
tadanena bādhyatvābādhyatve mithyājñānatattvajñānayorūpalakṣyete /

children.translated_text: This has been stated by others too —
The superiority of the subsequent over the prior is to be acknowledged
where the cognitions arise independently of each other.

Here he raises a doubt — 'how then?' False knowledge, having arisen first without an arisen contradictory [cognition], having preempted the domain, makes the subsequent knowledge of reality unable even to arise, let alone override the false knowledge — this is the sense. The answer — 'of false knowledge.' For therein, the subsequent is overridden by the prior cognition that has arisen first without an arisen contradictory [cognition], only where the subsequent arises in dependence on the prior. That indeed, in the case of contradiction with the prior, would not arise. Being unarisen, how could it override the prior, like inference contradicted by perception and the like? But here, both cognitions — one born from the contact of senses afflicted by defects, and one from the contact of senses unafflicted — arise independently of each other. Therein, what should the prior override, since it has arisen without an arisen contradictory [cognition], given that the future one, having not yet arrived, cannot be overridden, and given that [the subsequent], whose birth is being brought about by the force of its own cause, cannot have its arising prevented? Thus, having arisen, the subsequent, by virtue of being one with an arisen contradictory [cognition], whose nature is the overriding of the prior, overrides [the prior] without being assisted by the prior to arise. But that [false knowledge] is not [assisted] by the prior or by anything else — it exists as something assisted by its object. And false knowledge is not assisted by its object [i.e., it lacks object-support in reality]. By this, the susceptibility to being overridden and the non-susceptibility to being overridden of false knowledge and knowledge of reality respectively are indicated.

children.text:
iti /
tathā cānupajātavirodhitvamatra bādhyatve hetuḥ, upajātavirodhitvaṃ ca bādhakatva iti /
yadupalakṣaṇārthaṃ sasahāyatvābhidhānaṃ tajjijñāsuḥ pṛcchati--kasmāt? uttaram--tayātveneti /
anenābādhyatvaṃ tattvajñānasyoktamiti /
na kevalamabādhyatvam, dṛḍhamūlatvamapi tattvajñānasyetyāha--pramāṇāntarānugrahācca /
antaraśabdo viśeṣavacanaḥ /
ātmāditattvajñānaṃ hi phalaṃ pramāṇaviśeṣairāgamānumānapratyakṣairanugṛhyate /
tasmād dṛḍhamūlatvāt tadapi tattvajñānaṃ mithyājñānaṃ nivartayatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of having firm roots, that knowledge of reality too removes false knowledge — this is the meaning.
He analyzes this very point — 'scripture.'
He elaborates this very point — 'for when.'

children.text: āgamamayena hi jñānena prameyaṃ gṛhītvā śāstrīyeṇa ca nyāyavijñānenānumānāparanāmnā vyavasthāpya bhāvayato yadātmamanaḥsannikarṣād yogajadharmasahāyādutpadyate tattvaviṣayaḥ sākṣātkāraḥ pratyakṣaphalam, tatra trayāṇāmapi pramāṇānāṃ pratisandhānam astīti dṛḍhamūlatvāt tena mithyājñānaṃ bādhyate //
children.translated_text: For having grasped the object of knowledge through cognition based on scripture (<s>āgama</s>), and having established it through logical investigation belonging to the <s>śāstra</s>, also called inference, when one who contemplates [the object] produces, through the contact of self and mind aided by the <s>dharma</s> of <s>yoga</s>, a direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) having reality as its object — which is the fruit of perception — therein the convergence of all three <s>pramāṇas</s> exists. Therefore, because of having firm roots, false knowledge is overridden by it.

Thus, having arisen without an arisen contradictory [cognition] is the reason for being overridable, and having an arisen contradictory [cognition] is the reason for being the overrider. What was stated indicatively as 'being assisted' — wishing to know that, he asks — 'why?' The answer — 'because of being of such nature.' By this, the non-overridability of knowledge of reality is stated. Not only is it non-overridable, but knowledge of reality also has firm roots — he says — 'and because of the support of other <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge).' The word 'other' (<s>antara</s>) means 'particular.' For the knowledge of the reality of the self and the rest, which is the result, is supported by particular <s>pramāṇas</s> — scripture (<s>āgama</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).

children.text: samāhitatvena cetaso dhāraṇāṃ darśayati--ananyamanā iti pratyāhāram, cetasaḥ tattvaviṣayabuddhidhārāvipacyamānatvaṃ dhyānasya, tattvajñānasya sphuṭābhatvārambhāvasthā /
children.translated_text: He shows the mental concentration involved in being concentrated — '<s>ananyamanā</s>' (with undistracted mind) represents <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of the senses); the state of the mind's stream of reality-directed cognition being ripened is <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation); the stage of the inception of clear manifestation of knowledge of reality.

children.text: dhyānajanitabhāvanā saṃskāro dhyānabhāvanā, tasyā viveko mithyajñānavāsanāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: The impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) born of meditation is the cultivation of meditation (<s>dhyānabhāvanā</s>); its discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) is from the latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) of false knowledge.

children.text: pūrvaṃ hi mithyājñānavāsanā tattvajñānavāsanāyā balavatyāsīt, athābhyāsavaśāt tulyabalābhavat, atheyameva balīyasī tattvajñānavāsanāsaṃbhinnā mithyājñānavāsanayā sahānuvartate /
children.translated_text: For previously, the latent impression of false knowledge was stronger than the latent impression of knowledge of reality; then through practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) they became of equal strength; then this very [impression of knowledge of reality] became stronger, and being combined with the latent impression of knowledge of reality, it continues alongside the latent impression of false knowledge.

children.text: saṃprati tu tattvajñānavāsanayā atyantabalīyasya samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitatvāt mithyājñānavāsanāyā bhavati viviktā tattvajñānavāsanā tasyāmityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: But now, because the latent impression of false knowledge has been uprooted completely by the latent impression of knowledge of reality, which has become exceedingly strong, the latent impression of knowledge of reality becomes isolated from it — in that [state] — this is the meaning.
He explains 'one who contemplates the object' — 'one who is concentrated (<s>samāhita</s>).'

children.text:
nanvanena krameṇa nivartatāṃ mithyājñānam, nivṛttaṃ taṃ tattvasākṣātkārasamaye 'pi kasmāt punaḥ svavāsanāvaśānna jāyate? na khalu mithyājñānavāsanā anādikālapravṛttā ādimatā tattvajñānena tatsaṃskāreṇa vā śakyā nivartayitumityata āha--nivṛtte ceti /
tāvadeva puṃsāṃ buddhayo 'sthirā bhrāmyanti svocitaṃ ca saṃskārajātamātanvate, na yāvad bhūtamarthaṃ sākṣātkurvanti /
atha sākṣātkṛtya tatra sthirapadā bhavanti, kṣiṇvanti ca savāsanān mithyāpratyayān /
bhūtārthaṃpakṣapāto hi buddheḥ svabhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: As even the outsiders [i.e., non-Naiyāyika philosophers] say —
The intellect, whose nature is the unwavering real object, cannot be overridden by errors,
even with effort, because of its partiality toward that [reality].

Let false knowledge be removed by this process; even so, at the time of direct realization of reality, why does it not arise again through the force of its own latent impression? Surely the latent impression of false knowledge, having operated since beginningless time, cannot be removed by knowledge of reality or its impression, which has a beginning — therefore he says — 'and when it has ceased.' The cognitions of people waver and are unstable only so long as they do not directly perceive reality, and they extend the appropriate class of impressions. But when they directly perceive reality, they become firmly established therein, and they destroy the false cognitions together with their latent impressions. For partiality toward real objects is the very nature of the intellect.
(<s>Pra. Vā.</s> 212.3) Thus.
Therefore, false knowledge does not arise again.

children.text:
uktamevārthaṃ smṛtidāḍhrayāya pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
uktaṃ smārayitumuttaram--saheti /
bhavatu mithyājñānasya nivṛttiḥ savāsanasya, tato 'pi kimityata āha--mithyājñāneti /
atra pṛcchati--ye tāvaditi /
uttaram--teṣāmapīti /
vairāgyasvarūpaṃ pṛcchati--ki punariti /
rāgābhāvo hi vairāgyam /
na ca tasmādeva rāgādīnāmabhāva iti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--bhogānabhiṣvaṅgalakṣaṇamityuktam /
viṣayadoṣaparibhāvanāparipākāt khalu viṣayaparityāgecchā bhavati /
tayā virodhiguṇena viṣayatṛṣṇā ca tatparipanthini vidveṣaśca tadadhikaraṇāśrverṣyādayo nivartante /
asaktirviṣayaparityāgecchā, vaśitayā ca svayamupanateṣu viṣayeṣu mādhyasthyadarśanam /
doṣābhāve kiṃ bhavatītyata āha--doṣābhāva iti /
pṛcchati--kā punariyamiti /
yadi hi janmanaḥ pravṛttiḥ kāraṇaṃ syāt, tato janmanivṛttyai tannivṛttirarthyeta /
na punarasau kṣaṇikā sato āmuṣmikāya janmane kalpate /
ataḥ kimarthaṃ nivartyata iti bhāvaḥ /
viditābhiprāya uttaramāha--dharmādharmo /
kasmāt punarūpacāra ityata āha--janmasādhanatvāt /
etadvibhajate--nāsminniti /
upacāre prayojanaṃ darśayitvā nimittamāha--dharmādharmayostviti /
vartamānānāgatayoraviśeṣeṇa doṣāpāyāt nivṛttirūkteti bhrāntyā deśayati--yau tāvadanāgatāviti /
pariharati--na, anāgatayoriti /
anāgatābhiprāyametadityarthaḥ /
yadyevam, vartamānayoḥ kutaḥ prakṣaya
ityata āha--vartamānayoriti /
astu pravṛtterabhāvaḥ,tataḥ kimityata āha--pravṛttyabhāva iti /
uktaṃ vivekamihāpi yojayati--atrāpīti /
vartamānanivṛttihetu pṛcchati--atheti /
uttaram--saṃskāreti /
śrutiḥ,
tāvadevāsya ciraṃ yāvanna vimokṣye 'tha saṃpatsye /
# chāndogya 6.14.2 # iti /

children.translated_text: To the question 'what is accomplished by the absence of birth?', he says— 'absence of birth.'
On this very point he states the view approved by the elders— 'and this is what they say.'
The construction is: 'that is this.'
The duration limited by the division of time of breathing is <s>āyus</s> (lifespan).

He asks the already-stated meaning for the purpose of strengthening the memory— 'who then?' The answer, to recall what was stated— 'together with.' Granted that false knowledge together with its impressions ceases, but what follows from that?— to this he says— 'false knowledge.' Here he asks— 'those at first.' The answer— 'of those too.' He asks about the nature of dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>)— 'what then?' For dispassion is the absence of attachment (<s>rāga</s>). But the mere absence of attachment does not entail the absence of attachment and the rest— this is the purport. The answer— 'it is said to be characterized by non-clinging to enjoyments.' Indeed, from the maturation of the contemplation of the defects of sense objects, the desire to renounce sense objects arises. By that opposing quality, craving for objects, and hatred which obstructs it, and envy and the like directed at its substrate, all cease. Non-attachment is the desire to renounce sense objects, and mastery is the attitude of indifference toward objects that present themselves of their own accord. When there is absence of defects, what happens?— to this he says— 'absence of defects.' He asks— 'what then is this?' For if activity were the cause of birth, then for the cessation of birth, the cessation of activity would be sought. But that momentary [activity] of an existing being is not adequate for birth in the next life. Therefore, for what purpose is it to be ceased?— this is the purport. He answers, having understood the intention— '<s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.' Why is there figurative usage?— to this he says— 'because of being the means to birth.' He analyzes this— 'not in this.' Having shown the purpose of the figurative usage, he states the reason— 'but of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.' One mistakenly teaches that the cessation of both present and future [dharma and adharma] occurs indiscriminately from the removal of defects— 'those two which are future.' He resolves— 'no, of the future ones.' The meaning is that this is intended with reference to the future ones. If so, whence the destruction of the present ones?— to this he says— 'of the present ones.' Granted the absence of activity; what follows from that?— to this he says— 'absence of activity.' He applies the distinction already stated here as well— 'here too.' He asks about the cause of the cessation of the present ones— 'now.' The answer— 'impression.' The <s>śruti</s> (Vedic text): 'So long indeed shall he wait until he is freed, then he shall arrive' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.14.2).

children.text:
syādetat, mahāpralaye 'pi mithyājñānādinā duḥkhāntenāsti viyoga iti atrāpi muktiprasaṅga ityata āha--so 'yaṃ mithyājñānādineti /
sarvata iti tṛtīyārthe tasiḥ sarveṇeti /
na ca pralayāvasthāyāṃ sarveṇa viyogaḥ, karmāvidyāvāsanayoranavināśāt /
children.translated_text: And in the state of dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>), there is no separation from everything, because the impressions of <s>karma</s> and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are not destroyed.
But in liberation (<s>mukti</s>), even those two are destroyed.
And the impression of <s>karma</s> is the producer and sustainer of all effects.

children.text: tannivṛttau śarīrādivat tattvajñānasaṃskārasyāpi pralaya ityaśeṣaviśeṣaguṇavimukto mukta ityucyata iti saddhim //
children.translated_text: Upon the cessation of that, just as the body and the rest dissolve, so too the impression of the knowledge of reality dissolves— thus one freed from all particular qualities is called 'liberated' (<s>mukta</s>). This is in agreement [with the tradition].

An objection may arise: even in the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>), there is separation from suffering and the rest through false knowledge— and thus there would be the unwanted consequence of liberation there too. To this he says— 'this very [cessation] from false knowledge and the rest.' The word '<s>sarvatas</s>' (completely) uses the <s>tasi</s> suffix in the sense of the instrumental case, meaning 'by everything.'

children.text:
stādetat /
tattvajñānāt mithyājñānāpāya ityuktam /
kiṃ punastattvajñānamityata uktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā--tattvajñānu tviti /
tadanubhāṣya sarveṣāṃ jñānānāṃ bhāṣyoktānāmanugatamekaṃ svarūpatastviti /
codayati--kasmāditi /
no khlvayaṃ prekṣāvatāṃ samācāro yad duḥkhabhiyā sukhaparityāga iti, api tu sukhaṃ duḥkhād vivicya upādadate duḥkhaṃ ca varjayanti /
na hi mṛgāḥ santīti śālayo nopyante, bhikṣukāḥ santīti sthālyo nādhiśrīyanta iti /
uttaram--vivekahānasyeti /
yadyapi sukhaduḥkhe bhinne, tathāpyanityatvakṛtakatvavat parasparānuṣakte iti na khalu sukhasya kevalasyopādānaṃ duḥkhasya vā kevalasya parivarjanaṃ śakyamityarthaḥ /
kaḥ punarayamanuṣaṅgo yato vivekahānamaśakyamityata āha--anuṣaṅgo 'dhinābhāvaḥ /
tatsvarūpamāha--yatraikaṃ sukhaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ vā, tatretarat duḥkhaṃ vā sukhaṃ vā /
tadanenānityatvakṛtakatvayoriva sukhaduḥkhayoravinābhāvo darśitaḥ /
na cāvinābhāvo vinā saṃbandhāditi tatsiddhaye saṃbandhavikalpānāha--samānanimittatā vā anuṣaṅgo 'vinābhāvaḥ, vāśabdaśca vakṣyamāṇasaṃbandhāntarāpekṣayā, na tu pūrvāpekṣayā /
atra ca śarīrādyapekṣayā samānanimittatā, na tu dharmādharmāpekṣayā, na tu pūrvāpekṣayā /
atra ca śarīrādyapekṣayā samānanimittatā, na tu dharmādharmāpekṣayā tayorasādhāraṇyāditi /
mantavyam /
tayoravinābhāvasiddhyarthaṃ saṃbandhāntaram āha--samānādhāratā vā /
aparaṃ saṃbandhāntaramāha--samānādhāratā vā /
aparaṃ saṃbandhāntaramāha--samānopalabhyatā vā /
manogocaratvamubhayoḥ /
tataśca siddho 'navinābhāvāparanāmā anuṣaṅga iti /
yatraikaṃ tatretaraditi vā yatra yasminnimitte satīti vā yatrādhāra iti vā yatropalabdhisādhane satīti vyākhyeyam /
itiḥ sūtrasamāptiṃ sūcayati//2 //
children.translated_text: An objection may arise: it has been said that from the knowledge of reality, false knowledge ceases. But what is the knowledge of reality?— therefore the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) has stated— 'but the knowledge of reality.' Having restated that, the single essential nature common to all cognitions mentioned in the <s>bhāṣya</s> is 'reality' (<s>tattva</s>). He objects— 'why?' Surely the practice of discerning people is not to abandon pleasure out of fear of pain; rather, they discriminate pleasure from pain, accept pleasure, and avoid pain. For rice paddies are not neglected because deer exist, nor are cooking pots not put on the fire because beggars exist. The answer— 'because of the impossibility of discrimination.' Although pleasure and pain are distinct, nevertheless, like impermanence and being-produced, they are mutually connected, so that the acceptance of pleasure alone or the avoidance of pain alone is impossible— this is the meaning. What then is this connection, due to which discrimination is impossible?— to this he says— 'the connection is dependence.' He states its nature— 'where there is one— pleasure or pain— there too is the other— pain or pleasure.' By this, the inseparability of pleasure and pain, like that of impermanence and being-produced, has been shown. And inseparability is not without a relation— therefore, to establish that, he states the alternative relations— 'having a common cause is the connection, the inseparability'— and the word 'or' is with reference to the other relation to be stated, not with reference to the previous one. And here the common cause is with reference to the body and the like, not with reference to <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, since those are not common [to both]— this should be understood. He states another relation for establishing their inseparability— 'or having a common substrate.' He states yet another relation— 'or having a common substrate.' He states still another relation— 'or being apprehended by the same means.' Both are within the scope of the mind. And thus the connection, also called inseparability, is established. 'Where there is one, there is the other'— this should be explained either as 'where, when a certain cause exists,' or 'where, in a certain substrate,' or 'where, when a certain means of apprehension exists.' The word <s>iti</s> indicates the conclusion of the <s>sūtra</s>. // 2 //
<s>NyS</s> 1.1.3: Perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge).

children.text:
tadevaṃ pramāṇādipadārthatattvajñānasya niḥśreyasasaṃbandha uktaḥ parīkṣitaśca /
tatraitat syāt /
svapadebhyaḥ pramāṇādayaḥ padārthāstattvato jñātā yathāyathaṃ mithyājñānādinivṛttikrameṇa apavarge upayokṣyante, kṛtamuparitanena prabandhena iti /
ata uktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā--trivadhā cāsyeti /
na nāmadheyamātrāt pramāṇādīnāṃ tattvajñānaṃ bhavati, api tu lakṣaṇaparīkṣaṇābhyām ityasti prabandhasyottarasyopayoga iti bhāṣyārthaḥ /
tadetadbhāṣyamanubhāṣya pṛcchati---pravṛtteriti /
yadi puruṣakalpanā mātrāt traividhyam, athānantyameva kasmānna bhavati? sarvatra tasya sulabhatvāditi bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---arthasya tathābhāvāt /
arthasya prayojanasya sākṣāt, śāstrakāryasya tattvajñānalakṣaṇasya tathaiva trividhayaiva śāstrapravṛttyā bhāvāt /
tathā hi, lakṣaṇaṃ nāma vyatirekihetuvacanam /
taddhi samānāsamānajātīyebhyo vyavacchidya lakṣyaṃ vyavasthāpayati /
na cāsya dharmidarśanamantareṇa pakṣadharmatā sidhyatīti tadupadarśanāya nāmadheyamātreṇa dharmiṇāmuddeśaḥ /
yadyapi ca pratilakṣaṇamuddiṣṭā eva dharmiṇaḥ, tathāpi śāstrābhisaṃbandhaparādapi vākyāt samadhigamyanta ityuddeśo 'pyuktaḥ /
na cāparīkṣito heturvyatirekī catūrūpo bhavatīti parīkṣāpyavaśyaṃ kartavyā /

children.translated_text: Therefore, because the object— the knowledge of reality— is so constituted, the threefold [exposition] is justified.
He analyzes this— 'the named categories.'
'But rather'—

children.text: arthaḥ tattvajñānaṃ tathābhūtam, yenārthena hetunā śāstrasya pravṛttistredhā bhavati //
children.translated_text: The object is the knowledge of reality so constituted, by reason of which object the operation of the <s>śāstra</s> is threefold.

Thus the connection of the knowledge of the reality of the categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> with <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (the highest good) has been stated and examined. Here the following thought may arise: the categories such as <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest, being known in their true nature from their own words, will serve in their respective ways through the sequential cessation of false knowledge for <s>apavarga</s> (liberation)— so the subsequent exposition is unnecessary. Therefore the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) has said— 'and this is threefold.'
