The knowledge of the reality of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest does not arise from mere names alone, but rather from definition and examination— thus there is a use for the subsequent exposition. This is the meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s>. Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s>, he asks— 'of the operation.' If the threefold [exposition] were merely from human convention, why should there not be infinity? Since that [convention] is easily available everywhere— this is the purport. The answer— 'because the object is so constituted.' The object, i.e., the purpose— which is directly the knowledge of reality, the proper effect of the <s>śāstra</s>— exists precisely through the threefold operation of the <s>śāstra</s>. For a definition is a statement of the differentiating reason. For that discriminates the definiendum from things of the same and different kinds and establishes it. And the property-of-the-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>) of this [reason] cannot be established without observing the property-bearer— therefore, for the purpose of showing that, the enumeration is merely by name of the property-bearers. And although the property-bearers are enumerated for each definition, they are also understood from the sentence that pertains to the connection with the <s>śāstra</s>— therefore the enumeration too is stated. And an unexamined differentiating reason does not become a quadruply characterized [valid reason]— therefore examination too must necessarily be performed.

children.text: yadyapi pramāṇaṇādiśabdā api kārakaśabdā eva, tathāpyuddeśasamaye tadarthānāṃ sadapi kārakatvamavivakṣitam, api tu prātipadikārthamātram /
children.translated_text: Although the words <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest are also <s>kāraka</s> (action-related) words, nevertheless at the time of enumeration, the <s>kāraka</s>-meaning of their referents, though existing, is not intended; rather, only the meaning of the nominal stem (<s>prātipadikārtha</s>) is intended.

children.text: ghrāṇādisūtre # 1.1.12 # tu lakṣaṇapare kārakatvaṃ vivakṣitam anyathā lakṣaṇatvāyogāditi adoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: But in the <s>sūtra</s> on the organ of smell and the rest (1.1.12), which pertains to definition, the <s>kāraka</s>-meaning is intended; otherwise, the status of being a definition would not work— therefore there is no fault.

children.text: atra ca yadyapi sūtrakāreṇa saṃśayapramāṇaprameyeṣu parīkṣā sākṣāt kṛtā na prayojanādiṣu, tathāpi tatkaraṇādeva prayojanādiparīkṣāpi sūcitā sūtrakāreṇa iti trividhetyuktam /
children.translated_text: And here, although the <s>sūtrakāra</s> has directly performed examination with respect to doubt, <s>pramāṇa</s>, and <s>prameya</s>, and not with respect to purpose and the rest, nevertheless the examination of purpose and the rest is also indicated by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> through doing precisely that— hence it is said 'threefold.'
For this very reason, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) has carried out examination everywhere.
Having restated the <s>bhāṣya</s> that aims to explain the nature of enumeration (<s>uddeśa</s>), he raises an objection— 'by name.' He resolves— 'by the force of the word mātra (mere).'

children.text:
syādetat /
vibhāgaparametat sūtramiti vakṣyati /
na ca vibhāgo nyūnādhikasaṃkhyāvyavacchedārthamekaṃ kiñcidupasaṃgrāhakamantareṇa /
na ca pramāṇatvādanyadatropasaṃgrāhakam /
na cedamalakṣitamupasaṃgṛhṇāti /
na caitat sūtramasya lakṣaṇam, vibhāgaparatvāditi śaṅkānirākaraṇaparaṃ bhāṣyam--tatroddiṣṭasyeti /
tasyārthaḥ--yadyapi vibhāgaparametat sūtram, tathāpi pramāṇapadasamabhivyāhṛtaṃ sat sāmarthyāt pramāṇatvamapi lakṣayatīti /
tathā hi, pramīyate 'nenetyasya vākyasyārthe pramāṇapadaprayogaḥ /
pramā ca smṛteranyaḥ arthāvyabhicārī svatantraḥ paricchedaḥ tasmād vibhāgaparādapi sūtrāt pratīyamānaṃ pramāṇasāmānyalakṣaṇamapekṣitaṃ saṃgṛhītamiti pramāṇatvopagṛhītānāṃ pratyakṣādīnāṃ pramāṇānāṃ yukto vibhāgaḥ /
tathā ca vibhāgaparatvena sākṣāt sāmānyalakṣaṇānabhidhānād vibhaktasya lakṣaṇamucyata ityuktam tacceha /

children.translated_text: The specific definition is 'the contact of the sense organ with the object' and so on (1.1.4).
He explains this <s>bhāṣya</s>— 'of the enumerated one.'
With the intention of expressing merely the distinction between what is defined and what is undefined, it is said 'of the defined' and 'of the undefined.'

children.text: tacca chale sāmānyataḥ, pramāṇeṣu prameyeṣu ca viśeṣata iti gamayitavyam //
children.translated_text: And this should be understood as being general in the case of <s>chala</s> (equivocation), and specific in the case of the <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s>.

An objection may arise: it will be said that this <s>sūtra</s> pertains to division (<s>vibhāga</s>). And division— for the purpose of excluding a lesser or greater number— is not possible without some single unifying factor. And no unifying factor other than <s>pramāṇatva</s> (the nature of being a means of valid knowledge) is found here. And this [unifying factor] does not subsume what is undefined. And this <s>sūtra</s> is not a definition of it, since it pertains to division. To remove this doubt, the <s>bhāṣya</s> states— 'of the enumerated one.' Its meaning: although this <s>sūtra</s> pertains to division, nevertheless, being conjoined with the word <s>pramāṇa</s>, it also defines <s>pramāṇatva</s> by implication. For the word <s>pramāṇa</s> is used in the meaning of the sentence 'that by which something is ascertained.' And <s>pramā</s> (valid cognition) is a determination that is different from memory, non-deviating from the object, and independent. Therefore, the general definition of <s>pramāṇa</s> understood even from a <s>sūtra</s> pertaining to division is what is required and is subsumed— and thus the division of perception and the rest, which are subsumed under <s>pramāṇatva</s>, is justified. And since the general definition is not directly stated because of the <s>sūtra</s>'s pertaining to division, it is said that the definition of what has been divided is stated— and that is here.
Its meaning: the <s>sūtra</s> is the statement, the verbal expression, of the division— that which says 'by this.'
'Now' (<s>atha</s>) indicates that after the explanation of the threefold operation, the presentation of the distinguished [categories] is the statement of division.

children.text: na ca vivekaḥ svarūpa upayujyata ityata āha--athoddiṣṭavibhāgadvāreṇeti /
children.translated_text: One might object that distinction is not useful in itself— to this he says— 'or through the division of what has been enumerated.'

children.text: nātra vibhāgamātraṃ vivakṣitam, api tu taddvāreṇa nyunādhikasaṃkhyāvyavacchedastattvajñānāṅgamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Here it is not mere division that is intended, but rather through it, the exclusion of a lesser or greater number is a component of the knowledge of reality— this is the meaning.
Here the <s>bhāṣya</s> states— 'or the statement of the division of what has been enumerated.'

children.text:
avyākhyāne hetumāha--sūtreti /
codayati--uddiṣṭasya vibhāgānarthakyam vyāghātāt /
trividhā cāsya śāstrasya pravṛttirityasyānarthakyam /
anarthamarthaviparyayaṃ kāyati kīrtayatītyanarthakaḥ /
tasya bhāvastattvam /
kasmāt? vyāghātāt /
vyāghātam eva sphorayati--trividhā cāsya śāstryasyeti /
pariharati--noddiṣṭeti /
parasparaṃ vibhaktā nāmadheyamātreṇoddiśyanta ityuddeśentarbhāvaḥ /
tenāyamartho bhavati, sāmānyenoddiṣṭasya vibhāgavacanaṃ viśeṣeṇoddeśa iti /
vibhāgaprayojanaṃ pṛcchati--kiṃ punariti /
uttaram--niyamaḥ /
tadvibhajate--yadīti /
punaścodayati--lakṣaṇata iti /
pramāṇalakṣaṇakaraṇapravṛtto yat catvāryeva lakṣayati tadavagamyate na nyūnānyadhikāni vā pramāṇanītyarthaḥ /
pariharati--lakṣaṇasyeti /
ākṣepaṃ vibhajte--syādeṣeti /
parihāraṃ vibhajate--na, lakṣaṇasyeti /
anyaparamapi vākyaṃ tadevārthalabhyaṃ svīkaroti /
na ca pratyakṣādīnāṃ samānāsamānajātīyasya vyavacchede pañcamyādyabhāva upayujyate /
lakṣaṇakaraṇapravṛttasya kvacidakaraṇaṃ na tadabhāve pramāṇam, sato 'pyanupayogenākaraṇāpatteḥ /
children.translated_text: The non-formulation by one engaged in formulating definitions, regarding some [category], is not evidence for the absence of that, since even something that exists might not be formulated because of non-utility.
This is what he states—'because of the impossibility of anything else.'
But since the enumeration-division has no other purpose, the ascertainment of the absence of anything else follows from it.
He concludes—'therefore.'

He states the reason for not explaining—'<s>sūtra</s>.' He objects—'the purposelessness of dividing what has been enumerated, because of contradiction.' 'The activity of this <s>śāstra</s> is threefold'—this is purposeless. '<s>Anarthaka</s>' means one who proclaims (<s>kāyati</s>) what is contrary to the purpose (<s>arthaviparyaya</s>). Its nature (<s>tattva</s>) [is purposelessness]. Why? Because of contradiction. He expands the contradiction itself—'the activity of this <s>śāstra</s> is threefold.' He resolves—'not enumerated.' Those that are mutually distinguished are enumerated merely by name—thus they are included within enumeration. Therefore the meaning is: the statement of division for what has been enumerated generally is an enumeration in specific form. He asks the purpose of division—'what then?' The answer—'restriction.' He divides that—'if.' He objects again—'by definition.' The meaning is: when one engaged in formulating the definition of <s>pramāṇa</s> defines exactly four, it is understood that there are neither fewer nor more <s>pramāṇas</s>. He resolves—'of the definition.' He divides the objection—'it might be so.' He divides the resolution—'no, of the definition.' Even another statement accepts that very meaning obtainable [from the definition]. And in the exclusion of what is of the same and different class from perception etc., the ablative and such are not needed.

children.text:
akṣasyākṣasyeti bhāṣyamanubhāṣya tātparyamāha--ayaṃ ca sūtravivakṣāyāmiti /
akṣamakṣaṃ prati vartata iti vigṛhyāvyayībhāve kṛte sarvendriyāvarodho bhavati /
nanu yadir idṛśo vigrahaḥ, kasmāt punarbhāṣyakāreṇa akṣasyākṣasyeti vigṛhyata ityata āha--anyathā tu vastunirdeśa iti /
arthamātramanena pratipādyate, na punaḥ samāsa ityarthaḥ /
atha kasmāt samāsa eva tena vigraheṇa na pratipādyata ityata āha--samāse hi akṣasyeti ṣaṣṭhī na śrūyeteti /
yadi sūtragatasya pratyakṣapadasyāvyayībhāvaḥ samāsaḥ, anyatra punarasya kaḥ samāsa iti pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
uttaram--prādisamāsa iti /
tathā hi, prāptāpannālaṃpūrvagatisamāseṣu paravalliṅgatāpratiṣedhādabhidhayaliṅgopādānāt pratyakṣo 'rthaḥ pratyakṣābuddhiḥ pratyakṣaṃ jñānamityabhidheyaliṅgatā siddhā bhavati /
kvacit pāṭhaḥ samāse hi pratyakṣasyeti ṣaṣṭhī na śrūyeteti /
sūtravivakṣayāvyayībhāva ityuktam /
tatra śaṅkate, kasmāt punaḥ sūtravivakṣayetyucyate, yāvatā sarvatraiva kasmādavyayībhāvo na bhavatīti? tatredamupatiṣṭhate--samāse hi avyayībhāvasamāse hi, sarvatra pratyakṣasyeti ṣaṣṭhī na śrūyeteti /
vyutpattinimittamātraṃ cedaṃ pratyakṣaśabdasya, na tu pravṛttinimittam /
tasmāt nendriyagatairguṇasāmānyādibhirvyabhicāraḥ,
pravṛttihetustvarthasākṣātkārijñānajanakatvam /
tannimittaḥ khalvayaṃ pratyakṣaśabdastatra tatra laukikaparīkṣakaiḥ prayujyate /
children.translated_text: It is indeed on that basis that the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' is employed here and there by worldly people and examiners.

children.text: yathā mayūraśabdo mayūratvasāmānyanibandhanaḥ kāsucideva patatrivyaktiṣu vartamānaḥ, mahyāṃ rautītyanvākhyāyate /
children.translated_text: Just as the word 'peacock,' founded on the universal peacock-ness, occurring only in certain bird-individuals, is etymologically explained as '<s>mahyāṃ rauti</s>' (it calls to me).

children.text: tadidaṃ pratyakṣamuddhiṣṭamapi sat pramāṇatadābhāsasaṃkīrṇamiti tadvivekāya lakṣaṇamupayujyate /
children.translated_text: This <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), though enumerated, being mixed with both valid cognition and its semblance, requires a definition for its discrimination.

children.text: yadi tūddeśapadaṃ tadvivecayet, kṛtaṃ tarhi lakṣaṇapraṇayanena //
children.translated_text: But if the enumerating word itself could discriminate that, then the formulation of a definition would be unnecessary.

Having restated the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'of each sense organ,' he states its purport—'and this, regarding the intention of the <s>sūtra</s>.' When 'pratyakṣa' is analyzed as '<s>akṣam akṣaṃ prati vartate</s>' (operates with respect to each and every sense), and resolved as an <s>avyayībhāva</s> compound, it covers all sense organs. Now, if this is the analysis, why does the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> analyze it as '<s>akṣasya akṣasya</s>'?—therefore he says: 'but otherwise, it is merely stating the referent.' Only the meaning is conveyed by that, not the compound—such is the meaning. Then why is the compound itself not conveyed by that analysis?—therefore he says: 'for in the compound, the genitive "<s>akṣasya</s>" would not be heard.' If the <s>avyayībhāva</s> compound is the compound of the word 'pratyakṣa' occurring in the <s>sūtra</s>, then what compound does it have elsewhere?—he asks: 'what then?' The answer—'a <s>prādi</s> compound.' For thus, in compounds with <s>prāpta</s>, <s>āpanna</s>, <s>ālam</s>, and prefixes with <s>gati</s>, since the prohibition of taking the gender of the latter member applies, and since the gender of the expressed meaning is adopted, the forms '<s>pratyakṣo 'rthaḥ</s>' (masculine), '<s>pratyakṣā buddhiḥ</s>' (feminine), '<s>pratyakṣaṃ jñānam</s>' (neuter) are established through the gender of the expressed meaning. In some readings: 'for in the compound, the genitive "<s>pratyakṣasya</s>" would not be heard.' It was said that the <s>avyayībhāva</s> is by the intention of the <s>sūtra</s>. There he raises a doubt: 'why is it said "by the intention of the <s>sūtra</s>," when in fact why is the <s>avyayībhāva</s> not applicable everywhere?' Here this presents itself—'for in the compound, i.e., in the <s>avyayībhāva</s> compound, everywhere the genitive "<s>pratyakṣasya</s>" would not be heard.' This is merely the etymological ground of the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>,' not the ground of its actual usage. Therefore there is no deviation through qualities, universals, etc., which reside in the sense organs; the ground of actual usage is the capacity to generate cognition that directly apprehends the object.

children.text:
vigrahavākyagatā ca vṛttirbhāṣyakṛtā vyākhyātā /
vṛttistu sannikarṣo jñānaṃ vā /
vṛttiriti hi vyāpāraḥ /
sa tu vyāpāra ucyate, yaḥ kārakaiḥ phale janayitavye cāramabhāvī dharmabhedaḥ phalotpādānukūlo 'pekṣyate /
yathā paṭe janayitavye tantubhiścaramabhāvinaḥ saṃyogabhedāḥ, svarge vā janayitavye yāgenāpūrvamātmadharmaḥ, tathehāpi indriyādinā pramāṇena pramāyāṃ phale pravṛttena tadutpādanānukūlaḥ sannikarṣo jñānaṃ vā caramabhāvī dharmabhedo 'pekṣyata iti bhavati vyāpāraḥ /
sa eva vṛttirityākhyāyate /
vyavasthāṃ darśayati--yadā sannikarṣo vyāpāra indriyādeḥ pramāṇasya tadā jñānam ālocanaṃ vā savikalpakaṃ vā sākṣātkāravadvijñānaṃ pramitiḥ phalam, ubhayasyāpīndriyavyāpārāt sannikarṣāparabhidhānānutpatteḥ /
na cāntarālikena nirvikalpakenendriyavyāpāraviccheda iti pratyakṣavyākhyānāvasare nivedayiṣyate /
yadā jñānam ālocanaṃ vā vikalpo vā vyāpāra indriyādīnāṃ tadā hānopādānopekṣābuddhayaḥ phalam /
tatropādeyamidaṃ salilamiti buddhiranāgatopādānaviśiṣṭaṃ salilamālambamānā na sākṣātkāravatī, salilamātrasākṣātkārastu syāt /
na ca tanmātramasya phalam, api tūpādeyatā /
sā ca parokṣā, anāgatatvāt /
tasmādupādīyate anenetyupādānam upādānaṃ cāsau buddhiścetyupādānabuddhiḥ /
tatra toyālocanamatha toyavikaltaḥ, atha tajjātīyasya dṛṣṭacarapipāsopaśamanahetubhāvasya smṛtibījasaṃskārodbodhaḥ, atha tasya smaraṇam, atha liṅgaparāmarśaḥ tajjātīyaṃ cedamiti /
tadidaṃ liṅgaparāmarśavijñānaṃ sākṣātkāravat /
liṅge vinaśyadavasthavyāptismaraṇasahakāridṛśyamānasya salilasya pipāsopaśamanahetutayā anumānamukhenopādānabuddhirūcyate /

children.translated_text: Having inferred its nature thus, desiring to accept it, one who strives thus accepts it.

children.text: na ca vyāptismṛtivicchinnamālocanaṃ vā vikalpo vā na liṅgaparāmarśajñānaheturiti vācyam, tadudbodhitasaṃskāradvāreṇa vyāpsmiraṇe ca parāmarśe ca tasya tadānīmasato 'pi kāraṇatvāt /
children.translated_text: And it cannot be said that apprehension or determination, when separated from the recollection of pervasion, is not the cause of inferential-mark-consideration-cognition—since it is a cause of both the recollection of pervasion and the consideration through the medium of the awakened latent impression, even though not existing at that time.

children.text: na khalu kṛṣikarma śasyādhigatisamaye samasti, na ca yāgādikaṃ svargādyutpādasamaye, na ca trivṛtkaṣāyapānaṃ virekasamaye /
children.translated_text: Indeed, agricultural work does not exist at the time of obtaining the harvest, nor does sacrifice etc. exist at the time of the production of heaven, nor does the drinking of the triple decoction exist at the time of purging.
But through the series of intermediate effects, its being a means [to the result] is the same everywhere.

And the operation (<s>vṛtti</s>) contained in the etymological sentence has been explained by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>. <s>Vṛtti</s> is either contact or cognition. For <s>vṛtti</s> means activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>). And activity is said to be that differentiation of properties which is the last to arise among the <s>kārakas</s> (factors) in generating the result, which is conducive to the production of the result and is awaited. Just as in producing cloth, the differentiations of contact that are the last to arise in the threads [are the activity]; or in producing heaven, the <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented merit), a property of the self, that is the last to arise through sacrifice [is the activity]—similarly here too, in the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) such as the sense organ etc., which has engaged in the result, namely <s>pramā</s> (valid cognition), the contact or cognition that is the last differentiating property to arise, which is conducive to its production, is awaited—thus it is the activity. That very thing is called <s>vṛtti</s>. He shows the arrangement—'when contact is the activity of the sense organ etc., the means of knowledge, then cognition—whether indeterminate apprehension or determinate—a cognition possessing direct apprehension, is the result (<s>pramiti</s>),' since both arise from the activity of the sense organ, contact being another name for it, and nothing else arises. And there is no interruption of sense-organ activity by the intervening indeterminate cognition—this will be explained on the occasion of explaining perception. 'When cognition—whether indeterminate apprehension or determination—is the activity of the sense organs etc., then the cognitions of abandonment, acceptance, and indifference are the result.' There, the cognition 'this water is to be accepted,' apprehending water qualified by future acceptance, does not possess direct apprehension, though there may be direct apprehension of water alone. And not that alone is its result, but rather the quality of being-to-be-accepted. And that is remote, since it has not yet occurred. Therefore, 'that by which one accepts is <s>upādāna</s> (acceptance),' and that is a cognition too—hence '<s>upādānabuddhi</s>' (acceptance-cognition). There, [first] the apprehension of water, then the determination of water, then the awakening of the latent impression that is the seed of memory regarding the capacity of similar things previously observed to quench thirst, then the remembering of that, then the reflective consideration of the inferential mark—'this is of that type.' This inferential-mark-consideration-cognition possesses direct apprehension. Through the inferential mark—perceiving the water [currently] seen, with the aid of the recollection of the pervasion: the invariable immediately-prior-existence ascertained regarding similar things in their passing states—[the cognition] that it has the capacity to quench thirst is called <s>upādānabuddhi</s> (acceptance-cognition) through the medium of inference.

children.text:
syādetat /
kā punariyaṃ pipāsopaśamanaśaktistoyasya, yā anumānagocaraḥ? na tāvat mīmāṃsakavadatīndriyā śaktiryusmābhirabhyupeyate, kiṃ tu kāraṇānāṃ svarūpaṃ vā sahakārisākalyaṃ vā /
tatra svarūpaṃ hetūnāṃ pratyakṣameva /
sahakāriṇā pratyakṣāpratyakṣāṇāṃ sākalyaṃ kāryasamutpādaikavya/janīyam, na tu tat toyarūpadarśanamātrāt śakyānumānam /
tat kimaparamavaśiṣyate yadanumānasya gocara iti? atrocyate /
na vayamatīndriyaṃ sāmarthyam ātiṣṭhāmahe, nāpi sahakārisākalyānumānamācakṣmahe, kiṃ tu svarūpasya kāryasaṃbadhitām /
na ceyaṃ svarūpameva, ihasthasyeva nārikeladvīpādāgatasyāpi vahnidarśanamātrād grāhakatvāvagamaprasaṅgāt /
tasmāt kāryopahitaṃ svarūpamanumeyam /
idameva cāsya kāryopadhānaṃ yat kāryotpādāt pūrvamavaśyaṃbhāva ānantaryaniyamaḥ /
na ca tajjātīyasya dṛṣṭacarasya tathābhāvadarśane 'pi dṛśyamānasya toyasya tad dṛṣṭaṃ bhavati yena tatra smaryeta /

children.translated_text: Indeed, those who are undeluded do not remember in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> a palace perceived in <s>Ujjayinī</s>.
By [the explanation of] acceptance, abandonment has been explained.

And indifference is not placed in the category of abandonment by virtue of being non-acceptance—since there would be the undesirable consequence of its being placed in the category of acceptance by virtue of being non-abandonment.

children.text: upādānaprayatnāprasavahetutayā nopādānamiti cet? kimiyaṃ hānaprayatnamapi prasūte yato hānaṃ syāt? tasmād yā nobhayaprayatnaprasavahetuḥ sopekṣābuddhistṛtīyā lokaprasiddheti siddham //
children.translated_text: If it is said that it is not acceptance because it does not produce the effort of acceptance—then does it produce the effort of abandonment such that it would be abandonment? Therefore, that which does not produce either effort is the third cognition—indifference—well-known in the world. This is established.

It might be said: what then is this capacity of water to quench thirst, which is the object of inference? It is not the case that you accept, like the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, a supersensory power (<s>śakti</s>); rather, [you hold it to be] either the intrinsic nature of causes or the totality of auxiliary conditions. Of these, the intrinsic nature of causes is directly perceptible. The totality of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions can only be inferred from the actual production of the effect—but it cannot be inferred merely from seeing the form of water. So what else remains that would be the object of inference? Here it is said: we do not maintain a supersensory power, nor do we claim an inference of the totality of auxiliary conditions; rather, [we infer] the connection of the intrinsic nature with the effect. And this is not merely the intrinsic nature itself—since otherwise, even for someone who has come from a coconut island and is here, there would be the unwanted consequence of understanding capacity merely from seeing fire [for the first time]. Therefore, the intrinsic nature as qualified by the effect is what is to be inferred. And this qualification by the effect is nothing other than the necessary immediately-prior-existence before the production of the effect—the restriction of immediate succession. And even though the nature of a similar thing previously observed is seen to be so, the water being presently perceived has not been [previously] observed, so that [past experience] does not apply to it and cannot be remembered regarding it.

children.text:
pratyakṣapadavyutpattiṃ darśayitvā anumānādipadeṣvavi vyutpattigati diśati--evamanumānādiṣvapīti /
tatredamanumānadavyutpattibhāṣyam /
mitena liṅgena liṅgino 'rthasya paścānmānamanumānamiti /
mitirmānam /
tathā ca liṅgadarśanodbodhitasaṃskārajā smṛtirvyavacchinnā, tasyā miteranyatvena lokasiddhatvāt /
mitenetyajñānasandehaviparyāsā liṅgaviṣayā vyudastā bhavanti /
tathāpi mitenārthasya jñānaṃ śābde 'pyastītyata uktam--liṅgeneti /
apakṣadharmato nivartayati--liṅgina iti /
tathāpi dharmiṇaḥ pratyakṣagocaratvāt kṛtamanumānenetyata uktam--arthasyeti /
arthyate sādhyata ityarthaḥ /
na ca dharmo svarūpeṇārthyate, kiṃ tu jijñāsitadharmaviśiṣṭa ityarthaḥ /
paścāditi anuśabdasya vyākhyā /
tadetadbhāṣyamanubhāṣyākṣipati--miteneti /
kasmādayuktamityata āha--phalābhāvāditi /
etad vibhajate--etasminniti /
anumānajñānasya phalāvasthāyāmevārtho mita iti meyaṃ nāvaśiṣyate, yatraitat siddhaṃ sat pramāṇaṃ bhavedityarthaḥ /
tatra phalaviśeṣaṇapakṣamāsthāya yata ityadhyāhṛtya sāmadhatte---naiṣa doṣa iti /
anadhyāhāreṇāpyadoṣa iti samādhānāntaramāha---bhavatu veti /
pūrvoktaṃ doṣaṃ smārayatti---nanu ceti /
pariharati--na doṣa iti /
atha kasmāt hānādiviṣayaṃ pramāṇamucyate, na svagocaraṃ pratītyata āha--sarva ca pramāṇamiti /
yadyapi vahnijñānasyānumānasya sato heyatvādikaṃ viṣayaḥ, tatraiva vyāpārāt /
anyathā pramāṇaphalayorvibhinnaviṣayatvena vipratipattyā pramāṇaphalabhāvāyogāt /
na hi panasaviṣayeṇa paraśunā khadire dvaidhībhāvo bhavati /
tathāpi phalāntarānapekṣamutpattāveva vijñāne yat prakāśate sa tasya viṣayaḥ /
tatra tu na tat pramāṇam, phalāntarājanakatvādapi tu phalamevetyarthaḥ /
viṣayāntaraṃ prati tu pramāṇamityāha--viṣayāntaramiti /
codayati--yadīti /
bhāvasādhanaścet pramāṇaśabdaḥ phalamasyārtho na tu phalaṃ svaviṣaye karaṇam, tadvyāpārasya tajjanakenaiva kṛtatvāt /
na ca svaviṣayādanyad viṣayāntaramasya saṃbhavati, atiprasaṅgāditi bhāvaḥ /
pariharati--uktaṃ phalamiti /
yadyapi yatra phalaṃ so 'syautpattiko viṣayaḥ, tathāpi yatrānena pramāṇena satā hānādibuddhayo janayitavyāḥ, so 'pi vyāpāreṇa viṣaya iti bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: He states the reason for it being the result itself—'the known.'

children.text: parokṣārthāvagāhitayā heyādibuddhayaḥ pratyakṣaphalaṃ na bhavanti, bhavanti tvanumānasyeti /
children.translated_text: Cognitions such as 'to be abandoned' and the rest, which grasp imperceptible objects, are not the fruit of perception, but rather are the fruit of inference.
Having presented the view of the restrictionists, he refutes it—'some, however.'
Favoring the non-restriction view, he says—'both, however.'

Having shown the etymology of the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' (perception), he indicates the course of etymology in the words '<s>anumāna</s>' (inference) etc. as well—'thus in <s>anumāna</s> etc. also.' There, this is the <s>bhāṣya</s> on the etymology of <s>anumāna</s>: 'the subsequent measurement (<s>māna</s>) of the object possessing the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>), by means of the ascertained mark (<s>liṅga</s>), is <s>anumāna</s> (inference).' <s>Miti</s> is <s>māna</s> (measurement/cognition). And thus the recollection born of the impression awakened by seeing the mark, being discriminated—since its being other than that <s>miti</s> (the final inferential cognition) is well-established in the world. 'By the ascertained (<s>mitena</s>)'—this rules out ignorance, doubt, and error regarding the mark. Even so, 'by the ascertained' applies to knowledge of the object even in verbal testimony—therefore it is said 'by the mark (<s>liṅgena</s>).' He excludes what is not a property of the thesis—'of the possessor of the mark (<s>liṅginaḥ</s>).' Even so, since the property-bearer is an object of perception, what need is there for inference?—therefore it is said 'of the object (<s>arthasya</s>).' '<s>Artha</s>' means what is to be established (<s>sādhya</s>). And the property is not sought (<s>arthyate</s>) in its own form, but rather as qualified by the property under investigation—such is the meaning. 'Subsequently (<s>paścāt</s>)'—this is the explanation of the prefix '<s>anu</s>.' Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s>, he objects—'by the ascertained.' Why is it improper?—therefore he says: 'because of the absence of a result.' He divides this—'in this.' When the object is already measured at the stage of the result of inferential cognition, nothing measurable remains in which this, being established, would be a means of knowledge—such is the meaning. There, adopting the position of qualifying by the result, he supplies 'because' and resolves—'this is not a fault.' He states another resolution without supplying anything—'let it be so.' He reminds of the previously stated fault—'but surely.' He resolves—'this is not a fault.' Now, why is a means of knowledge said to be directed at abandonment etc., not at its own object?—therefore he says: 'and every means of knowledge.' Although the cognition of fire, being an inference, has as its object [fire's] being-to-be-abandoned etc., since its activity is directed there. Otherwise, since the means of knowledge and its result would have different objects, through disagreement, there would be the impossibility of the means-result relationship. For a breadfruit-directed axe does not split <s>khadira</s> (acacia) wood. Nevertheless, in the cognition that appears at the very moment of its arising, without awaiting another result—that is its object. But there, it is not a means of knowledge, since it does not generate another result; rather, it is itself the result—such is the meaning. But with respect to another object, it is a means of knowledge—he says: 'another object.' He objects—'if.' If the word <s>pramāṇa</s> has a bhāva-formation [meaning 'the act of measuring'], then its meaning is the result, and it is not an instrument regarding its own object—since the activity toward that has already been accomplished by that which generated it. And there is no other object possible for it, because of over-extension—such is the sense. He resolves—'the result has been stated.' Although where the result is, that is its natural object, nevertheless where valid cognitions of abandonment etc. are to be generated by this means of knowledge, that too is its object through its activity—such is the sense.

Thinking that the word '<s>upamāna</s>' (analogy), like the words '<s>anumāna</s>' (inference) and '<s>śabda</s>' (verbal testimony), should be etymologically explained by its result, he objects—'proximity' (<s>sāmīpya</s>).
He resolves—'there is no contradiction.'

children.text: neyamupamānaśabdasya phalena nirūktiḥ, api tu pramāṇena nirūktiriti na vayāghāta ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: This etymology of the word '<s>upamāna</s>' is not by its result, but rather by its instrument (<s>pramāṇa</s>)—therefore there is no contradiction—this is the meaning.

children.text: yat khalu caitra, gāṃ badhāneti vākyamidamityanusandhānātmakaṃ smārtaṃ vijñānamupajāyate, tat padārthasmaraṇasahakāri viśiṣṭārthaviṣayaṃ vijñānaṃ prasūte, tacchābdra pramāṇam /
children.translated_text: When the sentence 'O <s>Caitra</s>, tie up the cow' gives rise to a memorial cognition (<s>smārta vijñāna</s>) of the nature of connecting [the words], that cognition, aided by the memory of word-meanings, produces a cognition having a qualified meaning as its object—that is <s>śābda pramāṇa</s> (verbal testimony as a means of valid knowledge).
Having stated the means of valid knowledge, he states its result—'the result is that very thing.'

children.text: yadā hyetat pramāṇaṃ tadā vākyārthavijñānaṃ phalam /
children.translated_text: When this is the means of valid knowledge, then the cognition of sentence-meaning is the result.

children.text: yadānumānavad vākyārthavijñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ tadā hānopādānādibuddhayaḥ phalamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: When, like inference, the cognition of sentence-meaning is the means of valid knowledge, then cognitions such as abandonment, acceptance, and the like are the result—this is the meaning.
<s>Śābda</s> <s>pramāṇa</s> (verbal testimony as a means of valid knowledge) is the cognition whose object is verbal [testimony].

children.text:
atra pratyakṣādīnāṃ kramoddeśaprayojanaṃ prati ekadeśimatamupanyasyati---kecit tviti /
pratyakṣaparā hi pramāṇāntarajanyāḥ pramitaya iti pratyakṣasya prādhānyam /
yadyapi kiñcidanumānamanumānādipūrvakamapi, tathāpi prāyeṇa pratyakṣapūrvakam, upamānaṃ tu pratyakṣapūrvakamapi śabdapūrvakamevetyasyānumānādapakarṣaḥ /
smaraṇasahakāritā cānumānasādṛśyamupamānasyāstītyanumānānantaramuddeśaḥ /
alpajñānādhīnaṃ ca bahujñānamityalpaviṣayapratyakṣādyuddeśebhyaḥ paro bahuviṣayaśabdoddeśa iti /
tadetat ekadeśimatam ekadeśyantaramatena dūṣayati--taccāyuktamityapara iti /
ākliṣṭo hi prathamaṃ mahāviṣayameva duravadhāraṇatvānnirūpayati, alpaviṣayaṃ tu kliṣṭo 'pi śaknoti nirūpayitum /
ato mahāviṣayatvaṃ prāthamya eva heturna caramatva ityarthaḥ /
anantaramataṃ dūṣayati--etacceti /
etāvatā kramamātraṃ bhavet, na tu tadviśeṣaniyama ityarthaḥ /
//
children.translated_text: Here, regarding the purpose of the sequential enumeration of perception and the rest, he presents the view of one side—'some, however.' For cognitions produced by other means of valid knowledge are dependent on perception—hence the primacy of perception. Although some inferences are preceded by inference and the like, still, generally they are preceded by perception. <s>Upamāna</s> (analogy), though preceded by perception, is necessarily preceded by verbal testimony—hence its lower rank compared to inference. And since analogy shares with inference the characteristic of being aided by memory, it is enumerated immediately after inference. And since knowledge of many things depends on knowledge of few things, the enumeration of <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony), which has many objects, comes after the enumeration of perception and the rest, which have few objects. He refutes this partial view with another partial view—'and that is improper, say others.' For one who is at ease first examines what has many objects, since it is difficult to determine, while even one who is strained can determine what has few objects. Therefore, having many objects is a reason for primacy, not for being last—this is the meaning. He refutes the latter view—'and this too.' By this much, there would be merely some sequence, but not a fixed particular sequence—this is the meaning.

children.text:
saṃprati vimarśapūrvakaṃ svābhibhatakramaniyamahetumavadhārayanneva pūrvaikadeśimatamapākaroti--tasmādanya iti /
vimarśanimittaṃ vipratipattimāha--pratyakṣaṃ pūrvaṃ prādhānyāt ityekaḥ /
mahāviṣayatvāccādau śabdopadeśa ityaparaḥ /
tatra mahāviṣayatvamanaikāntikaṃ sannāgamasyaiva pūrvopadeśaṃ gamayatītyāha--ubhayamiti /
pṛcchati--kathamiti /

children.translated_text: The answer—'even by perception.'
He states the doubt caused by the observation of the common property characterized as having many objects—'therein.'
He determines the fixed particular sequence by his own preferred reason—'of perception, this.'

children.text: yadyapi pramiteḥ pratyakṣaparatvena pratyakṣasya prādhānyam, tathāpi śāstre vyutpādyatvenānumānasyāpi tadastīti sādhāraṇatayā na heturiti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: Although perception has primacy because cognitions are dependent on perception, nevertheless inference too has such primacy by being what is to be taught in the <s>śāstra</s>—therefore, being common to both, it is not a [decisive] reason—this is the purport.

Now, having deliberated, while determining the reason for the fixed particular sequence according to his own view, he sets aside the former partial views—'therefore another.' He states the ground for deliberation, namely the disagreement—'perception is first, because of primacy,' says one; 'because of having many objects, verbal testimony should be taught first,' says another. Therein, the characteristic of having many objects, being non-exclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), when present, leads to the prior enumeration of scripture itself—he says: 'both.' He asks—'how?'

children.text:
syādetat /
vyavasthitaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ nānumānaviṣaye pravartate /
na cānumānam agṛhītasaṃbandhamudeti /
na ca saṃbandhagrahaḥ saṃbandhigrahamantareṇa /
na cānumānaviṣaye sāmānyarūpe saṃbandhini pratyarkṣa pravartate /
anumānāntareṇa tu grahaṇe 'navasthā /

children.translated_text: Therefore, because there is no causal basis, inference does not exist.

children.text: etena śabdopamāne api parāste, tayorapi saṃbandhasaṃvedanādhīnajanmatvāt /
children.translated_text: By this, <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) are also refuted, since they too depend on the cognition of the relation for their arising.

children.text: tasmāt nāpratyakṣaṃ pramāṇamiti vibhāgavacanamanupapannamiti śaṅkāmapanetuṃ vimarśapūrvakaṃ vicārayati sma bhārūyakāraḥ---kiṃ punaḥ pramāṇānīti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, with the doubt that 'since there is no non-perceptual means of valid knowledge, the statement of division is unjustified,' the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> investigates with deliberation—'what then are the means of valid knowledge?'
Having echoed this <s>bhāṣya</s>, he states the reason for the explanation—'what then are these?'

There might be this [objection]: perception, having a fixed domain, does not operate in the domain of inference. And inference does not arise without the relation having been grasped. And the grasping of the relation is not possible without grasping the relata. And perception does not operate regarding the general form that is the relatum in the domain of inference. And if it were grasped by another inference, there would be infinite regress.

children.text:
sā ceyaṃ pramitiḥ pratyakṣapareti bhāṣyam /
tadanubhāṣya hetumāha--seyamiti /
ākāṅkṣābhāvapratipādanāya pratītisvarūpaṃ kramaṃ cāha--yathāyamiti /
āhita utpāditaḥ pratyayo niścayo yasya, saṃsargopadhānaṃ varhi prati sa tathā /
sandigdhena hi niścayāya pravartitavyameva /
niścitastu viniścayāya pramāṇāntare pravartamānastadabhyarhitataraṃ manyate /
dhūmāṅgatveneti /
aṅgatvaṃ vyāpakatvam /
vyāpyaṃ punarvyāptikriyāyāṃ karmatvena pradhānam /
tadanena dhūmavyāpakatvopadhānena dhūmād gamyamāno bahniḥ parokṣa iti darśitam /
anupahitaprakāśasatu pratyakṣeṇāvyavahitavahnisvarūpaprakāśaḥ /
sa hi sākṣātkāra iti /
tāvadayaṃ pramātā sākāṅkṣo yāvadupadhānavyavahitaṃ svarūpamupalabhate /
upadhānānapekṣastu pratyakṣeṇāvyavahitaṃ sākṣād varhina viṣayīkṛtya nirākāṅkṣo bhavati /
dhūmāṅgatvena dhūmaviśeṣaṇatveneti kecit /
tattu prakṛtānupayogitayā ayuktamiti /
upasaṃharati--ataḥ pradhānamiti /
so 'yaṃ guṇapradhānabhāvo bhedāśrayo vyavasthāyāṃ nāsti, vyavasthitānāṃ pratyekamekatvāt /
tasmād vyavasthāyāṃ guṇapradhānabhāvo na cintya iti /
itiḥ sūtrasamāptau//3 //
children.translated_text: The <s>bhāṣya</s> states: 'and this cognition is dependent on perception.' Having echoed that, he states the reason—'this.' To show the absence of expectancy, he states the nature and the sequence of the cognition—'just as this.' 'One in whom the determination has been produced'—whose determination regarding the connection is [already established], he is so. For one who is in doubt must indeed proceed to ascertain. But one who has ascertained, when engaging another means of valid knowledge for further ascertainment, considers it more worthy. 'By virtue of being a part of smoke'—'part' means being a pervader (<s>vyāpaka</s>). The pervaded (<s>vyāpya</s>), however, is primary in the act of pervasion by being the object. By this, it is shown that fire, being cognized through the presentation of smoke-pervasion from smoke, is imperceptible. But for one whose cognition has not been presented [through such mediation], perception directly reveals the unmediated nature of fire itself. For that is direct apprehension (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>). The knower has expectancy only so long as he apprehends the nature mediated by presentation. But one who, without dependence on presentation, directly cognizes fire through perception without mediation, becomes free of expectancy. Some say: 'by virtue of being a part of smoke' means 'by virtue of being a qualifier of smoke.' But that is improper as being irrelevant to the topic at hand. He concludes—'therefore, primary.' This relationship of subordinate and primary, based on distinction, does not exist in the fixed domain, since each [means of knowledge] in its fixed domain is singular. Therefore, the subordinate-primary relationship should not be considered in regard to the fixed domain. The word '<s>iti</s>' marks the completion of the <s>sūtra</s>.
Thus ends the <s>Nyāyatrisūtrītātparyaṭīkā</s> (commentary on the purport of the three <s>Nyāya sūtras</s>).

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.4: Perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is the cognition that arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object, which is non-verbal, non-errant, and of the nature of determination.

children.text:
pratyakṣādipramāṇaviśeṣalakṣaṇānām arthākṣiptasāmānyalakṣaṇavibhāgoddeśahetutvena tadanantarābhidhānamityāha--atha vibhaktānāmiti /
tatra teṣu madhye prāthamyāt pratyakṣalakṣaṇam indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam ityādi sūtram /
asya tātparyamāha--sūtrārthaḥ sūtraprayojanam /
samānāsamānajātīyaviśeṣakatvam /
samānajātīyamanumānādi, asamānajātīyaṃ pratyakṣābhāsaprameyādi /
tebhyo viśeṣakatvaṃ viśeṣaḥ /
tadasya sūtrasya prayojanam /
yaḥ khalu kutaścid vyāmohāt samānāsamānajātīyavyāvṛttaṃ tadrūpaṃ na śakroti grahītum, so 'nena lakṣaṇena bodhyate /
evaṃlakṣaṇakaṃ pratyakṣamiti /

children.translated_text: Therefore, this <s>sūtra</s> has as its primary purpose the prescription of a definition, through the mere restatement of perception as already generally established and distinguished.

children.text: itastvavagatalakṣaṇaḥ tenaiva vivicya pratyakṣatattvaṃ gṛhṇātīti samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedaḥ sūtrārtha ukta iti /
children.translated_text: But from this, one who has understood the definition, by distinguishing through that very definition, grasps the reality of perception—thus the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> has been stated as the exclusion from similar and dissimilar kinds.

children.text: atra ca yaha ityadhyāhṛtya yattadonityābhisaṃbandhāt tat pratyakṣamiti pramāṇavāci pratyakṣapadra yojanīyam /
children.translated_text: And here, by supplying the word 'that which' and connecting it with 'that' through the invariable relation, the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' (perception) should be construed as denoting the means of valid knowledge—'that is perception.'

children.text: evaṃ ca jñānapramāṇyapakṣe 'pi yat tadviśeṣyajñānaṃ pratyakṣaphalaṃ liṅgaparāmarśo vā tadapīndriyārthasannikarṣotvannatvādyupetatvena bhavati pramāṇaviśeṣaṇamiti nāvyāpakatvaṃ lakṣaṇasyeti //
children.translated_text: And thus, even on the view that cognition is the means of valid knowledge, the specific cognition that is the result of perception, or the apprehension of the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), since these too possess the characteristic of arising from the contact of sense organ and object, serve as qualifiers of the means of valid knowledge—therefore there is no under-extension of the definition.

He says that the specific definitions of means of valid knowledge such as perception and the rest should be stated immediately after [the general definition], because the general definition and the division that are implied by the subject-matter serve as reasons for the enumeration—'now, of those that have been divided.' Among those, because of primacy, the definition of perception is [given first]: the <s>sūtra</s> beginning with 'arising from the contact of sense organ and object.' He states its purport—'the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>' is the purpose of the <s>sūtra</s>: the capacity to distinguish from similar and dissimilar kinds. The similar kind is inference and the rest; the dissimilar kind is semblances of perception, <s>prameya</s>, and the rest. The capacity to distinguish from these is the distinguishing feature. That is the purpose of this <s>sūtra</s>. One who, due to some confusion, cannot grasp the form that is distinguished from similar and dissimilar kinds, is informed by this definition: 'perception is that which has such characteristics.'

children.text:
sūtrapadārthaṃ pṛcchati---atheti /
uttaram--indriyeti /
sannikarṣagrahaṇalabhyaṃ prakārabhedaṃ parisaṃcaṣṭe--sannikarṣaḥ punariti /
punaḥśabdena saṃyogasamavāyapadopādānāt vyavacchinatti /
saṃyogapadopādāne hi na samavāyo labhyate, samavāyapadopādāne vā na saṃyogaḥ /
sannikarṣapadopādāne tvabhimatalābhaḥ /
arthagrahaṇenārthyamāṇatayā jñeyasvarūpyogyatā darśitā /
na cāsāvaṇvākāśādīnāmastīti satyapi saṃyogādau nāsāvarthasannikarṣa iti tadvyudāsaḥ /
utpannagrahaṇena ca sannikarṣasyotpādakatvaṃ sūcitam /
tataḥ satyapyarthasvarūpayogyatve saṃyuktasaṃyogāderanutpādakasya sannikarṣasya vyudāsaḥ /
anyathā kuḍyādisaṃyuktenendriyeṇa kuḍyādivyavahitasya tatsaṃyuktasya ghaṭādeḥ tatsamavetasya ca rūpāderapi grahaṇaprasaṅgaḥ /
na caitāvatā trividha eva sannikarṣaḥ saṃyogaḥ saṃyuktasamavāyaḥ samavāyaśceti sāṃpratam /
svatantravyāghātādanubhavavyāghātācca /
ye hi dravyaguṇakarmāśrayaṃ sāmānyātiriktaṃ sādṛśsayamarthānataraṃ rocayante, teṣāṃ kathaṃ rūpādibhedānāmanyonyasya sādṛśyaṃ pratyakṣaṃ bhavet ? na hi tadindriyeṇa saṃyuktam /
nāpīndriyasaṃyuktasamavetam /
tasmāt caturthaḥsaṃyuktasamavetasamavāyo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ /
itarathā svatantravyāghātaḥ, anubhavavyāghātaśca /
anubhūyante hi rūpagandhatvādayaḥ sāmānyaviśeṣā anugatāḥ, tāsu tāsu vyaktiṣu parasparavyāvṛttimatīṣu ete nānubhūyeran asati sannikarṣāntare /
yadi tu vaiyātyādāhuḥ nānubhūyanta eveti, tadā prativaktavyaṃ kutastyo 'yamanantāsu rūpagandhādivyaktiṣu rūpamiti vā gandha iti vā vyapadeśabhedaḥ? cākṣuṣatvādyupādhinibandhana iti cet--na, ananusaṃhitopādherūpahitapratyayāyogāt /

children.translated_text: Indeed, no one designates <s>Caitra</s> as 'one with a staff' without having apprehended the staff.
And the sense organs, being beyond the senses, do not experience the state of being objects of sense-organ perception.

children.text: tasmādastīndriyeṇa rūpatvādisāmānyānubhavo yannibandhanāḥ kāsucideva kecideva vyaktiṣu vyapadeśebhedā iti siddhaṃ sannikarṣāntaram /
children.translated_text: Therefore, there does exist the experience of universals such as color-ness etc. through the sense organ, which is the basis for certain particular designations being applied to certain particular instances only—thus an additional kind of contact is established.

children.text: viśeṣaṇabhāvena ca saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇaṃ samavetaviśeṣaṇa ca saṃgṛhītam //
children.translated_text: And in the mode of being a qualifier, 'qualifier-of-the-conjoined' and 'qualifier-of-the-inherent' are also included.

He asks about the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> terms—'now.' The answer—'sense organ' (<s>indriya</s>). He explains the varieties of modes obtainable from the mention of 'contact' (<s>sannikarṣa</s>)—'contact, then.' By the word 'then' (<s>punaḥ</s>) he distinguishes from the inclusion of the words 'conjunction' (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and 'inherence' (<s>samavāya</s>). For if the word 'conjunction' were used, inherence would not be obtained; or if 'inherence' were used, conjunction would not be obtained. But by using the word 'contact' (<s>sannikarṣa</s>), the intended meaning is obtained. By the mention of 'object' (<s>artha</s>), the fitness of the nature of the knowable as something to be known is shown. And since atoms, space (<s>ākāśa</s>), and the like do not possess this, even when conjunction and the rest exist, that is not 'contact with an object'—thus they are excluded. And by the mention of 'arising' (<s>utpanna</s>), the productive nature of the contact is indicated. Therefore, even when there is fitness of the object's nature, the contact of conjoined-conjunction and the like, which is non-productive, is excluded. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that through a sense organ conjoined with a wall etc., one would apprehend a pot etc. hidden behind the wall, and also the color etc. inherent in it. And it is not the case that by this much, contact is of only three kinds—conjunction, inherent-in-the-conjoined, and inherence—for that would be proper. Because of contradiction with the system itself and with experience. For those who accept a similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>) as something different from the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), as a separate category residing in substance, quality, and action—for them, how would the mutual similarity of specific colors and the like be perceptible? For it is not conjoined with the sense organ. Nor is it inherent in what is conjoined with the sense organ. Therefore, a fourth kind—'inherent-in-the-conjoined-inherent' (<s>saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya</s>)—must be accepted. Otherwise there is contradiction with the system, and contradiction with experience. For universals and particulars such as color-ness and odor-ness are experienced as pervading in those various instances that are mutually distinguished—these would not be experienced in the absence of an additional kind of contact. But if some say due to misinterpretation that they are simply not experienced, then they should be asked: whence comes this differentiation of designation as 'color' or 'odor' among the infinite instances of color, odor, etc.? If one says it is based on the limiting condition of being apprehended by the eye etc.—no, because a cognition conditioned by an unapprehended condition is impossible.

children.text:
yasyendriyeṇa yādṛśaḥ sannikarṣaḥ tādṛśaṃ tatra darśayati--tatra cakṣuriti /
śabdassya ākāśaguṇatvam /
karṇaśaṣkulyavacchinnasya nabhobhāgasya śrotratvam /
ādyasyaiva śabdasya saṃyogavibhāgayonijatvam /
santānena śrotre samutpādaḥ samavāya ityādi dvitīye nipuṇataramupapādayiṣyate /
avayavāvayavinau guṇaguṇinau kriyākriyāvantau jātijātimantau ca mithaḥ saṃbaddhāvanubhūtete /
nānyathā tantuṣu paṭa iti ca, śuklaḥ paṭa iti ca, paṭaḥ spandate iti ca, paṭo dravyamiti ca buddhivyapadeśau syātām /
śuklaḥ paṭa ityādi sāmānādhikaraṇyajñānaṃ na tu saṃbandhijñānamiti cet? kiṃ punaridaṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyam? tādātmyamiti cet--na, dvitīyabuddhivyapadeśayoḥ paunaruktyāt /
apaunarūktyaṃ cābhimanyante pratipattāraḥ, yadanyataradupalabhyānyad bubhutsante /
na caikaṃ vastu dvyātmakamiti yuktam /
bhedādhiṣṭhānasya tannāntarīyakasya dvitvasyaikātmani virodhenāsaṃbhavāt /
tasmād bhinne eva vastunī saṃbaddhe sāmānādhikaraṇyena bhāsete, asaṃbandhe gauraśva itivat tadanupapatteḥ /
saṃbandhe 'pi kuṇḍe dadhītivadvaiyadhikaraṇyaprasaṅga iti cet--na, śabdavṛttibhedena saṃbandhābhede 'pi sāmānādhikaraṇyavaiyadhikaraṇyavyavasthāpanāt /
na hi jātu dadhiśabdaḥ kuṇḍe vartate kuṇḍaśabdo vā dadhni /
vartante tu surabhimadharaśuklādiśabdāḥ svābhidheyaṃ nimittīkṛtya paṭādiṣu, evaṃ paṭādiśabdā api jātyādi nimittīkṛtya dravye pravartante iti sāmānādhikaraṇyam /
tena sāmānādhikaraṇye 'pi pravṛttinimittānāṃ naikātmyaṃ parasparam /
nāpi dravyeṇa, kiṃ tu taistainvitamekaṃ dravyaṃ pratīyate /
śabdānāṃ tu tatraikasmin dravye pravṛtteḥ tadvācyānāmaikātmyabhramaḥ /
ayutasiddhyā tu kuṇḍe dadhītivat na sphuṭataro vivekaprakāśaḥ /
tadevamasti saṃbaddhānubhavaḥ, na cāsau saṃbaddhānubhavaṃ vineti saṃbandho 'nubhūyate, sa cāyutasiddhyādisaṃpattyā samavāyaḥ, na cāsyānyaḥ samavāyaḥ, avasthānāt /
na cendriyeṇāsya saṃyogaḥ adravyatvāt /
na cāsaṃbaddhasya grahaṇam, indriyāṇāṃ prāpyakāritvasamarthanāt /
tasmāt viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvaḥ pariśiṣyate /

children.translated_text: But this qualifier-qualified relation is seen elsewhere as preceded by another relation.

children.text: tat kimatra saṃbandhāntaraṃ kalpyatām? tathā cānavasthā ityuktam /
children.translated_text: Should then another relation be postulated here? And thus there would be an infinite regress — this has been said.
And there is no apprehension of what is not connected with the sense organ.

children.text: tasmād vinā saṃbandhāntaraṃ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva eṣitavya iti siddham //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the qualifier-qualified relation is to be sought without another relation — this is established.

He shows the kind of contact each sense organ has with its object — 'there, the eye.' Sound has the nature of being a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>). The portion of space delimited by the cavity of the ear is the organ of hearing (<s>śrotra</s>). The first sound itself is produced through conjunction and disjunction. Its arising in the organ of hearing through a series [of sound-waves] constitutes inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) — this and more will be established more precisely in the second [section]. Part and whole, quality and quality-bearer, action and action-possessor, universal and universal-possessor are experienced as mutually related. Otherwise, the cognitions and designations 'the cloth is in the threads,' 'the cloth is white,' 'the cloth moves,' and 'the cloth is a substance' would not be possible. If one objects that 'the cloth is white' and the like constitute knowledge of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) but not knowledge of a relation — then what is this co-referentiality? If one says it is identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) — no, because there would be redundancy in the second cognition and designation. And cognizers consider there to be non-redundancy, since having apprehended one thing, they desire to know the other. Nor is it proper that a single entity has a dual nature. For the duality that is the basis of difference and inseparable from it is impossible in a single nature, due to contradiction. Therefore, it is only two distinct entities, when related, that appear through co-referentiality; without a relation, it would be untenable, like 'the cow [is] a horse.' If one objects that even with a relation, there would be the undesirable consequence of different-substratum reference (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>), as in 'yogurt in the pot' — no, because even without a difference in relation, co-referentiality and different-substratum reference are established through a difference in the mode of word-application (<s>śabdavṛttibheda</s>). For the word 'yogurt' never applies to the pot, nor the word 'pot' to the yogurt. But words like 'fragrant,' 'sweet,' 'white,' and the like apply to cloths and such by taking their own designated meaning as the basis; similarly, words like 'cloth' also apply to a substance by taking universal and the like as their basis — this is co-referentiality. Therefore, even in co-referentiality, the bases of word-application are not identical with each other. Nor are they identical with the substance; rather, a single substance is cognized as endowed with all of them. But because the words apply to that single substance, there is the illusion of identity among what they denote. Due to inseparable existence (<s>ayutasiddhi</s>), however, as in 'yogurt in the pot,' there is no clear manifestation of discrimination. Thus, there is the experience of related things, and that experience itself — which cannot exist without the experience of relation — is the experience of relation. That, by virtue of the conditions of inseparable existence and the like, is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). And there is no other inherence of this [inherence], due to its being self-established. Nor is there conjunction of it with the sense organ, since it is not a substance. And there is no apprehension of what is not related [to the sense organ], because the sense organs are established as operating by contact. Therefore, the qualifier-qualified relation alone remains.

children.text:
evamabhāve 'pi yadindriyasaṃyuktaṃ vā yadvendriyasamavetu yathā bhūtale ghaṭo nāstīti vā nāstyakāre 'nudāttasvara iti vā tasya saṃyuktasya vā viśeṣaṇabhāvena, samavetasya viśeṣaṇabhāvena cendriyapratyāsattyā grahaṇam /
na ca bhūtalādirūpameva ghaṭābhāvo nārthāntaramiti sāṃpratam, satyapi ghaṭādau bhūtalasya bhāvāt /
na ca kaivalyaṃ tasya dharmo ghaṭabhāvavirodhī ghaṭābhāvādanyaḥ /
na ca dṛśye ghaṭādau bhūtalopalambhaḥ kaivalyamabhāvavyavahāraheturiti yuktam /
evaṃ hi ghaṭasaṃsṛṣṭabhūtalagraho 'pi kaivalyamiti ghaṭābhāvavyavahāraṃ pravartayet /
na hyadṛśyo ghaṭastadānīṃ dṛśyamānaḥ /
dṛśye 'nupalabhyamāna iti tu viśeṣaṇe kimaparāddhamupalabhyābhāvena yena tadapākaraṇāyopalambhābhāvo 'bhyupeyate? tasmāt sadivāsadapi tattvamabhyupeyam /
tacca pratyakṣamakṣavyāpāre sati tatpratyayāt /
na ca pratiyogismaraṇavyavahita indriyārthasannikarṣo nālamabhāvadhiyamupajanayitumiti sāṃpratamityagra darśayiṣyāmaḥ /
savikalpakassa pratyakṣatvasiddhau yathā śabdasmaraṇapūrvagṛhītapiṇḍānusandhānādayo nendriyavyāpāraṃ vyavadadhatīti, na ca śabdasmaraṇādīnāmanuyogitā, bhūtalavikalpaṃ pratyaṅgatvāt, svāṅgamavyavadhāyakamiti nyāyāt, ghaṭasya tu pratiyogiteti sāṃpratam /
kasya punaḥ pratiyogī ghaṭaḥ? tadabhāvasyeti ced bhavatu /
ghaṭābhāvānubhavasya tu ghaṭasmaraṇaṃ heturiti na pratiyogi, kiṃ tvanuyogyeva /
nanu svarūpamātraṃ dṛṣṭaṃ veśmādyarthaṃ smaranneva bahirnitaśrcaitro yadā pṛcchyate kenacit--vayasya, tava gṛhe tadā kimāsīt maitra iti ? sa caitraḥ pratiyogismaraṇavirahāt pūrvamapratipannamaitrābhāvo 'pi tatpraśnajanitamaitrasmṛtiḥ kṣaṇaṃ dhyātva tadabhāvamavagamyāha, mitra, tatra nāsīt maitra iti /
tadīyamasatīndriyārthasannikarṣe 'bhāvabuddhirbhavantī pratyakṣādyatiriktamabhāvākhyaṃ pramāṇa vyavasthāpayatīti /
naitat, saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇalakṣaṇena manaḥsannikarṣeṇa smartavyasya smaraṇābhāvaṃ maitrasya gṛhītvā tena liṅgena tadabhāvasya tadānīmanumānāt /
tathā hi tadgehaṃ tadā maitrābhāvavat
jñānārhasya maitrasyājñāne gehasya jñāyamānatvāt /
yad yasya jñānārhasyājñāne jñāyate tat tadabhā vavat /
yathā ghaṭabhāvavad bhūtalam /
tathā ca geham /

children.translated_text: Therefore it is so.

children.text: na ca yat kadācidānumānikaṃ tenenidrayagamyena na bhavitavyam, pramāṇasaṃplavavyavasthāpanāt /
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that what is sometimes known through inference can never be known through the senses, since the coordination of means of valid knowledge is established.
Therefore, absence (<s>abhāva</s>) is an object of the senses through being a qualifier, together with [the substrate].

He states the purpose of adopting the word '<s>sannikarṣa</s>' (contact/proximity) instead of the words '<s>saṃyoga</s>' (conjunction) and '<s>samavāya</s>' (inherence) — 'this word <s>sannikarṣa</s>.'

Thus, even in the case of absence (<s>abhāva</s>), whatever is conjoined with the sense organ, or whatever is in inherence with the sense organ — as when a pot does not exist on the ground surface, or the <s>anudātta</s> (grave accent) does not exist in the <s>nākāra</s> (the letter 'na') — by virtue of the qualifier-relation of what is conjoined, or by virtue of the qualifier-relation of what is in inherence, there is apprehension through proximity to the sense organ. And it is not proper that the ground surface itself is the absence of the pot and not a separate entity, because the ground surface exists even when the pot is present. Nor is the aloneness [of the ground surface] its property, contradicting the presence of the pot, something other than the absence of the pot. And it is not proper that the perception of the ground surface when the pot and the like are visible, being [mere] aloneness, is the cause of the usage of absence. For thus, even the apprehension of the ground surface in contact with the pot, being aloneness [in some respect], would occasion the usage of absence of the pot. For the pot, not visible at that time, is not being seen. But the qualifier 'not perceived though perceptible' — what fault does the absence of perception commit that the absence of perception itself must be accepted in order to remove it? Therefore, the non-existent too, like the existent, must be accepted as a reality. And that is perceptible, because of being a cognition arising when the sense organ operates. And it is not the case that the sense-object contact intervened by the recollection of the counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogi</s>) is unable to generate the cognition of absence — this we shall show later. In establishing the perceptual nature of the determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>), just as the recollection of the word, the recognition of a previously apprehended object, and the like do not obstruct the operation of the sense organ, and just as the recollection of the word and the like are not to be questioned — because with respect to the determinate cognition of the ground surface, they are subsidiary parts, and what is subsidiary does not obstruct — by the principle [that parts do not obstruct the whole], but the pot is indeed a counter-correlate — this is appropriate. Of what is the pot the counter-correlate? If of its absence — so be it. But the recollection of the pot is a cause of the experience of the absence of the pot; it is not a counter-correlate, but rather an ancillary factor. Now, when <s>Caitra</s>, who has seen only the bare form of a house and the like, and who remembers [only] its general purpose, having gone outside, is asked by someone — 'friend, was <s>Maitra</s> in your house at that time?' — that <s>Caitra</s>, not having ascertained the absence of <s>Maitra</s> earlier due to the lack of recollection of the counter-correlate, now, prompted by the question to recall <s>Maitra</s>, reflects for a moment, ascertains his absence, and says — 'friend, <s>Maitra</s> was not there.' His cognition of absence, arising in the absence of sense-object contact, would establish an additional means of valid knowledge called <s>abhāva</s> (absence), different from perception and the like — this is the objection. This is not so; by the mental contact characterized by a conjoined-qualifier, having grasped the absence of recollection of <s>Maitra</s> who should be remembered, that inferential mark leads to the inference of his absence at that time. Thus: that house at that time was characterized by the absence of <s>Maitra</s>, because of the non-cognition of <s>Maitra</s> who was fit to be cognized — the house being cognized [while he was not]. Whatever, when something fit to be known is not known, is itself known — that is characterized by the absence of that thing. Just as the ground surface [is characterized by] the presence of the pot. Similarly the house.

children.text:
tadanena prabandhena indriyasyārthena sannikarṣād yadutpadyate jñānaṃ tat pratyakṣamiti bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
saṃprati na tarhīti codyabhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---yadīndriyārtheti /
pratyakṣajñānakāraṇābhidhānapravṛttestadekadeśaṃ vadannakuśalaḥ sūtrakāraḥ syādityarthaḥ /
kāraṇāntarāṇi darśayati--tadyatheti /
viṣayasaṃyoti cakṣurālokaśca /
tatsthaṃ rūpam /
ātmīyena hi rūpeṇālokacakṣuṣī dravyaṃ darśayata iti sthitiḥ /
mahattvaṃ vā anekadravyavattvaṃ vā, anekadravyā avayavāḥ, tadvattvamavayavino mahata eva na dvyaṇukasya, tasmādanyonyanirapekṣatvaṃ mahattvānekadravyavattvayoriti vikalpa eva nyāyya iti /
satyapyevaṃlakṣaṇakatve cukṣuravayavinastaijasasya na cākṣuṣatvamityata uktam--upalabdhikalaḥ saṃskāra iti /
dharmādharmanimitta ubhdavasamākhyātaḥ saṃskāraḥ upalabdhiphalaḥ /
na cāsau cakṣuṣi, tasyādṛṣṭavaśenānudbhūtarūpasparśatvādityarthaḥ /
pariharati--na vaktavyāni iti /
pratyakṣalakṣaṇakaraṇapravṛtto hi sūtrakāraḥ tadeva brūyāt yadasyāsādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇam /
na tu sadapi sādhāraṇamasya kāraṇam /
na hi tat tasya lakṣaṇamativyāpterityarthaḥ /
tadanena nedam ityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ cet pratyakṣalakṣaṇāyopādeyaṃ hanta, anyadapyasyāsādhāraṇamasti kāraṇamiti tadapyupādeyamiti codayati--indriyamanaḥ- saṃyogastarhīti /
tadanena manasastarhītyasya bhāṣyasyārtha ukto veditavyaḥ /
pariharati-na, anenaiva indriyārthasannikarṣeṇaiva /
tasya---indriyamanaḥsannikarṣasya uktatvāt /
taduktisādhyaṃ yat tat tenaiva kṛtam /
tatsādhyaṃ tvindriyamanaḥsannikarṣo na śaknoti sādhayitum /
na ca sukhādijñāne mānase astīndriyamanaḥsannikarṣaḥ /
indriyārthasannikarṣastu sarvavyāpakaḥ /

children.translated_text: For it will be stated that the mind is a sense organ.
And that pleasure and the like are objects is already established.
Now, having accepted the all-pervasiveness [of the term 'contact of sense organ with object'], he states another response — 'sense organ and object.'

children.text: yadyapīndriyamanaḥsannikarṣe 'pīndriyam asti pratyakṣajñānasya viśeṣakam indriyeṇa vyapadeśādindriyajñānamiti, tathāpi manasā vyapadeśāmāvāt manasastatrāviśeṣakatvam indriyārthasannikarṣe tūbhayamapi viśeṣakam, ubhābhyāṃ pratyakṣajñānasya vyapadeśādityayamasyendriyamanaḥsannikarṣādviśeṣa iti //
children.translated_text: Although in the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind too there is a sense organ that is a distinguishing factor of perceptual knowledge — since it is designated by the sense organ as 'sense-knowledge' — nevertheless, because there is no designation by the mind, the mind is not a distinguishing factor there. But in the contact of the sense organ with the object, both are distinguishing factors, because perceptual knowledge is designated by both. This is the difference of this [formulation] from 'conjunction of sense organ and mind.'

By this extended discussion, the <s>bhāṣya</s> stating 'the cognition that arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object is perception' has been explained. Now he explains the objection-<s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'then it is not so' — 'if the sense organ and the object.' The meaning is: the <s>Sūtrakāra</s>, while engaged in stating the causes of perceptual knowledge, if he mentions only a part of them, would be unskilled. He shows the other causes — 'namely.' The eye conjoined with the object, and light. Form situated in that [object]. For it is established that through its own form, light and the eye make the substance visible. Or magnitude — or the property of having multiple substances; the multiple substances are the parts, and the possessor of them is the whole which is large alone, not the dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>). Therefore, magnitude and having multiple substances being independent of each other, the alternative is proper. Even when the definition is thus, the fact that the fire-composite, which is a luminous whole, is not an object of vision — therefore it is said — 'the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that enables perception.' The impression, whose origin is described as due to <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, has perception as its result. And that is not in the eye, because due to the unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), its form and touch are unmanifest — this is the meaning. He responds — 'they need not be stated.' For the <s>Sūtrakāra</s>, engaged in defining perception, should state only what is the uncommon cause of it. But even if it exists, a common cause should not [be stated]. For that is not a defining characteristic, due to over-extension — this is the meaning. By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'this is not' and so on has been explained. If the uncommon cause is to be adopted for the definition of perception, well then, there is also another uncommon cause — he objects: 'then the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind.' By this, the meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'then of the mind' should be understood as having been stated. He responds — 'no, by this very contact of the sense organ with the object.' Because that — the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind — has already been stated. What is accomplishable by stating that has already been accomplished by this. But what is accomplishable by that — the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind cannot accomplish. And in mental cognition of pleasure and the like, there is no conjunction of [external] sense organ and mind. But the contact of the sense organ with the object is all-pervading.

children.text:
codayati--yadā tviti /
tuśabdaḥ pūrvapakṣaṃ vyāvartayati /
yu/jānasya hi yogino yadātmamanaḥsayogādātmani buddhayo bhavanti tāḥ khalvātmanā vyapadiśyante ātmabuddhaya iti /
manasā ca vyapadiśyante manobuddhaya iti /
tasmādubhābhyāṃ vyapadeśād ubhayorviśeṣakatvamitīndriyārthasannikarṣavadātmamanaḥsannikarṣo vaktavya ityarthaḥ /
pariharati--yacceti /
co 'vadhāraṇe /
yadevāsādhāraṇaṃ tad vyapadeśabhāgbhavati, kāraṇatvena jñānaṃ vyapadiśyate ityarthaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati---yathā cukṣuṣā indriyatvena jñānaṃ vyapadiśyate cākṣuṣamiti, tathā manasāpīndriyatvena vyapadiśyate jñānaṃ mānasamiti /
children.translated_text: This is what has been stated: just as cognition is designated by the eye as a sense organ — 'visual' (<s>cākṣuṣa</s>) — so too cognition is designated by the mind as a sense organ — 'mental' (<s>mānasa</s>).

children.text: evaṃ yathā rūpeṇārthena vyapadiśyate jñānaṃ rūpajñānamiti, tathā ātmanāpyarthena vyapadiśyate ātmajñānamiti, tatra cāsādhāraṇatvameva tayoḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, just as cognition is designated by form as an object — 'cognition of form' — so too cognition is designated by the self as an object — 'cognition of the self.' And therein, it is precisely the uncommonness of these two [that is relevant].

children.text: yatra tvindriyāntaramevāsādhāraṇam, liṅgādi vā tatra cātmā nārtho 'pi tu pramātaiva /
children.translated_text: But where another sense organ itself is the uncommon factor, or an inferential mark and the like, there the self is not an object but merely the cognizer.

children.text: yathā rūpādijñāne 'numānādijñāne vā na tatra jñānaṃ mānasamiti vā ātmajñānamiti vā vyapadeśaḥ sa kasya hetāḥ, tayoḥ sādhāraṇyāt? ātmamanaḥsannikarṣastvindriyārthasannikarṣeṇa saṃgṛhīto na tvindriyārthasannikarṣasyaiṣa saṃgrāhako 'vyāpakatvāditi //
children.translated_text: Just as in the cognition of form and the like, or in inferential cognition and the like, the designation 'mental' or 'self-cognition' does not apply there — for what reason? Because of the commonness of the two [i.e., self and mind being common to all cognitions]. But the conjunction of the self and the mind is included within the contact of the sense organ with the object; however, the contact of the sense organ with the object cannot be included by that, because of its non-pervasiveness.

He objects — 'but when.' The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) distinguishes the prior view. For when a <s>yogin</s> (practitioner) who is in <s>yoga</s> has cognitions of the self through the conjunction of the self and the mind, those are designated by the self as 'self-cognitions.' And they are designated by the mind as 'mental cognitions.' Therefore, since there is designation by both, both would be distinguishing factors — and thus, just as in the contact of the sense organ with the object, the conjunction of the self and the mind should be stated — this is the meaning. He responds — 'that which.' The particle 'ca' is in the sense of emphasis (<s>avadhāraṇa</s>). Only what is uncommon becomes the basis of designation; that is, cognition is designated by its cause — this is the meaning.

children.text:
ekadeśinaḥ parīhāramupanyasyati--indriyamanaḥsaṃyogasya vā agrahaṇaṃ bhede 'bhedāt /
yadā hi nāgarayoṣitaḥ kutūhalāt praṇihitamanaso vikasitaniḥspandanayanotpalāḥ saudhamālāgavākṣakairavanipatiṃ sabalavāhanamaticiraparāvṛttaṃ gopureṇa niviśamānamālokayanti, tadā khlvāsāmekenaivendriyamanaḥsaṃyogena kramavadanekendriyārthasannikarṣasahakāriṇā bhinnāni kramavanti hāstikāśvīyādipratyakṣajñānāni jāyante /
tadidamāha--yasmād iti /
codayati--yadīti /
yadā hi mandaṃ gacchati gavi dūrataḥ saṃyuktasamavāyenendriyārthasannikarṣeṇa śuklo gaurityajñāsīt, atha pratyāsīdan gacchatītyapi vijānāti tenaiva saṃyuktasamavāyena sannikarṣeṇa, tena pratyakṣajñānasya śukla iti ca gacchatīti ca bhede 'pi indriyārthasannikarṣo na bhidyate /
tasmādindriyārthasannikarṣe tulyatvādindriyamanaḥsaṃyogo 'pi tatra vaktavya ityarthaḥ /
pariharati--na vaktavyaḥ /
kutaḥ--uktottaratvāditi /
tadvibhajate--ukteti /
nanu bhavatūktamuttaraṃ bhede 'bhedādityasyākṣepaḥ samādhātavyaḥ ityata āha--anabhyupagamācca /
ekadeśimatametadasmābhirnābhyupeyate /
tasmānna samādheyam ityarthaḥ /
tat kimidānīṃ bhidyamānasya pratyakṣajñānasya nāyaṃ bhidyata iti samānatvānnokta iti bhāṣyam anupapannameva? netyāha--indriyamanaḥsaṃyogasya cāgrahaṇaṃ samānatvāt /
pṛcchati--keneti /
uttaram"--ātmamana iti /
punaḥ pṛcchati--kiṃ punaḥ samānatvam, uttaram--vyapadeśābhāva ityuktam /
tena bhāṣyasyāyamarthaḥ /
pratyakṣajñānasya rūpajñānasya rūpajñānamiti vā cakṣurvijñānamiti vā vyapadeśena bhidyamānasya ātmamanaḥsaṃyoga iva ayam indriyamanaḥsaṃyogo na bhidyate /
evaṃ hi sa bhidyate, yadi svasaṃbandhivācakena vyapadeśena svamanyato vyāvartyate, na viśeṣaṇena viśiṣṭaṃ jñānamapyanyato vyāvartayet /
children.translated_text: For it would differ only if, through a designation expressing its own relatum, it distinguished itself from others; a qualifier would not distinguish even qualified cognition from others.

children.text: na tvasti indriyamanaḥsannikarṣādhārābhyāmindriyamanobhyāṃ pratyekamasya vyapadeśo yathendriyārthasannikarṣādhārābhyāṃ indriyārthābhyāṃ vyapadeśo rūpajñānamiti cakṣurjñānamiti vā /
children.translated_text: But there is no designation of this [contact of sense organ and mind] individually through the sense organ and the mind, which are the substrata of the contact of sense organ and mind, as there is a designation through the sense organ and the object, which are the substrata of the sense-object contact, such as 'form-cognition' or 'visual cognition.'
Therefore, the absence of designation constitutes the sameness of the contact of sense organ and mind with the contact of self and mind.
Therefore, because of sameness, it was not stated.

He presents the partial advocate's resolution—'or the non-apprehension of the contact between the sense organ and the mind constitutes non-difference amid difference.'
For when the city women, with minds intently focused out of curiosity, with wide-open unblinking lotus-eyes, gaze from the latticed windows of the upper terraces at the king entering through the gate with his army and vehicles after a long absence, then indeed with a single contact of the sense organ and the mind—sequential yet aided by a single sense-object contact—distinct and sequential perceptual cognitions of elephants, horses, and the like arise.
This is what is stated—'because.'
He objects—'if.'
For when a cow is moving slowly, from a distance, through the contact of conjunction-inherence (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>) between sense organ and object, one knew 'it is white cow,' and then as it approaches, one also cognizes 'it is moving' through that same conjunction-inherence contact—thus even though the perceptual cognitions 'white' and 'moving' are different, the sense-object contact does not differ.
Therefore, since the sense-object contact is the same, the contact of the sense organ and the mind should also be stated [as invariant]—this is the meaning.
He resolves—'it need not be stated.'
Why?—'because the answer has already been given.'
He analyzes that—'stated.'
But granted that the answer 'non-difference amid difference' has been stated; the objection must still be resolved—therefore he says—'and because of non-acceptance.'
This partial view is not accepted by us.
Therefore it need not be resolved—this is the meaning.
Then is the <s>bhāṣya</s> statement that 'this [contact of sense organ and mind] does not differ, due to sameness, while perceptual cognition differs' simply unjustified? No—he says: 'and the non-apprehension of the contact of the sense organ and the mind is due to sameness.'
He asks—'with what?'
The answer—'with the contact of self and mind (<s>ātma-manas</s>).'
He asks again—'what then is the sameness?' The answer—'absence of designation,' it has been said.
Thus the meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s> is:
Of perceptual cognition—of form-cognition—which differs through designations such as 'form-cognition' or 'visual cognition,' the contact of the sense organ and the mind does not differ, just like the contact of self and mind.

children.text:
prākarāntaraṃ samānatve darśayati--atīndriyādhāratā veti /
lakṣaṇaṃ hi prasiddhaṃ bhavati yathā dhūmo vahneḥ na cātīndriyadvayādhārasannikarṣastathā prasiddho yathendriyārthasannikarṣo 'rthasya saṃbandhina ekasnaya prasiddhatvāt, indriyamanasostu dvayoratīndriyatvāt /
ātmā tu yadyapi yu/jānasya śarīrādyatiriktaḥ pratyakṣaḥ, tathāpyasmadādīnāṃ na tathetyatīndriya uktaḥ /
tadanenātīndriyādhāratvaṃ svarūpeṇoktvā tadevaṃ viṣayāvṛttitvamanovṛttitvābhyām atīndriyādhāratvaṃ sāmānyamāha--viṣayāvṛttitvaṃ veti /
children.translated_text: Having thus stated the supersensory substrate nature in its own form, he states the commonality of the supersensory substrate nature through not operating on objects and operating through the mind—'or because of not operating on objects.'

children.text: upasaṃharati--tasmāditi samānatvāditi bhāṣyokto hetuḥ, caritārthatvāditi svoktaḥ //
children.translated_text: He concludes—'therefore.' 'Because of sameness' is the reason stated in the <s>bhāṣya</s>; 'because of having served its purpose' is his own stated reason.

He shows another reason for the sameness—'or because of having a supersensory substrate.'
For a <s>lakṣaṇa</s> (inferential mark) must be well-known, as smoke is for fire; but the contact of two supersensory substrata is not as well-known as the sense-object contact, because only one of the relata of the sense-object contact—namely the object—is well-known, whereas both the sense organ and the mind are supersensory.
And although the self (<s>ātman</s>) is perceptible for a <s>yogin</s> as distinct from body and the like, nevertheless for ordinary people like us it is not so—hence it is called supersensory.

children.text:
ākṣipati--indriyārthasannikarṣotpannamityayuktamiti /
sāntaragrahaṇāditi hetuṃ vibhajate--viprakṛṣṭeti /
nanu nārtho viprakṛṣṭaḥ, cakṣuṣastatra prāpterityata āha--na tu cakṣuṣa iti /
kasmādityata āha--bhūtaviśeṣasyeti /
bāhyo bhūtaviśeṣa ālokaḥ /
tasya prasāda indriyāvyavadhāyakatvam kuḍyādibhyo viśeṣaḥ yaḥ khalu kācābhrapaṭalādiṣu svaccheṣu samasti /
syādetat /
asti kṛṣṇasāralakṣaṇo bhūviśeṣaḥ prasannāndhasyāpi, atastasyāpi rūpopalabdhiḥ syāditpata āha--tattṛṣṇāpūrvaketi /
rūpopabhogatṛṣṇā hi tatsādhanaṃ kṛṣṇasāramapi viṣayīkaroti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati--bhūtaviśeṣaḥ karmāpekṣo rūpaṃ caṣṭa iti cakṣurityucyate /
karmakṣāyāt tu prasannāndhasya na rūpaṃ caṣṭa iti na cakṣuḥ /
children.translated_text: But for a person born blind, whose <s>karma</s> is exhausted, it does not 'show' form—hence it is not an eye.
Let the eyeball itself be the eye—what follows from this?—he says: 'and not...'
The meaning is: for the eyeball, being severed, is directly experienced [as separate from seeing].
Thus, the apprehension of what is at a distance has been stated as the reason for the non-contact theory (<s>aprāpyakāritva</s>).

He raises an objection—'it is improper to say that [perceptual cognition] arises from the contact of sense organ and object.'
He analyzes the reason 'because of apprehending what is at a distance'—'distant.'
But is it not the case that the object is not distant, since the eye reaches there?—therefore he says—'but not the eye.'
Why?—therefore he says—'because of a particular element.'
The external particular element is light (<s>āloka</s>).
Its transparency (<s>prasāda</s>) is its distinguishing feature from walls and the like, that is, the quality of not obstructing the sense organ—which indeed exists in clear things like glass, mica-sheets, and the like.
It may be objected:
There is a particular element in the form of the dark pupil (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>) even for a person born blind who has clear [eyes]—so even that person should perceive form. To this he says—'preceded by the craving for that.'
For the craving for the enjoyment of form makes even its instrument, the dark pupil, its object.
What is stated amounts to this: a particular element that is dependent on <s>karma</s> 'shows' (<s>caṣṭe</s>) form—hence it is called 'eye' (<s>cakṣus</s>).

children.text:
kecit tu sāntaramiti grahaṇaviśeṣaṇaṃ hentu bruvate, tanmatamupanyasyati---apare tviti /
sādhyaviparyayādasya vyatirekaṃ darśayati--na hi prāpyakāriṣviti pakṣadharmatāmāha--dṛṣṭaṃ tviti /
yaccoktamaprāpyakāritve sādhanaṃ pṛthutaragrahaṇāditi, tadvibhajate--pṛthutareti /
dvyāśrayo hi saṃyogo 'lpameva saṃyoginamanurudhyate, na mahāntam /
na jātu rathādisaṃyogā nabho vyaśnuvate, mā bhūt sarvatra rathādīnāṃ tatsaṃyogādīnāṃ copalabdhiḥ /
tena yāvanmātra rāṣṭravanādergolakena vyāptaṃ tāvanmātrasya grahaṇaprasaṅgaḥ /
hetvantaramāha--digiti /
asyāpi vyatirekamukhena gamakatvaṃ darśayati---yadi prāpyakārīti /
aparamapi hetumāha---sannikṛṣṭeti /
