yadyapi gatikṣaṇānāṃ pratyekaṃ spāśrayasya deśāntaravibhāgasaṃyogopajananaṃ prati kṣipratayā na viśeṣaḥ /
svāśrayapratyāsattau cāviśeṣaḥ tathāpyā cāpādānavibhāgāt ā ca prāpanīyadeśaprāpterantarālavartī yāvān gatikṣaṇapracayaḥ pūrvāparībhūto gatiriha vivakṣitaḥ /
tasya sāntaratvaṃ mandatvaṃ vilambaḥ nairantaryaṃ tu pāṭavaṃ kṣipratā /
tāmimāṃ gatimabhindad nairantaryeṇa kurvadapi sannikṛṣṭamāśu prāpnoti /
na viprakṛṣṭena tulyakālam, kiṃ tu viprakṛṣṭaṃ cireṇeti /
yathoktaṃ digrāgena--
sāntaragrahaṇaṃ na syāt prāptau jñāne 'dhikasya ca /
bahirvartitvādindriyasyopapannaṃ sāntaragrahaṇamiti cet?

children.translated_text: Therefore it has been said—
The sense organ does not [exist] outside the body-seat; rather, the sense organ is in the body-seat itself.
Why?
Because of medical treatment and such practices.

But some state '<s>sāntara</s>' (with an intervening gap) as a qualifier of apprehension and call that the reason. He presents their view—'others however.'
He shows the negative concomitance of this through the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s>—'for in the case of contact-operating [senses], this is not so.' He states the property of the subject—'but it is observed.'
Regarding what was stated as the proof for non-contact operation—'because of apprehending what is larger'—he analyzes that—'larger.'
For contact, being two-based, accommodates only the smaller of the two conjoined things, not the larger.
Surely the contacts of chariots and the like never extend to the sky; otherwise there would be perception of chariots and the like, and of those contacts, everywhere.
Therefore, to whatever extent a country, forest, and the like are covered by the eyeball, only to that extent would there be the occasion for apprehension.
He states another reason—'direction.'
He shows its probative force through negative concomitance—'if it were contact-operating.'
He states yet another reason—'what is proximate.'
Although for each moment of motion there is no difference in the speed of generating contact with another location and separation from the present location, since each is in its own substrate,
and although there is no difference in proximity to their own substrate, nevertheless, the accumulated collection of moments of motion—becoming earlier and later—from the departure-separation to the arrival at the destination, which is intervening, is what is meant by 'motion' here.
Its being 'with gaps' (<s>sāntaratva</s>) is its slowness, its delay; and its being 'without gaps' (<s>nairantarya</s>) is its swiftness, its quickness.
Even while performing this motion continuously, one reaches what is proximate quickly,
but does not reach the distant in the same time; rather, the distant is reached after a delay.
As stated by way of indication—
'There would be no apprehension-with-gap if there were contact, and [there would be] the additional [problem] of cognition.'
If it be said that the apprehension-with-gap is justified because the sense organ is located outside the body?
And even if it were outside, there would be no capacity for seeing objects.

children.text: yadi ca syāt tadā paśyedapyunmīlya nimīlanāt //
children.translated_text: And if there were, then one would see even with closed eyes, from the closing [not affecting an external organ].

children.text: yadi ca syāt unmīlya nimīlitanayano 'pi rūpaṃ paśyet, unmīlanādasti bahirindriyamiti //
children.translated_text: And if one could see form even with eyes closed, since from the opening [of eyes] the sense organ would be [proven] outside.

children.text:
tatra vārttikakāraḥ sāntaragrahaṇāditi hetuṃ vikalpya dūṣayati--yat tāvaditi /
sāntaratā khalvaprāptisāhacaryāt /
aprāptiṃ lakṣayati---hetvarthasya pratijñārthenākṣipratvāt amedena /
taduktam--na pratijñārthād bhidyata iti /
hetupratijñāpadavācyatvena bhedamupacaryākṣepyākṣepakabhāvo draṣṭavyaḥ /
tasya vyavadhāyakatvāditi rūpavato 'prasādasvabhāvasya kuḍyāderityarthaḥ /
yat tu prasādasvabhāvaṃ tejaḥ tanna gṛhyate, kiṃ tu tasya rūpamātraṃ visphāritākṣaṇa dṛśyate /
tadāśrayaṃ ca dravyaṃ sādhayiṣyate /
na ca guṇo dravyasyāntaram /
mā bhūd gandhādibhirantaraṃ dravyasya, mā na bhūtāṃ ca nirantare dravye, svaguṇābhyāmantaritatvāt /
na cāpātajanmālocanaṃ vā vikalpo vā dravyānumānaṃ pratīkṣate yena rūpajñānānumitaṃ dravyam indriyarthayordravyayorantaraṃ syāt /

api ca rūpamātramagṛhyamāṇe dravye svatantraṃ gandhādivad gṛhyamāṇaṃ kathamantarā svāśrayamanumāpayet, ākāśādīnāmāśrayāṇamagrahaṇāt? tasmād viṣaktāvayavatejodravyāpratyakṣatvasamāropamātreṇa dūṣaṇaṃ vakṣyamāṇaṃ tvanyathāsiddhatvadūṣaṇaṃ pāramārthikaṃ draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: Moreover, if form alone were apprehended without the substance being apprehended, being independent like smell and the like, how could it inferentially indicate its own substrate in between, given that no apprehension of the substrates of space and the like [occurs independently]? Therefore, the refutation based merely on the superimposition of imperceptibility of the element of light-substance that is in contact with parts is refutation by superimposition alone; but the refutation to be stated regarding being otherwise established should be seen as the real one.

children.text: athābhāvo 'ntaraśabdavācya iti, nāsmākaṃ mūrtadravyābhāvādanyat ākāśamastīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if the word 'gap' (<s>antara</s>) means 'absence'—our view is that there is no space (<s>ākāśa</s>) other than the absence of corporeal substance—this is the purport.

children.text: dūṣayati--sa svatantraśrcakṣurviṣayo na bhavati indriyaṃ cārthaṃ cāntarā abhāvo grāhyaḥ, tena sahārthasya grahaṇaṃ sāntaragrahaṇam /
children.translated_text: He refutes—'that absence, being independent, is not an object of the eye. The absence between the sense organ and the object is what is to be apprehended; the apprehension of the object together with that is apprehension-with-gap.'

children.text: na cendriyārthayormadhyate kasyacit saṃyuktasya vā samavetasya vā grahaṇamasti, yattantro 'yamabhāvo gṛhyeta iti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: The purport is: there is no apprehension of anything—whether conjoined or inherent—between the sense organ and the object, on which this absence would depend for being apprehended.

There the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> (author of the <s>Vārttika</s>) critiques the reason 'because of apprehension-with-gap' by presenting alternatives—'as for the first.'
The 'with-gap' nature is accompanied by non-contact.
He characterizes non-contact—'because the meaning of the reason is not different from the meaning of the thesis, they are identical.'
This is what is stated—'it does not differ from the thesis-meaning.'
The identity of what is implied and what implies should be seen through the figurative attribution of difference by virtue of being expressed by the words of reason and thesis respectively.
'Because of its obstructing nature'—meaning the wall and such, which have a form-bearing but non-transparent nature—this is the meaning.
But that which has a transparent nature—namely light (<s>tejas</s>)—is not apprehended [as obstructing]; rather, only its form alone is seen by one with wide-open eyes.
And the substance that is its substrate will be established.
And a quality is not an intervening gap for a substance.
Let there be no gap from smell and the like for a substance, and let there be no gap in a substance without gaps—since it is mediated by its own qualities.
And neither the immediate apprehension, nor thought (<s>vikalpa</s>), nor the inference of substance awaits [the gap]—whereby the substance inferred from form-cognition would be a gap between the sense organ and the object, both being substances.

children.text:
syādetat /
mā bhūdāntarālikaṃ saṃyuktaṃ vā samavetaṃ vā viśeṣyaṃ gṛhyamāṇameva tu rūpādiviśeṣyamiti /
tattantro 'yamabhāvaḥ tadviśeṣaṇatvena rirūpayiṣyate /
tataśrca sāntaragrahaṇamupapatsyata ityata āha--tena sahopalabdhāviti /
pratīyate hi tvagādibhiḥ apīndriyaiḥ prāpyakāribhirauṣṇyābhavaviśeṣaṇa śiṣirataraṃ pāthaḥ /
na cendriyāṇāmatrāprāpyakāritā,
tasmādanaikāntikam /
anvayābhyupagamenaitaduktam /
anvayābhāve tu viruddhamiti bhāvaḥ /
na ca taijasaṃ rūpamantaram, yena sāntaragrahaṇaṃ syādityāha--na cānyā gatirati /
yathā caitat tathopapāditamadhastāt /
ye tu sāntara iti grahaṇamiti hetumāhuḥ, tān prati dūṣaṇamāha---yairapīti /
anyathāsiddhatve hetumāha--śarīreti /
śarīrāvacchinnāḥ khalvātmānaḥ śarīrāyatanāḥ śarīramevātmānamabhimanyānā arthānanubhavanti /
tatra ya eva śarīrāsaṃbaddha ityanubhūyate tameva sāntara iti manyate /
indriyasaṃbandho bhavatu, mā vā bhūt, śarīrasaṃbandhena tasya sparśādau na sāntaratvābhimāna ityarthaḥ /
hetvantaraṃ dūṣayati--yadapīti /
saṃbandhamātreṇeti /
mātragrahaṇaṃ saṃbandhacatuṣṭayavyāptyartham /
tad yathā indriyeṇārthasya saṃbandhaḥ, indriyāvayavairarthasya, arthāvayavairindrayasya, indriyāvayavairarthāvayavānām /
na caitat niryatā vinā pṛthvagratāṃ bhavatīti pṛthvagratā sūcitā /
yathā vartideśe piṇḍitamapi tejaḥ prasarpat prāsādodaraṃ vyāpnoti /

children.translated_text: For what reason? Because of extensiveness.

children.text: svabhāvataḥ prasaradapi na svaparimāṇānuvidhāyinaṃ pratyayamādhatte, kiṃ tu viṣayabhedānuvidhāyinam /
children.translated_text: Even while naturally spreading, it does not produce a cognition conforming to its own measure, but rather one conforming to the differences of the object.
For cognitions are determined by the determination of the object, not by the determination of the sense organ.
This is what is stated—'cognition conforms to the differences of the object.'

It may be objected:
Let there be no intervening conjoined or inherent thing being apprehended; but rather, let a qualificand having form and the like be [apprehended].
Dependent on that, this absence will be presented as a qualifier of that.
And thus apprehension-with-gap will be justified—therefore he says: 'when it is apprehended together with that.'
For through touch and the other senses that are contact-operating, one perceives water that is cooler, qualified by the absence of warmth.
And the senses are not non-contact-operating here.
Therefore [the reason] is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).
This has been stated by accepting positive concomitance.
But in the absence of positive concomitance, it would be contradictory—this is the purport.
And the luminous form is not a gap, by which there would be apprehension-with-gap—he says: 'and there is no other movement.'
And as this is so, it has been established above.
Regarding those who state '<s>sāntara</s>' as [qualifying] apprehension and call that the reason, he states the refutation against them—'even by those.'
He states the reason for being otherwise established—'body.'
For selves, delimited by the body, having the body as their seat, identifying the body itself as the self, experience objects.
Therein, whatever is experienced as not connected with the body is considered to be 'with a gap.'
Whether there is a connection with the sense organ or not, through the connection with the body, there is no conception of 'with a gap' regarding touch and the like—this is the meaning.
He refutes another reason—'even that.'
'By mere contact'—
the word 'mere' is for the purpose of encompassing the fourfold contact.
Namely: the contact of the sense organ with the object, of the parts of the sense organ with the object, of the parts of the object with the sense organ, of the parts of the sense organ with the parts of the object.
And this does not occur without extension—thus extension is indicated.
Just as light, even though concentrated at the wick-location, when spreading out, pervades the interior of the palace.

children.text:
aparamapi hetuṃ dūṣayati--yat punariti /
dehamarthaṃ cāntarāvasthitasya pṛthivyādeḥ saṃyuktasaṃyogālpīyastvaṃ bhūyastvaṃ cāpekṣamāṇasyeti /
khagānāṃ coparyupari saṃcaratāṃ dūrāntikabhāvo bahulatamālokāvayavabhāgānāṃ saṃyuktasaṃyogālpatvabhūyastvābhyāmavagantavyaḥ /
sa ca tādṛgālokāvayavī pratyakṣo 'nyathā na rūpamātreṇa tadanumānaṃ śakyamityuktam /
children.translated_text: And such a whole consisting of portions of light is directly perceptible; otherwise it cannot be inferred merely from form— this is what is stated.

children.text: na ca khagānāmuparyupari saṃcaratāṃ dūrantikapratyayaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: And for birds flying higher and higher, there would be no cognition of far and near.

children.text: na ca patati patatriṇīha prāpto neheti bhavet /
children.translated_text: And it would not be the case that 'a flying bird has arrived here' or 'has not arrived here.'
Therefore, the refutation here too should be seen as: 'this is otherwise-established (<s>anyathāsiddhi</s>), because of apprehension together with an intervening medium'— just as stated before.

He refutes yet another reason— 'that which moreover.' The earth and the like situated within the body and the object, when having lesser or greater contact-by-conjunction (<s>saṃyuktasaṃyoga</s>)— and the far and near distances of birds flying higher and higher are to be understood through the lesser or greater contact-by-conjunction of the portions of the most extensive light.

children.text:
aparamapi hetuṃ dūṣayati--yat punariti /
yugapadgrahaṇamasiddham, tadabhimānastu anyathāsiddhaḥ /
acintyo hi tejaso lādhavātiśayena vegātiśayo yadudayagiriśikharam ārohatyeva mārtaṇḍamaṇḍale bhavanodareṣvāloka ityabhimāno laukikānām /
tādṛśaṃ cākṣuṣamapi teja iti krameṇāpi gacchad yugapattatra tatra lakṣyate /
na caikasmādeva karmaṇo yugapad durāntikasaṃyogā bhavantīti yuktam /
taddhi svakārye janayitavye svāśrayapratyāsattim apekṣate /
anyathā madhurāsthasya devadattasya karma pāṭaliputreṇa devadattaṃ yojayet /
vegākhyasaṃskārajamapi karmana sahasā śaramantarāladeśena ca lakṣyeṇa ca yojayati /
tasmāt mithyaiva yaugapadyābhimāna iti /
codayati--kathaṃ punariti /
asti hi śākhācandramasoḥ grahaṇe yaugapadyābhimānaḥ /
na cāyamasati bādhake mithyeti vaktuṃ śakyaḥ /
so 'yamabādhito bodho 'vabodhayatyaprāpyakāritāṃ cakṣuṣa ityarthaḥ /
pariharati--idamiti /
indriyaṃ yadyagatvānāgatamarthaṃ gṛhṇīyāt, kimasya kuḍyakaṭādyāvaraṇamapakuryāt yena tadāvṛtaṃ na gṛhṇīyāt /
gatau tu sparśavatā prasādarahitena saivāsya pratibaddheti na prāpnoti viṣayam, aprāptaṃ ca na gṛhṇāti /
prāyogastu, cakṣuḥśrotre prāpya svaviṣaye kāryaṃ kurutaḥ, janakatve sati tadaprāptāvajanakatvāt /
children.translated_text: The formal argument is: the eye and ear produce their effect upon reaching their respective objects, because when they have the capacity to produce [cognition] and do not reach [the object], they do not produce it.

children.text: yajjanakaṃ sad yadaprāptau yanna janayati tat tatprāptāveva tajjanayati, yathā kumbhajanakaḥ kumbhakāro mṛdo 'prāptāvakurvan kumbhaṃ tatprāptāveva karoti /
children.translated_text: Whatever, being a producer, does not produce something when it has not reached it, that produces it only upon reaching it— just as a potter who is a producer of a pot does not make the pot when he has not reached the clay, but makes it only upon reaching the clay.
And so it is in this case.
Therefore, it is so.

He refutes yet another reason— 'that which moreover.' Simultaneous apprehension is unestablished; the belief in it is otherwise-established. For the extraordinary speed arising from the extraordinary lightness of light is inconceivable— the common belief is that the sun's orb merely rises to the peak of the eastern mountain and there is light in the interiors of houses. And visual light too is of such a nature— even though traveling sequentially, it is perceived as if simultaneously here and there. And it is not reasonable that from a single action, conjunctions with far and near things arise simultaneously. For that [action], in order to produce its own effect, requires proximity to its own substrate. Otherwise, the action of <s>Devadatta</s> stationed in <s>Madhurā</s> would connect <s>Devadatta</s> with <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>. And action born of the impression called velocity suddenly connects an arrow with both the intermediate space and the target. Therefore, the belief in simultaneity is simply false. He objects— 'but how then?' For there is a belief of simultaneity in the apprehension of a branch and the moon. And this cannot be called false in the absence of a contradicting cognition. This uncontradicted cognition makes one understand the non-contact-based functioning (<s>aprāpyakāritā</s>) of the eye— this is the meaning. He resolves— 'this [is not so].' If the sense organ were to apprehend an object without going there and without contact, what would its obstruction by walls, mats, and the like do to it, such that it would not apprehend what is covered by them? But in the case of going, since it is obstructed by that which is tangible and opaque, it does not reach the object, and what is not reached is not apprehended.

children.text:
yuktyantaramāha--dūrāntikānuvidhānamiti /
dūre nopalabhyate, antike ca upalabhyate /
aprāpteraviśeṣeṇa dūre 'pyupalambhaḥ syāt /
anupalambhe vā antike 'pi na syāt /
prāptau tu dūraṃ gacchat prakṣīṇaṃ sat prāptamarthaṃ na gṛhṇāti ataijasam, taijasam apyabhibhūtaṃ na gṛhṇāti, yatholkāprakāśaṃ madhyandine /
anabhibhūtaṃ tu mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalaṃ gṛhṇātyeveti /
codayati--viṣayībhāvāditi /
yogyo hi tādṛśa indriyakṣaṇaḥ svakāraṇādupajātaḥ pariṇato vārthakṣaṇaśrca, yayoraprāptayoreva grahaṇagrāhyabhāvaḥ /
vyavahitaviprakṛṣṭau ca na tau tādṛśau /
tat kimapratīyamānaprāptikalpanayetyarthaḥ /
pariharati---tacca naivamiti /
niṣatsyete hi kṣaṇabhaṅgapariṇāmau bhāvānām /
tena sthemabhājāṃ bhāvānāṃ svarūpayogyatā vā mahattvādirviṣayībhāvaḥ sahakārisākalyaṃ vā jñānopajananaṃ prati pariśiṣyate /
tatra svarūpayogyatāmātraṃ cedāsthīyeta, tadā yadevāvyavahitaṃ sannihitaṃ sad ajanayad vijñānaṃ viprakṛṣṭamapi vyavahitamapi tadeveti tathaiva tena jñānaṃ janayitavyam /
asti hi tasya tadāpi svarūpayogyateti, sahakārisākalyaṃ tu prāptireva /
tasmāt na saṃbandhamantareṇa viṣayībhāva iti sūktam /
sandigdhaḥ pṛcchati--atha prāpyakāritva iti /
ayamabhisandhiḥ /
kulālādau prāpyakāriṇi dṛṣṭaṃ yathā viprakṛṣṭo vyavahitaśrca na karotīti, tasmāt aprāpyakāriṇi cācaskāntādau dṛṣṭaṃ yathā viprakṛṣṭo vyavahitaśrca lauhaṃ maṇirākarṣati, tasmāt tatra pramāṇaṃ vaktavyamiti uttaram--indriyatvameva pramāṇam /
tadeva pañcāvayavopapannamāha--prāpyakārīti /
yadi tu kaśrcit dṛṣṭāntasya sādhyavikalatvam ubhdāvayet tvagādīnāmaprāpyakāritvāditi, tu pratyāha--atha punarna kiñciditi /
pṛcchati--atheti /
yogyatayaiva hi kāraṇāni svakāryaṃ kurvanti, prāptistu svarūpyogyatāprayuktāṃ vyāptimupajīvati, na tvasyāḥ svābhāvikaṃ vyāpakatvamiti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--so 'pīti /
sahakārisākalyaṃ tāvat na prāpteratiricyata ityuktam /
kevalaṃ svarūpayogyatā vaktavyā /
sa ca vyastānāmapyastīti yatra tatra vyavasthitebhyo 'pi kāryotpādaprasaṅkaḥ /
ayaskāntamaṇerapi cakṣuṣa iva vṛttibheda eṣitavyaḥ,
anyathā vyavadhānaviprakarṣayorapi lauhākarṣaṇaprasaṅgāt /
na ca vyavadhānaviprakarṣābhāvasahito lauhamākarṣati, vyavadhānaviprakarṣayostu tadabhāvābhāvo nākarṣati saṃpratam /
prāptereva tatra tatra kāryotpādaṃ prati upayogasya viditasvāt /
yogyatāmātrasya copādherapākṛtatvāt /
yathā ca dravyātiriktastaddharmaḥ prāptistathāgrenivedayiṣyate /

children.translated_text: Therefore everything is clear.
He concludes— 'therefore.'

children.text: yadapi kṛṣṇasārānugrahopaghātābhyāṃ darśanādarśanāditi tatrocyate, tadadhiṣṭhānamindriyamityadhiṣṭhānānugrahopaghātābhyāṃ tasyānugrahopadhātau, yathā kūṣmāṇḍalatāsecanacchedanābhyāṃ tatphalasya anugrahopaghātau /
children.translated_text: And regarding what was said about perception and non-perception being due to the favorable and unfavorable conditions of the pupil of the eye (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>)— to that it is said: the sense organ is the basis of that, and through the favorable and unfavorable conditions of the basis, the favorable and unfavorable conditions of that [perception arise]— just as through the watering and cutting of a pumpkin vine, the favorable and unfavorable conditions of its fruit [arise].

children.text: ata eva bahirnisṛtāpyacchinnamūlā dṛṣṭiḥ kāryāya samarthā na chinnamūleti siddham //
children.translated_text: For this very reason, vision, even when it has emerged outward, if its root is uncut, is capable of producing its effect, but not when its root is cut— this is established.

He states another reasoning— 'conformity with far and near.' What is far is not perceived, and what is near is perceived. If there were no contact [required], then without distinction, even what is far would be perceived. Or if not perceived, even what is near would not be perceived. But in the case of contact-based functioning, [the visual ray] going far becomes diminished and, not being luminous, does not apprehend the object that has been reached; and even if luminous, when overpowered it does not apprehend— just as the light of a torch at midday. But the sun's orb, being unoverpowered, is indeed apprehended. He objects— 'because of becoming an object.' For a suitable sense-moment, having arisen from its own cause or having undergone transformation, and a suitable object-moment— the apprehension-apprehensible relation holds between these two even without contact. And one that is obstructed or remote is not suitable in that way. So why postulate an unperceived contact?— this is the meaning. He resolves— 'and that is not so.' For momentary destruction and transformation of things will be refuted. Therefore, for things that endure, what remains as the explanation for becoming an object is either the inherent suitability of their own nature, such as magnitude and the like, or the completeness of auxiliary conditions for the production of cognition. If one relies on inherent suitability alone, then whatever is unobstructed and proximate, having not produced cognition, even when remote or obstructed, being the very same thing, should produce cognition in the same way. For it has the same inherent suitability even then. But the completeness of auxiliary conditions is nothing other than contact itself. Therefore, it is well said that there is no becoming-an-object without a relation. One who is in doubt asks— 'now, contact-based functioning.' This is the intention: just as in the case of the potter and the like who function through contact, it is observed that one who is remote or obstructed does not produce— therefore it is contact-based functioning. And just as in the case of a magnet and the like, it is observed that even when remote or obstructed, the magnet attracts iron— therefore a <s>pramāṇa</s> (proof) must be stated. The answer— 'being a sense organ itself is the proof.' He states that very [argument] equipped with five members— 'functions through contact.' But if someone were to raise the objection that the example lacks the property to be proved, since the skin and the like function without contact— to that he replies— 'or alternatively, nothing.' He asks— 'now.' For causes produce their effects by suitability alone, and contact depends on the pervasion brought about by inherent suitability, but there is no natural pervading power of this [contact]— this is the purport. The answer— 'even that.' The completeness of auxiliary conditions does not differ from contact— this has been stated. Only inherent suitability [remains to be considered]. But that belongs even to the distributed [individual causes], and so there would be the unwanted consequence of effect-production from [causes] situated anywhere. A difference in the mode of operation (<s>vṛttibheda</s>) should be sought for the magnet too, just as for the eye; otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of attraction of iron even when there is obstruction or remoteness. And it is not the case that the magnet, combined with the absence of obstruction and remoteness, attracts iron, while in the presence of obstruction and remoteness the absence of that absence [i.e., the presence of those conditions] does not attract— at present. Because the usefulness of contact for the production of effects in each case is known. And because the objection of mere suitability as a limiting condition has been removed. And that contact is a property of substance distinct from substance itself— this will be explained later.

children.text:
pṛcchati--atha jñāneti, pratyakṣasamākhyātalakṣaṇānuvādena lakṣaṇe vidhīyamāne jñāyata evaitajjñānameveti loke sākṣātkārijñānahetoḥ pratyakṣatvāditi bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---sukhādivyudāsārtham /
tadeva hi lakṣaṇavāyamucyate, yasya lakṣyānapekṣo 'tivyāptyavyāptivyudāso lakṣaṇapadebhya eva pratīyate /
lakṣyānurodhena tu lakṣaṇavyavasthāpane anyonyāśrayatvamagatirveti bhāvaḥ /
sukhādīnāṃ vijñānābhinnahetujatvena vijñānatvādaśakyaṃ vyāvartanamiti cet--na, abhinnahetujatvāsiddhaḥ /
na khalu yaiva candanasparśajñānasyotpattau sāmagrī saiva sukhasyāpīti /
asti hi śītārtasyāpi candanendriyasaṃyogāt śītasparśajñānam iti tadvadevāsya sukhamapi bhavet /
avāntarasāmagrībhede 'pīndriyārthamanaskārajatvāt jñānajātīyatvamiti cet---na, kiñcitkāraṇābhede 'pi kāryabhedasyānākasmikatvopapatteḥ /
tadarthatvācca kāraṇabhedānusaraṇaprayāsasya /

children.translated_text: And it is not proper to say that there is non-difference [of effects] because of non-difference of the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>).
Because even you accept that different cognitions have a single immediately-preceding-condition as their material cause.

children.text: api copādānābhedaśrca kutaśrcit kāraṇabhedāt kāryabhedaśceti ko virodhaḥ? ata evāsmākamabhede apyupādānasya piṭharasyauṣṇyāparākhyasya ca vahinasaṃyogasya pūrvarūpādipradhvaṃsānāṃ kāraṇānāṃ bhedād bhinnajātīyā jāyante gandharūparasasparśā iti siddhāntaḥ /
children.translated_text: Moreover, even given non-difference of material cause, there is difference of effect from some difference of [other] causes— what contradiction is there? For this very reason, in our system, even though the material cause— the pot's prior form and the conjunction of fire called heat— is non-different, from the difference of causes such as the destruction of the prior form, the products of different kinds— smell, color, taste, and touch— are born.

children.text: tasmādarthapravaṇebhyo jñānebhyastadapravaṇatayā bhinnajātīyāḥ sukhādayo yathāsvamunakūlavedanīyatvādibhirlakṣaṇairanyonyamapi bhedavantastīvrasaṃvegatayā pramitsānapekṣamānasapratyakṣapravedanīyā iti ramaṇīyam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, pleasure and the like, being of a different class from cognitions which are directed toward objects, by virtue of not being directed toward objects, and being mutually different too by their respective defining characteristics such as being experienced as favorable and so on, and being experienceable by mental perception without requiring any desire to know because of the intensity of the experience— this is well-established.

He asks— 'now, cognition'— since in the definition being formulated through the restatement of the definition stated under the name 'perception,' it is already known in the world that this is simply cognition, because of being perception due to being the cause of direct apprehension— this is the purport. The answer— 'for the purpose of excluding pleasure and the like.' For only that is called a definitional effort whose exclusion of over-extension and under-extension, independent of the definiendum, is understood from the definitional words themselves. But if the definition is established with dependence on the definiendum, there would be mutual dependence or groundlessness— this is the purport. If one objects that since pleasure and the like are produced by causes not different from cognition, they cannot be distinguished because of being of the nature of cognition— no, because the claim of being produced by non-different causes is unestablished. Surely the aggregate of conditions for the production of the cognition of sandal-touch is not the same as that for pleasure. For even one who is suffering from cold, from the contact of the organ with sandal, has cognition of cold touch— and so he should also have pleasure. If one objects that even given the difference in subsidiary conditions, because of being produced by the sense organ, object, and mental attention, it belongs to the class of cognition— no, because even with some partial identity of cause, the difference of effects is non-accidental and tenable.

children.text:
syādetat /
asatyapīndriyārthasannikarṣe jñānamātrādeva sukhaduḥkhayoḥ svapnāntike darśanāt
yatrāpīndriyārthasannikarṣastatrāpi jñānamastīti tadeva sukhaduḥkhayoḥ kāraṇaṃ kluptasāmarthyāt /
indriyārthasannikarṣasya tu jñānamātropayogādanyathāsiddhau bhāvābhāvāviti /
tadayuktam, svapnāntike sukhaduḥkhotpādasyāsiddhestajjñānasyārthajñānasyeva mithyātvāt /
yathā hi tatra kāminīsmṛtiviṣaryāsa eva mupalabdhacaratajjanmasukhasmaraṇaviparyāsaḥ /
sukhaduḥkhabuddhyutpāda eva cātra dharmādharmopayogo na tu susaduḥkhotpāde /
na cāsatīndriyārthasannikarṣe jñānamanyanmanorathādi vā tādṛśaṃ sukhabhedaṃ vidhatte yādṛśo viṣayopabhogajanmā /
satīndriyārthasannikarṣe jñānamātrameva tasya hetuḥ /
jñānahetustu sukhabhedasyānutpādādityapyuktameva /
viṣayasākṣātkārastadutpādaheturna viṣayajñānamātramiti cet? hantar, iśvarasyāpyasti tatrabhavato yogarddhisaṃpannānāṃ ca mahādhiyāṃ samastavastusākṣātmāra iti teṣāmapi sukhaduḥkhotpādapracayaḥ prasajyet, asatyāṃ pratipakṣadhāraṇāyām /
tasmādindriyārthasannikarṣo 'pi sukhaduḥkhotpādahetureṣitavyaḥ /
sa ca satyapyarthasākṣātkāre nāsti siddhānāmiti na teṣāṃ sukhaduḥkhotpādaḥ /
api ca caramabhāvi kāraṇaṃ gṛhītvā pūrvabhāvināmakaraṇatvāpādane tantvādīnāmapi paṭādīn pratyakāraṇatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
saṃyogabhedādeva tādṛśapaṭātpatteḥ tantvādīnāṃ ca saṃyogabheda evopayogāt /
children.translated_text: Because such cloth is produced from the specific conjunction alone, and threads and the like are useful only for the specific conjunction.
But the causality of that [thread] combined with that [conjunction] is the same as the causality of the sense-contact combined with the cognition.

children.text: yathāhuḥ padārthavidaḥ stragādyabhiprataviṣayasānnidhye satīṣṭopalabdhīndriyārthasannikarṣadharmādyapekṣādātmamanasoḥ saṃyogāt yadanugrahābhiṣvaṅganayanādiprasādajanakamatpadyate tatsukham iti /
children.translated_text: As the knowers of categories say: when a desired object such as a garland and the like is proximate, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> (self) and <s>manas</s> (mind)— dependent on the desired perception, the contact of the sense organ with the object, <s>dharma</s> (merit), and the like— that which is produced, which generates attachment, delight, brightness of the eyes, and the like, is pleasure.
Therefore, it is well said that the mention of 'cognition' [in the definition] is for the purpose of excluding pleasure and the like.

An objection may arise: even without the contact of the sense organ with the object, pleasure and pain are observed in dream merely from cognition alone. And even where there is contact of the sense organ with the object, cognition is present there too— so cognition alone is the cause of pleasure and pain, because its capacity has been established. The contact of the sense organ with the object merely serves cognition, and so it is otherwise-established whether it exists or not. That is improper, because the production of pleasure and pain in dream is unestablished, since dream-cognition is false just like cognition of objects [in dream]. For just as there, the memory-based confusion regarding a desired woman alone is the confusion of the memory of pleasure experienced in past lives as actually being experienced. And here, only the arising of the belief in pleasure and pain is where <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> play a role, not in the actual production of pleasure and pain. And without the contact of sense organ and object, cognition or mere fancy and the like do not produce such a variety of pleasure as that born from actual enjoyment of objects. When there is contact of sense organ with object, cognition alone is the cause of it. But since the variety of pleasure is not produced by cognition alone as cause— this too has already been stated. If one objects that direct perception of the object is the cause of its production, not mere cognition of the object— well then, even <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and yogins possessed of yogic accomplishments, who are of great intelligence, have direct perception of all things— and so for them too there would be the production and accumulation of pleasure and pain, in the absence of a counteracting practice. Therefore, the contact of the sense organ with the object too must be sought as a cause of the production of pleasure and pain. And that [contact] does not exist for the liberated even though they directly perceive objects— and so there is no production of pleasure and pain for them. Moreover, if one takes the latest cause and declares the earlier ones to be non-causes, then there would be the unwanted consequence of threads and the like not being causes of cloth and the like.

children.text:
iha dvayī pratyakṣajātiravikalpikā savikalpikā ceti /
tatrobhayyapi indriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānamavyabhicārīti lakṣaṇena saṃgṛhītāpi svaśabdenopāttā, tatra vipratipatteḥ /

children.translated_text: There, the term for indeterminate [perception] is '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (inexpressible), and for determinate [perception] it is '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' (having the nature of determination).

children.text: tatra vyapadeśo viśeṣaṇamupalakṣaṇaṃ vā nāmajātyādi, tat karma vyapadeśyaṃ viśeṣyamiti yāvat /
children.translated_text: There, <s>vyapadeśa</s> (designation) is a qualifier or an indicating mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) such as name, class, and the like; its object (<s>karma</s>) is what is to be designated, i.e., the qualified— this much is meant.

children.text: tadyathā ḍittho 'yaṃ gaurayaṃ śuklo 'yaṃ kamaṇḍalumānayaṃ gacchatyayamiti sarvaṃ hi savikalpakaṃ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvena vastuṣu pravartate /
children.translated_text: For example, 'this one is <s>Ḍittha</s>,' 'this one is fair,' 'this one is white,' 'this one carries a water-pot,' 'this one is walking'—for all determinate cognition operates upon objects through the relation of qualifier and qualified.

children.text: avidyamānaṃ vyapadeśyaṃ yasmistadavyapadeśyaṃ jātyādisvarūpāvagāhi, na tu jātyādīnāṃ mitho viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvāvagāhīti yāvat //
children.translated_text: That in which the designable is not present is the undesignable (<s>avyapadeśya</s>)—it apprehends the own-nature of universals and the like, but does not apprehend the mutual qualifier-qualified relationship among universals and the like. This much is meant.

Here, the class of perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is twofold: indeterminate (<s>avikalpikā</s>) and determinate (<s>savikalpikā</s>). Of these, both are subsumed by the definition as 'cognition produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object, non-deviating'; and both are also taken up by their own specific terms, because there is disagreement regarding them.

children.text:
tatra nāmarahitamavikalpakaṃ nāstīti ye vipratipadyante tanmatamapacikīrṣurūpanyasyati bhāṣyakāraḥ yāvadarthaṃ vai nāmadheyaśabdāḥ /
sarve 'rthāḥ sarvathā sarvadā sarvatra nāmadhayānvitāḥ /
nāsti so 'rtho yaḥ kadācit kvacit kathañcit nāmadheyena viyujyate /
tadanena nāmadheyatādātmyamarthānāṃ pratijānīte /
atra hetumāha--tairarthasaṃpratyaya iti /
arthā hi pratīyamānāṃ nāmadheyairūpetāstatsāmānādhikaraṇyenāvagamyante gaurityartho 'śva ityartha iti /
na copāyatayā sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ ghaṭate /
na hi cakṣurādisāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ rūpādyanubhavati /
nāpi jñāyamāna upāya upeyasāmānādhikaraṇmanubhavati /
na hi bhavati dhūmo 'yaṃ vahinariti kiṃ tu dhūmo 'yaṃ dhūmatvāt vahinamāniti /
api cāśabdopāye 'numeyādau na śabdasaṃbhedenādhigamo bhavet, asti tu /
tasmāt tairnāmadheyaiḥ saha samānādhikaraṇasyārthasya pratyayo yata iti /
tasmāt nāmadheyātmānaḥ arthāḥ /
kiṃ ca gavādiṣu ṣaḍjādiṣu ca śabdāpakarṣe 'rthapratyayāpakarṣāt tadutkarṣe tvarthapratyayotkarṣāt pratyayasya ca pratyetavyotkarṣādhīnotkarṣatvāt nāmadheyotkarṣeṇārthasyotkarṣaḥ arthasya tādatmyaṃ gamayati /
tadidaṃ samaḥ prayojanaṃ saṃpratyaya iti samadhikaḥ pratyaya ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: This means: '<s>saṃpratyaya</s>' means equal utility, i.e., increased cognition—such is the meaning.

children.text: astyarthasaṃpratyayo nāmadheyasāmānādhikaraṇyena, na tvetāvatā nāmadheyātmatā sidhyati /
children.translated_text: There is comprehension of objects through co-referentiality with names, but this alone does not establish identity with names.

children.text: asti hi purovartidravyasāmānādhikaraṇyena rajatapratyayo na caitāvatā śuktī rajatātmikā bhavatītyata āha---arthasaṃpratyayācca vyavahāraḥ /
children.translated_text: For there is cognition of silver through co-referentiality with a substance present before one, yet by that alone the shell does not become identical with silver—therefore he says: 'and from the comprehension of objects, there is practical usage.'
And from that, because of non-discordance, the means of valid knowledge—once the identity of names [with objects] is assumed—establishes the identity of objects [with names]—such is the meaning.

There, in order to refute the view of those who disagree, saying 'there is no indeterminate cognition devoid of names,' the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> presents [their position]: 'Name-words exist for every object. All objects are in all ways, at all times, and everywhere connected with names. There is no object that is ever, anywhere, in any way separated from a name.' By this, he asserts the identity of objects with names. Here he states the reason—'because through them there is comprehension of objects.' For objects, when being cognized, are apprehended as endowed with names, through co-referentiality with them—'cow' is the object, 'horse' is the object. And co-referentiality does not work by way of being a means [of knowledge]. For one does not experience co-referentiality with the eye and such. Nor does a means being cognized experience co-referentiality with what is to be reached. For one does not say 'this smoke is fire,' but rather 'this is smoke, and from its smoke-ness one infers fire.' Moreover, in the case of inference and the like, where words are not the means, cognition mixed with words would not occur, yet it does. Therefore, since there is cognition of the object as co-referential with those names, objects have names as their nature. Furthermore, regarding cows and the notes <s>ṣaḍja</s> etc., when the word diminishes, the cognition of the object diminishes; when it increases, the cognition of the object increases; and since the increase of cognition depends on the increase of what is to be cognized, the increase of the object through the increase of the name indicates the identity of the object [with the name].

children.text:
tadevaṃ sāmānyato 'rthānāṃ nāmadheyatādātmyaṃ vyutpādya prakṛte yojanayati---tatredamindriyārthasannikarṣādutpannaṃ viṣayajñānaṃ rūpamiti vā rasa iti vā evaṃ rūpādyarthasāmānādhikaraṇyena bhavati /
bhavatu, kimetāvatāpītyata āha---rūparasaśabdāśrca viṣayanāmadheyam /
kimetāvatāpītyata āha--tena vyapadiśyate jñānam /
uktamapi vyapadeśaṃ savyākhyānamāha--rūpamiti jānīte rasa iti jānīte iti /
tathā cārthānāṃ nāmadheyātmakatvāt tadgocaramālocanamapi nāmadheyagocaramityarthavat nāmadheyena vyapadiśyamānaṃ śābdaṃ prasajyata iti /
na śabdapramāṇakatayā śābdam, api tu śabde jātaṃ śābdam /
śabdaśrcātra viṣayatvena janako 'rthatādātmyāt /
tathā ca nāvikalpakaṃ śabdarahitamastīti tātparyārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: And thus they say,

children.text: na so 'sti pratyayo loke yaḥ śabdānugamādṛte /
children.translated_text: There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words.
All knowledge is apprehended as if pervaded by words.

Having thus explained generally the identity of objects with names, he applies it to the present subject—'there, this cognition of the object, arising from the contact of sense organ and object, has co-referentiality with the object as form (<s>rūpa</s>), or taste (<s>rasa</s>), and so on.' Let it be so—what follows from this?—therefore he says: 'form, taste, sound, etc. are the names of the objects.' What follows from this?—therefore he says: 'by that, the cognition is designated.' He states the designation already mentioned, with explanation—'one knows as form, one knows as taste.' And since objects have names as their nature, the apprehension directed at them is also directed at names—thus, being designated by names as if it were verbal, the consequence follows that it is verbal (<s>śābda</s>). It is not verbal in the sense of being produced by verbal testimony as a means of knowledge, but rather verbal in the sense of being born in words. And words here, by being the object, are the producer, due to identity with the object. And thus the purport is: there is no indeterminate cognition devoid of words.
As he said,
The initial arrangement of the [speech] organs, the upward propulsion of breath,
and the striking of the places of articulation—these are not without the cultivation of words.
Even the cognition of infants, mutes, and the like is accompanied by words, due to the force of the cultivation of words from beginningless [time].
Thus.

children.text: tadasya nirākaraṇaṃ lakṣaṇagatenālocanajñānāvarodhārthenāvyapadeśyapadena sūcitam iti parīkṣāparvaṇi vacanārhamapi subhāṣitarucitayā tadvilambamasahamāno bhāṣyakāro lakṣaṇāvasara evāha /
children.translated_text: The refutation of this is indicated by the word '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (undesignable) in the definition, which is meant to include indeterminate apprehension-cognition. And the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>, relishing well-spoken [discourse], unable to bear the delay of [discussing] that until the occasion of examination, states it right at the occasion of the definition.
Therefore he says—'[the word] avyapadeśya [is used].'

children.text: tena sūcite 'pyarthe avyapadeśyapadaṃ cojayati---yadidamanumayukte śabdārthasaṃbandhe 'rthajñānam, na tat nāmadheyaśabdena vyapadiśyate //
children.translated_text: Though the matter is indicated, he elaborates the word '<s>avyapadeśya</s>'—'this cognition of an object, which is in an inferred word-meaning relation, is not designated by a name-word.'

children.text:
ayamabhisandhiḥ /
sāmānādhikaraṇyena śabdātmakatvaṃ rūpādīnāmabhidhīyānaṃ śabdabrahmātmakatvaṃ vocyeta śreyamāṇagaurityādipadabhedātmakatvaṃ vā? na tāvadādya /
kalpaḥ /
na salvasmadādisamastadarśanapathātivṛttena śabdabrahmaṇā rūpādīnāmasti sāmānādhikaraṇyapratītiḥ laukikānām /
śrūyamāṇaśabdasāmānādhikaraṇyena tu tādātmyaprasādhane anupayuktaśabdasaṃbandhasya bālamūkādeḥ rūpādijñāneṣu nāsti śrūyamāṇaśabdagandho 'pi, prāgeva tu tatsāmānādhikaraṇyam /
na ca teṣāmapi prāgbhavīyaśabdabhāvanānugamena tatsāmānādhikaraṇyamiti sāṃpratam /
na khalu rūpādyātmanaḥ śabdasya rūpādivaiśadyaināvaiśadyaṃ saṃbhavati /
yugapad vaiśadyāvaiśadyarūpaviruddhadharmayogena bhedaprasaṅgāt /
veśadye tu vyutpannavadavyutpanno 'pi śabdaiḥ vyavaharet, na tu saṃbandhagrahaṇapekṣeta /
na ca tādātmyādanyad vācakatvaṃ śabdānāṃ yatra saṃbandhagrahāpekṣā bhavet /
na ca tādātmye 'pi kalpitabhedānāṃ vācyavācakabhāvaḥ /
tathā sati na sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ syāt /
na hyasti saṃbhavo bhedakalpanā ca sāmānādhikaraṇyaprathā ceti /
tasmādavyutpannānāmasti śabdarahitaṃ rūpādiṣu nirvikalpakaṃ pratyakṣamiti /
na kevalamabyutpannānām, vyutpannānāmapyastītyāha--gṛhīte 'pi ca śabdārthasaṃbandhe iti /
ārddhekta eva sāmānādhikaraṇyanirāsāya saṃbandhagrahaṇasvarūpamāha--asthārthasya sāsnādimadrūpasya ayaṃ gakarādyokāro nāmadheyamiti /
itikaraṇo jñānaparāmarśapradhānaḥ /
tathā ca yo ḍittho nānādeśakālāvasthāsaṃsṛṣṭaḥ piṇḍabhedaḥ so 'yamiti sannihitadeśakāla ityarthaḥ /
na tvayaṃ piṇḍo ḍitthaśabda iti pratyayaḥ /
autsargikaṃ hi śabdānāmarthaparatvaṃ kvacit punarityādibhiḥ śabdaistadapodyate /
yatrāpi saṃbandhapratipādanamabhedena ayaṃ ḍittha iti, tatrāpi śabdo vācyatvaparo na svarūpaparaḥ yathā gaurvāhīka iti lakṣyamāṇaguṇayogaparaḥ /
na ca tanmātreṇa vāhīkasya gotvaṃ bhavati /
tasmād bhinnayoreva śabdārthayoḥ saṃbandhagrahāt tanmūlatvācca śabdavyavahārasya na śabdapuraḥsaramapi jñānaṃ śabdasāmānādhikaraṇyamātmano 'rthasyāvagamayati /
yattu śabdānupāye 'pi jñāne śabdaḥ pūrvaṃ bhavati tadgṛhītasaṅketasya prathamamindriyārthasannikarṣādālocanena śabdasaṃsargarahitenālocite 'rthamātretasyārthabhedasya śabdabhedena saṃbandhāt śabdaviṣayaḥ saṃskāraḥ prabodhyate /
prabuddhaḥ śabdasmṛtiṃ janayati /
tena vyutpannasya nirvikalpakāt parāñcaḥ pratyayāḥ śabdānupāyā api śabdapuraḥsarā jāyante /

children.translated_text: As they say,
The remembrance of the name there is not caused by anything else either.

children.text: piṇḍa eva hi dṛṣṭaḥ san saṃjñāṃ smārayituṃ kṣamaḥ //
children.translated_text: For the individual, having been perceived, is capable of bringing the name to memory.

Here the underlying intention is: does the identity with words of forms and the like, asserted through co-referentiality, refer to identity with <s>Śabdabrahman</s> (the Word-Absolute), or to identity with the distinct words like '<s>gaur</s>' etc. that are being heard? Not the first alternative. For worldly people have no apprehension of co-referentiality between forms and the like and <s>Śabdabrahman</s>, which transcends the entire cognitive range of all beings like ourselves. But if identity is to be established through co-referentiality with heard words, then for infants, mutes, and the like, who have no connection with words and for whom it is useless, there is not even a trace of heard words in their cognitions of form etc., let alone co-referentiality with them. Nor is it proper [to say] that even for them, because of the accompaniment of the cultivation of words from previous births, there is that co-referentiality. For it is not possible that words, being identical with forms etc., would share in the clarity or lack of clarity of forms etc. Because there would be the absurd consequence of difference, through the possession of contradictory properties—clarity and lack of clarity—simultaneously. And if there were clarity, even one who is not learned would transact with words just like one who is learned, and would not depend on grasping the convention. And there is no expressive capacity of words other than identity whereby the grasping of the convention would be needed. Nor is there a speaker-spoken relationship among things that are posited as identical. In that case, there would be no co-referentiality. For there is no possibility of positing difference and also maintaining co-referentiality. Therefore, for those who have not learned the convention, there exists an indeterminate perception regarding forms etc. that is devoid of words. Not only for the unlearned, but even for the learned there exists [such perception]—he says: 'even when the word-meaning relation has been grasped.' He states the nature of the grasping of the relation, precisely in order to refute co-referentiality—'of this object having dewlap etc. as its form, this sound consisting of ga-ka etc. is the name—thus.' The word '<s>iti</s>' primarily refers to the cognitive apprehension. And thus, the particular individual (<s>piṇḍa</s>) called <s>Ḍittha</s>, associated with various places, times, and conditions, is [known as] 'this one'—meaning present in place and time. But the cognition is not 'this individual is the word <s>Ḍittha</s>.' For it is natural for words to refer to objects; only sometimes, by words like 'punaḥ' (again) etc., that [referral] is reversed. Even where the teaching of the convention is done through identity—'this is <s>Ḍittha</s>'—even there, the word aims at what is to be denoted, not at its own form, just as '<s>gaur vāhīkaḥ</s>' (the Bāhīka is an ox) aims at the quality being indicated. But by that alone, the Bāhīka does not become a cow. Therefore, since the convention is grasped between word and meaning which are indeed different, and since verbal usage is based on that, cognition—even when preceded by words—does not indicate co-referentiality of the word with its own object. But as for the word occurring first even in cognition where words are not the means—for one whose convention has been grasped, first through the contact of sense organ and object, by apprehension devoid of word-association, when the mere object is apprehended, because of the relation between the distinctions of that object and the distinctions of words, the latent impression whose content is the word is awakened. Once awakened, it generates the memory of the word. Thereby, for the learned person, cognitions subsequent to the indeterminate—even though not having words as their means—arise as preceded by words.

children.text:
tasmād vyutpannasyāpi nāmadheyasmaraṇāya pūrvameṣitavyo vinaiva nāmadheyamarthapratyayaḥ /
tadidam uktam--gṛhīte 'pi śabdārthasaṃbandhe asyārthasyāyaṃ śabdo nāmadheyamiti /
yadā tu so 'rtho gṛhyate nāmadheyarahito nāmadheyasmaraṇāt pūrvamavikalpena tadā pūrvasmād avyutpannāvasthāyām arthajñānāt na viśiṣyate iti /
yato na viśiṣyate tasmāt tadarthajñānaṃ tādṛgeva bhavati /
nanu parapratipādanādilakṣaṇavyavahārāya svarūpeṇa jñāne vyapadeṣṭavye yadarthavyapadeśena vyapadiśyate tadavagacchāmo 'rthavyapadeśākāramiti /
kathaṃ cārthākāraṃ bhavati? yadyarthavyapadeśayornābhedaḥ, tasmāt punarapi tādātmyaṃ prasaktamityata āha--tasya tviti /
children.translated_text: And how does it have the form of the object? If there is no non-difference between object and designation, then identity is again entailed—therefore he says: 'but of that.'

children.text: arthākārameva tu jñānamarthavyapadeśena vyapadiśyate anyathā aśakyatvādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The cognition, which has the form of the object, is designated by the designation of the object because it is otherwise impossible—such is the meaning.
Being understood by another.
He concludes—'therefore.'

Therefore, even for the learned, for the sake of remembering the name, a cognition of the object without the name must first be sought. This has been said—'even when the word-meaning relation has been grasped, of this object, this word is the name.' But when that object is grasped without a name, prior to the remembering of the name, through indeterminate [cognition], then it is not different from the cognition of the object in the state of not having learned [the convention] before. Since it is not different, that cognition of the object is just like that [earlier one]. Now, when cognition is to be designated by its own form for the purpose of practical usage characterized by communicating to others, and it is designated by the designation of its object—we understand that it has the form of object-designation.

children.text: tadevamarthajñānakāle # sa # na samākhyāśabdo vyāpriyate pratīyamānatayā, vyavahārakāle tu parapratyāyanakāle tu vyāpriyate kāraṇatayā /
tadanena gopālāvipālādīnāṃ saṃjñāniveśanaṃ tāsu tāsu vyaktiṣu vyavahārotkarṣahetuḥ
children.translated_text: By this, it is indicated that the establishment of names by cowherds, shepherds, and the like for those various individuals is the cause of increased practical usage,
not the cause of increased reality of the object.
Therefore, since the word '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (undesignable) indicates the freedom from word-accompaniment of this very indeterminate [cognition]—with this intention, he concludes: 'therefore.'

Thus, at the time of object-cognition, the convention-word does not operate in the mode of being cognized, but at the time of practical usage—the time of making another understand—it operates in the mode of being a cause.

children.text:
tadetad bhāṣyaṃ vārttikakāraḥ tātparyato vyācaṣṭe---taccendriyārtheti /
viṣayabhedānuvidhāyi jñānamiti śabdātmatāmapāroti /
cākṣuṣaṃ hi rūpajñānaṃ rūpa eva niyataṃ na śabde pravartate /
evaṃ śrautramapi śabda eva niyataṃ na rūpādau pravartate /
yadi punaridaṃ śabdātmakaṃ rūpādi bhavet, śrotrajaṃ jñānaṃ śabdagrāhīti rūpādāvapi pravarteta /
apravartamānaṃ vā vidhurayati rūpādīnāṃ śabdātmatām /
api ca śrūyamāṇaśabdātmatve rūpādīnām, teṣāmapi śravaṇagrāhyatvamityandho 'pi rūpu gṛhṇīyāt /
asti hi tasya śrotraṃ ca śabdajñānaṃ ca /
evaṃ badhiro 'pi śabdaṃ gṛhṇīyāt /
asti hi tasya locanaṃ ca rūpajñānaṃ ca /
aśabdo 'bhāva iti ca vivakṣitaviparītāpattiḥ śabdābhāvasyārthasya śabdatvāt, aśabdatve vā sa evāsyārthaḥ śabdād bhinnaḥ prasajyate /
evamabhāvo 'pyartha iti śabdaḥ syāt /
tathā ca nābhāvaḥ, śabdasya sattvāt /

children.translated_text: And thus cognition would not follow the object.
But it does.
Therefore objects do not have words as their nature.
The phrase 'at the time of its arising' rules out the accompaniment by words in the primary [moment].

The <s>Vārtikakāra</s> explains this <s>bhāṣya</s> in its purport—'that which [arises from] sense organ and object.' Cognition follows the distinctions of objects—thus he refutes the identity with words. For visual cognition of form is restricted to form alone and does not operate on words. Similarly, auditory [cognition] is restricted to words alone and does not operate on form etc. If form etc. were identical with words, then cognition born of the ear, being a grasper of words, would operate on form etc. too. Or, not operating [thus], it refutes the identity of forms etc. with words. Moreover, if forms etc. had the nature of heard words, then since they too would be graspable by hearing, even a blind person would grasp forms. For he has an ear and cognition of words. Similarly, even a deaf person would grasp words. For he has eyes and cognition of forms. And the undesirable consequence opposite to what is intended—[the claim that] 'absence is non-word'—would arise, since absence, being an object, would be a word; or if it is non-word, then that very object, being different from words, is established.

children.text:
ekadeśivyākhyānamāha---apare tviti /
indriyārthasannikarṣeṇa hi liṅgena yadindriyagātijñānaṃ tadapi pratyakṣalakṣaṇopetamiti pratyakṣaṃ prasajyata iti tannivāraṇāya avyapadeśyapadam /
apadeśo hetuvacanam /
tadeva tadābhāsebhyo viśiṣṭaṃ vyapadeśaḥ /
tasya kāryaṃ hetupratyāyanadvārā anumeyajñānaṃ vyapadeśyam /
na vyapadeśyamavyapadeśyamaliṅgobhdavam ityanumānaṃ vyāvartitamityarthaḥ /
tadekadeśimataṃ dūṣayati---tacca naivamiti /
nanvindriyagatijñānamapi indriyārthasannikarṣālliṅgādutpannamityata āha---na hyanumeyasyeti naitadindrayārthasannikārṣādupajāyate, kiṃ tu tajjñānāt /
ata evātīte 'pi dhūmādau liṅge tatsmaraṇamātrādevānumeyajñāna bhavati /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, even when the inferential mark such as smoke has passed away, the cognition of the inferable arises from the mere memory of it.

children.text: na ca sannikarṣapadasya mukhyatve saṃbhavati jñānalakṣaṇā yuktetti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: And when the word 'contact' (<s>sannikarṣa</s>) is taken in its primary sense, the figurative contact known as '<s>jñānalakṣaṇā</s>' (cognition-based contact) is not possible—this is the purport.
He concludes—'therefore.'

And those who, not understanding this <s>vārttika</s> text, supply the words 'in the objects of the sense organs' into the <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of excluding cognition arising from sense-organ movement [are mistaken].

He states the partial view's interpretation—'others, however.' For since through the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), which is a form of sense-object contact, the cognition arising from sense-organ movement would also possess the characteristics of perception, and thus perception would undesirably follow—to prevent this, the word '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (non-verbal/non-demonstrable) [is used]. '<s>Apadeśa</s>' means the reason-statement. That very thing, distinguished from its semblances, is '<s>vyapadeśa</s>' (demonstration). Its effect—the cognition of the inferable through the medium of conveying the reason—is '<s>vyapadeśya</s>' (demonstrable). What is not demonstrable is '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (non-demonstrable)—that which has not arisen from an inferential mark—thus inference is excluded—this is the meaning. He refutes that partial view—'and that is not so.' But surely, even the cognition arising from sense-organ movement is produced from the inferential mark, which is a form of sense-object contact—to this he says: 'for not of the inferable'—this does not arise from sense-object contact, but rather from the cognition of it.

children.text:
kramaprāptasyāvyabhicāripadasya tātparyaṃ brūvāṇo bhāṣyasyāpi tātparyamāha--grīṣme marīcaya itīti /
yadyapi sāmānyalakṣaṇenaiva vyabhicāriṇo nirastāḥ pratyayāḥ tadapekṣaṃ ca viśeṣalakṣaṇam, anyathā anumānādipadeṣvapyabhicādipadamupādeyaṃ syāt, tathāpi siddhe satyārambho niyamārthaḥ /
dvayī hi pramāṇānāṃ gatiḥ /
kiñcit sattāmātreṇapramāsādhanaṃ yathā pratyakṣam /
na hi cakṣurādīnāṃ grahaṇamupayujyate, api tu sattaiva /
anumānādīna tu svajñānena pramāsādhanāni /
na khalvagṛhītaṃ liṅgaṃ vā śabdo vā āgamasahitaṃ sādṛśyaṃ vā yathāviṣayam ādadhāti pramām /

children.translated_text: There, inference requires the grasping of non-deviation from the object prior to generating valid cognition, and not otherwise.
From that, valid cognition is accomplished.

children.text: śabdādau tu yadyapi pramopajananaṃ prati nārthāvyabhicāragrahāpekṣā, tathāpi śakyamatirohitārthamantramadhyapatitasya drāgityeva pratīyamānārthasyāpi,
children.translated_text: But in the case of verbal testimony and the rest, although the grasping of non-deviation from the object is not required for generating valid cognition, nevertheless, even for a <s>mantra</s> whose meaning is not hidden yet has fallen amidst [other mantras], whose meaning is cognized merely rapidly,
'<s>Sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū</s>' (a Vedic mantra of obscure meaning),

While stating the purport of the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' (non-errant) that comes in sequence, he also states the purport of the <s>bhāṣya</s>—'in summer, the heat-mirages.' Although errant cognitions are already excluded by the general definition alone, and the specific definition is relative to that—otherwise the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' would have to be included in the definitions of inference etc. as well—nevertheless, the undertaking of what is already established serves the purpose of restriction. For the operation of means of valid knowledge is of two kinds. Some produce valid cognition merely by existing, like perception. For the apprehension of the eye and other [sense organs] is not required; rather, their mere existence [suffices]. But inference and the rest produce valid cognition through their being cognized. Indeed, an unapprehended inferential mark, or verbal testimony, or similarity accompanied by scripture, does not produce valid cognition in its respective domain.

children.text:
ityevamādermantrasyāptapraṇetṛkatayā sāmānyato 'rthāvyabhicāritvaṃ grahītum /
autsargikaṃ hi śabdānāmarthaparatvam /
ata eva nigamaniruktavyākaraṇasahāyāstato 'rthamavadhārayanti /
evaṃ yathā mudgastambastathā mudgaparṇīti āptavākyaśravaṇādeva mudgastambasādṛśyajñānasyānupajanitaphalasyāpi śakyaṃ tadarthāvyabhicāritvaṃ niśrcetum /
pratyakṣasya tu pramāṇasyātyantaparokṣasvarūpolambha eva tāvat pramopajananāt prāg durlabhaḥ, prāgeta tu tasyārthāvyabhicāritvam /
yadyapi ca saṃvedanaprāmāṇyapakṣe 'pi tatsaṃvedanaṃ manasā sulabham, tathāpi na tanmātraṃ pramāṇam /
api tu asādhāraṇendriyārthasannikarṣasahāyamiti tatsahāyasya tasya parokṣatvameva /
tena pratyakṣasya pramāṇasya phalāvyabhicāreṇaivāvyabhicārajñānam, na svarūpataḥ ityetat pramāṇāntarebhyo vyāvṛttamasādhāraṇaṃ pratyakṣasya rūpamādarśayitumavyabhicāripadopādānam /
atha vā pratyakṣāvyabhicāra evānumānādyavyabhicāre kāraṇam /
na hyasti saṃbhavo 'vyabhicaritapratyakṣagṛhītapakṣadharmatākaṃ tarkasahāyapratyakṣagṛhītāvinābhāvaṃ cānumānaṃ vyabhicāratīti /
yattu bādhitaviṣayaṃ satpratipakṣitaṃ cānumānam, tadapi yadyapi prathamaṃ vyāptigrahaṇadoṣeṇa na khaṇḍitam, tathāpi khaṇḍanottarakālaṃ so 'pi pratīyate /
tathā ca vyāptigrāhi pratyakṣaṃ tatrāpi vyabhicārīti /
evamāgamo 'pi sākṣāt kvacit pāramparyeṇa pratyakṣapūrvakastadvyabhicāreṇaiva vyabhicarati /
āgamavyabhicāreṇaivopamānavyabhicāro vyākhyātaḥ /
tadevaṃ pratyakṣāvyabhicāre pramāṇānāmavyabhicāro 'stīti pratyakṣasyaiva viśeṣaṇamavyabhicāripadaṃ cakāra, netareṣāṃ pramāṇānām /
na hyasti saṃbhavastanmūlaṃ pratyakṣam avyabhicāri, tāni ca vyabhicārīṇīti /
so 'yaṃ viśeṣaḥ pramāṇāntarebhyaḥ pratyakṣasya /

children.translated_text: As the author of the <s>Mīmāṃsāvārttika</s> says,
By the non-deviation of perception and by the force of its own particular character,
since non-deviation is well-established, inference is not examined.

—of such a <s>mantra</s> as this, the non-deviation from meaning can be grasped in general through its being composed by a trustworthy person. For the natural tendency of words is to be directed toward meaning. For this very reason, aided by the <s>Nigama</s> (Vedic glossary), <s>Nirukta</s> (etymology), and <s>Vyākaraṇa</s> (grammar), they ascertain the meaning from it. Similarly, from merely hearing the trustworthy statement 'the <s>mudgaparṇī</s> plant resembles the <s>mudga</s> (mung bean) stalk,' even though the knowledge of the resemblance between the <s>mudga</s> stalk and [the <s>mudgaparṇī</s>] has not yet produced its result, it is possible to ascertain its non-deviation from meaning. But for the means of valid knowledge that is perception, the very apprehension of its utterly imperceptible nature is itself difficult to obtain prior to the generation of valid cognition—how much more so its non-deviation from the object. And although on the view that awareness is the means of valid knowledge, that awareness is easily obtained by the mind, nevertheless that alone is not the means of valid knowledge; rather, it requires the aid of the extraordinary sense-object contact—and therefore that aid is itself imperceptible. Hence, for perception as a means of valid knowledge, the knowledge of non-deviation is through the non-deviation of its result alone, not through its own nature—this unique characteristic of perception, distinguishing it from other means of valid knowledge, is shown by the inclusion of the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>.' Or alternatively, the non-deviation of perception itself is the cause of the non-deviation of inference and the rest. For there is no possibility that an inference whose thesis-property has been grasped by undeviated perception, and whose invariable concomitance has been grasped by perception aided by <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), would deviate. As for inference that has a contradicted subject-matter or an equally strong counter-argument—even though it was not initially refuted by a defect in the grasping of pervasion, nevertheless that [defect] becomes evident subsequently. And thus the perception that grasped the pervasion deviates even there. Similarly, scripture too, directly or indirectly preceded by perception, deviates precisely through the deviation of that [perception]. The deviation of analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) is explained through the deviation of scripture. Thus, since the non-deviation of the means of valid knowledge depends on the non-deviation of perception, the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' has been made a qualifier of perception alone, not of other means of valid knowledge. For there is no possibility that perception, being their root, is non-errant while they are errant. This is the distinguishing feature of perception from other means of valid knowledge.
Thus.

children.text: tasmāt suṣṭhūkaṃ grīṣme marīcaya iti bhāṣyam, tatpratiṣedhārthamidamucyate---avyabhicārīti //
children.translated_text: Therefore the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'in summer, the heat-mirages' is well said—this is stated for the purpose of negating that—'non-errant' (<s>avyabhicāri</s>).

children.text:
pṛcchati--kimidamiti /
uttaram--yadatasminniti /
etaccopapāditaṃ dvitīyasūtre /
punaḥ dūṣayati--tacca naivamiti /
pṛcchati--kasmāt? uttaram--arthasyeti /
tadeva sphorayati--yattaditi /
atra ca na nirvikalmakaṃ bhrāntam, kiṃ tu savikalpakamityāha--tāṃstu marīcīniti /
indriyeṇālocya marīcīn uccāvacamuccalato nirvikalpakena gṛhītvā paśrcāt tatropaghātadoṣād viparyeti, savikalpako 'sya pratyayo bhrānto jāyate iti /
children.translated_text: Having perceived the heat-mirages with the sense organ, having first apprehended them indeterminately as rising up and down, afterwards, due to the defect of impairment there, one errs—a determinate erroneous cognition arises in that person.
Therefore, the deviation belongs to the cognition, not to the object.

children.text: yathāhuḥ niruktakārāḥ, naiṣa sthāṇoraparādho yadenamandhe na paśyati /
children.translated_text: As the etymologists (<s>Nairaruktakāras</s>) say: 'It is not the fault of the post that a blind person does not see it.'
'It is the fault of the person.'

He asks—'what is this?' The answer—'that which [apprehends] in what is not that.' And this has been established in the second <s>sūtra</s>. He again refutes—'and that is not so.' He asks—'why?' The answer—'of the object.' He elaborates that—'that which, that.' And here it is not the indeterminate (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) that is errant, but rather the determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>)—therefore he says: 'those heat-mirages.'

children.text:
avyabhicāripadenaiva saṃśayajñānamapi vyudastam /
no khalu saṃśayajñānaṃ vikalpyamānavastugocaraṃ tadrūpaṃ vastu prāpayati /
aprāpayaccopadarśitaṃ kathaṃ saṃvādam, asaṃvādakaṃ ca kathamavyabhicāri? tasmādavyabhicāripadenaiva saṃśayajñāne niraste savikalpakapratyakṣāvadodhārthamupādīyamānaṃ vyavasāyātmakapadaṃ saṃśayajñānapratyakṣatāpākaraṇamanvācinoti /
tadyathā edhānāhartumaraṇyaṃ gaccha, śākamapyāneṣyasīti śākānayanamanvācīyate /
na ca tadevāsya preṣiturvi dhitsitam, tathehāpi /
vyavasāyātmakapadaṃ sākṣātsavikalpakasya vācakam /
tathā hi vyavasāyo viniśrcayo vikalpa ityanarthāntaram /
sa evātmā rūpaṃ yasya tat savikalpakaṃ pratyakṣam /
tadetadatisphaṭatvāt śiṣyairgamyata eveti bhāṣyavārttikakārābhyām avyākhyātamapi asmābhiḥ,
children.translated_text: This, being extremely clear, is understood by the students themselves—therefore, though not explained by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> and <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, by us,
who are intent on following the path charted by the teacher of <s>Trilocana</s>,
this has been explained thus, properly and in accordance with the facts.

By the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' (non-errant) alone, doubtful cognition too is excluded. For doubtful cognition, having as its object a thing being deliberated upon, does not lead to that thing in its real form. And if it does not lead [to the object] and yet has been pointed out, how can it be in agreement [with reality]? And if not in agreement, how can it be non-errant? Therefore, with doubtful cognition already excluded by the word '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' alone, the word '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' (of the nature of determination), included for the purpose of confirming determinate perception, implies the exclusion of doubtful cognition from being perception. Just as [in the command] 'go to the forest to fetch firewood—you will also bring back greens,' the bringing of greens is implied. And that [bringing of greens] is not the primary intention of the one commanding—similarly here too. The word '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' directly denotes the determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>). For <s>vyavasāya</s> (determination), <s>viniścaya</s> (ascertainment), and <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition) are synonyms. That whose nature (<s>ātman</s>) is that [determination]—that is determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>) perception.

children.text:
syādetat /
na vyavasāyātmakaṃ pratayakṣaṃ bhavitumarhati /
abhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsaṃ hi tat /
na cendriyārthābhyāṃ labdhajanma vijñānamarthāvabhāsaṃ śakyamabhilāpena yojanayitum /
na hyarthe śabdāḥ santi, arthātmano vā, tathā satyavyutpannasyāpi vyutpannavad vyavahāraḥ syādityuktam /
na cābhilāpo 'rthāsaṃsparśo saṃvedanadharmaḥ, artheṣu tanniyojanāt /
tasmādarthādupajāyamānaṃ jñānamarthamevādarśayet nābhilāpam /
na hi rūpāt jāyamānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ rasasahitametadādarśayati /
tasmādabhilāpasaṃsargānapekṣamabhilāpasaṃsargiṇamādarśayad vikalpavijñānaṃ vikalpavāsanotthāpitamaniyatārthagrāhi mānasamātmīyamutprekṣālakṣaṇaṃ vyāpāraṃ tiraskṛtyānubhavaprabhavatayā anubhavavyāpāraṃ darśanu puraskṛtya pravartamānamanubhavatayā abhimanyante pratipattāraḥ /
tat siddhametat, yadarthasāmarthyalabdhajanma, na tat śabdakalpanānugatam, yathā nirvikalpakam /
arthasāmarthyalabdhajanmāraśrca vivādādhyāsitā vikalpā iti prasaṅgasādhanaviruddhavyāptopalabdhiḥ /
śabdakalpanānugatatvasya hi pratiṣedhyasya viruddhaṃ tadananugatatvam, tenārthasāmarthyajatvaṃ vyāptam /
tasyopalabdhistadananugatatvamutthāpayantī tadanugatatvaṃ virūṇaddhīti /
athaiṣāṃ pratyayānāṃ pratyakṣamabhi lāpānugatatvamaśakyāpahnavam, hanta bhoḥ, nārthasāmarthyajatvamiti prasaṅgaviparyayaḥ /
tathā hi yadabhilāpakalpanānugataṃ na tadarthasāmarthyajaṃ yatheśvarapradhānādivikalpavijñānam /
tathā caite vivādādhyāsitā vikalpā iti vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiḥ /
niṣedhyamarthasāmarthyajatvaṃ tadabhilāpakalpanānanugatatvena vyāptaṃ tadviruddhaṃ ca sadanugatatvamiti /
na ca sandigdhavyatirekitā, arthasāmarthyena hi tadutpadyamānamartharūpam anukuryād na śabdarūpam /
na hyarthe śabdāḥ santi tadātmāno vetyuktam /
asaṃbaddharūpānukāre tu vijñānasya sarvarūpānukāreṇa sarvasarvajñātāpattirati /
saṅketavaśāt śabdānāmarthasaṃbandhenārthopalabdhau tatsmaraṇāt tatsaṃsṛṣṭavedanamiti cet? yatra tarhi te kṛtasaṅketāḥ tadeva smārayedetān /
tatraiva ca te kṛtasaṅketā yadanugataṃ sāmānyam /
na ca taddṛṣṭam, kiṃ tu svalakṣaṇaṃ darśanagocaraḥ /
tadeva hi paramārthasadvijñānasya kāraṇam, na tu sāmānyam /
sarvasāmārthyayahitaṃ hi tat alīkatvāt /
tasmād yad dṣṭaṃ na tena śabdānāṃ saṃbandhaḥ, yena ca saṃbandho na taddṛṣṭam /
api ca dṛṣṭasya śabdavācyatve darśanādiva vahinaruṣṇa iti vākyādapi pratīyeta /
tathā ca śabdādapi tasmin pratīte śītāpanopanaprasaṅgaḥ /
sāmānyaviṣayauliṅgaśabdau vastubhūtasāmānyavacca svalakṣaṇam /
tādṛśaṃ ca taddarśanasya kāraṇamiti nirvikalpakena prathamākṣatannipātajanmanā jātimadvastuvedanāt tatropalabdhacarasaṃbandhasya śabdasya smaraṇam /
tathā ca tacchabdābhidheyajātiviśiṣṭadravyāvagāhīndriyārthasannikarṣajanmā vikalpapratyayo gaurayamityevamākāro jāyata iti cet? yathāhuḥ,
nirvikalpakabodhena dvyātmakasyāpi vastunaḥ /

children.translated_text: [Verse reference: <s>Ślokavārttika</s>, Pratyakṣa 118]
And then after that, the cognition by which the thing is determined through its properties—universal and the rest—
that too is accepted as being of the nature of perception.

There might be this [objection from the Buddhist side]: determinate cognition (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>) cannot be perception. For it has an appearance that is fit for association with verbal designation (<s>abhilāpasaṃsargayogya</s>). And a cognition born from the sense organ and object, having the appearance of the object, cannot be associated with verbal designation. For words do not exist in objects, nor are they of the nature of objects—otherwise, even for the unlearned, there would be the same usage as for the learned—as has been said. Nor is verbal designation, being unconnected with objects, a property of awareness—since words are applied to objects. Therefore, a cognition arising from an object would manifest only the object, not verbal designation. For perception arising from form does not manifest 'this is accompanied by taste.' Therefore, conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpavijñāna</s>), which manifests what is associated with verbal designation without depending on verbal designation, is a mental cognition of one's own—having the character of imagination, grasping no fixed object, arising from conceptual impressions—which, by setting aside its own imaginative operation and, by virtue of arising from experience, foregrounding the operation of experience, proceeds as if it were experience, and perceivers regard it as experience. Thus it is established that what is born from the power of the object is not accompanied by verbal conceptual construction, like the indeterminate (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>). And the concepts that are the subject of dispute are born from the power of the object—this constitutes the apprehension of a property pervaded by what is contrary to the probandum (<s>prasaṅgasādhanaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi</s>). For what is to be negated is accompaniment by verbal conceptual construction; its contrary is non-accompaniment by that; and being born from the power of the object is pervaded by that [non-accompaniment]. The apprehension of that [non-accompaniment], by establishing the non-accompaniment, undermines the accompaniment. If, then, the accompaniment of these cognitions by verbal designation is perceptually undeniable—well then, they are not born from the power of the object—this is the reversal of the consequence (<s>prasaṅgaviparyaya</s>). For thus: whatever is accompanied by verbal conceptual construction is not born from the power of the object, like conceptual cognitions of God, <s>Pradhāna</s>, etc. And these concepts are the subject of dispute—this is the apprehension of a property pervaded by what is contrary to the pervader (<s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s>). What is to be negated—being born from the power of the object—is pervaded by non-accompaniment by verbal conceptual construction; and its contrary, namely accompaniment, [is what is apprehended]. And this is not a case of doubtful negative concomitance: for what arises from the power of the object would replicate the form of the object, not the form of the word. For words do not exist in objects, nor are they of the nature of objects—as has been said. But if a cognition were to replicate an unconnected form, then by replicating all forms, there would be the unwanted consequence of everyone knowing everything. If one says: by virtue of convention, through the connection of words with objects, upon perceiving the object, the memory of that [convention] produces cognition associated with that [verbal designation]—then those words with which convention has been established should be recalled only regarding that [thing where the convention was established]. And it is regarding the universal that pervades those things that the convention was established. But the universal is not perceived; rather, the particular alone (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) is the object of perception. For only the particular, being ultimately real, is the cause of cognition—not the universal. For the universal, being unreal, is devoid of all causal power. Therefore, what is perceived has no connection with words, and what has connection with words is not perceived. Moreover, if what is perceived were expressible by words, then just as one would know 'fire is hot' from seeing, so too one would know it from a statement—and thus from a statement about it, one would experience heat-removal—which is absurd. The inferential mark and the word, having universals as their objects, and the particular, like a real universal [if it existed, would function like perception]. And since such [a universal] is the cause of perception, through indeterminate cognition born at the first moment of sense-contact, there is the cognition of a thing possessing a universal (<s>jāti</s>); and from the recollection of the word whose connection was grasped there, a conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) born from sense-object contact, having the form 'this is a cow,' arises, encompassing the substance qualified by the universal denoted by that word—if so? As they say: 'Even of a thing having a dual nature, apprehension by indeterminate cognition [occurs].'

children.text:
# ślo. vā. pratyakṣa. 120 # iti /
tanna, piṇḍavivekena jātyāderavikalpakenāgrahaṇāt /
na hi jātijātibhantau vā kriyākriyāvantau va guṇaguṇinau vā tatsamavāyo vā vivekena cakāsati /
children.translated_text: For neither the universal and what possesses the universal, nor action and what possesses action, nor quality and what possesses quality, nor their inherence, shine forth in distinction [in indeterminate cognition].

children.text: na ca vivekenāpratibhāsamānaḥ śakyā mitho yojayituṃ kṣīrodakavadatadvedinā /
children.translated_text: And things that do not appear as distinct cannot be combined with each other by one who does not know their [distinction], like milk and water.

Therefore, we see it as proper that a single, undifferentiated particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), upon which the distinctions of universal (<s>jāti</s>) and the like are superimposed by the latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) of beginningless conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), is conceptualized in that way.

children.text: api ca paramārthasadvastudvayavedane 'pi kuto viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvaḥ? na hyaṅgulyāvekavijñānaviṣayau mitho viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvamāpadyete //
children.translated_text: Moreover, even when two ultimately real entities are cognized, whence comes the qualifier-qualified relation? For two things that are objects of a single cognition, as in the case of a finger-ring, do not assume the qualifier-qualified relation with each other.
[Verse reference: <s>Ślokavārttika</s>, Pratyakṣa 120] Not so—because the universal and the rest are not grasped by the indeterminate [cognition] as distinguished from the concrete particular.

children.text:
viśeṣaṇa khalūpakārakam, upakāryaṃ ca viśeṣyam /
nānyathā tayostabhdāvaḥ /
na caikavijñānasamārūḍhayorjñāpyajñāpakabhāvo vā kāryakāraṇabhāvo vā saṃbhavī, samānakālayoḥ tayorūbhayorapi paurvāparyaniyamāt /
api ca vastuniveśe jātyādīnāmupādhīnāmekasya vastunaḥ sattvaṃ ca dravyatvaṃ ca pārthivatvaṃ ca vṛkṣatvaṃ ca śiṃśapātvaṃ copādhaya iti dūrādekopādhiviśiṣṭasya grahe sarvopādhiviśiṣṭagrahaprasaṅgaḥ /
tathā hyādhārādheyabhāva upakāragarbho bhavati /
patanadharmaṇo hi badarasyottarasya kuṇḍamadharaṃ pratayāsannamapatanadharmakaṃ badaraṃ vidadhadādhāraḥ /
tadvadihāpi dravyeṇa jātyādīnāmupādhīnāmupakartavyam /
na ca śaktyantarairūpakaroti /
śaktyantarapakāre 'pi śaktyantaraukalpanāyām anavasthāpātāt /
tasmāt svabhāva eva svakāraṇādhīnajanmā dravyasya sa tādṛśo yena bahūnāmupādhīnāmupakarotīti vācyam /
tathā ca sattvopakārasamartheṃ tasmin dravye gṛhyamāṇe dravyatvādyupakārasamartho 'pi sa evāsya svabhāva iti tatsvabhāvāvacchinnāḥ sattvavikalpakena paramārthasaddravyāvagāhinā sarva eva dravyatvapārthivatvavṛkṣatvaśiśapātvādayo viṣayīkṛtā iti vikalpāntarāṇāmānarthakyam /

children.translated_text: As he says:
Even for one who holds that the object, which is differentiated and apprehended by cognition, has diverse conditions,
in the apprehension of the intrinsically differentiated [substance] whose limbs of assisting by diverse conditions are capacities,
what undetermined distinction could there be for the entity that is to be assisted in its entirety?

The qualifier is what assists, and what is assisted is the qualified. Their relation is not otherwise. And for two things that have entered into a single cognition, there cannot be either a relation of the informing and the informed, or a cause-effect relation, because both being simultaneous, neither can have priority. Moreover, if universals and the like are conditions (<s>upādhi</s>) of a single entity — existence (<s>sattva</s>), substance-ness (<s>dravyatva</s>), earth-ness (<s>pārthivatva</s>), tree-ness (<s>vṛkṣatva</s>), and <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness being conditions [of a single thing] — then, upon apprehending something qualified by one condition from a distance, there would be the undesirable consequence of apprehending it as qualified by all conditions. For the container-contained relation involves assistance. For a container supports the lower jujube fruit that tends to fall, providing it with a non-falling jujube fruit above. Similarly here too, the substance must assist the conditions such as universal and the like. And it does not assist through other capacities. For even if it assisted through another capacity, the postulation of yet another capacity [to explain that] would lead to an infinite regress.
