Therefore, it must be said that it is the very intrinsic nature of the substance, born from its own causes, which is such that it assists many conditions. And thus, when that substance capable of assisting existence is being apprehended, that very intrinsic nature of it is also capable of assisting substance-ness and the like. Therefore, all [conditions] — substance-ness, earth-ness, tree-ness, <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness, and the like — being delimited by that intrinsic nature, are made objects by the conceptual cognition of existence, which grasps the ultimately real substance. Thus other conceptual cognitions are purposeless.
When the thing to be apprehended has a single assistance, the other [conditions] do not provide further assistance.
What is not seen when that [single assistance] is seen — in apprehending that, there is apprehension of the whole.

children.text:
iti /
asmākaṃ tu anādivikalpavāsanopādānā vikalpā yacca gṛhṇanti, yacca adhyavasyanita tayorūbhayorapyanyanivṛttirūpatayā avastutvāt matāgapi na paramārthasad vastu gāhante, pāramparyeṇa tu vastupratibandhāt tatra pravartayantaḥ prāpayantaśca na visaṃvādayanti lokam /
ato vastusabhdāvāviniveśād vikalpānāṃ na paunarūktyamasti /
api cālocite vastunīndriyeṇa tadanantarotpannaṃ śabdasmaraṇavyavahitavyāpāramindriyamarthaśrca na savikalpikāmapi dhiyamupajanayitumarhataḥ /

children.translated_text: As he says:
Even when the object is being utilized, the subsequent association with the word, which belongs to memory,
if the sense-cognition were to depend on it, that object would become mediated [i.e., non-perceptual].

Thus. But for us, the conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpas</s>), which arise from the material cause of beginningless conceptual latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), are such that both what they apprehend and what they determine — being of the nature of the exclusion of others (<s>anyānivṛtti</s>) — are non-entities. Therefore, even though accepted [by us], they do not grasp an ultimately real entity. But by indirectly being grounded in reality, they cause [people] to engage and attain [their goals] without misleading the world. Therefore, since conceptual constructions do not involve real entities and words, there is no redundancy among them. Moreover, when the object has been inspected by the sense organ, the sense organ and the object, whose operation is intervened by the recollection of the word arising immediately after, are not capable of generating even a determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>) cognition.

children.text:
na ca yadevālocanamajījanadindriyaṃ tadeva smaraṇasahakāri vikalpapratyayamādhatte /
na ca smṛtirvyavadhāyikā, svāṅgamavyavadhāyakamiti nyāyāt /
yato yaḥ prāgajanako buddherūpayogāviśeṣataḥ /
sa paśrcādapi /
iti no khalvatītaṃ bhavati gocaro 'kṣasya /

children.translated_text: And what is not in its domain, even a thousand means cannot cause it to operate upon.
And memory cannot make a present thing, which has not been previously experienced, the object of a past [cognition].
And if it could make it its object, then there would be the undesirable consequence that even blind persons would directly perceive form. As he says:
By that, even without the eye, there would be visual cognition.

And it is not the case that the very sense organ that generated the initial inspection (<s>ālocana</s>) then, becoming an associate of memory, produces a conceptual cognition. Nor does memory obstruct [the sense organ], by the principle that what is subsidiary does not obstruct. Because: that which did not generate [a determinate cognition] earlier, due to no difference in the utilization of the sense organ, does not generate [it] later either. And indeed the past is not the domain of the sense organ.
Even the conceptual construction of substance, as in 'the one with a stick' (<s>daṇḍī</s>)—

children.text: viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyaṃ ca saṃbandhaṃ laukikīṃ sthitim /
children.translated_text: having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the worldly convention,
combining all this, one cognizes in that way, not otherwise.
Thus, the conceptual constructions of name, universal, quality, and action have been dismissed as not being perceptual.

children.text: na caitāvantaṃ vyāpārakalāpaṃ vicārakanivartanīyamindriyajñānaṃ sahate, tasya sannihitaviṣayabalenotpatteravicārakatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the sense-cognition does not tolerate such an elaborate operational process that is to be rejected by critical examination, because it arises by the force of the proximate object without examination.

children.text: jātiguṇakriyāvatāṃ caitanna saṃbhavatyeva rūpavivekasaṃbandhayorapratibhāsanena ghaṭanāyogāt kṣīrodakavadatadvedinetyuktam /
children.translated_text: And for things possessing universal, quality, and action, this [conceptual construction] is simply impossible, because of the impossibility of combining them when the discrimination and relation between form are not manifest, like milk and water for one who does not know [their distinction] — this has been said.
Therefore, that conceptual construction is not perception.

children.text:
atrocyate /
yat tāvaduktam---arthasāmarthyajatvābhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsattvayoḥ virodha iti, tatra brūmaḥ /
syād virodho yadi svalakṣaṇamevārthaḥ, na tvetadasti /
upapādayiṣyati hi paramārthasantaṃ jātyādimantamarthaṃ sthemabhājamabhilāpasaṃsargayogyam /
tena tajjanitaṃ jñānamarthasāmarthyajaṃ cābhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsaṃ ceti na virodhaḥ /
tathā ca prasaṅgasādhanasya sandigdhavyatirekitā /
na ca dravyādyabhinnaṃ jātyādi bhinnaṃ kalpayanto vikalpā nārthasāmarthyajanmāna iti sāṃpratat /
dravyādapi hi bhedaḥ sādhayiṣyate teṣām /
yathā ca bhede 'pi teṣāṃ tadvācakānāṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tathopapāditamadhastāt /
na ca bhinnena śabdena ḍittho 'yamityabhedakalpanādarthasya vikalpānāmanarthajatvamiti yuktam /
uktametad avyapadeśyapadavyākhyānāvasare yathā na śabdābhedenārthayorekendriyajñānasaṃsargitā kiṃ tu prathamamālocito 'rthaḥ sāmānyaviśeṣavān saṅketagrahaṇsamayavartinīmātmano 'vasthāṃ smārayan tatkālabhāvinaṃ śabdamapi smārayatyavarjanīyatayā /
na tvindriyajavikalpotpādaṃ pratyastyupayogaḥ kaścit śabdasmaraṇasya /
anyathā bālamūkādīnāṃ nendriyajaḥ syādvikalpaḥ śabdasmaraṇābhāvāt /
saṅketasamayavartyavasthāsmaraṇaṃ tūpayujyate, vastunastadānīntanedānīntanāvasthābhedavata ekasyendriyajena vikalpenākalanāt /
śabdastu saṃpātāyāto na niveśayatyātmānam indriyaje vikalpe /

children.translated_text: As he says:
The word '<s>Devadatta</s>' and the like, present in the heart, by which [the person] is remembered —

children.text: cakṣuṣāpi sa evāyaṃ piṇḍaḥ saṃprati dṛśyate //
children.translated_text: that very same object is now seen by the eye directly.

Here we reply: As for what was stated — that there is a contradiction between arising from the force of the object and manifesting as fit for association with verbal expression — to that we say: there would be a contradiction if the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) alone were the object, but this is not so. For it will be established that the object is ultimately real, possessing universals and the like, enduring, and fit for association with verbal expression. Therefore, the cognition produced by it both arises from the force of the object and manifests as fit for association with verbal expression — and there is no contradiction. And thus the reductio proof has doubtful negative concomitance. And it is not proper that conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpas</s>), which construct universals and the like as non-different from substance and the like while [actually] being different, are not born from the force of the object. For the difference of universals from substance will also be established. And how, even with their difference, the words denoting them have co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) — that has been explained above. And it is not proper that, because a person named <s>Diṭṭha</s> is conceptualized as 'this is he' with a construction of non-difference using different words, conceptual constructions are not born from the force of the object. This has been stated at the occasion of explaining the word '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (inexpressible) — just as the oneness of the sense-cognition with the word is not established by the non-difference of the word, but rather the object first inspected, possessing universal and particular, causes the recollection of the state of the self at the time of learning the convention, and thereby inevitably also causes the recollection of the word present at that time. But the recollection of the word has no use for the generation of the sense-born conceptual cognition. Otherwise, infants, mutes, and the like would not have sense-born conceptual cognition, due to the absence of word-recollection. But the recollection of the state at the time of the convention is useful, because a single entity having different states at different times is not fully grasped by a sense-born conceptual cognition [of a single moment]. The word, however, arriving coincidentally, does not embed itself in the sense-born conceptual cognition.

children.text:
anena hi piṇḍasya pūrvāparāvasthāvartinīmekatāmindiyajavikalpagocaratvena darśayati, na tu śabdaniveśanamapi /
tathā,
saṃjñā hi smaryamāṇāpi pratyakṣatvaṃ na bādhate /
children.translated_text: For even a name (<s>saṃjñā</s>) being remembered does not obstruct the perceptual nature
of the named thing (<s>saṃjñin</s>).
Why?
That state of being at the bank [of memory] is not capable of covering form.
For by this, he shows the unity of the object across its prior and later states as the domain of sense-born conceptual cognition, but not the embedding of the word. Similarly,

children.text:
nārthendriyavyāpāraṃ vyavadhatte ityarthaḥ /
na ca prāgavasthāsmaraṇasāpekṣatayā nendriyārthasannikarṣaḥ kāraṇaṃ vikalpasyeti sāṃpratam /
yato,
na kiñcidekamekasmāt sāmagryāḥ sarvaṃsaṃbhavaḥ /
# pra. vā. 3.53 # iti bhavanto 'pyāhuḥ /

children.translated_text: Otherwise, [the sense organ and object], being dependent on light and attention, would not generate even a non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) [cognition].
That it did not generate [a conceptual cognition] at first is because of the absence of the cooperating factor of memory.

children.text: na hi nājījanat kuśūlasthaṃ bījamaṅkuramiti na samavahitakṣityādisahakārigrāmamapyasyājanakaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: For just because a seed stored in a granary does not produce a sprout, it does not follow that even with the full complement of cooperating factors such as soil and the like, it cannot produce one.

children.text: na ca janakatvājanakatvalakṣaṇo viruddhadharmasaṃsargo bhedaheturityupapādayiṣyate kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅge //
children.translated_text: And [the objection] that the co-occurrence of contradictory properties — being a producer and a non-producer — constitutes a reason for difference [of the seed] will be refuted in the refutation of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>).

That is, it does not obstruct the operation of the sense organ and the object — this is the meaning. And it is not proper that, because [conceptual cognition] depends on the recollection of a prior state, the contact of the sense organ with the object is not the cause of the conceptual cognition. Because: 'Nothing single arises from a single [cause]; everything arises from a totality of causes' (<s>Pra. Vā.</s> 3.53) — thus even you say.

children.text:
syādetat /
atītāvasthā nendriyagocarastasya vartamānārthe niyamāt /
na ca vartamāno 'rthaḥ smaraṇagocaraḥ smaraṇasyānubhavajanitasaṃskārodbodhajanmanaḥ pūrvānubhavagocaraṃ prati niyamāt /
tasmāt bhinnaviṣayatayā nendriyasahakāritā smaraṇasya /
na hi rūpaviṣayāḥ sahasramapi nayanapradīpādayaḥ śabdaviṣayasya śravasaḥ sahakāritāmāpadyanta iti /
tat kiṃ bhavatāṃ yatra gandhajñānānantaraṃ cākṣuṣaṃ rūpajñānaṃ jāyate tatra gandhajñānam na samanantarapratyayaḥ? tatrāpi hi cakṣūrūpaviṣayaṃ na gandhaviṣayasya jñānasya sahakāri bhavitumarhati, bhinnaviṣayatvādeva /
athānvayavyatirekanibandhanaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo na samānaviṣayatvamanuvidhīyate ityucyetra, tadasmākamapi samānam /
nanvatītāvasthāviśiṣṭatvam asya nendriyasannikṛṣṭamiti kathaṃ pratyakṣam? tat kiṃ yadindriyasaṃbaddhaṃ tat pratyakṣam? tathā satyākāśaparamāṇvādayo 'pi tatsaṃyuktā iti te 'pi pratyakṣāḥ prasajyeran /
tasmād yadevendriyajasya jñānasya gocarastat pratyakṣam /
na tvindriyasaṃbaddham /
nanvasaṃbaddhamindriyaṃ kathaṃ tatra jñānaṃ janayati? tacca jñānaṃ kathaṃ pratyakṣam?
children.translated_text: But then, how does a sense organ that is not connected [with the past state] generate cognition regarding it? And how is that cognition perceptual?

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ cet, kathamindriyārthasannikarṣotpannamiti lakṣaṇaṃ pratyakṣaṃ vyāpnoti, asyaiva pratyakṣasya lakṣaṇenāvyānāt? mā bhūdarthasya pūrvakālavartitā indriyagocaraḥ, tathāpi smaraṇasahakāriṇā saṃskārasahakāriṇendriyārthasannikarṣeṇopajanitaṃ tadindriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ na bhavati /
children.translated_text: If it is perceptual, how does the definition 'arising from the contact of the sense organ with the object' pervade perception, since this very perception is not pervaded by the definition? Let the past temporal state of the object not be the domain of the sense organ; even so, a cognition generated by the contact of the sense organ with the object cooperating with the impression cooperating with memory does not arise from the contact of the sense organ with the object [in that strict sense].
And thus the definition is not non-pervasive for it.

One might object: the past state is not the domain of the sense organ, since the sense organ is restricted to the present object. And the present object is not the domain of memory, since memory, arising from the awakening of impressions produced by prior experience, is restricted to the domain of prior experience. Therefore, due to having different objects, memory is not a cooperating factor of the sense organ. For even a thousand [factors] pertaining to form — such as the eye, lamp, and the like — do not become cooperating factors of the auditory sense, which pertains to sound. Then, according to you, when a visual cognition of form arises immediately after an olfactory cognition, is the olfactory cognition not the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>)? For there too, the eye pertaining to form-objects ought not to be capable of cooperating with olfactory cognition, precisely because of having a different object-domain. If it is said that the cause-effect relation is grounded in positive and negative concomitance and does not follow from having the same object-domain — that is equally our position. But [one might object:] since being qualified by the past state is not in contact with the sense organ, how is [such cognition] perceptual? Is it then the case that whatever is connected with the sense organ is perceptual? If so, space, atoms, and the like, being conjoined with it, would also be perceptual — and this would be an undesirable consequence. Therefore, whatever is the domain of a sense-born cognition — that is perceptual. But not [merely] whatever is connected with the sense organ.

children.text:
nanu pūrvāparāvasthāparāmarśijñānaṃ kathamekam, viṣayabhedāt pārokṣyāpārokṣyalakṣaṇaviruddhadharmasaṃsargācca? tathā hi taditi pārokṣyam, idamiti ca sākṣātkāraḥ /
na ca viruddhadharmasaṃsarge 'pyekatvam, trailākyasyaikatvaprasaṅgāt /
viṣayabhedaśrca pūrvadeśakālāparadeśakālasaṃbandhayorekasya virodhāt /
yathā hyekasmin padmarāgamaṇau gṛhyamāṇe tadabhāvo vyavacchidyate, yadi punarnaṃ vyavacchidyeta tadā bhāvo na paricchidyeta, tasya svābhāvavyavacchedarūpatvāt /
tadabhāvāvinābhāvinaśrca puṣparāgādaya iti te 'pi sarve vayavacchinna bhavanti /
yadi punarna vyavacchidyaran, sa eva puṣparāgādyatmeti tadavinābhāvī padmarāgābhāvaḥ padmarāgaśrca syāditi durghaṭamāpadyeta /
evaṃ tasyaiva pūrvadeśakālasaṃbandhe gṛhyamāṇe tadabhāvavyavacchedakrameṇāparadeśakālasaṃbandho vyavacchinnaḥ /

children.translated_text: being invariably concomitant with the absence of the relation to the prior place-time.
And thus it is not of the nature of the relation to the prior place-time.

children.text: tathāpi yadyasau taddeśakālasaṃbandhādanyasvabhāvo bhavet, tathā sati sa eva bhavet, na bhavecceti durghaṭamāpadyeta /
children.translated_text: Even so, if it were of a nature other than the relation to that place-time, then a contradiction would result — that it would both be and not be the same thing.

children.text: tasmāt pūrvadeśakālasaṃbandhādanyo 'paradeśakālasaṃbandha iti siddho viṣayabheda iti //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the relation to a later place-time is different from the relation to a prior place-time — thus the difference in object is established.

But how is the cognition that apprehends the prior and later states a single [cognition], given the difference in objects and the co-occurrence of contradictory properties characterized as mediate and immediate? For 'that' implies mediacy, and 'this' implies direct apprehension. And there is no unity amid the co-occurrence of contradictory properties, lest the three worlds become one. And the difference in object [is as follows:] because one entity's relation with a prior place-time and with a later place-time are contradictory. Just as when a single ruby is being apprehended, its absence is excluded; and if it were not excluded, then the presence would not be delimited, since [presence] has the nature of excluding its own absence. And things inseparable from that absence, such as topaz and the like, are also all excluded. But if they were not excluded, then the very one would be identical with topaz and the like, and its inseparable absence of ruby would be [identical with] the ruby — and an impossibility would result. Similarly, when the relation with a prior place-time of that very entity is being apprehended, through the sequence of excluding its absence, the relation with a later place-time is excluded.

children.text:
atrocyate /
yadi parokṣyāpārokṣyadharmabhedāt pūrvāparāvasthāparāmarśijñānaṃ bhidyeta, hanta bhoḥ, tadityapi vikalpo bhidyeta /
so 'pi hi parokṣaścāparokṣaśrca vikalpaścāvikalpaśrca /
arthe parokṣo vikalpaśrca svātmani tvavikalpo 'parokṣaśrca /
tasmād viṣayabhodāt virodha iti cet---na tvihāpi tadekaṃ jñānaṃ tasyaivaikasya vastunaḥ pūrvadeśakālasaṃbandhe parokṣamaparokṣaṃ vā paradeśakālasaṃbandha iti ko virodhaḥ? yo 'pi kāladeśasaṃbandhabhedena viṣayabheda uktaḥ, so 'pi ayuktaḥ /
yato yuktaṃ yat padmarāgasvarūpagrahe tadabhāvo vyavacchidyata iti, svābhāvavyavacchedātmakatvena bhāvānāṃ tadavyavacchede svarūpāgrahaṇaprasaṅgāt /
kasmāt punaḥ puṣparāgādayo vyavacchidyante, padmarāgābhāvāvinābhāvāditi cet? athaitadabhāvāvinābhāvajñānaṃ kutastyam? tayoḥ kadācidapi tādā tmyenānupalambhāditi cet---yatra tarhi tādātmyamupalabhyate na tatra tadabhāvāvinābhāvaḥ, tathā ca pūrvāparadeśakālasaṃbaddhastādātmyenānubhūyamāna indriyajena vikalpena padmarāgo na bhinno bhavitumarhati /
tasmāt parvāparadeśakālau tatsaṃndhau vā kāmaṃ bhidyeyātāṃ parasparābhāvāvinābhāvāt, tayorekadāpi tādātmyenāpratibhāsanāt /
na tu tadāliḍrigatasvabhāvaḥ padmarāgamaṇi/, tasya tābhyāmanyatvāt /
na cānyasya bhedo 'nyasya bhedamāpādayati, atiprasaṅgāt /
na cendriyārthasannikarṣābhāve 'pi pūrvāparāvasthāparāmarśātmano vikalpasya bhāvādanindriyajayatvamiti sāṃpratam, tathā satyavikalpakamapi kāmāturasya kāminīṃ bhāvayataḥ tadviṣayamindriyārthasannikarṣaṃ vināpi dṛṣṭamiti nīlādyanubhāvātmāno 'pi avikalpakā anindriyajāḥ prasajyeran /
yadi tu nīlādyanubhavānāṃ kāminyanubhavāt kathañcid viśeṣaṃ brūyāta, tadā asmākamapi anindriyajebhyo vikalpebhya utprekṣāvyāpārebhyo 'stīndriyajānāṃ darśanavyāpārāṇāṃ bhedaḥ /
na ca vikalpagato darśanavyāpāro 'nubhūyamānaḥ sati saṃbhave nirvikalpakopādhiriti yuktam /
sarvā eva hīndriyajā buddhayo vikalpikā avikalpikā vā dhārāvāhinyo 'mahamikayā parasparānapekṣā ekamarthamavagāhamānā udayante vyayante ca /
na tvamūṣāmanyonyamanugamyānugantṛtāmīkṣāmahe /
tasmāt indriyārthasannikarṣalabdhajanmāno vikalpā darśanavyāpārā nānya iti yuktamutpaśyamaḥ /
na ca śabdapratyakṣayorvastugocaratve satyapi pratyayābhedaḥ kāraṇabhedena pārokṣyāpārokṣyabhedopapatteḥ /
na ca vahinasaṃyogajanmā śītāpanodo vahinajñānād
bhavitumarhati /
na caikopādhinā sattvena viśiṣṭe tasmin gṛhīte upādhyantaraviśiṣṭatadgrahaprasaṅgaḥ /
svabhāvo hi dravyasyopādhibhirviśiṣyate, na tūpādhayo va tairviśiṣṭatvaṃ vā tasya svabhāvaḥ /
na ca yat svabhāvasaṃbandhi sa svabhāvaḥ /
tathā satyasaṃbandhitvameva /
na hi tadeva tena saṃbadhyate /
api ca rūpajñānaṃ viṣayagrahaṇadharma nānāparamāṇuviṣayaṃ na paramāṇusvabhāvaḥ /
tatsvabhāvatve vā teṣāṃ sarvān pratyaviśeṣāt sarvaireva te paramāṇavo viditāḥ syuḥ /
na cāsaṃbaddhā eva svajñānena rūpaparamāṇavo viṣayāstasyeti vācyam, asaṃbaddhasya viṣayatve 'tiprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: And it cannot be said that the atoms of form, unrelated [to a particular cognition], are its objects, since if the unrelated could be an object, there would be over-extension.

children.text: svabhāva evārthajñānabhedayoḥ saṃbandho yadartho viṣayo jñānaṃ ca viṣayīti cet? hantopādhyupādhimatorapi svabhāva eva saṃbandho 'stu tathāpi vijñānārthavanna svarūpābhedaḥ /
children.translated_text: If one says that the relation between object and object-cognition is just their essential nature—that whatever has an object is the cognition and whatever is an object is the object? Well then, let the relation between the conditioned and the condition also be just their essential nature—even so, there would be no identity of essential form, as in the case of cognition and object.
But in refuting momentary destruction and transformation, we shall establish a relation distinct from essential nature.
Therefore, when something is apprehended as possessing one condition, there is no absurd consequence of a cognition possessing all conditions.

Here it is said:
If the cognition that reflects on prior and subsequent states were to differ due to the distinction between the properties of being mediate and immediate, well then, even the conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) 'that' would differ.
For it too is both mediate and immediate, both conceptual and non-conceptual.
With regard to the object it is mediate and conceptual, but with regard to itself it is non-conceptual and immediate.
If one objects that the contradiction is due to difference of object—but here too, it is the same single cognition of the same single thing that is mediate in connection with a prior place and time, or immediate in connection with another place and time—so what contradiction is there? And the difference of object stated on the basis of difference in connection with time and place is also improper.
For it is proper that when the essential nature of a ruby is apprehended, the absence of that [other thing] is excluded; since the nature of things consists in the exclusion of their own absence, if that exclusion did not occur, there would be the absurd consequence of non-apprehension of their essential nature.
If one asks why topaz and the like are excluded—because of their invariable concomitance with the absence of the ruby? But whence comes this knowledge of invariable concomitance with its absence? If one says because they are never experienced as identical—then wherever identity is experienced, there should be no invariable concomitance with its absence. And thus the ruby, experienced as identical through the conceptual cognition born of the senses that is connected with prior and subsequent places and times, should not be capable of being different.
Therefore, the prior and subsequent places and times, or their connections, may freely differ from each other, because of their invariable concomitance with mutual absence, since they never appear as identical.
But not the ruby gem whose nature pervades those [times and places], since it is different from both.
And the difference of one thing does not bring about the difference of another, due to over-extension.
And it is not proper to say that because <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition), whose nature is reflecting on prior and subsequent states, exists even in the absence of sense-object contact, it is therefore not born from the senses. For if that were so, then even the non-conceptual experience of a man tormented by passion who visualizes his beloved—observed even without sense-object contact with that object—would entail that even non-conceptual cognitions having the form of experiencing blue and the like are not born from the senses.
But if one could state some distinction of the experiences of blue and the like from the experience of the beloved woman, then we too can state that sense-born cognitive operations of seeing differ from non-sense-born <s>vikalpas</s> and acts of imagination.
And it is not proper that the cognitive operation of seeing, present in <s>vikalpa</s> and being experienced, is, when there is the possibility [of being sense-born], merely a condition for the non-conceptual.
For all sense-born cognitions—whether conceptual or non-conceptual—arise and perish in a continuous stream, independently of one another, without any mutual regard, each plunging into a single object.
And we do not see among these any relation of following and being followed.
Therefore, we see it as proper that <s>vikalpas</s> born from sense-object contact are cognitive operations of seeing and nothing else.
And there is no identity of cognition between verbal testimony and perception even when they have the same object, since the difference of being mediate and immediate is justified by the difference of cause.
And the removal of cold born from the contact of fire cannot arise from the knowledge of fire.
And when something is apprehended as qualified by one condition (<s>upādhi</s>), namely existence, there is no absurd consequence of apprehending it as qualified by another condition.
For it is the essential nature of a substance that is qualified by conditions, but the conditions themselves, or the state of being qualified by them, is not its essential nature.
And it is not the case that whatever is related to the essential nature is the essential nature.
If so, there would be non-relatedness itself.
For the same thing is not related to itself.
Moreover, the cognition of form, having the property of object-apprehension, has multiple atoms as its object—it is not the essential nature of the atoms.
Or if it were their essential nature, since there is no distinction among them with respect to all [cognitions], all those atoms would be known by everyone.

children.text:
yaccaikavijñānagocarayorna viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva iti, tatra brūmaḥ /
bhinnajñānagocaratve 'pi nāsau saṃbhīti /
na hi viśeṣaṇajñānaṃ viśeṣyāviṣayaṃ viśeṣyamavacchettumarhati /
evaṃ viśeṣyajñānamapi viśeṣaṇāviṣayaṃ kena svaviṣayamavacchindyāt, tayoḥ parasparavārtānabhijñatvāt? tābhyāṃ vāsanā, tato mānasapratyayo viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvākara utpadyate /
na tvasti viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvo vāstava iti cet? astu tāvad vāstavāvāstavacintā /
children.translated_text: If one objects that there is no real qualifier-qualified relation? Let the question of real versus unreal be set aside for now.
For this will be dealt with later on.

children.text: yastu bhavatāmasya mānasatve prayāsaḥ, sa varamindriyajatva eva bhavatu, tathā sati darśanavyāpāratvamasya sākṣāt samarthitaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: But the effort you make to establish this as mental—that effort would be better directed toward establishing it as sense-born, since in that case its being a cognitive operation of seeing would be directly established.
For otherwise, one would have to posit a non-conceptual [cognition] as a basis.

And as for the claim that there is no qualifier-qualified relation among what are objects of a single cognition—to that we say:
Even when they are objects of different cognitions, that [relation] is not possible.
For a cognition of the qualifier that does not have the qualificand as its object cannot delimit the qualificand.
Similarly, a cognition of the qualificand that does not have the qualifier as its object—by what would it delimit its own object?—since the two are unaware of each other's affairs. From those two arise latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), and from those arises a mental cognition having the form of the qualifier-qualified relation.

children.text:
nanvavicārakamindriyajñānaṃ kathaṃ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyādi sakalaṃ saṃkalayet? hanta bhoḥ kiṃ mānasamapi jñānaṃ saṃkalayitumarhati? saṃkalayati manasastatkāraṇasya sarvaviṣayatvāt iti cet? yadi pūrvakaṃ vijñānaṃ manaḥ, kathaṃ tasya sarvaviṣayatā? asmākaṃ tu manaḥ sarvaviṣayamapi acetanatayā na vicārakam /
tasmādātmaiva sakalajñānatajjanitavāsanādhāraḥ smartā ca pratisandhātā ca /

children.translated_text: As it is said—

children.text: ātmanyeva sthitaṃ jñānaṃ sa hi boddhātra gamyate /
children.translated_text: Knowledge abides in the self alone, for it is understood that the self is the knower here.

children.text: smaraṇe cāsya sāmarthyaṃ sandhānādau ca vidyate //
children.translated_text: And it has the capacity for memory and for synthesis and the like.

But how can sense-born cognition, which is non-investigative, compile the entire qualifier-qualified relation and the like? Well then, can mental cognition compile it? It compiles because the mind, its cause, has all objects as its domain—if so objected? If the mind is a prior cognition, how can it have all objects as its domain? But for us, the mind, though having all objects as its domain, is not investigative, being non-conscious.
Therefore, the self (<s>ātman</s>) alone, being the substratum of all cognitions and the latent impressions born from them, is the one who remembers and connects.

children.text: # ślo. vā. pratyakṣa. 122 # sa salvindriyārthasannikarṣādālocya jātimantaṃ saṃmugdhamartham udbuddhasaṃskārasamupajātapūrvapiṇḍānusmṛtisahāyaḥ prāgeva cakṣuṣā vikalpayati, gaurayamiti /

children.translated_text: As it is said—

children.text: karaṇaṃ cendriyaṃ buddheḥ kartā cātma sacetanaḥ /
children.translated_text: The sense organ is the instrument of cognition, and the self, being conscious, is the agent.
And that [self], being capable of memory, will conceptualize all objects.

[<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Pratyakṣa</s> 122.] That [self], having perceived through sense-object contact an object possessing a universal but whose [particular nature is] confused, aided by the recollection of a prior composite occasioned by the awakening of latent impressions, conceptualizes through the eye itself, even at the outset: 'this is a cow.'

children.text:
tenaikavijñānavedyatve yadyapi jñāpyajñāpakabhāvarūpa upakāryopakārakabhāvo nāsti, tathāpi, tadarthālocanānugatasmaraṇayorviśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvāvagāhi vijñānaṃ pratyutpādakatvamevopakārakatvamasti /
arthau hi rūparūpibhāvena sthitāvapi nāpātajanmanā jñānena tathā gṛhītau, api tu svarūpamātreṇa /
na hi yāvadasti tāvad grahītavyam, tena tadekadeśagrahe 'pi nāpramāṇatā /
savikalpakaṃ tūktasāmagrījanma jātyādirūpatayā dravyaṃ ca rūpitayā kalpayat paścājjāyamānamapīndriyārthasannikarṣaprabhavatayā pratyakṣaṃ bhavatyeva /

children.translated_text: And even for what is non-sequential, producing effects sequentially due to the presence of different auxiliary factors will be established.

children.text: tat siddhametad vivādādhyāsitā vikalpāḥ svagocare pratyakṣā avyabhicāritve sati indriyārthasannikarṣajatvāt /
children.translated_text: Thus it is established: the disputed <s>vikalpas</s> (determinate cognitions) are perceptual in their own domain, because they are born from sense-object contact when there is non-deviation.

children.text: yo ya evaṃbhūtaḥ sa sarpaḥ pratyakṣo yathālocanam, tathā caitat /
children.translated_text: Whatever is of this nature is perceptual, like immediate apprehension—and so it is with these.
Therefore it is so.

Therefore, although when two things are known by a single cognition there is no relation of informer-informed or helper-helped, nevertheless, because the cognition generates the perception of the object and the accompanying recollection in the qualifier-qualified relation, its being a productive cause is itself its being a helper.
For the two objects, though existing in the relation of form and form-possessor, are not apprehended as such by the cognition born of immediate apprehension, but only in their bare essential form.
For it is not the case that everything that exists must be apprehended; therefore, even in apprehending only a part, there is no invalidity.
But the determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>) cognition, born from the stated aggregate of conditions, conceptualizing the substance as having the form of universal and the like, and as possessing form—though arising later—is indeed perceptual, because it originates from sense-object contact.

children.text:
tasmāt savikalpakapratyakṣāvarodhārthaṃ vyavasāyātmakapadamiti siddham /
tadasya savikalpakapratyakṣāvarodhārthasyānvācīyamāno vyavacchedaḥ /
tadvyavacchedyapratipādanārthaṃ bhāṣyamanubhāṣyānvācīyamānameva vyavasāyātmakapadasyārthamāha--dūrāccakṣuṣeti /
na caitanmantavyamiti bhāṣyaṃ vyācikhyāsuśrcodayati--na saṃśayasyeti /
nanu satīndriyārthasannikarṣe purovartini dravye dhūma iti vā reṇuriti vā jñānamutpadyamānaṃ kathamanindriyajamityata āha--na hīti /
kasmānmānasa ityata āha--saṃśītiriti /
saṃpūrvo hi śīḍ bhāvapratyayānto viśeṣāpekṣe vimarśe vartate sa caikādhikaraṇau smaryamāṇau mitho viruddhau dharmāvāropayan anyatarannāvadhārayati /
tathā cādhikaraṇamātrasamarpaṇamindriyajavyāpāraḥ /
manasā tu smaraṇasahakāriṇaiva puruṣaḥ saṃśete /
ata eva visphāritākṣāḥ saudāminīsaṃpātāt sakṛdālocya kañcit samānadharmavantaṃ dharmiṇaṃ samandhakāre sandigdhe, tasmānmānasa evaiṣa saṃśayo na tvindriyaja ityarthaḥ /
tadetat pariharan na caitadityādi bhāṣyaṃ vcācaṣṭe---tacca naivam /
kasmāt saṃśayasyeti--ubhayaṃ tviti /
tu śabdo manomātranimittatvaṃ vyavacchinatti /
tadanena cakṣuṣā hītyādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
paśyan samānadharmāṇaṃ dharmiṇaṃ nāvadhārayati /
viśeṣataḥ sandigdhe tasminnityarthaḥ /
indriyeṇopalabdhaṃ sannikṛṣṭaṃ sannikarṣapūrvakatvāduparladheḥ manasopalabhate jānīte cakṣuḥsahāyenetyarthaḥ /
atra bhāṣyaṃ yacca tadindrayānavadhāraṇapūrvakaṃ manasānavadhāraṇaṃ tadviśeṣapekṣaṃ vimarśamātraṃ saṃśayaḥ, na parvamiti /
anavadhāraṇaśabdo 'yaṃ saṃśayajñānavācakaḥ svakāraṇendriyārthasannikarṣe prayukta upacāreṇa /
uparatendriyavyāpārasya hi saṃśayajñānadarśanāt /
satyapīndriyavyāpāre saṃśayo nendriyaja iti codako 'bhimanyate /
tadanayoḥ saṃśayajñānayormadhye yat tadindriyāvadhāraṇapūrvakamindriyārthasannikarṣapūrvakaṃ manasānavadharaṇaṃ saṃśayajñānamityarthaḥ /
na pūrvam /
yaduparatendriyavyāpārasya saṃśayajñānaṃ dṛṣṭāntatayā hṛdi sthitaṃ śaṅkiturityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: the doubt-cognition that occurs when the operation of the sense organ has ceased is what stands in the mind as an illustration, i.e., as what is suspected.
He explains this <s>bhāṣya</s>—'there, what is of sense-object.'
The compound is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> (appositional compound): 'the sense-object contact which is itself the non-determination.'
The meaning is: the non-determination by the mind, preceded by that [sense-object contact], is doubt-cognition.

Therefore, the word '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' (of the nature of determination) is for the purpose of including determinate perception (<s>savikalpaka pratyakṣa</s>)—this is established.
That which is being additionally read as the exclusion of this [i.e., what is to be excluded by the word 'determination'].
To explain the meaning of the word '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' as an additional reading for the purpose of showing what is to be excluded, he comments on the <s>bhāṣya</s>—'from a distance, with the eye.'
'And this should not be thought'—wishing to explain this <s>bhāṣya</s>, he raises an objection—'not of doubt.'
But when there is sense-object contact with the object present before one, the cognition arising as 'is it smoke or dust?'—how is it not sense-born?—therefore he says—'for not.'
Why is it mental?—therefore he says—'deliberation (<s>saṃśīti</s>).'
For the root '<s>śīḍ</s>' with the prefix '<s>sam</s>,' ending in the suffix of state, refers to a deliberation that requires distinction; and that, imposing two mutually contradictory properties recalled as pertaining to a single substrate, does not determine either one.
And thus, the mere presentation of the substrate is the operation of what is sense-born.
But through the mind alone, assisted by memory, the person doubts.
For this very reason, those with wide-open eyes, having once perceived by a flash of lightning some property-bearer possessing a common property, [remain] in doubt in the darkness—therefore this doubt is mental only, not sense-born—this is the meaning.
Resolving this, he explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'and this is not so'—'and that is not so.'
'Why, of doubt?'—'but both.'
The word 'tu' (but) excludes the [view that doubt is caused by] mind alone.
By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'for by the eye' has been explained.
Seeing a property-bearer possessing a common property, one does not determine it.
The meaning is: when it is doubted with respect to its particular [nature].
What is apprehended by the sense organ is proximate, because apprehension is preceded by proximity; the mind apprehends, i.e., knows, with the aid of the eye—this is the meaning.
The <s>bhāṣya</s> here states: 'that non-determination by the sense organ, preceded by that very [non-determination], and the non-determination by the mind—that which is merely a deliberation requiring distinction—is doubt, not the former.'
The word 'non-determination' here denotes doubt-cognition, used figuratively with reference to its cause, the sense-object contact.
For doubt-cognition is observed even when the operation of the sense organ has ceased.
The objector holds that even when the operation of the sense organ exists, doubt is not sense-born.
Among these two doubt-cognitions, the one that is preceded by sense-determined non-determination, preceded by sense-object contact, and is the non-determination by the mind—that is doubt-cognition—this is the meaning.
Not the former.

children.text:
nanu smaraṇavyavahitavyāpāramasya kāraṇaṃ nendriyamityata āha--tasya hīti /
upapāditametadadhastāt yathā smaraṇaṃ nendriyavyāpāraṃ vyavadhatta iti /
pūrvaṃ tviti /
dṛṣṭantatayā pūrvatvam /
syādetat, mana evendriyānapekṣaṃ bāhye pravartate ityabhyupeyam, anyathā ghaṭamahaṃ jānāmīti jñānaṃ nirnimittaṃ syāt /
na tāvadindriyajam, āntare jñāne cakṣurādīnāmapravṛtteḥ /
nāpyanumānādiṣvantarbhavati, liṅgādyabhāvāt /
tasmānmānasabhevedam /
yadi ca ghaṭādau bāhye na manaḥ pravartena, kathaṃ ghaṭamiti bhavet? jānāmītyeva syāt /
na cārthanirupaṇamantareṇa jñānarūpanirūpaṇam, tasmād bāhyābhyantaraviṣayaṃ manaḥ, tathā ca sarva eva saṃśayo mānasa ityāśaṅkyāha bhāṣyakāraḥ, sarvatra ca pratyakṣaviṣaye iti /
children.translated_text: And the determination of the nature of cognition is not possible without the determination of the object; therefore the mind (<s>manas</s>) has both external and internal objects. And thus one might suspect that every doubt is mental. Anticipating this, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) says— 'and everywhere, regarding the object of perception.'

children.text: yadyapyayamīdṛśo 'nuvyavasāyo mānasastathāpyandhabadhirādīnāmabhāvāt tatpūrvaṃ vyavasāyotpattau cakṣurādyapekṣaṇīyam, anyathā andhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Although this kind of reflective determination (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>) is mental, nevertheless, for blind and deaf persons and the like, since they lack [such determinations], the eye and the rest must be required for the prior occurrence of the initial determination (<s>vyavasāya</s>); otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of there being no blind or deaf persons.

children.text: tathā ca saṃśayajñānotpāde apīndriyārthasannikarṣo 'pekṣaṇīya iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus, even in the production of the cognition of doubt, the contact of the sense organ with the object must be required— this is the purport.
This has been explained by the <s>vārttika</s> beginning with 'for of that.'

But is not the sense organ, whose operation is mediated by memory, not the cause of this?—therefore he says—'for of that.'
This has been established above—namely, that memory does not obstruct the operation of the sense organ.
'But the former'—
Its being 'former' is by way of illustration.
It may be objected: it should be accepted that the mind operates on external objects independently of the sense organs; otherwise, the cognition 'I know the pot' would be without a cause.
It is not sense-born, since the eye and the like do not operate on internal cognition.
Nor is it included under inference and the like, due to the absence of an inferential mark and the like.
Therefore this is mental.
And if the mind does not operate on the external pot and the like, how would 'pot' arise? There would only be 'I know.'

children.text:
avyāpakatvena lakṣaṇākṣepaparaṃ bhāṣyam ātmādiṣu ityāti /
tad vyācaṣṭe--indriyārtheti /
codayati--kathaṃ punariti /
pariharati--indriyeti /
mā bhūdindriyasūtre pāṭhaḥ /
taddhi bāhyendriyalakṣaṇam, āntaraṃ ca mana ityata āha--pṛthak ceti /
na ca sukhādau pramāṇāntaramasti /
tasmāt pāriśeṣyāt saddhiṃ pratyakṣatvamityāha---pratyakṣāśrceti /
nanu naite prameyāḥ svasaṃvedanasiddhatvāt, tat kimatra prameyārthena pramāṇena ityata āha---na ca teṣāmiti nanūktaṃ svasaṃvedanatayā na pramākarmabhāva eṣāmityata āha--na cānyā gatiriti /
saṃvedanatvena hi teṣāṃ svasaṃvedanatā, na caite saṃvedanamiti uktamadhastāditi bhāvaḥ /
ākṣepanupasaṃharati--tasmāditi /
bhāṣye cātmādiṣu sukhādiṣviti nityānityābhiprāyaṃ vargadvayam /
ātmasukhaduḥkhatvādayo nityāḥ anityāśca sukhaduḥkhādaya iti /
tadidamuktaṃ dignāgena,
na sukhādi prameyaṃ vā mano vāstvindriyāntaram /
na ca tat saṃbhavati, ghrāṇādisūtreṇa vibhāgapareṇa niṣedhāditi bhāvaḥ /
samādhibhāṣyam indriyasya vai sataḥ iti /
tadvyācikhyāsurgūḍhābhiprāyaḥ pṛcchati--kaścaivam iti /
ākṣepturuttaram--indriyārtheti /
samādhātā āha--naiṣa doṣa iti /
ākṣeptuḥ anuśayabījamudghāṭya dūṣayati--yattu sūtre iti /
nedaṃ vibhāgaparaṃ ghrāṇādisūtram, api tu lakṣaṇaparam /
tatra cendriyamapi mano na lakṣitam, vaidharmyādityarthaḥ /
vaidharmyamāha--vaidharmyamiti /
tatra pramāṇayati--sarvaviṣayaṃ tviti /
vaidharmyāntaraṃ dūṣayati---bhautiketi /
kāryasya hi viśeṣau bhautikatvābhautikatve, bhūtakāryaṃ bhautikam /
yad bhūtakāryaṃ na bhavati tadabhautikam /
bhūtakāryatvapratiṣedhaśrca tadanyakāryatvaṃ gamayati, viśeṣaniṣedhasya viśeṣāntarābhyanujñānahetutvāt /
itarathā tu akāryamevocyeta, na tvabhautikamiti /
tasmādakāryasya manaso 'bhautikatvaṃ kāryadharmo viruddhamityarthaḥ /
api ca vaidharmyāt manovat śrotramapi na vaktavyamityāha--śrotre ceti /
śaṅkate--svārtha iti /
bhūtāni hi ghrāṇādīni śrotrāntāni, manastu na bhūtamiti vaidharmyamityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti--tacca neti /
darśayiṣyati hi vārttikakāro yathā svārthiko na kaśrcidapi pratyaya ityarthaḥ /
ākṣepahetumanubhāṣate--yat purariti /
dūṣayati--na nāstīti /
tadadena sati cendriyārthasannikarṣe ityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
yaccāparaṃ vaidharmyaṃ ghrāṇādibhyo manasa uktaṃ bhāṣyakāreṇa tadapi siṃhāvalokanena dūṣayati---saguṇānāmiti /
ghrāṇādīni yathā svasvaguṇena gandhādinā bāhyaṃ gandhādi bodhayanti , naivaṃ svaguṇena śabdena śrotraṃ bāhyaṃ śabdaṃ bodhayati, tanmanovat śrotramapi ghrāṇādisūtre na paṭhitavyamityarthaḥ /
bhāṣyokteṣu madhya abhimataṃ vaidhamyamupasaṃharati--tasmāditi /
bhūtatvābhūtatvalakṣaṇaṃ vaidharmyaṃ na bhautikatvābhautikatvagrahaṇena śakyaṃ vaktumityavadhāraṇābhiprāyaḥ /
nanu yugapajjñānānutpatterjñānakāraṇaṃ manoḥ astītyavagamyate, na punarasyendriyatvamapi, tabhdāvānavagame ca nendriyārthasannikarṣajaṃ sukhādijñānaṃ śakyaṃ vaktumityata āha--tantrāntareti /
tantryate vyutpādyate anena tattvamiti tantraṃ śāstram /
tadanena manasaśrcetyādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
etad dūṣitaṃ dignāgena
aniṣedhādupāttaṃ cedanyendriyarutaṃ vṛthā /
iti /
taddūṣayitumupanyasyati----na śeṣeti /
taddūṣayati--na tantrayuktīti /
sarvasya tantrāntare loke ca siddhatvādavaktavyatāyāṃ svamatamiti nāsti /
children.translated_text: Since everything is established in other systems and in the world, there is nothing left to be stated as one's own view by mere non-statement.

children.text: vacanaliṅgaṃ hi matājñānaṃ na cānanumate niṣedhamātraṃ śakyaṃ vaktum, abhāvasya bhāvanirūpaṇādhīnanirūpaṇatvāditi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the indicator of a view is explicit statement; and regarding what is not approved, mere non-denial is not possible to assert, because the determination of non-existence depends on the determination of existence— this is the purport.
He concludes the established meaning— 'therefore.'
He concludes the topic at hand— 'that.'

The <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'regarding the self and the like' aims to raise an objection to the definition on the ground of under-extension (<s>avyāpakatva</s>). He explains that— 'sense organ and object.' He objects— 'how then?' He resolves— 'sense organ.' Let there not be a reading [of 'mind'] in the <s>sūtra</s> on the sense organs. For that is the definition of external sense organs, and the mind is an internal [organ]— therefore he says— 'and separately.' And regarding pleasure and the like, there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). Therefore, by elimination, their perception is established— thus he says— 'and perception.' Now, these are not objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>), since they are established by self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>); so what need is there of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for them as objects of knowledge?— to this he says— 'and of them there is not.' Now, it was said that by virtue of self-awareness, they do not have the status of being objects of valid cognition— to this he says— 'and there is no other way.' For their self-awareness is by virtue of being awareness (<s>saṃvedana</s>), but they are not themselves awareness— as has been stated below. This is the purport. He concludes the objection— 'therefore.' And in the <s>bhāṣya</s>, 'regarding the self and the like' and 'regarding pleasure and the like' are two groups intended to be eternal and non-eternal [respectively]. The self, pleasure-hood, pain-hood, and the like are eternal; while pleasure, pain, and the like are non-eternal. This is what <s>Dignāga</s> has stated: 'Pleasure and the like are not <s>prameya</s>, nor is the mind a real additional sense organ.' And that is not possible, because of the denial by the <s>sūtra</s> on the organ of smell and the like, which pertains to division— this is the purport. The reconciliation-<s>bhāṣya</s> is 'of the sense organ indeed, being present.' Wishing to explain that, one with a hidden intention asks— 'who then says this?' The answer of the objector— 'sense organ and object.' The reconciler says— 'there is no fault in this.' Uprooting the latent seed of the objection, he refutes it— 'but what is in the <s>sūtra</s>.' This <s>sūtra</s> on the organ of smell and the like does not pertain to division but rather to definition. And there, even the mind, though a sense organ, is not defined, because of its dissimilarity— this is the meaning. He states the dissimilarity— 'dissimilarity.' He proves that— 'but [the mind] has all things as its object.' He points out another dissimilarity— 'elemental.' For the specific properties of an effect are being elemental and non-elemental; what is an effect of the elements is elemental. What is not an effect of the elements is non-elemental. And the negation of being an effect of elements implies being an effect of something else, because the negation of one specific type is the basis for acknowledging another type. Otherwise, it would simply be called 'non-effect,' not 'non-elemental.' Therefore, for the mind which is a non-effect, non-elementality, which is a property of effects, is contradictory— this is the meaning. Moreover, because of dissimilarity, hearing too, like the mind, should not be stated [in the sense-organ <s>sūtra</s>]— thus he says— 'and regarding the ear.' He raises a doubt— 'in its own [element].' For the organs of smell and the rest up to hearing are elemental, but the mind is not elemental— this is the dissimilarity— such is the meaning. He refutes— 'and that is not so.' For the <s>vārttikakāra</s> will demonstrate that no cognition whatsoever is merely of its own element— this is the meaning. He restates the reason for the objection— 'that which moreover.' He refutes— 'it is not that there is not.' By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'when there is contact of the sense organ with the object' has been explained. And regarding the other dissimilarity of the mind from the organ of smell and the rest stated by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>, he refutes that too by the lion's backward glance method— 'of those possessing qualities.' Just as the organs of smell and the rest each make known the external smell and the like through their own respective quality— smell and the like— the ear does not similarly make known external sound through its own quality, sound. Therefore, just like the mind, the ear too should not be listed in the sense-organ <s>sūtra</s>— this is the meaning. He concludes the dissimilarity accepted in the <s>bhāṣya</s>— 'therefore.' The intention is that the dissimilarity characterized by being elemental and non-elemental cannot be stated through the mention of 'being material-elemental' and 'non-material-elemental.' Now, from the non-production of simultaneous cognitions, it is understood that the mind is a cause of cognition, but not that it is also a sense organ; and without understanding its sense-organ status, it is not possible to say that the cognition of pleasure and the like is born from the contact of a sense organ with its object— therefore he says— 'in another system.' A <s>tantra</s> is a system by which reality is elucidated— that is, a <s>śāstra</s> (treatise). By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'and of the mind' has been explained. This has been criticized by <s>Dignāga</s>: 'If it is accepted because it is not denied, then the statement "additional sense organ" is useless.' To refute that, he introduces— 'not by remainder.' He refutes that— 'the reasoning of the system is not [merely that].'

children.text:
tadevaṃ lakṣaṇapadāni vyākhyāya vimṛśati--samastamiti /
abhimatamāha--samastamityāha bhāṣyakāraḥ /
hetumāha--yasmāditi /
indriyārthasannikarṣotvannaṃ jñānamavyabhicārīti hi pratayakṣalakṣaṇamanavayavena samānāsamānajātīyebhyo vyāvṛttaṃ śakyameva lakṣayitum /
na khalvayamasāvaśva iti jñānamindriyajaṃ śabdajaṃ saṃbhavati /
taddhi dravyagocaraṃ vā ucyeta, vācyatvagocaraṃ vā, vācyatvaviśiṣṭadravyagocaraṃ vā /
tatra dravyamaindriyakameva na śābdamityaśakyaṃ hi jñānaṃ vyavacchettum, anabhimataṃ ca /
vācyatvagocaraṃ tu jñānaṃ śābdam eva, anyathā hyaśrutaśabdo 'pyāraṇyako 'śvamevendriyasannikarṣādaśvaśabdavācya iti gṛhṇīyāt /
vācyatvaviśiṣṭadravyajñānamapi śābdameva, vahniviśiṣṭadhūmajñānamivānumānikam, anyathā tadapyaindriyakamiti na tannirākaraṇāya yatnāntaramāstheyam /
atha na vācyatvaṃ nāma mīmāṃsakānāmiva kiñcidatīndriyam, api tu saṅketamātrametadasmādidaṃ pratyetavyamiti /
tathāpi śabda eva /
athāyamapyaindriyaka eva, tatra gurupadiṣṭā gāthā paṭhitavyā,
children.translated_text: Now if even this were sensory, then the verse taught by the teacher should be recited—
If it is verbal because of being born from words, then perception too [would be verbal] because of arising from the eye;
Because it has the nature of clear apprehension, it is proper that it is sensory.

Having thus explained the definitional terms, he deliberates— 'the composite.' He states what is accepted— 'the composite, says the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>.' He states the reason— 'because.' For the definition of perception— 'cognition produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object, non-deviating'— is indeed able to define [perception] as distinguished from things of the same and different kinds, without any component [being removed]. Surely the cognition 'this is not a horse' cannot arise both from the sense organs and from words. For that would either be said to have substance as its object, or the property of being expressible as its object, or substance qualified by expressibility as its object. Among these, substance as the object of the senses alone and not of words— for that purpose it is impossible to exclude such cognition, and it is also not intended [to exclude it]. But cognition having expressibility as its object is verbal alone; otherwise, even a forest-dweller who has never heard a word would apprehend through sense-contact that a horse is what is denoted by the word 'horse.' And cognition of substance qualified by expressibility is also verbal alone, just as cognition of smoke qualified by fire is inferential; otherwise, that too would be sensory, and no other effort would need to be made to refute it. Now if expressibility is not, as for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, something supersensory, but rather is merely a convention— 'from this, this is to be understood'— even so, it is verbal [cognition].
Thus.
Therefore, the term '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' (inexpressible) is not for the purpose of excluding cognition born from both [sense and word].

children.text: vyavasāyātmakapadena tu savikalpake jñāne 'varuddhe nirvikalpakasyāpratyakṣatā mā prasāṃkṣīditi tadavarodhārthenāvyapadeśyapadena nirvikalpake 'pi śabdasaṃbhedanirākaraṇamanvācitamiti śābdetyuktam /
children.translated_text: Rather, by the term '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' (having the nature of determination), when determinate cognition is included [in perception], lest the non-perceptual status of indeterminate [perception] be inferred, the term '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' includes indeterminate [perception] too. And thereby the exclusion of the admixture of verbal [cognition] in indeterminate [perception] is implied— hence it was said 'verbal.'

children.text: evam avyapadeśyapadena nirvikalpake 'varuddhe savikalpakasyendriyajasyāpratyakṣatvaṃ mā prasāṃkṣīditi tadavarodhārthena vyavasāyātmakapadena saṃśayajñānapratyakṣatvanirākaraṇamanvācitamiti saṃśayetyuktam //
children.translated_text: Similarly, by the term '<s>avyapadeśya</s>', when indeterminate [perception] is included, lest the non-perceptual status of determinate sensory [cognition] be inferred, the term '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' includes that too. And thereby the exclusion of the perceptual status of doubt-cognition is implied— hence it was said 'doubt.'

children.translated_text: In the context of providing specific prescriptions, the mention of the exclusion of the remainder is for the purpose of obtaining an illustration.
Acceptance of a partial position— among the thirty-one positions, the thirty-first position is the partial acceptance— this is the meaning.
'Or the prescription of the remainder'—
The word 'or' (<s>vā</s>) has the sense of 'indeed' (<s>iva</s>).

Having shown the positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), he states the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>)— 'if.' He concludes— 'therefore.' He counts the positions to be rejected, thirty-one in number— 'there.' With the inclusion of two terms, there are ten: keeping the term 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object' fixed, in connection with each of the other terms 'cognition' and so on singly, there are four positions; keeping 'cognition' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' and so on singly, there are three; similarly keeping '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' (non-deviating) and so on singly, there are two positions; and the connection of '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' with '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' is the tenth. With the inclusion of three terms also, there are ten. Keeping 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object' and 'cognition' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' and so on singly, there are three positions; keeping 'cognition' and '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' and so on, there are two; but keeping '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' and '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' fixed, in connection with '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>', there is one position; keeping 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object' and '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' and so on singly, there are two; but keeping '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' and '<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>' fixed, in connection with each of the terms 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object' and 'cognition' respectively, there are two— thus with the inclusion of three terms there are ten positions. With the inclusion of four terms, there are five. Keeping 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object,' 'cognition,' and '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' fixed, in connection with each of '<s>avyabhicāri</s>' and so on singly, there are two positions; dropping the '<s>avyapadeśya</s>' term gives another; dropping the 'cognition' term gives yet another; and dropping the 'produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object' term gives the fifth. He asks— why does the inclusion of all five terms, as the thirty-first position, exclude the other positions? For there is no word here that explicitly expresses that exclusion— this is the meaning. The answer— 'by specification.'

children.translated_text: As they say,
Restriction is justified because of contrariety, not from what is non-contrary.
Thus.

Having thus established the definition of perception, he first presents the definition of perception according to <s>Vasubandhu</s> for refutation—'others however.' He explains the definition—'from that very object.' That cognition which is designated as the cognition of whichever object, due to the permanent connection—if it arises from that very [object] and not from another object unconnected with the designation, that is perception. For this very reason, the cognition of shell that is designated as silver, arising from another object—the form of shell—unconnected with the designation, is not perception, because the designator has not arisen, since the designator, silver, is impossible there. The exclusion of this semblance of perception is well-known, so setting that aside, he states the exclusion of inference—'by this.' Why? For the cognition of fire that is inference does not arise from that very designator alone, but rather [it arises] where fire exists, there [the inference operates]. And thus, where smoke has ceased from the form of fire having been merely seen, there [the cognition] arises from something else—from the remembered smoke—when the designator, fire, is absent. In 'from that very object,' the word 'that' (<s>tataḥ</s>) is a qualifier of 'object.' And the particle 'eva' (alone), connected with that, functions as exclusion of disconnection (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>)—just as 'Caitra is the very one who holds the wealth.' Therefore, where there is disconnection from that, that is non-perception—such is the meaning. He refutes this definition—'here the word "object" is purposeless.' For the designation of cognition is not possible through the self or through the sense organ. He raises a doubt—'for the purpose of restriction.' This restriction is by the exclusion of disconnection, and the word 'that' is the qualifier. The particle 'eva,' connected with the qualifier, excludes disconnection. But without the word 'object,' of what would this be a qualifier?—so the particle 'eva,' not being connected with a qualifier, would not exclude disconnection—such is the sense. He refutes—'not so.' Because the pronoun 'that' (<s>tataḥ</s>) awaits a proximate qualified [noun]. Otherwise, since there is no end to what it could denote, the qualified [noun]—namely the one connected with the designation in 'of which that is designated'—is certainly obtained, and so its function as a qualifier is established. But accepting [the objector's position], thinking there is no fault even in mere restriction, the analogy of eating iron (<s>abbhakṣa</s>) is cited. For even in exclusion of something else, only what is contrary would be excluded, not just anything else.

children.text: bhinnakālaṃ kathaṃ grāhyamiti ced grāhyatāṃ viduḥ /
children.translated_text: 'How is what is of a different moment apprehended?'—the knowers of reasoning know apprehension to be
nothing other than being a cause capable of imparting its form to cognition.

It might be said: when 'from that' is said, it would mean 'from whatever that is'—and thus even inference etc., arising from the cognition of the mark etc., would be perception. To prevent that, 'from the object' must be said. For it [inference] does not arise from the object itself. Rather, [perception arises] from the very perceptible [object]. Therefore he says—'by this.' Having regard to 'of which that is designated,' by the force of the word 'from that,' the exclusion of inference etc. is also answered. And he also refutes the other exclusion stated for the word 'from that'—'but what is this again.' If whatever cognition is designated as [belonging to] something is perception, then even the cognition 'that is a pot' would be perception—for it too is designated as [belonging to] the pot. But it does not arise from that pot. Because [the pot], being unable to withstand analysis, lacks ultimate reality, and being conventionally existent, has no causal capacity toward cognition. Therefore, to refute that, 'from that' was said. We do not understand how this is refuted—such is [the objection]. He raises a doubt—'if.' The atoms of form etc. alone, arising in uninterrupted succession, being ultimately real and distinct, are the producers of their own indeterminate cognition. But the determinate conceptual cognition 'pot,' which arises subsequent to the indeterminate and conceals their multiplicity by its own form, showing those very forms etc. as if unified, capable of a single action like carrying water—is called convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>). He refutes—'for, from form etc.' He exposes the root assumption—'but even so.' He refutes—'a mental candy.' Let them be distinct—what follows from this?—therefore he says: 'and all.' Whatever is held by you to be conventional, and whatever is indeterminate—all of that arises from its own object. Therefore the word 'from that' for excluding convention is purposeless. 'Let it not be for excluding convention; it will serve for excluding false knowledge'—he objects: 'but false knowledge arises from something other than [its designator] too.' Just as a substance present before one is designated as 'this,' and designated as silver but not as shell—so although its cognition is designated in a general form and arises from that [object], nevertheless in the specific form by which it is designated, it does not arise from that—hence 'from something other than that too' is said. Therefore, what arises from that very thing alone is perception, and false knowledge is not thus. For it arises from both that and not-that—such is the meaning. He resolves—'for the false knowledge does not arise from that which is not it—the superimposed form which does not exist there; rather, it arises from that [which does exist]. From the general form of which it is designated as 'this'—from that very thing. But what is superimposed is its object in the form of the appearing aspect. This is what was said—'of that which is not it, that arises.' And thus, since only the definiendum remains, there is no definition—he says: 'the word "from that."' And thus there is over-extension—he says: 'and thus.' He states another fault by way of concession—'even if this.' That from which cognition arises is the apprehended object, the cause; and the apprehending cognition is the effect. Since the two cannot exist simultaneously, the cognition, appearing as present, would be false regarding the past [object], and so would not be perception. And since things simultaneous with each other cannot have a cause-effect relationship—from that very object, [the definition] fails—such is the sense. He raises a doubt—'destruction and arising.' Due to the momentariness of entities, the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect occur at one time; even so, the cause, though of a different moment, is apprehended—its being apprehended is nothing other than being the producer of cognition similar to itself,

children.text: sa cet kāraṇaṃ vinaṣṭasya pratyakṣateti tathā ca vartamānābhamavartamānaṃ gocarayati mithyātvamapratyakṣatvaṃ ca syāditi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: If that [object] is the cause, then the perished is [what is] perceived—and thus it objectifies something non-present as if present, so there would be falsity and non-perception—such is the sense.

children.text: yaugapadye 'pi nāstyudāharaṇam, sarvasya kṣaṇikatvapakṣanikṣepāditi codayati--tulyamiti cet /
children.translated_text: He objects that even in simultaneity there is no example, since everything is placed in the camp of momentariness—'if it is equal.'
He refutes—'and that [is not so].'

Thus in <s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> (2.2.47). And this does not entail falsity, because the blue form deposited by the object is present—such is the sense. He refutes—'and that is not so.' Momentariness, characterized by the parts of prior and posterior time, does not exist anywhere. For even lightning and the like, though quickly perishing, persist for two or three or more moments—such is the meaning. And the previously stated objection remains just as it was—he says: 'and what has perished.' The blue etc. is experienced as having a form that is non-ego, non-agreeable etc., and as different from cognition—not as having the nature of cognition. And thus, if the apprehension of distinctness is false, then how is the cognition 'this is false regarding that' perception—since a variety of valid cognition would be of that same nature? Nor is the experience of the form deposited by the object the same as the experience of the object—because there would be the consequence of being secondary (<s>bhākta</s>). And the modes of speech—figurative and primary—cannot be applied to cognitions, since they belong to different domains.

nanu yadi svarūpato nābhidhīyetānabhidheyaṃ tarhi vastu prasajyeta /
tathā cāvāstavaḥ syāt śābdo vyavahāra ityata āha--sarvasya ceti /
sāmānyaviśeṣatadvabhdedād vastutrayam /
tatra tadvadvastvadhikṛtyoktam--dvāvākārāviti /
sāmānyenaivākāreṇābhidhīyate sāmānyānvitamityarthaḥ /
brāhmaṇa iti /
manuṣyatvajātimānityarthaḥ /
viśeṣamākāramabhipretya svarūpato na vyapadeśyamityuktam, na tu sarvatheti bhāvaḥ /
prakṛte yojayati--evamiti /
āśaṅkya pūrvoktamatiprasaṅgaṃ samārayati--yadi ceti /
athāścakarṇādivadavyutpannaḥ kalpanāpoḍhaśabdaḥ pratyakṣasvarūpasya vācaka iti śaṅkate--atheti /
children.translated_text: He raises a doubt: perhaps the word '<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>' (free from conceptual construction), like '<s>āścakarṇa</s>' etc., is a conventional (<s>avyutpanna</s>) word denoting the own-nature of perception—'now.'
He refutes—'even so.'

children.text: bhavatu kalpanāpoḍhaśabdaḥ avyutpanno mā vā bhūt, avācyaṃ tu pratyakṣameṣitavyam, anyathā vikalpasya pratyakṣatvaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: Whether the word '<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>' is conventional or not, perception must be held to be inexpressible—otherwise there would be the absurd consequence that conceptual construction is perception.
And thus there is contradiction—such is the meaning.

Now he presents the definition of <s>Dignāga</s>—'another.' In order to refute it, he asks about the nature of conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>)—'what then is this?' The answer of the definition-proponent—'name.' For in conventional words (<s>yadṛcchā-śabda</s>), the object qualified by name is expressed—'<s>Ḍittha</s>.' In class-words, by class—'this is a cow.' In quality-words, by quality—'white.' In action-words, by action—'cook.' In substance-words, by substance—'one with a staff, one with horns.' This is conceptual construction; where in a cognition this does not exist—either in terms of meaning or in terms of own-form—perception is that which is free from such construction. This is what he says—'that which is indeed not designated by name—either in terms of meaning or in terms of own-form—and is not expressed by class etc.' For non-deviation, he states the cause being the object—'following the own-form of the object.' For being a means of valid knowledge, he says—'determining, establishing.' He shows its nature as cognition—'self-cognized'; from self-awareness alone, its freedom from conceptual construction is also [known]. As it is said: 'Perception, free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself.' 'That is perception.' He refutes this by analyzing the operation of the definiendum, definition, and their combination—'now this.' 'Now, is it not so?' For words are the sources of conceptual constructions and attach to their domain. What conceptual constructions grasp, and what [cognition] determines—both are in the form of exclusion from others (<s>anyavyāvṛtti</s>), [and thus] unreal. Therefore, neither indeterminate cognition nor its object—being ultimately real—is objectified by conceptual constructions or words. This is the underlying intention. Moreover, if [perception] is inexpressible, there would be contradiction with scripture accepted as authoritative by you—he says: 'impermanent etc.' He raises a doubt—'now.' Its own uncommon form—meaning, what is excluded [from others]. He refutes from that—'all objects.' For <s>Dignāga</s> did not formulate the definition of perception with reference to valid cognition in the way that <s>Kīrti</s> (i.e., <s>Dharmakīrti</s>) did—whereby [the restriction] 'free from conceptual construction' would be confined to cognition by virtue of the subject-matter—such is the sense. Now, if [perception] is not expressed by its own form, then the entity would be inexpressible. And thus verbal usage would be unreal—therefore he says: 'and of all.' The triad of entities: the universal, the particular, and what possesses both. There, regarding the entity possessing both, it is said—'two forms.' It is expressed by the form of the universal alone—meaning, as endowed with the universal. '<s>Brāhmaṇa</s>'—meaning one possessing the class of humanness. With regard to the specific form, 'it is not expressed by own-form' is said—but not in every respect—such is the sense. He applies to the present topic—'thus.' Having anticipated the previously stated over-extension, he reminds—'and if.'

children.text:
jaiminipratyakṣalakṣaṇaṃ dūṣayati--satsaṃprayoga iti /
yathāśrutasyātivyāptiḥ saṃśabdenāpi prayogasya samīcīnatā pratipādyate /
sā ca mithyāpratyaye 'pi tulyā, vyatyaye 'pi buddhyā boddhasyopasthāpanāt /
tad iti bodhyaṃ parāmṛśati /
asti ca mithyājñāne 'pi bodhyena saṃbandha indriyāṇām, bodhyaṃ hi purovarti dravyam /
atha yathā bodhyaṃ tādṛśo nāsti saṃbandha indriyāṇām, rajatatvasya prakārasyāsannidhānāt /
hantāvyāpakatvaṃ lakṣaṇadoṣaḥ /

children.translated_text: In recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), the mode of 'that' and 'this'
has no connection with the sense organ.

children.text: api ca prābhākare darśane anumānādijñānamātmani pratyakṣaṃ na bhavet, na hi tat satsaṃprayogajam /
children.translated_text: Moreover, on the <s>Prābhākara</s> view, knowledge of inference and the like in the self would not be perception, for it does not arise from contact with an existent.
Therefore, this too should be examined by the learned.

He refutes <s>Jaimini</s>'s definition of perception—'contact with an existent' (<s>satsaṃprayoga</s>). The over-extension of [the definition] as literally heard is shown: the propriety of the word '<s>sam</s>' (together) in the compound '<s>prayoga</s>' (connection) is demonstrated. And that [over-extension] equally applies to erroneous cognition, since even in error, the cognizable is presented to the intellect. The word 'that' (<s>tad</s>) refers to the cognizable. And even in erroneous cognition, there is a connection of the sense organs with the cognizable, for the cognizable is the substance present before one. Now, such a connection of the sense organs as the cognizable [truly is] does not exist, because of the non-proximity of the mode, namely silver-ness. Alas—under-extension is a defect of the definition.

children.text:
vārṣagaṇyasyāpi lakṣaṇamayuktamityāha--śrotrādivṛttiriti /
pañcānāṃ khalvindriyāṇāmarthākāreṇa pariṇatānāmālocanamātraṃ vṛttiriṣyate, sā ca saṃśayādivyāpakatvādalakṣaṇamiti /
tat siddhamindriyārthasannikarṣotpannamityetadeva lakṣaṇamiti pratyakṣalakṣaṇaṃ samāptam//4 //
children.translated_text: He says that even <s>Vārṣagaṇya</s>'s definition is improper—'the operation of the ear etc.' For the operation of the five sense organs, which have been transformed into the form of the object, is accepted as mere apprehension (<s>ālocana</s>), and that, because it extends to doubt and the like, constitutes a definitional defect. Thus it is established that 'arising from the contact of sense organ and object' is the only proper definition—thus the [discussion of the] definition of perception is completed.

children.text: NyS_1,1.5: atha tatpūrvakaṃ trividham anumānaṃ pūrvavaccheṣavatsāmānyato dṛṣṭaṃ ca //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.5: Now, inference (<s>anumāna</s>), preceded by that [perception], is threefold: <s>pūrvavat</s> (from cause to effect), <s>śeṣavat</s> (from effect to cause), and <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (based on general observation).

children.text:
pratyakṣalakṣaṇānantaramanumānalakṣaṇaparaṃ sūtraṃ paṭhati---atha tatpūrvakaṃ trividhamanumānamiti /
atrānumānamiti sidvavat pramāṇāviśeṣarūpalakṣyānuvāda eva nāpratyakṣaṃ pramāṇamityaprāmāṇyamanumānasya sudūdaṃ pratikṣipati /
dṛṣṭaprāmāṇyāprāmāṇyavijñānavyaktisādharmyeṇa hi kāsāṃcid vyaktīnāṃ prāmāṇyamaprāmāṇyaṃ vā vidadhīta /
dṛṣṭasādharmyaṃ cānumānam eveti kathaṃ tenaiva tasyāprāmāṇyam? api cānumānamapramāṇamiti vākyaprayogo 'jñaṃ vipratipannaṃ sandigdhaṃ vā puruṣaṃ pratyarthaṃvān /
na ca parapuruṣavartino dehadharmā api sandehājñānaviparyāsā gauratvādivat pratyakṣamīkṣante /
na ca tadvavacanāt prattīyante, vacanasyāpi pratyakṣādanyasyāprāmāṇyopagamāt /
puruṣaviśeṣamanadhikṛtya tu vacanamanarthaṅkaṃ prayu/jāno nāyaṃ laukiko na parīkṣaka ityunmattavadanavadheyavacanaḥ syāt /
pariśiṣṭaṃ tu parīkṣāparvaṇi nivedayiṣyate /
tasmādakāmenāpi pramāṇamanumānamupetavyamiti /
lakṣyaṃ pramāṇabhedamanumānamanūdya tatpūrvakamiti lakṣaṇaṃ vidhatte /
athetyānantarye uktaṃ pratyakṣam anumānasya hetuḥ /
athedānīmanumānaṃ hetumadvyutpādyate ityarthaḥ /
lakṣaṇasūtratātparyamāha---anumāneti /
tadeva sphuṭayati---aneneti /
samānajātīyāni pramāṇatayā pratyakṣādīni, asamānajātīyāni cānumānābhāsādīni, yathā kṣaṇikatvādiṣu sādhyeṣu sattvādīni /
syādetadativyāpakametat tatpūrvakatvam /
taditi hi pratyakṣaṃ parāmṛśatyānantaryāt /
tathā ca pratyakṣapūrvakatvamanumānasyevāgamasmṛtisaṃśayaviparyāsānāmapyastīti tānyapyanumānaṃ prasajyeran /
anumānādipūrvakaṃ cānumānaṃ na pratyakṣapūrvakamiti nānumānaṃ syāt, anumānalakṣaṇenāvyātatvāt /
tasmādavyāptyativyāptibhyāmalakṣaṇametadityata āha---tatpūrvakamiti /
tatpūrvakamityāvṛtyā vigrahatrayapradarśanam /
tatra prathame vigrahe tānītyanantaraṃ sūtram uvallaṅghya vibhāgasūtragatāḥ pratyakṣādayaḥ saṃbandhanīyāḥ yogyatvāt /
yathāhuḥ,
yasya yenārthasaṃbandho dūrasthasyāpi tasya saḥ /
iti tadanena lakṣaṇasyāvyāptiḥ parihṛtā /
tadidamāha---yadā tānīti /
nanvedaṃ pratyakṣapūrvakamiti bhāṣyavirodha ityata āha---pāramparyeṇeti /
pāramparyeṇa hi pratyakṣapūrvakatvamuktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā, tasmānna virodha iti /
ativyāptinirāsāya dvitīyaṃ vigrahaṃ vivṛṇoti---yadāpīti /
te iti vigrahe anantarasūtragatameva pratyakṣapadaṃ saṃbadhyate /
yathā ca dve pratyakṣe pūrve yasya pratyakṣasya liṅgaparāmarśajñānasya pratyakṣaphalasya /
tadidaṃ tatpūrvakaṃ pratyakṣam, taddhi svaviṣaye pratyakṣamapyanumeyārthapratyayaṃ kurvadanumānam /
tadidaṃ tadityucyate /
pratyakṣagrahaṇamupalakṣaṇārtham, anumāne ityādyapi draṣṭavyam /
syādetat /
saṃbandhagrahaṇasamaye padatadarthagocaraṃ pratyakṣaṃ prathamam /
atha tadarthaviṣaye dvitīye pratyakṣe sati yā tatpadaviṣayā smṛtirutpadyate sāpi pratyakṣadvayapūrvā /
evaṃ liṅgalliṅgsiṃbandhasmṛtirapi pratyakṣadvayapūrveti tadavasthaivātivyāptirityāśayavān pṛcchati--- katare dve iti /
uttaram---liṅgeti /
sarvasandeheṣvidamupatiṣṭhate /
vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattirna hi saṃndehādalakṣaṇamiti bhāvaḥ /
na ca dvitīyaliṅgadarśanaṃ vyaptismaraṇasamaye vinaśyadavasthamapyasti, vyāptisaṃskārobdodha samayajanmanā svajanitena saṃskāreṇāsya vyāptismaraṇasamaye vināśāt /
vinaśyadavasthasya dvitīyaliṅgadarśanasya vyāptismaraṇena saha yaugapadye 'pi tayoḥ parasparavārtānabhijñatayā mitho ghaṭanāyogaḥ /
na cātmā te ghaṭayatīti yuktam /
vṛttyā khalvayaṃ ghaṭayet, na svarūpataḥ / tasmād ubhābhyāmutpannaṃ parāmarśajñānamindriyārthasannikarṣajaṃ tṛtīyaṃ pratyakṣam eṣitavyam /
bubhutsāvato dvitīyāditi /
bubhutsāpyanumānajñānotpattau kāraṇamiti darśayituṃ bubhutsāvata ityuktam /
liṅgaliṅgisaṃbandhadarśanamādyaṃ pratyakṣam ityatra saṃbandhapadenānumānāṅga saṃbandhaṃ vivakṣan paroktān saṃbandhavikalpān anumānānaṅgabhūtān pratikṣipati---pratyakṣamiti ca tasya pramāṇamāha /
tathā hi kecidavinābhāvaṃ tādātmyatadutpattinibandhanamanumānāṅgamāhuḥ /
dvividho hyarthaḥ, pratyakṣaśca parokṣaśca /
tatra yo buddhau sākṣādātmīyaṃ rūpaṃ niveśayati sa pratyakṣaḥ /
sa hi svaviṣayāyā buddheḥ janaka iti tamantareṇa buddhirātmānamanāsādayantī tasya sattā niścāyayatīti yuktam /
parokṣastu buddhau sākṣāt svarūpopadhānasāmarthyarahito 'yuktapratipattireva /
na cānyadarśane anyakalpanā yuktā, atiprasaṅgāt /
nāntarīyakatayā tvanyo 'pyanyaṃ gamayet /
sa hi pratibaddhasvabhāvo yathāvidhaḥ siddhaḥ tathāvidhasannidhānaṃ sūcayati /
sa ca pratibandho na darśanādarśanamātrādavaseyaḥ, tathā sati sa śyāmo maitanayatvāt paridṛśyamānamaitratanayastomavadityapyanumānaṃ syāt /

children.translated_text: For here too there are observation and non-observation.
Therefore, the binding is based on identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>) alone.

children.text: yathāha kāryakāraṇabhāvād vā svabhāvād vā niyāmakāt /
children.translated_text: As it is said: 'From the causal relation or from the determining nature,
the restriction of invariable concomitance [arises]—from observation, not from non-observation alone.'

After the definition of perception, he reads the <s>sūtra</s> concerning the definition of inference—'now, preceded by that, threefold inference.' Here, by the word '<s>anumāna</s>' (inference), treated as already established, through the mere restatement of the definable as an unspecific means of valid knowledge, the invalidity of inference—[the claim that] 'non-perceptual means of knowledge are not valid'—is rejected from afar. For by the analogy of instances whose validity or invalidity of cognition has been perceived, one would determine the validity or invalidity of certain [other] instances. And the perceived analogy is inference itself—so how can inference itself establish its own invalidity? Moreover, the statement 'inference is not a means of valid knowledge' is meaningful only toward a person who is ignorant, in disagreement, or in doubt. And the bodily properties of another person—such as doubt, ignorance, and error—like heaviness, do not face perception. Nor are they understood from that person's statement, since the statement, being something other than perception, has itself been accepted as invalid. But one who employs a statement without addressing a particular person does it meaninglessly—such a one is neither a worldly person nor an examiner, and like a madman, his words would be disregarded. The remainder will be explained in the section on examination. Therefore, inference must be accepted as a means of valid knowledge, even unwillingly.
