Having restated the definable—inference as a type of means of valid knowledge—he prescribes the definition as 'preceded by that' (<s>tatpūrvaka</s>). 'Now' (<s>atha</s>) indicates sequence—the previously stated perception is the cause of inference. The meaning is: now inference, having a cause, is taught. He states the purport of the definition-<s>sūtra</s>—'inference.' He elaborates that—'by this.' The similar kinds are perception and the rest, by virtue of being means of valid knowledge; the dissimilar kinds are semblances of inference and the like, such as being-existent (<s>sattva</s>) etc. when the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is momentariness and the like. There might be this [objection]: this 'being preceded by that' is overly extensive. For 'that' refers to perception because of sequence. And thus being preceded by perception belongs not only to inference but also to scripture, memory, doubt, and error—so those too would undesirably become inference. And inference that is preceded by [another] inference and the like, not by perception, would not be inference, since it would not be covered by the definition of inference. Therefore, this is a defective definition due to under-extension and over-extension—to this he says: 'preceded by that.' By repeating 'preceded by that,' three analyses are shown. In the first analysis, the word 'those' (<s>tāni</s>) should be connected—skipping the immediately next <s>sūtra</s>—with perception and the rest mentioned in the division-<s>sūtra</s>, because of fitness. As they say: 'whatever has a meaningful connection with something, even if distant, has that connection.' By this, the under-extension of the definition is removed. He states this—'when those.' But is this not in contradiction with the <s>bhāṣya</s> which says 'preceded by perception'?—to this he says: 'indirectly.' For the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> said 'preceded by perception' in the indirect sense; therefore there is no contradiction. To remove the over-extension, he explains the second analysis—'but when.' In the analysis with 'those,' the very word 'perception' (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) in the immediately next <s>sūtra</s> is connected. And just as the two perceptions—[first] the perception of the mark and the mark-bearer's relation, and [second] the apprehension of the inferential mark—are prior to the cognition that is the result of perception, that is the inferential-mark-consideration-cognition (<s>parāmarśajñāna</s>). That is 'preceded by that'—that perception which, in its own domain, though being perception, produces the cognition of the inferable object, is inference. That is what is called 'that' (<s>tad</s>). The mention of perception is illustrative—inference etc. should also be understood [as possible precedents]. There might be this [objection]: at the time of grasping the relation, the perception of the word and its referent is first. Then, when the second perception regarding that referent occurs, the memory that arises regarding that word is also preceded by two perceptions. Similarly, the memory of the relation between mark and mark-bearer is also preceded by two perceptions—so the over-extension remains as before. With this intent he asks—'which two?' The answer—'the mark.' This applies in all doubtful cases: 'specific understanding [comes] from the explanation; a definition is not defective merely because of doubt'—this is the purport. And the second seeing of the mark does not exist even in its perishing state at the time of the memory of pervasion, because the impression deposited by the awakening of the pervasion-impression, by the impression it itself generated, causes its destruction at the time of the memory of pervasion. Even if there is simultaneity of the second seeing of the mark in its perishing state with the memory of pervasion, since they are unaware of each other's presence, their conjunction is impossible. And it is not proper that the self connects them. For it would connect them through an operation (<s>vṛtti</s>), not through its own nature. Therefore, the inferential-mark-consideration-cognition born from both—the third perception arising from sense-object contact—should be sought. 'From the second, for one who desires to know'—the desire to know is also shown to be a cause in the generation of inferential cognition, hence 'for one who desires to know' is said. Regarding 'the perception of the mark, the mark-bearer, and their relation is the first perception'—here, intending the relation that is a component of inference by the word 'relation,' he rejects the alternatives of relation stated by others as not being components of inference—'perception'—and states its means of valid knowledge. For some say that invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>) based on identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>) is the component of inference. For objects are of two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible. Among those, what directly places its own form in cognition is perceptible. It is the cause of its own cognition—so it is reasonable that without it, cognition, being unable to reach itself, ascertains its existence. But the imperceptible, lacking the capacity to directly present its own form in cognition, is merely an unjustified cognition. And the construction of one thing from the perception of another is not proper, because of over-extension. But through inseparability (<s>nāntarīyakatā</s>), one thing can make another known. For it, having a bound nature, when established as being of a certain kind, indicates the presence of what is of a corresponding kind. And that binding is not to be determined merely from observation and non-observation—for in that case, 'he is dark, because he is the son of <s>Maitra</s>, like the perceived son of <s>Maitra</s> who is <s>Soma</s>,' would also be an inference.

children.text:
tathā ca liṅgavikalpaṃ vinā na liṅgivikalpaḥ /
na liṅgavikalpo liṅgānubhavaṃ vinā /
na liṅgānubhavo liṅgaṃ vinā /
na cāvinābhūtaṃ liṅgaṃ vinā liṅginamiti liṅgisvalakṣaṇāpratibhāsyapi pāramparyeṇa tatpratibandhāt tatrāvisaṃvādako 'numānavikalpa iti /
kāryakāraṇabhāvaścedam /
asmin sati bhavati satsvapi tadanyeṣvasminnasati na bhavati evamākāro nānvayavyatirekābhyāmatiricyate /
tau ca pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvinā vikalpenāvasīyete /
tathā hi satyagnau dhūma iti pratyakṣameva vikalpānugatavyāpāramadhyavasyati /
asati cāgnau na dhūma ityapi pratyakṣameva, na hyagnidhūmānupalambhāvānyau /
children.translated_text: And 'when fire does not exist, there is no smoke'—this too is perception itself, for the non-perception of fire and smoke are nothing other [than perception].
Therefore, since what is distinct from those two is perceived, the negative concomitance of these two is also nothing other than a thing distinct from them.

children.text: evaṃ tādātmyamapi viparyaye bādhakapramāṇopapattyā niścetavyam, yathā sattvasya kṣaṇikatayā saha tādātmyaṃ vipakṣai'kṣaṇike kramākramayorvyāpakayoranupalambhanniścīyate /
children.translated_text: Similarly, identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) too is to be ascertained through the availability of a sublating means of valid knowledge in the contrary case—just as the identity of existence (<s>sattva</s>) with momentariness is ascertained through the non-perception of the two pervaders, namely sequence and simultaneity, in the counter-instance of the non-momentary.
Therefore, binding is only through identity and causal origination, not otherwise.

And thus, without the concept of the mark, there is no concept of the mark-bearer. Without the experience of the mark, there is no concept of the mark. Without the mark itself, there is no experience of the mark. And there is no mark without what is inseparable from the mark-bearer—thus, even though the particular of the mark-bearer does not appear [in the inferential cognition], because of indirect binding with it, the inferential concept is non-deceptive regarding it. And this [binding] is the causal relation. Its form is: 'when this exists, that exists; even when other things exist, when this does not exist, that does not exist'—this does not exceed positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>). And those two are determined by conceptual cognition that follows upon perception. For thus: 'when fire exists, there is smoke'—it is perception itself, accompanied by the operation of conceptual cognition, that determines this.

children.text:
atrocyate /
satyaṃ yat kiñcit kvacid dṛṣṭam, tasya yatra pratibandhaḥ tadvidastasya tadgamakaṃ tatretyanujānīmaḥ /
sa eva tu pratibandho na tāvat tadutpattyā saṃbhavati /
kā punariyaṃ tadutpattirdhūmasya? kiṃ vahnyanantaraṃ bhāvaḥ? sa tādṛśo 'sti rāsabhasyāpīti tatpratibaddho 'pi dhūmaḥ syāt /
atha tadanantarameva bhāvaḥ, na ca rāsabhānantaraṃ bhavannapi tadanantarameva bhavati, tasmin satyapyasatyagnau tadabhāvāt /
asatyapi tasmin sati ādrendhanavati vahnau tadbhāvāt /
atha yadyapi dhūmasya vahnibhāvābhāvānuvidhānaṃ tatropalabdhaṃ tathāpi deśāntarādiṣu tadbhāvo 'sya kutastyaḥ? tathā hi bhūyo bhūyo rāsabhe dṛṣṭe dhūmo dṛṣṭaḥ, tadabhāve cādṛṣṭaḥ /
na ca sa tatkāryaḥ /
tajjātīyasyaiva dhūmasya rāsabhaṃ vinā sati vahnau bhāvāt /
evaṃ satyapyagnau piśācena janito dhūmaḥ kvacit deśādau tajjātīya eva rāsabhavad vahnyabhāve 'pi piśācādeva bhaviṣyatīti,

children.translated_text: one must necessarily entertain doubt—for those who do not see a determining factor.

children.text: na ca sati bhāvamātraṃ niyāmakam, tasya rāsabhādiṣvaṣyaviśeṣāt /
children.translated_text: And mere existence when [fire] is present is not a determining factor, because of its being the same in [the case of] donkeys and the like.
And the definitive determination 'only after that' is impossible without removing the doubt.
But if the doubt is removed through definitive determination, there is the fault of mutual dependence.

Here it is said [in reply]: it is true that when something is observed somewhere, and its binding exists with something else, we accept that for one who knows [the binding], it is an indicator of that, there. But that very binding is not possible, first of all, through causal origination. What then is this 'causal origination' of smoke? Is it mere existence after fire? Such [existence after fire] belongs to a donkey too—so smoke would be bound to a donkey as well. If it means existence only after that [fire] and not [after anything else]—but even something that exists after a donkey does not exist only after that [donkey], because in the absence of that [donkey] but in the presence of fire with fuel, that [smoke] exists. And even in the absence of that, when there is fire with fuel, that [smoke] exists. Now, even though the conformity of smoke to the presence and absence of fire has been observed in some cases, whence comes this conformity in other locations etc.? For thus: smoke has been observed again and again in the presence of a donkey, and not observed in its absence. And yet it is not its effect. Because smoke of that very type exists when fire is present without a donkey. Similarly, even when fire is present, smoke generated by a demon (<s>piśāca</s>) in some location—being of the same type—would exist even in the absence of fire, just like [in the case of] a donkey, from the demon alone. Thus,

children.text:
syādetat /
yo yo dhūmo dṛṣṭaḥ sa sarvastāvadārdrendhanasahitavahnyanantarameva na piśācānantaram /
sa ca kādācitkatayā nimittamapekṣamāṇo yadanantarameva gamyate tadevāpratītavyabhicāraṃ nimittīkaroti, na tu pratīvyabhicāraṃ rāsabhādi /
nāpi sarvathā anupalabdhapūrvapiśācādi /
yadi na tannimittaṃ kasmāt vināpi vahni kvacid dhūmo nopalabhyate? athāsau sarvathā vahnisahitaḥ, tathā satyādrendhanavat kathaṃ vahnirapi na kāraṇam? kāraṇaṃ cet kathaṃ tadantareṇa dhūmabhāvaśaṅkā? akāraṇasya hi kāryasya nityaṃ sattvamasattvaṃ vā syāt, anapekṣatvāt, na kādācitkatvam /
nāpyanekakāraṇakam, akāraṇakatvaprasaṅgādeva /
vahnyanantarameva bhāva iti hi dhūmasya vahnikāryatvam /
sa cet avahnerapyanantaraṃ naivakārārthaḥ syāditi na vahneḥ kāryam /

children.translated_text: Similarly, it would not be an effect of anything else either.

children.text: na hi anyānantarameva bhavati, vahnerapyanantaraṃ bhāvāt /
children.translated_text: For it does not exist immediately after another thing alone, since it also exists immediately after fire.
And then smoke would be without a cause.
And thus there would be a contradiction with its occasional nature.

One might say: every smoke that has been seen is always immediately after fire accompanied by moist fuel, not immediately after a goblin. And being occasional, requiring a cause, it takes as its cause only that after which it is invariably understood without known deviation, not a donkey and the like where deviation is known. Nor goblins and the like which have never been observed at all. If [fire] is not its cause, why is smoke never observed anywhere without fire? If smoke is always accompanied by fire, then being so, how is fire not a cause, just as moist fuel is? And if it is a cause, how can there be doubt about the existence of smoke without it? For an effect without a cause would either always exist or never exist, being independent — it would not be occasional. Nor could it have multiple causes, precisely because of the undesirable consequence of being causeless. For the causality of smoke by fire consists in its existing immediately after fire alone. And if it existed immediately after non-fire too, it would be purposeless — so it would not be an effect of fire.

children.text:
satyam, tatkāryatvasiddhau syādevam /
tadeva tu tadanantarameva bhāva ityevaṃrūpaṃ nāsti /
yadyapi ca vinā vahni nopalabdho dhūmo yadyapi ca piśācānantaraṃ nopalabhyate teṣāmanupalabdheḥ, tathāpi piśācakārya eva dhūmasyatra tatra vahniḥ kutaścit svahetorūpanipatito rāsabha iva na tu dhūmasya janamaḥ /
tena tadabhāve 'pi tajjātīya eva kāraṇabhedajanmā kadācit kādācitko dhūmaḥ syāditi anivṛttireva śaṅkāyāḥ /
na dṛṣṭasaṃbhave nādṛṣṭaṃ kalpayituṃ yuktamiti śakyaṃ bhavadbhirvaktum, anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya aśakyanirākaraṇatvāt /
na cānupalabdhantarāṇyapi tanniṣedhe prabhavanti /
tasmāt anantaramevetyavadhāraṇābhāvāt naivaṃrūpaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvāvadhāraṇaṃ yuktam /
na ca yad yadanyasahitānantaram mupalabdhaṃ tat tadanyarahitāt tasmād bhavad bhinnajātīyaṃ bhavati /
uktaṃ hi rāsabhasahitād vahneryādṛśo dhūmaḥ tādṛśa eva tadvirahitād vahneriti /
tasmādevaṃvidhā śaṅkāpiśācī svanivārakaṃ tadutpattiniścayamāskandantī na śakyā nivārayitum /
api cāstu tadutpattiniścayaḥ, tathāpi kasmāt kāraṇamantareṇa na kāryaṃ bhavati? tathā ca satyanapekṣatayā kādācitkatvavihatiriti cet---yathāha,
children.translated_text: Moreover, let the determination of its production be granted; even so, why cannot the effect exist without the cause? And if so, being independent, there would be a contradiction with occasionality — if thus objected. As he says:
An [effect] would either always exist or never exist, because the cause does not depend on another.
For it is precisely because of dependence that the occasionality of things is possible.

True — this would be so if its being an effect of fire were established. But the very form 'it exists immediately after fire alone' does not hold. Even though smoke is not observed without fire, and even though it is not observed immediately after goblins — because goblins themselves are not observed — nevertheless, smoke is actually an effect of goblins, and fire is found here and there having fallen from some cause of its own, like a donkey, but is not the producer of smoke. Therefore, even in the absence of fire, smoke of the same kind, born from a different cause, might occasionally arise — and thus the doubt is not at all dispelled. You cannot say 'when a visible explanation is available, it is improper to postulate an invisible one,' because what is established by the criterion of non-observation (<s>anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>) cannot be set aside. Nor do other instances of non-observation avail to negate that. Therefore, in the absence of the restriction 'immediately after [fire] alone,' such a determination of cause-effect relation is not proper. And it is not the case that whatever is observed immediately after something else is of a different kind from [what arises from] that [thing] without the other. For it has been said: 'the smoke from fire accompanied by a donkey is of exactly the same kind as from fire without a donkey.' Therefore, this goblin-like doubt, attacking the very determination of its production, which would dispel it, cannot be dispelled.
Thus.

children.text: astu tarhi saṃbandhaḥ svābhāvikatayā anyānapekṣo 'vyabhicārī gamakāṅgam /
children.translated_text: Let there then be a relation that is natural, independent of another, non-deviating, and a component of the indicator.

children.text: sa ca yo vā sa vā bhavatu, kṛtaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvāvadhāraṇāyāsena /
children.translated_text: And let it be whatever it may be — let the effort for determining the cause-effect relation be done with.
And how this is so, we shall demonstrate at this very place.

children.text:
api ca kāryāt kāraṇamanumīyamānaṃ tataḥ pūrvamevānumīyeta, na tu vartamānakālam /
na hi hetusattā kāryakālā kāryotpādāṅgam, api tu tatpūrvakālā /
na hi nadīpūrabhedaḥ svasattāsamayavarti varṣaṃ gamayatyapi tu tatpūrvakālam /
tatkālaṃ tu na tasya kāraṇam /
ata eva sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvena tatkālavartina varṣe sandihānā na tadarthinaḥ pravartante /
evaṃ dhūmādapyagniḥ tatpūrvakāla evānumīyeta, na tu vartamānakālaḥ /
tathā ca sati na tadarthinaḥ tatra niḥśaṅkaṃ pravarteran /
api ca rasādanyadrūpaṃ rasasamānakālamanumimate 'numātāraḥ /
na cānayorasti kā kāraṇabhāvaḥ tādātmyaṃ vā /
yadyucyeta tatpūrvebhyo rūparasagandhasparśakṣaṇebhyo rasakṣaṇo jāyate, sa svakāraṇaṃ pūrvarūpakṣaṇamanumāpayan yādṛśā tena janitaḥ, tādṛśamevānumāpayati /
sa cānumāpakarasakṣaṇasamānakālarūpakṣaṇāntarajanaka eva svakāraṇam iti tādṛśameva gamayati /
tathā ca kāryasamānakālarūpānumānasiddhiḥ /
etena dhūmānumānaṃ vyākhyātam /

children.translated_text: As he says:
Form and the like, being non-existent yet dependent on a single aggregate, are reached
through inference of the property of the cause, like smoke and the transformation of fuel.

Moreover, a cause being inferred from an effect should be inferred as prior to it in time, not as existing in the present. For the existence of the cause at the time of the effect is not a factor in the production of the effect; rather, its existence prior to that time is. For the breaking of a river's flood does not indicate rain at its own time of existence, but rather rain at a prior time. Rain at that [same] time is not its cause. For this very reason, those who doubt about rain existing at the time [of the flood], due to the absence of establishing or refuting evidence, do not engage in activities aimed at it. Similarly, from smoke too, fire should be inferred as existing at a prior time only, not at the present time. And if so, those desiring fire would not proceed there with confidence. Moreover, inferrers infer form, which is different from taste and simultaneous with taste. But between these two there is no cause-effect relation or identity (<s>tādātmya</s>). If it is said that from the prior moments of form, taste, smell, and touch, a taste-moment arises, and that [taste-moment], while inferring its own cause — the prior form-moment — infers it as being of the very kind from which it was generated; and that its own cause, being a generator of another form-moment simultaneous with the inferring taste-moment, indicates itself as being just of that kind; and thus the inference of form simultaneous with the effect is established — by this, the inference of fire from smoke is also explained.
Thus.

children.text:
atrocyate /
yo 'yu gamakarasasamānakālo rūpakṣaṇaḥ, sa kiṃ tajjanakasya rūpakṣaṇasya svabhāva ata tatsvabhāvāvacchedako 'svabhāvabhūtaḥ? na tāvat svabhāvaḥ, ekasminnabhinne janyajanakabhāvānupapatteḥ, tasya bhedāśrayāt /
tadasvabhāvabhūtaḥ kathaṃ tadanumānaniveśī? tadavacchedakatvādita cet? nanu naitāvatāpyasya tulyakālasya rūpasya kāraṇabhāva iti kathaṃ kāryaṃ hetorgamyeta? viśiṣṭena kāraṇasvabhāvenāsvabhāvo 'pi asāvākṣipyate viśeṣaṇatayeti cet? nanvākṣipyate jñāpyata ityanarthāntaram /
sa kiṃ kāraṇānumiteḥ prāgathānumitisamaye paścād vā? na tāvat prāk na hi sattāmātreṇa kāraṇaṃ tad gamayatyatiprasaṅgāt, kiṃ tu svajñānena /
na ca kāryamasya gamakam, akāraṇatvādityuktam /
ata evānumitisamaye 'pyagamakam, svajñānena gamakatvāt /
ubhayośca jñānayoḥ sahabhavatoḥ savyetaraviṣāṇavat kāryakāraṇabhāvābhāvāt /
tathā ca rasāt kāryāt tatkāraṇaṃ rūpamanumātavyam /
tathā ca kāraṇāt kāryānumānaṃ tādātmyatadutpattibhyāmanyata iti nābhyāmeva pratibandhasiddhiḥ /
laukikānāṃ cedaṃ rasād rūpānumānam, na caite piśitacakṣuṣaḥ kṣaṇānāmanyonyabhedamadhyavasyanti /
na cānadhyavasyantaḥ pravṛttarūpotpādanasāmarthyaṃ rasahetuṃ rūpamanumātumutsahante /
na ca lakṣaṇānurodhena lakṣyasyānyathākaraṇaṃ yuktaṃ parīkṣakāraṇam /
atipatitalokamaryādānāṃ teṣāṃ tattvānupapatteḥ /

children.translated_text: As they say:
Investigators should properly only make claims that follow what is established.
They should not reject what is established for the whole world through a [technical] definition.

Here we reply: This form-moment that is simultaneous with the inferring taste — is it the essential nature of the form-moment that is its generator, or is it a delimiter of that essential nature while not being its essential nature? It is not its essential nature, because a cause-effect relation is untenable in what is one and undifferentiated, since that [relation] is grounded in difference. And if it is not its essential nature, how does it enter into the inference of that? If because it is a delimiter of that — but surely, just because of this, the form simultaneous in time is not shown to have a causal relation; so how is the effect knowable from the cause? If because it, though not its essential nature, is indicated by the distinctive causal nature as a qualifier — but to say 'it is indicated' and 'it is made known' is not a different meaning. Does it [become known] before the inference of the cause, at the time of inference, or afterwards? Not before, for fire does not indicate [smoke] by its mere existence — there would be over-extension — but through its own cognition. And the effect is not its indicator, since it has been said that it is not its cause. For this very reason, even at the time of inference, it does not indicate, since it indicates through its own cognition. And since the two cognitions co-exist simultaneously, like the left and right horns, there is no cause-effect relation between them. And thus from taste as the effect, its cause — form — is to be inferred. And thus inference of the effect from the cause by means other than identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal production (<s>tadutpatti</s>) means that the establishment of invariable connection is not through these two alone. And this inference of form from taste belongs to ordinary people, and these flesh-eyed folk do not ascertain the mutual difference of moments. And those who do not ascertain [this] are unable to infer form as the cause of generating an arisen form, having taste as the reason. And it is not proper that the investigator should alter the characterized object to conform to the definition. For the reality of those who have transgressed worldly conventions is untenable.

children.text:
iti /
api cādyatanasya saviturūdayasya hyastanena saviturūdayena, candrodayasya ca samānakālasya samudravṛddhyā, madhyanakṣatradṛṣṭyā cāṣṭamāstamayodayasya, na kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ tādātmyaṃ vā, atha ca dṛṣṭo gamyagamakabhāvaḥ /
api ca tādātmye 'pi kathaṃ gamyagamakabhāvaḥ? na hi tadeva karma ca kartṛ ceti yuktam /
tasya bhedāśrayatvāt /
yadyapi ca vṛkṣatvaśiṃśapātve paramārthato na bhinne tathāpi bhedāntarapratikṣepāpratikṣepābhyāṃ kalpitabhedayorgamyagamakabhāva iti cet---na, vāstavameva vṛkṣatvaśiṃśapātvayorbhedamupapādayiṣyāmaḥ /
api ca kālpanikamapi rūpaṃ vicāryamāṇaṃ na yathā bhinnamevamabhinnamapi na bhavati, vastuno 'pi tucchatvaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, even an imposed form, when examined, is not both different and non-different, since even the real thing would become void.
Because of the unreality of the imposed, its reality is untenable.
Therefore, what have entered into conceptual construction have neither real identity, nor mutual [identity with each other].
If so, there would be the undesirable consequence that the conceptual constructions of existent, substance, earthy, tree, <s>śiṃśapā</s>, and the like are synonymous.

Thus. Moreover, today's sunrise and yesterday's sunrise, or the simultaneously occurring rise of the moon and the swelling of the ocean, or the rising and setting of the eighth [lunar day] as observed through the mid-heaven star — between these there is no cause-effect relation or identity, yet an observed indicator-indicated relation exists. Moreover, even in the case of identity, how is there an indicator-indicated relation? For it is not proper that the very same thing is both the action and the agent. Because that [relation] is grounded in difference. Even if tree-ness and <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness are not ultimately different, nevertheless the indicator-indicated relation holds between them as having an imposed difference through the acceptance and rejection of another difference — if thus objected — no, we shall establish that the difference between tree-ness and <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness is real.

children.text:
syādetat /
kalpanābhedavirahiṇāṃ bhedamullikhantyapi parasparameṣāmabhedamapyavagāhate sāmānādhikaraṇyākāratvāt, abhedānullekhe tadanupapatteḥ /
tathā ca tādātmyaṃ siddhamiti /
tadayuktam /
uktaṃ hi yathā sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na bhāvānāmabhedasādhakam /
jātyādiśabdā hi jātyādīn nimittīkṛtya dravye vartante /
taccādhikaraṇamekamiti sāmānādhikaraṇyam aśnuvate, na punarjātyādīnapi mitho miśrayanti /
śabdasamānaviṣayāṇāṃ vikalpānām apīyameva gati /
tasmād yatra gamyagamakabhāvo na tatra tādātmyam, yatra tādātmyaṃ na tatra gamyagamakabhāva iti saddhim /
yattu viditaśiṃśapāvyavahāramaviditavṛkṣavyavahāramuccāyāṃ hi śiṃśapāyāṃ vṛkṣaśabdaḥ prayuktaḥ, tasmāduccatvameva vṛkṣaśabdapravṛttinimittamiti manyamānaṃ mūḍhaṃ prati śiṃśapātvena vṛkṣavyavahāramātraṃ sādhyate /
vāmanāyāmapi śiśapāyāṃ vṛkṣa iti vyavahartavyam, śiṃśapāmātrānubandhitvād vṛkṣatvasyeti /
tatrāpi ced vyavahāraḥ sādhyaḥ sa śiṃśapāyā bhinna iti, na tādātmyam /
children.translated_text: If even there the usage is what is to be proved, that is different from <s>śiṃśapā</s> — so there is no identity.

children.text: vyavahārayogyatā cet? sā śiṃśapāyā abhinneti na gamyagamakabhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: If it is the fitness for usage [that is to be proved] — that is non-different from <s>śiṃśapā</s>, so there is no indicator-indicated relation.
And regarding the difference of exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>), it has been stated [above].
Therefore, the invariable connection through identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal production (<s>tadutpatti</s>) is mere wishful thinking.

One might say: although the conceptual constructions, which lack the distinction of imposed [difference], inscribe difference among themselves, they also comprehend non-difference, because they have the form of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>); without inscribing non-difference, that [co-referentiality] would be untenable. And thus identity is established. That is improper. For it has been stated how co-referentiality does not establish non-difference among entities. Words for universal and the like apply to the substance by taking universal and the like as their basis. That substrate being one, they attain co-referentiality; but they do not thereby mix the universals and the like with each other. The same applies to conceptual constructions whose objects are the same as those of the words. Therefore, where there is an indicator-indicated relation, there is no identity; and where there is identity, there is no indicator-indicated relation — this is established. As for the case where one who knows the usage of <s>śiṃśapā</s> but does not know the usage of 'tree,' upon seeing a tall <s>śiṃśapā</s> and hearing the word 'tree' applied to it, thinks that tallness alone is the basis for the application of the word 'tree' — for that confused person, only the usage of 'tree' is established through <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness. One should use 'tree' even for a short <s>śiṃśapā</s>, since tree-ness invariably accompanies <s>śiṃśapā</s> as such.

children.text: yaśca vaiṣeśikaiḥ catuṣprakāraḥ saṃbandha ucyate, asyedaṃ kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ saṃbandhyekāryasamavāyi virodhi ceti laiṅgikam # vai. sū. 9/2/1 # //
children.translated_text: And the fourfold relation stated by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> — 'this is its effect, its cause, a co-inherent of the related, and its contrary' — constitutes the inferential [relation]. (<s>Vai. Sū.</s> 9/2/1)

children.text:
iti, atrāpi saṃbandhipadenaiva sarvāpasaṃgrahāt śeṣābhighānaṃ vyartham /
na ca saṃbandhipadopāttasyātiprasaktiḥ śeṣapadairnivāryate /
tathā sati śeṣapadānyeva santu kṛtaṃ saṃbandhipadena, tebhya eva saṃbandhibhedānāmadhigateḥ /
na caivaṃ cāturvidhyaṃ saṃbandhasyānumānaṅgasya /
tacceṣyate /
tathā ca saṃbandhipadasya saṃbandhimātrāvarodhe 'tivyāptiḥ /
api ca bhūtaṃ varṣam abhūtasya vāyvabhrasaṃyogasya kathaṃ virodhi? taddhi tadanukūlameva evam abhūtam varṣaṃ bhūtasya vāyyabhrasaṃyogasyāpratikūlam /
children.translated_text: Moreover, how is past rain contrary to the non-existent conjunction of wind and clouds? For that [conjunction] is actually favorable to it. Similarly, non-existent rain is not unfavorable to the existent conjunction of wind and clouds.

children.text: evaṃ bhūto nakulajayo na bhūtasya sarpaparājayasya virodhī /
children.translated_text: Similarly, a past mongoose-victory is not contrary to an existing snake-defeat.
Nor is that non-existent [victory] contrary to the non-existent [defeat].

children.text: yeṣāṃ punarvirodhaḥ, teṣāmanyatamadanyatamasya na liṅgamapi tu pratikṣepakameva //
children.translated_text: And for those things that are truly contrary, one is not an inferential mark of the other; rather, it is merely an excluder.

Here too, the word 'related' (<s>saṃbandhi</s>) alone encompasses everything, making the rest superfluous. And it is not the case that the over-extension of the word 'related' is restricted by the remaining words. If so, let the remaining words alone suffice — what need is there for the word 'related'? — since the varieties of relation are understood from them alone. And thus there would not be a fourfold nature of the relation that is a component of inference. And that is desired [by us]. And thus, if the word 'related' encompasses merely relations in general, there is over-extension.
By this very [reasoning],
through cause, accident, co-inherent, contrary, concomitant,
through master-servant, executioner-slayer, and the like — the sevenfold inference of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>
should also be understood as refuted.

children.text:
tasmād yo vā sa vāstu saṃbandhaḥ kevalaṃ yasyāsau svābhāviko niyataḥ, sa eva gamako gamyaścetaraḥ saṃbandhīti yujyate /
tathā hi dhūmādīnāṃ vahnyādisaṃbandhaḥ svābhāvikaḥ, na tu vahnyadīnāṃ dhūmādibhiḥ /

children.translated_text: For they [fire and the like] are observed even without smoke and the like.

children.text: yadā tvādrendhanādisaṃbandhamanubhavanti, tadā dhūmādibhiḥ saha saṃbadhyante /
children.translated_text: But when they are associated with moist fuel and the like, then they become related with smoke and the like.

children.text: tasmādvahnyādīnāmādrendhānādyupādhikṛtaḥ saṃbandho na svābhāvikaḥ, tato na niyataḥ svābhāvikastu dhūmādīnā vahnyādisaṃbandhaḥ, tadupādheranupalabhyamānatvāt /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the relation of fire and the like is conditioned by moist fuel and the like, and is not natural. Hence it is not invariable. But the relation of smoke and the like with fire and the like is natural, because no such condition is observed for it.

children.text: kvacid vyabhicārasyādarśanāt māno 'pi darśanānarhatayā sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhovana sandihyamāna upādhiḥ saṃbandhasya svābhāvikatva pratibadhnātīti sāṃpratam //
children.translated_text: Because of the non-observation of deviation anywhere, even doubt—which is worthy of observation but is neither established as valid nor as sublating by a <s>pramāṇa</s>—a suspected <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) obstructs the natural character of the relation—this is not proper.

Therefore, let the relation be whatever it may be; only that whose natural, invariable relation is with it is the indicator, and the other — the related — is what is indicated. This is proper. Thus, the relation of smoke and the like with fire and the like is natural, but not that of fire and the like with smoke and the like.

children.text:
avaśyaṃ śaṅkayā bhāvyaṃ niyāmakamapaśyatām /
iti dattāvakāśā khalviyaṃ laukikapramāṇāmaryādātikrameṇa śaṅkāśicī labdhrapasarā na kvacit nāstīti nāyaṃ kvacit pravarteta /
sarvatraiva kasyacit kathañcidanarthasya śaṅkāspadatvāt /
anarthaśaṅkāyāśca prekṣāvatāṃ nivṛttyaṅgatvāt /
antataḥ snigdhānnapānopayoge 'pi maraṇādidarśanāt /
tasmāt prāmāṇikalokayātrāmanupālayatā yathādarśanaṃ śaṅkanīyam /
na tbadṛṣṭapūrvamapi /

children.translated_text: But not what has never been observed before.
For doubt, requiring the recollection of a particular, does not arise from what has not been remembered.
And memory cannot occur regarding what has never been experienced.

children.text: tasmādupādhi prayatnenānviṣyanto 'nupalabhyamānā nāstītyavagamya svābhāvikatvaṃ saṃbandhasya niścinumaḥ //
children.translated_text: Therefore, diligently seeking <s>upādhis</s> (limiting conditions) and not finding them, we conclude they do not exist and ascertain the natural character of the relation.

One must necessarily entertain suspicion when one does not see a determining factor.
But this needle of suspicion, having been given room by transgressing the bounds of worldly <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means), once it finds passage, would never be absent anywhere—and thus one would never act.
Because everything, in some way, can be a ground for suspecting some harm.
And because the suspicion of harm is a factor in the cessation [of activity] for discerning people.
Ultimately, even in consuming wholesome food and drink, death and the like are observed.
Therefore, one who upholds the practice of life governed by valid means should entertain suspicion only in accordance with what has been observed.
But not what has never been observed before.

children.text:
syādetat /
anyenānyasya sahakāreṇa cet svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandho bhavet, sarvaṃ sarveṇa svabhāvataḥ saṃbadhyeta /
tathā ca sarvaṃ sarvasmād gamyeta /
athānyasya cedanyat kāryam, kasmāt sarvaṃ sarvasya na bhavati, anyatvāviśiṣāt /
tataśca sa evātiprasaṅgaḥ /
yadyucyeta, na bhāvasvabhāvāḥ paryanuyojyāḥ, tasmādanyatvāviśeṣe 'pi kiñcideva kāraṇaṃ kāryañca kiñciditi /
nanveṣa svabhāvānāmanuyogo bhinnānāmakāryakāraṇabhūtānāmapi svabhāvapratibandhe tulya eva /
tasmād yatkiñcidetat /
kaḥ punaḥ pramāṇena svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandho gṛhyate? pratyakṣasaṃbandhiṣu pratyakṣeṇa, yathāha---liṅgaliṅgisaṃbandhadarśanamādyamiti /
yadā tāvat prathamaṃ vahnidhūmayoḥ sahādrendhanayoḥ saṃbandhaṃ paśyati tadā dvayorapi kiṃ svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandha aupādhiko vā? atha dhūmasyaupādhiko vahneḥ svābhāvikaḥ, vahnervaupādhiko dhūmasya tu svābhāvika iti na śakyaṃ nirdhārayitum /
tatra vahneranārdrendhanasya vinādhūmamayogolakādau darśanād ādrendhanopādhirasya dhūmena saṃbandho, na tu svabhāvika iti niścīyate /
dhūmaviśeṣasya tu vinā vahnimanupalabhbhād upādhibhedasya cādṛśyamānasya kalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvād viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣasya ca saṃśayasyānupalabdhapūrve anutpādāt, utpāde vā atiprasaṅgāt prekṣāvatāṃ pravṛttyucchedāt svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandhaḥ avadhāryate /
tadidamavadhāraṇaṃ na mānasam, anapekṣasya manaso bāhye pravṛttāvandhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgāt /
bhūyodarśanasāpekṣasya ca pravṛttau pramāṇāntarāpātāt, na hi mano nimittam ityeva mānasaṃ pratyakṣaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: And since its operation depends on repeated observation, another <s>pramāṇa</s> would be involved—for it is not the case that merely because the mind is the instrument, it constitutes mental perception.

children.text: tathā sati na kiñcinmānasam, pratyayamātrasya manonimittatvāt /
children.translated_text: If that were so, nothing would be non-mental, since every cognition has the mind as its instrument.

children.text: tattadasādhāraṇakāraṇāpekṣayo tu tatpramāṇavyapadeśe atrāpi bhūyodarśanam asādhāraṇamiti pramāṇāntaraṃ jātam /
children.translated_text: But when the designation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> depends on the uncommon cause, here too repeated observation is the uncommon cause—so another <s>pramāṇa</s> has arisen.

Therefore, we see it as proper that the sense organ itself, aided by the impression generated through repeated observation—like an expert in gem classification who knows the reality of gem distinctions—apprehends the natural relation of smoke and the like with fire and the like.

It may be objected:
If the natural relation were to exist through the cooperation of one thing with another, then everything would be naturally related to everything.
And thus everything would be inferable from everything.
But if one thing is the effect of another, why is it not the case that everything is the effect of everything, since there is no distinction in their being 'other'?
And thus the same over-extension would follow.
If it is said that the natures of things should not be questioned—therefore, despite the non-distinction of otherness, only something particular is a cause and only something particular is an effect—
then surely this same questioning of natures applies equally to the natural restriction of things that are different and not in a cause-effect relation.
Therefore, all this is arbitrary.
By what <s>pramāṇa</s> then is the natural relation apprehended? For things related to perception, by perception—as stated: 'The observation of the relation between the mark and the mark-bearer is the first [step].'
Now, when one first sees the relation of fire and smoke in moist fuel, is the relation of both natural or conditional? Whether the conditional relation belongs to smoke and the natural to fire, or the conditional to fire and the natural to smoke—this cannot be determined.
There, from observing fire without smoke in hot coals where the fuel is not moist, it is ascertained that its relation with smoke is conditional upon moist fuel, not natural.
But since a particular kind of smoke is never observed without fire, and since no difference of <s>upādhi</s> is seen and there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for imagining one, and since doubt—which requires the recollection of a particular—does not arise regarding what has never been observed before, or if it did arise there would be over-extension and the cessation of all activity of discerning people—therefore the natural character of the relation is ascertained.
And this ascertainment is not mental, since if the mind operated independently on external things, there would be the absurd consequence that the blind and deaf and the like would not exist.

children.text: evaṃ mānāntaraviditasaṃbandhiṣu mānāntarāṇyeva yathāsvaṃ bhūyodarśanasahāyāni svābhāvikasaṃbandhagrahaṇe pramāṇamunnetavyāni /

svabhāvataśca pratibaddhā hetavaḥ svasādhyena yadi sādhyamantareṇa bhaveyuḥ, svabhāvādeva pracyaveranniti tarkasahāyā nirastasādhyavyatirekavṛttisandehā yatra dṛṣṭāḥ tatra svasādhyamupasthāpayantyeva /
children.translated_text: And causes that are naturally restricted to their probandum—if they were to exist without the probandum, they would deviate from their own nature—therefore, aided by <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), having removed the doubt regarding their occurrence in the absence of the probandum, wherever they are observed, they invariably present their own probandum.

children.text: na ca śyāmādiṣu maitratanayādīnāṃ svābhāvikapratibandhasaṃbhavaḥ, annapānapariṇatibhedasyopādheḥ śyāmatāyā maitratanayasaṃbandhaṃ prati vidyamānatvena maitratanayatvasyāgamakatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the natural restriction of dark complexion and the like with being the son of <s>Maitra</s> and the like is not possible, since the <s>upādhi</s> of the difference in the transformation of food and drink exists for the relation of dark complexion with being the son of <s>Maitra</s>, and thus being the son of <s>Maitra</s> is not indicative.

children.text: etena pakvānyasya vṛkṣasyāgravartīni phalāni etadvṛkṣaprabhavatvāt patitaphalavadityādayo 'pyaupādhikasaṃbandhā vyākhyātāḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, the conditional relations such as 'the ripe fruits at the top of another tree are from this tree, because of being tree-born, like fallen fruits' and the like are also explained.
Therefore, everything is clear.

Similarly, for things whose relation is known through other means of valid knowledge, those very other means—each aided by repeated observation—should be adduced as the <s>pramāṇa</s> for apprehending the natural relation.

children.text:
nanvantimapratyakṣamatītābhyāṃ pratyakṣābhyāṃ kathamanugṛhyate ityata āha---smṛtyā ceti /
co hetvarthe /
yadyapi svarūpato liṅgadarśane atīte, tathāpi tajjanitā smṛtiḥ anugṛhṇāti yasmādatastābhyāmanugṛhyate /
anugrahaśca karaṇameva /
saṃbandhasamṛtisahakāriṇā indriyeṇa svasādhyāvinābhūtaliṅgavijñānaṃ yadupajanyate tat parāmarśa
ityākhyāyate /
tathābhūtaliṅgagocara eva caturtho vākyāvayava upanaya ityākhyāyate /
atra pṛcchati---kaḥ punariti /
anumānaśabdasyārtho na tāvadanumitiḥ /
na khalu liṅgaparāmarśo 'numitiḥ, pratyakṣaphalatvāt /
tasmādanumīyate aneneti karaṇārtho vaktavyaḥ /
sa ca liṅgaviṣayaḥ kriyā ca liṅgiviṣayeti viṣayavaiṣamyāt na kriyākaraṇabhāva iti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---anumīyata iti /
tenaivābhiprāyeṇa pṛcchati---kiṃ punariti /
uttaram---agnīti /
praṣṭā svābhiprāyamudghāṭayati---kathaṃ punaranyaviṣayamiti /
ekadeśina uttaram---nāniyamāditi /
vṛkṣoddeśena pravartitaḥ paraśuḥ kartrā na tadavayavoddeśena, tasmād vṛkṣaviṣayaḥ paraśurna tadavayavaviṣayaḥ /
dvaidhībhāvaścāvayaveṣu na vṛkṣe, tasya tato vināśāt iti bhāvaḥ /
kvacit punaryadviṣayamiti /
auṣṇyāpekṣo vahnisaṃyogaḥ karaṇaṃ taṇḍuleṣu /
rūpādiparāvṛttirūpaḥ pākaḥ teppeva /
taṇḍulena piṭharaṃ lakṣayati /
na kevalaṃ samānaviṣayatvāniyamaḥ kartuḥ karaṇaṃ bhinnamityapi niyamo nāstītyaniyamābhidhānaprasaṅgenāha-kvacit punariti /
sthitiḥ sāvayaveṣu samavāyo vā pradeśaviśeṣe saṃyogo vā /
evamaniyamaṃ dṛṣṭānta uktvā dārṣṭāntike yojayati---evamanyaviṣayasyeti dhūmaviṣayasya pramāṇasyāgniviṣayā kriyā pramitiḥ /
yadā agniviṣayameva jñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ tatrāha---kvacit punariti /
ākṣipati---kiṃ punariti /
atra hetumāha---pramitatvāt /
uttaram---pramīyate /
tadvibhajate---heyatveneti /
aniyamavādina ekadeśino mataṃ niyamavādī dūṣayati---tanneti /
hetumāha---pramāṇaphalayoriti /
yadi anyaviṣayaṃ karaṇamanyaviṣayā kriyā bhavet tataśchedane khadiraṃ prāpte panasādāvapi cchidā syādityatiprasaṅgaḥ syāt /
yadyapi vṛkṣoddeśena kartrā paraśuḥ prayuktastathāpyayaṃ vṛkṣamiva tadavayavānapi prāpta iti tadviṣayo bhavati /
tena tadavayavadvaidhībhāvamukhena vṛkṣaviṣayāmapi dvaidhībhāvakriyāṃ janayatīti na vaiyadhikaraṇyaṃ karaṇaphalayoḥ /
evaṃ yadyapi liṅgaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣaphalatayā liṅgajñānam, tadanubaddhasya tasya mānasapratyakṣagocaratvāt, liṅganirūpaṇamantareṇa tadanirūpaṇāt /
na tu liṅgajñānaṃ liṅginaṃ vinā na nirūpyate /
tasmāt pratipattayanubandhitayā viṣayo na liṅgajñānasya liṅgī, kiṃ tu liṅgameva /
tathapi liṅgiviṣayapratipattijanakatvāt liṅgajñānaṃ bhavati liṅgiviṣayam /
na cātiprasaṅgaḥ, svābhāvikasaṃbandhaśālitvāt liḍsya liṅgini /
tasmād dvividho viṣayabhāvaḥ pratipattyanubandhitayā, pratipādyatayā ca /
tatra pūrvaḥ phalasya, uttarastu prāmāṇyasyeti vivekaḥ /
tasmāt suṣṭhuktam---pramāṇaphalayorviṣayabhadānabhyupagamāditi /
sthitau tu bhedo darśayiṣyate kartuḥ karaṇasya ceti /
children.translated_text: But in the case of stability, the difference between the agent and the instrument will be shown.

children.text: tadevaṃ tāni te iti vigrahadvayaṃ parasparāpekṣamupapādya tāni taditi vigrahadvayaṃ parasparāpekṣamupapādayati---yadā punariti /
children.translated_text: Thus, having established the two analyses 'those' and 'those' as mutually dependent, he establishes the two analyses 'those' and 'that' as mutually dependent—'when however.'

children.text: liṅgaliṅgisaṃbandhadarśanaṃ ca anantaraliṅgadarśanaṃ ca tatsmṛtiśceti vigrahaḥ /
children.translated_text: The analysis is: the observation of the relation between the mark and the mark-bearer, and the subsequent observation of the mark, and the memory of that.

children.text: atrāpi sarvasandeheṣvidamupatiṣṭhate, vyākhyānato viśaiṣapratipattirna hi sandehādalakṣaṇamiti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: Here too, in all doubts, this stands firm: particular understanding comes from explanation, for there is no lack of definition merely because of doubt—this is the purport.

But how is the final perception assisted by the two prior perceptions that have passed? Therefore he says—'and by memory.'
The word 'ca' (and) is in the sense of reason.
Although the observation of the mark in its own form has passed, nevertheless the memory generated by it assists—therefore by those two [prior perceptions] it is assisted.
And assistance is precisely the instrumental operation.
The cognition of the mark as invariably concomitant with its probandum, produced by the sense organ cooperating with the memory of the relation, is called <s>parāmarśa</s> (reflective consideration).
The fourth sentence-member directed at such a mark is called <s>upanaya</s> (application).
Here he asks—'what then?'
The meaning of the word '<s>anumāna</s>' (inference) is not the inferential cognition (<s>anumiti</s>).
For the reflective consideration of the mark is not <s>anumiti</s>, since it is a result of perception.
Therefore, the instrumental meaning 'that by which one infers' should be stated.
And that has the mark as its object, while the action [of inferring] has the mark-bearer as its object—and due to the difference in object, there is no relation of action and instrument—this is the purport.
The answer—'it is inferred.'
With that very intent he asks—'what then?'
The answer—'fire.'
The questioner reveals his own intent—'but how is it that something directed at a different object...'
The partial advocate's answer—'because there is no restriction.'
An axe, employed by the agent with reference to the tree, is not employed with reference to its parts—therefore the axe has the tree as its object, not its parts.
And the splitting occurs in the parts, not in the tree, since the tree is destroyed by that—this is the purport.
Sometimes, however, that whose object is [different]—
The conjunction with fire, dependent on heat, is the instrument in [cooking] rice grains.
The cooking—which is the transformation of form and the like—is in those very [rice grains].
By 'rice grains' he indicates the pot.
Not only is there no restriction that the instrument have the same object as the agent, but there is also no restriction that the agent and instrument be different—to indicate this absence of restriction he says—'sometimes however.'
<s>Sthiti</s> (stability) in composites is either inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) in a particular location, or conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>).
Having thus stated the absence of restriction with an example, he applies it to the case at hand—'thus, of one directed at a different object'—the <s>pramāṇa</s> directed at smoke has fire as the object of its action, i.e., the inferential cognition (<s>pramiti</s>).
When the cognition directed at fire itself is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, there he says—'sometimes however.'
He objects—'what then?'
Here he states the reason—'because of being measured (<s>pramitatva</s>).'
The answer—'it is measured.'
He analyzes that—'as what is to be abandoned.'
The advocate of non-restriction, a partial advocate, has his view refuted by the advocate of restriction—'that is not so.'
He states the reason—'of the <s>pramāṇa</s> and its result.'
If the instrument had one object and the action another, then when cutting a <s>khadira</s> tree, cutting would occur even in a jackfruit tree and the like—and this would be an over-extension.
Although the axe was employed by the agent with reference to the tree, nevertheless it reaches the parts of the tree just as it reaches the tree itself—so it has those as its object.
Therefore, by generating the cutting action on the tree through the splitting of its parts, there is no difference of domain (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>) between the instrument and its result.
Similarly, although the cognition of the mark has the mark as its object with perception as its result, because it [the mark] is the object of mental perception due to being connected with the mark-bearer, and because without the determination of the mark, the mark-bearer is not determined.
But the cognition of the mark is not determined without the mark-bearer.
Therefore, by being connected with understanding, the mark-bearer is not the object of the mark-cognition; rather, the mark itself is.
Nevertheless, because of generating the understanding directed at the mark-bearer, the mark-cognition is directed at the mark-bearer.
And there is no over-extension, because the mark has a natural relation with the mark-bearer.
Therefore, the object-relation is of two kinds: by being connected with understanding, and by being what is to be made known.
Therein, the former belongs to the result, and the latter to validity—this is the distinction.
Therefore it is well said—'because the difference of object of the <s>pramāṇa</s> and its result is not accepted.'

children.text:
nanu yadi pramāṇaphalayorekaviṣayatvaṃ tarhi parāmarśajñānaviṣayīkṛta evārtho viṣayīkartavyo nānyaḥ /
sa ca pratyakṣapramāṇaviṣaya eveti kṛtamanumānenetyāśayavān pṛcchati---kiṃ punariti /
tairviśiṣṭena liṅgaparāmarśenetyarthaḥ /
uttaram---śeṣo 'rthaḥ /
pratyakṣapramitāt liṅgādanyo liṅgī tadviṣayatvaṃ ca liṅgaparāmarśasyoktamiti /
pṛcchati---anumānamityatra kiṃ kārakam? anumīyate 'neneti karaṇakārakameva yuktaṃ, tasyaiva liṅgadarśanadvayasmṛtipūrvakatvāt, na tvanumitiranumānaṃ pramāṇavyāpāratvenātannimittatvāt karaṇakārakādanyatvād atatpūrvakatvācceti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---bhāvaḥ karaṇaṃ vā /
nanūktaṃ na bhāvaḥ kārakamityata āha---yadeti /
na dravyādīnāmeva kārakatvam, api tu vyāpārasyāpi /
anyathā karmanāmadheyeṣūdbhidādiśabdeṣu na kāraṇavibhaktiḥ śrūyeta, udbhidā yajeta darśamaurṇamāsābhyāṃ yajetetyādi /
saṃbhavati hi tasyāpi siddhasya phalabhāvanāyāṃ nimittatvam /
evaṃ vahnipramāyāḥ siddhāyāḥ saṃbhavati hānādibuddhinimittabhāvaḥ /
etasmiśca kalpe tatpūrvakamityatra tadā hānādisaṃbandhāvadhāraṇasamaye prathamaṃ vahnitvasya liṅgasya darśanam, athānumānikaṃ dvitīyam, atha saṃbandhasya smṛtiriti trayamekīkṛtya parāmarṣṭavyam /
tatpūrvako hi tathā cāyamanumīyamāno vahniriti liṅgaparāmarśaḥ /
tasmād dāhapākādikāritvādupādeyo vahniriti jñānamanumānasya phalam /
tataśca tatpūrvakatvamapi siddhaṃ bhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
karaṇakārakapakṣe phalamāha---yadā karaṇamiti /
atra vimṛśati-liṅgeti /
tatpūrvakatvānumitinimittatvasamānadharmadarśanāt saṃśayaḥ /
atra ācāryadeśīyamatamāha---eke tāvaditi /
satsvapītareṣu smṛterabhāvādanumiteranutpādanena smṛtireva anumānam, itare tu tadanugrāhakā ityarthaḥ /
matāntaramāha---apara iti /
satsvapītareṣu liṅgaparāmarśaṃ vinā anumityanutpādāt, liṅgaparāmarśa evānumānamitarairanugṛhīta ityarthaḥ /
svamatamāha---vayaṃ tviti /
anvayavyatirekābhyāmaśakyo guṇapradhānabhāvo vivektum, tayoḥ sarvatra tulyatvāditi bhāvaḥ /
tat kimidānīṃ nāstyeva guṇapradhānabhāva ityata āha---pradhāneti /
nānvayavyatirekāvatra prabhavato na tu nyāyāntaramiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: positive and negative concomitance are not effective here, but another method [of determination exists].
He asks—'what then here?'
The answer—'immediate succession (<s>ānantarya</s>).'
Nothing here is hidden.

Now, if the means of knowledge and the result have the same object, then the very object that is objectified by the reflective consideration (<s>parāmarśa</s>) cognition must be the object—not another. And that is an object of perception alone—so inference is unnecessary. With this thought, he asks—'what then?' The meaning is: by that specific inferential-mark consideration. The answer—'the remaining object.' The mark-bearer is different from the mark ascertained by perception, and the inferential-mark consideration has that [mark-bearer] as its object—this has been stated. He asks—'what <s>kāraka</s> (syntactic role) does the word "<s>anumāna</s>" have?' 'That by which one infers'—so the instrumental <s>kāraka</s> alone is appropriate, since that alone is preceded by the perception of the mark, pervasion, and memory. But <s>anumiti</s> (inferential cognition) is not <s>anumāna</s> (the means of inference), because it is not the cause of that [result], being the operation of the means of knowledge, and being different from the instrumental <s>kāraka</s>, and not being preceded by that—such is the sense. The answer—'the action (<s>bhāva</s>) or the instrument.' Now, it was said that the action is not a <s>kāraka</s>—therefore he says: 'that.' Not only substances and the like have <s>kāraka</s> status, but activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>) also does. Otherwise, in ritual-action-names like '<s>udbhid</s>' etc., the instrumental case would not be heard—'one sacrifices with the <s>udbhid</s>,' 'one sacrifices with the <s>darśapaurṇamāsa</s>,' and so on. For it is possible that the accomplished [action] too is a cause in producing the result (<s>phala</s>). Similarly, the accomplished cognition of fire can be the cause of abandonment-cognitions etc. And on this alternative, regarding 'preceded by that'—at the time of determining the relation with abandonment etc., first the perception of the mark, fire-ness, then the inferential [cognition] second, then the memory of the relation—these three combined are to be reflected upon. For the inferential-mark consideration 'thus this fire is being inferred' is preceded by that. Therefore, the cognition 'fire is to be accepted because of its capacity for burning, cooking, etc.' is the result of inference. And thus the 'being preceded by that' is also established—such is the sense. On the instrumental-<s>kāraka</s> alternative, he states the result—'when it is the instrument.' Here he deliberates—'the mark.' Because of observing the common property of being preceded by that and being the cause of inferential cognition, there is doubt. Here he states the view of the followers of the <s>Ācārya</s>—'some, first.' The meaning is: since without memory, even when the others exist, inferential cognition is not produced, memory alone is <s>anumāna</s>; the others are its auxiliaries. He states another view—'others.' The meaning is: since without the inferential-mark consideration, even when the others exist, inferential cognition is not produced, the inferential-mark consideration alone is <s>anumāna</s>, aided by the others. He states his own view—'but we.' The subordinate-principal relationship cannot be discriminated by positive and negative concomitance, since both are equal everywhere—such is the sense. Then is there no subordinate-principal relationship at all?—therefore he says: 'the principal.'

children.text:
ativyāpti codayati---yadīti /
nanu bhavatu pratyakṣadvayapūrvakaḥ saṃskāro 'numānam, tenāpi śeṣo 'rtho 'numāsyata ityata āha---smṛtihetuḥ nānumitiheturityarthaḥ /
pariharati---naiṣa doṣa iti /
viśiṣṭajñānaṃ vijñānam viśaṣaśca smṛteranyatvam, na hīndriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānaṃ smṛtiḥ /
tasyāḥ saṃskāramātraprabhavatayā anyasmādanutpatteḥ /
tena ca jñānena svakāraṇaṃ viśeṣitam, pratyakṣasūtre yata ityadhyāhārāt /
tasmādihāpi svakāraṇaviśeṣakaṃ smṛteranyad vijñānamadhikṛtam /
na ca saṃskāraḥ pratyakṣapūrvo 'pi tādṛśajñānakāraṇamiti na tasya prasaṅga ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He prevents the over-extension to determination (<s>nirṇaya</s>) that has not produced a result—'determination.'

children.text: vibhāgasūtrākṣiptapramāṇasāmānyalakṣaṇapūrvakaṃ viśeṣapramāṇalakṣaṇaṃ tadapekṣaṃ pravartamānaṃ nānupajanitaphale 'pramāṇe nirṇayamātre pravartitumarhati, janitaphalastu nirṇayaḥ pramāṇameveti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: The definition of a specific means of knowledge, which presupposes the general definition of means of knowledge implied by the division <s>sūtra</s>, being dependent on that, cannot apply to mere determination that has not produced a result (and is thus not a means of knowledge); but determination that has produced a result is a means of knowledge itself—such is the sense.
Because it determines its own object, the result is determination itself; and that which determines is the determiner.
The suffix is in the reflexive sense.

He raises over-extension—'if.' Now, let the latent impression preceded by two perceptions be <s>anumāna</s>; even by that, the remaining object could be inferred—therefore he says: 'the cause of memory is not the cause of inferential cognition'—such is the meaning. He resolves—'this is not a fault.' The specific cognition is <s>vijñāna</s> (understanding), and the specific feature is its being different from memory—for cognition produced from the contact of sense organ with object is not memory. Because memory arises solely from latent impressions and not from anything else. And that cognition, qualified by its own cause, [is what is meant]—because in the perception <s>sūtra</s>, 'from which' is to be supplied. Therefore, here too, the understanding that is different from memory, which qualifies its own cause, is what is intended. And the latent impression, though preceded by perception, is not the cause of such cognition—so there is no over-extension—such is the meaning.

children.text:
trividhamiti sūtrāvayavamarthagauravādarād vārttikakāra udbhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---trividhamitīti /
anvayavyatirekiṇaṃ lakṣayati---tatreti /
vivakṣitopapattiḥ pakṣadharmatā /
tajjātīyopapattiḥ anvayaḥ /
vipakṣāvṛttiḥ vyatirekaḥ /
anvayimātrāt vyatirekimātrācca vyāvṛtto 'nvayavyatirekī darśanīya iti hetutrayasādhāraṇe abādhitaviṣayatvātsatpratipakṣatve satī api heturūpe na darśite /
vivakṣitapratyayamantareṇa cānvayavyatirakayoḥ tajjātīyātajjātīyavṛttivyāvṛttyoraśakyapratītitvād vivakṣitopādānam /
tatprasaṅgena ca taddharmatā hetutrayasamānapi darśitā /
tasyodāharaṇamāha---yatheti /
pratyakṣatvāditi heturātmani nitye 'stītyata uktam---bāhyakaraṇeti /
tathāpi sāmānyaviśeṣairghaṭatvādibhirvyabhicāra ityata uktam--sāmānyaviśeṣavattva iti /
tathāpi paramāṇubhirbāhyakaraṇapratyakṣairyogināṃ vyabhicāra ityata uktam--asmadādīti /
tathā cāyaṃ nityebhya ākāśādibhyo ghaṭādiṣu cānityeṣvanvita iti bhavatyanvayavyatirekī /
anvayinaṃ lakṣayati--anvayīti, vipakṣahīna iti /
vipakṣābhāvena tato vyatirekābhāvaṃ darśayati /
sadbhyāmabhāvo nirūpyate naikena satetyuktam /
tena hetoryato vipakṣānnivṛttiḥ sa eva nāstīti kuto nivartatām, pakṣādanyasya sarvasyaiva sapakṣatvāt? na nivartata iti cet? astu tarhi hetostatra vṛttiḥ, nivṛttiniṣedharūpatvād vṛtteriti cet? yasyābhāvādhikaraṇatvamapi na saṃbhavati nirūpākhyasya tasya bhāvādhikaraṇatvaśaṅketi subhāṣitam /
na khalu mumurṣosatoyābhyavahāre 'pyasamarthasya śaṣkulībhakṣaṇaṃ śaṅkate cetanaḥ /
tat kimidānīṃ bhāvābhāvau na parasparābhāvātmānau yadekaniṣedhenānyavidhiḥ syāt? satyam, yatraikatara etayorniṣidhyate vidhīyate vā tatra taditaravidharniṣedho vāvaśyaṃ bhavet /
na tviha paramārthataḥ kasyacit niṣedhaḥ /
na cātra nirūpākhyo hetorvyatireko niṣidhyate /
nanu nirūpākhyo niṣedhādhikaraṇamiti ca vacaḥ svacaritaviruddham /
na caitat tattvato nirūpākhye hetorvyatirekaṃ vā hetuṃ vā vyāsedhāmo nāpyanvayaṃ vidadhmaḥ /
no khalvayaṃ sakalapratipattyabhājanaṃ kvacidapyupayujyate /
upayoge vā nirūpākhyo na bhavet /
kastarhi na nirūpākhye hetorvyatireka ityasyavacanasyārthaḥ? atha nirūpākhye hetorvyatireka ityasya bhavadbhāṣitasya ko 'rthaḥ? ahṛdayavācāṃ khalayahṛdayā eva prativāco bhavanti bhavanti /
yakṣānurūpo baliriti hi laukikānām ābhāṇakaḥ /
na cātyantādṛṣṭapūrvāṇāṃ kalpanājālagocaratvamiti copapāditamanyathākhyāti /
nirūpaṇavāsare /
kalpitagocaraśca vyatireko 'pi kālpanika iti nānumānāṅgam /
svābhāvikarūpasaṃpannaṃ hi pramāṇaṃ tattvajñānarūphalāya kalpate na kalpitarūpasaṃpadā, tasyāḥ sarvatra sulabhatvāditi /
tattvaviṣayatvaṃ cānumānasyopapādayiṣyate /
tasmādanupākhye vipakṣe hetorvyatirekanivṛttau vā vyatireke vā hetupravṛttau vā sahṛdayānāṃ mūkataivocitā /
na caitāvatā hetoragamakatvam /

children.translated_text: For it is not the case that the reason is probative only because negative concomitance exists.

children.text: mā bhūdasādhāraṇasyāpi gamakatvam, kiṃ tu svasādhyena saha svābhāvikasaṃbandhaśālitayā /
children.translated_text: Let the uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>) reason too not be probative—but rather, [it is probative] by virtue of possessing a natural relation with its own <s>sādhya</s> (probandum).

And that [natural relation] can be known through positive concomitance alone, free from limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>), just as through both positive and negative concomitance—so negative concomitance is unnecessary here.

children.text: vipakṣasaṃbhave tu tatrāpi hetuvṛttiśaṅkānirākaraṇāya vyatirekagrahaṇam upāsanīyamiti sarvamavadātam //
children.translated_text: But when a counter-thesis is possible, the acceptance of negative concomitance is to be sought for the purpose of removing the suspicion of the reason's presence even there—thus all is clear.

The <s>Vārtikakāra</s>, out of respect for profundity of meaning, explains the <s>sūtra</s>-component 'threefold' as something worth elaborating—'threefold, thus.' He defines the <s>anvayavyatirekin</s> (the reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance)—'there.' The fitness of the intended [conclusion] is being a property of the thesis (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>). The fitness of what is of that class is positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>). Absence from the counter-thesis is negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>). The <s>anvayavyatirekin</s>, distinguished from the merely positive and the merely negative, is to be shown. Among the three common characteristics of a reason—being of an uncontradicted domain—even when there is a counter-argument (<s>satpratipakṣatva</s>), the form of the reason that is not demonstrated [is excluded]. And since the occurrence and non-occurrence in things of the same and different class cannot be understood without [first understanding] the intended [conclusion], the intended is included. And incidentally, its being a property of the thesis, though common to all three types of reason, is also shown. He gives an example—'as.' 'Because of perceptibility'—since the reason exists in the eternal self, it is said: 'external instrument.' Even so, there is deviation through universals and particulars like pot-ness etc.—therefore it is said: 'possessing universals and particulars.' Even so, there is deviation through atoms, external perceptible instruments, and yogins—therefore it is said: 'for us and others.' And thus this [reason], being present in the eternal [things] like space etc. and in non-eternal things like pots etc., is an <s>anvayavyatirekin</s>. He defines the <s>anvayin</s> (merely positive)—'<s>anvayin</s>'—'devoid of counter-thesis.' He shows the absence of negative concomitance from the absence of a counter-thesis. Absence is determined by both [kinds of] presence, not by a single presence—this is said. Therefore, that counter-thesis from which the reason's withdrawal [would occur] simply does not exist—so from what would it withdraw? Since everything other than the thesis is a homologue. 'If it does not withdraw?'—then let there be the presence of the reason there; and since presence is of the form of negation of withdrawal—if so? It is well said: of something whose absence-locus-hood is not even possible—something nameless—to suspect its presence-locus-hood! Indeed, a conscious person does not suspect the eating of rice-cakes by one who is dying and incapable even of consuming waterless food. 'Then do existence and non-existence not have each other as their negation, such that the negation of one would establish the other?'—True; wherever one of these is negated or affirmed, there the affirmation or negation of the other necessarily follows. But here, nothing is truly negated. And here, the negative concomitance of the reason in the nameless [counter-thesis] is not negated. 'But saying "the nameless is the locus of negation" is self-contradictory!'—We do not truly negate the reason's negative concomitance in the nameless, nor do we affirm the positive concomitance. This [nameless counter-thesis] being utterly beyond all cognition, is not applicable anywhere. Or if it were applicable, it would not be nameless. What then is the meaning of the statement 'the reason has no negative concomitance in the nameless'? And what is the meaning of your statement 'the reason has negative concomitance in the nameless'? Heartless words indeed receive heartless responses. 'An offering befitting the <s>Yakṣa</s>'—such is the worldly proverb. And it has been established in the [discussion of] <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (error) that what has never been seen cannot be an object of the web of imagination. At the time of examination. And negative concomitance whose domain is imagined is also imaginary—and so is not a component of inference. For a means of knowledge endowed with natural form is capable of producing the result that is knowledge of reality—not through imagined form, since that is easily available everywhere. And the truth-directedness of inference will be demonstrated. Therefore, regarding the reason's negative concomitance or its absence in the nameless counter-thesis, or the reason's presence [there]—silence alone befits the wise. But this does not entail the non-probativeness of the reason.

children.text:
udāharaṇamāha---yatheti /
svamate tvabhidheyo viśeṣaḥ prameyatvāt sāmānyavat /
paramāṇvākāśādayaḥ kasyacit pratyakṣāḥ prameyatvāt ghaṭavadityādayo draṣṭavyāḥ, viśvasyaiva sadasatprabhedabhinnasya yathāsvaṃ pakṣasapakṣayorantarbhāvena vipakṣābhāvāditi /
vyatirekiṇaṃ lakṣayati---vyatirekīti /
tamimaṃ vyatirekiṇaṃ hetvavayavalakṣaṇavyākhyānāvasare vārttikakṛd upapādayiṣyatīti nehopapāditaḥ /
tadevaṃ trividhamityavacchidya vyutpādya saṃprati pūrvavadityādinā ekavākyatayā vyācaṣṭa---atha vā trividhamiti /
tisṛṣvapi vidhāsu sādhyavacanasya pūrvamapapādanāt pūrvaṃ sādhyaṃ tad yasyāstyadhikaraṇatayā tatpūrvavat /
tathāpyanityāḥ paramāṇavo gandhavattvād ghaṭavadityapi hetuḥ syāt /
asti hi sādhyaṃ tasyāpi, pārthivānāmapyaṇūnāmanityatvena siṣādhayiṣitatvādityata āha---vyāptyeti /
children.translated_text: For that too has a <s>sādhya</s>—since the impermanence of earthy atoms is also what is desired to be proved—therefore he says: 'by pervasion.'

children.text: asti gandhavattvasya sādhyaṃ na tu vyāptyā, pṛthivīmātravṛttitatayā caturṣu paramāṇuṣu tadabhāvāt /
children.translated_text: Odor-possession has a <s>sādhya</s>, but not through pervasion—since, being restricted to earth alone, it is absent in [the atoms of] the other three [elements].

children.text: sādhyasyopayuktatvāt tato 'nyastajjātīyaḥ śeṣaḥ, sādhyasāmānyena samāna iti yāvat /
children.translated_text: Because of the usefulness of the <s>sādhya</s>, what is other than it, being of its class, is the remainder—meaning, similar by sharing the general nature of the <s>sādhya</s>.
This is what he says—'the <s>sādhya</s> and what is of its class.'

He gives an example—'as.' But in our view, the particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>) is to be expressed: 'because of being knowable, like the universal.' Atoms, space, and the like are perceptible to some, because of being knowable, like a pot—and so on should be understood. Since everything, divided into existent and non-existent categories, is included within the thesis and homologue respectively, there is no counter-thesis. He defines the <s>vyatirekin</s> (merely negative)—'<s>vyatirekin</s>.' The <s>Vārtikakāra</s> will establish this <s>vyatirekin</s> at the occasion of explaining the definition of the components of the argument—so it is not established here. Having thus delimited and explained 'threefold,' he now explains through unity of sentence with '<s>pūrvavat</s>' etc.—'or, threefold.' Since in all three types, the expression of the <s>sādhya</s> is established first, 'first the <s>sādhya</s>'—that which has this as its locus is '<s>pūrvavat</s>' (preceded by that). Even so, 'atoms are impermanent because of possessing odor, like a pot' would also be a reason.

children.text:
padāni vibhajyārthamāha---pūrvavannāmeti /
sāmānyato 'dṛṣṭamiti na/mantarbhāvya vyācaṣṭa---sāmānyataśceti /
tathā ca bādhitaviṣayaṃ prakaraṇasamaṃ cānumānaṃ syādityata āha---caśabdāditi /
vārttike caśabdenāsatpratipakṣatvamati sūcitam /
tena sūtrasthena caśabdenābādhitaviṣayatvamasatpratipakṣatvamapi rūpadvayaṃ samuccitamityuktaṃ bhavati /
nanvevaṃ trividho 'pi hetuḥ pañcalakṣaṇaḥ syādityata āha---evamiti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati abādhitaviṣayamasatpratipakṣaṃ pūrvavaditi ca dhruvaṃ kṛtvā śeṣavadityekā vidhā, sāmānyatodṛṣṭamiti dvitīyā, śeṣavatsāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ ceti tṛtīyā /
trividhamanumānam /
tatra caturlatraṇa dvayam /
ekaṃ pañcalakṣaṇamiti /
tadevaṃ svamatena sūtraṃ vyākhyāya bhāṣyakṛnmatena vyācaṣṭa---atha veti /
ākṣeptuṃ svarūpato vyācaṣṭe---tatreti /
pūrvaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāryāt /
tad yasyāsti viṣayatayā parāmarśajñānasyānumānasya tat pūrvavadityarthaḥ /
vikalpyā ākṣipati---yadi tāvaditi sarvatrānumānaprasaṅgāditi bhāvaḥ /
atiprasaḍbhiyā kalpāntaramātiṣṭhate---atha punariti /
dūṣayati---etadapīti /
dūṣaṇāntaraṃ samuccinoti---kāraṇadarśanācceti /
nāsiddhāśrayo heturgamaka iti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati--neti /
dvayamapi nābhyupeyata ityarthaḥ /
kiṃ tarhi abhyupeyate ityata āha--kāryaṃ tviti /
enaṃ prakāramanyatrāpyatidiśati--evamiti /
pṛcchati--kathamiti /
uttaram--dvayoriti /
pūrvaśabdena kāraṇabhighāyinā pratisaṃbandhitayā kāryamapyupakṣiptam /
ato dvayorapyupakṣiptayoḥ kāraṇasyopayogādanumānabhāveneti yocanā /
udāharaṇamāha--udāharaṇamiti /
yadyapi kāraṇamātraṃ vyabhicārati kāryotpādam, tathāpi yādṛśaṃ na vyabhicarati tatra nipuṇena pratipatrā bhavitavyam /
anyathā dhūmamātramapi vahnisattāṃ vyabhicaratīti na dhūmaviśeṣo gamako bhavet /
rasādrūpānumāne tu vaināśikānāmāpāditaṃ kāraṇāt kāryānumānamasmābhiḥ /
api cāntyatantusaṃyogānantaraṃ paṭo jāyate tatrāpi śakyaṃ kāraṇāt kāryānumānam /
yadā khalvayamanyata evodbuddhasaṃskāro vyāptismṛtimān aviraleṣvitareṣu tantuṣu antyatantāvutpannāyāṃ kriyāyāmindriyasannikarṣāt prathamameva parāmṛśati tathā ceyamiti, tadaiva kriyāto vibhāga ityekaḥ kālaḥ /
atha yadā vibhāgāt pūrvasaṃyogavināśaḥ, tadā parāmarśāt tasmādavaśyaṃbhāvipaṭaviśiṣṭeyaṃ kriyetyanumānotpāda ityekaḥ kālaḥ /
athāntyasya tantostantusaṃyogaḥ, atha paṭotpādaḥ, tatra rūpādyutpādaḥ, atha pratyakṣadarśanam ityanumānotpādasya parastāccaturthe kṣaṇe pratyakṣam /
children.translated_text: Then the conjunction of the final thread with the other threads; then the production of cloth; therein the production of color and the like; then direct perception— thus perception [occurs] at the fourth moment after the production of inference.

children.text: yadi tu kriyotpādānantaramālocanamiṣyate, tathāpi tṛtīye kṣaṇe pratyakṣasya utpāda iti nānavasaramanumānam /
children.translated_text: But if observation immediately after the production of action is accepted, even so the production of perception is at the third moment— so inference is not without occasion.

children.text: api ca badhiro murajamukhamabhihatya svapāṇinābhighātādeva śabdakāraṇāt tatkāryaṃ śabdaṃ niḥśaṅkamanumimīte /
children.translated_text: Moreover, a deaf person, striking the face of a drum with his own hand, unhesitatingly infers sound— the effect— from the cause, namely the striking.
Similarly, other inferences from cause to effect should also be considered.

He analyzes the terms and states the meaning— 'pūrvavat by name.' Without subsuming 'sāmānyatodṛṣṭa' (based on general observation) under inference, he explains— 'and from the general.' And thus there would be inference with a contradicted subject and inference equal to the thesis (<s>prakaraṇasama</s>)— therefore he says— 'from the word ca (and).' In the <s>vārttika</s>, by the word 'ca,' the property of having no counterargument (<s>asatpratipakṣatva</s>) is indicated. Thus, by the word 'ca' in the <s>sūtra</s>, both the property of having an uncontradicted subject (<s>abādhitaviṣayatva</s>) and the property of having no counterargument are conjoined— this is what is stated. Now, if so, even the threefold reason would have five characteristics— to this he says— 'thus.' What is stated amounts to this: keeping 'having an uncontradicted subject,' 'having no counterargument,' and '<s>pūrvavat</s>' as fixed, '<s>śeṣavat</s>' constitutes one type; '<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' is the second; and '<s>śeṣavat</s> together with <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' is the third. Inference is threefold. Of these, two have four characteristics, and one has five characteristics. Having thus explained the <s>sūtra</s> according to his own view, he explains according to the view of the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>— 'or alternatively.' To raise an objection, he explains the essential nature [of each type]— 'therein.' The prior is the cause [which is prior to] the effect. That inference whose reflective cognition has that [cause] as its object— that is <s>pūrvavat</s>— this is the meaning. He raises an objection through alternatives— 'if indeed'— the purport being that there would be the unwanted consequence of inference everywhere. Out of fear of over-extension, he resorts to another interpretation— 'or alternatively.' He refutes— 'this too.' He adds another refutation— 'and because of seeing the cause.' A reason whose substrate is unestablished is not indicative— this is the purport. He resolves— 'no.' Neither of the two is accepted— this is the meaning. What then is accepted?— to this he says— 'but the effect.' He extends this pattern elsewhere as well— 'thus.' He asks— 'how?' The answer— 'of both.' By the word 'prior,' which denotes the cause, the effect too is implied through its correlative connection. Therefore, since the cause is useful when both [cause and effect] are implied, it has the nature of inference— such is the construction. He states the example— 'the example.' Although a cause in general deviates from the production of an effect, nevertheless, one must be skilled in identifying that specific [cause] which does not deviate. Otherwise, even mere smoke would deviate from the existence of fire, and so a specific kind of smoke would not be indicative. But in the inference of color from taste, the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (nihilists) have presented to us an inference from cause to effect. Moreover, after the final conjunction of threads, cloth is produced— there too an inference from cause to effect is possible. When this person, whose latent impressions have been awakened by something else, possessing the memory of pervasion, regarding the unbroken remaining threads, upon the arising of action in the final thread, first reflects through sense-contact— 'this action is such'— at that very time, from the action comes separation— this is one moment.

children.text:
śeṣavadudāharaṇamāha--nadyā iti /
codayati--kathaṃ punariti /
pariharati--neti /
anumīyate 'neneti anumānaṃ nadīpūraḥ /
na tu vṛṣṭiranumīyamānā pūraviśeṣāt nātītā śakyānumātum, anumānasamaye tadatyayasyāśakyaniścayatvāt /
nāpi vartamānā tadatyayasyāpi tadānīṃ saṃbhavāt /
evaṃ bhaviṣyantyapi sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvena sandigdhaiva /
tasmāt trekālyasyāśakyaniścayatvāt anupapannamanumānamityata āha--bhaviṣyatīti /
kāraṇasya hi kāryāt pūrvakālatā śakyā niścetum kāryeṇa liṅgena /
children.translated_text: For the priority of the cause to the effect can be determined with certainty through the mark which is the effect.
Therefore, the doubt regarding past, present, or future does not cause harm.
'Whatever'— this is intended in the sense of fitness.

children.text: sa ca kāryasya purastāt tato niścayavyāpta ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And that [rain], being prior to the effect, is encompassed by the certainty arising from it— this is the meaning.

He states the example of <s>śeṣavat</s>— 'of the river.' He objects— 'but how?' He resolves— 'no.' That by which something is inferred is the <s>anumāna</s> (means of inference)— the flooding of the river. But the rain that is inferred cannot be inferred as past from a particular type of flooding, since at the time of inference the passing of that [rain] cannot be determined with certainty. Nor [can it be inferred] as present, since even its passing is possible at that time. Similarly, even future [rain] remains merely doubtful due to the absence of either a proving or refuting <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, since none of the three times can be determined with certainty, the inference is untenable— to this he says— 'future.'

children.text:
sāmānyatodṛṣṭodāharaṇaṃ bhāṣyakārīyaṃ duḥkhabodham, śeṣavadudāharaṇāntargataṃ ca /
atrāpi kāryeṇa saviturdeśāntaraprāptyā tatkāraṇasya vrajyāyā anumānāt /
na caitāvatā anumānasya traividhyaṃ bhavati, udāharaṇamātrasyānantyenānantyaprasaṅgāt /
tasmād bhāṣyakāravyākhyānamarocayamāno vārttikakṛt anyathāvyākhyāyodāharaṇāntaramāha--sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ nāmeti /
sādhyadharmāvinābhāvinā viśeṣaṇena sādhanadharmeṇa viśiṣyamāṇo dharmo gamyate gamakatvena /
hetuviśiṣṭo hi dharmo gamakaḥ, jijñāsitadharmaviśiṣṭaśca gamyaḥ /

children.translated_text: As they say—

children.text: sa eva cobhayātmāṣa gamyo gamaka iṣyate /
children.translated_text: That very [property] which has both natures is accepted as what is indicated and what indicates.
By the unestablished portion it is what is indicated; by the established portion it is what makes known.

The example of <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> given by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> is difficult to understand and is subsumed under the example of <s>śeṣavat</s>. For here too, from the effect— the sun's arrival at another location— the inference of its cause, namely locomotion, is an inference [from effect to cause]. And this alone does not make inference threefold, since from the infinity of examples alone there would be the unwanted consequence of infinity [of types]. Therefore, not approving the explanation of the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> gives a different explanation and another example, saying— '<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> is named thus.' A property that is qualified by the qualifying property of the proving-term, which is inseparable from the property of the thesis (<s>sādhya</s>), is understood as indicative. For a property qualified by the reason is indicative, and one qualified by the property to be investigated is what is indicated.

children.text:
iti /
avinābhāvitvaṃ svabhāvapratibaddhatvaṃ sarveṣāmeva hetūnāṃ sāmānyam /
tatra dharmadharmiṇorabhedavivakṣayā hetureva sāmānyamuktaḥ /
sāmānyenāvinābhāvinā hetunā avacchinnaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ dharmirūpamanumānaṃ sāmānyato dṛṣṭamanumānam /

children.translated_text: The <s>tasi</s> suffix stands for the third [instrumental] case.

children.text: tadetat pūrvavaccheṣavatorapi prāpakamapi tatpadasannidhānāt gobalīvardanyāyena te parityajyānyatra niviśate /
children.translated_text: This [definition of <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>], though applicable to <s>pūrvavat</s> and <s>śeṣavat</s> as well, by virtue of the proximity of that term [in the <s>sūtra</s>], by the principle of 'cow and bull' (<s>gobalīvardanyāya</s>), abandons those and settles in something else.
This is what was stated— 'by what does not bear [the relation of] effect and cause.'
He states the example— 'just as with cranes.'

Thus. The property of inseparability— being bound by nature— is common to all reasons.
