There, by the intention of non-difference between property and property-bearer, the reason itself is called 'the general' (<s>sāmānya</s>). Inference that is ascertained through the general— the inseparable reason— is the form of the property-bearer seen (determined)— this is <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> inference.

children.text:
bhāṣyakārīyamudāharaṇamupanyasyākṣipati--apare punariti /
taditi gatimāniti /
parāmṛśati--upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatvāditi /
karmaṇo hi mahattvarūpaviśeṣaikārthasamavāya upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptiḥ pratyakṣopalabdhiyogyatā /
samādhatte--naivedamiti /
deśāntaraprāptimānādityaḥ dravyatve sati kṣayavṛddhipratyayāviṣayatve ca prāṅmukhopalabhyatve ca tadabhimukhadeśasaṃbandhād anutpannapādavihārasya parivṛtya tatpratyayaviṣayatvāt maṇyādivat, tatpratyayaviṣayatvād ityucyamāne puraḥsthitena sthāṇunā vyabhicāraḥ, so 'pi hi pratyabhijñāviṣayo bhavati tatraiva sthitaḥ /
tannivṛttyarthaṃ parivṛtyetyuktam /
tathāpi guṇādibhirvyabhicāraḥ /
tannivṛttyarthaṃ dravyatve satīti viśeṣaṇam /
tathāpi pradīpādibhirāśutaravināśibhirvyabhicāraḥ, tannivṛttyarthaṃ kṣayavṛddhipratyayāviṣayatve satīti viśeṣaṇam /
tathāpi pṛṣṭhato 'vasthitayā sthūṇayā vyabhicāraḥ, tannivṛttyarthaṃ prāṅmukhopalabhyatve satīti viśeṣaṇam /
upalabhyatā ca upalabdhikarmatā /
sā cehātītā vivakṣitā, anyathā pūrvāparajaladhivelāvagāhinā tuhinaśailena vyabhicāraḥ /
yadyapyayamapi parivṛtya tatpratyayavato 'tipatitopalambhakarmabhāvaḥ, tathāpi tadā narāntarasyopalabhyaḥ /
mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalaṃ tvastācalacūḍāvalambi na prācyāṃ kasyacidupalambhagocara iti vaiṣamyam, tathāpi yadi draṣṭaiva puro 'vasthitasya paścimābhimukhasaya prāsādasya svayumupanipatya pṛṣṭato bhavati, tadoktalakṣaṇasya hetorasti vyabhicāraḥ /
tannivṛttyarthamanutpannapādavihārasyeti viśeṣaṇam /
tadabhimukhadeśasaṃbandhāditi lyablope pañcamī /
svābhimukhadeśamuddiśyānutpannaḥ pādavihāro yasya sa tathoktaḥ /
tamuddiśya khalvayaṃ padbhyāṃ saṃcaramāṇaḥ prāsādasya pṛṣṭato bhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
deśāntaraprāptau sādhanāntaramāha---deśāntareti /
satyavināśa iti ca draṣṭavyam /
ye tvimāmanumānaparamparām amṛṣyamāṇā diśaḥ pratyakṣatāmicchanti, vipratipannaṃ cānumānena bodhayanti, tanmatamupanyasyati---eke tviti /
dūṣayati--tacca neti /

children.translated_text: One suspecting that even formless things like the self, pleasure, and the like are directly perceptible [objects: he says]— 'by an external instrument' was said [to exclude this].
He asks— 'how then?'
The answer— 'direction and location.'

children.text: anyathāsiddhatayā aṅgulyā nirdeśasya dikpratyakṣatvena na svābhāvikaḥ pratibandha ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is that pointing with a finger, being otherwise-established as perception of direction, does not constitute a natural binding [between direction and perception].

Having presented the example of the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>, he raises an objection— 'others however.' 'That'— meaning 'possessing motion.' He refers to— 'because of having attained the conditions for apprehension.' For the attainment of the conditions for apprehension of an action is the fitness for direct perceptual apprehension, [arising from] the co-inherence of magnitude, a specific form, and one meaning in the action. He reconciles— 'this is not so indeed.' The sun, which has arrived at another location— being a substance, not being the object of the cognitions of decrease and increase, being perceived when facing eastward, and because of the connection with the region facing toward it, for one whose walking has not been generated [i.e., who remains stationary], becomes the object of that cognition [of having moved] by turning around, like a gem and the like. If one were to say 'because of being the object of that cognition'— there would be deviation with a post standing in front [of the observer], for that too becomes the object of recognition while remaining in that very place. To prevent that, it is said 'by turning around.' Even so, there is deviation with qualities and the like. To prevent that, the qualifier 'being a substance' is stated. Even so, there is deviation with a lamp and the like which perish more quickly. To prevent that, the qualifier 'not being the object of the cognitions of decrease and increase' is stated. Even so, there is deviation with a pillar situated behind. To prevent that, the qualifier 'being perceived when facing eastward' is stated. And perceptibility means being the object of perception. And here, past [perceptibility] is intended; otherwise there would be deviation with the snow mountain that enters both the eastern and western oceans. Although that [mountain] too, by turning around, has passed beyond the object-of-perception status of one who has already perceived it, nevertheless at that time it is perceptible to another person. But the sun's orb resting on the peak of the western mountain is not within the scope of perception of anyone in the east— this is the difference. Even so, if the observer himself, standing before a palace that faces west but is situated in front, moves and comes behind it, then there is deviation of the stated reason. To prevent that, the qualifier 'for one whose walking has not been generated' is stated. 'Because of connection with the region facing toward it'— the fifth case is in the ablative sense after the absolutive [suffix being dropped]. One whose walking has not been generated toward the region facing oneself— he is so described. It is by walking with feet toward that [region] that this person comes behind the palace— this is the purport. He states another means of proving the arrival at another location— 'at another location.' And 'with real destruction' should also be observed. Those who, not tolerating this chain of inference, wish to hold that directions are directly perceptible, and who teach one who is confused by inference— their view is presented— 'some however.' He refutes— 'and that is not so.'

children.text:
syādetat /
apratyakṣāyāṃ diśi digdeśasaṃbandhiṣvityetadeva kuta ityata āha---ādityeneti /
tadvibhajane---prācītyayamiti /
tat punaridaṃ pratyakṣam ā codayāt ā cāstamayād deśāntaraṃ sañcaraṇaṃ mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalasya anākalitadravyatve satītyādidaṇḍakānumānānāmindriyavyāpārāntaramupajāyamānatvāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, this perception of the sun's orb traveling to another location from sunrise to sunset— in the absence of ascertaining it as a substance— and the series of inferences such as those involving a stick [used for shadow-measurement], arise as a different operation of the senses.

children.text: tatra mā bhūvannākāśadigādayaḥ pratyakṣāḥ, tathāpi parito viniṣpatadativiśadamayukhajālamadhyavartino helimaṇḍalasya ta eva mayukhabhāgabhedāḥ pratyakṣadeśā iti teṣāṃ pratyakṣāṇāṃ pratyakṣeṇa savitṛmaṇḍalena saṃyogavibhāgāḥ pratyakṣā bhaviṣyantīti yuktam /
children.translated_text: There, let space, direction, and the like not be directly perceptible; even so, those very portions of rays that are portions of the exceedingly clear net of rays spreading out in all directions from the center of the sun's orb, being perceptible locations— it is proper that the conjunctions and disjunctions of those perceptible [rays] with the perceptible sun's orb are perceptible.

children.text: idaṃ tvatisphuṭatayā nābhidhāya śiṣyavyutpādanāyākṣuṇṇaṃ mārgāntaraṃ darśitamiti mantavyam /
children.translated_text: But this, not being stated because of being extremely obvious, and another well-trodden path being shown for the instruction of students— this should be understood.

children.text: tadevaṃ rūpeṇa sparśānumānam, śiṃśapātvena śrutena vṛkṣatvānu mānamityādi sāmānyatodṛṣṭena saṃgṛhītaṃ veditavyam //
children.translated_text: Thus, the inference of touch from form, the inference of tree-ness from the heard word '<s>śiṃśapā</s>' (a type of tree), and the like should be understood as subsumed under <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>.

An objection may arise: if direction is not directly perceptible, then how [can one say] 'regarding things related to directional location'?— to this he says— 'by the sun.' He analyzes that— 'the eastern, this.'

children.text:
svamatena vyākhyāntaramāha--athavā trividhamiti /
taddhibhajate--prasiddhamiti /
pakṣaikadeśe sadapi siddham, pakṣavyāpakaṃ tu prakarṣeṇa siddhamityarthaḥ /
yadyapi avinābhāvaḥ pañcasu caturṣu vā rūpeṣu liṅgasya samāpyate ityavinābhāvenaiva sarvāṇiliṅgarūpāṇi saṃgṛhyante, tathāpīha prasiddhasacchabdābhyāṃ dvayoḥ saṃgrahe gobalīvardanyāyena tat parityajya vipakṣavyatirekāsatpratipakṣatvābādhitaviṣayatvāni saṃgṛhṇāti /
atrāpi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ caturṇāṃ pañcānāṃ vā rūpāṇāṃ liṅgeṣu saṃbandhaḥ /

children.translated_text: By this exposition, the disagreements of the theorists of inference regarding the essential nature, number, and result [of inference] have been refuted.
There, '<s>tatpūrvaka</s>' (preceded by that) is the disagreement regarding essential nature.
'<s>Anumāna</s>' (inference)— by the force of the etymology of the designation, the disagreement regarding the result is [refuted].
And 'threefold'— by the exclusion of a lesser or greater number, the disagreement regarding number has been refuted.

He states another explanation according to his own view— 'or alternatively, threefold.' He analyzes that— 'well-established.' Even though existing in a part of the thesis, it is established; but what pervades the entire thesis is 'prominently established'— this is the meaning. Although the inseparability of the mark is completed in five or four characteristics, and thus all the characteristics of the mark are subsumed by inseparability alone, nevertheless here, by the two words 'well-established' and 'existent,' when two [characteristics] are subsumed, by the principle of 'cow and bull,' setting those aside, it subsumes exclusion from the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣavyatireka</s>), having no counterargument (<s>asatpratipakṣatva</s>), and having an uncontradicted subject (<s>abādhitaviṣayatva</s>). And here too, the connection of four or five characteristics with the marks [is to be understood] as applicable.

children.text:
saṃpratyāntargaṇikabhedānantyenānantyād anumānasyāśakyalakṣaṇamiti yadi kaścidanumanyeta, tannirākaraṇāya traividhyamanumānasya ucyate iti trividhapadasyatātparyāntaramāha--atha veti /
trividhatvena yato niyatamataḥ śakyalakṣaṇamityarthaḥ /
anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvāditi sapakṣe sadeva /
anitya śabdo 'smadādipratnanāntarīyakatvāditi sapakṣe sadasat /
tadetadanvayavyatireki dvividham /
evamanvayyapi dvedhā /
tatra sapakṣe sadeva, yathā paramāṇvādayaḥ kasyacit pratyakṣāḥ prameyatvād ghaṭādivaditi /
tathā sapakṣe sadasad yathā tatraiva sādhye sattvād ghaṭādivaditi /
kālabhedaḥ traikālyam /
pratipanno 'pratipannaḥ sandigdho viparyastaśceti puruṣabhedaḥ /
pūrvaṃ siddhavat pūrvavadityanūdya tasyodāharaṇamuktam /
saṃprati praśnapūrvakaṃ tadarthābhāsanirākaraṇena tāttvikamasyārthamāha---pūrvavadityuktamiti /
bhāṣyavyāghāta ityarthaḥ /
pūrvavadityasya vyākhyānaṃ śeṣavadityatrāpi yojayati /
sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ ca jñānamatidiśati---evaṃ śeṣavadādiṣviti /
athavā pūrvavaditi bhāṣyam /
tasyārthaḥ, pūrveṇa tulyaṃ vartate iti pūrvavat /
kriyātulyatāyāṃ ca vatiriti kriyātulyatā darśitā /

children.translated_text: 'Where'—

children.text: pūrvamanyataradarśanena sahānyataradarśanaṃ dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi, yathāpūrvaṃ pratyakṣabhūtayoriti pramāṇamātropalakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: Previously, in the example-subject, the observation of one [property] together with the observation of another, as both were previously objects of perception—'by means of valid knowledge' is merely illustrative.

children.text: evaṃ sādhyadharmiṇi anyataradharmadarśanena sādhanadharmadarśanenānyatarasya sādhyadharmasyānumānamanumiti darśanamiti bhavati kriyātulyatā /
children.translated_text: Thus, in the thesis-subject, through the observation of one property, namely the proving property, the inference—the inferential cognition—of the other, namely the property to be proved, constitutes the similarity of action.
Having echoed this <s>bhāṣya</s>, he explains—'or alternatively.'

Now, if someone were to think that inference is incapable of being defined due to the infinity of its internal sub-types, he states another purport of the word 'threefold' for the purpose of refuting that—'or alternatively.' The meaning is: because it is restricted to being threefold, it is capable of being defined. 'Sound is impermanent, because of being produced'—[here the reason] exists only in the similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>). 'Sound is impermanent, because of being inseparable from effort by persons like us'—[here the reason] exists and does not exist in the similar instance. This is twofold as positive-and-negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireki</s>). Similarly, the purely positive (<s>anvayi</s>) is also twofold. Among those, [the reason] exists only in the similar instance, as in: 'atoms and the like are perceptible to someone, because of being knowable, like a pot and such.' And [the reason] exists and does not exist in the similar instance, as in the same probandum: 'because of being existent, like a pot and such.' The temporal division is the three times. The personal division is: one who has understood, one who has not understood, one who doubts, and one who is in error. Having previously restated '<s>pūrvavat</s>' (from antecedent) as if established, and having stated its example, he now, through questions and the removal of apparent meanings, states its true meaning—'it has been said <s>pūrvavat</s>.' The meaning is: [to resolve] the contradiction in the <s>bhāṣya</s>. He applies the interpretation of '<s>pūrvavat</s>' to '<s>śeṣavat</s>' (from remainder) as well. And he extends the knowledge to '<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' (based on general observation)—'thus in <s>śeṣavat</s> and the rest.' Or alternatively, the <s>bhāṣya</s> [says] '<s>pūrvavat</s>.' Its meaning: it operates in the same way as the antecedent, hence '<s>pūrvavat</s>.' And the suffix '<s>vat</s>' indicates similarity of action—thus the similarity of action is shown.

children.text: atra dignāgena dhūmādagnirūpadharmāntarānumānam agnideśayoḥ saṃbandhānumānaṃ ca dūṣayitvā agniviśiṣṭadeśānumānaṃ samarthitam /

children.translated_text: And thus he says—
Some hold that what is to be inferred is a property different [from the mark], because of the non-deviation of the mark.
Some desire [that what is inferred is] the relation, because the property and property-bearer are [already] established.

Here, <s>Dignāga</s>, having refuted both the inference of fire as a property different from smoke and the inference of the relation between fire and location, established the inference of a location qualified by fire.

children.text: liṅga dharme prasiddhaṃ cet kimanyat tena mīyate /
children.translated_text: If the mark is well-known in [connection with] the property, what else is measured by it?
If [it is well-known] in the property-bearer, why is not that very thing [the property-bearer] the inferable?

children.text: saṃbandhe 'pi dvayaṃ nāsti ṣaṣṭhī śrūyeta tadvati /
children.translated_text: Even in [the case of inferring] the relation, there is no duality; the genitive case would be heard in what possesses it.
It [the relation] is inexpressible because it is supported [by both], and it is not connected with the mark.

children.text:
na hi saṃbandhadharmatayā liṅgaṃ pratīyate, api tu deśasaṃgatamityarthaḥ, iti /
tatra liṅgasyāvyabhicārastu dharmeṇānyatra dṛśyate /
tatra prasiddhaṃ tadyuktaṃ dharmiṇaṃ gamayiṣyati //iti /
tatra dignāgadūṣitān kalpān anyāṃśca vikalpān dignāgasamarthitaṃ ca kalpamupanyasya dūṣayati---anye punariti dharmadharmibhāvānupapatteriti /
dharmeṇa hi dharmipratipattavyaḥ, anyathā atiprasakteriti bhāvaḥ /
deśasya ca svarūpeṇetyarthaḥ /
śaṅkate---athāpīdamiti /
nirākaroti---tacca naivamiti /
yaḥ kaścid vā deśo 'gnimān sādhyo, dhūmavān vā deśabhedaḥ? tatra pūrvasvin kalpe nirākaraṇamāha---ataddharmāditi /
yaḥ kaścidagnimattayā deśaḥ sādhyate na tasyāvaśyaṃ dhūmo dharma ityarthaḥ /
na caitat sādhyaṃ siddhatvādityāha---na cāgneriti /
dvitīyaṃ kalpamāśaḍte---ayamiti /
nirākaroti---na, tasyeti, śaṅkāṃ vibhajate---deśeti /
nirākaraṇaṃ vibhajate---na hyayamiti /
na hyayamevaṃvādī dignāgo dhūmādhāraṃ deśaviśeṣaṃ paśyati /
na hyasya mate parvato nāma kaścidavayavī yadādhāro dhūma upalabhyeta, kiṃ tu paramāṇavaḥ paramasūkṣmā atīndriyāḥ parvataḥ /
evaṃ dhūmo 'pi tādṛśa eva /
yathā vakṣyati---sarvāgahaṇam mavayavyasiddheḥ # 2/1/34 # iti /
yeṣāmapi deśabhedo 'vayavī darśanārhaḥ, teṣāmapi viyadvartinīṃ dhūmalekhāmabhraṃlihāmupalabhyānupalabdhadeśānāṃ nānumānasaṃbhava iti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkate---avinābhāveneti /
tadeva vibhajate---athāpīti /
nirākaroti---tanneti /
vikalpayati---agnidhūmayoriti /
kāryakāraṇabhāvamālambate---astviti /
dūṣayati---tanneti /
dhūmena hi vahniranumīyate, na ca kāryasattā nimittakāraṇasattāyā vyāptā /
na hi yadā yatra vā paṭaḥ, tadā tatra vā kuvindaḥ /
nāpyasamavāyikāraṇasattayā, na hi yadā yadā saṃyogastadā karma /
tasmāt samavāyikāraṇāvinābhāvaḥ kāryasya vaktavyaḥ /
tatredaṃ dūṣaṇam--atadvṛttitvāditi /
ekārthasamavāyamavinābhāvaṃ dūṣayati--naiketi /
ekārthasamavāya iti hi dvedhā, ekasyārthasya samavāyaḥ, ekasmin vārthe samavāya iti /
tatra prathamaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati---tābhyāmiti /
yadi hi vahnimābhyāmeko 'rthaḥ kaścit ārabhyeta tato 'sau tayoḥ samaveyāt, na tvetadastītyarthaḥ /
dvitīyaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati---na ca tāviti /
tat kimasaṃbaddhāveva vahnidhūmau, tathā ca pratītivirodha
children.translated_text: Then are fire and smoke simply unrelated? If so, there would be a contradiction with cognition.
To this he says—'mere relation.'
The meaning is: conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>).
That alone [is the relation] there.

For the mark is not cognized as having the relation as its property, but rather as being connected with the location—this is the meaning. 'But the non-deviation of the mark is seen elsewhere with the property. That [mark], well-known there, will make known the property-bearer qualified [by the property].' Having presented the alternatives refuted by <s>Dignāga</s> and other alternatives, and the alternative established by <s>Dignāga</s>, he refutes [the latter]—'others, however'—'because of the impossibility of the property-property-bearer relation.' For the property-bearer must be cognized through the property; otherwise there would be over-extension—this is the purport. 'And of the location, in its own form'—this is the meaning. He objects—'but even if this.' He refutes—'and that is not so.' Is it any location whatsoever that is to be proved as possessing fire, or is it a particular location that possesses smoke? In the first alternative, he states the refutation—'because of not being its property.' The meaning is: for whatever location is to be proved as possessing fire, smoke is not necessarily its property. And this probandum is not [already] established—therefore he says: 'and not of fire.' He takes up the second alternative—'this.' He refutes—'no, of that.' He divides the objection—'location.' He divides the refutation—'for not this.' For this <s>Dignāga</s>, who speaks thus, does not perceive the particular location that is the substrate of smoke. For in his view, there is no composite thing called a mountain that would be the substrate on which smoke is perceived; rather, atoms that are supremely subtle and beyond the senses constitute the mountain. Similarly, smoke too is of the same kind. As will be stated: 'non-apprehension of all, because of the unestablished composite' (2.1.34). Even for those who accept the composite as the particular location worthy of perception, when they perceive a streak of smoke extending into the sky and licking the clouds, inference is not possible for locations that are not perceived—this is the purport. He objects—'by invariable concomitance.' He elaborates that—'but even if.' He refutes—'not that.' He considers alternatives—'of fire and smoke.' He takes up the causal relation—'let it be.' He refutes—'not that.' For fire is inferred from smoke, but the existence of the effect is not pervaded by the existence of the efficient cause. For it is not the case that whenever and wherever cloth exists, there also exists a weaver. Nor by the existence of the non-inherent cause—for it is not the case that whenever there is conjunction, there is action. Therefore, the invariable concomitance of the effect with the inherent cause must be stated. Therein, this is the refutation—'because of not occurring in that.' He refutes the invariable concomitance as co-inherence in a single substrate—'not in one.' For 'co-inherence in a single substrate' has two meanings: the inherence of a single object, or inherence in a single object. He refutes the first alternative—'by those two.' The meaning is: if some single object were produced by fire and smoke together, then it would inhere in both—but this is not the case. He refutes the second alternative—'and not those two.'

children.text:
yavadhāryatāmityata āha---tadapīti /
pṛcchati--kathamiti /
uttaram--yadi tāvaditi /
kurute prayogam /
asti saṃbandho 'gnidhūmayordhūmāditi /
dūṣayati--tannāpratītatvāt /
tadanenānaikāntikatvaṃ darśayati /
saṃbandhāntaram āśaṅkate--rūpasparśavaditi /
na hi bauddharāddhānte dravyaṃ nāma kiñcidasti yatra rūpasparśai samavetau, kiṃ tvekasāmagryadhīnatayā niyatasāhacaryau, tathā vahnidhūmāvapi ityarthaḥ /
dūṣayati--nobhayoriti /
ubhayasahācaryanirākaraṇena yatra dhūmastatrāgnirityapi parākṛtam, tasyāpi sāhacaryaviśeṣatvādityāha--yatra dhūma iti /
gatyantarābhāvādupasaṃharati--na ceti /
śaṅkate--loka iti /
nirākaroti-- nāstīti /
yatra tāvat parvatanitambavartinī dhūmalekhā santatamudgacchantī dṛśyate, tatrāsau deśa eva tadviśiṣṭo 'numīyate iti lokaprasiddhameveti kimatra vaktavyam /

yatra tu bhūyiṣṭhatāyā tasya dhūmasya dūratvena deśo na dṛśyate, dhūma eva tvamraṃliho limpanniva abhramaṇḍalamavalokyate, tatra deśānumānaprayāsālasatayā dṛśyamāno dhūmaviśeṣa evāgnimattayā sādhyate dhūmatvaikārthasamavāyibhiḥ tadgataiḥ saṃtatyerdhvagamanādibhirityāha--dhūmaviśeṣeṇa iti /
children.translated_text: But where, due to the distance and predominance of that smoke, the location is not seen, and only the smoke licking the sky and seeming to smear the canopy of clouds is observed—there, out of the weariness of attempting to infer the location, the observed particular smoke itself is to be proved as possessing fire, through the properties co-inherent with smoke-ness in the same substrate, such as continuous upward movement and the like—therefore he says: 'by the particular smoke.'
What distinguishes it is the distinguishing feature (<s>viśeṣa</s>)—continuous upward movement and the like.

children.text: tena dhūmamātrād vahnivyabhicāriṇo vahnyavinābhāvī dhūmo viśeṣyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: by that [distinguishing feature], smoke that is invariably concomitant with fire is distinguished from mere smoke, which may deviate from fire.
The rest is self-evident.

'Let it be determined'—to this he says: 'even that.' He asks—'how?' The answer—'if, first.' He makes the argument: 'there is a relation of fire and smoke; from smoke' [one can infer fire]. He refutes—'not that, because it is not cognized.' By this he shows inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntika</s>). He anticipates another relation—'like form and touch.' For in the Buddhist doctrine, there is no substance whatsoever in which form and touch would co-inhere; rather, they are invariably accompanied due to dependence on a single causal aggregate—similarly fire and smoke too—this is the meaning. He refutes—'not of both.' By the refutation of mutual accompaniment, 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire' is also rejected, since that too is a specific form of accompaniment—therefore he says: 'where smoke.' In the absence of any other possibility, he concludes—'and not.' He objects—'in the world.' He refutes—'there is no [difficulty].' Where a streak of smoke is seen continuously rising from the slope of a mountain, there that very location qualified [by smoke] is inferred—this is well-known in the world, so what is there to say about it?

children.text:
śeṣavannāma pariśeṣaḥ /
dravyatvakarmatvayoḥ śabde nirākāryatvena upayuktatvāt tābhyāmanyad guṇatvaṃ śeṣaḥ /
sa yasyāstyanumānasya pratipādyatayā, taccheṣavat /
tatra na dravyaṃ śabdaḥ ekadravyatvāt /
dvividhameva hi dravyam, adravyamanekadravyaṃ ca /
adravyaṃ paramāṇvādi, anekadravyaṃ ca ghaṭādi /
śabdastvekadravyaḥ /
tasmāt na dravyaṃ rūpādivat /
na karma, śabdāntarahetutvāditi /
tadetad bhāṣyamākṣipati---karmeti /
pariharati---neti /
anyamasyārthaṃ darśayati---samānajātīyārambhakatvāditi /
yat samānajātīyārambhakaṃ na tat karma, yathā rūpādaya iti /
kāryatvāt tāvat śabdaḥ samavāyikāraṇavān /
tatra ca pṛthivyādiniṣedhāt nabho 'sya samavāyikāraṇam /
na caiṣa nabhovyāpakaḥ sarvatra upalambhaprasaṅgāt /
tasmādavyāpakaḥ /
karṇaśaṣkulyupasannihitaṃ ca nabhaḥ śrotram /
tālvādisaṃyogopadhānena ca nabhaḥpradeśe śabdaḥ samavetaḥ /
prāpyakāri ca śrotram /
na ca vaktṛvaktrāvaruddhaṃ nabhaḥpradeśaṃ tat prāpnoti /
na cādravyaṃ śabdo gatvā śrotreṇa saṃbadhyate /
tasmād vīcītaraṅgarītyā svadeśānantaradeśe śabdāntarārambhaṇaparamparayā śrotradeśotpannaṃ śabdaṃ gṛhṇātīti siddhaṃ sajātīyārambhakatvāditi /
idaṃ tu pariśeṣasya udāharaṇaṃ nādaraṇīyam /

children.translated_text: For elimination is just another name for negative concomitance (<s>vyatirekin</s>).

children.text: eṣa punaranvayavyatirekī dravyakarmānyatve sati sadādyabhedasya sapakṣe rūpādau sattvād, vipakṣe sāmānyādāvabhāvāt /
children.translated_text: And this [inference] is of the type that has both positive and negative concomitance: given that [sound] is other than substance and action, the non-difference from an existent etc. [quality] is present in the similar instance of form etc., and absent in the dissimilar instance of universals and the like.
Therefore, the inference by elimination that establishes the self-dependence of desire and the rest should be examined as the [proper] example of elimination.
And that will be stated immediately after.

<s>Śeṣavat</s> means remainder (<s>pariśeṣa</s>). Since substance-ness and action-ness have been employed in being negated with respect to sound, quality-ness, which is other than those two, is the remainder. That inference which has this as its content is <s>śeṣavat</s>. There, sound is not a substance, because of being a single substance. For substance is of two kinds only: non-substance (atoms and the like) and multi-substance (pot and the like). But sound is a single substance [i.e., inheres in a single substance]. Therefore, it is not a substance, like form and the like. It is not an action, because of being the cause of another sound. He objects to this <s>bhāṣya</s>—'action.' He resolves—'no.' He shows its other meaning—'because of being the producer of a homogeneous [entity].' That which produces a homogeneous entity is not an action, like form and the like. Sound, being a product, has an inherent cause. And since earth and the rest are negated, space (<s>nabhas</s>) is its inherent cause. And this [sound] does not pervade the entirety of space, since there would be the undesirable consequence of being perceived everywhere. Therefore it is non-pervasive. And the space proximate to the ear-cavity is the organ of hearing. And sound inheres in a region of space through the intermediary of conjunctions with the palate and the like. And the organ of hearing operates by reaching [its object]. And it does not reach the region of space enclosed in the speaker's mouth. Nor does sound, being a non-substance, travel and connect with the ear. Therefore, in the manner of waves and ripples, through the successive production of further sounds in regions adjacent to its own region, [the organ of hearing] apprehends the sound produced in the region of the ear—thus it is established that 'because of being the producer of a homogeneous entity.' But this example of elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>) should not be given importance.

children.text:
sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ nāmetyādi bhāṣyam anubhāṣyākṣipati--sāmānyata iti /
kathaṃ tarhi anumānamatra pravartate iti /
nityaparokṣeṇa saha kasyacit liṅgasaya saṃbandhādarśanādityarthaḥ /
vyāhataṃ ceti /
sa khalvatyantāparidṛṣṭaḥ svarūpato vā sādhyeta, dṛṣṭadharmiviśeṣaṇatayā vā? tatra pūrvasmin kalpe nānupalabdha iti vyāghātaḥ /
uttarasmin sandigdha iti, viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣo hi saṃśayo nātyantānupalabdhapūrvadharmavattayā kvacid bhavitum arhati /
na khalu saptamarasavattayā kecid dravye saṃśerata iti bhāvaḥ /
samādhatte--na viśeṣaṇabhūtasyeti /
na tāvat svarūpeṇānumīyate yena nānupalabdha iti vyāhanyeta, kiṃ tu dṛṣṭasya dharmiṇo viśeṣaṇatayā /
na caivaṃ sarvānumānāviśeṣaḥ /
sādhyadharmiṇyasyāsmadādibhiḥ kadācidapi pratyakṣeṇānupalambhāt /
tajjātīyena tu dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇordṛṣṭena pratyakṣato vā mānāntarād vā sādhanadharmasya svābhāvikapratibandhagrahasaṃbhādityarthaḥ /
udāharaṇamāha--yathecchādibhirātmā /
tadevaṃ vibhajate--icchādayaḥ khalu dharmiṇo bhavanti mānasapratyakṣadṛṣṭāḥ, teṣām ātmā viśeṣaṇam /
kutaḥ? guṇabhūto 'vacchedakatayā yataḥ, tasmādātmaviśiṣṭā icchādayaḥ sādhyā ityuktaṃ bhavati /
sādhanadharmaṃ tadvartinaṃ darśayati--icchādīnāṃ guṇatvamiti /
nanūktamanupalabdhacareṇa sādhyadharmeṇa na saṃdehaviṣayatvam, anupalabdhacaraścātmeti kathaṃ tadviśiṣṭā icchādayo nyāyaviṣayā iti śaṅkāmurīkṛtyata prayogaṃ sūcayati--paratantrā iti /
children.translated_text: But it was said that the <s>sādhya</s>-property, whose occurrence has not been perceived, cannot be the object of doubt—and the self's occurrence has not been perceived—so how can desire and the like qualified by it be the subject of <s>nyāya</s>? Accepting this objection, he indicates the argument—'dependent on another' (<s>paratantra</s>).

children.text: mā tatra saitsīdātmapāratantryam, pāratantryamātraṃ tu siddham ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Let the dependence on the self not be established there; but mere dependence is established—this is the meaning.

children.text: tena sāmānyatodṛṣṭasya pāratantryamātraviṣayatā, na pāratantryamicchādīnām anumeyātmavādīnāṃ kadācidapyasmadādipratyakṣagocaraḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference based on general observation) has mere dependence as its domain—the dependence of desire and the like, whose self is to be inferred, is never within the scope of perception for ordinary people like us.
Because the other [entity]—the self that is its substrate—is eternally beyond perception.

Having echoed the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with '<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' (inference based on general observation), he objects—'from the general.' How then does inference operate here? Because the connection of any mark with what is perpetually imperceptible has not been observed—this is the meaning. 'And it is contradictory'—is that which is utterly unperceived to be proved in its own form, or as a qualifier of a perceived property-bearer? In the first case, the contradiction is: 'not perceived [and yet inferred].' In the second case, [the contradiction is that it is] doubtful—for doubt, which depends on the memory of a distinguishing feature, cannot properly arise with respect to what has never at all been perceived as possessing a given property. For nobody doubts regarding a substance as possessing a seventh taste—this is the purport. He resolves—'not of the qualifier.' It is not inferred in its own form—which would lead to the contradiction of 'not perceived'—but rather as a qualifier of the perceived property-bearer. And this does not make all inference indistinguishable. Because the <s>sādhya</s>-property-bearer has never been perceived at any time by us and others through perception. But with respect to the example-subject, of the same type, the grasping of the natural binding of the proving property is possible through perception or through another means of valid knowledge—this is the meaning. He gives an example—'just as the self [is inferred] through desire and the like.' He elaborates this—'desire and the like are indeed property-bearers perceived through mental perception; the self is their qualifier. Why? Because, being a quality, it serves as a delimiter. Therefore, desire and the like qualified by the self are what is to be proved'—this is what is stated. He shows the proving property as residing in them—'the quality-ness of desire and the like.'
Having thus illustrated <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>, he shows through a question the genuine example of the method of elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>)—'dependence.'

children.text: icchādīno hi bādhakairapanīte dravyāṣṭakaguṇatve guṇatvameva vyatirekī hetuḥ ātmapāratantrye pramāṇam /
children.translated_text: For when the property of being a substance among the eight [categories of substance] has been removed for desire and the like by sublating cognitions, the property of being a quality itself is the negative concomitant reason—the <s>pramāṇa</s> for their dependence on the self.

children.text: yadyapi cāyaṃ svarūpeṇātmā na prasiddhaḥ, tathāpi dravyāṣṭakavyatirekādiśabdairadūraviprakarṣeṇa parāmṛṣṭaḥ śaknoti viśeṣṭuṃ dharmiṇi ca nyāyapravṛttyaṅgaḥ saṃśayam āpādayitumiti niravadyam //
children.translated_text: And although the self is not well-known in its own form, nevertheless, being referred to at no great distance through words such as 'what is different from the eight substances' and the like, it is capable of qualifying, and of producing doubt regarding the property-bearer, which is a component of the operation of <s>nyāya</s>—hence there is no fault.

children.text: atra bhāṣyaṃ vibhāgavacanādeva trividhamiti saddhi iti, tasyārthaḥ, trividham iti vibhāgavacanādeva trividhe pūrvavadādau siddhe kimarthaṃ pūrvavadādyupādānaṃ sūtreṇeti /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>bhāṣya</s> says 'from the very statement of division, the threefold [nature] is established'—its meaning is: when the threefold [nature] is already established by the statement of division alone, as with <s>pūrvavat</s> and the like, what is the purpose of the <s>sūtra</s>'s adopting '<s>pūrvavat</s>' and the rest?
The resolution there is: the statement of the threefold is the utterance, the expression, of the threefold <s>pūrvavat</s> and the rest.

children.text: mahataḥ trividhasya mahāviṣayasya atītānāgatavartamānaviṣayasya laghīyasā sūtreṇa tatpūrvakamityetāvataivopadeśe paraṃ vākyalāghavaṃ manyamānasyānyasmin vākyalāghave 'nādaraḥ sūtrakārasyeti śiṣyān vyutpipādayiṣoḥ atraiva nidarśanam--tathā cāyam /
children.translated_text: For the great threefold—the great subject-matter pertaining to past, future, and present—when [the <s>sūtrakāra</s>] thinks that supreme brevity of expression is achieved by instructing with just this much, namely '<s>tatpūrvakam</s>' (preceded by that), while disregarding other verbal economy—this very thing is the illustration for one who wishes to instruct the students. Thus this one—

children.text: asya samācāraḥ---itthaṃbhūtena vakyavikalpena vaicitryeṇa pravṛtta iti yojanā //
children.translated_text: his practice—the construction is: he has proceeded with such a variety of sentence-alternatives.

children.text:
evaṃ tāvat lakṣaṇabhedānumānaṃ bhinnaṃ pratyakṣād darśitam /
bhāṣyakārastu viṣayabhedādapi bhedamāha---sadviṣayaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ sadasadviṣayaṃ cānumānam /
co viṣayabhedaṃ samuccinoti /
saditi vartamānam /
asadityatītānāgate /
pratyakṣaṃ hi laukikaṃ vartamānaviṣayameva /
anumānaṃ tu traikālyaviṣayam /
yadyapi pratyakṣamapyatītānāgatayoḥ saṃprati niṣedhyaniṣedhayorniṣedhe pravartamānamasadviṣayaṃ tathāpi na pratiṣedhyayoḥ pravartate ityetāvatā sadviṣayamuktam /
anumānaṃ tu tayorapi pravartate ityetāvatā asadviṣayamuktam /
tadetadākṣipati---sadviṣayaṃ ceti /
na hyanupalabdhasāmānye iti sāmānyata upalabdho viśeṣataścānirṇīto dharmo nyāyapravṛttāvadhikriyate /
na tvanupalabdhasāmānya ityarthaḥ /
na cāsataḥ svatantrasya sāmānyena darśanamastīti /
dvitīyaṃ kalpamāśaṅkate---atheti /
etaddūṣayituṃ dharmatraividhyamāha---dharmā iti /
tadvibhajate---tatreti /
pṛcchati---kathaṃ punariti /
yadi hi svatantraḥ samavāyaḥ, na tarhi kasyacid viśeṣaṇam, tathā ca na viśeṣaṇatayā gṛhyeteti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---samavāyāntarābhāvāt /
na viśeṣaṇatvaṃ svātantryeṇa nirākurmaḥ, kiṃ tu vṛttimasyetyarthaḥ /
kasmāt punarasya na samavāyāntaramabhyupeyata ityata āha---atheti /
pṛcchati--kimidamiti /
anavasthāprasaṅgo hi nāma tarkaḥ /
naiṣa pramāṇamantareṇa nirṇayāya paryāpta ityarthaḥ /
uttaram--na saṃdehaḥ, kiṃ tvastyeva nyāyaḥ /
tamāha--pañceti /
ayaṃ pañcapadārthavṛttiśabdo bahuvrīhiṇā paramāṇau vartate, ṣaṣṭhīsamāsena tu samavāye /
na ca kathañcit śabdābhedamātramanumānāṅgam, mā bhūd gośabdasāmyena vāgādīnām api viṣāṇitvamityaparitoṣāt nyāyāntaramāha--anāśritaḥ samavāya iti /
iha buddhinimittatvaṃ kāraṇatvam /
saṃyogenānaikānto mā bhūdityata uktam---vyāpakatve satīti /

children.translated_text: Pervasiveness is being apprehended everywhere when the full complement of other causes of apprehension is present.

children.text: tacceha pratyayakāraṇe ātmāni ca samavāye cāvilakṣaṇamiti /
children.translated_text: And that is of uniform character here—in the cause of cognition, in the self, and in <s>samavāya</s>.
He asks about <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) that serves as the procedural component of <s>nyāya</s>—'but if.' The answer—'the effect.'
Having stated the charge of infinite regress, the charge of substratelessness has been stated to introduce it.

Thus far, inference has been shown to differ from perception by the difference in definition.
But the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> also states a difference by the difference in object—'perception has existing things as its object, and inference has both existing and non-existing things as its object.'
The word 'ca' (and) combines the difference in object.
'Existing' means present.
'Non-existing' means past and future.
For ordinary perception has only present things as its object.
But inference has all three times as its object.
Although perception too, in presently negating what is to be negated regarding the past and future, operates on non-existing things, nevertheless it does not operate on the things to be negated themselves—to that extent it is called 'having existing things as its object.'
But inference operates even on those [past and future things]—to that extent it is called 'having non-existing things as its object.'
He raises this objection—'having existing things as its object.'
For a property whose universal has not been apprehended—that is, one apprehended universally but undetermined in its particulars—is brought under consideration for the operation of <s>nyāya</s>.
But not one whose universal has not been apprehended at all—this is the meaning.
And there is no perception of the non-existent as independent through its universal.
He entertains the second alternative—'or else.'
To refute this, he states the threefold nature of properties—'properties.'
He analyzes that—'therein.'
He asks—'but how then?'
For if <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) were independent, then it would not be a qualifier of anything, and thus it would not be apprehended as a qualifier—this is the purport.
The answer—'because of the absence of another <s>samavāya</s>.'
We do not deny its being a qualifier by [invoking] its independence; rather, [we deny] its mode of subsistence—this is the meaning.
Why then is another <s>samavāya</s> not accepted for it?—therefore he says—'or else.'
He asks—'what is this?'
For the charge of infinite regress is a form of <s>tarka</s> (reasoning).
This alone, without a <s>pramāṇa</s>, is not sufficient for determination—this is the meaning.
The answer—'there is no doubt; rather, there is indeed a <s>nyāya</s> (logical proof).'
He states it—'the five [categories].'
This word 'subsisting in five categories' functions as a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> (possessive compound) with reference to the atom, and as a <s>ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa</s> (genitive compound) with reference to <s>samavāya</s>.
And mere verbal similarity is not a component of inference—lest by the similarity of the word 'go' (cow), even speech and the like have horns—being unsatisfied, he states another proof: '<s>samavāya</s> is without a substrate.'
Here, being a cause of cognition is causality.
Lest there be inconclusiveness through conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), it is said—'when there is pervasiveness.'

children.text:
syādetat /
bhavatu vṛtteḥ prāganāśritaṃ kāryaṃ paścāt samavaiṣyati, turīsaṃyuktebhya iva tantubhya utpadya paṭaḥ paścāt turyā ityata āha--samavāyaśceti /
anavasthāprasaṅgaḥ pūrvokta ityarthaḥ /
śaṅkate--prāptitvāditi /
pramāṇavattvāt prāptā samavāyasya vṛttirna śakyā anavasthābhiyā parityaktumityarthaḥ /
vimarśapūrvakaṃ śaṅkāṃ nirākaroti--kimiyamiti /
saṃyoge prāptitvasya nivṛttyā svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandhaḥ kāryatvasyopādheḥ tatprayojakasya vidyamānatvādityarthaḥ /
atha prāptidharmo 'pi kasmāt na bhavatītyata āha---yadi punariyamiti /
nanviyamanavasthā kasmād bījāṅgurādiṣvivehāpi nābhyupeyate ityata āha---na caināmanavasthāmiti /
anidaṃprathameṣvanāditvāt śakyā pratipādayitumanavasthā pramāṇena, na tvidaṃprathameṣvādimattvena tasyāśakyaniścayatvāt /
tadidam uktam---pramāṇābhāvāditi /
śāstravirodhaśca samavāyāntarābhyupagama ityāha---samavāyaśceti /
tattvamekatvaṃ samavāyasya bhāvena sattvayā vyākhyātamiti śāstramāha, tadanekatvamupapādayatā bādhyetetyarthaḥ /
codayati---saṃbandhinivṛttāviti /
tathā ca vinaśyati, vinaṣṭe ca tasmin yo dṛśyate sa tato 'nya utpanna iti siddhaṃ samavāyasya nānātvamityarthaḥ /
pariharati---na nāstīti /
khyātirūpalabdhiḥ /
kasmāt? akṛtakatvāt /
akṛtakatvameva kuta ityata āha---akṛtaka iti /
kārya svāpādānena akṛtakasaṃbandhavad ādhāravattvāditi vyatirekī hetuḥ /
vyatirekāvyabhicāramāha---yadyayamiti /
utpadyamānaḥ khalvayaṃ samavāyaḥ sahakāryeṇa, na kāryasya /
na hi sahotpannau rūpasparśau mithaḥ saṃbadhyete /
ekārthasamavāyastu tayoḥ /
so 'pi samavāye nāsti /
sannapyasau na kāryamādhāravat karoti /
tasmāt sahotpāde kāryamanādhāraṃ syāditi /
śaṅkate---atheti /
kāryāt pūrvamutpannaḥ samavāyaḥ paścādutpadyamānaṃ kāryamupādānādhārakaṃ kariṣyati kāryahetubalādityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti--tathāpīti /
tribhyo hi kāraṇebhyaḥ kāryaṃ bhāvarūpaṃ jāyate /
kāryakāraṇasamavāyasya ca kāryakāraṇe samavāyikāraṇe vaktavye, kāryāt prāg jātasya ca samavāyasya na kāryaṃ kāraṇam /
na ca nimittakāraṇamātrādasya janmeti sāṃpratam, bhāvotpādasya sarvatra kāraṇatrayapūrvakatvaniyamāt /
tasmāt samavāyasya samavāyyasamavāyikāraṇābhāvat na kāryāt prāg utpāda iti suṣṭhūktam--tathāpi kasyeti vācyamiti /
śaṅkate--atheti /
dūṣayati--kāryeti /
na ca paṭaturīsaṃyogavat samavāyasya paścāt kāryakāraṇasamavāya iti yuktam /
saṃyogajasya saṃyogasya kāraṇatrayasaṃbhavād asya tu samavāyāntaramantareṇa kāraṇatrayāyogāt /
anyathānavasthāprasaṅgāditi bhāvaḥ /
upasaṃharati--tasmāditi /
tataśca na jñāyate kimabhipretyata asadviṣayamityuktamityākṣepa iti /
samādhatte--tatra pratiṣidhyamāneti /
atītānāgate saṃprati pratiṣidhyamāne tadviṣayamanumānam asadviṣayamuktam /
tanniṣedhastu bhavatu pratyakṣagocaraḥ, tathāpi siddho viṣayabheda ityarthaḥ /
atra caiṣa dharmatraividhyakramo dvedhā tāvat, vidhīyamānaḥ pratiṣiśyamānaśca /
vidhīyamāno 'pi dvedhā, paratantraḥ svatantraśceti /
svatantrasya ca dharmatvaṃ viśeṣaṇatvamātravivakṣayā draṣṭavyam /
nanu vidhīyamāno 'pyasan pratyakṣaśca kvacit /
yathā vyāpriyamāṇe kulāle jāyamāno ghaṭaḥ /
visphāritākṣo hi tadā ghaṭo bhavatīti pratyeti /
na cāsau tadā san, sato bhavanaṃ pratyakartṛkatvāt, gamanavaditi śaṅkate---bhavatīti /
nirākaroti---na, jāyamāneti /
jāyamānasyārthasya vidhiviṣayasya sattayāsattayā vānabhyupagamāt /

children.translated_text: But as the object of negation, its non-existence is indeed accepted.
What then is the meaning of the word 'comes into being'?—therefore he says—'comes into being.'

children.text: dhaṭo jāyata iti tu laukikaḥ prayogo ghaṭaśabdaṃ ghaṭārtheṣu tadavayaveṣūpacarya teṣāṃ ca siddhatayā kartṛtvādupapādanīya iti /
children.translated_text: But the common usage 'the pot comes into being' is to be justified by figuratively transferring the word 'pot' to the parts of the pot, which are its material, and by their being established [as existent] and having agency.
He concludes—'thus far.'

It may be objected:
Let the effect, prior to its subsistence, be without substrate; afterwards it will inhere—just as a cloth, arising from threads conjoined with the loom, afterwards [separates from] the loom—therefore he says: 'and <s>samavāya</s>.'
The charge of infinite regress has been stated previously—this is the meaning.
He raises a doubt—'because of being established (<s>prāptitvāt</s>).'
The subsistence of <s>samavāya</s>, being established through a <s>pramāṇa</s>, cannot be abandoned out of fear of infinite regress—this is the meaning.
He removes the doubt after deliberation—'what is this?'
Since in conjunction the established nature ceases, the relation is natural, because the <s>upādhi</s> of being an effect—which is its activating condition—is present—this is the meaning.
But why does it not also have the property of being established?—therefore he says—'but if this too.'
But why is this infinite regress not accepted here as in the case of seeds and sprouts?—therefore he says—'and this regress.'
In things that have no first beginning, the infinite regress can be established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> because of their beginninglessness; but in things that have a first beginning, it cannot be determined because of their having a beginning.
This is what is stated—'because of the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>.'
And accepting another <s>samavāya</s> contradicts the <s>śāstra</s>—he says: 'and <s>samavāya</s>.'
The <s>śāstra</s> states that the reality of <s>samavāya</s> is its oneness, explained by its existence—the meaning is that one who establishes its multiplicity contradicts it.
He objects—'when the relatum ceases.'
And thus it perishes; and when it has perished, what is seen is another [<s>samavāya</s>] that has arisen—thus the multiplicity of <s>samavāya</s> is established—this is the meaning.
He resolves—'it does not not exist.'
<s>Khyāti</s> means apprehension.
Why? Because of being uncreated (<s>akṛtakatva</s>).
But why is it uncreated?—therefore he says—'uncreated.'
The negative concomitant reason: an effect possesses a substrate through its material cause in the manner of something related to what is uncreated.
He states the non-deviation of the negative concomitance—'if this.'
Indeed, this <s>samavāya</s>, when being produced, would be produced along with the effect, not of the effect.
For form and touch, produced simultaneously, are not related to each other.
Rather, their inherence in a single substance [relates them].
But that [inherence] too does not exist in <s>samavāya</s> [itself].
Even if it exists, it does not make the effect possess a substrate.
Therefore, in the case of simultaneous production, the effect would be without a substrate.
He raises a doubt—'or else.'
The meaning is: <s>samavāya</s>, having been produced prior to the effect, will subsequently make the effect possess a substrate through the force of the cause of the effect.
He removes the doubt—'even so.'
For an effect having a real form arises from three causes.
And for the <s>samavāya</s> of cause and effect, the material cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) must be stated as the cause and effect [themselves]; and for <s>samavāya</s> produced prior to the effect, the effect is not its cause.
And it is not proper that it is born from merely the efficient cause, since the production of any existent thing is necessarily preceded by all three causes.
Therefore, since <s>samavāya</s> lacks a <s>samavāyin</s> (co-inherent) and a material cause, it is not produced prior to the effect—this is well said: 'even so, of what [material cause] is it to be stated?'
He raises a doubt—'or else.'
He refutes—'effect.'
And it is not proper that there be a <s>samavāya</s> of cause and effect [of samavāya itself] subsequent [to samavāya], as there is a conjunction of cloth with the loom.
Because for conjunction born of conjunction, all three causes are available, but for this [second samavāya], without another <s>samavāya</s>, the three causes are unavailable.
Otherwise there would be the charge of infinite regress—this is the purport.
He concludes—'therefore.'
And thus it is not known with what intention it was said that 'it has non-existing things as its object'—this is the objection.
He resolves—'there, what is being negated.'
The past and future, being presently negated—the inference that has those as its object is said to have non-existing things as its object.
But let the negation of those be within the scope of perception; even so, the difference of object is established—this is the meaning.
And here, this sequence of the threefold nature of properties is twofold: what is being affirmed and what is being negated.
What is being affirmed is also twofold: dependent and independent.
And the property-nature of the independent should be understood as intended merely in the sense of being a qualifier.
But is not what is being affirmed also non-existent sometimes, and perceptible?
As when a potter is working, the pot being produced.
For one with wide-open eyes cognizes 'the pot comes into being.'
And it is not existent at that time, since coming-into-being of the existent would be without an agent, like motion—he raises this doubt: 'comes into being.'
He removes it—'no, because the object that is coming into being [is neither accepted as existent nor as non-existent].'

children.text:
svalakṣaṇaṃ samādhāya pareṣāmanumānalakṣaṇaṃ dūṣayitumupanyasyati---apare tviti /
tasyārthamāha---asyārtha iti /
dūṣayati---atreti /
yathāsaṃbhavaṃ samāsaṃ vikalpya dūṣyati--nāntarīyakārtha iti ceti /
sattvaṃ vidhiviṣayajñānagamyatvam, na tu sāmānyam /
sattvādibhiranityatvānāntarīyakaiḥ tannāntarīyakakṛtakatvadharmairanityatvānumānaṃ syāt, na ca śakyam, teṣāmākāśādiṣu nityeṣu vyabhicārādityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Even so, the compound is incapable [of yielding the desired meaning].
Previously, only the excess of meaning was stated as the refutation.
But now, through the reason of excess of meaning, the impossibility of the qualificative compound is stated—hence there is no repetition.
'The qualifier with the qualified' is common [in Sanskrit grammar].

Having established his own definition, he presents the definition of inference by others in order to refute it—'but others.'
He states its meaning—'its meaning.'
He refutes—'here.'
Analyzing the compound in alternative ways, he refutes each—'not in the sense of inseparability.'
<s>Sattva</s> (existence) means being knowable through the cognition of what is to be affirmed, not the universal [existence].
Through existence and the like—through impermanence which is inseparable from those, through the property of being produced which is inseparable from impermanence—there would be inference of impermanence. But this cannot be, because of the deviation of those [properties] in space and the like, which are permanent—this is the meaning.

children.text:
ityatra viśeṣaṇapadopādādamātreṇa vā viśeṣyapadopādānamātreṇa vā anyatarasyārthāt prāpterūbhayapadopādānasyaitat prayojanam---yatrobhayoḥ pratyekaṃ vyabhicāraḥ samudāye tvavyabhicāraḥ, tatra samāso yathā syāditi /
sa cātra nāstīti samāsānupapattirityarthaḥ /
sāmarthyaṃ prayojanābhisaṃbandhaḥ /
codayati---ekapadeti /
pariharati---atrāpīti /
pradhānaṃ vyaktirviśeṣyatvāt aṅgaṃ jātirviśeṣaṇatvāt /
pṛthivītyukte bhavati saṃśayaḥ, kiṃ pṛthivītvaṃ sāmānyamasya vivakṣitaṃ yathā paśunā yajeta iti, kiṃ vā tadviśeṣyaṃ dravyam, grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭīti /
atredamupatiṣṭhate--dravyamiti /
taddhi pṛthivītvāt sāmānyaviśeṣāt pṛthivī vyavacchinatti /
evaṃ dravyamityapyukte dravyatvaṃ vā sāmānyaṃ vyaktirveti vimarśe pṛthivītyetadupatiṣṭhate /
na dravyatvaṃ sāmānyaṃ kiṃ tu pṛthivī /
na ca dravyatvapṛthivītvayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyamasti /
na hi bhavati pṛthivītvaṃ dravyatvamiti /
tasmāt sāmānādhikaraṇyasaṃbhavāt pradhānaikavyaktilābhaḥ /
iha tvartho nāntarīyakatvaṃ vyabhicarati /
nāntarīyakatvaṃ tu nārtham /
na hyasti saṃbhavo nāntarīyakaśca syāt na cārtha iti, nāntarīyakaśabdavācyasyānabhidheyatvāsaṃbhavāt /
vastuvacanatve 'pyarthaśabdasya lakṣyāsaṃbhavād aviṣayaṃ lakṣaṇam, na hi dignāgasya mate kiñcidasti vastu yannāntarīyakaṃ saddheturbhavati /

children.translated_text: As he says —

children.text: sarvo 'yamanumānānumeyabhāvo buddhyārūḍhena dharmadharmibhāvena na bahiḥ sadasattvamapekṣate iti /
children.translated_text: This entire relation of inference and the inferable, being a relation of property and property-bearer that has entered the intellect, does not depend on external existence or non-existence.

children.text: avyāpakaṃ ca, na hi vastveva nāntarīyakamasato 'pi nāntarīyakatvāditi bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: And it is non-pervasive — for it is not only real things that are inseparable; even non-existent things have inseparability — this is the sense.

Here, by the mere adoption of the qualifier-word or by the mere adoption of the qualified-word, the other is obtainable by implication. The purpose of adopting both words is this: where there is deviation in each individually but non-deviation in the aggregate, the compound should occur. But that does not exist here — hence the compound is unjustified — this is the meaning. The capacity is the connection with purpose. He objects — 'with a single word.' He responds — 'here too.' The principal is the particular (<s>vyakti</s>), because it is the qualified; the subsidiary is the universal (<s>jāti</s>), because it is the qualifier. When 'earth' (<s>pṛthivī</s>) is said, doubt arises: is the universal 'earth-ness' intended, as in 'one should sacrifice with an animal,' or the substance that is its qualified, as in 'he sweeps the sacrificial vessel'? Here what presents itself is — substance. For that, by means of earth-ness — the distinction between universal and particular — distinguishes earth. Similarly, even when 'substance' is said, when there is the deliberation whether it is the universal substance-ness or the particular, 'earth' presents itself — not substance-ness the universal, but earth. And there is no co-referentiality between substance-ness and earth-ness. For it is not the case that earth-ness is substance-ness. Therefore, because of the possibility of co-referentiality, a single principal particular is obtained. But here [in <s>Dignāga</s>'s definition], the meaning does not deviate from being inseparable (<s>nāntarīyakatva</s>). But inseparability does not deviate from meaning. For there is no possibility that something is inseparable yet not meaningful — since what is denoted by the word 'inseparable' cannot be inexpressible. Even if the word 'meaning' (<s>artha</s>) denotes a real thing, the definition is without scope because the characterized object is impossible — for in <s>Dignāga</s>'s view, there is no real thing that, being inseparable, would be a valid reason.

children.text:
dūṣaṇāntaramāha---tadvida iti ceti /
nāntarīyakadarśanamityucyamāne śabdasāmarthyādeva labhyate nāntarīyakatvaviśiṣṭārthadarśanamiti, sati saṃbhave śabdārthaparityāgābhāvāt /
atastrirūpaliṅgadarśanasya siddheḥ kimaparamavaśiṣyate yadavarodhāya tadvida ityupādīyate ityarthaḥ /
etadeva vyatirekamukhena nirūpayati--na hīti /
etallakṣaṇadūṣaṇaṃ lakṣaṇāntare apyatidiśati--eteneti /
pṛcchati--ka iti /
na hyasmin lakṣaṇe tadvida ityasti, tena tadatiricyate iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: For in this [other] definition, there is no 'known to the expert' — the sense is that it is surpassed by that [critique].
The answer — 'as.'
He refutes their example — 'the example.'

children.text: tadanena dignāgasya lakṣaṇaṃ dūṣayitvā anyeṣāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ dūṣitam //
children.translated_text: Thus, having refuted <s>Dignāga</s>'s definition, the definitions of others are also refuted.

He states another refutation — 'known to the expert' and so on. When 'the observation of the inseparable' is said, by the force of the words alone one obtains 'the observation of the meaning qualified by inseparability,' since when there is a possible [simpler] interpretation, there is no abandoning of the word's meaning. Therefore, the establishment of the observation of the triple-characterised mark being accomplished, what else remains that requires the adoption of 'known to the expert'? — this is the meaning. He demonstrates this same point through negative concomitance — 'for not.' He extends this refutation of the definition to other definitions as well — 'by this.' He asks — 'which?'

children.text:
saṃprati dignāgasya svakīyalakṣaṇaprapañcārthaṃ vākyam anumeye 'tha tattulya ityādyupanyasya dūṣayati--apare tviti /
anantaralakṣaṇakāramapekṣyāpara ityuktam /
codayati--anumeya iti /
na hi yo 'numeye saṃścāsaṃśca sa śakyaḥ sanniti vaktum
ityarthaḥ /
samādhatte--nāprasaṅga iti /
yadyevaṃ syātad yo vipakṣe dvedhā sa vipakṣāvṛttiriti hetureva syāt na savyabhicāra ityarthaḥ /
punaścodayati--na kartavya iti /
kutaḥ? avadhāraṇāt nivṛtteḥ /
anumeye sadbhāva evetyavadhāraṇenānumeye sadbhāvasya niyatatvāt kutaḥ pakṣaikadeśavṛtteḥ prasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ /
evannirākartuṃ yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vikalpayati---anumeye iti /
tatra pūrvakalpasya tātparyaṃ vikalpayati--kiṃ punaraneneti /
asaṃbhavaḥ atyantāsaṃbhavo nirākriyate, yathā nīlaṃ sarojaṃ bhavatyeva nātyantaṃ na bhavatīti gamyate, na tu nīlameva sarojaṃ nānīlamiti, nāpi sarojameva nīlaṃ nānyaditi /
atha saṃbhava iti /
anvayaparo na vyatirekapara ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He refutes both alternatives — 'in both ways.'
He states another refutation — 'and one that occurs only in a part is not [excluded].'

children.text: na hyatyantāyogavyavacchedenāyogo vyavacchinno bhavati, nāpi saṃbhavamātravidhānenāsaṃbhavo vyavacchinno bhavati /
children.translated_text: For the exclusion of complete non-connection does not exclude [mere] connection; nor does the mere prescription of possibility exclude impossibility.
Therefore, since connection is not excluded, the pseudo-reason that occurs only in a part [of the thesis] is not excluded — this is the meaning.

Now, he presents <s>Dignāga</s>'s statement for elaborating his own definition — 'in the inferable, and in what is similar to that' — and refutes it: 'others however.' 'Others' is said with reference to the immediately preceding definition-maker. He objects — 'in the inferable.' For that which is both present and absent in the inferable cannot be said to simply exist — this is the meaning. He resolves — 'there is no over-extension.' If this were so, then whatever is two-fold in the counter-instance would be merely 'absent from the counter-instance' — i.e., it would be a valid reason and not inconclusive — this is the meaning. He objects again — 'it need not be done.' Why? Because of the restriction. Since the restriction 'existence in the inferable alone' necessitates that existence in the inferable is fixed, whence comes the over-extension to a part of the thesis? — this is the sense. In order to refute this, he proposes alternatives as far as possible — 'in the inferable.' Therein, he proposes the purport of the first alternative — 'what then by this?' The impossibility — i.e., complete impossibility — is being refuted. Just as 'a blue lotus does indeed exist, it is not entirely non-existent' — this is understood, but not 'a lotus is only blue, not non-blue,' nor 'only a lotus is blue, nothing else.' Or if [it means] possibility —

children.text:
syādetat /
viśeṣyasaṃgato 'yamevakāro 'numeya eva saṃbhavati /
yathā pārtha eva dhanurdhara iti /
na cāyamanyayogavyavacchedo vinaivakāraṃ labhyate /

children.translated_text: Therefore the restriction is not purposeless — hence he says — 'and it contradicts the subsequent word.'

children.text: na hyasti saṃbhavo 'numeya evāsti tattulye ceti /
children.translated_text: For it is not possible that something exists in the inferable alone and also exists in what is similar to it.
Therefore, 'in what is similar to that' is contradicted.
And the particle 'ca' (and) gathers the [earlier] refutation that 'the part-occurring [reason] is not excluded.'

One might say: this restrictive particle 'eva' (alone) is connected with the qualified: 'it occurs in the inferable alone.' Just as 'only <s>Arjuna</s> is the archer.' And this exclusion of other connection cannot be obtained without the particle 'eva.'

children.text:
anumeya eva sadbhāva iti pakṣaṃ yathāsaṃbhavaṃ dūṣayitvā anumeye sadbhāva eveti dvitīyaṃ pakṣaṃ dūṣayitumupanyasyati---athottaramiti /
tasya prayojanaṃ daśayati---tasya vayāptirityarthaḥ /
sadbhāva eveti kila viśeṣaṇasaṃgatamavadhāraṇamayogam avyāpti vyavacchindat vyāpti darśayati /
tathā ca vyāptirasyārtha ityarthaḥ /
dūṣayati---tathāpyanumeyamavadhāritaṃ saṃbhavasya vyāptyā na dharmaḥ sadbhāvaḥ /
hetumāha--yata evakārakaraṇaṃ tato 'nyatrāvadhāraṇamiti /
mā vadhāri sadbhāvo 'vadhāryatāṃ cānumeyam /
kimetāvatāpītyata āha---saṃbhavavyāptyā ceti /
anumeyaṃ khalvavadhāritaṃ saddhetusaṃbhavaṃ parityajya nānyatra vartate, tataścānumeyaṃ hetusaṃbhavavyāptyāvadhāritaṃ bhavati /
hetusaṃbhavastvanavadhāritaḥ sarvatraiva tattulye ca vipakṣe ca prasṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: But the possibility of the reason is unrestricted, spreading everywhere — in the similar and in the counter-instance.

children.text: sa ca kaścit tattulyavipakṣau vyāpnoti, kaścit tadekadeśavṛttiḥ /
children.translated_text: And some of that possibility pervades the similar and the counter-instance, while some occurs only in a part of them.

children.text: tadasya hetusaṃbhavasya vipakṣe 'pi prasaktasya pratiṣedhāya yuktamasati nāstīti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, to negate the possibility of this reason as extending even to the counter-instance, 'it does not exist where it does not exist' is proper.

children.text: tattulye tu prasaktamapratiṣiddhamanumatameveti tattulye sadbhāva iti vyarthamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: But being extended to the similar and not negated, it is simply accepted — therefore 'existence in the similar' is purposeless — this is the meaning.

Having refuted the interpretation 'existence in the inferable alone' as far as possible, he introduces the second interpretation to refute — 'now the latter.' He shows its purpose — 'its pervasion — this is the meaning.' [According to this view,] the restriction connected with the qualifier — 'existence alone' — excludes non-pervasion, i.e., non-occurrence, and shows pervasion. And thus pervasion is its meaning — this is the meaning. He refutes — 'even so, the inferable is restricted by the pervasion of possibility, but not the property — existence.' He states the reason — 'because the function of the restrictive particle is to restrict something other [than itself].' Let existence not be restricted, but let the inferable be restricted. What is the point of even this? — therefore he says — 'and by the pervasion of possibility.' For the inferable, being restricted, does not occur elsewhere abandoning the possibility of a valid reason — and thus the inferable is restricted by the pervasion of the reason's possibility.

children.translated_text: One might say: even when the existence of the valid reason in the similar is established, in order to state that the reason exists in the similar with pervasion, the statement 'existence in the similar' is purposeful — therefore he says — 'and in the similar.' But if pervasion were intended, then when the probandum is 'being produced,' 'being immediately after effort' (<s>prayatnānantarīyakatva</s>) would not be a valid reason. For this does not pervade the homologous instances — this is the sense. He demonstrates — 'now in the similar.' He proposes alternatives to refute — 'what then here?' The former is contradicted because of contradiction, the latter because of redundancy. Regarding the contradiction with the former word, he gives an illustration — 'for it is not possible.' When 'existence in the inferable' has already established the occurrence of the reason in the inferable, the restriction being aggregated with 'existence in the similar alone' excludes occurrence only from the counter-instance, not from the inferable. Just as in 'he first begat two sons, <s>Nara</s> and <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> alone' — if so objected, therefore he says — 'similarly here too.' For in the aggregated restriction, just as the particle 'eva' is connected with 'similar' by the exclusion of other connection, it would also be connected with 'inferable.' And thus even a reason occurring only in part of the inferable would be a [valid] reason. For the particle in '<s>Nara</s> and <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> alone' is not connected with <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> by the exclusion of other connection while being connected with <s>Nara</s> by the exclusion of non-connection — this is the sense. But if one, desiring a uniform connection of the restriction, says that just as there is exclusion of other connection for the inferable, so too for the similar there should be exclusion of non-connection — he anticipates — 'now the similar.' He refutes — 'the similar.' He elaborates that — 'they.' 'They' means 'in your view' — this is the meaning. Nor can one, having first stated 'existence in the inferable alone' as an anuvāda (reiteration), then prescribe 'existence in the similar alone.' For inference cannot be qualified [in this way], since if so, there would be the need for a separate effort to qualify it, leading to sentence-splitting. Just as in 'for one who has both [the Havis-bearing affliction], one should prepare a five-vessel porridge for <s>Indra</s>' — here, although the affliction, being unascertainable by its own nature, requires qualification by the Havis, nevertheless the Havis cannot be qualified by 'both-ness' without a separate effort, and so out of fear of sentence-splitting, the 'both-ness' though understood is treated as unintended. Similarly here too, 'in the inferable' is to be treated as unintended. Or, having accepted sentence-splitting with the intention of expressing that, thereafter the establishment of the intended meaning through the single-sentencehood of both sentences is to be resorted to. But the absence of single-sentencehood due to contradiction of the sentences is not [a valid objection]. Because, since the exclusion of other connection in 'in the similar alone' can also be justified as concerning only the counter-instance, contradiction is not established. Therefore, since words have the meaning of mutual exclusion (<s>anyāpoha</s>), contradiction must be stated. Thus, the word-meaning of 'existence in the inferable' is: 'in the inferable alone, not in the non-inferable; existence alone, not non-existence.' And thus the absence of the reason in both the similar and the counter-instance has been shown. Similarly, the word-meaning of 'existence in the similar' is: 'in the similar alone, not in the non-similar; existence alone, not non-existence.' And thus 'non-existence in the inferable' is being stated. And the aggregation of the meanings of the words 'inferable' and 'similar,' which mutually exclude each other, is not possible. If it is said that since both are concerned only with the exclusion of the counter-instance, being of identical meaning, they can be aggregated as co-referential — no, because there would be the undesirable consequence of co-referentiality even for 'tree' and 'cow,' which are also concerned only with excluding elephants and the like. Therefore, due to contradiction, the aggregated restriction is not proper. And <s>Dignāga</s> did not hold the aggregated restriction, since he said thus on the occasion of refuting the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> definition: 'If form alone is visual, then substance would not be visual. And thus the statement [in the <s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s>] that substance is visual because of perception arising from form and from [its being] a great thing co-inhering with multiple substances (<s>Vai. Sū.</s> 8/1/6) would be contradicted.'

children.text: atra hi rūpavaddravyasahitaṃ rūpameva cākṣuṣaṃ na gandharasādīti śakyaṃ samuccīyamānāvadhāraṇam /

Therefore, the statement of the aggregated restriction is <s>Kīrti</s>'s own, independently.
And that is improper — enough of the elaboration.

children.translated_text: When [only] 'exists in the similar and the non-existent does not exist' is stated, even what is not a property of the thesis would be a reason—as in 'atoms are impermanent because of being produced.'
The purpose of adopting the composite is so that none of these [fallacies] would occur.
He refutes this—'even this.'
Through pervasion and non-pervasion of the homologue, the duality of the merely-positive reason which has a twofold form.

He refutes [the idea that] 'it does not exist in the non-existent'—'in the non-existent.' Why? What is non-existent is void—it itself does not exist; it cannot be said to be 'existent' or 'non-existent.' Let it be so; even so, why is there no withdrawal of the reason from it?—therefore he says: 'for the non-existent.' And as this is, so it has been stated by us at the occasion of establishing the merely-positive reason. Having refuted [the definition] in terms of its own nature, wishing to refute the restriction contained in it, he restates and presents alternatives—'what is being restricted?' He refutes the first alternative—'if first.' The meaning is: 'existence in what is similar' is understood by this. He refutes the second alternative—'but again.' The reason 'this is a cow because of possessing horns' does not exist in the counter-thesis alone, because it pervades both the thesis and the homologue. But it is not that [the counter-thesis] simply does not exist—since [the reason] occurs in a part of the counter-thesis, such as buffaloes etc. Therefore 'does not exist in the counter-thesis alone' would also be a reason [on this account]. Having thus refuted the meaning of the components, he presents [a refutation of] the composite meaning—'also by the exclusion of one or two terms.' There, by the exclusion of one term there are three positions; by the exclusion of two terms there are also three—thus six. By the exclusion of that [combination], the inclusion of seven [positions] results. For example, when [only] 'existence in what is inferred' is stated, even that which is absent in the similar and present in the counter-thesis would be a reason—as in 'sound is permanent because of being produced.' When [only] 'exists in the similar' is stated, even what is present in the counter-thesis and not a property of the thesis would be a reason—as in 'sound is permanent because of being visible, like the universal.' When [only] 'absence is absent' is stated, even what is not a property of the thesis and not present in the similar would be a reason—as in 'sound is permanent because of non-existence.' When [only] 'in what is inferred and in the similar' is stated, even a reason present in the counter-thesis would be valid—as in 'sound is impermanent because of being knowable.' When [only] 'exists in what is inferred and the non-existent does not exist' is stated, even a reason lacking occurrence in the similar would be valid—as in 'sound is permanent because of being auditory while possessing a universal.'

children.translated_text: Now he refutes the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> definition of inference—'by this.' The relation is the invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>) of the proving mark with the probandum. From that—from perception, ascertained by a firmer means of knowledge. Even so, where there is a mark invariably present, if for you there are two mutually contrary [marks] in a single property-bearer that are non-deviating, then their being reasons would also follow—therefore it is said: 'from a single.' The establishment of the remainder—the inferable. It is said 'by this, it is not employed' because of the similarity of merely being impossible. He asks the impossibility—'how?' He states the impossibility according to the case—'for it is not so.' If the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' (perception) denotes cognition, and cognition is qualified by oneness, then this refutation [applies]. But if 'from a single' is a qualifier of the relation, and the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' refers to what is to be known and not the knowing—he presents this and refutes: 'but if from the relation.' He raises a doubt—'now.' The meaning is: the relation has been said to be [known] from perception previously, not at the time of inference. He refutes—'even so, for one whose relation was previously apprehended, and whose mark is not apprehended at the time of inference, inference would follow.' It might be said: the <s>liṅga</s> (mark) is the <s>saṃbandha</s> (relation) by the etymology 'that which is related.' Therefore, from the reason—the invariably present mark—perceived from a single [perception]—the inferable is established. And thus the definition is appropriate: 'from a mark whose invariable concomitance has been grasped, presently perceived'—therefore he says: 'and there is no other interpretation.' Even on this explanation, 'from a single' is superfluous. For thus: is <s>avinābhāva</s> (invariable concomitance) merely the possession of positive and negative concomitance, or the possession of all qualifications? On the first alternative, let there not be a mutually contradictory non-deviating [reason], but a reason with a contradicted subject-matter would be [possible]. On the second alternative, a reason with mutual contradiction and non-deviation cannot exist, so 'from a single' is redundant. Therefore it is well said—'there is no other interpretation.' He states the fault of under-extension in the definition—'and by form.' These two [form and touch] are not identical in nature, since they are apprehended by different sense organs and known by different cognitions. Nor is any other relation between these non-identical things apprehended. And on the doctrine of momentary transformation, even between bowls and plums, no relation exists—this too should be noted. He raises a doubt—'now.' He refutes—'that too.' For in the system of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> or the Buddhists, there is no relation called <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). Nor is substance, the locus of that, [accepted by them]. Therefore there is contradiction with one's own system—such is the meaning. If it were said that since forms and the like are produced from <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter), <s>Pradhāna</s> alone is the single substrate, and thus 'where there is form, there is touch'—therefore he says: 'where form.' Why? 'Not anywhere.' For <s>Pradhāna</s> is not the container of its effects; rather, these are held to be of the nature of <s>Pradhāna</s>. And thus 'where that, there this' is impossible. And identity has also been denied. And difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one thing, due to contradiction—such is the sense. He raises a doubt—'mutual support.' Just as the parts of a seat, though different and not arranged as upper-and-lower, do not fall because of mutually supporting each other—so form and touch too are mutually supporting—such is the meaning. He refutes—'even in mutual support, [while it occurs] elsewhere in seat-parts and the like, it does not [occur] in form and touch.' Why? 'Form is not [in touch], and touch is not in form.' The parts of a seat, bound by their mutual contacts dependent on gravity, are stable and are designated as mutually supporting. But the stability of form, touch, and the like is not caused by each other; rather, it is caused by the human purpose characterized by experience and liberation—such is the sense. By this, the sevenfold relation of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> is also refuted. The rest is easy to understand.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.6: <s>Upamāna</s> (analogy) is the means of establishing what is to be known, based on well-known similarity.

children.text:
vibhāgasūtre anumānānantaramupamānasyoddeśād yathoddeśaṃ ca lakṣaṇādanumānalakṣaṇānantaramupamānalakṣaṇamāha---athopamānamiti bhāṣyam /
sūtraṃ paṭhati---prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanamupamānam /
atrāpi yata ityadhyāhāryam /
siddhiḥ sādhanam /
tadetad bhāṣyakāreṇa vyākhyātam /
prajñātena prasiddhena /
gavā sādharmyāt sāmānyād gavayasya /
sādharmyaṃ ca sāmānyamabhidadhatā na sāmānyātiriktaṃ sādṛśyaṃ nāma padārthāntaramastītyuktaṃ bhavati /
sādharmyaṃ cāprasiddhaṃ na sādhyasāghanāyālamiti sādharmyaprasiddhirapi draṣṭavyā /
sā ca yathā gaustathā gavaya ityāptavākyāt /
tadidamuktam---yathā gauriti /
sādhyasādhanapadavyākhyānam---prajñāpanīyasya gavayaśabdavācyatayā pratyakṣadṛśyamānagosādṛśyasya gavayatvasāmānyaviśeṣavataḥ piṇḍasya prajñāpanamupamānam /
piṇḍasya hi gavayaśabdavācyatāṃ puruṣo 'tideśavākyasmaraṇasahakāriṇaḥ pratayakṣād gavayagatād gosādṛśyāt prajānan tena prajñāpyata iti pramāṇasya vyāpāraḥ prajñāpanamuktamiti /
tatra vārttikakāraḥ prathamaṃ tāvat sūtratātparyamāha---sūtrārthaḥ pūrvavat /
samānāsamānajātīyavyavaccheda ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: When '<s>sādhyasādhana</s>' (means of establishing what is to be known) is said, there would be over-extension to perception and the like as means of establishing, and to pleasure, pain, etc. as what is to be established.
Therefore it is said 'based on well-known similarity.'

children.text: yadyapi prasiddhasārmyamupamānamityucyamāne pramāṇaviśeṣābhidhāyyupamānapadasāmānādhikaraṇyāt karaṇatvalābhaḥ, tathāpi tadābhāsanirākaraṇāya sādhyasādhanapadopādānam /
children.translated_text: Although when 'well-known similarity is <s>upamāna</s>' is said, instrumentality is obtained due to co-referentiality with the word '<s>upamāna</s>' which denotes a specific means of valid knowledge, nevertheless the words '<s>sādhyasādhana</s>' are included for the purpose of excluding semblances of analogy.
By that, the semblance of analogy is excluded.

Since in the division <s>sūtra</s>, <s>upamāna</s> is enumerated immediately after <s>anumāna</s>, and the definition is to follow the order of enumeration, the definition of <s>upamāna</s> comes immediately after the definition of <s>anumāna</s>—'now <s>upamāna</s>' is the <s>bhāṣya</s>. He reads the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Upamāna</s> is the means of establishing what is to be known, based on well-known similarity.' Here too, 'from which' is to be supplied. Establishment (<s>siddhi</s>) is proof (<s>sādhana</s>). This has been explained by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>. 'By the well-known, the familiar'—from the cow, 'by similarity,' i.e., by the common property (<s>sāmānya</s>), of the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox). And by expressing similarity as common property, it is said that there is no separate category called resemblance (<s>sādṛśya</s>) apart from the universal. And since unfamiliar similarity cannot serve to establish what is to be known, the familiarity of the similarity should also be understood. And that [familiarity comes] from the trustworthy statement 'the <s>gavaya</s> is like the cow.' This is what is said—'just as the cow.' The explanation of the words '<s>sādhya</s>' (what is to be established) and '<s>sādhana</s>' (the means of establishing): <s>upamāna</s> is the establishing (<s>prajñāpana</s>) of the individual possessing the specific universal <s>gavayatva</s>, which is perceptually seen as having cow-resemblance, and which is to be made known as denoted by the word '<s>gavaya</s>.' For the person, knowing through perception—aided by the memory of the comparative statement—the cow-resemblance present in the <s>gavaya</s>, is made to know that that individual is denoted by the word '<s>gavaya</s>'—this operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the establishing, is stated. There, the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> first states the purport of the <s>sūtra</s>—'the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is as before.' The meaning is: exclusion from what is of the same and different class.

children.text:
avayavārthaṃ vibhajate---prasiddheti /
vārttikakāreṇa bahuvrīhidvayasaṃbhavo darśitaḥ, na tu tṛtīyāsamāso bhāṣyakārīyo nirastaḥ /
bhāṣyakāreṇa hi saṃjñitayā gavayapratipattiḥ phalaṃ sādhyasādhanapadavācyamuktā, ākṣiptaprayojyavyāpāratvāt /
prayojakavyāpārasya prajñāpanasya paścāt niṣkṛṣyābhidhānaṃ kṛtam---samākhyāsaṃbandhapratipattipattirūpamānārtha iti /
