etadeva sādhyasādhanapadārthatayā vārttikakāro vyācaṣṭe---samākhyāsaṃbandhapratipattirūpamānārthaḥ phalam /
sādhyaśabdena samākhyāsaṃbandha ucyate /
tasya sādhanaṃ siddhiḥ pratipattiriti /
nanu pratipadyatāmayaṃ gosādṛśyayuktaṃ gavayam /
samākhyāsaṃbandhapratipattistu kutastyā? na hi yo yatsadṛśaṃ yaṃ pratipadyate, sa tasya samākhyāmapyavagacchati ityāśayavān pṛcchati---kimuktaṃ bhavati /
uttaram---āgameti /
āgamānubhavāhitāt saṃskārāt smṛtiḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, na kevalaṃ sārūpyajñānaṃ samākhyāsaṃbandhapratipattihetuḥ, api tvāgamārthasmṛtyapekṣamiti /
nanvasatyāgamānubhave kutaḥ smṛtirityata āha---yadā hyaneneti /
prasiddhasādharmyādityatra prasiddhirūbhayī śrutamayī pratyakṣamayī ca /
śrutamayī yathā gaurevaṃ gavaya iti /
pratyakṣamayī ca yathā gosādṛśyaviśiṣṭo 'yamīdṛśaḥ piṇḍa iti /
tatra pratyakṣamayī prasiddhirāgamāhitasmṛtyapekṣā samākhyāsaṃbandhapratipattihetuḥ /
yadyapi yathā gaurevaṃ gavaya ityetasmādapi gosadṛśasya gavayaśabdaḥ samākhyeti śakyamavagantum, na khalu pratyakṣa eva saṃjñākarma, samānajātīyavyavacchinne hi tadbhāvati /

tacca yadi mānāntareṇāpi tathāvagamyate, kastatra saṃjñākarma nivārayet? gosādṛśyena copalakṣitaḥ piṇḍo ya iti sarvanāmnā parāmṛṣṭaḥ śakyo ghaṭādibhyo 'samānajātiyebhyo mahiṣādibhyaśca samānajātīyebhyo vyavacchinno 'vagantuṃ gavayaḥ, tathāpi yāvadayamasau gavaya iti sākṣāt pratīte saṃbandhini saṃjñāṃ na niveśayati, tāvadayaṃ pariplutamatiḥ pramātā kaccit khalu drakṣyāmi tādṛśaṃ piṇḍaṃ yatra gavayasaṃjñā pratipatsya iti pramotsuka evodīkṣate /
children.translated_text: And if that is understood through another means of knowledge too, who would prevent the naming-act there? An individual, indicated by cow-resemblance, referred to by the pronoun 'that,' can be understood as <s>gavaya</s>—distinguished from dissimilar things like pots etc. and from similar things like buffaloes etc. Even so, until this person directly establishes the name in a directly perceived related entity—'this one is that <s>gavaya</s>'—until then, this person of agitated mind, wondering 'will I indeed see such an individual in which I shall comprehend the name <s>gavaya</s>?', looks on with eagerness.

children.text: na cāsau vākyamātrasahāyo 'pratyakṣīkṛtagosadṛśagavayatvajātimatpiṇḍo 'sau gavayākhya iti pratipattumarhati /
children.translated_text: And that person, aided by the statement alone without having directly perceived an individual possessing the <s>gavaya</s>-universal endowed with cow-resemblance, is not able to comprehend that it is called <s>gavaya</s>.
And without the statement, from perception alone [the comprehension does not arise].

Therefore, this knowledge of resemblance, accompanied by scripture and memory, being different from both scripture and perception, should be accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) called <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).

He divides the meaning of the components—'well-known.' The <s>Vārtikakāra</s> has shown the possibility of two <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compounds, but has not rejected the genitive compound (<s>ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa</s>) of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>. For the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> has stated the comprehension of <s>gavaya</s> as a designated entity (<s>saṃjñita</s>) as the result, expressed by the words '<s>sādhyasādhana</s>'—because the incited operation is implied. The inciting operation, namely the establishing, was subsequently extracted and stated—'the result of <s>upamāna</s> is the comprehension of the name-relation.' This very thing is explained by the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> as the meaning of the words '<s>sādhyasādhana</s>'—'the comprehension of the name-relation is the result of <s>upamāna</s>.' By the word '<s>sādhya</s>' (what is to be established), the name-relation is meant. Its establishment, i.e., comprehension, is the proof. Now, let him comprehend the <s>gavaya</s> as endowed with cow-resemblance. But whence the comprehension of the name-relation? For it is not the case that whoever comprehends something similar to something thereby also knows its name—with this thought he asks: 'what is being said?' The answer—'from scripture (<s>āgama</s>).' The memory arises from the latent impression deposited by the experience of scripture. What is said amounts to this: not merely the cognition of resemblance is the cause of comprehending the name-relation, but [that cognition] is dependent on the memory of the meaning of scripture. Now, in the absence of the experience of scripture, whence the memory?—therefore he says: 'for when this one.' In 'based on well-known similarity,' the familiarity is of two kinds: based on what is heard and based on what is directly perceived. The heard-based familiarity is 'the <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow.' The perception-based familiarity is 'this individual of such a form possesses cow-resemblance.' There, the perception-based familiarity, dependent on memory deposited by scripture, is the cause of comprehending the name-relation. Although even from the [statement] 'the <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow,' it can be understood that the word '<s>gavaya</s>' is the name for what resembles a cow, nevertheless the object of the naming-act is not directly perceived alone—for that [naming] occurs only when [the object] is distinguished from things of the same class.

children.text:
nanu yadodīcyena kramelakaṃ nindratoktam, dhik karabhamatidīrghavakragrīvaṃ pralamboṣṭhaṃ kaṭhoratīkṣṇakaṇṭakāśinaṃ kutsitāvayavasanniveśamapasadaṃ paśūnāmiti, tadupaśrutya dākṣiṇātya uttarāpathaṃ gatastādṛśaṃ vastūpalabhya nūnamasau karabha iti pratyeti, tat katamadeteṣu pramāṇam? na tāvadupamānaṃ sādharmyābhāvāt /
nāpi pañcamaṃ pramāṇamupagamyate /
yadyucyeta nindāparaṃ vākyaṃ karabhasya tādṛśatve na pramāṇam, na hyanyaparāt śabdādanyasyāvagama iti /
yatra tarhi tādṛktve paryavasyati vākyaṃ tatra kā gatiḥ? atha tatrāpi tādṛk karabha āgamāvagataḥ pratyakṣeṇa pratyabhijñāyate, karabhaśabdavācyatā tu tasya tatpūrvaṃ tādṛkvarabhaparatve apyāgamasya prayogamātrādavagatā anumānāt /
yo hi yatra prayujyate śabdo 'sati vṛttyantare sa tasya vācakaḥ, yathā gośabdo gotve /
prayuktaścāyaṃ tādṛśi /
tasmāt tasya vācaka iti /
tadidaṃ prāgeva prayogānumitaṃ vācakatvamasya pratyakṣasamaye kevalaṃ smaryate iti /

children.translated_text: This is the same [objection]—

children.text: upamānavākye 'pi tatrāpi vākyādavagataḥ sādharmyavān piṇḍaḥ pratyakṣeṇa pratyabhijñāyate /
children.translated_text: even in the sentence of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), there too the entity possessing the common property, known from the sentence, is recognized by perception.

children.text: prayogānumitaṃ ca gavayapadasya vācakatvaṃ smaryate iti na phalāntaramavaśiṣyate yatropamānaṃ pramāṇamiti //
children.translated_text: And the denotability of the word <s>gavaya</s>, inferred from usage, is [merely] remembered—so no separate result remains for which <s>upamāna</s> would be a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

But suppose a northerner has disparaged the camel, saying 'Shame on the <s>karabha</s> (camel)—with its excessively long curved neck, drooping lips, covered with hard sharp thorns, with an ugly arrangement of limbs, the lowest of animals!' A southerner, having heard this, goes to the northern region and upon perceiving such a thing thinks 'surely this must be a <s>karabha</s>'—then which of these <s>pramāṇas</s> is it? Not <s>upamāna</s>, due to the absence of positive similarity.
Nor is a fifth <s>pramāṇa</s> to be accepted.
If it is said that a statement aimed at censure is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> for the camel being of such a nature, since from a statement directed at something else, knowledge of something else does not arise—
then where the statement does culminate in establishing something as being of such a nature, what is the recourse? Well, even there, the <s>karabha</s> known through scripture as being of such a nature is recognized by perception; but its denotability by the word <s>karabha</s> is understood through inference, having been known earlier from the mere usage of the scripture even though the scripture was directed at 'a <s>karabha</s> being of such a nature.'
For whatever word is used for whatever thing, in the absence of another convention, that word is its denoter—just as the word 'go' (cow) for cow-hood.
And this word has been used for something of such a nature.
Therefore it is its denoter.
Thus this denotability, inferred earlier from usage, is merely remembered at the time of perception.

children.text:
atrocyate /
na tāvadākāśādiśabdavadeṣa gavayaśabdaḥ sākṣāt piṇḍasya vācakaḥ, kintu gavayatvaṃ nimittīkṛtya piṇḍe vartate iti paramārthaḥ /
na ca yathā gaurevaṃ gavaya iti vākyād gavayatvamavagatam, na hyanavagatasaṃbadhaṃ gavayapadametadavabodhayati /
tatastadavagamāt tu saṃbandhavedane parasparāśrayaprasaṅgaḥ /
na ca gosādṛśyenopalakṣyate gavayatvam /
na khalvanupalabdhacareṇa gavayatvena gosādṛśyaṃ saṃbaddhaṃ dṛṣṭam /
na cādṛṣṭasaṃbandham upalakṣakam /
na hi puruṣeṇādṛṣṭasaṃbandho daṇḍaḥ puruṣamupalakṣayitumarhati /
tasmāt saṃbandhino gavayatvasya sarvathānupalabdheḥ kuto vākyād vā anumānād vā vācyavācakasaṃbandhāvasāyaḥ? kutastarāṃ ca saṃbandhasmṛti? gavayatvasāmānyaviśeṣavati tu piṇḍe pratyakṣe yuktaḥ saṃbandhāvagamaḥ, saṃbandhino gavayatvasya pratyakṣatvāt vākyārthasya ca smaryāṇatvāt /
tathāpi kiṃ gavayatvajātimān piṇḍo vācyaḥ, uta gosādṛśyavāniti kuto vinigamaneti cet? vākyārthasmaraṇasahakāri gavayatvajātimataḥ piṇḍasya gāsādṛśyadarśanameva tarkasahāyaṃ gavayatvābhidhāne pramāṇam /
tarkaśca gosādṛśyaviśiṣṭapiṇḍābhidhāne kalpanāgauravaprasaṅgaḥ tathā hi sādṛśyaviśiṣṭa piṇḍābhidhāne, nāpratītaṃ sādṛśyaṃ piṇḍaṃ viśinaṣṭīti tatpratipattavyam /
na ca śabdādanyatastadavagama iti śabdaśya tatra vācakatvaṃ kalpanīyam /
na cāviśiṣṭaṃ sādṛśyamapi piṇḍaviśeṣe gavayapadam avasthāpayitumarhati, yasya kasyacid yena kenacit saha sādṛśyāditi tadapi gavā viśeṣaṇīyam /
na cānyato gotvasyāpi pratipattiriti tadapi gavayapadenābhidhātavyam iti kalpanāgauravam /
gavayatvajātimatpiṇḍābhidhāne tu lāghavamiti tadanujānāti /

children.translated_text: And the mention of 'common property' (<s>sādharmya</s>) is merely indicative of property in general—thus even the knowledge of the name <s>karabha</s> is a result of <s>upamāna</s> alone—hence there is no non-pervasion.
Nor is there acceptance of a fifth <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text: ata eva bahunyudāhaṇānyuktvāpyāha sma bhagavān bhāṣyakāraḥ, evamanyo 'pyupamānasya loke viṣayo bubhutsitavya iti /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, even after citing many examples, the revered <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> said: 'Thus other applications of <s>upamāna</s> in the world should also be investigated.'
Therefore, everything is in order.

Here we reply:
This word <s>gavaya</s> is not, like the words for space and the like, directly a denoter of the individual entity; rather, in the ultimate analysis, it refers to the individual through the intermediary of <s>gavayatva</s> (gavaya-hood).
And <s>gavayatva</s> is not known from the sentence 'a <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow,' for the word <s>gavaya</s>, whose relation [with its referent] has not been understood, does not convey this.
And from understanding that [<s>gavayatva</s>] to the knowledge of the relation, there would be mutual dependence.
Nor is <s>gavayatva</s> indicated by cow-resemblance.
For <s>gavayatva</s>, being beyond apprehension, has never been observed in relation with cow-resemblance.
And what has an unobserved relation is not an indicator.
For a staff with an unobserved relation to a person is not fit to indicate that person.
Therefore, since the relatum <s>gavayatva</s> is entirely unapprehended, whence the determination of the denoter-denoted relation from either the sentence or from inference? And whence, still less, the memory of the relation? But when the entity possessing the universal and particular of <s>gavayatva</s> is perceived, the knowledge of the relation is justified, since the relatum <s>gavayatva</s> is perceptible and the meaning of the sentence is being recalled.
Even so, what is denoted—is it the entity possessing the universal <s>gavayatva</s>, or one possessing cow-resemblance? Whence the determination?—if so objected. The perception of cow-resemblance in the entity possessing the universal <s>gavayatva</s>, cooperating with the memory of the sentence-meaning, aided by <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the denotation by <s>gavaya</s>.
And the <s>tarka</s> is: in the denotation of an entity qualified by cow-resemblance, there would be the charge of excessive complexity of supposition. For in denoting an entity qualified by resemblance, the resemblance that is not independently apprehended must be understood as qualifying the entity.
And since there is no understanding of it from anything other than verbal testimony, the denotability of the word for that must be posited.
Nor can unqualified resemblance establish the word <s>gavaya</s> in a particular entity, since anything has resemblance with anything—so that too must be qualified by 'cow.'
And since cow-hood too is not understood from anything else, that too must be said to be denoted by the word <s>gavaya</s>—this is excessive complexity of supposition.
But in the denotation of an entity possessing the universal <s>gavayatva</s>, there is simplicity—hence he accepts that.

children.text:
tadīdṛśamupamānaphalamavidvān sādṛśyaviśiṣṭavastujñānaṃ copamānaphalamiti bhrānto bhadanto dignāga ākṣipati---pratyakṣeti /
pṛcchati---kathamiti /
uttaram---yadā tāviti /
upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat, ubhau pratyakṣeṇa paśyatīti /
yadā tu gavayamekaṃ pratyakṣeṇa paśyati, smarati ca gām, tadāpi gosādṛśyaṃ gavayasthaṃ pratyakṣameva /
gagosthamapratyakṣam, apratyakṣatvād goriti cet? hanta bhoḥ kimabhimataṃ sādṛśyamāyuṣmato yadapratyakṣāyāṃ gavi na pratyakṣam? sāmānyabāhulyaṃ jātyantaravarti jātyantarasya /

children.translated_text: As they say—
The very multitude of commonalities of qualities, parts, and actions,
subsisting in the universal of what has a different principal—that is called resemblance.

Not knowing this nature of the result of <s>upamāna</s>, the confused venerable <s>Dignāga</s> objects that the knowledge of the object qualified by resemblance is a result of <s>upamāna</s>—'perception.'
He asks—'how?'
The answer—'when indeed.'
And this is indicative: both are seen by perception.
But when one sees a single <s>gavaya</s> by perception and remembers the cow, even then the cow-resemblance residing in the <s>gavaya</s> is perceptible.
The cow-resemblance residing in the cow is not perceived, because the cow is not perceived—if so objected? Well then, what is resemblance as understood by you, that when the cow is not perceived it is not perceptible? It is the abundance of common universals that one kind possesses in relation to another kind.

children.text:
iti cet? tat kimidānīṃ karṇatvādisāmānyaṃ gogavayagatakarṇādibhedena bhinnamityapi vaktumadhyavasito 'si? tasmād
yathā kālākṣyāṃ gavi gotvamīkṣitavataḥ svastimatyāṃ pratyabhijñāyamānaṃ tadevedamiti, etadeva tadityavagataṃ bhavati, tathehāpīti na phalātirekaḥ /
tasmāt na sādṛśyapratītiphalamupamānaṃ pratyakṣād vākyād vā vyatiricyate iti sūktam /
bhadantabhrāntimudghāṭayati---gaveti /
gavayasattāṃ sādṛśyaviśiṣṭam ityarthaḥ /
arthatattvamuktaṃ smārayati---gavayeti /
upasaṃharati---tasmāditi /

children.translated_text: The formal argument is: <s>upamāna</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s> different from perception and the rest, because it generates a valid cognition unlike the valid cognitions generated by those.

children.text: yadi tu na tebhyo vilakṣaṇamabhaviṣyad na tadvilakṣaṇāṃ pramāmakariṣyat, tathā tānyeva /
children.translated_text: For if it were not different from them, it would not have produced a valid cognition different from theirs—and similarly those [would not have produced their own].
But this is not the case.
Therefore it is so. // 6 //

If so? Then are you also prepared to say that ear-hood (<s>karṇatva</s>) and the like, common to cow and <s>gavaya</s>, are different on account of the difference of ears in cow and <s>gavaya</s>? Therefore,
just as for one who has seen cow-hood in a black cow, when it is recognized in a white cow—'this is the very same as that'—so too here, there is no surplus result.
Therefore it is well said that <s>upamāna</s>, having the result of apprehending resemblance, is not different from perception or from verbal statement.
He exposes the venerable one's confusion—'cow.'
The meaning is: the existence of the <s>gavaya</s>, qualified by resemblance.
He reminds of the true nature of the matter—'<s>gavaya</s>.'
He concludes—'therefore.'
<s>NyS</s> 1.1.7: The instruction of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>).

children.text:
atha śabda iti bhāṣyam /
upamānānantaraṃ śabdoddeśāt upamānalakṣaṇānantaraṃ śabdasya lakṣaṇamityarthaḥ /
lakṣaṇasūtraṃ paṭhati---āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ /
atra śabda iti lakṣyapadam /
āptopadeśa iti lakṣaṇam /
upadiśyate 'neneti upadeśo vākyajñānaṃ vā tadarthajñānaṃ vā abhighīyate /
tatra vākyajñānapramāṇyapakṣe tadarthajñānaṃ phalam, padārthasmṛtyādayastvāntarālikā itikartavyatāḥ /
tadarthajñānaprāmāṇyapakṣe tu hānādibuddhiḥ phalam /
yadyapi vidhirūpadeśaḥ pravartanamityanarthāntaram, yadyapi cāyaṃ niyojyaprayojane pravṛttinivṛttī vidadhadājñādhyeṣaṇābhyāmatiricyate, te hi niyoktṛprayojane pravṛttinivṛttī vidhattaḥ, tathāpi bhūtārthaparopaniṣadādiśabdavyāpakatvāt paraprayojanavadvacanamātravivakṣayopadeśapadaṃ vyākhyeyam /
yadyapi sadeva somyedamagra āsīd
ityādi vacanaṃ kvacit na pravartayati, kutaścid vā nivartayati puruṣam, tathāpi puruṣaśreyo 'bhidhatte ityupadeśa ityucyate /

children.translated_text: Even so, there is over-extension, since even statements about worshipping <s>Caityas</s> (Buddhist shrines) and the like would have this definition.
Therefore it is said—'<s>āpta</s>' (trustworthy).

children.text: āptānāṃ ṛṣyāryamlecchānāmupadeśaḥ śabdo na tvanāptānāṃ māyāmohanirmitānāṃ buddharṣabhādīnāṃ pramāṇaviruddhakṣaṇikasarvadharmanairātmyavādināmiti /
children.translated_text: The instruction of trustworthy persons—<s>ṛṣis</s> (seers), <s>āryas</s> (noble ones), and <s>mlecchas</s> (foreigners)—is <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony), but not of untrustworthy persons—those conjured by <s>māyā</s> (illusion) and delusion, such as <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Ṛṣabha</s>, and the like, who teach that all <s>dharmas</s> are momentary and without self, which contradicts the <s>pramāṇas</s>.
This very thing the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> says—'Not mere verbal statement'—this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>.

Now, the <s>bhāṣya</s> on verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>).
After <s>upamāna</s> has been enumerated, and after the definition of <s>upamāna</s>, the definition of <s>śabda</s> follows—this is the meaning.
He reads the definition-<s>sūtra</s>: 'The instruction of a trustworthy person is verbal testimony.'
Here, the word '<s>śabda</s>' is the term for what is to be defined.
'<s>Āptopadeśa</s>' (instruction of a trustworthy person) is the definition.
'That by which instruction is given'—<s>upadeśa</s> denotes either the sentence-cognition or the cognition of its meaning.
In the view that takes sentence-cognition as the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the cognition of the meaning is the result, and the recollection of word-meanings and the like are intermediate procedural steps.
But in the view that takes the cognition of the meaning as the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the cognition of what is to be abandoned and the like is the result.
Although injunction is <s>upadeśa</s> as prompting action—and this is not something different [from instruction]—and although this, by bringing about action and cessation in the person being directed through command and request regarding the intended purpose, differs from what merely serves the commander's purpose, nevertheless, because the word <s>upadeśa</s> must pervade statements about past facts, <s>Upaniṣads</s>, and the like, the word <s>upadeśa</s> should be explained as merely intending a statement for another's benefit, like a statement serving another's purpose.
Although the statement 'Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.2.1)
does not in some cases prompt action or restrain a person from something, nevertheless it speaks of human welfare—hence it is called <s>upadeśa</s> (instruction).

children.text:
sūtrasthāptalakṣaṇaparaṃ bhāṣyam---āptaḥ khalu sākṣātkṛtadharmā /
sudṛḍhena pramāṇenāvadhāritāḥ sākṣātkṛtā dharmāḥ padārthā hitāhitaprāptiparihāraprayojanā yena sa tathoktaḥ /
tathāpi tattvaṃ vidvān akārūṇikatayā vā alasatayā vā anupadiśan, matsaritayā vā viparītamupadiśan nāptaḥ syādityata āha---yathādṛṣṭasyārthasya cikhyāpayiṣayā prayuktaḥ /
yathādṛṣṭasyeti matsaritayā viparītopadeśo nivāritaḥ /

children.translated_text: 'By the desire to communicate'—this rules out lack of compassion and self-interest.
'Motivated' means one in whom effort has been produced—this [rules out] laziness.

children.text: tathāpi sthānakaraṇapāṭavābhāvena varṇaniṣpādanāsāmarthyenāptaḥ prasajyeta, ityata āha---upadeṣṭā /
children.translated_text: Even so, one who, due to lack of skill in the place and manner of articulation, is unable to produce the phonemes correctly would qualify as an <s>āpta</s>—therefore he says: 'an instructor.'
The meaning is: one possessing skill in the places and manners of articulation.

The <s>bhāṣya</s> defining <s>āpta</s> in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'An <s>āpta</s> is one who has directly realized <s>dharma</s>.'
One who has ascertained through a firmly established <s>pramāṇa</s>—i.e., directly realized—the <s>dharmas</s>, i.e., the objects that serve the purpose of attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful—such a one is so called.
Even so, one who knows reality but out of lack of compassion or laziness does not teach, or out of envy teaches the opposite, would not be an <s>āpta</s>—therefore he says: 'one who is motivated by the desire to communicate what has been seen as it was seen.'
'As it was seen'—this rules out teaching the opposite out of envy.

children.text:
āpta iti prakṛtipratyayasamudāyāt prakṛti niṣkṛṣya tadarthamāha--sākṣātkaraṇamiti /
anena yathoktarūpasaṃpadupalakṣitā /
pratyayārthamāha--tayeti /

children.translated_text: He states the pervasiveness of the definition of <s>āpta</s>—'<s>ṛṣis</s>.'
One who 'sees' (<s>darśanāt</s>) is a <s>ṛṣi</s> (seer).

children.text: karatalāmalakaphalavat sākṣātkṛtatraikālyavarttiprameyamātraḥ, ārād yātaḥ pātakebhya ityāryo madhyamo lokaḥ, mlecchaḥ prasiddhaḥ /
children.translated_text: One who has directly realized objects existing across all three times, as clearly as an <s>āmalaka</s> fruit on the palm of one's hand. One who has gone far from sins (<s>ārād yātaḥ pātakebhyaḥ</s>) is an <s>ārya</s> (noble one)—an ordinary person. A <s>mleccha</s> (foreigner) is well-known.

children.text: mlecchā api hi paripathamavasthitāḥ pānthānāmapahṛtasarvasvānāṃ mārgākhyāne hetudarśanaśūnyā avantyāptā iti pareṣāmāptalakṣaṇamavyāpakamityuktaṃ bhavati //
children.translated_text: For even <s>mlecchas</s>, when standing by the roadside and telling the way to travelers who have been robbed of everything—without any self-interested motive—are trustworthy. Thus it is stated that others' definition of <s>āpta</s> is non-pervasive.

From the compound '<s>āpta</s>' consisting of base and suffix, he extracts the base and states its meaning—'direct realization.' By this, the possession of the stated qualities is indicated.
He states the meaning of the suffix—'by that.'

children.text:
tadetad bhāṣyam ākṣeptumanubhāṣate---āptaḥ khalviti /
ākṣipati---svargeti /
ākṣeptā bhāṣyam ākṣipya sūtraṃ samādhatte tasmāditi /
āptaḥ prāpto yukta iti yāvat /
apauruṣeyo vaidika upadeśaḥ svargāpūrvadevatādiviṣayaḥ svataḥprāmāṇye siddhe nirdeṣatayā yukta upapannaḥ /
laukikaścāryamlecchānāṃ pramāṇāntaramūlo yuktaḥ /

children.translated_text: But in the absence of [support from] other <s>pramāṇas</s>, [the person is] not trustworthy, not fitting.
He resolves—'we do not say [so].'
The personal authorship (<s>pauruṣeyatva</s>) of the <s>Vedas</s> will be established in the second chapter.

children.text: tasmāt puruṣasyaivāptasyopadeśa āptopadeśa iti sādhu vyākhyānaṃ bhāṣyakārīyamiti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the instruction of a trustworthy person alone is <s>āptopadeśa</s>—thus the explanation of the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> is good—this is the purport.

He restates this <s>bhāṣya</s> in order to raise an objection—'an <s>āpta</s> indeed.'
He objects—'heaven.'
The objector, having objected to the <s>bhāṣya</s>, resolves the <s>sūtra</s>—'therefore.'
<s>Āpta</s> means 'attained,' i.e., 'fitting.'
The Vedic instruction, being non-personal (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), having heaven, <s>apūrva</s> (unseen potency), deities, and the like as its objects, when its intrinsic validity (<s>svataḥprāmāṇya</s>) is established, is fitting as an object of definition.
And the worldly [instruction] of <s>āryas</s> and <s>mlecchas</s>, being grounded in other <s>pramāṇas</s>, is fitting.

children.text:
pṛcchati--kaḥ punariti /
asti hi svargādīnāmapratyakṣatve nyāyaḥ, yogipratyakṣaṃ na svargādiviṣayaḥ pratyakṣatvāt asmadādipratyakṣavaditi bhāvaḥ /
uttaram--brūmo nyāyam /
tamāha--samānyaviśeṣavattvāt kasyacit pratyakṣā iti /
atra yāvati pakṣe yo hetuḥ siddhaḥ, tasya tanmātre pakṣīkāryam /
yogaje ca pratyakṣe siddhe tatsādhakādeva pramāṇāt tasya svargādiviṣayatvamapi siddhamiti dharmigrāhakapramāṇaviruddhaṃ mīmāṃsakānām anumānaṃ nodetumapyutsahate prāgeva tad bādhitum /
asiddhe tu yogaje pratyakṣa āśrayāsiddho heturābhāsaḥ /
asmākaṃ tu samyañco bahavaśca nyāyā iti bhāvaḥ /
anityatvaṃ hetumākṣipati--asiddhamiti /
pariharati--neti /
nitye cāpūrva iti /
atra trayaḥ kalpāḥ, kimekamapūrvaṃ sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇam, āho asādhāraṇam? yadāpi asādhāraṇaṃ tadāpi kiṃ pratipuruṣamekaikamapūrvam, āho pratipuruṣamanekamiti? tatra prathamaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati--yadi sādhāraṇateti /
na hi kadācidapyayamapūrvaṃ paśyati laukikaḥ puruṣaḥ /
yoginastvanabhivyaktamapi paśyantīti bhāvaḥ /
dvitīyaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati--etena pratipuruṣamiti /
utkarṣa ādhikyamavayavopacaya iti yāvat /
śaṅkate--vya/jaketi /
ekamapi vya/jakabhedāt utkarṣanikarṣavad dṛṣṭam /
tad yathā mahati darpaṇatale mahanmukham, tadeva kanīnikāyām aṇviti bhāvaḥ /
vakṣyamāṇenābhiprāyeṇa nirākaroti--na hyekamiti /
śaṅkitā svābhiprāyamuddhāṭayati--nanu ceti /
svābhiprāyeṇa nirākaroti---na dṛṣṭa iti brūma iti /
śaṅkitā pṛcchati--kiṃ punastat yadi na dṛṣṭam? tatra yadi bhedena na dṛṣṭam, dṛṣṭirnāsti /
kiṃ punastat, yad bhedena bhedadarśanamiti bhāsate? samāghātā svābhiprāyamāha--mithyāpratyaya iti /
na bhedadarśanamapajānīmahe, kiṃ tu pāramārthikaṃ bhedam /
na ca kalpito 'pūrvabhadaḥ pāramārthikāya kāryāyālamiti bhāvaḥ /
utkarṣāpakarṣakartṛtvaṃ veti karmaṇa iti śeṣaḥ /
tṛtīyaṃ kalpamātiṣṭhate---pratipuruṣamaneka iti /
dūṣayati---anivṛtta iti /
athottarakālamiti /
aśvamedhakriyayā tāvat tadapūrvaṃ svakāla evābhivyaktaṃ phaladānābhimukhīkṛtam, abhivya/jakasamānakālatvādabhivyakteḥ, pradīpādiṣu darśanāt /
tathāpi phalaṃ tāvat na datte, yāvat kriyā na nivartate /
nivṛttāyāṃ tu phalaṃ datte ityarthaḥ /
dūṣayati---asatīti /
tat khalu pūrvaṃ sadapi phalaṃ nākārṣīt caramabhāvinyāḥ kriyāyāḥ tajjanyāyā ābhivyakteranutpādāt /
utpannāyāṃ tu kriyāyāmabhivyaktau vā kasmāt na karoti? na hi kriyāyā vināśasya kaścidupayogaḥ /
tasmādakāmenāpi tvayā asatyā eva kriyāyā vya/jakatvamanugrāhakatvaṃ cāṅgīkartavyam /

children.translated_text: And both of these are strange—this is the meaning.

children.text: api ca sāsatī cet kriyābhivyanakti, tathā sati asattāyāḥ sarvatra sulabhatvāt na kiñcidapūrvaṃ nābhivyaktamiti /
children.translated_text: Moreover, if the non-existent action manifests [the <s>apūrva</s>], then since non-existence is readily available everywhere, no <s>apūrva</s> would remain unmanifested.
The cessation of action means the cessation of effort—this is the meaning.

He asks—'what then?' For there is an argument that heaven and the like are imperceptible: 'yogic perception does not have heaven and the like as its object, because of being perception, like our ordinary perception'—this is the purport. The answer—'we state the argument.' He presents it—'because of possessing universals and particulars, some things are perceptible.' Here, the reason that is established in any domain of the thesis should be made the thesis only in that much [of the domain]. And when yogic perception is established, its having heaven and the like as its object is also established from the very <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes it—thus the inference of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, which contradicts the <s>pramāṇa</s> that apprehends the thesis-subject, does not dare even to arise, let alone to override [yogic perception]. But if yogic perception is unestablished, then the reason is a fallacy of unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddha</s>). But for us, the arguments are numerous and correct—this is the purport. He objects to impermanence as a reason—'unestablished.' He resolves—'no.' 'And in what is permanent, <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented merit)'—here there are three alternatives: is the <s>apūrva</s> one and common to all persons, or uncommon? Even when uncommon, is there one <s>apūrva</s> per person, or many per person? He refutes the first alternative—'if common.' For no ordinary person ever sees the <s>apūrva</s>. But yogins perceive even what is unmanifest—this is the purport. He refutes the second alternative—'by this, one per person.' Increase (<s>utkarṣa</s>) means surplus, that is, accumulation of parts. He objects—'manifestation (<s>vyañjaka</s>).' Even a single thing, due to differences in manifestation, is seen as having increase and decrease. Just as a large face [appears] on a large mirror surface, and the same [face appears] tiny in the pupil of the eye—this is the purport. He refutes with the intention to be stated later—'for a single thing cannot.' The objector reveals his own view—'but surely.' He refutes with his own view—'we say: it is not perceived.' The objector asks—'but what is that, if it is not perceived? If it is not perceived as different, there is no perception [of it at all]. What then is that which appears as the perception of difference in difference?' The resolver states his own view—'erroneous cognition.' 'We do not deny the perception of difference, but [we deny] the real difference. And an imagined difference of <s>apūrva</s> is not adequate for a real effect'—this is the purport. 'Or the agency of increase and decrease'—the word 'of action' (<s>karmaṇaḥ</s>) should be supplied. He takes up the third alternative—'many per person.' He refutes—'not ceased.' 'But at a later time'—the <s>apūrva</s> produced by the <s>aśvamedha</s> sacrifice is manifested and directed toward giving its fruit at its proper time, because manifestation is simultaneous with the manifester, as seen in lamps and the like. Even so, it does not give its fruit so long as the sacrificial action has not ceased. But when the action has ceased, it gives the fruit—this is the meaning. He refutes—'when it does not exist.' For that [<s>apūrva</s>], even though previously existing, did not produce the fruit, because the manifestation produced by the final phase of the action had not arisen. But when the action arises, or when the manifestation [arises], why does it not produce [the fruit]? For the cessation of the action has no utility. Therefore, even unwillingly, you must accept that the non-existent action itself is the manifester and the supporter [of the <s>apūrva</s>].

children.text:
atra śabdaṃ pramāṇāntaramasahamāno dignāgaḥ tallakṣaṇaṃ vikalpyākṣipati---āptopadeśa iti /
anyasmādanyasya niścayo na tāvadasaṃbandhādatiprasaṅgāt /
na ca śabdaḥ arthātmā, nāpyarthakāryaḥ /
vināpyarthaṃ puruṣavivakṣāmātrādeva tadutpādāt /
tasmāt na sākṣāt śabdādarthaniścayaḥ, vivakṣākāryantayā tu vivakṣāṃ gamayet /
sā cārthābhiprāyapūrvā /
abhiprāyaśca kaścinmanomātrayoniḥ, aparastu pramāṇamūlaḥ /
tatra yaḥ pramāṇaniścitamarthaṃ vivakṣati, yathāvivakṣaṃ coccārayati sa āptaḥ /
tasya vacanāt kāryāt kāraṇaṃ vivakṣā anumīyate /
tasyāśca kāraṇamarthajñānam /
tataścārthajñānasyārthakāryatvāditi pramāṇagatiḥ /
tatrāptopadeśa ityatropadeśakriyayā upadeṣṭāra upasthāpitāḥ /
te ca prāyeṇa visaṃvādakā dṛṣṭā ityāptagrahaṇena teṣāmavisaṃvāditvam /
tataśca upadeśādarthaviniścayo bhavatvityetadarthaṃ yadyucyeta ityāha---yadyāptānāmiti /
upadeṣṭaṇāmityarthaḥ /
imaṃ kalpaṃ dūṣayati---tadanumānāt /

children.translated_text: The non-deceptiveness of the instructor is inferred; the statement of such a person is inference itself regarding the determination of the object.

children.text: tathā hi yad yannirdeṣasattvīyaṃ vacanaṃ tatsarvamarthavat, yathā buddhasya kṣaṇikanairātmyādiviṣaya upadeśaḥ, tathā cāyaṃ vivādādhyāsita upadeśa iti /
children.translated_text: For thus: whatever statement belongs to a speaker who possesses that quality [of non-deceptiveness], all of that is meaningful—just as the teaching of the <s>Buddha</s> regarding momentariness, selflessness, and the like. And this teaching, which is the subject of dispute, is also [of that kind].
As the venerable [<s>Dignāga</s>] has said—
'From the general [property of] non-deceptiveness of trustworthy statements, [verbal testimony has] the status of inference.'

Here, <s>Dignāga</s>, being unable to tolerate verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) as a separate means of valid knowledge, proposes alternatives regarding its definition and objects—'the instruction of a trustworthy person' (<s>āptopadeśa</s>). First, the determination of one thing from another is not possible from something unrelated, because of over-extension. And a word is not of the nature of the object, nor is it an effect of the object—for it is produced merely from the speaker's wish to communicate, even without the object. Therefore, there is no direct determination of the object from the word; but as an effect of the wish to communicate, [the word] could lead to [knowledge of] the wish. And that [wish] is preceded by the intention regarding the object. And the intention is sometimes born merely from the mind, and sometimes rooted in a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Among those, one who wishes to communicate an object ascertained by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, and who utters in accordance with his wish—he is a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>). From his statement, as an effect, the cause—the wish to communicate—is inferred. And the cause of that is the knowledge of the object. And from that, the knowledge of the object is known to be an effect of the object—thus the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> [is traced]. Therein, 'instruction of a trustworthy person'—by the action of instruction, the instructors are indicated. And since they are mostly seen to be deceptive, the mention of 'trustworthy' (<s>āpta</s>) [ensures] their non-deceptiveness. And thus, 'let there be determination of the object from the instruction'—this is what it would mean if stated—he says: 'if of trustworthy persons.' The meaning is: of the instructors. He refutes this alternative—'because of being inference from that.'

children.text:
iti /
dvitīyaṃ kalpamātiṣṭhate---athārthasya tathābhāvaḥ /
atra hi upadiśyata ityupadeśa iti vyutpattyā artha ucyate /
āptaḥ prāpta upadeśo yasmāt sa tathoktaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati yasmāt śabdādavagamyārthaṃ pravartamānaḥ prāpnoti tamevārtha sa āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ pramāṇam /
evaṃ ca yathā śabdena yo 'rtho darśitaḥ, tasyāptyā tathātā darśitā bhavati /
tadidamuktam--athārthasya tathābhāva iti /
dūṣayati--so 'pīti /
tadeva sphuṭayati--yadā hīti /
āptyā hi tathātvaṃ viniścanvan arthasya nāpratipannatayā niścetumarhati /
pratipattiśca prāyeṇa pratyakṣeṇeti pratyakṣata ityuktam /
tamimamākṣemapākaroti--tanneti /
nāptatvasahāyaḥ śabdo 'rthaṃ bodhayatīti sūtrārthaḥ /
nāpi śabdārthaprāptyā śabdārthatathātvamiti /
kastarhi ityata āha--api tviti /
indriyasaṃbaddhāsaṃbaddheṣviti dṛrūṭadṛṣṭeṣvityarthaḥ /
yathoktaṃ sa dvividho dṛṣṭādṛṣṭabhedāditi /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, nāptatvahetukamavisaṃvāditvamanena sūtreṇāgamārthatayā pratipādyate /
nāpyarthatathātvam āgamārthatayā pratipādyate /
nāpyāgamaḥ pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ na bhidyate, kiṃ tu upadeśaḥ śabda ityuktam /
upadeśa iti ca kārakapadam, upadiśyate jñāpyate prayojanavānartho 'neneti /
tathāpi vātikādyupadeśo 'pi śabdaḥ syādityata uktam---āpteti /
tenopadeśapadādevāgamasya vākyārthapratipattiḥ phalamuktam /
tadidamuktam---yā śabdollekhena padārthasmaraṇāvāntaravyāpārāt śabdādevārthaṃ pratyemītyanenollekhena pratipattiḥ sāgamasyārthaḥ phalamiti /
āptatvaṃ ca na vākyārthaṃ pratyāyayati api tvāgamasyāvyabhicāritām /
na ca yataḥ prāmāṇyamavagamyate tataḥ prameyamapi /
tathā ca sati prāmāṇyajñānahetoranumānādeva pratyakṣādiprameyāvagatiriti pratyakṣādīnāmapramāṇyaprasaṅgaḥ /
tathāsati kasyānumānamapi prāmāṇyamavadhārayet /
na cāptavākyaṃ kāryaṃ sad vaktṛjñānānumānadvāreṇārthe 'pyanumānameva, na tvarthasya pratyāyakamiti sāṃpratam /
yadi hi nārthaṃ pratyāyayet jñānamātramanumāpayet, tathā ca nārthaviśeṣasiddhiḥ /
na ca jñānasyārthādanyo 'sti kaścid viśeṣaḥ /
tasmāt vaktṛjñānaviśeṣaṇāya pūrvaṃ śabdādeva kevalād vākyārthajñānam eṣitavyam /
evaṃ ca kṛtaṃ vaktṛjñānānumānenārthapratipattyarthena kevalaṃ prāmāṇyajñānāya tadupayoga iti /
na cāvinābhāva eva saṃbandho yena śabdārthayorasaṃbandhena gamyagamakatvaṃ na syāt /
asti hi sāṅketikaḥ saṃbandho 'nayoriti vakṣyate /
na cāvinābhāvaḥ eva pratyāyanāṅgam, cakṣurādayo nīlādibhedavyabhicāriṇo 'pi dṛṣṭāḥ tatpratipādakā ityuktam /
tasmāt padāni kṛtasaṃketāni svārthān smārayanti, ākāṅkṣāyogyatāsattisadhrīcīnāni adṛṣṭapūrvaṃ vākyārthaṃ bodhayanti, na saṃgatigrahaṇamapi pratīkṣanta iti dūre 'numānād bhavanti /
yathā caitat, tathoddeśe leśata uktam /
upapāditaṃ ca tattvabindau /
tasmāt sarvamavadātam//7 //
children.translated_text: He takes up the second alternative—'or the object has such a nature.' Here, by the derivation 'what is instructed is the instruction,' the object is referred to. '<s>Āpta</s>' (trustworthy) means 'obtained' (<s>prāpta</s>)—the instruction by which one obtains [the object]. This is what is meant: the word whose [denoted] object, when one acts having understood it from the word, is obtained—that verbal testimony with trustworthy instruction is a means of valid knowledge. And thus, just as the object shown by the word, its actuality is shown by its being obtained. This is what was said—'or the object has such a nature.' He refutes—'that too.' He elaborates that—'for when.' For one who ascertains the actuality of the object through obtainment cannot ascertain it as not [yet] understood. And understanding is mostly through perception—hence 'from perception' was said. He removes this objection—'not that.' The meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is: verbal testimony does not convey the object aided by [the speaker's] trustworthiness. Nor is the actuality of the object of the word [established] through the obtainment of the object of the word. What then?—therefore he says—'but rather.' 'Regarding things connected and unconnected with the senses'—the meaning is: regarding things seen and unseen. As was said: 'it is twofold because of its having seen and unseen objects.' This is what is meant: this <s>sūtra</s> does not teach non-deceptiveness caused by trustworthiness as the content of scripture. Nor does it teach the actuality of the object as the content of scripture. Nor is scripture not different from perception and inference; rather, 'instruction' means 'word' (<s>śabda</s>). And the word 'instruction' is a <s>kāraka</s> (instrumental) word—'that by which something is instructed, made known, [namely] a purposeful object.' Even so, the instruction of a madman would also be verbal testimony—therefore 'trustworthy' (<s>āpta</s>) was said. By the word 'instruction' alone, the result of scripture—the comprehension of sentence-meaning—has been stated. This is what was said: 'that comprehension which, through the intermediate operation of remembering word-meanings by means of the imprint of the word, [arises] from the word alone'—by this imprint, the comprehension is the content, the result of scripture. And trustworthiness does not convey the sentence-meaning, but rather [establishes] the non-deviation of scripture. And it is not the case that from what the validity is understood, the knowable object is also [understood] from that. For if so, from inference, which is the means of knowing validity, the knowable objects of perception and the like would be understood—and thus perception and the like would be rendered invalid. And in that case, inference too—from what would its validity be determined? And it is not the case that the trustworthy statement, being an effect, is merely inference through the door of inferring the speaker's knowledge, and is not a conveyor of the object. For if it did not convey the object but merely led to the inference of knowledge, then there would be no establishment of a particular object. And knowledge has no particular feature other than its object. Therefore, from the word alone—prior to [the need for] qualifying the speaker's knowledge—the knowledge of sentence-meaning must first be sought. And thus, the inference of the speaker's knowledge, [which is sought] for the purpose of understanding the object, has been rendered unnecessary—it is useful merely for the knowledge of validity. And the relation [between word and meaning] is not merely invariable concomitance, such that in the absence of a relation between word and meaning, there would be no indicator-indicated relationship. For there is a conventional relation between them—as will be stated. Nor is invariable concomitance alone the component of conveying [meaning]—for the eye and the like, though deviating regarding the distinctions of blue and the rest, are seen to convey those—as has been said. Therefore, words, when their conventions have been established, recall their own meanings; and when aligned with expectancy, fitness, and proximity, they convey sentence-meaning never perceived before—they do not even wait for the grasping of the co-occurrence. Thus they are far removed from inference. And as this is, so it has been briefly stated in the enumeration (<s>uddeśa</s>). And it has been established in the <s>Tattvabindu</s>. Therefore, everything is clear.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.8: It [verbal testimony] is twofold, because of having seen and unseen objects.

children.text:
sa dvividho dṛṣṭādṛṣṭārthatvāt iti sūtrasya tātparyamāha---niyamārtham /
tadvibhajate---anekadheti /
dṛṣṭādṛṣṭārthatvāditi bhāṣyamatena vyācaṣṭe---pratyakṣeti /
āptapraṇītatvaliṅgānumitaprāmāṇyaśabdaikaviṣayasvargayāgādisaṃbandhādīnāmanumānaviṣayatā /
yathāha bhāṣyakāraḥ, yasyāmutra pratīyate so 'dṛṣṭārtha iti /
adṛṣṭārtho 'pi pramāṇamarthasyānumānāditi /
tena dṛṣṭo 'rtho yasyāgamasya sa tathā /
evamitaro 'pīti /
tadevaṃ bhāṣyamatena vyākhyāya svamatena vyācaṣṭe---vaktṛbhedenati /
dṛṣṭo 'rtho yena saṃ dṛṣṭārthaḥ pravaktā, evamadṛṣṭo 'rthonumito yena sa tathā /
tatra dṛṣṭārthā ṛṣayo 'smadādayaśca /
anumitārthā asmadādaya eveti /
evamapi śabdadvaividhyasādhane mā bhūdapakṣadhargateti pravaktṛpadena pūrayati---dṛṣṭādṛṣṭārthapravaktṛkatvāditi /
adṛṣṭārthaḥ pravaktā yasyāgamasya sa tathoktaḥ /
asyārthamāha na vigrahaṃ karoti pratyakṣata iti /
śeṣaṃ subodham /
sa na manyeta dṛṣṭānāṃ vākyānāṃ prāmāṇyam /
children.translated_text: He would not accept the validity of statements regarding seen [objects].
'He'—
the extreme <s>nāstika</s> (nihilist) is being referred to—this is the connecting interpretation of the <s>bhāṣya</s>.
The remainder will be explained in the section on examination.

He states the purport of the <s>sūtra</s> 'it is twofold because of having seen and unseen objects'—'for the purpose of restriction.' He divides that—'in many ways.' He explains according to the view of the <s>bhāṣya</s>—'perception.' The objects that are within the scope of inference—such as the connection of heaven with sacrifice and the like—which are the object of the single verbal testimony whose validity has been inferred through the mark of being composed by a trustworthy person—their being objects of inference. As the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> says: 'that whose object is understood there is of unseen object.' Even what has an unseen object is a means of valid knowledge, because the object [can be established] through inference. By this, that scripture whose object is seen is described. And similarly the other. Having thus explained according to the view of the <s>bhāṣya</s>, he explains according to his own view—'by the difference of speakers.' The speaker by whom the object has been seen is one whose object has been seen; similarly, the one by whom the unseen object has been inferred is described thus. Among those, the <s>ṛṣis</s> (seers) and we and others are those whose objects are seen. We and others alone are those whose objects are inferred. Even so, lest there be the fault of the reason not being a property of the thesis in establishing the twofold nature of verbal testimony, he completes with the word 'speaker'—'because of having speakers whose objects are seen and unseen.' That scripture whose speaker has an unseen object is described thus. He states its meaning—he does not analyze it—'from perception.' The rest is easily understood.

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.9: The <s>prameyas</s> (objects of valid knowledge) are: <s>ātman</s> (self), body, sense organs, objects, cognition, mind, activity, defects, transmigration, fruit, suffering, and liberation.

children.text:
iha prameyaṃ heyopādeyabhāvenāvasthitaṃ mumukṣuṇā pratipitsitam /
tacca parīkṣitasvapramāṇaviśeṣādhīnapratipatti /
lakṣaṇaṃ cāsya pramāṇaviśeṣaḥ /
na cāvāntarapramāṇasāmānyapratyakṣādilakṣaṇamantareṇātmādipramāṇāvatāraḥ kartuṃ śakyaḥ, tasya pratyakṣādisāmānyaviśeṣatvāt /
ataḥ pratyakṣādilakṣaṇānantaraṃ tadavatāraḥ /
aparīkṣitaṃ ca na tattvanirṇayāya paryāptamiti parīkṣā vidhāyiṣyate /
tatparikaraśca saṃśayādaya iti yuktaṃ teṣāṃ paścāllakṣaṇam /
tadiha prameyalakṣaṇāya tadvibhāgoddeśasūtramavatārayituṃ bhāṣyakāraḥ pṛcchati sma---kiṃ punaranena pramāṇeneti /
jātyabhiprāyamekavacanam, prakṛte prameye yathāyathaṃ pramāṇānāmupayogāt /
tadetad bhāṣyam anūdya vārttikakāra ākṣipati---kiṃ punariti /
prameyanāntarīyakatvaṃ pramāṇānāṃ sāmarthyam /
samādhatte--neti /
pratyakṣādilakṣaṇasāmarthyāt prameyamātraṃ sidvam, siśiṣṭaṃ tu prameyamadyāpi na sidhyatīti tadarthaṃ praśnaḥ /
sa ca viśeṣo yathāvaditi na darśita iti /
ayameva ca sūtrārtha iti /
yeṣāṃ tattvātattvajñānābhyām apavargasaṃsārau bhavataḥ, ta etāvanta eva /
na nyūnā nādhikā ityarthaḥ /
prathamasūtravyavasthām atidiśati---atrāpīti /
uktamarthamanākalayannākṣipati---ubhayeti /
digādīnāmiti /
dravyeṣu dikkālaparamāṇūnāmanabhidhānāt /
vṛkṣastiṣṭhatīti /
itiśabda ādyarthe tena vṛkṣaṃ paśyati, vṛkṣeṇa candramasaṃ paśyatītyādayo veditavyāḥ /
samādhatte---na sūtrārthāparijñānāditi, na prameyapadaṃ prameyamātre pravartate, kiṃ tu yat tattvato jñāyamānamapavargasādhanaṃ tasmin, taccātmādyeva nānyaditi yukto 'nyayogavyavaccheda ityarthaḥ /
ayogavyavacchede 'pi na doṣa ityāha---prameyameveti /
nanvasmin pakṣe na kadācidapi pramāṇatā syādityasti doṣa ityata āha---kimuktaṃ bhavatīti /
nāsya puruṣamātraṃ prati prameyatvaṃ vidhīyate, api tu mokṣamāṇaśiṣṭaṃ prati vidhīyate /
anūdyata iti pramāṇāntaramūlakatvena vidhānasya dārḍhyaṃ darśayati /
upasaṃharati---tasmāditi /
kauśalamātramātmanaḥ khyāpayitumabhyupetya samādhānāntaramāha--upetyeti /
pravṛttisaṃskārakatvamasti dikkālayoḥ,
prāṅmukho 'nnāni bhu/jīta //
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>prameya</s> (knowable object), being situated in the form of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, is desired to be known by one who seeks liberation (<s>mumukṣu</s>). And its cognition depends on the specific <s>pramāṇa</s> that has been examined. And its definition is that specific <s>pramāṇa</s>. And without the definition of the subsidiary general <s>pramāṇa</s> such as perception and the like, the introduction of the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the self and the rest cannot be accomplished, since that [pramāṇa for ātman] is a specific type of the general category of perception and the like. Therefore, after the definition of perception and the like, its introduction [follows]. And what has not been examined is not sufficient for the determination of reality— so examination will be prescribed. And the apparatus for that is doubt and the rest— so it is proper that their definition comes afterwards. Therefore, in order to introduce the <s>sūtra</s> of enumeration and division for the purpose of defining <s>prameya</s>, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) asked— 'what then, by this <s>pramāṇa</s>?' The singular number is intended in the sense of the class, since the <s>pramāṇas</s> are useful respectively for the <s>prameya</s> under discussion. Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s>, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> raises an objection— 'what then?' The capacity of the <s>pramāṇas</s> is their inseparability from <s>prameya</s>. He reconciles— 'no.' By the capacity of the definition of perception and the like, <s>prameya</s> in general is established; but the specific <s>prameya</s> has still not been established— so the question is for that purpose. And that specific nature has not been shown as it truly is. And this very thing is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>: those by whose knowledge of reality and non-reality, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) and <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) arise— they are exactly this many, neither fewer nor more— this is the meaning. He extends the arrangement of the first <s>sūtra</s>— 'here too.' Not grasping the meaning that was stated, he objects— 'both.' 'Of direction and the like'— because among substances, direction, time, and atoms are not mentioned. 'The tree stands'— the word <s>iti</s> is in the sense of 'and so on'; by this, 'he sees the tree,' 'he sees the moon by the tree,' and the like should be understood. He reconciles— 'because of incomplete understanding of the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>': the word <s>prameya</s> does not apply to <s>prameya</s> in general, but rather to that which, when known in its reality, is a means to <s>apavarga</s>— and that is only the self and the rest, not anything else— so the exclusion of disconnection (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>) is proper. He says that even in the exclusion of disconnection there is no fault— '<s>prameya</s> indeed.' Now, in this position, there would never be <s>pramāṇa</s>-status [for other things]— so there is a fault— to this he says— 'what has been said.' The <s>prameya</s>-hood of this is not prescribed for just any person, but rather is prescribed for the liberated and the learned. 'Is restated' shows the firmness of the prescription through being rooted in another <s>pramāṇa</s>. He concludes— 'therefore.' Having conceded that it is merely a display of skill on his part, he gives another reconciliation— 'having accepted.' There is the property of being a cause of the impression for activity for direction and time: 'One should eat food facing east.'
'One should sacrifice with the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> on an eastward-sloping [ground].'
'On the full-moon day, one should sacrifice with the full-moon offering.'
'On the new-moon day, one should sacrifice with the new-moon offering.'

children.text:
ityevamādi śravaṇāt /
kauśalamātramidaṃ na tu samādhānamityāha---na punaridamiti /
vihitavidhānāditi /
pramāṇavidhānasāmarthyena vihitamityarthaḥ /
na kevalaṃ pramāṇavidhānākṣiptam, api tvādyasūtragamaprameyapadādapi labdhamityāha---ādyena ceti /
etasmiścārthe sūtrakārasya anumatimāha---enaṃ cārthamiti /
bhāṣyam---sarvasya sukhaduḥkhasādhanasya, draṣṭā sarvasya sukhaduḥkhasya bhoktā, yataḥ sukhaduḥkhasādhanaṃ sarvam, sarvaṃ ca sukhaduḥkhaṃ jānāti, ataḥ sarvajñaḥ /
na cāprāptānyetāni jānātītyata āha---sarvānubhāvī /
anubhavaḥ prāptiḥ /
tadetad vairāgyotpādāyoktam, evamuttaratrāpi boddhavyam /
ātmanyayaṃ viśeṣo yadanena rūpeṇa heyaḥ, kaivalyena copādeyaḥ /
śarīrādīni tu heyānyeva /
apavargastūpādeya eveti /
avidyamānaṃ pūrvaṃ śarīraṃ yasya tadapūrvaṃ śarīram /
tanniṣedhati---nāsyedamiti /
prameyatattvamaviduṣa ātmana avidyamānamuttaraṃ śarīraṃ yasya tad anuttaram /
tadapi niṣiddhaṃ cena, netyanukarṣaṇāt /
nanu yathā pūrveṣāṃ śarīrāṇām anāditā evamuttareṣāmapyanantatā, tathā ca mokṣamāṇānāṃ pravṛttayaśca tadarthāni śāstrāṇi cānarthakāni prasajyerannityata āha---uttareṣāmiti /

children.translated_text: The meaning is: because of the understanding of the reality of <s>prameya</s>.

children.text: nanu sūkhe 'pyuddeṣṭavye duḥkhamātroddeśaḥ kiṃ sukhaṃ pratyācaṣṭe? tathā cānubhavavirodha ityata āha--nedamiti /
children.translated_text: Now, when pleasure too is to be enumerated, why is only suffering enumerated? Does that deny pleasure? And thus there would be contradiction with experience— to this he says— 'this is not.'

children.text: tadetad bhāṣyaṃ vārttikakāra ākṣepasamādhānābhyāṃ vyācaṣṭe---sukhaṃ punariti na cānyata ātmādipadāt, upalabdhiḥ, asmādeva ātmādibhyo bhedena pratyātmamupalabhyamānatvādeva, nirvidyate ityasya vyākhyānam---tāṃ copāsīnasya tayaiva virodhiguṇena tṛṣṇā vicchidyate, sukhānabhidhānena duḥkhapakṣanikṣepaṃ sūcayati /
children.translated_text: The <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains this <s>bhāṣya</s> through objection and resolution— 'but pleasure.' 'And not from elsewhere than the word <s>ātman</s> and the rest'— 'apprehension,' because it is apprehended by each individual self as distinct from the self and the rest. The explanation of 'becomes dispassionate' is: 'and for one who contemplates that, by that very opposing quality, craving is cut off.' By not mentioning pleasure, the inclusion of pleasure in the category of suffering is indicated.

children.text: tathā ca sukhe 'sya vairāgyaṃ bhavatīti tātparyārthaḥ //9 //
children.translated_text: And thus the purport is that dispassion toward pleasure also arises for this [seeker]. // 9 //

And so on from hearing such [injunctions]. He says this is merely a display of skill, not a proper resolution— 'but this is not.' 'Because of what has been prescribed by prescription'— meaning: prescribed by the capacity of the <s>pramāṇa</s>-prescription. Not only is it implied by the <s>pramāṇa</s>-prescription, but it is also obtained from the word <s>prameya</s> in the first <s>sūtra</s> as understood— thus he says— 'and by the first.' And the <s>sūtrakāra</s>'s approval of this meaning he states— 'and this meaning.' The <s>bhāṣya</s>: '[The self is] the seer of all that is a means to pleasure and pain, the experiencer of all pleasure and pain; since all is a means to pleasure and pain, and it knows all pleasure and pain, therefore it is omniscient.' And it does not know these without having attained them— therefore he says— 'experiencing all.' Experience (<s>anubhava</s>) means attainment. This is stated for the purpose of producing dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>); the same should be understood in what follows as well. The specific nature of the self is that in this form it is to be abandoned, and in its isolated state (<s>kaivalya</s>) it is to be accepted. The body and the like are simply to be abandoned. And <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) is simply to be accepted. That whose prior body was non-existent— that is an unprecedented body. He negates that— 'this is not its.' For one who does not know the reality of <s>prameya</s>, that self whose subsequent body is non-existent— that is 'without a subsequent.' And if that too is negated— 'no,' by the force of continuation. Now, just as prior bodies are beginningless, so subsequent ones too are endless; and thus the activities of those who seek liberation and the <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures) meant for that purpose would be purposeless— therefore he says— 'of the subsequent ones.'
<s>NyS</s> 1.1.10: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (<s>liṅga</s>) of the self (<s>ātman</s>).

children.text:
apavargasyāpyātmārthatvena prameyeṣvātmanaḥ prādhānyāt prathamamātmalakṣaṇasūtram icchetyādi /
tadavatārārthaṃ bhāṣyam---tatrātmeti /
ahamiti jñānaṃ gaurādyākāraṃ śarīrāvabhāsaṃ na śakyaṃ ghaṭādijñānavad drāgātmani pramāṇayitumityabhiprāyaḥ, paradehavartyātmābhiprāyaṃ vā /
tadatra vārttikāraḥ sūtratātparyamāha---samāneti /
samānajātīyaṃ śarīrādi, asamānajātīyaṃ pramāṇasaṃśayādi /
satyevāsmin prayojane prayojanamanvācinoti---āgamasyeti /
tataścātpoktatvānumānasiddhamapi prāmāṇyaṃ śabdasya anena tadarthasaṃvādakenānumānena dṛḍhataraṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ /
prayojanāntaraṃ cānvācinoti---pramāṇasaṃplavasyeti /
dvāvapi vāśabdau cārthe 'nvācaye draṣṭavyau /
tadanena vārttikena anumānācca pratipattavya iti bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam icchāyā ātmaliṅgatvakathanaparaṃ bhāṣyaṃ yajjātīyasyeti /
yajjātīyasyeti vyaptismṛtikathanam /
tajjātīyaṃ paśyanniti pakṣadharmopanayaḥ /
tasmādayaṃ sukhaheturityanumāyādātumicchati /
seyamicchedṛśī vyāptigrahaṇatatsmaraṇapakṣadharmatāgrahaṇānumānecchādīnāmekakartṛtvaṃ sūcayati, bhede pratisandhānābhāvena tadanupapatteḥ /
tadidamuktam---ekasyeti /
yaścāsāveko 'nubhavitā ca smartā cānumātā caiṣitā ca sa ātmā /

children.translated_text: And it cannot be merely the body, since that too is different due to the distinctions of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age.

children.text: nendriyam, indriyāntaragṛhīta indriyāntareṇāpratisandhānaprasaṅgāt yamaham asprākṣaṃ ta paśyāmīti /
children.translated_text: Nor the sense organ, because there would be the unwanted consequence of non-recognition by one sense organ of what was grasped by another— as in 'what I touched, that I now see.'
Nor the mind (<s>manas</s>), since the mind is inferred only as an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>).
For it will be stated: 'all this is tenable as an instrument of knowledge belonging to a knower'—

Since <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) too is for the sake of the self, and since the self has primacy among the <s>prameyas</s> (knowable objects), the definition-<s>sūtra</s> of the self comes first— 'desire' and so on. The introductory <s>bhāṣya</s> for that is— 'there, the self.' The intention is that the cognition 'I,' having the form of a cow and the like, or appearing as the body, cannot quickly be established as pertaining to the self, like the cognition of a pot and the like; or the intention refers to the self residing in another's body. There the <s>vārttikakāra</s> states the purport of the <s>sūtra</s>— 'similar.' Of the same kind is the body and the like; of a different kind is <s>pramāṇa</s>, doubt, and the like. Even when this purpose exists, he traces another purpose— 'of scripture.' The meaning is that the validity of verbal testimony, though already established by the inference stated as trustworthy, is made more firm by this confirmatory inference. He traces yet another purpose— 'of the confusion of <s>pramāṇas</s>.' Both uses of the word 'or' (<s>vā</s>) should be seen as being in the sense of 'and' for inclusion. By this <s>vārttika</s>, the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'and it should be understood from inference' has been explained. The <s>bhāṣya</s> that discusses desire being a mark of the self— 'of whatever type.' 'Of whatever type' is the statement of pervasion. 'Seeing something of that type' is the presentation of the property of the subject. 'Therefore this is a cause of pleasure'— he desires to infer and take. This desire of this kind indicates the unity of agent for the grasping of pervasion, its recollection, the grasping of the property of the subject, inference, desire, and the like— since without [unity of agent], due to the absence of recognition, that [inference] would be untenable. This is what was stated— 'of one single.' And that one who is the experiencer, the rememberer, the inferer, and the desirer— that is the <s>ātman</s> (self).
in the <s>sūtra</s> at 3.1.17.

children.text:
syādetat /
asatyapi ātmani jñātari satyapi ca buddhyādīnāṃ bhede, tatsantānābhedena pratisandhānavyavasthopapatsyata ityata āha---niyataviṣaye iti /
niyataviṣaya iti buddhibhedasya pratisandhānamapākaroti /
mātragrahaṇena ca saṃtānaṃ saṃtānivyatiriktamapākaroti /
tadabhyupagame vā sa evātmeti siddhaṃ naḥ samīhitam /
tadetad bhāṣyam anubhāṣya vārttikakārastātparyamasyāha---yajjātīyasyeti /
tatra vicāramārabhate---tatreti /
pūrvapakṣamāha---kathamicchādīti /
pariharati---smṛtyeti /
nanvekaviṣayāṇāṃ smṛtyādīnāṃ nānākartṛkatve ko virodha ityata āha---na hīti /

children.translated_text: He gives an example of multiplicity of objects— 'for it does not happen that the form [I touched is what I see].'

children.text: nānānimittatva udāharaṇamāha---nāpi bhavatīti, yad yasmāt nimittāt tvagindriyāt sparśamahamasparkṣaṃ tat tasmāt nimittāt cakṣuṣo rūpaṃ paśyāmīti /
children.translated_text: He gives an example of multiplicity of causes— 'nor does it happen that': that which was touched from one cause— the organ of touch— 'what I touched, that from that cause, the eye, I see the form.'

children.text: nānākartṛtva udāharaṇamāha---na hi bhavati devadatta iti /
children.translated_text: He gives an example of multiplicity of agents— 'for it does not happen: <s>Devadatta</s> [remembers what <s>Yajñadatta</s> experienced].'
This recognition, it is said, establishes the unity of agent through the force of negative concomitance from the difference of agents in the case of <s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s>.

An objection may arise: even without a self as knower, and even given the difference among intellects (<s>buddhi</s>) and the like, recognition could be accounted for through non-difference of their continuum— to this he says— 'regarding a restricted object.' 'Regarding a restricted object' removes the [possibility of] recognition of different intellects. And by the word 'mere' (<s>mātra</s>), a continuum distinct from what possesses the continuum is removed. Or if that [continuum] is accepted [as distinct], then that itself is the self— and thus our desired [conclusion] is established. Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s>, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> states its purport— 'of whatever type.' There he begins deliberation— 'therein.' He states the prima facie view— 'how are desire and the like?' He resolves— 'through memory.' Now, what contradiction is there in memory and the like having a single object but multiple agents?— to this he says— 'for it is not the case.'

children.text:
tadetadanupapannam, bhinnakartṛkatvād vyatirekasyopādhisaṃbhavena svābhāvikapratibandhavijñānavaikalyāt, asti hi devadattayajñadattavijñānānāṃ bhinnakartṛkatvamakāryakāraṇabhāvaśca, tatra kimakāryakāraṇabhāvāt pratisandhānasya vyatireka uta bhinnakartṛkatvāditi sandigdhavyatirekatvādasādhanāṅgaṃ pratisandhānamityāśayavāṃścodayati---kāryakāraṇabhāvāditi /
tadidamuktam---tadidaṃ pratisandhānamanyathā bhavaditi /
gūḍhābhiprāyaḥ pariharati---na nānātvasyeti /
codaka āha---akāryeti /
gūḍhābhiprāya eva parihāravādyāha---tadayuktamiti, anaikāntikatvaṃ sandigdhavyatirekitā /
codaka āha---tulyaṃ bhavato 'pīti /
siddhāntī gūḍhābhiprāya evāha--abhyupagamāditi /
codaka āha--nāsādhanāditi /
asiddhārthatā anyathāsiddhārthatā /
hetoḥ hetuvacanasyetyarthaḥ /
saṃprati samādhātā svābhiprāyamāviṣkaroti--na, hetvarthāparijñānāt /

children.translated_text: He analyzes that very point— 'it does not happen.'

children.text: kaḥ punarasau hetuviśeṣa ityata āha---viśeṣitaṃ caitatpratisaṃdhānam /
children.translated_text: What then is that specific reason?— to this he says— 'and this recognition is specified.'

children.text: tat kathayati--- smṛtyā saha pūrvāparapratyayayorekaviṣayatvena pratisaṃndhānam yajjātīyaṃ candanavanitādi sukhahetuṃ pratītaṃ smarāmi tajjātīyamimu pratyemīti pratisandhānam /
children.translated_text: He explains that— recognition is the unity of object between a prior and a subsequent cognition together with memory: 'I remember having perceived sandal, butter, and the like of this type as a cause of pleasure; and I now perceive something of this same type'— this is recognition.

children.text: tadanena śālibījāṅgurasya paramparayā śālibījāntarajananalakṣaṇāt pratisaṃdhānāt kāryakāraṇabhāvaniyamād vyavacchinatti //
children.translated_text: By this he distinguishes [genuine recognition] from the recognition characterized by the successive production of another rice-seed from a rice-seed-sprout, through the rule of cause-effect relation.

This is untenable, because the negative concomitance from the difference of agents is subject to a possible limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>), and hence there is a deficiency in the knowledge of natural binding. For the cognitions of <s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s> have both different agents and no cause-effect relation. The question arises: is the negative concomitance of recognition due to the absence of a cause-effect relation, or due to the difference of agents? Since the negative concomitance is doubtful, recognition is not a component of proof— with this intention the objector objects— 'because of the cause-effect relation.' This is what was stated— 'this recognition, being otherwise.' One with a hidden intention resolves— 'not [because] of plurality.' The objector says— 'non-cause-effect.' The resolver, still with hidden intent, says— 'that is improper'— the inconclusiveness is the doubtful negative concomitance. The objector says— 'it is the same for you too.' The <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent), still with hidden intent, says— 'because of acceptance.' The objector says— 'not from what is a non-proof.' Non-establishment of meaning, or otherwise-establishment of meaning— of the reason, of the statement of the reason— this is the meaning. Now the reconciler reveals his intention— 'no, because of incomplete understanding of the meaning of the reason.'

children.text:
nanviyaṃ pūrvāparapratyayasaṃhitā smṛtirapi kāryakāraṇabhāvādevopapatsyate, kṛtamekena kartretyata āha---sā ca smṛtirbhavatpakṣe 'nupapannā /
pṛcchati---kasmāt? uttaram---anyena nimittena anubhūtasya anyena nimittena asmaraṇāt /
na hi bhavati yenaiva cakṣuṣā ghaṭamadrākṣam, tenaiva tvagindriyeṇa taṃ spṛśāmīti /
nimittabhede pratisaṃdhānābhāvamuktvā viṣayabhede 'pyāha---na hyanyena svabhāvena ghaṭatvādinānubhūtasya anyena vṛkṣatvādinā smaraṇam /
na hi bhavati yamahaṃ ghaṭamadrākṣaṃ so 'yaṃ vṛkṣa iti /
kartṛbhede pratisaṃdhānābhāvamāha---na hyanyena devadattena anubhūtamanyo yajñadattaḥ smarati /
na hi bhavati yo 'haṃ devadatto 'drākṣaṃ so 'haṃ yajñadattaḥ paśyāmīti /
na cedaṃ satyapi bhede kāryakāraṇabhāvāt pratisaṃdhānaṃ bhavitumarhati /
na hi yatra sphuṭataraḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ tantupaṭayorghaṭakapālayorvā dṛśyate tatra pratisaṃdhānaṃ bhavati, ye tantavaḥ sa eva paṭa iti vā yo ghaṭākṣaṇaḥ sa eva kapālakṣaṇa iti vā /
vastutaḥ kāryakāraṇabhūtānāmagṛhītabhedānāṃ pratisaṃdhānahetubhāvaḥ sabhāgeṣu kṣaṇeṣu tathā darśanāditi cet? tanna, āmalakaphalasyaikasyāpanayane tatraiva sthāne āmalakāntarāvasthāpane bhavati pratisaṃdhānam /
na ca tayorāmalakayorasti kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ /
pūrvāparapratyayayoḥ smṛtyā sahaikaviṣayatvaṃ kartari kāryakāraṇabhāvanibandhanaṃ na karmaṇīti cet? hanta, nairātmyasākṣātkārasātmībhāve 'pyasti vijñānānāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāva iti tannibandhanaṃ pratisaṃdhānaṃ pūrvavadeva prasajyeta /
saiva cātmadṛṣṭirdeṣāṇāṃ nidānaṃ paramiti vyartho nairātmyasākṣātkārasātmībhāvaprayāsaḥ /
athāsadapi pratisaṃdhānaṃ kāryavaśādāharati tathāgato naṭa iva rāmatvamātmanaḥ, yadi tat kāryakāraṇabhāvanibandhanam, kathamasat, kathamāhāryam? atha kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'pyavastusan kalpanāmātranibandhanaḥ, sa tarhi tādṛśaḥ śālibījasyotpādaṃ vāstavaṃ na niyantumarhati, na jātu kalpitavahnibhāvo māṇavako dahanapākayorūpayujyate /
na ca pratyayānāṃ bhedāgrahāt pratisaṃdhānamiti sāṃpratam, pravṛttivijñānānāṃ rūpādiviṣayāṇāṃ bhedena pṛthagjanairapi pratiyamānatvāt, ālayavijñānasya ca pravṛttivijñānātiriktasyānupalabdheḥ /
children.translated_text: And it is not proper that recognition arises from the non-apprehension of the difference among cognitions, since even ordinary people recognize the difference among the active cognitions (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>) that have form and the like as their objects; and since the store-consciousness (<s>ālayavijñāna</s>), as something distinct from the active cognitions, is not observed.

children.text: ahamiti ca sattvadṛṣṭeḥ kṣaṇikatvanirākṛtāvasati bādhake sthiravastuviṣayatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the 'I'-cognition, being directed toward an enduring entity due to its being the object of the cognition of a self — when the sublater, namely the proof of momentariness, has been refuted — is not overridden.

children.text: tasmāt smṛtyā saha pūrvāparapratyayayoḥ ekaviṣayatvalakṣaṇasya pratisandhānasyānekakartṛkatvād vyatireko nirūpādhirekakartṛkatvaṃ sādhayati /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because the recognition characterized by the single-objecthood of prior and subsequent cognitions together with memory requires more than one agent, the negative concomitance establishes that there is a single agent that is unconditionally so.

children.text: sa caikaḥ kartā śarīrendriyabuddhibhyo bhinna ātmeti siddham //
children.translated_text: And that single agent is the self (<s>ātman</s>), distinct from body, sense organs, and intellect — this is established.

But this memory, connected with prior and subsequent cognitions, will also be explained by the cause-effect relation alone — a single agent is sufficient for it. To this he says — 'and that memory is untenable in your position.' He asks — 'why?' The answer — 'because what has been experienced through one cause is not remembered through another cause.' For it does not happen that 'with the very eye by which I saw the pot, with that very tactile organ I touch it.' Having stated the absence of recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>) when the cause differs, he states it also when the object differs — 'for what has been experienced through one essential nature, such as pot-ness, is not remembered through another, such as tree-ness.' For it does not happen that 'the pot I saw — that is this tree.' He states the absence of recognition when the agent differs — 'for what has been experienced by one <s>Devadatta</s>, another <s>Yajñadatta</s> does not remember.' For it does not happen that 'I who am <s>Devadatta</s> saw it — that I, <s>Yajñadatta</s>, now see.' And this recognition cannot arise from the cause-effect relation even when there is difference. For where the cause-effect relation is most manifest — as in threads and cloth, or pot and potsherds — no recognition occurs: 'the threads are the very same cloth,' or 'the pot-moment is the very same potsherd-moment.' If one objects that the cause-effect relation among things whose difference is not apprehended serves as the cause of recognition in homogeneous moments, as observed — that is not so. For when one <s>āmalaka</s> (myrobalan) fruit is removed and another <s>āmalaka</s> is placed in the very same spot, recognition occurs. But between those two <s>āmalakas</s> there is no cause-effect relation. If one says that the single-objecthood of prior and subsequent cognitions along with memory is grounded in the cause-effect relation in the agent, not in the object — well then, even when the direct realization of non-self (<s>nairātmyasākṣātkāra</s>) has been internalized, there still exists a cause-effect relation among cognitions, and recognition grounded in that would occur just as before. And that very view of a self is the supreme root of defects — so the effort to internalize the realization of non-self would be pointless. If one says that the <s>Tathāgata</s> conjures even unreal recognition through the force of its effects, like an actor [conjuring] the identity of <s>Rāma</s> for himself — if it is grounded in the cause-effect relation, how can it be unreal, how can it be conjured? If the cause-effect relation too is a non-entity, grounded in mere imagination, then being of such a nature, it cannot regulate the real production of a rice seed. A boy with an imagined fire-nature is never useful for burning and cooking.

children.text:
tadanenāśayenāktam---asti ca smṛtiḥ uktarūpa /
tasmād yasmin pakṣe smṛtiḥ saṃbhavati tatra pratisaṃdhānaṃ nyāyyamiti /
sa ca kartrekatvapakṣa iti bhāvaḥ /
āśayamavidvān punaḥ paraḥ pratyavatiṣṭhate---bhavāniti /
para evaikagranthenāha---kathamiti /
kathaṃ na saṃbhavatītyarthaḥ /
syādetat, yogicittamapi sarvajñasya cetasa ālambanapratyaya iti /
tasyāpi yogicittena pratisandhānaṃ syādityata āha---yatkāyeti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, upādānopādeyabhāvenāvasthitaḥ cittapravāhaḥ santānaḥ /
na ca yogicittamupādānaṃ sarvajñasya cetasaḥ /
ālambanapratyayo hi taditi /
kāyagrahaṇaṃ ca ekasantānopalakṣaṇaparam /
tena janmāntare 'pi smṛtirūpapanneti /
tamimamasmadabhiprāyānabhijñaṃ paramanyathāpi bodhayituṃ vibhavāma iti siddhāntī anyathā smṛtyanupapattimāha---na, asthiratvāt buddhīnām /
na hyajātānanvayadhyastayorasti kaścid viśeṣa iti pūrvotpanno 'nubhavaḥ kāñcana vāsanāmādhāya dhvaṃsate, yayā kālāntare smṛtirādhīyate ityabhyupagantavyam /
na cāsthirā buddhiḥ śakyā vāsayitumityātmā sthiro 'bhyupeya ityarthaḥ /
yuktyantaramāha---asaṃbandhācceti /
na ca buddhīnāmasamānakālānāmasti saṃbandha ityarthaḥ /
punaḥ paraḥ pratyavatiṣṭhate---śaktīti /
nāsmākaṃ kṣaṇikavastuvādināmasti tajjagati yadavasthitaṃ vāsakena vāsyamānaṃ dṛṣṭamiti bhāvaḥ nanu tathāpyasamānakālayatā saṃbandharahitamaśakyaṃ vāsayitumiti grahaṇakavākyavivaraṇavyājenāpākaroti---athāpīti /
pūrvacittaṃ pravṛttivijñānaṃ yattat ṣaḍvidham, pañca rūpādijñānānyavikalpakāni, ṣaṣṭhaṃ ca vikalpavijñānam /
tena saha jātaḥ samānakālaḥ cenāviśeṣaḥ tadālayavijñānamityucyate /
ahaṅkārāspadaṃ smṛtiśaktiḥ /
sā ca na śaktāt tajjñānādatiricyate /
tena kathañcid

children.translated_text: But with the intention of expressing difference, it is said to be 'qualified by capacity.'
The <s>Siddhāntin</s> says — 'here it has been stated.'

children.text: upapādayiṣyate hi bhāvānāṃ sarvajanapratītisiddhā stharatā kṣaṇabhaṅganirākaraṇena /
children.translated_text: For the stability of things, established through the universal cognition of all people, will be demonstrated by the refutation of momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>).

children.text: tathā ca sthirasya saṃbaddhasya ca vastrādeḥ mṛgamadādinā vāsyatvaṃ dṛṣṭamiti nāsthire 'saṃbaddhe ca bhavitumarhatītyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And thus, the imprinting of stable, connected things like cloth and the like by musk and the like has been observed — therefore it cannot occur in what is unstable and unconnected — this is the meaning.

With that intention it has been said — 'and memory exists, of the stated form.' Therefore, in whichever position memory is possible, therein recognition is justified. And that is the position of a single agent — this is the sense. The opponent, not knowing the intention, again objects — 'you.' The opponent himself says in a single passage — 'how?' — meaning 'how does it not occur?' One might think: even the cognition of the <s>yogin</s> is an object-condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) for the mind of the omniscient — therefore he says — 'of what body.' This is what is stated: the stream of consciousness established in the relation of cause (<s>upādāna</s>) and caused (<s>upādeya</s>) is the continuum (<s>santāna</s>). And the cognition of the <s>yogin</s> is not the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of the omniscient's consciousness. For it is [merely] its object-condition. And the mention of 'body' (<s>kāya</s>) is for the purpose of indicating a single continuum. Therefore, memory is justified even in another life. 'We are able to instruct this opponent, who does not know our intention, in another way as well' — with this thought, the <s>Siddhāntin</s> states the impossibility of memory in another way — 'no, because cognitions are unstable.' For there is no distinction between what has never arisen and what has arisen and perished without a trace. Therefore, it must be accepted that a previously arisen experience deposits some latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) and then perishes, and that through that impression memory is produced at a later time. And an unstable cognition cannot be imprinted — therefore a stable self must be accepted — this is the meaning. He states another reason — 'and because of the absence of connection.' And there is no connection among cognitions that are not simultaneous — this is the meaning. The opponent again objects — 'capacity.' 'For us who hold the doctrine of momentary entities, there is nothing in the world that is seen as stable and being imprinted by an imprinter' — this is the sense. But even so, what is not simultaneous, being without connection, cannot be imprinted — with this implication, he refutes through the device of explaining the opponent's statement — 'even if.' The prior consciousness is the sixfold active cognition (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>): five non-conceptual cognitions of form and the like, and the sixth is conceptual cognition. What is born simultaneously with that — co-temporal and hence non-different — is called the store-consciousness (<s>ālayavijñāna</s>). The basis of the ego-sense is the capacity for memory. And that does not differ from the cognition that possesses it.

children.text:
syādetat /
asthirayorapi jñānayoḥ samānakālatayā asti saṃbandha iti kasmāt anyataracittavāsitamanyataraccittaṃ smṛtiṃ nādhatte ityata āha---yaścāsāviti /
vakṣyamāṇāpekṣo 'piśabdaḥ /
nanu vartamāne cetasi mā kārṣodupakāram, anāgate tu kariṣyati ityata āha---nāpīti /
pṛcchati---kathamiti /
uttaram---vartamānaṃ tāvaditi /
prakṛtamupasaṃharati---tasmāditi /
ito 'pyasatyātmani vijñānamātrāt kāryakāraṇabhāvena smṛtirnotpadyate ityāha---itaśceti /
kasmāt? bhāvasya bhavitrapekṣatvāt /
bhāva utpattimān dharmaḥ /
bhavitā dharmo /
pāko viklittiḥ saṃyogabhedaḥ /
sa ca taṇḍulāvayavasamaveto 'pyavayavāvayavinorabhedopacārāt taṇḍulānāmityuktam /
gatiḥ parispando devadatte kartarīti /
siddhāntī kṣaṇikavādinamutthāpyākṣaṇikatvābhripāyeṇa dūṣayati---anādhāraiveti /
pūrvapakṣī kṣaṇikatvābhiprāyeṇāha---kāryeti /
siddhāntavādyakṣaṇikatvābhiprāyeṇa pariharati---tacca neti /
samānakālayorādhārādheyabhāvo dṛṣṭaḥ, yathā kuṇḍavadarayoḥ /
sthirameva hi kuṇḍaṃ sthirasyaiva vadarasya gurutvena patato gurutvaṃ pratibadhnadadhaḥpatanaṃ nivārayadādhāro bhavati /
yadyucyeta na smṛtirbhāvaḥ, kiṃ tu bhavitrī utpattirasyā bhāvaḥ /
na tu bhaviturbhavitrantarāpekṣā yuktā anavasthāpātāditi āśaṅkate---athāpīdamiti /
nirākaroti---tacca neti /
virodhāditi vivṛṇoti---yadīti /
kasmād vyāhatamityata āha---svarūpaṃ ceti /
co hetvartha /
svarūpamutpatterūcyamānaṃ svatantraṃ bādhate yataḥ, tasmād virodha ityarthaḥ /
anabhyupagamāditi vivṛṇoti-na hi bhavanta iti /
virodhāditi sphorayati---vyatiriktāṃ ceti /
tantraṃ śāstram /
śaṅkate---atheti /
tathā ca na virodho nāpyanabhyupaga ityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti---kiṃ kveti /
abhidhānasvarūpamāha-utpattitirati /
api cotpatterbhāvatve 'pi na smṛtirna bhāvaḥ, bhāvatvasya kāryamātrānubandhitvāt smṛteśca kāryatvāt /
na cānavasthā, nitye vyavasthānāt /
tathā ca smṛteḥ bhāvasya bhavitā ātmaika nityaḥ pariśiṣyate ityāśayavānāha---yadā cotpattiriti /
prakṛtamupasaṃharati---tasmāditi /
tat siddhametat---smṛtiḥ pūrvāparapratyayābhyāmekakartṛkā, tābhyāṃ sahaikaviṣayatvena pratisandhīyamānatvāt /
children.translated_text: This is established: memory has a single agent together with prior and subsequent cognitions, because it is recognized as having a single object together with them.

children.text: yā punarnābhyāmekakartṛkā sā nābhyāṃ tathā pratisandhīyate, yathā devadattasya smṛtirna yajñadattapratyayābhyām /
children.translated_text: But what does not have a single agent together with them is not recognized in that way with them — just as the memory of <s>Devadatta</s> is not [recognized] with the cognitions of <s>Yajñadatta</s>.
And this [memory] is not like that.
Therefore it is so.

One might object: even between unstable cognitions, because of their simultaneity, there is connection — so why does one consciousness, imprinted by the other, not produce memory? Therefore he says — 'and that which.' The word 'also' (<s>api</s>) anticipates what is to be stated. Let it not assist the present consciousness; but it will assist the future one — therefore he says — 'nor.' He asks — 'how?' The answer — 'the present, for its part.'
