He concludes the topic at hand — 'therefore.' From this too — even without a self, memory does not arise from mere cognitions through the cause-effect relation — he says — 'and from this.' Why? Because that which exists depends on that which is to become. 'That which exists' (<s>bhāva</s>) is a property that has arisen. 'That which is to become' (<s>bhavitṛ</s>) is a property. Cooking, dissolution, conjunction, and separation. And that, though inhering in the parts of the rice grains, is said to be 'of the rice grains' by the figurative identification of parts with the whole. Motion (<s>gati</s>) is vibration, in <s>Devadatta</s> as the agent. The <s>Siddhāntin</s>, having raised the momentarist, refutes with the intention of non-momentariness — 'without a substrate.' The prior advocate states with the intention of momentariness — 'the effect.' The <s>Siddhāntin</s> responds with the intention of non-momentariness — 'and that is not so.' The container-contained relation between simultaneous things is observed, as in the case of a pot and jujube fruits. For it is precisely a stable pot that, by opposing with its own heaviness the heaviness of a stable jujube fruit that tends to fall, preventing its falling, becomes its container. If one says that memory is not a 'that which exists' (<s>bhāva</s>), but rather its arising is its 'that which exists' — and that it is not proper that 'that which is to become' depends on another 'that which is to become,' because of the infinite regress — he anticipates — 'even if this.' He refutes — 'and that is not so.' He explains 'because of contradiction' — 'if.' Why is it contradicted? Therefore he says — 'and the essential nature.' The particle 'ca' is in the sense of reason. Because the essential nature of arising being stated independently subverts [the thesis], therefore there is contradiction — this is the meaning. He explains 'because of non-acceptance' — 'for you do not.' He elaborates 'because of contradiction' — 'and distinct.' <s>Tantra</s> means <s>śāstra</s> (treatise). He raises a doubt — 'if.' And thus there is neither contradiction nor non-acceptance — this is the meaning. He refutes — 'what, where?' He states the form of the expression — 'arising.' Moreover, even if arising were a 'that which exists,' memory is not not a 'that which exists,' because 'being a that-which-exists' invariably accompanies anything that is an effect, and memory is an effect. And there is no infinite regress, because of the stable ground in the permanent [self]. And thus, for memory as a 'that which exists,' the 'that which is to become' is the single, permanent self — with this intention he says — 'and when arising.' He concludes the topic at hand — 'therefore.'

children.text:
tadevaṃ vyatirekisamarthanaṃ kṛtvā anvayavyatirekiṇamatrārthe pramāṇayati---atha veti /
anekagrahaṇamanekanibhittapratiṣedhaśaṅkānivṛttyarthaṃ yena mayā rūpādayo 'nūbhūtāḥ tenaiva gandha upalabhyate iti khalu mayeti smṛtyā saha pratisandhānaṃ tasmād bharatamatābhyāsenābhinaye ye kṛtasaṅketāḥ, teṣām /

children.translated_text: And what has been said by the opponents:
The raising of the eyebrow-creeper of a dancer is not truly one thing;
because of being an aggregate of atoms, its unity is merely imagined.

Having thus accomplished the negative concomitance reasoning, he validates as a <s>pramāṇa</s> the argument combining both positive and negative concomitance for this purpose — 'or.' The word 'multiple' is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt of negation based on multiple substrates. 'The very one by whom forms and the like were experienced, by that very one smell is perceived' — this recognition together with memory, 'by me indeed' — therefore, for those who have learned the conventions through the practice of <s>Bharata</s>'s [system] in dramatic performance,

children.text:
iti /
tatrāha---bhrūkṣepasyaikatvāt /
na bhrūḥ paramāṇusamūho 'pi tu avayavidravyamekam, tadgataṃ ca recitakamapi kriyaikaiva /
bhavatu vā paramāṇusamūha eva bhrūkṣepaḥ, tathāpi samūhasya samūhibhyo 'nanyatvāt paramāṇava eva, teṣāṃ ca pratyekamekatā cānekabharatamatanipuṇapratipattṛsādhāraṇatā ca /
asti ca teṣāmapi svagocarāvikalpotpādanadvāreṇa paraṃparayā mayeti pratisandhānahetubhāva iti yatkiñcidetadekatvaṃ tasya kalpitamiti /
tadevaṃ pratisandhānadvāreṇecchādīnāmātmaliṅgatvamuktvā saṃprati guṇatayā liṅgatā vārttikakṛd āha---atha veti /
guṇatvenecchādīnāṃ pāratantryaṃ rūpādivat sādhanīyam /
taccānityatvenaiva sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyebhyo vyāvartakena siddham /
na hyanityo bhāvo dravyāt svatantro bhavati /
tasmād guṇatvaprasādhakādeva hetoḥ pāratantryasiddheḥ kṛtaṃ guṇatvena pāratantryasādhakeneti hṛdi nidhāya vārttikakāraḥ tadapi pūrvamuktamiti siddhena pāratantryeṇa guṇatvamapi sādhayati /
na caitadanityasya pāratantryaṃ dravyeṇa sidhyati, dravyavakarmaṇorapyanityayoḥ pāratantryāt /
tasmādanityatvasiddhena dravyapāratantryeṇa dravyakarmabhyāṃ vyatirecayati---na dravyaṃ karma vā icchādayaḥ,
vyāpakadravyasamavāyāt śabdavad ityādi /
yadyapyanityatvena dravyasamavāyamātraṃ sidhyati, tathāpi dravyakalpanamātreṇaivopapattau tadavayayavakalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvena tad dravyamanavayavaṃ tāvat siddham /
anavayavaṃ ca dravyaṃ dvedhā, vyāpakam aṇu ca /
na tāvadaṇu, tatrecchādīnāmupalabdheḥ /
kvacidanyatarakarmaṇā kvacit svabhāvataḥ tatsaṃyogopapattau tadgatikalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāt siddhamasya vyāpakatvam /
tadetadādigrahaṇavyākhyānam /
tadanayā vakroktyā nityatvaṃ paramamahattvaṃ cātmano darśitaṃ bhavati /
etacca sāmānyatodṛṣṭamanumānaṃ sūtrayatā sarvaṃ darśitamityāha---sāmānyata iti /
yat tatpūrvaṃ hṛdi sthitamicchādīnāṃ dravyapāratantrye sādhye 'nityatvahetukānumānam taduddhāṭayati, kāryatvamapi hetuṃ samuccinoti---eteneti /
nanvastu dravyapāratantryaṃ tathāpi śarīrapāratantryamastu, kṛtamanupalabdhacareṇātmanā ityata āha---ayāvaditi /
children.translated_text: Even granting dependence on substance, let there be dependence on the body; what need is there for an unperceived self? — to this he says: 'as long as' etc.
And because there would be the unwanted consequence of [desire etc.] being common to all persons, they are not qualities of earth and the rest.
And because of the [mere] postulation that the mind (<s>manas</s>) is the instrument in their production, [one cannot say that] the mind, which is not an agent, [is their substrate].

children.text: tasmād aṣṭadravyātiriktaṃ dravyāntaram, tatrecchādayaḥ, sa cātmeti siddhamityāha---tatpratiṣedhāditi //10 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, there is a substance distinct from the eight substances [earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, and mind], in which desire and the rest inhere, and that is the <s>ātman</s> — thus it is established, he says — 'by the negation of those' etc. //10//

Thus.
To this he says — 'because the raising of the eyebrow is one.'
The eyebrow is not an aggregate of atoms but rather a single composite substance (<s>avayavidravya</s>), and the gesture (<s>recitaka</s>) belonging to it is also a single action.
Or let the raising of the eyebrow be indeed an aggregate of atoms; even so, since the aggregate is non-different from its constituents, they are just the atoms, and of each of them there is unity and commonality among multiple skilled practitioners versed in the doctrine of <s>Bharata</s>.
And even of those [atoms], through the door of producing a non-conceptual cognition of their own domain, there is indirectly a causal relation for the recognition 'by me' — thus whatever unity there is, it is merely imagined.
Having thus stated that desire and the rest are marks of the self (<s>ātman</s>) through the door of recognition, now the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> states their being marks in the capacity of qualities — 'or alternatively.'
The dependence of desire and the rest as qualities must be established, like color and the rest.
And that is established by the differentiator [that distinguishes them] from universals, particulars, and inherence — namely, by their being non-eternal.
For a non-eternal entity is not independent of substance.
Therefore, since dependence is established by the very reason that proves quality-hood, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, keeping in mind that 'the [separate] proof of dependence through quality-hood is redundant,' also establishes quality-hood through the already-established dependence, saying 'that too has been previously stated.'
But this dependence of the non-eternal on substance cannot be established [as distinguishing quality alone], since substance and action, which are also non-eternal, are also dependent.
Therefore, through the dependence on substance established by non-eternality, he differentiates [qualities] from substance and action — 'desire and the rest are neither substance nor action,
because of inherence in a pervading substance, like sound' and so forth.
Although through non-eternality only the bare inherence in substance is established, nevertheless, since the matter is explained by merely positing substance and there is no evidence for positing parts of that [substance], that substance is first established as partless.
And partless substance is of two kinds: pervading and atomic.
[Desire etc.] are not [in an] atomic [substance], for desire and the rest are apprehended in that [pervading substance].
Since the conjunction [of the self with bodies] is possible sometimes through the action of one of them and sometimes by nature, and there is no evidence for positing its movement, its pervading nature is established.
This is the explanation of the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.).
Thus by this indirect reasoning, the eternality and supreme magnitude of the <s>ātman</s> have been demonstrated.
And the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (the author of the <s>sūtras</s>) has shown all this by the inference from general observation (<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>) — he says '<s>sāmānyataḥ</s>' etc.
That inference based on the reason of non-eternality, which was previously held in mind for establishing the dependence of desire etc. on substance — that he now brings forth, and he also adds the reason of being an effect (<s>kāryatva</s>) —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.11: The body (<s>śarīra</s>) is the substratum of effort (<s>ceṣṭā</s>), sense organs (<s>indriya</s>), and objects (<s>artha</s>).

children.text:
ātmānaṃ lakṣayitvātmano duḥkhanidānānāmindriyādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa ca śarīramāśritya tannidānatvamiti tadevāsya duḥkhamūlakāraṇamityanantaraṃ śarīraṃ lakṣayituṃ sūtram---ceṣṭetyādi /
tadavatārāya bhāṣyam---tasyeti /
tasyetyāmānaṃ parāmṛśati /
bhogaḥ sukhaduḥkhasaṃvit /

children.translated_text: The substratum of that [experience] is the body (<s>śarīra</s>).
By this, the body is the ultimate cause of the entire mass of suffering.
Therefore it has been said that the body should be defined before the sense organs and the rest.

children.text: atra ceṣṭāśrayatvenendriyāśrayatvenārthāśrayatvena ca pratyekaṃ samānajātīyebhya ātmendriyādibhyo 'samānajātīyebhyaḥ pramāṇasaṃśayādibhyaḥ śarīraṃ vyavacchidyate //
children.translated_text: Here, the body is differentiated — by being the substratum of effort, by being the substratum of sense organs, and by being the substratum of objects — from things of the same class such as the self and the sense organs, and from things of a different class such as <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt), and the rest.

Having defined the <s>ātman</s>, since all the causes of suffering such as sense organs etc. depend on the body either directly or indirectly, and since the body is thus the root cause of suffering, the <s>sūtra</s> next defines the body — '<s>ceṣṭā</s>' etc.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> introduces this — 'of that' etc.
'Of that' refers back to the <s>ātman</s>.
<s>Bhoga</s> (experience) means the awareness of pleasure and pain.

children.text:
kathaṃ ceṣṭāśrayaḥ iti bhāṣyam /
tasyārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe---kā punariti /
ceṣṭā vyāpāraḥ /
sa cātivyāpakatayā avyāpakatayā ca na lakṣaṇam, vṛkṣādiṣu bhāvāt, abhāvācca pāṣāṇamadhyavartimaṇḍūkādiśarīre iti bhāvaḥ /
atrottarabhāṣyarm---ipsitamityādita /
tad vyācaṣṭe---hitāhiteti /
prayuktasya utpāditaprayatnasya /
na ca vyāpāramātraṃ ceṣṭā abhimatā, api tu viśiṣṭo vyāpāraḥ /
children.translated_text: And it is not mere activity that is intended by '<s>ceṣṭā</s>,' but rather a specific kind of activity.
And that [specific activity] does not exist in trees and the like, so there is no over-extension.

children.text: yadyapi ca dārūyantrādiṣur idṛśo vyāpāro 'sti, tathāpi mūrtāntarāprayoge satīti viśeṣaṇāt na vyabhicāraḥ, teṣāṃ śarīreṇa mūrtena prayogāt /
children.translated_text: And even though such activity exists in wooden machines and the like, there is no deviation because of the qualification 'when not employed by another material body,' since those [machines] are operated by a material body.

children.text: śarīrasya tu mūrtāntarāprayuktasyar idṛśavyāpārāśrayatvam, pāṣāṇamadhyavartinaśca maṇḍūkadehasya tadvyāpārāyoge 'pi tadyāgyatvāt, pāṭite pāṣāṇe tādṛśasya tadvyāpārasya darśanāditi bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: But the body, when not operated by another material body, is the substratum of such activity; and even though the body of a frog inside a stone lacks such activity, it has the capacity for it, since when the stone is split open, such activity is observed — this is the purport.

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> asks: 'How is it the substratum of effort?'
He explains its meaning — 'what then?' etc.
<s>Ceṣṭā</s> means activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>).
And that, due to being either too broad or too narrow, is not a defining characteristic — because it is present in trees and the like, and absent in the body of a frog situated inside a stone — this is the purport.
The subsequent <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage [begins] — 'the desired' etc.
He explains that — 'beneficial and harmful' etc.
'Of one who has engaged' means one who has produced effort.
He explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage 'how is it the substratum of sense organs?' — 'how?' etc.

children.text: saṃyogitayā tvindriyāśrayatve ghaṭādīnāmapi śarīratvaprasaṅgaḥ, teṣāmapīndriyasaṃyogitvāditi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if being the substratum of sense organs means merely being in conjunction [with them], then even pots and the like would absurdly be bodies, since they too are in conjunction with sense organs — this is the purport.
He explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage that provides the solution — 'of which' etc. — with 'body' etc.

children.text:
eteneti /
tadvṛttitvenānupapattyā arthānāmapyānyādṛśa āśrayārtho vyākhyeyaḥ /
yadyapi gandhādayo viṣayā na svarūpeṇa śarīramāśrayante tathāpi yadeṣāṃ sukhādyupalambhahetutvaṃ kāryaṃ prayojanaṃ tadarthamāśrayante ityarthaḥ /
tadanena yasminnityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
codayati---kathaṃ punariti /
pariharati---sāmānyeti /
viśeṣeṇa bubhukṣitatvādināprakaraṇāpannaṃ niyantriyaṃ sāmarthyam /
prakaraṇādītyatrādipadasaṃgṛhītamaparamapi sāmarthyaśabdārthamāha---sāmarthyaṃ ceti /
aparamāpyāha---pramāṇeti /
atra prathame pakṣe ceṣṭāśabdo vyāpāraviśeṣe spandādivanmukhyārthaḥ /
tadetat---lokastāvadityādinā tathā cāyaṃ ceṣṭāśabda ityantena darśitam /
pramāṇāsaṃbhavo veti dvitīyaṃ pakṣaṃ vivṛṇoti---sāmānyavācyapīti /
apirabhyupagame /
pramāṇāsaṃbhavo/nupapattiḥ /
sā ca na kriyāmātra ityanena darśitā /
children.translated_text: And it has been shown by this that [<s>ceṣṭā</s>] is not mere action.
With this explanation of the word '<s>ceṣṭā</s>,' there is no unwanted consequence of pots and the like being bodies.

'By this' etc.
Because [the objects] cannot function in that [merely conjunctive] manner, the word 'substratum' in relation to objects must also be explained differently.
Although odor and other sense-objects do not in their own form take the body as their substratum, nevertheless, their function of being the cause of the apprehension of pleasure etc. — for the sake of that purpose they take it as their substratum — this is the meaning.
By this, the <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage beginning with 'in which' has been explained.
He raises an objection — 'but how then?' etc.
He resolves it — 'by capacity' etc.
The capacity that is contextually determined by specific [conditions] such as being hungry etc. is what restricts [the definition].
In 'by context etc.' the word '<s>ādi</s>' includes another meaning of the word 'capacity,' which he states — 'and capacity' etc.
He also states yet another — 'and <s>pramāṇa</s>' etc.

children.text:
evaṃ bhāṣyānusāreṇa svamatena ca pratyekaṃ ceṣṭāśrayatvādi śarīrasya lakṣaṇamiti varṇayitvā samastamevedaṃ śarīralakṣaṇamiti ye varṇayāṃbabhūvuḥ, tanmataṃ nirākaroti---yairapīti /
yadyādyaṃ padaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ ceṣṭāśraya iti, tadā ghaṭena vyabhicāraḥ /
tadarthaṃ dvitīyapadopādānam indriyāśraya iti, indriyasaṃyogītyarthaḥ /
tathāpi tenaiva ghaṭādinā vyabhicāraḥ, prāpyakāritvenendriyāṇāṃ ghaṭādīnāmapi indriyasaṃyogitvāt /
ata āha---arthāśraya iti /
evamapi vyabhicārastadavastha
eva, ghaṭādīnāmapi rūpādyarthasamavāyenārthāśrayatvāt /
atha samavāyābhiprāyeṇāśrayatvam, tathāpi na samavāya indriyāṇāṃ śarīre /
ghrāṇasya pārthivatvena samavāyo na viruddha iti cet---na, tasya śarīrāvayavasamavāyitvena śarīrāsamavāyāt /
yadi nāsikāgrameva ghrāṇam, atha tadādhāramatīndriyam, tathāpi na tatsamavetaṃ śarīram, pratyakṣāpratyakṣavṛttervāyuvanaspatisaṃyogavadapratyakṣatvaprasaṅgād dehasya /
api ca yadā ceṣṭendriyārthasya samavāyena śarīratvam, hanta bho indriyasamavāyikāraṇeṣu paramāṇuṣu samastam etadastīti teṣāmapi śarīratvaprasaṅga ityāha---samasteti /
syādetat /
bhavanmate 'pi cukṣurādibhirindriyairvyabhicāraḥ, teṣāmapi yathoktavyāpārādhāratvādityata āha---yathā tviti /

children.translated_text: The qualification 'when not employed by another material body' [resolves this].

children.text: cakṣurādayastu unmīlanānmūrtena śarīreṇa prayujyante iti na prasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: But the eye and other [sense organs] are operated by the material body through the opening [of the eyelids etc.], so there is no unwanted consequence.

children.text: śrotraṃ tu ceṣṭādhāra eva na bhavati /
children.translated_text: The ear, however, is simply not a substratum of effort [requiring bodily operation].
Thus, contemplating this body as a characterizing mark, one becomes dispassionate — this is established. //11//

Having thus described substratumship of effort etc. as the definition of body both in accordance with the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and according to his own view, individually, he refutes the view of those who held that all these together constitute the definition of body — 'even by those' etc.
If the first term '<s>ceṣṭāśraya</s>' (substratum of effort) were the definition, then there would be deviation with respect to a pot.
For that purpose, the second term '<s>indriyāśraya</s>' (substratum of sense organs) is added, meaning 'that which is in conjunction with sense organs.'
Even so, there is deviation with respect to the same pot etc., since the sense organs, being contact-requiring in their operation, are also in conjunction with pots etc.
Hence he says — '<s>arthāśraya</s>' (substratum of objects).
Even with this addition, the deviation remains exactly the same, since pots etc. also possess color and other
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.12: The <s>indriyāṇi</s> (sense organs) are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear, [arising] from the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>).

children.text: na ca viśeṣalakṣaṇamakṛte sāmānyalakṣaṇe śakyamiti bhāṣyakāraḥ prathamamindriyāṇāṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ nirvedopayuktamāha---bhogasādhanānīti /
children.translated_text: And since the specific definition cannot be given without first giving the general definition, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> first states the general definition of the sense organs, which is conducive to dispassion — 'instruments of experience' etc.

children.text: anena yaccharīrasaṃyuktaṃ satkārakadoṣavyatiriktaṃ sākṣātpratītisādhanaṃ tadindriyamiti sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ sūcitam /
children.translated_text: By this, the general definition is indicated: that which is conjoined with the body, distinct from meritorious and demeritorious dispositions, and is the direct means of cognition — that is a sense organ (<s>indriya</s>).
The reason for saying 'instruments of experience' instead of 'direct means of cognition' is that it serves the purpose of dispassion.

children.text: pāramparyeṇa ca bhogasādhanatvaṃ ghrāṇādīnām sākṣānmanasa eva tatsādhanatvāt, sukhaduḥkhasākṣātkārasya bhogatvāt //
children.translated_text: And the nose and the rest are instruments of experience only indirectly, since the mind (<s>manas</s>) alone is directly the instrument of that [experience], experience being the direct realization of pleasure and pain.
Since the sense organ serves as the conveyor [of cognition], the definition of sense organs, being distinct from objects etc., comes before [the definition of] objects etc.

children.text:
ghrāṇa---bhyaḥ //12// atrendriyāṇīti lakṣyanirdeśaḥ ghrāṇādīnītyarthaḥ /
teṣāṃ pañcānāṃ pañcaiva lakṣaṇānīti kathayati---lakṣaṇasūtrāṇīti /
āpātataḥ sūtram, vicāryamāṇāni tu sūtrāṇītyarthaḥ /
samānajātīyaṃ ghrāṇāde rasanādi pratiniyataviṣayatvāt /
asamānajātīyaṃ tu mana ādi sarvaviṣayamiti /
jighratītyādibhāṣyanirākaraṇīyaśaṅkāmāha---uddeśeti /
pramāṇādyuddeśena sāmānyādityarthaḥ /
lakṣaṇaṃ hi vidheyam /
lakṣyaṃ coddeśyam /
jñātaṃ coddiśyate, ajñātaṃ ca vidhīyate iti /
na caikasya yugapajjñātājñātatve saṃbhavataḥ /
nāpi lakṣyalakṣaṇatve iti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati---nedaṃ tathā yathoddeśa ityarthaḥ /
kasmāt? karaṇabhāvāt svaviṣayagrahaṇalakṣaṇatvaṃ yato ghrāṇādīnām /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, indriyāṇāmatīndriyatvāt sarvadā svasvaviṣayopalabdhikaraṇatvenaivānumātavyāni /
tasmāt svasvaviṣayopalabdhisādhanatvameva samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakatayā lakṣaṇam /
tadekārthasamavāyi tu ghrāṇatvādi lakṣyam /
atra ca ghrāṇādiśabdāḥ paṅkajādipadavadavayavārthaṃ nimittīkṛtya kvacit, kvacit sāmānyaviśeṣe vartante, avayavārthasaṃbandhasya pratīyamānasyāsati bādhake parityāgāyogāt /
aśvakarṇādau vṛkṣaviśeṣavācake vājikarṇāyogena bādhakenāvayavārthaparityāgāt /
avayavārthage 'pi ca gandhādyupalabdhisādhane sannikarṣādau ghrāṇādiśabdāprayogāt avayavārthānvitaṃ ghrāṇatvādyeva ghrāṇādiśabdapravṛttinimittam /
tathā ca ghrāṇādipadameva ghrāṇatvādiparaṃ lakṣayanirdeśaḥ /
tacca indriyāṇi ityanena sūcitam /
tadeva tvavayavārthaparaṃ lakṣaṇanirdeśo ghrāṇetyādi /
na ca sannikarṣeṇa gandhopalabdhisādhanena ca vyabhicāraḥ, indriyasāmānyalakṣaṇayuktasya gandhopalabdhisādhanatvaṃ na sannikarṣasyāsti /
tadanena jighratītyādi svaviṣayagrahaṇalakṣaṇāni ityantaṃ bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
children.translated_text: By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> from 'one smells' up to 'are defined by the apprehension of their own objects' has been explained.
By the inclusion of the etymological derivation (<s>nirvacana</s>), only the mere basis for the application of the word is stated.
By that, the word '<s>tvak</s>' (skin) is also included.

children.text: tasyāpi tvaksthāne indriye sparśopalabdhisādhane eva upacāra iti //
children.translated_text: For that [word] too involves a figurative transfer (<s>upacāra</s>) to the sense organ located in the skin, which is the instrument for apprehending touch.

The nose— from [the elements]. //12// Here, 'sense organs' is the indication of the <s>lakṣya</s> (definiendum), meaning the nose and the rest. He says that for these five, there are exactly five definitions— 'definition-<s>sūtras</s>.' At first glance it is one <s>sūtra</s>, but when examined, they are [multiple] <s>sūtras</s>— this is the meaning. What is of the same class as the nose is the tongue and the like, because of having a restricted object-domain. What is of a different class is the mind (<s>manas</s>) and the like, because it has all things as its object-domain. He states the objection to be refuted by the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'one smells'— 'enumeration.' The meaning is: because of the enumeration beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, [it is known] from generality. For the definition is what is to be predicated, and the definiendum is what is to be indicated. What is known is indicated, and what is unknown is predicated. And it is not possible for one and the same thing to be simultaneously known and unknown, nor to be both definiendum and definition— this is the import. He resolves— 'this is not so,' meaning it is not as in the enumeration. Why? Because of being an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>): the nose and the like have the character of being defined by the apprehension of their own respective objects. What has been stated amounts to this: since the sense organs are supersensible (<s>atīndriya</s>), they must always be inferred only through being instruments of the apprehension of their respective objects. Therefore, being the instrument of apprehending one's own respective object is the definition, serving to distinguish from what is of the same and different class. What co-inheres in one and the same object with that [definition]— namely nose-ness and the like— is the definiendum. And here, the words '<s>ghrāṇa</s>' (nose) and the like, like the word '<s>paṅkaja</s>' (lotus, lit. 'born in mud'), sometimes function with the component-meaning as their basis, and sometimes denote the universal-particular, since when the connection with component-meaning is understood, it cannot be abandoned in the absence of a sublating cognition. In the case of '<s>aśvakarṇa</s>' (a kind of tree, lit. 'horse-ear') and the like, which denote a specific kind of tree, the component-meaning is abandoned because of the sublating fact that horse-ears are inapplicable. And since the words '<s>ghrāṇa</s>' and the like are not used for sense-object contact and the like, which are [also] instruments for apprehending smell and the like based on component-meaning, the basis for the application of the words '<s>ghrāṇa</s>' and the like is nose-ness and the like connected with the component-meaning. And thus the word '<s>ghrāṇa</s>' and the like, referring to nose-ness and the like, constitutes the indication of the definiendum. And this is indicated by [the word] 'sense organs.' But that same [word], referring to the component-meaning, is the indication of the definition— '<s>ghrāṇa</s>' and so on. And there is no deviation with respect to sense-object contact as an instrument for apprehending smell, since sense-object contact does not possess the property of being an instrument for apprehending smell that is endowed with the general definition of sense organ.

children.text:
bhūtebhya iti sūtrāvayavatātparyavyākhyānaparaṃ bhāṣyaṃ bhūtebhya itīti /
nānāprakṛtīnāmityādi /
tad vārttikakāro vyācaṣṭe---bhūtebhya iti /
pṛcchati---kaḥ punariti /
uttaram---bhūtaguṇaviśeṣagrahaṇasādhanatvam ghrāṇenaiva hi pṛthivyā yo guṇaviśeṣo gandhaḥ sa gṛhyate, na rasanādinā /
evaṃ rasanenaivāpāṃ yo mādhuryaṃ guṇaviśeṣaḥ sa gṛhyate, na ghrāṇādinā /
children.translated_text: Similarly, by the tongue alone is sweetness, which is the specific quality of water, apprehended, not by the nose and the like.
Similarly, by the eye alone is the bright, luminous form (<s>rūpa</s>) of fire [apprehended].
Similarly, by the skin alone is the non-hot and non-cold touch that is not produced by heating— the [natural touch] of wind [apprehended].

children.text: evaṃ śrotreṇaiva śabdo nabhasa iti hi niyamaḥ //
children.translated_text: Similarly, by the ear alone is sound, [the quality] of space, [apprehended]— this is indeed the rule.

The <s>bhāṣya</s> 'from the elements' explains the purport of a portion of the <s>sūtra</s>— 'from the elements.' 'Of different material natures' and so on. The <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains that— 'from the elements.' He asks— 'what then?' The answer— 'being the instrument for apprehending the specific quality of each element': for by the nose alone is smell, which is the specific quality of earth, apprehended, not by the tongue and the like.

children.text:
atra ca prayogaḥ, gandhopalabdhiḥ karaṇasādhyā kriyātvāt chidikriyāvaditi /
evaṃ sā tadanyakriyākāraṇātiriktakaraṇaniṣpādyā, tadanvayavyatirekānanuvidhāne sati kāryatvāt /
yā yatkriyākaraṇānvayatirekānanuvidhāne sati kāryā, sa sarvā takriyākaraṇātiriktakaraṇaniṣpādyā, yathā paṭādikriyā ghaṭadikriyākaraṇacakradaṇḍādyatiriktavemādikaraṇaniṣpādyā /
tathā ceyam /
tasmāt tatheti /
tacca karaṇaṃ cakṣurādyatiriktaṃ ghrāṇam /
tad dravyam, saṃyogādhāratvād ghaṭadivat /
tacca pārthivam, dravyatve sati rūpādiṣu madhye gandhasyaiva vya/jakatvāt, pārthivāntaravat /
evaṃ rasanādiṣvapi yojyam /
tadidamuktam---yajjātīyamindriyaṃ pārthivaṃ pārthasīyaṃ vā bhavati, tasya pṛthivyāḥ pāthaso vā yo guṇaviśeṣo gandho vā madhura eva vā rasabhedaḥ, tena hi pṛthivī abādibhyaḥ, āpo vā pṛthivyādibhyo vyavacchidyante iti /
itaretarabhūtavyavacchedahetuḥ sa tenaivendriyeṇa gṛhyate nānyeneti /
na caive rasanā apāmiva pṛthivyā api rasabhedaṃ gṛhṇātīti pārthivī bhavati /
tathātve tayā gandho 'pyupalabhyeta /
tena tenaivendriyeṇeti niyamo guṇaviśeṣamavadhārayati, na tvindriyamimi /
atra ca karṇaśaṣkulīsaṃyogopādhinā śrotrasya nabhasaḥ kathañcid bhedaṃ vivakṣitvā bhūtebhya iti pa/yamyartho vyākhyeyaḥ //
children.translated_text: And here the argument is: the apprehension of smell is an action accomplished by an instrument, because it is an action— like the action of cutting. Similarly, that [action] is accomplished by an instrument distinct from the causes of other actions, because it is an effect while not conforming to the presence and absence of those other instruments. Whatever action is an effect while not conforming to the presence and absence of the instruments of a given action, all of that is accomplished by an instrument distinct from the instruments of that action— just as the action of producing cloth is accomplished by instruments like the loom and the like, which are distinct from the instruments of the action of producing a pot, such as the wheel and stick. And so is this. Therefore, it is so. And that instrument, distinct from the eye and the like, is the nose. That is a substance, because it is a substrate of conjunction— like a pot and the like. And that is earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>), because, being a substance, among form and the like it is a manifester of smell alone— like other earthy substances. The same should be applied to the tongue and the like as well. This is what has been stated: whatever class the sense organ belongs to— whether earthy or watery— for that earth or water, whichever specific quality it has— whether smell or a particular kind of taste— by that quality earth is distinguished from water and the like, or water from earth and the like. That which is the cause of mutual distinction among the elements— that is apprehended by that very sense organ and not by another. And it is not the case that the tongue, because it apprehends the specific taste of earth just as it does that of water, is therefore earthy. If it were so, it would also apprehend smell. Therefore the rule 'by that very sense organ' determines the specific quality, but not the sense organ [itself]. And here, having intended some kind of distinction of the organ of hearing— which is space— from space by means of the limiting adjunct of conjunction with the ear-cavity, 'from the elements' should be explained in the sense of a plural.

children.text:
anena khalvāhaṅkārikāṇīndriyāṇi iti yadāhuḥ sāṃkhyāḥ, tat nirākṛtam /
nirākaraṇahetumāha---aikātmya iti śliṣṭaṃ padam /
sāṃkhyānāṃ kila rāddhānte kāraṇātmakaṃ kāryam /
tacca kāraṇamindriyāṇāmahaṅkāra eva ityaikātmyamekakāraṇakatvam /
tathā caikātmyamekatvaṃ ghrāṇādīnāmityaniyamaḥ syāditi /
tadetad vibhajate---yadi punariti /
śaṅkate---eketi /
vibhajate---atheti /
ekaḥ pākya eko 'gnisaṃyogaḥ ekaṃ coṣṇyamityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti---na brūma iti /
yadyapyauṣṇyaṃ nimittaṃ sādhāraṇam, tathāpi gandhādyutpattau pūrvagandhādidhvaṃsānāṃ nimittānāṃ bhedādutpannaṃ bhedādutpannaṃ kāryanānātvamiti /
tadidamuktaṃ ye pūrve rūpādayaḥ teṣāṃ svagato viśeṣaḥ pradhvaṃsa ityarthaḥ /
atha rūpatvādisāmānyameva kasmāt svagato viśeṣo na bhavatītyata āha---evaṃ ca kṛtveti /
rūpatvādisāmānyānāṃ tādavasthye na pakvataratamādibhedaḥ /
pradhvaṃsānāṃ tu stokabhūyastvaṃ niḥśeṣatve nopadyate iti bhāvaḥ /
punarāśaṅkate---ekaṃ karmeti /
nirākaroti---neti /
samavāyikāraṇaṃ svāśrayapratyāsatti vāpekṣata iti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkate---yadi tarhīti /
lakṣaṇahāniḥ tathā ca lakṣaṇahānirityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He refutes— 'no.'
The meaning is: the final subsidiary instrumental cause (<s>nimittāntara</s>) has a positive nature (<s>bhāvarūpa</s>).
But it requires the absence of the [prior] conjunction for the production of the subsequent conjunction.
He concludes— 'therefore.' //12//

By this, what the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> say— that the sense organs originate from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle)— has been refuted. He states the reason for the refutation— '<s>aikātmya</s>' (identity of nature) is a compact expression. For according to the established doctrine of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, the effect is of the nature of the cause. And the cause of the sense organs is <s>ahaṅkāra</s> alone— so identity of nature means having a single cause. And thus, because of the identity and oneness of the nose and the like, there would be no restriction [of each to its own object]. He analyzes that— 'if, however.' He raises a doubt— 'one.' He analyzes— 'now then.' One thing to be cooked, one fire-conjunction, and one heat— this is the meaning. He refutes— 'we do not say.' Although heat as the instrumental cause is common, nevertheless, in the production of smell and the like, because the instrumental causes— namely the destructions of prior smells and the like— are different, the effects produced are diverse because they arise from diverse [causes]. This is what has been stated: 'the prior forms and the like'— meaning: their own specific destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>). Now, why should the universal such as form-ness and the like not be the specific [distinguishing feature]?— therefore he says— 'and having done so.' When the universals such as form-ness remain unchanged, there would be no distinction of 'more cooked' and 'most cooked.' But for destructions, degrees of partial and complete [destruction] do not arise when destruction is total— this is the import. He again raises a doubt— 'one action.' He refutes— 'no.' The import is that the inherent cause requires proximity to its own substrate. He raises a doubt— 'if then.' 'Deficiency of the definition'— meaning: and thus there would be a deficiency of the definition.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.13: Earth, water, fire, wind, and space (<s>ākāśa</s>)— these are the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>).
But it should be understood that being the material cause of the sense organs is the definition of the elements. //13//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.14: Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound are qualities of earth and the rest— they are the objects (<s>artha</s>).
The <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) introduces the definition of <s>artha</s> (object), which comes in due order— 'but we.'
By the word 'but' (<s>tu</s>), he distinguishes [the object] from the mere [category of] object.

children.text: yeṣāmindriyaviṣayatvena bhāvyamānānāṃ niḥśreyasasādhakatvam, mithyājñānaviṣayīkṛtānāṃ tu saṃsāranimittatā, ta ime ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: those [objects] which, when apprehended as objects of the sense organs, serve as means to the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), but when made the objects of false knowledge, become causes of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration)— they are these.

children.text:
gandhar---thāḥ //14// atra coddeśakramasmāritā arthā lakṣyatayā pratipattavyāḥ, teṣāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ tadarthā iti /
tadityanantaralakṣitānīndriyāṇi parāmṛśati, teṣāmindriyāṇām arthāḥ /
indriyairaryamāṇatvamarthānāṃ lakṣaṇam /
etāvataiva lakṣaṇe paryavasite suhṛdbhāvena pravibhāgābhidhānaṃ pṛthivyādiguṇā iti /
pṛthivyaptejāṃsi ca guṇāśca dharmāḥ saṃkhyākarmādayaḥ /
pravibhāge 'pyetāvatāvagate ganadhādyabhidhānaṃ suhṛdbhāvenendriyaviṣayaniyamajñāpanārtham /
pṛthivyādīnāmiti bhāṣyaṃ na ṣaṣṭhīsamāsajñāpanārtham, api tvarthābhidhānamātram /
yathāviniyogamiti /
yathākramaṃ pṛthivyādiṣvanilānteṣu gandhādayaḥ sparśāntāḥ catustridvyekaniyamena viniyuktāḥ /
śabdaścākāśa evetyarthaḥ /
tadarthā iti lakṣaṇapadaṃ vyācaṣṭe---indriyāṇāmiti /
yena krameṇa ghrāṇādaya indriyasūtre paṭhitāḥ yena ceha gandhādaya, tadanatikrameṇetyarthaḥ /
atra vārttikakāraḥ pṛthivyādiguṇā ityatrānekasamāsapratibhāsanāt saṃśayaṃ kṛtvā dvandvasamāsamavadhārayati---pṛthivyādiguṇā iti /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsenābhinnārthatvāt saptamīsamāsasyetyasau na darśitaḥ /
nanu kaṇṭhekāla itivad vaiyadhikaraṇyena bahuvrīhirbhaviṣyati pṛthivyādīnāṃ guṇā yebhyo gandhādibhyaḥ, te tathā /
tathā hi paramāṇugatā gandhādayo 'vayavini gandhādyārabhante, nabhogataśca śabdo nabhasi samānajātīyaṃ śabdamityata āha---na cānyatheti /
jñāpakavaśāt kvacid vyadhikaraṇānāṃ bahuvrīhiḥ /
jñāpakakṛtaṃ ca na sarvatra /
na ca gandhādīnāṃ pṛthivyādiguṇahetutvapratipādanaṃ kvacit nirvedādāvupayujyata iti bhāvaḥ /
anyasamāsaḥ karmadhārayādiḥ /
dvandvamavadhāritamākṣipati---na dvandva iti /
samādhatte---na, ubhayasyāpīti /
pṛthivyādigrahaṇeneti /
yadyādiśabdena vāyvādayo gṛhyeran, tadarthā iti lakṣaṇamavyāpakaṃ syāt, teṣāṃ bāhyendriyārthatvābhāvādityarthaḥ /
guṇagrahaṇena sarva iti āśritānāśritatvābhiprāyam, guṇaśabdasya dharmavacanatvāt /
viśeṣastu rekhoparekhādiḥ na tvantyaḥ, tasyātīndriyatvāt /
eteṣāṃ ca yathāyogaṃ mithyājñānasamyagjñānaviṣayāṇāṃ rāgavairāgyahetutvamūhanīyam /
codayati---gandheti /
pariharati---na kartavyaṃ laghusūtram /

children.translated_text: The meaning is: a separate statement of smell and the like should be composed.
He states the restriction— 'sense organs.'

children.text: tatretyaniyateṣu madhye, pṛthivyaptejāṃsi dvīndriyagrāhyāṇi, śeṣaśca guṇarāśiḥ saṃkhyādirviśeṣānto dvīndriyāgrāhya ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: There, among the unrestricted [qualities], earth, water, and fire are apprehensible by two sense organs; and the remaining group of qualities— from number up to <s>viśeṣa</s> (distinguishing feature)— is not apprehensible by [just] two sense organs— this is the meaning.
Similarly, [some qualities are] apprehensible by all sense organs— this is the meaning.

Smell— objects. //14// Here, the objects recalled by the order of enumeration should be understood as definienda, and their definition is 'objects of those' (<s>tadarthāḥ</s>). The word 'tad' (that) refers to the sense organs defined immediately before; 'their objects' means the objects of those sense organs. Being apprehended by the sense organs is the definition of the objects. When the definition has been completed by just this much, the further specification 'qualities of earth and the like' is stated out of friendly concern. Earth, water, fire— and their qualities, i.e., properties such as number, action, and the like. Even when the specification has been understood to this extent, the mention of smell and the like is for the friendly purpose of indicating the restriction of sense organs to their objects. The <s>bhāṣya</s> 'of earth and the like' is not for the purpose of indicating a genitive compound, but merely for stating the meaning. 'According to their respective assignment'— meaning: smell and the like, up to touch, are assigned to earth and the rest up to wind, in the restriction of four, three, two, and one [qualities] respectively. And sound belongs to space alone— this is the meaning. He explains the definitional expression 'objects of those'— 'of the sense organs.' The meaning is: in whichever order the nose and the like were listed in the sense-organ <s>sūtra</s>, and in whichever [order] smell and the like [are listed] here, [the correspondence is] without transgressing that order. Here the <s>vārttikakāra</s>, having raised a doubt because of the appearance of multiple possible compounds in 'qualities of earth and the like,' determines it to be a <s>dvandva</s> (copulative) compound— 'qualities of earth and the like.' The genitive compound is not shown because its meaning is identical with that of the locative compound. Now, as in '<s>kaṇṭhekāla</s>' (one with time at the throat, i.e., near death), there could be an exocentric (<s>bahuvrīhi</s>) compound with different substrates: 'those [objects] from which— namely smell and the like— there are qualities of earth and the like; they are so.' For the smells and the like residing in atoms produce smells and the like in the composite substance, and sound residing in space [produces] a sound of the same kind in space— therefore he says— 'not otherwise.' By the force of an indicatory sign (<s>jñāpaka</s>), the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> of words with different substrates [is possible] in some cases. But what is established by indicatory signs is not [applicable] everywhere. And indicating that smell and the like are causes of the qualities of earth and the like is not useful anywhere, such as in producing dispassion— this is the import. The other compound is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> (appositional) and the like. He objects to the determined <s>dvandva</s>— 'not a <s>dvandva</s>.' He reconciles— 'no, because both.' By the inclusion of 'earth and the like'— the meaning is: if by the word 'and the like' (<s>ādi</s>), wind and the like were included, the definition 'objects of those' would be non-pervasive, since they are not objects of the external sense organs. By the inclusion of 'quality'— the intention is regarding what is dependent and what is independent, since the word <s>guṇa</s> (quality) has the meaning of property (<s>dharma</s>). And the distinguishing feature (<s>viśeṣa</s>) refers to lines and the like, not the ultimate <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), since that is supersensible. And the fact that these, according to their respective applicability, serve as causes of attachment and detachment when they are objects of false knowledge and right knowledge, should be inferred. He objects— 'smell.' He resolves— 'a concise <s>sūtra</s> should not be composed [separately].'

children.text:
atra bauddhamutthāpayati---darśanasparśanābhyāmiti /
tasya paryanuyogamāha---sa iti /
svasaṃvedanena vā mānasena vā jñānena rūpāddhālambanaḥ, pratyayo rūpādiviśiṣṭo yathānubhūyate, evaṃ rūpādyatiriktaghaṭādiviśiṣṭo 'nubhūyata ityarthaḥ /
atra para āha---rūpādibhyastathā sanniviṣṭebhya iti /
tathetyākāraṃ nirdiśati /
sanniveśo vyavasthānam /
rūpādiparamāṇava eva tena tenākāreṇa utpannā ekayodakāharaṇakriyayā vyavacchinnā ghaṭa ityucyante /
anura/janādikayā tu rūpādivyapadeśaḥ /
yathāha ghaṭa ityapi ca rūpādaya evaikārthakriyākāriṇastathā vyapadiśyante iti /
nirākaroti---na, ākārārtheti /
tathārthasya yathāpadārthena nityābhisambandhāt yathā ghaṭaḥ, tathā sanniviṣṭā rūpādaya ityartho gamyate /
tena ghaṭākāreṇa ghaṭasādṛśyenetyayamarthaḥ /
tathā ca dūṣaṇamiti /
dūṣaṇāntaramāha---rūpādimātre ceti /
na tāvad rūpādikṣaṇa eko ghaṭaḥ, kṣaṇāntare tatprayogābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
tasmād
rūpādimātramavivakṣitabhedam tathā satyetaddūṣaṇamityarthaḥ /
śaṅkate---saṃsthānabhedāditi /
yathāsaṃsthānāṃ rūpādayo 'rthā anubhūyante, tathā sanniviṣṭebhyo ghaṭādipratyayā ityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti---naitaditi /
anyatve tadevāvayavīti saṃjñābhedamātram /
ananyatve vyarthābhidhānam /
śaṅkate---ghaṭādipratyayā iti /
ekānekavicārāsahatvād asanta eva ghaṭādayo 'nādivikalpavāsanājanitavikalpapratyayapratibhāsinaḥ /
śabdaśabdena vikalpamupalakṣayati---śabdavāsanāvaśāditi /
nirākaroti---tadayuktamiti /
bījaṃ mithyāpratyayasya samyakpratyayaviṣayo 'rthaḥ /
tasya kvacidabhyupagame 'bhimatārthahānamityarthaḥ /
yastu bhinnalokamaryādatayā brūte ādimān mithyāpratyayaḥ samyagjñānaṃ nimittīkaroti, ayaṃ punaranādi /
pūrvapūrvamithyāpratyayajanmā mithyāpratyayapravāhaḥ, kṛtamatra samyagjñāneneti, taṃ pratyāha---mityāpratyayāścaita iti /

children.translated_text: The meaning is: the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is non-different from form and the like /
But the opponent states a proof for non-difference— 'it is not non-existent' /
For there is no thing called 'broth' (<s>yūṣa</s>) distinct from meat and water /
Nor is there anything called a 'row' distinct from trees, humans, and trees //

Here he raises the Buddhist [objection]— 'by seeing and touching' /
He states the cross-examination of that— 'that' /
The meaning is: just as a cognition having form and the like as its object, qualified by form and the like, is experienced through self-awareness or through mental cognition, so too something qualified by a pot and the like, distinct from form and the like, is experienced /
Here the opponent says— 'from forms and the like arranged in such a way' /
He indicates the meaning of 'in such a way' /
<s>Sanniveśa</s> (arrangement) means disposition /
The very atoms of form and the like, produced in a particular configuration and demarcated by a single activity such as fetching water, are called a 'pot' /
But the designation 'form and the like' is due to coloring and so on /
As it is said: 'even what is called a pot is just forms and the like performing a single purposive action, and is thus designated' /
He refutes— 'no, because of the form-meaning' /
The meaning understood is: since the word 'such' (<s>tathā</s>) is always connected with its referent, just as there is a pot, so too forms and the like are arranged /
Therefore, 'in the form of a pot' means 'by resemblance to a pot'— this is the meaning /
And thus there is a fault /
He states another fault— 'in mere form and the like' /
A pot is not a single entity at the moment of form and the like, because there would be the unwanted consequence of no use of it at the next moment /
Therefore, when 'mere form and the like' without intended distinction is meant, this is the fault— this is the meaning /
He raises a doubt— 'because of difference in configuration' /
The meaning is: just as objects of form and the like are experienced according to their configuration, so too cognitions of pot and the like arise from those arranged [atoms] /
He refutes— 'this is not so' /
If [the whole is] different [from the parts], then calling it 'the whole' (<s>avayavin</s>) is merely a difference of name /
If not different, the designation is pointless /
He raises a doubt— 'cognitions of pot and the like' /
Since they cannot withstand the analysis of being one or many, pots and the like are simply non-existent, appearing in conceptual cognitions generated by beginningless latent impressions of conceptualization /
By the word 'word' (<s>śabda</s>) he indicates conceptualization— 'due to the force of verbal latent impressions' /
He refutes— 'that is improper' /
The seed of false cognition is the object that is the content of correct cognition /
The meaning is: if that [object] is accepted somewhere, the intended thesis is abandoned /
But one who, transgressing worldly norms, says that false cognition has a beginning and takes correct knowledge as its cause— this [stream of false cognition] is beginningless /
The stream of false cognition, born from each preceding false cognition— 'correct knowledge has nothing to do here'— to him he replies— 'and these false cognitions' /

children.text:
dūṣayati---nāyaṃ heturiti /
ye ghaṭādibhāvamāpannā bhavatāṃ darśane iti /
kāme 'ṣṭadravyako 'ṇuraśabdaḥ rūpadhāturarūpadhātuḥ kāmadhāturiti traidhātukaṃ jagat /
tatra kāmadhātusvarūpamuktam /
kāme kāmadhātau /
aṣṭadravyako 'ṇuḥ /
rūparasagandhasparśā iti catvāri dravyāṇi, pṛthivyaptejovāyava iti catvāri /
dravyaśabdo vastuvacanaḥ /
tenāṣṭadravyako 'ṇurityāgamaḥ /
so 'yaṃ rūpādyatiriktapṛthivyādyanabhyupagame bādhyeta /
atha vaiyātyāducyate---pṛthivyādīnāmiti /
tataśca sāṃvṛtatvenāṣṭasaṃkhyāsiddhernāgamavirodha iti bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: The reply— 'even so' /

children.text: mā bhūvan vastutaḥ, ubhaye 'pi sāṃvṛtā bhaviṣyantītyata āha---saṃhanyamānasyeti /
children.translated_text: Let them not be real; both will be merely conventional— to this he says— 'of what is being combined' /

children.text: yo hi yattantraḥ sa tadabhāvamabhyupagamyāśakyābhyupagamaḥ, na khalu saṃyujyamānānāmabhāve saṃyogaḥ śakyābhyupagama ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: one who depends on something cannot accept its non-existence; for indeed, combination cannot be accepted when the things being combined are non-existent /

children.text: na ca saṃvṛtiḥ, sā hi pararūpaṃ svarūpeṇa saṃvṛṇoti, saṃhanyamānābhāve ca na saṃghātaḥ, nāpi saṃhanyamānā iti kimanayā svarūpeṇāvriyeteti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: And there is no convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) either; for convention conceals another nature by its own nature, and when the things being combined are non-existent, there is no aggregate, nor are there things being combined— so what would be concealed by its own nature?— this is the purport //

He refutes— 'this is not a [valid] reason' /
Those who have attained the status of pots and the like in your view— /
In the realm of desire (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), the atom has eight substances and is without sound; the form-realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>); the formless realm (<s>arūpadhātu</s>); the desire-realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>)— thus the three-realm world /
Therein the nature of the desire-realm is stated /
In the desire-realm: the atom has eight substances /
The four substances are form, taste, smell, and touch; and the four are earth, water, fire, and air /
The word 'substance' (<s>dravya</s>) means 'entity' /
Thus 'the atom has eight substances'— this is the scriptural tradition (<s>āgama</s>) /
This would be contradicted if earth and the like, distinct from form and the like, are not accepted /
But if it is said through a different interpretation— 'of earth and the like' /
Then, because the number eight is established conventionally (<s>sāṃvṛta</s>), there is no contradiction with scripture— this is the purport /

children.text:
tadevaṃ tadagrahe tadbuddhyabhāvād ityasya vyāghātadoṣaṃ darśayitvā svasāmarthyālocane na vivakṣitaliṅgābhidhāyitā, kiṃ tvasaṃbaddhārthatā hetuvacanasyetyāha---tadagrahe iti /
evaṃ kilātrābhimatam, pṛthivyādayo rūpādibhyo 'bhinnā, rūpādyagrahe pṛthivyādibuddhyabhāvāditi /
tannṛ tadettatadagrahe tadbuddhyabhāvādityanena na śakyaṃ vaktum /
tadagraha ityatra tacchabdaḥ pradhānaparāmarśī , pṛthivyādayaśca dharmitayā pradhānamiti ta eva parāmarṣṭavyāḥ /
tathā ca pṛthivyādyagrahe pṛthivyādibuddhyabhāvāditi syāt /
tathā ca pratijñātasteṣāṃ rūpādyabhedo na sidhyedityasaṃbaddham /
atha rūpādayaḥ pakṣīkriyante, tathāpi rūpādyagrahe rūpādibuddhyayabhāvāditi syāt /
tathāpi na pratijñātārthasiddhirityasaṃbaddhārthamityarthaḥ /
evaṃ śabdāntareṇāpi pratijñāprayoge tulyaḥ prasaṅga ityāha---evaṃ rūpādimātramiti /
pratijñādoṣamāha---sarvatra ceti /
nānātvaikārthasaṃbandhaniyatāyā bahutvasaṃkhyāyā abhedaikārthaniyataikatvasaṃkhyayā sāmānādhikaraṇyavirodha ityarthaḥ /
tadetadanaikāntikamiti codayati---nanviti /
nirākaroti---tanna, anabhyupagamāditi /
samānaṃ dharmasādhanam /
yamāḥ pañca /
niyamāśca pañca /
brahmacārigṛhasthavānaprasthayatīnāmaviśeṣeṇaiva daśa dharmasādhanam /
teṣāṃ dharmasādhanatvamekaṃ cāturāśramyamiti prakṛtigatā vibhaktirāha /
āśramaprakṛtigatā tu vibhaktiḥ prakṛtyarthasamavetāmeva bahutvasaṃkhyāmāha, samānārthānāmapi prakṛtīnāṃ rūpabhedena tatparasya pratyayasya sāmarthyabhedāt /
yathāptoyaśabdayostulyārthatve 'pi toyaśabdāt parā vibhaktistoyānīti toyasamavetāmeva bahutvasaṃkhyāmāha /
āpa iti na toyagatām, api tu tatsaṃbaddhagatām /
tatsaṃbaddhāśca tadavayavāḥ,
tadgatarūpādayo vā bahava ityekasyāmapi pāthaḥkaṇikāyāṃ bahuvacanopapattirāpa iti /
na ca sorastāḍaṃ krandato 'pi lokasyāvinivṛtternaivamiti sāmpratam /
loko hi dṛṣṭavyavahāramātraprayojano na vivecayati, parīkṣakāstu tadanusāriṇo vivecayantyeva /
anyathā hi pratyakṣādilakṣaṇapraṇayanavaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ /
etena dārāḥ ṣaṇṇagarītyādayo 'pi vyākhyātāḥ /
ṣāṅguṇyamiti ṣaṇṇāṃ guṇānāmekaṃ rājaprayayojanasādhakatvam /
vaiśeṣikamityatrāpi viśeṣāṇāṃ samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakatvamekamacyate iti gamayitavyam /
hetudeṣamāha---asiddho 'pīti /
sphaṭikasya dhavalaṃ rūpam /

children.translated_text: And that, being overpowered by contact with the substance indigo, is not perceived /
But the crystal is perceived /

children.text: na ca nīlasya sphaṭikalakṣaṇasyotpattiriti tṛtīye nivedayiṣyate /
children.translated_text: And the arising of the blue [appearance] is not [the arising] of something with the nature of crystal— this will be explained in the third [book] /
Therefore, the reason is unestablished— this is the meaning //

Having thus shown the fault of self-contradiction in 'when that is not apprehended, the cognition of it is absent,' he says that when one's own capacity is examined, the intention is not the statement of an intended mark (<s>liṅga</s>), but rather the incoherent meaning of the statement of the reason— 'when that is not apprehended' /
What is intended here is this: earth and the like are non-different from form and the like; when form and the like are not apprehended, the cognition of earth and the like is absent /
But that cannot be stated by 'when that is not apprehended, the cognition of it is absent' /
In 'when that is not apprehended,' the word 'that' refers to the principal [subject], and earth and the like, being the subject of the proposition (<s>dharmin</s>), are the principal— so they alone should be referred to /
And thus it would be: 'when earth and the like are not apprehended, the cognition of earth and the like is absent' /
And thus the non-difference of those [earth etc.] from form and the like, which was the thesis, would not be established— hence it is incoherent /
If form and the like are made the subject, even then it would be: 'when form and the like are not apprehended, the cognition of form and the like is absent' /
Even then the thesis would not be established— hence the meaning is incoherent /
The same problem arises when the thesis is formulated with different words too— thus he says— 'likewise, mere form and the like' /
He states the fault of the thesis— 'and everywhere' /
The meaning is: there is a contradiction in co-reference between the number 'plurality,' which is restricted to the meaning of difference and multiplicity, and the number 'unity,' which is restricted to the meaning of non-difference and single purpose /
He objects that this is inconclusive— 'but is it not' /
He refutes— 'not so, because of non-acceptance' /
The means of <s>dharma</s> (righteous conduct) are the same [for all] /
The <s>yamas</s> (restraints) are five /
And the <s>niyamas</s> (observances) are five /
The ten are means of <s>dharma</s> without distinction for the celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the renunciant /
Their being a single means of <s>dharma</s> and the fourfold system of life-stages (<s>cāturāśramya</s>)— thus the inflection pertains to the base /
But the inflection pertaining to the base of the life-stage expresses the number 'plurality' as inherent in the meaning of the base itself, because even among bases with the same meaning, due to the difference in form, the suffix following has a difference in capacity /
Just as, though the words <s>ap</s> and <s>toya</s> have the same meaning, the inflection following the word <s>toya</s> expresses the number 'plurality' as inherent in <s>toya</s> [yielding <s>toyāni</s>] /
But <s>āpaḥ</s> does not express [plurality] as residing in water, but as residing in what is connected with it /
And what is connected with it are its parts, or the many forms and the like residing in it— thus even for a single drop of water, the plural is justified in <s>āpaḥ</s> /
And it is not proper [to dismiss this] saying 'this is not so, because even when one beats one's chest and cries, the world does not desist [from such usage]' /
For the world, having only the purpose of observed convention, does not discriminate; but examiners, following that [convention], do indeed discriminate /
Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of the pointlessness of formulating definitions of perception and the like /
By this, [expressions like] <s>dārāḥ</s> ('wife,' always plural) and <s>ṣaḍ nagarī</s> ('six cities') and the like are also explained /
<s>Ṣāṅguṇya</s> means: the six <s>guṇas</s> (political expedients) have a single capacity to accomplish the king's purpose /
In '<s>vaiśeṣika</s>' too, it should be understood that the <s>viśeṣas</s> (individuators) have a single [function] of differentiating things of the same and different kinds /
He states the fault of the reason— 'even if unestablished' /
Crystal has a white form /

children.text:
dṛṣṭāntaśca sādhyavikala ityāha---yo 'pyayamiti /
utpannapākajānāṃ taile sartiṣi vā bhṛṣṭamāṃsapiṇḍāvayavānām, dravyāntareṇa toyena saṃpṛktānāṃ pākajotpattau satyām /
na cāsau sahaseti /
ata uktam---kālaviśeṣānugrahe satīti /
sa ca saṃyogabheda eva toyamāṃsayoḥ, na tvavayavī vijātīyayoranāmbhakatvāt /
nāpi yūṣajātīyaṃ toyasaṃyogi dravyaṃ kṣīrajātīyamiveti yuktam /
toyavirahe kāṭhinyapi kṣīrabuddhivyapadeśayostādavasthyat /
iha tu kāṭhinye na yūṣabuddhivyapadeśāviti saṃyogabheda eva toyamāṃsayoryūṣa iti nyāyyam /
sa cānubhavasiddhaḥ saṃyogivyatiriktaḥ /
evaṃ bahutvasaṃkhyā saṃkhyeyātiriktānubhavasiddhaiveti /
evaṃ tatra tatra vyākhyeyam /
anādyanteṣu anāravdhāvayaviṣviti draṣṭavyam /
na ca parakīya sādhanadoṣodabhāvanamātrāt svapakṣasiddhiriti siddhāntinaṃ sādhanaṃ pṛcchati---atha rūpādibhyo 'rthāntare dravye kiṃ pramāṇamiti /
yato 'yaṃ paro rūpādibhyo 'rthāntaraṃ dravyaṃ pratyakṣeṇa vidvānapi svasiddhāntābhyāsāhitavyāmohāpasmāro na tathā vyavaharati, ato 'nenānumānena sa vyavahāryate /
asti hi sarveṣāmeva laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ brāhyaṇasya kamaṇḍaluritivat candanasya rūpādaya iti vyapadeśaḥ /
tatra ca paro rūpādyupalambhamabhyupagacchati candanopalambhamapi /
anyathā tadbuddhyabhāvādityetāvanmātre vaktavye kathamāha tadagraha iti? tenāvagacchāmo rūpādigrahe 'sya candanabuddhirabhimateti /
na cāsau manomātrayoniḥ smārtīti nyāyyam /
upapāditametasyāḥ savikalpikāyā indriyajanyatvaṃ vyavasāyātmakapadavyākhyānāvasare /
dravyabādhakapramāṇāni ca parīkṣāparvaṇi nirākariṣyante /
tasmāt siddhamupalabhyatvaṃ candanasya /
so 'yaṃ candano vivādagocarebhyo rūpādibhyo bhinnaḥ, svayamupalabhyasya ca samastairūpalabhyairvyapadiśyamānatvāt /
pradhānamapi sāṃkhyairvyapadiśyate, pradhānasya rūpādaya iti /
tannivṛttyartham upalabhyasyeti /
pradhānaṃ tu kālpanikaṃ nopalabhyam, tathāpi rūpādīnāṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ pradhānamityasti sāṃkhyānāṃ vyapadeśaḥ /
ata uktam---upalabhyairiti /
tathāpi rūpādīnāṃ parasparabhinnānāmanyonyaṃ vyapadeśyavyapadeśakabhāva upapatsyata ityuktam---samastairiti /
ataḥ samastebhyo vyapadeśakebhyaścandanaṃ bhinnaṃ bhavati /
upalabhyasyopalabhyeneti vaktavye pratyakṣsya pratyakṣeṇeti vacanaṃ rūpāvagamasamaye 'numeyebhyo rasādibhya ekāntato vyapadeśaṃ vyāvartayitum, na tvasyānumāna upayoga iti /
asyānaikāntikatvamudbhāvya nirākaroti---senāvanādibhiriti /
saṃkhyāyāmasattvamāśaṅkya nirākaroti---tadasattvamiti cediti /
vidhīyamānaṃ pratiṣidhyamānamiti yathāsaṃkhyaṃ niṣedhasya vidhyadhīnanirūpaṇatayā niṣedhyamekatvam aṅgīkāryam, tacca saṃkhyetyarthaḥ /
nanu santvamī pratyayāḥ, te tu dravyamātranibandhanā bhaviṣyanti, kṛtaṃ saṃkhyetyata āha---viśiṣṭāśceti /
na dravyātiriktanimittapratyākhyānena ityarthaḥ /
prayogāntaramāha---tatpratyayaviṣayanimittapratyayavyatirekeṇeti /
ghaṭapratyayasya viṣayaśca, nimittaṃ ca, ghaṭapratyayaśca tadvyatirekeṇeti, tadviśiṣṭasaṃkhyādipratyayasya nimittāntarākāṅkṣitvāt /
tat kimarthamat uktam---utpattāviti /
carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti itivad ghaṭādiviṣayanimittavyatirekabhāja ityatrāpi pratyayagrahaṇaṃ kartavyam /
codayati---mahatpuṣpiteti /
na saṃkhyāyā guṇasya parimāṇapuṣpayogasambhava ityarthaḥ /
pariharati---naiṣa deṣa iti /
sthānaśabdena tiṣṭhatīti vyutpattyā saṃkhyocyate /
sā yeṣāmasti te gajavājipadātiprabhūtayaḥ sthāninaḥ pratyekaṃ mahāntaḥ /
tatra te kvacicchatameva, kvacit punaḥ svajātīyasthānyaṅgāntarasannidhāne satyupacitāḥ sahasraṃ bhavanti /

children.translated_text: Therefore, the number 'plurality' being the instrument of augmentation, by the figurative attribution of the greatness that inheres in the single object of that [plurality], it is called a 'great army.'

children.text: na caitāvatā yatra śataṃ gajādayaḥ yatra ca sahasraṃ tayoḥ senayormahattvāviśeṣaḥ, upacayāpacayopakaraṇatvena viśeṣitatvāt /
children.translated_text: And by this much, there is no lack of distinction in greatness between an army where there are a hundred elephants and the like, and one where there are a thousand, because it is differentiated by being the instrument of augmentation and diminution.
Similarly, 'a flowering forest' and the like should also be understood.

children.text: pratyayabhedād dravyādibhyaḥ saṃkhyāyā bhedamuktvā vyapadeśādabhedādapyāha---ata eveti //
children.translated_text: Having stated the difference of number from substance and the rest due to the difference in cognition, he also states [the difference] from the perspective of designation — 'therefore.'

And the example is deficient in what is to be proved — he says 'even this one.'
When the parts of fried meat balls, produced by cooking in oil or ghee, are mixed with another substance, namely water, and a cooking product arises —
and that does not occur simultaneously —
therefore it is said 'when there is the assistance of a particular time.'
And that is merely a difference of conjunction between water and meat, not a whole (<s>avayavī</s>), because dissimilar things do not have the nature of having no water.
Nor is it correct that a substance conjoined with water belonging to the broth class is like one belonging to the milk class.
In the absence of water, even with hardness, the cognition and designation of milk remain the same.
But here, with hardness, there is neither the cognition nor the designation of broth — therefore it is proper that broth is merely a difference of conjunction between water and meat.
And that is established through experience as distinct from the things conjoined.
Likewise, the number 'plurality' (<s>bahutvasaṃkhyā</s>) is established through experience as distinct from the things numbered.
This should be explained similarly in each case.
Regarding things without beginning and end, it should be understood as 'in things whose parts have not begun.'
And since one's own position is not established merely by showing the absence of defects in the opponent's proof, the <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent) is asked for his proof — 'then what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for <s>dravya</s> (substance) being something different from <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the rest?'
Since this opponent, even though knowing through perception that substance is different from form and the rest, does not behave accordingly due to a kind of confused forgetfulness caused by habitual adherence to his own doctrine, he is made to behave so through this inference.
For there is a designation by all worldly examiners, just as 'the <s>kamaṇḍalu</s> (water-pot) belongs to the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>,' so too 'the <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the rest belong to the sandalwood.'
And therein the opponent accepts the apprehension of form and the rest, and also the apprehension of sandalwood.
Otherwise, since there would be no cognition of it — when only this much need be said, why does he say 'the non-apprehension of that'? From this we understand that in his view, the apprehension of form and the rest constitutes the cognition of sandalwood.
And it is not proper that this [cognition] is merely mind-born, i.e., based on memory.
It has been demonstrated that this determinate cognition (<s>savikalpikā</s>) is produced by the sense-organs, in the context of explaining the term 'having the nature of determination' (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>).
And the <s>pramāṇas</s> that would negate substance will be refuted in the section on examination.
Therefore the perceptibility of sandalwood is established.
This very sandalwood is different from form and the rest which are the objects of dispute, because what is itself perceptible is designated by all perceptible things.
<s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) too is designated by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, saying 'the form and the rest belong to <s>pradhāna</s>.'
To negate that, the qualifier 'perceptible' is used.
But <s>pradhāna</s> is imaginary and not perceptible; nevertheless, the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> have the designation that <s>pradhāna</s> is the root cause of form and the rest.
Therefore it is said 'by perceptible things.'
Even so, the mutual designation-designator relationship among form and the rest, which are mutually distinct, would be possible — thus it is said 'by all.'
Therefore sandalwood is distinct from all that designates it.
Where one should say 'of a perceptible thing by a perceptible thing,' the statement 'of a directly perceived thing by a directly perceived thing' is made to exclude entirely the designation from things inferred, such as taste and the rest, at the time of apprehending form — not that inference has no use here.
Having raised the fault of inconclusiveness in this, he refutes it — 'by army, forest, and the like.'
Having raised the suspicion of the non-existence of number, he refutes it — 'if that non-existence.'
What is being prescribed and what is being negated — by this correspondence, since negation is determined in dependence on affirmation, the object to be negated, namely oneness, must be accepted — and that is number: this is the meaning.
But let there be these cognitions; they would be based on substance alone, making number unnecessary — to this he says 'and qualified.'
The meaning is: not by rejecting a cause beyond substance.
He states another formulation — 'by the distinction from the cause of the cognition that is the object of that cognition.'
The object and the cause of the pot-cognition — by the distinction from the pot-cognition — since the cognition of number and the rest, qualified by that, requires a different cause.
What purpose does this serve? He says 'in origination.'
Just as in 'he kills the leopard for its skin,' here too in 'distinct from the object-and-cause that is the pot and the like,' the word 'cognition' should be supplied.
He raises an objection — 'large, flowering.'
The meaning is: number, being a quality, cannot have size or the connection with flowers.
He resolves it — 'this is not the fault.'
By the word 'location' (<s>sthāna</s>), derived as 'that which stands,' number is meant.
Those which possess it — elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and the like — are individually large as 'possessors of location.'
Among these, sometimes there are only a hundred, but sometimes, when there is the proximity of additional members of the same kind as possessors of location, they become augmented to a thousand.

children.text:
sthaṇuśabdenāpīti /
mūrtānāṃ samānadeśatvābhāvāt na parvasu khadiraśca sthāṇuśca samavetau /
na cāvasthitasaṃyogebhyastarūvināśāpekṣebhyaḥ sthāṇorūtpattiriti yuktam /
yasya dravyasya yāvān saṃyogapracayo 'samavāyikāraṇaṃ sa tāvānutpannamātra eva tajjanakaḥ, tasya kṣepāyogāt /
tasmāt parvaṇāṃ saṃsthānaviśeṣa eva sthāṇuriti gamayitavyam /
athāvasthitasaṃyogānāṃ dravyavināśāpekṣāṇāṃ janakatvam, tataḥ saṃyogapracayapadena sthaṇutvasāmānyaviśeṣavad dravyamupalakṣaṇīyam /
tacca khādiratarorbhinnamiti /
pratimāyā mahārajatamayyā avayavinyāḥ śarīraṃ saṃsthānameva, evaṃ śilāputrakasya avayavinaḥ saṃsthānameva śarīram /
śaṅkate---guṇasamudāyeti /
atādātmyenāgrahaṇaṃ vyatirekeṇāgrahaṇam pṛthak śabdo 'pyatādātmyameva brūte /
dūṣayati---agrahaṇasyeti /
satāmapi vastūnāmanupalambho yathā mūlakīlodakādīnāṃ pramāṇābhāvena, śaśaviṣāṇādīnāṃ cānupalambho grāhyābhāvena /
tasmād vyatirekāgrahaṇamātraṃ heturanekānta iti /
śaṅkate---grāhyābhāvāditi cet? grāhyābhāve satyagrahaṇāditi hetuḥ, na tvagrahaṇamātramityarthaḥ /
dūṣayati---pratijñārtheneti /
pratijñārthasyāsattvena /
tadviśiṣṭo heturasiddha ityarthaḥ /
śaṅkate---grahaṇeti /
grahaṇaṃ pramāṇam /
nirākaroti---na pramāṇābhāvamātrād vyatirekapratiṣedhaḥ, yastu yogyapramāṇābhāvāditi viśeṣayet taṃ pratyāha---yaśca tadagraha iti /
asiddhatā hetordeṣaḥ /
darśanasparśanābhyāmekārthapratisandhānameva rūpādivyatiriktadravyagrahaṇam /
ato guṇasamudāyavyatirekeṇāgrahaṇādityasiddho heturiti /

children.translated_text: Regarding otherness in one [locus] —
Because of the validity of the <s>pramāṇas</s>.
And because of the impossibility of non-otherness in one [locus].
He concludes the topic under discussion — 'therefore.' (14)

Also by the word '<s>sthāṇu</s>' (post/stump) —
Since corporeal things cannot occupy the same space, the <s>khadira</s> (acacia) tree and the stump are not co-inherent in the joints.
Nor is it proper that the stump originates from the stable conjunctions that require the destruction of the tree.
The aggregate of conjunctions that is the non-inherent cause of whatever substance — that aggregate, when merely not yet produced, is the generator of it, because of the impossibility of its being thrown away.
Therefore it should be understood that the stump is merely a specific configuration (<s>saṃsthānaviśeṣa</s>) of the joints.
If the conjunctions, which are stable and dependent on the destruction of the substance, have generative capacity, then by the term 'aggregate of conjunctions,' substance should be indicated, just like the universal and particular of stump-ness.
And that [substance] is distinct from the <s>khadira</s> tree.
The body of a large silver idol, which is a whole possessing parts, is merely a configuration — likewise the body of a stone figure (<s>śilāputraka</s>), which is a whole, is merely a configuration.
He raises a doubt — 'an aggregate of qualities.'
Non-apprehension as non-identical is non-apprehension through distinction; the word 'separately' also expresses non-identity.
He refutes — 'of non-apprehension.'
Even of existing things there is non-apprehension, as of roots, pegs, water, and the like due to absence of <s>pramāṇa</s>; and of hare's horns and the like, non-apprehension is due to absence of the object to be apprehended.
Therefore, mere non-apprehension of distinction is an inconclusive reason.
He raises a doubt — 'if due to absence of the apprehensible?' When there is absence of the apprehensible, then there is non-apprehension — this is the reason, not mere non-apprehension: this is the meaning.
He refutes — 'by what is to be proved.'
Due to the non-existence of what is to be proved,
the reason qualified by that is unestablished: this is the meaning.
He raises a doubt — 'apprehension.'
Apprehension means <s>pramāṇa</s>.
He refutes — not merely from the absence of <s>pramāṇa</s> is the distinction negated; and to one who would specify 'from the absence of a competent <s>pramāṇa</s>,' he replies — 'and one who [claims] non-apprehension of that.'
The fault is the unestablished nature of the reason.
The synthesis of a single object through seeing and touching is itself the apprehension of substance distinct from form and the rest.
Therefore, the reason 'because of non-apprehension distinct from the aggregate of qualities' is unestablished.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.15: <s>Buddhi</s> (cognition), <s>upalabdhi</s> (apprehension), <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) — these are synonymous.

children.text:
ātmādīnāṃ buddhihetūnāṃ lakṣaṇasyānantaraṃ hetumatī buddhirlakṣaṇīyetyāha vārttikakāraḥ---atha buddheravasaraprāptāyā iti /
lakṣaṇaṃ tāvat prakṛtatvādapadeṣṭavyameva, tadapadeśadvāreṇānyadapi kiñcit sūcanīyam /

children.translated_text: Therefore it is said — 'the <s>sūtra</s>.'
And another [purpose is] the refutation of the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine.
As stated by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) — 'of the unconscious instrument, cognition.'

children.text: ivakāreṇa nedaṃ pratyākhyānaparam, api tu lakṣaṇaparādayamapyarthaḥ pratīyamāno 'pekṣitaśca nopekṣaṇīya ityuktaṃ bhavati //
children.translated_text: By the particle 'as if' (<s>iva</s>), this [sūtra] is not aimed at rejection; rather, it means that this meaning too, being understood from the definition and being relevant, should not be disregarded.

After the definition of <s>ātman</s> and other causes of cognition, cognition which has causes is to be defined next — thus says the <s>vārttikakāra</s> (author of the <s>Vārttika</s>): 'Now, of <s>buddhi</s>, the occasion having arrived.'
First, the definition must certainly be stated since it is the topic under discussion; through the occasion of stating the definition, something else too is accomplished.

children.text:
buddhi---ram //15// sūtratātparyamāha---etairiti /
pṛcchati---kathamiti /
samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakaṃ hi lakṣaṇamavyabhicāritayā /
paryāyaśabdāśca saṃketamātrādhīnapravṛttayaḥ kva nāma na sambhavanti? tasmāt naite lakṣaṇamiti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---vyavacchedeti /
nanu vyabhicārasambhavena vyavacchedakatvamayuktamityata āha---etaiśceti /
saṃketo hi dvedhā, sarvajanīno yathā gauriti gojātīyasya vāyakaḥ, prādeśikaśca yathā caitra iti puruṣabhedasya /
tatra sarvajanīnaḥ śaknoti vyavacchedabuddhi bhāvayitum, tadvivakṣayaivoktam---etaiśceti /
upapattisāmarthyāditi bhāṣyāvayavaṃ vyācaṣṭe---paryāyeti /
acetanasyetyādi bhāṣyam /
tad vyācaṣṭe---ya āhurbuddheriti /
buddhiḥ kilatraiguṇyavikāraḥ /
traiguṇyaṃ cācenamityacetanā kevalamindriyapraṇālikayā arthākāreṇa pariṇamate /
citiśāktiścāpariṇāminī nityacaitanyasvabhāvā /
tasyāḥ sannidhānād ayaskāntamaṇikalpā buddhistatpratibimbodgrāhitayā caitanyarūpatāmāpannevārthākārapariṇatārthaṃ cetayate /
tena yo 'sau nīlākāraḥ pariṇāmo buddheḥ, sa jñānalakṣaṇā vṛttirityucyate /
ātmapratibimbasya tu buddhisaṃkrāntasya yo buddhyākāranīlasambandhaḥ, sa ātmano vyāpāra ivārthopalabdhirātmano vṛttirityākhyāyate /
tadidaṃ buddhitattvaṃ jaḍaprakṛtitayā indumaṇḍalam iva svayamaprakāśaṃ caitanyamārtaṇḍamaṇḍalacchāyāpattyā prakāśate, prakāśayati cārthāniti /
tannirākaraṇāya paryāyopanyāsaḥ /
nātmavṛtterūpabdheranyāsti buddhiḥ /
nāpi buddhivṛttirjñānam anyaditi /
ayamabhisandhiḥ /
na tāvad buddherātmācchāyāpattirindāviva mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalatejaḥsaṃkrāntiḥ pāramārthikī, citerapariṇāmitayā saṃkramāyogāt /
tasmād bhrāntiḥ /
sā ca na tāvad buddheḥ, tasyā acaitanyāt /
nāpyātmanaḥ, tasyāvṛttikatvāt, tathātve vā pariṇāmāpatteḥ /
tasmāt kṛpaṇadhanamivātmacaitanyaṃ na svaparopakārīti buddheḥ svābhāvikaṃ caitanyamāstheyam /
tathā ca ubhayacaitanye dūṣaṇamuktam /
pratyayavyavasthayā yadekakartṛtvānumāna tanna syādityarthaḥ /
atha dvayoścetanayorekā vṛttirbhedāgraho vā, tenaikakartṛkatvābhimāna ityata āha---buddhivṛttyaviśiṣṭāyāmiti /
children.translated_text: If two conscious entities have one activity, or if there is non-apprehension of difference [between them], and from that the notion of a single agent arises — to this he says 'when there is no distinction in the modification of <s>buddhi</s>.'
<s>Buddhi</s> (cognition) is the instrument of knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>).
By the etymological derivation 'that by which one knows,' <s>manas</s> (mind) is referred to.

children.text: gandhādiviṣayatayā sukhaduḥkhaviṣayatayā ceyaṃ buddhirbhāvyamānā nirvedāya kalpata iti //15 //
children.translated_text: This <s>buddhi</s>, when contemplated as having objects such as smell and the like, and as having pleasure and pain as objects, conduces to dispassion (<s>nirveda</s>). (15)

<s>Buddhi</s> (cognition) — (sūtra 15). He states the purport of the <s>sūtra</s> — 'by these.'
He asks — 'how?'
For a definition, by its non-deviating nature, distinguishes from both similar and dissimilar classes.
And synonymous words, whose usage depends merely on convention, where indeed are they not possible? Therefore these are not a definition — this is the meaning.
The answer — 'distinction.'
But since deviation is possible, the capacity for distinction would be improper — therefore he says 'and by these.'
For convention is of two kinds: universal, as 'cow' (<s>gauḥ</s>) is the designation of what belongs to the cow class; and particular, as '<s>Caitra</s>' is [the designation] of a specific person.
Among these, the universal [convention] is able to produce the cognition of distinction — with the intention of expressing that, it is said 'and by these.'
He explains the component of the <s>bhāṣya</s>, 'by the force of logical reasoning' — 'synonym.'
The <s>bhāṣya</s> reads 'of the unconscious' and so forth.
He explains that — 'those who say, of <s>buddhi</s>.'
<s>Buddhi</s>, they say, is a modification of the three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities of <s>prakṛti</s>).
And since the three <s>guṇas</s> are unconscious, it is unconscious, and merely transforms into the form of the object through the channel of the sense-organs.
And the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) is non-transforming, of the nature of eternal consciousness.
Due to its proximity, <s>buddhi</s>, like a magnet-gem, having assumed the appearance of consciousness through reflecting its image, cognizes the object that has transformed into the form of the object.
Thus, that particular transformation of <s>buddhi</s> into the form of blue is called the 'cognitive modification' (<s>jñānalakṣaṇā vṛttiḥ</s>).
But the connection of the reflection of the <s>ātman</s>, which has transferred to <s>buddhi</s>, with the blue form of <s>buddhi</s> — that is called 'the activity of the <s>ātman</s>' as if it were the apprehension of the object, 'the modification of the <s>ātman</s>.'
This reality of <s>buddhi</s>, being of inert material nature, like the disc of the moon, is itself non-luminous, but shines through the falling of the light of consciousness as if of the sun's disc, and illuminates objects.
To refute that, the synonyms are presented.
There is no cognition other than the modification of the <s>ātman</s>, i.e., apprehension.
Nor is the modification of <s>buddhi</s>, i.e., knowledge, anything different.
This is the intended meaning.
First, the falling of the <s>ātman's</s> reflection on <s>buddhi</s> is not real, like the transfer of the sun's radiance to the moon, because of the impossibility of transference due to the non-transforming nature of consciousness (<s>citi</s>).
Therefore it is an illusion.
And that [illusion] does not belong to <s>buddhi</s>, because it is unconscious.
Nor to the <s>ātman</s>, because it has no modifications — or if it did, transformation would follow.
Therefore, like a miser's wealth, the consciousness of the <s>ātman</s> benefits neither itself nor others — hence the inherent consciousness of <s>buddhi</s> should be accepted.
And the objection against both having consciousness has been stated.
The inference of a single agent from the regularity of cognitions would not hold — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.16: The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of <s>manas</s> (mind).

children.text: bhāṣyakāraḥ kramaprāptaṃ manolakṣaṇasūtramavatārayan utsūtramanyānyapi lakṣaṇāni āha---smṛtītyādi /
children.translated_text: The <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator), introducing the <s>sūtra</s> on the definition of <s>manas</s> which comes next in order, states other definitions as well beyond the <s>sūtra</s> — '<s>smṛti</s> (memory)' and so forth.
By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) in 'direct perception of pleasure etc.,' desire and the rest are included as objects [of perception].
By the word '<s>ādi</s>' in 'desire and the rest,' pleasure and the rest are included as effects.

children.text:
yuga---ṅgam //16// anindriyanimittā abāhyendriyanimittā ityarthaḥ /
smṛtītyādibhāṣyasya vārttikakāraḥ tātparyamāha---smṛtīti /
anindriyetyādibhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---yasmāditi /

children.translated_text: 'Conjoined with a sense organ' is justified for the purpose of excluding form and other [qualities] that belong to the sense organs.

children.text: tathāpi ākāśādīnāmapi manastvaṃ māṃ bhūdityata uktam---sahakārīti /
children.translated_text: Even so, lest ether (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the rest also become mind (<s>manas</s>), it is said — 'an auxiliary cause' etc.
Even so, lest light also [be considered mind], it is said — 'another cause' etc.
Even so, lest the self (<s>ātman</s>) also [be considered mind], it is said — 'non-pervading' etc.

Simultaneously //16// 'Not caused by sense organs' means 'not caused by external sense organs' — this is the meaning.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the purport of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'memory' — 'memory' etc.
He explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage beginning with 'not by sense organs' — 'since' etc.
