children.text:
ākṣipya bhāṣyaṃ samādhatte---kathaṃ punariti /
cakṣurādibhyo 'nutpattau satyāṃ kriyātvāt /
atra ca ya ātmano viśeṣaguṇāste sarve indriyajanmāno yathā gandhādipratyayāḥ, tathā ca vivādādhyāsitāḥ smṛtyādayaḥ /
tasmāt te 'pīndriyajanmānaḥ /
evaṃ ca saṃskārādiṣu na karaṇatvaprasaṅga iti /
sautraṃ hetumākṣipya samādhatte---athāyugapaditi /
sambandhibhedāditi /
yadā tasyaiva manaḥsaṃyuktasyendriyasya krameṇa nīlādayo 'rthāḥ sambadhyante tadā tatkramāt krama
ityarthaḥ /
bubhutsākramaṃ gṛhītvā siddhānte 'pi manaḥparityāgo mā bhūditi bhiyā uktam---satyāṃ bubhutsāyāmayugapadgrahaṇa iti /
na hi kiñcitkaraṇaṃ sambaddhamapi saditi syāt /
yadyevaṃ dhārāvāhikajñānotvattirna syāt, dvitīyādijñāneṣvapi saiva sāmagrīti sakṛdeva yāvat kartavayakaraṇāt samarthasya kṣepāyogāt /
kṣepayoge vā paścādapi na janayet, aviśeṣāt /
na ca karturapyayaṃ kramakāritādharmaḥ sa hyanekakaraṇādhiṣṭhānena yugapannānākāryāṇi karoti /
yathā yugapanmāṇavako gacchati, paṭhati, panthānaṃ vīkṣate, vahati cācāryasya kamaṇḍalumiti /
tasmāt sarvamavadātam /
tadidamapimanaḥ smṛtyādisādhanatayā bhāvyamānaṃ nirvedāya kalpata iti saddhim//26 //
children.translated_text:
Having raised an objection, the <s>Bhāṣya</s> resolves it — 'but how then?' etc.
When there is non-origination from the eye and other [external sense organs], [memory etc. still arise] because they are actions.
And here, all the specific qualities of the self are born of the sense organs, just as cognitions of smell and the rest [are], and similarly memory and the rest, which are the subject of dispute, [are also sense-organ-born].
Therefore they too are born of the sense organs.
And thus there is no unwanted consequence of <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression) etc. being instruments.
Having raised the reason from the <s>sūtra</s>, he resolves it — 'but not simultaneously' etc.
'Due to difference in the related [objects]' etc.
When the very sense organ that is conjoined with the mind (<s>manas</s>) is sequentially related to objects like blue etc., then from that sequence arises the sequence [of cognitions] — this is the meaning.
Accepting the sequence of desire to know, lest the mind be abandoned even in the established doctrine, it is said — 'when there is a desire to know, there is non-simultaneous apprehension.'
For no instrument, even when connected, would [produce cognition] without [the desire to know].
If so, there would be no continuous stream of cognitions, since in the second and subsequent cognitions the very same aggregate [of causes exists], and that which is capable [of producing all at once] cannot be delayed.
Or if delay is possible, it should not produce [cognitions] even later, since there is no difference [in conditions].
Nor is this property of causing sequence attributable to the agent [soul] either, for he, presiding over multiple instruments, performs various actions simultaneously.
Just as a boy simultaneously walks, recites, watches the road, and carries the teacher's water-pot.
Therefore everything is clear.
Thus this mind (<s>manas</s>) too, being contemplated as the instrument of memory and the rest, serves the purpose of dispassion — this is established //16//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.17: Activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) is the initiation of speech, cognition, and body.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says] 'but in the order of enumeration' — to introduce the definition of <s>pravṛtti</s> (activity).
The activity of the mind (<s>manas</s>) too needs to be shown.

children.text: na cāpratipādite manasi śakyā darśayitumiti manaso 'nantaratvaṃ pravṛtterityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And since [the activity of the mind] cannot be shown without first establishing the mind, the mind [is defined] immediately before <s>pravṛtti</s> — this is the meaning.

children.text:
pravṛ---mbhaḥ //17// ārambha pravṛttiḥ /
sā ca dvividhā jñānahetuḥ kriyāhetuśca /
tatra yā jñānotpādadvāreṇa puṇyapāpahetuḥ sā vākpravṛttiḥ /
vāgiti ca jñāpakahetūpalakṣaṇam /
tena manasā iṣṭadevatādyanucintanaṃ cakṣurādibhiśca sādhvasādhudarśanādi sūcitaṃ bhavati /
kriyāheturdvayī kāyanimittā manonimittā ceti /
tadetad vārttikakāro vibhajate---śarīreṇeti /

children.translated_text: But it has been stated in the second <s>sūtra</s> that activity is the cause of birth.

children.text: na ceyaṃ kṣaṇikā satī āmuṣmikaṃ janma sādhayitumarhati /
children.translated_text: And this [activity], being momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), cannot be capable of bringing about birth in a future life.
Therefore, [this would constitute] a contradiction with the second <s>sūtra</s> — he raises this objection with 'because of being momentary' etc.
He resolves it — 'no' etc. //17//

Activity is initiation //17// <s>Ārambha</s> means activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>).
And that is of two kinds: that which is the cause of cognition, and that which is the cause of action.
Among these, that which is the cause of merit and demerit through the production of cognition is verbal activity (<s>vākpravṛtti</s>).
And 'speech' (<s>vāk</s>) is a figurative designation for the cause of making known.
Thus, mental contemplation of one's chosen deity etc. through the mind, and seeing virtuous and non-virtuous things through the eye and other [senses], are indicated.
The cause of action is twofold: that caused by the body and that caused by the mind.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> classifies this — 'by the body' etc.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.18: Faults (<s>doṣas</s>) are characterized by [their power of] impelling.
Since the operation of the impeller is determined as being preceded by the operation of the impelled, the definition of faults (<s>doṣa</s>) comes immediately after activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>).

children.text:
prava---ṣāḥ //18// rāgadveṣau mohaprabhavau puruṣaṃ pravartamānaṃ pravartayataḥ /
tayordharmaḥ pravartanā /
sā ca mohaikārthasamavāyaḥ /
tāvaddhi ayaṃ rāgādivaśaḥ spandate, yāvadasya moho vartate iti /
pratyātmavedanīyā ityādi codyabhāṣyam /
tasyārthaḥ /
lakṣaṇaṃ khalvanumānam /
na pratyātmavedanīyeṣu samānāsamānajātīyavyāvṛtteṣu sphuṭatareṣu tad yuktamiti bhāvaḥ /
parihārabhāṣyam---karmalakṣaṇā ityādi /
tasyārthaḥ /
svarūpataḥ sphuṭatve 'pi na nirvedaviṣayatayā sphuṭatā /
tathā ceha prayojanam /
pravartanāvattvena caite nirvedaviṣayāḥ /
sā ca pravṛttyā kāryeṇa lakṣyata iti karmalakṣaṇā ityuktam /
yataḥ karmaṇā pravṛttyā pravartakarāgādiyuktāḥ puruṣā lakṣyante, ato rāgādīnāṃ pravartanāvatvattmapi lakṣitaṃ bhavati /
bahu noktaṃ bhavatīti /
svarūpamātraṃ rāgādīnāmuktaṃ bhavati, na tu pravartanāvatvamapi teṣāmityarthaḥ /
tadetat sarvaṃ vārttikakāraḥ praśnapūrvakaṃ vyācaṣṭe---kā punariti /
avaśo 'svatantraḥ /
sā punariyaṃ pravartanā pravartakānāṃ doṣāṇāṃ vyāpāraḥ kathaṃ gamyate? doṣā hi gamyante, na tu teṣāṃ pravṛttihetutvamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: But how is it known that this impelling is the operation of the faults that are the impellers? For the faults are known, but not their being the cause of activity — this is the meaning.
The answer — 'by each individual self' etc.
In one's own and others' selves, respectively, through direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>).

children.text: mauhaikārthasamavāyo hi rāgādīnāṃ mānasa pratyakṣavedanīya ityarthaḥ //18 //
children.translated_text: For the co-existence of attachment and the rest with delusion in a single purpose is directly perceived by mental perception — this is the meaning. //18//

Faults //18// Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), which arise from delusion (<s>moha</s>), impel a person who is [already] inclined to act.
Their function is impelling (<s>pravartanā</s>).
And that [impelling] is the co-existence with delusion in a single purpose.
For a person acts under the influence of attachment and the rest as long as delusion persists in him.
'Perceived by each individual self' etc. is the objection-<s>Bhāṣya</s>.
Its meaning [is as follows]:
A definition is indeed an inference.
But it is not appropriate for things that are perceived by each individual self, that are differentiated from things of the same and different classes, and that are most manifest — this is the purport.
The resolution-<s>Bhāṣya</s> [begins] — 'characterized by action' etc.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.19: Transmigration (<s>pretyabhāva</s>) is being born again.
He defines <s>pretyabhāva</s> (transmigration), which comes next in the order of enumeration — 'again... state' //19//

children.text:
satvanikāyaḥ prāṇinikāyaḥ /
nanvātmano notpattiḥ saṃbhavati nityatvādityata āha bhāṣyakāraḥ---utpannasya saṃbaddhasyeti /
tadetad vārttikakāro vyācaṣṭe---pūrveti /
punargrahaṇamiti /
punarityabhyāsamāha, tathā cānāditā sūcitā bhavati /
tadetad vārttikajātaṃ dvitīyasūtre kṛtavyākhyānam /
pūrvābhyastasūtre cāyamartha upapādayiṣyate /
ājara/jarībhāva ityāyamabhāṣayā asyārthasyāgamikatvaṃ sūcayati /
kriyāmiti upasarpaṇamapasarpaṇaṃ cetyarthaḥ//19 //
children.translated_text:
A class of beings (<s>satvanikāya</s>) means a class of living creatures (<s>prāṇinikāya</s>).
Since the <s>ātman</s>, being eternal, cannot have origination, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says — 'of one who has been born, who has been connected.'
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this — 'previous' etc.
'The word <s>punar</s> (again)' etc.
He says that <s>punar</s> (again) indicates repetition, and thus beginninglessness (<s>anāditā</s>) is suggested.
This <s>Vārttika</s> passage has been explained in connection with the second <s>sūtra</s>.
And this meaning will be established in the <s>sūtra</s> that recapitulates the preceding.
'Up to old age / the process of aging' — by this he indicates the future relevance of this meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.20: The fruit (<s>phala</s>) is the result produced by activity and faults.

children.text: yadyapi śarīrendriyabuddhisukhaduḥkhopabhogātiriktaṃ gauṇamukhyaphalaṃ bhinnaṃ nāsti, te ca yathāyogaṃ pūrvaṃ lakṣitāḥ, tenāpi ca rūpeṇa te nirvedopayoginaḥ, tathāpi pravṛttidoṣajanitatvenāpi rūpeṇāmī nirvedopayogina iti tena rūpeṇa lakṣyante //
children.translated_text: Although there is no fruit, whether primary or secondary, distinct from the experience of body, sense organs, cognition, pleasure, and pain — and these have already been defined in their respective places, and even in that form they serve the purpose of dispassion — nevertheless, since they also serve the purpose of dispassion in the form of being produced by activity and faults, they are defined in that form as well.
Activity... fruit //

children.text:
atra ca pravṛttijanita iti vaktavye doṣagrahaṇaṃ na kevalaṃ pravṛtti prati doṣāṇāṃ hetubhāvaḥ,
api tu pravṛttikārye sūkhaduḥkhe api prati iti darśanārtham /
doṣasalilāvasiktāyāṃ khalvātmabhūmau dharmādharmabīje sukhaduḥkhe janayataḥ, nānyathā /
na cāsti sambhavo na tatra tṛṣyati tacca tasya sukham, na ca tad dveṣṭi tacca tasya duḥkhamiti /
sūtre arthagrahaṇaṃ gauṇamukhyaphalāvarodhārtham /
bhāṣye ca niṣṭhā samāptiḥ /
sā ca mahāpralaye 'ṣyastītyata uktam---paryavasānamiti /
avasānamātramasti, na tu paritaḥ punarapi sargahānopādānayorbhāvādityarthaḥ /
subodhaṃ vārttikam//20 //
children.translated_text:
And here, the mention of 'faults' when it would suffice to say 'produced by activity' is for the purpose of showing that faults are not merely causes of activity,
but are also causes of pleasure and pain, which are the effects of activity.
For in the ground of the self irrigated by the waters of faults, the seeds of merit (<s>dharma</s>) and demerit (<s>adharma</s>) produce pleasure and pain — not otherwise.
And there is no possibility that one does not thirst for that which is one's pleasure, nor that one does not hate that which is one's pain.
The word '<s>artha</s>' (object/result) in the <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of encompassing both primary and secondary fruits.
In the <s>Bhāṣya</s>
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.21: Pain (<s>duḥkha</s>) is characterized by affliction (<s>bādhanā</s>).

children.text:
nānukte śarīrādau teṣāṃ duḥkhatvaṃ śakyaṃ lakṣayitumiti tallakṣaṇebhyaḥ paramidanduḥkhalakṣaṇam ---
bādha---kham //21// atra ca bādhaneti bādhanāviṣayāṃ buddhimupalakṣayati /
tena bādhanā ca tadanuṣaṅgiṇaśca śarīrādayo gauṇamukhyabhāvena lakṣitā bhavanti /
saiva hi bādhanā buddhirduḥkhe mukhyā, śarīrādau gauṇīti /
alamebhiriti pratyayo nirvedaḥ, vaśitayā yoginaḥ svayamupalabhante svayamupanīteṣvapi viṣayeṣu audāsīnyamupekṣābuddhirvairāgyam /
lakṣaṇaśabda iti vārttikam /
anuṣaṅgaśca sambandhaḥ /
sa ca bādhanāyāṃ viṣayaviṣayībhāvaḥ /
śarīrādiṣu uktaḥ /
kecid
viraktaṃmānyā mānyante na sukhaṃ nāmāsti svarūpata iti /

children.translated_text: Wishing to reject those [views], he says — 'but in its own nature, pain' etc.
<s>Vikalpa</s> (alternative) means distinction.
Because there would be the unwanted consequence that [<s>dharma</s>] has non-existence as its fruit.

children.text: yadyapyupāttaduritakṣayahetavo 'pi dharmāḥ santi, tathāpyadhikādhikotkarṣaphalānāṃ darśapaurṇamāsādīnāṃ sahasrasaṃvatsaraparyantānāṃ vidhāyakebhyo vacanebhyo bhāvaphala eva dharmo gamyate bhāvasyaibotkarṣaśālitvāditi //21 //
children.translated_text: Although there are <s>dharmas</s> (meritorious acts) that are causes of the destruction of previously accumulated sin, nevertheless, from the Vedic injunctions prescribing rituals such as <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> and others extending up to a thousand years, which produce progressively greater excellence as their fruit, <s>dharma</s> is understood as having a positive result, since positive [existence] alone possesses excellence. //21//

Since the nature of suffering in body and the rest cannot be defined without first describing them, this definition of suffering comes after those definitions —
Affliction... pain //21// And here, '<s>bādhanā</s>' (affliction) figuratively indicates the cognition that has affliction as its object.
Thus, affliction and the body etc. that accompany it are defined in a primary and secondary sense.
For the cognition of affliction is primary in [the definition of] pain, while [its application to] body etc. is secondary.
Dispassion (<s>nirveda</s>) is the conviction 'enough of these'; yogins attain it through mastery, even regarding self-produced [experiences].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.22: <s>Apavarga</s> (liberation) is the absolute release from that [suffering].
The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> introduces the definition of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), which comes next in order — 'where, however' etc.

children.text:
tadar---gaḥ //22// tadityanantaraṃ gauṇamukhyabhedabhinnaṃ duḥkhaṃ parāmṛśatītyāha bhāṣyakāraḥ---tena duḥkheneti /
mukhyameva duḥkhamiti bhramo mā bhūdata āha---janmaneti /
anena jāyamānā duḥkhaśabdena sarve śarīrādaya ucyanate ityuktaṃ bhavati /
abhayamiti punaḥ saṃsārabhayābhāvamāha,
abhayaṃ vai brahma
ityasakṛdabhayaśruteḥ /
ye tu brahmaiva nāmarūpaprapañcātmanā pariṇamata ityāhuḥ, tān pratyāha---ajaramiti /
sarvātmanā vā pariṇāma, ekadeśena vā? pūrvasmin kalpe sarvātmanā brahmaṇo 'nyathātvād vināśaprasaṅgaḥ /
ekadeśapariṇāme tu sāvayavatvāt ghaṭadivadanityatvaprasaṅgaḥ iti sūktam---ajaramiti /
vaināśikāḥ prāhuḥ
iti /

children.translated_text: To them he responds — 'the state of deathlessness' etc.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> will establish this further on.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage — 'by that' etc.
The word '<s>ātyantika</s>' (absolute) is for the purpose of excluding the state during the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>).

That... liberation //22// The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says that the word 'that' refers to suffering in both its primary and secondary senses — 'from that suffering' etc.
Lest there be the misconception that only primary suffering [is meant], he says — 'birth' etc.
By this it is stated that all [categories] beginning with body etc. are denoted by the word 'suffering' as they are being produced.
'Fearlessness' — he further states the absence of fear of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth),
since [the <s>Upaniṣad</s>] repeatedly declares '<s>abhayaṃ vai brahma</s>' (Brahman is indeed fearlessness).
To those who say that <s>Brahman</s> itself transforms into the manifold world of name and form, he responds —

children.text:
atra bhāṣyaṃ nityaṃ sukhamātmana ityādi /
asyārthaḥ---
vijñānamānandaṃ brahma
iti sāmānādhikaraṇyaśruteḥ brahmasvabhāvaṃ sukham, tayā ca brahmaṇo nityatvāt tadapi nityamityarthaḥ /
ātmana iti ca ṣaṣṭhī rāhoḥ śira itivat mantavyā /
tadetad bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---ātyantikīti /
teṣāmityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---tanneti /
atrānumānamupanyasyātiprasaṅgena nirākaroti---na, neti /
athātmani duḥkhādikaṃ nityaṃ necchati, tatrāha---anaikāntikatā vā /
nityasyābhivyaktirityādibhāṣyārthamāha---nityamiti /
ayamabhisandhiḥ /
sukhaṃ tāvadātmano guṇo nātmā /
upapādito hi guṇaguṇinorbhedaḥ /
evaṃ vijñānamapyātmaguṇaḥ,na hyudayavyayavatībhyo vijñānavyaktibhyo 'nudayavyayadharmā bhavitumarhatyabhinna ātmā /
na cātmaiva vijñānasvabhāvaḥ tattadviṣayopadhānenodayavyayadharmeva bhavatīti sāṃpratam /
ghaṭamahaṃ jānāmīti mānasyāṃ buddhau trayāṇāmapi jñānajñeyajñātaṇāṃ bhedenānuvyavasāyāt /
viṣayatajjñānabhede 'pi ca jñāturekasya pratisandhīyamānatvāt /
na caitadasati bādhake bhedajñānaṃ bhrāntamiti yuktam /
na cāgantukajñānātiriktaṃ svābhāvikamātmani caitanyamanubhūyate /
na cātmaiva tatsvabhāvaḥ, suṣuptatvānupapatteḥ /
acetayanneva hi suṣupata ityucyate /
na ca tadā viṣayaśūnyaṃ svaniṣṭhamātmacaitanyamiti yuktam /
children.translated_text: And it is not proper [to say] that at that time there is self-consciousness resting in itself, devoid of objects /
Because there would be the unwanted consequence that one who has awoken from deep sleep would remember that state as distinct [from waking], just as one remembers the end of a dream /
And it has been established in the <s>sūtra</s> on perception that pleasure is not of the same class as cognition /

children.text: na ca kiñcidapi sava prakāśamastīti caturthe vijñāna vādaṃ nirākurvan vakṣyati //
children.translated_text: And he will say in the fourth [book], while refuting the doctrine of consciousness (<s>vijñānavāda</s>), that nothing whatsoever is self-luminous //

Here the <s>bhāṣya</s> [reads]: 'pleasure is eternal, belonging to the self' and so on /
The meaning of this is:
From the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) stating co-reference— '<s>Brahman</s> is consciousness and bliss'—
pleasure has the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, and since <s>Brahman</s> is eternal, that [pleasure] too is eternal— this is the meaning /
And the genitive in '<s>ātmanaḥ</s>' (of the self) should be understood as in '<s>Rāhoḥ śiraḥ</s>' (the head of <s>Rāhu</s>) [i.e., an appositional genitive] /
This <s>bhāṣya</s> he explains— '<s>ātyantikī</s>' (absolute) /
The <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'of those' he explains— 'that, no' /
Here, presenting an inference, he refutes by overextension— 'no, no' /
Now, if one does not accept that suffering and the like in the self are eternal, to that he says— 'or inconclusiveness' /
The meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'the manifestation of what is eternal' he states— 'eternal' /
This is the purport:
Pleasure, for one thing, is a quality of the self, not the self itself /
For the difference between quality and quality-possessor has been established /
Likewise, cognition too is a quality of the self; for the self, which has the nature of not arising and not perishing, cannot be non-different from the manifestations of cognition that arise and perish /
And it is not proper that the self itself has the nature of consciousness and simply becomes subject to arising and perishing through the superimposition of various objects /
Because in the mental cognition 'I know the pot,' all three— knowledge, the knowable, and the knower— are ascertained as distinct in reflective awareness /
And even when the object and its cognition differ, the single knower is recognized [as the same] /
And it is not proper to say that this cognition of difference is erroneous when there is no sublating cognition /
And no natural consciousness inherent in the self, distinct from adventitious cognitions, is experienced /
And the self itself does not have that nature [of consciousness], because deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>) would be inexplicable /
For one who is not conscious at all is said to be 'in deep sleep' /

children.text:
tadevaṃ vyavasthite dūṣaṇa bhāṣyavārttikoktaṃ draṣṭavyaṃ yathāyamātmamanaḥsaṃyoga iti /
saṃsārāvasthāyāṃ tāvadayamātmamanaḥsaṃyogo dharmaṃ nimittamapekṣamāṇaḥ sukhajñānam ākārṣīt /
yadi tu muktyavasthāyāṃ tadanapekṣa eva sukhajñānaṃ karoti, hanta rūpādijñāneṣu indriyāntarāṇyapi nāpekṣeteti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkate---yogajeti /
na vayaṃ viṣayamātrāpekṣāṃ brūmo yena rūpādiṣvapi jñānamutpādayet, api tu saṃsārāvasthāyāṃ yat sukhajñānāyānenāpekṣitaṃ tadapekṣate /
dharmaśca tadā tenāpekṣita iti muktyavasthāyāmapi dharmamevāpekṣate /
etāvān viśeṣo yadayaṃ yogaja iti /
tathā ca na rūpādivijñāna prasaṅga iti /
śaṅkate---nityo 'sāviti /
nirākaroti---yogeti /
nanu tvanmate yathā sukhasaṃvedanaṃ jihāsitam, evamasmanmate 'pi sukhasaṃvedanahānāya ghaṭiṣyata ityata āha---na cāyaṃ sukhamiti /
asmanmate hi duḥkhahānāyaiva tadanuṣaktaṃ sukhaṃ jihāsitam /
nityaṃ tu sukhaṃ sarvaduḥkhavinirmuktaṃ sanna duḥkhahānāya jihāsitaṃ saṃbhavati ityarthaḥ /
na kevalamānukūlyāt pratibandhakatvaṃ nāsti śarīrādīnām, pratyuta muktyavasthāyāmapi kalpanīyatā ityāha---nityaṃ śarīrādi iti /
siddhāntino vacanamanubhāṣya deśayeti---pramāṇābhāvādityuktaṃ tacca neti /
śāstreṇa hi mokṣasādhane lokaḥ pravartanīyaḥ /
apravartamānaśca pravartanīyaḥ /

children.translated_text: And one who desires a desired object engages in the means for it /
And pleasure is desired /
The meaning is: liberation has the nature of pleasure /
He resolves [the objection] that this worldly engagement is a cause of doubt through inconclusiveness— 'no, because of engagement' //

Thus, when this has been established, the refutation should be seen as stated in the <s>bhāṣya</s> and <s>vārttika</s>: 'this conjunction of the self and mind' /
In the state of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), this conjunction of the self and mind, requiring <s>dharma</s> (merit) as its cause, produces the cognition of pleasure /
But if in the state of liberation it produces cognition of pleasure without requiring that [dharma], then it should not require other sense organs either for the cognition of form and the like— this is the purport /
He raises a doubt— 'born of <s>yoga</s>' /
We do not say it requires merely objects, such that it would produce cognition even of form and the like; rather, in the state of <s>saṃsāra</s>, whatever was required by it for the cognition of pleasure, that it requires [in liberation too] /
And <s>dharma</s> was required by it at that time— so even in the state of liberation, it requires <s>dharma</s> alone /
The only difference is that this [cognition] is born of <s>yoga</s> /
And thus there is no unwanted consequence of cognition of form and the like /
He raises a doubt— 'that is eternal' /
He refutes— '<s>yoga</s>' /
Now, just as in your view the experience of pleasure is to be abandoned, so in our view too one may strive to abandon the experience of pleasure— to this he says— 'and this is not pleasure' /
For in our view, pleasure is to be abandoned only for the sake of abandoning suffering, to which it is attached /
But eternal pleasure, being completely free from all suffering, cannot possibly be abandoned for the sake of abandoning suffering— this is the meaning /
Not only is there no obstruction from the body and the like due to [pleasure's] favorability, but on the contrary, [the body etc.] must be posited even in the state of liberation— he says— 'eternal body etc.' /
Having restated the <s>Siddhāntin</s>'s statement, he teaches— 'it has been said: because of the absence of proof, and that is not so' /
For people must be motivated toward the means of liberation by the <s>śāstra</s> /
And one who is not motivated must be motivated /

children.text:
syādetat /
mukhyāsaṃbhave gauṇamarīyate /
sukhaśabdaśca sukhe mukhyaḥ, bhāktastu duḥkhanivṛttau /
tasmāt nityānanda eva mokṣa ityata āha---yadi punariti /
saṃcakṣāṇakaḥ saṃkhyānapravṛtto yogī /
dharmādharmau tāvadātmani pāramārthikau, na tvavidyākalpitau /
tau ca vītarāgeṇāsaktena satā śakyau bhogena kṣetum, na tu śaktane /
sa hi saktasteṣu teṣu viṣayeṣu upāttamupāttaṃ bhu/jānaḥ tyaktaṃ tyaktaṃ copādadānaḥ saṃsārāt na mucyeta /
tasmādayaṃ rāgo bandhanamiti samājñātaḥ /
tannibandhanā ca pravṛttiḥ parihartavyā /
anyathā tu nityasukhāvadhāraṇalāliteyaṃ tṛṣṇāpiśācī labdhaprasarā viṣayasukheṣvapi pratyāsanneṣu purūṣaṃ pravartayantī mokṣamasya sūdūraṃ pratikṣipediti manāgapi prasaro 'syā na dātavyaḥ /
tasmāt nityānandapratipādakaśrutirātyantike duḥkhaviyoge bhāktīti yuktamiti bhāvaḥ /
codayati---yadyapīti /
rāgavad dveṣasyāpi prasaro na dātavyaḥ /
tasya ca tvayā prasaro datta iti tulayo doṣa iti /
pariharati---na, apratikūlatvāt /
yathā nityasukhopādānaṃ mokṣam apratikūlayā saktyā sapratikūlaṃ naivamātyantikaduḥkhahānaṃ duḥkhadveṣānuṣaktam /
dveṣaḥ krodho manyurityanarthāntaram /
jvalanātmako hi sa bhavati /
naivaṃ vairāgyam /
alaṃ pratyayo hi sa ityapratikūlaṃ duḥkhahānamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For it has the cognition 'enough'— so the cessation of suffering is not adverse— this is the meaning /

children.text: tadanena nityaṃ sukhamātmano mokṣe 'bhivyajyate ityādi tasmin prahīṇe nāsya nityasukharāgaḥ pratikūlo bhavatītyevamantaṃ bhāṣyajātaṃ vyākhyātaṃ veditavyam /
children.translated_text: It should be understood that by this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> from 'eternal pleasure belonging to the self is manifested in liberation' up to 'when that [suffering] has been abandoned, this eternal-pleasure-attachment is not adverse to him' has been explained /
The meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning 'if thus' is as follows: /

children.text: evaṃ vairāgyeṇa mokṣamāṇasya pravṛtto satyām, muktasya yadi nityaṃ sukhaṃ bhavati kāmaṃ bhavatu mā vā bhūt, ubhayorapi pakṣayoḥ vītarāgasya pravṛttau na mokṣādhigamo vikalpyate, na sandigdho bhavatītyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: When one who is being liberated through dispassion is engaged in practice, whether there is eternal pleasure for the liberated one or not— let it be or let it not— in both alternatives, for one who is dispassionate, the attainment of liberation through practice is not subject to doubt, is not uncertain— this is the meaning //

It might be objected:
When the primary meaning is impossible, the secondary meaning is resorted to /
And the word 'pleasure' is primary for [actual] pleasure, but secondary (figurative) for the cessation of suffering /
Therefore, liberation is nothing but eternal bliss— to this he says— 'if, however' /
The 'one who expounds' is a <s>yogin</s> engaged in enumeration /
<s>Dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) are indeed real in the self, not merely superimposed by ignorance /
And they can be exhausted through experience by one who is dispassionate and unattached, but not by one who is attached /
For such a person, being attached to various objects, consuming whatever is taken up and grasping whatever is relinquished, would not be freed from <s>saṃsāra</s> /
Therefore, this attachment (<s>rāga</s>) has been recognized as bondage /
And the activity based on it must be avoided /
Otherwise, this she-demon of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), pampered by the certainty of eternal pleasure and having gained free rein, would, by driving a person toward even the proximate pleasures of sense-objects, push his liberation far away— so not even the slightest scope should be given to her /
Therefore, it is proper that the <s>śruti</s> teaching eternal bliss is figurative, [meaning] the absolute cessation of suffering— this is the purport /
He objects— 'even if' /
Just as attachment should not be given scope, so too aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) should not be given scope /
And you have given scope to that [aversion]— so the fault is equal /
He resolves— 'no, because of not being adverse' /
Just as the acceptance of eternal pleasure in liberation, through adverse attachment, is adverse— not so is the absolute cessation of suffering accompanied by aversion toward suffering /
Aversion, anger, and indignation are the same thing /
For that [anger] has the nature of burning /
Dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) is not like that /

children.text:
vaināśikānāṃ mokṣamupanyasyati---cittaṃ vimucyata iti /
saṃsārī hi mucyate /
rāgādayastaddhetavaḥ /
na cātmani nitye rāgādayaḥ saṃsāraṃ kartumutsahante, nityasyāvikāryatvena tādavasthyādupaneyāpaneyābhāvāt /

children.translated_text: As they say: /
What do rain and sunshine do to space? Their effect is on leather /
If [the self is] like leather, it is non-eternal; if like space, the result is void //

He presents the view of the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (Buddhist annihilationists) on liberation— 'the mind is released' /
For it is the one in <s>saṃsāra</s> who is released /
Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the like are its causes /
And attachment and the like cannot bring about <s>saṃsāra</s> in an eternal self, because what is eternal, being unmodifiable, remains in the same state, and thus there is nothing to be added or removed /

children.text:
iti /
cittaṃ tu kāryaṃ rāgādivaśāt saṃsārī, tadviyogācca mucyate iti yuktamityarthaḥ /
devamanuṣyādijātiḥ gatiḥ tatrotpattiḥ /
tadetad dūṣayati---na, ayatnata iti /
kṣaṇikatvāt cittasya, janmavināśaprayojanameva /
janmāntaraṃ hi vināśa iti kṣaṇasyābhedyatvenopaneyāpaneyābhāvāt /
svarasabhaṅgitvācca vaiyarthyamityarthaḥ /
śaṅkate---santateriti /
anādiḥ khalu kāryakāraṇapravāharūpā buddhīnāṃ santatiḥ /
sā cātmasākṣātkāronmūlitasavāsanakleśajālasya nivartate /
nivṛttiśceyameva tasyā yat tatsantānavartinaścetaso 'nāgatasyānutpāda iti bhāvaḥ /
nirākaroti---na, tasyāśakyatvāt /
utpannasyānutpādo na śakyaḥ, nāpi santānanivṛttiḥ śakyā kartum, antyakṣaṇānupapatteḥ /
sa hi antyaḥ kṣaṇaḥ kiñcidārabhate na vā? ārambhe nāntya iti na kāryakāraṇapravāhanivṛttiḥ, pravāhaśca santāna iti na santānanivṛttiḥ /
anārambhe tasyāsāmarthyenāsattvam /
tataḥ pūrve sarve 'pi kṣaṇā asantaḥ syuriti kasyoccheda iti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkate---anāgatānutpāda iti /
tathā satyanāgatānutpādalakṣaṇārthakriyākāritvādantyakṣaṇopapattiriti bhāvaḥ /
nirākaroti---anāgateti /
prāgabhāvasyānāditvādityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He asks— 'then whose [liberation is it]?' /
Because what is eternal cannot be benefited, there is nothing to be removed— this is the purport /
The reply— 'that which' /

children.text: yathā cākṣaṇikasyopakāryatvaṃ tathā kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅge upapādayiṣyata iti saddhim //22 //
children.translated_text: And how a non-momentary entity can be benefited will be established in the refutation of momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>)— along with [the sūtra] //22//

Thus /
But the mind, being an effect, transmigrates through the influence of attachment and the like, and is released by separation from them— this is proper— this is the meaning /
Birth in the species of gods, humans, and the like is <s>gati</s> (destiny); birth there [is the result] /
He refutes this— 'no, because of effortlessness' /
Because of the momentariness of the mind, its very birth is its destruction /
For the next birth is [the same as] destruction, since a moment, being indivisible, has nothing to be added or removed /
And because of its natural tendency to perish, [effort toward liberation] is pointless— this is the meaning /
He raises a doubt— 'of the continuum' /
The continuum of cognitions, in the form of a stream of cause and effect, is indeed beginningless /
And it ceases for one whose entire net of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) together with latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) has been uprooted by the direct realization of the self /
And this cessation is precisely the non-arising of the future [moment of] consciousness belonging to that continuum— this is the purport /
He refutes— 'no, because of its impossibility' /
The non-arising of what has arisen is impossible; nor can the cessation of the continuum be brought about, because of the impossibility of a final moment /
For does that final moment produce something or not? If it produces something, it is not the final one— so there is no cessation of the cause-effect stream; and since the stream is the continuum, there is no cessation of the continuum /
If it does not produce anything, then it does not exist due to its incapacity /
Then all prior moments too would be non-existent— so whose cessation would it be?— this is the purport /
He raises a doubt— 'the non-arising of the future' /
If so, since it has the efficacy characterized by the non-arising of the future, the final moment is possible— this is the purport /
He refutes— 'of the future' /
The meaning is: because prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) is beginningless /

<s>NyS</s> 1.1.23: Doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) is inquiry characterized by expectation of a specific [determination], arising from the apprehension of common properties belonging to many, from conflicting testimony, and from the irregularity of perception and non-perception //

children.text:
saṃśayalakṣaṇāvatāraṇaparaṃ bhāṣyaṃ sthānavata etarhi iti /
tasyārthaḥ /
sthānaṃ kramaḥ /
tadvataḥ /
etarhi idānīmiti /
kkacit pāṭhaḥ sthānavata eva tarhīti /
tarhi tadānīmuddeśasamaye, kramavataḥ saṃśayasya prameyānantaramuddiṣṭasya, prameyalakṣaṇānantaraṃ sthānaṃ kramo lakṣaṇasyetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Then' means at the time of enumeration; of doubt which has sequence, having been enumerated after <s>prameya</s>, the proper place, i.e., the sequence of its definition, is after the definition of <s>prameya</s>— this is the meaning /
This the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains— '<s>prameya</s>' /
Clarifying this very point— 'since' /
The word '<s>sthāna</s>' (place) has been explained by the word 'sequence' (<s>krama</s>), and the meaning of the possessive suffix (<s>matup</s>) by the word 'arrival' (<s>prāpti</s>) //

The <s>bhāṣya</s> introducing the definition of doubt is '<s>sthānavata etarhi</s>' (of one having a [proper] place, now) /
Its meaning: /
<s>Sthāna</s> (place) means sequence /
'Having that' /
'Now' means 'at this point' /
In some readings the text is '<s>sthānavata eva tarhi</s>' /
<s>Samā</s>— 'which' //

children.text:
atra ca vimarśaḥ saṃśaya iti saṃśayasāmānyalakṣaṇam /
tatra saṃśaya iti lakṣyanirdeśaḥ, vimarśa iti lakṣaṇapadam /
ekasmin dharmiṇi virodhinānārthāvamarśo vimarśaḥ, kiṃ sviditi jñānam /
tadanenāsamānajātīyebhyaḥ pramāṇādibhyaḥ samānajātīyebhyaśca viparyayādibhyaḥ saṃśayo nivartito bhavati /
samānetyādīni tu trīṇi viśeṣalakṣaṇāni /
teṣu ca vimarśaḥ saṃśaya ityetadanuvartanīyam /
atra viśiṣṭo 'vamarśo vimarśaviśiṣṭaḥ saṃśaya iti lakṣyapadam /
samānadharmopapatteranekadharmopapattervipratipatteriti trīṇi pratyekaṃ śeṣaiḥ padairūpetāni lakṣaṇānīti /
tadetadāha vārttikakāraḥ---tatra samāneti /
trividha eveti ye pañcavidhamācakṣate te nirākṛtāḥ /
tadanavadhāraṇajñānaṃ sa saṃśaya iti saṃśayasāmānyalakṣaṇaparaṃ bhāṣyaṃ vyācaṣṭe---tatra viṣayasvarūpeti /
pratyayo 'navadhāraṇātmakaśceti /

children.translated_text: The objection and resolution have already been explained in the first <s>sūtra</s> itself /
The explanation proceeds by accepting that the word <s>pratyaya</s> means ascertainment /
But in reality, the word <s>pratyaya</s> is a synonym of cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) /

children.text: jñānatvaṃ ca sāmānyaṃ saṃśayādiṣvapyastīti na virodha iti //
children.translated_text: And cognition-hood is a universal that exists even in doubt and the like— so there is no contradiction //

And here, '<s>vimarśa</s> (inquiry) is doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>)'— this is the general definition of doubt /
Therein, '<s>saṃśaya</s>' is the indication of the definiendum; '<s>vimarśa</s>' is the defining term /
<s>Vimarśa</s> is the deliberation upon mutually contradictory meanings with respect to a single subject (<s>dharmin</s>)— the cognition 'what could this be?' /
By this, doubt is distinguished from non-homogeneous things like <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, and from homogeneous things like error (<s>viparyaya</s>) and the like /
But '<s>samāna</s>' (common) and the rest are three specific definitions /
And in those, '<s>vimarśa</s> is doubt' must be carried over [from the general definition] /
Here, the definiendum term is: doubt that is characterized by a specific inquiry /
'From the apprehension of common properties,' 'from the apprehension of multiple properties,' 'from conflicting testimony'— these three, each joined with the remaining words, are [three separate] definitions /
This the <s>vārttikakāra</s> states— 'there, common' /
'Of three kinds only'— by this, those who declare five kinds are refuted /
The <s>bhāṣya</s> 'that cognition of non-determination is doubt' he explains as pertaining to the general definition of doubt— 'there, of the nature of the object' /
And the cognition has the nature of non-determination /

children.text:
samānadharmopapatteriti vyācaṣṭe---samāneti /
vikalpyākṣipati---kiṃ punariti /
kasmāditi /
mā kārṣīd dravye saṃśayam, guṇa eva kasmāt na karotīti praśnārthaḥ /
samādhatte---na, sādhāraṇeti /
yādṛśaṃ saṃkhyāpracayaparimāṇabhadayoni parimāṇaṃ sthāṇupurūṣayoḥ, tādṛśamāsyāpi purovartino dravyasya parimāṇam /
tasmāt sadṛśaparimāṇadharmasya dharmiṇa upapatterityarthaḥ /
mahatvadīrghatvasāmānyadharmayogastu sannapi na saṃśayakāraṇam, asādṛśye tadyoge 'pi saṃśayābhāvāditi bhāvaḥ /
syādetat /
upapattiḥ sattā /
na ca sadṛśo dharmaḥ sattāmātreṇa saṃśaye hetuḥ, api tūpalabdhaḥ /
na copalabdhivācakamatrāsti padamityata āha---tasyopapattiradhyavasāya iti /
yadyapyayamupapattiśabdaḥ sattāvacanastatparaśca, tathāpi padāntarasamabhivyāhārādavagamyate sattāmātrābhidhāne 'pi tadupalabdhirvivakṣiteti /
viṣayaviṣayiṇorabhedavivakṣayā sāmānādhikaraṇyamupapattirūpalabdhiriti /
pṛcchati---kasmāditi /
asmadāyatte hi śabdaprayoge kimityavācakaṃ prayokṣyāmaha ityarthaḥ /
uttaram---anuktamapīti /
viśeṣāpekṣā iti vacanena viśeṣasyāpekṣā ucyate /
apekṣāśabdaśca yadyapīcchāyāṃ vartate, tathāpīha jighṛkṣāyāṃ vākyasāmarthyāt /
na ca sā saṃśayasya hetuḥ, tasyāḥ saṃśaye sati bhāvāt /
tasmād viśeṣāpekṣayā vighṛkṣālakṣaṇayeha viśeṣayoḥ purovartivastusādṛśyāt smaraṇe satyagrahaṇaṃ lakṣaṇīyam, yathā gaṅgāśabdastīraṃ saṃbaddhameva lakṣayati, na tu tīramātram /
anenaivābhiprāyeṇa vakṣyati bhāṣyakāraḥ viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣa iti /
tasmād viśeṣagrahaṇapratiṣedhāt sāmānya grahaṇamabhyanujñātaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ /
parihārāntaramāha---atha veti /
syādetat, upapattiśabdaḥ sattāvacanaścopalabdhivacanaśca /
tathā ca vinigamanāyāṃ ko heturityata āha---yaḥ punariti /
nanvabhāvaḥ pramāṇālambanamuktaḥ, tat kuto na virodha ityata uktam---svatantramiti /
children.translated_text: Now, non-existence has been stated [by others] as the object of <s>pramāṇa</s>; so why is there no contradiction? — to this it is said — 'as independent' etc.
Or alternatively, this word <s>upapatti</s>, though meaning existence, indicates the apprehension that pertains to its own denoted object — thus he says — 'by the word viṣaya (object)' etc.
And this indication is not extra-ordinary — thus he says — 'worldly' etc.

children.text: yathā ca dhūmo na sattāmātreṇa hetustathoktaṃ prāgiti //
children.translated_text: And just as smoke is not a reason by mere existence [but by being apprehended], so it was previously stated. //

He explains 'because of the occurrence of a common property' — 'common' etc. / He raises an objection through an alternative — 'what then?' / 'Why?' / The meaning of the question is: let him not raise doubt about substance; why does he not raise it about quality alone? / He resolves — 'no, because of being common' etc. / Whatever magnitude — generated by number, accumulation, and dimension — belongs to the post and the person, the same kind of magnitude belongs to the object standing before one. / Therefore the meaning is: because of the occurrence of the subject possessing the common property of similar magnitude. / But the connection with the common properties of largeness, length, and the like, even though it exists, is not a cause of doubt, because even in the absence of similarity, when those are present, there is no doubt — this is the purport. / One might say this: occurrence (<s>upapatti</s>) means existence. / And a common property is not a cause of doubt by mere existence, but rather when it is apprehended. / And there is no word here that denotes apprehension — therefore he says — 'its occurrence is ascertainment.' / Although this word <s>upapatti</s> means existence and is used in that sense, nevertheless, from the co-occurrence with other words, it is understood that even when mere existence is expressed, apprehension of it is intended. / The co-referentiality [of the terms] 'occurrence' and 'apprehension' is by the intention of non-difference between the content and the cognition [of it]. / He asks — 'why?' / The meaning is: since the use of words is within our control, why should we use a non-expressive [word]? / The answer — 'even though unexpressed.' / By the statement 'expectation of a specific [distinguishing feature],' the expectation for the specific is expressed. / And the word 'expectation' (<s>apekṣā</s>), although it ordinarily means 'desire,' here [means] 'desire to grasp' by the force of the sentence. / And that [desire] is not the cause of doubt, since it comes into being [only] when doubt exists. / Therefore, by 'expectation of the specific' — characterized as the desire to grasp — what should be indicated is the non-apprehension [of the distinguishing features] when there is memory [of the two alternatives] due to the similarity of the object standing before one to the specific [features], just as the word <s>Gaṅgā</s> indicates only the bank that is connected [with the river], not just any bank. / With precisely this intention, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> will say 'dependent on the memory of the specific.' / Therefore the meaning is: from the prohibition of the apprehension of the specific, the apprehension of the general is implicitly permitted. / He states another resolution — 'or else' etc. / One might say: the word <s>upapatti</s> means both existence and apprehension. / And thus, what is the reason for deciding [between them]? — therefore he says — 'whoever then' etc.

children.text:
ekadeśināmupasaṃkhyānamupanyasyati---avyavacchedeti /
te kila manyante vyavacchedaheturapi dharmaḥ samāno bhavati /
yathā kṛtakatvaṃ sādhyadharmiṇi śabde dṛṣṭānta dharmiṇi ca ghaṭādau samānam, na cāsau nityānityatvasaṃśayahetuḥ, api tvanityatvasyāyogaṃ sādhyadharmiṇi vyavacchinatti /
ato 'vyavacchedahetoriti vaktavyamityarthaḥ /
tadetad vaktavyaṃ dūṣayati---na samāneti /
samāno hi dharmaḥ pratisaṃbandhinamapekṣate---keneti /
saṃśayapadena ca svaviṣayopasthāpakena parasparavirodhinau tāvupasthitau /
tena tābhyāṃ samāna iti gamyate /
tena vivakṣitatajjātīyavṛttitve satyanyajātīyavṛttireva gamyate /
na caiva kṛtakatvam /
tasmāt na vaktavyamavyavacchedahetoriti /
samānaśabdārthaḥ sādṛśyaṃ tatra nāstītyarthaḥ /
atraivopalabdhītyādipadadvayaṃ śaṅkāpūrvakaṃ yojayati---so 'yaṃ sādhāraṇa iti /
upalabdhyanupalabdhī na vyavatiṣṭhete iti /
śiraḥpāṇyāderanupalabdhirvakrakoṭarāderūlabdhiḥ purūṣasya bādhakaṃ pramāṇam, taddhi purūṣa evāyaṃ vā, idantayā vyavatiṣṭhate, idantāniṣedhena vā /

children.translated_text: 'This is not a person' — it settles through negative determination.
The absence of that [settlement] is non-determination.
By this, the absence of both establishing and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s> has been shown.
And 'when there is expectation of the specific' shows the memory of the specific [feature]. //

He presents the supplementary addition of the partial interpreters — 'non-exclusion' etc. / They hold that the common property is also a cause of exclusion. / Just as the property of being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) is common to the <s>dharmin</s> of the thesis — sound — and to the <s>dharmin</s> of the example — pot and the like — and yet it is not a cause of doubt regarding permanence and impermanence, but rather excludes the non-connection of impermanence with the <s>dharmin</s> of the thesis. / Therefore, the meaning is that it should be said 'of a property that is a cause of non-exclusion.' / He refutes this addition — 'not common' etc. / For a common property requires [specification of] its correlates — 'common to what?' / And by the word 'doubt' (<s>saṃśaya</s>), which presents its own object [i.e., the two alternatives], the two mutually contradictory [alternatives] are brought to mind. / Therefore, 'common to those two' is understood. / Hence, when there is occurrence in a thing of the intended type, occurrence in another type alone is understood. / But that is not so for the property of being produced. / Therefore, it is not necessary to say 'of a property that is a cause of non-exclusion.' / The meaning of the word 'common' is similarity — which does not exist there — this is the meaning. / Here itself he construes the pair of words 'apprehension-non-apprehension' together with an objection — 'this common [property]' etc. / 'Apprehension and non-apprehension do not settle' — the non-apprehension of head, hands, and the like, and the apprehension of crookedness, hollows, and the like is the sublating <s>pramāṇa</s> for [determining] a person; for it settles either through positive determination — 'this is indeed a person' — or through the negation of positive determination.

children.text:
vimarśapūrvakaṃ samastamityavadhārayati---kimidamiti /
tatraikapadaparigrahe doṣamāha---yadi samāneti /
viśeṣaḥ śiraḥpāṇyādiḥ /
viśiṣyate hyanena purūṣaḥ sthāṇoriti anupalabdhasāmānyasyāpi kvacidupalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthāstīti /
yathā saptame rase, daśame vā dravye /
na hi tatra sādhakaṃ bādhakaṃ vāsti pramāṇam /
children.translated_text: For there is no establishing or sublating <s>pramāṇa</s> in that case.
And yet there is no doubt.
'Expectation of the specific' — just this much [is needed].

children.text: tad yathā hastinaṃ dṛṣṭvā tatsaṃbandhino sthūṇāhastipakau smarati na ca tatra saṃndigdhe //
children.translated_text: For example, seeing an elephant, one remembers the pillar and the elephant-keeper associated with it, but there is no doubt about that. //

He ascertains through deliberation that the whole [set of conditions is required] together — 'what is this?' / There he states the fault in taking a single term [as sufficient] — 'if common' etc. / The specific [feature] is head, hands, and the like. / For by this, a person is distinguished from a post — so even for one whose common [property] has not been apprehended, there is somewhere a non-settlement of apprehension and non-apprehension. / As in [the case of] a seventh taste, or a tenth substance.

children.text:
dvipadaparigrahe doṣamāha---evaṃ samāneti /
naudolārūḍho hi gacchan vidūre ārohapariṇāvadvastudarśane 'pi satyapi ca sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāve viśeṣasmṛtyamāvāt naga iti vā nāga iti vā na sandigdhe /
evamupalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthāto viśeṣāpekṣa iti padadvaye vidhīyamāna'nyataḥ smaryamāṇād viśeṣāt sadṛśadharmavati dharmiṇyanupalabhyamāne saṃśayaḥ syāt /
asti hi tadā viśeṣasmṛtiḥ sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvaśca, no khalvanupalabhyamāne samānadharme dharmiṇi tadgatā vakrakoṭarādayo vā śiraḥ pāṇyādayo vā śakyagrahā iti /
yadāyaṃ draṣṭeti /
yadā khalvayaṃ draṣṭā pratiparūraḍakurodbhedapukakitābhirmandamalayamārūtāndolanalalitalāsyaśālinībhiḥ śākhābhirmadhumadamuditamadhupamālāśiñjitavallakīvādyamanoharābhirmattapuṃskokilakulavipañcyamānapañcamābhirārabdha-
saṃṅgītakaṃ sahakāratarūmanubhūyātha vidūravartī ku/jarasadṛśadharmavantamanubhavati, tadāsyāsti samānadharmolabdhiḥ /
asti ca karitarurūpaviśeṣasmṛtiḥ, na tu sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāva iti na saṃśete /
katipayavyaktyāśrayatvaṃ sahakāratvāderviśeṣasyālpaviṣayatvam /
ārohapariṇāhādestu bahuvyāpitvaṃ mahāviṣayatvam /
nānārthāvamarśanaṃ ca virūddhārthāvamarśanaṃ draṣṭavyam /
tadanena sthāṇupurūṣayorityādi bhāṣyaṃ vyākhyātam /
paśyan ityupapattivivaraṇam /
viśeṣaṃ bubhutsamāna iti viśeṣāpekṣa ityasya vivaraṇam /
kiṃ sviditi vimarśavivaraṇam /
syādetat /
saṃśayottarakālā bubhutseti, kathaṃ bubhutsamānaḥ saṃśeta ityata uktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā, samānamanayoriti /

children.translated_text: The purport is: by the word 'expectation of the specific' — which denotes desire — what is indicated is the memory of the specific that has not been grasped.

children.text: seyaṃ sādhakabādhakapramāṇānupapattau satyā samānadharmopalabdhirvinaśyadavasthā viśeṣasmṛtyā sahāvinaśyadavasthā ekasmin kṣaṇe satī saṃśayajñānasya heturiti siddham /
children.translated_text: This is established: when there is the non-establishment of establishing and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s>, the apprehension of a common property — which is in a state of passing away — together with the memory of the specific — which is in an enduring state — being [present] at a single moment, is the cause of the cognition of doubt.
He also applies this to the three-term interpretation 'because of the occurrence of multiple properties' and 'because of conflicting claims' — 'by this' etc.
The first two [terms] should be seen as combined into pairs. //

He states the fault in taking two terms [together] — 'thus common' etc. / For one riding a boat, while traveling, even upon seeing a distant object having the properties of height and girth, and even when there is an absence of establishing and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s>, one does not doubt whether it is a mountain or a serpent (<s>nāga</s>), because there is no memory of the specific. / Thus, when the two terms — 'non-settlement of apprehension and non-apprehension' and 'expectation of the specific' — are prescribed, from the specific that is remembered from one of them, doubt would arise regarding a <s>dharmin</s> possessing a common property but whose [specific feature] is not apprehended. / For then there is memory of the specific and absence of establishing and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s>, but the common property of the <s>dharmin</s> is not apprehended — neither the crookedness and hollows belonging to it nor the head and hands are graspable. / 'When this observer' etc. / When this observer, having experienced a mango tree whose branches — bristling with fresh buds and sprouts, gracefully swaying in gentle <s>Malaya</s> breezes, with intoxicated bees buzzing like <s>vallakī</s> (lute) music delightful to the mind, their garlands humming with the joy of honey, and mad male cuckoos singing the fifth note initiating a concert — then perceives from afar [something] possessing properties similar to an elephant, then there is for him the apprehension of a common property. / And there is memory of the specific features of the elephant and the tree, but there is no absence of establishing and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s> — so he does not doubt. / The fact that the specific features such as being a mango tree and the like belong to only a few individuals is what is meant by 'small scope.' / But height, girth, and the like, being widely applicable, have 'great scope.' / And 'deliberation of various meanings' should be seen as 'deliberation of contradictory meanings.' / By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> passage 'of the post and the person' and so on has been explained. / 'Seeing' is the explanation of 'occurrence' (<s>upapatti</s>). / 'Desiring to know the specific' is the explanation of 'expectation of the specific.' / 'What might this be?' is the explanation of deliberation. / One might object: the desire to know (<s>bubhutsā</s>) comes after doubt — so how can one who desires to know have doubt? — therefore it has been said by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> — 'common to these two' etc.

children.text:
anekadharmopapatterityatra bhāṣyakṛto vyākhyāṃ grahītum ekadeśivyākhyānamupanyasya dūṣayati---aneketi /
śabdo hi saṃyogajaḥ /
saṃyogajatvaṃ hi kārye dravye guṇe ca rūpādau śarīrādikriyāyāṃ cāstīti dravyaguṇakarmaṇāṃ samānam /
tasmādanekasya dharmaḥ caritārthaḥ /
evaṃ śabdagato 'neko 'pi dharmaḥ samānatayaiva dravyatvādisandehahetuḥ triṣu, saṃyogajatvaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ sattvādinā nirbhaksya, nirguṇatvaṃ guṇakarmaṇāḥ /
evaṃ kṣaṇikatvaṃ dravyaguṇakarmaṇāmiti samānadharmopapattyā gatārthaṃmityarthaḥ /
pṛcchati---atheti /

children.translated_text: The <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> explains through the answer — 'uncommon' etc.
He asks again — 'how?' etc.
The meaning is: by the word 'aneka' (multiple) within the compound, that component 'aneka' is indicated by the compound word — i.e., by 'aneka' as part of the compound.
The answer — 'common' etc. //

In [the phrase] 'because of the occurrence of multiple properties,' he presents and refutes the partial interpretation of the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>'s explanation — 'multiple' etc. / For sound is produced from conjunction. / And the property of being produced from conjunction exists in the effect-substance, in the quality such as color and the like, and in the action such as bodily movement — so it is common to substance, quality, and action. / Therefore the property 'multiple' [i.e., belonging to many] has fulfilled its purpose. / Similarly, the multiple property residing in sound is also a cause of doubt among the three [categories] only through commonality — the property of being produced from conjunction being common, [and] being separated from existence (<s>sattva</s>) and the like; the property of being without quality [separating it] from quality and action. / Likewise, momentariness [being common to] substance, quality, and action — so the meaning is that the purpose is fulfilled by the occurrence of a common property. / He asks — 'then' etc.

children.text:
etaduktaṃ bhavati /
yato 'nekasmāt samānāsamānajātīyādeṣa svāśrayaṃ vyāvartayati, ato 'nekāpādānakavyāvṛttihetukatvāt lakṣaṇayānena ityucyate /
tadanena samānajātīyam asamānajātīyaṃ cānekamiti bhāṣyaṃ tasmād viśeṣa ityadhyāhṛtya vyākhyātam /
adhyāhṛtaviśeṣapadavivaraṇaṃ viśeṣako dharma iti /
saṃbandhasāmānyavivakṣayā tu ṣaṣṭhī tasyānekasyeti /
lakṣaṇābījāntaramāha---tasya cānekasyeti /
nivartyanivartakasaṃbandhenānekaśabdena dharmoḥ lakṣyata ityarthaḥ /
tadanena vinaivādhyāhāraṃ samānajātīyamasamānajātīyaṃ cānekam /
tasya dharme nivartakatayeti vyākhyātam /
na tvatra samāsabhrāntiḥ kartavyā /
darśayiṣyati hi bahuvrīhimihaiva vārttikakāraḥ /
tadevaṃ lakṣaṇābījadvayopanyāsena asādhāraṇo dharma iti grahaṇakavākyaṃ vyākhyātam /
prakārāntareṇānekadharmapadaṃvyācaṣṭe---ekāṃneketi /
ekaṃ cāneka ca tadubhayamanekaṃ tasyānekasya pratyayaheturdharmo 'nekadharmaḥ bhedābhedapratyayaheturityarthaḥ /
vibhāgajatvaṃ vibhāgajānāṃ śabdānāmanyonyasyābhedapratyayahetuḥ, taditarebhyaśca bhedapratyayahetuḥ /
tadidamāha---yato vibhāgajatvāt eṣa pratyayo bhavatīdaṃ vibhāgajaṃ śabdajātam ekam /
idaṃ ca tato 'nyad anekaṃ bhinnam /
tatra ya eva ekapratyayahetuḥ dharmo 'bhedaḥ sa eva anekapratyayaheturviśeṣaḥ /
jātyabhiprāyaṃ caikavacanam, sadādirhi dharmo duvyaguṇakarmaṇāmabhedapratyayahetuḥ, sāmānyādibhyaśca śabdaṃ nirbhajati /
tadidamāha---yataḥ sadādereṣa pratyayo bhavatīdamekaṃ yataśca vibhāgajatvādepa pratyayo bhavatīdamanekamiti, tasmāt siddhamekaṃ cānekaṃ ca /

children.translated_text: 'Multiple' — by figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>), the cause of the cognition of multiplicity is called 'multiple.'
This is the explanation corresponding to the <s>bhāṣya</s>.
He gives an example here — 'for instance' etc.
The [examples] 'from universal, particular, and inherence' are stated for the purpose of showing doubt regarding the three categories of substance, quality, and action. //

This is what has been stated: / Since 'multiple' differentiates its substrate from [things of] the same and different types, and since it is the cause of differentiation from multiple sources, it is said [to function] through indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>). / By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> passage 'of the same type and of a different type, multiple' has been explained by supplying the word 'specific' — [i.e.,] 'therefore the specific [feature].' / The elaboration of the supplied word 'specific' is 'the differentiating property.' / But the sixth case [genitive] 'of that multiple' is by the intention of the general relation [between property and substrate]. / He states another basis for indication — 'and of that multiple' etc. / The meaning is: by the word 'multiple,' through the relation of what is to be excluded and its excluder, the property is indicated. / By this, without any supplementation, 'of the same type and of a different type, multiple; of that [multiple], in the property, by the capacity to exclude' — this has been explained. / But here no confusion regarding the compound should be entertained. / For the <s>vārttikakāra</s> himself will show that it is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound right here. / Thus, by presenting the two bases for indication, the introductory statement 'uncommon property' has been explained. / He explains the term 'multiple-property' (<s>anekadharma</s>) in another way — 'one and multiple' etc. / 'One and multiple' — both together are 'aneka'; the property that is the cause of the cognition of both [unity and multiplicity] is the 'anekadharma' — meaning: the cause of the cognitions of both difference and non-difference. / The property of being produced from disjunction (<s>vibhāgajatva</s>) is the cause of the cognition of non-difference among sounds produced from disjunction with respect to each other, and it is the cause of the cognition of difference from other [categories]. / This is what he says: because of being produced from disjunction, the cognition arises — 'this class of sounds produced from disjunction is one.' / 'And this other is multiple, different [from it].' / There, the very property that is the cause of the cognition of unity — namely non-difference — is itself the cause of the cognition of multiplicity — namely the specific [differentiator]. / And the singular number is with the intention of the universal (<s>jāti</s>): for the property of existence (<s>sat</s>) and the like is the cause of the cognition of non-difference among substance, quality, and action, and differentiates sound from universals and the like. / This is what he says: because of existence and the like, the cognition arises — 'this is one'; and because of being produced from disjunction, the cognition arises — 'this is multiple.' Therefore it is established that [there is] both one and multiple.

Existent, non-eternal, possessing substance, being an effect, being a cause, possessing universal and particular — these are the non-differentiating [common properties] of substance, quality, and action. //
The meaning is: [the property] that has been separated, differentiated, by this [set of common properties] such as existence and the like. //

children.text:
syādetat /
yad yena sahacaritaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tat kkacid dṛśyamānaṃ tat smārayat tadviyaruddhenāpi ca saṃbandhānaniścāyayat saṃśayaheturbhavati, yathā samāno dharmaḥ /
asādhāraṇastu dharmo vibhāgajatvaṃ narte śabdāt kkacit pṛthivyādau vā utkṣepaṇādau vā gandhādau vā dṛṣṭa iti kathra smārayet, asmārayad vā kathaṃ tatra saṃśayaṃ janayet? tasmāt ko 'yaṃ bhavedityayo dharmāditi jijñāsāmātramutpādayet na tvayaṃ vāyaṃ veti saṃśayamityata āha---na hīti /
kasmāt na dṛṣṭamityata āha---sarvatrāsaṃbhavāt /
na hi dravyādervibhāgato janma saṃbhavati, tadanvayavyatirekānanuvidhānādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For birth from disjunction is not possible for substance and the like, because [sound] does not conform to their presence and absence — this is the meaning.

children.text: nanvata evoktaṃ na saṃśayaheturityataḥ āha---vibhāgajatvaṃ saṃśarye karoti sarvato vyāvṛtteriti /
children.translated_text: But then, from this very fact, it has been said that it is not a cause of doubt — to this he says — 'being born of disjunction causes doubt because of exclusion from all [categories].'

children.text: ayamarthaḥ, yadyapi vibhāgajatvaṃ na dravyādau kvacid dṛṣṭam, tathāpi tadvyatirekaḥ pratyekaṃ dravyādau dṛṣṭa iti vibhāgajatvena sadādyaviśeṣavān śabdo dravyakarmabhyā vyāvartamānaḥ kiṃ guṇaḥ, guṇakarmabhyāṃ vyāvartamānaḥ kiṃ dravyam, guṇadravyābhyāṃ vyāvartamānaḥ kiṃ karmeti vyatirekamukhena tattat smārayan asādhāraṇo dharmo bhavati saṃśayakāraṇamiti /
children.translated_text: The meaning is as follows: although being born of disjunction has not been seen in substance and the like anywhere, nevertheless its absence has been seen in each of substance and the like individually. Therefore, sound — possessing the general properties of being existent and the like, yet [also possessing] being born of disjunction — when being distinguished from substance and action [one asks] 'is it a quality?'; when being distinguished from quality and action [one asks] 'is it a substance?'; when being distinguished from quality and substance [one asks] 'is it an action?' — thus, by causing the recollection of each through the method of exclusion (<s>vyatireka</s>), the uncommon property becomes a cause of doubt.
He shows — 'but is it not so?' //

One might object: that which has been seen as concomitant with something, when seen somewhere, causes the recollection of that [concomitant], and by also not determining the connection even with its contrary, becomes a cause of doubt — just as a common property does. But the uncommon property — namely, being born of disjunction (<s>vibhāgajatva</s>) — has not been seen anywhere apart from sound, neither in earth and the like, nor in throwing and the like, nor in smell and the like. So how could it cause recollection? And if it does not cause recollection, how could it produce doubt regarding that? Therefore, it would merely produce a desire to know — 'what could this be? From which property [does it arise]?' — but not doubt of the form 'is it this or that?' — to this he says — 'for it is not so.' Why has it not been seen? — to this he says — 'because of the impossibility in all [categories].'

children.text:
ayamabhisandhiḥ /
vaṃśe pāṭyamāne vaṃśadalayoḥ kriyā, tatastayormitho vibhāgaḥ, tato vaṃśadalāvaruddhanabhobhāgavibhāgaḥ /
so 'yaṃ vibhāgajo vibhāgo na vaṃśadalakarmajaḥ /
avayavakriyā hi tadavayavāvaruddhanabhobhāgavibhāgajanikā dravyārambhakasaṃyogāpratidvandvivibhāgajanakatvena vyāptā vikasatkamalakuṅmaladaleṣu dṛṣṭā /
na hi tatra tatra mukulitād vikāsi kamalamanyat, ākuñcitaprasāritāṅgulikaratalavat tattvena pratyabhijñāyamānatvāt /
vaṃśadalakriyāpi cet tādṛśī, nūnamanayāpi dravyārambhakasaṃyogāpratidvandvivibhāgajanikayā bhavitavyam /
tathā ca dravyaṃ kāryamapi na naśyet /
tasmāt nānayā vaṃśadalākāśavibhāgo janayitavyaḥ /
na cānyadasya kāraṇaṃ saṃbhavati /
tasmād vaṃśadalakriyājanito dalayorvibhāgaḥ kāryaikārthasamavetaḥ tadavaruddhākāśapradeśavibhāgasyāsamavāyikāraṇameṣitavyaḥ /
heturiti siddhaṃ bhavatīti /
pariharati---anabhyupagatavibhāgajavibhāgasyaitad vibhāgajatvam evaṃ saṃśayakāraṇaṃ bhavati /
anabhyupagamabījaṃ ca kutaḥ punarevadevamavagataṃ padmapatrāvayavakriyā vibhāgadvayajaniketi, vibhāgadvayakramakalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāditi cet? hanta, vaṃśadalavibhāgayorapi tulyam /
nanūktaṃ dravyārambhakasaṃyogāpratidvandvivibhāgajanakaṃ syāt karma, tataśca dravyanāśo na bhavediti /
athaṃ viparyayaḥ kasmāt na bhavatīti vaṃśadaladvayakriyaiva vibhāgadvayajanikā, padmapatravayavakriyā tvavayavavibhāgajanikā, tadavayavākāśavibhāgastvavayavavibhāgajanmā /
yadi tu padmapatrāvayavakriyā ubhayajanikā bhavet, vaṃśadalakriyaiva dravyārambhakasaṃyogapratidvandvinaṃ vibhāgaṃ janayediti /
na cānyataratra vibhāgadvayayaugapadyaniścayaḥ kramapramāṇābhāvaśca tulyaḥ /

children.translated_text: Therefore, because of the doubt about the capacity of lotus-petal-part action to produce disjunction, the relation of pervaded and pervader cannot be ascertained.

children.text: kriyāvailakṣaṇyāt tu svahetuvailakṣaṇyajanmanaḥ kāryasya vibhāgasya vailakṣaṇyaṃ syāt, yadeko dravyārambhakasaṃyogapratidvandvī apratidvandvī cetaraḥ, tathāpi caitadvailakṣaṇyaṃ kriyāyā abhyupetavyam yadekā vibhāgamekaṃ janayati /
children.translated_text: But due to the dissimilarity of the actions, there would be dissimilarity of the effect — the disjunction — since it arises from dissimilar causes: one [disjunction] is opposed to the substance-constituting conjunction, and the other is not opposed to it. Even so, this dissimilarity of the action must be accepted: that one [action] produces a single disjunction,
while the other produces two disjunctions.
Therefore, by the force of this example, disjunction born of disjunction is not established. //

The intention is as follows. When a bamboo is being split, there is an action of the two bamboo-halves, from which there is mutual disjunction between them, and from that there is disjunction of the space-portions obstructed by the bamboo-halves. This disjunction is born of disjunction, not born of the action of the bamboo-halves. For the action of the parts, which produces disjunction of the space-portions obstructed by those parts, is pervaded by the capacity to produce disjunction that is not opposed to the conjunction that constitutes a composite substance — as seen in the petals of a blooming lotus bud. For there, the blooming lotus is not different from the closed [bud], since it is genuinely recognized as the same — like a hand with fingers curled and extended. If the action of the bamboo-halves too is of that same kind, then it too must produce a disjunction not opposed to the substance-constituting conjunction. And thus even the composite substance, being an effect, would not be destroyed. Therefore, by this [action] the disjunction between the bamboo-halves and space should not be produced. And no other cause of it is possible. Therefore, the disjunction of the halves produced by the action of the bamboo-halves, co-inhering in one and the same effect, must be accepted as the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) of the disjunction of the space-portions obstructed by them. Thus it would be established that [disjunction born of disjunction] is a reason [for something other than sound]. He resolves — for one who does not accept disjunction born of disjunction, this very property of being born of disjunction becomes a cause of doubt in this way. And the seed of non-acceptance — how exactly has it been ascertained that the action of lotus-petal parts produces two kinds of disjunction? — because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the postulation of a sequence of two disjunctions — if so, the same applies equally to the disjunction of bamboo-halves. But has it not been said that the action could produce a disjunction not opposed to the substance-constituting conjunction, and thus the substance would not be destroyed? — why then does the reverse not obtain: the action of the two bamboo-halves produces two kinds of disjunction, while the action of lotus-petal parts produces only the part-disjunction, and the disjunction between the parts and space is born of part-disjunction? But if the action of lotus-petal parts were to produce both, then the action of the bamboo-halves too would produce the disjunction opposed to the substance-constituting conjunction. And the certainty of simultaneity of the two disjunctions in one case and the absence of evidence for sequence is the same in both.

children.text:
yastvaṅgulikarmānantaramaṅgulitaruvibhāgo hastataruvibhāgaḥ, śarīrataruvibhagāśca daśyate, tatrāṅgulitaruvibhāgamaṅgulyāśrayā kriyā karotu, hastataruvibhāgaṃ tu na śaktā janayitum, tasyāḥ svāśrayasamavāyāt, svāśrayasamavetakāryajanane ca kriyāyāḥ sāmarthyāvadhāraṇāt /
tasmāt hastāditaruvibhāgaḥ kriyato 'saṃbhavannaṅgulyāditaruvibhāgameva kāryaikārthasamavāyalakṣaṇayā pratyāsattyā nimittīkarotīti vibhāgajavibhāgasiddhiṃ manyate, taṃ pratyāha---yaḥ punariti /
astu vā vibhāgajo vibhāgaḥ, tathāpi vibhāgajatvamīdṛśamasādhāraṇamevetyata āha---astu vā tasya abhyupagatavibhāgasya api vibhāgajatvamasādhāraṇaṃ viśiṣṭam /
tadeva deśayati---vibhāgajeti /
pāṭyamāne hi vaṃśe śabdotpattau vaṃśadalayormitho vibhāgo nimittakāraṇam /
vaṃśadalāvaruddhākāśavibhāgastvasyāsamavāyikāraṇam, na tu bheryākāśasaṃyogavat vaṃśadalākāśasaṃyogo 'samavāyikāraṇaṃ bhavitumarhati /
tathā hi prayogaḥ, yo 'yaṃ vaṃśadalavibhāganimittaḥ śabdaḥ, sa nimittasamānajātīyāsamavāyikāraṇajanyaḥ, tadasādhāraṇanimittajanyaśabdatvāt /
yo yaḥ śabdo yadasādhāraṇanimittajanmā, sa sarvastajjātīyāsamavāyikāraṇajanyaḥ, yathā bherīdaṇḍasaṃyoganimittaḥ śabdo bheryākāśasaṃyogāsamavāyikāraṇakaḥ /
tathā cāyam /
tasmāt tatheti /
tadevaṃ vaṃśadalavibhāgalabdhajanmanā vaṃśadalākāśavibhāgenāsamavāyikāraṇena janitaḥ śabdaḥ /

tadevaṃ vibhāgajavibhāgāsamavāyikāraṇakatvaṃ śabdasya, tadapi yadyapyaṅgulyākāśavibhāgajahastākāśavibhāgāsamavāyikāraṇe kāyākāśavibhāge 'sti, tathāpi kāraṇamātravibhāgajavibhāgāsamavāyikāraṇakatvāditi hetuḥ bhāṣyakāreṇa vibhāgajatvāt ityanena sūcitaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, sound has the property of having disjunction-born-disjunction as its non-inherent cause. And this, even though it exists in the case of body-space disjunction born from finger-space disjunction, [is uncommon] because the reason indicated by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> with the expression 'because of being born of disjunction' is: having as its non-inherent cause a disjunction born from a cause-only disjunction.
And the body-space disjunction preceded by finger-space disjunction is not of this kind.

children.text: sa hi kāraṇākāraṇavibhāgapūrvako, na tu kāraṇamātravibhāgapūrvakaḥ /
children.translated_text: For that is preceded by a disjunction of both cause and non-cause, not preceded by a disjunction of cause alone.
This is what has been stated: sound has disjunction-born-disjunction as its non-inherent cause, and no other category does. //

Now, the one who holds that immediately after the action of a finger, there is the disjunction of the finger from a tree, then the disjunction of the hand from the tree, and then the disjunction of the body from the tree — and that for this, let the action residing in the finger produce the disjunction of the finger from the tree, but it is not capable of producing the disjunction of the hand from the tree, since that [action] inheres in its own substrate, and the capacity of action is determined only for producing effects co-inhering in its own substrate — therefore, the disjunction of the hand and the like from the tree, being impossible from action, makes the disjunction of the finger and the like from the tree its cause through the proximity characterized by co-inherence in one and the same effect — and thus considers disjunction born of disjunction to be established — to him he replies — 'but what.' Let there be disjunction born of disjunction; even so, this property of being born of disjunction is uncommon — therefore he says — 'let there be, for that accepted disjunction too, an uncommon and distinguished property of being born of disjunction.' He shows precisely that — 'born of disjunction.' For when a bamboo is being split and sound arises, the mutual disjunction of the bamboo-halves is the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>). But the disjunction of the space obstructed by the bamboo-halves is its non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>), not the conjunction of bamboo-halves with space like the conjunction of a drum[-stick] with the drum-space. For the argument is: this sound, caused by the disjunction of bamboo-halves, is produced by a non-inherent cause of the same class as its efficient cause, because it is a sound produced by an uncommon efficient cause. Whatever sound is born of whatever uncommon efficient cause, all of that is produced by a non-inherent cause of that same class — just as sound whose efficient cause is the conjunction of drum and stick has the conjunction of drum and space as its non-inherent cause. And so is this. Therefore, it is so. Thus, the sound is produced with the disjunction of bamboo-half-space — born from the disjunction of bamboo-halves — as its non-inherent cause.

children.text:
nanu sahacarito dṛṣṭaḥ smārayan viśeṣasaṃśayaheturbhavati, na tu yo vyāvṛttaḥ tena sahāsyāsāhacaryāditi śaṅakāmapanetuṃ bhāṣyakārīyamuttaramāha---tulyajātīyeṣvitiṃ /
yadyapi vyatirekamukhenāsādhāraṇaḥ śaktaḥ smārayitum,
tathāpi bhāṣyoktamapyuktam /
yat khalu sadādirūpasaṃpannaṃ viśeṣavat tatsamānajātīyebhyo 'samānajātīyabhyaśca vyāvṛttam, yathā pṛthivīdravyam /
abādibhyaśca dravyāntarebhyāṃ guṇakarmabhyaśca vijātīyebhyo gandhavattvena vyāvṛttaṃ dravyajātīyam /
evaṃ rūpatvena rūpaṃ guṇaḥ /
utkṣepaṇatvenotkṣepaṇaṃ karma /
tathāvidhaḥ śabdaḥ sadādirūpasaṃpanno vibhāgajatvena samānāsamānajātīyebhyo viśiṣyate /
tasmād bhavati dravyaṃ guṇaḥ karma veti saṃśaya iti /
pūrvavyākhyānato 'nekaśabdenāsādhāraṇadharmo lakṣyata ityuktam /
saṃprati samānaśabdaparyālocanayāpyanekapadamasādhāraṇe vartate lakṣaṇayaivetyāha---samānadharmasya saṃśayakāraṇatvena upayogād veti /
samānaṃ hi pratigogitayā asamānaṃ buddhau sannidhāpayati /
tatra dvayasyāpi samānaśabdena śrutyarthābhyāmupāttasya samānasya dharmasyāsamānasya ca, samānasya saṃśayakāraṇatvenopayogāditi yojanā /
pṛcchati---kasmāditi /
asmadāyatte śabdaprayoge kimityavācakaṃ prayokṣyāmaha iti bhāvaḥ /
uttaram---naivamiti /
asādhāraṇo hi dharmo vyatirekamukhena saṃśayahetuḥ /
sa cānekasmād vyāvṛttyā sidhyati /
sā ca lākṣaṇikānekapadādhīnā nāsamānapadāt labhyata iti prayojanavallākṣaṇikapadopādānam /
lakṣaṇaiva ceyam anekasmādvyāvṛtto dharmo 'nekadharma iti vigraheṇa nirvarṇyate iti /
abhyuccayamātramāha---lāghavaṃ veti /
asādhāraṇasya saṃśayakāraṇatve vyāvṛttiḥ prayojiketi manvānaścodayati---yadyaneketi /
pariharati---naiṣa doṣa iti /
vyabhicārāvyabhicārau hi saṃśayanirṇayayoḥ prayojakau, nānvayavyatirekamātramityarthaḥ /
codayati---yadi tarhīti /
sapakṣāsapakṣasādhāraṇyaṃ hi hetorvyabhicāraḥ /
sa cet saṃśayasya kāraṇam, hanta, samānadharmopapattireva sarvatra saṃśayakāraṇamiti kṛtam anekagrahaṇenetyarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He resolves — 'true.'
For the commonness of a reason to the similar and dissimilar instances is deviation.
And that is the operative factor for doubt.
Nevertheless, the positive concomitance of one [property] is common, while the exclusion of the other [constitutes the uncommon] — and the adoption of both is just this much — this is the meaning. //

Now, it is a concomitant property that, when seen, causes recollection and becomes a cause of doubt regarding a particular [category] — but not one that is excluded [from all], since there is no concomitance of it with that [category]. To remove this objection, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> states this reply — 'among those of the same class.' Even though the uncommon [property] is capable of causing recollection through the method of exclusion, nevertheless what has been said in the <s>bhāṣya</s> is also stated. What indeed possesses the general properties of being existent and the like, together with distinguishing features, and is excluded from things of the same and different classes — that is like an earthly substance: excluded from water and the like among other substances, and from quality and action which are of different classes, by the possession of smell. Similarly, form (<s>rūpa</s>) is a quality by virtue of form-ness. Throwing (<s>utkṣepaṇa</s>) is an action by virtue of the property of throwing. In the same way, sound, possessing the general properties of being existent and the like, is distinguished from things of the same and different classes by the property of being born of disjunction. Therefore there is doubt: 'is it a substance, a quality, or an action?' As stated in the previous explanation, the uncommon property is indicated by the word 'multiple' (<s>aneka</s>). Now, by considering the word 'common' (<s>samāna</s>) too, the word 'multiple' applies to the uncommon [property] through secondary signification — thus he says — 'because of the utility of the common property as a cause of doubt.' For the common, by being a counterpart, brings the uncommon into mental proximity. There, both — the common property and the uncommon one, taken up by the word 'common' through its literal and secondary meanings — are applied: the common one serves as a cause of doubt — this is the construction. He asks — 'why?' The import is: when the usage of words is within our control, why would we use a non-designative one? The answer — 'it is not so.' For the uncommon property is a cause of doubt through the method of exclusion. And that is established by exclusion from multiple [categories]. And that [exclusion] depends on the secondary-signification word 'multiple,' not obtainable from the word 'uncommon' — therefore the adoption of the secondary-signification word is purposeful. And this very secondary signification is analyzed by the explanation: 'a property excluded from multiple [categories] is a multiple property.' He states a mere additional point — 'or, for brevity.' Thinking that exclusion is the operative factor when the uncommon [property] is a cause of doubt, he objects — 'if multiple.' He resolves — 'this is not a fault.' For deviation and non-deviation are the operative factors for doubt and determination respectively, not mere positive and negative concomitance — this is the meaning. He objects — 'if then.' For the commonness of a reason to the similar and dissimilar instances is deviation. If that is the cause of doubt, then the occurrence of the common property alone is in all cases the cause of doubt — so the word 'multiple' is unnecessary — this is the meaning.

children.text:
evamanekadharmopapatteriti svamate vyākhyāya paramatavyākhyānaṃ dūṣayitumupanyasyati---na /
iti /
nityaḥ śabdaḥ śrāvaṇatvāt śabdatvavadityekaḥ pañcarūpopapanno 'vyabhicārī hetuḥ1 anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvād ghaṭavaditi cāyamaparaḥ pañcarūpopapanno 'vyabhicārī heturiti /
tadetad dūṣayati---tadayuktamiti /
na hyavyabhicāriṇau pañcarūpopapannāvityarthaḥ /
na cāyaṃ prativādinaḥ prayogo 'pi yuktaḥ iti /
viruddhaśabdasyārtho viruddhārtha iti, svarūpamanayorviruddhaṃ parasparābhāvavadityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: 'Arisen from the perception of a distinguishing feature.'

children.text: saṃśayasya hi viśeṣādarśanaṃ janakam, viśeṣadarśanaṃ ca nivartakamiti /
children.translated_text: For the non-perception of a distinguishing feature is the producer of doubt, and the perception of a distinguishing feature is its remover.

children.text: sa cet tvanmate nivartakādutpadyata, avyabhicārihetujanitādviśeṣadarśanāt nāsya nivṛttiḥ syādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: If, in your view, [doubt] arises from a remover, then its removal would not occur from the perception of a distinguishing feature generated by a non-deviating reason — this is the meaning.

children.text: na ca yadā nivartakatvamasyāsti tadā janakamapītyāha---na hi viśeṣadarśane satīti //
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that when [perception of a distinguishing feature] is a remover, it is also a producer — thus he says — 'for when the perception of a distinguishing feature is present.' //

Having thus explained 'because of the occurrence of multiple properties' according to his own view, he presents the opponent's explanation in order to refute it — 'no.' 'Sound is eternal, because of being auditory, like sound-ness' — this is one reason possessing the five characteristics and non-deviating. 'Sound is non-eternal, because of being produced, like a pot' — and this is another reason possessing the five characteristics and non-deviating. He refutes that — 'that is improper.' The meaning is: they do not [both] possess the five characteristics and are non-deviating. 'And this formulation of the opponent is also not proper.' The meaning of the word 'contradictory' (<s>viruddha</s>) is 'having a contradictory meaning': their essential natures are mutually contradictory, being like the mutual absence [of each other] — this is the meaning.
One might object:

children.text: pratyakṣameva sa evāyaṃ gakāra ityevamākāraṃ pratyabhijñāsamājñātaṃ śabdasya sthemānamākalayat,
children.translated_text: Perception itself, in the form of the recognition 'this is the very same <s>ga</s>-sound,' having ascertained the permanence of sound,
Who could afterwards destroy that which is stable for that long a duration? //

children.text:
iti nityatvaṃ paricchetsyatītyata āha---nāyamarthaḥ pratyakṣasya viṣayaḥ /
