children.translated_text: Therefore, by "not the contradiction of all <s>pramāṇas</s>" — with this word accompanied [by the prefix <s>vi-</s>] — what is stated?
What is stated is: "some" [<s>pramāṇas</s> are negated, not all].
Having examined the <s>pramāṇas</s> relied upon by the components, he examines the aggregate.
And so forth. //14//

Regarding the validity of those [means of knowledge] —
The meaning of this is as follows:
If the <s>Mādhyamika</s> (Buddhist) says that perception and the rest are not valid because the three times are not established — then the <s>pramāṇas</s> relied upon by the components of his own statement, being established through ordinary worldly cognition, are themselves unexamined and accepted as established, and by those [pramāṇas] the validity of the others is negated.
To this it is said:
Regarding the validity of those — i.e., regarding the validity of the perception and the rest relied upon by the components [of his statement] — there is no negation of all <s>pramāṇas</s>, since the validity of those relied upon by the components is accepted.
Now, what is this "being established without examination"?
Is it inability to withstand examination, or is it being beyond the scope of doubt because established for all people?
In the first alternative — it is well said that what is itself poorly established through inability to withstand examination negates the validity of others.
Therefore the latter alternative [holds], and thus not the validity of all [is negated], precisely because of the validity of that [relied upon by the components].
Here the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [states]: the prefix <s>vi-</s> has the meaning of agreement; it accepts the meaning of the negation-word while specifying a particular — but it is not a word expressing something different [from negation], not a contradictory statement — this is the meaning.
This is what was stated — "there is no contradiction."
Why? Because of the absence of the meaning.
For the contradiction of negating all <s>pramāṇas</s> when the <s>pramāṇas</s> relied upon by the components of one's own statement are accepted as valid has been stated before — that negation contradicts the former.
"And it is impossible" — this means "absence of the meaning."
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this.
"The prefix <s>vi-</s> [operates] in the negation of the specific."
What is stated amounts to this: insofar as it means "negation specifically regarding all <s>pramāṇas</s>," so far it means "contradiction" — because the syllable <s>vi-</s> accepts the meaning of the negation-word.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.15: And the non-negation across the three times — [the three times are established] like the establishment of sound from [musical instruments such as] the lute.

children.translated_text: like a sound previously apprehended as caused by the lute.
This is what was stated — "because of being caused by the lute."
"From the observation of smoke" —

children.text: saṃyoginā hi vahninā viśiṣṭo dhūmo 'numīyate na kāraṇena, astīti varttamānāvabhāsānupapatteriti // 15 //
children.translated_text: For the smoke is inferred as qualified by the fire with which it is in conjunction, not [qualified] by the cause — because the appearance as existing in the present would be impossible. //15//

Thus the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, having shown the non-contradiction with <s>pramāṇa</s> through similarity even in the non-negation of the subsequent [time] from the non-establishment of the three times, now reads a <s>sūtra</s> aimed at showing the non-establishment.
"Non-negation of the three times" <s>sūtra</s> 15. He objects to its reading.
"For what purpose?" —
If the meaning of this <s>sūtra</s> has already been stated independently before, then the reading of the <s>sūtra</s> is unnecessary — this is the meaning.
He resolves.
"Previously stated" —
We did not state that beyond the <s>sūtra</s>, but rather it is the very meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> — the reading of the <s>sūtra</s> by us is for the purpose of making known — this is the meaning.
He negates the [view] that the negation [of the three times] is restricted to either before, after, or simultaneously.
"Without restriction" —
The particle <s>khalu</s> here has the meaning "because."
Because the sage demonstrates the lack of restriction.
The <s>Vārttika</s> shows that the reading of the <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of indicating its derivation.
Why is it placed here, crossing the order of reading?
And here too, why was the <s>Bhāṣya</s> on it not stated [earlier]? — this should be considered.
He resolves.
"Because there is no distinction" —
Now, if sound is inherent in the aperture of the ear, how does it indicate a musical instrument with which it is not in contact? — to this
he says: "that which, of the sounds of the lute and the flute."
This sound is the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>); "preceded by the sound born from the contact of the finger with the lute"
is the property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>); because it possesses an uncommon property caused by that,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.16: And [the objection of non-establishment is refuted by] the knowability [of the three times], just as the validity of a balance [is established].

children.translated_text: Now, the objection is raised: what is indeterminate is not ultimately real — just as serpent-hood superimposed upon a rope: one person imagines the very same rope to be a serpent at the very same time, while another imagines it to be a stream. The same person, having first imagined it to be a serpent, later imagines it to be a stream. Similarly, the relation of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s> [is indeterminate]; therefore it is not ultimately real. To this, the next <s>sūtra</s> is addressed: '<s>Prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is the scale too, like its validity' (<s>sū</s>. 16). He construes it: '<s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) is also <s>prameya</s>' — this. The intention is as follows: when momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>) and transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) have been refuted, a stable entity that has arisen from its own cause, upon the proximity of various other entities, being connected with various properties, undergoes various cognitions and designations. To show this convergence (<s>samāveśa</s>), he asks — 'but when.' The answer — 'then, because of the instrumental cause.' And for the purpose of indicating this very meaning, the <s>sūtra</s> is: '<s>prameya</s> is the scale too, like its validity.' Not only is the <s>pramāṇa</s> a scale in the aggregate-weight [sense], but when there is doubt about its own validity, the scale [itself] is an object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) — [tested] by another scale with established <s>pramāṇa</s>-status, by which gold and the like have been examined — 'like its validity.' Just as the scale is <s>prameya</s> with respect to its validity, so too every other <s>pramāṇa</s> is <s>prameya</s> with respect to its own validity — this is the meaning. This the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> states: 'thus, without remainder, in its entirety.' The purport of the doctrine — the meaning of the treatise. In some cases there is convergence of knower-hood, knowable-hood, and <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood — as in the self (<s>ātman</s>). For it is the knower, and being known it is the knowable, and through what is known about it, its qualities are a <s>pramāṇa</s> in subsequent inference. In some cases there is convergence of <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood, knowable-hood, and result-hood — as in cognition (<s>buddhi</s>). In some cases there is convergence of <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood and knowable-hood — as in doubt and the like. This is the pervasion of convergence throughout the doctrine. 'And thus the <s>kāraka</s> (agent-factor) words' — here the <s>vārttikakāra</s> completes and explains. 'And just as <s>pramāṇa</s>.' 'As many' — wherever the instrumental causes are present, the invariable occurrence of their effects is the rule (<s>niyama</s>). 'Standing in space, the tree is an agent independently' — this is the <s>bhāṣya</s>. There the <s>vārttikakāra</s> asks about independence — 'what then is independence?' Not being directed by other agent-factors, and being the director of other agent-factors — this is stated as the independence of the agent. But here, because of the absence of other agent-factors, such independence does not exist — this is the import. The answer — 'not depending on other agent-factors': for one who depends on other agent-factors, independence is spoken of in some manner through being a director; for one who does not depend [on them], independence is even more [pronounced] — this is the meaning. When the word 'standing' (<s>sthiti</s>) means the negation of going — as long as 'it does not go' is said, so long 'it stands' is said. And here, since negation is determined in dependence on what is negated, the prior-posterior sequence is a limiting condition of the negation, but in its own nature the negation cannot have prior-posterior sequence. When, however, [the root '<s>as</s>'] denotes existence — meaning it denotes the universal 'existence' (<s>sattā</s>) — '<s>asti</s>' manifests [existence]. For the tree, possessing largeness and form, the inherence of existence alone is what manifests existence — and in that [the tree] is independent — this is the meaning. The experience of connection with the house — the obtaining of connection with the house — is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). The action pertaining to that — the effort that holds and sustains — by that it stands. 'The pot stands in the house' — but this is a figurative usage. When, however, [the word means] 'not broken' — here too the prior-posterior sequence of what is negated is merely a limiting condition for the negation's being so. Alternatively, even in 'it stands,' there may be, with some intention, a dependence on other agent-factors; even so, independence is precisely through being the director — thus he says — 'aggregate.' The collection of parts is the aggregate; a portion of that is a part. '<s>Dhriyate</s>' — the verbal ending is in the agent sense. Or, stability is being the object of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>). Even when that [recognition] depends on other agent-factors, independence is through being the director — thus he says — 'prior-posterior.' Many cognitions connected with a synonym [i.e., the same entity], experienced before and after, and then re-experienced by the same property-bearer — this is [called] memory, or recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>). The momentarist (<s>vaināśika</s>) teaches — 'the wheel.' The very same spinning of the wheel caused by the conjunction with the stick [continues] even when the conjunction with the stick has ceased — this is the meaning. He resolves — 'not a <s>pramāṇa</s>.' When there is no powerful defeater (<s>bādhaka</s>), the falsity of recognition cannot be [established]; but in the case of flames and the like, such [a defeater] exists — this is the meaning. And when the falsity of all recognition-cognitions [is proposed], a false recognition-cognition cannot arise [to support that claim], since it would lack a seed (<s>bīja</s>) — thus he says — 'and false cognitions.' The momentarist asks — 'but in your view.' One who says this, while invalidating perception as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, cannot be instructed by it — therefore he states inference as a <s>pramāṇa</s>. 'The <s>pramāṇa</s> has been stated in the definition of the self.' 'Form' — he states another inference. 'It will cause to act' — the experiencing at the time of the effect is the attaining of the time of the effect. The momentarist raises a doubt — 'without a substrate.' Having depended on the prior state and having been transformed — this is the meaning. He criticizes — 'that is not so.' The co-temporality of the thing to be placed with its substrate is established through experience; therefore the substrate, being a cause, must persist until the time of the effect. But the substratelessness of the effect is not within the scope of experience; rather, it is to be proved by reasoning, and that [reasoning] is untenable because of the absence of an example. And recognition cannot be dismissed merely because of disagreement [about it]. And the proofs for momentary destruction will be refuted. For if the substrate-hood of forms and the like is denied, then there is contradiction with [the Buddhist's] own acceptance: 'the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) are earth and the like; the elemental derivatives (<s>bhautikas</s>) are forms and the like.' He states a contradiction with another acceptance — 'and what has been said by you.' Not only is the dependent-nature (<s>āśritatva</s>) of forms and the like accepted by you, but it is also tenable — thus he says — 'because of being without a substrate.' He asks — 'in the [grammatical] object (<s>karman</s>), what is the <s>kāraka</s> (agent-factor) meaning?' — meaning the meaning of the <s>kāraka</s> word. For <s>kāraka</s> is that which is the instrumental cause of an action; but what is merely pervaded by the action is not an instrumental cause of it, and hence is not a <s>kāraka</s>. And how can a non-<s>kāraka</s> be a [grammatical] object? Since the designation 'object' falls within the domain of <s>kāraka</s> — this is the import. The answer — 'being the domain of action.' Being the domain of action — being that whose result belongs to an action not inhering in the self — is object-hood. For by the action of seeing (<s>darśana</s>), which inheres in <s>Devadatta</s>, an experience with the tree as its object is produced — and this very thing, the experience's having the object as its domain, is [defined as] having its determination dependent on the object — as stated in the definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, for the domain of an action, the existence prior to the action justifies its <s>kāraka</s>-status. And thus the object-status of what is transformable (<s>vikārya</s>) and what is to be reached (<s>prāpya</s>) is justified. For what is to be produced (<s>nirvartya</s>), however — such as cloth and the like — even though there is no prior existence of the action, nevertheless the prior existence of the threads that constitute it [justifies it]; and since their purpose is cloth-hood, by figurative identification, the usage 'he makes cloth' is justified. As will be stated in the <s>sūtra</s> on co-occurrence and the like: 'in the reeds intended for a mat.' By this definition of object, [expressions like] 'he walks through the village, approaching the roots of trees,' and the like should also be understood as included. In '<s>Caitra</s> goes to the city' — just as the attaining inheres in the city, so too it inheres in <s>Caitra</s> — lest <s>Caitra</s> too, having the result of the action, become an object, it has been said 'not inhering in the self.' And even in mental perception pertaining to the self, although the self does not become an object, nevertheless the action of knowing is indeed transitive — since there is some object of knowledge other than the self as a property of the self — thus everything is clear. 'The tree becomes a recipient (<s>sampradāna</s>)' — following the definition of <s>Pāṇini</s> and following common usage, '<s>sampradāna</s>' is [used as] a designation consistent with meaning — this is the import. 'The cause in the obstruction by gravity' — this is with the intention of the example at hand. And thus, since the property of being a support (<s>ādheya</s>) is understood for qualities and the like too, their support-relation with substance and the like is established. Therefore [the statement] 'the substance in its own nature is not a <s>kāraka</s>' — what was said by the <s>Mādhyamika</s> is actually what we accept. But a purely imagined <s>kāraka</s> we do not tolerate — with this intention the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> has spoken. 'And this being so' — 'not mere action' — not mere subsidiary action. 'That which is the means of accomplishing the principal action, endowed with a specific subsidiary operation.' Having repeated this, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains — 'and this being so.' By this, the general [definition of] <s>kāraka</s> has been stated. The <s>bhāṣya</s> pertaining to the specific definition — 'that which is the instrument of action, independently' — he explains — 'but when the specific.' One might think: let 'instrument of action' suffice, or 'endowed with a specific action' — why adopt both? — therefore he says — 'and of every <s>kāraka</s>.' If mere subsidiary action were stated, then since all [factors] have agency in that, there would be no diversity among <s>kārakas</s>. And if only the principal action were adopted, then without mentioning the subsidiary operation, there would be no diversity among all [factors] — therefore the adoption of both is purposeful. He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'thus, by definition' — 'and thus the <s>śāstra</s> (grammar).' He teaches — 'if.' He resolves — 'not from capacity.' He teaches again — 'from capacity.' He resolves — 'this is not a fault.' Now, intellect and the like too are causes of the manifestation of capacity, and they are not in the form of action but in the form of quality — therefore it has been said 'by the word action.' Capacity (<s>sāmarthya</s>) means strength (<s>bala</s>). For even one who knows the means, being weak, does not act — like one with a lame hand and an axe. Therefore, the <s>kāraka</s> word is primary for the connection of capacity and action, but secondary for capacity alone. He applies to the case at hand — 'and these <s>kāraka</s> words.'

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.17: If [<s>pramāṇas</s>] are established through [other] <s>pramāṇas</s>, there would be the unwanted consequence of [needing] another <s>pramāṇa</s> to establish the <s>pramāṇas</s>.

children.translated_text: From what source does the property of being a cause of apprehension [arise]? — therefore he says.
'They are experienced' — the particle 'ca' is in the sense of reason.
From what does the property of being an object of apprehension [arise]? — therefore he says.
'My cognition is perception.' // 17 //

Now, the <s>pramāṇas</s> are objected to and resolved in another way. / 'Sir, there is [the usage] of action-words (<s>kārakaśabda</s>)' etc. / Here, the following alternatives present themselves: is the apprehension of the <s>pramāṇas</s> — perception and the like — with a means of proof or without? / Even when it is with a means of proof, is it by these very [pramāṇas] — perception and the like — or by another <s>pramāṇa</s>? / Even when it is by these very [pramāṇas], is it by that very particular instance of perception [or by another]? / Or [is it that] one instance [is apprehended] by another instance? / In the case of accepting another <s>pramāṇa</s>, there would be a breach of the division-<s>sūtra</s> [which enumerates only four pramāṇas], / and also the fault of infinite regress. / For if perception and the like are apprehended by [other instances of] perception and the like, there is infinite regress. / But if apprehended by that very particular instance, there is the contradiction of self-operation. / For the very sword-edge does not cut that same sword-edge. / Therefore the apprehension of <s>pramāṇa</s> is without a means of proof; / and if so, done with <s>pramāṇas</s> as means of proving <s>prameyas</s> — let the apprehension of <s>prameya</s> too be without a means of proof, like that of <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the first position. / [The resolution:] The establishment of <s>pramāṇa</s> is not without a means of proof, nor is there the acceptance of a <s>pramāṇa</s> other than perception and the like, by which there would be a breach of the division-<s>sūtra</s>. / Nor is it accepted that that very instance [of perception] apprehends itself, / by which there would be the contradiction of self-operation. / Rather, we maintain that one of the same class as perception etc. apprehends one of the same class as perception etc. / And there is no infinite regress: some <s>pramāṇa</s> is not known but is a cause of knowing another, / like smoke and the like. / And some [pramāṇa] is itself unknown yet is a means of cognition, like the eye and the like. In that case, the eye and the like, for their own cognition, depend on the eye and the like, but the eye and the like are means of cognition without depending on [prior] cognition — so where is the infinite regress? / And the desire to know [the pramāṇa] — that too is knowable, and that [desire] arises only sometimes and somewhere — so in saying that there is infinite regress due to the need for another <s>pramāṇa</s> for that purpose [of knowing the pramāṇa], / it has been shown in the first <s>sūtra</s> that since even regarding seen objects, engagement occurs even from doubt, and since through the capacity for engagement, [the pramāṇa's] being easily known [is established] — for unseen objects, since [the pramāṇa] is not impossible to know through the similarity with <s>pramāṇa</s> whose validity has been ascertained through the capacity for engagement. / Therefore, the established conclusion is: the <s>pramāṇas</s> — perception and the like — are apprehended by [other instances of] perception and the like, and there is no infinite regress. / The <s>bhāṣya</s> — 'bhoḥ' is an interjection of address.
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.18: Or, when that [objection] ceases, the establishment of <s>prameya</s> is like the establishment of <s>pramāṇa</s>. //
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.19: [The establishment of <s>pramāṇa</s>] is not like the establishment of the light of a lamp. //

children.translated_text: Because vision's being so [i.e., self-luminous] corresponds to the presence and absence of the lamp; / and because a knower and a mind are observed [as necessary conditions] — this is the <s>bhāṣya</s>; the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains it. / 'And this is not definitive' etc. / 'The knower knows' — this is intended in the sense of having an object; for the act of knowing is not inherent in another thing such that the self would be the object; rather, it is inherent in the knower alone. For it has been stated that the object is that which bears the fruit of the action inherent in another. Therefore, it is the qualities of the self such as pleasure and the like that are the objects here; but the self has the property of being illuminated. By that intention, it is called 'knowable.' But the mind, although it is both an instrument and an object with respect to its own cognition, even so, there is no contradiction of self-operation. / For if what is known were the instrument, then there would be the fault of self-dependence. / But by its own existence it is an instrument for cognition, and its cognition is different and its existence is different; and the act of knowing is not inherent in the mind / but inherent in the self — therefore the knowability and the property of being a means of cognition of the mind do not entail a fault. / But those teachers of the [Buddhist] school who think that just as the light of a lamp does not require another light, so too there are and will be <s>pramāṇas</s> that do not require another <s>pramāṇa</s> — / against them he says:

children.translated_text: but another fault does arise — this is the meaning.
And the rest of the text, which presents the established conclusion, has been substantiated by us
and so is not explained [further]. / 'So that he might bring up the infinite regress' — [this is said] with a touch of humor. // 19 //

Just as this consequence — the consequence of the independence of <s>pramāṇas</s> — [follows from the lamp analogy]: since the lamp is observed to be capable of illumination without depending on another lamp, the <s>pramāṇas</s>, like light, will be established as not depending on another <s>pramāṇa</s>; for this purpose the consequence is brought forth. [Similarly,] even the <s>prameyas</s> will be established as independent — for this purpose too [the consequence] should be brought forth; and thus there would be the non-existence of <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning. / Having thus stated, by resorting to the lamp-example, the consequence of the non-existence of <s>pramāṇa</s>, he says that if one resorts to the example of a pot and the like, then even <s>pramāṇa</s> would require another <s>pramāṇa</s>. / 'And just as the form of a pot and the like is apprehended' etc. / The <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains this <s>bhāṣya</s>: just as the light of a lamp does not depend on one of its own class, so too <s>pramāṇas</s> do not depend on one of their own class; but it does not follow that just as the form of a pot and the like depends on <s>pramāṇa</s>, so too <s>pramāṇas</s> depend on <s>pramāṇa</s>. / Why then does the form of a pot and the like depend on <s>pramāṇa</s>? — therefore he says. / 'And in the illumination of the form of a pot and the like' etc. / The light of the lamp there is the <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is well-known in the world — this is the meaning. / Why are the <s>pramāṇas</s> not like the form of a pot — let them too be illuminated by another <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning. / By this, it has been said that through the lamp-example there is no restriction to independence, nor through the pot-example is there a restriction to dependence — there is no reason for either restriction. / He states the absence of a reason for the other restriction. / 'And this lamp-light example' etc. / For just as the <s>pramāṇas</s> are independent by the lamp-example, why should not the <s>prameyas</s> too be so by that very example? — and then there would be the consequence of the non-existence of <s>pramāṇa</s>. / For there is no reason for the restriction that the lamp is an example only for <s>pramāṇas</s> and not for <s>prameyas</s>. / By this, the <s>bhāṣya</s> passage 'just as the consequence' has been explained. / By saying 'let the lamp-light be the example,' the restriction 'this example only and not that example' has been refuted; by the former, the restriction 'through the lamp-example only independence, not through the pot-example dependence' has been refuted — so there is no repetition. / But by the reason of being illuminating and the like, one can say that the lamp-example is captured [as relevant] by that restriction. / Only, the illuminating nature, when it is to be proved in respect of independence from another of the same class, needs to be analyzed: is it [independence from] something absolutely of the same class, or from something merely of the same class? If absolutely of the same class, then it proves what is already established, / for the eye and the like as <s>pramāṇas</s> do not depend on another eye and the like for their own apprehension. / But if [independence from] something merely of the same class, then even light has that dependence, / since it too depends on the eye and the like — and therefore the example lacks the <s>sādhya</s>, and the reason is contradictory: visual cognition is not apprehended by another visual cognition, but by a cognition that has [visual cognition] as its object — so it is not [independence from] something absolutely of the same class. With this intention, what the <s>vārttikakāra</s> stated as 'inconclusive' [means:] this fault does not arise,
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.20: [The objection of] the non-establishment of the definition of perception [arises] because of the incomplete statement. //
'pratya—t' (<s>sūtra</s> 20) //

children.translated_text: And by this <s>sūtra</s>, is it the definition of perception that is stated, or the nature of perception? Not the cause of perception, to begin with — thus he says: / 'This definition of perception that you state' etc. / The meaning is: the cause of perception. / When the cause is present, the effect — cognition — is indicated. / He raises a doubt about the second alternative — 'or else' etc. / The <s>siddhāntin</s> says: / 'Not in either way' etc. / The definition-position alone is the accepted established doctrine; the acceptance of the cause-position should be seen as a bold assertion. / An uncommon cause that pervades all instances of perception is being ascertained. / For there is no other such cause of perception — neither the conjunction of self and mind, nor the conjunction of sense organ and mind — the former being common [to all cognitions, not just perception] and the latter not pervading [all perception]. / He states another resolution: 'or, by the meaning' — up to 'the contact with mind is also a cause.' / // 20 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.21: Perception does not arise in the absence of the conjunction of self and mind. //

children.translated_text: Having thus stated the essence of the established doctrine, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> explains [the matter] even without reading the <s>sūtra</s> 'not of self and mind' etc. / 'And [when] the substance is not in conjunction' etc. / For the entire set of causes requires the mutual concurrence [of its members] for the production of the effect; otherwise, effects would arise from causes situated anywhere whatsoever. / Therefore, the self too must produce the effect in conjunction with the mind, / and the conjunction of self and mind is precisely conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>). / Or let cognition be born from conjunction — why can it not be born from the conjunction of object, sense organ, and self, without the need for the conjunction with mind? — therefore / he says: 'in the contact with mind' etc. / Therefore, the conjunction of self and mind too must be stated — this is the prima facie view. / This is the <s>sūtra</s> 'not in the absence of the conjunction of self and mind' etc., for which the <s>bhāṣya</s> was composed before its reading. / The <s>vārttikakāra</s>, having restated the <s>bhāṣya</s>, reads the prima facie <s>sūtra</s>. / 'nātma—ttiḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 21) // He states the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. / 'Of self and mind' etc. / The <s>vārttikakāra</s>, unable to bear even a moment's standing of the prima facie view, reminds [the reader] of the refutation that has already been stated. / 'It has been stated' etc. / // 21 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.22: The same consequence [would follow] for direction, space, time, and <s>ākāśa</s> (ether) too. //

yadyapi tatrāpi tejasyauṣṇyamasti tathāpyatyantābhibhavena svocitārthakriyānupayogādasatkalpatvamityarthaḥ
// 22 //
children.translated_text: When the prima facie view has been thus established by two <s>sūtras</s>, a bystander, thinking that by mere existence / the sense-object conjunction and the like have been stated to be causes, objects. / 'If from the mere existence of sense-object [conjunction]' (1). / Not by mere existence is causality [established]; for then even <s>ākāśa</s> (ether) and the like would be causes — and of such a nature are the conjunction of self and mind / and the conjunction of sense organ and self — so they are not proper causes — this is the meaning. / He refutes: / 'even if it is not a cause' etc. / Ascertainment of causality is not from positive concomitance alone, / but from both positive and negative concomitance. And in direction and the like, there is no negative concomitance, since their presence is unavoidable due to being eternal and all-pervading. But the conjunction of self and mind, operating in a body endowed with sense organs, has its capacity ascertained through both positive and negative concomitance, / since for a sleeping person, cognition does not arise. / But in the conjunction of sense organ and object, when the [object] is far away or concealed, cognition does not arise; / and in the absence of the conjunction of sense organ and mind, simultaneous cognitions do not arise — therefore there is no over-extension from <s>ākāśa</s> and the like. / The <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains this. / Those who describe causality from mere co-existence — whether prima facie advocates or <s>siddhāntins</s> — 'when there is absence, there is no existence' — the negative concomitance that comes as if by accident. / But it is not operative [for them] — against them the bystander speaks. / 'For them, direction, space' etc. / 'Just as the form of the moon' etc. / Although even there [in moonlight] there is heat in the luminous [body], nevertheless, due to extreme overpowering, because of the non-usefulness for the appropriate activity, it is as if non-existent — this is the meaning. / // 22 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.23: Because the self has cognition as its mark, there is no exclusion [of the self-mind conjunction as a cause]. //

children.text:
evaṃ pārśvasthe niraste pūrvapakṣī brūte /
yadyevamiti (204/2) siddhāntyāha /

children.translated_text: 'It need not be additionally enumerated' etc.
Cognition... (sūtra 23) // Here it is stated that cognition is the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the <s>ātman</s> (self).

children.text:
jñānaṃ tāvatkāryamanityatvād ghaṭavat /
(tacca)
kva cit samevataṃ kāryatvād ghaṭavat /
na ca tatpṛthivyādyāśritaṃ mānasapratyakṣatvāt /
yatpunaḥ pṛthivyādyāśritaṃ tat pratyakṣāntaravedyamapratyakṣameva vā /
na ca tathā jñānaṃ dravyāṣṭakātiriktāśritam /
tadāśrayaśca dravyajātīyaḥ, samavāyikāraṇatvādākāśavat /
tasya ca vibhutvamātmalakṣaṇe 'smābhiruktam /
ato guṇajātīyaṃ jñānaṃ, kāryatve mati vibhudravyasamavāyāc śabdavat /
evaṃ vyavasthite praśnottare vārttikagate vyākhyātavye /
ātmasamavāyāditi /
kāryatve sati vibhudravyasamavāyādityarthaḥ /
vibhudravyasamavāya evāsiddha iti vadatu āha /
na pṛthivyādiguṇaḥ svasaṃvedyatvāta /
mānasapratyakṣavedyatvādityarthaḥ /
svaparasaṃbaddhaṃ pratyakṣāntaravedyaṃ draṣṭavyam /
anyathā pṛthivyādiguṇena dvitvādinā vyabhicāraḥ syāditi /
tasmāj jñānaliṅga ātmā, na tvasāvasaṃyukto jñānaṃ janayati /
tasya sadātanatve sadā jñānotpādaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text:
Cognition, first, is an effect, because of being non-eternal, like a pot.
(And it)
is inherent in something, because of being an effect, like a pot.
And it does not inhere in earth and the like, because of being perceptible by mental perception (<s>mānasapratyakṣa</s>).
But what inheres in earth and the like is either knowable by another perception or entirely imperceptible.
And cognition is not like that — it does not inhere in [any substrate] other than the eight substances.
And its substrate belongs to the class of substances, because of being a material cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>), like <s>ākāśa</s> (space).
And we have stated its all-pervasiveness in the definition of the <s>ātman</s>.
Therefore cognition belongs to the class of qualities; when it is an effect, [it inheres] in an all-pervading substance through inherence, like sound.
Thus having established [this], the question and answer found in the <s>Vārttika</s> are to be explained.
"Because of inherence in the <s>ātman</s>" —
The meaning is: because of inherence in an all-pervading substance, when [cognition] is an effect.
Let one who says that the very inherence in an all-pervading substance is unestablished speak — he says.
It is not a quality of earth and the like, because of being known by self-awareness.
The meaning is: because of being knowable by mental perception.
"Known by itself and by what is connected with another" should be understood as "knowable by another perception."
Otherwise there would be deviation [in the reason] through duality and the like, which are qualities of earth and the like.
Therefore the <s>ātman</s> is inferred through cognition as its mark; but if it were unconnected, it could not produce cognition.
If it were eternally connected, there would be the absurd consequence of the perpetual production of cognition.
Therefore it requires an occasional difference in conjunction — from the meaning it is established.
The conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> (mind) is [thus established] — [it was] not stated by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> [explicitly].
To show that this resolution is made with confidence in debating, he reminds [us] of the supreme resolution already stated.
And it has been stated here. //23//
When the bystander has been thus refuted, the prima facie advocate speaks: / 'If this is so' etc. / The <s>siddhāntin</s> says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.24: And because of the non-simultaneity [of cognitions] being its mark, [the conjunction] is not of <s>manas</s> (mind) [alone].

children.text:
anyārthamiti /
prameyabhūtamanaḥsvarūpapratipādanārtham /
anyārthasyāpipa tadarthaprakāśakatvam (105/2) upapattiḥ /
liṅgam /
īdṛśaṃ hi talliṅgaṃ yadanyārthamapi manaso jñānakāraṇatvaṃ pratipādayatīti /
na hi jñānaṃ svatantraṃ yena svakāraṇaṃ mano nāpekṣeta, nāpi cakṣurādi svatantraṃ jñānajanane yena manojñānakaraṇaṃ na syādityāha /
na cakṣurādīti /
tasmādarthaprāptatvādātmanaḥsaṃyoga
indriyamanaḥsaṃyogaśca noktau sūtrakāreṇa
// 24 //
children.translated_text:
"For another purpose" —
For the purpose of demonstrating the nature of <s>manas</s> as an object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>).
Even what serves another purpose has the capacity to illuminate that purpose — this is the justification.
"Mark" —
For such is the mark of that [ātman] — that even while serving another purpose, it demonstrates the causality of <s>manas</s> with respect to cognition.
For cognition is not independent, such that it would not depend on <s>manas</s> as its cause; nor are the eye and the other [sense-organs] independent in producing cognition, such that <s>manas</s> would not be an instrument of cognition — he says.
"Not the eye and the rest" —
Therefore, since it is already obtained by the meaning, the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> [with manas]
and the conjunction of the sense-organs with <s>manas</s> were not stated by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>.
//24//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.25: Because [the contact of the sense-organ and the object] is the cause of perception, the contact of the sense-organ and the object is stated by its own word.
The meaning is: even regarding the contact of the sense-organ and the object, the derivation [of its being a cause] from the meaning is not different [from the others].
He resolves.

children.text: pratyakṣeti sarvānamidhāne hi pratyakṣaṃ na lakṣitaṃ syāditi tallakṣaṇāya kiñcidvaktavyam /
children.translated_text: If all [causes] are named in the definition of perception, then perception would not be defined — therefore something must be stated for its definition.

children.text: tatrendriyārthasannikarṣa eva vaktavyaḥ, samastapratyakṣavyāpakatvāt netarāvavyāpakatvādativyāpakatvācceti paramaḥ samādhiḥ // 25 //
children.translated_text: Among those, the contact of the sense-organ and the object alone must be stated, because it pervades all perception — not the others, because they either do not pervade or over-pervade — this is the supreme resolution. //25//

He teaches.
"But why?" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.26: And because it [cognition] is caused by the contact of the sense-organ and the object even in the case of those who are asleep or whose minds are occupied.

children.text:
supta-t (sū. 26) // jñānotpatteriti sūtraśeṣaḥ /
praṇidhāya saṅkalpya /
pradoṣe supto 'rddharātre mayotthātavyamiti,
so 'rdharātre evāvabudhyate /

children.translated_text: "Awakening-cognition" —

children.text: prabodhe nidrāvicchede sati dravyasparśasya saṃjñānaṃ prabodhajñānamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: awakening-cognition is the awareness of the touch of a substance when the interruption of sleep occurs at the time of awakening.
He explains "of those whose minds are sleeping."
"At one time, this [mind] goes to another object." //26//

Sleeping... (sūtra 26) // "Of the arising of cognition" is the supplement of the <s>sūtra</s>.
"Having concentrated" means having resolved.
Having resolved at dusk while sleeping, "I must wake up at midnight,"
he wakes up at exactly midnight.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.27: And the designation of specific cognitions is by those [sense-organs].

children.text:
prādhānye ca hetvantaram /
taiścā-ṇām (sū. 27) // indriyairvyapadeśaṃ vigrahasamāsābhyāṃ jñānasya darśayati /
ghrāṇeti /
indriyaviṣayasaṅkhyānurodhāttajjñānasya tadvyapadeśa ityāha /
indriyeti /
vārttikaṃ-yaccā-sādhāraṇaṃ teneti /
digādirapyupādhikalpitena prācītvādinā kāryaṃ viśeṣayannasādhāraṇamevetyabhiprāyaḥ
// 27 //
children.translated_text:
And another reason for [the contact of sense-organ and object's] primacy.
By those... cognitions (sūtra 27) // He shows the designation of cognition by the sense-organs through both analysis and synthesis of the compound.
"By the nose" —
In accordance with the enumeration of sense-organs and objects, the cognition of each is designated by that [sense-organ] — he says.
"By the sense-organ" —
The <s>Vārttika</s> — "and what... uncommon, by that" —
The intent is: even direction and the like, qualifying through conditionally attributed properties like "eastern" etc., [function as] uncommon [causes].
//27//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.28: [The contact of ātman and manas is not the cause of cognition alone,] because of contradiction.
By this connected [series of sūtras], the contact of the sense-organ and the object
alone is the cause of cognition, not the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>,
nor the conjunction of the sense-organ and <s>manas</s> as the cause of cognition — thinking that this is what has been stated, he teaches.
Contradiction... (sūtra 28) //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.29: No, because of the predominance of the object-[contact].

parihārasūtram // nārtha-t (sū. 29) // anenendriyārthasannikarṣasya prādhānyamātramucyate /
na tvātmamanaḥsaṃyogasyendriyamanaḥsaṃyogasya vā 'kāraṇatvamucyata iti na vyāghāta ityarthaḥ /
pṛcchati /

saṅkalpa icchā /

yathaiveti /
nanvasya jātyāyurbhoganimittatvamavagataṃ,

tena hyapreryamāṇe manasīti /
bhogo hyadṛṣṭasya pradhānaṃ prayojanaṃ tannāntarīyakatayā janmāyuṣī ākṣipati /
svasaṃbandhisukhaduḥkhasākṣātkāraśca bhogaḥ, tadāyatanaṃ ca śarīram /
aprāptaṃ ca mano na tatra bhogaṃ ca bhogaviṣayau sukhaduḥkhe ca tayoḥ kāraṇaṃ ca jñānaṃ janayitumarhati,
nūnaṃ tatprāptihetormanaḥkarmaṇaḥ kāraṇamadṛṣṭaṃ vaktavyam /
anyathāsya sarvadravyaguṇakarmakāraṇatā na syāt /
mā mūtsarvārthatetyata āha /
eṣitavyaṃ cāsyeti /
aṇūnāṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ bhūtasūkṣmāṇāmiti /
vyāhatatvāditi pūrvapakṣāsūtram /
asya tātparyamāha vārttikakāraḥ /
aneneti /
(206/7) nanviyaṃ trisūtrī indripayārthasannikarṣasya prādhānyamāha, na punaḥ saṃyogāntarasya kāraṇatvaṃ pratyācaṣṭa
ityata āha /
iyaṃ kileti /
kāraṇatvaṃ pratiṣidhyata
ityabhimānaḥ pūrvapakṣiṇa ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: "Observed contradiction"
Non-simultaneity is observed; its contradiction — this is the meaning.
The rest has been explained through the explanation of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. //29//

The resolution-<s>sūtra</s>. // No... predominance (sūtra 29) // By this, only the predominance of the contact of the sense-organ and the object is stated.
But the causality of the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, or of the conjunction of the sense-organ and <s>manas</s>, is not denied — therefore there is no contradiction: this is the meaning.
He asks.
"In the absence of resolve and concentration" —
Effort is concentration (<s>praṇidhāna</s>).
Resolve is desire (<s>saṅkalpa</s>).
The answer.
"Just as" —
But the causality of this [<s>adṛṣṭa</s>] in terms of birth-class, lifespan, and enjoyment is understood,
not its capacity to impel the mind — therefore he says.
"For when the mind is not impelled by that" —
For enjoyment is the primary purpose of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit), and as its necessary accompaniment it implies birth and lifespan.
And enjoyment is the direct experience of pleasure and pain connected with oneself; and the body is its seat.
And <s>manas</s>, not having reached [a given sense-organ], cannot produce enjoyment there, nor pleasure and pain which are the objects of enjoyment, nor the cognition which is their cause —
therefore <s>adṛṣṭa</s> must be declared the cause of the activity of <s>manas</s>, which is the cause of its reaching [the sense-organ].
Otherwise, it would not be the cause of all substances, qualities, and actions.
Lest it be [the cause of] all things [indiscriminately] — therefore he says.
"And this should be sought" —
The qualifier of atoms is "of the subtle elements" (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>).
"Because of contradiction" is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's) <s>sūtra</s>.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states its purport.
"By this" —
But this triad of <s>sūtras</s> states the predominance of the contact of sense-organ and object, it does not deny the causality of the other conjunction
— to this he says.
"This, they say" —
The meaning is that the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (opponent) has the notion that causality is being denied.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.30: Perception is inference, because of the apprehension of a part of the apprehended [object].

children.translated_text: For <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation) operates when a dyad (<s>dvika</s>) is established through direct perception.

children.text: trikasya tu pratyakṣeṇa prasiddhau pratyakṣatodṛṣṭamiti viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: But the distinction is that when a triad (<s>trika</s>) is established through direct perception, it is called <s>pratyakṣatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference from direct observation).
Since everything [in the atomist view] is imperceptible, tree-cognition arises neither from inference based on direct observation nor from inference based on general observation — he says.
"But in your position" etc. //30//

Hereafter, regarding this —
(207/12) For there is no composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) that is a separate entity from the parts;
rather, the parts alone truly exist. Among them, having grasped some parts and inferred the parts that accompany them, the tree-cognition arisen from recognition is just an inference resting on those very parts — and since direct perception is thus subsumed within inference, the classification-<s>sūtra</s> cannot demarcate a lesser or greater number [of <s>pramāṇas</s>] — this is the meaning.
He refutes.
"Not so, because the alternatives are untenable as the case may be."
For a part of the composite is a support —
(208/14) One (<s>eka</s>) and that (<s>ca</s>) is a region (<s>deśa</s>), hence "one-region" (<s>ekadeśa</s>).
And a region is a support, but there is no composite whole to be supported — so how can it be a support? — this is the meaning.
Or else he states verbal-referential skill.
"Skill in words or in meaning" — this is the meaning.
First, he states the lack of skill regarding meaning.
"Non-effectual" etc.
For the causes of a single effect have mutual proximity for producing that single effect.
Just as clay, stick, wheel, and thread have proximity for producing a pot.
And effects born from a single causal aggregate have mutual proximity,
like form, taste, smell, and touch; or cause and effect,
like fire and smoke. But for things that are neither cause and effect, nor having a single effect, nor having a single cause — how can there be a fixed proximity for them? — this is the meaning.
He states the lack of verbal skill.
"Nor mutually" etc.
A part, in supporting the composite, depends on another part.
Thus the parts are mutually helpful.
But in the absence of a composite, the parts are not mutually helpful — so how are they parts? — this is the meaning.
"Nor is [the tree-cognition] born from the recognition of a non-tree" etc.
For having grasped a cow with a white mark, the recognition "[this is a] cow" is seen in a black cow, but having grasped a horse, the recognition "[this is a] cow" in another horse is not seen — for what reason?
Because those two [horses] are not cows. Similarly, since the lower portion, upper portion, etc. are not trees, the recognition "tree" would not arise in a part — this is the meaning.
If one were to say: let there be no grasping of a property-bearer in the form of a tree; rather, having first inferred the property-bearer — a particular tree — from the lower portion, one will recognize it — to this he says.
"Nor is there inference."
(209/6) Why? — to this he says.
"Inference" etc.
This inferrer does not first perceive fire and then, through inference, apprehend the fire qualified by smoke and recognize: "this is smoke and this is fire."
But if one objects that recognition comes first and inference afterward — to this he says.
"Nor having recognized" etc.
Since fire is known at the very time of recognition, the inference "there must be fire here" would be purposeless — this is the meaning.
Granting [the opponent's view], he says.
"Even having recognized" etc.
"What then of the lower portion?" etc.
That which has parts is not itself a part but is only partitioned.
Why does he not see [it]? — to this he says.
"The lower and upper portions are not connected."
(210/4) For they would be connected through inherence in a single composite, but there is no composite.
Nor are they even conjoined, since conjunction has been refuted through the same method as the refutation of the composite — this is the meaning.
He asks.
"But how then?" etc.
The answer: "always with the lower portion" etc.
That there is no connection has already been stated.
But granting it, the answer is: even if they are connected, even with the connection, that [tree] is impossible to grasp — this is the meaning.
"Even if connected" — this is indeed a statement of concession.
As for what is said "born from the recognition-cognition" etc.
Earlier, even when a tree exists, it was said that tree-cognition born from recognition does not arise in a part because parts are not trees; now, however, since the tree does not exist, the recognition "tree" in a part does not arise — so there is no repetition.
"And the form perceived by me, and the taste" etc.
The very one who is colored by the taste-cognition is the same one colored by the form-cognition — this is the meaning.
"Because of the <s>pramāṇa</s> determining the object as it truly is" etc.
Just as even a mistaken inference is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> due to its connection with the object — so it was shown in the first chapter.
"Error through imitation of the principal" —
(211/1) when there is the erroneous cognition (<s>viparītakhyāti</s>),
and that was established in the first chapter.
"Not so, because the word does not express that meaning" etc.
What then is the meaning of the word "thus" (<s>tathā</s>)?
[It could mean] the form of the atoms, or their contiguity, or their difference in conjunction, or their difference in origination.
If merely form — then there would be tree-cognition even in pots etc.
If difference of form — then in the next instant it would be a non-tree.
For that prior form does not [continue].
If contiguity — that exists in pots etc. too.
Or nowhere at all, due to the intervening atoms of smell, taste, form, and touch.
Since conjunction is not accepted by you, how can there be a difference in it?
Difference in origination is also just the form of the atoms.
For there is no origination of theirs apart from the atoms.
And form has already been considered.
If somewhere there were a real arrangement of parts that served as the basis for the use of words like "lower portion," "upper portion," etc., then the meaning of the word "thus" would be understood; but for you, this [arrangement] is nowhere real, since the atoms that truly exist are partless — this is the meaning.
The questioner, confused into thinking that even for <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation), there is no direct perception regarding the property-bearer, asks.
"Of <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>" etc.
(212/6) The answer.
"This is the distinction" etc.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.31: Not [subsumption under inference], because there is apprehension by direct perception of at least that much.

children.translated_text: "The sense organ" etc.
And direct perception arises from the connection of the sense organ with the object,
but inference does not [arise] in this way — this is the meaning. //31//

Not direct perception (sū. 31) // Direct perception does not become inference.
Why?
As much of the class of objects as is a part — the grasping of that part is the apprehension; and in the reason "because of the apprehension of that part," that much too [is apprehended] by direct perception.
Otherwise, due to the non-arising of inference in the absence of part-grasping.
Or, if that grasping is [achieved] through another inference, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, the thesis — "the apprehension of that much of the class of objects by direct perception is itself inference" — is contradicted by the reason "because of the non-apprehension of part-grasping [by inference]." Or alternatively, if part-grasping is not accepted as [occurring through] direct perception, then since no other <s>pramāṇa</s> is tenable for that, the reason is unestablished — this is a rope that binds from both sides, as it were.
Lest the reason be unestablished because part-grasping [occurs] through inference — to this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "nor is part-grasping" etc.
Inference (<s>anumiti</s>) is the inferential cognition.
"Because of the absence of a reason through the consequence of infinite regress in producing" etc.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this <s>sūtra</s>.
"And this is contradictory" etc.
But even if parts are perceptible, only that much would be perception, not everything — to this he says.
"And it is not thus asserted — everything" etc.
"Without any particular form" etc.
For inference has three forms, and direct perception is not of that kind.
"Because of having objects in all three times" etc.
By this he indicates that inference has objects that are beyond [direct perception], while direct perception has objects that are not beyond — hence the difference — this is the meaning.
Even the cognition of the mark-grasping, which is the fruit of direct perception and is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, receives the assistance of the memory of the connection between mark and marked in its origination;
but direct perception as a <s>pramāṇa</s> does not [receive such assistance] — therefore [inference] depends on the memory of the mark-marked connection either in its origination or in its effect — this is the meaning.
"And otherwise" etc. — he explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with this — "moreover" etc.
(213/4) He states the meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with "but this is not inference" etc.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.32: Nor is the apprehension of a part [possible without a composite], because of the real existence of the composite (<s>avayavin</s>).

tathaiva darśanāditi /
va hi dṛśyamānasya dṛśyamānāntaravaidharmyeṇa rūpamupalabhyamānaṃ śakvamapākartum, mā bhūd dṛśyamānavaidharmyeṇa dṛśyamānarūpāntarāpākaraṇamaviṣeṣāt /
tasmāddarśanānurodhātprameyavaicitryasiddherūpavannaḥ saṃyogaśabdabuddhyādīnāṃ tatraiva tadānīmabhāvo bhāvaśceti /
atra evaiṣāmavyāpyavṛttitvamāsthīyate /
rūpādīnāṃ tu na dṛṣṭastatraiva tadānīmabhāvo bhāvaśceti teṣāṃ vyāpyavṛttīnāṃ bhāvābhāvau yugapadekatra viruddhāviti siddham-raktāraktayorekatrāvirodhaḥ sahadarśanāditi /
yatpunaryadanekavṛtti tannānā,
anekavṛttiścāvayavyabhyupagata iti prasaṅgasādhanaṃ svabhāvahetuḥ, nānātvābhāvādanekavṛttitvābhāva
iti prasaṅgaviparyayo vyāpakānupalabdhiriti /
tatra brūmaḥ /
ekatvānekavṛttitvayoravirodhena nānātvasya vyāpakatvasiddherna prasaṅgo nāpi viparyaya iti /
yathaiva nīle paricchidyamāne tadabhāvo vyavacchidyate, anyathā na nīlaṃ paricchinnaṃ syāt, evaṃ tadabhāvāvinābhāvi pītamapi nīlaparicchedakaṃ pratyakṣaṃ vyavacchinatti, tathaikāvayavasaṃsarge avayavinaḥ paricchidyamāne tadabhāvo vyavacchidyate,
tadabhāvāvinābhūtāścāvayavāntarasaṃsargā iti tepi vyavacchettavyāḥ, tadavyavacchede tadabhāvo na vyavacchidyeteti sa eva tadānīmeva tatra bhavenna bhavedveti durghaṭamāpadyeta, so 'yamekatvānekavṛttitvayorvirodha
iti cet /
hanta bhāvaparicchede tadabhāvo vyavacchidyat iti yuktam /
bhāvaparicchedalakṣaṇatvāttadabhāvavyavacchedasya /
na hi bhāvādanyastava bhāvābhāvo nāma /
bhāvāntarāṇi tu kasmādvyavacchidyante /
tadabhāvāvinābhāvāditi cet /
kutaḥ punarayaṃ bhāvāntarāṇāṃ bhāvābhāvāvinābhāvaḥ /
pītādibhāvatādātmyena kadācidapi nīlasya bhāvasyānupalambhāditi cet /
yatra tarhyekāvayavavṛtterapyekasyāvayavāntareṣu varttamānasya tādātmyaṃ dṛśyate na tatraikāvayavasaṃsṛṣṭābhāvāvinābhāvo 'vayavāntarasaṃsṛṣṭasya,
tasmānnaikatvanānāvṛttitvayorvirodhaḥ /
api ca ekaṃ vijñānamanekai rūpacakṣurālokamanaskāraiḥ kathaṃ sambadhyate, sambadhyamānaṃ vā, na vāstavaḥ kaścitkāryakāraṇabhāvo nāmāsti sambandhaḥ /
pratītya kathamekam /
samutpādamātraṃ taditi cet /
atha kasmādrūpādyeva pratītya rūpajñānaṃ jāyate na punā rasādyapi /
svabhāva eva tādṛśo yatastāneva pratītya jāyate na punā rāsabhādīniti cet /
hanta bhoḥ svabhāvān bhinnān pratītya kathameko bhāvo jāyate /
ko virodho na hi kāryakāraṇayostādātmyaṃ yena kāraṇasvabhāvānurodhaḥkāryasya bhavediti cet /
tatkimavayavāvayavinorapyabhedaḥ samavāyasya vā tābhyāṃ, yenāvayavabhadeḥ'vayavino vā samavāyasvaya vā bhedo bhevaditi samaḥ samādhiḥ /
tasmādyadyadavayavini pramāṇaṃ vakṣyāmaḥ
tattadasati bādhake 'pratyūhamavayavinamavasthāpayiṣyatīti siddham /

children.translated_text: But one who thinks that the aggregate of parts
is itself the composite whole (<s>avayavī</s>) — to him the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> replies.
"The remainder after aggregation" and so forth.
This is easily understood. //32//

Moreover, by you who think the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is non-existent, it was said that the cognition of a tree from the apprehension of a mere part is inferential; but this is not a mere apprehension of a part, but rather the establishment of the whole, which is concomitant with it and which has obtained the defining characteristic of apprehension— he says: /
'And it is not the apprehension of a part' /
Having restated this <s>bhāṣya</s>, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains /
'And not'— here the indicative <s>bhāṣya</s> /
'Because of non-complete apprehension'— if [one objects] /
The subsequent <s>bhāṣya</s>: 'not because of the cause' /
The explanation of the indicative /
'And not the parts' /
For by you, the apprehension of the whole is maintained in order to negate the apprehension of a part; but by this much alone, the possibility of complete apprehension, which would negate the apprehension of a part, does not arise /
For in the apprehension of the whole, not all parts are apprehended /
Nor is the whole [completely apprehended], since even when the near side is apprehended, the middle and far sides remain unapprehended— this is the meaning of the indicative <s>bhāṣya</s> /
This <s>bhāṣya</s> the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains /
'The apprehension of the whole is not [complete]' /
Now, what exists in many things exists either in each one completely, like the throat-quality of the <s>kalaviṅka</s> bird,
or in a part, like the garland-thread in the flowers /
And there is no mode other than complete and partial /
Because the negation of either entails the assertion of the other— like eternality and non-eternality /
And when [the whole] is completely contained in one [part], it cannot exist in another; for then there would be no complete containment /
Therefore, what is seen between the parts is not the whole;
and thus only the parts [exist]— this too is the intended [conclusion] /
'For there is no [part] other than its cause' /
(214/5) For if it had other portions, then in those too the search for yet other portions would lead to an infinite regress— this is the meaning /
The prima facie objector himself states the overextension, preceded by a question /
'Now if it is apprehended' /
The <s>bhāṣya</s> explaining the subsequent <s>bhāṣya</s>: 'the complete, indeed certainly' etc. /
That, as a single text, is the <s>bhāṣya</s> arranged beginning with the address 'but you, sir' /
This the <s>vārttikakāra</s> explains /
'In one' /
The intent is: as to what was said— that the [thread] exists in the flowers by a part— that is unjustified; for if the parts of the thread exist in the flowers, what need is there for the thread as a whole? /
For it has been said: when one thing exists [in something], another does not exist [there] /
And even [the saying] 'when the whole is absent, it does not exist' is also that the thread exists by its parts /
Now, let there be no such thing as a thread-whole; we say that the parts exist in the flowers /
And that being so, it is not the case that one thing exists in many by a part— rather, many things [exist] in many things /
And thus, one thread-atom exists in one flower-atom— this is what has been said; and the existence too does not go beyond the atoms, so that one could say 'it exists'; therefore, mere co-origination of the two atoms should be spoken of as their existence,
but no existence that is a real entity distinct from the intrinsic nature of the atoms /
And thus, like the throat-quality of the <s>kalaviṅka</s> bird, the complete containment in each individually as the mode of existence— this too has been explained /
And thus, because existence [as described] does not obtain, [the dichotomy of] 'existing by a part or by the whole' is empty talk /
But if, in accordance with ordinary experience, existence is accepted, then the thread does not exist in the flowers by a part; rather, the parts of the thread and the thread [itself] exist in the flowers— this is the ordinary experience /
Therein, the existence of the thread in the flowers is neither by a part nor by the whole,
but by its own nature; likewise the whole exists in its parts by its own nature /
But this is the difference: for the thread's existence in the flowers, there are parts, so both the thread-form and the parts exist in the flowers;
but for the whole's existence in its own parts, there are no other portions, so it exists there merely by its form alone /
Therefore, since nothing is seen to exist anywhere either by the whole or by a part, the all-pervasiveness of those [categories] with respect to existence is unestablished /
Only form is the pervader /
And that exists in the whole too; so since the non-apprehension of the pervader is unestablished, the negation of the whole's existence in the parts is established [as refuted] /
And how the words 'complete' and 'partial' do not apply to the form of the whole— that has been stated by the <s>vārttikakāra</s>: /
'It does not exist by a part, nor does it exist by the whole, and yet it exists'— this is the proper formulation, if the object as it truly is were designated thus— this is the construction /
'Because of contradiction by both' /
(215/4) The meaning is: there is contradiction in one thing existing in many either by a part or by the whole /
For only that property is to be analyzed which, when analyzed, does not contradict the property-bearer— just as 'sound is eternal or non-eternal'; but that which contradicts the very substrate-property-bearer is not a proper analysis of properties /
Because of the impossibility [of such an analysis] due to unestablished locus /
Whatever entity exists, all of it is without parts—
like cognition; and since it is existent and never experienced as blue and the like— this is a svabhāva-reason (natural reason), because existence-as-such pervades what is without parts /
For the existence of a single thing is pervaded by the non-association with contradictory properties; and the association with contradictory properties, which is the opposite of that, leading to the unwanted consequence that blue and the like have parts, negates its own opposite— the non-association with contradictory properties— and thereby negates the existence pervaded by it /
For example, when the palm and the like tremble, the whole that is in their location also trembles— so the whole, which has its location also in the shanks and other parts and which is uniformly present [everywhere], would be apprehended as trembling; but it is not apprehended— therefore, it [the whole] both trembles and does not tremble at the same time— this is the association with contradictory properties /
Alternatively, if even when the parts tremble, the whole inhering in them does not tremble, then there would be the unwanted consequence of a separately-established [relation] of moving and non-moving, like cloth and water /
When one part is concealed, the whole having its location in that part is concealed— so there would be the unwanted consequence of concealment even of [the whole] at the location of other parts,
because of non-difference /
Or it would never be concealed anywhere, and would be seen as undiminished /
The concealment of the part is not the concealment of the whole, because [the whole] is different from it;
but if the concealment of one does not entail the concealment of the other, there would be over-extension— to this [the objection]: no /
Even with half-concealment, since the whole is not concealed, there would be the unwanted consequence of undiminished apprehension as before /
If [one says] the whole is perceived through the perception of parts, so when parts are unseen the whole is not cognized— no, because of inability to withstand analysis /
Is the cognition of the whole through the perception of all parts, or through the perception of some parts? /
In the first alternative, the whole would never be seen at all /
For one who is not omniscient cannot apprehend all parts, since the far side is obstructed by the middle and other sides /
But in the perception of some parts, since it is manifested by them, even the perception of few parts would lead to the unwanted consequence of gross perception as in the perception of many parts /
And when one part is colored red, the whole having its location there would also be red— so there would be the unwanted consequence of perceiving redness even in other parts, because of its non-difference /
Or if only the part is red, the form of the whole at that location is seen as non-red— this is the association with contradictory properties /
With this intention, the <s>vārttikakāra</s>, through the association with contradictory properties characterized by apprehension and non-apprehension, indicates all associations with contradictory properties /
'Apprehension and non-apprehension' /
He refutes: /
'Not difference' /
Here, this much should be said first: /
If blue, which is experienced and determined, is to be proved as without parts, then this is proving what is already established;
for even for us, the specific color blue and the like is without parts, because it is a quality /
If [one says] its substrate is a pot—
but 'that which is called a pot is also just forms, smells, and touches performing a purposive action, and is so designated'— and those, being qualities, are indeed without parts; and there is no such substrate /
If [one says] the substance accepted by the opponent is made the subject as the substrate of form and the like— then proving its partlessness by the very existence accepted by the opponent is proving the unestablished by the unestablished, and [such a person] demonstrates his own great logicianship /
For what is not itself cognized as the <s>sādhya</s>-property-bearer is not fit for convincing the other party /
As they say: /
'Even one who is unestablished for the other party but self-established—
there may be a remedy for that; but for what is unestablished for oneself, what action [is possible]?' /
And this cannot be so even in a reductio ad absurdum proof /
Nor [can it be proved] by having parts, because of the absence of contradiction /
And the contradictory property of a single thing is not a sublating <s>pramāṇa</s> /
There is no apprehension and non-apprehension of a single whole /
Even in the concealment of parts, because of the apprehension of the [whole's] existence in some parts /
And it is not proper [to say] that in the apprehension of [the whole's] existence in some parts there is no manifestation of the whole, unlike in the apprehension of existence in many parts, because of the non-manifestation of such magnitude /
For magnitude is a difference in size, a property of the whole; and when that [magnitude] of such a kind is not manifested, the whole is not thereby unmanifested, because the whole is different from it /
Therefore, the whole is apprehended from the mere contact of the sense organ /
The apprehension of differences in magnitude comes from the contact of the sense organ with the object, of parts of the sense organ with the object, of the sense organ with parts of the object, and of parts of the sense organ with parts of the object— so from the difference in the aggregate of conditions, the apprehension and non-apprehension of the whole and its differences in magnitude are explained /
By this it has been said: even when the near side is apprehended, the non-apprehension of [the whole] with the middle side does not in any way bring about a contradiction /
Nor does the whole tremble when a part trembles, so there is no unwanted consequence of trembling in other parts, because the part and the whole are different /
If that leads to the unwanted consequence of separate establishment (<s>yutasiddhi</s>)—
what then is this 'separate establishment'? Is it the difference between part and whole,
or the existence of something unconnected? /
If difference— that is desired by us /
If the existence of something unconnected— even though there is separate movement, that does not apply to the whole,
for being born and being connected is a single moment /
For the whole is never unconnected with its parts /
For what possesses a universal is never unconnected with the universal /
Qualities and actions are not unconnected with substance /
And the individuator (<s>viśeṣa</s>) is not unconnected with substance /
But those who define separate establishment as non-arrival and non-conjunction must state a reason for the non-conjunction of part and whole /
If [they say] non-separate-establishment (<s>ayutasiddhi</s>)— no,
for the very thing to be ascertained is the non-conjunction /
And being-red and being-not-red do not belong to a single whole, because the [whole] is simply not-red /
But the lac (<s>mahārajana</s>) that is in contact with it is red; and that [lac] is different from the cloth, which is not-red /
'The cloth is red'— that is an error; but this error should not be extended everywhere, since it is caused by the contact with lac, and since lac exists in the cloth, and since the cloth is the same everywhere;
if there is no contact [with lac] somewhere in the cloth, there would be the unwanted consequence of the distinction between contacted and non-contacted [parts] /
For it does not happen that the very same thing at the very same time in the very same place both exists and does not exist /
Therefore, it follows that the cloth not in contact is different from the cloth in contact /
To this we say: /
This is the nature of knowable objects: /
Existence and non-existence have the nature of mutual absence; the cessation of existence is itself non-existence,
and the cessation of non-existence is itself existence /
But the cessation of those two is not something other than existence and non-existence /
Therefore, the two can never have the nature of each other— because it is never observed /
Likewise, the unity and plurality of their substrates should be established in accordance with observation— just as the very same white dog at one time exists on the terrace and at the very same time is absent from the crow /
And thus, the pot is dark; that very same [pot] later, through contact with fire, is non-dark;
but its difference in magnitude does not perish when the pot exists; so even when the size-condition changes, [the pot] does not perish /
Thus, in the variety of knowable objects established by the variety of observations, as one accepts, so the existence and non-existence of that very same conjunction should be established at one and the same time in the same [entity],
because that is what is observed /
For the form of what is seen, being apprehended, cannot be denied by the dissimilarity with something else that is seen; nor should the form of what is seen be denied by dissimilarity with what is seen, because of non-distinction /
Therefore, from conformity with observation, since the variety of knowable objects is established— having form— the non-existence and existence of conjunction, words, cognitions, and the like in the very same [entity] at the very same time— /
here, their non-pervading occurrence (<s>avyāpyavṛttitva</s>) is maintained /
But for form and the like, since their non-existence and existence at the very same place at the very same time has not been observed, for those that have pervading occurrence, existence and non-existence simultaneously in one place are contradictory— this is established /
The non-contradiction of being-red and not-being-red in one place is due to their being observed together /
As to the reductio argument: 'whatever exists in many is manifold;
and the whole is accepted as existing in many'— this is a <s>svabhāva-hetu</s> (natural reason); and the reductio in reverse— 'because of the absence of manifoldness, there is absence of existence in many'— is a non-apprehension of the pervader /
To that we say: /
Since unity and existence-in-many are not contradictory, the pervasiveness of manifoldness is unestablished— so there is neither the reductio nor its reverse /
Just as when blue is determined, its absence is excluded— otherwise blue would not have been determined— so too yellow, which is inseparable from the absence of blue, is excluded by the perception that determines blue; likewise, when the whole's connection with one part is determined, its absence is excluded,
and the connections with other parts, which are inseparable from that absence, would also have to be excluded; and if they are not excluded, that absence would not be excluded— so the very same thing at the very same time would both exist and not exist there, which is an absurdity— this is the contradiction between unity and existence in many—
if [one argues thus]: /
Indeed, it is proper that when existence is determined, its absence is excluded /
Because the exclusion of the absence of existence has the defining characteristic of the determination of existence /
For your 'absence of existence' is nothing other than existence /
But why should other existing things be excluded? /
If [one says] because of inseparability from the absence of that [existence]—
then whence comes this inseparability of other existents from the absence of that existence? /
If [one says] because blue as an existent is never observed in identity with the existence of yellow and the like—
then wherever the identity of a single thing existing in one part with [what exists in] other parts is seen, there the existence of what is connected with one part is not inseparable from the absence of what is connected with other parts;
therefore there is no contradiction between unity and existence in many /
Moreover, how does a single cognition connect with many [causes]— form, eye, light, and mental attention? And even if it connects, there is no real causal relation that constitutes a connection /
If [one says] it is single because of dependent [origination]—
and mere co-origination is that?
Then why is it that only from form and the like does form-cognition arise, and not from taste and the like? /
If [one says] its nature is simply such that it arises dependent on those alone and not on donkeys and the like—
then, well sir, how does a single entity arise dependent on different natures? /
What contradiction is there? For there is no identity of cause and effect such that the effect would follow the nature of the cause— if [one argues thus]:
then why not also non-difference of part and whole, or of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) with them? For then the difference of parts from the whole, or of inherence from itself, would occur— so the resolution is the same /
Therefore, whatever <s>pramāṇa</s> we shall state for the whole,
that, in the absence of a sublating [cognition], will establish the whole without obstruction— this is established /
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.33: Because it is [itself] what is to be proved, there is doubt regarding the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>).
