children.translated_text:
That which is to be proved (sū. 33) // The very fact that the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is unestablished for the opponent constitutes its being to-be-proved.
For he held thus: the determination of an object rests upon cognition.
That alone is established by cognition which is its object.
And that alone is the object which imparts its form to it [the cognition].
And we do not observe a cognition bearing the form of a composite that is distinct from the atoms of form etc. arising in continuous succession; rather, [we observe cognition bearing] the form of atoms of form etc. arising in continuous succession.
And although bulk does not exist in each individual atom,
nevertheless it is a property of appearance, like multiplicity, and cannot establish a single composite.
As they say: this [composite], like a priceless gift-purchaser, imparts its own form to cognition and wishes to claim perceptibility — that is the composite!
Thus, the erroneous understanding regarding the composite arises from its non-establishment for the opponent.
Therefore, in the absence of establishing or defeating <s>pramāṇa</s>, there is doubt — this is the meaning.
Thinking that being-to-be-proved is not in its own nature a cause of doubt, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "this being so" etc.
The meaning is: when it is unestablished for the opponent.
"Because of being to-be-proved" — taking the <s>sūtra</s> literally, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> considers alternatives and objects.
"What then here" etc.
(217/1) It deserves the acceptance of the property-bearer from some reason, [but] every reason would have an unestablished locus — this is the purport.
"Or, non-exclusion" etc.
Even when the property-bearer exists, its non-difference from the parts is the property to be proved — this is the meaning.
"Because of depending on the composite" etc.
For threads are parts relative to cloth; threads lying in a basket are not called parts.
"Nor is the genitive" etc.
(218/1) "The parts of cloth are threads" — there is no genitive [relation without the composite]; and if the qualification "of cloth" is absent, mere part-hood would be the reason, and that would be contradictory — this is the meaning.
The example for "part-hood is not something different [from the whole]" [follows].
"Nor is a thread [a part] of a thread" etc.
In the absence of the genitive meaning, the next example follows.
He states that threads have thread-hood.
Because the word "that" refers back to the principal — this is the meaning.
"And of the word part" etc.
Previously, without intending causality, the word "part" was used merely as a relational term given by the words "prior" and "posterior";
now, with causality intended, [the different usage] is stated — so there is no repetition.
He teaches.
"For indeed not" — what is non-existent is not being made; it is what is being produced.
And for us who hold <s>satkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause), it does not exist — this is the meaning.
He criticizes.
"This" etc.
For the cognition having the form of cloth does not rest on mere threads, since it would then apply even to threads lying in a basket.
Nor does it rest on a difference in the measure of threads, since that too was present even before [the weaving].
He states the established doctrine.
"The <s>pramāṇa</s> that has been experienced is the determinative cause."
Form and the rest do not possess contact in the form of conjunction, because of being qualities — like conjunction itself. When this is not accepted, regarding form and the rest, the certainty [arises]; the illusion of contact in form and the rest, caused by not seeing that [distinction], is [merely an illusion]; while the cognition of contact in substances is ultimately real — this is the determination.
With this intent, he concludes.
"Therefore it is established" etc.
(238/8) The rest has a transparent meaning. //33//
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.34: The non-apprehension of everything [follows] from the non-establishment of the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>). //

children.translated_text: 'sarvā—ddheḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 34) / One might say: just as the opponent does not accept the composite whole, so too [he would not accept] quality, action, and the like. / Then how does this consequence [apply to] the opponent's [view that there is] non-apprehension of everything? — therefore he states this <s>sūtra</s>. / For even one who does not accept quality, action, and the like does not deny the cognition of them. There is in the world, for both ordinary people and critical examiners, the cognition of composite-substance, quality, action, and the like. This [cognition] is impossible to deny. And its being perceptual has been justified in the definition of perception. / And the <s>pramāṇas</s> that would sublate the composite substance have been refuted below. / This [composite], being co-apprehended with qualities and the like when there is no sublating [evidence], and being itself [directly perceived], cannot be rejected — this is the topic-meaning. // 34 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.35: And because of the justification of supporting and attracting. //

children.text: samūhamātratvena tulyatve 'pi yathā kaścidviśeṣe heturevamavayavitvena tulyatve 'pīti samānamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: just as, even though [heaps and solid bodies] are alike in being mere aggregates, some specific [condition] is the reason [for the difference in behavior] — so too, even though [things] are alike in being composite wholes, it is the same [i.e., some specific condition accounts for the difference].
The specific relation accompanying that [supporting and attracting] is [the property of] being caused by cohesion (<s>sneha</s>) and fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>).
Therefore, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s>'s objection to the <s>sūtra</s> should be understood as [made] according to the opponent's view. // 35 //

'dhāra—śca' (<s>sūtra</s> 35) // These two — supporting and attracting — being observed, prove the composite whole, as in cows, pots, and the like. From what [evidence]? Because they are not observed in what is partless, such as consciousness and <s>ākāśa</s> (space), / nor in the atoms, which are [ultimate] parts. / This amounts to the following argument: / This observed [thing] — a cow, pot, and the like — which is the composite whole that is the subject of dispute as to whether it is a mere aggregate of atoms — / it is not partless, because of the unwanted consequence of the impossibility of supporting and attracting. / Whatever is partless — in that, there is no supporting or attracting on your part, as in consciousness and the like. And this cow, pot, and the like is not of that nature — therefore it is not partless. / 'There is no contradiction' — / The fault characterized by deviation is [what is meant by] 'contradiction.' / 'Of the composite whole itself, each individually' — / The meaning is: but in a mere aggregate of atoms, even individually, the atoms are not [entities possessing] a composite whole. / 'Because of the absence of a differentiating reason' — / For a differentiating reason would exist only if, apart from the composite whole, supporting of the described kind and the capacity for attraction had been observed somewhere in consciousness, space, and the like. / But that is not observed — sticks, grass, stones, and the like are each [parts] of a composite whole alone / — this is the meaning. / One might say: even though they are alike in having a composite whole, why is there supporting and attracting in one [case] and not in another? — therefore he says:
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.36: If [it is said that] the apprehension [of the whole] is like [that of] an army or a forest — no, because atoms are beyond the senses. //

atrāntare vārttikakāra āha sma---ko vā virodho bahavaḥ saṃjātātiśayāḥ pṛthakbhaveyuḥ kāraṇaṃ buddheryadi nānmendriyādivaditi /
etadapi vārttikakṛtaivāthānupajātaviśeṣā iti vadatā parāstam /
na khalu sthairyasiddhau bhāvānāmayavavidravyotpādamantareṇāstyanyo 'tiśayaḥ paraṃmāṇūnām /
na ca yamāgantukamāsādya paramāṇavo 'vayavinaṃ janayanti tenaiva sthūlabuddhiṃ,
kṛtamavayavineti sāṃpratam /
yadābhāsā hi buddhistadasyā ālambanapratyayaḥ /
na ceyaṃ parasparavyāvṛttaparamasūkṣmaparamāṇvālambanā tathā sati sthūlabhedāttadekamiti ca syāt /
na caiṣa pratyayo vikalpaḥ spaṣṭapratibhāsatvāt /
na vāvikalpopādhirasya viśadatā nirvikalpakenāpi tasyāgrahaṇāt /
na ca pratibhāsadharmaḥ sthaunyam /
nānādigdeśasthitasya nirantarasyaikena vijñānena grahaṇaṃ sthaulyam /
tatkhalvīdṛśatvaṃ paramāṇūnāṃ pratibhāsasamayabhāvīti pratibhāsadharma
ityucyate /
tathā caiṣa samīcīna evānubhavaḥ
na hi te na paramāṇavo na ca na nirantarotpannā na ca na digdeśabhinnā na vaikasminvijñāne na cakāsati /
tasmāt kasyātrānyathātvam /
yathāha---
children.translated_text: Now then, the positive-and-negative-concomitant [reason] — / The positive-and-negative-concomitant — / 'This is a cloth' — a cognition having a single object is a single cognition; / 'these are threads' — a cognition having multiple objects is a multiple cognition. / Because they have non-aggregated and aggregated objects respectively — / a single cognition [arises] because its object is non-aggregated, and a multiple cognition [arises] because its object is aggregated. / From the apprehension [of this], / the <s>sūtra</s> [is read]: 'senā—nām' (<s>sūtra</s> 36) // 'As stated' etc. / The numerical property of 'many-ness' is itself what constitutes an army and a forest. / But as for one who thinks: for the designation 'army' or 'forest,' or for the cognition produced [by such designation], the numerical property of plurality can somehow be a cause — but this perceptual cognition, which arises instantly grasping a single forest in respect of trees whose individual unity has not been previously grasped and in which the cognition of unity has not [yet] arisen — since plurality does not arise [first] due to the absence of its cause, it cannot be the object of the plurality-number — he is not satisfied. To him he says: / 'And of the false cognition of non-difference' etc. / In things whose forms are being apprehended, due to some cause, when their distinctness is not being apprehended, a false cognition of non-difference arises. / But not in things that are entirely unapprehended — this is the purport. / But to one who thinks that nothing accepted by both parties that is a single [entity] exists in the world — to him he says: / 'There is no single [entity]' etc. / One might say: / Sticks, clods, grass, stones, and the like, when individually separated from a distance, are not apprehended. / But their aggregate is seen. / And they do not produce another substance, because of being of different kinds — so let atoms too be individually invisible, but let their aggregate be visible without the production of any further effect — therefore he says: / 'And of what is apprehended, the non-apprehension' etc. / Of those very [things] — even when not individually apprehended, [their aggregate is] seen when combined — [this is because] the form by which they are fit for apprehension [exists in them, but] due to another cause they are not apprehended. But atoms, due to their extreme subtlety, are not fit for apprehension by their own nature — so even when combined, they should not be apprehended at all. For never are aggregates of wind visually perceived, even when combined. / The greatness of things, like [their] form, is [required for] the fitness of their own nature with respect to apprehension — this is the purport. / And thus, they would be both sensible and non-sensible — which is a great contradiction. / At this juncture, the <s>vārttikakāra</s> had said: 'What contradiction is there? Many [atoms] having acquired a surplus [of magnitude] individually could be a cause of cognition, as in the case of sense organs and the like.' / Even this has been set aside by the <s>vārttikakāra</s> himself, saying 'but if no surplus has arisen.' / For when the stability of things has been established, there is no other surplus of atoms apart from the production of a composite substance. / Nor do the atoms, by acquiring some adventitious [property], produce a composite whole — that very [adventitious property] would [already] produce gross cognition. / 'Done with the composite whole' — this is appropriate. / For that of which a cognition has appearances is the object-condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) of that [cognition]. / And this [gross cognition] does not have the appearance of atoms that are mutually excluded, maximally subtle — for if so, it would be [indistinguishable from] the distinction of gross [objects], and [the cognition] 'this is one' would also [apply]. / And this cognition is not a conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), because of its vivid appearance. / Nor is vividness a property of conceptual construction, since even by non-conceptual [cognition] it is not grasped [as such]. / And grossness (<s>sthaulya</s>) is not a property of [mere] appearance. / Grossness is the apprehension by a single cognition of something that occupies different directions and locations without interval. / And this being-of-such-a-nature of atoms exists at the time of appearance — so it is called a property of appearance. / And thus this is a perfectly valid experience: / for they are indeed atoms, and they are indeed produced contiguously, and they are indeed distinct in direction and location, and they do indeed shine forth in a single cognition. / Therefore, what is erroneous here? / As it has been said —

children.translated_text: Here, to begin with, like sesame seeds and rice grains, because of being separated by the atoms of smell, color, taste, and touch, there is no contiguity among these [atoms]. / Therefore, in the non-apprehension of what is in between, this is a false cognition — like the cognition of a single dense forest from a distance — because of the atoms of color and the like being with gaps, and because of their plurality. / And it is not proper [to call something] false in the absence of a sublator (<s>bādhaka</s>). / And the absence of a sublator has been stated, and the stability of entities will be established. / Therefore, this too is untenable. / 'This very [point] is being examined' / — thus the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. / For one who denies the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) everywhere, / or who holds that [everything] is merely a collection of atoms beyond the senses — because even the parts of an army, a forest, and the like — elephants, <s>kusumbha</s>-pots, and the like — would be merely collections of atoms beyond the senses, / there is an absence of an example — this is the import. / He raises a doubt: 'if [one says] it is observed' — / The parts of an army, a forest, and the like, to begin with, / cannot be denied because of being observed — so the example is established — this is the meaning. / He refutes: / 'But that is not so' — / If what is observed cannot be denied, then the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) too is observed — so it too should not be denied. / But if this [whole] is denied after examination, then the parts of an army, a forest, and the like too should be denied — so there is an absence of an example, because of being equal to what is to be proved — this is the meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'and this [cognition] of the one in many' — / A non-existent particular — silver-ness in a shell — the seeing of that, in the jeweler's street and the like, has [as] its gateway the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>); by that [impression], a property contrary to [that of] the shell — namely silver-ness — is superimposed. That by which the generic perception [occurs] — its being that way [as stated] — the nature of the generic perception — this [is the explanation]. / When the distinction is concealed, the comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) itself is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>); when known with the indication of distinction, [it is] analogical (<s>aupamika</s>) — this is the distinction. (The cognition of the name is the analogical example.) / As in '<s>siṃho māṇavakaḥ</s>' ('the boy is a lion'). / (244/5) Now, this too, because of having concealed distinction, is merely figurative — he says: / '<s>siṃha iva siṃhaḥ</s>' ('a lion as it were, a lion'). / The meaning is this: / From the word '<s>siṃha</s>' used as a standard of comparison, in conventional usage, from all nominal stems — / with the <s>kvip</s> suffix — from the <s>kvip</s>-suffixed [form], in the agent [sense], even when the [suffix] <s>kṛt</s> is applied, the word '<s>siṃha</s>' has the meaning of a standard of comparison. / He explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'and when the atoms are different' — / 'Even the false cognitions' — / 'But in the absence of that' — / But in the absence of the principal [substrate], regarding pots and the like, [there are] false cognitions. / 'When the atoms are collected' — / Even for those for whom the pot is the whole, the collection of atoms is to be accepted; and even for those for whom the whole does not exist, the collection of atoms is to be accepted — for this collection is accepted by both [parties] — this is the meaning. / 'Those too are just collected' — / The <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s> indeed, [who are] <s>Vātsīputrīyas</s>, hold that from the collection of elements (<s>bhūta</s>) and derivative [substances] (<s>bhautika</s>), even cloth and the like, as well as sounds and the like, [arise] — therefore, in their view, sounds and the like do not have primary oneness as a number, since the quality of number does not inhere in qualities such as sound and the like. / Rather, [oneness] is merely figurative — therefore / he says: 'and the cognition of oneness regarding sound and the like.' / He raises a doubt: 'everywhere' — / (245/1) He refutes: / 'Not two — herein' — / If oneness is merely the negation of aggregation, [then] by the negation of two-ness, the aggregation is negated — so that negation is oneness alone — then there would be no doubt as to 'one or many?' / Nor would the answer 'it is one alone' have a restrictive purpose. / 'In the going' — / 'In the arriving' — / He raises a doubt: 'everywhere' — / He refutes: / 'Not one — herein' — / The intention is this: / In the absence of two-ness and the like, there would be mere aggregation, / but there would be no sub-distinctions among aggregations. And thus, 'not one' — the aggregation accompanied by the negation of aggregation and oneness — is already obtained — so there would be no doubt. / But here, this must be said: / In the absence of two-ness and the like regarding sound and the like, how is the usage of two-ness and the like [explained]? / If [one says] it is figurative — / What is the basis of the figurative [usage]? / If [one says] it is mere aggregation — whence the restriction of 'two'? / If [one says] from a particular aggregation — but it has been said: one who does not know [this] has no apprehension of difference. / And two-ness does not exist here that would distinguish [it] — and thus, even unwillingly, the intrinsic (<s>svābhāvika</s>) sub-distinction of aggregations must be stated. / And let that very [sub-distinction] be the subject of doubt — there is no need for two-ness and the like in the substance. / Therefore, cognition itself — the blessed [cognition] — is our refuge in accepting real entities, comprehending two-ness and the like, and is the establisher of two-ness and the like; and the manner of tracing those [numbers to cognition] — by the profusion of reasoning, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> has accomplished [this] — this is to be understood. / But one who, while experiencing oneness, does not acknowledge the experienced oneness and also the experienced two-ness and the like — for this denier of experience, because of his unboundedness, even the substrate of oneness does not exist — so whose aggregation or two-ness and the like would there be? / Even in the absence of aggregation, whose absence would oneness be? — he says: / 'But one who' — / Moreover, for one who does not accept oneness and the like as primary, this figurative usage too would apply — he says: / 'Oneness, two-ness, and the like' — / He explains by restating the <s>Bhāṣya</s>: / 'And regarding those, thus' — / (246/2) 'Because of the non-determination of the quantity' — / The determination of quantity for what is of perceptible size; but for those of maximally great [size], whose size is imperceptible, even though there is non-determination of quantity, there is no absence-of-size, because the size of substances like <s>ākāśa</s> (space) and the like can be inferred from their substance-hood. / 'As in "great size"' — / The worldly [people] designate the size of an <s>āmalaka</s> (myrobalan) as 'great' relative to the size of a <s>kuvala</s> (jujube). / As in 'the <s>āmalaka</s> is great compared to the <s>kuvala</s>.' / And there is no size of a size — / because of the consequence of infinite regress. / Therefore, this designation 'great' in reference to greatness is figurative. / In that [figurative usage], the word 'that' [refers to what] has the figurative word 'great' — [it is] a quality, because of being like greatness. And the quality-hood of sound has been established in the definition of inference. / And the figurative [usage] presupposes the primary [usage] — so somewhere [there must be] a primary [sense of] greatness, and that, in the absence of a sublator, is primary in [the category of] substance — this is established. / 'Not because of being the object of the cognition of "great"' — / (247/16) Not from that alone — but rather from that which is unsubtracted and otherwise unaccounted for — that alone he says: / 'But rather' and so on — / By this, the otherwise-unaccounted-for [nature] of the cognition of 'great' with respect to substance has been shown. / 'And thus the cognitions of one, and the like, and of great' — / (248/10) The remainder is: 'relying on the aggregate as one.' / 'And the aggregate [being one with] another aggregate through attainment' — / For when the constituents of the aggregate, though different, are unified through attainment into one aggregate, then another aggregate too, having attained [proximity with] yet another aggregate, becomes one aggregate. But there is no attainment of a single [thing] with itself. / For indeed, the very same fingertip is not attained by that very same fingertip. And therefore the non-attainment of two aggregates [to form one] is untenable — this is the meaning. / He objects: / 'There is no universal (<s>jāti</s>) at all' — / The intention is this: / There is no real entity called a universal, whose substrate, being a real entity, could be traced. / For thus: does it reside in that individual, or everywhere? If everywhere, then all things would be cows — for just as <s>Śābaleya</s> and the like are cows because of their connection with cow-ness, so everything connected with it would be a cow. / But if it resides only in certain individuals, then one must say: when an individual is born in some place, one must then say: whence does this cow-ness come to it? / For it was not there even before the production of the individual, nor has it come from another individual — because of its being without action and because of the consequence of abandoning the other individual. / And it is not born when the individual is born — because of the consequence of being non-eternal, and because of the consequence of the superimposition of contradictory properties — birth and non-birth — upon another individual having cow-ness, and in the case of difference, the consequence of not being a universal. / Therefore, being afraid of this great calamity, one should maintain only conventional (<s>sāṃvṛta</s>) universality, not ultimate [universality]. / He resolves: / 'Of the specific universal' — / (249/2) Although the recurrence of cognition is perceptual, still, with respect to one who disputes, that very [recurrence] is stated as an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>). / For some entities indeed, though co-existing, are mutually unconnected — just as smell, taste, color, and touch that exist at the same time, and, for others, many consciousnesses that exist at the same time are non-intermingling; / and direction, time, space, and the selves, though co-existing, are mutually non-intermingling according to the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> — so too, the universal, though unconnected with everything, co-exists with everything. / But the particulars (<s>vyaktis</s>) through which [it is manifested] — with those it is connected. / And thus, wherever particulars are born, there, though unconnected, both the universal and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) [are present]. / The very birth of those [particulars] is the delimiter of the universal and <s>samavāya</s>. / And that [birth] is not to be questioned [about its origin] from its own cause / — thus, those who know the course of real entities as established by <s>pramāṇa</s> do not fear this objection. / And other objections have been refuted by the explanation of the whole (<s>avayavin</s>). / 'So much, then, is the extent of the substrate of the universal' — / Those which, without depending on a specific universal such as tree-ness and the like, manifest [it] — they are mutually differentiated as tree-particulars and the like. / Just as <s>kiṃśuka</s>, <s>aśoka</s>, <s>campaka</s>, and the like are different trees, so the front part, middle part, and rear part too would be [different] parts of it. / But when the whole comes into being, this defect does not [arise], / because of its being recognized as common to all parts. / Nor should one say: even of the whole, there would be that many [parts]. / Because of that single [whole] being recognized as common to all parts. / But one further part is not recognized in another further part. / If those [parts] were the cause of being a tree-particular, there would be the consequence of the multiplicity of [the] tree. / 'And the most removed is the aggregator' — this is a contradiction: / meaning: because of the non-removal with respect to what is being aggregated. / He states the argument against the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, who thinks the whole is merely a property of the parts and not absolutely different from them: / 'A different entity' — / (250/18) The covering capacity belongs to the cloth, while the capacity to produce the cloth belongs to the threads. / 'The color of the thread and the cloth' — / The color of the threads is blue, yellow, red, and the like; but the color of the cloth is variegated. Therein, the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of the blue and the like is the threads, while the inherent cause of the variegated [color] is the cloth. / Thus, even in the sameness of color between thread and cloth, some distinction is to be inferred. / And the possession of distinction [is established] by being cognized as having different substrates; and by that, having different causes; and by that, having different inherent causes — [this] is proved. So it is neither proving-what-is-already-proved nor inconclusive. / As for those who, having construed the thesis-subject and the reason in a different manner, attempted to show [a flaw] — / having presented their view, he refutes: / 'Some however' —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.37: Because of deviation through obstruction, destruction, and similarity, inference is not a [valid] means of knowledge. //

children.translated_text: But if without even understanding the cause-effect relation, then it should be considered as an example of <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation) due to the absence of the cause-effect relation.
"Through the gate of deviation in the example" —
The meaning is: the refutation of the definition through the gate of refuting the definiendum.
For there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever for the deviation of the inference that demonstrates the non-<s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of inference through the characteristic of deviation. //37//

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads] "inference, now." Here the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the meaning of the word "now" (<s>idānīm</s>).
"Now, the occasion having arrived" —
The meaning is: the order of enumeration itself is the connection between definition and examination.
Examination... inference (sūtra 37) // "Of what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>," etc. — this <s>Bhāṣya</s> that is to be set aside [as belonging to the opponent].
"Demonstrating" means "determining."
Since the definition is aimed at the definiendum, and since the definiendum that possesses the definition deviates [from being a valid means of knowledge], the definition itself is thereby refuted as establishing non-<s>pramāṇa</s>-hood — this is the meaning.
The <s>Vārttika</s>:
"As before, the examples beginning with" etc.
And here, the examples of a river flood, the cry of a peacock, and the remainder — the movement of ant-eggs is not the effect of rain that is about to come soon, for the future cannot be the cause of what has already arisen.
Nor are a curved nose and the like caused by future death; otherwise even a son would be the cause of his father — so everything is clear.
Let the establishment of the cause-effect relation be worldly.
For a regular prior existence is the establisher of causality, and a regular posterior existence is the establisher of effectuality. A curved nose and the like are prior effects of that which is the cause of death — and through this proximity they make death inferable.
But the movement of ant-eggs is not the cause of rain, because its capacity is not observed.
Since rain arises even in its absence.
But the movement of ant-eggs is a prior effect of the great elemental disturbance that is the root cause of rain — for ants, being heated by terrestrial warmth, carry their eggs that are on the ground upward.
Therefore, if having inferred the cause of rain from the movement of ant-eggs, the inferrers then infer rain as an effect from the cause of rain, then the example is as before.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.38: [Inference is not invalid] because of [the objection being based on] a part, fear, or similarity, since [each involves] a different matter.
In the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, "like the ants" —
The word "mostly" (<s>prāya</s>) is used in the sense of continuation. //38//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.39: The non-existence of the present [is objected to], because for what is falling, the times of having-fallen and about-to-fall are tenable.

children.translated_text: Of the effect, namely remoteness and proximity and the like, and of the cognition — the specific cause, which is the conjunction of substance with a time-portion delimited by a greater or lesser number of elapsed solar revolutions, is what [time] depends upon. Time, though one, is the cause of the cognitions of remoteness, proximity, and the like through the production of the qualities characterized as remoteness and proximity — thus it is established. It is made manifest by the cause; because of its being fully accomplished, the justification of demonstrating [its] instantiation is established.

children.text: na tu kriyāvyaṅnya tasyāḥ sādhyatayā asiddhatvādvyaktiṃ prati hetubhāvābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: But it is not made manifest by action, because that [action] is what is to be proved and hence unestablished — due to the absence of the capacity to be a cause with respect to instantiation.

children.text: tathā cātītānāgatamātradarśanādvarttamānābhāvena na traikālyaviṣayamanumānaṃ tayośca pitāputravatparatvāparatvavadūdhrasvadīrghavacca parasparāpekṣāsiddhirantareṇāpi varttamānakālamiti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ // 39 //
children.translated_text: And thus, from observing only the past and future, since the present is absent, inference does not have the three times as its object; and those two [past and future] are established through mutual dependence, like father and son, like remoteness and proximity, like short and long — even without the present time: this is the opponent's position. //39//

Having thus examined the definition of inference through the examination of the definition, now the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> introduces the examination of inference through the examination of the object of inference.
"Having the three times as its object" —
Therein the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> [says]: when the existence of time is established, the present is examined — [but] that [time] itself, being unexamined, has not been established even today — so he examines the nature of time.
"Therein, first" —
"Of the three aspects of time" —
The deficiency of another cause, the unsuitability of the object, or the non-existence of the object — these are the three causes of non-apprehension.
"Even if the property [does not exist]" —
For a positive entity as a reason cannot have non-existence as its locus; but there is no contradiction in a negative entity having non-existence as its locus — this is the meaning.
He resolves.
"The force of the proof is diminished."
For non-existence as accepted by the opponent, being devoid of all capacity, cannot be a proof of anything. But non-existence as accepted by us is dependent [on a positive entity], has non-existence itself as its locus, is not without a locus, and is not located in non-existence — this is the meaning.
Having thus stated the absence of a refuting <s>pramāṇa</s> for time, he states the establishing <s>pramāṇa</s>.
"Remoteness, proximity" etc.
Of two persons existing by themselves, not located in a fixed direction, or located in the same direction, or spatially proximate and remote, or remote and proximate — of an elder and a younger — in a single person:
having taken the elder, whose birth is separated by a multitude of elapsed sunrise-sunset cycles inferred from the differences in bodily states, as the benchmark, the cognition "remote" arises; relative to that, through connection with a time-portion distinguished by a greater number of sunrise-sunset cycles, remoteness (<s>paratva</s>) arises in the more-aged.
Similarly, having taken the more-aged as the benchmark, the cognition "proximate" arises in the younger; relative to that, having taken one whose birth is separated by fewer elapsed sunrise-sunset cycles as the benchmark, the cognition "remote" arises; relative to that, through connection with a time-portion distinguished by a greater number of sunrise-sunset cycles, remoteness arises in the younger [relative to an even younger one].
And the perception of those two — the conjunctions of time and individual substance — is not established in the world; these two, remoteness and proximity, arising from the conjunction of time and substance, indicate themselves as effects and thereby lead to [the inference of] a cause distinguished by time.
[Objection:] Remoteness and proximity will arise from the substance itself, distinguished by the scarcity and abundance of sunrise-sunset cycles — what need is there for a separate substance called time?
No — because the action (<s>kriyā</s>) inhering in the sun has no connection with the [individual] substance, [only] through the relation of conjunction-with-the-conjoined (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>) does it have this connection with time, which is all-pervading; but space (<s>ākāśa</s>), though all-pervading, does not serve as the cause of remoteness-proximity distinction.
Because of non-difference in its own nature.
Moreover, space and <s>ātman</s> are not the causes of the remoteness-proximity distinction, because they possess uncommon qualities, like earth and the like.
Therefore, when a cause of the remoteness-proximity distinction is to be posited —
those [causes] are substances independent [like space and ātman]; like space, they are called direction (<s>dik</s>) and time (<s>kāla</s>). Similarly, the cognitions of simultaneity, non-simultaneity, quickness, and slowness are also marks of time — for these cannot belong to the action or to its causal agents, since even when those exist, [these cognitions] are only occasional.
But this time too is eternal, so even when it exists, these are only occasional — how is time not a non-cause?
Moreover —
If it were said: actions connected with a time-portion delimited by a single solar revolution are simultaneous; actions connected with a time-portion delimited by many solar revolutions are sequential — [these are] the objects of the cognition of simultaneity.
Similarly, an action connected with a time-portion delimited by very many solar revolutions is the object of the cognition of long duration.
An action connected with a time-portion delimited by very few solar revolutions is the object of the cognition of quickness.
Then the solar revolution would suffice for delimiting time.
But this [solar revolution] would directly delimit the actions themselves.
And thus the cognitions of simultaneity and the like would arise.
No — because the solar revolution has no connection with [other] actions and thus cannot delimit them; nor does it delimit them through the medium of connection with space and the like.
For space and the like are not the causes of the cognition of simultaneity and the like of actions,
because they possess uncommon qualities, like a pot.
Similarly, the cognitions of simultaneity and the like are not caused by direction, because of depending on the determination of directional location.
The conjunction of time and substance [produces] remoteness and proximity.
Therefore the solar revolution and the revolution of <s>Devadatta</s> and the like have a connection characterized as conjunction-with-the-conjoined (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>) with all-pervading time.
And through this, there is a connection between the two revolutions as well.
And the apprehension of the revolution of <s>Devadatta</s> and the like as delimited by the solar revolution occurs without depending on the knowledge of the connection with time.
Just as from the word "staff-bearer" (<s>daṇḍin</s>), having cognized a person delimited by a staff, then, through the otherwise-impossibility of that [cognition], the difference of conjunction between staff and person is subsequently understood — but the cognition of the staff-bearer is not preceded by the knowledge of the connection.
Similarly, remoteness and proximity too — having grasped them as based on the conjunction of time and substance, time is inferred — but the knowledge of them is not preceded by the knowledge of time. Thus it is established that time, being formless, is imperceptible, and is to be inferred through remoteness, proximity, and the like.
Therefore it is well said: "of the cognitions of remoteness and the like."
"Depending on the specific cause-effect [relation]"
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.40: Their [past and future's] non-existence too [would follow] in the absence of the present, because they depend on it.

children.text:
tayo--tvāt (sū. 40) // nātītādirūpatā kālasya kārakavyaṅnyā tayostādavasthyāt /
api tu kriyāvyaṅgyā tāṃ khalūrarīkṛtya pravartamānānayamatītānāgatavartamānān pratipadyate nānyathā /
yadā khalvayaṃ puruṣaḥ phalaṃ pravartamānapatanakriyāviśiṣṭaṃ pratipadyate tadā vyapadiśatipatati phalamiti /
tanmūle cāsyātītānāgatatve apatat phalaṃ patiṣyatīti /
na ca vartamānapatanamasiddhaṃ yena na kālaṃ vyaña jyāt (taddvayostādavasthyāt api tu kriyāvyaṅgyatā) tadasattve kasyedaṃ kāraṇaṃ gurutvaṃ kasya ca phalaṃ kārakaṃ kasya ca phalaṃ bhūmisaṃyogaḥ kāryaḥ /
na ca paratvāparatvādīnāmapi siddhiḥ parasparāpekṣā /
kiṃ tarhi ? sannikṛṣṭabuddhyapekṣamaparatvaṃ viprakṛṣṭabuddhyapekṣaṃ paratvaṃ pūrvasaṃkhyāvacchinnatā ca saṃyuktasaṃyogānāṃ sannikarṣaḥ /
parasaṃkhyāvacchinnatā ca viprakarṣaḥ /
evaṃ hrasvatvadīrghatve api parimāṇabhedau na parasparāpekṣau pitāputrau ca pramāṇaprameyavyākhyayā vyākhyātau /
tasmādatītānāgatayorvartamānāpekṣatvādvartamānasya ca tadanapekṣatvādasti traikālyamiti siddhāntaḥ
// 40 //
children.translated_text:
Their... dependence (sūtra 40) // The nature of being past and the like does not belong to time as made manifest by causal agents — since those [causal agents] remain in the same state.
Rather, [the nature of being past etc.] is made manifest by action — only by accepting that does the person operating [in the world] cognize past, future, and present — not otherwise.
When indeed this person cognizes a fruit as qualified by the present action of falling, he then designates: "the fruit falls."
And based on that, its past and future states [are cognized]: "the fruit fell" and "the fruit will fall."
And the present falling is not unestablished, such that it could not make time manifest. (In the absence of that [present], whose cause would this gravity be? Whose effect would the fruit be? Whose product would the conjunction with the ground be?)
Nor is the establishment of remoteness, proximity, and the like mutually dependent.
What then? Proximity depends on the cognition of nearness, and remoteness depends on the cognition of distance. And the proximity of the number delimited by the preceding [number] is the conjunction-with-the-conjoined.
And the distance of the number delimited by the succeeding [number] is the distance.
Similarly, shortness and longness too are differences of measure, not mutually dependent. And father and son have been explained through the explanation of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s>.
Therefore, since the past and future depend on the present, and the present does not depend on them, the three times exist — this is the established doctrine.
//40//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.41: The establishment of the past and future is not through mutual dependence.

children.text:
bhāṣyam athāpīti /
kasmādatītānāgatāvitaratarāpekṣau na bhavataḥ kṛtaṃ vartamāneneti śaṃṅkā sūcayati /
tannirākaraṇānaya sūtram--- nātī--ddhiḥ (sū. 41) // parasparāpekṣasiddherhi vartamānābhāvaḥ saiva tu nāstīti sūtrārthaḥ /
kayā yuktyeti praśnaḥ /
uttaraṃ kena kalpena prakāreṇātītaḥ
tadanena vartamānābhāve 'tītasvarūpākṣepaḥ kṛtaḥ /
hrasvadīrghatvādīnāṃ parasparāpekṣasiddhitvamaṅgīkṛtyāha /
tannopapadyate viśeṣahetvabhāvāditi /
paramārthatastu na cetaretaratarāpekṣā hrasvadīrghatvādīnāmapi siddhiriti /
svakīyāṃ yuktiṃ vārtikakāra
āha /
na ca vartamānakālānabhyupagame patata
itīti /
( 255 / 6 ) // 41 //
children.translated_text:
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads] "even if" —
He indicates the doubt: why should the past and future not depend on each other, making the present unnecessary?
The <s>sūtra</s> for refuting that — "Not... establishment" (sūtra 41) // For the non-existence of the present [would follow] from mutual dependence of establishment — but that [mutual dependence] does not exist: this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>.
"By what reasoning?" is the question.
The answer: "by what alternative, in what manner, is the past [established]?"
By this, in the absence of the present, the very nature of the past is challenged.
Accepting the mutual dependence of the establishment of shortness, longness, and the like, he says.
"That is not tenable, because of the absence of a specific reason" —
But in the ultimate sense, the establishment of shortness, longness, and the like too is not through mutual dependence.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states his own reasoning.
"And in the non-acceptance of the present time, [the cognition] falling" etc.
//41//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.42: In the absence of the present, there would be non-apprehension of everything, because of the impossibility of direct perception.

children.text:
vakṣyamāṇasūtrāvatāraparaṃ bhāṣyam /
arthasadbhāvavyaṅnyaścāyiti /
asyārthaḥ na kevalaṃ patanādikriyāvyaṅnyo vartamānaḥ kālaḥ api tvarthasadbhāvo 'rthasya sattā 'stikriyeti yāvat /
tayā vyaṅnyaḥ kālaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati patanādayaḥ kriyāḥ
vartamāneṣvapayāntyapayāntica /
asti kriyātu sarvavartamānavyāpinī /
tadevamastikriyāviśiṣṭasya vartamānasyābhāve sarvāgrahaṇaṃ pratyakṣānupapatteḥ /
na cāvidyamānaṃ tasya vivaraṇamasaditi /
na ca varttamānābhāvavādī vidyamānaṃ satkiṃ cidanujānāti /
atra vārtikakāraḥ pṛcchati /
kathaṃ punariti /
( 255 / 17 ) na hi sarvaṃ pratyakṣaṃ varttamānaviṣayamatītānāgatayorapi yogipratyakṣatvāditi bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: The answer — 'because.'
We do not say that direct perception is impossible because of having past and future objects; rather, [it is impossible] because of having past and future as substrates — this is the meaning.

children.text: bhāṣyamapi varttamānābhāve pratyakṣanimittaṃ sannikarṣaḥ asmādipratyakṣaviṣayo vidyamāno ghaṭādiḥ pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇamanādhāraṃ satsarvaṃ nopapadyata iti draṣṭavyam // 42 //
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṣya</s> too should be understood as follows: 'in the absence of the present, the proximate connection (<s>sannikarṣa</s>) that is the cause of direct perception — everything that exists, such as pots and the like, which is the object of our direct perception — all of this, being without a substrate, cannot be a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).' //42//

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> introductory to the forthcoming <s>sūtra</s>. 'And the existence of the object is the indicator' — its meaning: not only is the present time indicated by actions such as falling and the like, but the existence of the object — the being of the object, the activity of 'existing' (<s>asti</s>-<s>kriyā</s>) — by that too time is indicated. What is said [amounts to] this: actions such as falling and the like come and go in present [moments]; but the activity of 'existing' pervades all present moments. Thus, in the absence of the present qualified by the activity of 'existing,' there would be non-apprehension of everything, because of the impossibility of direct perception. 'And what does not exist is its explanation as non-existent' — and one who holds the absence of the present does not acknowledge anything existent as real. Here the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> asks — 'but how then?' (255/17) For not all perception has a present object, since past and future things too are objects of <s>yogi</s>-perception — this is the import.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.43: But because of the tenability of what-has-been-done and what-is-to-be-done, apprehension is in both ways.

children.translated_text: 'Mere' means 'pure.'
The statement of a synonym shows the absolute absence of connection.

children.text: yadi kva cinmukhyaṃvartamānatvaṃ nābhyupeyate tatastatpūrvako bhākto 'pi vartamānaprayogo 'pi na syādityata āha /
children.translated_text: If primary present-ness is not accepted anywhere, then even the figurative usage of the present based on it would not be possible — therefore he says.
'And there is common usage' — this is the meaning. //43//

Here the <s>Bhāṣya</s> is 'the present is apprehended in both ways' — having introduced that, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains. 'And being tenable, it is divided in two ways': sometimes [the present] is indicated by mere activity, as in '<s>asti</s>' (it exists); sometimes it is indicated by a continuum of activity, as in '<s>patati</s>' (it falls), '<s>chinatti</s>' (it cuts) — (256/3) for here a prior-posterior sequence is understood. And it is not the case that for a single action having completion at each moment — a single cooking or a single cutting — there is a prior-posterior sequence. Rather, the continuum of actions is to be relied upon; and that too does not exist without a single unifying [principle] — therefore the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> has said: 'a single-purposive action is the continuum of actions' — meaning: delimited by a single purpose. And here, let the preparatory heating and the like be subsidiary to the meaning of 'cooking,' as the <s>Mahābhāṣyakāra</s> states: 'the intentional command or request — all of that is subsidiary to the meaning of cooking.' Or, only the transformation of form and the like is the meaning of the verbal root '<s>pac</s>' (to cook) as denoted by the verbal ending. Let all this requesting and the like denote <s>bhāvanā</s> (bringing into being) — in neither way is there any loss to our view. '[The present] distinguishes from the future — non-commencement': non-commencement is non-performance — the intended sense is as in '<s>pakṣyati</s>' (he will cook). '[It] distinguishes from the past — non-cessation is intended' — the intended sense is as in '<s>apākṣīt</s>' (he cooked). 'When the intention is the commencement of the continuum' — here 'commencement' refers to the desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>), so there is no contradiction. Having stated that very present as the existence of action, he states the present-ness of the <s>kāraka</s> (agent-factor) as indicated by its connection [with action]. 'And this which is being cut' — (not) that which is being acted upon. [It is] present through its connection with a present action, not in its own nature — this is the meaning. And the present-ness of that <s>kāraka</s>'s connection with present action, considered independently of past and future — the manifestation of the action and of the <s>kāraka</s> too, the manifestation of its state — and the duality caused by that — the <s>sūtra</s> is introduced for the purpose of demonstrating this. 'In that which is being acted upon — done (<s>kṛta</s>)' (sūtra 43) // <s>Bhāṣya</s>: The continuum of actions, commenced for the purpose of attaining the desired result, [is expressed by] '<s>pacati</s>' (he cooks). For the purpose of the forthcoming [discussion], he states the nature of the action-continuum in terms of its connection [with time]. 'In that' — in the action-continuum. '(Not) is it not the case that even in <s>vidyate</s> (it exists) there is understanding of prior-posterior sequence, and so it is connected with past and future?' — to this the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says. 'For here, merely' — the connection is due to the power of language, not real; but the present-ness is real — therefore he says. 'Mere, pure' — the connection is due to the power of language, not real; but the present-ness is real — therefore he says.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.44: Because of complete, predominant, or partial similarity, <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) is not established.

children.text:
atya--ddhiḥ (sū. 44) // yathā gaurevaṃ gavaya ityatideśavākyārthasmṛtisahakāri sārūpyadarśanaṃ sādhyasya gavayo 'yamiti saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandhasya sādhanamupamānaṃ taccedaṃ nopapadyate vikalpānupapatteḥ /
kiṃ yathā gaurevaṃ
iti gavā 'tyantasādharmyaṃ vivakṣitaṃ tathā sati gavāntaramevagavayaḥ syāt /
tadidamāha bhāṣyakāraḥ na caivaṃ bhavati yathā gaurevaṃ gauriti /
co yasmādarthe /
tasmādyathā gaurevaṃ gavaya iti vākyasyārtho bhavati yathā gaurevaṃ gauriti /
gavā prāyasādharmyādapi gavayopamānaṃ na sidhyati /
mahviṣasyāpi gavā prāyasādharmyasya vidyamānatvena tasyāpi gavayābhidhānaprasaṅgāt /
tadidamāha /
na hi bhavati yathā 'naḍvānevaṃ mahiṣa itīti /
yathā 'naḍvānevaṃ gavaya
ityasya vākyasyārtho yathānaḍpavānevaṃ mahiṣa iti yasmānna bhavati /
ekadeśasādharmyādupamānaṃ na bhavati /
ekadeśopamānasyaivānupapatteratiprasaṅgāt /
tadidamāha na hi sarveṇa sarvamupamīyate tathā sati sumerorapisarṣapeṇopamānaprasaṅgāt
// 44 //
children.translated_text: Complete... established (sūtra 44) // 'Just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox)' — the perception of resemblance, which is an auxiliary to the memory of the meaning of the prescriptive statement, is the instrument (<s>sādhana</s>) for establishing the connection between the name and the named (<s>saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandha</s>), namely 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>' — this is <s>upamāna</s> (analogy). But this is untenable, because of the untenability of the alternatives. Does 'just as a cow, so' intend complete similarity with a cow? In that case, the <s>gavaya</s> would be just another cow. This the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> states: 'and it is not the case that just as a cow, so is a cow.' The word 'and' [means] 'because.' Therefore the meaning of the statement 'just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>' becomes 'just as a cow, so is a cow.' Even through predominant similarity with a cow, <s>upamāna</s> for the <s>gavaya</s> is not established — because even the buffalo has predominant similarity with a cow, there would be the unwanted consequence of it too being called '<s>gavaya</s>.' This the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> states: 'for it is not the case that just as a bull, so is a buffalo' — the meaning of the statement 'just as a bull, so is a <s>gavaya</s>' does not become 'just as a bull, so is a buffalo,' because that is not the case. Through partial similarity, <s>upamāna</s> does not hold either — because partial analogy itself is untenable, due to over-extension. This he states: 'for not everything is compared with everything — otherwise, even [Mount] <s>Sumeru</s> could be compared with a mustard seed.' //44//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.45: Because of the establishment of <s>upamāna</s> from well-known similarity, the stated faults do not arise.

children.text:
prasi--ttiḥ (sū. 45) // prakaraṇādyapekṣaṃ hi vākyaṃ svārthaṃ pratipādayati, na kevalam /
tadvaśācca kva cidatyantasādharmyaṃ pratīyate kva cidbhūyaḥsādharmyaṃ kva cidekadeśasādharmyaṃ, tadiha pratītamahiṣādikaṃ puruṣaṃ prati yathā gaurevaṃ gavaya iti vākyamuccāryate tadā mahiṣādipariharārāya bhūyaḥ sādharmyaṃ vivakṣitamityavagataṃ vākyārthaṃ smaran mahiṣādiṣu vane gosādharmyaṃ paśyannapi na gavayasaṃjñāṃ niveśayati /
api tu sādharmyavati gavaya eva tāṃ niveśayati /
yastvapratītamahiṣādistaṃ pratyetadvākyamupamānaṃ na bhavatyeveti paramārthaḥ /
yathā ca prakaraṇādivaśādatyantaprāyaikadeśasādharmyamāśrityātideśavākyāni pravarttante tathā coktaṃ vārttikakṛtā /
nasādharmyasyatyādi bhāṣyaṃ niyamaṃ niṣedhati na sādharmyasya kṛtsnabhāvameva vā 'lpabhāvameva vā āśrityātideśavākyaṃ pravarttate /
kiṃ tarhi ? prasiddhasādharmyāddhetoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvamāśrityoddiśyeti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati /
na niyamaḥ, kiṃ tu kva citkiṃ citsādharmyamāśrityātideśavākyaṃ pravarttate tacca prakaraṇādyunneyamiti /
anabhyupagamāditi ca vārttikaṃ niyamābhiprāyameva /
tatkriyayaiva
( 257 / 23 ) tatkriyāntaramityarthaḥ // 45 //
children.translated_text: Well-known... non-arising (sūtra 45) // For a statement conveys its meaning in dependence on context and the like, not merely [on its own]. And by the force of that [context], sometimes complete similarity is understood, sometimes predominant similarity, sometimes partial similarity. Here, when the statement 'just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>' is uttered to a person who knows buffaloes and the like, then predominant similarity is understood as intended, in order to exclude buffaloes and the like; and remembering the meaning of the statement thus understood, even when seeing cow-similarity in buffaloes and the like in the forest, he does not apply the name '<s>gavaya</s>' — rather, he applies that [name] only to the <s>gavaya</s> which possesses [the appropriate] similarity. But for one who does not know buffaloes and the like, this statement is indeed not an <s>upamāna</s> at all — this is the ultimate meaning. And just as prescriptive statements operate by relying on complete, predominant, or partial similarity depending on the context — this too the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> has stated. The <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'not of similarity etc.' negates a restriction: it is not the case that the prescriptive statement operates relying only on complete similarity or only on partial similarity. What then? From well-known similarity as the reason, relying on the relation of what-is-to-be-proved and the means-of-proving, it is directed — this has been said. What is meant is: there is no restriction; rather, in some cases relying on some particular similarity, the prescriptive statement operates, and that [similarity] is to be inferred from the context and the like. And the <s>Vārttika</s> 'because of non-acceptance' also has the intention of [negating] restriction. 'By that very action' — (257/23) meaning: by another action of that [same kind]. //45//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.46: Because what is imperceptible is established through the perceptible.

children.text: pratya--ddheḥ (sū. 46) // yathā gauravaṃ gavaya iti hi vākyaṃ pratyakṣeṇa gavā gavayapratyakṣaṃ pratipādayati /
na khalu śrutavākyo 'pi yadā pratyakṣeṇa gavayaṃ paśyati tadā vākyārthādhigamādadhikaṃ kiṃ citpratipadyate /
children.translated_text: Surely one who has heard the statement, when he perceives the <s>gavaya</s> directly, does not come to know anything more than what is known from the meaning of the statement.
Even the connection of name and named (<s>saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandha</s>) is already known from this [statement] alone.

children.text: tasmātpratyakṣeṇa gavā pratyakṣasya gavayasya gavayasaṃjñāviśiṣṭasya pratīterupamānasyānumānaneti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ // 46 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the cognition of the <s>gavaya</s> — qualified by the name '<s>gavaya</s>' — through the perceptible cow, is [just] perception and not analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) distinct from inference — this is the first objection. //46//
Perceptible... established (sūtra 46) // For the statement 'just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>' conveys, through the perceptible cow, the perception of the <s>gavaya</s>.

children.text: NyS_2,1.47: nāpratyakṣe gavaye pramāṇārthamupamānasya paśyāma iti //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.47: We do not see the purpose of <s>upamāna</s> as a <s>pramāṇa</s> when the <s>gavaya</s> is not [yet] perceived.

children.text:
siddhāntastu--- (sū. 47) // gavayatvaṃ hi saṃjñi, na ca tadyathā gaurevaṃ gavaya iti vākyātpratīyate /
api tu kasya cidgatā sādṛśyaṃ, na ca vākyagatopava gavayaśabdastasya vācakaḥ /
tathā tadānīmagṛhītasaṃgatitvāt /

etadeva darśayati bhāṣyakāraḥ bhavati bhoḥ svayamapyuccārayiturvākyādadhyavasāya

children.translated_text: — this.
The <s>siddhāntin</s> replies.

children.text: nādhyavasāvaya uccārayituḥ pratiṣidhyate upamānam uccārayitāraṃ prati na bhavati /
children.translated_text: The ascertainment of the speaker is not denied — [but] <s>upamāna</s> does not function as a <s>pramāṇa</s> for the speaker.
As to why — he says: 'because of well-known similarity.' //47//

The <s>siddhānta</s> (established view), however — (sūtra 47) // For <s>gavayatva</s> (gavaya-hood) is the named entity (<s>saṃjñin</s>), and it is not cognized from the statement 'just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>.' Rather, [what is cognized is] the similarity belonging to something [encountered later]; and the word '<s>gavaya</s>' occurring in the statement is not the designator of that [entity at that time] — because at that time the connection [between name and named] has not been grasped. Nor is similarity the named entity. Therefore, the determination of the connection between name and named — the purpose of the <s>pramāṇa</s> — is through direct perception alone, because <s>gavayatva</s> is perceptible. And this was demonstrated in the definition of <s>upamāna</s>. Therefore, the <s>gavaya</s> is perceptible, [but] it is cognized through the imperceptible [i.e., previously unseen] cow — this is the established meaning. The <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (objector) says: 'If you think, O <s>siddhāntin</s>, that <s>upamāna</s> serves another's [purpose], that is not so. Why? Because one ascertains [the meaning] oneself as well. For <s>upamāna</s> would serve another's purpose [only] if the statement "just as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>" generated ascertainment only in the other person; but inasmuch as it generates ascertainment in the speaker too, it serves one's own purpose as well — this is the meaning.' This very thing the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> shows: 'Sir, the speaker too has ascertainment from the statement.'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.48: Because of the conclusion 'thus,' the establishment of <s>upamāna</s> is not indistinct [from inference].

children.text:
vārttikaṃ tu parārthatvenānumānādupamānabhedamāha /
parārthatvācceti /
( 258 / 19 ) nanu pratyakṣaṃ sārūpyajñānamupamānaṃ na caitatparārthamityata āha /
na hi yathāgauriti /
astu tarhi vākyamevetyata āha /

children.translated_text: 'For not scripture (<s>āgama</s>)' — [it is not <s>āgama</s> either].
Even though inference and <s>upamāna</s> are different, under the pretext of concluding what is to be established by just this much, he says —
'Therefore, just as' — [this is the conclusion].
The rest is easy to understand. //48//

The <s>Vārttika</s>, however, states the difference of <s>upamāna</s> from inference by virtue of its serving another's purpose. 'Because of serving another's purpose' — (258/19) Now, the perception of resemblance is <s>upamāna</s>, and that is not for another's purpose — therefore he says. 'For not just as a cow' — but let it be the statement itself [that is <s>upamāna</s>] — therefore he says.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.49: Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is inference — because of the object being apprehended through inference.

children.translated_text: Inference is verbal testimony
— thus.
Verbal... because (sū. 49) //

For the <s>sūtrakāra</s> here first examined the subsumption [of testimony] within inference; and since that [examination] is not proper without first examining its status as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> first examines its very status as a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
The objection to that is: verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> — (259/8) that upon which, when it is present, valid cognition invariably arises and never fails to arise, that is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because of being the most effective instrument.
But even when verbal testimony is present, valid cognition sometimes does not arise — thus he dismantles its effectiveness.
"Because of the absence of an object" etc.
For validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is pervaded by having an object; when that [objecthood] ceases in the case of verbal testimony, validity too ceases — just as when tree-hood ceases, <s>śiṃśapā</s>-hood (being a particular species of tree), which is pervaded by it, [also ceases].
And the object is of two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.
Among these, the former is the object of the <s>pramāṇa</s> of direct perception.
And the imperceptible is to be understood from a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that is invariably concomitant.
If one disregards that [requirement], then due to the absence of any specific connection, everything would be known from everything.
And thus every cognition of an imperceptible object would be pervaded by inference.
And there is no third class besides the perceptible and imperceptible.
Therefore, even due to the absence of an object, verbal testimony is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
As for what was said: "even when there is no valid cognition" —
That is not so.
"Because of being unestablished" etc.
Not the mere word alone is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, but the word together with the grasped and remembered connection.
And when such a word is present, valid cognition does not fail to arise.
But that kind of word from which valid cognition does not arise — that is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning.
"Because of being the producer of the cognition of magnitude" etc.
(260/3) Magnitude is the attribute of the large; it is the qualifier of the large. That which is not known — the <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding the large as the qualified.
Thus, having established the status of verbal testimony as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, he now examines its difference from inference, presenting the prima facie view.

children.text:
yaj jñānaṃ pratyakṣeṇānupalabhyamānārthaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣasya paścādupajāyate tadanumānaṃ yathā 'gnimaddhūmajñānaṃ tathā ca śabdajñānaṃ tasmādanumānamityarthaḥ
// 49 //
children.translated_text: That cognition which has as its object a matter not apprehended by direct perception and which arises after direct perception — that is inference, just as the cognition of fire from smoke; and the cognition from verbal testimony is likewise — therefore [verbal testimony] is inference — this is the meaning. //49//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.50: Because apprehension does not function in two ways.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.51: And because of the connection.

children.text: advipravṛttikatvaṃ prakārabhedarahitatvaṃ pratyakṣānumāne tu parokṣāparokṣāvagāhitayā prakārabhedavatī ityarthaḥ // 50-51 //
children.translated_text: Not functioning in two ways means being devoid of difference in mode — but direct perception and inference, through grasping the imperceptible and the non-imperceptible, have a difference in mode — this is the meaning. //50-51//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.52: From the capacity of the teaching of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>), there is understanding of the meaning from the word.
He begins [stating] the nature of the established doctrine.

children.translated_text: 'As for the first' etc. / By this — the deviation in doubt and the like, since they too have objects in all three times. / The bare justification of positive and negative concomitance exists in perception too. / But the knowledge of positive and negative concomitance that is a component of communication is of one kind in verbal testimony and of another kind in inference — for in inference it depends on being a property of the thesis-subject, but in verbal testimony it does not depend on that — on this point there is a <s>sūtra</s>: / 'The trustworthy person who' (<s>sūtra</s> 52) // For what is completely unprecedented and never before seen — heaven (<s>svarga</s>), the unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>), deities, and the like — that is in the form of sentence-meaning. Thus: / 'That pleasure which is not mixed with pain, nor consumed by what follows after, / and is brought about by desire — that is the pleasure which is the abode of the word <s>svaḥ</s> (heaven).' / // Heaven is a sentence-meaning. / Similarly, the unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>) too: / it is indeed the cause of heaven, hell, and the like, enduring through future time, a special quality of a person, opposed to its own contrary effect — this is the sentence-meaning. Similarly for deities too: / for they too — partakers of the hymns and oblations, possessed of bodies endowed with thousand-eyed [Indra] and the like — are sentence-meanings alone. / None of these is within the scope of the perception and the like of persons such as ourselves, apart from verbal testimony. / And an unapprehended mark (<s>liṅga</s>) cannot operate [as a basis of inference] in this [domain]. / And a relation cannot be grasped when the relatum is not grasped. / But the word, although it requires the awareness of the mutual connection of word-meanings, / and although the sentence-meaning is nothing other than word-meanings qualified by other word-meanings — / even those who, in [producing] the sentence-meaning at the time of creation and the like, operating through the medium of the recollection of word-meanings, produce the sentence-meaning in the form of heaven without depending on the grasping of [mutual] connection — they point to what is established in their own world as belonging to the class of pleasure, designate what is denoted by the word 'heaven' as qualified by the well-known [properties of] non-mixture with pain and the like, and do not make a non-word-meaning into a sentence-meaning. And the use of the word in the sentence-meaning is [analogous to] 'heaven,' just as [saying] 'a <s>śrotriya</s> is one who has studied the <s>Chandas</s> (Vedas).' / Just as the eye and the other [sense organs] operate with respect to form and the like without having grasped [their mutual] connection — so too, words, even though they require the grasping of the mutual connection of word-meanings, do not require the grasping of connection in producing the awareness of sentence-meaning, since the status of being a <s>pramāṇa</s> is indicated by the effect, and since the effect of producing awareness of sentence-meaning is observed even from word-fragments that do not depend on the grasping of connection. / Therefore, neither the word nor its meaning is a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) in the awareness of sentence-meaning, because of not depending on the grasping of a relation — just as the eye and the like [do not function as a mark] in the awareness of form and the like. / One might say: / let it not be inference based on direct observation (<s>pratyakṣatodṛṣṭa</s>) in the case of sentence-meaning; it will be inference based on general observation (<s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>). / And although the words do not have the property of being a property of the thesis-subject when the sentence-meaning is what is to be proved, and although the word-meanings recalled by words deviate [from the sentence-meaning], nevertheless, word-meanings qualified by expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>), and proximity (<s>satti</s>), being in [mutual] connection, will be the mark. / Thus: by words such as 'that which is not [mixed] with pain' and the like, the recalled word-meanings, established in the relation of principal and subordinate, possessing [mutual] connection — since they are possessed of expectancy, fitness, and proximity and are recalled by words, like the word-meanings recalled by words in 'one should drive the cow' — / And the specific nature of the connection is nothing other than the things being connected, not something that a knower [grasps] as a separate specific. / And the things being connected are recalled by the words alone — so the specific connection is obtained [thereby]. / And that alone is the sentence-meaning — so it is established that the sentence-meaning is inferential. / And in 'one should drive the cow,' the fact that the word-meanings possess [mutual] connection is understood from the cognition of the connection of word-meanings inferred from the activity of elders immediately following the hearing of the sentence. / This is clumsy. / Because the words themselves, having the intermediate function of recalling word-meanings, are instruments (<s>karaṇa</s>) for the awareness of sentence-meaning, and hence are <s>pramāṇas</s>. / And since they do not have the property of being a property of the thesis-subject, their being a mark is unjustified. / But if the words had a function terminating merely in [recalling] word-meanings and were not directed toward sentence-meaning-cognition, then the word-meanings would have no expectancy, and sentence-meaning-cognition would not arise. / For without expectancy, word-meanings are not connected merely by proximity and fitness — as in 'this son is coming; the king's man should be removed' — where the king, being without expectancy through his relation to the son, is not connected with the man [for the purpose of sentence-meaning]. / And without the words being directed toward sentence-meaning-cognition, the word-meanings recalled by them do not have expectancy. / For it is not the case that whatever cannot exist without something else has expectancy for it — for then a <s>kāraka</s> (action-factor) would have expectancy for the action, or a substance for a quality, and in that case 'the cloth exists' would not be a complete sentence / because cloth, as a substance, has expectancy for a quality. / Therefore 'the red cloth exists' — of which this is a partial [expression] — 'the cloth exists' — being incomplete because of expectancy — would not be a <s>pramāṇa</s>. But 'the cloth exists' as a sentence grasps some quality or other and is complete, and is indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And when 'the red cloth exists' — of this, the partial [expression], grasping some quality or other, is complete — and thus, when divided, there would be a difference of sentences because of completeness. / And 'red' too would be a sentence that, grasping some possessor-of-quality and some action, would complete [itself]. / And it is not proper [to say] that when a specific is seen, there is no implied [reference] — / for when there is unity of sentence, upon seeing the specific, there is no implied [reference]; / and when there is no implied [reference], there is unity of sentence — so there would be mutual dependence. / Therefore, we consider it proper that the expectancy of word-meanings is nothing other than their non-termination [of function], since they are recalled by the cluster of words uttered together for the purpose of communicating sentence-meaning. / And thus, 'the cloth exists' — just this much alone, being complete, produces [awareness] by implying some quality or other. But in 'the red cloth exists,' because of the co-utterance of the word 'red' too, since [all words] are directed toward sentence-meaning-connection, cloth and the like, not terminating without connection with redness, and redness, not terminating without connection with cloth and the like — being mutually related — [establish] the unity of sentence. / Therefore, the words themselves, through the medium of recalling word-meanings, indicate their mutual connection — they are the <s>pramāṇa</s> for sentence-meaning — and since they do not have the property of being a property of the thesis-subject, they are not a mark. / One might say: / this specific cluster of words, being possessed of the connection of recalled word-meanings, since it has the property of being a word-cluster and is endowed with expectancy and the like, [functions] like the word-sequence 'one should drive the cow' — so there is no [fault of] not being a property of the thesis-subject. / Not so. / Because of mutual dependence. / For the object-<s>kāraka</s> (accusative action-factor) — cloth and the like — being in reality established as different from [the sentence-meaning], serves the purpose of a cognition characterized by a defining mark (<s>jñānalakṣaṇā</s>). / Just as the possession of fire by smoke or the conjunction of smoke with the mountain — not the capacity to generate the cognition of fire — is its possession of fire. / For the indication by the effect does not work unless the effect has arisen. / And thus, when the effect has arisen, the possession-of-fire [is established]; but the production of the effect requires the object (<s>karman</s>) of the possession-of-fire — so there is mutual dependence. / For the effect and the object are not identical. / For the tree itself is not the cutter [of the tree]. / So here, the property of the words having connection and their capacity to generate the cognition [of the connection] — these cannot be what is to be proved by inference. / For it has been said that the capacity of smoke to generate the cognition of fire is not what is to be proved by inference. / And their capacity to generate recollection too is posited for the purpose of communicating sentence-meaning — it does not reveal another relation. / Therefore it is established: words are not a mark in the awareness of sentence-meaning, because of not being a property of the thesis-subject, like the mind. / Moreover, it is the worldly meaning that is followed by critical examiners — they do not adhere to the extra-ordinary in accordance with self-made definitions. / And the world does not, with difficulty, by some contrivance, construct the property of being a property of the thesis-subject and then understand sentence-meaning from words — rather, [it understands] from those [words] themselves, independently. So the difference of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) as a <s>pramāṇa</s> from inference is established. / But the property of being spoken by a trustworthy person (<s>āptoktatva</s>) is indeed a mark for the validity of that particular <s>āgama</s> (scripture) that communicates [things like] heaven and the like. / And this does not make its object inferential for that reason. / For the object of perception, whose validity has been inferred through the capacity for engagement, does not become inferential. / For the <s>pramāṇa</s> has an object that is the thing [itself], and with respect to its validity, the [marks are] the capacity for engagement and being spoken by a trustworthy person. / Having thus established [the matter], we should consider that what was presented by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> and the <s>vārttikakāra</s> — the dependence and non-dependence on being spoken by a trustworthy person as the ground of the difference between verbal testimony and inference — was presented merely as an additional [consideration]. / By this account of the difference in operation, non-dual-operation has been explained — through the refutation [of the opposing view]. / Having restated the prima facie view that verbal testimony is inference because of the relation [between word and meaning], he refutes it. / 'But this again' etc. / 'Of this to that' — the genitive-qualified [relation] — this <s>bhāṣya</s>, its explanation is: 'the relation of expression and expressed' etc. / For the relation between word and meaning, if intrinsic, could be either one of identity, or the relation of being the conveyed and conveyor, or one of contact (<s>prāpti</s>). Among these, by the word 'undesignatable' — which pertains to the definition of perception — identity has been removed. / And below, the naturally-arisen (<s>autpattika</s>) relation of conveyed and conveyor will be refuted by the argument for the refutation of the contact between word and meaning. / Therefore the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> refutes contact — 'the relation characterized by contact' etc. / For the contact of things apprehendable by a single sense organ is perceptual, as between fingers — but word and meaning are not apprehendable by a single sense organ. Therefore the contact between them is not perceptible through the senses, like [the contact] between wind and trees — this is the meaning. / Now, the meaning of a word is apprehendable by the same sense organ [as the word] — so why is it not grasped by a sense organ? The word [is auditory], and its object, passing beyond that [auditory] domain — therefore he says: / 'And there is a super-sensory object, even if dead' etc. / The sense organ that grasps the word has been transcended — the mere sense organ, and what transcends it is super-sensory; and that [super-sensory thing], being an object — this is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> compound. / This has been explained by the <s>vārttika</s> 'because of this, of the word' etc.
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.53: And from the non-observation of filling, burning, and splitting, there is absence of relation [between word and meaning]. //
