children.translated_text: The answer [is]: 'this is the very same' etc.
<s>Nirukta</s> (etymology) and the rest would have the capacity to instruct regarding the connection of [words] with meaning.
But it is that very [connection] which is being examined — this is the meaning. //53//

He explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'and when [the relation is] characterized by contact' etc. / 'Not by inference either' — this completes [the thought]. / 'Reaches' — goes, that is, arrives. / Coming, it should be observed — like a sweetmeat and the like — but it is not observed; therefore the meaning of words does not come [to the word]. / And thus, in this position, worldly transaction through words would be destroyed. / 'Now, the word' etc. / To begin with, the movement of sound, which is a quality, is not tenable — therefore it should be said that sound reaches a place through a succession of [similar sounds] — and thus there would be a contradiction with permanence [of sound] — this is the meaning. / He raises a doubt: / 'Now, it does not come' etc. / 'Exists' means 'is present.' / Thinking that 'coming into being without previously existing' is the meaning of 'exists' (<s>bhavati</s>), he refutes: / 'And [if] it is eternal, it exists' — etc. / The doubter states his own intention: / 'Now, it does not come' etc. / He refutes: / 'Not of all meanings' etc. / For it is not observed that things in the same location, apprehendable by the same sense organ, and having specific manifestors and manifestations, are restricted [in this way] — this is the intention. / The apprehension of the substrate of a universal is the cause of the manifestation of an individual — / but there is no apprehension of the substrate of sound from which sound could be manifested. / Rather, it is by the word itself that the substrate should be manifested. / And thus, [the word] sound, residing in the meaning [i.e., the object], being manifested by the palate and the like which do not reach [the meaning], manifests all [objects] — so the previously stated fault arises. / And it is not the case that the inherence of the word in the meaning is within the scope of experience — thus he says: / 'And there is no inherence in the expressed.' / 'One will understand from scripture' — the scripture (<s>āgama</s>) is that beginning with the etymological tradition (<s>nirukta</s>).
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.54: Because of the fixed correspondence of words and meanings, there is no denial [of verbal testimony].
The proponent of the prima facie view says:
"Word and meaning" etc. //54//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.55: Not so, because the understanding of the meaning from words is based on convention (<s>sāmayika</s>).

children.translated_text: "And from common usage" etc.
Having ascertained the convention through the practice of the learned, one then understands the distinction of correct and incorrect [usage] from grammar — this is the meaning.
He classifies this.
This is the <s>śāstra</s> (science/treatise). //55//

The proponent of the established doctrine says:
"Because of being conventional" etc.
"The fixed rule of expression and expressed" — the fixed correspondence of expression and expressed is this: the word "cow" (<s>go</s>) refers only to that which possesses a dewlap etc.; the word "horse" (<s>aśva</s>) refers only to that which possesses a mane etc.
The injunction to understand that [correspondence] — the convention of the Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) at the beginning of creation is this convention — this is the meaning.
When that is employed and known, the fixed correspondence of word and meaning obtains.
Even for those who hold the view of [an inherent] connection, this [convention] is unavoidable.
Even those <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> and grammarians who maintain that the connection between word and meaning is natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>) — for them too, not by the mere existence [of the connection] does it [the word] make known [the meaning]; rather, only when known — "this is the expression of that" or "from this, that is to be understood" — this convention alone is the means.
Even the usage of the learned with respect to words like "cow" etc. is preceded by convention, just like words such as "<s>Devadatta</s>" etc.
Therefore, let there be convention alone; the natural connection is unnecessary, since the transactions of usage, understanding, and application are explained by convention alone — this is the meaning.
But this convention, for some words, cannot be made when there is no natural connection with meaning — for one would have to point out the meaning and say "this is to be understood from this."
And pointing out is not possible for some words without a natural connection.
But if the expressive capacity [of all words] depends on convention, then since no convention has been made for any [word at the start], what would anything be pointed out with?
Therefore, the very act of making a convention demonstrates the natural connection of words — to this he says:
"Because of grasping while being used" etc.
For the convention that <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord) made at the beginning of creation for words like "cow" etc. in relation to their meanings — that can be grasped even by children who do not know the convention, when they observe words being used in the practice of the learned.
For thus: after hearing the speech of an elder, the child, observing the comprehension of activity, cessation, fear, sorrow, joy, etc. in another elder who has heard it, infers the cognition that is its cause.
And of that [cognition], among other existing meanings — whether real or unreal — immediately upon hearing,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.56: And because of the non-restriction to universal and particular.

children.translated_text:
Thus, since the establishment of the fixed correspondence of word and meaning is explained by the very convention that is seen and accepted by both parties, the postulation of a natural connection that is entirely unseen is not justified — this has been said. Now he says that this natural connection is also untenable.
"Universal and particular" (sū. 56) // For a natural connection would be of a word with some [particular] universal or particular.
But there is no restriction [to either] —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.57: Its invalidity [results] from the faults of untruth, contradiction, and redundancy.

children.translated_text: Likewise, the remaining Vedic statements are not <s>pramāṇa</s>, because of being Vedic statements — like the statement of the <s>Putrakāmeṣṭi</s> (sacrifice for obtaining a son).
Having stated the to-be-proved in the form of exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), he states the to-be-proved in the form of implicative negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>) using the same reason.
Of the statements of <s>Agnihotra</s> and the like, or —
The other statement is the one about <s>Putrakāmeṣṭi</s> etc. //57//

Its... faults (sū. 57) // If verbal testimony were subsumed under inference, it could sometimes have validity due to the invariable concomitance with the meaning. But when it falls outside [inference], its invalidity would be easy — thinking thus, the prima facie view states its invalidity immediately after stating its being a variety of inference.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with "of that" etc. — the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains.
Taking "that" as the governing word,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.58: Not so, because of the deficiency in the action, the agent, and the instrument.

children.translated_text: But the non-communication of meaning was what was asserted [as the thesis], and that very same thing is the "falsity" — so there is no difference in meaning between the thesis and the reason.
To this he says:
"And [it is] falsity." //58//

The non-observation of the result, being explicable otherwise too, does not establish the falsity [of the Vedas] — therefore the falsity is unestablished as a reason: this is the meaning.
One might say: since the <s>iṣṭi</s> (sacrifice) is enjoined [by the Veda], it is independent — it [itself] brings about the result of a son — so what deficiency of the action or the agent could affect it? To this he says:
"Because the <s>iṣṭi</s> has the nature of being an instrument" —
An <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen) cause that has been observed [to require] seen auxiliaries is not [effective] alone;
therefore, from the deficiency in the seen [auxiliaries], the non-arising of the result is explicable — this is the meaning.
He states the agent to be considered — "the parents" —
He states the instrument.
"By the <s>iṣṭi</s>" —
He states the action.
"Being properly united" —
The <s>Bhāṣya</s>: "depending on the <s>iṣṭi</s>."
Desire — the performance of subsidiary acts like fuel-offering and the like; its failure is non-performance.
"An ignorant performer" —
For the qualified person has authority by capacity.
Hence women, <s>śūdras</s>, and animals, being incapable, have no authority.
Even a learned person, if he has committed an act that causes the loss of twice-born status, such as the killing of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> and the like — even a ritual performed by him is not fit to produce results, due to deficiency in the agent — this he shows.
"One of bad conduct" —
<s>Kapūya</s> means censured action;
one who practices it is a person of [bad] conduct.
"Offering" — unpurified, not consecrated or not sprinkled.
"Contaminated" — by dogs, cats, and the like.
"Mantras" — deficient in the specific sequence.
"<s>Dakṣiṇā</s>" (sacrificial fee) — obtained through wicked means such as messenger-service, gambling, bribery, and the like: this is the meaning.
<s>Anvāhārya</s> means the <s>dakṣiṇā</s>.
That is given as less than what would satisfy the person — and that person, fed on human food, is censured for being decrepit, dull, and incapable of [retaining] cooking.
Improper sexual union — acting in the manner of a woman with one's mother, and various defects of the womb that are obstacles to the generation of a son.
The impairment of the seed consisting of blood and semen, from which the birth of a son does not occur.
Faulty churning, from which fire is not produced.
Regarding the deficiency of the action and the deficiency of the agent, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says.
"Thus of the <s>iṣṭi</s>, of what is to be accomplished" —
"Due to the incapacity of the mantras and the like" —
Meaning: of the rituals such as the <s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s> and the like, whose instruments are mantras and the like.
But if the <s>iṣṭi</s> is independent and not the means [alone], then the parents alone, when properly united, without depending [on anything else], would generate a son — what need then for the <s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s>? And for this very reason the birth of sons to barbarians (<s>mlecchas</s>) and the like is also explicable — to this he says:
"Because of being an auxiliary to that" —
The auxiliary nature of the <s>iṣṭi</s> is not known through positive and negative concomitance alone, but through scripture. The birth of sons to barbarians and the like is due to the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) from a previous life.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.59: [No contradiction,] because the statement of fault is made having accepted a distinction of time.

Regarding what was said — that statements like "one should offer when the sun has risen" and the like mutually contradict each other — to this he says:
"Both" —
Among the sentences that have injunction as their purpose, since a single sentence does not negate the meaning of both sentences, there is no multiplicity of authorities for different [results] — this is the meaning.
Although one offering cannot be performed simultaneously through combination, nevertheless it will be performed alternatively — for frequently
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.60: And because of the possibility of restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>).

children.translated_text: Therefore, even a result that is desired does not, because of not being the object of activity, prompt by its own cognition with respect to oneself; but the means to it, because of being the object of activity and because of being desired, does prompt through its own cognition — this we consider proper.

But for infants, the knowledge of the means that is needed for [taking] breast-milk and the like is inference itself — produced by the cognition of the mark of being-of-that-kind, arising in those who have the recollection of invariable concomitance produced through the continuity of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by the grasping of the invariable concomitance in previous lives.
And this will be demonstrated in the context of "from the recollection connected with traces of previous practice."

children.text: ata eva prayojanalakṣaṇaṃ vyācakṣāṇenoktaṃ vārttikakṛtā ... idaṃ sukhasādhanamiti vuddhā sukhāvāptaye yatate idaṃ duḥkhasādhana miti cāvagamya duḥkhahānāyeti ... //
children.translated_text: For this very reason the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, in explaining the definition of purpose (<s>prayojana</s>), said: "understanding that this is a means of pleasure, the wise person strives for the attainment of pleasure; and understanding that this is a means of suffering, [he strives] for the avoidance of suffering." //

Injunction is that which enjoins (sūtra 63) // Its explanation is: "that sentence which."
"Prompting" means "causing to act."
And here, upon hearing the instruction "one who desires health should eat wholesome food" and the like, a child, observing an elderly person acting upon it and engaging in eating wholesome food, infers the cognition that is the cause of his activity — "his activity is preceded by a prompting cognition" — spontaneously.

children.translated_text: making known the being-a-desired-means for the agent, is an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>); that very [sentence] permits the activity of obtaining the means — materials and the like — for accomplishing that.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati -- ye hi dravyārjananiyamavidhayo brāhmaṇasya pratigahādinetyevamādayaḥ te ca rāgato dhanārjane pravṛttānāṃ brāhmaṇānāṃ laukikānekopāyaprayuktau satyāṃ niyamaparāḥ puruṣārthā na kratvarthāḥ kratuvidhayastu dhanasādhanāste 'nūditāḥ paryavasyantopa 'pi na dhanārjjaṃnaṃ tanniyamaṃ vā prayujjate puruṣārthatvenaiva tasya prayuktatvāt kevalamanujānanti, tasmāttadevāgnihotrādivākyamaprāpte 'gnihotrādau vidhiranyataḥ prāpte sādhdhane 'nujñeti siddham /
children.translated_text: What is said amounts to this: those injunctions that prescribe restrictions on the acquisition of wealth for a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, such as 'by acceptance (<s>pratigraha</s>) and the like' — these, since <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> who are engaged in acquiring wealth out of desire have many worldly means available, are restrictive and serve the person's purpose, not the sacrifice's purpose. But the sacrifice-injunctions, being means for wealth — even though when traced they terminate in wealth-acquisition or its restriction — do not enjoin [wealth-acquisition] because that is already enjoined as serving the person's purpose; they merely permit it. Therefore, that very <s>agnihotra</s>-statement, being an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) with respect to the <s>agnihotra</s> which has not been [previously] arrived at, is a permission (<s>anujñā</s>) with respect to the means that have been arrived at from elsewhere — this is established.
The word 'or' (<s>vā</s>) indicates aggregation. //63//

Therefore, the child who is learning understands that the being-a-desired-means, namely the prompting, which is established in oneself, is the cause of activity even for an elder.
And that [understanding], arising immediately after hearing the indicatory mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the like, ascertains the meaning of the indicatory mark and the like.
But mere being-a-desired-means is not the cause of activity — for indeed, the <s>kārīrī</s> sacrifice performed by the sacrificer is a desired means for the farmers, yet they do not engage in it, because it is already accomplished.
Therefore, one should maintain that it is the being-a-desired-means for the agent that is the cause of activity.
And there is no agency with respect to what is already accomplished.
As the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> has said:
'The result of scripture [accrues] to the performer, because of that being its defining characteristic.'
And in ordinary usage too, action alone is the desired means — this being the meaning of the word; and following that, Vedic injunctions such as 'one who desires heaven should perform the <s>agnihotra</s>' also designate action alone as the desired means.
And this [action], though perishable at the next moment, being connected with an intermediate <s>apūrva</s> (unseen potency), serves even a long-lasting result,
just as agriculture, born in the summer season, [serves a result] produced in the winter season.
One need not postulate <s>apūrva</s> as the desired means here.
Or, even if that very [<s>apūrva</s>] is the desired-means-as-cause-of-activity, even so, the injunctive word (<s>vidhiśabda</s>), having the common qualifier of being-a-desired-means-for-the-agent, by virtue of connection with that single qualifier, sometimes operates with respect to action, sometimes with respect to <s>apūrva</s> — thus there is no harm to [either] view.
Thus, having learned the meaning of instruction (<s>upadeśa</s>) regarding the enjoined-person, the purpose, and the action, upon perceiving those very words being used in commands and the like to enjoin the purpose and action, he also understands their capacity to express request (<s>adhyeṣaṇā</s>) and permission (<s>anujñā</s>).
But statements like those about the <s>agnihotra</s>, which express the enjoined-person, purpose, and action, are indeed instructions (<s>upadeśa</s>).
Therefore, although commands, requests, invitations, and instructions are all injunctions (<s>vidhi</s>), still, instruction is the intended form of injunction here.
Therefore, it is well said that 'a sentence is injunctive' —
meaning: it makes known the being-a-desired-means for the agent.
Having restated the <s>Bhāṣya</s> 'injunction, however, is enjoining and permission,' he explains.
'Injunction, however' —
(269/11) This sentence 'one who desires heaven should perform the <s>agnihotra</s>,' having the characteristic of prompting one who has not [yet] commenced,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.64: Praise, censure, the practice of another, and ancient precedent — these are <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage).

children.translated_text: First of all, in these sentences that denote what is [already] established, there is no injunctive expression.

children.text: tatra kimaśrūyamāṇo vidhiḥ kalpyatāmāho pratītena vidhinaikavākyateti /
children.translated_text: So then, should an injunction be postulated even though not heard, or should there be syntactic unity with a cognized injunction?

children.text: tatra kalpanālāghavātpratītena vidhinaikavākyataiva jyāyasī--pūrvapakṣe vidhikalpanā tadekavākyatākalpanamiti dvayaṃ kalpanīyam, uttarasmiṃstu ekavākyatāmātramiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Between these, syntactic unity with a cognized injunction is preferable, because of economy of postulation — in the prima facie view, two things must be postulated: an injunction and syntactic unity with it; in the established view, only syntactic unity [need be postulated] — this is the import.
And more clearly, because of the absence of the cognition of praise and censure [in them], <s>parakṛti</s> and <s>purākalpa</s> are presented separately from praise and censure. //64//

Praise has a twofold utility: being an auxiliary to the activity [of the person] when the duty is to be performed as enjoined by the injunction, and when that activity is to be performed; persons who engage [in action] having known 'this is praiseworthy' engage all the more, and that activity of a faithful person produces <s>dharma</s>, not of an unfaithful one.
As the <s>śruti</s> declares: '... whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the <s>upaniṣad</s>, that indeed becomes more powerful ...'
Regarding the auxiliary role in the effect of activity, he says:
'That which is being praised' —
Regarding the auxiliary role in the effect of the injunction, he says:
'And it is promotive' —
As to how <s>parakṛti</s> (another's practice) and <s>purākalpa</s> (ancient precedent) are <s>arthavāda</s>:
Since one hears of the connection of the <s>Caraka</s>-<s>adhvaryu</s>-person, the difference in sequence between the sprinkling (<s>vapā</s>)-oblation and the <s>pṛṣadājya</s>-sprinkling, being unobtained [from elsewhere], is enjoined as a property of a particular person through the <s>parakṛti</s>-statement; similarly, since the connection of the <s>bahiṣpavamāna</s>-<s>soma</s>-<s>stoma</s>-<s>mantra</s> is heard through connection with a person of the past, why should the <s>purākalpa</s>-statement not be injunctive as a property of a present-day person? — this is the import.
The answer:
'Because of connection with a statement of praise or censure, being subsidiary to some injunction' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.65: The restatement of what has been enjoined by an injunction is <s>anuvāda</s> (restatement).

children.translated_text: For example, <s>Soma</s> has been enjoined, [and then] 'having sacrificed with the <s>darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, one should sacrifice with <s>Soma</s>.'
Similarly, 'the <s>adhvaryu</s>, having consecrated the householder, consecrates the <s>Brahman</s> [priest].'
Because of apprehending the meaning through differentiation, validity is appropriate.
The meaning is: validity obtains. //65//

Injunction... restatement (sūtra 65) // What has been enjoined is taken up [again] for the purpose of praise or censure.
For example, the <s>arthavāda</s> of the injunction 'one should sacrifice with the <s>aśvamedha</s>' is: 'he who sacrifices with the <s>aśvamedha</s>' —
For what purpose? To praise: 'he crosses over death, he crosses over sin' — this is the praise.
The <s>arthavāda</s> of the injunction 'one should offer at sunrise' is: 'he who offers at sunrise' —
For what purpose? To censure: 'the dark one devours his oblation' — this is the censure.
He states another purpose:
'Or a subsidiary of the injunction is designated' —
As follows: through originating sentences like '... that which is an <s>āgneya</s> eight-<s>kapāla</s> [offering] ...' and the like, the <s>ṣaḍāgneya</s> and other sacrifices, connected with the full-moon and new-moon times, are enjoined — and those injunctions, being of the form of being-a-desired-means, not obtaining their desired [object] within their own sentences, are expectant.
Similarly, the originating injunctions for the <s>āghāra</s> and the like too, having no connection with a specific time, are expectant of the desired [object]. There,
'He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon' — this is the restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) of the <s>āgneya</s> and the like that have arisen through connection with a specific time.
For what purpose? For the purpose of restricting the desired-object-connection expected by the originating injunctions like 'that which is an <s>āgneya</s> eight-<s>kapāla</s>,'
so that the fruit-connection may belong only to the six <s>āgneya</s> and the like that have arisen through connection with a specific time and been restated, and not to the <s>āghāra</s> and the like that have arisen without time-connection — for this purpose.
Thus the <s>āghāra</s> and the like, by the maxim 'what is fruitless in proximity to what is fruitful is subsidiary to it,'
remain as subsidiaries (<s>aṅga</s>) of the <s>darśapūrṇamāsa</s> — and this is established.
This fruit-connection-restriction is a subsidiary-of-injunction (<s>vidhiśeṣa</s>); restatement serves that purpose — this is the meaning.
Similarly, the oblation enjoined as 'one performs the <s>agnihotra</s>' is restated.
For what purpose? For the purpose of enjoining specific qualifications such as curd and the like:
in [sentences like] 'one offers with curd,' 'one offers with milk,' and so on.
This qualification-injunction is a subsidiary-of-injunction — thus he states another purpose of restatement.
'For the purpose of what comes after what has been enjoined' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.66: There is no difference between restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) and repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), because the repetition of words is possible.
Not... [possible].
(Sūtra 66) // The prima facie view of one who does not know the purpose of restatement stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. //66//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.67: Just as in the instruction to go faster, there is no non-difference because of repetition.
Faster... non-difference.

children.translated_text: And it is not the case that the speaker's cognition is one thing and the hearer's another, such that one could postulate that the hearer's cognition is mistaken because of contradiction — he says:
'And just as for the hearer' —

As in 'village after village is delightful' and the like. //67//

(Sūtra 67) The <s>Vārttika</s> [says] 'as follows' —
(270/5) Just as when 'go quickly' is said, 'go more quickly' is not a mere repetition,
because the comparative suffix (<s>tarap</s>) conveys an excess of action; similarly, the repetition in 'go quickly, quickly' conveys an excess of action through repetition, and since the excess of action is not understood from a single utterance, the repetition is purposeful.
The excess of the qualifier of the action is also an excess of the action — this is the meaning.
Granted, in 'go quickly, quickly,' the difference of restatement from the understanding of excess through repetition is understood.
But what is the difference in 'cooks, cooks' and the like?
To this he says: 'What then is that difference which exists in "cooks, cooks" and the like?'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.68: Just as the validity of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, so is that [Vedic] validity, because of the validity of trustworthy persons (<s>āpta</s>).

children.translated_text: — this. For the purpose of drawing in the prior [quality of] being worthy of consideration as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, namely the property of having a division of meaning. For a thesis that has been rendered plausible by a reason is then proved, not one that has not been rendered plausible. As they say: 'A thesis rendered plausible in the proposition would be proved by a reason; there is no protection by reasons for one who is struck down as he rises.' // He explains the <s>sūtra</s>: 'as in the statements of <s>mantras</s> (sacred formulae) and <s>Āyurveda</s> (medical science).' The distinctive qualities of <s>Puruṣa</s> — the blessed Lord who is the maker of the <s>Vedas</s> — are: having directly perceived what is to be avoided and what is to be pursued; compassion for beings which is the root of that [perception]; the desire to communicate things as they are; and skillfulness of expression. For it is precisely by this that the <s>Puruṣa</s> is distinguished from other persons who are not trustworthy (<s>āpta</s>). 'By a threefold qualification' is illustrative — the lack of skill in expression should also be considered. The purport here is as follows: living beings of diverse kinds are observed to have infinite varieties of internal pleasures and pains. And that this diversity is not natural will be explained in the third [book]. Nor is it caused solely by visible causes, since those are observed to deviate. Therefore, an unseen [force] (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) assisted by the visible is the cause of this diversity — and that is called <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented merit), and also <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit). And that is directly perceptible to certain persons such as <s>Manu</s> and the like — this has been demonstrated. The maker of effects characterized as bodies, worlds, and the like — one who is capable of their creation, who knows the reality of all things, who is untouched by afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), actions (<s>karma</s>), fruitions (<s>vipāka</s>), and latent impressions (<s>āśaya</s>), who is supremely compassionate — is inferred from the very effects characterized as bodies and worlds — this will be demonstrated in the fourth [book]. This very [Lord], seeing living beings who do not know the means of attaining their own benefit and avoiding harm, and moreover beholding them being burned by the fires of manifold sufferings — how could he not be pained? And being pained, knowing the reality of the means of attaining benefit and avoiding harm, how could he not teach? Or teach otherwise? Therefore, by this supremely compassionate [Lord], having created earth and the like and the four kinds of creatures, the means of attaining benefit and avoiding harm must be taught to them. For he cannot remain without teaching. And his instruction to creatures — for whom he is like a father — has as its scope gods, sages, and humans, and is to be respectfully received through the four classes (<s>cāturvarṇya</s>) and the four stages of life (<s>cāturāśramya</s>). And it is to be upheld for the practice of the means of attaining benefit and avoiding harm. Therefore, the <s>āgama</s> (scripture) that establishes the conduct of classes and stages of life, that is accepted by the great community of people — that is composed by Him and is a <s>pramāṇa</s> because of being the utterance of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>), like the statements of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s> — this is being established. Which <s>āgama</s> is that, spoken by a trustworthy person? Are they the scriptures of the <s>Śākya</s> monks, <s>Digambaras</s> (Jains), those who claim liberation from <s>saṃsāra</s>, and the like? Or are they the <s>Vedas</s>? Regarding this: the <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Ṛṣabha</s> and the like are remembered clearly as the authors of the scriptures of the <s>Śākyas</s> and the like — but it is not [established] that the Lord of the described characteristics is their author. And these [persons] beginning with the son of <s>Śuddhodana</s> are not the creators of bodies, worlds, and the like, by which they could be ascertained as omniscient. Through the practice of the means [of knowledge], their omniscience may be considered possible, but by mere possibility alone, discerning persons cannot have confidence in the scriptures composed by them. Nor are their scriptures the basis for establishing the conduct of classes and stages of life — for indeed these do not prescribe the rites beginning from the sacrament of conception (<s>niṣeka</s>) and ending at the cremation ground for the creatures. For even those who accept Buddhist and other scriptures as authoritative do not, in worldly affairs, proceed by those scriptures alone without regard for <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, <s>Itihāsa</s>, and <s>Purāṇa</s>. Rather, even they, saying 'this is conventional [truth],' follow the <s>Śruti</s> and the like in worldly affairs. Therefore, whether or not there exists a memory of the <s>Vedas</s> having a world-creator as their author — we maintain that these [Vedas] alone are composed by the Lord. For these are not remembered as being authored by someone else, like statements about worshipping <s>caityas</s> (Buddhist shrines) and the like. And no other scripture is seen that sustains worldly order, is accepted by the great community, and is remembered as composed by the Lord. And it has been said that the Lord cannot remain without teaching. Therefore, by the method of residual elimination, the <s>Vedas</s> alone, sustaining the entire worldly order and teaching the means of attaining benefit and avoiding harm, are composed by the Lord — this we understand. For indeed, it is for this reason that they are diligently received and upheld to this day by the three upper classes (<s>traivarṇika</s>). And for the preservation of their meaning, the treatises of the auxiliary sciences (<s>aṅga</s>), subsidiary sciences (<s>upāṅga</s>), <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> have been composed through the lineage of great sages. But the words of <s>Buddha</s> and the like do not sustain worldly order. Nor is there absence of dissent regarding them among worldly people; and even those who dissent do not practice their meaning merely by saying 'this is conventional.' Therefore, because of their acceptance only by certain barbarians (<s>mleccha</s>) and the lowest of men who are like animals, the possibility of these [scriptures] being the utterance of a trustworthy person does not exist. Nor is the validity of these [Buddhist etc. scriptures] established through having the <s>Veda</s> as their root, like the statements of <s>Manu</s> and the like — this is appropriate. Because the inferential mark of having the <s>Veda</s> as root — namely, the commonality of students, teachers, and practitioners — which exists equally in <s>Smṛti</s> and the <s>Vedas</s>, is absent in the statements of <s>Buddha</s> and the like. And because of doubt about their omniscience, there is no certainty of [their scriptures] having experience as their root either. Since in the <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, whose validity is inferred from efficacy in practice, there is approval of Vedic rites such as pacificatory and prosperity-bringing rituals; and since at the commencement of procedures like rejuvenation therapies (<s>rasāyana</s>), the <s>Āyurveda</s> too, being composed by a trustworthy person, prescribes expiatory rites (<s>prāyaścitta</s>) such as the <s>cāndrāyaṇa</s> fast ordained by the <s>Veda</s> — thereby the validity of the <s>Vedas</s> is accepted [even by the <s>Āyurveda</s>]. Thus it is established that the <s>Vedas</s>, composed by a trustworthy person, are a <s>pramāṇa</s>. But the concordance in matters such as agriculture and the like is merely a surplus. Having intended this very [point], the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the formal argument: 'the argument for this — the Vedic statements are a <s>pramāṇa</s>.' He states another argument: 'because of having a single author.' The statements of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s> have an omniscient author, when there is acceptance by the great community, because of conveying suprasensory meanings — the positive concomitance. But those that do not have an omniscient originator are not of this kind, like the statements of the <s>Vātaputrīyas</s> — this is the negative concomitance. And just as the statements of <s>Buddha</s> and the like, though suprasensory, are not accepted by the great community — this has been stated immediately [after]. And regarding the statements of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, even though there is efficacy in practice, a non-omniscient person could not, even in a thousand human lifespans, first establish the positive and negative concomitances of those various herbs, their different combinations, and the different arrangements of their respective syllables. Nor is the objection 'this is not unprecedented' a refutation [of this], since that [independent discovery] is impossible at the beginning of creation. And the [cycles of] creation and great dissolution will be demonstrated through inference and scripture — thus everything is well-established. Therefore, when the authorship of an omniscient [being] is established, the validity of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s> is established by virtue of being the utterance of a trustworthy person, just as worldly statements like 'one who desires food should cook' — this is the meaning. If [the Vedas] are not eternal, how are they a <s>pramāṇa</s>? For if non-eternal, since human beings are capable of various deceptive compositions, the suspicion of error cannot be removed — therefore non-authoredness by any person (<s>apauruṣeyatva</s>) alone, by removing the defects dependent on persons, establishes the validity of the <s>Vedas</s> — this is the import. The answer — 'because of being a means of conveying [truth]': even what is non-eternal is a means of ascertainment by virtue of being the utterance of a trustworthy person — this is the meaning. 'Some, however' — (272/5) that which performs the efficacious action (<s>arthakriyā</s>) that constitutes valid cognition is a <s>pramāṇa</s>; and what is eternal has no efficacious action — therefore it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning. He refutes — 'but we do not consider that correct.' And how the efficacious action is possible even for what is eternal — that we shall state in the third [book] — this is the import. 'And the self (<s>ātman</s>)' — with the intention of merely being a cause of valid cognition, not with the intention of instrumentality. 'Of the word <s>pramāṇa</s>' — here too, it should be understood that the intention is merely of being a cause of valid cognition, not of instrumentality. 'By the establishment of the other entity' — meaning: by the establishment of the very corporality (<s>mūrtatva</s>) and the like belonging to the atom — this is the meaning. Having thus refuted the partial view, he states his own view — 'therefore.' 'And that, because <s>saṃsāra</s> is beginningless' — (273/17) although the letters, words, and sentences are different at each utterance, nevertheless for the letter <s>ga</s> and the like, delimited by the universal <s>gatva</s> (g-hood) and the like, and for the sentences that are their aggregates, the convention can be grasped through the individuals such as <s>Śābaleya</s> and the like, which are delimited by the universal <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) and the like — this is the import. 'At [the change of] a <s>manvantara</s>' —

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> introductory to the next <s>sūtra</s> [begins with] 'what then is the denial' —
having restated that, he explains.
'What then' —
The answer is 'no' —
He asks:
'For what reason?'
The answer is 'not without a means of proof' —
He asks again: 'whence then?'
(271/1) The answer: 'from a <s>pramāṇa</s>.'
He asks: 'what is that <s>pramāṇa</s>?'
Regarding that, first, concerning the hypothetical ground for Vedic validity, he states the <s>pramāṇa</s>:
'Having meaningful differentiation' —
Thus, in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Miśra Vācaspati</s>,
the first section (<s>āhnika</s>) of the second chapter [is concluded].

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.1: There is no fourfold [classification of <s>pramāṇas</s>], because <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>saṃbhava</s> (inclusion), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) are [themselves] <s>pramāṇas</s>.

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says:] "not according to the real meaning."
The classificatory enumeration of <s>pramāṇas</s> — that is not according to the real meaning.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this — "direct perception" etc.
(274/3) Having thus explained the <s>sūtra</s> as the objection of one who is confused, according to the <s>Bhāṣya</s> view, he also explains it in another way.
Or the context is for the purpose of removing doubt.
But the <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of [expressing] doubt.
And the number four cannot be ascertained. Why?
Because of the validity of <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>saṃbhava</s> (subsumption), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) [as <s>pramāṇas</s>].
Due to the doubt that arises for us from what is accepted by others — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>.
He states another purport.
"Injunction" etc.
The classificatory enumeration is aimed at the negation of additional [<s>pramāṇas</s>] — this was previously explained as the prima facie view that the <s>pramāṇa</s>-enumeration is not according to the real meaning. But now, that very beginning [of the <s>sūtra</s>] is aimed at the injunction of direct perception and the rest: "direct perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the <s>pramāṇas</s>."
And the negation of additional ones is obtained from the meaning — stating this intention avoids repetition.
He states another purport — "of those having faults" etc.
He states yet another purport — "in direct perception and the rest" etc.
The meaning is: from the context that is aimed at subsuming [other <s>pramāṇas</s>], the truth of the classificatory enumeration is established by implication.
He teaches.
"Because of being established" etc.
For not everything that is indicated by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> must necessarily be demonstrated by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> and others, since their demonstration of it is [already] accomplished — this is the purport.
He resolves — "not because the purpose of determination — the negation of additional <s>pramāṇas</s>" etc.
What is obtainable from mere indication, even without being stated, is not stated by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>; but what, though indicated, remains as if concealed — that must be brought to light by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>.
For there is no certainty there — "the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> and others say only what we hold and nothing else" — this is the purport.
The question: what is obtained here from the meaning?
The answer: "when [something] exists, [something else] comes into being" etc.
(275/1) "From the grasping of the opposite" etc.
From the grasping of what has been taken as the opposite of the falling of water — from that, the grasping of the conjunction of wind and cloud, which contradicts the falling — this is reportedly the <s>pramāṇa</s> called <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence), by which it is known that even when clouds arise, the conjunction of wind and cloud [explains] the non-falling of water.
He states the established doctrine — "these very" etc.
But the object will be beyond the scope of the <s>pramāṇas</s> having the stated definitions, and <s>aitihya</s> and the rest, being additional <s>pramāṇas</s>, will operate there — to this he says.
"Because of the absence of an object" etc.
He objects — "but because of the difference in purpose" etc.
He refutes this by showing an unwanted consequence.
"Then there would be eight" etc.
There are no such general and specific purposes by which purposeful <s>pramāṇas</s> could be differentiated from one another; rather, one must say they differentiate merely by difference. And thus, by unwanted consequence, the number eight would not be excluded — this is the meaning.
"But if the commonality of the object" etc.
The commonality of the object, such as form-ness — its non-exclusion from its own instances

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.2: Verbal testimony [subsumes] <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), because [tradition] is not something different in meaning; and <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>saṃbhava</s> (subsumption), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) are not denied because they are not different in meaning from inference.

children.translated_text: The word "other" (<s>antara</s>) means specific/particular.

children.text: tena bhojanakriyāyā yadantaraṃ viśeṣaḥ kriyāntararahitatvaṃ bhuṅkta evaṃ tasya pratiṣedha ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, what is the specific difference of the action of eating — being devoid of another action — "he eats alone" — the negation of that — this is the meaning.
"<s>Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>" (inference from general observation) etc.
Where there is no cause-effect relation between what is to be known and the means of knowing — that is <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>. //2//

"If these" etc.
If <s>aitihya</s> and the rest are <s>pramāṇas</s>, then it must be stated: in which — direct perception etc. — does <s>aitihya</s> etc. get subsumed?
"Of a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>" — a non-<s>pramāṇa</s> is not subsumed within a <s>pramāṇa</s> — hence it was said "<s>pramāṇas</s>."
Now, the succession of discourse whose speaker is unspecified is <s>aitihya</s> (tradition); if its author is a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) who has not been ascertained, then it simply does not become a <s>pramāṇa</s> — this was stated in one way.
But if through the succession of syllables it is understood — then it does not exceed the definition of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>), which is "the instruction of a trustworthy person" — this is what has been said.
"Because of having the same definition" etc.
He asks: "how is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) [subsumed]?" etc.
(276/1) When there are no clouds, rain does not occur; when there are [clouds], it occurs — this is <s>arthāpatti</s>: how is it subsumed within inference?
The answer: "of both" etc.
Here he gives an example.
"Wherever" etc.
He shows that the example is deficient in what is to be proved.
"But one" etc.
If the negation of a specific time is ascertained as "he does not eat during the day," then the injunction of eating at another time — "he eats at night" — is understood. But the ascertainment of a specific time is not [what occurs]; rather, "he simply does not eat during the day."
Of the action of eating and the like, what is another action such as sitting etc. — by the negation of the negation of that, the eating at night is implied.
When the single [statement] "he does not eat during the day" is obtained, "he eats at night" would be [established]; and the negations of other actions, [being] obtained through negation, need not be stated as "he eats at night" — this is the meaning.
He refutes this.
"But this is not correct" etc.
For negations are preceded by a prior establishment [of the thing negated].
And here, neither for one who is eating nor for one who is not eating is the absence of another action established, such that it could be negated by "he simply does not eat."
For no one who is eating is [simply] not looking.
Because even the activity of existing and the like is present.
One who is engaged [in something] may sometimes not perform another activity, let alone one who is not engaged — for he, being unattached, does perform other activities — this is the meaning.
He concludes — "therefore" etc.
The time-negation — the negation of "he does eat during the day" — this is the meaning.
Since the negation of other-action-negation is impossible, having been refuted, [and] since [it is] unobtained, there is no negation — this is the purport.
"Negation of another action" etc.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.3: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because of being inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).

children.translated_text:
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says:] "True, these" etc.
Its meaning:
True, these <s>aitihya</s> and the rest are <s>pramāṇas</s>, but they are not additional <s>pramāṇas</s> — they are simply not additional <s>pramāṇas</s> distinct from inference and the rest — this has been said.
But we do not deny that they are <s>pramāṇas</s> at all — this is the purport.
The <s>Vārttika</s>: "of <s>arthāpatti</s> alone" etc.
(277/2) Because the <s>arthāpatti</s> such as "he does not eat during the day" etc. is conclusive (<s>aikāntika</s>). //3//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.4: Because of the presumption of <s>arthāpatti</s> even where there is no [genuine] <s>arthāpatti</s>.
Having refuted [the opponent] according to his own view, he states the refutation from the <s>sūtra</s>.
"Whatever you too" etc.

children.text: na satsu megheṣu vṛṣṭirbhavatyevetyartho yena vyabhicāro deśyetāpi tu asatsu na bhavatīti /
children.translated_text: The meaning is not that when there are clouds, rain invariably occurs — which would show deviation — but rather that when there are no [clouds], it does not occur.
And thus there is no deviation — this is the meaning. //4//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.5: And the denial [itself] would be invalid, because of being inconclusive.

children.text:
yadi tu yatra viṣayer 'thāpattiraikāntikī tato viṣayāntaraṃ kalpayitvā 'naikāntikaṃ deśyeta tato yaḥ pratiṣedhaviṣayaḥ prāmāṇyamarthāpatteḥ
tato viṣayāntaramarthāpatteḥ sattvaṃ pratiṣedhaviṣayaṃ kalpayitvā pratiṣedhasyāprāmāṇyaṃ śaknumo vaktuṃ tathā ca pratiṣedhāprāmāṇyānnārthāpatteraprāmāṇyamityāha /
prati--t ( sū. 5 ) // evaṃ hyekāntikaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ syād yadyarthāpatteḥ prāmāṇyaṃ sattāṃ ca pratiṣedhati /
na tu sattvaṃ pratiṣeddhumarhatyanaikāntikatvāt /
na hi yadanaikāntikaṃ tat sarvaṃ nāsti prameyatvādīnāṃ nityatvasādhane anaikāntikānāṃ satvāt /
yasmādarthāṣatterviśeṣa iti /
( 278 / 1 ) arthāṣatterviśeṣaḥ prāmāṇyaṃ na hyarthāpattimātraṃ satteti // 5 //
children.translated_text:
If <s>arthāpatti</s> is conclusive in some domain, then by postulating another domain and showing it to be inconclusive [there], then regarding the domain where the denial [of <s>arthāpatti</s>'s] validity [is made], by postulating the existence of <s>arthāpatti</s> in another domain as the object of denial, we can say that the denial itself is invalid. And thus, from the invalidity of the denial, <s>arthāpatti</s> is not invalid — he says.
Denial... (sū. 5) // For the denial would be conclusive only if it denies both the validity and the existence of <s>arthāpatti</s>.
But it cannot deny its existence, because of being inconclusive.
For not everything that is inconclusive is non-existent, since <s>prameyatva</s> (being an object of knowledge) and the like, though inconclusive [as reasons] for proving eternality, exist.
"Because of the specific [nature] of <s>arthāpatti</s>" etc.
(278/1) The specific nature of <s>arthāpatti</s> is its validity — <s>arthāpatti</s> is not merely existent [but specifically valid]. //5//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.6: Or if the denial [itself] is valid, then the invalidity of <s>arthāpatti</s> does not follow.

children.text:
na cānaikāntikatvaṃ pramāṇatvapratiṣedhe 'stīti yadi manyate pūrvapakṣī, evaṃ tarhi---
tatprāmā--ṇyam ( sū. 6 ) // vipratipattirapratipattirvā nigrahasthānamiti vadata ityarthaḥ /
yā 'pi mīmāṃsābhāṣyakṛtār 'thāpattirudāhṛtā jīvataścaitrasya gehābhāvadarśanena bahirbhāvasyādṛṣṭasya kalpaneti /
tadapyanumānameva yadā khalu sannekatra nāsti tadā 'nyatrāsti yadā vā 'vyāpaka ekatrāsti tadā 'nyatra nāsti so 'yaṃ svaśarīra eva vyāptigrahaḥ sukaraḥ /
tathā ca sato gehābhāvadarśanena liṅgena bahirbhāvadarśanamanumānam /
na ca tasya satvena gehābhāvaḥ śakyo 'pahnotuṃ yenāsiddho gehābhāvona vā sattvamapanhūyeta yena sattvamevānapapadyamānaṃ na svātmānaṃ bahiravasthāpayet /
tathā hi sattvamātraṃ vā virudhyate caitrasya gehābhāvena mehasattvaṃ vā caitrasya /
na tāvadyatra kva cana sattvasyāsti virodho gehe asattayā samānaviṣayatvābhāvāt /
deśasāmānyena gṛhaviśeṣākṣepo 'pi pākṣika
iti samānaviṣayatayā virodha iti cet /
na pramāṇaviniścitasya sāṃśayikena pratikṣepāyogāt /
nāpi pramāṇaviniścito 'bhāva eva pākṣikaṃ tasya gṛhasatvaṃ pratikṣipansatvamapi pratikṣeptuṃ sāṃśayikatvaṃ vā 'panetumarhatīti yuktam /
gṛhāvacchinnābhāvena gṛhasattvaṃ viruddhatvātpratiṣidhyate na tu sattvamātraṃ tatra tasyaudāsīnyāt /
tasmādgṛhābhāvena siddhena sato bahirbhāvo 'numīyata iti yuktam /
etena viruddhayoḥ pramāṇayoravirodhāpādanaṃ viṣayavyavasthayā arthāpattiviṣayaḥ parāstaḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, the reconciliation of two non-contradictory <s>pramāṇas</s> through the assignment of domains — the subject-matter of <s>arthāpatti</s> — has been set aside.
Because what is delimited and what is undelimited are not in contradiction.
Therefore
<s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> separate from the <s>pramāṇa</s> of inference — this is established. //6//

If the prima facie view holds that there is no inconclusiveness in the denial of <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood, then —
If the denial is valid (sū. 6) // The meaning is: [then the opponent] is told that erroneous understanding or failure to understand constitutes a point of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>).
As for the <s>arthāpatti</s> cited by the author of the <s>Mīmāṃsābhāṣya</s> — the postulation of the unseen going-out, from seeing the absence of <s>Caitra</s>, who is alive, from his house — that too is just inference. When something that exists is not in one place, it is in another; or when what is non-pervasive is in one place, it is not in another — this pervasion-grasping within one's own body is easy.
And thus, from the mark of seeing the absence from the house of one who is [alive], the inference of going-out is [just] inference.
And his existence cannot be denied by [pointing to] his absence from the house, lest his absence from the house be unestablished; nor can his existence be denied, lest his existence, being itself untenable, would not establish his going-out by itself.
For thus: either mere existence is contradicted by <s>Caitra</s>'s absence from the house, or <s>Caitra</s>'s house-existence [is contradicted].
Mere existence is not anywhere contradicted by absence from the house, because they do not share the same domain.
If one objects that by the general [notion of] place, the specific house is implied — and thus by sharing the same domain there is contradiction —
no, because what is ascertained by <s>pramāṇa</s> cannot be overturned by what is doubtful.
Nor does the absence [from the house], which is itself ascertained by <s>pramāṇa</s>, in overturning his house-existence, also have the power to overturn his existence or to remove the doubtfulness [of his being outside] — this is proper.
The absence delimited by the house contradicts house-existence because of mutual opposition, but not mere existence, since [the absence] is indifferent toward that.
Therefore, it is proper that the going-out of the one who exists is inferred from the established absence from the house.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.7: <s>Abhāva</s> (non-existence) is not a valid <s>pramāṇa</s>, because the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is not established.

children.text:
nābhā--ddheḥ
( sū. 6 ) // nābhāvajñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ, kasmāt prameyasyābhāvasyāsiddheḥ /

children.translated_text: Indeed, nothing that is devoid of all attributes is experienced as an object of <s>pramāṇa</s>-cognition.
The usage of non-existence by ordinary people is merely conventional — this is the prima facie view. //7//
<s>Abhāva</s>... not established (sū. 6) // The cognition of <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Why? Because the <s>prameya</s> — i.e., <s>abhāva</s> — is not established.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.8: Since the unmarked is marked among the marked, the establishment of those [unmarked ones] as objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) [is achieved].

children.text:
siddhāntamāha /

yathoktaṃ dūṣayati /
kaścaivamāheti /
abhāvo hi prameyamucyate na tatsvarūpeṇa pramāṇamapi tu tadviṣayā pratipattiḥ /
sā ca pratyakṣaphalamupādānānadibuddhau pramāṇaṃ yathā 'gre tathā vakṣyate /
varṣābhāvapratyayastu vāyvabhrasaṃyoge 'numānamuktam /
pratipadya cānayatīti /
( 279 / 4 ) lakṣaṇābhāvena viśeṣaṇenāvacchinnānyānetavyatvena pratipadyānayati /
etaduktaṃ bhavati lakṣaṇābhāvajñānaṃ viśiṣṭe vāsasi pratyayaṃ janayatsādhakatamatvātpramāṇaṃ bhavati // 8 //
children.translated_text: What is said amounts to this: the cognition of the absence of the distinguishing mark, generating a cognition of the specific cloth, is a <s>pramāṇa</s> because of being the most effective instrument. //8//

He states the established view. 'Because of the greater [strength] of absence' — the cognition and conventional usage of absence, being universal, cannot be merely imagined. Nor can even imagination take as its object something devoid of all designation — this was said in the context of establishing erroneous cognition (<s>viparītakhyāti</s>). And in the context of refuting momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>), it will be demonstrated that [absence] is an object of designation. Therefore, because of its being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, its subsumption within [another] <s>pramāṇa</s> is appropriate. This entire [argument] the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains. 'Absence is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>' — he refutes what was stated. 'Who says this?' — for indeed absence is said to be a <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), not a <s>pramāṇa</s> in its own nature; rather, the cognition directed toward it [is the <s>pramāṇa</s>]. And that [cognition], when it is the result of direct perception in the beginningless cognition of the material cause, is a <s>pramāṇa</s> — as will be stated later. But the cognition of the absence of rain is inference, through the conjunction of wind and clouds — this has been stated. 'And having cognized, it brings' — (279/4) by the qualifier 'absence of the distinguishing mark,' [it] brings [the cloth] as that which is to be brought, having cognized it as delimited [by that qualifier].

children.text: NyS_2,2.9: asatyarthe nābhāva iti cen nānyalakṣaṇopapatteḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.9: If [it be said that] there is no absence when the object is unreal, [we reply:] no, because of the tenability of another definition.
Unreal... tenability (sūtra 9) //

children.text:
bhāvādhīnanirūpaṇatvātprāptipūrvakatvācca pradhvaṃsa evābhāvaḥ /
tasya bhāvapūrvakatvāt /
nānyo 'stya bhāva iti manvānasya pūrvapakṣaḥ /
nāparijñānāditi /
pratyakṣaṃ hi pramāṇaṃ prameyābhāvaṃ vyavasthāpayati /
tacca pradhvaṃsavatprāgabhave 'pi tulyam /
pratiyanti hi laukikā dadhni kṣīrābhāvamiva kṣīre dadhyabhāvam /
nanu sūtramanyeṣu vāsassu lakṣaṇābhāvarūpāṇāmupapattiṃ sadbhāvamāha /

ata uktārthaṃ sūtramiti /

children.translated_text: The meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> has been stated by way of the negative [concomitance] (<s>vyatireka</s>).
For this very reason the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says:
'Not so in those that are not marked' —
For by the non-seeing of the distinguishing mark, the seeing of the absence of the distinguishing mark is indicated. //9//

The prima facie view of one who thinks: since the ascertainment [of absence] depends on a [prior] positive entity, and since [absence] presupposes [prior] occurrence, only destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>) is absence — because it is preceded by a positive entity — and no other absence exists. 'Not because of non-recognition' — for direct perception as a <s>pramāṇa</s> establishes the absence of the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge). And that [direct perception] is equal for prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) as for destruction. For ordinary people cognize the absence of curd in milk just as [they cognize] the absence of milk in curd. Now, the <s>sūtra</s> states the tenability — the existence — of [the absence of] distinguishing marks in other cloths. But you are not speaking of the cognition of absence — so how is there no contradiction? — to this he says: 'therefore the <s>sūtra</s> has the stated meaning.'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.10: Because of the establishment of those [marks], [the argument] is not a valid reason regarding unmarked [cloths].

children.text:
yāni tāni lakṣiteṣviti /
na kasya cillakṣitasya na santi yāni ca santi teṣāmabhāvo vyāhataḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati yatra lakṣaṇāni santi tatra teṣāmabhāvo vyāhataḥ
yatra ca na santi tatrāpyabhāvo 'nupapannaḥ /

children.translated_text: because absence, whose ascertainment depends on a positive entity, cannot be ascertained in the absence of that [positive entity].
He refutes: 'not because of non-recognition.'

children.text: bhāvajñānādhīnanirūpaṇo bhavatyabhāvo na tu bhāvādhīnanirūpaṇaḥ prāgabhāvo 'pi ca śakyo bhaviṣyadbhāvajñānenānyatrāvasthitabhāvajñānena vā nirūpayitumiti na prāgabhāvābhāva
children.translated_text: Absence has its ascertainment dependent on the cognition of the positive entity, but not dependent on the [actual] positive entity. And even prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) can be ascertained through the cognition of the positive entity that will come into being, or through the cognition of the positive entity existing elsewhere — therefore there is no [denial of] prior absence.
— this is the meaning. //10//

'Those that are marked' — it is not the case that certain marked [cloths] do not have [marks]; and those that do have [marks] — their absence is contradictory. What is said amounts to this: where the distinguishing marks exist, the absence of those [marks] is contradictory; and where they do not exist, absence is also untenable —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.11: Not [so], because of the non-establishment of the expectation of the persistence of the distinguishing mark.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.12: And because of the tenability of absence prior to origination.

children.text:
abhāvadvaitamiti /
prakṛtāpekṣaṃ prakṛtaṃ pradhvaṃsamātravādinaṃ prati prāgabhāvapratipādanaṃ paramārthatastu prathamamabhāvedvaitaṃ tādātmyābhāvaḥ saṃsargābhāvaśceti saṃsargābhāvo 'pi prākpradhvaṃsātyantābhāvabhedena trividha
iti catasro vidhā abhāvasyeti /
asatyarthenābhāvaḥ /
tatsiddheralakṣiteṣvaheturiti cobhe apyete chalasūtre iti /
( 280 / 3 ) yo yo 'bhāvaḥ sa sarvaḥ satyarthe bhavati yathā pradhvaṃsaḥ na ca tathā lakṣaṇābhāva
iti sāmānyacchalam // 10 // tatsiddheriti tu vākchalaṃ yāni lakṣaṇāni bhavanti kathaṃ tānyeva na bhavantīti hi tasyārthaḥ // 11-12 //
children.translated_text: 'The duality of absence' — with reference to the topic at hand, the demonstration of prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) is directed toward the one who maintains only destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>) as absence. But in ultimate reality, first, absence is twofold: absence of identity (<s>tādātmyābhāva</s>) and relational absence (<s>saṃsargābhāva</s>). And relational absence too is threefold — as prior absence (<s>prāk</s>), destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>), and absolute absence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>) — thus there are four kinds of absence. 'Absence [is only] of an unreal object' [and] 'because of the establishment of those, it is not a valid reason regarding the unmarked' — both of these are quibbling <s>sūtras</s> (<s>chalasūtra</s>). (280/3) Every absence whatsoever occurs with respect to a real object, like destruction; but the absence of a distinguishing mark is not like that — this is generality-quibbling (<s>sāmānyacchala</s>). //10// 'Because of the establishment of those' is verbal quibbling (<s>vākchala</s>) — 'how can those very marks that exist not exist?' — this is its meaning. //11-12//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.13: Because of having a beginning, because of being sensory, and because of figurative usage as with what is produced.

children.translated_text: — this.
The self-attainment of the effect — the state of being connected with its own cause — its cause is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>).

children.text: samavāyo hi samavetatvaṃ bhavati samavāyaḥ kāraṇaviśiṣṭakāryatvamiti /
children.translated_text: For inherence is the state of being inherent; inherence is the state of being an effect qualified by [its] cause.

The conformity to the differences in efficient causes, the property of having origination [as a characteristic], is [stated] with the intention of non-difference between what is to be known and the means of knowing. //13//

Having thus commenced the examination of <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and examined its validity, and having examined the classification-enumeration, he now continues with the remainder of the examination of <s>śabda</s> — 'verbal testimony is the teaching of a trustworthy person.' Showing the disagreement that is the cause of doubt, he states the view of the ancient <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>: '<s>śabda</s> (sound) is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> (space).' For by the wind impelled by a blow, rushing as far as its momentum [carries it], the eternal sound, inherent in the portion of space delimited by the cavity of the ear, is manifested — this [is their view]. This the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains: 'some, first...' Even though its substrate does not perish, it is non-eternal like conjunction and the like — therefore he says: 'inhering in a single substance.' Even so, [the argument] is inconclusive because of form and the like belonging to earthen atoms — therefore he says: 'and a quality of <s>ākāśa</s>.' When it is a quality of a single substance and is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> — by just this much the intended [conclusion] is established; the non-perishing of the substrate is an elaboration of that and should be so understood. 'From conjunction, disjunction, and sound' — the wind impelled by the conjunction of the drum and the stick, reaching the space terminating in the ear-cavity, is the manifester of sound; similarly, the wind impelled by the disjunction of a bamboo leaf is the manifester of sound — this should be understood. Conjunction and disjunction [are causes] indirectly; but sound [itself is a cause] directly. He states the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view: 'co-occurring with smell and the like.' Sound is a modification of earth and the like — [entities] that are themselves modifications of the aggregate of subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>) produced from the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) — and occurs in cows, pots, and the like; the sense-organ of hearing, which pervades the relevant region due to being derived from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), apprehends [sound] even while it remains in place. This he states: 'others, however...' 'From the striking of specific elements' — meaning: from the striking of a drum and stick. He states the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view: 'a quality of <s>ākāśa</s>.' He states the Buddhist established doctrine: 'born from the disturbance of the great elements.' (281/2) 'Not because of the absence of connection' — when a positive entity exists, because of the absence of prior-absence and destruction-absence, it is not non-eternal. And because of the unwanted consequence [of non-eternality applying] to what has not arisen and what has been destroyed. First, prior absence and destruction do not coexist [with the entity]; therefore, [considering] each separately, non-eternality [would apply] — and thus in an entity that has not arisen or in one that has been destroyed, there would be the unwanted consequence of non-eternality. And this is neither observed nor accepted, because non-eternality is understood as a property of a positive entity: 'the pot is non-eternal.' Not only is non-eternality not a property of a positive entity [alone], but in the opponent's view the genitive relation too does not hold. Why can absence not be a property of a positive entity? — to this he says: 'nor at the time of the property.' The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is in the sense of a reason. He raises a doubt: 'but if...' For it is precisely the existing [entity] that, because it did not exist before and will not exist afterward, has absence; thus the genitive is tenable — this is the meaning. The answer: 'even so' — true, the existing [entity itself] does not exist [at those times], but the connection of the entity with its absence does not [obtain] thereby, because they belong to different times. Therefore nothing that we have said is refuted — this is the meaning. He brings out the contradiction with common experience: 'prior absence of the pot.' When there is no [real] connection, this genitive usage is figurative; and the figurative basis is the dependence of [absence's] ascertainment on the positive entity — this is the meaning. Moreover, a presently existing thing is said to be eternal; its being (<s>bhāva</s>) is eternality. Let that be so — what follows even from that? — to this he says: 'and in the present.' (282/1) Since its destruction will necessarily come about, the use of the possessive suffix (<s>matup</s>) is by figuratively attributing the connection with the destruction that will necessarily come — this is the meaning. 'Of that which has the conditions for being perceived' — (283/7) for a real entity does not have destruction, by which a non-connection of the entity could be indicated; rather, just as the manifestation (<s>āvirbhāva</s>) of what exists is birth, so too the absolute concealment (<s>atyantatirobhāva</s>) of what exists is destruction — and this is called non-eternality; and the connection of concealment with the entity, through their being simultaneous, is tenable — this is the import. And since concealment is possible even for pots and the like, it has been said 'of that which has the conditions for being perceived.' He then refutes this <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view: 'this, however, is an empty statement.' Since the world is a transformation of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter), and since the transformation is non-different from its material cause, through the perception of some <s>Prādhānika</s> [entity], there is no entity whatsoever that is absolutely imperceptible — this is the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine, and it contradicts [the proposed account] — this is the meaning. Moreover, just as there is no destruction of what exists, so too there is no birth of what does not exist; and thus the concealment of an entity whose specific [qualities] have not arisen is not tenable; and how can there be origination of what exists through the arising of specific [qualities], since those specific [qualities] either did not exist before — or if they did exist, there would be the unwanted consequence of their being perceived even before [manifestation]. 'Those, however, who...' — [the view that] non-eternal itself is non-eternality, with the reflexive suffix (<s>svārthika</s>) having a self-referential meaning — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'but this is not proper — for even the <s>smṛti</s> (grammatical teaching) of <s>Pāṇini</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s> when not in conflict with [other] <s>pramāṇas</s>, [and] is the ground for establishing reality, but not when it conflicts [with them]; and there is indeed a conflict with <s>pramāṇa</s> in [treating] <s>ṭhag</s> and the like as self-referential. For there would be no co-occurrence of the base and the suffix — for indeed, co-occurrence of synonymous [terms] is not observed; one does not say "tree wood" (<s>vṛkṣas taruḥ</s>) as one says "a tree, a <s>śiṃśapā</s>." But then, what about "one, two, many" (<s>eko dvau bahavaḥ</s>)? No — because the use of inflectional endings is for the purpose of [expressing] specific gender and individuality. Similarly, in the case of <s>yāvaka</s> (barley gruel) and the like, the meaning of the suffix should be understood as the exclusion of a different, conflicting class. As they explain: "the words that are <s>yāva</s> are indeed <s>yāvaka</s>." This has been stated: 'even for those whose difference is not perceived, there is difference from inference.' What is the inference? It is that the genitive has difference as its object — [this] leads to [the suffix] <s>tvatal</s>, since eternality and non-eternality are under discussion. 'Its being is <s>tvatal</s>' — since <s>tvatal</s> originates from the genitive with the meaning of difference, the inference stated is applicable to all [cases]. 'Whether or not [it] requires a limit-point' — (284/3) existence bounded at both ends — requiring a limit-point — is non-eternality; that very [existence] not requiring [a limit-point] is eternality. And the limit-point is an indicator, not a qualifier; and even that which is at a different time can [serve as indicator] — just as when the mother <s>Devadattā</s> has died, <s>Yajñadatta</s> is [called] the son of <s>Devadattā</s>; <s>Devadattā</s>, having gone to a past state, indicates her own son. And when causality [is the criterion], inherence — then existence bounded at both ends is eternality. But when existence bounded only at the prior end is origination, then existence bounded at the posterior end is non-eternality — thus there is no contradiction with the explanation given here. Inherence is the cause of the effect's self-attainment

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.14: Not [established] because of the generality of absence [like] the absence of a pot, because of non-eternality, and because of figurative usage even in eternal [entities] as with non-eternal ones.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.15: Because of the differentiation of diversity between what is literal and what is figurative, there is no deviation.
