children.translated_text: Having thus stated his own position, he presents the opponent's position —
"Some, however" —
The remainder is: "when the speaker is imperceptible."

children.text: yadyapi jātyandhānāmapi kathaṃ cidabhimukhapṛṣṭhapārśvataḥ śabdavivekaḥ saṃbhavati tathāpi pūrvāparadigvibhāgo nāstītyata uktaṃ jātyandhānāmiti // 13-14 //
children.translated_text: Although even for those born blind there is some discrimination of sound from the front, back, and sides, nevertheless there is no distinction of the eastern and western directions — therefore it is said "for those born blind." //13-14//

The efficient causes (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) are the conjunction of the drum-stick and the like.
From the difference of those [causes], sound is indeed different.
He raises the doubt: 'conjunction and disjunction' —
(285/2) For just as difference is observed from difference of cause, so too difference of a face reflected in gems, swords, mirrors, and the like is observed from difference of the manifestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>) — therefore there is doubt.
'The ear, first of all, does not go to the location of sound, because of being incorporeal' —
For the ether delimited by the ear-cavity is the organ of hearing; and the ear-cavity, though corporeal, does not approach the mouth of the speaker — for the ear-cavity is directly perceived as situated in the organ of hearing. Therefore, even if something goes, since the ether alone — apart from the ear-cavity — is not the organ of hearing due to the absence of the ear-cavity's support, this should be seen as stated against one who thinks that the ether aided by the ear-cavity goes [to the sound].
'Because of inherence in the quality that is the cause of action' —
The meaning is: because of inherence in impulse (<s>nodana</s>) and strike (<s>abhighāta</s>).
'This is not meant without qualification' — even though the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) — gravity — requires [something else] when falling is to be accomplished, still it does not require any final efficient cause — this is the meaning of 'without qualification.'
Even though the removal of an obstruction is the last efficient [cause], still it is not [truly] an efficient cause — for when there is an obstruction, gravity does not produce its natural effect; but it is not reasonable to postulate the obstruction-removal as having the status of an efficient cause, since its co-presence and co-absence [with the effect] are otherwise established — or, [gravity] does not require any final efficient cause of a positive nature — this is the meaning of 'without qualification.'
'Because of the absence of a substrate' —
(286/3) The fitness for the production of action is the substrate of action; relying on that, action exists — that is corporeality (<s>mūrti</s>). And that does not exist in all-pervading substances whose magnitude is of the nature of ether and the like, which are all-pervading — therefore these are not possessed of action — this is the meaning.
'Therefore, because of the extreme sluggishness of the last [sound]' —
The last [sound] does not originate another sound; not only does it not destroy its own cause — the [prior] sound — but it too is destroyed by the sound that is its own cause. This is the mutual opposition of cause and effect between them.
The first [sound], however, is destroyed by the effect alone; for the intermediate [sounds], there is no fixed rule.
He raises the view of the ancient <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>: 'if indeed, indeed' —
Their sound is one alone, a quality of ether; ether is extended and abiding, like magnitude — this is the meaning.
Taking up the position of sound-impression (<s>śabdasaṃskāra</s>), he states the refutation:
'Because of the unwanted consequence of apprehension by all' —
The meaning of the question 'is it not?' (287/2) —
'Because sound exists in ether' —
Since ether is all-pervading, [sound] manifested therein would be manifested everywhere — so there would be apprehension everywhere, things being the same — this is the meaning.
Having accepted one part [of the argument], he says:
'And in the manifestation at one location, there would be no apprehension of meaning;
because the effect produced by phonemes cannot be accomplished by one location alone;
just as in a word of multiple phonemes, when only one phoneme is manifested, there is no apprehension of meaning.'
One might think: the phoneme exists at just one location, and thus the effect produced by phonemes can be accomplished by one location — therefore he says:
'All [phonemes] would be pervading' —
In this view, one-location-manifestation of a phoneme is accepted; therefore, from the pervading phoneme, the one-location is something different — this is the meaning.
'But let there be apprehension of meaning from just one location' — therefore he says:
'In this view, one-location-manifestation of a phoneme is accepted, but the one-location of a phoneme cannot be delimited.
For the mind does not grasp a phoneme uttered with too little effort, or if it does grasp it, it grasps the phoneme itself, never its one-location' — this is the meaning.
Accepting the delimitation, he says:
'And not from the delimited [one-location]' —
'Then let many phonemes be manifested, and from their delimitation let the meaning be understood' — therefore he says:
'By this' —
Now, one who thinks: there is no one-location in reality for sound; rather, the non-pervasive existence of the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) alone is the one-location — against him, he states a different fault: 'and there would be cacophony (<s>kolāhala</s>).'
If one says: some particular resonance (<s>dhvani</s>) manifests only a particular sound, and therefore there is no cacophony — to that he says:
'And there would be no restriction' —
(288/5) Since even among things at the same location and graspable by the same sense-organ, such as color, taste, and the like, there is restriction of manifestor and manifested — therefore it is said 'graspable by the same sense-organ.'
Even so, among things at different locations [yet] graspable by the same sense-organ, not all are manifested simultaneously — therefore it is said 'at the same location.'
He raises the doubt: 'if this has a manifestor' —
For the manifestor-status of manifestors is not known from anything other than manifestation, and that [manifestation] is fixed — therefore the fixedness of manifestors too is established — this is the meaning.
He resolves: 'that is not [valid], because of not being observed' —
For among other elements — manifestors and things manifested — non-restriction alone is observed; [that observation] undermines restriction here too.
But for effects — colors and the like, numbers and the like — even among those at the same location and graspable by the same sense-organ, restriction of causes is observed — therefore for sounds too, restriction of production through fixed causes is tenable — this is the import.
He doubts, [arguing from] the totality of objects being contiguous with universals — 'like the universal' — thinking: the totality of objects contiguous [with universals] is the entire totality.
Even when all objects are contiguous, some particular object is connected with some particular universal, not everything with every [universal] — with this intent he refutes:
'Because of non-acceptance' —
Although for being (<s>sattva</s>), humanity (<s>naratva</s>), and Brahmin-hood (<s>brāhmaṇatva</s>) — which are at the same location, graspable by the same sense-organ, and have form-difference, bodily constitution, and birth as their respective manifestors — there is fixed manifestor-manifested relationship, nevertheless, because of the absence of being-at-the-same-location, there is no deviation.
Because <s>sattva</s>, through its inherence in the three categories [substance, quality, action], exists at a greater number of locations; because <s>naratva</s>, like Brahmin-hood, exists in <s>Kṣatriyas</s> and the like;
because <s>brāhmaṇatva</s>, being absent from <s>Kṣatriyas</s> and the like, exists only in [those of the] <s>Kaṭha</s> [branch] and the like — being at fewer or more locations, there is no being-at-the-same-location.
By this, the same reasoning should be understood regarding the impression on the organ of hearing:
just as the sense-organ, prepared by opening [the eyes], shows at once all its own objects at the same location that are graspable by it — not just some particular [objects] — thus everything is clear.
Moreover, if all sound has tongue-palate-conjunction and the like as its manifestor, then upon their cessation, sound should be apprehended at a distance — but it is not apprehended.
But if the wind-continuum (<s>vāyusaṃtāna</s>) is the manifestor, then the previously stated fault of absence of restriction applies — he shows through the objection and reply:
'If indeed' —
Moreover, is this eternal sound localized or all-pervading? In either case there is a fault — he shows through the objection and reply:
'And in the proximity of the efficient cause' —
(289/10) One might think: let the wind-continuum not be the manifestor; there are indeed wind-qualities called resonances (<s>nāda</s>) — those are the manifestors of this sound — therefore he says:
'And in the apprehension of resonance' —
First of all, no quality of wind called resonance is apprehended.
Even accepting [it], we say:
Even when resonance is apprehended, wherever there is wind, its quality [resonance] must be accepted there; but when a distant person apprehends sound, there is no wind there nor any quality of wind called resonance. And the traversal of a wind-continuum is not accepted in this [eternalist] view — since by the distant person's apprehension of sound, [what is established is merely that] the manifestor is resonance.
One might think: let it not be the wind-continuum, nor its quality resonance, that is the manifestor of sound; but let the conjunctions and disjunctions of wind be the manifestors — therefore he says:
'By this' —
Now, one who thinks: recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) itself, that blessed [faculty], is the accomplisher of the proof of sound; and to accommodate it, the all-pervading sound — whether a quality or a substance — is postulated as having efforts-impelled winds, proceeding as far as their momentum carries, preparing the organ of hearing or the specific sound delimited by the organ of hearing, as manifestors.
And [he might say]: the observation that things at the same location, graspable by the same sense-organ, have fixed manifestors and manifested [entities] — recognition does not tolerate this objection; [the objection], having its domain refuted by recognition, dissolves.
To him he replies:
'Like what is produced — because of figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>).'
(290/1) And here, by 'figurative usage' — by conventional usage — he indicates the cause of that [perception], namely the cognition of difference in sound.
For among the sounds <s>ga</s> and the like produced by parrots, <s>śārikā</s> birds, and human mouths, people have quite clear cognitions of form-difference.
Similarly among those produced by females and males, and those produced by the difference between females and males.
And one should not say 'this is merely incidental (<s>aupādhika</s>), not [belonging to the sound] in its own nature.'
For that incidental character would be either experiential — as in 'the young woman is saffron-colored' —
or within the scope of rational explanation — as in the case of the face in a sword-blade or in water: the face does not have elongation and darkness [in itself], given a reflective cause.
Now, the experiential [case] requires knowledge of the condition: one for whom the condition — saffron — is known, for him it is [merely] conditional, as 'saffron-colored' for one who knows the saffron.
But even for one who does not know the difference [in source] among parrots and the like, when the parrot and the like are hidden behind a curtain or cloth, the cognition of sound-difference occurs — whence one infers: 'that is the most melodious song, uttered by a parrot.'
Nor is the incidental character within the scope of rational explanation —
for there is no evidence that the difference inherent in the very nature of sound is merely incidental, as [there is for] a face in a gem, mirror, or sword.
For in mirrors and the like, which have contradictory magnitudes, the production of reflections of contradictory magnitudes is not possible.
But for sounds, which arise from conjunctions and disjunctions, form-difference through the difference of those [causes] is reasonable.
One might think: the properties of intensity (<s>tīvratva</s>), softness (<s>mandatva</s>), and the like are what differ — not the sound which is their substrate. For the difference of one thing cannot require the difference of another — because of over-extension.
For the difference of colors, tastes, and the like — whether simultaneous or successive — or of conjunctions and the like, does not [entail] the difference of the substance.
'How can one and the same sound have the contact of contradictory properties like intensity and softness simultaneously?' — if this be asked:
For this very reason, let it be incidental — just as a face, though non-different, [appears to have] contradictory properties like elongation and roundness in swords and the like.
To this we say: we do not assert the difference of the property-bearer merely from the difference of properties. Rather, let it be examined whether only the appearance of property-difference spreads, or whether the difference of the property-bearer too spreads. For even when the appearance of 'cow, cow' follows [a universal], in white, brown, and pigeon-colored cows, there is an appearance that penetrates the difference of property-bearers.
And there is an appearance that penetrates only the difference of properties, reckoning the property-bearer as non-different — as in '<s>Śāla</s>-tree-tall, broad-chested, long-armed, dark as a blue lotus petal, lion-faced, with a voice deep and sweet as a fresh cloud, with <s>cakora</s>-like eyes — a <s>Kṣatriya</s> youth.'
Now this appearance — when parrots, <s>śārikā</s> birds, and humans simultaneously utter the sound <s>ga</s> — that penetrates the intense, soft, nasal, and other [varieties of] <s>ga</s>: does it rest upon one single <s>ga</s>-sound having multiple properties, like a single <s>Kṣatriya</s> youth? — one <s>ga</s>-sound with diverse properties — or, just as 'this is a white cow, this is a brown cow,' so 'this is an intense <s>ga</s>, this is a soft <s>ga</s>, this is a nasal one'? — let the learned decide for themselves.
And this recognition, resting upon <s>gatva</s> (g-hood) — like <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) among particular cow-individuals — among the particular different sounds of intense, soft, and the like, will be compatible with both recognition and the appearance of difference.
Moreover, from the simultaneous contact of contradictory properties characterized by intensity, softness, and the like, we infer the mutual difference of <s>ga</s>-sounds from one another, like the sun and the firefly.
And [the objection that] this contact of contradictory properties does not belong to <s>ga</s> and the like but is merely incidental, and [that] the conditions alone differ, not the <s>ga</s>-sound — this is not tenable,
because of the impossibility of postulating incidental character for what is perceived as inherent in the phoneme, in the absence of a defeating cognition (<s>bādhaka</s>).
And because recognition is explained as having the universal <s>gatva</s> as its object.
Moreover, in the position of incidental character, one must maintain that intensity, nasality, and the like — whether a property of the tongue-palate conjunction or a property of the resonance (<s>dhvani</s>) impelled by that contact — are superimposed upon the sound.
But superimposition is not possible for those who do not know [the thing being superimposed].
And the properties of resonances or of tongue-palate conjunctions and disjunctions cannot be grasped by the ear, like the properties of other things.
And these are not presented [to the subject] by another <s>pramāṇa</s>, nor are they remembered, such that they could be superimposed.
Nor does such a capacity-difference of the ear arise from the force of impressions of resonance-differences,
by which, even without grasping [the conditions], error could occur.
And it is not tenable [to compare this] to the case of people whose eyes are smeared with frog-fat, who superimpose snakes on bamboo reeds even though the [snake] has not been cognized or remembered at the first contact of the sense — 
because all errors invariably require as their prerequisite the grasping of both the superimposed and the substrate of superimposition through a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Following that, the snake-error on bamboo reeds for those whose eyes are smeared with frog-fat should be explained [accordingly]:
Bamboo reeds indeed have considerable resemblance with snakes; and by that resemblance alone, having been grasped [in that form], they are capable of producing the memory of a snake.
Even so, the reason that others do not have this error is the grasping of the bamboo reed's form as distinct from the snake-form; and the frog-fat ointment merely causes the concealment of the bamboo-form.
And it is not authoritative [to say] that error occurs from the very first contact of the sense, since the momentary distinction is difficult to know.
And it is possible to say that [the snake] has not been grasped — [but] the possibility of grasping a snake exists either in this life or in a previous life.
But the property of resonance — nasality and the like — is impossible to grasp either in this life or in a previous life.
Therefore, nasality and the like, being perceived as inherent in the phoneme, are indeed properties of the phoneme, not incidental; and thus, from the simultaneous contact of contradictory properties, the mutual otherness of <s>ga</s>-sounds and the like is reasonable.
With this intention it was said: 'like what is produced — because of figurative usage.'
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this:
'Intense, soft' — [these terms], being produced [differently], are figuratively applied —
He indicates the contradictory properties as pertaining to sound.
He states other reasons for the non-eternality of sound as well:
'By [the argument] "like what is produced, because of figurative usage"' and so on —
Since the refutation of <s>jāti</s> (universal) is accomplished by 'like the universal' alone, the specification [of <s>viśeṣa</s>] is for the purpose of refuting the confusion that 'similarity is a universal.'
For that [similarity] — such as being a <s>prameya</s> (knowable), being (<s>sattva</s>), and the like — exists in qualities and the like just as in universals.
But by the word <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), the reference to <s>jāti</s> is excluded.
'Of the apprehended' — this will become clear further on.
He raises the doubt: 'of the intense sound' —
The word 'intense' (<s>tīvra</s>), having its usage governed by the co-presence and co-absence of the property of intensity, is not competent to denote the sound as property-bearer — this is merely a restatement of the objection as stated — this is the meaning.
He refutes:
'Not, because of being co-referential (<s>samānādhikaraṇa</s>) with the word "sound"' —
And this will be established in the context of 'individuals, form, and universals are the objects of words.'
He raises the doubt: 'of the manifestor' —
From its own cause, namely the manifestor, the cognition of sound arises as intense or soft.
Therefore, the sound that is the object of intense cognition appears as if intense, and the sound that is the object of soft cognition appears as if soft — but one who does not know [the source] does not [truly] know its intensity or softness, by which [sounds] could be differentiated — this is the meaning.
He refutes: 'not, because of overpowering (<s>abhiśrava</s>)' —
One thing is overpowered by another of the same kind, but not that very thing by itself. For a cloth associated with the light of the midday sun does not overpower itself — its own illumination — by the keen solar light.
Similarly, the <s>ga</s>-sound would overpower itself — the <s>ga</s>-sound illuminated by an intense resonance — [which is absurd].
But if this <s>ga</s>-sound illuminated by a soft resonance is different from the <s>ga</s>-sound illuminated by an intense resonance,
then, just as the midday sunlight, being lesser [in some comparison], is overpowered by solar light — this is reasonable. This remainder is as stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>.
'Granted, one thing is overpowered by another; even so, there is no multiplicity of <s>ga</s>-sounds, but rather the overpowering-overpowered relationship belongs to their cognitions, not to the <s>ga</s>-sound' — with this intent he raises the doubt:
'Of the cognition' —
He refutes:
'Not, because of the difference of cognitions' —
The difference of cognitions, whose delimitation depends on the difference of objects, cannot be delimited without the difference of objects; and what is not delimited as different cannot be understood as having the overpowering-overpowered relationship — this is the meaning.
'The difference of cognitions would always exist' —
If the acceptance of difference of cognitions [is granted], then necessarily the difference of objects must be accepted.
And thus, everything would be different — nothing would be non-different.
Even difference would not exist, since difference depends on non-difference as its substrate — this is the meaning.
'And the impossibility of overpowering' —
(291/1) At the very moment when the prior cognition, [about to be] overpowered by the subsequent one, arises — at that very moment it is destroyed by it; and there is no overpowering of what does not exist — this is the meaning.
Even in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view, there is no overpowering — he says:
'Overpowering' —
The <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>, seeing the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> defeated, thinks 'this objection does not apply to us' and raises the doubt again:
'Everywhere' —
He refutes: 'no.'
The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> objects:
'If it exists as a continuum' —
He resolves:
'Because of the arrival of the sound-continuum's proximity to the difference of efficient causes.'
(291/8) The difference of efficient causes is the drum, conch, tongue-palate, and the like; and by their orientation, that portion of the ether delimited by the ear-cavity — the organ of hearing — in which the sound first arises, from its arrival [there], 'this sound is born from a conch situated in such-and-such a direction and location' — this is inferred.
What is said amounts to this: some particular property-difference of the sound that is produced by a sound-continuum originating from a conch and the like situated in a specific direction and location falls within the scope of the organ of hearing, from which its origination from a conch and the like situated in a specific direction and location is inferred. And that [property] is not a universal or a particular — [but it exists], because it cannot be denied due to being inexpressible.
For the sub-universal differences of sweetness among sugarcane, milk, and molasses — though perceptually experienced — cannot be denied merely because of their inexpressibility.
And the experience is the same [in both cases].
Therefore, the cognition of direction and location regarding sound is inferential.
'That which is the sound-continuum' —
That which extends is the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>); the first sound that arises is what extends — this is the connection. 'From that efficient cause, [it proceeds] toward [the hearer]' — this is the construal.
'The first sound' —
A sound having a portion [of ether] oriented toward that [cause] — this is [the meaning].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.16: Because of the qualification by the inference of continuity. //
"And this, in the absence" means: there is neither the connection with existence (<s>sattā</s>), nor the delimitation by both ends — this is the meaning. //15-16//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.17: Because the causal substance is denoted by the word "region" (<s>pradeśa</s>), there is no deviation even in the case of eternal [substances]. //

children.translated_text: Thus, the situation being such, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states his own answer to the question of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> —
"Because of being understood from the meaning" —
He states the different subject matter of the question and answer — "the continuity of sound" —

children.text: bhāṣyakārīyamuttaramāha dvau pakṣau na vyavasthāpayatīti bhāṣyasyārthaḥ niṣpradeśatvamātmādīnāṃ śabdasaṃtānaṃ ca sākṣādācakṣāṇaḥ sūtrakāraḥ pakṣaṃ vyavasthāpayenna tu tenedamabhihitamiti anumānatarośca pañcānāṃ rūpāṇāṃ catarṇāṃ vā saṃpadaḥ śākhā bahava ityarthaḥ // 17 //
children.translated_text: He states the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>'s answer: "the meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> is that he does not establish both theses" — the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, directly stating the partlessness of the self (<s>ātman</s>) and the like, and the continuity of sound, establishes the thesis; but that is not what is expressed by this [sūtra]. And the fullness of inference — [meaning] the fulfilment of four or five of its members — has many branches — this is the meaning. //17//

Objection: If pervasion by another does not exist, then how do you maintain that some things are pervasive and some are non-pervasive? To this he says:
"We, however, [maintain] pervasion of finger-form" —
Wherever the substratum is apprehended, there whatever object is fit to be apprehended and exists is apprehended — that is pervasive. Therefore, whiteness, though non-pervasive of a crane, is not apprehended even when the crane is apprehended in dim light, because of the absence of fitness [for apprehension].
Such pervasion of conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and the like cannot be established as a quality — because of contradiction with non-apprehension — thus he says:
"Not, however, sound and the like" —
The remainder is: "fit to be apprehended."
And summarizing his own accepted view regarding pervasion and non-pervasion with respect to all objects, he says:
"Of those that occupy a common locus" —
For <s>sattā</s> (existence) and the like, <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) and the like, which occupy a common locus, are pervasive, because they are apprehended even when a single member of the aggregate is apprehended. But conjunction and the like, though occupying a common locus, are non-pervasive,
for these are not ascertained in a single member of the aggregate, but only in the aggregated [members] themselves. The construction is: for color (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like that belong to a single substratum, which are pervasive, and for sound, cognition, and the like, which are non-pervasive — the apprehension and non-apprehension upon apprehension of the substratum [constitute respectively] pervasion and non-pervasion.
The word "one" in "one aggregate" is for the purpose of excluding the totality of aggregate-members,
and the intended meaning is not a single [member] nor the grasping of it; therefore, the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>), being apprehended upon the apprehension of some parts and also upon their non-apprehension, is stated to be pervasive.
By the word "and the like" in "because of corporeality and the like," tangibility, non-pervasiveness, and the like are included.
"The conjunction of produced space is a matter of dispute" —
If mere conjunction of produced space is made the subject of dispute, then since the conjunction existing in a perishing substratum-substance [lasts] as long as the substance lasts, there would be a counter-thesis (<s>apasiddhānta</s>) — therefore it is said "a matter of dispute."
Moreover, it would be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — therefore it is said "because of being in an imperishable substratum."
Even so, with respect to a cloth, the conjunction with the indigo-substance, which lasts as long as the substance, would make it inconclusive — therefore
it is said "because of being in an active substance."
What is to be understood here is activity that is the cause of the intended mutual separation.
Somewhere it is read: "The disputatious ones — space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like — have parts, because of being conjoined with active substances, like an atom." Here, if it were to be proved that space and the like have parts, then the self (<s>ātman</s>) and the like would also have parts, resulting in a counter-thesis — therefore it is said "a matter of dispute."
Therefore, the intended view that separation is from a corporeal [substance] alone is obtained.
"And because conjunction is a non-pervasive property" —
Indeed, the conjunction of two objects possessing regions, like two <s>āmalaka</s> fruits, involves pervasion; the conjunction in space and the like also involves the universal of being a substance-possessing-regions, and by that [universal] there is a figurative attribution of regions to space and the like — this was stated. Now he states the basis for another figurative attribution:
"Of a single [entity]" —
Just as a pot, being a single [thing], is conjoined with many corporeal substances and is [thereby treated as] possessing regions, so too is space (<s>ākāśa</s>) — this is the meaning.
"On what point is the question?" — this is the query.
Its answer: "... of the reality and figurative [uses], from the diversity of separation..."
"... because of the qualification by the inference of continuity..."
"... because of the causal substance being denoted by the word 'region'..."
— by these very sūtras, the inconclusiveness is resolved, [so] in this matter no [additional] sūtra is heard — thus it is inappropriate.
The answer: "space is without regions" —
The meaning is: the sūtra "because the causal substance is denoted by the word 'region'" does not directly state that space and the like are without regions.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.18: Because of non-apprehension before utterance, and because of non-apprehension due to obstruction and the like. //

"The absence of a cause for the non-apprehension of what exists" —

atra jātivādinaḥ sūtradvayaṃ ... tadanupalabdheranupalambhādāvaraṇopapattiḥ ...

anupalabdhisvarūpavirodhāt /

jñānasya nirālambanatvāyogāt /
children.translated_text:
Here, the proponent of universals [argues with] the two sūtras: "because of the non-apprehension of the non-apprehension of that, the explanation of obstruction is valid" —
First, the apprehension of the non-apprehension of obstruction is not possible,
because of contradiction with the very nature of non-apprehension.
Therefore, one must state the non-apprehension of obstruction; and if so, when the non-apprehension of obstruction obtains, there is the apprehension of obstruction, and by that the existence of obstruction [is established],
because a cognition cannot be without a support.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.20: Just as from non-apprehension the existence of non-apprehension is [established], so too the explanation of obstruction is not invalid because of non-apprehension. //

children.translated_text: He illuminates the element of concession contained even in the sūtra —
This very [point] the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> states —
"Even if you concede" —
Thus it is established that inconclusiveness is stated by these two sūtras. //19-20//

If, out of fear of the previously stated defect, the non-apprehension of obstruction exists even though not apprehended, then, since non-apprehension would be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), the absence of obstruction [cannot be proved] from non-apprehension.
Herein, the inconclusiveness is demonstrated by two sūtras.
The introductory <s>Bhāṣya</s> to this is: "and this being the case, the reality."
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains that with "and this being the case."
He shows the purport of the two sūtras through a question: "what is the meaning of this statement?"
Here the <s>Siddhāntin</s> [asks]: what is to be known in this matter, since [non-apprehension] is known through individual inner experience?
The <s>Siddhāntin</s> says "this being the case" —
If the non-apprehension of obstruction is apprehended by mental perception (<s>mānasa pratyakṣa</s>), then there is neither inconclusiveness nor the existence of obstruction.
"The latter statement" —
meaning: the statement of the opponent (<s>jāti</s>).
"There is no ground for it" —
meaning: there is no ground for either of the two sūtras.
Now, since the explanation of obstruction has been shown by the previous sūtra itself, what is the purpose of this sūtra [beginning with] "from non-apprehension"?
To this he says: "by way of concession" —
By the previous sūtra, the absence [of sound] was stated from the non-apprehension of non-apprehension. But here, [the argument is:] even if from non-apprehension there is no absence of non-apprehension, then by this concession, the inconclusiveness is stated —
therefore this sūtra is not purposeless — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.21: Because non-apprehension has the nature of non-apprehension, it is not a valid reason. //

The answer-sūtra to this is:
"Non... reason" (sūtra 21) //

children.text: tathā 'pyā tmasamavāyitvasyeti amūrttatvādityucyamāne ghaṭādibhiḥ pradeśavadbhiḥ prathame kṣaṇe vyabhicāro 'ta uktaṃ sarvadeti /
children.translated_text: Even so, if one says "because of incorporeality" (<s>amūrtatva</s>), there would be deviation through pots and the like, which possess regions, at the first moment [of their existence] — therefore it is said "always."

children.text: tathā 'pi kriyāguṇādibhirvyabhicārasteṣāmapi hi samavāyikāraṇaṃ pradeśa ityata uktam /
children.translated_text: Even so, there would be deviation through action (<s>kriyā</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), and the like, for their inherent cause is also a region — therefore it is said:
"Of a substance that exists." //21//

The proponent of universals (<s>jātivādin</s>) thinks: the non-apprehension of non-apprehension does not exist, because of contradiction. In that case, the perception-status (<s>pramāṇagocaratā</s>) of being in the domain of a positive cognition would contradict [the nature of] non-apprehension.
Objection: but the perception-status of being in the domain of a negative cognition also [applies], and therefore the apprehension of non-apprehension by the mind (<s>manas</s>) through a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose domain is negation does not bring about contradiction. The meaning of the sūtra is thus:
Because the non-apprehension of obstruction-non-apprehension has the nature of non-apprehension — that is, the nature of being the negation of the apprehension of obstruction — the [reason] "from the non-apprehension of that non-apprehension" is not a valid reason for establishing the existence of obstruction,
because of being unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), since the non-apprehension whose domain is negation [establishes it].
The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains this: "what is apprehended" —
What is apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose domain is positive [cognition] — that exists; what is not apprehended — what is apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose domain is negation — that does not exist.
Therefore, it is established that what has the nature of non-apprehension, being accessible to a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose domain is negation, is non-existent.
And the absence of apprehension is non-apprehension; that, being of the nature of absence, is not apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose domain is positive [cognition].
The rest is easy to understand.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the ultimate purport of this: "by one not of that kind" —
meaning: the opponent's (<s>jāti</s>) rejoinder is without a [valid] counter-argument.
"Of that kind" —
For indeed, sound, which has been apprehended, being analogous to what is impermanent — since before and after utterance it is not apprehended when there is no cause for the non-apprehension of what exists — is impermanent.
Objection: let sound not exist before and after utterance — even so, why is it not eternal due to dissimilarity with other impermanent things like the self (<s>ātman</s>), space (<s>ākāśa</s>), and the like?
To this he says: "and it has been stated" —
He states the means of proving impermanence: "impermanent" —
If one says "because of being perceptible" (<s>pratyakṣatva</s>), there would be deviation through <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) and the like — therefore it is said "when there is inherence in a pervasive substance."
Even so, there would be deviation through oneness (<s>ekatva</s>) which inheres in the self (<s>ātman</s>) — therefore it is said:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.22: Because of intangibility (<s>asparśatva</s>). //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.23: Not because of action, since [action] is impermanent. //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.24: Not because of atoms, since [atoms] are eternal. //

children.translated_text: The meaning is: between the two — identity and difference — non-identity is established dependently on difference. / And it is not proper that what is non-different from its own nature is also non-different from something else — / for blue, being non-different from itself, is not therefore also non-different from yellow. / For the ultimate truth is that blue is indeed different from yellow. / This cognition, to begin with, is observed as ceasing in another person — thus: / (302/9) When indeed one person has that cognition, then necessarily another person does not; / therefore, the non-cessation of cognition is itself unestablished. / 'This is so' — / True, the perception of a specific [difference] is the cause of the cessation of that cognition; but in the absence of that [perception], the non-perception-of-a-specific-difference cannot be prevented from being a cause of doubt — this is the meaning. / As for 'the word go (cow)' — / The cognition of one form 'go-word, go-word' cannot arise without a single [referent]. / Then why is it not erroneous? — to this he says: / 'And not of the go-word' — / For if it were erroneous, then from that go-word the cognition of meaning would be erroneous, just as the inference of fire from a firefly whose smoke-nature has been superimposed. / Therefore, the non-erroneous cognition of the unity of the go-word indicates its permanence — this is the meaning. / He refutes: 'This too' — / 'But the non-cessation of that cognition is justified because of the commonality of the cause' — the cause of the go-word-cognition is its substrate, and its commonality is <s>gatva</s> (g-hood), <s>otva</s> (o-hood), <s>gośabdatva</s> (go-word-hood) — so much is meant. / Therefore, the cessation of that cognition is justified, being of the form 'go-word, go-word.' / 'How?' is the question. / In the go-cognition, the go-cognition-awareness does not cease — the singular 'in go-cognition' is with reference to the universal. / For just as in go-cognitions, even though they differ among themselves, the persisting awareness 'go-cognition, go-cognition,' being based on the commonality of go-cognition-hood, takes as its object the go-cognitions that are its own cause — so too the cognition 'go-word, go-word,' being based on go-word-hood, [takes as its object] go-word-particulars, not a single go-word-particular pervading multiple places and times. / And in 'of this go-word-cognition' here too, the singular is with reference to the universal. / The persistence of the cognition 'go-word, go-word' is grounded in commonality, because, being persistent, it is connected with go-word-cognition — / like the persistent cognition 'go-word-cognition, go-word-cognition.' / One who, knowing what is different as non-different, ceases [to discriminate] without having apprehended the specific [difference] — to such a person, does the thing have a specific [difference] or not? — the opponents themselves should be asked. / He states the fault in both [alternatives]: 'If it exists' — / 'Having a dual nature' — / the meaning is: both different and non-different. / 'By being the object of all persons' — / the meaning is: by being the substrate [of cognition for all]. // 32 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.33: Because of the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction. //
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.34: Because of the non-apprehension of a cause of non-hearing, the consequence of perpetual hearing [follows]. //
By separation, the destruction of the non-inherent-cause-contact is indicated, because of being an effect of that. // 33-34 //
[The cause of destruction is] the separation of the causal substance — / thus: / (303/5)
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.35: And when [the cause of destruction] is being perceived, because of the non-existence of non-perception, [the argument] is inconclusive (<s>anapadeśa</s>). //

children.translated_text: And then from the motion [arises] an impression, and from the impression again motion and sound — this too should be understood.
The rest is easy [to understand]. // 35 //

'Inconclusive' means 'not a [valid] reason' — this is the meaning. / 'Both' — / When one proves horse-hood by means of 'having a horn like a camel,' then for him neither the horn nor the connection with it [exists] — / just as 'having a horn' is unestablished in a camel, so too by inference, when the perception of the cause of destruction is [supposed to be] established, the non-perception of that [cause] is unestablished. / 'Because of the absence of the connection of a horse with a horn' — / Since there is absolutely no connection between horse-hood and horn-hood established among horses, therefore, due to contradiction, this inference is unfounded — this is the meaning. / Therefore, just as inference from a contradictory reason is invalid, so too from an unestablished [reason] — this is the meaning. / He raises a doubt: 'If [one says] like <s>karmatva</s> (action-hood)' — / He refutes: / 'And that is not [valid], because of the impermanence of the substrate.' / The substrate of <s>karmatva</s> is <s>karma</s> (action), and because of its impermanence — this is the meaning. / We say: the non-hearing of eternal sound is unjustified, because of the impossibility of a cause of non-hearing. / 'Not [so], because of the impermanence of the substrate' — he divides this statement of the objector: / 'Of <s>karmatva</s>, however' — / The <s>Bhāṣya</s> says: 'The contact with an obstructing substance is the destroyer of the ultimate sound.' / Its meaning: / An obstructing substance is a wall and the like; its contact is with <s>ākāśa</s> (space). / What is said amounts to this: <s>ākāśa</s> that is conjoined with a denser substance does not serve as the inherent cause [of sound]; and thus, even though [a sound] exists, being without a non-inherent cause, the sound does not produce another sound, and its own cause [likewise ceases] — therefore destruction occurs — this should be understood. / Similarly, in other cases too, such a cause of the destruction of sound should be inferred. / And for another reason sound is impermanent — he says: / 'When a bell is not being struck' — / If sound, being eternal, were manifested by a manifesting agent residing in the bell — whether that agent is stationary and located [there] or is a continuing succession — then the distinction of hearing as louder, louder still, loudest, soft, softer, and so on would not arise. / And for eternal sound, there is neither a natural distinction nor an adventitious one — this has been demonstrated below. / But if the louder [sounds] and the like are just so many eternal sounds, then they should all be heard simultaneously, because of the absence of a distinguishing [factor] — for their manifesting agent is one and stationary. / Now if [the agent] is a continuing succession, even so, all [sounds] falling within that succession would be capable [of manifesting] — so they should all be manifested by the very first [agent]; but a restriction of manifestors to sounds in the same location and apprehensible by the same sense organ is not justified — this has been demonstrated below. / But if [sound is produced as] an effect, then the distinction of hearing by the difference of louder and softer sounds, because of the difference of cause, being effectual, and being occasional, is justified — this is the meaning. / 'And that cause' — / (305/8) meaning: the instrumental cause. / 'Requiring the contact of the hand' — / From the contact of a substance that has touch and velocity, motion arises in the bell; from that motion, which is like a motion, the contact of the bell with <s>ākāśa</s> (space) [produces] sound of that kind — this is one moment. That motion, requiring the impulse of the hand-strike, simultaneously with the separation, produces a residual impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) called vibration in the bell. / That bell, moving, gathers the internal air — the air-atoms conjoined with the bell and its parts alone are the internal air; their being gathered is [the effect of] the bell, requiring its own velocity, producing motion in the air through contact with the air; and then from the motion of the wind, the contact of bell-air, requiring the velocity imparted to the air, originates motion in the bell.
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.36: Because of the contact caused by the hand, in the absence of sound, there is no non-apprehension. //

children.translated_text: He resolves: 'We do not say'
— thus.
Although upon the cessation of the instrumental cause too, the effect ceases — as the number two and the like [cease] upon the destruction of the apprehending cognition —

children.text: dvitvādi tathā 'pi nimittanivṛttāvapi tadanivṛttimabhyupagamyaiva parihāra iti mantavyam // 36 //
children.translated_text: nevertheless, the resolution should be understood as conceding [the opponent's point that] even upon the cessation of the instrumental cause, that [effect] does not [always] cease. // 36 //

He instructs: 'Now, the one residing in the bell' — / For it is not the case that upon the destruction of the cause, there is annihilation of the effect — lest upon the cessation of the potter and the like, there be cessation of the pot and the like too — this is the meaning.
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.37: And because of the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction, if [the sound] persists, then the consequence of its being eternal [follows]. //

children.text:
siṃhāvalokitanyāyena pūrvoktaṃ hetu dūṣayati /
vināśeti /
( 306 / 3 ) pratyakṣeṇa śabdavināśakāraṇānupalabdheścāvasthāne śabdasya śabdopalabdherapi nityatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
na hi tasyā api vināśakāraṇaṃ pratyakṣeṇopalabhyata iti tadanena vināśakāraṇānupalabdhirityasyānaikāntikatvamudbhāvitam
// 37 //
children.translated_text: By the method of the 'lion's backward glance' (<s>siṃhāvalokitanyāya</s>), he refutes the previously stated reason. / 'Destruction' — / (306/3) And because of the non-apprehension by perception of a cause of destruction of sound, if the sound persists, then even from the perception of sound there follows the consequence of its being eternal — / for the cause of the destruction of that [perception] too is not apprehended by perception. Thus, the inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>) of 'the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction' has been brought out by this [argument]. // 37 //
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.38: Because of being intangible, there is no refutation. //

children.translated_text: 'For when there is difference of substrate' —

children.text: dravyapraśleṣāsamānādhikaraṇasyaivava saṃskārasyocchedaḥ syād na vyadhikaraṇasya śabdasya, vyadhikaraṇasya tūcchedābhyupagame 'tiprasaṅgaḥ syāt tasmāt kampasaṃtānasaṃskārasamānāśrayaḥ śabdo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: The destruction would be of an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that has the same substrate as the contact with substance, not of sound which has a different substrate; but if the destruction of what has a different substrate were accepted, there would be over-extension. Therefore, one should accept that the sound shares the same substrate as the vibration-succession-impression.
By this, the property of sound having <s>ākāśa</s> (space) as its substratum has been refuted. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this —
"Because of being in different substrata, [it is] unjustified" //

Now the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> philosopher objects. / 'Of what shares the same substrate as vibration' — / The persisting sound is called <s>nāda</s> (resonance), and the sound is the after-sound (<s>anunāda</s>) —
The next <s>sūtra</s> answers this —
"Without touch..." (sū. 38) //

children.translated_text: then by the very first contact with a corporeal substance, since [the <s>saṃskāra</s>] is destroyed, the arrow would fall without having traversed [even] what is to be traversed — this is the unwanted consequence of the arrow's fall.

children.text: dvitīye tu kalpe kṛtakasyāpi saṃskārasya vināśakāraṇābhāvenāvināśānna kadā cidapi pātaḥ syāt prayogaśca iṣvādivegaḥ kṣaṇikaḥ vegatvāt ghaṭādigatavegavaditi // 38 //
children.translated_text: But on the second alternative, since even a produced <s>saṃskāra</s> would never be destroyed due to the absence of a cause of destruction, there would never be a fall [of the arrow]. And the argument is: the velocity of an arrow and the like is momentary, because it is velocity, like the velocity belonging to a pot and the like. //38//

The contact-dependent nature (<s>prāpyakāritva</s>) of the sense organs has been previously established. Sound, which has a bell and the like as its locus, does not reach the ear. For it would reach [the ear] only if the bell came to the ear-cavity or the ear-cavity [went] to the bell — but neither of these obtains. And it has been said that the sense organ born of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> is not all-pervading. Therefore, the substratum of sound is intangible and all-pervading — namely <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — and sound, having that as its substratum, reaches the ear through a propagation of successive [impulses] (<s>saṃtānavṛtti</s>). And thus hearing is explained — not otherwise. The <s>Vārttikakṛt</s> analyses this: "without touch" etc. "By whatever" etc. The meaning is: by a weaker or weakest causal sound. "Multiple <s>saṃskāras</s> (impulses)" — the truth is "because of the difference of sounds." For if there were a single <s>saṃskāra</s>, the postulation of property-differences would involve an excess of postulation — the <s>saṃskāra</s> would be one entity, the property-differences another, and so on. Rather, let there be a difference of <s>saṃskāras</s> in place of property-differences — one property-bearer suffices here. And in the case of different <s>saṃskāras</s>, property-differences need not be postulated, since the difference of effects is explained by the mere difference of <s>saṃskāras</s> as cause, making the postulation of property-differences belonging to them futile — this is the purport. And for the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> who holds a single <s>saṃskāra</s>, the fall of the arrow follows as a consequence — for the <s>saṃskāra</s> of the arrow [involves] contact with a corporeal substance that is either destructive [of the saṃskāra] or non-destructive;  if destructive,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.39: And because of the possibility of another case-ending, [sound is not a quality] of a composite [substance].
"Case-ending... composite" (sū. 39) //

children.text: saṃkhyānāṃ rūparasagandhasparśaśabdasamudāyo vīṇāveṇuśaṅkṣādidravyaṃ tatra samāse samudāye sthita eva vyajyata iti darśanaṃ tasminsamudāye sāṃkhyābhimate vibhaktyantaropatteśca na vyajyeta śabdaḥ yadi samudāye vyajyeta śabdaḥ vibhaktiśca ṣaḍjadhaivatagāndhārādibhedena vibhāgāntaraṃ ca ṣaḍjajātīyasyaiva tāramandrādirūpaṃ nopapadyate na hi tadgatānāṃ gandhādīnāmekasminneva dravye vīṇādau nānājātīyānāṃ ca pratikṣaṇaṃ bhedo dṛśyate tasmādvibhaktyantarotpatterna samāse vyajyate śabdaḥ api tvākāśaguṇaḥ kriyata iti sāṃpratam /
children.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> [hold that] the aggregate of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound [constitutes] a substance such as a <s>vīṇā</s>, flute, conch, and the like. The view is that in such a composite — an aggregate — [sound] is manifested while remaining within it. In that aggregate accepted by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, because of the possibility of another case-ending and because sound would not be manifested if it were manifested in the aggregate — [furthermore,] case-division (<s>vibhakti</s>) by the differentiation of <s>ṣaḍja</s>, <s>dhaivata</s>, <s>gāndhāra</s>, and other [notes], and further division (<s>vibhāgāntara</s>) such as high (<s>tāra</s>), low (<s>mandra</s>), and other forms of [notes] belonging to the very <s>ṣaḍja</s> class — these would not be possible. For within a single substance like a <s>vīṇā</s>, no differentiation of diverse kinds is observed at each moment for the smell and other [qualities] residing therein. Therefore, because of the occurrence of another case-ending, sound is not manifested in a composite, but rather is produced as a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> — this is correct.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> and <s>Vārttika</s> are explained by the very explanation of the <s>sūtra</s>. //39//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.40: Because of the teaching of transformation and substitution, there is doubt.
