children.translated_text: By the word '<s>sattā</s>' (existence), substances, qualities, and actions are not included — the meaning is: by virtue of being fit for co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>). Without that, they cannot be established. But the mere inclusion can be stated — he says: 'it can be stated.' Having asked, he determines the three meanings of the word '<s>sat</s>' (existent), in accordance with the method of the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, through [distinguishing] the principal and subordinate senses. 'And this <s>sat</s>' — 'caused by the purpose (<s>artha</s>)' — the purpose is the effect, and [what is] caused by that [is principal]. What is said amounts to this: that which is connected with an effect is principal; that which has the property of delimiting the effect-connection is subordinate. 'By this' — (325/9) by the statement of the three meanings. For the cognition of being-a-master does not arise regarding a servant; rather, merely through being the cause of the servant's purposive activity, the designation 'master' [is applied] — this is the meaning. 'Here there is neither sequence nor simultaneity of cognition' — (326/3) because in a substratum of difference, sequence and simultaneity cannot obtain in a single cognition of a qualified substance. 'By this' — by the statement that <s>śabda</s> (word) denotes a substance qualified by existence (<s>sattā</s>), since there would be the unwanted consequence of the arising of erroneous cognition — this has been refuted. For in a crystal that is in reality pure white, the cognition of blueness arises due to the placing of a blue substance [near it] — let that be erroneous, because of the absence of real inherence of the quality of blue in it. But the inherence of existence in substances and the like is ultimately real — therefore the cognition 'existent' with respect to substances and the like is not erroneous — this is the meaning. 'For there is no word whatsoever' — the meaning is: since particular instances (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) cannot have a convention [assigned to them], no word whatsoever is accepted by you as being a designator of them. 'Nor of the word for a universal (<s>jāti</s>)' — because of the non-existence of universals — this is the import. The word for a universal is not a designator of particulars — then of what? Previously, this was said with emphasis on the particulars; but now, just this much — that the word for a universal [has no referent] — is [sufficient for showing] that it is not of human origin. 'There is no dispute' — (327/20) the meaning is: when the definitions of <s>anyāpoha</s> (exclusion of the other) and <s>jāti</s> (universal) are not different, there is no dispute. But the co-referentiality of the words '<s>dravya</s>' (substance) and '<s>sat</s>' (existent) [is problematic], and [to say that] words are not designators of positive entities is contradictory — (328/4) for the word '<s>dravya</s>' has a positive form, and likewise '<s>sat</s>' has a positive form; those two words are their designators; the claim that they have the meaning of exclusion-of-the-other is contradictory; and that positive-form words have the meaning of exclusion-of-the-other is impossible. Nor is the co-referentiality of [two words that] do not designate differences even tenable. For operating with respect to a single referent that has the form of [a] difference, by virtue of two different grounds of application, they would be co-referential; but if they do not designate difference, they would not operate in a single [referent]. And not operating [in a single referent], being restricted to different grounds of application, they cannot be co-referential, like 'cow' and 'horse.' This is another contradiction: non-designation of differences and co-referentiality. Thus by this, a twofold contradiction has been stated. Wishing to remove this twofold contradiction, he raises the doubt: 'if there is no contradiction because of figurative usage.' He analyzes this: 'the words <s>dravya</s> and <s>sat</s>.' By this, the first contradiction is resolved. The objector who raised the doubt resolves the second contradiction: 'those two' — 'state' means 'convey' or 'determine.' The purport here is this: words are the sources of conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpa</s>), and they are directed toward precisely what is the domain of conceptual constructions. [This is so] because of the cognition of cause and effect through co-referentiality. And this fourfold classification of conceptual constructions that apprehend existent-and-non-existent property-bearers and existent-and-non-existent properties: '<s>Gaurī</s>, the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), blue, eternal' and so on. But the domain of conceptual constructions is not that which is conceptually constructed — [the particular] which, through differences of place, time, and state, is cognitively synthesized as one: 'this is that very thing.' And that is the domain of words, because the convention can be assigned to [words] with respect to it. But particular instances (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), being absolutely unique in all three worlds, are not [the things] of this kind — so they are not the domain of conceptual constructions. Nor is there any real entity called a 'universal' that could be their domain. Therefore, even the particulars that possess [universals] are not ultimately real either, because in the absence of those universals, their possession-of-universals does not exist in the particulars. Moreover, even if the universal exists as a real entity, even so, being eternal, since it cannot be assisted, the tenability of its being a substrate for particulars [fails] — for being a substrate is indeed a form of being a cause. For plums and the like, which have the nature of falling, are made not-having-the-nature-of-falling by baskets and the like. But what is eternal cannot be 'made' [into anything] — therefore it is not a supported entity (<s>ādheya</s>). Similarly, <s>vṛkṣatva</s> (tree-hood) and <s>śiṃśapātva</s> (being-a-<s>śiṃśapā</s>-tree), being independent universals each cognized by their own words, should not have co-referentiality like 'cow' and 'horse.' Moreover, even if an eternal [entity] can be a supported entity by being assistable — even so, this must be examined: does [the particular] assist <s>śiṃśapātva</s> by the very same nature by which it assists <s>vṛkṣatva</s>, or by a different nature? If by a different nature, then because of the difference of natures, one particular is the substrate of <s>śiṃśapātva</s> and another is the substrate of <s>vṛkṣatva</s> — and so again there would be no co-referentiality, like 'cow' and 'horse.' But if by a single nature the particular assists all universals, even so, since the natures are non-different, among the universals whose natures depend on [the particular's] assistance, when one particular possessing one universal is grasped by a single word or conceptual construction, all universals whose natures are bound to that single assistance would be grasped — and then the unwanted consequence that the conceptual constructions and words '<s>sat</s> (existent), <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>pārthiva</s> (earthen), <s>vṛkṣa</s> (tree), <s>śiṃśapā</s>' would be synonymous. As stated: 'When one assisted [entity] is grasped, the other assistances [follow]; / What is unseen in the seen — in the grasping of that, there is the grasping of all.' Therefore, conceptual constructions that have differences possessing universals as their domain do not exist. By the negation of their having particular-differences as domain, the [view that] they have cognition-images (<s>jñānākāra</s>) as domain is also removed. If one says: a conceptual construction, superimposing its own image — which is not external — onto the external [object], has both its own image and the external as its domain — as stated: 'activity toward what is not a [real] object [occurs] through the determination of [it as] an object in one's own appearance' — then what is this 'determination' (<s>adhyavasāya</s>)? Is it grasping? Or is it producing? Or is it connecting? Or is it superimposing? Regarding these: how could a conceptual construction grasp or produce its own appearance, which is a non-object, as an object? For not even a hundred craftsmen can grasp or produce yellow as blue. Nor can a conceptual construction connect its own image with a particular that has not been grasped. And it has been demonstrated that a particular is not within the domain of conceptual construction. Nor does it superimpose its own image — a non-object — onto the real object. First, an image that has not been grasped cannot be superimposed — so one must accept that it is grasped. Then what — does it grasp [first] and then superimpose? Or at the very moment it grasps, does it superimpose? The first alternative is not [tenable] — for a momentary conceptual cognition cannot perform grasping and superimposition sequentially. In the latter alternative, however, the conceptual construction that is superimposed — from the conceptual-construction-image which is the seat of ego-sense — onto [something that is] not the seat of ego-sense, being perceived by the self-awareness of the conceptual construction, is not outside its own domain, nor can it be cognized as non-different [from the external particular], nor can it be cognized as identical with the external particular by a conceptual cognition — because the external particular does not appear in the domain of conceptual cognition — this has been stated. If one says: because of arising from a non-conceptual [perception] as its immediately preceding cause, through the causal chain of that [perception's] operation, [the conceptual construction,] though not having that as its domain, appears as if having that as its domain — [we reply:] this way [of thinking] is possible in the case of experiential impressions (<s>anubhavavāsanā</s>) even by your own admission, but it is not possible in the case of <s>avidyā</s>-impressions (<s>avidyāvāsanā</s>) that apprehend the absence of what is beyond [perception]. Moreover, even for what arises from experiential impressions, the assumption of having that as its domain, when [the object] does not appear [in the cognition], cannot arise merely from its origination [from a prior cognition]. But when the particular of fire is not being grasped, then by the non-grasping of difference from it, if its form were superimposed [onto something else], there would be the unwanted consequence of superimposing the form of the entire three worlds, because of the absence of a ground for restriction. For at that time, there is no difference between the particular of fire and the three worlds by virtue of their not being grasped. If one says: [the conceptual construction] is restricted to fire by virtue of arising from a non-conceptual [perception] pertaining to the particular of fire, [but] in conceptual constructions about <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter), <s>Īśvara</s> (Lord), and the like, which arise from <s>avidyā</s>-impressions, such [restriction] would not exist — [so] the restriction would not hold. And it has been stated that by non-grasping, the superimposition of that is not possible. Therefore, the externality of the unreal as a domain of conceptual construction is empty talk. Moreover, the unreal cannot be the domain of conceptual construction, just as it [cannot be] graspable as a cognition-image or as a particular — for this is dependent on conceptual construction: when the construction arises, it [seems to have] arisen; when it perishes, it [seems to have] perished; when the constructions differ, it [seems] different — and it cannot be rendered as one. If one says: because of the non-discernment of difference — is its true nature, even when not discerned, [real]? If yes — then it is not constructed. Surely, its difference too is not natural — for what is natural is compatible with both difference and non-difference, but not what is unreal. Let its difference not be natural; but that unreal [entity], being dependent on construction, must be cognized as different because of [the construction's] difference — otherwise, dependence on it would not follow. For this is precisely what it means for the constructed [entity] to be dependent on construction: its conformity with the differences and non-differences of the constructions; but if it were [independent of] dependence [on construction], since its being-constructed would not be tenable, the consequence of its being non-unreal [would follow]. Therefore, let there not be natural diversity or unity in it; but [what is] conforming to different constructions cannot be cognized as one — so it must be cognized as different. Thus it is established that the unreal external [entity] is not within the domain of conceptual constructions — because of being unfit for connection with verbal expression (<s>abhilāpasaṃsarga</s>), like the particular of pleasure and the like. For that [particular] is unfit for connection with verbal expression, and therefore, because of being incapable of having a convention [assigned], it is like the particular of pleasure and the like. For the fitness for connection with verbal expression is pervaded by the capacity to have a convention — otherwise there would be over-extension. The absence of being-an-unreal-external, which differs for each conceptual construction, by being negated, also negates the fitness for connection with verbal expression — thus the [logical] entailment is established. Moreover, is this unreal [entity] the form of the exclusion of non-cow (<s>agovyāvṛtti</s>), or a property of it? If it is the form of the exclusion of non-cow — it cannot be grasped in a cow, since it is unestablished. And a non-cow, being of the nature of the negation of cow, depends on the establishment of cow — so the mutual dependence [objection] is irrefutable. Or, if it is a property [of the cow], then let <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) itself be the natural [property], which is of a positive form; what need is there for the unreal non-positive-form [exclusion]? And the proof that properties belong to their bearers has been refuted, and the commonality of that [exclusion] with existence and non-existence has been demonstrated — therefore, fearful of an even more extensive elaboration, we have fallen into it — so let us set aside this refutation of the <s>Nāstika</s> (Buddhist) view. The <s>Vārttika</s> that resolves the doubt 'if there is no contradiction because of figurative usage' — 'because of the impossibility of the primary [sense]' — (328/11) everywhere, figurative usage or superimposition is observed to be preceded by a primary [usage]; but in your established doctrine, there is no primary word or conceptual construction that has a positive entity as its object, since everything is within the domain of negation. And it has been demonstrated below that the positive as 'determined' (<s>adhyavasita</s>) is not possible — this is the import. Nor is figurative usage appropriate in the <s>anyāpoha</s> (exclusion) thesis, since both [words] are primary — the meaning is: for indeed, there is no such thing as 'lion-hood' existing in [actual] lions that would not [also] exist in a [metaphorical] boy. Rather, by the exclusion of the [quality of] acting with force and the like, since [that exclusion] does not exist in the boy, the word 'lion' would be primary even in the boy, just as in [actual] lions — this is the meaning. 'What, cow, non-cow?' — (329/5) meaning 'horse and the like.' The activity of the command in the object of the command, preceded by the cognition of the command, is the concurrence; and since the existence of what is other than the subsidiary — the principal, such as army, forest, multitude, number, and the like — is accepted by you — this is the meaning. 'And since <s>apoha</s> (exclusion) has the form of an action, its object must be stated' — action has an object (<s>karman</s>) — that must be stated — this is the meaning. 'How from what has another [thing] as domain?' — how does the cognition of a cow arise from the exclusion (<s>apoha</s>), which has a non-cow as domain, with respect to a cow? — this is [the question]. 'But [by the word] non-cow (<s>ago</s>)' — (330/2) for there is indeed some action that, belonging to one thing, has another thing as its object — just as cognition cognizes the meaning (<s>artha</s>) of the self (<s>ātman</s>) — meaning: it cognizes its object — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'by what, a cow?' — for action, belonging to conscious beings, is preceded by effort. And the action characterized as exclusion has the form of negation; and negation is preceded by applicability — for indeed, the cow-hood of a cow has not been proposed by anyone such that a discerning person would exclude it — this is the meaning. 'And how, in a non-cow?' — the negation [expressed by] the word 'non-cow' (<s>agavī</s>) does not exist without [prior] cognition of a cow — this is the meaning. 'Because of the impossibility of superimposition, the cognition of the object is not tenable' — the cognition of the object that has the form of exclusion (<s>apoha</s>) is not tenable — this is the meaning. 'Is <s>apoha</s> (exclusion) what is expressed or what is not expressed?' — meaning: by the word <s>apoha</s> and the like. 'If what is expressed' — then <s>apoha</s> is expressed in its own form, not by the exclusion of the exclusion (<s>apohāpoha</s>) — this is the meaning. One might say: if the word does not operate through the exclusion of the other, then how does a single word operate in many specific instances such as two and the like through a single exclusion? For here, multiplicity is not some real universal like cow-hood — therefore he says: 'and of this word "many" (<s>aneka</s>), because of having two and the like as its objects' — (331/2) the specific [number] within the universal of number-hood-excluding-oneness, cognized through a universal-word, must be resorted to; the universal of number-hood-excluding-oneness alone is the ground for cognizing the specifics of two and the like — not mere exclusion-of-the-other — this is the meaning. For when the universal-word designating the universal of number-hood-excluding-oneness does not exist, the specific [number] cannot be cognized from the word '<s>aneka</s>' (many) [by] resorting to the specific from mere exclusion-of-the-other — this should be the construction. The same applies to words like '<s>abrāhmaṇa</s>' (non-Brahmin) and the like. There too, the universal of manhood (<s>puṃstva</s>) alone is the meaning of the word '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>.' And of the words '<s>nīla</s>' (blue) and '<s>utpala</s>' (lotus), because of being primary — for the words '<s>nīla</s>' and '<s>utpala</s>' convey the exclusions of non-blue and non-lotus as primary [meanings]; for indeed, these [two words] do not have the relation of qualifier and qualified with each other, because of the absence of mutual connection — this is the import. By this, the words '<s>nīla</s>' and '<s>utpala</s>' in this established doctrine, having been explained as having their primary meanings through exclusion, explain [by analogy] the words '<s>rāja</s>' (king) and '<s>puruṣa</s>' (man) — with the primary sense. Here too, the exclusions of non-king and non-man do not have the relation of delimited and delimiter, nor the relation of master and servant — this is the meaning. 'And of co-referential [words]' — because of the impossibility of contact with an ultimately real entity by words and conceptual constructions — this is the meaning. //65//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.66: An individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is a substance possessing specific qualities — a corporeal entity (<s>mūrti</s>). //

children.translated_text: Or alternatively, the words are: "the substrate of specific qualities" —

children.text: atha vā guṇaviśeṣāṇāmāśraya iti guṇā rūpādayaḥ viśeṣāḥ karmāṇi guṇebhya ityarthāt /
children.translated_text: Or alternatively, "the substrate of specific qualities" — qualities are color (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like; specifics are actions (<s>karman</s>), [which are specifics] of qualities, i.e., [distinguished] from qualities —
and [the compound] "their substrate" is a <s>dvandva</s> (copulative compound) — "their" is understood from the context.

children.text: tatra mūrcchita itimūrchanaṃ saṃbandha iha cāsau samavāya iti // 66 //
children.translated_text: Therein, "consolidated" (<s>mūrcchita</s>) — consolidation here means connection, and that is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). //66//

For where individual, configuration, and universal converge, there is a definition that distinguishes the individual without difference [from the others].
By this, there is no fault even when space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like are not included, because of the absence of configuration in them — this is the view of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>.
As the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "Not every substance is an individual."
Although heaviness (<s>gurutva</s>) and the like are general qualities, still, being distinguished from other qualities, they are called "specific qualities" (<s>guṇaviśeṣa</s>).
"Non-pervasive" — this delimits the measure of an all-pervading substance.
"Having consolidated parts" (<s>mūrcchitāvayava</s>) — that whose parts are mutually conjoined.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> raises an objection against the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with "but how" —
"Because of being [already] understood" —
The intent of the objection is: since the understanding of the intrinsic nature [of the individual] is prior and the sentence-exposition is subsequent, the understanding of the intrinsic nature too is established as a necessary consequence of [that exposition].
He refutes:
"Not [so], because when there is a threefold ground, [the definition] has the purpose of conveying knowledge of the specific [differences]."
When there is a threefold ground for the application of the word, the question has as its scope precisely the specific [differences among them]; the definition has as its purpose the conveying of knowledge of those [specific differences] — thus it is called [a definition with that purpose]. What is being said is this: taking the distinction [of the three] as established, the denotability of [all] three has been demonstrated; now that very distinction is being demonstrated.
"<s>Sūtra</s>" — the import is: because it indicates many meanings.
He presents an alternative <s>Bhāṣya</s>-interpretation:
"Is manifested" —
(332/2) He refutes it: "But this" —
The subject under discussion is that the individual is a word-referent. Therein, just as the word-referent-status of the individual as a composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) [is defined], so too the definition should be explained in such a way that it encompasses space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like, as well as throwing (<s>utkṣepaṇa</s>) and the like — otherwise the <s>sūtrakāra</s> would be unskilled — for that purpose he says:
"We, however, maintain" —
Here is this interpretation:
"Individual" is the indication of the definiendum; the rest is the definition.
"Specific qualities" (<s>guṇaviśeṣa</s>) — the compound can be analyzed in two ways. The first analysis: "qualities and particulars" — by this, configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) is excluded and color (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like are included.
Even so, since the individual [as] throwing and the like is not included, there is a second analysis:
"Specifics [distinguished] from qualities" — that is, throwing and the like, which are distinguished from qualities.
Even so, since substance (<s>dravya</s>) is not included, he says:
"Substrate" (<s>āśraya</s>) —
By supplying the word "that" [i.e., substance], the meaning is: the substrate of specific qualities is substance.
"Word by word" —
The words are: "quality" (<s>guṇa</s>), "particular" (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and "substrate" (<s>āśraya</s>).
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.67: Configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) is that which is called the indicator of the universal (<s>jātiliṅga</s>). //

children.translated_text: Although <s>gotva</s> (cow-hood) is directly perceptible and not indicated by configuration, nevertheless this is said in response to one who disputes [it]: "they infer" — but it is not the case that every universal is indicated by configuration.

children.text: mṛtsuvarṇarajatādikā hi rūpaviśeṣavyaṅgyā jātirnākṛtivyaṅnyā brāhmaṇatvādijātistu yonivyaṅgyā ājyatailādīnāṃ jātistu gandhena vā rasena vā vyajyate /
children.translated_text: For the universal of clay, gold, silver, and the like is indicated by specific color (<s>rūpaviśeṣa</s>), not by configuration; the universal of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-hood and the like is indicated by birth (<s>yoni</s>); and the universal of clarified butter (<s>ājya</s>), oil (<s>taila</s>), and the like is indicated by smell or taste.

children.text: ata eva na sārṣapādīnāṃ tailatvamasti tadvyañjakayorgandharasayorabhāvāt /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, mustard-oil and the like do not have oil-hood (<s>tailatva</s>), because of the absence of the smell and taste that indicate it.

children.text: bhāktastu tailaśabdaprayogaḥ kṣīrajātirapi rasavyaṅgyaiva ata evāmikṣāyāḥ kṣīratvaṃ na tu vājinasya tavyañjakasya rasabhedasya vājine 'bhāvād āmikṣāyāṃ ca bhāvāditi // 67 //
children.translated_text: Rather, the usage of the word "oil" [for mustard-oil] is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>). The universal of milk (<s>kṣīra</s>) too is indicated by taste alone — for this very reason, <s>āmikṣā</s> (curdled milk) has milk-hood, but a mare does not, because the taste-difference that would indicate [milk-hood] is absent in the mare but present in <s>āmikṣā</s>. //67//

The universal and the indicators of the universal are <s>jātiliṅga</s>; that by which they are designated is configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>).
The arrangement of head, hands, and the like —
configuration designates the universal such as humanity (<s>manuṣyatva</s>) and the like.
The arrangement of head, nose, forehead, and the like is the indicator of the universal of humanity; the head designates [it].
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: "They infer the cow by head and foot."
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.68: A universal (<s>jāti</s>) is that which has the nature of producing a common cognition (<s>samānaprasava</s>). //

children.translated_text: Elsewhere, the cognition accords with the grammatical gender.
"A neuter [noun] with a non-neuter [noun]" — the neuter gender should not be suspected.
Thus, in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Vācaspati Miśra</s>,
the second section (<s>āhnika</s>) of the second chapter is concluded.

That which produces (<s>prasūte</s>) is <s>prasava</s> (production); the universal (<s>jāti</s>) that is the producer of a common cognition in different [individuals] necessarily produces a common cognition — but it is not the case that whatever produces a common cognition is a universal,
because of deviation in the case of cooks and the like.
And this definition is to be understood only as distinguishing [the universal] from individual and configuration, not as [exhaustively defining it] in every respect.
But for one who, out of contrariness, disputes even what is perceptible, he states the inferences:
"The persisting cognition in cows and the like" —
(333/18) "Designation" (<s>vyapadeśa</s>) — a relation is designated by a relatum: "the person is designated by [the expression] 'of the king'" — thus.
"The persisting cognition of cow-hood in a cow" —
Previously, merely the persisting cognition was made the subject [of dispute]; here, however, "the persisting cognition of cow-hood in a cow" — thus there is no redundancy.
"Mentioned" (<s>kīrtita</s>) — as the grammatical gender is intended, because of being different [in gender].
The second chapter is complete. //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.1: Because of the apprehension of a single object through sight and touch. //

children.translated_text: Here the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says:] "The <s>pramāṇas</s> have been examined; now the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is to be examined." The recapitulation of what has been done is for the purpose of showing the causal relation of the completed examination of <s>pramāṇas</s> to the forthcoming examination of <s>prameya</s>. For <s>prameya</s> is examined by means of <s>pramāṇa</s>, not by anything else. And that [<s>pramāṇa</s>], if unexamined, is not capable of [serving in] the examination of <s>prameya</s>. Therefore, the examination of <s>pramāṇas</s> is the cause; the examination of <s>prameya</s>, having that cause, [follows]. The <s>prameya</s> is twelvefold — then why is the <s>ātman</s> (self) alone examined first, and not another <s>prameya</s>? To this he says: "And that, beginning with <s>ātman</s> — the <s>ātman</s> is being investigated." (335/5) For it is the <s>ātman</s> that was first enumerated and defined among the <s>prameyas</s>; and in accordance with that, the <s>ātman</s> alone is examined first, not the other <s>prameyas</s>. And here, although the examination is professed regarding the <s>ātman</s> in its own nature, nevertheless, since the examination of the defined entity proceeds through the examination of the definition, it should be seen as an examination of the definition [itself]. How this is an examination of the definition of the <s>ātman</s> will be shown below. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this: "from contiguity" etc. What then is the purpose of the examination of <s>prameya</s>? For discerning persons do not examine what is purposeless — to this he says: "that which is the object of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense)." The word <s>ahaṅkāra</s> indicates false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>) having the <s>ātman</s> and the like as its object. Indeed, seeing the <s>ātman</s> as non-different from the body and the like sets <s>saṃsāra</s> in motion — this was stated in the second <s>sūtra</s>. By this, the purposefulness of the examination of <s>prameya</s> has been shown. Here the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> has shown the doubt, which is the preliminary form of investigation: "Is the <s>ātman</s> merely an aggregate of body, sense organs, mind, and intellect?" And the cause of doubt has been stated: "because of designation." Although with respect to a tree and a palace — which are composites and aggregates that are different [from their parts] — the designation is by parts or by the aggregate, nevertheless, for the opponent who considers the composite to be absent and the aggregate to be non-different from its members, the example should be seen [in that light]. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, in order to object, asks: "what then is this?" The answer: "is it the body?" He objects: "no" — the meaning is that doubt arises from the observation of common properties in a property-bearer, not from non-observation. He resolves: "nor the <s>sūtra</s> about desire (<s>icchā</s>) and the like." For desire and the like, being effects, have been shown to be inferential marks of the <s>ātman</s>. But those very marks point to the agent of desire — the investigation is whether the agent of desire is established as different from body and sense organs, or as non-different — this is a proper inquiry. Moreover, this property-bearer designated by the word <s>ātman</s> is accepted in all systems (<s>sarvatantrasiddha</s>); the dispute among theorists is merely about its difference or non-difference from the body — he says: "and because of non-disagreement" etc. (336/1) But objectors have presented arguments such as non-production (<s>ajātatva</s>) and the like to prove the non-existence of the <s>ātman</s> — how then is there no disagreement about its existence? To this he says: "because of the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing non-existence." One who disagrees about the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) itself is not even a proper disputant, for one who disagrees about the property-bearer has no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever, since everything for such a person suffers from the fallacy of unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>). And since <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence), whose determination depends on <s>bhāva</s> (existence), cannot be determined in case of absolute non-existence — therefore, one who asserts the non-existence of the property-bearer is neither a worldly person nor a proper examiner, and should be disregarded like a madman. He presents the <s>pramāṇa</s> of those who assert the unestablishedness of the property-bearer: "it does not not exist" etc. He refutes: "therein, the <s>ātman</s> does not exist" etc. As for what others have maintained: "The object-word (<s>śabdārtha</s>), grounded in conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) born of beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), is threefold as the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) — having existence (<s>bhāva</s>), non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>), or both as its ground." Having existence as ground — as in "blue"; having non-existence as ground — as in "hare's horn"; having both as ground — as in "non-corporeal." For what is non-corporeal can be consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), and it can also be a hare's horn. "Of that [<s>ātman</s>], when the external origin is the object to be proved, the non-apprehension of it is the reason — not the non-existence of that very [<s>ātman</s>], because of the usage of the word" — thus, this conceptual construction of the <s>ātman</s> does not have an external origin. Just as the conceptual construction of "blue" has an external blue as its origin, the conceptual construction of the <s>ātman</s> does not similarly have an external origin — this is the meaning. Regarding this, the following question arises: is it merely the external origin of the <s>ātman</s>-construction that is denied, or is the external <s>ātman</s> [itself] as origin denied? In the first case, there is proving what is already established — let the <s>ātman</s>-construction not have an external blue and the like as its origin — what harm does that do to us? But in the second case, where is this external <s>ātman</s> established, such that its being the origin of the construction is denied? If established somewhere, then its denial is not absolute. And if unestablished, how can what is not cognized be denied? If you say: "it is cognized in the construction and denied in the external [realm] — just as <s>Caitra</s> [is cognized] in the house and denied on the courtyard" — even so, where it is cognized, there it is not denied, as you yourselves have said: "not the non-existence of that very [thing], because of the usage of the word." And the external <s>ātman</s> has not been presented by the construction — hence, since there is no basis [for denial], it cannot be denied. If you say: "though not presented, it is determined — hence there is indeed a basis" — well, what is this 'determination' (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) of a construction? If it is a superimposition of the external upon the grasped, whether upon its own form or upon the false — then it is remarkable that constructions that do not have the external as their object should superimpose the external! For it has been repeatedly demonstrated that one who does not know the object of superimposition and what is superimposed upon cannot superimpose. Moreover, just as what appears falsely cannot be denied precisely because it appears, so too its externality [cannot be denied]. If you say it is denied because of being false — then is even the false true, that you are determined to deny its externality, bypassing it? The grasping of external-difference — its determination is not a basis [for denial], hence it is not within the scope of denial. Nor is it correct that the <s>ātman</s>, which is the form of cognition and ultimately real, is denied as being superimposed as external. For in the consciousness-only [doctrine], since there is absolutely no grasping of the external in any way, there is no possibility of its superimposition. And if the external, being absolutely non-existent, were grasped in consciousness — then what wrong has that non-existent [entity], which is of the nature of consciousness and is graspable by consciousness, committed, that it should not be the object of that grasping? Thus the consciousness-only position would have given up [its case]. Nor can this <s>ātman</s>, which persists through earlier and later times, be of the form of a momentary construction, such that its form would be denied as external. Therefore, it is proper that what is observed in one place is superimposed onto another and then denied. And that superimposition sometimes arises from its own cause [and] is sometimes denied — as when the silver-cognition produced from a defect of the sense organ and the like is denied regarding the mother-of-pearl: "this is not silver." But sometimes it is removable — as in "<s>Caitra</s> is not here." Therefore, since the construction of the <s>ātman</s> in another place and time is impossible in consciousness, and in the case of absolute non-existence the superimposition — and since in the absence of that [superimposition] it simply does not exist in the <s>ātman</s>; and if it does exist, how can there be an absolute denial? Therefore, the words "the <s>ātman</s> does not exist" are self-contradictory. Even though the words are "the <s>ātman</s> does not exist," still, by intending the single-word status of "does not exist" (<s>nāsti</s>), the dual number usage "two words" (<s>pade</s>) is justified. And intending that a <s>pada</s> (word) is that by which meaning is reached (<s>padyate</s>), even an aggregate of words is called a <s>pada</s>. Although for pots and the like, the denial is from another place and so on, still for the <s>ātman</s> it would be absolute [denial] — for a denial of one kind does not necessarily entail a denial of another kind — to this he says: "and all this" etc. It has been demonstrated below that what has not been experienced cannot be superimposed — and nowhere has the <s>ātman</s> been said to have another as its substratum; rather, aggregates and the like are its substrata. He asks: "what is this?" (337/2) What does not exist anywhere is absolutely non-existent, and this [<s>ātman</s>] is such — therefore it is absolutely non-existent — this is the purport. The answer: "it does not not exist" etc. The sentence "it does not not exist anywhere" does not deny the <s>ātman</s> in its own nature, because it denies [only] a specific place and form. The questioner says: "what is this verbal trick?" The answerer says: "this verbal trick" etc. — this [trick] has the meaning to be stated. For that purpose he says: "that which is as it really is" etc. For the existence of entities is not pervaded by the force of place, such that the removal of place-ness would remove that [existence] — this is the purport. "Nor is the denial of a specific time" etc. — a specific time is each time that has another time as its counterpart; its denial too is unjustified regarding the <s>ātman</s>. For time does not serve as a delimiter for the eternal <s>ātman</s> in the way it does for pots and the like. A pot that possesses destruction-absence (<s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s>) does not exist [later]; likewise a pot possessing prior-absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) will come to exist — but not so the <s>ātman</s>. A pot is present [when it has] past prior-absence and future destruction — but not so the <s>ātman</s>. Therefore, the three times, in the sense of delimitation, do not apply to it. There exists a time — the present — distinguished from the past and future by the manifestation of activity, for eternal things always exist: the <s>ātman</s> exists, <s>ākāśa</s> (space) exists — therefore, since the delimiting three times do not apply, there is no denial of the three times. And since the present — distinguished from past and future by the manifestation of activity — cannot be denied, the denial of time with respect to the <s>ātman</s> is established [as unjustified]. "And the denial of the <s>ātman</s>" — for the word <s>ātman</s> is established in the world; by it some meaning is reached; that by which no meaning is reached should be meaningless. "What commonality does the non-existent have with the existent?" — well then, in your own doctrine, the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) that is devoid of all designations is also non-existent — this is the purport. Now, if what is denied is the <s>ātman</s>-hood superimposed on body and the like — "the body and the like are not the <s>ātman</s>" — to that he says: "and the universal of <s>ātman</s>-hood" etc. "Now, the body and the like" — the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) is, in ultimate reality, directed toward the body and the like, from cognitions such as "I am stout, I am fair." Having constructed this [body etc.] as the <s>ātman</s>, one erroneously [identifies with it], designates and transacts accordingly. This very error is denied by "the <s>ātman</s> does not exist." He refutes: "thus, the body and the like" etc. (338/1) For one who does not accept the existence of the object of the superimposition of the ego-sense, the superimposition itself is not possible — therefore, from the denial of that [object], there is a contradiction — this is the meaning. "Because of the four [elements] having the nature of material cause, of darkness (<s>tamas</s>)" — form, taste, smell, and touch — these four, having transformed into the form of pots and the like — their material-cause form is that which is taken up, i.e., that which is to be taken up (<s>upādeya</s>). In some readings, "because of having the nature of what is to be taken up" — that reading is equally good. This is the doctrine of the <s>Vātsīputrīyas</s>, a <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> [Buddhist] school — and there is a contradiction with it — this is the meaning. The rest is easy. "Now this is a denial of existence" — (339/16) It is not merely a denial of birth, but rather the existence — the being — of the <s>ātman</s> is denied — this is the meaning. "Because of not observing any [property] other than inherence, which is an independent property" — a <s>nikāya</s> (class) is an assemblage of gods, humans, animals, and the like arranged without hierarchy; "by those distinguished [by those classes]" — this is the meaning. "Whether an effect or a cause" — (340/14) if the horn is a part, then it is a cause; but if, being like hair and nails, it is non-constitutive and hence not a part, then it is an effect — therefore it arises from that — this is the meaning. He states a previously stated meaning again, reconsidering it for the purpose of cross-examination: "one who says 'this hare's horn does not exist'" etc. "General denial" means: denial of mere connection with horns. "Specific denial" means: denial of the connection characterized as the cause-effect relation. "Following the nature-difference of the object" — the mental cognition "I" has as its object the <s>ātman</s>; the nature-difference of that [<s>ātman</s>] — characterized as agency and experiencership — "I know, I enjoy" and the like — [the cognition] follows that. What is being said is this: not merely the own-nature of the <s>ātman</s> is the object of <s>ātman</s>-knowledge; for if so, since action and its fruit, which inhere in another [entity], would not be fruitful, and since the <s>ātman</s> would lack object-hood (<s>karmatva</s>), and since the knowledge pervaded by that [object-hood] would also cease — this would follow. But when the knowledge having the <s>ātman</s> as its object includes its properties, then because the properties, being fruitful through action and result inhering in another, the knowledge pervaded by them also ceases. And "knows" — this verb having the <s>ātman</s> as agent and its properties as object — also has the <s>ātman</s> within its scope — thus it is well said "following the nature-difference of the object." "Having the ego-sense as support" — (341/16) that by which [something] is supported is the support (<s>ālambana</s>), i.e., knowledge; and through the ego-sense as the cognizer, it apprehends the object. He teaches. "But surely, 'I am fair' [is experienced]." He resolves: "we say it does not obtain" — mere designation is not what we have said to be the proof of the existence of the <s>ātman</s> as different from the body and the like, lest it be inconclusive. Rather, [it is] experience. And that [experience] does not exist in the body and the like, which are objects of "this" (<s>idam</s>). Rather, the "I"-cognition has "this" (<s>idam</s>) as its distinct object; the body and the like, however, are made objects of "I" through figurative usage by the elision of the possessive suffix (<s>matup</s>) or by differentiation. But the designation "my <s>ātman</s>" is merely conventional, and the possessive marker (<s>ma</s>-kāra) is not primary there as it is with the body and the like, because it does not appear as different [from the <s>ātman</s>]. Rather, the possessive usage regarding the <s>ātman</s> should be seen as like "<s>Rāhu</s>'s head" [where the head is not different from <s>Rāhu</s>]. For this very reason he says: "the 'my'-cognition" etc. (342/2) But the mere possessive usage is not therefore entirely pleasing. Contradictory cognition is disagreement, which is overridden — and so on. "What is the meaning of <s>sādhana</s> (proof)?" — what is the meaning of the word <s>sādhana</s>? "Now, does even non-apprehension not exist?" — a positive property is contradicted by non-existence, not a non-existent property, because both [non-existence and the non-existent property] share the same nature — this is the meaning. He refutes: "what is the proof-meaning of non-apprehension?" — for a non-apprehension that is void (<s>tuccha</s>) and non-existent, what proof-nature is there? — this is the meaning. He raises a doubt: "now, of what is constructed" etc. — non-apprehension is not void; rather, it is a real entity; but as having a constructed [entity as] its locus, there is no fallacy of unestablished locus — this is the meaning. Having considered this, he refutes: "how, of what is constructed" etc. — for real non-apprehension, having an ultimately real locus, cannot be a property of a property-bearer whose existence is merely constructed — this is the meaning. He raises the second alternative as a doubt: "now, by non-existence" etc. He refutes: "non-apprehension is established" etc. — the ultimate existence of [the <s>ātman</s>] whose existence is [said to be merely] constructed must be accepted through its [very] non-existence. Since the construction of non-existence is unjustified [for something truly non-existent], and thus the real non-apprehension having an existent locus is indeed established. But the very thing for which that [non-apprehension was intended] — that ultimate non-existence of the <s>ātman</s> — is not established, because you yourselves accept the constructedness of non-existence — this is the meaning. Moreover, this person, having constructed the <s>ātman</s> as existent through [its] non-existence, has undertaken to prove the absolute non-existence [of the <s>ātman</s>] through non-apprehension. And that is not established for him by the property of non-apprehension that belongs to the existent [<s>ātman</s>]. For never can the ultimate post-nature be proved in a person through a constructed property of a post — he says: "for what purpose is this, the <s>ātman</s>?" etc. "When there is difference from words like <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like" — for if one says "because of being a word" (<s>padatvāt</s>), it would be inconclusive with respect to words like <s>rūpa</s> and the like — therefore it is said "when there is difference from words like <s>rūpa</s> and the like." If one says "because of being a single word," it would be inconclusive with respect to words like <s>rūpa</s> and the like — therefore it is said "when there is difference from words like <s>rūpa</s> and the like." Even so, the word that denotes <s>rūpa</s> (form), <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), <s>vedanā</s> (feeling), <s>saṃjñā</s> (perception), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (formations) — the word that is the collective denoting <s>rūpa</s>, <s>vedanā</s>, <s>saṃjñā</s>, <s>vijñāna</s>, and the like — one that is different from that is non-collective; one that is different from the collective — therefore, because of inconclusiveness, it is said "single" etc. So, whatever single word is different from single words denoting <s>rūpa</s> and the like, that single word denotes what is different from <s>rūpa</s> and the like — just as the words "pot" and the like; and so too the word "<s>ātman</s>" — therefore it too is such. "By this" etc. — the "I"-cognition, distinct from the "this" (<s>idam</s>)-cognition, has been explained as having the very word <s>ātman</s> as its object to be proved. He raises a doubt: "unestablished" etc. — "<s>ghaṭa</s>" (pot), it is said, denotes merely <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like delimited by water-carrying and the like. But there is no entity called "pot" different from <s>rūpa</s> and the like — this is the meaning. He refutes: "here it has been said" etc. — "because of the four [elements] having the nature of material cause, of darkness" etc. — just as <s>dāya</s> (gift) means what is to be given (<s>deya</s>), so <s>upādāya</s> (taking up) means what is to be taken up (<s>upādeya</s>). The opponent, thinking that "having an object" means "having an existent object" as stated by the <s>siddhāntin</s>, objects: "the word <s>tamas</s> (darkness) has an object" — even though having <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) as its object does not make it objectless, still, complying with the concern about place-convention, he resolves: "but as for the <s>sūtra</s>-meaning, the example is not absent" etc. (344/10) The absence of an example was previously stated when proving the <s>ātman</s>'s non-contributoriness — here it is stated again — this is the meaning. He teaches: "now, the word <s>ātman</s>" etc. — whatever consists of phonemes, all of that has a non-eternal referent, like the word "pot" and the like. And thus, being non-eternal, it would be merely its cognition, not the <s>ātman</s> — in effect, a denial of the <s>ātman</s> — this is the meaning. He refutes this too: "even so" etc. — the word "eternal" (<s>nitya</s>) at least denotes the eternal; otherwise there would be no denial of that [eternality] — this is the meaning. He raises a doubt: "now" etc. — for the purpose of removing the proving of what is already established, [the word <s>ātman</s>] has an object different from the body and the like. He refutes: "even so" etc. — your established doctrine is that nothing exists beyond the five aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>) of <s>rūpa</s> and the like — accepting something beyond them is contradictory — this is the meaning. "If, differing from the intended meaning" etc. — (345/8) The speaker's intended meaning is the purposiveness of the aggregate of body, sense organs, intellect, and feeling — saying "the eyes and the like serve another" — his [intended meaning] is not directly that the aggregate serves another; but here, by the force of the thesis, it would be entailed — not directly intended. Similarly here, what is entailed by intention and imputed as intended — if concomitance and contradiction are shown regarding that, then all inference would be destroyed. And this will be more carefully demonstrated in the proof of <s>Īśvara</s> (God). "Now, if overridden by inference" etc. — the inference from being an aggregate itself — the thesis that the aggregate serves another, which is the opposite of what was intended — the inference from the existence of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and the like, assisted by <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) in the form of the unwanted consequence characterized by the criterion of regularity, is its overrider. And the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, who says "by a part, of other parts," intends that from houses, walls, palaces, and the like, the composite of heterogeneous [parts] is not constitutive. "And of those that are not in a cause-effect relation" etc. — (347/19) Just as for one who has seen a black cow, there arises recognition regarding a white cow — and these two are not in a cause-effect relation — this is the meaning. "But the consciousness of the <s>ātman</s> — when there is independence, because of non-regularity, like the eye and the like" — this is the reason. That one who is continuous through <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), doubt, error, and memory, who is perceived as one — he is conscious; because of non-regularity when there is independence. But what is non-conscious is not regular when independent, like the eye and the like — this is the negative concomitance reason. If only "because of non-regularity" were said, then the mind (<s>manas</s>) would make it inconclusive — therefore it is said "when there is independence." Or alternatively, regularity is not needed — let independence alone be the proof of consciousness — he says: "a non-conscious <s>ātman</s>" etc. — it indicates what has been experienced as continuous through <s>pramāṇa</s>, doubt, error, and memory. Having presented a previously refuted meaning again in another form, he refutes it: "in proving the eternality of earth and the like" etc. The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says:] "they have different causes" — they have different sense organs as their causes; they are not by infinite agents but by a single agent, the <s>ātman</s>; they have the same object — a single substance is the object — this is the meaning. //1//
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.2: Not so, because of the fixity of the sense-objects. //

children.text: pūrvapakṣasūtram--- na vi--t (sū. 2) // yadbhāvābhāvānuvidhāyinau jñānabhāvābhāvau taccetanam /

children.translated_text: Since the presence and absence of the sense organs determine those [cognitions], that very [sense organ] is the sentient [entity] — this is the purport.

children.text: siddhāntabhāṣyaṃ saṃdigdhatvādahetuḥ ananyathāsiddhāvanvayavyatirekau kāraṇatvāmātre pramāṇaṃ na tu kartā na cetanaścetanaṃ karaṇamityatretyarthaḥ // 2 //
children.translated_text: The <s>siddhānta</s>-<s>Bhāṣya</s> [says]: 'because of being doubtful, it is not a [valid] reason' — positive and negative concomitance that are not otherwise-established are a <s>pramāṇa</s> only for mere causality, but not in [establishing] that 'the agent is not the sentient [entity], [but rather] the sentient [entity] is the instrument' — this is the meaning. // 2 //
The prima facie view <s>sūtra</s> — 'na vi--t' (<s>sūtra</s> 2) // That whose presence and absence determine the presence and absence of cognition is the sentient [entity]. /
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.3: Because of the fixity of that very [sense-object], from the existence of the self (<s>ātman</s>), there is no refutation. //
And the fixity of sense-objects is contradictory [to the opponent's view] — because it would prove the non-sentience of the sense organs and the like — he says:
'What was stated' — thus.
'tadvya--dhaḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 3) //

children.translated_text: — indeed.
'Mere configuration, however' —
The meaning is: mere universal (<s>sāmānya</s>).

children.text: tadetaccetanavṛttaṃ dehādibhyo vyāvartamānaṃ tadatiriktaṃ cetanaṃ sādhayatīti sthitaṃ necchādyādhāratvaṃ dehādīnāmiti // 3 //
children.translated_text: This very [distinguishing mark] that belongs to the sentient [entity], being distinguished from the body and the like, establishes a sentient [entity] distinct from them — it is thus established that the body and the like are not the substrate of desire and the like. // 3 //

The explanation of 'omniscient' is: one who grasps all objects — one who grasps the objects of all sense organs; and the other sense organs and other <s>pramāṇas</s> have fixed objects — therefore even in that limited sense, it is established that [the self] is omniscient. / Therein, 'this is the distinguishing mark (<s>abhijñāna</s>)' — / An uncommon sign is called <s>abhijñāna</s>; and that cannot be denied, because it is established by experience. / The construction is: the distinguishing mark that belongs to the sentient [entity] is illustrated as undeniable. / 'Of non-fixed sequence' means of non-fixed order — this is the meaning. / 'A multitude of objects having multiple contents' — / that multitude of objects which has multiple referents is so described. / In some readings, 'a multitude of objects having multiple contents' — that is easy [to understand].
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.4: Because of the absence of sin (<s>pātaka</s>) in the burning of the body. //

children.text: sūtrāntaramavatārayati bhāṣyakāraḥ itaśca dehādivyatirikta ātmā na dehādisaṃghātamātramiti /
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> introduces another <s>sūtra</s>: 'And for this further reason, the self (<s>ātman</s>) is distinct from the body and the like — [it is] not a mere aggregate of body and the like.'
'śarīra--vāt' (<s>sūtra</s> 4) //

children.translated_text: Because of the impossibility of the production of an incapable moment being either dependent or independent of auxiliary causes.
And as this is so, it will be demonstrated in the context of the refutation of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>). // 4 //

Because of the consequence of the absence of sin in the destruction of life — / Although this is not an undesired consequence for the proponents of elemental sentience (<s>bhūtacaitanika</s>), nevertheless it should be viewed as directed against the <s>Śākyas</s> (Buddhists), for they accept sin arising from the destruction of life. / And thus, where one should say 'not cognition is the self,' the use of 'body and the like' is due to the diverse intentions of people — / if some proponent of elemental sentience does not accept sin arising from the destruction of life, let this refutation be understood as having that very meaning. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: / 'The fault of the arrival of what is not done and the destruction [of what is done]' — / (350/17) The meaning is: for one by whom the <s>karma</s> (action), namely the destruction of life, has not been done, there would be the arrival of sin; and for one by whom it has been done, there would be the destruction [of its result]. / The general rule is that the result enjoined by scripture [belongs] to the performer. But where the scripture declares the result of another [person's act] — as in the <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral rite), the <s>vaiśvānarī</s> sacrifice, and the like — there let the result of the <s>śrāddha</s> performed by the son accrue to the father, or the result of the <s>jāteṣṭi</s> (birth-sacrifice) performed by the father accrue to the son. / The impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is the cause of recollection, [also called] <s>bhāvanā</s>. / 'By which body' — / (351/2) The meaning is: a certain mental continuum identified by a particular body enjoys the result even when in another body. / 'Because of the reconnection of cognitions having a single cause' — / This has been said: just as in the bending of a dancer's eyebrow, there is the reconnection of many [cognitions] with respect to a single [cause]. / 'Because of the apprehension of all states' — / (352/7) Because of the apprehension of the parts of the seed in all states; but in the state of atoms, there would be non-apprehension. / Therefore, the parts of the seed, while undergoing transformation, do not reach the atomic state at the time of sprout-production; / rather, the composite wholes themselves undergo transformation — this is the meaning. / Thinking that the <s>siddhāntin</s> has said that the parts of the seed in their atomic state cannot produce the specific universal of seed-hood and the like, he shows [the objection]: / 'If so, then' — / He resolves: 'Not so, because of having been answered by this very [argument]' — / The division of the seed's parts into atoms has been prohibited by us in order to mark the parts as belonging to the class of seed-hood for the purpose of reconnection; but at the beginning of a cosmic cycle (<s>kalpa</s>), at the [first] creation, there is no reconnection of atoms — for it is not the case that only those [atoms] that produced the seed in a previous creation produce it now too, and not others — there is no such restriction of reconnection; / rather, [seeds] arise from other [atoms] too — this is the purport. / The Pailuka (atomist) raises a doubt: / 'If [one says]: the impossibility of transformation from the uncooked' — / He resolves: 'Not so, because of non-obstruction' — / The meaning is: composite substances have interstices. / Now, if this entry of parts [into interstices] were to be a destroyer of the substance, why would it not be so? — to this he says: / 'And if this entry of parts' — / (353/6) The water contained in a vessel would not remain at all upon the destruction of the vessel. / But when there are interstices, just so many drops of water move in the vessel as produce the tactile perception of coldness outside; and by a measure, there too, because of the power of temporal ripening, there may be displacement — but upon destruction, there would be sudden displacement of the water contained in the vessel — this is the meaning. / He raises a doubt regarding the perception [being] not the same in a transparent substance like a crystal vessel: / 'If [one says]: one would be happy, and that is its action' — / Although the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) are suffering, nevertheless, by the force of the impression of beginningless ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), this [being], wrongly identifying a single entity as the locus of the sense of 'I,' thinking 'may I be happy, may I not be unhappy,' acts out of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) — this is the meaning. / He refutes: 'Not so, because of not having been experienced' — / And just as momentary cognitions, being unaware of each other's states, are not capable of reconnection — this has been demonstrated by us in the context of the definition of the self. / 'Because of the non-arising of future [cognitions], from [their mere] existence' — (354/17) And it is not the case that a cognition-moment endowed with the maturation of celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>) and the like generates an incapable cognition-moment, and that [incapable one] does not produce another cognition — this is the non-arising of the future; and the destruction of the incapable moment is by its own nature — this is justified.
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.5: That absence [of sin] would follow even in the burning of what possesses a self, because of the permanence of that [self]. //

children.translated_text: If such transformation — of the kind that exists in pots and the like, where upon the cessation of dark color there is the arising of red — does not [occur] in the self — if this is the doubt — this is the meaning.
He refutes:
'In the self too' —

children.text: na bāhyendriyagrāhya eva vikāro 'pi tu dharmāntarotpādamātraṃ taccātmanyapyastīti // 5 //
children.translated_text: Transformation is not only what is grasped by the external sense organs; rather, it is merely the arising of a different property — and that exists in the self too. // 5 //

The annihilationist (<s>vaināśika</s>), just as he has shown the impossibility of violence and its result for the <s>Naiyāyika</s>'s position, attempts to show the same for the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position too, and presents the prima facie view regarding violence and the possibility of its result. / 'This, however, is violence' — (355/7) '[of] the individual (<s>vyakti</s>)' — / The meaning is: the effect already exists and is merely manifested by the cause, not [newly] created when non-existent. / He resolves: 'No' — / This threefold transformation — of property (<s>dharma</s>), of characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and of state (<s>avasthā</s>) — does not differ from the permanent substratum (<s>dharmin</s>); so the impermanence of transformation is contradicted by the permanence of the substratum. / Or, if the impermanence of the substratum is accepted in order to avoid contradiction, the faults stated in the annihilationist's position would follow — this is the meaning. / 'Quality (<s>guṇa</s>)' — / Indeed, straightness and crookedness are qualities [that are] specific varieties of accumulation, conjunction, and separation; while the conjunction that produces a substance persists, they are experienced as subject to arising and passing away — this is as follows: / having applied this very refutation of the <s>Naiyāyika</s>'s position to the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position too, he asks the <s>Naiyāyika</s>: 'if so, then of the eternal self' — / (356/10) The <s>Naiyāyika</s> says: / 'Pleasure and pain' — / From the eternal self, through merit (<s>puṇya</s>) and demerit (<s>pāpa</s>), which are distinct [from the self], which are properties of the self and are impermanent — pleasure and pain, which are also properties of the self, are produced — this is the meaning. / What is said amounts to this: / The service of the permanent [self] is merely being the substrate of impermanent properties, not the making of its own permanent nature [into something else] — by which it would become impermanent. / And a property is different from the property-bearer, not [identical with] the nature of the property-bearer. / And just as, even when there is no difference in [the fact of being] different, the causal relation obtains only between fire and smoke, not between fire and a camel — because of the restriction of the nature of things — / so too, even when there is no difference in [the fact of being] different, the property-property-bearer relation obtains only between the self and merit/demerit, not between the self and space, or between merit and space — this much has been briefly indicated; the elaboration will come in the refutation of momentariness. / 'Because of inconclusiveness' — / The inconclusiveness is stated by the strength of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps the permanence of atoms accepted by the opponent — not [by accepting] that in the Buddhist doctrine the atom is permanent. / For this very reason, expressing dissatisfaction, he states the alternative establishment: / 'And of leather being impermanent' — / 'And because of the stability of stones and the like that possess that [quality]' — / There is no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever for destruction in the absence of a cognition of destruction. / And in stones and the like, no destruction is experienced prior to the separation of parts or [their] destruction — and momentariness will be refuted — this is the purport. / 'Of [atoms] whose effects have been produced, not producing other substances' — / (357/15) The distinction from the conjunction that produces the composite whole has been stated. / 'And the absence of an example for transformation' — / The meaning is: transformation of the nature of the property-bearer without the arising of a property and without the destruction of the property-bearer's nature. / He raises a doubt: 'If so, then' —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.6: Not [so], because of the killing of the substrate of the effect, the agent, and the <s>kārakas</s>. //

children.translated_text: [is not an agent]; and similarly, one who desires to act but, being lazy, does not exert effort — he is not an agent either.
'The co-occurrence of the experience of pleasure and pain' —
This should be understood as one's own pleasure and pain.

children.text: asti hi parakīyasukhaduḥkhasākṣātkāro yogināṃ na caite bhoginaḥ // 6 //
children.translated_text: For there is direct perception of others' pleasure and pain for <s>yogins</s>, but they are not the experiencers [of those]. // 6 //

'Either maiming or killing' — / (358/8) Just as one injures the body by striking it, so too one injures by destroying the eye and the like — / He asks: 'From what [evidence]?' — / When violence to the intrinsic nature is impossible, figurative violence is not justified — this is the intention aligned with the annihilationist's (<s>vaināśika</s>) view. / The reply: 'Because of the enjoyment of the fruit of violence' — / For the annihilationist too, there is no violence to the intrinsic nature of transient entities — therefore, 'the production of a different [entity] is violence' must be stated, because of the possibility of causal operation there. And thus, there too violence is figurative — since the figurative nature is the same in both [positions], / the position in which there is no fault of loss of what is done and arrival of what is not done should be accepted. / And that is the position of permanence [of the self] — / therefore, by elimination, that is established. / 'The co-occurrence (<s>samavāya</s>) of cognition, desire-to-act, and effort is agency' — / (359/3) For one who does not know the means and their operation, even though desiring to act, is not an agent; similarly, one who knows but does not desire to act
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.7: Because of the recognition by another [sense organ] of what was seen by [one side, e.g.,] the left [eye]. //
And for this further reason the self (<s>ātman</s>) is distinct from the body and the like — from what [evidence]?
'savya--t' (<s>sūtra</s> 7) //
'That very one at this time' —
He states the recognition that is born from the external sense organs as a determinate cognition (<s>vyavasāya</s>):
'This is that very same object' —
And the after-cognition of this very [external recognition] is prior [to the mental one]. // 7 //
Therein, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> shows that the recognition is a mental after-cognition (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>).
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.8: Not [so], because of the sense of duality with respect to a single [entity] in which bone, sinew, and flesh are interposed. //
He objects to this by [arguing] the unity of the eye:
'naika--t' (<s>sūtra</s> 8) //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.9: Because upon the destruction of one, the second is not destroyed, there is no unity [of the eyes]. //
He resolves:
'eka--tvam' (<s>sūtra</s> 9) //
The meaning is: plurality [is established] because of the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by destruction and non-destruction. // 9 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.10: Because of the apprehension of the composite whole even upon the destruction of a part, [the argument] is not a [valid] reason. //
The objector says:
'ava--tuḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 10) //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.11: Because of the contradiction with the example, there is no refutation.
The proponent (<s>samādhātā</s>) says:
Example... refutation (sūtra 11) //
