children.translated_text: And [it should] not [be objected that] when pressed by the bridge of the nose, there would be the unwanted consequence of the error of seeing double moons for all people at all times and in all places.
Adventitious pressing is the cause of error, not what is natural — this is postulated from the observation of the effect. //11//

He states the third explanation:
'Or alternatively, because of the non-restriction of the destruction of one [eye]' —
If [the eye] were one, there would be no restriction in the destruction of the eye:
[one could not say] 'of the left eye only, not the right' —
because, being one, upon the destruction of the left [eye], the destruction of the right too would follow.
But this restriction is observed.
Therefore, there are two objects, separately covered and separately damaged.
Moreover, if the eye is one, when pressed by the left bridge of the nose, and then further pressed by a finger, [one sees] as though the single [object] appears as two.
When the pressing ceases, those two appearances are reunited into those [single] objects.
Similarly, when pressed by the bridge of the nose, [the eye] would show [things] as if split, and upon cessation [of the pressing], would reunite them — he says:
'Because of pressing — of the single eye' —
The meaning is: from the difference of the ray, there is difference of the sense-object contact.
The meaning is: because of contradiction with the example of the eye pressed by a finger.
'Either the destruction of one [causes] the destruction of the other' is the example;
'because of contradiction with that' — for that [one-eyed person] indeed, being seen, is [known] from definite ascertainment from one [direction] only — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> criticizes this entire discussion:
'Because of being already established, [there is] no need to begin [the discussion]' —
A different aggregation is appropriate in the treatise.
The intent is this:
A one-eyed person or one with one eye closed does not see in the same way as one with an impaired sense-organ.
If the eye were differentiated by the difference of left and right substrates, then this pair cannot be simultaneously controlled by the minute mind — therefore only one of the two should be controlled.
And thus, everyone would see with only one eye at a time — so one with one eye closed would have unequal apprehension compared to one with unimpaired eyes.
But this is not the case. If [the eye is] one, then [the visual faculty], issuing from both substrates, wherever controlled by the mind — that alone [functions] — therefore, for one with unimpaired eyes, there is no unwanted consequence of apprehension like one with impaired eyes.
Therefore, the eye is one with multiple substrates.
'And contradiction with the discussion [arises] because of the fivefold nature of the sense-organs' (360) —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.12: Because of the modification of another sense-organ.

children.text:
tadevaṃ pratisandhānadvāreṇātmani pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇayitvā anumānamidānīṃ pramāṇayati /
anumīyate cāyamiti /
( 361 / 15 ) vipratipannaṃ hi prati yatisandhānamuktaṃ paramārthatastu anubhavānusārasārgo 'yamiti mantavyam //
children.translated_text:
Thus, having validated direct perception as a <s>pramāṇa</s> for the self through the door of reconnection (<s>pratisaṃdhāna</s>), he now validates inference.
'And this is inferred' —
(361/15) For the reconnection was stated with respect to one who is in disagreement [about the self]; but in ultimate reality, this should be understood as following experience. //
Sense-organ... [modification] (sūtra 12) //

children.text: kasya cidamlacirabilvāderanubhūtasya tena sahacaritaṃ rūpaṃ vā gandhaṃ vā 'nubhavati /
children.translated_text: When someone experiences the color or smell associated with some sour <s>cirabilvā</s> fruit and the like that has been previously tasted,

children.text: atha tatsahacaritaṃ rasamanusmarati smṛtvā cecchati icchāto rasanendriyavikāro dantodakasaṃplavalakṣaṇaḥ pravartate taddarśanāccāsyecchānumīyate icchayā ca smṛtiḥ seyaṃ smṛtirasatyātmani sarvendriyaviṣayavedini na bhavitumarhatīti // 12 //
children.translated_text: then he remembers the taste associated with that [fruit]; having remembered, he desires [it]; from the desire, a modification of the taste sense-organ — characterized by salivation and watering of the teeth — occurs; and from observing that, his desire is inferred, and from the desire, [his] memory. This memory, in the absence of a self that cognizes the objects of all sense-organs, cannot exist. //12//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.13: Not [so], because memory has what-is-to-be-remembered as its object.
This is the objection-<s>sūtra</s>.
Not... memory (sūtra 13) // Memory could make the self known either as a cause

children.text:
viṣayatveca vā /
na tāvatkāraṇatvena tasyāḥ saṃskārakāraṇatvāt /
na viṣayatvena smartavyaviṣayatvāt /
smṛtācca tasmādindriyāntaravikārotpattirityarthaḥ
// 13 //
children.translated_text:
or as an object.
Not as a cause, because [memory's] cause is the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) [alone].
Not as an object, because [memory] has what-is-to-be-remembered as its object.
And [the sense-organ modification arises] from the remembered [object] — therefore, 'because of the modification of another sense-organ' — this is the meaning.
//13//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.14: Because of the existence of that [memory] as a quality of the self, there is no refutation.

He resolves:
That... refutation (sūtra 14) //

children.text: asatyātmani smṛtyanutpattindarśayitvā smartavyārthaviṣayaiva smṛtirnātmaviṣayeti pūrvapakṣiṇo 'vathāraṇaṃ khaṇḍayati /
children.translated_text: Having shown the non-arising of memory in the absence of the self, he demolishes the prima facie view that memory has only the object-to-be-remembered as its object, not the self.
'And because of the non-enumeration of the object of memory' (sūtra 15) //

children.text:
mānasānuvyavasāyajanitasaṃskārakāraṇāsu catasṛṣvapi smṛtiṣu nārthamātraṃ viṣayo 'pi tu jñānajñātṛjñeyāni sarva eva viṣayāḥ caturṣu vākyeṣu ekatra jñānaṃ kriyā kārakānniṣkṛṣṭā yathā amuṣmin mama jñānamabhūditi agṛhyamāṇo 'pyarthaḥ smṛtisannidhāpanādamuṣminnityucyate kārakādaniṣkṛṣṭāpyekatra pūrvāparībhūtabhāvanāpradhānā jñānakriyāgamyate ajñāsiṣamahamamumarthamiti /
anyatra tu jñānabhāvane kārakādaniṣkṛṣṭe katṛpradhāne yathā jñātavānahamamumarthamiti /
anyatra jñānabhāvane kārakādaniṣkṛṣṭekarmapradhāne yathā 'sāvartho mayā jñāta iti /
samānārthamiti /
jñānajñeyajñātṛprakāśanaṃ samānamityarthaḥ /
evaṃ tāvadagṛhyamāṇer 'the smṛtiḥ pradarśitā /
ata pratyakṣer 'the smṛtiḥ pradarśyate /
atha pratyakṣer 'tha iti /
smṛtiriti pratyabhijñānamāha smṛticchāyāvāhitvāt /
adrākṣamiti /
pūrvārthamarthadarśanaṃ parāmṛṣapi tenārthadarśanānubhavaḥ kalpyatāmanubhavakalpanā tu kutastyetyata āha /
na khalvasavidite sve darśane iti /
api tvarthadarśanaṃ taddarśanaṃ ca saṃvidite evetyarthaḥ /
kuta etadityata āha /
etadadrākṣamiti /
yasmādanubhavapuraskṣaraṃ yadatrādrākṣamiti bhavati nūnaṃ tatrānubhavaprathā 'pyabhūditi kalpanīyamityarthaḥ /
ito 'pi na śarīraguṇaḥ smṛtiḥ bālye anubhūtasya vārdhake smaraṇāt /
anyaddhi bālaśarīramanyacca vṛddhaśarīramiti /
āstāṃ tāvatpratyabhijñātaṃ,
sādṛśyamapi durvijñānam /
na ca paramāṇūnāṃ caitanyaṃ, te hi pratyekaṃ vā cetayeran militā vā /
pūrvasmin kalpe anekacaitanye ekasmin śarīre naikamityaniyamo bhavet /
na hi nānācetanānāmaikamatyaniyamo dṛṣṭaḥ
militānāṃ tu caitanye paramāṇūnāmāvāpodvāpabhedena melakaspaya nānātvātsa evānyopalabdhasyānyena smṛtyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ /
tasmānna śarīrādhārā cetaneti /
pareṣāṃ kārikāṃ dūṣayati vārtikakāraḥ /
etena na taccakṣuṣi norūpa iti pratyuktam /
( 263 / 6 ) ātmanaḥ pāriśeṣyātsiddheḥ smṛtyādhāratvavyutpādanenetyarthaḥ /
yatrādhikaraṇe tajjñānaṃ niṣṭhitaṃ bhavenna tadadhikaraṇamasti na ca nāstīti vyāhatam /
syādetad nāyaṃ viśeṣapratiṣedho na cakṣuṣi vijñānaṃ na rūpa iti, kiṃ tu ye cakṣurādyāśrayaṃ vijñānaṃ manyante tanmataṃ pratiṣidhyate /
ādhāravattaṃ tu na pratiṣiddhamaprasaktatvādityata āha /
kasya veti /
api caiṣā kārikā ātmābhāvavivakṣayā prayuktā ātmasattvameva pratipādayanto vivakṣitaviruddhetyāha /
ayaṃ ca vijñānasyeti /
tadevaṃ bhāṣyamatenendriyāntaravikārāditi sūtraṃ vyākhyāya vārtikakāraḥ svamatena vyācaṣṭe /
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the <s>sūtra</s> 'because of the modification of another sense-organ' according to the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains it according to his own view.
'Or alternatively, of one' —

children.text: uktameva pratisaṃdhānaṃ punanindriyāntaravikāradvāreṇa darśayati sūtraṃ yathā ca pratisaṃdhānaṃ dehendriyādivyatiriktamātmānaṃ pratipādayati tathā 'dha stādeva vivṛtamityāha /
children.translated_text: He shows the same reconnection (<s>pratisaṃdhāna</s>) again through the door of the modification of another sense-organ. And just as the reconnection establishes the self as distinct from body, sense-organs, and the like — that has been explained from this very [perspective] — he says:
'By the reasoning already stated.' //12-15//

In all four types of memory — generated from the impression produced by mental reflective cognition (<s>mānasānuvyavasāya</s>) — not the object alone is the content, but cognition, the cognizer, and the cognized — all of these are contents. In four [grammatical] sentences: in one, when the cognition is extracted as the action and the <s>kārakas</s> [are separated], as in 'I had a cognition of that [object]' — even though the object, not being explicitly grasped, is brought near through the proximity of the memory, it is expressed as 'of that [object].' In another, where the cognition-action is not extracted from the <s>kārakas</s>, [it is] predominantly the past-future <s>bhāvanā</s> (bringing-into-being) [expressed as]: 'I knew that object.'
In another, [with] the cognition-<s>bhāvanā</s> not extracted from the <s>kārakas</s>, predominantly the agent: 'I was a knower of that object.'
In another, [with] the cognition-<s>bhāvanā</s> not extracted from the <s>kārakas</s>, predominantly the object: 'that object was known by me.'
'Having the same meaning' —
The illumination of cognition, cognized, and cognizer is the same — this is the meaning.
Thus, memory where [the self is] not explicitly grasped has been demonstrated.
Now, memory where [the self is] directly perceived is demonstrated:
'Now, in the sense of direct perception' —
By 'memory' he means recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), because it bears the trace of memory.
'I saw' —
He touches upon the earlier seeing of the object; thereby the experience of seeing the object is postulated. 'But whence is the postulation of experience?' — therefore he says:
'For surely, one's own seeing is not unseen' —
Rather, both the seeing of the object and the seeing of that [seeing itself] are known — this is the meaning.
'Whence is this?' — therefore he says:
'This [I] saw' —
Since the experience-preceded [cognition] 'I saw this' arises here, surely the spreading of experience too must have occurred there — this is the meaning.
For this reason too, memory is not a quality of the body: because of remembering in old age what was experienced in childhood. For the child's body is one thing and the old person's body another.
Setting aside recognition,
even similarity is difficult to discern [between them].
And atoms do not have consciousness; for they would be conscious either individually or collectively.
In the first alternative — many consciousnesses in one body — there would be no restriction that there is one [consciousness]; for the non-unanimity of multiple conscious entities has never been observed.
But if consciousness [arises] in the aggregate, since the aggregate of atoms varies with the addition and subtraction [of atoms], it being different [at different times], the same unwanted consequence follows — the absence of memory by one of what was experienced by another.
Therefore, consciousness does not have the body as its substrate.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> refutes the opponent's verse:
'By this, [the objection] "not in the eye, not in form" is answered.'
(263/6) The meaning is: by the demonstration that the self is established by the method of residual elimination through being the substrate of memory.
'The substrate in which that cognition is completed — it is not the case that that substrate exists, and it is not the case that it does not exist' — this is contradictory.
One might think: this is not a denial of a specific [substrate] — 'not in the eye is consciousness, not in form' — but rather, the view of those who hold consciousness to be dependent on the eye and the like is being denied; however, the having-of-a-substrate is not denied, because it is not under consideration — therefore he says:
'Of what, then?' —
Moreover, this verse, being uttered with the intention of denying the self, actually establishes the very existence of the self — [the opponent] states the opposite of what is intended — he says:
'And this, of consciousness' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.15: Not [so], because of the possibility of the causes of self-cognition [being] in the mind.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.16: Because of the tenability of the instrument of the knower's knowledge, [it is] merely a difference of name.

children.text:
matiḥ smṛtyanumānādijñānam /
yadyapi cedaṃ prātisvikasaṃskārādikāraṇakaṃ tathāpyavaśyametenendriyajena bhavitavyaṃ jñānatvādrūpādijñānavaditi, taccendriyamasati cakṣurādau bhāvānmateścakṣurādyatiriktaṃ mana
ityucyate /
nanu bhavatu karaṇāntaraṃ manaḥ tattu kathamindriyāntarasahakāri kathaṃ cāṇuparimāṇamityata
children.translated_text: Granted, let the mind be another instrument — but how is it an auxiliary to another sense-organ, and how is it of atomic magnitude? — therefore
he says:
'And that [is established] by the mark of the non-simultaneity of cognitions.' //15-16//

<s>Mati</s> (thought) is knowledge consisting of memory, inference, and the like.
Even though this [thought] is caused by its own particular impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) and the like, still it must necessarily be produced by a sense-organ, because of being a cognition — like the cognition of color and the like. And that sense-organ, since it exists in the absence of the eye and the like, and since <s>mati</s> exists [even then] — [that sense-organ] distinct from the eye and the like is called the mind (<s>manas</s>).
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.17: And the restriction [of the mind to one cognition at a time] is without [need for further] inference.

children.text:
vārtikaṃ yadi sarvaṃ vijñānaṃ samādhanamucyate manasyapīti /
( 364 / 17 ) na ca tatra mana eva karaṇamātmani vṛttivirodhāditi tadanyasya karaṇatve tajjñānāyāpīndriyāntaramupāsanīyamityanavasthā,
anindriyajatve tu matāvapi saṃskārādyeva kāraṇamastīti kṛtaṃ manaseti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati -- omitīti /
yathā kāraṇasattayā kāryaṃ janitaṃ kāraṇaṃ jñāyate evaṃ manaḥsattayā manoliṅgajñānaṃ janitaṃ mano jñāpayati /
tacca liṅgajaṃ manojñānaṃ manaḥsattāhetukam /
na ca svātmani vṛtivirodhaḥ
na hi manaḥsattāyāṃ manaḥkaraṇaṃ manojñāne vā manojñānaṃ karaṇaṃ yena svātmani vṛttivirodhaḥ syāt /
kevalaṃ vā manaḥ svajñāne karaṇaṃ yenaikatra karmakaraṇatve syātām /
api tu manojñāne liṅgajñānasahitaṃ manaḥ karaṇaṃ tatsvarūpaṃ tu liṅgajñānasāhityāditi na svātmani vṛttivirodhaḥ /
nāpyekasyava kevalasya karmakaraṇabhāva
iti bhāvaḥ /
syādetad liṅgajñānasahitasya manasaḥ karaṇatve mā bhūdekasyaiva karmakaraṇabhāvaḥ svarūpeṇa karmatvāda liṅgajñānasāhityena ca karaṇatvāt /
yadā tu yoginā pratyakṣeṇa mano gṛhyate tadā kathamekasya karmakaraṇabhāva
children.translated_text: But when the <s>yogin</s> grasps the mind by direct perception, how then [is the problem of] a single [entity] being both object and instrument [resolved]?
Therefore he says:
'For one whose mind is directly perceptible.' //17//

The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'if all cognition is called a settled state, then [this applies] to the mind too' —
(364/17) And therein, the mind alone being the instrument — because of the contradiction of operating upon itself — if another instrument is required for the cognition of that [mind], then for the cognition of that [other instrument] too, yet another sense-organ must be postulated — and thus there is an infinite regress.
But if [the mind's self-cognition] is non-sensory, then even for <s>mati</s> (thought), the impression and the like alone are the cause — so what need is there for the mind? — this is the import.
He resolves: 'yes' —
Just as the existence of a cause is known through the production of an effect, so too the existence of the mind, through producing the cognition that is the mark of the mind, makes the mind known.
And that cognition — born of the mark — of the mind, is caused by the existence of the mind.
And there is no contradiction of operating upon itself —
for it is not the case that the existence of the mind is the instrument in the cognition of the mind, or that the cognition of the mind is the instrument in [another] cognition of the mind — which would cause the contradiction of operating upon itself.
The mind is merely the instrument in its own cognition — [but] that would [require] the same [entity] to be both object and instrument [in a single act].
Rather, the mind together with the mark-cognition is the instrument in the cognition of the mind; and its own nature is [known] from its association with the mark-cognition — therefore there is no contradiction of operating upon itself.
Nor is there the state of a single [entity] being both object and instrument — this is the import.
One might think: granted, when the mind together with the mark-cognition is the instrument, there is no [problem of] a single entity being both object and instrument — because [the mind] is the object by virtue of its own nature, and the instrument by virtue of its association with the mark-cognition.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.18: Because of the apprehension of joy, fear, and sorrow in a newborn, from the connection with the memory-trace of what was practiced in a previous life.

hānānaśakyateti /
(366/1) viṣayeṇa viṣayiṇīṃ buddhimupalakṣayati /
aniṣṭo viṣayo maraṇādistasya sādhanamahivnayāghrādistasyopanipātaḥ sannidhānaṃ tasminsati vyāghrādijihāsoraśakyahānametaditi buddhirbhayaṃ sā hi kasyāpi janayati /

ya iṣṭo viṣayaḥ prāptumaśakyastatra prārthanā idaṃ me upapadyatāṃ bhavatviti itthaṃbhūtā ceyaṃ prārthapanā na svarūpeṇa śoka ityata āha /

anarhaṇeneti yāvat /

pratyakṣagrahaṇena grahaṇamātramupalakṣayati /
tadanugṛhītaḥ smṛtyanugṛhītaḥ /
tadanusaṃdhānaviṣaya iti /
anusaṃdhīyataityanusaṃdhānaṃ smṛte yadanusaṃdheyaṃ tadviṣaya ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Even so, there would be no difference between memory (<s>smṛti</s>) and recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>)
— therefore he says:
"Having as its object the being-such of a present, visible object" —

children.text: dṛṣṭo hi nirālambano bālaḥ skhalanmāturaṅkātpatanasyāniṣṭasādhanatvamanusmṛtyedaṃ ca patanamiti parāmṛṣya tasyāniṣṭasādhanatvamanuprāya rudanmāturmaṅgalyabhuraḥ- sūtraṃ vikṣipya hastau vepamāna upādadānaḥ tasyānayā ceṣṭavayā bhayaśokāvanumīyete ityarthaḥ // 18 //
children.translated_text: For a helpless child is observed — stumbling and falling from his mother's lap — recollecting that falling is a means of undesirable [consequence], and recognizing "this is [indeed] falling," and then inferring its undesirable consequence, he cries, pulls at his mother's auspicious breast-ornament, and trembles while grasping [her] with his hands — by this behavior of his, fear and grief are inferred — this is the meaning. //18//

Wishing to examine the other world (<s>paraloka</s>), which is conducive to prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) and final liberation (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) — the subject matter of the science — he states the doubt that is the ground for examination:
"But what is this" —
(365/8) Here the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, while criticizing the doubt, raises an objection against the commencement of a new topic:
"On this matter" —
By showing that the <s>ātman</s> is distinct from the body, sense-organs, intellect, and sensations, and by incidentally establishing the continuous identity of the single <s>ātman</s> even through the different stages of childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, the existence of the <s>ātman</s> after the destruction of the body has been demonstrated.
And that much serves our purpose — so what remains about which there is doubt and for the sake of which a new topic is commenced? — this is the meaning.
He resolves:
"It is not [merely] commenced" —
Even though the distinctness from body and the like is established and the continuity through childhood and the like is established, [the question remains:] does this <s>ātman</s> exist only as long as the bodily continuity lasts — from the origination of the body to death — or does it continue even when the bodily continuity has ceased?
This deliberation has not yet been resolved — therefore this topic is commenced for its resolution — this is the meaning.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: "from the difference of bodies" —
The fifth case-ending is due to the elision of the <s>lyap</s> suffix.
The meaning is: having considered the difference of bodies in childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, the continued existence [of the <s>ātman</s>] is established from the recognition [of self-identity].
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]:
"Upon the attainment of the desired object that is longed for" —
Where one should say "upon the attainment of the desired object," the inclusion of the word "longing" (<s>prārthanā</s>) indicates the superlative degree of desirability.
Not upon the attainment of what is [merely] desired, but upon the attainment of what is most desired — therefore the meaning is: upon the attainment [of what is most desired], when there is longing for the desired object.
"The impossibility of avoidance" —
(366/1) By "object" he figuratively refers to the cognition that has it as its object.
An undesired object is death and the like; its means is a snake, tiger, and the like; their encounter is proximity. When that occurs, the cognition "this impossibility of avoiding the desire to flee from the tiger and the like" — that cognition is fear (<s>bhaya</s>); for it arises in anyone.
Grief (<s>śoka</s>) is the longing for the unattainable when separated from a desired object.
For that very person, the longing directed toward what is unattainable for him is grief —
what is a desired object that is impossible to attain, the longing directed toward it — "may this be mine, let it be so" — and since this kind of longing is not grief in its own nature, therefore he says:
"When there is separation from a desired object" —
meaning: by virtue of unworthiness.
The meaning, then, is this: grief is the cognition of the impossibility of attaining [what is desired] when separated from what is desired.
The unworthiness indicates the cognition of impossibility of attainment in one who grieves.
"The cessation of perceptual cognition" —
By the word "perceptual" he figuratively refers to apprehension in general.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.19: Just as there is modification (<s>vikāra</s>) in lotuses and the like — blooming and closing — so too is [the soul's] modification. //

children.translated_text: Pots and the like too, at the first moment [of their existence], are incorporeal — for corporeality (<s>mūrti</s>) is a specific measure (<s>parimāṇaviśeṣa</s>), and qualities do not arise simultaneously with the substance — therefore "always" is said, to exclude that [objection]. //19//

"Because of being qualified by what is observed" —
(367/14) The meaning is: the cause-effect relation, being qualified — i.e., established — by observation, cannot be set aside.
Now, the inference for the origination and destruction of the <s>ātman</s>:
What undergoes modification is subject to origination and destruction, as is observed — like a lotus. And the <s>ātman</s> is such [i.e., it undergoes modification]. Therefore it is impermanent — this is the meaning.
If mere arising of properties is modification, that would be inconclusive (<s>anekānta</s>), since it occurs in space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like too. And because of the difference between a property and its possessor, the arising and cessation of a property cannot be attributed to its possessor — therefore there is no inference of impermanence from modification.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.20: Not [so], because the modifications of what is composed of five [elements] are caused by the seasons of heat, cold, and rain. //
The modifications of lotuses and the like, which are composed of five [elements] (<s>pañcātmaka</s>), are called "modifications of what is composed of five elements" — this is [the meaning]. //20//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.21: Because of the desire for breast-milk, which is accomplished through practice in a previous life (<s>pretyāhāra</s>). //
"For the purpose of specifying what has been generally understood" —

Iron... approach (sūtra 22) // The previous practice based on memory-connection alone is not the cause of activity.
Because of the absence of that [memory-connection] in the approach of iron to a magnet.
And if the child had a memory-connection based on previous practice, then those born blind and deaf would also describe the smells and touches experienced since birth, as well as the colors and touches experienced in other births — this is the intent.

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.23: Not [so], because of the absence of activity elsewhere. //

children.translated_text:
The contemplation of a previously experienced object" —
A flow of memories directed toward a single object, uninterrupted by cognitions of a different kind, is contemplation (<s>cintana</s>),
and that [contemplation] occurs after the experience — hence "re-contemplation" (<s>anucintana</s>),
and that does not occur without the memory [of it]; for indeed, there is no flow without something that flows — that very re-contemplation, having the purpose of longing for the previously experienced object, is volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>); longing is volition, and that is directed toward a previously experienced object
— this is the meaning.
Now, if the sensory experience of objects in this very life, together with the ascertainment of desirable means [established] through positive and negative concomitance, is the cause of attachment, why is it not the cause of attachment? — to this the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says:
"Not for those incapable of apprehending objects" —
By this, the <s>Bhāṣya</s> statement "and the previous experience of objects in another birth" is explained. //25// Here the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads] "this is a restatement of what has been stated."
Its meaning: this objection has been stated by the example of the magnet; nevertheless, its restatement serves the purpose of illustration.
Previously, the magnet was the illustration; now, the colors and the like of pots and the like being produced are the illustration — for that purpose — this is the meaning.
Because the restatement of the objection has been stated, the refutation too is a restatement of what has been stated.
"Because of being constituted by that" — attachment [arises] —
(370/3) Having conceded [for argument's sake] that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) is the cause of attachment and the like, the refutation was stated [above]; but in ultimate truth, attachment [arises] "because of being constituted by that" — this is the meaning.
This might be [objected]: if attachment and the like arise from the memory-connection of previous practice, then after a human birth, one who has attained the state of a camel should have attachments corresponding to what is appropriate for human birth — due to the immediacy of the human-birth dispositions — and not attachments corresponding to the camel state, since the camel species is separated from him by hundreds of births of different kinds.
To this he says:
"Because of the specific birth" —
Because <s>karma</s> (action) is the awakener of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), by the <s>karma</s> whose purpose is the camel birth, even the camel-disposition that is separated by hundreds of births is awakened — but not the human disposition, even though immediate, because it is overpowered by the death-[process] — this is the import.
//24//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.25: Is [the soul's] origination like the origination of a substance possessing qualities? //

children.translated_text: Objection: let the [argument] "like the origination of a substance possessing qualities" not be inconclusive in the thesis-proving position; but in the position of raising an inconclusiveness-charge, what is the fault? — to this the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says:

— this is [the meaning]. //25//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.26: Not [so], because attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the like are caused by volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>). //

// Moreover, even though [all people] are equal in humanity, because of the observation of differences in the degrees of intelligence and understanding, one should postulate practice in a previous life. For even now, the practice of scripture, enhancing the intelligence directed toward its subject matter, is experienced through positive and negative concomitance. Thus, for one who has not undertaken the practice of scripture in this life, the excellence of intelligence and understanding directed toward that subject matter makes known the excellence of practice in a previous life as its cause. For a person whose previous-life impressions have faded due to the intervening obstacle of hundreds of births in animal and other species, the deficiency in intelligence and understanding should be postulated. Therefore, the beginningless stream of the eternal <s>ātman</s>'s assuming and abandoning various bodies — bound by <s>karma</s> (action) and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — [continues] until final liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.27: The body is earthen (<s>pārthiva</s>), because of the apprehension of qualities other [than smell]. //

children.translated_text:
The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>, wishing to examine the body — which was mentioned immediately after the <s>ātman</s> — states the subsidiary connection:
"The connection of the conscious being with the body is beginningless" — this has been stated.
He states its utility for examination as a means to detachment (<s>nirveda</s>):
"By one's own <s>karma</s>" —
He states the doubt, which is the preliminary form of examination:
"Is it like the nose and the like?" —
The disputants who maintain that the body is constituted of one, two, three, four, or five elements — this is the dispute about their number.
Here the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> independently states the connection for the examination of the body:
"Immediately after the <s>ātman</s>" —
He states the connection according to the view of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>:
"Or alternatively" —
He states the purport of the subsidiary connection: "when that is being examined" —
The human body is earthen (<s>pārthiva</s>), because of possessing smell (<s>gandhavattvā</s>), like an earthen atom (<s>pārthiva paramāṇu</s>).
[Objection:] A cause is not the self (<s>ātman</s>) of the effect — so how is [the body] composed of a single element? — to this he says:
"Composed of a single element" means "having a single nature" — the nature of things is the universal (<s>jāti</s>) of what will come into being; [the body would be] of a single universal if its inherent cause were of a single universal — not otherwise — this is the meaning.
First, with a friendly intent, he presents the opponents' reasons as otherwise-established: "but indeed, this is not [refuted] by [the arguments] beginning with smell" —
(371/3)
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.28: [If] earthen, [it would be] watery or fiery, because of the apprehension of those qualities.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.29: And because of the apprehension of inhalation and exhalation, [the body is composed] of four elements.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.30: Because of smell, moisture, heat, spatial arrangement, and the providing of space, [the body is composed] of five great elements.

children.translated_text: Having stated the opponent's proof as otherwise-established, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> states the defeating [argument]; the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> restates that and explains. 'This indeed has many material causes' — because [a body] originated from earth and water would be smell-less, since a single smell that is a cause cannot originate [it]. The intent is as follows: first, two earthen atoms cannot originate a single dyad — because, even though the origination of that [dyad] is possible by virtue of their having form, taste, and touch, there would be the unwanted consequence of the absence of smell. Similarly, because of the single smell inherent in earthen atoms being incapable of originating [the body]. Nor is it proper that two earthen atoms and one water-atom, as three atoms, are capable of origination — and thereby the possession of smell would be established. For many atoms are incapable of origination. As follows: three atoms do not originate an effect-substance, because of the absurd consequence that a multitude-number would be appropriate for [entities with] atom-hood, like the collection of atoms contained in a pot. If they were capable of origination, then in the destruction of the pot, the succession of sherds, pebbles, and powder contained in the pot would not be apprehended. And since the incapacity of a dyad to be originated from atoms of different classes has been established, by that very example, origination from a different class should be denied elsewhere too. By this, the origination of the body from large earthen parts together with watery parts is also refuted — because the incapacity of different-class [elements] for origination has been ascertained in the exemplified subject. Thus, by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, twenty-six alternatives have been refuted. If, however, there were a single cause for each [element], then what would follow? — to this he says: 'but if there is a single cause.' (372/6) Since the single cause is eternal and non-dependent, there would be perpetual production of the effect. A substance perishes from the destruction of its cause or from disjunction of [the cause]; but there is no destruction of a single eternal cause; nor is there disjunction, because that [disjunction] requires a substrate consisting of a substance accompanied by a second [substance], and the single [cause] has no second. Because of the absence of a cause of destruction, [there would be] the absurd consequence of the eternal nature of what is produced — the form [quality], being unaccompanied, does not originate in a single [substrate] the form in the composite whole — therefore the composite whole would be formless; and thus, because of the absence of form and the impressions [produced by form], the composite whole would not be apprehended — this is the meaning. //28// //29// //30//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.31: And because of the authority of <s>śruti</s> (scripture).
Meaning: '<s>Spṛti</s>' [here means] origination.

children.text: nyāyasiddhamarthaṃ śrutirūpodbalayati na punarasya prāpikā sāṃkhyarāddhāntābalambanenāpyasyāḥ kathaṃ cidupapatteḥ // 31 //
children.translated_text: The <s>śruti</s> merely corroborates what has been established by reasoning; it is not the originator [of the proof]. Even by relying on the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine, this [scriptural passage] can somehow be made to fit. //31//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.32: There is doubt because of the apprehension [of the pupil image] in the dark pupil (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>), and also because of apprehension apart from it.

children.text:
uddeśakramānurodhāccharīrānantaramindriyāṇāṃ parīkṣāṃ pratijānīte bhāṣyakāraḥ /
athedānīmindriyāṇi prameyakramaṇeti /
tatra parīkṣāpūrvarūpaṃ saṃśayamāha /
kimāvyaktikāni āho svidbhautikānīti /
upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat /
yadāpi bhautikāni tadāpi kiṃ kṛṣṇasāraṃ yadetadupalabhyate tadevendriyam
āho tadadhiṣṭhānaṃ taijasamityapi saṃśayo draṣṭavyaḥ /
vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ /
tatra pūrvaḥ sāṃkhyanaiyāyikayorvipratipatteḥ /
uttarastu saugatanaiyāyikayoriti /
āvyaktikatvamāhaṅkārikatvaṃ draṣṭavyam /
ahaṅkārāddhi buddhivikārādvaikārikāpadekādaśendriyāṇi jāyanta iti sāṃkhyāḥ /
āvyaktikatvaṃ tvavyaktasya mūlakāraṇatvāduktam /
vipratipattibījaṃ pṛcchati /
kutaḥ saṃśaya iti vipratipattimāha kāraṇe kāryopacārāt /
uttaraṃ kṛṣṇasāre satīti /

children.translated_text: because of the apprehension in the dark pupil, the dark pupil itself is the eye — so say the Buddhists.
'And because of apprehension apart from it' — what transcends it, and that is derived from <s>ahaṅkāra</s>,
because <s>ahaṅkāra</s>, being all-pervading, cannot be obstructed.
If [the sense-organs were] elemental, there would be the unwanted consequence of obstruction by elemental [substances] such as glass, clouds, and coverings — so say the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>. //32//

In accordance with the order of enumeration, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> undertakes the examination of the sense-organs after [that of] the body — 'now, the sense-organs in the order of the objects of knowledge.' There he states the doubt, the preliminary form of the examination: 'are they non-manifest (<s>āvyaktika</s>) or elemental (<s>bhautika</s>)?' And this is illustrative. For even when they are elemental, there is a further doubt to be considered: is it the dark pupil that is apprehended that is itself the sense-organ, or is the luminous [element] that is its substrate [the sense-organ]? The doubt arises from disagreement. Of these, the first is from the disagreement between the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>; the latter is from the disagreement between the Buddhists and the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>. '<s>Āvyaktika</s>' should be understood as 'derived from <s>ahaṅkāra</s>' (ego). For from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> — which is a modification of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) — the eleven sense-organs of the <s>vaikārika</s> type are born: so say the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>. But '<s>āvyaktika</s>' has been said because of <s>avyakta</s> (the unmanifest) being the root-cause. He asks about the seed of the disagreement: 'whence the doubt?' He states the disagreement: 'because of the figurative attribution of the effect to the cause.' The answer: 'because of the apprehension in the dark pupil' —

children.text:
na pradīpādibhiranekāntāditi /
vartideśasyena piṇḍitena tejasā pradīpenānekāntāt /
prabhā hi visāriṇī tamarvaṃ prāpya prakāśayatiṃ na tu pradīpa ityarthaḥ /
viṣayībhāvāditi cediti /
utpādaviśeṣa eva sa tādṛk cakṣurarthakṣaṇayoryato 'prāptayorapi viṣayaviṣayibhāvādvedyavedakatvaṃ,
na cāyaṃ vyavahitaviprakṛṣṭayoriti na tayorvedyavedaka bhāva ityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti noktottaratvāt /
sa evārtho viprakaṣṭo na viṣayaḥ sannikṛṣṭaśca viṣaya ityekasya viṣayībhāvastadabhāvaścāyuktaḥ kṣaṇabhaṅgaśca niṣetsyata iti bhāvaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Not, because of inconclusiveness through lamps and the like' — because of inconclusiveness through the lamp, which is light (<s>tejas</s>) congealed in the region of the wick. For the radiance, being diffuse, reaching the darkness, illuminates — but not the lamp [itself] — this is the meaning. 'If because of becoming an object' — this is a particular origination, such that between the eye and the object, even though they do not come into contact, the subject-object relation arises because of the eye being an object — but this [relation] does not obtain between what is screened or distant — therefore there is no knower-known relation between them — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'not so, because [this has] already been answered.' That very object which is distant is not an object [of perception]; but the same [object] when proximate is an object — thus it is unjustified that the same [entity] both has and lacks object-status. And momentary destruction will be refuted — this is the import.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.33: Because of the grasping of the large and the small.
There, having raised the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> [view], he refutes the Buddhist position.
'Not elemental' — [the sense-organs are not elemental].

children.text: kṛṣṇasārādhikagrahaṇe vivakṣiter 'thagrahaṇaṃ saṃpātāyātaṃ na tu tadatra vivakṣitam asādhakatvāditi /
children.translated_text: Since the intention is the grasping of more than just the dark pupil, the word 'object' (<s>artha</s>) has been introduced for completeness, but it is not intended here, because it would not prove [the point].
Grain [and] sprout. //

children.text:
abhautikatvaṃ tu vpayāpakatvāditi /
( 374 / 2 ) tadyathā vijñānādyabhautikaṃ mahaccāṇu ca gṛhṇātītyarthaḥ /
ekadeśimatena dūṣaṇamāha /

sāṃkhyaḥ śaṅkate /
vṛttiriti /

yadyapi sāṃkhyīyarāddhānte dīrghāṃ śaṣkulīṃ bhakṣayato gugapadanekajñānotpattirabhimatā tathā pi kvacit kramo 'pi dṛśyate sa na syād
vṛttimato 'vasthāne tadabhinnā vṛttirapyavatiṣṭhata iti tanmātrādhīnotpattīnāṃ vijñānānāṃ kramo na syāditi bhāvaḥ /
ubhayaṃ neṣyata iti /
( 376 / 4 ) vṛttibhyo 'nanyatvaṃ vṛttimato neṣyate nāpi vṛttīnāmananyatvaṃ vṛttimata ityarthaḥ
// 33 //
children.translated_text: 'But being non-elemental is because of being all-pervading' — (374/2) just as cognition and the like, being non-elemental, grasp the large and the small — this is the meaning. He states a refutation from the partial view: 'not in earthen lamps and the like.' Now, if intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) illuminates both the large and the small, then what — does it not illuminate everything? — to this he says: 'of the object that is limited.' And there is no [question whether] the cognitions of abandoning, acquiring, and equanimity are small or large — this is the import. The <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (opponent) says: 'not even regarding the sense-organ, because of the same [difficulty].' Thus, having shown that the <s>ekadeśin</s>'s (partial-view-holder's) attribution of uncommonness is itself refuted even by the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s>, the <s>siddhāntin</s> says: 'not consisting of the non-elemental self, and being all-pervading.' The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> raises a doubt: 'the functions (<s>vṛtti</s>)' — the functions of the sense-organs, which are causes of knowledge, are being denied — this is the meaning. 'Because of the unwanted consequence of simultaneous multiple grasping' — although in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> established doctrine, the simultaneous arising of multiple cognitions is accepted — as when someone eats a long piece of food — nevertheless, sequence too is observed, and that would not [be possible]. For when the function-possessor remains in place, the function which is non-different from it also remains — and thus there would be no sequence in cognitions whose origination depends solely on the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) — this is the import. 'Neither is accepted' — (376/4) the non-difference of the functions from the function-possessor is not accepted, nor is the non-difference of the function-possessor from the functions — this is the meaning. //33//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.34: Because of the specific contact of the ray with the object, the grasping of that [object occurs].
The <s>Naiyāyika</s> refutes the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>. // Ray... grasping (sūtra 34) //

children.text:
āhaṅkārikatve cakṣurna pratihanyate yadi tat kācābhrapaṭalāntaritaprakāśavat kuḍyāntaritamapi prakāśayet /
na caivamasti,
tasmātkṛṣṇasārādhiṣṭhānaṃ teja eva bhautikaṃ prāpya gṛhṇāti kuḍyāntaritaṃ tvarthamaprāptaṃ na gṛhṇāti /
kācābhrapaṭalāntarite tu vakṣyati /
children.translated_text: If, being derived from <s>ahaṅkāra</s>, the eye is not obstructed, then it should illuminate [objects] behind a wall too, like light obstructed by glass and clouds. But it is not so — therefore, the [eye's] substrate being the dark pupil, light itself, being elemental, grasps [the object] by reaching it; but an object behind a wall, not being reached, is not grasped. As for [objects] obstructed by glass, clouds, and coverings, he will state:
'because of the assistance of the contact with more parts'
— thus.
The parts of the sense-organ [contact] the parts of the object; the parts of the sense-organ [contact] the object;
the parts of the object [contact] the sense-organ; the sense-organ [contacts] the object. //34//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.35: Because of the non-apprehension of that, [the argument] is not a valid reason.
'Because of the non-apprehension of that' —

What satisfies the conditions for being perceived (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>) yet is not perceived cannot be inferred — because there would be the unwanted consequence of inferring even human horns and the like — this is the meaning. //35//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.36: The non-apprehension by direct perception of what is being inferred is not a reason for [its] non-existence.
The resolution: 'not of what is being inferred' —

children.text: satyamanupalabdhinalakṣaṇaprāptamanupalabhyamānaṃ na śakyamanumātuṃ na tu mahattvādyevopalakṣaṇaprāpterapi tu rūpaviśeṣo 'pi /
children.translated_text: True, what satisfies the conditions for being perceived yet is not perceived cannot be inferred; but the conditions for being perceived are not only largeness and the like, but also a specific form (<s>rūpaviśeṣa</s>).

children.text: na cāsau viśeṣa udbhavasamākhyātaḥ kṛṣṇasārādhiṣṭhānaspaya cakṣuṣo 'stītyarthaḥ // 36 //
children.translated_text: And that specific [form] has not been established as manifest — [yet] it does belong to the eye whose substrate is the dark pupil — this is the meaning. //36//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.37: And because of the difference in substance, quality, and property, the condition for apprehension [varies].
The meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is: where there is apprehension, there is this [specific condition].

children.text: tato mahattvādiṣu madhye yatkiṃ cidekaṃ vaktavyaṃ sūtrakāreṇa yatropalabdhistatraitadityakasmādeva siddheranekopādānavaiyarthyaṃ tasmātsambhāvanāyogyatābhidhānapadaṃ sūtram //
children.translated_text: Since 'where there is apprehension, there is this' is established without further ado, the <s>sūtrakāra</s> should state just one from among largeness and the like — [but] the mention of many would be purposeless. Therefore, the <s>sūtra</s> is a statement of the conditions worthy of consideration.

children.text: nanu yathāśrutaṃ mahattvādyupalabdhikāraṇamasti cākṣuṣasya raśmeriti kasmādayaṃ nopalabhyata ityata āha /
children.translated_text: Now, according to the literal reading, largeness and the like are the causes of apprehension; and the visual ray exists — so why is it not apprehended? — to this he says:
'Because of the difference in substance, quality, and property' (sūtra 37). //37//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.38: The arrangement of the sense-organs, caused by action, is dependent on the purposes of the person (<s>puruṣa</s>).

children.text:
anekaraśmisannidhāne sparśasyodbhūtau satyāṃ dravyaṃ dahyeta rūpodbhūtau satyāṃ vyavahitatvādādau nipatitena cakṣurantareṇa dravyasyānupalabdhyā bhavitavyam /
śaṅkate athāneketi /
( 379 / 9 ) nānānayanāvayavaireko 'sau nayanāvayavyārabhyataityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He refutes: 'this being so' —
that single composite whole of the eye, originated by many parts of the eye, would be common to those who have complete or incomplete eyes
— and thus the apprehension would be equal — this is the meaning.

When many rays are proximately present, if touch were to become manifest, the substance would be burned; if form were to become manifest, first the [intervening] substance, being screened, would have to be not-apprehended by another eye — [this is the problem]. He raises the doubt: 'now, many' — (379/9) meaning: by many parts of the eye, that single composite whole of the eye is originated.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.39: Just as the non-apprehension of a midday-meteor's light, so is the non-apprehension of that [ray].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.40: Not [so], because of non-apprehension even at night.

children.text:
na hi yadyasyābhibhāvakaṃ tattasya vyañjakamiti /
( 380 / 17 ) rātrau yad loṣṭatejaso 'bhibhāvakaṃ divā kathaṃ tadevāsya vyañjakaṃ yena tadabhāvādrātrau loṣṭatejo nopalabhyeta ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: It is understood from the word 'also' (<s>api</s>)
— thus.
'Not even at night' — [this is understood] from the word in the <s>sūtra</s> — this is the meaning. //39-40//

For it is not the case that what overpowers something is also the manifester of that [same thing]. (380/17) What overpowers the light of a clod [of fire] during the day — how can that same [sunlight] be its manifester, such that in its absence at night the light of the clod would not be apprehended? — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.41: Because of the dependence on external light for the apprehension of an object, the non-apprehension is due to non-manifestation.

children.text:
so 'yaṃ cakṣuṣo raśmiḥ kimabhāvānnopalabhyate kiṃ vā 'nudbhūteratrāha bhāṣyakāraḥ upapannarūpā ceyamanabhivyaktito '
nupalabdhiriti yojanā /
anabhivyaktito 'nudbhūterityarthaḥ /
atra heturbāhyaprakāśānugrahādviṣayopalabdheḥ
viṣayaśca svaṃrūpamātmano 'nyacca /
etaduktaṃ bhavati yadupalabdhau bāhyaprakāśamanugrāhakamapekṣate tasyānudbhūterevānupalabdhirna tvabhibhūteḥ
yathā hemante viṣaktāvayavasyāpyasya dravyasya /
āpyaṃ hi dravyaṃ viṣaktāvayavaṃ svaviṣayopalabdhau bāhyaprakāśānugrahamapekṣamāṇaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ cakṣurapi ca viṣayopalabdhau bāhyaprakāśamapekṣate nirāloketasyāpravṛtteḥ /
children.translated_text: For a watery substance with congealed parts, requiring the auxiliary of external light for the apprehension of its own object, has been observed; and the eye too requires external light for the apprehension of objects — because it does not function in the absence of light.

children.text: tasmādviṣayopalabdhau bāhyaprakāśāpekṣatvāttadanudbhūtyā na pratīyate na punarabhibhūtyeti siddhaṃ prakṛtam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of requiring external light for the apprehension of objects, [the ray] is not perceived due to non-emergence, not due to being overpowered — thus the point under discussion is established.
This the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains:
'Of that which exists' — //41//

This ray of the eye — is it not apprehended because of non-existence, or because of non-manifestation? Regarding this, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: 'and the non-apprehension due to non-manifestation is well-established in this form' — this is the construction. 'Due to non-manifestation' means 'due to non-emergence.' Here the reason: 'because of the dependence on external light for the apprehension of an object.' And the object is its own form and what is other than itself. What is said amounts to this: that which, for its apprehension, requires external light as an auxiliary — its non-apprehension is due to non-emergence only, not due to being overpowered — just as a watery substance with congealed parts [is not apprehended] in winter.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.42: And because of overpowering at the time of manifestation.

children.translated_text: The construction is: the reason for establishing [plurality], which is other than [i.e., immediately after] the refutation, is what is immediately [subsequent].
'Or alternatively' —
A negative-concomitance reason (<s>vyatirekī hetu</s>) establishes one of two contradictory [alternatives] by the negation of the other.
Just as by the negation of non-self-hood (<s>nairātmya</s>), the living body is [established as] possessing a self. // 54 //

Since from the very refutation of unity, plurality will be established by elimination — to this he says: 'the action is not without a means of proof' — / (389/7) 'And how [is] unity [established]?' — / It has been said that the thesis [of unity] cannot be refuted. / He asks: / 'How then?' / The answer: / 'From refutation, what is immediately [next]' — / Although the ablative case is not traditionally recalled in the usage of the word 'immediately' (<s>anantara</s>), nevertheless, by the elliptical supply of the word 'other' (<s>anya</s>), the ablative should be explained.
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.55: Because of the fivefold nature of the sense-object. //
He raises an objection to the <s>sūtra</s>:
'But this <s>sūtra</s>' —

children.text: eṣa nyāyo mayā vāco bhaṅgyā sūtrita
children.translated_text: 'This reasoning has been formulated by me through an indirect mode of speech'
— this is the meaning. // 55 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.56: Not so, because of the multiplicity of objects of that. //
The prima facie objector's <s>sūtra</s>:
'na ta--t' (<s>sūtra</s> 56) //
He raises an objection to the prima facie view: 'not, because of contradiction' —
The prima facie objector's resolution: 'not, because it is not without a means of proof.' // 56 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.57: Because of the non-distinction of smell-hood and the like from smell and the like, there is no refutation. //
The <s>siddhānta</s> — 'gandha--dhaḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 57)
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.58: Because of the non-distinction of being-an-object, [there is] unity. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.59: Not from [the distinctions of] cognition, characteristic, substrate, movement, configuration, universal, and fivefold [classification]. //

'Desirable, undesirable, and to-be-ignored' —

children.translated_text: The experience of the world is that action is suffering; but when [something is recognized as] to-be-ignored, that [suffering] does not befall him. // 58-59 //

'Whose substrate is different' — / (391/10) 'Different' means 'fixed.' / What is said amounts to this: the substrate of the manifester of color is only the pupil of the eye (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>), not the ear-lobe and the like — and similarly in other cases too. / But for the <s>siddhāntin</s> whose substrate is non-different — and thus, there is also non-difference of the sense organ belonging to that substrate — for him, even upon the destruction of one substrate, although the sense organ belonging to it is destroyed, the sense organ belonging to another substrate persists; so it is not the case that upon the destruction of one substrate, the destruction of all substrates and hence the destruction of all sense organs — characterized as
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.60: Because of the apprehension of the specific qualities of the elements, [the sense organs have] identity [with those elements]. //

children.translated_text: the uncommon effect of these must be stated.
It has been stated: 'speech, grasping, locomotion, excretion, and pleasure are the [functions] of the five [action-organs].'
But grasping, locomotion, and excretion can also be performed by the mouth, hands, and the like.

children.text: api cāsti kaṇṭhahṛdayāmāśayapakvāśayādīnāṃ giraṇāditattadasādha raṇaṃ kāryamiti tānyapīndriyāṇi prasajyeranniti tasmādyatkiñcidetadapīti // 60 //
children.translated_text: Moreover, the throat, heart, stomach, intestines, and the like have their own uncommon functions such as swallowing and the like — so they too would have the consequence of being sense organs — therefore, whatever this [argument is], it is [only] this much [i.e., inconclusive]. // 60 //

Therein, the organ of smell is earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>), because among smell, color, taste, and touch, it specifically manifests smell — like an external earthy [substance]. / Just as rooster-droppings and the like, being earthy, are manifesters of musk-smell — this is the meaning. / And there is no inconclusiveness through heat (<s>ātapa</s>) — / for heat is not a manifester of smell; rather, the smell, being overpowered by water, is not apprehended in substances; [heat] merely removes the water, but does not manifest the smell of the substance — therefore there is no inconclusiveness. / Similarly, the sense organ of taste is watery (<s>āpya</s>), because among smell and the like, it specifically manifests taste — / like a drop of water trickling between the teeth. / For one whose mouth is dry does not experience the taste of a sweetmeat and the like. / Similarly, the eye is fiery (<s>taijasa</s>), because among smell and the like, it specifically manifests color — like a lamp and the like. / Similarly, the sense organ of touch (skin) is airy (<s>vāyavīya</s>), because among smell and the like, it specifically manifests touch alone — like a fan whose waving manifests the touch of hundreds of drops of perspiration. / The mention of 'specifically' (<s>niyama</s>) is for the purpose of excluding the mind (<s>manas</s>). / And the [word] 'among' (<s>madhye</s>) is for the purpose of establishing exclusion — / otherwise, the exclusive [attribution] of smell-hood and the like as manifesting powers of the nose and the like would not be [obtained]. / This is what he states: / 'Similarly in the remaining [cases]' — / (392/19) And thus, by the fivefold nature of the sense organs, the refutation of the sense-organ-status of the hands, feet, anus, genitals, and speech is also indicated — because of the absence of the definition of a sense organ. / For the definition of a sense organ is: that which is conjoined with the body, which is distinct from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) and defects (<s>doṣa</s>), and which is a direct instrument of cognition — that is a sense organ; and this [definition] does not apply to the hands and the like. / 'These are action-organs (<s>karmendriya</s>)' — if so, / well then, a different definition of sense-organ-hood must be stated for them. / 'If [the definition is]: a sense organ is that which resides in the body and produces an uncommon effect' —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.61: Of earth — smell, taste, color, touch, and sound, up to touch. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.62: Of water, fire, and air — [the qualities are obtained] by removing the prior one successively; of space, the last [alone]. //

children.translated_text: Or let there be a reference with the comparative suffix (<s>tarap</s>); even so, there is no fault — he says:
'Let it be so' —
In some readings, 'or alternatively, the system' — as per the <s>Bhāṣya</s>,
the meaning is self-evident. // 61-62 //

Desiring to examine the definition of the object (<s>artha</s>) which has come in order, he reminds [us] of the definition of the object. / 'Smell and the like are the qualities of earth and the like — this has been enumerated' — / Where one should say 'defined' (<s>lakṣitam</s>), the confused expression 'enumerated' (<s>uddiṣṭam</s>) is used because of the generality [of the terms]. / Therein, he states the doubt, which is the preliminary form of examination: / 'And the enumeration is a directive (<s>niyoga</s>)' — / He states the nature of the directive and the like: / 'Therein, the directive' — / Thus, having deliberated, setting aside the directive and the collective, he adopts the alternative through two <s>sūtras</s>: 'therefore, for the purpose of qualification' — / (393/2) 'gandha---vyāḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 61), 'apta---raḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 62) / / 'For the purpose of qualification' — / The purport of the two <s>sūtras</s> has been stated; he now makes it explicit. / 'In the sense of restriction' — / In the subsequent [elements] — water and the like — there is a successive removal, one by one, of [the qualities] from smell and the like up to touch. / As follows: among the four [elements], there is a removal of smell [from water onwards] — and the smell that has been removed does not arise again — so in fire, which is subsequent to water, there is a removal of taste; / and similarly, when smell and taste have been removed, they do not arise again — so in air, which is subsequent to fire, there is a removal of color; / and similarly, when smell, taste, and color have been removed, they do not arise again — so in space, which is subsequent to air, there is a removal of touch. / This is what is said: 'one by one.' / The non-standard word 'uttara' (subsequent) means 'immediately next' (<s>anantara</s>); by that, even though the extraction is of many [elements], the meaning is appropriate.
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.63: Not [so], because of the non-apprehension of all qualities [in each element]. //
The prima facie objector raises the directive-view:
'na sa--bdheḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 63) //

children.text: pṛthivyādiprakṛtīnāṃ ghrāṇādīnāṃ gandhādiprativyaktiniyama evamupapadyate yadi gandhamātraguṇā pṛdhivī rasamātraguṇā āpa

and so on — but not otherwise.

children.text: anyathā tu pārthivena ghrāṇena gandhavadrasarūpasparśā api vyajyeran aviśeṣādityarthaḥ // 63 //

<s>NyS</s> 3.1.64: Because of the successively higher existence of qualities one by one in each, the non-apprehension of those in the higher [elements]. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.65: For the lower is pervaded by the higher. //
'viṣṭaṃ ṇa' (<s>sūtra</s> 65) //

children.translated_text: Although the relation [of pervasion] has two relata, there is not equal [pervasion] in both — just as in the relation of fire and smoke: it is otherwise for fire, for fire is the pervader — in smoke, the nature of being marked by smoke (<s>dhūmadhvaja</s>) exists and does not not exist; / but smoke is the pervaded — it exists only in fire and nowhere else. / Similarly, the lower — earth and the like — is pervaded (<s>viṣṭa</s>) by the higher — water and the like — earth does not exist without water and the like. / Therefore, in earth, the qualities of water and the like — taste and the like — are apprehended by restriction; but in water and the like, the qualities of earth are not [apprehended]. / Similarly, in water, the quality of fire and the like is explained. / 'Pervasion' (<s>viṣṭattva</s>) is a specific conjunction — pervasion — this is the meaning. / The <s>Bhāṣya</s>: 'and this [is seen] in the creation of the elements' — / In the <s>Purāṇas</s> that teach the creation of elements — 'not at this time' — / The meaning is: not now, because of non-experience [at present]. // 64-65 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.66: Not [so], because of the perceptibility of earthy and watery [things]. //
The <s>siddhāntin</s>, [being] a proponent of the alternative view, this
[he] refutes.
'napā--t' (<s>sūtra</s> 66) //

children.translated_text: because of the absence of a pervader-pervaded relation between those two.

children.text: dhūme ca gaganatalāvalambini bhūmiṣṭhena vahninā vyāpteragnerguṇāgṛhyeran tayorvyāpyavyāpakabhāvāt /
children.translated_text: And in smoke suspended in the sky, the qualities of fire would be grasped [even when] the fire is on the ground, because of the pervader-pervaded relation between those two.
Therefore, the conjunction with another [element] is the cause [of the apprehension of qualities]; and that [conjunction] is the same in both [cases]

children.text: iti tejasā saṃyuktasya vāyorapi rūpavattvena cākṣuṣatvaprasaṅga iti // 66 //
children.translated_text: — so there would be the consequence that air too, being conjoined with the fiery [substance], would be visible because of possessing color. // 66 //

For a threefold substance is accepted as visible: earthy, watery, and fiery. / Therein, if only what possesses color — the fiery — were visible, / the others, not possessing color, [would not be visible]. / And it should not be said that the visibility of the earthy and the watery is due to [their] contact with a substance possessing color — / for then even space and air would have the consequence of being visible, / since they too are in contact with the fiery [substance] that possesses color. / Or alternatively, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: because of the perceptibility of the difference of taste and the difference of color, whether of one kind or many kinds, which belong to earthy and watery [substances] — / 'Of the two tastes' etc., up to 'is not justified.' / He then states another interpretation: / 'Of the two touches' — / Because 'of the earthy and the watery' is merely illustrative, / the interpretation 'of the earthy and the fiery' is also stated. / He states yet another interpretation: / 'Or alternatively' — / Because of seeing that the effect has fixed qualities, the cause too is inferred to have fixed qualities. / And there is not contact everywhere, such that the quality of one [element] is apprehended in another — because of the observation of distinction, i.e., non-contact. / He states another interpretation: / 'And it is seen' — / The 'and' (<s>ca</s>) has the sense of the alternative. / 'But the directive [view] is without inference' — he says: / 'Without inference, [the view that] the lower is pervaded by the higher — this' — / The directive means: smell alone belongs to earth, and so on. / There is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means) for that [directive], since only the <s>pramāṇa</s> that contradicts it has been stated. / Therefore, the creation of elements should be explained somehow figuratively. / 'Pervasion is conjunction, and that is equal in both' — / The quality of one [element] is apprehended in another — is that because of conjunction or because of pervasion? If because of pervasion, then the qualities of fire would not be grasped in a log conjoined with fire,
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.67: Because of the excellence of the prior qualities in each case, each [element] is predominated by that [quality]. //
'pūrva--nam' (<s>sūtra</s> 67) //

children.translated_text: "But one who [holds] that it is because of having smell as its [sole] quality" —

children.text: gandhamātraguṇatvodeva ghrāṇaṃ gandhasya vyajjakaṃ na tu mandhasyotkarṣādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: the nose is the manifester of smell merely because of having smell alone as its quality, not because of the excellence of smell.
For that theorist, there follows the consequence of apprehending all the earthen qualities,
the consequence of [all earthen qualities] being graspable by the nose — this is the meaning. //67//

The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains the meaning of the word 'predominance': the capacity to grasp objects — smell and the like are the objects. That very capacity to grasp objects — whence does it arise? To this he says: "from the excellence of the quality, from the capacity for its manifestation." If the capacity to grasp objects is predominance, then all sense organs have that capacity — with this intention, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, not accepting the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>'s explanation, asks: "what is predominance?" (395/8) He answers according to his own view: "because of having four qualities" etc. What is being said is this: because the nose (<s>ghrāṇa</s>), being earthen, possesses four qualities and is thus predominant over the tongue and the like, which are watery and so forth, it does not lack the property of possessing smell, by which it would fail to grasp smell. But does the nose not also possess taste and the like in the same way, such that it would also grasp taste and the like? To this it is said: "from the excellence of the quality." Even though there is no difference in inherence for all [qualities], the nose has excellence only with respect to smell — therefore it grasps only smell. Thus, the statement of predominance is aimed at denying the absence of smell-possessing [in the nose], not at saying that the possession of smell is the operative cause for grasping smell; rather, the excellence of smell [in the nose] is established [as the operative cause]. Thereupon the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> asks about the meaning of the word 'excellence': "what is the excellence of quality?" The answer: "the capacity to manifest its own quality" — the own quality of the nose is smell; a smell of the same kind, even one inhering in sandalwood and the like, is called 'own.' But the nose does not manifest only its own smell; for the smell inhering in the nose, by the power of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit), has such a constructional difference that it manifests a smell of the same kind inhering in sandalwood and the like — just as the smell inhering in another earthen substance [manifests] the smell of musk and the like. For this very reason he says: "that quality by which a substance is made excellent — that [quality], because of being a manifester of [qualities] of the same kind, is excellent." "In that substance" is the remainder.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.68: But the regularity of that [grasping] is because of preponderance.

children.text: nanu bhavato 'pi kuto vyavasthitiriti sūtramavatārayituṃ pṛcchati /
children.translated_text: "But for you too, whence comes the regularity?" — he asks, in order to introduce the <s>sūtra</s>.
"For what reason?" —
"That regularity... preponderance" (sū. 68) //
"Of what is distinguished" —
of what is distinguished from the others.
"Produced by <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression)" —
produced by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit). //68//
"For the accomplishment of the purpose" — the purpose is the human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.69: Because of the sense-organ status of things possessing qualities.

children.text:
śaṅkate /
yadi punarindriyasya gandha iti ( 396 / 6 ) nirākaroti /
tenaiva tasyeti /
children.translated_text: He raises an objection: "but if the sense organ has smell" — (396/6) He refutes: "by that very [smell], of that [smell]" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.70: And because that [sense organ] does not grasp by that very [quality of its own].

children.text:
tadetadgrahaṇakavākyaṃ sopaskāraṃ vyācaṣṭe /
yadīnidrayaṃ svagandhaṃ gṛhṇīyātte tava darśanenāsāvindriyagandhaḥ, athendriyagandhastato nendriyagrāhyaḥ syāt /
kasmānnendriyagrāhya indriyagandha
ityata āha /
gandhaṃ ca gṛhṇaditi /
co hetvarthe /
na cātmasādhanaṃ karaṇamastīti manastu liṅgavadātmani karaṇaṃ na kevalamityuktam /
tulyatvamāpādayituṃ siddhāntī pūrvapakṣiṇamanuyuṅkte kasmātpunaridaṃ na codyata iti /
children.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent), in order to establish parity, presses the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (objector): "why is this not objected to?"
The <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> says: "it is not objected to."
The <s>siddhāntin</s> says: "the parity is that the nose does not grasp its own smell."
He establishes the very parity: "this too is to be indicated" — [meaning:] this too is open to the same challenge. //70//

He explains this statement about grasping, with its supplement. If the sense organ were to grasp its own smell — then by your view, this smell of the sense organ [would be grasped]; but if it is a smell of the sense organ, then it should not be graspable by the sense organ. Why is the smell of the sense organ not graspable by the sense organ? To this he says: "and grasping smell" — the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is in the sense of a reason. And there is no instrument that proves itself — but the mind, like an inferential mark, is an instrument with respect to the <s>ātman</s>, not solely [self-referential] — this has been said.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.71: Not [so], because of the apprehension of the quality of sound.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.72: The apprehension of that [sound] is because of the dissimilarity of qualities from the qualities of other substances.

children.text:
( 397 / 11 ) śabdaguṇatvameva dikkālayoriti ceda nāmni vivādaḥ dikkālayorhi śabdaguṇatve satyasādhāraṇayogitvena na parāparavyatikarakāraṇatvaṃ pṛthivyādivadbhavitumarhatīti /
tathā ca śabdaguṇaṃ parāparapratyayakāraṇaṃ cākāśameveti nāmni vivādaḥ /
dikkālau tu parāparavyatikarakāraṇe kalpanīyau tena vyatiriktāvityarthaḥ /
api cākāśamicchata
ākāśapratyākhyānaṃ ca sāmarthyānupalabdheriti /
rūpādisākṣātkāre hi indriyāṇāmindriyatvameva svarūpasāmarthyaṃ taccakṣurādidravyasya dṛṣṭaṃ na guṇādīnāmityarthaḥ // 75 // iti miśraśrīvācasyativiracitāyāṃ nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkāyāṃ
children.translated_text: (397/11) If it is [objected that] direction (<s>dik</s>) and time (<s>kāla</s>) also have sound as their quality — [the answer is:] the dispute is merely about the name. For if direction and time have sound as their quality, then because of their non-shared connectivity (<s>asādhāraṇayogitva</s>), they cannot be the cause of the distinction of near and far, as earth and the like [can]. And thus, what is the substratum of sound-quality and the cause of the cognition of near and far is <s>ākāśa</s> (space) alone — the dispute is merely about the name. But direction and time, being the causes of the distinction of near and far, must be postulated as different from that [<s>ākāśa</s>] — this is the meaning. Moreover, for one who accepts <s>ākāśa</s> — and the refutation of <s>ākāśa</s> is because of the non-apprehension of [its] capacity. For in the direct perception of form and the like, the very sense-organ-ness of the sense organs is their intrinsic capacity, and that is observed in the substance of the eye and the like, not in qualities and the like — this is the meaning. //75// Thus, in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Miśra Vācaspati</s>,
the first section (<s>āhnika</s>) of the third chapter is completed.
In the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Vācaspatimiśra</s>,
the third chapter.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.1: Because of the similarity with action (<s>karma</s>) and <s>ākāśa</s> (space), there is doubt.

parīkṣitānīndriyāṇyarthāśca buddheridānīṃ parīkṣākramaḥ /
kramaḥ sthānaṃ /
vṛttavarttivyamāṇānukīrttanaṃ hetuhetumadbhāvajñāpanārtham /
arthondriyaparīkṣā ca buddhiparīkṣaṇaṃ ( ca ) yathopayujyate tathā buddhiparīkṣāyāmeva sphuṭapībhaviṣyati /
saṃśayamākṣipati /
anupapannarūpa iti /
(398 / 12) yadyupalabhyamānajñānaviṣayaḥ saṃśayaḥ so 'nupapannaḥ sāṃkhyānāmapi tadanityatvasyābhyupagamāt /
atha sāṃkhyābhimatamahattattvaviṣayaḥ tasya sattva eva vipratipattiriti kutastadgatadharmavicāraḥ sati dharmiṇi dharmāścintyante na sandigdhasattvā iti bhāvaḥ /
samādhate dṛṣṭipravādeti /
sāṃkhyānāṃ hi darśane pravādo mahadantaḥ karaṇaṃ buddhiriti tadupālambhārthaṃ dūṣaṇārthaṃ prakaraṇamiti /
ayamabhiprāyaḥ
neha nityānityavicāro 'pi tavanayā dvārā vṛttaratiriktā sāṃkhyābhimatā buddhirnirākriyate sāmānyato buddhimātrasya nityānityatvavicāreṇa /
yadi hi nityā buddhiḥ syāttato vṛttibhya
children.translated_text: For if <s>buddhi</s> were eternal, then the <s>mahat-tattva</s>, the inner instrument,
which is different from the mental modifications that arise and perish, would be [established].

children.text: atha tu nityatvasādhanāni pratisandhānādīni na buddhinityatvasyeśate tato vṛttaya eva buddhayo na tu tadatiriktaṃ buddhitattvaṃ sidhyatīti sidhyati buddhirupalabdhirjñānamityanarthāntaramiti buddherlakṣaṇaṃ tathā cāspaya lakṣaṇe saṅgatiḥ
children.translated_text: But if the proofs of eternality — such as recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>) and the like — cannot establish the eternality of <s>buddhi</s>, then the mental modifications themselves are <s>buddhis</s> (cognitions), and no <s>buddhi-tattva</s> (principle of intellect) different from them is established. Thus it is established that <s>buddhi</s>, apprehension, and <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) are synonymous — this is [in accordance with] the definition of <s>buddhi</s>, and thus the [sūtra's] relevance is to the definition.

children.text: itarathā tu pradhānato nityānityatvavicāro na lakṣaṇena saṅgacchata iti // 1 //
children.translated_text: Otherwise, if the investigation of eternality and non-eternality were primary, it would not be connected with the definition — this is [the meaning]. //1//

The sense organs and objects have been examined; now is the turn for the examination of <s>buddhi</s> (cognition/intellect). 'Turn' means 'place.' The recapitulation of what has been done, what is being done, and what is to be done is for the purpose of making known the cause-effect relation. And the examination of sense organs and objects — and the examination of <s>buddhi</s> — how they are mutually useful will become clear in the examination of <s>buddhi</s> itself. He raises a doubt: "of an impossible form" — (398/12) If the doubt concerns cognition as apprehended [by all], that [doubt] is impossible, since even the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> accept its non-eternality. But if it concerns the <s>mahat-tattva</s> (great principle) accepted by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, the dispute is about its very existence — so whence the investigation of its properties? For properties are investigated when the property-bearer is [established as] existent, not when its existence is doubtful — this is the purport. He resolves: "the doctrinal assertion" — for in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> system, the assertion is that the <s>mahat</s> (the great [principle]), the inner instrument, is <s>buddhi</s> — and the topic is for the purpose of criticizing and refuting that. The intent is this: here, the investigation of eternality and non-eternality is not primarily [about buddhi in general]; rather, through that means, the <s>buddhi</s> accepted by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> — which is different from the mental modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>) — is refuted, by the general investigation of the eternality or non-eternality of <s>buddhi</s> in general.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.2: Because of the recognition of objects.

children.text:
sādhanaṃ ca pracakṣate /
viṣayapratyabhijñānāditi /
( 399 / 3 ) vṛttimān kila viṣayaṃ pratyabhijānannātmānamapi pratyabhijānāti /
na ca cetano vṛttimān tasya kūṭasthanityatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the conscious being who has mental modifications is not [himself subject to modification], because of his immutable eternality (<s>kūṭasthanityatva</s>).
Otherwise, if he had different states in earlier and later [moments], he would not be immutably eternal.

children.text: pariṇāminityā tu buddhirudayavyayavadanekavṛttimatī yujyata iti bhāvaḥ // 2 //
children.translated_text: But <s>buddhi</s>, being eternal as undergoing transformation (<s>pariṇāminityā</s>), possessing many modifications that arise and perish, is consistent — this is the purport. //2//
And they state a proof: "because of the recognition of objects" — (399/3) Indeed, one who has mental modifications, when recognizing an object, also recognizes himself [as the same perceiver].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.3: [This is] not a [valid] reason, because of being equal to what is to be proved.
