children.text: pratyabhijñānasvarūpāvadhāraṇe ca sati viruddho hetvābhāso buddhyanityatvasādhanāditi /
children.translated_text: And when the nature of recognition is ascertained, [the argument from recognition] is a contradictory pseudo-reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) with respect to proving the non-eternality of <s>buddhi</s>.
The rest is explained by the mere recitation [of the text].
The non-difference of consciousness (<s>cetana</s>) and determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) in the definition of <s>buddhi</s> has been investigated by us. //3//

The <s>siddhāntin</s> says: "not a [valid] reason, because of being equal to what is to be proved." For the mental modifications are different from the one who has modifications; therefore, even if they are eternal, the one who has modifications does not lose his immutability. And thus, it is the very <s>ātman</s> that is recognized through recognition, and would be eternal through recognition — not the inner instrument called <s>buddhi</s>, for that does not appear in recognition — this is the meaning. "And because the instrument is not the substratum of the primary action" — the instrument is not the substratum of the primary action; and this primary action is apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>); whatever is spontaneously (<s>svataḥ</s>) cognized as the substratum of that [apprehension] is the agent, not the instrument. And thus, through apprehension such as recognition, its substratum — the agent, the <s>ātman</s> — is established as eternal, not the instrument — this is the meaning. He raises a doubt using the word 'action' in general. He refutes by taking it as 'primary action.' "True, it obtains" — now, if the intention is that the words 'agent' and the like function with the intention of difference, and the word '<s>kāraka</s>' (case-relation) functions with the intention of non-difference — how then is the co-predication "the agent is a <s>kāraka</s>, the instrument is a <s>kāraka</s>" [possible], since the intentions of difference and non-difference have contradictory meanings? To this he says: "by the word <s>kāraka</s> also" — (440/4) The intention is not of non-difference of the specific [<s>kārakas</s>], but of the general. 'What is differentiated' is the differentia; 'what is not a differentia' is 'non-differentia' — i.e., the general — because the general is denoted [by <s>kāraka</s>]. And thus, a word functioning with the intention of the general, entering into co-predication with a word denoting its differentia — a word expressing difference — operates with respect to a specific [<s>kāraka</s>] such as <s>apādāna</s> (ablative) and the like, which is distinguished from each other [specific <s>kāraka</s>], because co-predication of another specific <s>kāraka</s> with the word <s>kāraka</s> is impossible [in that context]. "As before" — he reminds [us] of the definition of a specific <s>kāraka</s> stated in the second chapter. He objects: "if the other <s>kārakas</s>" — the agent, prompted by the taking up of <s>kārakas</s>, takes up the <s>kārakas</s>. Therefore, its not being prompted by the others is unestablished — this is the meaning. He resolves: "it is not prompted, because the fruit is the prompter" — we do not say that the agent is not prompted at all, but that it is not prompted by the <s>kārakas</s>; and the fruit is not a <s>kāraka</s> — this is the meaning. "Having conceded the recognition in the inner instrument, of that" — if the recognition is perceptual, then [the question is] not about unity, but if it is inferential, then there is no example for "whatever is recognized is one" — for its unity is not ascertained from anything else, but from recognition.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.4: Because of non-simultaneous grasping.
— this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. //4//
Because of the persistence of the one who has modifications, there follows the consequence of the persistence of modifications
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.5: And in the case of non-recognition, the consequence of destruction [would follow].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.6: Non-simultaneous grasping is because of having successive operation.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.7: And non-recognition is because of engagement with another object.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.8: Not [so], because of the absence of movement.

children.translated_text: He states what is relied upon for the denial: "the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) knows, not the internal organ."
By [this] reason, the occupation of the internal organ with another object is refuted.

children.text: vyāsakto hi sa bhavati yo jānīte /
children.translated_text: For one who knows is the one who is occupied [with something].

children.text: na cāntaḥkaraṇaṃ jānīte kiṃ tu puruṣa iti tasyedṛśavyāsaṅgo nāntaḥkaraṇasya, anyādṛśastvantaḥkaraṇasya vyāsaṅgo na niṣidhyataityarthaḥ // 8 //
children.translated_text: And the internal organ does not know, but rather the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) does — therefore such occupation belongs to the person, not to the internal organ. But a different kind of occupation of the internal organ is not denied — this is the meaning. //8//

The statement of the objector: "why not the same for me too?" — (403/15) The statement of the resolver: "not so, because difference of cause is observed."
For when there is difference of cause, a single agent is observed to produce many effects simultaneously.
And for the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) is the agent and is all-pervading — therefore the sense-organs, being presided over by the all-pervading internal organ, should produce effects simultaneously.
But for us, since the internal organ has the status of an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), even when grasping a single sense-organ's object, there is no simultaneous production of effects — this is the difference.
And because of the absence of motion, the non-simultaneous apprehension of the all-pervading internal organ, which has been denied, is not inferred by another mark — he restates the <s>Bhāṣya</s> pratīka "because of the absence of motion, of the all-pervading internal organ" and states its meaning: "because of the absence of going, which serves the purpose of reaching."
And there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the non-simultaneous production of cognitions, by which <s>pramāṇa</s> the non-simultaneity of cognitions, which has been denied, could be established.
Therefore, when the internal organ is all-pervading, the simultaneity of cognitions is inevitable; but this is not observed — therefore the internal organ is atomic — this is the meaning.
Objection: when eating a long pastry (<s>śaṣkulī</s>), the simultaneous arising of all five cognitions is observed — so what is this consequence that simultaneity would follow if the internal organ were all-pervading? — to this he says:
"And there is no simultaneous arising of cognitions" —
The meaning is: the impression of simultaneous arising is due to extreme rapidity, but there is no real simultaneity there.
"The person knows, not the internal organ" — he explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, which is directed toward the resolution of his own view: "for one whose activity is the activity of that which has activity" —
(404/12) And what the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> have stated — that when the internal organ is occupied with another object, even though there is connection with the eye and the like, the ignorance belongs to the internal organ; and the activity of the internal organ is knowledge — the <s>Bhāṣya</s> directed toward refuting that is: "by this, the occupation with another object."
Having restated that, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains:
"By this" —
"Therein" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.9: Just as there is the false impression of otherness in a crystal, so is the false impression of otherness of that [internal organ]. //

children.translated_text: "Not so" —

children.text: api ca pratyayābhede prakāravattvābhāvād yathādhyavasyati buddhistathā cetayate puruṣa iti vyāghātaḥ /
children.translated_text: Moreover, if there is no difference of cognitions, then because of the absence of modes (<s>prakāra</s>), there is a contradiction: "as the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) determines, so the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) experiences."

children.text: kuto 'prakāravattvād bhinno hi prakāravān bhavati nābhinna ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Why [contradiction]? Because of the absence of modes — for what is different possesses modes, not what is non-different — this is the meaning.

children.text: antaḥkāraṇasya buddheḥ pratyayānāmabhede buddhistaṃ pratyayamupalabhate iti virodha iti // 9 //
children.translated_text: When there is no difference of cognitions belonging to the internal organ, namely <s>buddhi</s>, the [claim that] <s>buddhi</s> apprehends that cognition involves a contradiction. //9//

The objection-<s>Bhāṣya</s> "the internal organ is one, its activities are many" — he explains that:
"The internal organ is one, its activities are many" —
"This is not so" —
The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> speaks correctly, [the one who] elucidates.
For <s>Sāṃkhya</s> means: one who proceeds by correct understanding (<s>samyak buddhi</s>).
What is being said is this: although the activities appear as many, nevertheless this is an error — because the impossibility of plurality of what is non-different from the single internal organ.
Therefore, just as a crystal, though single, has merely adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>) difference due to the placement of different flowers such as <s>tāpiccha</s>, <s>japā</s>, <s>karṇikāra</s>, and the like, so too the internal organ — a gem-like transparent [entity] — being colored by the respective objects through the channels of the sense-organs, has merely adventitious plurality, which is called "activity" (<s>vṛtti</s>), "cognition" (<s>pratyaya</s>), and "knowledge" (<s>jñāna</s>) — this is the meaning.
He refutes this: "not, because of inconclusiveness" —
(405/4) Even one who asserts merely adventitious difference of activities must accept that the objects — the adventitious conditions — are different, as known [by the cognizer].
And thus, since difference is seen in two ways [i.e., both real and adventitious], the example is inconclusive and does not prove a single meaning.
"Not, because of the absence of a reason" — he explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s>: "the sūtra according to the literal meaning" —
Not only is there an absence of proof, but there is also a defeating argument — thus he says: "and because of the impossibility of [the proposed] alternative" —
With the intent that the mere negation of the opponent's position does not establish one's own position, he asks:
"But for you" —
The answer: "cognitions arise in sequence" —
This might be [objected]: the impression of plurality of cognitions will be the reason for the unity of activities — since the activities are one, being the object of the impression of plurality, like a crystal — therefore there is no absence of reason. To this he says:
"And because the impression of plurality of cognitions pertains to one-and-many objects —
how is the apprehension of one-and-many objects [to be explained]?"
The impression of plurality too, like the example, is non-probative because of inconclusiveness.
Having thus refuted the opponent's objection in between, he again establishes the difference of activities:
"And this [impression of] non-difference" —
If the difference in cognitions is not recognized as arising from the placement of different objects, then there would be no difference of cognition regarding a single object, because of the absence of difference in the placement of cognitions — this is the meaning.
Someone teaches:
"A crystal" —
He refutes: "because of the observation of contiguity" —
(406/1) Even the application of indigo-dye has gaps — "the crystal is blue" — this is to be inferred from direct observation — this is the import.
Moreover, [there is] difference of cognition — thus he says:
"And for one in whom there is non-difference of cognition" —
The difference of the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) is to be inferred from the difference of its effect, characterized as cognition — it cannot exist without difference of cognition.
He raises a doubt: "because of the difference of objects" —
What is being said is this:
If even the specific difference of objects is the cause of the difference of <s>pramāṇas</s>,
then, since those [specific differences] are infinite, there would be an infinite difference of <s>pramāṇas</s>, not just three. Therefore, one should accept a subsidiary commonality of objects. But that too cannot be based on the mere intrinsic nature of objects, because of the confluence of [multiple] <s>pramāṇas</s> even in a single [object].
Therefore, objects — having a commonality characterized by difference of cognition — standing in a threefold [division], also establish the <s>pramāṇas</s> in a threefold [division].
And cognitions, conforming to the positive and negative concomitance of three sets of causal conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>), are three.
And thus, because of having three objects, the <s>pramāṇas</s> are three — this is what is said by "because of the difference of objects."
He refutes:
"Not so" —
Because when there is no difference of <s>pramāṇas</s>, there is no difference of the three sets of causal conditions, and [hence] no difference of cognitions that conform to them.
For the difference of causal conditions cannot be known without the difference of cognitions. Therefore, even when the difference of cognitions and causal conditions [is assumed], without the ascertainment of the difference of objects, there is no ascertainment of the threefoldness of objects — or rather [there is no ascertainment] without the difference of cognitions.
He raises a doubt: "because of the identity of object and cognition" —
The meaning is: the difference of cognition is justified because of the non-difference of cognition and its object.
He refutes:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.10: Even in a crystal, because of the successive arising of one thing after another, because of the momentariness of individuals, [the argument] is not a [valid] reason. //

children.text: tadevaṃ svamatena sāṃkhyapakṣaṃ dūṣayitvā bauddhairyatsāṃkhyarāddhānte dūṣaṇamuktaṃ tad
children.translated_text: Having thus refuted the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position by his own doctrine, the refutation that the Buddhists raised against the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> established view —
that he presents and refutes by setting forth the Buddhist view.
Unable to tolerate the [argument of] false impression of otherness in a crystal, the proponent of momentariness says:
"Crystal... reason" (sūtra 10) //

children.text:
yatsattatsarvaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ yathā śarīraṃ tathā ca sphaṭika iti jaranto bauddhāḥ /
śarīrasyā ca ca kālaparipākavaśena sthaulyasya hrāsasya ca darśanāt pratikṣaṇaṃ sūkṣmaḥ pariṇatibhedo 'numīyate sa cāntarā vināśa
eveti /
yasyāpi sphaṭikādestādṛśaṃ sthaulyaṃhrāso vāna dṛśyate tasyāpi sattvena śarīravadeva pratikṣaṇaṃ vināśotpādāvanumīyete iti /
syādetad yadaivopacayāpacayau śarīrasya dṛśyete tadaivotpādavināśau bhaviṣyataḥ pūrvaṃ tu tatprabandhakalpanāyāṃ kiṃ pramāṇamityata
āha /
yaspaya khalu pratikṣaṇamiti /
( 407 / 9 ) asya prayogaḥ pratikṣaṇamanyaccānyacceti /
paṭasya kuṅkumādidravyasaṃyoge satyante 'ruṇimalakṣaṇo viśeṣo dṛśyate na cāsyāruṇimā pratikṣaṇabhāvītyata uktaṃ bāhyapratyayābhedesatīti /
children.translated_text: When there is conjunction with a saffron-substance and the like, a specific feature characterized as reddishness is observed at the end [of the cloth] — and yet this reddishness is not present at each moment [prior to the conjunction] — therefore it is said "when there is no difference of external condition."

children.text: abhinno hi śarīropacayahetuḥ pratidinamupayujyamāno 'nnapānapracathoyathā pākajotpattāvauṣṇyāpekṣo vahnisaṃyogo bāhyaḥ pratyayaḥ kāraṇaṃ, paṭe ttu rāgotpattau kuṅkumadravyasaṃyogaḥ sāṃpratiko viśiṣṭa ityarthaḥ // 10 //
children.translated_text: For the cause of the body's increase, being non-different [over time], is the food and drink consumed daily — just as in the production of what arises from cooking, the external condition (<s>pratyaya</s>) is the conjunction with fire that requires heat; but for the cloth, the production of coloring is from the present conjunction with saffron-substance, which is a specific [external condition] — this is the meaning. //10//

Whatever exists is entirely momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), like the body — and so too the crystal — thus proclaim the Buddhists.
And because of the observation, through the ripening of time, of increase and decrease of the body's bulk, a subtle modification at each moment is inferred — and that is nothing but destruction in the interval.
And even for the crystal and the like, in which such increase or decrease of bulk is not observed, because of [their] existence, destruction and origination at each moment are inferred just as for the body.
This might be [objected]: at the very time when increase and decrease of the body are observed, origination and destruction will occur — but previously, what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for postulating such a continuum? — to this he says:
"Of that which indeed at each moment" —
(407/9) The formal argument for this is: "at each moment, one thing and another" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.11: Because of the absence of a reason for restriction, acceptance [should be] as observed. //
This is the <s>siddhānta</s>-sūtra.
"Restriction... acceptance" (sūtra 11) //

children.translated_text:
He explains that:
"This is [the argument] — augmentation and diminution" —
For just as fire inferred from the observation of smoke does not operate everywhere — so too, even when smoke is not observed, the inferrers do not infer fire in another mountain merely on the basis of its being a mountain — this is the meaning.
He raises a doubt: "where there is apprehension" —
Momentariness is the state of lasting only a portion of time devoid of prior and subsequent parts.
And such momentariness is not accepted by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> anywhere — therefore there is no proving of what is already established — this is the meaning.
He refutes: "true" —
But why does the momentariness as accepted by us not get established from the observation of the continuum of augmentation and diminution? — to this he says:
"And the observation of the continuum of augmentation and diminution is otherwise [explainable]" —
The word "and" has the force of a reason.
He raises a doubt: "[the situation is] equal" —
(408/5)
He refutes: "not so, because it does not prove" —
Without a one-sided determination, there is no proof; but a refutation can be achieved even by generating doubt —
this is the difference between proof and refutation — this is the meaning.
//11//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.12: Not [so], because of the apprehension of a cause of origination and destruction. //
He introduces the next sūtra:
"Now, a proof must necessarily be stated" —
"Not, origination... apprehension"
(sūtra 12) //

children.translated_text: But as for the action of the composite whole, there is neither simultaneity nor cause-effect relation, because of being a single [entity] — this is the meaning.
'Gravity, effort, and conjunction are [the causes] of rising' —

children.text: vidhārakaḥ prayatnastulādhārasya tadapekṣaḥ saṃyogaḥ sayuktaṃsaṃyogo gurutvaṃ ca tatsaṃyuktāvayavāntaravartikāraṇamunnatestulāvayavasya
children.translated_text: The sustaining effort belongs to the balance-holder; the conjunction dependent on that [effort] — namely the conjunction with the conjoined — and gravity, which belongs to another part conjoined with it, are the causes of the rising of the balance-part.

children.text: anavaterapi dravyaṃ gurutvavatsuvarṇādi parimayimāṇaṃ tatsaṃyogānugṛhīto rajjutulāsaṃyogaḥ kāraṇam // 12 //
children.translated_text: For the [opposite] part that is not rising, the substance being weighed — gold and the like — which possesses gravity, and the conjunction of the cord-balance assisted by that conjunction, are the causes. //12//

The cause of origination and destruction is the indicator; but the aggregation and disaggregation of parts are not tenable in the momentariness (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) thesis — because in [the case of] origination and destruction that leave no residue (<s>niranvaya</s>), there is no basis for the cognition of aggregation and disaggregation. 'Because of the apprehension of the cause of origination and destruction through aggregation and disaggregation' — aggregation and disaggregation are themselves the causes of origination and destruction — this is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> (appositional compound). He states an alternative interpretation of 'because of the apprehension of the cause of origination and destruction': 'or, the cause' — (409/1) for the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) is commonly established as being prior to the effect and present at the time of the effect — and this is untenable if [things are] momentary — this is the meaning. 'Experienced at the same time' — experience is contact (<s>prāpti</s>); experienced at the same time means contacted at the same time — this is the meaning. One transgressing the bounds of the world raises a doubt: 'of the substrate-superstratum relation' — He refutes: 'not, because of inconclusiveness.' In your own established doctrine too, form (<s>rūpa</s>) is resisted, is an effect, and is like a substrate. But if form too is without a substrate in a person, then there would be a violation of your own doctrine — he says: 'and contradiction in "touch, its substrate"' — Everything experienced at the same time is established — [this is the point]. He raises a doubt: 'the cause-effect relation is established even among momentary [entities]' — through the absurd consequence that the effect would be without a substrate — for it is not the case that in the momentariness thesis, the cause-effect relation is not established. Rather, it is established even in the momentariness thesis, because the origination of the effect is simultaneous with the destruction of the cause — and therefore cause and effect are simultaneous — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'not, because of the misunderstanding of the reason.' With so much effort you establish the cause-effect relation of momentary [entities]; but this [argument of yours] is not a reason against non-momentariness — rather, the substrate-superstratum relation [is at issue], and that cannot be proved [by you]. What then is this destruction of the cause? Is it the absence of the cause, or the proximity of a cause of destruction? In the first alternative, how can cause and effect be simultaneous? In the second alternative too, when what has arisen [subsequently encounters] the proximity of the cause of destruction, how can what exists be momentary? And the simultaneous-ness of being-originated and being-destroyed is contradicted by experience. And if the effect originates at that very [same] time, there would be no cause-effect relation — like the right and left horns [of an animal] — this is the import. Moreover, the example too is deficient in the property to be proved — he says: 'of the balance-holder' — (410/1) the two [movements] that are actions of the parts — the rising and sinking — of those two there is no cause-effect relation.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.13: Just as the non-apprehension of the cause in the destruction of milk, and just as the origination of curd — so is the tenability of that.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.14: Because of apprehension through a mark (<s>liṅga</s>), there is no non-apprehension.
