na ca kāryakāraṇayorabhedo yena kāraṇabhedābhedāvanupatetāṃ kāryabhedābhedau /
tasmādyathā kebhyaḥ kaścideva bahubhyaḥ kāryamekaṃ jāyate tathaikasmādeva kutaścidbahūni janayiṣyante kāryāṇīti cet /
mudhaiva tarhi nānādeśavṛttireko 'vayavisāmānyasaṃyogādirarthastapasvī bhavatāyāsitaḥ na hi nānātve 'pi deśānāṃ tadāśritaḥ sāmānyādirartho nānā bhavitumarhati /
tasya tebhyo 'bhinnatvāt /
rūpāntareṇa bījamaṅkurāditareṣāṃ kṣityādīnāṃ janakam tathā hi bījamaṅkurasyopādānaṃ tatsārabhāgavikriyayā 'ṅkurasyotpatteḥ kṣityādiṣu tu janayitavyeṣu sahakāri pūrve tu kṣityādayaḥ kṣityādīnāṃ yathāsvamupādānāni tadvikriyayā tadutpattiriti cet /
atha sahakāritopādānate kimekaṃ tattvaṃ nānā vā /
ekaṃ cet kathaṃ rūpāntareṇa janakaṃ nānātve tayorbījādbhedo 'bhedo vā bhede kathaṃ bījasya janakatvaṃ tābhyāmevāṅkurādīnāmutpatteḥ /
abhede vā kathaṃ na bhedo bījasya bhinnatādātmyāt /
tayorvaikarūpatvameva tādātmyāt /
tasmādaṅkurādbhinne kṣityādau janayitavye tadupādānaṃ pūrvameva kṣityādisamasamayabhāvi bījenāpekṣyate /
evaṃ bījamapi samasamayabhāvyeva sahakārikāraṇaṃ kṣityādibhirapekṣyate nānyathā kāryabhedasiddhirityanicchatā 'pyabhyupeyam /
na cānupakārakamapekṣāgocara
iti bhavadbhirevopapāditam /
na ca kṣaṇikasyopakārakatavasaṃbhavo 'nyatra jananāt tasyābhedyatvāt /
na ca samasamayabhāvinorjanyajanakatvamasti savyetaraviṣāṇayoriva /
tasmātsvasaṃtānamātrādeva kāryotpādaprasaṅgātkāryabhedānupapatteścānupakāriṇyapekṣāvirahācca kṣaṇikasyāpi sāpekṣasyānapekṣasya vā nārthakriyā saṃbhavinītyasādhāraṇasattvaṃ na kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhāvaṅgam /
atha mā bhūdasādhāraṇatā sattvasyetyanupakārakeṣvapi kāryakaraṇāyāpekṣābhyupeya te teṣāmapi kāryeṇānukṛtānvayavyatirekatvāt /
na tvanena krameṇākṣaṇiko 'pi bhāvo 'nupakārakānapi sahakāriṇaḥ kramavataḥ kramavataiva kāryeṇānukṛtānvayavyatirekānapekṣiṣyate /
kariṣyate kramavatsahakārivaśaḥ krameṇa kāryāṇi /
samarthasyāpyapekṣaṇīyāsannidheḥ kāryakṣepaupapatsyate /
na caitāvatā sahakārisamavadhānādevotpattimataḥ kāryasiddhiḥ kṛtameṣāṃ rūpeṇeti vācyam /
tatsahitādeva tata utpattidarśanāt /
rūpe satyapyanutpādāt /
samavadhāne (hetu) satyutpādādeva kāryasvasamavadhānameva heturna punā rūpamapīti cet tatkimidānīṃ rāsabhāditulyatābījarūpasya /
oṃmiti cet /
atha kasmādgardabhādīnantareṇeva bījarūpaṃ vināpi nāṅkuro jāyate /
tatsamavadhānasya tatkāraṇatvāditi cet /
tatsamabadhāne kāraṇe kathaṃ tanniveśi rūpamapi na kāraṇam /
na cāvarjanīyatayā tanniveśaḥ /
samavadhānamātrasya bījarūpamantareṇāpi tatra tatra bhāvāt /
viśeṣastu samavadhāne rūpameva bījādīnām /
tasmādya thobhayādhīnanirūpaṇā vyāptirayogavyavacchedena vyāpake nirūpyate vyāpye bhāva eva vyāpakasya nābhāva iti vyāpye punaranyayogavyavacchedena vyāpaka
eva bhāvo vyāpyasya nānyatreti evaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'pyubhayādhīnanirūpaṇo 'pi kāraṇe ayogavyavacchedena nirūpyate /
kāryotpādasya purastādbhāva
eva kāraṇasya nābhāva iti /
kārye punarayogavyavacchedena /
kāraṇa eva sati bhāvo nānyasminniti anubhavānusārānniścīyate /
tathaiva hi laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ saṃpratipatteḥ /
na ca kāraṇataiva sattā kiṃ tu svarūpaṃ nīlāderanubhūtāvasitaṃ taddhi tenaiva rūpeṇa svābhāvavyavacchinnaṃ tāsu tāsvarthakriyāsūpayujyate na punararthakriyākāritaivava tvarūpaṃ mā bhūdanekārthakriyākāriṇo 'paryāyeṇa rūpabhedaḥ /
tasmādyadyasti sarvajñastataḥ svarūpeṇaiva sanbhāvaḥ tajjñānasyālambanapratyayo bhaviṣyati /
atha tu nāsti tathāpi tadrūpo janitvā āpātato 'kiñcitkaro 'pi paścātkutaścinnimittādāsādya sahakāripratyayān tāsu tāsvarthakriyāsūpayokṣyate /
tatsiddhametat kṣaṇikasyāpi kramākramābhyāṃ yathāyogamarthakriyopapattervyāpakānupalabdherasiddheḥ saṃdigdhavyatirekamanaikāntikaṃ sattvaṃ śākyānāṃ kṣaṇikatve sādhye bhāvānām /
asmākaṃ tvanyathāsiddhamasiddhaprabheda
eveti /
na ca janakatvājanakatvalakṣaṇaviruddhadharmasaṃsargo nānātve heturbhavitumarhati /
janakatvaṃ nāma na vastusvabhāvo 'pi tu taddharmaḥ /
dharmaśca dharmiṇo vastuto bhidyate /
na cānyasya bhedo 'nyasya bhedāyālamatiprasaṅgāt /
anyattvāviśeṣe kathaṃ tasyaiva dharma iti cet /
atra vastusvabhāvairevottaraṃ vācyam /
yathā 'nyatvāviṃśeṣe 'pi kāryaṃ dhūmo hutabhuja eva na bījasyetyuktam /
na ca kṛtakatvamapi kṣaṇikattve heturanyathāsiddheḥ /
sahetuke vināśe tadupapatteśca /
na cotpattivināśayostādātmyaṃ bhāvasyātyantābhāvaprasaṅgādityuktam /
tadidamuktaṃ vārtikakṛtatā te 'pyasiddhā anyathāsiddhā viruddhā vā bhavantītyahetava iti /
( 416 / 15 )
antyakṣaṇaviśeṣadarśanaṃ pūrvakṣaṇadharmatvenāsiddhatvādasiddham /
sattvakṛtakatve anyathāsiddhe /
viruddhatvaṃ ca sarvasyaiva hetoḥ kṣaṇikatve sādhye /
tathā hi sattvaṃ kṛtakattvaṃ vā traipalokyavyāvṛttatayā 'nanugataṃ deśataḥ kālato vā na sādhanaṃ tasyāśakyāvinābhāvajñānatayā liṅgabhāvābhāvāt /
anvayamukhena vyatirekamukhena vā 'vinābhāvagrahasyaikasmin kṣaṇe 'śakyatvāt /
tasmāddeśakālānugataṃ sattvaṃ kṛtakatvamanyadvāhetūkartavyam /
tacca vidhirūpaṃ vā bhavatvanyavyāvṛttirūpaṃ vā nānākālamekamakṣaṇikaṃ kṣaṇikatvena sādhyena virudhyataityuktaṃ viruddhā veti /
ante viśeṣadarśanādityasya tu viruddhatvamanantaraṃ vakṣyati /
upetya viśeṣavattve siddhatvamanaikāntikatvamāhapa upetya vetañ
hetorisiddhatvaviruddhatve darśayitumāha /
ante viśeṣeti /
darśanādarśanalaṇasya hetoranyathāsiddhatetyāha /
yo 'pyayaṃ heturiti /
bhāvābhāvayostadvattvāditi ( 417 / 7 ) saṃyogābhāvābhāvayorihabuddherbhāvavattvādityarthaḥ /
pradīpasya deśāntare utpāda ityetadapi na budhyāmaha iti /
kṣaṇikasya pradīpasya yadi saṃtānamātraprabhavatvaṃ nibaddhaṃ deśāntare kāryotpādakatvaṃ tataḥ sarva eva pradīpakṣaṇā deśāntare pradīpamutpādayeyuḥ /
na ke cana pradhanodara eveti /
athoḥ pasarpaṇapratyayavaśātpraghanodarādanyatrāpi kāryamutpādayanti /
nūnapasarpaṇapratyayaḥ pradīpe kaṃ cidupakāramādhatte na vā, na tāvadādhatte kṣaṇasyābhedyatvenopakṛtānupakṛtatvāsambhavāt /
anādhāne ca sahakāribhāvābhāvāt /
anupakārakaspaya sahakāritve 'tiprasaṅgāditi bhavatāmeva giraḥ /
na ca viśiṣṭapradīpakṣaṇajananamevopakāraḥ sahakāriṇāṃ tasya pūrvasmādevopādānādupapatteḥ sahakāryanapekṣaṇāt /
na khalu tasyeva tatkāraṇasyāpyupakārakāḥ sahakāriṇo bhavitumarhanti /
evaṃ pūrveṣāmapi pradīpakṣaṇānāṃ pūrvapūrvapradīpamātrasāmarthyabhuvā na sahakāriṇā kiñcidādhīyata iti sarva evaikasmin pradhānaṃ kāryaṃ kuryuḥ deśāntare vā /
yadi punaranupakāriṇo 'pi kāryānuvihitabhāvābhāvatayā kṣaṇikena pradīpena kāryakriyāṃ pratyapekṣyante tadakṣaṇikapakṣe 'pi tulyamiti saṃkṣepaḥ /
vipañcitaṃ caitadasmābhirbrahyatattvasamīkṣānyāyakaṇikābhyāmityuparamyate /
na kilākāśe patato loṣṭāderiti /
loṣṭaśyenādestulyagurutvavatāṃ dravyāṇāmekasya gurutvaprayatnakṣepāḥ kāraṇam /
tathā hi saudhasyoparisthena puruṣeṇa bhūmau carantaṃ pārāvatamuddiśya yadā 'dhaḥ śyenaḥ kṣipyate tadā śyenasya pārāvatajidhṛkṣājanitaḥ prayatno gurutvaṃ ca kṣepaścāśutarapatanahetavaḥ /
akṣiptasya tu gurutvaprayatnāvāśupatanahetū aprayatamānasya gurutvamātraṃ patanaheturiti /
aulūkyamate 'pi na doṣa ityata āha /
ekaśca saṃskāra iti /
( 418 / 7 ) ayugapatkālāḥ pratyayā ekaviṣayā ityucyamāne ghaṭapaṭādipratyayāḥ pradīpādipratyayāśca kramavanta ekaviṣayāḥ prasajyerannityata
āha /
vipratipannā iti /
samānaśabdavācyatvādityanekāntaḥ
bhavanti hi samānaśabdavācyāḥ pratyayāḥ akṣo 'kṣa iti, na ca samānaviṣayāḥ devanādīnāṃ tadvipayāṇāṃ bhedādata āha /
tatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇye satīti /
tathā 'pi pradīpapratyayairevānekānta
ityata āha /

children.translated_text: "Non-deviating" —

children.text: vyutthātuṃ bhramituṃ śīlaprasyeti vyutthāyi bhrāntamiti yāvat /
children.translated_text: That whose nature is to deviate (<s>vyutthāna</s>), i.e., to err, is "deviating" — meaning: erroneous.
And its non-erroneousness should be understood through the refutation of the proof of momentariness.
Since [non-erroneousness] is already established by co-predication with the non-deviating cognition, the expressibility by the same word is [merely] an elaboration. //13-14//

He objects: 'it is not the case that the difference of cold and hot touch does not exist' —
(411/5) He resolves: 'but that is from another cause' —
He objects again:
'The interpenetration of the parts of water and fire is not tenable' —
The specific great elements are intrinsic to [each substance]; their parts are earth and the like —
for they are distinguished from each other, hence they are 'specifics' (<s>viśeṣa</s>).
He resolves:
'That is not tenable' —
If difference arises merely from being other at each moment, then even among the moments of wood, there should be apprehension of difference just as with earth, stone, and iron.
For just as iron-moments suddenly differ from wood-moments, so too other wood-moments [should differ from each other].
Therefore, even while being earthy, two specifics must be maintained as intrinsic, by which [wood] is distinguished from earth, stone, and the like, but wood-moments are not distinguished from other wood-moments. Therefore, by that very specificity, even without momentariness, the successive differences among wood, earth, stone, and iron are tenable — hence the postulation of momentariness is futile.
'The nature of being an element is not a means of proof' —
meaning: for establishing momentariness.
He states another refutation:
'And this reason is contradictory' —
'Because of observing successive differences' —
According to you, the defining characteristics that mutually distinguish the elements are: roughness, unctuousness, heat, and impulse — these are the natures of the elements.
Earth is rough, water is unctuous, fire is hot, wind is impelling — that is, possessing motion.
But if the production [of wood, earth, stone, iron] is accepted, then one single [entity] would be rough-hot or rough-hot-impelling — and thus, because of conflation, there would be a contradiction in the defining characteristics of the elements.
'Hard' — he indicates earth, which is rough.
'But in our view there is no contradiction' — he says: 'for one who, however' —
Not only is there contradiction with the defining characteristics of earth and the like, but also with the previously stated proof of multiplicity through the difference of cold and hot touch — he says:
'And this is contradictory' —
(413/1) He asks: 'how?'
The answer:
'Because of accepting the specificity of one [entity]' —
By the very specificity through which difference from the prior [moment] was accepted — namely, through the distinction of cold, hot, and the like — by that very [specificity], there is now unity — this is the meaning.
'Accepting the established doctrine' —
The meaning is: the thesis accepted by the prior reason is contradicted, hence it is 'contradictory.'
He raises the doubt: 'if you think it is not mere specificity' —
Let form, which is resistant, not be the material cause — thus one form alone would be multiple — this is the import.
He refutes: 'not the intended [meaning]' —
But one who teaches the interpenetration of parts — in hot water, the grasping of the touch of fire too would occur, as in an iron ball — against him, he states a resolution from the partial-view standpoint:
'In water, the unwanted consequence of grasping the form of fire' —
He refutes that: 'that is not [so]' —
It is reasonable that at midday, the dim light of a meteor is overpowered by the intense radiance of the sun, because of the intensity [of the latter] when they are of the same kind.
But the form of water is not intense, nor is it of the same kind [as fire], because of being non-luminous.
Fire, however, is luminous — therefore there is no overpowering — this is the meaning.
He states the ultimate resolution:
'But rather, because of the fourfold nature of fire' —
Some fire has manifest form and touch, as the light of the sun in autumn during the day; some has non-manifest form and touch, as the fire in the eye; some has manifest form but non-manifest touch, as the fire in the radiance of a lamp; and some has non-manifest form and non-manifest touch, as the fire in water, or the fire in the summer midnight from which corpulent persons sweat.
Dividing the thesis according to possibility, he refutes:
'And this thesis' —
Now, accepting the present crystal, taking as the thesis the past different crystal, he proves: 'it is different from the present one.'
He refutes:
'If that were so' —
(413/5) If the mark [of inference] is the indicative of its own existence and cognition, then even when there is cognition, since the existence of the past property does not [currently] exist, it would not be indicative — this is the import.
If, on the other hand, the mark is said to be indicative merely by its own cognition, then he states another refutation:
'From the present [moment]' —
[It perishes] by following the destruction of its contradictory-substrate —
'Contradictory' has the intention of [referring to] a quality.
For a quality is destroyed by another contradictory quality — that is what is meant by 'contradictory.'
'And upon the destruction of the substrate' — this is common to all [cases].
The mention of 'substrate' is indicative — thereby, destruction through the non-inherent cause or the efficient cause should also be inferred as appropriate.
He raises the doubt: 'in the state of being destroyed' —
Let the lamp not be the example; but in a substance that is in the state of being destroyed, action that has arisen is destroyed immediately after arising — therefore such action will serve as the example — this is the meaning.
He refutes: 'not of action' —
For this refutation of momentariness is grounded on the denial of action; if [action] is accepted, [the refutation] cannot stand.
Because the production of the effect is tenable only from a stable substance possessing adventitious action — [not from a momentary entity].
He states another refutation:
'And because of non-acceptance' —
Because such action too is momentary, [we maintain]:
For the destruction of the substance and the production of action are one moment; and the destruction of the substance [occurs] — and the effect is not produced at the same time as the cause — so the destruction of action follows immediately after the destruction of the substance.
Thus, the two-moment duration of action is established.
He raises the doubt:
'If [one says]: because of the absence of a cause of destruction' —
The intent is this: does this entity arise from its own cause as destructible or as indestructible? If destructible, it would not require a cause for its destruction — for blue, having arisen from its own cause, does not require a cause for its being blue, since it is of that very nature.
But if indestructible, even so, not even by a hundred causes could its destruction be effected — for when blue has arisen, not even by a hundred artisans can yellow be produced [from it].
Moreover, is this destruction, being brought about by causes with respect to the entity, produced as different from the entity or as non-different?
If non-different, then it is just the entity itself — and so the entity, [supposedly] destroyed, would produce apprehension and efficacious action as before.
And when the causes of existence and non-existence are different, non-difference is impossible.
For a cloth arises from the conjunction of threads, while the non-existence of the cloth [arises] from the disjunction of threads or the destruction of threads — thus the causes are different.
But if [the destruction is] different from the entity, let non-existence arise — what has befallen the entity? For upon the production of a camel, lotuses do not cease.
'If [one says] the entity is concealed by non-existence' —
No, for if the concealment is non-different from the entity, there is the unwanted consequence of apprehension and the like as before.
Even if different, when the concealment is [merely] the production of another, nothing has been produced or destroyed in the entity itself — so from the unchanged state of the entity, there is the unwanted consequence of apprehension and the like as before.
Moreover, if [destruction] is inevitable for them, then they do not require another cause for it — as an iron sword [does not require a cause] for its iron-nature.
And destruction is inevitable for produced entities — this is the apprehension of concomitance with the contradictory (<s>viruddhavyāptopalabdhi</s>).
For inevitability — being apprehended as pervading the non-requirement-of-another-cause, which contradicts the denied requirement-of-another-cause — when perceived here, presents non-requirement, thereby rejecting requirement-of-another-cause.
For those that require another cause are not inevitable — like the colors of a garment, which depend on conjunction with saffron and the like and are not necessarily present.
Therefore, since non-existence — being devoid of all designation, being postulated, and being incapable of action — 'produces non-existence' [means]: the connection of the action 'produces' with non-existence is untenable, hence the negative particle applies — 'it does not produce' — [rather] 'it brings about.'
As it is said: '... nothing becomes of his, only [it] merely becomes ...'
Therefore, because of the absence of a cause of destruction, destruction [occurs] at the very moment of production — thus momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>) is established — so [says the Buddhist].
He refutes this:
'Not, because of the impossibility of the alternatives.'
The intent is this: as for the alternative postulated — that entities arise from their own causes either as destructible or as indestructible —
regarding that we say: what indeed is this destructibility of entities according to you? Is it having-destruction-as-nature? Or is it being-worthy-of-destruction — a form distinguished from eternal [entities]?
The first alternative is not [tenable], because identity between an entity and its destruction — which are mutually exclusive — is impossible.
And if there were identity, the entity too, like destruction, would continue in the second and subsequent moments — so you have nicely established the eternality of entities while claiming to prove their momentariness!
Or, at the time of the entity, destruction too, having the nature of the entity, would exist — so there would be absolute non-existence of the entity — thus the truth of entities has been thoroughly cleansed by you!
Nor is it tenable that the entity persists for one moment while destruction [begins] in the second and subsequent moments —
because of their difference through the contact of contradictory properties characterized by the delimitations of first and second [moments].
But the second alternative we accept.
'But if entities arise from their own causes as worthy-of-destruction, they should be destroyed immediately after arising!' — No, they are not destroyed; though worthy of destruction, cloths and the like will be destroyed by the destruction or disjunction of threads — by their own causes dependent on [the current] causes.
For rice grains, though cookable, do not soften without the combination of fire, water, and container.
Nor do logs, though splittable, split without the strike of an axe.
One who thinks 'those very rice grains are cookable which have come into conjunction with a competent fire, water, and pot — for after that, husked rice appears;
but those after which [husked rice] does not appear are not cookable' —
to him we shall reply by demonstrating the efficacious action of non-momentary [entities].
Therefore, it is reasonable that entities, being produced as destructible, do not require a cause of destruction from their own causes [alone].
But you who say that nothing other than the entity is a cause [of destruction] are to be questioned:
Does the non-causality of the destruction please you as [implying] its non-existence, or as [implying] its eternality? Regarding that, the direct refutation has been stated by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>: in the thesis of the <s>Śākyas</s> (Buddhists), what is without a cause is of two kinds — eternal like space, or unreal (<s>tuccha</s>) like a hare's horn and the like.
But for us, it is eternal alone — since we do not accept your alleged unreal (<s>tuccha</s>) absolute non-existence; and since what we accept [as non-existence] is not accepted by you, it has been declared 'non-existent' by superimposition, as belonging to one category.
'Destruction of what has arisen' — this is universally accepted; the opposite follows in your view.
'But what is the fault if entity and non-existence coexist?' — therefore he says:
'And then, of entities' —
(414/5) He raises the doubt: 'if, because of indestructibility' —
The damage to the purpose is this: if destruction is without a cause, this is the fault — but through fear of fault, one cannot accept the causality of destruction when it is contradicted by a clearer <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the import.
The <s>siddhāntin</s>, with hidden intent, asks: 'whence is it that destruction does not perish?'
The objector says: 'of destroyed [entities]' —
The <s>siddhāntin</s>, relying on the Buddhist view, says:
'For the non-existence of destruction' —
For one for whom the non-existence of a cloth is itself unreal (<s>tuccha</s>), what discussion is there about its non-existence — since it is even more unreal than the unreal — this is the import.
Taking his own view, he says:
'Moreover, destruction has causes' —
The rest is easy to understand.
As for what was said as a reason for non-causality — 'if non-existence is different from the entity, [its] arising would leave the entity unchanged' —
to that we say: upon the arising of non-existence, there is no further cessation of the entity; rather, the very arising of non-existence is its cessation. 'How does the arising of one [cause] the cessation of another?' — here the answer must be given through intrinsic natures (<s>svabhāvabheda</s>): those that exist in mutual exclusion arise from their own causes.
For it is not the case that, merely because fire is other than the sprout, it is not a cause [of the sprout's destruction] — for by the non-specificity of otherness, it would not be a cause of the ashes either.
But the delimitation of the cause-effect relation through intrinsic natures is equally [applicable] to the delimitation of mutual-exclusion.
And just as, even though the prior-non-existence of the sprout, being devoid of all capacity, is not assisted by the seeds and the like, they still originate the sprout — because the very production of that [sprout] is of the nature of the cessation of its prior-non-existence —
so too, the causes of the entity's non-existence, though not doing anything to the entity's form, produce that non-existence. But if the causes of non-existence do nothing to the entity's form, why does the entity not produce apprehension and efficacious action as before, at the time of its own non-existence?
By the same token, why does the sprout, even before arising, not produce apprehension and efficacious action?
'Before arising, the sprout did not exist — therefore it did not [produce them]; but having arisen, it exists — therefore it does' — if so,
well then, the entity too — when it existed, it [produced them]; but now, being destroyed, it does not exist — therefore it does not [produce them].
And just as the very production of the entity is the non-existence of its prior-non-existence, so the very production of non-existence is the non-existence of the entity.
'But destruction, being of the nature of arising-and-perishing, is non-different from entities — therefore the universe does not divide into the two categories of existent and non-existent' — if so: what is this 'arising'? If it is the inherence of one's own cause, or the inherence of <s>sattā</s> (being) — that does not exist in non-existence.
If it is the attainment of one's own nature —
even so, since there is equality in that much [between entity and non-existence], the division into two categories is tenable through the sub-differences.
Therefore, just as, though being (<s>sattva</s>) is common [to all], substance, quality, and action differ from each other by that very nature, so too, though there is no difference in being-a-<s>prameya</s>, being-denotable, and being-a-cause, the difference of non-existence from them is established through the difference in form characterized by the presence of <s>sattā</s> versus the absence of <s>sattā</s>.
As for the inevitability of destruction —
regarding that we say: one who says that destruction, by its inevitability, does not require another cause, should not be able to say that it has no cause at all —
because the negation of another cause does not negate cause-in-general;
because the negation of a specific [cause] has the result of permitting the remainder.
Moreover, inevitability is either unestablished or inconclusive.
Let this gentleman answer this question: is the homogeneous (<s>sabhāga</s>) continuum of potsherds inevitable from the pot-continuum, or not?
If not,
then the destruction of the pot too is not inevitable — for we who have physical eyes do not observe the destruction of the pot without the production of a heterogeneous moment (<s>visabhāgakṣaṇa</s>). And thus, the inevitability of destruction is unestablished.
But if [the potsherd-continuum] is inevitable, then even in that inevitable heterogeneous continuum, a hammer and the like as causes would be required — and so inevitability is inconclusive, not pervaded by non-requirement-of-another-cause — hence it cannot negate the requirement of another cause.
This is what was indicated by the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'and the fault of causeless destruction is irremediable.'
Thus, the fault has been stated when difference [from the prior moment] is the thesis to be proved.
(415/11)
Even though momentariness too was previously stated and refuted, still the statement of momentariness is for your benefit — difference is indeed the primary [thesis] there.
But now, momentariness itself is the primary thesis to be proved — by this much there is a difference of context.
'The qualifier contradicts the established doctrine' —
If some entities were slowly destructible [rather than instantly], then the qualifier 'quickly destructible' could be postulated — and thus there would be contradiction with the established doctrine — this is the meaning.
'Having the possessive suffix' —
(416/2) 'Momentary' (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) — [the suffix] <s>iṇ</s> or <s>ṭhan</s>, being a possessive suffix —
meaning: characterized by destruction at the immediately subsequent [moment].
'The ultimate time of all' —
The smallest time-unit, lacking prior and subsequent parts — established by the science of astronomy — is merely a designation 'the ultimate time'; but the intended momentariness is real.
Having refuted the thesis-statement, he refutes the reason: 'those too' —
Here, the word 'and the like' should be understood as including <s>sattva</s> (being), <s>kṛtakatva</s> (being produced), and the like.
Therein, 'whatever has being is all momentary — like a pot; and the disputed sound and the like [also have being]' — this is the <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (nature-reason), because momentariness follows from being alone.
'But how is the invariable concomitance of momentariness with being alone established?'
It is said: <s>sattva</s> (being) is nothing other than the capacity for efficacious action (<s>arthakriyākāritva</s>) of entities.
For it is impossible that something exists and yet does not perform efficacious action.
For consider: is it or is it not a supporting condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) for the cognition of an omniscient being?
If not, then either it does not exist, or the omniscient is not omniscient — because of ignorance of that very thing.
If it is a supporting condition, how does it not perform efficacious action?
And there is nothing called the universal of being (<s>sattāsāmānya</s>);
nor is there its inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), by which [something] is called 'existent.'
Even if that [universal] existed, the universals, particulars, and inherences belonging to entities would not exist —
because their being substrates of universals is not accepted [by the Buddhists].
And apprehensibility by a <s>pramāṇa</s> too is being-an-object-of-a-<s>pramāṇa</s>, which is nothing but being a supporting condition for a <s>pramāṇa</s> — and that is nothing other than the capacity for efficacious action — thus it is established that being (<s>sattva</s>) is nothing but the capacity for efficacious action.
And that [capacity] is pervaded by the sequential (<s>krama</s>) and the simultaneous (<s>akrama</s>), because of the absence of a third mode.
For the sequential and the simultaneous modes of efficacious action of entities are observed to be mutually exclusive.
And thus, if a third mode — partaking of both the sequential and the simultaneous — is accepted as compounded of these very experienced and ascertained sequential and simultaneous [modes],
then even the observed sequential and simultaneous [modes] would be subject to mutual conflation.
For these sequential and simultaneous [modes], being compounded, would be such that the observed sequence would appear as having the nature of simultaneity, and the simultaneous as having the nature of sequence.
But it does not so appear.
By this, direct perception itself, distinguishing the mutually exclusive sequential and simultaneous [modes], rejects their conflation everywhere.
If there were identity [of sequential and simultaneous] anywhere, then even here, these very sequential and simultaneous would be grasped as conflated.
Therefore, the non-apprehension of their conflation here negates conflation in other places and times as well.
And in negating identity, because of the non-apprehension of what is qualified by being visible —
because the denial of what is visible, like a post, as identical [with other things], does not discriminately deny [identity for] both the invisible, like ghosts and the like, and the visible, like monkeys and the like.
As it is said: 'and the qualifier is inexpressible.'
[A mode] not being of the nature of [ordinary] sequence and simultaneity, a third mode — is it sequence and simultaneity, or not? — it is not, for the difference of a thing is not [negated] merely by the difference of a word.
Lest there be the unwanted consequence of horns for speech and the like merely from the co-referentiality with the word 'cow.'
One might think: let the sequential and simultaneous [modes] not be [the answer]; let there be some other mode, distinct from sequence and simultaneity, described as 'sequence-simultaneity,' by which even stable entities could serve for efficacious action.
But the efficacious action of these too, like [that attributed to] a third mode, is itself becoming phantom-like.
If so, what is cut for us? The observed, experienced, and ascertained efficacious action — having a form embraced by two modes characterized by mutually exclusive sequence and simultaneity — cannot exist from a third mode.
And there is no third mode either.
For wherever the denial of one mode necessitates the establishment of the other mode, there a third mode is impossible —
just as, when the denial of the blue mode necessitates the establishment of the non-blue mode in yellow, between those two — when either mode is denied, the other is established — the denied mode is the domain of every cause and effect — this is the apprehension of concomitance with the contradictory (<s>viruddhopalabdhi</s>).
For the rule that upon the denial of either of two [modes] the other is established is contradictory to the possibility of a denied third mode — and therefore the efficacious action of entities, being impossible from a third mode, is pervaded by the sequential and the simultaneous. And those two, being negated for what is stable, negate efficacious action too — like <s>śiṃśapā</s>-hood ceasing when tree-hood ceases, visible from a single-stone mountain-plateau — thus the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) is established.
For a non-momentary [entity] first cannot perform efficacious action sequentially.
For entities are observed to serve efficacious action through their own form.
Whatever entity has its existence and non-existence governed by the positive and negative concomitance of a particular effect — that entity's form is capable of producing that effect, and that form is [the same] whose concomitance is replicated by the effect — therefore form alone is capable. And that [form] exists in the first moment just as in the second and subsequent moments — so it should accomplish the entire complex of effects producible in the second and subsequent moments in the very first moment alone — because for what is capable, delay is impossible — therefore sequential operation is not possible for a non-momentary [entity].
'One might think: even though capable, it acts sequentially because of the sequential availability of auxiliary conditions' —
This has been answered:
'Because of the impossibility of the alternatives.'
Does the auxiliary condition confer some benefit upon it or not? And if conferring benefit, [does it produce] something different from the entity or non-different?
If a different benefit is conferred, then since the entity exists [without it] and the benefit has not yet arisen [without it] — thus the benefit alone is the producer of the effect when it arises, not the entity.
Nor should one say: 'the entity together with the auxiliary benefit is the producer of the effect, not the benefit alone' —
because there would be an infinite regress in the benefit requiring another benefit.
And when there is no [further] benefit [to be produced], there is no auxiliary status.
If a non-different benefit is conferred, then the entity alone would produce — and it existed before [the auxiliary arrived] — so the auxiliary is purposeless.
Or, if the auxiliary confers no benefit, then entities would not depend on [auxiliaries] — and so the entity would produce the effect at the very moment of its own production.
If one thinks: even though non-benefiting, auxiliaries exist, because the entity performs the effect together with them, and because without them the effect does not arise — they are not not-depended-upon —
surely, if the entity produces the effect by its own form, why does it not produce [it] even without those [auxiliaries], since its own form exists even before those [auxiliaries]?
Or, if it produces by virtue of the auxiliary's form, then the auxiliaries alone are the producers, not the entity.
'But because the existence and non-existence of the efficacious action follows the presence and absence of both, and because of deviation from either one alone, it depends on both' — this is not tenable.
When the entity exists but the effect is not produced — this deviation [exists]; but when, upon the conjunction of the final auxiliary condition, the effect arises from the entity itself — the deviation is from the conjunction of the final auxiliary alone, not from the entity — because cause-status is ascertained by [the conjunction's] being the final [condition].
By this, what some say — '... the entity, having arisen from its own cause, acts with delay — therefore it does not act at the very moment of arising ...' — is refuted.
For that delay-action-nature — is it or is it not its own nature? If it is its own nature, even at the time of conjunction with auxiliaries it exists — so it would not act even then.
If it is not its own nature, then it has been destroyed — how has the entity not perished when its own nature has perished?
But if delay-action is not its own nature, why would it not produce the effect at the very moment of arising?
Therefore, entities do not perform efficacious action sequentially, nor simultaneously —
therefore, whatever effect is accomplished by that non-momentary [entity] in the first moment — all of that it should accomplish in the second and subsequent moments.
Because the form that accomplishes that much effect exists in the second and subsequent moments too.
And what has been accomplished cannot be accomplished again — so what it accomplishes in the second and subsequent moments is different from what was accomplished in the first moment — and thus sequences would recur — and the fault already stated [applies].
Or, if [the entity] has accomplished all its work simultaneously, then in the second and subsequent [moments], having nothing left to do, it has no capacity for efficacious action — and by being non-existent [in that sense], momentariness follows.
Therefore, since the sequential and the simultaneous — which pervade being — are not apprehended in a non-momentary [entity], by the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>), being, being negated from the non-momentary, is pervaded by momentariness — thus the invariable connection is established.
Blue itself — without the experienced and ascertained [modes] — superimposed upon a non-momentary [entity], [remains] non-momentary. The non-apprehension of sequence and simultaneity in that non-momentary [entity] is like the very apprehension of the blue's own form; just as the apprehension of the ground's own form is the non-apprehension of the pot whose visibility has been superimposed.
And the ground, having thus arisen, is the non-existence of the pot — but non-existence is not some embodied entity that could be the object of cognition.
Rather, it is merely to be spoken of conventionally.
One might think:
Is the momentary entity of a nature that produces efficacious action, or not? If not, then it is non-existent. If it is of such a nature, what need has it of auxiliaries?
The seed, at the very moment of arising, should produce the sprout.
'But the seed-moment, having arisen with capacity, does produce the sprout! Whence comes the capacity of the capable [moment]? From the prior seed-moment.'
Then, since all [moments] in that continuum have equally the nature of seed, they should all have the capacity to produce a sprout — so the seed, at the moment immediately after the flower, should produce a sprout.
Not so!
The final seed-moment, whose birth is obtained through the succession of subsequent moments arising with a surplus produced by the conjunction of prior moments of earth, seed, wind, and the like — that capable [moment], not requiring capable earth and the like as co-present auxiliaries, produces the sprout.
And it is not the case that, despite not requiring its co-present earth and the like, it [could produce] without them — because, its arising being dependent on their single aggregate, it would not exist in their absence.
Or rather, there is no auxiliary status of earth and the like, because the sprout is produced only together with them.
Because their prior-existence-to-the-effect too, being invariable, is not different [from the seed's].
And because cause-status consists in just that much [invariable prior-existence].
Or, even for non-requiring [entities], there is no individual production of a different effect [without the others] — because that much alone is apprehended from them, and the capacity is restricted to that alone.
And it is not the case that, because the others have already done their job, they are inactive — because [the notion that] in joint action, [some have] already done [their part] is impossible.
And entities whose proximity is obtained from their own causes are not intelligent [beings who could think]: 'even one of us alone could do this — what need of the proximity of all of us?' — and desist.
And the cause of the difference of effects is not merely the difference of individual causes, but the difference of the aggregate — because the difference of effects is observed when that [aggregate-difference] exists.
Where the aggregate is non-different, there is no unwanted consequence of effect-difference.
And the co-presence (<s>parasparasamavadhāna</s>) of earth and the like is [inferred] from the cognitions of approach.
And because of the non-contradiction of efficacious action for the momentary, the reason [<s>sattva</s>] is not uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>).
And when the thesis-subject [sound and the like] is observed, since the establishment of the thesis follows from the establishment of the pervasion alone, the statement of the reason is not a non-component of the proof.
For a pervasion with complete enumeration cannot have only visible things as its domain.
For the opponent can doubt: 'you have not excluded being from the non-momentary among the non-visible — so being is inconclusive as a proof of momentariness.'
Therefore, the pervasion should be demonstrated as: 'whatever is — visible or invisible — all that is momentary.'
'But even so, since the momentariness of the disputed sound and the like is established by the very force of the pervasion-demonstration, the statement of the reason remains equally a non-component [of proof].'
Not so. Just as, even when hare-horns and the like are non-existent, the pervasion with complete enumeration is: 'whatever is existent — visible or invisible — all that is momentary'; and hare-horns and the like are not momentary either — so too, even when the disputed sound and the like exist, and even when the pervasion is established, momentariness is not established [for them].
Therefore, being must necessarily be demonstrated for these [entities] to prove their momentariness — so the statement of the reason is not a non-component [of proof].
To this we say:
Being (<s>sattva</s>) is not a component in establishing momentary destruction — because of being uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>), or because of having a doubtful negative concomitant (<s>saṃdigdhavyatirekitva</s>).
For being, pervaded by the sequential and the simultaneous, is excluded from the non-momentary by their non-apprehension; and that same [being], pervaded by dependence and non-dependence [on auxiliaries], is excluded from the momentary too by their non-apprehension. Therefore, like 'having-smell' [which proves only earth], it is uncommon — non-conducive and not a component [of proof].
For the earth, wind, water, fire, and seed — having reached their final moments, being capable, being determined by their prior existence — are accepted by you as the causes of earth, water, fire, and sprout, which have determined final productions. Do those [causes] produce [the effects] independently of each other, or dependently?
'But independent! The earth and the like, having reached their final moments, are to produce [the effect] in the next aggregate' — this has been said.
Then what — by the unaccepted alternative [of dependence] are they dependent? And [by the accepted alternative] independent?
Then what of this: is the seed-moment that produces the capable seed-moment also independent?
If yes,
then all seed-moments are independent producers of their own effects — so what need of auxiliaries?
'But it has been said: these are not intelligent; rather, having a proximity determined by their own conditions, they cannot intervene [to prevent co-presence].'
Then is this farmer too not intelligent? He is intelligent — because he deliberately takes the seed from the granary and sows it in the plowed ground,
precisely because the seed-moment, when co-present with earth and the like, has the capacity to produce the sprout through the succession of surplus-production — while from seed stored in the granary, even after a thousand years, no sprout arises — therefore he sows there.
If so —
Then is this capable seed-moment not produced from its own continuum alone? If so, why would it not require another continuum for its own effect?
'It does require [others] — but for its own production, not for its own effect. The non-requirement is maintained for its effect, not for its production.'
But even in its production, it is the prior moment within its own continuum alone that is independent and [fully] active in producing [it]. Similarly, the prior moment of that [moment], and the prior of that — each falling within its own continuum, is independent and active in production. So the seed deposited in the granary alone should [suffice for] a successful farmer — what need of his laborious agricultural work!
Therefore, even unwillingly, one must accept that it is only when mutually dependent [factors] reach their final moments that the production of the effect [occurs].
Moreover, does the seed that has reached its final moment, independently [of earth and the like], produce sprout, earth, wind, water, and fire? If so, by the very form by which it produces the sprout, does it produce the others too, or by a different form?
Not by the very same form — for then earth and the like would have the unwanted consequence of having the same nature as the sprout.
For according to you, when causes are non-different, the effect cannot be different — because the difference of effects would then be without cause.
As you yourselves have said: 'this very difference, or the cause of difference, is the superimposition of contradictory properties and the difference of causes.'
Nor is there difference of aggregate — because that [aggregate] too is non-different.
Otherwise, there would be no rule of co-existence [of the factors].
A certain intrinsic nature-difference alone, acquired from one's own causes — being of such a kind that from it diverse effects arise — is such that there is no absence-of-cause for the diversity of effects, nor over-extension, because such [a nature-difference] is not universal.
And it is not the case that cause and effect are non-different, such that the non-difference and difference of causes would entail the non-difference and difference of effects.
Therefore, just as from some many [causes] one effect is produced, so too from some one [cause] many effects will be produced — if so,
then the painstaking entity — the composite whole, universal, conjunction, and the like, existing at many locations — is uselessly tormented by you. For even when the locations are many, the entity such as the universal and the like that is dependent on them need not be many — because of its non-difference from them.
If by a different form the seed produces earth and the like, which are other than the sprout — consider: the seed is the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of the sprout, because the sprout arises from the transformation of the seed's essential portion; but with respect to the earth and the like that are to be produced, it is an auxiliary. But the prior earth and the like are themselves the material causes of [the subsequent] earth and the like — those arise from their transformation — if so:
Is auxiliary-status and material-cause-status one nature or many? If one, how does it produce by a different form? If many, are those two different from the seed or non-different? If different, how is the seed a producer — since the sprout and the like would arise from those two alone.
If non-different, how is the seed not different — because of having the nature of those different [two]?
Their having a single form is because of identity.
Therefore, for producing earth and the like, which are different from the sprout, their own prior material cause — the earth and the like co-temporal [with the seed] — is required by the seed.
Similarly, the seed too is required as a co-temporal auxiliary cause by the earth and the like — otherwise the difference of effects cannot be established — even unwillingly, this must be accepted.
And a non-benefiting [factor] is not within the scope of requirement — this has been demonstrated by you yourselves.
And for a momentary [entity], the possibility of benefiting is impossible other than through production — because of its being unmodifiable.
And between co-temporal [entities], there is no producer-produced relation — like the left and right horns.
Therefore, from the unwanted consequence that the effect would arise from one's own continuum alone, from the impossibility of effect-difference, and from the absence of requirement even of non-benefiting [auxiliaries] — for a momentary [entity], whether dependent or independent, efficacious action is not possible — hence being (<s>sattva</s>), being uncommon, is not a component in establishing momentary destruction.
'But let being not be uncommon' — then even for non-benefiting [factors], requirement for producing effects must be accepted, because even they have positive and negative concomitance replicated by the effect.
But by this reasoning, even a non-momentary entity would require non-benefiting auxiliaries — because even sequential [auxiliaries] have positive and negative concomitance replicated by the effect.
[The non-momentary entity] would produce effects sequentially, conditioned by sequential auxiliaries.
And for what is capable, delay is tenable because of the non-proximity of what is to be required.
Nor should one say: 'since its production depends solely on the conjunction of auxiliaries, what need of its form [as a cause]?' —
because production is observed from that [conjunction] only when it [the entity] is present.
Because even when the form exists, there is no production [without the conjunction].
'Since production occurs only when the conjunction exists, the conjunction alone is the cause, not the form' — if so, then what — is the form of the seed equal to a donkey?
If yes,
then why does the sprout not arise without the form of the seed, just as it does not arise without [the seed's presence among] donkeys?
'Because the conjunction of that [seed] is the cause [of the sprout]' — if so,
when the conjunction is the cause, how is the form that inheres in that [conjunction] not also a cause?
And the inherence of that [form] in [the conjunction] is not inevitable —
because the conjunction alone [can exist] without the form of the seed, being present here and there.
But the specific [factor] in the conjunction is precisely the form of the seeds and the like.
Therefore, just as pervasion, whose determination depends on both [pervader and pervaded], is determined in the pervader by the method of 'exclusively-that' (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>) — 'in the pervaded, there is only the existence of the pervader, not its non-existence' — and in the pervaded again by the method of 'exclusively-that' — 'only in the pervader does the pervaded exist, not elsewhere' — so too the cause-effect relation, whose determination depends on both, is determined in the cause by 'exclusively-that':
'before the production of the effect, only the cause exists, not its non-existence.'
And in the effect, by 'exclusively-that':
'only when the cause exists does [the effect] exist, not when something else [exists]' — this is ascertained by following experience.
For that is indeed the settled view of worldly investigators.
And being is not causality itself, but the intrinsic form of blue and the like as experienced and ascertained — for that, by that very form, delimited by its own nature, serves those various efficacious actions; but the capacity for efficacious action is not itself the form — lest there be unwanted consequence of form-difference for what performs multiple efficacious actions simultaneously.
Therefore, if an omniscient [being] exists, then the entity, existing by its own form, will be a supporting condition for his cognition.
But if no [omniscient being] exists, even so, [the entity], having been born with that form, though initially non-productive, later, from some cause or other, having obtained the auxiliary conditions, will serve in those various efficacious actions.
Thus it is established: since even for the momentary, efficacious action is tenable through the sequential and the simultaneous as appropriate, the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>) is unestablished; therefore, being (<s>sattva</s>), as a proof of momentariness for the Buddhists, is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) because of doubtful negative concomitance.
But for us, it is of the type unestablished-through-being-otherwise-established (<s>anyathāsiddha</s>).
And the contact of contradictory properties characterized by being-a-producer and being-a-non-producer cannot serve as a reason for difference [of moments].
For being-a-producer is not the intrinsic nature of a thing, but its property.
And a property is different from the property-bearer in reality.
And the difference of one thing is not sufficient for the difference of another — because of over-extension.
'If there is no difference of otherness, how is it the property of that [thing] alone?' — if so,
here the answer must be given through intrinsic natures themselves:
just as, despite non-specificity of otherness, the effect — smoke — belongs to fire alone, not to the seed — as has been said.
And being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) too is not a reason for momentariness — because of being otherwise-established,
and because [momentariness] is tenable when destruction has a cause.
And the identity of production and destruction is not [tenable] for the entity — because of the unwanted consequence of absolute non-existence — as has been said.
This is what was stated by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>: 'those too are either unestablished, otherwise-established, or contradictory — hence they are non-reasons.'
(416/15)
The observation of specific difference at the final moment — being a property of the prior moment — is unestablished because of being unestablished [as pertaining to the prior moment].
Being and being-produced are otherwise-established.
And every reason, when momentariness is the thesis to be proved, is contradictory.
For being or being-produced, not being continuous across the three worlds — in space or in time — is not a means of proof, because of the absence of the status of an inferential mark due to the impossibility of knowing invariable concomitance.
Because the grasping of invariable concomitance — whether through the positive or the negative method — is impossible in a single moment.
Therefore, being, being-produced, or whatever else is made a reason — must be continuous across place and time.
And whether that [reason] is of the form of a positive entity or of the form of exclusion-from-others — being one across many times, it is non-momentary — and contradicts the thesis of momentariness — thus it was said: 'or contradictory.'
But the contradictory nature of 'from the observation of specific difference at the end' will be stated next.
Accepting [for argument's sake] the existence of specificity — [the reason] is established, [hence] inconclusive — he says:
'Or, accepting' —
To show the unestablished-ness and contradictory-ness of the reason, he says:
'At the end, specific [difference]' —
The otherwise-established-ness of the reason characterized by observation-and-non-observation — he says:
'And this reason' —
'Because of both entity and non-entity having that [property]' — (417/7) the meaning is: because the cognition here — of the non-existence of conjunction-non-existence — has entity-hood.
'We do not even understand the production of a lamp in another location' —
If it is determined that a momentary lamp is produced solely from its own continuum, then all lamp-moments should produce a lamp in another location.
Not [just] some, within the interior of the wick alone.
'But through the conditions of approach, [the lamp-moments] produce an effect in [locations] other than the interior of the wick too.'
Now, does the approach-condition confer some benefit on the lamp or not? It does not confer — because of the impossibility of being benefited or non-benefited, since a moment is unmodifiable.
And when there is no conferring [of benefit], there is no auxiliary status.
And 'there is over-extension when what confers no benefit has auxiliary status' — these are your very own words.
And it is not the case that the production of a specific lamp-moment is itself the benefit of the auxiliaries — because that [specific lamp-moment] is tenable from the prior material cause alone, without requiring auxiliaries.
For the very auxiliaries of that [lamp-moment] cannot be the benefactors of its cause either.
Similarly, even for the prior lamp-moments, since from the capacity of the prior-prior lamp alone, nothing is conferred by auxiliaries — all [moments] should produce their primary effect in one [location] or in another.
But if even non-benefiting [auxiliaries] are required by a momentary lamp for efficacious action, by virtue of their existence and non-existence following the effect — then the same [reasoning applies] in the non-momentary view too — this is the summary.
And this has been elaborated by us in the <s>Brahmatattvasamīkṣā</s> and the <s>Nyāyakaṇikā</s> — so we desist.
'For a clod falling through space' and the like —
For clods, hawks, and other substances of equal gravity — the cause [of falling] for one is gravity, effort, and throw.
For when a person standing on a terrace throws a hawk downward, targeting a pigeon walking on the ground, the effort born of the desire to seize the pigeon, together with gravity and the throw, are the causes of [the hawk's] swifter falling.
But for what is not thrown, gravity and effort are the causes of swift falling; for one not exerting effort, gravity alone is the cause of falling.
'There is no fault even in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view' — therefore he says:
'And a single impression' —
(418/7) When it is said that 'cognitions are non-simultaneous and have a single object,' the cognitions of pot, cloth, and the like, and the cognitions of lamp and the like, being sequential, would have the unwanted consequence of having a single object — therefore he says:
'Contradictory' —
'Because of being denoted by the same word' is inconclusive —
for there are cognitions denoted by the same word — '<s>akṣa</s>, <s>akṣa</s>' [meaning both 'die' and 'axle'] — yet they are not of the same object. Because of the difference of those who have them as objects — <s>Devanādi</s> and the like — therefore he says:
'When there is co-referentiality of that cognition' —
'Even so, [there is] inconclusiveness from lamp-cognitions' — therefore he says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.15: Not [so], because of the manifestation of another quality through the transformation of milk.

children.text:
bhāṣyaṃ guṇāntaraprādurbhāva
iti /
dravyaṃ tāvatsadeva guṇo 'pi san kevalamanudbhūta
āsīt /
ekaścodbhūto guṇaḥ tatra ya udbhūtastirobhavati pūrvaguṇasyanivṛttau tirobhūtau guṇāntaramutpadyatetadbhavatītyarthaḥ
// 15 //
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads:] "the manifestation of another quality" — the substance at any rate existed [all along]; the quality too, though existing, was merely unmanifested. And when one quality is manifested among those [qualities], the one that was manifested disappears; upon the cessation of the prior quality, when [that quality] has disappeared, another quality is produced — this is what happens — this is the meaning. //15//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.16: The observation of the origination of a different substance from a different configuration is an inference of the cessation of the prior substance.

children.text:
atra tu pratiṣedha iti /
kṣīrāvayavā eva hi kṣīravināśe satyutpannapākajā vilakṣaṇaṃ dravyamutpādayanti /
yadi tu sarvaṃ kāryaṃ sadeva kāraṇavyāpārātprāgapi vyarthaḥ kāraṇavyāpāraḥ abhivyakterapi kāryāyāḥ sattvāt /
asattve vā yathā saiva na satī kriyate evaṃ kāryāntarāṇyapīti /
vipañcitaṃ caitadasmābhirnyāyakaṇikāyām
// 16 //
children.translated_text: "But here there is a denial" — for the very particles of milk, when the milk is destroyed, having produced maturation-born [qualities], produce a substance of a different character. But if every effect already exists [in the cause], then even before the causal operation, the causal operation is purposeless, since even the manifestation that is the effect already exists. Or, in the case of non-existence, just as that [manifestation] itself, though non-existent, is not produced, so too other effects [would not be produced]. And this has been elaborated by us in the <s>Nyāyakaṇikā</s>. //16//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.17: Because of the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction in some cases, and the apprehension [of such a cause] in other cases, [the argument is] inconclusive.

children.text:
abhyanujñāya ca niṣkāraṇamiti /
vināśotpādavattvātsamānadharmātsaṃśayaḥ
dadhikṣīrayorvināśotpādāvakāraṇau dṛṣṭau kumbhasya cotpādavināśau sakāraṇakau, tadiha sphaṭike vināśotpādau sakāraṇau niṣkāraṇau veti saṃdehaḥ /
tadyadi sakāraṇāveveti pramāṇato niścīyate tato vināśakāraṇānupalabdheḥ sphaṭikasya kumbhavadvināśo nāstīti niścīyate /
tadidamuktaṃ bhāṣyakāreṇa /
na punaryathā vināśakāraṇāprāvāditi /
niradhiṣṭhānaṃ ceti /
dharmiṇamāśritya tatsamānadharmā dṛṭānto bhavati sphaṭikotpādavināśau ca dharmiṇau tatsamānadharmatayā kṣīradadhivināśotpādayordṛṣṭāntatvena bhavitavyam /
na punaḥ sphaṭikotpādavināśau dharmiṇau gṛhyete /
tasmānna tatsamānadharmatayā dṛṣṭāntau bhavata iti /
yadi tu dravyasamavāyādityucyeta tatastoyādiparamāṇuvisamavetai rūpādibhiranekāntaḥ syādityata āha /
vyāpaketi /
( 420 / 17 ) tathāpyātmatvasāmānyenānekānto 'ta āha /
guṇatve satīti /
tathā 'pyātmaparimāṇenānekānto 'ta āha /
pratyakṣatayeti /
asmadādīnāmiti śeṣaḥ /
guṇatvādiviśeṣaṇayogātprāgvyāpakagrahaṇasyopayogaḥ /
asmadādipratyakṣatvādityucyamāne sāmānyasamavāyābhyāmanekāntaḥ syādata āha jātimattve satīti /
āśritatvādityatrāpijātimatve sati pratyakṣattve cetyanuṣañjanīyam /
anityā buddhiḥ pratyakṣatvādityurcyamāne manasā vyabhicāro 'ta āha /
ayogīti /
tathā 'pyātmanā vyabhicāro 'ta
uktaṃ karaṇabhāve satīti /
hānādibuddhiḥ karaṇaṃ bhavati /
śabdaśca pratyaye karaṇam /
atrā pi jātimattve satītyanuṣañjanīyaṃ tena na gandhatvādibhiranekāntaḥ
// 17 //
children.translated_text: "And having conceded that [destruction is] causeless" — the doubt [arises] from the common property of having destruction and origination: the destruction and origination of curd and milk are observed to be without a cause, while the origination and destruction of a pot are observed to have a cause. So here, regarding a crystal, is its destruction and origination with a cause or without a cause? — this is the doubt. Now, if it is determined by <s>pramāṇa</s> that [destruction] is only with a cause, then from the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction, the destruction of the crystal — like that of a pot — is determined to be absent. This is what the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> has said: "but not that there is no cause of destruction." "And without a basis" — a supporting example is [drawn] from the common property of the property-bearer; and the destruction and origination of the crystal, being property-bearers, should serve as examples for the destruction and origination of milk-curd by having a common property with them. But the destruction and origination of the crystal are not taken as property-bearers [here]. Therefore they cannot be examples by having a common property with those [milk-curd destruction-origination]. But if it is said "because of inhering in a substance" — then because of the inconclusiveness [that would arise] from the form and the like inhering in atoms of water and the like, he says: "pervading" — (420/17) Even so, because of inconclusiveness through the commonality of substance-hood (<s>ātmatva</s>), he says: "when there is quality-hood" — Even so, because of inconclusiveness through the measure of the <s>ātman</s>, he says: "through perceptibility" — "of ourselves and the like" is the remainder. Before the qualification of quality-hood and the like, the statement of "pervading" is useful. When it is said "because of being perceptible to ourselves and the like," there would be inconclusiveness through [the commonality of] universal and inherence — therefore he says: "when there is possession of a universal" — In "because of being dependent" too, the qualifications "when there is possession of a universal" and "when there is perceptibility" should be connected. When it is said "<s>buddhi</s> (cognition) is non-eternal because of being perceptible," there is deviation through the mind (<s>manas</s>) — therefore he says: "for non-yogins" — Even so, there is deviation through the <s>ātman</s> — therefore it is said: "when there is instrument-status." Cognition of abandonment and the like is an instrument. And word (<s>śabda</s>) is an instrument in cognition. Here too, "when there is possession of a universal" should be connected — by that, there is no inconclusiveness through smell-hood (<s>gandhatva</s>) and the like. //17//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.18: Not [derived] from the sense organ and the object, because even upon the destruction of those, cognition persists.

children.text:
cintāntaramavatārayati /
idaṃ tu cintyata iti /
nanvātmaparīkṣāyāmātmaguṇatvaṃ buddhervyavasthāpitaṃ tatkasmātpunaḥ parīkṣyata
ityata āha bhāṣyakāraḥ /
prasiddho 'pīti /
yadyapyayamarthaḥ parīkṣitastathā 'pyavāntaraviśeṣaparijñānārthaṃ punaḥ parīkṣyata ityarthaḥ /
codayati vārtatikakāraḥ /
na guṇeti /
pariharati /
anitvatve satīti /
vimṛṣya siddhāntī(ya)pakṣaṃ gṛhṇāti sannikarṣotpattariti /
codayati adrākṣamityetanneti /
( 421 / 3 ) pariharati smṛtāvapīti // 18 //
children.translated_text: He introduces another investigation: "but this is to be investigated" — Objection: in the examination of the <s>ātman</s>, the quality-status of <s>buddhi</s> in relation to the <s>ātman</s> has been established — so why is it examined again? To this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "even though well-known" — even though this matter has been examined, it is examined again for the purpose of understanding subsidiary details — this is the meaning. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> objects: "not a quality" — He resolves: "when there is non-eternality" — Having considered, the <s>siddhāntin</s> adopts the thesis: "born from contact (<s>sannikarṣa</s>)" — He objects: "'I saw' — this does not" — (421/3) He resolves: "even in memory" — //18//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.19: And because of the non-apprehension of simultaneous knowables, [<s>buddhi</s> is] not [the property] of the mind.

children.text:
deśayati astu tarhīti /
pariharati yugapaditi /
yatkaraṇatvenānumitaṃ tatkaraṇatvamapodya na kartṛ bhavitumarhatītyarthaḥ /
yugapaj jñeyānupalabdhyā yatsamadhigatamiti bhāṣyamākṣipati /
viśeṣaṇopādānāditi /
samādhatte na sarvasyeti /
punarākṣipati /
evamapīti /
viśiṣṭasya karaṇasya jñānaguṇatvaniṣedhaḥ karaṇāntarasya jñānaguṇatvamāpādayati na cātmā karaṇamityarthaḥ /
samādhatte anayasyopapatteriti /
etadeva vivṛṇokti /
anavasthitatvāditi /
pramātaiva kadā citpramāṇaṃ kadā citprameyamityarthaḥ /
puruṣāntareṇa puruṣāntaraṃ paricchinattīti /
yādṛśo 'yaṃ puruṣastādṛśo 'vamapīti puruṣāntareṇa prasiddhena puruṣāntarapariccheda iti /
pṛcchati /
yadi na karaṇasya kaspaya tarhīti /
uttaraṃ jñasya vaśitvāt /
kartuḥ svātantryādityarthaḥ /
kartṛkaraṇādisamavadhāne hi caitanyaṃ kartaryeva dṛṣṭaṃ na karaṇādau /
yathā mṛddaṇḍacakrasalilasūtrakulālasamavadhāne kartureva kulālasya na tu mṛdādīnāmiti /
vaśī jñātā vaśyaṃ karaṇamiti bhāṣyaṃ tadanupannaṃ jñāturapi kva cidvaśyatvadarśanāt /
yathā devadattaṃ kaṭaṃ kārayati yajñadatta ityata āha /
na cāyaṃ jñātarīti /
yadi tu kaścij jñānaguṇaṃ mana
icchettaṃ prati bhāṣyaṃ jñānaguṇatve ceti tadvyācaṣṭe /
jñānaguṇatveveti /
( 422 / 3 ) ghrāṇādisādhanasyeti bhāṣya vyācaṣṭe /
yathā ca jñāturiti /
tathā ca manturmatisādhanaṃ yattanmanaḥ karaṇam /
atha tadapi kasmāccetanaṃ na bhavatītyata āha /
ubhayoriti /
vibhu cāntaḥkaraṇaṃ jñānamantaḥkaraṇāntararahitamitiśeṣaḥ
// 19 //
children.translated_text: He teaches: "let it be so, then" — He resolves: "simultaneously" — that which has been inferred as having instrument-status — the denial of that instrument-status [shows that it] cannot become an agent — this is the meaning. He objects to the <s>Bhāṣya</s> "what has been ascertained by the non-apprehension of simultaneous knowables": "because of the inclusion of a qualifier" — He resolves: "not of everything" — He objects again: "even so" — the denial of the knowledge-quality-status of a specific instrument implies the knowledge-quality-status of another instrument — and the <s>ātman</s> is not an instrument — this is the meaning. He resolves: "because of the tenability of this reasoning" — He elaborates on this: "because of non-fixity" — the very knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) is sometimes the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) and sometimes the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) — this is the meaning. "By one person, another person is determined" — a person already known [serves to] determine another person of similar type — thus by one already established person, the determination of another person [is made]. He asks: "if not of an instrument, then of what?" The answer: "because of the mastery of the knower" — because of the independence of the agent — this is the meaning. For when agent, instrument, and the like are present together, consciousness is observed only in the agent, not in the instrument and the like. Just as when clay, stick, wheel, water, thread, and potter are all present, [the agency belongs] only to the potter as agent, not to the clay and the like. "The master is the knower, the mastered is the instrument" — this <s>Bhāṣya</s> is challenged, since mastery is observed even in the knower [being mastered by another], as in "<s>Devadatta</s> causes <s>Yajñadatta</s> to make a mat" — to this he says: "and this [mastery is] not in the knower" — But if someone wishes [to hold that] the mind has knowledge as its quality, then against him the <s>Bhāṣya</s> "and if it has knowledge as its quality" — he explains that: "if it has knowledge as its quality" — (422/3) He explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> "of the instrument such as the nose and the like": "and just as of the knower" — And thus, that which is the instrument of the thinker (<s>mantṛ</s>) and of thought (<s>mati</s>) — that is the mind (<s>manas</s>), the instrument. Now, why is that too not conscious? To this he says: "of both" — And the inner instrument is all-pervading — cognition is without another inner instrument — this is the remainder. //19//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.20: Even if it [<s>buddhi</s>] is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, the same [objection applies].
Now, one who does not see the mind as the inner instrument objects: "if it is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.21: Because of the absence of contact of the mind with the sense organs, [cognition] does not arise from that [mind alone].

children.text:
pariharati na prasaṅga iti /
vikaraṇadharmeti bhāṣyaṃ'pīti /
viśiṣṭaṃ karaṇaṃ dharmo yasya sa vikaraṇadharmā asmadādikaraṇavilakṣaṇakaraṇaḥ
yena vyavahitaviprakṛṣṭasūkṣmādidarśī bhavatītyarthaḥ
// 21 //
children.translated_text: He resolves: "there is no unwanted consequence" — the <s>Bhāṣya</s> too [says:] "having a distinctive instrument as its property" — one whose distinguished instrument is his property is one who has a distinctive-instrument-property — [meaning:] one whose instrument is unlike our instruments, by which he perceives what is hidden, remote, subtle, and the like — this is the meaning. //21//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.22: Not [so], because of not indicating a cause of origination.

children.text:
yadi punarityādi bhāṣyaṃ pūrayitvā vyācaṣṭe /
yadi punariti /
notpattīti /
nātra pramāṇamapadiśyate /
pratyuta bādhakaṃ pramāṇamastītyarthaḥ /
vyākhyānāntaramāha /
ayugapadutpattau veti /
vyākhyānāntaramāha /
ayugapadutpattau veti /
vyākhyānāntaramāha /
videheti /
śarīravṛttitve hi manasaḥ sarvaṃ jñānaṃ śarīrāyatanasyātmano bhavet /
yadā tu mana eva nāsti tadendriyārthasannikarṣasyātmanaśca śarīrādbahirapi bhāvādvidehapratyayotpādaprasaṅga
iti /
antaḥkaraṇapratyākhyāne ceti /
yadyapi sarvāṇyapi jñānāni na yugapadupajāyante tathāpi smṛtīnāmavaśyaṃ yugapadutpādaprasaṅga iti pūrvasmādasya viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Although all cognitions indeed do not arise simultaneously, nevertheless the consequence of the simultaneous origination of memories is inevitable — this is the difference from the previous [argument].
He states another interpretation:
"And when the sense organ and the <s>ātman</s> are simultaneously connected with the object" —
In the absence of the contact between sense organ and mind, when postulating the causality of deviating [factors], there is no basis for determination — this is the purport. //22//

He completes and explains the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with "but if": "but if" — "not origination" — no <s>pramāṇa</s> is adduced here [for origination]. Rather, there is a defeating <s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning. He states another interpretation: "or, in the case of non-simultaneous origination" — He states [yet] another interpretation: "disembodied" — For if the mind operated [only] within the body, all cognition would belong only to the <s>ātman</s> that has the body as its seat. But when the mind does not exist [independently], since the contact of sense-organ and object with the <s>ātman</s> exists even outside the body, the consequence would be the arising of disembodied cognition. "And in the refutation of the inner instrument" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.23: And if, because of the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction, [cognition] persists, the consequence of its eternality [follows].
"Destruction... consequence" (sū. 23) //

children.text:
atra pūrvapakṣasūtre cakāraḥ pūrvapūrvapakṣasūtrāpekṣayetyāha /
tadātmaguṇatva iti /
ataḥ( 423 / 6 ) parasya nigada

children.translated_text: is itself the explanation. //23//

Here, the word "and" (<s>ca</s>) in this prima facie <s>sūtra</s> is in reference to the preceding prima facie <s>sūtras</s> — he says: "if it is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>" — (423/6) Beyond this, the mere recitation [of the text]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.24: From grasping non-eternality, the destruction of <s>buddhi</s> is from another <s>buddhi</s>, like sound.

children.text:
yadanantaramapavṛjyate puruṣaḥ sā 'ntyā buddhiḥ /
sthitihetvabhāvādvinaśyatīti /
sthitihetū ( 424 / 6 ) dharmādharmau tayorabhāvāditi /
atha tayorabhāvaḥ kasmādityata āha /
kālāt /
antyasukhaduḥkhopabhogākalaṃ prāpyetyarthaḥ /
atha vā svajanitātsaṃskārādevāntyāyā buddhervināśa
ityāha /
saṃskārādvā /
saṃskārasya tu sthitihetvadṛṣṭābhāvādvināśo bhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
pṛcchati /
kathaṃ kālāt /
uttaraṃ yāvantyasya janmana iti caramasya dehasyetyarthaḥ
// 24 //
children.translated_text: That [<s>buddhi</s>] which ceases immediately after [the attainment of] <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) — that is the final <s>buddhi</s>. It perishes because of the absence of a cause of persistence. (424/6) The causes of persistence are <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit); because of the absence of those — why then is there an absence of those? To this he says: "from time" — meaning: upon reaching the time of the final experience of pleasure and pain. Or alternatively, the destruction of the final <s>buddhi</s> is from the <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) produced by itself — he says: "or from <s>saṃskāra</s>" — but the <s>saṃskāra</s> perishes because of the absence of the unseen [force] (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) that is the cause of its persistence — this is the purport. He asks: "how from time?" The answer: "for as long as this birth" — meaning: of the final body. //24//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.25: Memory arises from the contact of the mind with the region of the <s>ātman</s> in which knowledge inheres — therefore [cognitions] do not arise simultaneously.

children.text:
deśayati yadi kāraṇasyeti /
atra tāvadekaḥ parihāra iti /
ekaḥ pradhānaḥ parihāraḥ parihārāntaraṃ tvekadeśimatenāpradhānamityarthaḥ /
api ca na smṛtayo yuga padutpadyante paricchedakatvād
children.translated_text: Moreover, memories do not arise simultaneously, because of being delimiters —
that is, [delimiters of] cognitions of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound — he says "because of being delimiters."
He states the partial resolution: "others, however" — //25//
He teaches: "if of the cause" — "here, one resolution is primary" — one primary resolution; but another resolution, according to a partial view, is secondary — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.26: Not [so], because the mind does not operate [only] within the body.

children.text:
dūṣayati etattu na samyagiti /
na hi manaḥ kva cidāśritamiti (425/2)na kva citsamavetaṃ saṃyogamātraṃ tvatiprasaktamityarthaḥ /
nāpi vṛttiḥ svakāryasāmarthyamiti /
śarīra eva manaḥ svakāryaṃ karoti nānyatreti śarīrāśritaṃ mana ityucyata ityetadapi nāsti /

children.translated_text: Because the contact of sense organ and object, which is the effect of the mind, exists outside the body too — this is the meaning.
He resolves this objection:
"Here we say" —

children.text: yenātmanā yaccharīraṃ karmopārjitaṃ tatsaṃyuktasya manaso vaiśeṣikajñānādilakṣaṇakāritve na tadasaṃyuktasyeti śarīrāśritatve manaso nānyadityarthaḥ // 26 //
children.translated_text: The <s>ātman</s> by which a particular body has been acquired through <s>karma</s> — the mind conjoined with that [body] has the capacity to produce specific cognitions and the like; but [the mind] not conjoined with that [body] does not — therefore, 'the mind is dependent on the body' means nothing other than this — this is the meaning. //26//

He criticizes: "but this is not correct" — for the mind is not located anywhere — (425/2) [meaning:] not inhering anywhere; but mere conjunction is over-extended — this is the meaning. "Nor is the function the capacity for its own effect" — it is not the case that the mind produces its own effect only within the body and not elsewhere, such that the mind would be called 'dependent on the body' — this too is not [the case].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.27: [This is] not a [valid] reason, because of being something to be proved.
An objection.
"To be proved... reason" (sū. 27) //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.28: Because the tenability of body-sustenance for one who remembers, [the position is] not refuted.
A resolution.
"One who remembers... sustenance"
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.29: Not [so], because of the swift movement of the mind.
Another objection.
"Not that... mind" (sū. 29) //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.30: Not [so], because of the non-restriction of the time of remembering.
A resolution.
"Not... remembering" (sū. 30) //

cintanaṃ smaraṇam /

children.translated_text: "Accomplished" means established — [meaning:] the mark-possessor becomes a cause of memory.
And for this further reason, the mind, which depends on conjunction with the body, is the cause of memory and not otherwise — he says:
"Not depending on conjunction with the body"

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads:] "a flow of thought is a flow of memory" — of some specific object that serves as a sign (<s>liṅga</s>), that serves as a mark (<s>cihna</s>), that is distinctive (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>) — this is the meaning. Thinking is remembering.

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.31: Because of the impulsion by the <s>ātman</s>, because of chance, and because of the knowledge [of the yogin], there is no specific conjunction [of mind with body as the cause of memory].
"<s>Ātman</s>... conjunction" (sū. 31)
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.32: Of one whose mind is absorbed, [the non-simultaneous recollection is explained] by the movement of the foot — through a specific conjunction — as the same [principle]. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.33: Because of the non-simultaneity of attentive cognition, inferential cognition, and the like, there is non-simultaneous recollection. //
He refutes:
'vyāsa--nam'

children.text: prātibhavaditi smṛtyutpādasva purastātpraṇidhānādīnāṃ smṛtikāraṇānāmasaṃvadanādātmamanaḥ saṃyogātsaṃskārāpekṣāt smṛtīnāṃ yugapadutpādaprasaṅgaḥ // 32-33 //
children.translated_text: Before the arising of recollection, the non-concordance of the causes of recollection — attentive cognition (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) and the like — gives rise to the consequence that, from the conjunction of the self with the mind requiring impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), recollections would arise simultaneously as an intuitive flash. // 32-33 //
