children.translated_text: The answer: 'We do not say'
— thus.

children.text: niṣpradeśatve 'pyātmanaḥ saṃskārasyāpyavṛttitvamupapāditaṃ tena śabdavatsahakārikāraṇasya sannidhānāsannidhāne kalpete evetyarthaḥ // 33 //
children.translated_text: Even when the self has no spatial parts, the non-pervasiveness of the impression has been justified — by this, the proximity and non-proximity of the cooperating cause is postulated just as for sound — this is the meaning. // 33 //

'An intuitive flash (<s>prātibha</s>)' — this is the objection. / He states the resolution: / 'Of a cause of recollection that exists' — / (426/21) Even an unseen instrument and its sequential operation are inferred from the sequential production of effects — thus, even an intuitive [cognition], arising from the self-mind conjunction that requires specific <s>karma</s> of the person, is not without a cause nor without a sequence — the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> asks in order to introduce the principal justification: / 'The intuitive [cognition], now' — / Having given an unclear answer to this, he raises a doubt: / 'If it is said: because of the absence of a reason, it is unjustified' — / He states the essence of the answer: / 'Not, of the instrument' — / Even if somewhere, when a cutting-instrument is simultaneously conjoined with two pieces of wood, two simultaneous cuts occur, still, the difference of the instrument should be inferred from the difference of the parts of the cutting-instrument. / Or alternatively, let other instruments produce effects simultaneously — but the instrument that is the cause of cognitions produces cognitions only sequentially — there is no deviation here; as stated: 'in the series of cognitions.' / Therefore, a single instrument is never adequate for producing simultaneous effects. / But a single agent, even when there is difference of instruments, produces many effects simultaneously — he says: / 'Not, because of the simultaneous cognitions when the knower has multiple instruments and different bodies' — / One who has diverse instruments as his property is so described — the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this: / 'And this is not a restriction' — / (427/5) For a <s>yogin</s>, when supernatural powers have manifested, creates sense-endowed bodies in various worlds, taking the minds of liberated selves, and hurrying toward liberation, simultaneously enjoys pleasures and pains produced by accumulated <s>karma</s> without attachment or aversion — for him, even as a single [agent], because of the difference of instruments, simultaneous cognitions arise. / And this second negation [pertains to] the difference of portions of the self conditioned by cognition, [which was posited as] a cause of non-simultaneous cognition. / 'Residing [in a fixed body]' — / Where the portion of the self that has produced various cognitions and their impressions — [this is] of one residing in that very body. / By this, the conjunction of the mind, which is within the body, with that portion [of the self] has been justified. / This is what the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states: / 'And if from the conjunction with the portion of the self in which the cognition inheres' — / And therefore, because of being non-pervasive [as a reason], there is no resolution. / He states the consequence of simultaneous recollection for the followers of the preceptor: / 'It is improper that the impressions residing [in the self] are in the same location' — / How so? Because the portions of the self are not different substances, there is the unavoidable consequence of simultaneous cognitions when all impressions are in the same location. / For the self does not have portions that are different from itself, like a pot — rather, the self alone is that [portion], and it is one — so all impressions residing in the self are in the same location — this is the meaning. / This is what the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> has stated: / 'Because the portions of the self are not different substances, when there is no distinction between the inherence in a single entity, the negation of simultaneous recollection is unjustified.' / 'But in the continuum of sounds' — the <s>Bhāṣya</s> that resolves the doubt — the word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) removes the doubt. / The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains this <s>Bhāṣya</s>: / 'By the proximity of the impression' — / He asks: / 'What is this proximity?' —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.34: Because desire and aversion are the causes of initiation and cessation [of activity] on the part of the knower. //

children.text:
saṃprati buddhireva kimicchādisamānādhikaraṇā na veti vicāryate /
tatra sākhyadarśanavaināśikānāṃ vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ /
tadvipratipattimāha /
puruṣadharmo jñānamantaḥkaraṇasyatviti /
puruṣacaitanyamekameva kūṭasthanityaṃ sattattadarthākārapariṇatabuddhitattvapratibimbavibhramavaśādbhinnamivopajanāpāyadharmakaṃ vijñānamiti ca vṛttiriti cākhyāyate /
children.translated_text: The consciousness of the <s>puruṣa</s> is single, immutably eternal, and due to the confusion of the reflection in the <s>buddhi-tattva</s> that transforms into the form corresponding to each object, it appears as if different, and is called <s>vijñāna</s> (cognition) possessing the property of arising and perishing, and also called <s>vṛtti</s> (activity).
But desire, aversion, and the like, possessing the property of arising and perishing in reality, belong to the inner instrument — this is the [<s>Sāṃkhya</s>] view, and it is being refuted.
'jñasye--tyoḥ'

Now it is investigated whether <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) is or is not the co-substrate of desire and the like. / Therein, the doubt arises from the disagreement between the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position and the annihilationist's (<s>vaināśika</s>) position. / He states their disagreement: / 'Cognition is a property of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person), but of the inner instrument...' —

children.text: prativṛttyañcatīti sa cātmā ceti pratyagātmā tasmin /
children.translated_text: That which goes inward (<s>pratyak</s>) is the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) — in that [inner self].
What is said amounts to this:

Because desire and the like that belong to another [person] cannot be made directly perceptible by another — or if they could, there would be the consequence that <s>Caitra</s> would also grasp the [desires] belonging to <s>Maitra</s> — they are apprehended through their co-substrateness with cognition.

children.text: antaḥkaraṇavṛttīnāṃ ca guṇāntarāṇāṃ nityāpratyakṣatvādātmāśritā evecchādayo nāntaḥ-- karaṇāśrayā iti // 34 //
children.translated_text: And since the activities of the internal organ, being other qualities [of it], are eternally imperceptible, desire and the like reside in the self alone, not in the internal organ. // 34 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.35: Because desire and aversion are the marks of that [sentience], there is no refutation in earthy [substances] and the like. //
At this juncture, the proponent of elemental sentience (<s>bhūtacaitanika</s>), having found an opening, objects.
'talli--dhaḥ' (<s>sūtra</s> 35) //

children.text: ( 428 / 4 ) yadi yasyārambhanivṛttī tasyecchādveṣau yasya caitau tasya caitanyaṃ hantāyātamanena krameṇa bhūtacaitanyamasmadabhimataṃ bhūteṣveva kāyākārapariṇateṣu ārambhanivṛttidarśanādityarthaḥ // 35 //
children.translated_text: (428/4) If desire and aversion belong to that in which initiation and cessation [of activity] are [observed], and if sentience belongs to that which has these [desire and aversion] — well then, by this sequence, elemental sentience, as maintained by us, [is established], since initiation and cessation are observed in the elements themselves when they have taken the form of bodies — this is the meaning. // 35 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.36: Because of the observation of initiation and cessation in axes and the like. //

children.translated_text: The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the purport of 'in axes and the like': / 'In axes and the like' — / (428/9) The proponent of elemental sentience explains the reason 'because of being the mark of that' in a different way to prove his own position: / 'This, then' — / From the observation of the difference of part-arrangements in bodies as compared to clods of earth and the like, a difference of activity in the atoms that produce the body is inferred — and from that, desire and aversion, and from those, sentience. / 'Mobile (<s>trasa</s>)' means 'moving,' 'perishable,' 'unstable' — the body of worms and the like; 'stationary' (<s>sthāvara</s>) means 'stable' — the body of gods, humans, and the like, for it endures longer. / He refutes this: / 'Of the clay-parts of pots and the like' — / From the observation of different part-arrangements in the clay [atoms] that produce pots and the like, and the observation of non-production in [the case of] sand-grains, the inconclusiveness of [the reason for] initiation and cessation [follows]. // 36 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.37: But restriction and non-restriction are what differentiate that [sentience from non-sentience]. //

children.text: tadevaṃ bhūtacaitanyasādhanaṃ dūṣayitvā tebhyo 'nyasya caitanye sādhanamāha /
children.translated_text: Having thus refuted the proof of elemental sentience, he states the proof of the sentience of something other than the elements:

children.translated_text:
Of those two — desire (<s>icchā</s>) and aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) — restriction and non-restriction are the distinguishing [criteria].
And this is the very distinguishing feature of desire and aversion: excluding their being properties of elements (<s>bhūta</s>) and establishing their being properties of something other [than elements].
Therein, he first states the non-restriction:
The activity and cessation caused by desire and aversion of a conscious being — [i.e.,] movement and rest —
are not in their own substrate — not in the substrate of desire and aversion — but rather in the substrate that is the thing being impelled, such as another dog and the like. There, activity and cessation would occur only in those elements that are being impelled, not in all [elements], even in the impelling ones such as the body and the like.
This is the justification of non-restriction.
"Non-restriction is universality" —
What is being said is this: the body is not the substrate of desire, knowledge, and aversion,
because it is the substrate of the movement generated by desire and the like — just as another dog and the like.
Having thus explained the distinguishing [criterion] in the case of non-restriction, he explains the restriction:
But for the <s>Cārvāka</s>, in whose view the elements, being conscious, have activity and cessation caused by desire and aversion in their own substrate — the body and the like — for that <s>Cārvāka</s>:
Just as the activity of elements, characterized by falling and the like, is caused by another quality such as heaviness (<s>gurutva</s>) and the like, and the cessation of that very quality of heaviness and the like is through the obstruction by conjunction with a supporting substance — hence cessation characterized as non-falling and the like —
that [activity and cessation], occurring in elements as such, is pervaded by restriction — not only in those elements that are taken up in a body. Similarly, activity and cessation in elements as such, caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion in their own substrate, should [also] obtain.
What is being said is this: whatever properties belong to earth and the like, those are observed in everything that has the nature of earth and the like — such as heaviness and the like. If knowledge, desire, and the like are also properties of earth and the like, then they too must necessarily belong to everything that has the nature of earth and the like — but they are not observed in pots and the like — therefore knowledge and the like are not properties of earth and the like.
And here, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> used the word "restriction" (<s>niyama</s>) with the intention of the consequence of universality (<s>sārvatrikatva</s>), and the word "non-restriction" (<s>aniyama</s>) with the intention of non-universality.
But the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, intending the limitation "only in what is impelled," used the word "restriction" for the partial [case],
and the word "non-restriction" for the universal [case], because of the absence of such restriction-like limitation [in the universal case] — thus there is no contradiction, since the difference is based on different intentions.
But one who would counter the restriction through the power of intoxication — saying: just as ferment (<s>kiṇva</s>) and the like, having undergone a specific transformation, having attained the state of liquor, intoxicate — similarly, the elements, transformed in the form of the body, become conscious and not otherwise, and therefore there is no consequence [of consciousness] in pots and the like — to him he responds: "and in a single body" —
Just as in the parts of liquor, each individual [part] has the power of intoxication and not [only] the aggregate as a whole, so too in the parts of the body, each individual [part] should possess consciousness.
And it cannot be maintained, out of mere contrariness, that consciousness belongs only to the body-aggregate and not to the parts — because consciousness is observed even when three or four parts are cut off.
Therefore, if each part has consciousness, there would be many conscious beings in a single body.
"Let it be so — what harm does it do to us?" — No.
Because, having contradictory intentions, being independent [agents], no effect whatsoever would be produced [by them cooperating].
And the rule that many [beings] have a single intention is not observed — by the maxim of the crow and the palm-fruit, there might be single-intentionedness, but its rule is not observed in practice — since this [objection] is well-known,
having disregarded this refutation, the argument from the orderly arrangement of cognitions is stated.
We observe the mutual connection (<s>pratisandhāna</s>) of cognitions within a single body, but not across different bodies — this is the orderly arrangement.
This [orderly arrangement obtains] if there is a single conscious being in a single body, and that [being] is not in another body — then it would be [so explained], and not otherwise — this is the meaning.
Somewhere the reading is "there would be an inference from the orderly arrangement of cognitions" — that is easily understood.
"Restriction and non-restriction" — regarding what was stated, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> indicates the inference itself:
"And a specific activity caused by another quality is observed" —
The specific activity that is the cause of attaining benefit and avoiding harm — that movement — is the specific activity.
The formal argument is: in the bodies of mobile and stationary [beings], the activity is caused by a quality belonging to a substrate different from its own, because of being a specific activity — like the specific activity observed in another dog and the like.
Not only is the specific activity of the body caused by another quality,
but even the specific activity of the elements that compose it is due to another quality — thus he says:
"The mark of the arrangement of its parts" —
"And because knowledge persists even when the sense-organ and object are destroyed, it is the same [argument]" —
For just as knowledge persists even when sense-organ and object are destroyed, and therefore knowledge is not a quality of the sense-organ and object — similarly, because knowledge persists even when the body is destroyed through the stages of childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, knowledge is not a quality of the body — this is the meaning.
Moreover, in the [argument] "the activity and cessation [of the body] are caused by the desire and aversion of a conscious being" — by the words "activity and cessation" we do not intend mere activity and cessation, but rather the specific movement aimed at attaining benefit and avoiding harm.
The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "You have responded with activity in general without understanding this specific activity — therefore your failure to understand is a ground for censure (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>)" —
"Mere action" —
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains that.
"Because of designating otherwise" — the remainder is: "it is inappropriate."
This might be [objected]: the reasons stated as "because of the stated reasons" and the like — the reasons found in the forthcoming sūtras — are equally applicable even to the denial of consciousness in elements and sense-organs. So why is consciousness denied only in the mind (<s>manas</s>) and not in elements and sense-organs? — to this he says:
"Of elements, sense-organs, and mind" — (429/3) //37//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.38: Because of the stated reasons, because of dependence (<s>pāratantrya</s>), and because of the unwanted consequence of experiencing the fruits of unperformed actions (<s>akṛtābhyāgama</s>) — [consciousness does] not [belong to] the mind (<s>manas</s>). //
"Stated... mind" (sūtra 38) //

children.translated_text: — therefore the non-conscious <s>ātman</s>'s experiencer-ship of that [fruit] must be accepted,

children.text: tathā ca taiḥ śarīrādibhiḥ karma kṛtaṃ puruṣeṇa bhujyata iti śāstrapratikṣiptākṛtābhyāgamakṛtanāśadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: and thus, the <s>karma</s> performed by those [bodies and the like] would be experienced by the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) — this leads to the faults of <s>akṛtābhyāgama</s> (experiencing fruits of unperformed actions) and <s>kṛtanāśa</s> (loss of performed actions), which are rejected by scripture.

children.text: acaitanye tu śarīrādīnāṃ dehādyatiriktasya ca puruṣasya caitanye puruṣaḥ svātantryātkartā tatprayojyatayā śarīrādīni tatsādhanānīti tatsādhanasya svakṛtakarmaphalopabhoga iti na śāstravyākopaḥ nāpi prekṣāvatpravṛttivirodha
children.translated_text: But when the body and the like are non-conscious, and the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) who is distinct from the body and the like is conscious, the person is the performer by virtue of independence, the body and the like are his instruments as things impelled by him — therefore the experience of the fruit of one's own performed actions through those instruments [is established] — thus there is no violation of scripture, nor any contradiction with the purposeful activity [of rational agents]
— this is the import. //38//

He explains "because of the stated reasons":
"Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and knowledge are the marks of the <s>ātman</s>" — from the definition of the <s>ātman</s> onward, whatever has been stated up to the conclusion of the examination of those marks is encompassed.
And here, by the word "reason" (<s>hetu</s>), the sūtra on desire and the like is well encompassed; and by the abstract suffix (<s>bhāvapratyaya</s>), the examination concerning the domain of reason-hood is figuratively indicated.
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: "because of the stated reasons" —
The construction is: from the fact that the reasons stated as "because of the apprehension of a single object through sight and touch" and the like have the status of stated reasons — therefore.
By this, the meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>-word "from the beginning onward" is elaborated.
Lest [one think] the stated reasons have been refuted by the opponents — therefore he says:
"Because of non-refutation" —
The meaning is: they have been refuted only verbally, not in substance.
In the activities of sustaining, impelling, and arranging, the body and sense-organs are dependent as appropriate — because of being material (<s>bhautika</s>), like a pot and the like. And the mind is dependent, because of being an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), like an axe and the like. They operate through someone's effort — but if [they were] conscious, they would be independent.
And thus there is contradiction with the inference establishing dependence — this is the meaning.
But for one who, accepting the authority of the <s>Vedas</s>, accepts the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) as non-conscious and as the experiencer of fruits, and favors the consciousness of the body and the like — to him, he states the reason for their non-consciousness:
"And because of the unwanted consequence of experiencing the fruits of unperformed actions" —
For the fruit of instruction (<s>upadeśa</s>) [accrues] to the performer, because instruction has the character of communicating the means desired by the performer.
As the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> has said: "the fruit of scripture [accrues] to the performer, because of that being its defining characteristic."
And this has been established by us in the context of "injunction is enjoining."
And from the comprehension that "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" conveys a fruit intended for the agent,
and from the recollection of the <s>ātmanepada</s> (middle voice) in this very [context], it must be accepted by all who follow the path of orthodoxy (<s>āstika</s>) that the very performer of an action is the experiencer of its fruit.
If the body and the like are conscious, then because of their independence, they alone are the performers of actions; and for them, having been reduced to ashes, there is no possibility of bearing the other-worldly fruit
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.39: By the method of residual elimination, and because of the justification of the stated reasons. //

children.translated_text: For in the <s>Vaiśyastoma</s>, only a <s>Vaiśya</s> is qualified [to perform it], not a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> or a <s>Kṣatriya</s>. children.text: eveti pariniṣṭhā sā buddhisaṃtatimātre na syāt, kutaḥ sallakṣaṇānāṃ sarveṣāmeva trailokyavailakṣaṇyena bhedāt anyāpohasāmānyasya ca vyāvartitatvādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: — thus the determination. That [determination] would not be possible in a mere continuum of cognitions (<s>buddhisaṃtati</s>), because all [continuums] that have the same characteristic are different from each other by the distinctness of the three worlds, and because the commonality [based on] exclusion (<s>anyāpoha</s>) has been refuted — this is the meaning.
He states the reason for non-recognition:
"Because of the absence of recollection." //39//

Now this is the summary of what has been established — meaning: the concluding recapitulation.
The explanation of the meaning of the word "justification" is: "because of non-refutation."
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: "because of the difference and destruction of the body."
"Not connected by recognition" (<s>apratisaṃhita</s>) —
The completion on the following day of [works] half-done on the previous day is observed — "what was begun by me must be completed by me" — having recognized [the identity of the agent]. But without such recognition, they would not complete [the work]; or even if they did complete it, <s>Maitra</s> would complete what was begun by <s>Caitra</s>,
since, without being distinguished from what was begun by oneself, the aggregate of actions begun by another would be undetermined and unestablished even for oneself, because of one being other [than oneself at another time].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.40: But recollection [belongs] to the <s>ātman</s>, because of its inherent nature of being a knower (<s>jñasvābhāvya</s>). //

children.text: trikālavyāpinī jñānaśaktireva jñasvābhāvyaṃ taccākāśādibhyo vyāvṛttaṃ trikālavyāpi svarūpamevātmanaḥ // 40 //
children.translated_text: The capacity for knowledge pervading all three times is the inherent nature of being a knower; and that, being distinguished from space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like, is the very inherent nature of the <s>ātman</s> pervading all three times. //40//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.41: [Memory arises] from attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>), binding (<s>nibandha</s>), repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>), inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), distinguishing feature (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>), possession (<s>parigraha</s>), substrate-dependent relation (<s>āśrayāśrita</s>), relation (<s>sambandha</s>), proximity (<s>ānantarya</s>), separation (<s>viyoga</s>), single-effect-relation (<s>ekakārya</s>), opposition (<s>virodha</s>), excellence (<s>atiśaya</s>), attainment (<s>prāpti</s>), intervening factor (<s>vyavadhāna</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), fear (<s>bhaya</s>), need (<s>arthitva</s>), action (<s>kriyā</s>), attachment (<s>rāga</s>), merit (<s>dharma</s>), and demerit (<s>adharma</s>). //

children.translated_text: And from <s>dharma</s> (merit) — by the <s>dharma</s> generated through the practice of meditation on the gods, one remembers a previous birth.
Similarly, the remembering of the means to pleasure and the like by one who is just born should be understood as [arising] from <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit).

children.text: nanūnmādādayo 'pi smṛtihetavo lokasiddhāstatkiṃ te 'pi noktā ityata āha /
children.translated_text: Now, madness and the like too are commonly established as causes of memory — then why are they not mentioned? — to this he says:
'This is merely an illustration of the causes of memory.' //41//

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: 'the retention of <s>manas</s> (mind) through the desire to remember.' The meaning is: the withdrawal of the mind from those various objects in which it is engaged. Or, the contemplation of the mark that is desired to be remembered, or directly the effort applied to the retention [of the object], or to its mark — this is the meaning. 'The binding, indeed' — just as, in this very [treatise], the topics beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, taken up in a single work, are causes of mutual recollection. Or [it is] through sequence: just as having remembered the topic of <s>pramāṇa</s>, one remembers <s>prameya</s>. Or otherwise: just as having remembered the points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) among the <s>pramāṇas</s>, one remembers <s>prameya</s>. He states an alternative explanation of 'binding' (<s>nibandha</s>): '<s>dhāraṇā</s>' (concentration). The branch of <s>dhāraṇā</s> taught by <s>Jaigīṣavya</s> and the like: [it involves] the superimposition (<s>samāropa</s>) — the placing — of deities bearing seed-forms (<s>bījarūpa</s>), configurations, weapons, and ornaments, onto the <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels), <s>cakras</s> (energy centers), lotus of the heart (<s>hṛtpuṇḍarīka</s>), cavity of the throat (<s>kaṇṭhakūpa</s>), tip of the nose (<s>nāsāgra</s>), [the points of the] forehead, <s>brahmarandhra</s> (crown aperture), and the like, with respect to objects already known. When the deities have thus been superimposed there, they are remembered through the apprehension of their respective parts — this is the meaning. The latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>) — which is a quality of the self (<s>ātman</s>) — is here denoted by the word '<s>abhyāsa</s>.' Thereby, attention (<s>ādara</s>) and resolve (<s>pratyaya</s>) too are included. Because even those [attention and resolve] are causes of memory only through the channel of implanting impressions, just like repetition. Moreover, the non-convergence of the causes of memory is not intended — for by the impression, all the causes of memory — concentration (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) and the rest — converge. But through binding and the like, convergence and non-convergence should be considered as appropriate. 'Here, a mark that has been perceived again' — the example for what is [connected] through conjunction: 'smoke from fire.' The example for what is [connected] through inherence: the horn, which is not directly perceived because of being screened by a wall and the like, is with the cow through inherence of the horn — thus [the horn] is called 'the inherent [mark].' But [the horn] is not inherent in the cow; rather, the cow itself [inheres] in its own parts such as the horn, because of the cow's inherence in [its parts]. 'Inherent in a single object' — its meaning: the inherence of a single composite whole — that is 'single-object-inherence'; that which possesses it is 'possessing single-object-inherence.' The example of this: 'as the hand of the foot' — for one composite whole has inherence in both foot and hand; those hand and foot possess single-object-inherence; by one [of them], perceived, which possesses single-object-inherence, the other, unperceived, is remembered. But when the meaning is 'inherence in a single object,' then the example is 'form of touch.' The mark that has a natural invariable relation is distinct from the conventional mark (<s>cihna</s>), which is a symbol. '<s>Grāmaṇī</s>' means leader. Although everywhere in concentration and the like, connection (<s>sambandha</s>) pervades [as a cause of memory], still, by setting aside concentration and the like, the word 'connection' is used for another [kind of] connection, by the maxim of the cow and the bull. Nor should one say that, because the word 'connection' includes everything, the mention of other terms is purposeless. It has been said here by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>: 'the <s>sūtrakāra</s> does not care for brevity of expression elsewhere.' And the clarity of the student's understanding arises from specific mention. 'From succession' — for at the <s>Brāhma</s> hour, immediately after waking there is rising, then urination, then purification, then comfortable washing, teeth-cleaning, and the like. 'From separation' — [this] indicates grief. From that too, one remembers the object of grief. 'From a common effect' — just as seventeen or fewer [persons] who desire prosperity have a single sacrificial session (<s>satra</s>) as their common work. Having seen one sacrificer there, one remembers another sacrificer. 'From excellence' — just as a student of celibacy (<s>brahmacārin</s>) remembers the teacher who produced the excellence of his investiture, learning, and discipline. 'From one who has provided' — just as one who has obtained or will obtain delicious food from someone remembers that person constantly. 'Desire' is affection. That is toward brothers and the like. 'Aversion' is toward an adversary, wife, and the like. And by both of these too, one remembers the respective object. 'Through action' — meaning: through effect.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.42: Because of the apprehension that action is non-persistent.

children.translated_text: 'from that' —
'namely, from concentration and the like.'
It is not the case that memory [arises] merely because the impression exists; rather, [it arises] from the awakening of that [impression].
And the awakening is occasional, because concentration and the like are occasional — this is the meaning. //42//

Having thus fully considered the retrospective review (<s>siṃhāvalokita</s>), he commences the investigation of the topic at hand — <s>buddhi</s> (cognition). 'And <s>buddhi</s> being non-eternal' — (430/9) When it is said 'because of inhering in substance,' there would be deviation through form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like [inherent] in the eye and the like — therefore he says: 'because of inhering in a pervading substance.' Even so, there would be inconclusiveness through <s>ātmatva</s> (self-hood) and the like — therefore he says: 'when possessing a universal (<s>jāti</s>).' Even so, there would be inconclusiveness through the measure characterized as all-pervasiveness — therefore he says: 'when being perceptible to us and the like.' Cognitions whose objects are the continua of action and the like perish more quickly. Here, if it were said 'because of being an illuminator,' there would be inconclusiveness through the self (<s>ātman</s>) — therefore he says: 'when being an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>).' Even so, there would be inconclusiveness through <s>manas</s> (mind), the ear, and the like — therefore he says: 'restricted to each object.' A single cognition has a single object and is not directed toward another object — and so too other cognitions, being restricted to their own objects alone, are not like <s>manas</s> and the ear and the like, which have multiple objects. Now, the restriction to each object is non-pervasive: when there is simultaneous contact with multiple objects, a single cognition having multiple objects may arise — therefore he says: when at each moment, the action — the object — the <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented [entity]) — arises, then, because of the origination of that effect — the <s>buddhi</s> — not being simultaneous, because of the sequential [nature] of the effect following the sequence of the cause, and because perceptual <s>buddhi</s> has a causal object — each such object, arising in sequence, is a cause — therefore the restriction of all cognitions, which arise in sequence, to each object is established. And the restriction is with respect to another action of the same class, not with respect to substance — therefore the restriction to each object does not conflict with the cognition of action having substance and the like as its object. And because of the qualification 'restricted to each object,' since there was previously a suspicion of inconclusiveness through the self, instrumentality is [given as] a qualifier. He states another formulation: 'or' — lest there be inconclusiveness through pleasure and the like, it is said 'when being a quality (<s>guṇa</s>)' (431/1). To prevent deviation through form and the like, it is said 'not external.' Even when there is apprehension of a persistent [object], [<s>buddhi</s>] is destructible — although one could say: 'the cognition of touch and the like is a single [cognition] persisting for that long a time, and it will perish when the contact with the object ceases due to screening and the like; and the destruction of the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) too has been observed as a cause of the destruction of the effect — as in the destruction of the number two upon the destruction of the apprehending cognition' — even so, since momentariness is established by another reason, this should be regarded as merely corroborative. For indeed, the demonstration of the momentariness of cognition whose object is a momentarily-destructible thing itself implies the demonstration of the momentariness of cognition whose object is a persistent thing. Cognitions with stable objects are momentary — because of being cognitions, like cognitions of action and the like. [Objection:] <s>buddhi</s> itself is the rememberer and the grasper — thus, superimposing self-hood onto <s>buddhi</s>, he raises a doubt: 'if memory persists.' He refutes: 'not for this very [reason].' For <s>buddhi</s> is not the rememberer, such that in its absence memory would not arise; rather, the self (<s>ātman</s>) [is the rememberer], and it is eternal. But the existence of <s>buddhi</s> is contrary to memory — this is the meaning. Now, if <s>buddhi</s> does not exist, then from what does memory arise? For an effect cannot be without a cause. And the self alone is not sufficient as a cause — lest, because of the eternality of the self, the arising of memory too be eternal. Therefore, the arising of memory too is a mark of the persistence of <s>buddhi</s> — to this he says: 'and because of its state arising from another [cause].' One might say: if the impression born from <s>buddhi</s> is the cause of memory, then memory would last as long as the impression — to this he says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.43: The grasping of what is indistinct, because of non-persistence, is like the grasping of an indistinct form at the moment of a lightning flash.
The advocate of the persistence of <s>buddhi</s> says:
'If [<s>buddhi</s> is] non-persistent' — //43//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.44: By adopting the reason, [there is] an approval of what is to be refuted.

children.translated_text: 'not otherwise' —
He states another fault:
'and because of inconclusiveness.' —
The explanation of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> is accomplished by the explanation of the <s>Vārttika</s> itself. //44//

He refutes: 'not, because of contradiction.' (432/5) Having proposed the persistence of <s>buddhi</s> in general, the statement that <s>buddhi</s> arising from a lightning-flash regarding pots and the like is non-persistent — this is contradictory — this is the meaning. And he states the otherwise-established nature (<s>anyathāsiddhatva</s>) of the grasping of the indistinct: 'of the grasping of the indistinct' — because of the difference in the cause of the grasping of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>). The cause [of grasping] that is indistinct grasps the property-bearer as possessing only the universal; accordingly, the grasping is indistinct. But the cause that [grasps] as possessing both the universal and the particular — accordingly, the grasping is distinct — this is the meaning. But without depending on the property-bearer, the grasping of the respective objects is not possible — 'because of being distinct' — this is the meaning. Not depending on the property-bearer — an ignorant person raises the doubt: 'if there is a contradiction with common experience.' Depending on the grasping of the property-bearer, he refutes:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.45: The grasping of that is not like the grasping that is manifested by a lamp-flame-succession.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.46: Because of the apprehension of its own qualities and of another's qualities in a substance, there is doubt.

śarīreti(433/9) /
pūrvaṃ hi bhūtendriyamanasāṃ caitanyaṃ sākṣānnirākṛtamupakṣepāttu śarīrasya,
saṃprati tu śarīrasyaiva sākṣāccaitanyaṃ nirasyata iti tātparyabhedādapunaruktam /
children.translated_text: But now, the consciousness of the body itself is directly refuted — thus, because of the difference in purport, there is no repetition.

children.text: vastutastu paunaruktyaparihāraṃ bhāṣyakāraḥ prakārāntareṇa prakaraṇānte vakṣyati /
children.translated_text: In reality, however, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> will state the resolution of the repetition in another manner at the end of the section.
The property of being its (<s>ātman</s>'s) quality is established through apprehension in that [body].
The supplement is: 'through undefeated [apprehension].' //44-45//
'The body' — (433/9) Previously, the consciousness of the elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> was directly refuted, but [that of] the body was refuted only by implication.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.47: Because [cognition] lasts as long as the body, [it belongs] to [things having] form and the like.

children.text: śarīramasyāḥ kāraṇaṃ taccānucchinnaṃ, saṃskārasya tu kāraṇasyoccheda iti draṣṭavyam // 47 //
children.translated_text: The body is its cause and is not destroyed [throughout life]; but the cause that is the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is destroyed — this should be understood. //47//
Not because of the non-cessation of the cause — [does] consciousness [persist].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.48: Not [so], because of the origination of different qualities produced by heating (<s>pākaja</s>).
'And that is not [the case], because of the origination of different qualities produced by heating' —

children.text: nātyantikaḥ paramāṇau vā piṭhare vā rūpābhāva
children.translated_text: the absence of form in the atom or in the pot is not absolute
— this is the meaning. //48//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.49: Because of the establishment of a counterpart, there is no refutation of [qualities] produced by heating.

Having thus stated the dissimilarity of absoluteness and non-absoluteness, he states another dissimilarity — that of having and not having a counterpart — 'and for this reason.' 'Because of the establishment of a counterpart, of [qualities] produced by heating' — (435/8) by bringing out the deviation in that [argument], there is no refutation of consciousness lasting as long as the body. //49//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.50: Because of pervading the body.

<s>NyS</s> 3.2.52: Because the body is bounded by the skin, there is no applicability [of sentience] to hair, nails, and the like. //
'Because of being bounded by the skin' —

children.text: śarīrāvayavatvaṃ keśanakhādīnāṃ heturasiddhaḥ indriyāśrayatvaṃ śarīralakṣaṇaṃ, tadyatra śarīraṃ samavetaṃ tenendriyāśrayeṇāvaśyaṃ bhavitavyam /

And the aggregate of parts bounded by the skin is of that nature,

<s>NyS</s> 3.2.55: Because of being perceived by the sense organs, there is no refutation of color and the like. //

children.translated_text: 'Because of being imperceptible to external sense organs' —
And there is no inconclusiveness through gravity (<s>gurutva</s>) and the like —
for those are simply imperceptible,
not perceptible to external sense organs — this is the purport. // 55 //

The mutual dissimilarity of color and the like, however, has not been taken into account — that is, [it is] not connected with [the argument about] being a quality of the body — this is the meaning. / For it is not observed that those which have the dissimilarity of color characterized by being visible, tasteable, and the like are therefore not qualities of the body. / And the observation of such dissimilarity among the qualities of the body is uncontested. / Therefore, because of the absence of positive and negative concomitance with not-being-a-quality-of-the-body, this is mere dissimilarity. / The dissimilarity of qualities of the body — being perceptible and imperceptible to external sense organs — [where] being perceptible to the mind is [the quality] that has positive and negative concomitance, is the proof that consciousness is a quality of the body — [but this does not work]; / rather, it is the proof that [consciousness] is a quality of something other than [the body] — this is the meaning. / Because the negation of a specific [quality] is a reason for the acceptance of the remainder. / 'The reasons' — (437/2) the plural is with the intention of referring to parts of the reason. / When it is said 'consciousness is not a quality of the body, because of not lasting as long as the substance,' there would be inconclusiveness through impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — therefore it is said 'in the absence of another cause.' / Even so, there would be inconclusiveness through the quality produced by cooking (<s>pākajaGuṇa</s>) — therefore it is said 'and when a contrary quality is not observed.' / 'Because of pervading the body' — / [This] is not a [valid] proof — for an absurd consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>) is not a proof, because of the absence of a [proper] reason. / As they say: 'there is an absurd consequence, but the absurd consequence is not a proof.'
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.56: Because of the non-simultaneity of cognitions, the mind (<s>manas</s>) is one. //
In the examination of the nature of the mind, the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and <s>Vārttika</s> are explained by mere recitation. // 56 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.57: Not [so], because of the apprehension of non-simultaneous multiple actions. //
'Establishment' means 'position.' // 57 //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.58: Just as the perception of a firebrand-circle, so is the apprehension of that [simultaneity], because of the rapid movement [of the mind]. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.59: And because of the aforementioned reason, [the mind] is atomic. //
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.60: Because of the connection with the results of previously done [<s>karma</s>], the origination of that [body occurs]. //
