children.translated_text: <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is the instrumental cause of the world, whose material cause is atoms, and who depends on the <s>karma</s> of persons; and the <s>karma</s> of persons that is required by Him is also caused by <s>Īśvara</s> alone. / And it is not the case that what is depended upon [by Īśvara] is not caused by Him — this we shall explain from what has been taught. / Therefore, since the human effort (<s>puruṣakāra</s>) is caused by <s>Īśvara</s>, and [<s>Īśvara</s>] is assisted by that [human effort], the [reason] 'because of the absence of fruit when human <s>karma</s> is absent' is not a [valid] reason for refuting the thesis that <s>Īśvara</s> is the instrumental cause of the world — / the meaning is: it is a [valid] reason only for refuting the [thesis that] <s>Īśvara</s> is the instrumental cause independently [of <s>karma</s>]. / The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says:] 'a self other [than worldly selves], distinguished by qualities.' / The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> will establish the qualities of <s>Īśvara</s> — cognition and the like. / 'From a self-like [being]' — here, 'from a self-like mode, from a self-type' — this is the extent [of the meaning]. / He states the distinction from worldly selves: / 'Without <s>adharma</s>' — / Objection: since He has no performance of [ritual] actions, whence [would He have] <s>dharma</s>? And thus, the sovereign power (<s>aiśvarya</s>) such as <s>aṇimā</s> (atomization) and the like, being an effect, [would arise] without any <s>karma</s> — so there would be the consequence of the arrival of what is not done (<s>akṛtābhyāgama</s>). / To this he says: / 'And His <s>dharma</s> follows His will (<s>saṃkalpa</s>)' — / One might ask: what does this much accomplish? — to this he says: / 'And thus, without violating [the principle of] the arrival of what is done by oneself' — / Let there be no external performance [of rituals]; the <s>aiśvarya</s>, which is the fruit of <s>dharma</s> generated by the performance characterized as will, has the creation of the world as its fruit — so there is no consequence of the arrival of what is not done — this is the meaning. / One might think: / Without a purpose, discerning persons do not act; and for <s>Īśvara</s>, who has attained everything to be attained, there is nothing further to be attained — therefore, what has He accomplished by creating the world? — to this he says: / 'And He is like a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>)' — / Let there be no self-interest for this blessed [Lord]; He will engage in the creation of the world for the benefit of others — this is the meaning. / He gives an example for this very [point]: / 'This one, just as a father [acts] for his children.' / This father [acts] for his own children, just as a father [does] — this is the meaning. / He applies [the example] to the illustrated: 'So <s>Īśvara</s>, having become like a father.' / Objection: other selves are observed to be endowed with non-eternal cognition, and because of His dissimilarity from them, <s>Īśvara</s> cannot be of the self-type (<s>ātmajātīya</s>) — to this he says: 'but not because of being self-like' — / Although other selves are endowed with non-eternal cognition, and He is endowed with eternal cognition and the like, still He is indeed of the self-type, because of possessing qualities such as <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and the like. / Otherwise, there would be the consequence that water-atoms and the like would not be water, because of possessing eternal form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like. / [The non-eternity is established] because of the observation that the forms and the like belonging to pots and the like are non-eternal. / And if He were not characterized by qualities such as <s>buddhi</s> and the like, then because of the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> [for His existence], He would simply be unestablished — he says: 'and through <s>buddhi</s> and the like.' / One might think: if <s>Īśvara</s> engages in the creation of the world out of compassion, then, good sir, He should create only happy [beings], not unhappy ones. / And it should not be said that the diversity of creation is due to His acting as a cooperator with the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> belonging to the individual selves (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), because the compassionate [Lord], by not presiding over (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) <s>dharma</s> that is not presided over by Him, would [thereby] not produce its effect. — Therefore, from the observation of the diversity of the world as happy, unhappy, and the like, [one concludes that] <s>Īśvara</s> does not act impelled by compassion — to this he says: / 'Of one who acts without violating [the principle of] the arrival of what is done by oneself' — / The intention is this: / This [Lord], though compassionate and though His glory surpasses that of other selves, is not able to make the capacity of things otherwise [than what they are]. / Therefore, even what has originated through <s>adharma</s> cannot, even by the power of <s>Īśvara</s>, become eternal [if it is by nature non-eternal]. / And [<s>adharma</s>] cannot be destroyed without delivering its fruit, which contradicts its own result. / Therefore, <s>Īśvara</s>, not transgressing the regularity of individual selves, is unable to not preside over <s>adharma</s>; / therefore, though compassionate, conforming to the nature of things, cooperating with <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, He brings about the diversity of the world — this is what is said by 'of one who acts without violating the arrival of what is done by oneself.' / The meaning is: of one who acts without violating the arrival of the fruit of <s>karma</s> done by persons. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'the procedure regarding <s>Īśvara</s>' — / (457/9) 'Procedure' means 'topic' — the investigation of <s>Īśvara</s> being the instrumental cause — this is the meaning. / 'Now, though existing, He does not activate [<s>Prakṛti</s>] because of obstruction' — / (458/12) When <s>Prakṛti</s> is to be activated by human purpose for the sake of pleasure, <s>adharma</s> is the obstructor of human purpose — similarly, when <s>Prakṛti</s> is to be activated by human purpose for suffering, <s>dharma</s> [is the obstructor] — this is the meaning. / 'And this reason does not withdraw from that' — / (459/14) This very reason, characterized as non-sentience, does not withdraw from milk [i.e., applies to milk too] — this is the meaning. / Thinking that movement (<s>parispanda</s>) is action, that it conforms to what has form (<s>mūrti</s>), and hence is not possible in the formless, all-pervading <s>Īśvara</s>, he raises a doubt: / 'If [it is said]: because of the non-entry of action, [He] is not a cause' — / (460/16) The resolution is made with the intention that cognition, desire-to-act, and effort, though without physical movement, are actions inasmuch as they are denoted by verb-words, and [thus exist] in <s>Īśvara</s>. / 'Not, because of the impossibility of the alternative' — / 'And when many substances are simultaneously combined, from conjunctions that are distinguished from [those producing] uncommon effects' — / (461/8) The uncommon effect — of each conjunction of two threads, a two-thread [fabric]; distinguished from those [conjunctions], from the conjunctions [of all threads] together, only the common effect — characterized as cloth — is produced — this is the meaning. / Not only is substance produced from substances in which action has arisen and ceased, but even in substances in which action has not arisen, from persistent conjunctions, upon the cessation of the prior substance, another substance is produced — he says: / 'But upon the separation of a single part' — / The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) shows the distinction from the previous [case] of action that has arisen and ceased. / 'Does not the production [occur] only of what has no action?' — he says: 'but some' — / From the conjunction that is produced by the impulsion (<s>nodana</s>) born of the action of one [part], when the action in the other substance has ceased, at the very time of the cessation of that action, a substance is produced and proceeds from its own nature — so this is unobjectionable. / This [Lord], though sentient, though by nature beneficent to others, conforming to the nature of things, brings about the diversity of the world in accordance with the <s>karmāśaya</s> (accumulated <s>karma</s>). / And He does not necessarily obstruct the activity of persons who have done evil — this is the meaning. / Even at the present time, the diverse nature of sentient beings is observed — of good, bad, and middling people. / 'Now, if the sovereignty is eternal, there would be the purposelessness of <s>dharma</s> — [for it] does not arise from that <s>dharma</s>' — / (464/3) And thus, [the argument that] the sovereignty of <s>Īśvara</s> should be understood as the fruit of His own <s>karma</s> — the <s>Bhāṣya</s> is inappropriate — this is the purport. / He resolves: 'We say it is eternal' — / For His power of knowledge and power of action are eternal — hence His sovereignty is eternal. / But [the sovereignty characterized by] <s>aṇimā</s> (atomization) and the like is non-eternal; and it is with that intention that the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>'s statement about its being the fruit of <s>dharma</s> [is to be understood]. / The <s>dharma</s> of <s>Īśvara</s>, which follows His will (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) directed toward the sustenance of [the world], has as its purpose the presiding over the accumulation of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> that functions in each individual self. / Having accepted [for the sake of argument] the <s>dharma</s> of <s>Īśvara</s>, this was stated by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>. / But in ultimate truth, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the existence of <s>dharma</s> in <s>Īśvara</s>, since the production of all effects is accomplished by His eternal powers of knowledge and action alone — with this intent he says: / 'And there is no <s>dharma</s> in <s>Īśvara</s>' — / 'Because of possessing intellect, then, [He is] another self' — / 'Another self' is intended as 'another embodied being' — / And that bodily connection, being present for some — namely, worldly beings (<s>saṃsārins</s>) — and past for some — namely, liberated beings such as <s>Śuka</s>, <s>Prahlāda</s>, and the like — / by this, [the argument is:] <s>Īśvara</s>, being an intelligent being, must necessarily be an embodied being — this is the intended meaning. / [The answer:] 'Not another self, another embodied being' — this is the meaning. / Why? Because of the difference of qualities. / If His <s>buddhi</s> and the like are eternal, then the mention of the body is accomplished — for the purpose of [explaining] the production of that [non-eternal <s>buddhi</s>] — this is the purport. / Objection: is it not the case that atoms, presided over by an intelligent cause, proceed [to create]? / The meaning is: from the force of the thesis-property, assisted by <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), His eternal-knowledge-possessing-agent-hood is established. / The <s>tarka</s>, assisted by <s>pramāṇa</s>, has been shown by [the argument beginning with] 'because of the impossibility of restriction for each object' and the like. / Thus, the bodilessness of <s>Īśvara</s> has been shown through the difference of qualities; and that His connection with a body does not even admit an alternative — he says: / 'Now, by virtue of possessing intellect' — / (465/4) 'Having as its object past, future, and present — perception' — / The meaning is: having direct awareness (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>). / But not sense-organ-based, because of [His cognition's] eternality. / And this is indicative [i.e., not exhaustive] — / 'And not inferential' — / it should be understood as also: not sense-based, not analogical. / 'Unafflicted (<s>akliṣṭa</s>)' — / (466/4) <s>Kleśa</s> is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>); 'not tainted by that' — this is the meaning. / 'Because of being connected with a corporeal substance' — / The meaning is: because of being in conjunction. / And thus, there is no deviation through form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like. / This much is the intention of the teacher [<s>Uddyotakara</s>]: indeed, there are three kinds of entities in the world — those well-known as having a sentient creator, / such as palaces, towers, gateways, and arches; / those well-known as [having] the opposite of that, / such as atoms, space, and the like; / and those of doubtful sentient creatorship, such as bodies, mountains, and great mountains. / Regarding those [of the third kind], doubt [arises] about sentient creatorship — because of being a <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), or because of the disagreement of disputants, and because of the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> that either proves or contradicts [sentient creatorship]. / And mere non-apprehension by perception cannot be a contradicting [<s>pramāṇa</s>] here, / because even of things that exist but are remote from their own nature, there is non-apprehension by perception — as of atoms and the like. / And thus, the disputed bodies, mountains, and great mountains — / they have a creator who knows their material cause — because of having originated, or because of having a non-sentient material cause; whatever has originated or has a non-sentient material cause — all that is preceded by a creator who knows its material cause, like palaces and the like; and so too the disputed bodies, mountains, and great mountains — therefore they are likewise. / And their having-originated is not unestablished — / it is established either through being composite (<s>sāvayavatva</s>), or through being great in size and possessing action, like cloth and the like. / And this does not amount to proving what is already established for the annihilationists (<s>vaināśika</s>) through <s>karma</s> as the sentient [cause], or for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> through the individual self (<s>kṣetrajña</s>) as the sentient [cause] — even in [accepting] the sentience of [the cause of] earth and the like, because [those selves] do not know the material cause. / Or, if they do know it, then that is precisely our <s>Īśvara</s> — let there be such proving of what is already established! Who, without distress, would not welcome the establishment of what is desired? / And the example is not deficient in the property to be proved — / because cloth and the like too have a creator who knows the material cause, such as a weaver and the like. / For this very reason, the reason is not contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>) — for it would be so / only if cloth and the like did not have a creator who knows the material cause — and that is not accepted even by the opponents. / One might object: / because of the contradiction by <s>pramāṇa</s> of a specific [property] entailed by the [thesis-]meaning, namely having a body and the like, [the reason would be] contradictory. / Just as in 'because of being a producer of transformations of grass and the like, [the mountain] possesses fire' — here, the warm touch belonging to the fire that is entailed [as useful for] the production of grass-transformations is contradicted by the perceptual apprehension of the cold touch [of the mountain] — so the reason is contradicted. / Similarly, His cognition regarding the material cause of earth and the like has as its cause the conjunction of the self with the mind, the body, and the like — it does not arise without that; thus, [a body] is entailed by this [reason]; / and that [entailment] is here contradicted by <s>pramāṇa</s>; and upon the removal of that [body], His cognition would cease — just as fire that burns necessarily ceases when the production of warm touch ceases. / No — / because when a non-pervader ceases, the non-cessation of what is not pervaded [is justified]. / If the cause is a non-pervader of the effect — well then, the discussion of pervader and pervaded is destroyed! / This would be so if His cognition of the material cause of earth and the like were also an effect — but that is accepted as eternal — so even upon the removal of the body and the like, it need not cease. / Because upon the cessation of a non-pervader, what is not pervaded does not cease. / Otherwise, '<s>Maitra</s> does not have a horse' would entail that he does not have a cow either. / And it is not proper [to say] that an eternal <s>buddhi</s> is impossible merely because non-eternal [forms of] <s>buddhi</s> are frequently observed. / For the [atoms of] water and the like that are observed as [constituting] the lunar orb — being perceptible — and the forms and the like belonging to them are non-eternal — [this] does not entail that the atoms that produce them or the forms and the like belonging to [those atoms] must also be so [i.e., non-eternal]. / But as for being eternal without a cause, the [situation is] the same in both cases [atoms and Īśvara's buddhi]. / And it is not proper [to argue] that because cognition is apprehended in co-existence with the body and the like everywhere, the body and the like are what pervade (<s>vyāpya</s>) cognition. / For pervadedness (<s>vyāpyatā</s>) is the possession of a natural relation, and that obtains in the absence of limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>); / and there is a limiting condition for the co-existence of cognition with the body and the like, namely: being an effect. / Cognition that is an effect does not outlast its own cause, the body and the like; but eternal [cognition], even while outlasting them, does not obstruct the observation of co-existence — therefore, just as when someone argues 'sound is non-eternal, because of having originated, like a pot,' someone might resist because of the difference of properties between what is to be proved and the example: / 'If sound is non-eternal because of the similarity with a pot due to having originated, well then, for that very reason it must possess form and the like too — / and if this [sound] does not possess form and the like by virtue of similarity with a pot, then let it also not be non-eternal!' — and one who resists thus is defeated as a proponent of the pseudo-refutation of 'equality-of-excellence' (<s>utkarṣasamajāti</s>) — / just so, here too, the one [who objects] is to be defeated as a proponent of 'equality-of-excellence,' because of resisting by means of a mere similarity that is non-probative, / and because of its easy availability in all inferences and [its consequently] destroying all inference. / One might object: / 'Having-originated' is pervaded only by 'being preceded by a creator who knows the material cause' as observed in pots and the like — it should establish just that much for earth and the like — but whence would the creator have eternal, all-object-cognition? / For that is not observed in the example's subject [i.e., the pot-maker]. / Now, if from the apprehension of form and the like, even sense-organs are inferred as actions — how [is this justified]? For cutting and the like are not actions accomplished by sense-organs — / they are accomplished by axes and the like. / But even though the sense-organ-accomplishment, which is not observed in the example's subject, is established from the force of the thesis-property — / for the action-hood belonging to the apprehension of form and the like would establish only that instrument which is capable of accomplishing apprehension; / and axes and the like are not capable [of that] — so from the force of the thesis-property, even an unseen-operating [instrument] like the eye and the like is established. / Then the same applies here [to <s>Īśvara</s>] too! / For the simultaneity of the production of effects characterized by bodies, trees, mountains, and the like — which are in indeterminate directions and locations, sensory and non-sensory, mobile and immobile — cannot be inferred without all-object-cognition and its eternality. / Indeed, such cognition of the supreme Lord cannot be an effect [requiring] a body and the like — because before the origination of the body and the like, His [supposed] non-sentience would entail the postulation of another <s>Īśvara</s> for the production of prior effects. / Thus, by the extraordinary postulation of [Īśvaras] 'before that, before that,' it is better to postulate the eternality of <s>buddhi</s>. / By this, the postulation of the eternality of body and sense organs is also answered. / By this, what some say —
Although everything possessing configuration and the like would be established as having an intelligent cause, whence the sole causality of configuration and the like?

children.text: īśvaraprerito gacchetsvargaṃ vā śvabhrameva vā' akāraṇatvena ceśvarajñānanityatāṃ darśayati śrutiḥ 'apāṇipādo javano grahītā paśyatyacakṣuḥ sa śṛṇotyakarṇaḥ sa vetti viśvaṃ na hi tasya vettā tamāhuragryaṃ puruṣaṃ purāṇa' mityādikā /
children.translated_text: impelled by <s>Īśvara</s>, goes either to heaven or to the abyss of hell." And the <s>śruti</s> demonstrates the eternality of <s>Īśvara</s>'s cognition through its being uncaused: "Without hands and feet, swift is he and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears; he knows all, yet there is none who knows him — they call him the first, the great <s>Puruṣa</s>, the ancient" — and the like.
By this very [passage], his bodilessness is also demonstrated.
But the remainder has been elaborated by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> himself, so [the commentary] desists. //21//

Thus — that too has been refuted. Their fond hope of refuting omniscience would [be realized] if those with the eyes of flesh could see the atoms, the <s>kṣetrajñas</s> (embodied souls), or the <s>karmāśayas</s> (accumulated stores of karma) inherent in them — but this is not the case. Therefore, many [beings] of such a nature, characterized as 'us and the like,' who perceive supersensible objects, would have to be posited — but it is better to posit just one such [being], for the sake of economy of postulation. Nor should one say: 'because of the occasional ripening of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit), the production of bodies, worlds, and the like is explained by the conjunction of <s>kṣetrajñas</s> and atoms alone, [so] there is no need for a conscious agent.' [This is so] because, for what possesses origination, the natural invariable connection (<s>svābhāvika-pratibandha</s>) with [having] a maker knowledgeable of its material cause and the like is established — without any limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>). Nor is there deviation through observing the independent origination of unconscious milk — which is the cause of the growth of the calf — without supervisory control, and [the origination] of the senses and mind, which are the means of producing cognition, without knowledge, or [the origination] of plants and trees in the forest without effort — [for this is] not [valid], since all of these very [examples] have been placed in the thesis [as disputed objects]. Nor is there the fault of the property not residing in the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>) through [the argument] that the existence of <s>śaśaśṛṅga</s> (hare's horn) is contradicted by non-apprehension — because the blessed Lord, being worthy of being perceived, the contradiction through that [non-apprehension] is untenable. Otherwise, the consequence would be the destruction of all inference. But the horn existing on the hare's head — [being] worthy of perception like that [existing] in a calf and the like — is rejected by non-apprehension and therefore is not fit to serve as a proof. One might say: it is not mere origination that is invariably connected by nature with having an intelligent cause; rather, it is a specific [kind of origination] — namely, that upon seeing which, even one who does not [ordinarily] see deliberate activity develops the conviction of purposeful creation, and [that specific origination] is associated with that perception. What is seen to have its presence and absence follow the presence and absence of an intelligent [agent] — such as pots and the like — is [of that specific kind], but not merely anything that possesses origination; bodies, worlds, and the like [need not be such], because the correspondence of their existence and non-existence [with an intelligent agent] is not observed. [Response:] This [argument], relying on the general [fact of] origination that subsists on the pervading relation of 'having an intelligent cause' furnished by that specific limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>), [holds that] origination is not invariably connected by nature with that [intelligent causation], and so [origination] cannot indicate it — otherwise, there would be the consequence of inferring a fire-banner (<s>dhūmadhvaja</s>, i.e. fire) even from pallor and the like existing in jasmine, pigeons, and the like, by relying on the pervading relation of fire-banner [to smoke] furnished by smoke. To this we reply: let the wise ones examine this more carefully — is the specific [feature] the correspondence of presence and absence with an intelligent [agent], or is it the observation thereof? If the former, then it must be conceded by those who maintain [this objection] that bodies, worlds, and the like have an intelligent cause. For no one other than one who does not accept [causation] can say that a cause does not have its presence and absence correspond to its effect. But if [the specific feature is] the observation [of correspondence], then the conviction of purposeful creation cannot arise in one who does not see deliberate activity. For the very cloth that was seen by this person as corresponding in presence and absence to an intelligent cause — that very same [cloth] is its effect, not [the cloth] found in the market. [Objection:] Because in things of the same class, the correspondence of presence and absence is observed, even that of the same class whose correspondence of presence and absence is unobserved is also so [i.e., has an intelligent cause]. [Reply:] Well then! A pot and the like, possessing origination, correspond in presence and absence to an intelligent [agent] — and other things of the same class, such as bodies, worlds, and the like, are likewise — [so your argument] is not deflected by your own stick! [Objection:] What possesses origination and is of the same class as a pot is preceded by an intelligent [agent]. [Reply:] Then a mansion and the like would not be caused by that, because of not being of the same class as a pot. But if [you say:] whatever is of the same class [as something] that was seen to correspond in presence and absence to an intelligent [agent] — that alone, even with unobserved correspondence, has an intelligent cause — then what [class of] effect, such as mansions and the like, preceded by an intelligent [agent], has not been seen, such that bodies, worlds, and the like, possessing origination, should not be so? There is indeed no distinction regarding being of the same class. As for [the objection] that an anthill, being a modification of clay, is not the product of a potter like a pot and the like — that is because of the contradiction of direct non-perception of a potter [in the anthill's case]. But when [the cause is] an invisible conscious [agent], that [intelligent causation of the anthill] is indeed to be accepted. One might say: mere origination is not pervaded by having a maker knowledgeable of its material cause; rather, [only] that whose material cause and the like are knowable by us and the like [is so pervaded] — and bodies, worlds, and the like, even though possessing origination, are not like that; therefore, because of the absence of pervasion, they are not preceded by that. This is unjustified. When the pervasion between possessing origination and having a maker knowledgeable of its material cause has been established first by positive and negative concomitance, the postulation of the knowability of its material cause and the like [only by us] is settled in the domain of knowledge of the effect. It has been said: through the force of pervasion, the general [fact of] knowledge is established; through the force of the property residing in the thesis-subject, the eternality of that [knowledge] is established. Therefore, since the limiting condition is not tracked [i.e., not found following the property], because of non-apprehension [of the limiting condition], the possessing of origination is invariably connected by nature with having an intelligent cause. Nor can one suspect that the [fact of] possessing origination, being invariably connected by nature, might extend beyond its own correlates — in that case, there would be the consequence of the loss of the invariable nature. One might say: the inferences 'the earth and the like are not preceded by an omniscient [being], because of being objects of knowledge (<s>prameyatva</s>), existence (<s>sattva</s>), and the like — like pots and the like' are counter-proofs (<s>satpratipakṣa</s>), and therefore the inference in question is a pseudo-inference. To this we reply: does this [counter-inference] negate omniscient-precededness, or merely knower-precededness — with the word 'all' being illustrative? If the former, then precededness by a partial-seer would be established [instead]. And thus there would be the fault of <s>apasiddhānta</s> (undermining one's own established doctrine) — and this is also impossible, for earth and the like cannot be made by one of limited vision like us. But if knower-precededness in general is what is negated, there is deviation through pots and the like. And as for [the inference] '<s>Īśvara</s> is not the controller of atoms and the like, because of being bodiless, like a liberated soul,' and '<s>Īśvara</s>'s cognition does not have all things as its object and is non-eternal, because of being a cognition, like our cognition and the like' — these [inferences], requiring for their thesis-property's establishment the very proof of <s>Īśvara</s> and his possessing cognition, are contradicted by the very validating means (<s>pramāṇa</s>) that establish those [i.e., Īśvara's existence and cognition], and so cannot even establish themselves, let alone contradict that [proof]. For scripture and inference do not establish a mere bodiless [entity] to the exclusion of world-creatorship and possessing eternal, all-encompassing cognition. And thus your inference, being contradicted by those [scripture and inference], cannot arise — this is established. Just as with <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), <s>icchā</s> (desire) and <s>prayatna</s> (effort) too are eternal in him, and should be understood as included within the proofs of his being a creator — because creatorship is defined as the conjunction of cognition, desire-to-act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>), and effort, and because these are mutually inseparable, the establishment of any one [of them] entails the establishment of the others. Thus it has been said: from the mere [fact of] possessing origination, through the assistance of the thesis-property, the proof of <s>Īśvara</s> of such a nature [is established]. Or let there be merely the establishment of having a maker knowledgeable of the material cause and the like [from that argument]; from the inference by residual elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>), however, through the establishment of the negative concomitance, the specific [nature of Īśvara] is established. Namely: the maker knowledgeable of bodies, worlds, and the like does not possess non-eternal, non-all-encompassing cognition — because of the consequence that such a maker would not know their material cause and the like. For one of such a [limited] nature has not been seen to know their material cause and the like — as in our own case. But this one does know their material cause and the like — therefore he is so [i.e., possesses eternal, all-encompassing cognition]. For indeed, no one other than such an <s>Īśvara</s> is capable of knowing the distinctions among atoms and the <s>karmāśayas</s> (accumulated karmic stores) inherent in each <s>kṣetrajña</s> — as has been elaborated below. He is also able to govern the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> inhering in other persons, through connection — for not only direct conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) are the [only] connections, since <s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s> (conjunction-cum-inherence) also has that status. Indeed, <s>Īśvara</s> is conjoined with atoms and the like, and the <s>kṣetrajñas</s> [are conjoined] with those [atoms], and <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> inhere in those [<s>kṣetrajñas</s>] — thus it is either <s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s> (conjunction-cum-inherence), or because of the conjunction of <s>Īśvara</s> with the <s>kṣetrajña</s>, since even distal conjunction has been shown to be tenable. And even without the assistance of his own <s>dharma</s>, <s>Īśvara</s> will direct the <s>dharma</s>, <s>adharma</s>, and atoms toward their respective effects — just as one who knows the science of poisons [directs] a fragment of poison toward the commencement of action. By this, the [view of] <s>Brahman</s> as conscious material cause (<s>cetanopādāna</s>) is also explained. But the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> has stated consciousness as a reason, as an illustration. The reasons such as possessing origination and the like should also be inferred [as applicable here]. And having invoked this method, he corroborates [it] with scripture:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.22: The origination of entities is without a cause, because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like. //

children.text: kaṇṭakādīnāṃ saṃsthānaviśeṣavatāṃ nimittādarśanenānimittattāṃ manvānasyenaiva dṛṣṭāntena śarīrādīnāmapi saṃsthānabhedavatāmanimittatāṃ manvānaḥ pūrvapakṣayati /

children.translated_text: "Without a cause" —
Because of the placement in the thesis of bodies, thorns, and the like whose cause is not visible, and because of the non-exposure of deviation by the thesis,

children.text: udbhāvane vā sarvānumānocchadaprasaṅgāt sarvatra tasya sulabhatvāt /
children.translated_text: or [alternatively], because if deviation were exposed, there would be the consequence of the destruction of all inference, since that [objection] is easily available everywhere.

children.text: ubhayasiddhena nimittatatpaṭādidṛṣṭāntena saṃsthāna bhedavattvātkaṇṭakaśarīrādīnāmapi nimittavattvamiti siddhāntaḥ // 22 //
children.translated_text: By the example of cloth and the like, which is accepted by both sides as having a cause and which possesses differences in configuration — bodies, thorns, and the like also have a cause, because of possessing differences in configuration — this is the <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion). //22//

One who, upon not seeing a cause for thorns and the like which possess specific configurations, considers them to be causeless — and by this very example considers bodies and the like, which also possess differences in configuration, to be causeless — presents the prima facie view:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.23: Because of having a causeless [entity] as the cause, [it is] not without a cause. //
Having brought out and refuted the view of one who partially agrees with the <s>siddhānta</s> — 'but others' — (468/9) //23//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.24: Because of the otherness of what has a cause and what lacks a cause, there is no refutation. //

children.text:
svayaṃ vārtikakāraḥ kaṇṭakādīnāmanimittatāṃ vikalpya dūṣayati /
kaṇṭakādīnāmanimittaṃ janmeti /
pratipādyapratipādakanyāyasyeti /
( 469/2 ) pratipādyaḥ puruṣaḥ karma, pratipādakaśca puruṣaḥ kartā, kartṛkarmaṇī ca kārake, kārakaṃ ca kriyāyā nimittamiti pratipādyapratipādakaviṣayo nyāyaḥ sa cāyamanimittaṃ śarīrādīnāṃ janmeti pratijānānenānenābhyupeyate /
anyathā temūkataiva syāditi /
tadidamuktaṃ sarvaṃ cāmimittaṃ pratipādayasi ceti vyāhatam /
na kevalaṃ pratipādyapratipādakanyāyābhyupagamādito 'pītyāha /
vākyopādānācceti /
pratipādananimittaṃ vākyamupādatse abhidhatsecānimittaṃ sarvamiti vyāghāta ityarthaḥ /
tathā 'pyanyataradharmāsiddha
iti /
anyatareṇa sādhyadharmeṇānimittatvākhyenāsiddho 'nimittatvasyaivāsiddheḥ /
nanu prativādino vāṅnyātreṇa na siddhamasiddhaṃ bhavatyatiprasaṅgādityata āha /
children.translated_text: Now, one might say that what is non-established (<s>asiddha</s>) is not made established by the opponent's verbal concession, because of over-extension — to this he says:
Because of the existence of possessing specific configuration —
because the fact that thorns and the like have a cause is established as authoritative through the example of cloth and the like — there is no unestablishedness [of the reason] from any other source.

children.text: kasmātpunaḥ pūrva pakṣaḥ svayaṃ sūtrakāreṇa na nirākṛta ityata āha bhāṣkāraḥ sa khalvayaṃ vādo 'karmanimititta iti // 24 //
children.translated_text: "But why was the prima facie view not refuted by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> himself?" To this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "this view indeed [states that things are] not caused by <s>karma</s>." //24//

The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> himself, having considered the possibility that thorns and the like are causeless, refutes [it]: 'The birth of thorns and the like is without a cause.' [He refutes it] by the maxim of the expressible and the expresser (<s>pratipādya-pratipādaka-nyāya</s>). (469/2) The expressible (<s>pratipādya</s>) is the person as the object of action (<s>karma</s>), and the expresser (<s>pratipādaka</s>) is the person as the agent (<s>kartā</s>); the agent and the object are <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations), and the <s>kāraka</s> is the cause of the action — thus the maxim concerns the expressible and the expresser. And this [maxim] is accepted by the one who asserts that the birth of bodies and the like is causeless. Otherwise, there would be mere dumbness [i.e., inability to express anything at all]. Thus it is stated: 'You are presenting everything as causeless, yet you are [also] expressing [this thesis]' — this is contradictory. Not only because of the acceptance of the maxim of the expressible and the expresser, but also for this [additional] reason, he says: 'because of the employment of a sentence' — you employ a sentence, which is the cause of expression, and yet you declare 'everything is without a cause' — this is a contradiction — this is the meaning. 'Even so, [there is] the non-establishment of one of the properties' — [the property of] being without a cause, which is the property to be proved (<s>sādhyadharma</s>), is non-established, because causelessness itself is non-established.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.25: Everything is non-eternal, because of having the nature of origination and destruction.

children.text:
anye tu manyante /
sarvamanityamutpattivināśadharmakatvāditi /
hetorgakatvaṃ darśayituṃ pṛcchati /
kimanityamiti /
utaraṃ yasya kadā cidbhāvaḥ /
hetvarthaṃ vivṛṇoti utpattīti /
yad utpattidharmakarmanutpannaṃ nāsti tad utpannaṃ cāsti vināśadharmakaṃ ca vinaṣṭaṃ nāsti avinaṣṭaṃ cāsti tasmātpūrvāparayoḥ kālayorabhāvānmadhye ca bhāvātsiddhaṃ kadācidbhāvalakṣaṇamanityatvamutpattivināśadharmakatvādityarthaḥ /
sādhyadharmirūpaṃ pṛcchati, kiṃ punariti /
uttaraṃ bhautikaṃ ceti /
atra tāvatsvayaṃ vārtikakāra
uttaramāha /
sarvamanityamiti sūtrasya dṛṣṭāntārthatvāditi /
( 470/1 ) arthaśabdo nimittavacanaḥ dṛṣṭāntanimittatvāt sūtrasya pratijñāhetūpanyāsaparasya /
na dṛṣṭāntaṃ vinā hetuḥ pratijñātārthasya gamako yata
children.translated_text: For without an example, the reason cannot convey the meaning of the thesis —
this is the meaning.
He analyses this very [statement]: "everything is non-eternal" —
He states the subsequent refutation: "and 'because of having the nature of origination and destruction'" etc. //25//

Others, however, think: "everything is non-eternal, because of having the nature of origination and destruction." To show that the reason is too narrow (<s>agata</s>), he asks: "what is non-eternal?" The answer: "that which has occasional existence." He elaborates the meaning of the reason: "origination" etc. — that which has the nature of origination — what has not arisen does not exist; but what has arisen does exist. And that which has the nature of destruction — what has been destroyed does not exist; but what has not been destroyed does exist. Therefore, because of non-existence at earlier and later times and existence in between, the non-eternality characterized as occasional existence is established because of having the nature of origination and destruction — this is the meaning. He asks about the form of the property-bearer to be proved: "what then?" The answer: "what is material" etc. Here, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> himself first gives the answer: "because the <s>sūtra</s> 'everything is non-eternal' has the purpose of [providing] an example." (470/1) The word "purpose" (<s>artha</s>) means "occasion" — because the <s>sūtra</s>, which is aimed at presenting the thesis and reason, has the [additional] occasion of [providing] an example.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.26: Not [so], because of the non-eternality of non-eternality itself.
Having presented and criticized a partial view within the <s>siddhānta</s>:
"Not, because of the non-eternality of non-eternality itself." //27-28//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.27: The non-eternality of that is like the destruction of combustible [material] following the [destruction of] fire.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.28: The non-refutation of what is eternal, because of its establishment as apprehended.

children.text:
paramasiddhāntaṃ sūtroktamāha /
ayaṃ khalviti /
athoccate na vayaṃ sarvamanityaṃ sādhayāmo 'pi tu yaspaya yasyānityatā nāmāsti dharmastatsarvamanityamiti /
tataścākāśādīnāṃ nityatve 'pi nāsmatpakṣakṣatiriti tadetatsiddhasādhanena dūṣayati /
anityatābhāvācca sarvamanityamiti na doṣa iti /
( 471/5 ) yasya san dharmīsvaṃ tadyogādanityaḥ syātsa eva kadācinnāstītyata āha /
anityatvaṃ nāma dharmaḥ so 'sati dharmiṇi na bhavatīti /

children.translated_text: It might be [objected]: when non-eternality is understood through the apprehension of the nature of origination and destruction,

children.text: ghaṭādi bhavatvanityaṃ tenaiva dṛṣṭāntena sattvādākāśādayo 'pi bhaviṣyantyanityā iti deśayati /
children.translated_text: let pots and the like be non-eternal; and by that very example, <s>ākāśa</s> and the like too will be non-eternal because of [their] existence — he teaches [this objection].
He resolves: "but then" —
because, when the latter term [of the <s>sūtra</s>, "non-eternality"] is established, the meaning of that term — eternality — is also established. //28//

He states the ultimate <s>siddhānta</s> as expressed in the <s>sūtra</s>: "this indeed" etc. Now, if it is said: we do not prove that everything is non-eternal; rather, everything that has the property called non-eternality is non-eternal. And thus, even if <s>ākāśa</s> (space) and the like are eternal, our position is not damaged — he refutes this with the [charge of] proving what is already established: "and because of the absence of non-eternality, [the statement] 'everything is non-eternal' is not faulty." (471/5) The property-bearer that exists and would be non-eternal by the connection with its own [non-eternality] — that very [thing] sometimes does not exist — to this he says: "the property called non-eternality, in the absence of the property-bearer, does not exist."
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.29: Everything is eternal, because of the eternality of the five elements.
This is another extreme position: everything is eternal — why? — because of the eternality of the five elements.

children.text: pañcabhūtātmakaṃ khalvetad goghaṭādikāryamupalabhyate vyapadiśanti hi mṛd ghaṭo sṛccharīramiti /
children.translated_text: For this world of effects such as cows, pots, and the like is observed to consist of the five elements — indeed, they designate [things as]: "the pot is clay," "the body is [made of] earth."
And the elements are eternal, because the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> do not accept their destruction.

children.text: tena bhūtānāṃ goghaṭādīnāṃ nityateti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ // 29 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of [being identical with] the elements, cows, pots, and the like are eternal — this is the prima facie view. //29//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.30: Not [so], because of the apprehension of causes of origination and destruction.

children.text: bhūtebhyo bhautikāni bhinnāni na hi paramasūkṣmāḥ paramāṇavo goghaṭādayaḥ /

children.translated_text: If they were beyond the senses like atoms, because of their supreme subtlety, there would be the consequence of non-apprehension of everything — this was stated in the second chapter.
Therefore, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties of being apprehended and not being apprehended, the elemental products are different from the elements.

children.text: tathā ca teṣāmutpattivināśakāraṇopalabdherna nityatvaṃ bhūnityatve 'pīti siddhāntamāha /
children.translated_text: And thus, because of the apprehension of causes of their origination and destruction, [the elemental products] are not eternal even though the elements are eternal — he states the <s>siddhānta</s>:
"not, because of the apprehension of causes of origination and destruction." //30//
The elemental products (<s>bhautika</s>) are different from the elements (<s>bhūta</s>) — for the atoms, being supremely subtle, are not cows and pots.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.31: Because of being included in the definition of that, [their eternality is] not refuted.
The prima facie opponent, thinking that identity [with the elements] is established through similarity with the elements, says again:
"because of being included in the definition of that [i.e., the elements], the eternality of cows, pots, and the like, by virtue of the eternality of the elements, is not refuted." //31//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.32: Not [so], because of the apprehension of the origination and its cause.

children.text:
bhūtasāmyaṃ goghaṭādīnāṃ bhūtakāryatve 'pyupapadyamānaṃ na bhūtātmakatvamavagamayatītyāśayavānāha /
notpattitatkāraṇopalabdheriti /
(32) api ca yadyutpattivināśau na bhāvānāṃ vastusantau katha prekṣāvatāmabhimatotvapattikāraṇe 'nabhimatavināśakāraṇe ca tadarthināṃ pravṛttirityāha /
utpattivināśakāraṇeti /
api cāvyāpako heturityāha śabdakarmabuddhyādīnāṃ cāvyāptiḥ /
avyāpakaścānaikānta uktaḥ /
pakṣo hi sarvaṃ nityamiti /
( 471/ 0 ) tasminsatvāsattvābhyāmanekāntaḥ
naikaḥ sattvāsattvalakṣaṇo 'nto 'syetyanekānta iti /
tadetadvārttikakāro vakṣyatyarthadṛṣṭyā pakṣasyāntadvaye 'vasthānāditi /
hetorantadvaye sattvāsattvarūpe pakṣasyāvasthānāditi yojanā /
asati bādhake mithyātvakalpanāyāmatiprasaṅga ityamumarthaṃ śaṅkānirākaraṇābhyāmāha svapnaviṣayetyādi /
bhāṣyoktamarthamuktvā svayaṃ vārtikakāra
āha /
sarvasya ceti /
yāvadyena pratipādyata iti /
pratipādanena kriyata ityarthaḥ /
śeṣamatirohitārtham /
children.translated_text: With the intention that the similarity of cows, pots, and the like with the elements is consistent even when they are effects of the elements, and does not establish identity with the elements, he says: "not, because of the apprehension of the origination and its cause." (32) Moreover, if origination and destruction do not really belong to entities, how can discerning persons engage [in action] when they desire a particular cause of origination but not a particular cause of destruction? — he says: "the cause of origination and destruction" — Moreover, the reason is non-pervading — he says: "and the non-pervasion regarding sound, action, <s>buddhi</s>, and the like." And a non-pervading [reason] has been said to be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). For the thesis is "everything is eternal." (471/0) In that [thesis], because of [the presence of] both existence and non-existence [of the reason], there is inconclusiveness — one whose boundary (<s>anta</s>) has the two characteristics of existence and non-existence is <s>anekānta</s> (inconclusive). The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> will express this: "because of the thesis's standing on both sides from the perspective of the meaning." The construction is: because of the thesis's standing on both sides — the side of existence and the side of non-existence — of the reason. In the absence of a defeating [argument], the postulation of falsity would be over-extended — he states this point through doubt and refutation: "regarding the object of a dream" etc. Having stated the meaning expressed in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> himself says: "and of everything" — "by which it is demonstrated" — meaning: by which it is accomplished through demonstration. The rest has a transparent meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.33: Not [so], because of the impossibility of ordered arrangement.

children.text:
tadevaṃ sāṃkhyānāṃ matamapāsya svāyambhuvānāṃ matamapākartumupanyasyati /
apare sarvaṃ nityamityanthā varṇayanti /
trividhaḥ khalvayaṃ dharmiṇaḥ pariṇāmodharmalakṣaṇāvasthārūpaḥ
tadyathāsuvarṇaṃ dharmi tasya pariṇāmo vardhamānarucakādiḥ
dharmasya tu lakṣaṇapariṇāmo 'nāgatādi /
yadā khalvayaṃ suvarṇakāro vardhamānakaṃ bhaṅktvā rucakaṃ racayati tadā vardhamānako varttamānalakṣaṇaṃ hittvātītalakṣaṇamāpadyete rucakaṃ tvanāgatalakṣaṇaṃ hitvā varttamānatāmāpadyate vattamānatāpanna
eva tu rucako navapurāṇabhāvamāpadyamāno 'vasthāpariṇāmavān bhavati /
navapurāṇāvasthāśca varttamānalakṣaṇāśrayā lakṣaṇapariṇāmāḥ so 'yaṃ trividhaḥ pariṇāmo dharmiṇaḥ dharmalakṣaṇāvasthāśca dharmiṇo bhinnāścābhinnāśca /
tathā ca te dharmyabhedānnityāḥ
bhedāccotpattivināśaviṣatvamityubhayamupapannam /
nanu yadyupajanāpāyadharmakatvaṃ dharmiṇāṃ hantotpatteḥ prākteṣā masatvādvināśāccorddhamasatvātkathaṃ sarvanityatvasiddhirityata āha yaccopajāyate tatprāgapyupajanādasti /
dharmirūpeṇeti śeṣaḥ /

children.translated_text: "And that which has ceased also exists" —
here too, "in the form of the property-bearer" is the remainder.
He refutes:
"not, because of the impossibility of ordered arrangement" (sū. 33) //

Having thus set aside the view of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, he presents the view of the followers of <s>Svāyambhuva</s> [i.e., the <s>Yoga</s> school] in order to refute it. Others explain "everything is eternal" differently. The transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) is indeed threefold — in the form of property (<s>dharma</s>), characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and state (<s>avasthā</s>). For example: gold is the property-bearer; its transformation [in the form of property] is into a <s>vardhamāna</s> [ornament], bracelet, and the like. But the transformation of the property in the form of characteristic is [into] the future and the like. When the goldsmith breaks the <s>vardhamāna</s> and fashions a bracelet, then the <s>vardhamāna</s>, having abandoned the characteristic of being present, assumes the characteristic of being past; but the bracelet, having abandoned the characteristic of being future, assumes the characteristic of being present. And the bracelet, having assumed the present characteristic, undergoing the states of newness and oldness, has transformation of state. And the states of newness and oldness, being situated in the present characteristic, are transformations of characteristic. This is the threefold transformation of the property-bearer — and the property, characteristic, and state are both different from and non-different from the property-bearer. And thus, by virtue of their non-difference from the property-bearer, they are eternal; and by virtue of their difference, they are subject to origination and destruction — so both [eternality and non-eternality] are justified. Now, if the property-bearers have the nature of arising and perishing — well then, before origination they are non-existent because of non-being, and after destruction they are non-existent because of non-being — so how is the establishment of the eternality of everything [possible]? To this he says: "and what arises, even before arising, exists" — "in the form of the property-bearer" is the remainder.

upajanāpāyayoḥ svarūpataḥ kālato viśeṣataḥ sambandhito 'nāgatatvādivyavasthānupapattirityarthaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati na tāvadbhedābhedo parasparaparīhāravyavasthitadharmāvekatra samāviśataḥ /
tasmādupajanāpāyavyavasthāyai bhedaṃ dharmalakṣaṇāvasthānāṃ dharmiṇa icchatā teṣāmatityatvamabhyupetavyaṃ, sāṃkhyavatsakāryābhyupagamena tu nityatvavyavasthāpane vārttikakāra āha /

children.translated_text: "And one who says that what has ceased, even when ceased, exists" —
[he quotes this statement].
The rest is easy. //33//

The ordered arrangement of arising and perishing — in terms of their own nature, time, specific character, and relational status such as futurity and the like — is impossible — this is the meaning. What is being said is this: difference and non-difference, being properties established through mutual exclusion, cannot coexist in a single [entity]. Therefore, for one who, in order to establish the ordered arrangement of arising and perishing, wishes for the difference of properties, characteristics, and states from the property-bearer, their being beyond [the property-bearer] must be accepted. But for establishing the ordered arrangement of eternality through the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>-like acceptance of <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existent effect), the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.34: Everything is distinct, because of the distinctness in the form of existence.

children.text: ayamapyanya ekānto bauddhānāṃ sarvaṃ pṛthak kasmād bhāvalakṣaṇapṛthaktvāt /
children.translated_text: This is yet another extreme view, [held by] the Buddhists: everything is distinct — why? — because of the distinctness in the form of existence.

children.text: na rūpādyatiriktaṃ dravyaṃ nāma kiṃ cidasti nāpyavayavātiriktaḥ kaścidastyavayavīti sautrāntikā vaibhāṣikāśca prapatipedire // 34 //
children.translated_text: There is no substance whatsoever called [something] different from form and the like; nor is there any composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) different from the parts — thus the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> and <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s> have maintained. //34//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.35: Not [so], because of the production of a single entity from [things with] many characteristics.
He refutes them:
"not, because of the production of a single entity from [things with] many characteristics" (sū. 35) //
because of the production of a single entity — the pot and the like, a composite whole — that is connected with many kinds of characteristics. //35//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.36: But even so, because of the ordered arrangement of characteristics, [there is] no refutation.

children.translated_text: "But even so" — the meaning is: "moreover." "And in an aggregate of atoms, when not apprehended" — meaning: because of being beyond the senses due to supreme subtlety. "But even though this has been said subsequently" — moreover, the reason "because of the distinctness in the form of existence" having been stated in an earlier [<s>sūtra</s>], this is stated afterwards — what is that [subsequent statement]? To this he says: "there is no single entity, because [of the usage of the word <s>bhāva</s> for] an aggregate." He criticizes what has been said subsequently: "because of the impossibility of unity, the aggregate simply does not exist." He elaborates on the subsequent [statement]: "there is no single entity, because of the usage of the word <s>bhāva</s> (entity) for an aggregate." He elaborates on its criticism: "because of the impossibility of a single [entity]." He expands this: "for a collection of single [entities]" etc. — "There is no single entity" — the entity whose unity is denied in the thesis, by the very person who says "the word <s>bhāva</s> is used for an aggregate" is himself accepting that [entity]. Now, what is accepted is the aggregate, not a single entity — to this he says: "for a collection of single [entities] is an aggregate." By this, the contradiction between the thesis and the reason has been stated. Now he states the contradiction of the thesis with the reason: "and because of the usage of the word <s>bhāva</s> for an aggregate" — the <s>Vārttika</s> [reads:] "the usage of this" — (475/9) The word "pot" has many referents — meaning: in ultimate reality, it has many referents. But the conventional unity of the pot is not denied. And thus, "a single word" — with the word "single" there is deviation, because that too ultimately has many referents — this is the meaning. It might be [objected]: from words like "pot" and the like, many things are understood — form and the like, bottom and the like — so how can there be a single referent? To this he says: "because of the substrate-superstratum relation" — even if the words "pot" and the like have multiple referents, still the unity of each of those referents is undeniable — therefore the prima facie opponent's desired conclusion is not established. But taking [the argument] up, it is said: "even multiplicity of referent is not possible here" — "and because of the infinite regress of difference in the aggregate" — (476/19) If only an aggregate exists and no single [entity] whatsoever, then when the aggregate characterized as a pot is differentiated, no difference of lesser degree and the like would be apprehended — because pots, potsherds, gravel, powder, and atoms, being aggregates, have infinite parts — [so] the distinction "this is large, this is small, this is smaller" would not exist. Therefore, one who justifies gradation must at some point accept the cessation of aggregation — and that is not [possible] without a single [entity] other than the aggregate — therefore a single [entity] must be accepted — this is the meaning. Not understanding the stated meaning, [the opponent] raises a doubt: "if you think" etc. (477/5) "The aggregate of form and the like" and "four substances" — this should be seen with the intention of distinguishing sub-varieties of views. The answer is by showing the stated meaning. "In this view" — "if you accept an infinite aggregate" — the re-raising of a doubt about what has already been refuted is to bring about a contradiction with scripture. "Because of the impossibility of unity, the impossibility of plurality" — "that which was called 'many' — that is to be abandoned." The rest is explained by the explanation of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. //36//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.37: Everything is non-existent, because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among existents. //

children.text:
samprati śūnyatāvādinamutthāpayati /
ayamapara ekāntaḥ /
(478/1) sarvamabhāva iti pratijñā /
atra heturbhāveṣvitaretarābhāvasiddheriti /
sarvamidaṃ pramāṇaprameyapramitirūpamabhāvastuccham /
bhāveṣvitaretarābhāvasiddheriti /
vārttikakāro vyācaṣṭe asatpratyayabhāvapratiṣedhābhyāṃ bhāvaśabdasāmānādhikaraṇyāt /
pramāṇādayaḥ khalvamī parasparānātmakatayā asaditi pratyayasya nañaśca gocarā ityanubhūyante atastadvācināṃ śabdānāṃ tatsāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tataḥ pramāṇādayo 'santaḥ anutpannapradhvastapaṭavat /
api cāmī bhāvā nityā anityā vā nityatve sarvasāmarthyarahitasyāsattvam /
na hi nityaṃ kva citkāryaupayujyate kramākramānupapatterityuktam /
anityatve tu vināśasvabhāvāśced dvitīyādikṣaṇaiva prathamakṣaṇe 'pi na syuḥ /
sattve vānāmī vināśasvabhāvāḥ
atatsvabhāvattve vā kṣaṇāntare 'pi na vinaśyeyuḥ /
no khalu nīlaṃ svakāraṇādupajātaṃ jātu kāraṇasahasrairapi śakyaṃ pītaṃ karttumiti vināśasvabhāvakatvamakāmenāpi anityānāmeṣitatyam /
tasmādbhāvānāṃ śūnyataiva pāramārthikī kalpanayā tvavastusatyā santaivāvabhāsanta iti yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ /
tathā ca sarve bhāvā iti /
sarve bhāvaśabdā ityarthaḥ /
prayogaśca sarvebhāvaśabdā asadviṣayāḥ asatpratyayapratiṣedhābhyāṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyāt /
anutpannapradhvastapaṭaśabdavat /
atra tāvadutsūtraṃ bhāṣyoktaṃ dūṣaṇa vārttikakāra āha /
pratijñāpadayoḥ pratijñāhetvośca vyāghāta iti /
abhinnavibhaktikatvamabhinnārthakavibhaktikatvaṃ na tvabhinnavibhaktikatvameva, bhinnavibhaktikānāmapi sāmānādhikaraṇyāt /
yathā caitraḥ paṭhatīti /
yathā ca na tvāṃ tṛṇāya manya iti /
nāmati tatpratyayena bhavitumiti /
na hyatyantāsannirūpākhyaṃ sarvamiti vā bhāva iti vā 'bhidhānaspaya gocaraḥ upapāditaṃ hi dvitīyasūtra eva yathā 'sadvā 'nirvacanīyaṃ vā na khyātigocaro 'pi tu sadeva sadantarātmanā,
children.translated_text: For what is absolutely non-existent and indescribable is not the object of the expressions "everything" or "existent" — for it has been established already in the second sūtra that what is non-existent or indescribable is not even the object of cognition; rather, what exists alone [appears] as having the nature of another existent,
and thus, how can even the status of being an object of conceptual construction belong to the absolutely non-existent?
The rest is [explained] in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> —
the contradiction of thesis and reason is elaborated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. //37//

Now he raises the <s>Śūnyavādin</s> (proponent of emptiness):
"This is another extreme" —
(478/1) "Everything is non-existent" — this is the thesis.
Here the reason is: "because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among existents."
All this — in the form of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), and <s>pramiti</s> (cognition) — is non-existent, empty.
"Because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among existents" —
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains: "because of the co-referentiality of the word 'existence' (<s>bhāva</s>) with the cognition of non-existence and the negation [particle]."
For these <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like, being experienced as objects of the cognition 'non-existent' and of the negation-particle, by virtue of their mutual non-identity — therefore the co-referentiality of the words denoting that [non-existence] with the word 'existence' — therefore <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like are non-existent, like an unproduced or destroyed cloth.
Moreover, these existents are either eternal or non-eternal. If eternal, their non-existence [follows] from being devoid of all causal efficacy.
For indeed, what is eternal is never useful for any effect — because of the impossibility of both sequential and simultaneous [operation] — this has been stated.
But if non-eternal, then, since their nature is destructive — if [they perish] at the second and subsequent moments, they would not exist even at the first moment.
Or, these [entities] are either existent when [they are said to be] of a destructive nature,
or, if not of that nature, they would not perish even at a subsequent moment.
For indeed, what is blue, having arisen from its own cause, can never be made yellow even by a thousand causes — therefore the destructive nature of non-eternal [entities] must be accepted, even unwillingly.
Therefore, the emptiness of existents alone is the ultimate reality; but through conceptual construction — which is unreal — they merely appear as existing — this we see as reasonable.
And thus "all existents" —
the meaning is: all words denoting existence.
And the formal argument: all words denoting existence have a non-existent object, because of the co-referentiality with the cognition of non-existence and the negation [particle],
like the words for an unproduced or destroyed cloth.
Here, first, the refutation stated by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> that goes beyond the sūtra — the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says:
"Contradiction in the thesis-words and in the thesis-and-reason" —
"Having non-different case-endings" means "having case-endings with non-different meaning" — but not necessarily having identical case-endings, since even words with different case-endings can be co-referential.
As in "<s>Caitra</s> reads."
And as in "I do not consider you [worth even] a straw."
"Because it is not possible to have the suffix of that" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.38: Not [so], because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of existents. //
Having stated the refutation that goes beyond the sūtra, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> is about to state the refutation that is within the sūtra —
"And the refutation is connected with the sūtra."
"Not, because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature of existents" (sūtra 38) //

pūrvasūtrasyeti /

bhāvaśca kaścinnityaḥ kaścidanityaḥ tatra nityasyārthakriyākāritvamupapāditaṃ kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga eva /
anityo 'pi na vināśasvabhāvo bhāvaḥ kiṃ tu svakāraṇādayaṃ satsvabhāvo jātaḥ kāraṇāntarāttu vinaśyati /
yatūktaṃ nīlaṃ śakyaṃ na pītaṃ karttumiti /
tatra brūmaḥ śakya eva nīlaḥ paṭaḥ pītaḥ karttum āmaśyāmo ghaṭo vahnisaṃyogādraktaḥ /
atha nīlatvaṃ na pītatvaṃ śakyaṃ kartuṃ nanu bhāvo 'pi nābhāvaḥ karttuṃ śakya iti /
yathaiva kumbhādhikaraṇe śyāmaraktatve paryāyeṇa bhavataḥ evaṃ kapālādhikaraṇau kumbhabhāvābhāvāvityadoṣaḥ
// 38 //
children.translated_text:
"Everything is non-existent" — this is not so.
Why? Because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature of existents. The intrinsic nature is the property of substances and the like — being (<s>sat</s>) and the like.
Or alternatively, the intrinsic nature is the own-form (<s>svarūpa</s>) of existents, by which these existents are distinguished from their own [other] natures.
Or alternatively, because of the qualifier "as [possessed of] a cow-nature, horse-nature, etc." in the cognition "non-existent" —
just as the word <s>agau</s> ("not a cow"), by excluding the cow, establishes the existence of horse and the like through connection [with them] — similarly, even in the case of horse and the like — thus, because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature of existents, there is no non-existence — this is the meaning.
Having restated the sūtra "because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature," the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, explaining it merely by its own form, shows its purport through a question:
"Of the previous sūtra" —
(479/5) By "what is the intrinsic nature?" and ending with "the established existent," the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> shows three interpretations of the sūtra belonging to the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>.
"A common property" — meaning: a common [property] such as eternality and the like.
Through a question, he establishes the co-referentiality of "existence" with the cognition of non-existence and the negation [particle]:
"How then?" —
(480/2) The word "non-existent" (<s>asat</s>) indeed, being a qualifier of existence, denotes what is existent itself — it operates with respect to a cloth qualified by the white quality. And thus, the co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence and its expression with the word denoting existence is justified — this is the meaning.
And some existents are eternal, some non-eternal. Among these, the causal efficacy of the eternal has been established [already] — in the very refutation of momentariness.
And the non-eternal existent too is not of a destructive nature; rather, it arises from its own cause with the nature of existence, but perishes from another cause.
As for what was said — that blue cannot be made yellow — to that we say: a blue cloth can indeed be made yellow — we observe a pot becoming red from conjunction with fire.
Now, if [one says] blue-ness cannot be made into yellow-ness — [we respond:] well then, an existent too cannot be made into a non-existent. Just as in the substrate of a pot, dark and red colors alternately exist, so too in the substrate of potsherds, the existence and non-existence of the pot [alternate] — thus there is no fault.
//38//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.39: The establishment of intrinsic nature is not [valid], because of relativity (<s>āpekṣikatva</s>). //
The <s>Śūnyavādin</s> objects to what was said about the establishment of intrinsic nature:
"Not the establishment of intrinsic nature, because of relativity" (sūtra 39) //

children.text: sarva evaṃ hi bhāvā bhinnasvabhāvā bhinnatvaṃ ca teṣāmanyāpekṣam /
children.translated_text: For all these existents have different intrinsic natures, and their difference is relative to something else.

children.text: tathā hi nīlaṃ bhinnaṃ pītādyapekṣayā na tu svabhāvataḥ evaṃ hrasvatvadīrghatvaparattvāparatvapitāputratvādayaḥ parasparāpekṣā draṣṭavyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, blue is different only relative to yellow and the like, not intrinsically. Similarly, shortness, tallness, remoteness, proximity, fatherhood, sonhood, and the like are to be seen as mutually relative.

children.text: yacca parāpakṣaṃ tanna svābhāvikaṃ yathā japākusumāpekṣaṃ sphaṭikasya raktatvamityākṣepārthaḥ // 39 //
children.translated_text: And what is relative to something else is not intrinsic — just as the redness of a crystal is relative to a <s>japā</s>-flower — this is the intent of the objection. //39//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.40: Because of self-contradiction, [the objection is] inappropriate. //
He resolves:
"Because of self-contradiction, inappropriate" (sūtra 40) //

nanu yadyanena krameṇobhayābhāvo bhavati bhavatu siddhameva naḥ samīhitamityata āha /

children.translated_text: The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> himself states the refutations: "And this [objection] is self-contradictory in every way" —
Explained by mere recitation [of the text]. //40//

He explains that: "if" —
Objection: if by this method the non-existence of both [relativity and what it qualifies] follows, let it follow — our desired [conclusion] is indeed established — to this he says:
"In both dependence and non-dependence" —
For the difference of measure — tallness and shortness — is intrinsic (<s>autpattika</s>) to existents; merely the [cognition of] its excess and non-excess is dependent on mutual apprehension.
Thus, the shortness of a sugarcane-stalk relative to a bamboo-stalk — being measured by a lesser number of hand-spans — is the non-excess;
the tallness of the bamboo-stalk is the excess — being measured by a greater number of hand-spans. And this [characterization] has its ascertainment dependent on the ascertainment of the counterpart,
but its origination is not dependent on the counterpart — therefore this real property is not relative to something other.
And difference (<s>bhinnatva</s>) — which is distinction — is a qualifier of real things and does not depend on another thing for its origination, but [only] for its ascertainment.
Similarly, fatherhood too is an established generative capacity, whose ascertainment depends on the ascertainment of the son, but whose origination does not depend on the son.
And this has been elaborated by us in the <s>Brahmatattvaparīkṣā</s>.
But remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), and the like, being produced dependent on something else because of being caused by a cognition of dependence, while sustaining worldly transactions, cannot be rejected.
Nor is it the case that merely because of this, the existent that is their substrate is not independent [in nature] — thus everything is clear.
This might be [objected]: tallness and the like will be mere relativity; their intrinsic nature as real things is dispensed with — to this he says:
"And if the establishment of intrinsic nature does not [hold]" —
(481/1) Relativity means capacity; the connection with the purpose of relativity [is meant].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.41: The establishment of the exclusive [view on] number is not [valid], because of the impossibility and possibility of causes. //

children.text: prakṛtipuruṣāviti vā pañcaskandhā iti vā paśupāśataducchedeśvarā iti vetyādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Such as the doctrines of] '<s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>,' 'the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>),' 'the bound soul (<s>paśu</s>), the bond (<s>pāśa</s>), their cessation, and the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>),' and so on.
He shows the examination — culminating in the refutation of numerical absolutism — through the <s>sūtra</s>. //

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> is introductory to the next <s>sūtra</s>.
'Now, these are the doctrines of numerical absolutism' — those doctrines in which number is absolutized are so called.
'Now, after the doctrine of emptiness (<s>śūnyatāvāda</s>), they are examined' — this is the meaning.
There, he first raises the <s>Brahman</s>-non-duality (<s>brahmādvaita</s>):
'Everything is one — why? Because of the absence of difference in being (<s>sat</s>).'
The purport of this is as follows:
This manifold of name and form cannot be illuminated as different from consciousness (<s>prakāśa</s>);
because of the impossibility of self-illumination for what is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>).
Nor is it reasonable that [the inert] shines forth from contact with consciousness;
for there is no possible contact of this [manifold] with consciousness in any other way.
'The subject-object relation is the connection' — if so, no;
because of the impossibility of object-status for what produces no effect [on consciousness].
Nor is it tenable that cognition produces a real result in the object;
because of the impossibility of that for past and future objects.
Yet it is not the case that they do not have object-status.
Therefore, since the illumination of the manifold of name and form that is different from consciousness is impossible, we rightly see that this [manifold] is a transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) of consciousness itself.
Nor is it tenable that the pot and the like, being of the nature of consciousness, are subject to origination and destruction and mutually distinguished —
because of the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for grasping their mutual distinction.
For distinction is grasped through the grasping of both — that from which [something] is distinguished and that which is distinguished. But cognitions, being different [from each other], resting merely in their own nature, and unaware of each other's affairs, are not able even to grasp another cognition, much less to distinguish [themselves] from it.
And the grasping of distinction — which requires as its cause the grasping of the substrate of what is negated and the negation-locus — cannot arise simultaneously with its own cause;
because of the absence of a cause-effect relation between what is co-temporal, like the left and right horns.
Nor is it reasonable that one cognition, being momentary, first grasps the substrate of negation and the negation-locus, and then grasps the negation —
because of the impossibility of sequential operation for what is momentary and non-sequential.
Nor is it reasonable that one cognition grasps the substrate of negation and the negation-locus, while another cognition negates —
because even what is grasped by <s>Caitra</s>, <s>Maitra</s> could have the cognition of its negation [which is absurd].
Nor is it tenable that the very grasping of one's own nature is the grasping of its negation [from others] —
for that would be so only if one's own nature and its distinction from others were identical.
Regarding that: is the entity of the nature of distinction, or is the distinction of the nature of the entity?
In the first alternative, since distinction is unreal (<s>tuccha</s>), entities that have it as their nature would be unreal;
and then, without saying another word, the doctrine of emptiness (<s>śūnyavāda</s>) would follow.
In the second alternative, however, the entity, being of a positive nature, is itself the distinction — and since they are distinguished by virtue of having a positive nature, entities are not really distinguished from each other. This is what was said: 'because of the absence of difference in being.'
(482/1) But we do not deny the difference of entities that is grounded in beginningless, indescribable <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
And there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps difference between the knower and cognition either — for the very same reason.
Therefore, there is no difference of the knowable things from each other or from cognition.
Nor is there difference of the knower from cognition.
Nor is there difference of cognitions from each other. Therefore, consciousness (<s>prakāśa</s>) alone, self-luminous, eternally immutable (<s>kūṭasthanitya</s>), a mass of bliss (<s>ānandaghana</s>), displaying the varied and wonderful manifold of name and form through beginningless <s>avidyā</s>, is <s>Brahman</s> — thus non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) is established.
For this very reason, the <s>śruti</s> texts declare:
'<s>Brahman</s> is one alone, without a second. There is no multiplicity here whatsoever.
He who sees as it were multiplicity here goes from death to death' — and so on.
Having thus presented absolute oneness, he states absolute duality: 'everything is twofold — why? Because of the division into eternal and non-eternal.'
For there is no other category apart from the eternal and the non-eternal, depending on which entities could be established as threefold and so on.
He states another view: 'everything is threefold.'
He shows that: 'the knower, the knowable, and cognition.'
Cognition too, being known, does not transcend the knowable — this is the import.
He states another view: 'everything is fourfold.'
He shows that: 'the <s>pramātā</s> (knower), the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), and <s>pramiti</s> (the resultant cognition).'
If the reality called <s>pramiti</s> is not accepted as different from <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like — then in the absence of the principal action of valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), how could there be <s>pramātā</s> and the like?
And how could there be syntactic unity or the diversity of <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations) without the principal action?
We do not prohibit the designation of 'object of knowledge' (<s>prameya</s>) for the resultant state of valid cognition.
But by that much [alone], it does not become a separate category.
'The non-establishment of numerical absolutism, because of the untenability and tenability of reasons' (sūtra 41) //
