children.translated_text:
Is the thesis 'everything is one, twofold, threefold, or fourfold' without a component [that serves as] the reason? Then a means of proof distinct from [the thesis] should be stated.
For the thesis itself cannot be the means of proof.
And because the means of proof is different from that [thesis], numerical absolutism is not established.
And there is no such thing as self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>), since even cognition, lamp, and the like are cognized by another.
And that the object too, though different from cognition, is its content — this will be stated at the occasion of refuting the doctrine of consciousness-only (<s>vijñānavāda</s>).
And the difference of the object from cognition is not impossible to grasp.
For when one cognizes blue, that which is the object of self-awareness — the form that is blue, [i.e.,] non-white and the like — is within the range of one's own experience as belonging to the self. Similarly [the difference] of blue and the like from each other.
Otherwise, when instructed 'bring the pot,' one would close one's eyes and lie down; and when instructed 'lie down,' one would bring water.
Because there would be no distinction of anything from anything in any way.
Nor is it tenable that this differentiated usage is grounded in beginningless, indescribable <s>avidyā</s> —
because the doctrine of indescribable cognition (<s>anirvacanīyakhyāti</s>) has already been refuted.
Therefore, this cognition of difference, established by the experience of all people, cannot reasonably be refuted by looking to the face of [its] cause [alone].
Rather, from the clearly observed effect — characterized by the cognition of difference — one should postulate a cause of such a kind that the cognition of the manifold arises unobstructedly from it.
And that [cause] is direct perception itself.
For [perception], discriminating that blue [from others], discriminates its difference from yellow and the like — through the sense-object contact characterized by qualified-qualifier-relation and the like.
For one who experiences blue as blue, and yellow and the like as yellow and the like — whether currently or through memory — is able to apprehend them as the substrate of negation and the negation-locus, even when their mutual difference has not been grasped by form alone.
For it is not the case that because [blue] does not appear with difference, it appears with non-difference — for there is no [logical basis] for these two, blue and yellow, whose own forms have been grasped, not to stand in the relation of delimited and delimiter.
And having grasped them by perception, one can grasp their difference — so it is not tenable [that difference is imperceptible].
'Because of mutual dependence, difference is not provable by another <s>pramāṇa</s>;
without difference, no cognition of "this is not this"' —
By this, the difference of the knower too from valid cognition is explained.
And the knowers are inferred as different — because of the orderly distribution of diverse pleasures and pains among experiences, and because of the tenability of the distinction between deaf, blind, one-eyed persons, experts, dullards, those in <s>saṃsāra</s>, and the liberated.
Because the simultaneous contact of contradictory properties in one [entity] is impossible.
Even if made somehow possible through postulation, this [explanation] carries the weight of the maxim of cow-dung-and-milk-pudding [i.e., produces an absurd result].
Thus, because of contradiction with perception, the <s>śruti</s> texts like 'one alone, without a second' and the like, being of untenable meaning, transcend the primary [literal] meaning and take recourse to a secondary [figurative] meaning — like 'the sacrificer is the bundle of sacred grass' and 'the sun is the sacrificial post' and the like.
As the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> has said: 'but [it is] a statement of praise (<s>guṇavāda</s>)' and 'its establishment [is as such]' —
therefore, non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) is not [established].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.42: Not [so], because of the reason being a part of what is to be proved.

advaitādiṣvekānteṣu pretyabhāvo na tāttviko bhavedapi tu kālpanikaḥ
na kevalaṃ pretyabhāvo 'pi tu ṣoḍaśāpi padārthāḥ /
tasmādeteṣāṃ yattattvajñānaṃ tasya pravivekārthaṃ jñeyapravivekena jñānapraviveka
children.translated_text: Therefore, for the purpose of discerning the true knowledge of these [categories], the discernment of knowledge through the discernment of the knowable
— for this purpose, these have been examined.
By this extended discussion, afterlife (<s>pretyabhāva</s>) has been investigated. //43//

'Because of being a part' — if some part of the thesis were [available as a reason], then numerical absolutism would not hold. In the thesis 'everything is one,' nothing is excluded — nothing can be separated off — from which it could be a means of proof — this is the meaning.
'Then why is the thesis itself not the reason?' — therefore he says:
'And in oneself' — (402/20) the word 'and' [means] 'in the reason.'
Moreover, these numerical absolutisms are false statements, because of contradiction with <s>pramāṇas</s> such as perception and the like — he says:
'These, indeed, are the numerical absolutisms' —
The word 'indeed' (<s>khalu</s>) is for aggregation.
The difference of meaning caused by specific [properties] such as [the arrangement of] tree-cavity, hands, and the like — [the difference between] a post, a person, and the like — by the denial of that [difference], this is the meaning.
But if they proceed by accepting the specific-caused difference of meaning, even so, they abandon absolutism — the meaning being: because of the non-absoluteness of the number one and the like.
'But if only the general-caused [identity] is accepted' —
(483/5) meaning: mere number is accepted, but its absoluteness is not.
'That is just what we accept' — he says: 'even so, nothing is contradicted.'
Against those who say 'the universal of being (<s>sattāsāmānya</s>) alone is reality, while differences are merely constructed,' he says:
'And not without difference' —
As they say:
'Without difference, the universal would be [non-existent] like a hare's horn.'
One might think: in the investigation of afterlife (<s>pretyabhāva</s>), what occasion is there for examining these absolutist doctrines? — therefore he says:
'Those' —
In the absolutisms such as non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) and the like, afterlife would not be real but merely constructed —
and not only afterlife, but all sixteen categories as well.

children.text: NyS_4,1.44: sadyaḥ kālāntare ca phalaniṣpatteḥ saṃśayaḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.44: Because of the production of results immediately and at a later time, there is doubt.

children.text:
athoddeśakramānurodhātphalamidānīṃ parīkṣyate /
tatrāgnihotrādīnāṃ phalamanantarabhāvi kālāntarabhāvi veti saṃśayaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati /
karmānantaraṃ duḥkhaṃ ca lokapaṅktyādi copalabhyate praśaṃsanti hi laukikā dhārmiko 'yaṃ sādhutama iti,
tatkimetāvadevāsya phalamastu athāmuṣmikaṃ svargādīti /
kiṃ prāptaṃ svargādiphalatve karmaṇaḥ svarūpeṇākāraṇatvācciranivṛtte tasmiṃstadutpatteḥ apūrvakalpanāyāṃ ca pradhānāṅgāpūrvāṇi bhūyāṃsi kalpanīyāni na ca tānyutpannamātrāṇi janayanti phalamiti tatsahakāryantarāṇi kalpanīyānītyadṛṣṭakalpanāgauravāt tadanantaradṛṣṭaphalābādhanācca, nāsyā'bhuṣmikaṃ phalaṃ svargādi, api tvanantaradṛśyamānameva /
tatrāpi duḥkhaphalatve upadeśavyāghātāl lokapaṅktilābhakhyātyādikameva phalaṃ tacca sukhahetutayā kathaṃ citsvargādipadenocyate /
dṛṣṭo hi sukhahetau svargapadaprayogo loke yathā candanaṃ svargaḥ sūkṣmāṇivāsāṃsi svarga iti prāptam /
evaṃ prāpte brūmaḥ /
svarga padasya tāvadarthavādato--- 'yanna duḥkhena saṃbhinnaṃ na ca grastamanantaram /
abhilāṣopanītaṃ ca tatsukhaṃ svaḥpadāspada'miti sukhaṃ prati vācakatvamavadhāritam /
na ca tadvācakatvenaiva candanādau tatprayogopapattāvanekārthatvakalpanāpa yuktā /
yadāhuranyāyaścānekārthatvamiti /
tasmānmukhyo 'yaṃ svargaśabda uktabhede sukhe /
tathā ca svargakāma ityatra mukhyārthasaṃbhave nopacaritārthatā yuktā /
na cānekādṛṣṭakalpanābhayānmukhyārthaparityāgo nyāyyaḥ pramāṇasiddhe niyogaparyanuyogānupapatteḥ /
yathā 'huḥ /
'śrutisiddhyarthamaśrutopalabdhau yatnavatā bhavitavyaṃ na tu śrutaśaithilyamādaraṇīya'miti /
tathā--- 'pramāṇavantyadṛṣṭāni kalpyāni subahūnyapi' /
na cānantaradṛśyamānaṃ lokapaṅktyādi homādyanuṣṭhānaphalamapi tu tadupalambhaphalam /
adāmbhikānāṃ pracchannamanutiṣṭhatāmapi lokapaṅkyāderabhāvāt /

naiṣa puruṣasaṃskāraḥ snānādijanya
iva boddhavyo 'pi tu puruṣadharmatāmātreṇa saṃskāra ityucyate paramārthatastvayaṃ dharmaḥ puruṣāśrayo 'pi karmaṇā phale janayitavye tasyāvāntaravyāpāra iti /
vārtikaṃ sadyastāpādiphaletañ
(484/1) atidguṇasaṃvijñāno 'yaṃ bahuvrīhistāpādīti /

children.translated_text: By that, social esteem and the like are indicated. // 44 //

Now, following the order of enumeration, the fruit (<s>phala</s>) is now being examined. / Therein, the doubt [is]: is the fruit of the <s>agnihotra</s> and the like one that arises immediately or one that arises at a later time? / What is said amounts to this: / Immediately after the [ritual] action, suffering and social esteem and the like are observed — for worldly people praise [the performer saying] 'this one is righteous, most virtuous' — / so is this much alone his fruit, or is it the otherworldly [fruit] such as heaven and the like? / What is obtained [by the prima facie view]? If the fruit is heaven and the like — since the action, by its own nature, is not a cause [of a distant effect], and since [heaven] arises only long after [the action] has ceased — in postulating <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented potency), many <s>apūrvas</s> — of the principal [rite] and the subsidiaries — would have to be postulated, and since they do not generate the fruit merely upon arising, further cooperating [conditions] would have to be postulated — so because of the excessive postulation of unseen [entities], and because the fruit observed immediately is not contradicted — / [the conclusion is:] there is no otherworldly fruit such as heaven and the like for this [action]; rather, only what is immediately observed. / Among those [immediately observed results], if the fruit is suffering — because of contradiction with the teaching [that enjoins the action] — the fruit is social esteem, fame, and the like alone; and that, because of being a cause of pleasure, is called 'heaven' and the like in some way. / For the use of the word 'heaven' for a cause of pleasure is observed in the world — as in 'sandalwood is heaven,' 'fine garments are heaven' — this is the prima facie view. / To this established view we say: / To begin with, the denotative power of the word 'heaven' with respect to pleasure of the described kind has been determined from the explanatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>): 'That pleasure which is not mixed with pain, nor consumed by what follows after, and is brought about by desire — that is the pleasure which is the abode of the word <s>svaḥ</s> (heaven).' / And when its denotative power [with respect to that pleasure] is [thus] established, the postulation of multiple meanings with respect to sandalwood and the like — where its usage is justified [as figurative] — is not proper. / As they say: 'And multiple meanings are improper.' / Therefore, this word 'heaven' is used in its primary sense for the described kind of pleasure. / And thus, in '<s>svargakāma</s>' ('one who desires heaven'), when the primary meaning is possible, figurative meaning is not justified. / And the abandonment of the primary meaning out of fear of postulating many unseen [entities] is not proper, because of the impossibility of questioning what is established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding its [supposed] directive [function]. / As they say: / 'For the establishment of what is heard [in scripture], one should make effort to discover what is unheard [but required], and should not [instead] weaken what is [already] heard.' / And also: 'Things unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) that have a <s>pramāṇa</s> [behind them] should be postulated, even if very many.' / And the immediately observed social esteem and the like are not the fruit of the performance of the <s>agnihotra</s> and the like, but rather the fruit of its being known [publicly]. / Because for those who perform [the rites] secretly without ostentation, social esteem and the like are absent. / Therefore, well said is the <s>Bhāṣya</s>: 'Not [an immediate fruit], because of being enjoyable at a later time.' / And also: 'Through activity, an impression characterized as <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> is generated' — / This impression should not be understood as a person's purificatory impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) like that generated by bathing and the like; rather, it is called an 'impression' merely by virtue of being a property of the person. In ultimate truth, this is <s>dharma</s>, which, though residing in the person, has an intermediate operation in generating the fruit through <s>karma</s>. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'having burning pain and the like as immediate fruit' — / (484/1) This is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound with the qualification of excessive quality — 'burning pain and the like' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.45: Not [an immediate fruit], because of being enjoyable at a later time. //
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.46: The non-accomplishment at a later time [is objected], because of the destruction of the cause. //
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.47: That would be [possible] before accomplishment, like the fruit of a tree. //

children.text:
svargaḥ phalaṃ śrūyate ityayuktam, svargakāma iti svargasya puruṣaviśeṣaṇatvena śravaṇādasādhyatvādata
āha /
deśitayā ca kriyayā nānarthikayā śravitavyam /

iti /

śeṣamatirohitārtham // 45 // 46 // 47 //
children.translated_text: That heaven is heard [in scripture] as the fruit — [the objection that] this is improper [is answered]: since 'one who desires heaven' is heard, and since heaven is thereby heard as a qualifier of the person, it is [indeed] something to be accomplished — / to this he says: / 'And what is taught by instruction is not purposeless — it should be heard [as such].' / The instruction of a trustworthy person states the being-a-desired-means of the enjoined action — therein, when the action requires [the specification of] what is desired, the qualifier of the person too is required — and thus its being-something-to-be-accomplished is established. / For social esteem and the like would be the accomplishable [fruit] of the performance of the <s>agnihotra</s> and the like if the instruction 'one who desires that should perform the <s>agnihotra</s>' and the like were taught for one who desires that [social esteem], just as for one who desires heaven — but this is not the case — he says: 'And not one who desires burning pain and the like' — / The meaning is: not one who desires social esteem and the like. / The rest has a transparent meaning. // 45 // 46 // 47 //

children.text: NyS_4,1.48: nāsan na san na sadasat sadasatorvaidharmyāt //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.48: [The fruit before origination is] not non-existent, not existent, not both existent and non-existent — because of the dissimilarity of the existent and the non-existent. //

children.translated_text: he says:
'And not the opposite of both' —
The <s>siddhāntin</s> says:
Before origination, [the fruit] possessing the property of origination is certainly non-existent. // 48 //

Now this is being considered: what is this fruit before its origination? — non-existent, existent, both existent and non-existent, or neither? / Herein, wishing to state the non-existence of the fruit by rejecting all [four] alternatives, the prima facie opponent presents: / This fruit, before its accomplishment, / is not non-existent, not existent, not both existent and non-existent. / Why is it not both existent and non-existent? — to this he says: / 'Because of the dissimilarity of the existent and the non-existent' — / Because of having mutually contradictory properties — 'property' means 'intrinsic nature' — / the meaning is: because of contradiction. / And why is it not neither? — to this

children.text: NyS_4,1.49: prāgutpatterutpattidharmakam asad ity addhā, kasmād utpādavyayadarśanāt //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.49: Before origination, [the fruit] possessing the property of origination is certainly non-existent — why? — because of the observation of origination and destruction. //

children.text: nanu nāsadutapadyate na sanniruddhyataityācakṣate sāṃkhyāḥ tatkathametadityata āha /
children.translated_text: Objection: the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> declare 'the non-existent does not originate, the existent does not cease' — so how is this [position tenable]? — to this he says:
'Because of the observation of origination and destruction'

children.translated_text: The concealment of ignorance [means]: the concealment of doubt and error.

children.text: kāraṇasya hi pradhānasya lakṣaṇaṃ mahān lakṣyate hi mahatā pradhānamiti /
children.translated_text: For the definition of the cause, namely <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) — '<s>Mahat</s> (the Great) is defined' — for <s>Pradhāna</s> is defined by <s>Mahat</s>.
Similarly, of that [<s>Mahat</s>] too, <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) [is the definition]; 'its nourishment' means 'its grossness' — this is the meaning.
'Comes to be afterwards' — meaning: after the state of being the cause alone. // 49 //

Just as there is no origination and no destruction of the eternal nature of the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) — so too, if the fruit were eternal, there would be neither [origination nor destruction] of it — this is the meaning. / 'For not the <s>sat</s>-thesis' — / (486/1) The meaning is: not the <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existent effect) thesis. / 'Nothing whatsoever is born' — / From the mere thesis-statement, no knowledge of reality is possible. / 'And some doubt and the like does not perish' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.50: But that non-existent [fruit] is established by the intellect. //

children.translated_text: What has arisen as qualified by that [universal]
is said [to be] "arisen."

children.text: yeṣāṃ sāmānyagrahapuraḥ saraṃ viśeṣajñānaṃ tanmate na sāmānyaṃ vyanakti taduttarakālaṃ ca svapratyayaṃ janayatītyuktam /
children.translated_text: For those who hold that specific cognition is preceded by the grasping of the universal — according to that view, [it is said that the universal] does not manifest; and subsequently [the disjunction] generates its own cognition.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati na vayaṃ bauddhā iva pūrvāparakālamātrāvasthitilakṣaṇāṃ kṣaṇikatāṃ vibhāgādīnāmācakṣmahe kiṃ tvāśutaravināśalakṣaṇāṃ sā ca dvitrādikṣaṇasthāyināṃ cirasthāyibhyova ghaṭādibhyo vyāvṛttātmā śakyāvaktumiti // 50 //
children.translated_text: What is being said is this: we do not speak of the momentariness of disjunction and the like in the manner of the Buddhists — characterized as persistence for merely a prior and subsequent moment; rather, [we speak of] a momentariness characterized by rapid destruction. And that [rapid momentariness] can be predicated of [things] lasting two, three, or more moments, as distinguished from long-lasting [entities] like pots and the like. //50//

As for what was said, "because of the restriction of the material cause" — if there is a restriction of the material cause for a person — one who desires cloth takes up only threads, not <s>vīraṇa</s> grass; one who desires a mat [takes up] <s>vīraṇa</s> — then, from the knowledge of the capacity of those material causes in their respective effects, and since that capacity is inferential — this is what is said: sū. "But that is established through cognition as non-existent" //50// The effect that is to come into being as non-existent is produced by this cause alone and not by another — [this restriction] is established merely through inference — this is the meaning. Now, if on the <s>asatkārya</s> (non-pre-existent effect) position, you say the restriction that only threads are the material cause of cloth and not <s>vīraṇa</s> and the like would not hold — that is unjustified. Even though there is no difference in non-existence [of the effect prior to production], only a certain [specific] effect produced from its own cause is capable of producing a certain [specific other effect], not another — this is justified by the specific nature [of things]. Moreover, on the <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existent effect) position, since <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) is the material cause of the world, and since the class of effects is of the nature of the cause without any separation, everything would be the self of everything — and the restriction "this is here, not that; this is now, not that; this is of this kind, not of that kind" would not hold, because of the absence of any basis for discrimination anywhere. Therefore, even in a donkey there would be a horn — and one who says "the horn does not exist there, because of its non-existence" contradicts his own established doctrine — he says: "and one who says 'the donkey's horn is not produced because of its non-existence.'" When the existence [of everything in everything] and the non-existence [distinction] are equal, whatever has a cause is produced — this is a deceptive quibble (<s>guḍajihvikā</s>). In ultimate truth, however, when [the effect is] non-existent, the restriction of origination is justified through the restriction of the capacity of the cause; but when everything has the self of everything [as in <s>satkārya</s>], there is no basis for restriction — as has been stated and demonstrated. He teaches: "then what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the non-pre-existent effect?" For indeed, inference cannot be a <s>pramāṇa</s> in this matter, because of unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>). Nor can perception [be a <s>pramāṇa</s>], because by that too the non-existent cannot be determined independently — this is the purport. Understanding the intention, he gives the answer: "there is no inference either for non-existence or for existence." Just as for us, because of the fault of unestablished locus, there is no inference for the non-existence of the effect [before production], similarly, even for the existence of the effect, there is no inference, because of the very same unestablished locus. "Where then is there inference?" To this he says: the construction is "there is inference when there is no disagreement about the property-bearer." When there is [no disagreement about the property-bearer], its locus is not unestablished — this is the meaning. He asks again: "where?" If there is no disagreement about the property-bearer, where then is the dispute? The answer: "whatever both [accept]" — he divides the varieties of positions of the <s>satkāryavādins</s> on the basis of the property-bearer — "against those." "The cloth is nothing but threads" — meaning: non-different from threads. "As having the nature of an effect" — meaning: the effect is both different and non-different from the cause. But the <s>asatkārya</s> position, being his own accepted [view], is not presented because of its clarity and because of the absence of subsidiary controversy. "Has been demonstrated" — in the second chapter. "Before the time of apprehension" — meaning: before the causal operation. "With the intention of merely the absence of a specific configuration" — the example of a bed and the like [is given], not with the intention of prior-absence. "Established in a specific capacity" — meaning: before the causal operation, is the remainder. Here [we reply:] proving what is already established — we too say that before their own operation — the cause of the cloth's origination — the threads are delimited by a specific capacity. He presents the <s>satkārya</s>-proof of the opponents: "the threads are taken up with the intention of manifesting what [already] exists, necessarily by one who desires that, like a spade and the like." (489/1) For just as a spade, by removing mud, reveals water that already exists — thus. He refutes this: "the manifestation of what exists is non-existent" — the consequence applies to the effect too, like the manifestation. Just as the manifestation [of the water], being non-existent [before], arises, so too the non-existent cloth arises — this is the meaning. "Like the spade and the like" — the example is deficient in the property to be proved — he says: "and that" — "whence does that non-attainment arise? — this is to be stated." Attainment (<s>prāpti</s>) is indeed conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), and that is a quality (<s>guṇa</s>). A quality perishes either from the destruction of its substance or from a contrary quality. Of these, neither the covering substance nor the water being covered is destroyed — such that their conjunction would perish. Therefore, the origination of another quality contrary [to conjunction] must be stated — and that very quality contrary to conjunction is called disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>) — this is the meaning. Having refuted the position of non-attainment as absence of attainment, he raises and refutes the exclusion-position: "now, if [it is said that] attainment" — He raises another doubt: "now, if [it is said that it involves] origination in different locations" — And we do not accept conjunction or disjunction as a quality; rather, disjunction is [simply] the substance's originating in a different location, and conjunction is its originating without interval — this is the meaning. He refutes: "in a different location" — because of the inclusion of a qualifier, origination in a different location is not disjunction. Why? "What has arisen has arisen" — "as being in a different location, as different" — for a qualifier generates a cognition in the qualified [entity] that is consonant with itself, not one consonant with another. Indeed, the qualifier "blue" does not generate the cognition "red" in a lotus, for one who is not mistaken — this is the meaning. Moreover, since we who refute the momentariness of entities deny origination in different locations, disjunction is not origination in a different location. He raises a doubt: "because of the momentariness of disjunction" — for having arisen through the contact of the sense organ, disjunction must generate a cognition of its own object. But it does not exist for that much time, because of being momentary — having arisen, it ceases — this is the meaning. He refutes: "not, because of the manifestation of the universal" — (490/1) He analyses this: "first, the disjunction that has arisen manifests the universal" — the origination is the inherence in its own cause, or the inherence of <s>sattā</s> (existence) [in it].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.51: Because of the separation from the substratum, [the argument is] not a [valid] reason, like the production of fruit on a tree.
One who holds that the <s>ātman</s>, [supposedly] distinct from the body and the like, eternal, and going to another world, does not exist — says:
"Because of the separation from the substratum, like the production of fruit on a tree, [the argument is] not a [valid] reason"

children.text:
mūlasekaphalotpādayorekavṛkṣāśrayatvam /
karmaṇastu homāderāśrayaḥ śarīram /
na cāmuṣmikasya svargādeḥ śarīramāśrayaḥ tasminnaṣṭe 'sya bhāvāt /
tasmādāśrayavyatirekātsvargādervṛkṣaphalotpattivadityayaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ svargaphalatve homasyāheturityarthaḥ
// 51 //
children.translated_text: The watering of the root and the production of fruit have the single tree as their substratum. But the substratum of <s>karma</s> (action) such as the <s>homa</s> (fire-offering) and the like is the body. And the other-worldly [result] such as heaven and the like does not have the body as its substratum, since it exists even when that [body] has been destroyed. Therefore, because of the separation from the substratum, the example is "like the production of fruit on a tree" — the meaning is: the <s>homa</s> is not a [valid] reason for the heavenly fruit. //51//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.52: Because pleasure has the <s>ātman</s> as its substratum, [the argument is] not refuted.

With the intent that it has been demonstrated that the <s>ātman</s> exists, is capable of enjoying heaven, is distinct from the body and the like, and is the agent — he says: "because pleasure has the <s>ātman</s> as its substratum, [the argument is] not refuted" (sū. 52).
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.53: Not [so], because of the indication of results such as sons, cattle, wife, possessions, gold, food, and the like.

children.text: astu svargādyātmāśrayaṃ tathā 'pyavyāpako hetuḥ putrādiphalebhyo nivṛtteriti deśayati /
children.translated_text: Granted that heaven and the like have the <s>ātman</s> as their substratum; still, the reason is non-pervading (<s>avyāpaka</s>), because of its non-application to results such as sons and the like — he teaches:
"not, because of the indication of results such as sons, cattle, wife, possessions, gold, food, and the like" (sū. 53) //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.54: Because of the production of results from the connection with those, the designation 'fruit-bearing' is figurative in those [sons etc.].
He resolves:
"because of the production of results from the connection with those, the designation 'fruit-bearing' is figurative in those" (sū. 54) //

children.text: svargo 'pi tāvatsvargatayā na kāmyate kiṃ tu bhogyatayā /

children.translated_text: This being so, what need is there to speak about sons and the like?

children.text: te 'pi bhogyatayaiva kāmyante na tu svarūpaṃ bhogyamiti tatsādhyaṃ sukhaṃ bhogyam /
children.translated_text: They too are desired only as objects of enjoyment — but it is not their own nature that is enjoyed; rather, the pleasure produced by them is what is enjoyed.

children.text: tasmātputrādisambadhāttadutpatteḥ sukhotpatteḥ teṣu yathā phalaśabdaprayogastathā teṣu putrādiṣvityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of the production of pleasure from the connection with sons and the like, just as the word "fruit" is used [figuratively] for them, so too [it is used figuratively] for sons and the like — this is the meaning.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> and <s>Vārttika</s> are explained by the mere statement of the <s>sūtra</s>'s meaning. //54//
Even heaven is not desired as heaven [per se], but as something to be enjoyed.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.55: Because of connection with diverse afflictions, birth — i.e., origination — is nothing but suffering.

children.text:
phalānantaraṃ duḥkhaparīkṣaṇaṃ, tatreyaṃ parīkṣā bhavatu duḥkhaṃ bādhanālakṣaṇamanubhūyamānaṃ,
yatpunaridaṃ sukhaṃ pratyātmamanukūlavedanīyaṃ tatkathaṃ duḥkhamanubhavavirodhāt /
śarīrendriyabuddhayaśca yadi duḥkhahetutayā duḥkhaṃ kasmātsukhahetutayā sukhameva na bhavanti /
seyamatibhīrutā sakalalokayātrāvirodhinī /
yathāhuḥ 'na hi mṛgāḥ santīti śālayo nopyante /
na hi bhikṣavaḥ santīti sthālyo nādhiśrīyanta'iti /
tasmānmāṃsārthīva kaṇṭakānuddhṛttya māṃsamaśnannānarthaṃ kaṇṭakajanyamāpnotītyevaṃ prekṣāvān duḥkhamuddhṛttyendriyādisādhanaṃ sukhaṃ bhokṣyate, santi ca vividhaduḥkhaparivarjanahetavo dṛṣṭāḥ paridṛṣṭasāmarthyā anvayavyatirekābhyāmityabhiprāyavān pūrvapakṣī guḍajivhikayā saṃśayāna iva pṛcchati /
tatkimidamiti /
siddhāntina uttaram
anya ityāha sūtrakāra iti /
tenaivābhiprāyeṇa pūrvapakṣī pṛcchati katham /
uttaraṃ na vai sarvalokasākṣikamiti /
ayaṃ tu duḥkhabhāvanopadeśaḥ kimarthamityata
āha bhāṣyakāraḥ duḥkhahānārthaḥ /
kiṃbhūtasya duḥkhahānamityata āha /
janmamaraṇaprabandhasyānubhavaḥ prāptiḥ tannimittād duḥkhopadeśapariśīlanena nirviṇṇasyālaṃpratyayavataḥ ata eva duḥkhaṃ jihāsata
iti yojanīyam /
svābhiprāyeṇa pūrvapakṣī pṛcchati /
kayā yuktyā /
uttaram /
sarve khapalu sattvanikāyā iti /
utpattiḥ sukhaduḥkhahetubhūtā viṣayasaṃpattiḥ tasyāḥ saṃsthānāni bhuvanāni /
ā satyalokādā cāvīceriti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati /
yadi duḥkhavarjanena śakyate sukhamupādātuṃ tatastādṛśaṃ sukhamanakūlavedanīyaṃ kaḥ prajñāvān prajahyāt /
children.translated_text: If pleasure can be taken up by abandoning suffering, then what wise person would abandon such pleasure — which is felt as agreeable?

children.text: na ca tādṛśamasti sukhaṃ kva cidapi sarvasya duḥkhāvinābhāvinaḥ kevalasyopādātumaśakyatvāt /
children.translated_text: But no such pleasure exists anywhere, because all pleasure is inevitably accompanied by suffering and cannot be taken up in isolation.

children.text: na hi madhuviṣasaṃpṛktamannaṃ viṣamapahṛtya śakyaṃ madhumātramupādātumiti /
children.translated_text: For one cannot take honey alone from food mixed with honey and poison, having removed the poison.

children.text: tasmānnedaṃ sukhasya pratyākhyānamapi tu sukha eva duḥkhabhāvanamupadiśyate // 55 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, this is not a rejection of pleasure, but rather the contemplation of suffering is taught with respect to pleasure itself. //55//

After [the discussion of] fruit, there is the examination of suffering. Therein, this is the examination: granted that suffering, characterized as affliction, is experienced. But what about this pleasure — personally felt as agreeable? How is that suffering, since it contradicts experience? And if body, sense-organs, and intellect are suffering because of being causes of suffering, why are they not pleasure because of being causes of pleasure? This is excessive timidity, conflicting with the entire course of the world. As they say: "one does not refrain from planting rice because deer exist; one does not refrain from placing pots on the fire because mendicants exist." Therefore, just as one who desires meat — having removed the thorns, eats the meat without incurring the harm caused by thorns — so too, a discerning person, having removed suffering, will enjoy the pleasure that is accomplished through the sense-organs and the like. And various means of avoiding diverse sufferings have been observed, their efficacy established through positive and negative concomitance — with this intent, the prima facie opponent, as if doubting through a deceptive quibble, asks: "what then is this?" The <s>siddhāntin</s>'s answer — "another [speaks]" — the <s>sūtrakāra</s> says. With that very intent, the prima facie opponent asks: "how?" The answer: "surely, not all the world witnesses [suffering in everything]." But what is the purpose of this teaching of the contemplation of suffering? To this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "for the purpose of abandoning suffering." Of what kind [of person] is suffering to be abandoned? To this he says: the experience — i.e., attainment — of the continuum of birth and death; one who, through the cultivation of the teaching of suffering motivated by that, has become disenchanted (<s>nirviṇṇa</s>), who has attained the conviction "enough" — precisely because of this, one who desires to abandon suffering — this should be the construction. The prima facie opponent asks according to his own intent: "by what reasoning?" The answer: "indeed, all classes of living beings" etc. Origination is the attainment of sense-objects that are causes of pleasure and pain; the forms of that [origination] are the worlds. From <s>Satyaloka</s> to <s>Avīci</s> [hell] — this is what is being said:

children.text: atra heturupādīyate ṛṣiṇā / vividhabādhanāyod duḥkhameva janmotpattiḥ (sū. 55) //
children.translated_text: Here the reason is adduced by the <s>ṛṣi</s> (sage): "because of connection with diverse afflictions, birth — i.e., origination — is nothing but suffering" (sū. 55) //

children.text: janmana utpattiḥ sā dukhameva bhāvayitavyā vividhabādhanāyogāditi // 55 //
children.translated_text: The origination of birth — that is to be contemplated as nothing but suffering, because of connection with diverse afflictions. //55//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.56: Not [so], because of the production of pleasure in the intervals.
Why then is [birth] not suffering in its own nature? To this he says:
"not, because of the production of pleasure in the intervals" (sū. 56) //

children.text: na khalvayaṃ duḥkhoddeśo duḥkhakayanaṃ sukhasya pratyākhyānam // 56 //
children.translated_text: Indeed, this enumeration of suffering is not the teaching of suffering as the rejection of pleasure. //56//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.57: Because of the non-cessation of affliction, because of the fault of seeking on the part of the experiencer, [the argument is] not refuted.

children.text:
itaśca duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanaṃ na sukhasya pratyākhyānaṃ duḥkhoddeśenetyāha /
yasmādidaṃ me sukhasādhanamiti vedayan prārthayate sukhasādhanam /
tacca uktādbahuprakārādbādhanāheturiti duḥkhabhāvanayopadeśanamiti /
kāmaṃ kāmyaṃ kāmayamānasya yadā kāmaḥ samṛdhyati saṃpanno bhavati /

children.translated_text: Then immediately, another desire

children.text: icchā kṣipraṃ bādhate svargādiprāptāvapi svarājyādi kāmayate /
children.translated_text: — [another] wish — quickly afflicts this person: even upon attaining heaven, he desires sovereignty over it and the like.

children.text: evaṃ tatprāptau prājāpatyādīti asyecchā tadupāyaprārthanādinā duḥkhena prabādhataityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, upon attaining that, [he desires] the status of <s>Prajāpati</s> and the like — thus his desire afflicts him through the suffering of longing for the means [of attaining them] and the like — this is the meaning.

children.text: samantādudanemi yathā bhavati tathā bhūmiṃ labhati iti yojanā // 57 //
children.translated_text: "He goes around in all directions" — the construction is: just as it happens, so he obtains a realm. //57//

And for this further reason, the contemplation of the notion of suffering is not a rejection of pleasure — [it is stated] in the context of listing suffering — thus he says:
"Since, knowing 'this is my means of pleasure,' one longs for the means of pleasure.
And that [means of pleasure], as stated, being a cause of affliction (<s>bādhana</s>) of many kinds" — therefore the instruction is by way of the contemplation of suffering.
"When a desire — a desirable [object] — is fulfilled for a desiring person, it is accomplished" —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.58: And because of the false impression of pleasure in what is a variety of suffering. //

children.text: nanvayaṃ yadyapyantarāle sukhānyanubhavati tathā 'pi duḥkhasaṃbhedamākalayan anupadiṣṭo 'pi svayameva nivartsyati kṛtamasya duḥkhabhāvanopadeśenetyata āha //
children.translated_text: Objection: even though [a person] experiences pleasures in the interval, still, contemplating the admixture with suffering, he will desist by himself even without being instructed — so what is the use of the instruction in contemplating suffering? — to this he says: //
"And because of the false impression of pleasure in what is a variety of suffering" (sūtra 58) //

children.text:
śāstraniṣṭhānāṃ vivekināṃ khalu vividhabādhanānuṣaṅgād
anavayavena sukhamātraṃ duḥkhameveti viniścayo 'kṣipātrakalpā hi te /
tadyatheṣīkātūlasamparkādapyakṣipātra dūyate na gātrāvayavāntarāṇi tathā mṛducittatayā vivekino dūyante avivekinastu praṇayakalahakupitakuraṅgaśābalocanāṅganālaktakarasārdrapodapallavapātamapi śirasi rahasi sukhamabhimanyamānā dhanapulakakañcukāñcitatanavaḥ sāndrānandāśruplutanayanā nirvṛṇvantīti tān pratyayamupadeśor 'thavānityarthaḥ /
jāyasva mriyasva ceti saṃdhāvatīti /
punarjāyate punarmriyate janitvā mriyate mṛtvā jāyate tadidaṃ saṃdhāvanavyāpārapracaya ityarthaḥ /
codayati /
kasmād duḥkhaṃ janmeti nocyata iti /
yadi duḥkhabhāvanopadeśo janmani evaṃ satyevakāraḥ kimartha ityarthaḥ /
pariharati /
janmavinigrahārthīya
iti vinigraho vinivṛttiḥ sa evārthaḥ pravartata
iti janmavinigrahārthīyaḥ /

children.translated_text: And just as [the suffix] having the sense of "possessing"
— thus.
What is being said is this:

children.text: janma duḥkhameveti bhāvayitavyaṃ nātramanāgapi sukhabuddhiḥ kartavyā anekānarthaparamparāyāmapavargapratyūhaprasaṅgāditi // 58 //
children.translated_text: One should contemplate that birth is nothing but suffering — not even the slightest cognition of pleasure should be entertained regarding it, because of the consequence of the chain of manifold calamities being an obstacle to liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). //58//

For those who are devoted to scripture and are discerning, because of the association with manifold afflictions,
the determination that pleasure in its entirety is nothing but suffering [is already established] — for they are like [one with] sensitive eyes. Just as one with sensitive eyes is pained even by contact with a fiber of reed, but not other limbs [of the body], so too, by the delicacy of their minds, the discerning ones are pained. But the undiscerning, considering even the fall on their heads, in secret, of the reddish lacquer-juice-moist foot-petals of a woman whose doe-like eyes are angry from a lovers' quarrel as pleasure — their bodies bristling with the goose-bumps of delight, their eyes flooded with tears of intense joy — [these undiscerning ones] are delighted. Therefore, this instruction is meaningful for them — this is the meaning.
"Be born, die" — thus he runs about —
He is born again, dies again; having been born, he dies; having died, he is born — this accumulation of the activity of running about — this is the meaning.
He objects:
"Why is it not said that birth is suffering?" —
If the instruction in contemplating suffering concerns birth [itself], then what is the purpose of the word "alone" (<s>eva</s>) [in the text]? — this is the meaning.
He resolves:
"Having the purpose of restraining birth" —
Restraint (<s>vinigraha</s>) is cessation; that very [cessation] is the purpose for which [the instruction] operates — therefore it has the purpose of restraining birth.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.59: Because of the continuation of debts (<s>ṛṇa</s>), afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), and activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), there is no liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). //
After the listing of suffering, liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)
has been listed and defined — this is the remainder.
It is now being denied [by the prima facie view]:
"Because of the continuation of debts, afflictions, and activity, there is no liberation" (sūtra 59) //

children.text:
tadvyācaṣṭe bhāṣyakāraḥ /
ṛṇānubandhāditi /
asti hi /
 ... ṛṇāni trīṇyapākṛtya mano mokṣe niveśayed /
anapākṛtya mohena mokṣamicchan vrajatyadhaḥ/ ...

children.translated_text: The meaning is: because one's entire lifespan is consumed by the discharge of the three debts alone, there is no occasion for turning [the mind] to liberation — therefore there is no liberation.
Because of the continuation of afflictions, there is no liberation.
The meaning is: <s>saṃsāra</s> whose root cause has not been severed cannot be severed.
The interpretation of "because of the continuation of activity" is the same. //59//

The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains that:
"Because of the continuation of debts" —
For indeed:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should turn one's mind to liberation.
One who, through delusion, desires liberation without discharging them, falls downward."

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.60: Because of the inapplicability of the word "principal" (<s>pradhāna</s>), because there is no contradiction through the word "quality" (<s>guṇa</s>), and because of the tenability of censure and praise. //

children.text:
evaṃ pūrvapakṣayitvā siddhāntamupakramate /

children.translated_text: And for this reason too, the doctrine of [limitation by] old age and death [applies to] one who desires the fruit —
he says:
'And of one who desires the fruit' — //60//

Having thus presented the prima facie view, he commences the <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine). 'Here it is stated' — 'As for [the statement] "because of the binding of debts"' — In order to establish the secondary (<s>guṇa</s>) sense of the word '<s>jāyamāna</s>' (being born), since the primary sense is untenable, [and] in order to obtain an example, he first states the secondary sense of the word '<s>ṛṇa</s>' (debt): 'because of the untenability of the primary word.' He explains that: 'by debts.' 'This is not a primary word' — (491/1) Like one bound by debts, he is not independent and not qualified for those various rites — this is the censure. But in the absence of those [debts], [he is] independent — this is the praise. Thus, '<s>jāyamāna</s>' is a secondary word, not primary — this [is established]. Why is it not primary? — to this he says: because a mere newborn from the mother has no qualification [for rites]. Why is there no qualification? — to this he says: because qualification belongs to one who desires [the fruit] and is capable. Why must one desire? — to this he says: because in the injunction of rites, [there is] the <s>śruti</s> (scriptural statement) connecting [the rite] with desire, as in 'one who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>' and the like. And a child, even though desiring to obtain pleasure and avoid pain, does not with discernment desire heaven, sons, cattle, food, and the like. 'And engagement of one who is capable' — for indeed the <s>Veda</s>, being in the form of instruction from a trustworthy person, is not able to enjoin upon an incapable [person] an object that cannot be accomplished. And a child is not capable, because of lacking learning and the like. For this very reason, animals, sages among the gods, the lame, <s>Śūdras</s>, and those of <s>ṛṣi</s>-lineage are not qualified, because of lacking capability. Not only is such a <s>Vedic</s> convention [limited in this way], but the worldly [convention] too — he says: 'And this does not differ from the worldly [convention].' He explains that: 'The worldly [convention], first' — 'justified and faultless speech' — justified [means] by a means of valid knowledge; faultless [means] that which does not require what has already been said as a defect, i.e., what does not [need to] become something to be instructed — this is the meaning. He says that an observation of an indicative sign corroborates this point, which is already established by reasoning: 'And the <s>mantra</s>-<s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts declare the indicative sign of householdership as the rite.' The wife is the indicative sign of householdership — the rite in which that [wife participates] is thus stated: '<s>ājya</s> (clarified butter) is that which is looked upon by the wife'; 'the wives chant the <s>Udgītha</s>'; 'wearing linen garments, they should establish the sacred fires' — and the like. By this it is stated that the stage prior to householdership is not bound by debts. Now he says that the subsequent stage too is not bound by debts: 'And when the qualification belongs to one who desires, then, when the desire does not change, the doctrine of [limitation by] old age and death is justified.' Therefore, what was said — that because of repaying the debts until the end of one's lifespan, there is no opportunity for liberation — that is refuted. The explanation of the meaning of the word 'non-change' does not cease [to apply] — the explanation of 'the fourth' (<s>turīya</s>) is 'the fourth [stage].' Generally, after seventy-five years have been passed, the thirst for worldly objects becomes attenuated. But in the case of permanent conjunction [with desire], 'by old age indeed' — this is purposeless — because of its being already established by 'or by death' alone — this is the remainder. If it is said: this [phrase 'by old age indeed or by death'] is an illustration of incapability, [then] by that, whose purposelessness [is indicated]? — to this he says: 'The [statement] that the incapable one is released — even that is untenable.' One might say: although the householder has injunctions for sacrifice and the like, still the statement 'being born, one is [born] with three debts' will enjoin sacrifice and the like even for a child — he removes this doubt after deliberation: 'But even so, would what is enjoined be restated, or would its meaning be constructed as optional?' Now, in '<s>jāyamāno ha vai</s>' (being born indeed), the verb-form can [express] injunction when it is possible [to be primary], so a restatement of what is established (<s>siddhānuvāda</s>) is naturally understood. But if the establishment of that meaning cannot be devised in any way — either from another statement or from another means of valid knowledge — then only from the principle 'because of being unprecedented, non-statements [would become] injunctions' would its injunctive status be devised. But there are hundreds of statements with [injunctive] verb-forms that enjoin that very meaning — so who would ever devise injunctive status for this by mere whim? Therefore, it is reasonable that it is merely a restatement of what is [already] enjoined — thus we rightly see that the word '<s>jāyamāna</s>' has a secondary sense. One might say: the word '<s>jāyamāna</s>' in its non-figurative meaning naturally denotes separation from the mother's womb. How can it, [merely] out of conformity with some restatement, be devised as having a secondary sense? Better to devise, out of conformity with the primary meaning, [that it is] an injunction itself. In that case, the <s>śruti</s> is accommodated. And even a child has the fitness to produce the fruit, because the self is the <s>samavāyikāraṇa</s> (inherent cause) in relation to the fruit. Therefore, although a mere newborn does not have the fitness to perform the means to the fruit, still there is fitness in relation to producing the fruit; and the purpose is [served] by the fruit, not by the means to it — to this he says: 'for the means to the fruit are the domain of effort, not the fruit [itself].' This is the intention: an injunction indeed assigns a person as agent to its own operation, and effort is his operation; [effort] is possible [only] with respect to [its proper] domain and cannot be turned away from that domain — so [the injunction] requires its own domain. And the fruit cannot directly be its domain — it can be [so] only as something aimed at. But [mere] aiming does not fulfill [the role of] effort until one reaches what is directly to be accomplished. The means to the fruit is what is directly to be accomplished — thus the effort of a person who has set out with the fruit as [his] aim is fulfilled [only] when the means becomes [his] domain. And a child, not knowing the means, has no capability in that [domain]. And one who is incapable is a non-agent — how can he pervade himself with effort? And one who does not pervade [himself with effort] — how can he be qualified? — thus it is established that the word '<s>jāyamāna</s>' having a secondary sense alone is reasonable. 'And what is enjoined for the one being born' — means: it is enjoined [as applicable] before the debt-statement, and is enjoined [as applicable] after the debt-statement — this is the meaning. As for what was said — 'for therein <s>pravrajyā</s> (renunciation) is enjoined' — he addresses what is being examined: 'if [you object] because of the absence of an explicit injunction' — He removes the doubt: 'not, because of the absence of a prohibition as well.' He classifies the doubt: 'explicitly' — For the supremely trustworthy blessed <s>Īśvara</s>, having set out with compassion to instruct beings, teaches that householdership alone is to be resorted to — from that we understand: there are no other <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) beneficial to beings — this is the meaning. For this very reason they say: 'the <s>ācāryas</s> (teachers) [hold] that there is only one <s>āśrama</s>, because of the explicit injunction of householdership.' He classifies the refutation: 'not [so] because of the [absence of] prohibition' — The <s>smṛtis</s>, <s>itihāsas</s>, and <s>purāṇas</s> are found to prescribe the four <s>āśramas</s> without dispute. If they are prohibited by explicit <s>śruti</s>, then, because of contradiction with that [śruti] — like covering everything with <s>udumbara</s> [bark] — they would be unauthoritative in that [regard]. But the prohibition of that [four-āśrama system] is not directly understood from <s>śruti</s>. Therefore, the four-<s>āśrama</s> system, prescribed by <s>smṛti</s> and the like and not prohibited by <s>śruti</s>, cannot be abandoned — this is the meaning. And the inference of that prohibition from [mere] non-injunction [does not hold] — he says: 'because of the qualification' — Because of the qualification of the instruction of householdership, the injunction is of that [householdership] alone, not of other <s>āśramas</s> — but not because of the non-existence of other <s>āśramas</s>. For grammar, in expounding words, does not thereby deny the existence of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) and the like. Moreover — let there be no explicit injunction [in śruti]; but in the <s>śruti</s>, statements describing <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) together with its means, and statements describing the four <s>āśramas</s>, are explicitly found — those, being unprecedented, will be injunctions of <s>apavarga</s> together with its means and of the four <s>āśramas</s> — he says: 'And the <s>Ṛc</s>-<s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts declare <s>apavarga</s>' — '<s>mṛtyuḥ</s>, beyond action' — this suggests that abandonment of action is the means to <s>apavarga</s>. And immortality — by this <s>apavarga</s> is shown. He clarifies, through another <s>śruti</s>, the suggested means to <s>apavarga</s> — [which is] abandonment of action: 'not by action, not by progeny' — 'beyond the sky (<s>nāka</s>)' — the word '<s>nāka</s>' (sky/heaven) here illustratively denotes <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). The meaning is: beyond <s>avidyā</s>. 'Placed in the cave' — shows that it is beyond the scope of ordinary means of knowledge. 'Beyond darkness' — <s>avidyā</s> is darkness; beyond that. 'Of the color of the sun' — meaning: of eternal luminosity. By this, it is stated that meditation on <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>īśvarapraṇidhāna</s>) is the means to <s>apavarga</s>. Having cited the <s>Ṛc</s> (verse), he cites the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> (prose): 'now, the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>' — By '<s>yajña</s>' (sacrifice) and the like, the householder's <s>āśrama</s> is shown. By '<s>tapas</s> (austerity) alone,' the <s>vānaprastha</s> (forest-dweller) <s>āśrama</s>. By '<s>brahmacārin</s>' (celibate student), the <s>brahmacarya</s> <s>āśrama</s>. He states the fruit of these, characterized as worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>): 'all these indeed.' He states the fourth <s>āśrama</s>: '<s>brahmasaṃstha</s>' (established in <s>Brahman</s>). And thus '<s>akratu</s>' — <s>kratu</s> means resolve (<s>saṃkalpa</s>). One who was desiring — he himself then becomes non-desiring. Non-desiring — abandoning desire; upon the accomplishment of that abandonment, he is non-desiring; its explanation is: desireless (<s>niṣkāma</s>). '<s>Ātmakāma</s>' (self-desiring) — desiring the self endowed with <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation); by obtaining that, he becomes one whose desires are fulfilled (<s>āptakāma</s>). 'His <s>prāṇas</s> do not [depart]' — meaning: he becomes eternal. He concludes the topic: 'there, what was said.' He cites another <s>śruti</s> too that describes the four <s>āśramas</s>: 'and these four.'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.61: Because of the superimposition [of the fires] upon the self, there is no prohibition. //
Having asked —
how is the <s>sūtra</s> to be read? —
'Because of the superimposition upon the self, there is no prohibition' (<s>sūtra</s> 61). //

children.translated_text: 'Enough of these pursuits that are causes of misfortune' — [this is the conviction] of one who has arrived at [right] understanding —

children.text: ata eva nivṛtte phalārthitve samāroṣaṇamātmanyagnīnāṃ vidhīyate iti /
children.translated_text: for this very reason, when the desire for fruits has ceased, the superimposition of the fires upon the self is enjoined.

children.text: evaṃ brāhmaṇānīti yadaiṣaṇābhyo vyutthitasya pravrajyāvidhānaṃ tadā tadabhidhāyīni brāhmaṇānyupapannānītyarthaḥ // 61 //
children.translated_text: Thus, 'the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>' — when <s>pravrajyā</s> (renunciation) is enjoined for one who has risen from the [three] pursuits, then the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts that describe that [renunciation] are justified — this is the meaning. //61//

Because of the superimposition of the fires of the self — there is no prohibition of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) through the binding of debts. By this stratagem (<s>chala</s>), the injunction of <s>pravrajyā</s> (renunciation) too is shown to have an explicit [scriptural basis]. [For] one who has risen from the [three] pursuits (<s>eṣaṇā</s>), whose intellect is reversed —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.62: And because of the impossibility [of merit] at the end of the succession of recipients (<s>pātracaya</s>), there is absence of fruit. //

buddhādismṛtayastu vedaninditairmlecchādibhiḥ parigṛhītā na tvāryairiti na tāḥ pramāṇaṃ bhavitumarhantītyarthaḥ /
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmānyāccāprāmāṇyānupapattiḥ /
ya eva vedasya draṣṭrāro 'nuṣṭhātāraśca tadarthasya ta evetihāsādīnāṃ pravaktāraḥ prācetasakṛṣṇadvaiyāyanamanuprabhṛtayaḥ /
api ca vaidikāni karmāṇi smārtīmitikartavyatāmapekṣante smārtani ca vaidikāni mantrādīnīti sarvametadapramāṇye dharmaśāstrāṇāṃ nopapadyate /
yadyapi ca manvādayo 'pi dharmajñānavairāgyaiśvaryaśālitayā anubhūyāpyupadiśantīti saṃbhavati tathāpi vedamūlakatvamevetihāsapurāṇādināṃ yuktam /
children.translated_text: Although it is possible that <s>Manu</s> and the like too, possessing <s>dharma</s>, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, teach even from direct experience, nevertheless it is appropriate that <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and the like have the <s>Veda</s> as their root.
For thus [it is stated]:
'The entire <s>Veda</s> is the root of <s>dharma</s>, as well as the <s>Smṛti</s> and conduct of those who know it.
Whatever <s>dharma</s> of anyone has been proclaimed by <s>Manu</s>,

When the sacrificer has died, the sacrificial vessels are placed on the sacrificer's body according to their respective limbs, and the final offering (<s>antyeṣṭi</s>) is performed.
If the rituals [extending to] old age and death were postulated without distinction, then it would follow that everyone's rituals extend to the [final] arrangement of vessels — meaning: it would follow that rituals extend until death.
'But the ending-with-vessel-arrangement of rituals is indeed desired' — therefore he says:
'Therein, the rising from the pursuit (<s>eiṣaṇāvyutthāna</s>)' —
Therefore, fruit does not indiscriminately motivate the agent.
'The absence of fruit' — the meaning of this component of the <s>sūtra</s> is: the absence of fruit indiscriminately being the motivator of the agent.
By this, the contradiction with the <s>śruti</s> on the rising from pursuit has been shown.
Thus, the <s>śruti</s> regarding the four stages of life (<s>cāturāśramya</s>) has been stated.
Now, <s>Smṛti</s> and the like too are teachers of the four stages of life — he says: 'because of the prescription of the four stages of life.'
He raises the doubt: 'if that is not authoritative' —
Let the scripture (<s>āgama</s>) of the Lord — the creator of the world, supremely compassionate, omniscient, the blessed <s>Parameśvara</s> — be authoritative, because of being the utterance of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>).
But because there is no certainty about the trustworthiness (<s>āptatva</s>) of <s>Manu</s>, <s>Vyāsa</s>, and the like, how can there be certainty about the authority of what they composed? — this is the meaning.
The answer: 'by a <s>pramāṇa</s>' —
One might think: granted, the authority of <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s> [is established] through endorsement by the <s>Veda</s>; but how is the authority of the <s>Dharmaśāstras</s> composed by <s>Manu</s> and the like established? — therefore he says:
'And in the case of non-authority' —
The meaning is: their authority too [is established] because of universal acceptance by all people.
But the <s>Smṛtis</s> of <s>Buddha</s> and the like are accepted by <s>mlecchas</s> (barbarians) and the like who are censured by the <s>Veda</s>, not by the <s>Āryas</s> — therefore they cannot be authoritative — this is the meaning.
'And the impossibility of non-authority, because of the commonality of seers and speakers' —
The very seers and practitioners of the <s>Veda</s> and its meaning are themselves the speakers of the <s>Itihāsa</s> and the like — <s>Prācetasa</s> [Vālmīki], <s>Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana</s> [Vyāsa], <s>Manu</s>, and the like.
Moreover, Vedic rituals require <s>Smṛti</s>-based procedural details (<s>itikartavyatā</s>), and <s>Smṛti</s>-based rituals require Vedic <s>mantras</s> and the like — all this would be untenable if the <s>Dharmaśāstras</s> were not authoritative.

'But why is this subject matter, which is within the scope of <s>Itihāsa</s> and the like, not stated by the <s>Veda</s> that is directly known?' — from its not being stated [in the <s>Veda</s>], we understand that surely this [subject matter] is not intended by the maker of the <s>Vedas</s>.
Though already refuted, this is refuted again for the sake of firmness — 'and because of the orderly arrangement of subject matters.' //62//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.63: Because of the absence of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) in dreamless sleep, [there would be] liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).

children.translated_text: The state of dreamless sleep is cited because it is well-known in the world.

children.translated_text: Even in the state of the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>), the selves are indeed free from afflictions — but since that [state] is not well-known in the world, it is not cited.

children.text: etāvāṃstu muktāvasthāyāṃ viśeṣaḥ yadasyāṃ kleśavāsanāpi nāsti /
children.translated_text: But in the state of liberation, there is this much distinction: in it, even the latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) of afflictions does not exist.
In the state of dreamless sleep and the state of dissolution, even though there is cessation of afflictions, their latent impression exists. //63//

As for what was said — 'because of the unbroken continuity of the connection with afflictions' — he refutes that:
'Because of the absence of afflictions in dreamless sleep, liberation' (sūtra 63). He explains that: 'of one in dreamless sleep, indeed.'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.64: There is no activity for [the sake of] reconnection [with the body] for one whose afflictions have been destroyed.

children.text: yadapi pravṛttyanubandhāditi tatrāha--- na pravṛttiḥ pratisaṃdhānāya hi hīnakleśasya (sū. 64) //
children.translated_text:
As for what was said — 'because of the connection with activity' — regarding that he says: 'there is no activity for reconnection for one whose afflictions have been destroyed' (sūtra 64) //
Of the embodied being.
He explains that: 'when passion (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>) have been destroyed, even though [the body] exists, there is no activity for one's own reconnection [with a new body].'
'This has been demonstrated by us' — meaning: just as the rice-grains of <s>karma</s>, enveloped in the husk of faults (<s>doṣa</s>), are capable of [producing] the sprout of birth — not the bare [grains] alone.
He raises the doubt: 'the fruitlessness of <s>karma</s>' — [if <s>karma</s> cannot produce fruit without kleśas], then there would be the unwanted consequence of non-authority of scripture, which teaches that rituals are means to results

children.translated_text: — this is the import.
He refutes: 'not, [because] the fruition of <s>karma</s> [is not denied].'
Fruition is the result; its experience is enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>). //64//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.65: Not [so], because of the natural character of the continuum of afflictions.
The prima facie opponent says:
'Not, because of the natural character of the continuum of afflictions' (sūtra 65) //
A partial proponent (<s>siddhāntyekadeśin</s>) says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.66: Just as the non-eternality of [what existed as] non-existence before origination, so too non-eternality even for what is natural.
'Before... non-eternality' (sūtra 66) //
The construal is: just as the non-eternality of the state that exists in milk and the like before the origination of curd and the like. //66//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.67: Or, [the non-eternality is] like that of the darkness of atoms.
Another partial proponent presents the entity itself as the example — he says:
'Or, like the non-eternality of the darkness of atoms' (sūtra 67) //

children.translated_text: The darkness of atoms is produced, because of being a form of earth,
like redness and the like — thus, rather, there is a reason for non-eternality.

But due to the difference from forms such as redness produced by human effort, fire, and water — merely by virtue of not being preceded by effort — the statement of beginninglessness [is made] — therefore there is no contradiction with scripture. //67//

'That dark color belongs to food' — this is the scriptural tradition. Since the word 'food' (<s>anna</s>) denotes clay, [the <s>śruti</s>] states the beginninglessness of the darkness of earthen atoms — this is the import.
Here, he first refutes the first partial proponent: 'of the existent, indeed' —
He refutes the second partial proponent:
'The beginningless darkness of atoms' — because of the non-hearing of a reason, this is not tenable.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.68: Not [so], because passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the like have volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) as their cause.
Having thus refuted the two partial proponents, he states the ultimate resolution:

children.text:

na saṃkalpanimittatvācca rāgādīnām (sū. 68) //
children.translated_text:
'This, however, is the resolution:
Not, because passion and the like have volition as their cause' (sūtra 68) //

children.translated_text: Just as <s>karma</s> accompanied by false cognition is the cause of passion and the like, so too, [<s>karma</s>] accompanied by that [false cognition] is the cause of fruit — and thus, for one who possesses true knowledge, even existing <s>karma</s> should not be the cause of fruit — this is the meaning.
He resolves:
'Not, because of being non-expectant' —

children.text: karmāśayaprapañcamucchettumamūḍho 'pyasakto 'pyadviṣṭo 'pi mūḍha iva sakta iva dviṣṭa iva tatphalaṃ bhuṅkta iti rāgādyanapekṣaṃ karma svaphalaṃ janayati tenāsau phaloṣabhogo na bandhahetuḥ mūḍhādīnāṃ bandhahetuḥ mūḍhādīnāṃ bandhahetuphalopabhogaḥ sa catādṛśo rāgādisahāyaiḥ karmabhiḥ kriyate na rāgādinirapekṣairityavadātam // iti miśraśrīvācaspativiracitāyāṃ nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkāyāṃ caturthādhyāyasyādyamāhnikam //
children.translated_text: To exhaust the expanse of <s>karma</s>-residue (<s>karmāśaya</s>), even one who is undeluded, unattached, and free from aversion — though like a deluded, attached, or averse person — experiences its fruit. Thus <s>karma</s>, not requiring passion and the like, produces its own fruit. Therefore, his experience of fruit is not a cause of bondage. But for the deluded and the like, the experience of fruit that causes bondage — that is produced by <s>karmas</s> accompanied by passion and the like, not by <s>karmas</s> independent of passion and the like — thus everything is clear. // Thus, in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Vācaspati Miśra</s>, the first section (<s>āhnika</s>) of the fourth chapter [is concluded]. //

He explains the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) as serving to aggregate what is unmentioned:
'And because of having <s>karma</s> as a cause, and because of having each other as cause.'
The remainder is: 'the aggregation of what is unmentioned.'
Regarding 'because of having volition as a cause,' he analyzes:
'From false volitions' —
Although volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) is the desire for a previously experienced object, still its prior component — experience — should be taken [as relevant].
Because the desire [itself] has the nature of attachment (<s>rāga</s>).
Therefore, false experience is volition — this is the meaning.
'But how can the diversity of effects arise from a single false cognition?' — therefore he says:
'From what produces attachment, what produces anger, and what produces delusion' —
In [terms like] <s>bhavya</s> (charming), <s>geya</s> (singable), and the like, the agent-suffix is applied [indicating the object's capacity to evoke these responses].
The delusion-producing volition is the impression of false cognition.
He analyzes the causality of <s>karma</s> for passion and the like:
'And <s>karma</s>' — by 'community' (<s>nikāya</s>), birth-species is indicated.
He states the mutual causality of passion and the like:
'Each other' —
One might think: granted, the afflictions are non-eternal; but the false cognition that produces them has no cause for its cessation — and because of the continuation of afflictions, liberation is impossible — therefore he says:
'All... from the absence of false volitions' —
Moreover, it was said that the continuum of afflictions is beginningless. Whence [are they beginningless]? 'All these are psychophysical (<s>ādhyātmika</s>) states' —
Those that operate with reference to the self — the body, sense-organs, and the like — are <s>ādhyātmika</s>.
'But if even beginningless things can cease, there would be the consequence of cessation even for things that by nature never arise' — therefore he says:
'And it is not the case that, this being so, anything is of the nature of never arising' —
Because of accepting that only those that have the nature of arising also have the nature of perishing — namely, passion and the like — this is the meaning.
'Now, let passion and the like not have false cognition as their cause when false cognition has not ceased;
but those that have <s>karma</s> as their cause — whence their cessation? For there is no cessation of passion and the like without the cessation of <s>karma</s>,
because of the impossibility of the cessation of <s>karma</s> without [the cessation of] passion and the like — therefore there is no liberation' — therefore he says:
'And <s>karma</s>, which determines the birth-species, does not become the cause of the arising of passion and the like, because of the destruction of the volition in the form of false cognition through the true knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>).'
False cognition alone is the cause of all passions and the like.
But <s>karmas</s> prompt passions and the like through the determination of birth-species — thus the causality-of-<s>karma</s> was stated — this is the import.
'But just as passions and the like cease through the cessation of false cognition even when <s>karma</s> exists, so too, when <s>karma</s> exists, should not the fruit also not arise through the cessation of false cognition?' — therefore he says:
'But the experience of pleasure and pain — the fruit — does arise' —
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'as long as the connection with life [lasts], for by old age or' — this is meaningless.
(495/9) 'Or by death' — since the point is already made by this alone, [the first part] is not stated; the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the second reasoning mentioned in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>:
'Because of his own incapacity' — by this.
'Because of being a means for the sacrifice' —
(496/7) meaning: because of being a performer of the sacrifice.
He elaborates this very point:
'Because the sacrificer becomes a subsidiary (<s>aṅga</s>) of the sacrifice.'
As the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> has said: 'and the person is for the purpose of the ritual.'
'<s>Karma</s>, requiring volition and the like, is the cause of passion and the like' —
(498/20) The <s>karma</s> that is the cause of a particular type of birth makes manifest the latent impression of false cognition appropriate to that birth — and through that [latent impression], it becomes the cause of passion and the like.
He objects:
'Of pleasure and the like' —
The second section of the fourth chapter.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.1: From true knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), [there is] the cessation of egoism (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), which is caused by faults (<s>doṣa</s>).
