children.translated_text: The stating of synonyms — 'cultivating (<s>āsevamānasya</s>), practicing (<s>abhyasyataḥ</s>), contemplating (<s>bhāvayataḥ</s>)' — is for the purpose of showing the firmness [required] in contemplation (<s>bhāvanā</s>).
Having purified the meaning of the passage, he reads the <s>sūtra</s> on that topic:
From the true knowledge of the reality [of things] that are the causes of defects (<s>doṣa</s>), the cessation of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) [follows]
(<s>sūtra</s> 1) //

Thus, doubt, means of valid cognition, and objects of knowledge have been examined. And purposes and the like — wherever there is doubt — have been examined by extension through the successive occasions [of their discussion]; thus all sixteen categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been examined. It was stated that the true knowledge of these is the cause of attaining the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>). Moreover, it was said that the true knowledge of the <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) is the direct cause of <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, while the true knowledge of the other [categories serves] as auxiliaries to that. Now this is being examined here: is the true knowledge of each <s>prameya</s> individually — <s>ātman</s> and so on — the cause of attaining <s>niḥśreyasa</s>, or is it the [true knowledge] of some particular subset of these? The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> introduces this examination: 'Now, are there indeed as many objects as there are <s>prameyas</s>, [and is true knowledge needed] in each one individually' — meaning: for each individual living being, as many <s>ātmans</s> as there are, and as many sense organs and so on. A bystander asks the prima facie opponent: 'And what is the distinction here?' The prima facie opponent answers: 'Not indeed in each single one' — because of the impossibility from both the aggregate and a part [of it]. 'From the true knowledge of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, the attainment of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> [follows]' — this being inappropriate is the prior position. He states the <s>siddhānta</s>: 'False knowledge indeed is delusion (<s>moha</s>).' The word 'vai' is for [indicating the rejection of the] previous position; the word 'khalu' is in the sense of 'because.' The prior position is inappropriate because false knowledge is <s>moha</s>. True knowledge is not conducive to <s>niḥśreyasa</s> merely by the removal of ignorance, but rather through the cutting off of the root cause of <s>saṃsāra</s> — as directly [observed]; and it is not ignorance of reality (<s>tattvājñāna</s>) that is the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, but rather false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>). Because true knowledge opposes and cuts off that [false knowledge], it is the cause of liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). 'Let it be so — still, what bearing does this have on the prior position?' — to this he says: 'And that false knowledge, regarding whichever object it operates' — for indeed, one's own associated <s>ātman</s> and the like, when apprehended in a distorted manner, are causes of <s>saṃsāra</s>; therefore, only the false knowledge regarding those [specific objects] is to be removed, not knowledge regarding other <s>ātmans</s> and the like. Therefore, regarding those [other objects], let false knowledge cease or not cease — as illustrated by the example of one's own <s>ātman</s> and the like — but that [other knowledge] has no use for the cessation of [one's own] <s>saṃsāra</s>. But regarding that [specific object] for which it does have use, true knowledge is difficult [to attain]. He asks: 'What then is that false knowledge?' — for indeed there are various disagreements among the disputants. Some say: the direct realization of the non-dual <s>Brahman</s> — which is pure consciousness and a mass of bliss, whose manifold of varied names and forms has been shaken off and dissolved — that is true knowledge. Others, however, [say it is] the discrimination between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> (<s>sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti</s>). Still others [say it is] the knowledge of the selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> and the person (<s>dharmapudgalanairātmya</s>). The elders [say it is] the perception of the eternal <s>ātman</s> as distinct from the body, sense organs, and the like, which are impermanent. Thus, because of this disagreement, the question [is raised]. The answer: 'The apprehension of <s>ātman</s> in what is not <s>ātman</s> — "I exist" — this delusion is <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense).' First, the knowledge of <s>ātman</s> as non-dual and a mass of bliss is not true knowledge — because difference (<s>bheda</s>), being established by perception, cannot be denied in the absence of a sublating cognition. Nor can luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>) and bliss (<s>ānanda</s>) reasonably be the very nature of <s>ātman</s> rather than properties distinct from <s>ātman</s>'s [essential] nature. The <s>śruti</s> 'Truth, knowledge, bliss is <s>Brahman</s>' — with its intent being the powers of bliss and consciousness — [refers to] difference itself, and the co-referential predication (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) is somehow possible through the relation of possessor and possessed. But if there were non-difference, then since <s>ānanda</s> and <s>vijñāna</s> would be synonyms of 'that' [i.e., <s>Brahman</s>], their being used together [in the same sentence] would be impossible. Nor [is this like the statement] 'the sun is of surpassing luminosity,' where there is identity of the surpassing and the luminous — because even for what is not luminous, surpassingness is possible; and because even for what is not surpassing — such as a firefly — luminosity is possible. Therefore, this [Advaita view] amounts to nothing. The discrimination of <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, however, is untenable because <s>sattva</s>, i.e., <s>Prakṛti</s> itself, does not exist — since it is rooted in the <s>satkāryavāda</s> (doctrine of pre-existent effect), and since the existence of <s>Pradhāna</s> has already been refuted, it is refuted by that very [refutation]. The selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> and the person, however, has been refuted by the statement of the existence of the eternal <s>ātman</s> when the [doctrine of] momentary destruction was refuted. Therefore, it is well said: 'The apprehension of <s>ātman</s> in what is not <s>ātman</s> — "I am" — this delusion is <s>ahaṅkāra</s>.' For this very reason, every being has the wish for self-[preservation] — even a worm [thinks] 'may I not cease to be, may I continue to be.' This clinging (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) of such a kind arises for one who determines the body and the like as <s>ātman</s>, not for one who knows the true nature of <s>ātman</s>. For he, seeing the body and the like as distinct from <s>ātman</s> — like a discarded snakeskin — does not become attached to them; because of the absence of attachment, he is not tormented, nor does he grieve. Having shown <s>saṃsāra</s> for one who lacks true knowledge, he states the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> for one who possesses true knowledge: 'But one who [knows] suffering' — Thus, since in the manner explained, <s>moha</s> and true knowledge are the causes of <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>apavarga</s> respectively, he concludes: 'Therefore, those who are seeking liberation should know the sufferings that are the fruits of afterlife (<s>pretyabhāva</s>)' — this is the summary of the preceding [discussion].

children.text:
śāstrārthasaṃgraho 'nūdyate śāstratātparyasaṃgraho dvitīyasūveṇānūdyataityarthaḥ /
kiṃ nu khalu bho iti bhāṣyaṃ tadanupapannaṃ yato na viṣayamātrajñānamapavargaheturapi tu prameyatattvajñānamityata
āha vārtikakāraḥ /
tatra viṣayāntarāṇāmiti /
(500/8) yāvanto viṣayā iti na viṣayamātrābhiprāyamapi tu prameyābhiprāyamityarthaḥ /
sugamamanyadvārtikam
// 1 //
children.translated_text: A summary of the meaning of the treatise is being restated — the summary of the purport of the treatise is being restated by the second <s>sūtra</s> — this is the meaning. 'Now, are there indeed' — this <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage is inappropriate because not mere knowledge of objects is the cause of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), but rather the true knowledge of <s>prameyas</s> — therefore the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says: 'Of the other objects, then' — (500/8) 'as many objects' — the intent is not mere objects but rather <s>prameyas</s> — this is the meaning. The rest of the <s>Vārttika</s> is easy [to understand]. // 1 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.2: The objects such as form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like, which are the causes of defects, are produced by mental construction (<s>saṃkalpa</s>). //
By the sequence of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (meditative contemplation), indeed.

children.text: prasaṃkhyānaṃ samādhijaṃ tattvajñānaṃ tacca viṣaye sukaramiti tatraiva prāthamikasya prathamaṃ prayatno yuktaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Prasaṃkhyāna</s> is the true knowledge born of <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption); and that is easy regarding sense-objects — therefore the initial effort should first be directed there.
The <s>sūtra</s>:
The objects such as form and the like, which are the causes of defects, are produced by mental construction (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) (<s>sūtra</s> 2) //

It was stated that the apprehension of <s>ātman</s> in what is not <s>ātman</s> — namely the body and the like — is to be removed. Now, the question arises: in which [object] should the apprehension of <s>ātman</s> first be removed? In response, he says:
False knowledge is <s>saṃkalpa</s> (mental construction); by that [the objects are] made into objects [of attachment] — this is the meaning.
Desires are [objects that are] desirable. //2//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.3: But the cause of that [desire] is the false identification with the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>). //

children.text:
anye khalu avayavisaṃjñāṃ nivartayanto 'vayavinameva pratyācakṣate tān pratyācakṣāṇa āha /
ataḥ paraṃ kāciditi (502/2) sūtram--- tannimittaṃ tvavayavyabhimānaḥ (sū. 3) //
children.translated_text: Now, others who would eliminate the designation of parts (<s>avayava</s>) reject the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) itself. Refuting them, he says: 'Henceforth, a certain [objection]' — (502/2) the <s>sūtra</s>: 'But the cause of that [desire] is the false identification with the composite whole' (<s>sūtra</s> 3) //

children.translated_text: domain — that characterized by the appearance of a woman — exists indeed; nevertheless, for the purpose of abandoning attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the like, relinquishing the status of being the domain of the designations of parts and subsidiary features, the status of being the domain of the contemplation of impurity is adopted [instead] for it — for the purpose of generating dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) — this is the meaning.
He gives an illustration for this very point:
'Just as mixed with poison' —

children.text: na hi viṣamadhunī paramārthato na staḥ api tu vairāgyāya viṣasaṃjñā tatropādīyataityarthaḥ // 3 //
children.translated_text: For it is not the case that poison and honey do not ultimately exist; but the designation of 'poison' is adopted regarding them for the sake of dispassion — this is the meaning. //3//

The cause is [the specific properties] such as having teeth and the like; the objects qualified by those [properties] are the designations (<s>saṃjñā</s>). A lustful man, experiencing the parts (<s>avayavas</s>) — teeth, lips, nose, and the like — of his beloved becomes attached to her. The subsidiary features (<s>vyañjana</s>) are the parts of the composite whole; because of being perceived together with them, there is a resemblance (<s>anuvyañjana</s>) to those [parts], and through that, a superimposition (<s>āropa</s>) [of beauty onto the whole]. And thus is the conduct of those infatuated with women: 'If the beloved — whose splendor is like pure, flowing gold, whose bearing rivals the sport of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the god of love), whose body is languid with the weight of breasts that rival the temples of a great elephant — is not embraced, how shall we endure the agony of the arrows of <s>Madana</s> (Cupid), she who equals the life-giving <s>Siddha</s> herbs?' 'This world, plunging into the river of passion (<s>Madana</s>), delightful with the whirlpool-eddies of the navel on the sandbank of the hips, graced by the lotus of the face, [flowing] with the waves of playful eyebrows — has cast off the fatigue of the fire of long separation.' But the discriminating ones, cultivating the contemplation of impurity (<s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s>), say: 'Filled with marrow, bones, spleen, liver, and excrement, sewn with sinews and veins — women are but sheaths of skin.' The sages too have said: 'Because of [its origin from] a place, a seed, [its need for] sustenance, [its] inertness, and [its] death — the body, being of dependent purity, is known by the wise as impure.' He states the purpose of cultivating the contemplation of impurity: 'Contemplate that [impurity].' 'Then is there no domain for the designations of parts and subsidiary features — does only the domain of the contemplation of impurity exist ultimately?' — to this he says: 'Even though the twofold domain exists indeed' — the twofold
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.4: Because of the twofold [nature] of knowledge and ignorance, there is doubt. //

children.text:
tadevaṃ svamatena prasaṃkhyānopadeśamuktvā parābhimataprasaṃkhyānaṃ nirākarttumupanyasyati /
athedānīmarthaṃ nirākariṣyatā vijñānavādinā 'vayavinirākaraṇamupapādyate /

children.translated_text: The designations of parts and subsidiary features pertain to a particular [external] object.

children.text: tatrārthamātrasyābhāvātkuto 'vayavānuvyañjanasaṃjñe, tannirākaraṇāya prathamamavayavī nirākriyate paścātparamāṇuḥ, tataśca jñānamātramartharahitaṃ siddhaṃ bhavatītyabhiprāyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Since the [external] object as such does not exist at all, how can there be designations of parts and subsidiary features? For the refutation of that, first the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is refuted, then the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>); and then consciousness alone (<s>jñānamātra</s>), devoid of [external] objects, is established — this is the intent.
Since the demonstration [requires] being preceded by doubt, he first states the doubt:
'Because of the twofold [nature] of knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) and ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), there is doubt' (<s>sūtra</s> 4) //

Having thus stated the instruction of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (meditative contemplation) according to his own doctrine, he introduces [the objection] in order to refute the <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> accepted by others: 'Now then, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (consciousness-only advocate), wishing to refute the [external] object, propounds the refutation of the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>).'

children.text:
upalabdhirvidyā anupalabdhiścāvidyā /
saccopalabhyate yathā taḍāge toyam /
asaccopalabhyate yathā marumarīcikāyāmudakam /
sacca nopalabhyate yathā ciranikhātaṃ bhūmau nidhyādi /
asacca nopalabhyate yathā bhūtale dṛśyamāne tattulyopalambhanayogyato ghaṭādiḥ /
tadevaṃ vidyāvidyādvaividhyādavayavini saṃśayaḥ /
yadyavayavyupalabhyate tathāpi saṃśayaḥ
atha nopalabhyate tathā 'pi saṃśaya ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Apprehension is knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), and non-apprehension is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). What exists is apprehended — as water in a pond. What does not exist is also apprehended — as water in a mirage. What exists is also not apprehended — as a treasure long buried in the ground. And what does not exist is also not apprehended — as a pot and the like [which are absent] on a visible ground-surface equally suitable for their perception. Thus, because of the twofold [nature] of knowledge and ignorance, there is doubt regarding the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>). If the composite whole is apprehended, even so there is doubt; and if it is not apprehended, even so there is doubt — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.5: There is no doubt regarding that, because of the prior establishment of the reason. //
There, the <s>Siddhāntin</s>, with the intention 'I shall refute even the forthcoming reason for the refutation of the composite whole,' says:
'There is no doubt regarding that, because of the prior establishment of the reason' (<s>sūtra</s> 5) //

children.text:
avayavinaḥ /
vārtikakārastu svayaṃ saṃśayaṃ nirākaroti /
na vidyāvidyādvaividhyaṃ saṃśayasya kāraṇamiti (502/21)// 4-5 //
children.translated_text: Regarding the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>). The <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, however, himself removes the doubt: 'The twofold [nature] of knowledge and ignorance is not the cause of doubt' — (502/21) //4-5//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.6: If [the reason is] inapplicable because of the impossibility of occurrence, then there is no doubt [either]. //
The prima facie opponent says: 'Because of the impossibility of occurrence' — //6//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.7: Because of the impossibility of the parts (<s>avayavas</s>) inhering in the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) either entirely or partially, there is no composite whole. //

children.text:
vṛkṣastiṣṭhati śākhādiṣu śākhādayo vā vṛkṣa iti laukikīṃ pratipattimanurudhyamāno vikalpayati vārttikakāraḥ /
avayavā avayavinīti /
(503/10) ekadravyaścāvayavaḥ prāpnoti /
kutaḥ ekāvayavivṛttitvāt /
bhavatu ko doṣa ityata āha /
na caikadravyaṃ dravyamavinaśyadādhāramasti /
kṛtakasya nityatvaprasaṅgāditi śeṣaḥ /
avayavyekadeśeneti /
avayavino ya ekadeśāstenāvayavo 'vayavini varttataityarthaḥ /
na hyasyāvayavino 'nye avayaveṣu ekadeśā avayavāḥ santīti
children.translated_text: Accommodating the common understanding — 'the tree stands in the branches and the like' or 'the branches and the like [stand] in the tree' — the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> presents the alternatives: 'The parts in the composite whole' — (503/10) A part that is one substance would follow. Why? Because of inhering in one composite whole. 'Let it be so — what is the fault?' — to this he says: 'And a substance that is one substance does not, without being destroyed, have a substrate.' The remainder is: because of the consequence that what is produced would be eternal. 'By one part of the composite whole' — meaning: the part inheres in the composite whole by that which is one part of the composite whole. For this composite whole has no other parts — i.e., the parts that are in the parts — that are distinct [from those parts themselves].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.8: And because of non-inherence in those [parts], there is no composite whole. //
If [the composite whole] is produced by a single part, the consequence would be perpetual production.
For the activity of the [last] part — which is destined to be the final one — [operates] for the sake of conjunction, and [that activity] requires [certain] conditions as its causes.

children.text: ekadravyasyotpattiṃ prati na saṃyogāpekṣeti yāvadavayavamavayavyutpadyetetyavayavyanavaruddho na kadācidavayavo dṛśyetetyarthaḥ // 7-8 //
children.translated_text: There is no dependence on conjunction for the origination of a single substance — [this means] that as far as each part goes, the whole originates, so a part that is not obstructed by the whole is never perceived — this is the meaning. //7-8//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.9: And because of [its] not subsisting separately from the parts. //

children.text: avayavyatirekeṇa varttamāno 'vayavyupalabhyeta na cāsyādhārāntamupalabhyate dṛśyamānaścāvayavo nādhikaraṇamasyeti bhavataiva vādinā 'bhyupagatamityabhiprāyeṇāha /
children.translated_text: The whole (<s>avayavin</s>) would be perceived as subsisting apart from the whole — but no other substrate of it is perceived, and the perceived part is not its substrate — since this has been conceded by you, the proponent yourself — with this intent he says:
And it would be eternal. //9//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.10: And the whole is not [identical with] the parts. //

children.text: yastu manyate avayavānāṃ dharmamātramavayavī na tvavayavebhyo 'tyantaṃ bhinno 'bhinno vā bhinnatve gavāśvavadvarmadharmibhāvānupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: But one who thinks: the whole is merely a property (<s>dharma</s>) of the parts, not absolutely different from the parts nor non-different — [arguing that] in the case of difference, like a cow and a horse, the relation of property and property-bearer would be untenable;
and in the case of non-difference too, because of the untenability of that [relation] as it would be like the form of the property-bearer [itself];

children.text: tasmātkathaṃ cidbhinno 'bhinnaśca kathaṃ ciddharmamātramavayavānāmamayavīti taṃ pratyāha /
children.translated_text: therefore, somehow different and somehow non-different, the whole is merely a property of the parts — to him he replies:
"And the whole is not [identical with] the parts" (<s>sūtra</s> 10). //

and those are not different [from the parts] — so the whole would amount to a mere aggregate of parts.

children.text: ekasmiṃścāvayave ekadeśe varttamāno 'vayavīti na tāvadavayavī kvacidavayave varttata iti tadekadeśānāṃ tatra tatrāvayave vṛtteḥ tāvanmātreṇa cāvayavino grahaṇamiti yatraivāsyaikadeśo varttate tatraiva grahītavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: And [if] the whole subsists in one part by one portion, then to begin with, the whole does not subsist in any particular part — so because of those portions subsisting in each respective part, and because the whole is grasped only by that much, it should be grasped only where its portion subsists.

children.text: tathā caikasmin tantau paṭaikadeśo varttata iti tantāvekasmin paṭo dṛśyetetyarthaḥ // 10 //
children.translated_text: And thus, since one portion of the cloth subsists in one thread, the cloth is perceived in just one thread — this is the meaning. //10//

To begin with, difference and non-difference, whose natures are the mutual absence [of each other], are not co-inherent in one [thing] — this has been stated. / Nor is the relation of property and property-bearer [possible] in absolute non-difference; therefore, just as in absolute difference too, only some [things] have the relation of cause and effect, so too only some [things] have the relation of property and property-bearer — this is to be accepted. / And thus the refutation [stands] — this is the meaning. / And [if it is said that] the whole subsists in the parts by one portion, [then] the whole would amount to a mere aggregate of parts — / This is the argument: / For that which subsists in the parts is called 'the whole.' / If the portions of the whole subsist in the parts, then [they are] merely portions
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.11: Because of the absence of difference in one [thing], the use of the word 'difference' is untenable — [hence] the question does not arise. //
The <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent of the established view) says:
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.12: Even in the absence of further parts, [the argument about] non-subsistence is not a [valid] reason. //

children.translated_text: That the whole does not subsist in its own parts through portions — for this thesis, 'because of the absence of further parts' is not a [valid] reason. / Why? Because even if the whole has further parts, still, the further parts of the whole subsist in the further parts — so what follows regarding the subsistence of the whole? / And one who is committed to [the thesis that] one [thing] subsists in many is not to be questioned 'is it by wholeness or by portions?' — why? / Because of the contradiction for the one whole being-in-many through both — through wholeness or through portions — [since] oneness of the whole [would be violated]. / Relying on this, he says: 'If the whole subsists neither by a portion nor by wholeness, / then how does it subsist?' / He raises a doubt: 'if [one objects] because of the non-indication of another form' — / (506/7) With ridicule, he gives an example: / 'Just as non-variegated threads produce a variegated cloth.' / For indeed, the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> accept that a variegated cloth is produced by non-variegated threads. / And this is improper. / To begin with, the variegated color is not one [thing] co-inhering in the cloth — because of contradiction with one's own statement. / For 'variegated' means 'many' — so how can it be one? / Therefore, what is said amounts to saying 'the many is one' — [which is] saying 'the variegated is one.' / As they say: '... if the variegated is one, this is even more variegated, great [absurdity].' / Nor is it right [to say] that the many — blue, yellow, and the like — having non-pervading occurrence are the referent of the word 'variegated.' / Because colors have pervading occurrence [in their substrates]. / Those blue, yellow, and the like that are the subject of dispute are [qualities] that must pervade [their substrate], being of the color-class, subsisting in [their] substrate — like the color in a white cloth — thus the ridicule is well-founded: 'just as non-variegated threads produce a variegated cloth.' / He refutes: / 'Not [so], because of being the substrate of perceived color.' / By one saying 'let the color of the whole be indicated' — / [The response is:] something has parts — that is the whole (<s>avayavin</s>); and the part is the cause, or without [parts] is the effect (<s>avayavin</s>) — whence does the acceptance of the cause-effect relation arise? / And an <s>absurd consequence</s> (<s>prasaṅga</s>) is not any kind of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). / As for <s>tarka</s> (hypothetical reasoning), it could be [relevant], but without being accompanied by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, <s>tarka</s> is not capable of establishing a real entity — this is the meaning. / And as for what was ridiculingly presented by you — the cloth's variegated color as an example — the intention therein, whatever it may be, is not relevant, because this example does not [even] appear [valid]. / And an example must be undisputed between the proponent and the opponent — so proving it is pointless. / Nevertheless, accepting the variegation doctrine, we say — with respect to you, we establish that the variegated color is a property of the cloth, for the purpose of refuting the ridicule that pervades your intention — this is the meaning. / The uncontradicted experience 'the cloth has a variegated color' is the <s>pramāṇa</s> here — this is the purport. / The Buddhist reveals his own intention: 'if [you say] the consequence of multiplicity' — / He refutes: / 'Because of the word "variegated" having both singular and plural referents.' / If 'variegated' were said only of the many, then there would be a contradiction; but the word 'variegated' is also used of a single [thing]. / Therefore, there is no contradiction through oneness — this is the meaning. / The adversary says: 'not [so], because [variegated] of a single [thing] is not observed.' / Because the experience of a variegated-grasping [cognition] of a single [thing] has not been observed. / But words, whose usage depends on the speaker's intention — where indeed are they unavailable? — this is the purport. / He resolves: 'not, because of the loss of what is conceded.' / (507/1) To begin with, the word 'variegated' is not a synonym of the word 'many' — [so it] cannot be understood as being in co-referential usage (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with [the word] 'many' in 'the many is variegated.' / Because of the impossibility of co-usage of synonym-words. But the usage 'the many is variegated' is observed. / Therefore, just as 'whites are many,' so 'variegateds are many' — this must be accepted. / And thus, just as for one who does not accept a single white, the acceptance of the multiplicity of whites is lost — in exactly the same way, for one who does not accept a single variegated, the acceptance of the multiplicity of variegateds is lost — this is the meaning. / He raises another doubt: / 'But if [variegated] is many, [then it is] non-variegated.' / He refutes: 'even so.' / He objects: / 'But if non-variegated.' / He resolves: 'and thus nothing whatsoever [exists].' / We accept precisely this: that the variegated color is produced in the whole by the white, green, red, and the like colors co-inhering in the parts as non-inherent causes. / The adversary teaches: 'from the other side' — / 'The other side' means 'the other flank.' / He resolves: / 'This has been said by you yourself.' / Even if a single quality is produced — he objects with this thought: / 'The cognition of variegatedness therein' — / He resolves: 'not applicable.' / Objection: the color of the whole that is produced by the variegated and non-variegated [colors] — that too, like yellow and the like, should be indicated. But it cannot be indicated — therefore it does not exist — to this he says: / 'This much [is enough]' — / Even what is indescribable, being experienced, cannot be denied. / Just as the great difference in the sweetness of sugarcane, raw sugar, and the like — this is the meaning. / It is not proper that the color of the part should be the means of grasping the whole. / For it is not observed that one substance is perceptible through the color of another substance — just as air is not perceptible through the color of earth and the like — this is the meaning. / He concludes the topic: / 'Therefore' — / 'Undifferentiated' means 'unexamined' — this is the meaning. / (508/5) //12//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.13: Like the perception by one afflicted with <s>timira</s> (eye-disease) regarding a mass of hair, so is the perception of that [whole]. //

children.text: NyS_4,2.14: svaviṣayānatikrameṇendriyasya paṭumandabhāvād viṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāvo nāviṣaye pravṛttiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.2.14: Because of the keen and dull states of the sense organ without transgressing its own object-domain, [there is] such a [varying] state of object-apprehension — not engagement with a non-object. //
The prima facie opponent, having taken his stand at [the position that] non-apprehension of everything [proves] the non-establishment of the whole, now says this:

The <s>sūtras</s>, <s>Bhāṣya</s>, and <s>Vārttika</s> on 'like the perception by one afflicted with <s>timira</s> regarding a mass of hair' and the like, for both the prima facie view and the established view, have a transparent meaning. //13-14//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.15: And thus [there is] the consequence of parts-of-parts up to dissolution. //
Moreover, this alternative regarding [the mode of] subsistence
is untenable because of the contradiction [regarding] the substrate — he says:
"And thus the consequence of parts-of-parts up to dissolution" (<s>sūtra</s> 15). //

upalakṣaṇaṃ caitadā pralayāditi /
ā paramāṇorityapi draṣṭavyam /
paramāṇūnāmapyatīndriyatvena darśanaviṣayatvābhāvādanāśrayatā vikalpasya tadavasthaiva /
tadidamuktaṃ niravayavādvā paramāṇuto nivartteteti // 15 // athāpīti /
children.translated_text: Here, three alternatives are possible: / This consequence of the non-existence of the whole — [derived] from the untenability of the alternative regarding the subsistence of the whole in its parts — either ceases at dissolution, or ceases at the atom, or does not cease anywhere. / Therein, relying on the first and second alternatives, this <s>sūtra</s> [is stated]: / Just as the alternative regarding subsistence [applies] in gross [things] like pots and the like, [so it applies] in the parts, and in their parts — so because of its [the whole's] absence, [the regress] would terminate at dissolution. / But at that time, dissolution — being devoid of all designations — cannot be an object of perception, and because of the absence of an object of perception, the alternative [regarding subsistence] has no substrate and thus cannot even sustain itself. / And this 'up to dissolution' is illustrative: / 'Up to the atom' should also be understood. / Because of the atoms too being beyond the senses and hence not being objects of perception, the substratelessness of the alternative remains just the same. / This has been said: 'or it would cease at the partless atom.' //15// 'Moreover' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.16: There is no dissolution, because of the existence of atoms. //
'Moreover' — this is the meaning.
Moreover, having accepted dissolution, this was said: 'up to dissolution.'
But in reality:
"There is no dissolution, because of the existence of atoms" (<s>sūtra</s> 16). //
He states the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for [the atoms'] partlessness:
The partlessness of the atom, however, [is established by this]. //16//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.17: Or, [a limit] beyond the <s>truṭi</s> (smallest particle). //
Now, why is it not the case that this division into parts-and-wholes is infinite? — to this he says:
"Or, [a limit] beyond the <s>truṭi</s>" (<s>sūtra</s> 17). //

children.translated_text: Therefore, even if there is something smaller, it is not the atom qualified by ultimacy — this is the meaning.

children.text: atha bhinnaparimāṇāḥ paramāṇvavayavāstato nyūnaparimāṇā iti yāvat /
children.translated_text: Now, if the parts of the <s>paramāṇu</s> (ultimate atom) have different sizes, then they are of smaller size — this is the meaning.

children.text: tato na paramāṇuḥ pratiṣidhyate paramāṇvavayavā eva paramāṇavaste cānavayavatvādakāryāḥ /
children.translated_text: Then the <s>paramāṇu</s> is not denied — [rather,] the parts of the <s>paramāṇu</s> themselves are the <s>paramāṇus</s>, and they, being partless, are not effects.

children.text: tvayā ca paramāṇvārabdhaṃ kāryaṃ paramāṇuriti kṛtvā āropya vṛttitrikalpena pratiṣidhyata iti // 17 //
children.translated_text: And what you have done is: having attributed the status of '<s>paramāṇu</s>' to the effect produced by <s>paramāṇus</s>, you have denied it through the threefold-subsistence alternative. //17//

A <s>truṭi</s> is a <s>trasareṇu</s> (triple-atom) — this is not a different [meaning]. / 'The dust particle standing in the sunlight [coming through] a lattice-window is known as a <s>trasareṇu</s>.' / If the division of parts does not terminate at the <s>truṭi</s> — at the two-or-three-atom stage — then, because of the non-termination of the division of parts, / because of the innumerability of substances, the <s>truṭi</s>-nature would cease [to be distinctive], / and the <s>truṭi</s> too would be equal in size to Mount <s>Meru</s>. / For indeed, in infinite-partedness, there is no distinction — this is the meaning. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'either up to dissolution, [the alternative] does not cease' — / In the dissolution-atom alternative, the cessation of the alternative [regarding subsistence] does not exist, but the object of perception does not exist [either] — so the alternative has no substrate. / In the case of infinite partedness, because everything is ungraspable by the alternative, the absence of an object of perception [means] the alternative has no substrate — this is the meaning. / The enumeration example: / 'And those atoms, being so many, having combined, attain the state of a <s>truṭi</s>' — (510) / But when [the atom] has parts, the meaning of the word '<s>paramāṇu</s>' (ultimate atom) must be stated: / What is meant by '<s>paramāṇu</s>'? — For <s>paramāṇu</s> is an atom qualified by ultimacy (<s>paramatva</s>), meaning: beyond which there is nothing smaller.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.18: Because of the interpenetration with <s>ākāśa</s> (space), the untenability of that [whole]. //

children.text:
athedānīmānupalambhikastasya vyākhyānaṃ sarvaṃ nāstīti manvānaṃ āha /
ākāśavyatibhedāttasya paramāṇorniravayavasyānupapattiḥ /
sāvayatve tu vṛttivikalpāttadabhāva iti śūnyataiva tattvaṃ bhāvānām /
anāśritopi vikalpo yathā lokapratītikalpanāmātranirmitastāttvikīṃ śūnyatāṃ gamayati /
mithyājñānānāmapi tattvāvagamahetutvadarśanāt /
yathā dūrādvanaspatau hastipratyayapravāho vanaspatitattvapratipatterddetuḥ /
yathā rekhāgavayo vā gavayatvapratipatterityādi bahūtprekṣitavyamiti bhāvaḥ /
tedatadvārttikakārodūṣayati /
ākāśavyatibhedādanityaḥ paramāṇurityabhidhāno vyatiśredārthaṃ praṣṭavya
iti /
children.translated_text: Now, the explanation of the <s>ānupalambhika</s> (one who [argues from] non-apprehension), who thinks 'everything is non-existent,' [is stated]: because of the interpenetration with <s>ākāśa</s> (space), the atom, being partless, is untenable. But if [the atom] has parts, then because of the alternatives regarding its mode of existence (<s>vṛtti</s>), its non-existence [follows] — therefore emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) alone is the reality of entities. Even conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), though without a real basis, being merely fabricated by worldly conventional imagination, leads to the ultimate reality of emptiness — because it is observed that even erroneous cognitions can be causes for apprehending reality. Just as, from a distance, the stream of cognitions [perceiving] an elephant in a tree leads to the apprehension of the reality of the tree; just as a drawn [image of a] <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) [leads to] the cognition of <s>gavaya</s>-hood — and so on, much is to be reflected upon — this is the import. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> refutes that: 'Because of the interpenetration with <s>ākāśa</s>, the atom is non-eternal' — having stated [this objection], one should ask for the purpose of [clarifying] the interpenetration —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.19: Or, the non-omnipresence of <s>ākāśa</s>. //

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.20: Because of the statement of another cause for an effect-substance [existing] both inside and outside, in the absence of the effect, [the cause of that interpenetration] is absent. //

children.text:
(511/4) antarbahiriti vacanaṃ kāryasya kāraṇāntaravacanamiti (512/3) kāraṇāntaraṃ kāraṇaviśeṣaḥ tasya vacanamityarthaḥ /
upetya paramāṇoravayavānna tadvibhāgasyākāśaṃ kāraṇamiti ākāśavyatibhedādityākāśahetukaṃ vyatibhedaṃ vibhāgamāha /
na cākāśaṃ vibhajyamānayordravyāntarayorvibhāgasya kāraṇamapi tu karmetyarthaḥ /
sarvato 'vyavahitasya yasya madhye avayavā na santīti tatsupiramiti /
sarvato 'vyavahitaspaya nirantarasyāvayavinaḥ svāvayavadvāreṇa /

children.translated_text: This is what is being said:

children.text: yasyāvayavāḥ parito nirantaramavasthitā madhye ca na santi tatsuṣiramiti /
children.translated_text: That whose parts are situated on all sides contiguously without gaps, and [whose parts] do not exist in the middle — that is hollow (<s>suṣira</s>).
That which is conjoined with everything that possesses corporeality (<s>mūrtimat</s>) —

children.text: mūrtimatā sarveṇa sambaddhattvaṃ sarvatatvaṃ vadato vārtikakārasyājasaṃyogasyābhyupagamaḥ prauḍhivādatayeti lakṣyate // 19-20 //
children.translated_text: The <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, in saying that being conjoined with everything corporeal is omnipresence (<s>sarvagatva</s>), appears to accept distal conjunction (<s>ajasaṃyoga</s>) as a bold assertion. //19-20//

(511/4) The statement 'inside and outside' is the statement of another cause of the effect — (512/3) 'another cause' means a specific [kind of] cause; its statement — this is the meaning. Having conceded the parts of the atom, [the argument is:] the cause of their separation is not <s>ākāśa</s> — thus 'because of interpenetration with <s>ākāśa</s>' means the separation caused by <s>ākāśa</s>. But <s>ākāśa</s> is not the cause of the separation of two substances being divided — rather, it is action (<s>karma</s>) — this is the meaning. 'Hollow' (<s>suṣira</s>) [means:] that in whose interior there are no parts, being contiguous on all sides without gaps — this is [the meaning of] '<s>suṣira</s>' (hollow). Being contiguous on all sides without gaps, [i.e.,] of a continuous composite whole, through its own parts —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.21: And [<s>ākāśa</s>] is omnipresent, because of universal conjunction and because of [the universal range of] sound. //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.22: Non-rearrangement, non-resistance, and all-pervasiveness are the properties of <s>ākāśa</s>. //

children.text: ākāśaṃ cetsarvagataṃ tato mūrtimatāṃ dravyāṇāṃ tena pratibandhādgaterāvaraṇaṃ vyūhāntarāpādanaṃ ca jalaughasyeva nāvādinā bhavenna cāsti,
children.translated_text: If <s>ākāśa</s> is omnipresent, then, because of the obstruction of corporeal substances by it, there would be an impediment to movement, and a change in arrangement — as when a flood of water [is impeded] by a boat and the like — but this does not [happen].
Therefore [<s>ākāśa</s>] is not omnipresent — to this he says:
'Non-rearrangement, non-resistance, and all-pervasiveness are the properties of <s>ākāśa</s>' (<s>sūtra</s> 22). //
One might say:
therefore its all-pervasiveness is unimpeded — this is the meaning. //22//
Because there is non-rearrangement and non-resistance,
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.23: And because of the tenability of configuration for corporeal [entities], the existence of parts [is established]. //
Again, the <s>Śūnyatāvādin</s> (proponent of emptiness) objects:
'And because of the tenability of configuration for corporeal [entities], the existence of parts' (<s>sūtra</s> 23). //

children.text:
castvarthaḥ siddhāntaṃ nivarttayati /
yadyapi mūrtimatāmiti saṃbandhitvamātreṇopāttaṃ sūtraṃ tathāpi hetupadatayā vārtikakārovyācaṣṭe /
sāvayavāḥ paramāṇavomūrttimattvād ghaṭādivaditi /
(513/19) prayogāntaramāha saṃsthānavattvāditi // 23 //
children.translated_text: The word 'ca' (and) serves the purpose of reversing the <s>siddhānta</s>. Although the <s>sūtra</s> employs [the word 'corporeal'] merely as a correlative, still the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains it as a reason-word: 'atoms have parts, because of being corporeal (<s>mūrtimat</s>), like pots and the like.' (513/19) He states an alternative formulation: 'because of possessing configuration (<s>saṃsthāna</s>).' //23//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.24: And because of the tenability of conjunction. //
He reads another <s>sūtra</s> together with the continued [phrase]:
'And because of the tenability of conjunction' (<s>sūtra</s> 24). //
Thus —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.25: Because of producing an infinite regress, and because of the untenability of an infinite regress, there is no refutation. //

children.translated_text: by this, [they are refuted] as unestablished —
for one who does not accept the pot and the like as a composite whole, the pot and the like do not exist — this is the meaning.
"And the possessive suffix [is seen] in a different sense — therefore [the argument is] contradictory" —
for one who does not wish the activity of the atom to be something different [from the atom], the use of the possessive suffix is contradictory — this is the meaning. //25//

He points out the repetition. "Is this not" — (514/4) He resolves: "not having served its purpose" — <s>mūrti</s> (corporeality) is indeed the sixfold measure (<s>parimāṇa</s>) of a non-pervading substance. Supreme shortness (<s>paramaḥhrasvatva</s>) and atomic size (<s>paramāṇutva</s>) exist only in the supremely subtle substance; but taking the pervading [substance] too, with supreme magnitude (<s>paramamahattva</s>) and supreme length (<s>paramadīrghatva</s>), measure is eightfold. And supreme magnitude and supreme length, being all-pervading, are not <s>mūrti</s>. <s>Mūrti</s> is the measure of a non-all-pervading substance — from the authoritative statement of the sage. Configuration (<s>saṃsthāna</s>) is the conjunction called accumulation (<s>pracaya</s>), which exists in pots and the like, and is the cause of the manifestation of universals such as pot-hood and the like. Conjunction means mere conjunction — not attainment preceded by non-attainment. Therefore, there is no repetition. He refutes this [part of the] <s>Śūnyavāda</s> doctrine: "as for [the argument] 'because of possessing corporeality'" — The <s>Śūnyavādin</s>, with the intention of [things] having dissolution as their end, says: "now, for the time being" — The <s>siddhāntin</s> says: "the end is partless" — the purport is: the [claim of] dissolution-as-end has been refuted below. But from the refutation below, let [the argument of] dissolution-as-end not hold; disjunction-as-end will hold instead — what need for accepting atomic termination? — he raises this doubt: "now, if the end is disjunction" — He refutes: "that is not justified" — meaning: in the absence of the quality-bearer, there is no quality. And these many alternatives are possible. Among them, in the first alternative, there is inconclusiveness and self-contradiction; in the second, the consequence of disjunction having no substratum; in the third, the consequence of the immeasurability of the fragment — he says: "and this much would be the [set of] alternatives." One who says that disjunction terminates in the atom accepts a partless, corporeal atom. But if [division were] infinite, the consequence of immeasurability of the fragment would be self-contradictory. And if [division] terminated in dissolution, the consequence of disjunction having no substratum would be self-contradictory. The meaning of the word 'having parts' (<s>sāvayava</s>) is: having parts of the same class — not only produced from them but also supported by them. A substance like cloth and the like is produced from threads and the like, and also supported by threads and the like. But even so, whence the property of having parts? To this he says: a part (<s>avayava</s>) is the support of that — the support of the effect-substance that is produced from [parts of] the same class. Therefore, the property of having parts is a specific [feature] of effects. Therefore, by one who says excessively "atoms have parts," it has been said that the atom is a specific effect. And "the atom is a specific effect" is self-contradictory. (515/2) But if [division were] infinite, there would be the consequence of immeasurability of the fragment. Indeed, the designation "atom" (<s>paramāṇu</s>) [belongs to] what is postulated as partless, because of its supreme subtlety; therefore what is said by [the designation] "atom"? — "partless and not an effect." And what is said by "having parts"? — "having parts and being an effect." [There is] self-contradiction in the thesis-words — this is the meaning. Now, if you accept that an atom is preceded by a single atom, lest there be immeasurability of the fragment — the rest has a transparent meaning. "If it is stated with reference to two substances" — for the conjunctions of the lateral atoms with the middle atom are such that the conjunction of the middle [atom] with the front atom is not based on the middle-and-rear atom; similarly, the conjunction with the rear atom is not based on the middle-and-front atom. And the same should be seen elsewhere. Thus, all six [conjunctions] are in different locations — so the same-location-ness is not established. Now, if the middle atom is stated with reference to [another] atom related to those atoms, [then] the conjunctions based on it are indeed six — to this he says: "nothing is contradicted." (517/2) It might be said: because the conjunctions are in the same location, the atoms too, being conjoined, are in the same location — and thus the consequence that the aggregate is merely atomic in size — he restates the opponent's argument: "and as for this" — He refutes it: "not so" — wherever something inheres, that is its locus — just as substance is the locus of form and the like. But atoms do not inhere anywhere; rather, their conjunctions [do]. Therefore, let the conjunctions, which have spatial location, be in the same location — but not the atoms, since they have no [inherent] location — this is the meaning. He teaches: "but effect and cause" — just as in "the berry is in the bowl" — just as the berry is in the location of the bowl, so its parts are in the locations of its parts. And it is not the case that inherence alone is the basis for the designation of spatial location — conjunction too [serves that purpose]. For the cognition of the container-contained relation is not differentiated [between] "the berry is in the bowl" and "whiteness is in the cloth." Therefore, because of the observation of the same-location-ness of many substances, the example is not unestablished — this is the meaning. He refutes that: "this is countered by non-acceptance." We deny the same-location-ness of substances in a single [locus] through inherence, but not through conjunction. For same-location-ness through inherence obstructs bulkiness (<s>sthaulya</s>). Just as smell, taste, form, and touch, being in the same location, do not produce bulkiness — for what reason? — because of the inherence in the same location of these non-corporeal [qualities]. But corporeal, tangible [entities], being in different locations through inherence and being mutually conjoined — if they produce bulkiness, what is contradicted? Therefore, same-location-ness through conjunction is not denied; but same-location-ness through inherence is denied — for that obstructs bulkiness — this is established. Having made this concession, it is said: "conjunctions are in the same location." But in ultimate truth, the conjunction of bowl and berry has the bowl and berry as its locus; the conjunction of the parts of the bowl and berry has the parts of the bowl and berry [as its locus] — thus it is established that even conjunctions are in different locations — he says: "and conjunctions too are not" [in the same location]. He concludes: "because of the same-location-ness of the six" — "the statement" — As for what was said: "for that which has a difference of directional parts, unity is not justified" — the atom, as accepted by you, being one, has six directional parts. And there is no difference of directional parts in what is one — therefore there are [in fact] six atoms. He refutes this: "who says this — 'that which has a difference of directional parts'" — direction is one in its own nature and all-pervading — it has no difference — this is the meaning. If direction is one, then whence [arise] the cognitive and verbal differences "this atom is eastern, this is western" and the like? To this he says: "and the directional-part-differences are the conjunctions of direction" — even though direction is one, that [atom] which is conjoined with the location proximate to the place of sunrise — that, relative to the conjunction of another atom with a distant location, is "eastern." Similarly, that which is conjoined with the location proximate to the place of sunset — that, relative to the conjunction of another atom with a distant location, is "western." And relative to those two — the eastern and western atoms — that which has conjunction with a location distant from the sunrise and sunset locations, that is "the middle one." Similarly, the two [atoms] that are related to lateral locations of these [two], established on each side of the middle one, are the "southern" and "northern" atoms. Similarly, proximity to and distance from the sun at midday [determine] the upper and lower [atoms]. And fewness is delimitation by a lesser number; multiplicity is delimitation by a greater number. Therefore, even of a single atom, the conjunctions with other atoms, being non-pervasive, are themselves its parts. Similarly, even of a single direction, the conjunctions are themselves its parts. This simultaneous conjunction of the atom with six [others] is occasioned solely by corporeality (<s>mūrtatva</s>), not by having parts (<s>sāvayavatva</s>) — therefore it cannot establish the property of having parts. By this, the proof by unwanted consequence stated by the opponents — "what is partless is not conjoined with six, like consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>); and the atom [is partless]" — this <s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s> (apprehension of what contradicts the pervader) is refuted, because the pervasion of conjunction with six by having parts is not established, given that [conjunction with six] is occasioned by corporeality. The conjunction of shadow and sunlight with the atom is also explained by the non-pervasive nature of a single conjunction. Objection: but it has been said that there is no infinite regress — how then [is it avoided]? To this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: "in the infinite regress, with respect to each substratum, because of the infinity of the parts of substance." The <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, having considered in every way the reasons such as "because of having activity" and the like, refutes them: "those who [argue] 'because of having activity'" —

children.text: NyS_4,2.26: buddhyā vivecanāttu bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhistantvapakarṣaṇe paṭasadbhāvānupalabdhivattadanupalabdhiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.26: But because of the analysis by cognition, the non-apprehension of the true nature of entities — like the non-apprehension of the existence of cloth upon the removal of threads — [so is] the non-apprehension of that.

children.text:

buddhyā vivecanādbhāvānāṃ yāthātmyopalabdhirityata
āha /

iti (519/17) /
bhavantu paramāṇavo 'navayavāḥ saṃyogebhyastu ṣaḍbhyo buddhyā vivicyamānasya yāthātmyamupalabhyata iti // 26 //
children.translated_text: Let atoms be partless; still, when the atom is analyzed by cognition as separated from its six conjunctions, the true nature is apprehended. //26//

The <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (consciousness-only proponent) says: "that which you, sir, [call] cognitions" — If the cloth were different from the threads, it would be apprehended apart from them, as a cow is apprehended apart from a horse. But it is not so apprehended — therefore the cognition "cloth" is false. The cognition "thread" too is a false cognition, because of non-apprehension as different from fibers. Similarly the cognition "fiber" too. Thus, by this procedure, even in atoms — when analyzed by cognition — because of the non-apprehension of their true nature, there exists no external entity, whether gross or minute. And so all cognitions — grasping their own form, which is non-external, as if external — are false. Now, let cloth and the like have parts; still, because atoms are partless, the apprehension of the true nature of entities through analysis by cognition [is possible] — to this he says: "atoms too, being divided into parts, [are analyzed] until dissolution" — (519/17)
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.27: Because of self-contradiction, [the argument is] not a [valid] reason.

(250/5) pramāṇasyāpi bhāvāt tadgatatvena tadanupapattau sarvabhāvānupapattirityarthaḥ // 27 //
children.translated_text: He refutes this: "because of self-contradiction, not a [valid] reason." That whose true nature is not apprehended when analyzed — that must be analyzed starting from something. Because, in the absence of a terminus (<s>avadhi</s>), that [analysis] is impossible. And thus, one must stop at some terminus. In the case of infinite regress, there would be the consequence of immeasurability of the fragment — as has been said. Therefore, one must stop either at atoms or at their conjunctions. And thus, the entity from which [the analysis] proceeds — that very terminus of the analysis is apprehended in its true nature. Therefore, the self-contradiction [lies in this:] the impossibility of all entities through the [claimed] non-apprehension of the true nature of what is analyzed by cognition — this is established. He states another fault: "the impossibility of all entities" — (250/5) because even the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) is an entity, and being included in that [class of entities], upon its impossibility, there would be the impossibility of all entities — this is the meaning. //27//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.28: Because of being the locus of that [cloth], [there is merely] non-separate apprehension.
"Because of being the locus of that, non-separate apprehension" (sū. 28) //

children.text: tasmāttantubhyo 'nyatrādarśanamapṛthaggrahaṇaṃ tacca bhede 'pi tadāśritatvenopapadyamānaṃ nābhedaṃ gamayitumarhatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the non-separate apprehension is [merely] the non-observation [of cloth] elsewhere than in threads; and that, being consistent even when there is difference — because of being supported by that [threads] — cannot establish non-difference — this is the meaning.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: 'But because of discrimination by the intellect, the separate apprehension of entities [is possible] in the case of atoms that are beyond the senses.'

children.text: yatra khalvavayavāvayavināvaindriyakau tatra pṛthaggrahaṇamavivecakānāmasphuṭataramatīndriyebhyo 'ṇubhya ānumānikebhyaḥ pratyakṣadṛśyānāṃ tadāśritānāmavayavināṃ pṛthaggrhaṇamityatisphuṭamityarthaḥ // 28 //
children.translated_text: Where both the part and the composite whole are perceptible to the senses, there the separate apprehension of them by the undiscerning is [already] very clear; [and] the separate apprehension of composite wholes that are perceptible and dependent on [atoms] — from atoms that are beyond the senses and knowable [only] through inference — is [all the more] exceedingly clear — this is the meaning. //28//

One who says "because of non-separate apprehension" should be asked: is it the absence of a distinct transaction, or the absence of difference, or the non-apprehension in a location other than the threads? Not the first — for threads are cognizable by a cognition of the distinct, but cloth is cognizable by a cognition of the non-distinct. Nor the second —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.29: And because of the cognition of objects through the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). //

children.text:
saṃpratyaindriyake 'pyavayave 'vayavino vivicyamānasya yāthātmyena pṛthaggrahaṇamāha /

children.translated_text: what does not exist — the horn of a hare and the like — and how [it does not exist] — through the [absence of a] cause-effect relation;
all of that is established through the means of valid knowledge, [i.e.,] through apprehension.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> is easy [to understand]. //29//

Now he states the separate apprehension, in their true nature, of the part and composite whole even when the parts are perceptible: 'And because of the cognition of objects through the means of valid knowledge.' What exists — substances that are composite wholes, such as cloth and the like — and how [they exist] — through inherence in their own parts and through being the substrate of qualities;
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.30: By the tenability and untenability of the means of valid knowledge. //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.31: This conviction about means of valid knowledge and objects of valid knowledge is like the conviction about the objects of a dream. //

children.text:
yaduktaṃ pramāṇopapattyanupapattibhyāṃ na sarvabhāvānupapattiriti /

children.translated_text: What was said — that through the tenability and untenability of the means of valid knowledge, the non-tenability of all entities [cannot be established] — to that the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (proponent of consciousness-only) objects:
'This conviction about means of valid knowledge and objects of valid knowledge is like the conviction about the objects of a dream' (<s>sūtra</s> 31). //

children.text: na khalu vāstavaḥ pramāṇaprameyabhāvaḥ kiṃ tvanādivāsanānibandhanakalpanādhīnaḥ /
children.translated_text: Indeed, the relation of means of valid knowledge and objects of valid knowledge is not real, but rather dependent on conceptual construction grounded in beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>).

children.text: yathā hi na svapne santi viṣayā atha ca pratibhānti kalpanāmatreṇa tathā ca sāṃvṛtenāparamārthasatā pramāṇaprameyabhāvena bāhyārthaśūnyatā sidhyati paramārthasatī pratyayānāṃ dṛṣṭā mithyāpratyayānāmapi tattvapratipattihetutetyāveditaṃ purastādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For just as in a dream, objects do not exist and yet they appear through mere conceptual construction — so too, through a conventional [relation] of means of valid knowledge and objects of valid knowledge that is not ultimately real, the emptiness of external objects is established, [this emptiness] being ultimately real. [The point that] even false cognitions have been seen to be causes for apprehending reality in the case of cognitions — this has been previously indicated — this is the meaning.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> explains that:
'Just as in a dream, objects do not exist' — //31//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.32: Or, [this is] like illusion (<s>māyā</s>), the city of the <s>Gandharvas</s>, and a mirage. //

children.text: nanu svapnapratyayānāmastvevandharmakatvaṃ ye punarabhī jāgratyatprayāḥ stambha iti vā kumbha iti vā kimāyātaṃ teṣāmatyantavailakṣaṇyādityata
children.translated_text: Now, granted that dream-cognitions have such a character. But those [cognitions arising] in the waking state — 'this is a pillar' or 'this is a pot' — since they are entirely different in character from those [dream-cognitions], what basis is there [for equating them]? — therefore
he says:
'Illusion, the city of the <s>Gandharvas</s>' — etc.

children.text: jāgratpratyayā apyevaṃvidhāḥ sahasraśo dṛśyante na caite stambhakumbhādipratyayāstato vilakṣaṇā ityarthaḥ // 32 //
children.translated_text: Even waking cognitions of this kind are seen by the thousands — and those [waking illusions] are not different in character from cognitions of pillars, pots, and the like — this is the meaning. //32//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.33: Because of the absence of the reason, [the thesis is] not established. //

'Because of the absence of the reason, not established' (<s>sūtra</s> 33). //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.34: And the conviction about dream-objects is like memory and volition. //
