The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains that:
'As in dream, [there is] the conceit of objects' —
The word 'anta' (end), though meaning 'part,' is used merely by virtue of being situated in [the state]; thus 'in the state of dream' is the meaning.
This is what is being said: one who wishes to establish the veridicality of dream-cognition must state that the waking cognition is its sublator, through the impossibility [of establishing veridicality] by another sublator;
and since that [waking cognition] is not unsound, it is capable of sublating [dream-cognition] — thus the soundness of waking cognition must be accepted.
And thus 'as in the waking state, [there is] perception of objects' — this is untenable.
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: '<s>khyāti</s>' — if it be said [that this is the definition]:
'Cognition-hood itself, along with the dream example, is the reason for the conceit regarding the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) and <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge)' — this is the meaning.
'And in the contrary case, because of the absence of capacity' —
Previously, 'by one who has awakened' was stated as a qualification with that in mind;
now, 'because of non-apprehension' is stated with this in mind — thus there are no two [incompatible] explanations.
Here, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (Buddhist idealist) states the proof for his own position:
'Objects do not exist apart from consciousness, because of being apprehended,
like sensation (<s>vedanā</s>).'
This is the purport:
For the external object that is to be apprehended by consciousness, if it exists as a formless [relation], it would be so either merely by existence, or by being a cause, or by being dependent on the same aggregate, or by being a substrate of the fruit deposited by cognition.
Now, first, it is not the case that one thing is the object of another merely by existence — since mere existence pertains to other objects [as well], all things would be objects of all [cognitions], resulting in universal omniscience.
Nor does mere existence serve even to establish objecthood,
since even non-existents have objecthood.
For this very reason, objecthood is not through being a cause.
Moreover, the sense-organs like the eye too are causes of cognition — so they would absurdly become objects of color-cognition;
and cognition would not illuminate the present —
because, given momentariness, the object-moment that is the producer has perished at the time of the produced cognition.
Through dependence on the same aggregate, however, objecthood would explain the illumination of the present.
But that [account] does not work — because even past and future non-existents are grasped, it over-pervades; and because of over-pervasion also [in this sense], [it would follow that] sense-organ moments etc., being dependent on the same aggregate, would have the unwanted consequence of being <s>ālambana</s> (cognitive support).
If it be said that the <s>ālambana</s> is the substrate of the fruit deposited by cognition — then what is it that cognition produces in the object? Manifestation? But that is not even a property of the object — like whiteness, it would be common to all persons.
Because it is observed that even a property of an object deposited by cognition is uncommon only to one possessing that cognition —
just as the duality that is an object-property, generated by the cognition of comparison, is uncommon only to the person possessing the cognition of comparison.
That is wrong — because of non-pervasion.
Indeed there are thousands of cognitions about past and future objects — born of verbal testimony and inference —
and none of them is capable of depositing a fruit in the object, because of the impossibility of the object at that time.
Indeed there is no possibility — a property whose bearer, unperished and present in form, does not exist — [such a property] does not arise from a bearer that is non-existent and unoriginated.
If it be said that cognition arises from its own cause, endowed with the power of self-and-non-self-illumination, of such a kind that only something specific is its object and not everything:
Well then, since power resides in the capable object, what should be stated as its capable [object]?
If [you say] the object — no.
First, the object is not produced by it — for it is the object itself that produces cognition.
Nor does it deposit a fruit residing in the object — as was stated.
And without a capable object, there is no possibility of power. Therefore, [the claim that] formless cognition has an external referent is mere fantasy.
Let it then be that cognition [which is] with-form has an external referent.
For instance, cognition with the form of blue has blue as its referent;
because blue is its own nature.
Here, one should ask:
Is objecthood due to complete identity of form, or due to some [partial] identity of form?
First, there cannot be complete identity of form between the object, which is of inert nature, and cognition, which is of luminous nature — for in such identity, cognition too would become inert, resulting in the destruction of cognition-hood.
And if [there is only] partial identity of form — where is it absent? Thus all cognition would cognize everything.
Moreover, a cognition arisen from the immediately preceding condition that is a blue-cognition is not so identical in form with the blue object as it is identical in form with the blue-cognition — so by identity of form with and origination from the immediately preceding condition, that [preceding cognition] should be the object — but this is not the case. Therefore, identity of form and [corresponding] origination are not the defining mark of objecthood either.
Let it be [said that] cognition has identity of form and [corresponding] origination through attention (<s>manaskāra</s>), sense-organs, and the like — still, that which it determines (<s>adhyavasyati</s>) is its object, and it determines the object; therefore the object alone is its object, not attention and the like.
But then, what is this determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>)?
First, it is not apprehension — for two forms are not apprehended; the experience is 'blue,' not 'in blue.'
If it be said that determination is the superimposition of one's own form upon the external:
Does that occur upon an apprehended external, or upon an unapprehended one?
For it was stated that two blues are not illuminated.
And one cannot superimpose a superimposandum without apprehending the substrate of superimposition.
For no one superimposes silver on a shining white [shell] that is in front without perceiving it.
Moreover, if the external is unapprehended, there would be no restriction of activity [toward specific objects] —
because all [objects] being equally unapprehended, there would be the unwanted consequence of activity toward all of them.
And on the with-form cognition view, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the existence of externals, because they are unapprehended.
But, it is said, the occasionality of the blue-form and the like is itself the proof.
For if something occurs only sometimes even when [another thing] exists, then it depends on something else.
Just as — even when the staircase exists — cognitions with disconnected spatial arrangement appearances depend on another continuum; similarly, even when the <s>ālaya</s>-continuum exists, all six active (<s>pravṛtti</s>) cognitions [depend on another] — thus [this is] a natural reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>).
If it be said that occasionality [arises] from the ripening of <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) as the condition:
Now, the <s>vāsanā</s> is the capacity of the <s>ālaya</s>-cognitions falling within a single continuum to generate the respective active cognitions; its ripening is the readiness to produce the effect; and its condition is the preceding moment within its own continuum as the cause — because dependence on another continuum is not accepted.
And thus all [moments] falling within the <s>ālaya</s>-continuum would be ripening-causes,
or none at all, because there is no distinction.
If it be said that because of the difference of moments there is a difference of capacities, and because of the occasionality of that, the occasionality of the effect:
Now, one and the same [moment] has both the capacity to generate blue-cognition and the capacity to generate the awakening of [another] capacity — a different moment would not have those.
Or, if it does, how can there be a difference of capacity from a difference of moments?
Thus all [moments] within the <s>ālaya</s>-continuum are capable — and when capable causes exist, the impossibility of the postponement of the effect [follows].
But if [the system] depends only on its own continuum, the always-present-ness [of the effect contradicts] the occasionality that was to be refuted; and through the apprehension of that [occasionality], as the ever-present-ness is overturned, [the argument] settles on dependence on something else — thus the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) is established.
And the active cognitions, being conditioned by another continuum, [should arise also from] other continua — since cognitions of other continua are always present, and being non-spatial in nature, remoteness is untenable, and since nothing separate [from consciousness] is accepted.
Nor is temporal remoteness possible, because the emergence of a previously non-existent entity is not accepted.
Thus this inference belongs to the <s>Sautrāntikas</s>' acceptance of externals.
That is unjustified.
Even when [the cause] is only its own continuum, since the occasionality of blue-cognitions and the like can be explained, the reason [used] is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) due to being of doubtful exclusion.
But it was said: 'momentary difference is not the cause of effect-difference' — the difference of a conceptually posited continuum, devoid of all capacity, is the cause of effect-difference — but [to say] that a real moment is not the cause of effect-difference — who other than the Venerable [Buddhist] would dare say this?
Now, if momentary difference is the cause of capacity-difference, then different moments would not have one capacity; and so, when blue-cognition is generated by some one [moment], that blue-cognition would not arise from other moments —
if different [moments] do not have one capacity.
But for proponents of external objects too — how do different blue-lotus continua have the capacity for a single stream of blue-lotus-form cognitions?
If it be said that it is a different blue-cognition that arises from a different blue-lotus continuum —
we too say: it is a different blue-cognition that arises from a different moment.
Therefore, some such <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>-distinction arises that generates only some particular effect-distinction and not another effect — [this must simply be accepted].
Therefore, even for cognition with form, the object is not a referent.
And what is not a referent cannot be inferred.
And, like perception, inference too does not have an object as referent. Therefore, well said by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>: 'objects do not exist apart from consciousness, because of being apprehended, like sensation.'
For the objects such as blue are established by both parties; the disagreement is about their identity with or difference from consciousness.
Therein, the difference from consciousness accepted by the opponents is being refuted; and all that is refuted [is refuted] through non-apprehension — thus 'because of being apprehended' is a reason [consisting in] the apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory: the difference from consciousness that is to be refuted, its contradictory being non-difference from consciousness, 'apprehendedness' being pervaded by that — its apprehension is itself the non-apprehension of what is to be refuted.
Here, first, this should be said:
Given that apprehendedness is pervaded by non-difference, it would negate difference — but there is no pervasion of this by non-difference.
For what is perceived as blue, gross, and delimited — its delimitedness and grossness are not the nature of cognition,
for grossness means being spread across various directions and places.
And a single, non-spatial, partless cognition cannot possibly pervade various directions and places.
As is said:
'Therefore, the gross appearance belongs neither to the object nor to cognition as its own nature;
being precluded in one, it is impossible in many [as well].'
Similarly, object-delimitedness too is not of the nature of cognition.
If it were so, cognition would be delimited from the ultimate object.
Therefore, this [feature] too is not cognition — and thus must be accepted as non-existent.
But since identity of existent and non-existent is not possible, even what is not the self [of cognition] is illuminated in cognition — [this] must be accepted even by one unwilling.
And thus what is existent too will be illuminated [in cognition].
But if cognition does nothing regarding the non-self object, how can it be the illuminator of the object?
And if cognition does nothing, how can it illuminate grossness?
If [you say] by its own nature — here too the [same objection] is not averted.
For whatever is the own nature of something requires nothing else [to explain it] — like the relation of the inferential mark to its own provable.
And by its own nature, cognition belongs to the object — hence for its belonging, it does not require anything else.
If it be said: how can cognition belong to the object if they are unrelated? — well then, how is a relation [established] between the two relata?
If one posits another relation, there is infinite regress.
Therefore, just as a relation itself [relates] the two relata without another relation,
so too cognition [relates to] the object without another relation — the case is the same.
And there is no over-extension:
a cognition arisen from its own causes has only some specific object and not another.
Own natures do not merit cross-examination: 'be this way,' 'don't be that way,' 'why are you not this way?'
If it be asked: how does a color-cognition that does nothing have color as its object?
Is color-cognition being discussed as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), or as a <s>phala</s> (result)?
If as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then it is not inactive regarding that — for it is the cause of action, acquisition, and indifference.
If as a result — that is unjustified.
Where indeed does a result do something? For the arrival at a city produced by walking does not do anything for the conjunction-inherence between the person and the city.
Similarly, for the natural objecthood of cognition regarding the object, cognition need not produce anything further.
The object-boundedness of cognition is cognition's objecthood — for cognition, when examined by a subsequent reflective cognition (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>), cannot be ascertained without the ascertainment of the object — this was stated.
How can what is not inherent in an action (<s>karman</s>) [be a property] of the action?
If [you say:] because of its dependence on that — what is this dependence?
If [you say:] having its ascertainment dependent on the ascertainment of that — the same applies here too; [the objection arises] from attachment to [a position] elsewhere.
Therefore, since apprehendedness does not pervade non-difference, apprehendedness, being pervaded by the contradictory, does not merit negating difference — and while this major refutation already stands, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states a further refutation: '<s>vedanā</s> is pleasure and pain; <s>citta</s> is cognition.'
He speaks by way of acceptance: 'then if cognition is non-different from sensation' —
(522/1) Just as a fingertip cannot be touched by that very fingertip, so cognition cannot be grasped by that very cognition.
But apprehension (<s>gṛhīti</s>) is not what is to be apprehended — for it does not have the status of an object; what has an effect-producing function (<s>kriyāphala</s>) becomes an object, and this [apprehension] has no further result; rather, being of self-manifest nature, apprehension, whose illumination is not dependent on another, is called the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>).
For if apprehension itself were not self-luminous, objects too would not be illuminated,
since their illumination depends on its illumination.
Thus: whatever has its illumination dependent on the illumination of another is illuminated when that other is illuminated — like the illumination of the staff-bearer (<s>daṇḍin</s>) being dependent on the illumination of the staff; and the object's illumination is dependent on the illumination of cognition — thus [this is] a natural reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>). And it is not the case that nothing other than cognition is observed as self-awareness — mere non-observation does not mean that cognition cannot be self-aware; for it is not through observation and non-observation that a reason is probative, but through invariable concomitance with its own provable — and that [concomitance] is established through the operation of a sublating <s>pramāṇa</s> in the contrary case — thus what need is there of an example? Here,
he says:
'An action (<s>karma</s>) and an activity (<s>kriyā</s>) cannot be one and the same.'
This is the purport:
What indeed is this 'dependence of the illumination of objects on the illumination of awareness'? For awareness's illumination does not generate another illumination in the object.
Moreover, the illumination of the inferential mark's bearer (<s>liṅgin</s>) depends on the illumination of the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) — yet the bearer is not illuminated when the mark is illuminated, but rather when the illumination of the mark has perished.
If it be said that the illumination of the object is not something different from cognition, and cognition's illumination is nothing other [than this] — rather, cognition itself is the self-awareness and [the awareness] of the object — then:
What is achieved by this? For the self is not dependent upon itself.
And it is not established that cognition itself is the illumination of both self and other.
For the illumination of cognition [by subsequent cognition] is mental, while the illumination of the object is sensory.
And the illumination of the object does not depend on the illumination of the <s>pramāṇa</s>-cognition; rather, it depends on the existence of the <s>pramāṇa</s>-cognition — but nothing depends on the result — this is not understood [by the opponent].
Thus it is established — this, which is the subject of debate — cognition — is illuminated as different from its own illumination, because of being illuminated;
like the illumination of one entity by another entity.
By this, the following is also indicated: 'An action and an activity cannot be one and the same.'
By this, [the Buddhist thesis] 'from the invariable co-apprehension, there is non-difference of blue and the cognition of blue' is refuted — it should be understood.
For the co-apprehension of the object, the cognition, and the apprehension simply does not exist — whence, then, its invariability?
But if co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambha</s>) as literally understood is stated as the reason — then it is contradictory, because of the impossibility of 'co-' in non-difference.
And this topic has been elaborated in the <s>Nyāyakaṇikā</s>; here, out of fear of prolixity, it is not elaborated —
thus [the discussion] concludes.
'That too — the observed difference of cognitions — he should state the reason' —
The difference of cognitions — in the form of blue, yellow, etc. — cannot be based merely on the continuum, nor based on the dominance and proximity of another continuum — because cognitions, being non-spatial in nature, cannot have spatial remoteness.
Nor is temporal remoteness [possible] — because the emergence of a previously non-existent entity is not accepted — this is the import.
He raises an objection: 'like dream, the stream of cognitions' —
[The idea is:] even in the absence of externals, there is an internal cause of the differentiation of cognitions — this is the import.
He refutes: 'that too' —
Even dream-cognition is indirectly based on externals — this is the meaning.
Having accepted the non-external-causedness of dream-cognitions, he says:
'Now, even in the dream camp' —
'Camp' means 'side/party.'
And it should not be said that one cognition is the object of reflection while another is the reflector —
because the acceptance of a separate <s>ālambana</s> (cognitive support) is not [admitted by this school] — this is the import.
But having accepted the non-external-causedness of dream-cognitions, this was stated.
That the external-causedness alone is the ultimate [truth] — he says:
'And these dream-cognitions' —
The conclusion is stated.
The word 'api' (even/also) is for supposition: 'In my position, this is supposable —
that all cognitions whatsoever are false' — this is the meaning.
The rest is easy.
'False sleep' —
And the clarity of cognition without an object is inexplicable —
The apprehension of universal, particular, and their bearer is clarity; the apprehension of merely the universal is unclarity; and this, in the absence of an object, is difficult [to explain], because of the impossibility of the generation of that form — this is the meaning.
He raises an objection: 'A stream of cognitions regarding a non-existent object is observed.'
(523/12) In dream, illusion, mirage, and the like, while cognitions continue, let there be the non-causation by the object-sense-organ-mind-defect [conjunction];
but those perceptions of all subjects that possess persistence — cognitions of a pus-filled river — these cannot have an external object, because of having a defect as cause.
Because of the defect-causedness, the persistence [experienced] by many [subjects] would not occur.
But if [caused by] the contact of an undefective sense-organ with an object, then there would be a contradiction with the appearance of water and luster.
Therefore, beginning from beginningless diversity of <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions), diverse-formed cognitions arise and cease independent of objects — thus the current [view] is correct — this is the objection's import.
'There is no river there' — [the opponent] says this with confidence in his own position.
He refutes: 'Not, because of contradiction' — this is the intention.
From the difference of flavor, potency, post-digestive effect, and the like of human blood, and from the observation of flavor, potency, and ripening in the water of the river, when the fullness of the river with water is ascertained, the ascertainment of its fullness with pus by the <s>pretas</s> (hungry ghosts) is false — and in the ascertainment [of this] as false, the persistence of that [cognition] [is due to] the persistence of the defect; and the defect is the very <s>karma</s> that determines the body of a <s>preta</s>.
As stated: 'the <s>pretas</s> are born from the ripening of similar <s>karma</s>.'
'The <s>vāsanā</s> of <s>karma</s> is in one [place], while its fruit is posited in another.'
(524/6) The fruit is children, cattle, food, and the like.
If that is cognition, then in whichever cognitive continuum the <s>karma</s>-<s>vāsanā</s> resides, there the cognition with the form of children and the like is the fruit — thus the co-residence (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) is tenable.
But if the fruit is of the nature of the object — children, cattle, food, and the like — there would be different-residence (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>), and thus over-extension — this is the import.
He refutes: 'Not, because of non-acceptance' —
Children and the like are not in their own form the fruit; rather, the pleasure occasioned by them [is the fruit].
Because that [pleasure] alone is desired by the sentient being, and because fruit is defined by that — this is the import.
Having freely established the thesis, he states the formal arguments:
'From my own cognition' —
If cognition-only (<s>cittamātra</s>) is taken as the thesis, then there would be no example — therefore it is said 'from my own cognition.'
The qualification 'when not being the locus of my egoism' [prevents] deviation through one's own cognition.
And because the reasons serve the purpose of removing superimposition — there is no fault of an unestablished qualificand.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.35: The destruction of false apprehension [occurs] from knowledge of reality, like the destruction of the conviction regarding dream-objects upon awakening. //

children.text:
api ca mityopalabdhīnāṃ bāhyānālambanatvamāsthāya tattvabuddhīnāṃ bāhyānālambanatvaṃ sādhanīyam /
tāsāṃ bāhyānālambanatvaṃ bādhakādhīnaṃ bādhakaṃ cātra samāropitarajatādyabhimānaṃ nivarttayati na tu puro 'vasthitamarthasāmānyaṃ śuklabhāsvaram /
tasmānna bādhakānurodhādapi mithyājñānaṃ bāhyānālambanamiti svapnavaditi dṛṣṭāntaḥ sādhyavikala ityāha /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even from the conformity with the sublator, false cognition is not without an external object — thus the example 'like a dream' is deficient in the property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>) — he says:

children.text: evaṃ sati mithyājñānasya pradhānāśrayatve mithyopalabdhervināśastattvajñānādbādhakāt svapnaviṣayābhimānapraṇāśavat pratiṣedho na sāmānyasyāpīti śeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: This being so, when false cognition has <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) as its substrate, the destruction of false apprehension from the sublating knowledge of reality is like the destruction of the conviction regarding dream-objects — [this] negation [applies] not even to the universal [object] — this is the remainder.
The rest [is found] in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>.
The <s>Bhāṣya</s> is easily understood. //35//

Moreover, having maintained the non-externality of objects for false apprehensions, one should establish the non-externality of objects for veridical cognitions as well. / The non-externality of their objects depends on a sublator (<s>bādhaka</s>), and the sublator here removes the superimposed conviction of [falsely perceived] silver and the like, but not the object-universal that is present before [one] — white and shining.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.36: And of cognition too, similarly, because of the apprehension of the existence of a cause. //

children.text: yastu mādhyamiko mithyābuddhi dṛṣṭāntena bāhyāpahnavaṃ kṛtvavā tenaiva dṛṣṭāntena vijñānābhāvaṃ kṛtvā vicārāsahatvaṃ tattvambhāvānāṃ vyavasthāpayāṃbabhūva taṃ pratyāha /
children.translated_text: But the <s>Mādhyamika</s>, having denied external [objects] through the example of false cognition, or having denied the existence of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) through that very example, undertook to establish that the inability to withstand analysis is the reality of entities — to him he replies:
"And of cognition too, similarly, because of the apprehension of the existence of a cause" (<s>sūtra</s> 36). //

children.text:
arthe hi niṣiddhe bhavedapyetat /
tadvyavasthāpane tadvadevāpratyūhaṃ buddhisadbhāvo 'pi sidhyati /
na caivaṃ vādinaḥ pramāṇamastyasatā ca pramāṇena vicārāsahattvaṃ bhāvānāṃ vyavasthāpayan
ślāghanīyaprajño devānāṃpriya itañ ni ca kalpanāmātrarmita
upāyastattvajñānāya paryāptaḥ /
na ca vanaspatyāditattvajñānasya mithyāhastijñānaṃ nibandhanamapi tu praṇihitamanasa
indriyārthasannikarṣaviśeṣaḥ /
na cāsau mithyājñānasamaye āsīt /
na ca mohābhyāsaḥ samīcīnāya jñānāya kalpate sa hi māhemeva draḍhayatīti sarvamavadātam /
so 'yaṃ mādhyamiko 'nubhūyamānāṃ mithyābuddhiṃ nāpahnotumarhati /
tathā ca mithyābuddhiṃ pratipadyamānena tasyā nimittaṃ vaktavyamityuktam
// 36 //
children.translated_text: For if the [external] object were negated, this might [follow]. / But when its [the object's] existence is established, the existence of cognition too is established in the same unimpeded way. / And one who argues thus has no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), and one who establishes the inability of entities to withstand analysis through a non-existent <s>pramāṇa</s> / is a 'friend of the gods' worthy of praise for his intelligence — this is nothing but a fabrication of imagination, / and is not a sufficient means for knowledge of reality. / And the cognition of a false elephant is not the basis for knowledge of the reality of trees and the like; rather, [the basis is] a special contact between the sense organ and the object by a mind that is attentive. / And that [special contact] did not exist at the time of the false cognition. / And the practice of delusion is not fit to produce correct knowledge — for it only strengthens delusion itself — thus everything is pure [in our position]. / This <s>Mādhyamika</s> cannot deny the experienced false cognition. / And thus, while acknowledging false cognition, he must state its cause — this has been said. //36//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.37: And because of the distinction between <s>tattva</s> (reality) and <s>pradhāna</s> (principal substrate), the tenability of the twofold nature of false cognition. //
"And because of the distinction between <s>tattva</s> and <s>pradhāna</s>, the tenability of the twofold nature of false cognition" (<s>sūtra</s> 37). //

children.text:
mithyābuddhyā svanimittaṃ lakṣyate tena mithyājñānanimittasya dvaividhyamityarthaḥ /
yatra sthāṇau puruṣa iti jñānaṃ bhavati tatra tattvaṃ sthāṇuriti pradhānaṃ puruṣa iti yaḥ pūrvaṃ puruṣo 'bhūdityarthaḥ /
evaṃ tāvadrūpabuddhīḥ pratipādya gandhādibuddhīrapi pratipādayati bhāṣyakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the cognitions of form, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> also explains the cognitions of smell and the like:
And regarding smell and the like, [one says] '<s>prameya</s>' (object of knowledge).
He concludes:
Therefore, this is untenable — this. //37//

By the false cognition, its own cause is indicated — therefore the cause of false cognition is twofold — this is the meaning. / Where the cognition 'this is a person' occurs with respect to a post, therein the <s>tattva</s> (reality) is the post, and the <s>pradhāna</s> (principal [misperceived object]) is the person — meaning: one who was formerly a person — this is the meaning.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.38: Through the practice of a special <s>samādhi</s> (meditative concentration). //

children.text:
doṣanimittānāṃ tattvajñānādahaṅkāranivṛttirityuktam /
atha tattvajñānaṃ kathamutpadyata iti /
(525/9) na tāvadāgamata
upapattito vā tattvajñānamahaṅkāranivṛttiṃ kartu mutsahate /

children.translated_text: Because even for those in whom knowledge has arisen regarding the causes of defects, the continuation of ego-sense and defects persists as before; and direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) is untenable because of the absence of a means [to it]
— thus.
The answering <s>sūtra</s> to this:
"Through the practice of the special <s>samādhi</s> of reality" (<s>sūtra</s> 38). //

It has been said that the cessation of ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) [occurs] from the knowledge of reality, which has defects (<s>doṣa</s>) as its cause. / Now, how does the knowledge of reality arise? / (525/9) To begin with, the knowledge of reality [arising] from scripture / or from reasoning is not capable of producing the cessation of ego-sense.

children.text:
samādhipadaṃ vyācaṣṭe bhāṣyakāraḥ /
sa tu pratyāhṛtasyendriyebhyo manasa iti /
anena vikṣepaṃ nivarttayati /
indriyebhyaḥ pratīpamāhṛtasya manasaḥ kva cit hṛtpuṇḍarīkapradeśe ātmano nijaukasi dhārakeṇa prayatnena dhāryamāṇasyātmanā saṃyogo 'yam /

children.translated_text: Now, that [conjunction] exists [already] in the state of sleep — therefore
it has been said: 'qualified by the desire to know reality.'

And the practice of that [<s>samādhi</s>] is the repeated generation of effort directed toward that [concentration] — from that [practice], qualified by diligence, continuity, and long duration, the cognition of reality arises. //38//

The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains the word '<s>samādhi</s>': / 'That [state] of the mind withdrawn from the sense organs' — / By this he removes distraction. / Of the mind that has been drawn back from the sense organs in the reverse direction — [placed] somewhere in the region of the heart-lotus — the self's own abode — [when it is] held by the effort of the holder, the conjunction of that [mind] with the self — this is that [<s>samādhi</s>].
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.39: Not [so], because of the predominance of sense-objects [which are] not weak. //
He introduces this objection-<s>sūtra</s>: 'what has been said — "since that exists"' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.40: And because of engagement [of the mind] through hunger and the like. //

children.text:
indriyaviṣayairapahṛtamanaso dhāraṇā /
tathā ca tadabhyāsābhāvānna sattvasākṣātkāra
iti sūtrārthaḥ // 39 // 40 //
children.translated_text: The holding [in concentration] of the mind that has been carried away by sense-objects — / and thus, because of the absence of practice of that [holding], there is no direct realization of reality / — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. //39//40//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.41: Because of the connection with the fruit of what was previously done, its [<s>samādhi</s>'s] arising [occurs]. //
He introduces the resolution-<s>sūtra</s>:
Let this be [granted as] the cause of the disturbance and the arising of <s>samādhi</s> —
The <s>sūtra</s>:
"Because of the connection with the fruit of what was previously done, its arising" (<s>sūtra</s> 41). //

children.text:
pūrvakṛtaḥ samādhiḥ tasya phalaṃ saṃskāraḥ
tasyānubandhaḥ sthemā tasmāditi sūtrārthaḥ /
tadvyācaṣṭe bhāṣyakāraḥ /
pūrvakṛta iti /
pravivicyate 'neneti pravivekaḥ prakṛṣṭaḥ saṃskāraḥ sa tvātmadharma
iti /
kasmātpunaradṛśyamānaḥ saṃskāraḥ kalpyataityata
āha /
niṣphale hīti /
prayatnaviśeṣā hi viśarāravo bahavo 'pi parasparamasahabhavanto na tattvasākṣātkārāpaya pāryāptā iti tajjanitāḥ saṃskārāḥ kalpyante teṣāṃ sthemnā sambhavati sambhūyakāritetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The previously performed <s>samādhi</s> — its fruit is the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>); / its connection (<s>anubandha</s>) is its stability — from that — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. / The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> explains that: / 'Previously performed' — / 'Discrimination' (<s>praviveka</s>) is that by which one discriminates — [it means] an excellent impression; and that is a property of the self. / Why then is an unseen impression postulated? — to this / he says: 'for when fruitless' — / For the many diverse special efforts, though mutually non-coexistent, are not sufficient for the direct realization of reality — therefore the impressions generated by them are postulated; through the stability of those [impressions], the collective efficacy becomes possible — this is the meaning.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.42: The instruction for the practice of <s>yoga</s> [is given as being performed] in forests, caves, riverbanks, and the like. //
The culmination of accumulation is the limit of accumulation —
beyond which there is no further accumulation.

children.text: tatsahakāriśālitayā prakṛṣṭāyāṃ samādhibhāvanāyāṃ samādhiprayatnaḥ samādhibhāvanā tasyāmityarthaḥ // 42 //
children.translated_text: Because of being an auxiliary to that [accumulation], in the cultivation of the excellent <s>samādhi</s> — '<s>samādhi</s>-effort' means 'the cultivation of <s>samādhi</s>' — therein [the practice is to be done] — this is the meaning. //42//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.43: In [the case of] liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) too, the same consequence [applies]. //
The prima facie opponent says:
'If [one objects] because of the predominance of sense-objects' —
Indeed, such is the power of external objects that
even without depending on sense organs and the like, [external objects] generate cognition in the self itself — this is the conviction of the prima facie opponent. //43//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.44: Not [so], because [the fruit] does not necessarily arise [simply] from what has been accomplished. //
The <s>siddhānta</s> (established view) <s>sūtra</s>:
"Not [so], because [the fruit] does not necessarily arise [simply] from what has been accomplished" (<s>sūtra</s> 44) — this has been explained.

children.text: na khalu taṇḍulā atyantaṃ phalīkṛtā api piṭharodakadahanasaṃyogapracayamantareṇa pulākā bhavantīti bhāvaḥ // 44 //
children.translated_text: Indeed, rice grains, even though completely husked, do not become porridge without the combination of a pot, water, and fire — this is the purport. //44//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.45: And the absence of that [cognition occurs] in liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). //

<s>NyS</s> 4.2.46: For that purpose, the purification of the self through <s>yama</s> (restraints) and <s>niyama</s> (observances), and through <s>yoga</s> and the means of inner knowledge (<s>adhyātmavidyā</s>). //

children.text:
kiṃ samādhiviśeṣa eva tattvajñānasādhanam /
maivam /
kiṃ tu /
tadarthaṃ yamaniyamābhyāmātmasaṃskāro yogaccādhyātmavidhyupāyaiḥ (sū. 46) samānamāśramiṇāṃ dharmasādhanam /
ahiṃsā satyamasteyaṃ brahmacaryamaparigraha
iti yamaḥ /
niyama iti /
yasyāśramiṇo 'sādhāraṇo dharmopāyaḥ /
yoga iti viṣayeṇa yogaśāstraṃ pātañjalaṃ lakṣayati /
yogācāraḥ ekākitā āhāraviśeṣaḥ
ekatrānavasthānamityādi yatidharmoktam /
ete 'pi tattvajñānakramotpādakrameṇāpamargasādhanamityarthaḥ
// 46 //
children.translated_text: Is the special <s>samādhi</s> alone the means to the knowledge of reality? / Not so. / Rather: / 'For that purpose, the purification of the self through <s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>, and through <s>yoga</s> and the means of inner knowledge' (<s>sūtra</s> 46) — the common means of <s>dharma</s> for all <s>āśramins</s> (those in the stages of life). / Non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>), truthfulness (<s>satya</s>), non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>), celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), non-possessiveness (<s>aparigraha</s>) / — this is <s>yama</s> (restraint). / '<s>Niyama</s>' (observance) — / [means] the particular means of <s>dharma</s> specific to [each] <s>āśramin</s>. / '<s>Yoga</s>' — by the word [<s>yoga</s>], the <s>Pātañjala</s> (of <s>Patañjali</s>) <s>yoga</s> scripture is indicated as the object [of study]. / '<s>Yogic conduct</s>' [means] solitude, special diet, / not remaining in one place — and the like, as stated in the <s>dharma</s> of the renunciant (<s>yati</s>). / These too are means to liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) through the sequence of producing the knowledge of reality — this is the meaning. //46//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.47: Study and practice of [spiritual] knowledge, and dialogue with those learned in it. //

children.text: nanu yadyete tattvajñānotpādakrameṇāpavargopāyaḥ kṛtaṃ tarhyānvīkṣikyetyata āha /
children.translated_text: Objection: if these are the means to liberation through the sequence of producing the knowledge of reality, then what is the use of <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic/philosophy)? — to this he says:
"Study and practice of [spiritual] knowledge, and dialogue with those learned in it" (<s>sūtra</s> 47). //

children.text:
tadvyācaṣṭe tadarthamiti prakṛtam /
ātmavidyā'nvīkṣikī /
abhyāsaḥ satatakriyā tatra prayatna ityarthaḥ /
prayojanamāha prajñāparipākārtham /
paripākastu saṃśayacchedanam /

children.translated_text: Whether the self is distinct from the body and the like
or not — this is the doubt.

children.text: tasya cchedanaṃ lokasya tattvajñānamātmani tadavarodhaḥ adhyavasitaṃ pramāṇena /
children.translated_text: Its resolution [is] the knowledge of reality for the world — its containment in the self — [meaning] what is determined through a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge);
its confirmation through <s>tarka</s> (reasoning). //47//

He explains that: 'for that purpose' — this is the topic under discussion. / '<s>Ātmavidyā</s>' (knowledge of the self) is <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic/philosophy). / 'Practice' (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is constant activity — effort therein — this is the meaning. / He states the purpose: 'for the purpose of the maturation of wisdom.' / And maturation is the resolution of doubt.
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.48: One should approach that [knowledge] together with pupils, teachers, fellow students, and those who are seekers of the excellent good, who are free from envy. //
'Fellow student' (<s>sabrahmacārin</s>) means 'co-learner' (<s>sahādhyāyin</s>).

children.text: guruśiṣyasahādhyāyibhyo 'nyaḥ śāstreṇānuśiṣṭaḥ śiṣṭaśreyorthinaḥ śreyasi mokṣalakṣaṇe śrāddhāḥ /

children.translated_text: From observing their faith in liberation, it is inferred that they have the practice of the means to it from a previous birth.
Therefore, through the force of their impressions from previous births, their intuitive insight (<s>pratibhā</s>) is to be relied upon.
'One should approach' (<s>abhyupeyāt</s>) — having approached face to face, one should learn — together with the teacher and the like — this is the meaning.
'Of ascertained meaning' (<s>nītārtha</s>) means 'having arrived at [its] meaning.' //48//

Other than the teacher, pupil, and co-learner — one who is instructed by the <s>śāstra</s> (scripture); 'seekers of the excellent good' [means] those who have faith in the highest good characterized as liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>).
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.49: Or, even [a discussion] lacking a counter-position, when there is a purpose, for the sake of [that] purpose. //
By that [method], having debated with the teacher and the like, the determination of reality has been stated.

children.text: yadi ca manyeta pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahaḥ pratikūlaḥ parasya gurvādestasmānna vādo 'pyucita
children.translated_text: And if one thinks: the adoption of a thesis and counter-thesis is disagreeable to the other — the teacher and the like — therefore even debate is not proper
— thus.
To that, this <s>sūtra</s> applies:
"Or, even [a discussion] lacking a counter-position, when there is a purpose, for the sake of [that] purpose" (<s>sūtra</s> 49). //
He explains: 'one should approach' — this [verb] continues [from the previous <s>sūtra</s>].

children.text: parato gurvādeḥ prajñāmupāditsamānastattvabubhutsāprakāśanenātmanaḥ śarīrādibhyo bhedaṃ bubhutsaityabhidadhānaḥ svapakṣamanavasthāpayan svadarśanaṃ gurvādikṛtādvicārātpūrvapakṣocchedena siddhāntavyavasthāpanalakṣaṇāt svadarśanaṃ pariśodhayet /
children.translated_text: Wishing to acquire wisdom from the other — the teacher and the like — manifesting one's desire to know reality, stating one's own thesis that the self is distinct from the body and the like, without establishing one's own position [polemically], one should purify one's own view through the examination conducted by the teacher and the like — characterized by the destruction of the prima facie view and the establishment of the <s>siddhānta</s>.

children.text: anyonyapratyanīkāniṃ ca prāvādukānāṃ darśanānyayuktaparityāgena yuktaparigrahaṇena ca pariśodhayediti saṃbadhyate // 49 //
children.translated_text: And one should purify [one's views] regarding the mutually opposed doctrines of debaters — by abandoning what is unjustified and accepting what is justified — this is the connection. //49//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.50: <s>Jalpa</s> (wrangling) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavilling) serve the purpose of protecting the conviction of reality, like a thorn-fence for the protection of a seed-sprout. //

children.text: nanu yatra vādasyaiva daśeyamīdṛśī tattvanirṇaye dattajalāñjalī tarhi jalpavitaṇḍe ityata āha /
children.translated_text: Objection: if the condition of debate (<s>vāda</s>) itself is such [as described] in determining reality, then having dispensed with [debate], what about <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavilling)? — to this he says:
Some, through attachment to their own position, transgress proper reasoning.
In that case:

children.text: tattvādhyavasāyasaṃrakṣaṇārthaṃ jalpavitaṇḍe bījaprarohasaṃrakṣaṇārthaṃ kaṇṭakaśākhāvaraṇavat (sū. 50) iti sūtram /
children.translated_text: "<s>Jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> serve the purpose of protecting the conviction of reality, like a thorn-fence for the protection of a seed-sprout" (<s>sūtra</s> 50) — thus the <s>sūtra</s>.
He explains that: 'for those in whom the knowledge of reality has not yet arisen.' //50//
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.51: Hostile disputation through those two [<s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s>]. //

children.text: na kevalaṃ tadarthaṃ ghaṭamānānāṃ jalpavitaṇḍe api tu vidyānirvedādibhinaśca pareṇāvajñāyamānasya /
children.translated_text: Not only [are <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> useful] for those who are striving for that purpose, but also for one who is scorned by another because of disenchantment with learning and the like.

children.translated_text: Objection: if the conjunction or effort existing in one portion of <s>ātman</s> — how does it initiate an effect in another location where there is no conjunction and no effort? — to this
he says:
'And <s>ātman</s> does not have portions' —
The remaining <s>Vārttika</s> is explained by the commentary on the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. //51//

'Disputation through those two' (<s>sūtra</s> 51) — this is the <s>sūtra</s>. But one who, through the arrogance of pride in false knowledge displayed in his own doctrinal position, or from dispassion toward true knowledge, or from desire for gain, honor, and fame, engages in the disparagement of the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, the other world, and the like before lords and leaders of people, using fallacious reasons — toward him, a debater who sees that a proper refutation does not come to mind, brings him down to <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (caviling), and through those two, engages in the exposition of truth for the protection of knowledge. 'Let there not be, through the confusion of mind of the lords, a subversion of <s>dharma</s> among the people who follow their conduct' — this too is the purpose of <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s>. But the visible [purpose] is not gain, fame, and the like. For the supremely compassionate sage, who acts for the welfare of others, does not teach a means of defaming others for a visible [worldly] purpose. The doubt-<s>vārttika</s>: 'Because of the pervasiveness of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>)' — (525/13) its intended meaning will be stated [later]. He refutes: 'Because it has already been answered' — meaning: by those who refute the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> [position]. The objector reveals his own intent: 'The observation of the movement of one's own limbs' — as long as effort (<s>prayatna</s>) does not arise in the portion of <s>ātman</s> delimited by the hand, there is no action there; and there is no effort there without the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>; and there is no observation by <s>manas</s> without its conjunction with the sense organ; and there is no possibility of the atomic <s>manas</s>, the sense organ, and the hand [being connected] simultaneously. Therefore <s>manas</s> is all-pervasive — this is the intent of the objection. He refutes: 'Because of the simultaneity of the conjunction of body, <s>ātman</s>, and <s>manas</s>, and because the arising of effort and observation is admitted.' Regarding that, because of <s>ātman</s>'s connection with the body, the movement of one's own limbs [is explained]: through the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, which is dependent on the desire to move the hand, effort arises in the form 'I am moving the hand'; and there, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> that possesses effort, action arises in the hand. Although the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> with all limbs is not differentiated, nevertheless, effort of a specific kind, arising from a specific desire, produces action in the hand alone, not elsewhere. The impelling of the eye [occurs] from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> possessing effort [with it]. And although the arising of these two efforts is not simultaneous, nevertheless, because of their extreme subtlety, the temporal difference is not noticed.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Vācaspati Miśra</s>. //

// 1 //
children.translated_text: Now, the categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been enumerated and defined — so what else remains for the sake of which the fifth chapter is commenced? — to this he says: The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: 'Because of the alternatives in counter-argument through similarity and dissimilarity, the <s>jātis</s> (futile rejoinders) are many.' The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states the meaning of that: '<s>Jāti</s>, having been stated in summary' — and so on. (529/1) Although the specific distinctions of <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (grounds of defeat) are appropriate to define immediately after the general definitions of <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> in the first chapter, nevertheless, because of their multiplicity, there should be no delay in the examination of <s>prameyas</s> — and that [examination] was sought by the students. But without the examination of doubt and the like, the examination of <s>prameyas</s> is not possible. Therefore, the sage, in deference to the students, continued the examination first. After that, he continues [with] the remaining specific definitions of <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>. And the examination of <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> was conducted immediately [before this], and <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> are parts of those — so there is a proximate connection — thus everything is clear. He states the general definition that is useful for the specific [definitions]: 'A <s>jāti</s> is namely' — the remainder is: 'employed with the intention of refutation.' He raises an objection to the commencement of the section: 'Because of the prohibition of the use of <s>jāti</s>' — but avoidance arises from general knowledge and does not require specific knowledge — this is the import. He resolves: 'Because the purpose of the commencement has [already] been stated.' He reminds of this very [point] and [adds]: 'And the use [of <s>jāti</s>] is easy by oneself.' When questioners ask 'Which is the <s>jāti</s>?' — the use is easy by oneself. Alternatively: when truth is assailed by one hostile to true knowledge, and the means for its refutation does not become clear in that instant, before the witnesses, [thinking] 'rather than certain defeat, let there at least be some doubt — perhaps somehow the defeat of the opponent [will result]' — with this thought, one employs <s>jāti</s>, scattering [arguments] like dust. For by that, truth is established in the world. Otherwise, the world would proceed on a wrong path. And when one hostile to knowledge is refuted by [mere physical means like] nail-strikes and slaps, the common people do not have the understanding to refute the fallacious reasons raised by him. Therefore, the author of the treatise should not teach nail-strikes and the like — with this intent he says: 'For the purpose of refuting a proper proof' — even a proof that is actually improper — being directed at something other than truth — is called 'proper' because no refutation comes to mind [at that moment]. 'And desire for gain, honor, and fame' — the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is for inclusion. It means: the purpose of protecting truth is well-known; that being the case, this too is additionally included. He introduces in order to refute another view: 'An improper proof' — (503/2) one who has understood that even a proof directed at truth is improper, and at the time of debate, the demonstration of its impropriety does not come to mind. Remembering 'this is improper,' he employs <s>jāti</s> — this is what was said: 'because of not recognizing the defect of the proof.' Alternatively, even knowing [the defect], one employs <s>jāti</s> for the purpose of demonstrating the defect of that proof — by way of <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio): 'if my refutation-semblance is [valid], then your proof-semblance too [would be valid]; if your proof is correct, then mine too would be correct' — by this method of <s>prasaṅga</s>, he refutes the proof — this is the meaning. He criticizes this alternative view: 'But this' — for in the statement of a <s>jāti</s>, [both] neglecting the [proper] respondent and questioning the [person who should] not [be questioned] — these two are grounds of defeat; therefore it is said 'having understood.' But if one does not understand, then why would one employ <s>jāti</s>? — For one who forgets even what was previously practiced merely from looking at an equal [opponent], what can be said of one who brings up a <s>jāti</s> never previously considered? — this is the import. By this, since the alternative of 'having understood' or 'not having understood' is impossible, the use of the five <s>jātis</s> — <s>sādharmyasama</s>, <s>vaidharmyasama</s>, <s>vikalpasama</s>, <s>sādhyasama</s>, and <s>saṃśayasama</s> — when an inconclusive reason is employed, is [hereby] answered. 'The former is the counterpart of the latter' — for a correct proof, the correct answer [is the counterpart]; for an incorrect proof, the incorrect answer [is the counterpart]. 'But it is called <s>sādharmyasama</s> and the like' — and there is no real equality of the <s>sādharmyasama</s> and the like, since in that case, because of the establishment [of the thesis], it would follow that it is not a <s>jāti</s> — therefore he says: 'The use is for the purpose of equalization' — the equality is imagined, not real — this is the meaning. The remainder is: 'in which use similarity alone is equal.' This is what was said: 'the use whose meaning is equalization (<s>sama</s>), whose meaning is <s>sādharmyasama</s>, whose meaning is equalization — should be seen [as such].' Similarly, in the analysis where 'dissimilarity alone is equal,' having stated equality by nature, he states equality by the absence of specific reason: 'or the absence of a specific reason' — Against those who say 'all <s>jātis</s> can be employed in all types of arguments,' he replies: 'The pervasion of all <s>jātis</s>' employment across all arguments' — (531/2) argument (<s>apadeśa</s>) means the statement of reason. And those who think that in '<s>sādharmyasama</s>' and the like, the word '<s>sama</s>' (equal) means that the <s>jāti</s>-proponent and the proof-proponent are of equal status — 'just as the proponent is, so is the respondent; the two are equal by similarity' — to them he replies: 'The equality of proponent and respondent is not the meaning of <s>sama</s>' — the intended <s>jāti</s>-proponent is the respondent. //1//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.2: Because of the tenability of the opposite property of that [reason] in the conclusion through similarity and dissimilarity, [these are] the similarity-based and dissimilarity-based equal [rejoinders]. //

tenaitadupekṣya vārtikakāra
udāharaṇāntaramāha /

children.translated_text: For instance: 'Sound is eternal, because of possessing the property of origination.'
But this is a correct proof, while the rejoinder is a semblance —
When [the argument is] stated through similarity, [the rejoinder is] <s>sādharmyasama</s>; when stated through dissimilarity, [it is] <s>vaidharmyasama</s>.

children.text: evaṃ sādharmyokte vaidharmyasamaḥ vaidharmyokte sādharmyasama iti // 2 //
children.translated_text: Similarly, when [the argument is] stated through similarity, [there can be a] <s>vaidharmyasama</s> [rejoinder]; and when stated through dissimilarity, [there can be a] <s>sādharmyasama</s> [rejoinder]. //2//

By supplying 'refutations' to complete the <s>sūtra</s>, he justifies the masculine gender [of the word]. Otherwise, since <s>jāti</s> is the topic [and is feminine], it would be '<s>sādharmyavaidharmyasame</s>' [in feminine form] by co-referential predication. 'Because of the tenability of the opposite property' means: for the purpose of [showing] the tenability of the opposite of what is to be proved — this is the meaning. The illustration in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>: '<s>ātman</s> possesses action, because of the conjunction of a substance with a quality that is the cause of action.' Indeed, <s>ātman</s> has a quality that is the cause of action — namely effort (<s>prayatna</s>) or the unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>); and a clod of earth also has a quality that is the cause of action — namely, conjunction with a substance possessing the quality of touch and velocity. When thus concluded [by similarity], the opponent counter-argues by similarity itself: '<s>ātman</s> is without action, because of being all-pervasive, like <s>ākāśa</s> (space).' And here, the proof is a semblance and the rejoinder is not a [genuine] <s>jāti</s> — because there is no intrinsic necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) between all-pervasiveness and actionlessness. Therefore, setting this aside, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> gives another example:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.3: Just as a cow is established from cow-ness, so is the establishment of that [property]. //

children.text: kathaṃ punariyaṃ jātiḥ, atha prakaraṇasamodbhāvanaṃ samyaguttarameva kasmānna bhavatītyata āha /
children.translated_text: How is this a <s>jāti</s>? And why is the raising of <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (equivocation-based equal) not a correct answer? — to this he says:
And the answer to these two — <s>sādharmyasama</s> and <s>vaidharmyasama</s> —
'Just as a cow is established from cow-ness, so is the establishment of that' (<s>sūtra</s> 3). //

children.text:
bhavedevaṃ yadyanvayavyatirekamātrāddhetorgamakatvaṃ syāt tato viśeṣagrahaṇābhāvātprakaraṇasamatvaṃ bhavet /
na tvevaṃ bhavati svābhāvikasambandhabhājo gamakatvāt /
svabhāvasaṃbaddhaṃ ca kṛtakatvamanityatvena,
na tvamūrttatvasya nityatvena svābhāvikaḥ sambandhaḥ buddhikarmādau vyabhicārāt /
tasmādgṛhyamāṇaviśeṣatvānna prakaraṇasamaḥ /
yathā gotvādgauḥ sidhyati svābhāvikapratibandhāt /
natu sāsnādisaṃbandhāditi bhāṣyaṃ sāsnādītyatadguṇasaṃvijñano bahuvrīhiḥ /
tena vyabhicāriṇaḥ śṛṅgādayo gṛhyante /
vārttikam ekasyānanvayādekasyāvyāvṛtteḥ /
(532/11) ekasya sattvasya gavā 'nanvayād aśvādau vyabhicārādananvayaḥ /
ekasyaikaśaphatvādervaidharmyasya goṣvevāvyāvṛtteḥ mahiṣādāvapi vyāvṛtterityarthaḥ
// 3 //
children.translated_text: It would be so if the indicative power of the reason were due merely to [observed] co-presence (<s>anvaya</s>) and co-absence (<s>vyatireka</s>) — then, because of the absence of [any] apprehension of specificity, there would be equivocation (<s>prakaraṇasama</s>). But it is not so, because the indicative power belongs to [a reason] that has an intrinsic necessary connection (<s>svābhāvikasambandha</s>). And being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) has an intrinsic connection with impermanence, but incorporeality (<s>amūrtatva</s>) does not have an intrinsic connection with permanence — because of deviation [from the rule] in the case of mental acts (<s>buddhikarma</s>) and the like. Therefore, because of the specificity being apprehended, it is not <s>prakaraṇasama</s>. Just as a cow is established from cow-ness — because of the intrinsic necessary connection. But not from the connection with dewlap and the like — the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [says]. 'Dewlap and the like' — this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound meaning 'that which has those as its [non-essential] qualities.' By that, deviating [properties] such as horns and the like are understood. The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'because of the non-co-presence of one, and the non-exclusion of the other' — (532/11) because of the non-co-presence of one — namely being (<s>sattva</s>) — with cows, [i.e.,] because of deviation [of <s>sattva</s>] in horses and the like, [it is] non-co-presence. And because of the non-exclusion of one — namely single-hoofedness (<s>ekaśaphatva</s>) and the like [representing] dissimilarity — from cows alone, since there is exclusion [of it] from buffaloes and the like too — this is the meaning. //3//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.4: Because of the difference of properties between what is to be proved and the example, and because both would [then] be what is to be proved, [these are] the excess-based, deficiency-based, describable, indescribable, alternative-based, and established-as-proved equal [rejoinders]. //

'Because of the difference in properties between the thesis-subject and the example, and because of [the thesis] being provable by both, the [futile rejoinders] comparable-by-excellence, comparable-by-deficiency, comparable-by-describability, comparable-by-indescribability, and comparable-by-provability are equal [in fault]' (<s>sūtra</s> 4). //

sādhyadṛṣṭāntayordharmavaicitryātsvarūpeṇā sādhyāsādhanatvaprasaṅgajanane varṇyāvarṇyasamau /
sādhyadṛṣṭāntadharmavikalpahetukavarṇyatvanibandhanaṃ tu hetvādyavayavogitvaprasañjanaṃ sādhyasamaḥ /
ata evobhayasādhyattvāditi sādhyatvaṃ hetumāhamādhya samasya sūtrakāraḥ /
bhāṣyakāro 'pi hetvādyavayavasāmarthyayogīti bruvāṇastatprasañjanaṃ sādhyasamaṃ manyate /
tadetadvārttikakṛdāha /
ghaṭā vā 'nitya ityatra ko heturiti /
(533/9) na ca yadi samākhyābhedena viśiṣyamāṇaṃ lakṣaṇapadaṃ bhinnārthaṃ tarhi samākhyāpadānyeva lakṣaṇāni santu kṛtaṃ lakṣaṇapadeneti vācyam /

children.translated_text: Because only those [names] together with the definition-word are capable of indicating the difference in what is defined — //4//

Because of being provable by both — [this is] the comparable-by-provability (<s>sādhyasama</s>). The five <s>jātis</s> (futile rejoinders) have their five definitions indicated by [the phrase] 'because of the difference in properties between the thesis-subject and the example.' And they are mutually distinguished by the names of the <s>jātis</s>. When it is said 'sound is non-eternal, because of being produced, like a pot' — whenever the opponent objects by extension (<s>prasaṅga</s>) thus: 'if, because of similarity with a pot, sound is non-eternal due to being produced, then, by that very similarity with a pot, sound should also possess form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like. And if it does not possess form, then let it not be non-eternal either. And there is no distinguishing reason [to say that] because of being produced, it must be non-eternal but not possess form and the like' — this [objection], arising from the variety of properties between the thesis-subject and the example, when it occasions [an attribution of] excellence (<s>utkarṣa</s>), is the comparable-by-excellence (<s>utkarṣasama</s>). Similarly, that very variety of properties between the thesis-subject and the example, when distinguished by deficiency (<s>apakarṣa</s>), is the definition of comparable-by-deficiency (<s>apakarṣasama</s>). When the variety of properties between the thesis-subject and the example occasions, through its own nature, the [claim of] provability or non-provability of the thesis — [these are] the comparable-by-describability (<s>varṇyasama</s>) and comparable-by-indescribability (<s>avarṇyasama</s>). But the comparable-by-provability (<s>sādhyasama</s>) is the occasioning of the thesis-subject's having [the conjunction of] reason and the other members [of the syllogism], grounded in describability caused by the difference in properties between the thesis-subject and the example. For this very reason, the <s>sūtrakāra</s>, by saying 'because of being provable by both,' [indicates that] provability serves as the reason for the comparable-by-provability. The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> too, saying 'having the conjunction of the capacity of reason and other members,' considers this occasioning to be the comparable-by-provability. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> states this: 'What is the reason in [the argument] "the pot too is non-eternal"?' (533/9) Nor should one say: if the definition-word, being distinguished by the difference in names, has different meanings, then let the names alone be the definitions — what need for the definition-word? —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.5: Because of some similarity, and because [the argument] is established through positive correlation, there is no refutation through dissimilarity. //
The refutation of these six <s>jātis</s>:
'Because of some similarity, and because [the argument] is established through positive correlation, there is no refutation through dissimilarity' (<s>sūtra</s> 5). //

// 5 //
children.translated_text: A property that has a natural connection with the property to be proved in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) — that property is tenable [as a reason]; having become tenable, that property is a proof of the property to be proved and is correlated with the property to be proved. And thus, 'with sound' — meaning: by the connecting statement (<s>upanaya</s>). Now, as for this being [objected to as] an alternative between being produced by disjunction and not produced by disjunction, like the alternative between eternal and non-eternal — to that he says: 'the property of being produced (<s>utpattidharmakatva</s>) has positive and negative concomitance, [but] not so being-produced-by-disjunction (<s>vibhāgajatva</s>).' The meaning is this: the one who gives the reply of comparable-by-alternative (<s>vikalpasama</s>) says: 'just as, given that [sound] possesses origination, the pot is not produced by disjunction — this alternative is established — so too, given that [it] possesses origination, sound too, though produced by disjunction, will be eternal, while the pot will be non-eternal.' In response: the property of being produced is observed in non-eternal things like pots and the like, and is not observed in eternal things like <s>ākāśa</s> and the like, when non-eternality is absent — therefore it is ascertained as invariably connected by nature with non-eternality. But the natural connection of the property of being produced with being-produced-by-disjunction or not-being-produced-by-disjunction has not been grasped, such that some things possessing origination would be produced by disjunction and some not. Therefore, the one who gives the reply of comparable-by-alternative, with excessive insistence, must assert the eternality of sound through being-produced-by-disjunction — and against that the following objection stands: 'the property of being produced has positive and negative concomitance with non-eternality, [but] not so being-produced-by-disjunction with the eternality of sound.' For that [being-produced-by-disjunction] is an uncommon [reason] — this is the meaning. He states the uncommonness: 'For nothing other than sound that is produced from disjunction has been observed to be eternal or of that nature.' (534/1) Now, disjunction produced by disjunction is indeed observed as non-eternal — to this he says: 'with the stated qualification.' Sound is preceded by the disjunction of the cause alone; but the disjunction that is produced by disjunction is preceded by the disjunction of both cause and non-cause — thus it is established that being-preceded-by-the-disjunction-of-the-cause-alone is the uncommon [feature] — this is the meaning. //5//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.6: And because of the attribution of the provable [property to the example], the example is tenable. //

// 7 //
children.translated_text: Having stated the refutation of the six <s>jātis</s>, he states another refutation of the comparable-by-describability, comparable-by-indescribability, and comparable-by-provability: 'And because of the attribution of the provable, the example is tenable' (<s>sūtra</s> 6). He explains that: 'one who says the example is provable.' He presents here the criticism of the proponents of fourteen <s>jātis</s>: 'As for what was said here about the repetition of <s>jātis</s>' — By the difference and non-difference of definitions, there is difference and non-difference of what is defined. If 'this is one definition,' then there are not six <s>jātis</s>; therefore the comparable-by-excellence and the rest are subsumed under the comparable-by-alternative alone — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'There is no repetition.' The five definitions together with their respective defined-terms, [and] together with 'because of being provable by both' — six definitions — and not merely from the difference in what is defined, but also from observation of difference in application. He raises a doubt: 'If, because of the difference in what is defined, there is difference in the <s>jātis</s>, then [there would be] infinity.' He refutes: 'Not, because of non-delimitation' — there is no delimitation of what is defined, because of their infinity. But with the help of definitions, there are twenty-four <s>jātis</s> — this is the meaning. He gives an illustration of difference in what is defined even when there is non-difference in definition: 'Thus, the comparable-by-topic (<s>prakaraṇasama</s>)' — etc. The rest is easy. //7//

children.translated_text: 'Not because of incomplete understanding of the <s>sūtra</s>'s meaning' —

children.text: sūtre nodāharaṇasādharmyaṃ vivakṣitamapi tu yena kena cidvidyamānenāsādhyena sādharmyam /
children.translated_text: In the <s>sūtra</s>, the intended similarity is not with the example, but rather similarity with something existent that is not the provable [property].

children.text: aprāptena vā hetunā sādhamaryamiti na sāmānyalakṣaṇāyoga
children.translated_text: Or [it means:] the provable is [proved] by a reason that has not attained [it] — therefore there is no [defect of having] the general definition —
this is [the conclusion]. //8//

'The comparable-by-attainment-and-non-attainment' — this is the term for what is being defined. The rest is the definition. What is non-existent is to be proved, not what is existent. What has been attained is existent. For what is non-existent, attainment is impossible. Therefore it is not provable. Moreover, that by which something attains something — just as the <s>Gaṅgā</s> has attained the ocean, is united with the ocean, is non-different from the ocean — so too in [the case of] what is non-different: if the provable and the proof are [non-different], there is no relation of provable and proof, because that [relation] is grounded in difference — this too should be considered. The comparable-by-non-attainment is indeed clear. Now, since in the comparable-by-attainment and comparable-by-non-attainment combined, the negation of proof is one [and the same], how are the comparable-by-attainment and comparable-by-non-attainment different? — to this he says: 'The teaching of their distinction is [based] on the intention [of the speaker]' — (535/9). Even though the negation of proof is one, because of the difference in the alternatives 'having attained or not having attained,' the intention is to distinguish — this is the meaning. But when non-distinction is intended, then it is one single reply. Just as, intending the plurality of trees, one uses the plural 'trees' (<s>vṛkṣāḥ</s>), [and] intending the unity of the number-of-that-plurality, one uses the singular 'one forest' (<s>ekaṃ vanam</s>). One who, thinking that the general definition of <s>jāti</s> is 'the counter-argument against the example through similarity or dissimilarity,' teaches [it] — He refutes: 'Because of the absence of the definition of <s>jāti</s>' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.9: Because of the observation of the production of pots and the like, and because of the operation [of the reason] in cases of affliction, there is no refutation. //
