children.translated_text: He resolves:
'Not, [because it is] attributed by the opponent' —
Correctly —

children.text: sādhane jātyuttare datte tasya jātitvamanudbhāvayaṃstattvavādyapi nigṛhyataityarthaḥ // 1 //
children.translated_text: when a <s>jāti</s>-rejoinder is given against a [correct] proof, one who does not demonstrate its <s>jāti</s>-character is defeated even though he is a truth-speaker — this is the meaning. //1//

'Because of the alternatives in counter-argument and non-counter-argument, the grounds of defeat are many, due to variety' — having stated this in summary, now it must be analyzed.
Therein, to those who say 'all this procedure of proof and refutation is merely a mental construct, not real' — he replies: '[these are] the bases of defeat.'
'Defeat resides in these' — hence they are the grounds of defeat — this is the meaning.
Because if [they were] merely conceptual, then since conceptualization is easily available everywhere, the systematization of proof and refutation would not be possible — this is the import.
He clarifies the grounds of defeat by an alternative term:
'Faults' —
To those who say 'a statement that is not a member of proof, and a non-demonstration of defects — these two alone are grounds of defeat, and nothing else is proper' — he replies:
'In general, there are two grounds of defeat.'
When generality is intended, the twenty-two [items] beginning with abandonment of the thesis do not differ [from this two-fold classification] — [the opponent's view that] 'a statement that is not a member of the proof, and a non-demonstration of defects' — is subsumed [under these two] by you [the opponent], and by the sage [it is subsumed] through counter-argument and non-counter-argument — there is no difference.
He examines this: 'of agent, object, and instrument' —
Therein, some explain: 'of the thesis' —
(549/13) Just as the proof, operating with reference to the thesis, [is a fault] of the thesis, so too the refutations, operating with reference to that [thesis], are [faults] of the thesis itself.
Thus they say: 'the refutations' —
For deficiency and the like all operate with reference to the thesis, and are therefore [faults] of the thesis alone — this is the meaning.
He criticizes: 'But this is not correct' —
We do not deny that, because of operating with reference to the thesis, [these faults] pertain to the thesis; but we deny their direct pertaining to [the thesis].
Because the real entity [i.e., the thesis] remains as it is [regardless of the debater's faults].
Similarly, even a proof, when employed where it is incapable, is not itself defective; but where it is capable, it proves [the thesis] indeed. Therefore the fault belongs to the agent alone — he says:
'Therefore, of those who are incapable' —
(550/1) Not only by independence is there defeat of the agent, but also because of being the substratum of counter-argument and non-counter-argument — he says:
'Of counter-argument and non-counter-argument' —
But one might say: the faults of deficiency and the like reside in the statement, not in the person — therefore he says:
'Counter-argument and non-counter-argument' —
The statement is not defective in its own form — because it remains as it is — as was said. Rather, through the person's counter-argument or non-counter-argument, it appears so; therefore, from observing deficiency and the like in the statement, counter-argument and non-counter-argument are inferred in the person, and through that means the person is defeated — but the statement [itself is not defeated]. And to this extent, it is called a thesis-fault.
And there is no rule that the person is defeated only through the medium of the statement — because of the absence of that [medium] in ignorance and the like — therefore he says:
'Some grounds of defeat' —
He raises a doubt: 'the impossibility of the two-fold [classification]' —
Is generality intended, or specificity? If generality is intended, let 'ground of defeat' be the [general term] — since that is without distinction in all [cases], whence the two-fold [classification]? If specificity is intended, the [items] beginning with abandonment of the thesis are many — so the statement of a two-fold [classification] is inappropriate — in both cases — this is the meaning.
He refutes: 'Not, because [the discourse] proceeds from the intention of distinguishing between the general and the specific' —
Even when generality is intended, it was not said that 'ground of defeat' [alone is the term] — because of the consequence of non-distinction from the enumeration.
Therefore, one who formulates the definition, because of the impossibility of that [non-distinction] otherwise, intended the two-fold [classification] by intending the intermediate generality;
but the specific distinctions were elaborated as abandonment of the thesis and the like with the intention of [showing] their extension — this is the meaning.
But the infinity of the intra-group specific distinctions — he says:
'Because of being merely illustrative' —
The specific distinctions delimited by the number twenty-two are merely illustrative.
But with the intention of [showing] the intra-group specific distinctions, there would be infinity — this is the meaning.
He paraphrases the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and raises an objection: 'generally, thesis' —
He resolves: 'through the medium of faults in action and statement' —
(551/1) When it would have sufficed to say 'through the medium of faults in statement,' the mention of 'faults in action' is for the purpose of illustration.
But one might say that the attribution [of the fault] to a substratum is also inappropriate, because [the fault] resides in the person — therefore he says:
'And there is no relation of container and contained' —
He paraphrases another <s>Bhāṣya</s> [passage] and raises an objection: 'of the truth-speaker and the non-truth-speaker' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.2: Acceptance of a property of the counter-example for one's own example is abandonment of the thesis. //
But the definition [is as follows] —
The concession of the property of the counter-example in one's own example [constitutes] the abandonment of one's thesis (sūtra 2). //

children.translated_text: "Therefore, because the perceptibility, being present in both the eternal and non-eternal theses, deviates, and because of employing what is not a component of proof, the defeat [results] — not from the concession of the counter-thesis's property."
He refutes:
"Not so, because of the conflict — the tenability of that [thesis-abandonment comes] from the resolution of the inconclusiveness-fault."

children.text: yadā hi sāṃkhyapakṣāvalambanena śabdanityatvamabhyupa iti tadā pratijñāhāniḥ na viruddho heturnāpyanaikāntiko vipakṣābhāvāt kevalaṃ pratijñātārthahānamevāsya parājayasthānaṃ, vipratipatteḥ svasādhyaviruddhapratipatteriti sarvamavadātam // 2 //
children.translated_text:
For when [the proponent], relying on the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position, accepts the eternality of sound, then [what occurs is] the abandonment of the thesis — not a contradictory reason, nor an inconclusive [reason], because of the absence of the counter-thesis. The ground of his defeat is solely the abandonment of the asserted thesis-object,
because of the conflict — the cognition that contradicts one's own provable — thus everything is clear. //2//

He first explains this <s>sūtra</s> according to the view of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>: "When one concedes in one's own example the property of the counter-example."
Having presented this explanation of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> criticizes it:
"But this we do not understand — how is the thesis abandoned here?"
When the proof is formulated — "sound is non-eternal, because of being perceptible to the senses (aindriyakatva), like a pot" — and the opponent raises the inconclusiveness generally, the proponent, having fallen to the third position, says:
"Let it then be the case that the universal, like pot and the like, is eternal."
When this is so, being perceptible to the senses would not be inconclusive, because it pervades only non-eternal [things]; [and this is so] because, by accepting the eternality of pot and the like as well — this is the intention. Although this is so, nevertheless, without directly stating the fault of inconclusiveness in so many words, [the proponent] accepts eternality in his own example, and because of accepting eternality, the fault in the example becomes unestablishedness due to the absence of the provable — this is the meaning.
This [situation involves] either an example-fault or a reason-fault — either contradictoriness through the acceptance of eternality even of pots and the like, [since] the reason of perceptibility being pervaded by eternality which contradicts the provable non-eternality — [hence] the defeat of the proponent [is the issue], not the abandonment of the thesis.
For he has not abandoned his thesis "let sound be eternal"; rather, he has said "let pot too be eternal."
If it is said that the abandonment of the thesis [is called so] because of the non-establishment of the asserted meaning through the abandonment of the example — then every fault would be an abandonment of the thesis, since from every fault the abandonment of the thesis follows.
Therefore, since the abandonment of the thesis through abandoning the example is only figurative, and since that [abandonment of the example] cannot exist without its principal — the abandonment of the thesis proper — he says:
"And abandoning the example" —
(552/3) Having thus criticized the explanation of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>, intending to explain according to his own view, he asks:
"How then?" —
A <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) is what is seen and established at the end in the conclusion — hence [it is called] example.
Example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) and counter-example (<s>pratidṛṣṭānta</s>) are called thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) and counter-thesis (<s>pratipakṣa</s>).
This means the following:
One concedes in one's own thesis — [i.e.,] in sound — the property of the counter-thesis, i.e., the property of the counter-thesis (<s>pratipakṣa</s>), namely the universal, which is eternality.
He gives an illustration:
"For example, 'sound is non-eternal, because of being perceptible to the senses'" —
The second-thesis proponent — who, when the [objector] has counter-argued generally with inconclusiveness — [the proponent,] standing in the third position, [says]: "if the universal is perceptible and eternal, let sound too be so."
[This constitutes] the abandonment of the thesis.
And here, "counter-argued with inconclusiveness" is merely illustrative — the essential point is that whoever, by whatever means, seeing the non-accomplishment of his own asserted thesis, abandons the thesis-object, incurs the abandonment of the thesis.
As for what is also said — having himself cited pot as non-eternal and perceptible, and seeing the perceptibility of the pot, how could anyone who is not insane,
merely from seeing the perceptibility of the eternal universal, accept the eternality of sound? Rather, from observing [perceptibility] in both, he would be in doubt. In response to that: even [motivated by] reliance on the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine that "everything is eternal," the engagement in extracting the inconclusiveness is possible even for a discerning person who sees the accomplishment of his own thesis.
And extreme discernment should not be required here,
because of the impossibility of such a [person] being a subject of defeat.
Therefore, just as inquiry has no place with respect to a dull-witted [person], so too there is no place for defeat with respect to one who is truly authoritative — [rather,] the middling person is the subject of defeat.
And such lapses are indeed possible for him.
He raises the doubt:
"If [one says] because of the method of reductio (<s>prasaṅga</s>)" —
He refutes: "And that is not so, for that very reason, because of the obtaining of that."
One who wishes to point out a reason-fault, while [temporarily] adopting [the opponent's position] through reductio, does accept [it] — for without accepting the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine, one cannot extract the inconclusiveness — this is the import.
With this, he presents the opposing view, which is largely refuted, in order to refute it directly:
"Others [say that] because the purpose is served by the reason-fault characterized as inconclusiveness, the abandonment of the thesis is not a ground for defeat." (553/1) As <s>Kīrti</s> says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.3: When the asserted thesis-object is negated, because of the distinction of properties, the specification directed at that object is a shifted thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>). //

aindriyakatvād ghaṭavadityetāvavaduktvā nirākāṅkṣo vādī na tvasarvagatatve satīti sādhanaṃ viśeṣitavān na cāviśiṣṭaṃ sādhanamatrārthe 'samarthaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ tu samarthaṃ tasya sāmarthyamaparijñāyāviśiṣṭe tadāropyāviśiṣṭasādhanaṃ prayuktavān /

yadi tu vādinyaparyavasitavāda eva madhye prativādinā hetoranaikāntikatve udbhāvite tamevahetumasarvagatatve satīti viśeṣṭuṃ mīmāṃsake prati śabdasyāsarvagatatvaṃ pratijātīte /
asarvagataḥ śabda iti pratijñāya ca na hetuṃ bravīti tadānaikāntikatvoddhārāya pratijñāntarakaraṇānnānaikāntikatvena parājīyate api tu pratijñāntarādeva, na hi pratijñā pratijñāntaraṃ sādhayitumarhatīti /

tena pratijñā yatrārthe samārthā tadaparijñānātpañcāvayavasādhye ca sāmarthyāropaṇādaparijñānāditi śliṣṭanirddeśaḥ prasajyapratiṣedhaparyudāsau vivakṣitau tenājñānādviparītajñānācca pratijñāntaraṃ nigrahasthānamiti /
yatpunarucyate paraiḥ atyantāsambaddhametad yatpratijñā pratijñāsādhanāyeti yo hi prāk pratijñāmuktvā hetūdāharaṇādikaṃ vaktuṃ jānāti sa kathaṃ cidanukramaṃ sādhanasya jānātyeva jānan kathamavi kalāntaḥkaraṇaḥ pratijñāmeva pratijñānasādhanāyopādadīteti /
tatra brūmaḥ

nāyaṃ pratijñayā pratijñā sādhanīyeti buddhyā pravṛttaḥ kiṃ tvasarvagatatvaṃ śabdasya mīmāṃsakaṃ prati sādhayitvā tenaindriyakatvaṃ viśiṣyānaikāntikatvamuddharaṇīyamiti manorathena pravṛttaḥ pratijñāṃ kṛtavān asarvagataḥ śabda iti /
children.translated_text: This [proponent] has not proceeded with the intention "I must prove a thesis by a thesis"; rather, having proceeded with the aspiration "I should prove the non-all-pervasiveness of sound to the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>, and then qualify perceptibility with that, and [thereby] extract the inconclusiveness" — he has made the thesis "sound is non-all-pervading."

children.text: athāsya prativādyavaṣṭambhātpariṣaddarśanādvā stambhitatve sādhanāpratibhanayā tūṣṇīṃ bhavataḥ prekṣāvato 'pi pratijñāntaraṃ bhavati nigrahasthānam /
children.translated_text: But when, because of the opponent's pressure or from seeing the [reaction of the] assembly, he becomes paralyzed and, due to failure of [further] proof to come to mind, remains silent — even for a discerning person, the shifted thesis becomes a ground for defeat.
And this defeat of one whose inner faculty is impaired has been acknowledged even by you,

children.text: eva tadabhyupagamyāpratibhayā tūṣṇīṃbhāvāditi vadadbhiḥ so 'yamīdṛśo 'satpralāpo bhavadbhiḥ śāstre nibandhanīyona tvasmābhiriti vyaktamiyaṃ rājakulasthitiriti sarvaṃ caturasam // 3 //
children.translated_text: who say "because of remaining silent from failure of [proof to come to] mind, having conceded that" — this kind of nonsensical talk is to be inscribed in the treatise by you, not by us — "clearly, this is the way of the royal court" — everything is well-turned. //3//

He explains this: "The thesis asserted by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> against the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> is 'sound is non-eternal'; the proof for it is 'because of being perceptible to the senses, like a pot.' When [the proof] has been stated thus, the negation is made by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> through a counter-example — the deviation of the reason — he says: 'The universal is perceptible and eternal.'
When that negation has been made by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>, 'because of the distinction of properties, the specification directed at that' — until this much is uttered, it is only half-stated. Having cited 'because of the distinction of properties,' he explains:
Of the example and counter-example — of the pot and the universal — the common property (<s>sādharmya</s>) is perceptibility; and when that [property] is shared, because of the difference of their [other] properties — the universal is perceptible and all-pervading, but the pot is perceptible and not all-pervading — because of the distinction of properties, the specification directed at that object, i.e., for the purpose of establishing the asserted thesis-object, is to demonstrate to the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> the non-all-pervasiveness of sound — for indeed, the non-all-pervasiveness of sound is unestablished for them.
He states the form of the specification preceded by a question: 'How?'
'Just as the pot is non-all-pervading and non-eternal' — so too sound is non-all-pervading and non-eternal.
For this statement — like the thesis-statement 'sound is non-eternal' — 'sound is non-all-pervading' [made] as a specification to the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> who holds the contrary view — is [merely] a specification, not [having] the characteristic of a reason like 'because of being produced' nor the characteristic of an example-similarity — it is a statement of what is to be proved. But because it possesses the characteristic of a thesis, it is indeed a shifted thesis. Even though in his mind he intends: 'having proved non-all-pervasiveness, I shall qualify the reason "perceptibility" with "when non-all-pervasive"' — nevertheless, he has not done this; rather, having merely said 'sound is non-all-pervading, like a pot,' he has stopped. And in inference-for-others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>), the merits and faults of the statement are examined, not the object independent of the statement. This he states:
'"Sound is non-all-pervading" — the second thesis, devoid of reason.'
He states its ground-of-defeat status preceded by a question: 'How then?'
'Purposeless — without utility, because of the non-establishment of the desired object.'
The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'therein, the first thesis is "sound is non-eternal."'
It is to be connected [thus]: when, with respect to this [thesis], the proponent is blocked by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>'s pointing out the inconclusiveness of the reason through the universal being perceptible [and eternal], the proponent makes a shifted thesis — 'sound is non-all-pervading and non-eternal' — for the purpose of establishing the former thesis.
He asks: 'How?' —
Answer:
'Because of the non-comprehension of the capacity of the proof.'
Having said just this much — 'sound is non-eternal, because of perceptibility, like a pot' — the proponent is without remainder [i.e., his proof is complete]; he has not qualified the proof with 'when non-all-pervading.' And the unqualified proof is incapable of [establishing] this object, whereas the qualified [proof] is capable — not comprehending its capacity, he has attributed [capacity] to the unqualified [proof] and employed the unqualified proof.
In that case, the proponent, being without remainder, is defeated because of the very employment of the deviating reason — not because of the employment of a shifted thesis.
But if the proponent, being one whose discourse is not concluded, when the opponent raises the inconclusiveness of the reason in the middle [of the debate], formulates the thesis against the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> that sound is non-all-pervading, in order to qualify that very reason with 'when non-all-pervading' —
and having made the thesis 'sound is non-all-pervading,' does not state a reason for it — then he is defeated not by inconclusiveness but by the shifted thesis itself; for a thesis cannot prove another thesis.
This [proponent] is defeated through the non-comprehension that a mere thesis is not a prover, or through the comprehension that what is in fact a non-prover is a prover.
This he states: 'And a thesis does not prove another thesis.'
Therefore, the thesis — 'because of the non-comprehension of the object in which it is capable, and because of the attribution of capacity to [the thesis in establishing] a five-membered provable' — [these words] 'because of non-comprehension' form a condensed expression, with both the force of simple negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>) and exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) intended. Thus, the shifted thesis is a ground for defeat both from ignorance and from erroneous knowledge.
As for what is said by others — 'This is entirely irrelevant, that a thesis [should serve] for proving a thesis' — for one who, having first stated a thesis, knows how to state reason, example, and the like, certainly knows the order of proof; and knowing it, how would one who is not confused in mind employ a thesis itself for proving a thesis? —
To that we say:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.4: The contradiction between the thesis and the reason is the contradiction of the thesis. //

children.translated_text: Nor is it the case that the <s>sūtrakāra</s>'s preference for brevity is rigid everywhere —
thus it has been said.
Therefore, everything is satisfactory. //4//

Here, 'of the thesis and the reason' is intended as merely indicative of the two counter-parts. By that, the example and the like too should be understood as counter-parts. What this means is: the mutual contradiction (<s>vyāghāta</s>) of the meanings of the words occurring in the statement that is perceived, together with another means of valid knowledge as the basis of the contradiction — that contradiction is the ground of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) called [contradiction]; because the mention of 'thesis' is also indicative even for [contradiction] established in the thesis-subject. Nor is this a case of the 'jar-painting' maxim (<s>bhāṇḍālekhyanyāya</s>); for that [maxim applies] when the aggregate is comprehended by a part that is non-pervasive, not when comprehended by what is pervasive. And what is pervasive is 'without a constituent part' — the contradiction of these two counterparts, each designated by 'this.' Therefore, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> first explains the <s>sūtra</s> according to its literal meaning: 'Where the thesis is contradicted by the reason.' When two [elements] are in contradiction, that which has the support of another means of valid knowledge — by that, the other is sublated; therefore it is said 'by that, that is contradicted.' He illustrates [the case] where the reason is contradicted by the thesis: 'For instance, substance is different from quality, because of the non-apprehension through difference.' For here, by [the phrase] 'because of the non-apprehension through difference,' the negation of apprehension indicates the absence of what is to be apprehended. Thus, the meaning of the reason becomes: 'substance is different from quality, because of non-difference.' This contradiction between the thesis and the meaning of the reason exists — as between the words 'is' and 'is not' — without depending on the recollection of pervasion. And such is not the case between eternality and being-produced in [the case of] sound, such that being-produced would be a fallacious reason called 'contradictory' (<s>viruddha</s>). For there, contradiction is perceived only through depending on the recollection of the pervasion of being-produced with non-eternality — but this [present case] is not so, because of the contradiction of the very natures [of 'is' and 'is not'], like the [contradiction of] 'exists' and 'does not exist.' And even though this reason is also unestablished, nevertheless, its non-establishment is to be understood by recourse to another sublating means of valid knowledge, while the contradiction with the thesis is understood immediately from the mere utterance itself. Therefore, by this very defect, [subsequent] non-establishment is posterior [in logical order] and does not serve as a [separate] ground of refutation — like fire after [something has already been] reduced to ashes. And since the ground of defeat is established merely by the contradiction of thesis and reason, the greater strength of the thesis is established merely by [its having] the nature of a friendly [proposition, i.e., one's own accepted view]. And the greater strength of the thesis here [derives] from the support of another means of valid knowledge. For indeed, through visual and tactile perception, from the coordinated apprehension of a single object, substance as different from qualities like form and the like is established — and thus the thesis supported by that [perception] sublates the meaning of the reason. 'By this very' — definition. 'A female ascetic (<s>śramaṇā</s>) is pregnant' — a female ascetic is a celibate; she cannot possibly be with child, for celibacy is the restraint of the sexual organ by one who has conquered the senses. Nor is [the objector] defeated merely by stating the thesis, which is not a member of proof — [for that would be] sufficient without raising the contradiction; in [an act of] refutation whose function has [already] been accomplished, the statement of a refutation that says nothing specific would transgress the method of refutation — this is correct. Because the thesis's being a member of proof has already been shown in the first chapter itself. The contradiction of the reason too [occurs] where the thesis is sublated by a reason supported by another means of valid knowledge. For instance: the thesis 'everything is separate' — meaning 'nothing is one.' The reason: 'because of the use of collective terms in an assemblage' — meaning: because of the use [of words like] pot and the like in a single collection. The statement 'there is no one [thing]' and 'there is one collection' are mutually contradictory without any recollection of pervasion. Nor should one say that for the proponent of the non-existence of everything, there is no collection either — because of the impossibility of establishing the provable in the absence of a reason. And [the principle that] a contrived reason is not a member of proof has been explained in the respective [contexts]. And here, because of the support by means of valid knowledge for the [existence of the] single collection, the thesis 'nothing whatsoever is one' is sublated by the reason. By this same definition, the contradiction of the example with the thesis should also be stated. For instance: 'sound is eternal, because of being an object of knowledge; whatever is an object of knowledge is eternal, like <s>ākāśa</s> (space)' — this is the similarity-based example. Although here the reason is actually inconclusive, nevertheless, [the debater] is defeated by the very contradiction of the example with the thesis — because the contradiction in the statement is understood first. [To see] the inconclusiveness, one would have to infer non-eternal things like pots and the like [as counter-examples] — and the understanding of inconclusiveness is subsequent to that. And the contradiction of the reason with the example and the like should be stated by connecting [the principle] with this. For instance: 'sound is eternal, because of being perceivable by the senses, like a non-perceivable dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>).' Here too, the contradiction of 'perceivable by the senses' and 'non-perceivable' is perceived from the words [themselves]; but the deficiency of the proof [is perceived only] by examining the nature of things — this is the distinction. Similarly, contradiction through the application (<s>upanaya</s>): 'and sound is non-perceivable by the senses.' Here too, by examining the nature of things, the non-establishment of non-perceivability is perceived; but from the words [themselves], [only] the contradiction [is perceived]. And the contradiction with a means of valid knowledge should be stated for both the thesis and the reason. (554/1) Although [the case of] a sublated object is included within [other] fallacious reasons, nevertheless, it exists here too — so let there be inclusion of [both] the contradiction and the fallacious reason in these grounds of defeat; there is no purposelessness from inclusion in some [common] domain, because of the purposefulness [arising] from the absence of inclusion in other domains. And the difference in domain has been shown immediately [above]. Thus, having stated 'contradiction' as the ground of defeat for the proof-proponent, he states that the ground of defeat for the respondent too is comprehended by this same [definition]: 'by what is established in the opponent's position, like cow-ness for the proponent of cow-ness.' For when a Buddhist proves against a <s>Prābhākara</s>: 'sound is non-eternal, because of being audible' — and the <s>Prābhākara</s>, intending to raise [the objection of] inconclusiveness, says: 'if non-eternality were not [the case], audibility would not be [the case either]' — then his raising of inconclusiveness [involves the claim that] 'the audible, [i.e.,] sound-ness, is eternal' — and that is contradicted by his own [acceptance of] sound-ness [as non-eternal]. That which is established in the opponent's position, such as cow-ness and the like, should be seen as [applying] in precisely such a domain of contradiction. And a proof that contradicts the accepted doctrine (<s>siddhānta</s>) is [called] contradicted — he says: 'And independent of one's own position.' Now, if even raising inconclusiveness is contradicted, then what is the domain of [the legitimate] establishment of inconclusiveness? — to this he says: 'But what is accepted by both parties.' He teaches: 'the semblances of examples.' For the example is a member [of the syllogism] different from the thesis, reason, and the like; therefore, by the statement of 'fallacious reason,' that [example-semblance] is comprehended. But indirectly, since the semblance of an example vitiates the reason, everything [in the fallacious example] vitiates the reason — this is the import. He resolves: 'Because [it is] preceded by the fallacious reason.' Here, the word 'reason' in 'fallacious reason,' without abandoning its own meaning, also indicates the example. The reason is stated as indicative [of all members]: because [the example-semblance is] preceded by the fallacious reason, because it has the fallacious reason as its principal — since even through the semblance of an example, it is the reason itself that is vitiated. Nor does this [extension] lead to the consequence of indicating defects of the thesis and the like [through the same term]. For it is not the case that wherever there is a ground [for indication], everything is to be indicated; rather, only when something is being indicated must a ground necessarily be stated.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.5: When the thesis is denied, the withdrawal of the meaning of the thesis is the abandonment of the thesis (<s>pratijñāsaṃnyāsa</s>). //

children.text: yadapi tenoktaṃ pakṣapratiṣedhe tūṣṇīṃbhavatastūṣṇīṃbhāvo nāma nigrahasthānaṃ pralapataśca pralapitaṃ nāmetyādyapi vācyaṃ syāditi /
children.translated_text: And what he also said — 'When the thesis is denied, if [the debater] falls silent, the ground of defeat called "silence" (<s>tūṣṇīṃbhāva</s>) [applies]; and if [the debater] babbles, [the ground of defeat called] "babbling" (<s>pralapita</s>) [applies]' — and so on, [that too] would need to be stated.
But that too is incorrect.

children.text: na hi tūṣṇīmbhāvena pralapitādibhirvā śakyamanaikāntikatvamuddhartuṃ yathā pratijñārthāpahnavena, na caite hetvābhasodbhāvanasya purastāttanāḥ tasmādetadapyanirūpitābhidhānādyatkiñciditi // 5 //
children.translated_text: For by silence or by babbling and the like, it is not possible to raise inconclusiveness [as effectively] as by the repudiation of the meaning of the thesis; nor are these [i.e., silence and babbling] prior to the raising of the fallacious reason. Therefore, this too is a statement of uncertain purport — [amounting to] whatever [one wishes to say]. //5//

When the perceivability-by-senses of the reason has been shown to be inconclusive, and the thesis of the non-eternality of sound is rejected — the proponent, intending to raise inconclusiveness, might say to the respondent: 'Who indeed says that sound is non-eternal?' If he is able to repudiate [his own] thesis that 'sound is non-eternal,' then [he thinks]: 'In general, my eternal [thesis being maintained], the reason does not become inconclusive for me' — with this thought, he repudiates [his thesis]. This type of disputant cannot be defeated by [raising] inconclusiveness. Because of the disclosure of his repudiation — having raised inconclusiveness of [his] repudiation — therefore, for the establishment of the inconclusiveness of the inconclusiveness [raised by the opponent], one should expose the repudiation of the repudiator. Now, [the question arises:] should one defeat [the opponent] by first exposing the repudiation and then establishing the inconclusiveness, or [should one defeat him] by the repudiation alone? — In the case of this doubt, by the mere exposure of the repudiation, he is defeated as self-contradictory in terms of his earlier and later [statements] — not by inconclusiveness, because the establishment of inconclusiveness presupposes that [exposure]. Therefore, what was said by <s>Kīrti</s> — 'What then? — Considering that a fallacious reason and the subsequent abandonment of the thesis are [both] grounds of defeat for the respondent, the fallacious reason itself is the primary ground of defeat' — that too is set aside,

children.text: NyS_5,2.6: aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣamicchato hetvantaram //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.6: When the reason has been stated without specification and is refuted, desiring a specification [constitutes] a different reason (<s>hetvantara</s>). //

children.translated_text: He gives an illustration to explain: 'The illustration is this — the manifest [world] — elements, derivative substances, and sense organs — is of one material cause (<s>ekaprakṛti</s>); [this is known] from the limitedness of modifications of one material cause.' / For example: having a single lump of clay as their material cause, pots, shallow vessels, water-jars, and the like are observed [to be] limited — the extent of the arrangement, i.e., the configuration, of the material cause is the extent of the modification. / And this illustration is not deficient as a proof — he says: 'and it is observed.' / He states the connecting statement (<s>upanaya</s>): 'there is this.' / He states the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>): 'therefore, of those of one material cause.' / The prima facie opponent's counter-argument through the deviation of this reason of 'limitedness': / Of things of different material causes — pots and bracelets and the like — and of things of one material cause — pots and shallow vessels and the like — limitedness is observed equally. / When the prima facie opponent has thus counter-argued, the proponent subsequently qualifies the reason 'limitedness': 'when there is co-occurrence with one material cause, because of observing the limitedness of modifications such as shallow vessels and the like.' / '<s>Prakṛti</s>' means 'intrinsic nature' — meaning: when there is co-occurrence with a single intrinsic nature. / He makes clear the co-occurrence with one material cause: / For all this manifest [world] is apprehended as limited, accompanied by pleasure, pain, and delusion. / For example: / <s>Maitra</s> has a cognition of pleasure regarding his wife <s>Narmadā</s>; her co-wives have a cognition of pain; and <s>Caitra</s>, who has not obtained her, afflicted with agitation, has delusion — this is the confusion. / By the [example of] <s>Narmadā</s>, other entities are explained. / Thus, where there is limitedness when there is co-occurrence with a single intrinsic nature, there is the property of having a single material cause — just as in pots, shallow vessels, water-jars, and the like, which have a single lump of clay as their intrinsic nature. / But pots, bracelets, and the like do not have a single intrinsic nature, because of the difference of their intrinsic natures — clay, gold, and the like. / Having shown [this], he connects the <s>sūtra</s>: 'thus, when the reason is stated without specification, [it is] refuted.' / He states its being a ground of defeat: / 'And when there is an alternative reason.' / Moreover, if, upon stating an alternative reason, the entire [universe] is to be proved as having a single material cause, then there is no illustration — because everything is included in the thesis. / But if something is excluded from the thesis for the purpose of establishing the illustration, then by that very [excluded thing], [there is] inconclusiveness. / [That is:] because of those that are co-occurrent [with pleasure-pain-delusion] and limited having different material causes — he says: / 'When, upon the statement of an alternative reason, if the illustration of reason and [its] object' — / 'Reason' (<s>hetu</s>) means 'proof'; 'object' (<s>artha</s>) means 'what is to be proved'; these two — reason and object — are shown by the illustration in the relation of pervaded and pervader / — [that is] the illustration. / The illustration that shows the reason and its object — if that is employed, then this manifest [world] would not be of a single material cause, because the illustration involves another material cause. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'upon the employment of another proof, the former' — / When the proponent has had the opportunity to respond, if the opponent shows the deviation of the reason-and-object, and the proponent, standing at the third stage, qualifies the reason — then should he be defeated because of employing another proof, or because of employing an inconclusive proof? / To begin with, he is not defeated for [employing] an inconclusive proof, because [the inconclusiveness] is removed by the qualification of the reason. / Therefore, he is defeated precisely because of stating another reason — because of making known the actual inadequacy of the former [reason] that was in reality inadequate. / Or, if [the former reason] is adequate, [then] the alternative reason would be purposeless — thus it is well said. //6//
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.7: An irrelevant statement (<s>arthāntara</s>) is one whose meaning is unconnected with the topic under discussion. //

children.translated_text: Verbal prefixes are [also] understood as adding to the meaning or reversing the meaning.

children.text: yathā 'bhyāgacchati pratiṣṭhataityādiṣu tadasya nigrahasthānatvaṃ vārtikakāra upapādayati /
children.translated_text: As in '<s>abhyāgacchati</s>' (he approaches), '<s>pratiṣṭhate</s>' (he stands firm), and the like. The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> establishes its being a ground of defeat:
'Because of [the thesis] being accepted' —
And just as an irrelevant statement is a ground of defeat for the proof-proponent, so too it should be seen for the respondent. //7//

He explains: when there is the adoption of thesis and counter-thesis as described — meaning: in debate (<s>vāda</s>), <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling), or <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavilling). / When the establishment of the provable from the reason is the topic, the proponent should state his proof: 'Sound is eternal, because of being intangible.' / In the meanwhile, seeing the inadequacy of the reason through deviation in pleasure and the like, he brings up one topic after another by [the technique of] attachment-to-attachment, presenting this and that subject in order to conceal that [inadequacy] — and is defeated by [the charge of] irrelevant statement. / The meaning of what is denoted — because of the connection of the action with another action, i.e., because of the connection with a specific action — [a word] whose form is differentiated, i.e., whose form is divided — is called a 'name' (<s>nāman</s>). As in: 'the tree stands,' 'he cuts the tree,' 'he sees the moon through the tree,' 'he waters the tree' — and so on. / Thus, because of the connection of the thing denoted with a specific action, [a word] whose form is differentiated — is called a 'name.' / He states the nature of the verb (<s>ākhyāta</s>): / 'The aggregate of action and agent (<s>kāraka</s>)' — / By the object, the subject is indicated. / Words like '<s>pacati</s>' (he cooks), '<s>pacyate</s>' (it is cooked), and the like express the action, the agent, and the object. But this definition is unestablished and over-extensive — for the agent and the object are not denoted by the verb; / they are obtained only through the import of the action itself; / and only what is not obtainable otherwise is the meaning of a word. / And because of the established rule that agents and objects, being the most deserving among the <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations) for the verbal force (<s>bhāvanā</s>), are denoted by their [case-] number — [the claim of] denoting <s>kārakas</s> is unestablished. / And it is over-extensive, because even nouns like '<s>pācaka</s>' (cook), '<s>pākya</s>' (to-be-cooked), and the like denote an aggregate of action and <s>kāraka</s>. / Therefore, being unsatisfied with this definition, he grasps verb-words (<s>ākhyātapada</s>) through two other definitions: / 'An <s>ākhyāta</s> (verb) denotes an action qualified by the number of the <s>kāraka</s> and connected with time.' / In '<s>pacati</s>' (he cooks), '<s>pacyate</s>' (it is cooked), and the like, the action is understood as qualified by the number of the agent or the object, and by tense — present and the like. / And 'time is [present] somewhere' — only this much is stated, / but it is not intended as part of the definition — because in '<s>pacata</s>' (cook! [imperative]), '<s>yajeta</s>' (let him sacrifice), and the like, its connection is not understood. / By this definition, the non-inclusion of [forms like] '<s>supyata</s>' (let him sleep) and the like among verbs arises — because the <s>kāraka</s> and its number are not understood. To include those, he states a second definition: / 'What denotes merely the meaning of the verbal root, qualified by the denotation of tense — that [too] is an <s>ākhyāta</s>.' / 'In usages' — / Particles (<s>nipāta</s>) are [words] whose form is not denoted from the meaning of either a noun or a verb. / Just as, by the aggregating words and alternative words — 'the aggregation of them,' 'the alternative of them' — aggregation and the like are expressed as different from the noun-meaning or the verb-meaning, with the genitive usage [indicating this]. / [But] 'and' (<s>ca</s>) and the like do not express their own meanings as different from the noun-meaning or the verb-meaning [in the same way as those noun-phrases]. / '<s>Rūpa</s>' (form) [means:] the meanings — [the forms] being presented, i.e., the form being presented from the noun-meaning or the verb-meaning — of those particles that are so called. / '<s>Upasargas</s>' (verbal prefixes) are [words] used near [the verb], i.e., used before [it], illuminating the action. And 'illumination' is illustrative.
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.8: Like the utterance of a sequence of phonemes, [it is] meaningless (<s>nirarthaka</s>). //

// 8 //
children.translated_text: The word '<s>vat</s>' in 'like the utterance of a sequence of phonemes' [functions as a comparative suffix]. / Here, when a <s>Drāviḍa</s> (South Indian) explains the eternality of sound to an <s>Ārya</s> (North Indian) who does not know his language, using his own language, that is the meaningless ground of defeat. He, [the <s>Drāviḍa</s>,] indeed knowing the <s>Ārya</s> language, either to conceal [his] lack of capacity, or because of not knowing that [the other] does not know his language, employed the proof in his own language — in the first case, he is defeated through wrong understanding (<s>vipratipatti</s>); in the second, through non-understanding (<s>apratipatti</s>). / In reality, even when the proof has capacity [to prove], like a mute person, because of the non-apprehension of words that would convey [the meaning] to the <s>Ārya</s>, the commencement of conveying that [meaning] is purposeless. / Here, by the <s>vat</s>-suffix, the sequence of phonemes is shown only as an analogy — but this is not the [only] illustration of the ground of defeat, such that the consequence would apply even to cheek-drums and the like. / For just as the speech of the <s>Drāviḍa</s> arises from the intention to express a difference in meaning — not so the utterance of a sequence of phonemes, nor cheek-drums and the like; [but] because of the commonality of non-conveyance, 'like the utterance of a sequence of phonemes' [is used as] an analogy. / For this very reason the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> says: / 'Of this kind' — / meaning: not only this [example] — this is the meaning. / The <s>Vārttika</s>: 'the illustration is in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>' — / (555/3) meaning: 'of this kind' is the illustration. / 'Because of the non-employment of the proof' — / The five-membered sentence that conveys [the meaning] to the other party is the proof; that was not employed by him — meaning: because, even though it has the capacity to convey according to his own convention, it is incapable of conveying [the meaning] to the <s>Āryas</s>. //8//
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.9: What is unintelligible (<s>avijñātārtha</s>) is that which, even though uttered three times to the assembly and the opponent, is not understood. //

children.text:

vārtikaṃ bhāṣyavyākhyayā gatārtham
// 9 //
children.translated_text: A statement that is not understood by the assembly and the opponent — uttered three times, with a common convention, by the proponent — [this is] uttered 'three times' because three times is generally the number [of repetitions] by which the assembly and the opponent come to understand the meaning. / Now, [one might say:] it is impossible that it be uttered three times with a common convention by the proponent and [yet] be unintelligible. / Or, if possible, then the assembly and the opponent are dull — and a dull person's failure to understand is not the fault of the teacher. / For the singer is not at fault if a deaf person does not hear the song — therefore he says: / 'An ambiguous word (<s>śliṣṭaśabda</s>), when there is no determining factor such as context and the like' — as in '<s>śveto dhāvati</s>' ('the white one runs' or '<s>Śveta</s> runs'). / 'An expression with unfamiliar usage' — like '<s>jarbharīturpharītū</s>.' / 'Uttered too rapidly' — and the like are the causes of its being unintelligible. / He states its being a ground of defeat: / 'Because of incapacity' — / The <s>Vārttika</s> is understood through the <s>Bhāṣya</s> explanation. //9//
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.10: Because of the absence of sequential connection, what has unconnected meaning is purposeless (<s>apārthaka</s>). //

// 10 //
children.translated_text: Where a word — that is unambiguous, with understood usage, not rapidly uttered — and a sentence, being multiple, lack sequential connection, i.e., have no mutual relation — therefore the unconnectedness of meaning is grasped. That [statement is] purposeless (<s>apārthaka</s>) — a ground of defeat, [i.e.,] lacking purpose. Why? / Because of the failure of the aggregate-meaning or the sentence-meaning — for the purpose of the employment of words or sentences is the conveyance of sentence-meaning or larger-passage-meaning; when that [purpose] is absent, [the statement is] purposeless — this is the meaning. / He gives an illustration of the absence of sequential connection of sentences: / 'As in: "ten pomegranates, six cakes."' / He gives an illustration of the absence of sequential connection of words: / '<s>Kuṇḍam ajājinam</s>' — / '<s>Rauruka</s>' means 'related to a <s>raru</s> (deer).' / '<s>Pārya</s>' means 'to be made to drink.' / '<s>Apratiśīna</s>' means 'old.' / The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> raises a doubt: / 'Regarding the meaningless (<s>nirarthaka</s>) and the purposeless (<s>apārthaka</s>)' — / For the purpose of uttering speech is the conveying [of meaning] to the other party; and by both the meaningless and the purposeless, the other party is not made to understand — so there is no difference between the two. / Nor is the adoption [of a distinction] merely on the ground that in one case there is just a sequence of phonemes and in the other case there are words — a justified basis for positing a difference. / Because, even among the purposeless [statements], the consequence of positing a difference by sub-distinction — one having [unconnected] sentences and another having [unconnected] words — [would follow] — this is the meaning of the doubt. / He refutes: / 'They are different' — / He asks: / 'How?' / The answer: / 'In the meaningless, there are merely phonemes — devoid of anything denoted. But here, in the purposeless, there are words — "words" meaning those through which meaning is reached — and sentences too possess denotation, [but they are] unconnected.' Between the meaningless, which is devoid of denotation, and the purposeless, which is devoid of purpose, the distinction is great. / But there is not such a [great] distinction between [two kinds of] purposeless [statements] — with unconnected sentences and unconnected words — that we should pay attention to a sub-distinction. / If one intends [to identify the two] merely by the commonality of the absence of the purpose of conveying [meaning] to the other party, then in the non-distinction [of these two], there would be non-distinction of all grounds of defeat — because in all [of them] the conveyance to the other party is absent. / Or, if present, the ground of defeat would be untenable. //10//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.11: The statement of the disorder of the members [of the syllogism] is untimely (<s>sūtra</s> 11). //

children.translated_text: Therefore, although worldly people apprehend the meaning of cow and the like from the words '<s>gāvī</s>' and the like alone — this being the understanding of those who deal only with what is directly observed — still, for examiners who deliberate, the process of inquiry is as follows: when the most senior [speaker], [who should have] used the word '<s>go</s>,' inadvertently used the word '<s>gāvī</s>,' then the next senior [person], having elevated [it to] the word '<s>go</s>,' understood cow-ness [from it].
As they say:
'When a child, while learning, says "<s>ambāmba</s>" (a corrupted form of "mother"),

children.text: avyakte tadvidāṃ tena vyakte bhavati nirṇayaḥ //
children.translated_text: what is unclear to those who know becomes clear through [the correct understanding underlying] that [corrupted speech] —

He explains: the order of the members — <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis) and the rest — is [determined] by the force of their meanings in accordance with their definitions. The order that does not violate [their] definitions — we stated this in the first chapter: because [the audience] understands from the statement of what is relevant, not from [the statement of] something else. In that [context], the indication of what is to be proved is what is first required by others, not the indication of the proof. In that case, if this person were to employ the proof first, how could he state what is required [by the audience]? And one whose statement does not concern what is required — how can he be called an 'informer'? Thus, all [statements] beginning with the statement of the reason too require order and cannot communicate effectively without order. But even from [syllogistic members stated in] reversed order, there is understanding of the meaning by following the order of [their] meanings. This is the nature of the meaning of the <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest — that it cannot be known without their [proper] order. In the disorder of the members, because of the absence of expectation on your part, and because the connection of word-meanings depends on that [expectation], the disconnection [of meanings] is a ground of defeat — this is the meaning. The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'Some [say:] not even thus, because of the [eventual] establishment [of meaning].' As they say: here too there is no restriction of order, because of the establishment of the desired meaning in both cases [ordered and disordered] without distinction. If it were said: 'This is our convention, like the conventional assignment of words to meanings — that the meaning should be understood through this particular order and not through another — therefore it is indeed understood only in that way, not through another order' — to this he says: 'And because of the non-acceptance of that convention.' The convention applies to words alone, not to sentences, because the understanding of meaning from a sentence arises without depending on any convention — as from a sentence composed by a new poet. One might say: in sentences too, a restriction of order is observed, as in '<s>pācayāṃ babhūva</s>' (he had cooked) but never '<s>babhūva pācayām</s>' — to this he says: 'because of usage' — there the worldly usage is fixed; but here, the usage of disorder-of-members is also observed — this is the meaning. He refutes that: 'As for [the objection that] not even thus, because of [eventual] establishment [of meaning]' — the answer to that: like a word deviating from [correct] usage. He elaborates on this very [point]: just as the word '<s>gāvī</s>' (a corrupt form), being used for the meaning of the very word '<s>go</s>' (cow), makes known an object possessing a hump and the like. (556/1) Although the capacity of words to convey meaning is not natural, still, being preceded by the convention established by the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>), it continues to this day. Therefore, correct words (<s>sādhu</s>) are those for which the Lord's convention [assigns them to particular] meanings at the distinction of [those] meanings; but words that operate without that convention, even when referring to the [same] meaning, are incorrect words — corruptions (<s>apabhraṃśa</s>). And [the scriptural injunctions] such as 'one should speak with correct words' and the like are injunctions regarding <s>dharma</s> (religious duty), and censure-passages (<s>nindārthavāda</s>) like 'a <s>mantra</s> deficient in accent or phoneme [destroys the sacrificer]' and the like, and the authoritativeness of the <s>Vedas</s> was established in the second chapter. And the meaning of this is not 'all correct words are causes of <s>dharma</s>'; rather, the performance of <s>dharma</s> — when it requires speaking in the appropriate manner — is restricted to correct words alone. This being established, words like '<s>go</s>' and '<s>gāvī</s>' and the like are indiscriminately used by cultured persons (<s>ārya</s>). Regarding these: are they all indiscriminately incorrect, or is some one [of them] correct, and from that the others derive their [capacity to convey] understanding? In the case of postulating correctness for a single word, since the understanding of meaning from the other [word] is tenable as being grounded in that [correct word], it is not reasonable to postulate correctness for all [words]. As the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> says: 'It is wrong that there are multiple [correct] words' [<s>Mīmāṃsā Sūtra</s>]. Even there, regarding which of these [alternatives] is incorrect — when one inquires about one among these — 'The truth there would depend on the particular expertise [of the users]' — whichever is remembered as correct without dispute by the most expert [grammarians] beginning with <s>Indra</s>, <s>Pāṇini</s>, and the rest — that is correct; the other is incorrect — this is determined.

children.text:
evaṃ sādhau prayoktavye yo 'pabhraṃśaḥ prayujyate /
tena sādhuvyavahitaḥ kaścidartho 'bhidhīyate/'
pārśvasthāścāto 'nena mūlaśabdamunnīyārthaḥ pratīta ityagṛhītvaiva gāvīśabdādevāyamamumarthaṃ pratītavāniti tameva gotvasya vācakamavagamyānyeṣāṃ vṛddho babhūva /
tataḥ prabhṛtyananusṛtamūlaśabdānāmayaṃ vācakatvabhramo 'pabhraṃśe vartate na vṛddhatarasyobhayavedino mūlaśabdānusāriṇasī padarthapratipattiridānīntanānāṃ tvapabhraṃśādeva ata evānavākhyānamapi prayojanavat /
asatyasmin vācakāpabhraṃśavibhāge jñānānabhāvātsādhubhirbhāṣitavyamiti niyamavidherna mlecchitavai nāpabhāṣitavai iti niṣedhasya ca viṣayasaṃśayena duradhigamatvena dharmānuṣṭhānasyāśakyatvaprasaṅgāt /
yatrārthe yasya śabdasya bhagavateśvareṇa saṅketaḥ kṛtaḥ sa tatra sādhurasādhuranyatra yathā ya evāsvaśabdo daridre sādhuḥ sa evāsādhurvājini prayujyamānaḥ
yathā nakuladaṃṣṭāgraspṛṣṭā yā kā cidoṣadhirasau sarpaviṣaṃ hanti evamīśvareṇa kṛtasaṅketaḥ śabdaḥ sādhurdharmaupayujyate nānya iti /
yavavarāhādiśabdānāmāryamlecchayorarthavivāde vaidikādvākyaśeṣādāryasaṃmator 'tho grahītavyo na mlecchasaṃmataḥ tatra vaidikavākyaśeṣavirodhāt /
yeṣāṃ tu śabdānāmāryeṣu na dṛṣṭacaraḥ prayogaḥ kevalairmlecchairevārthabhede prayujyante yathā pikanematāmarasādayaḥ vede tu prayuktāsteṣāṃ mlecchavyavahārādevārtho 'vadhāraṇīyaḥ
tatra teṣāmabhiyopagāditi āryavyavahārāparipanthitvācceti /
tadevaṃ vyavasthite nyāyamīmāṃsāpariśīlanavikalānāṃ bāhyatarāḥ pralāpā upekṣaṇīyāḥ tasmātsuṣṭhūktaṃ prayogāpetaśabdavaditi /
na ca śabdānvākhyānaṃ vyarthamiti ceti /
pratijñādīnāṃ kramaniyamakāraṇaṃ praśnapūrvakaṃ darśayati /
tadetatkathaṃ pūrvaṃ tāvaditi /
dvitīyaṃ deśyamanubhāṣya pariharati /
yatpunaretatsamayānabhyupagamāditi /
so 'yamarthasyānurvīṃ pratitibalapravṛttāmanvācakṣāṇo nābhyākhyeya iti--- nopālabhyaḥ /
śāstre vākyānyarthasaṃgrahārthamupādīyanta iti /
na hiśāstre kṛtsnāsadivādarabhūtadivetyarthasaṅgraho yathā kathaṃ cit kriyata iti vāde 'pi tathā kriyatāmiti yuktaṃ vādādiṣu pakṣapratipakṣavadvakrorapi parīkṣyamāṇatvāt parīkṣitasya ca śāstritatvāt
// 11 //
children.translated_text: similarly, when a corruption is used where a correct [word] should be employed, some meaning, mediated by the correct [word], is expressed.' The bystanders too, having elevated the root-word through this [corrupt usage], understood the meaning — and not having grasped [the meaning from] the word '<s>gāvī</s>' itself, [they mistakenly conclude] 'this person understood this meaning from this [word] alone' and, apprehending that very [word] as the denoter of cow-ness, become seniors for others. From then on, this delusion of denotative capacity for those who do not trace the root-word persists in the corruption — but the understanding of the word-meaning by the more senior [person] who knows both [the correct and corrupt forms] follows the root-word. For those of the present day, however, [the understanding comes] from the corruption alone. For this very reason, even the grammatical explanation (<s>anvākhyāna</s>) serves a purpose. In the absence of this [analysis of] the distinction between correct denoters and corruptions, [there would be] uncertainty regarding the domain of the restrictive injunction 'one should speak with correct words' and the prohibition 'one should not speak barbarously, one should not speak incorrectly,' [and] because of the difficulty of ascertaining [the domain], there would be the consequence of the impossibility of performing <s>dharma</s>. The word for which the convention was established by the blessed Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) in [connection with] a particular meaning — that is correct [in that context] and incorrect elsewhere. Just as the very word '<s>aśva</s>' (horse) that is correct [when applied] to a poor person [in the sense of 'one who has horses'] is incorrect when applied to a horse [in its literal sense, since the convention differs]. Just as whatever herb has been touched by the tip of a mongoose's fang — that [herb] destroys snake-venom — so too, the word for which the convention was established by <s>Īśvara</s> — being correct — is useful for <s>dharma</s>, and no other. In cases where there is a dispute between the <s>ārya</s> (cultured) and <s>mleccha</s> (barbarian) regarding the meaning of words like '<s>yava</s>' (barley), '<s>varāha</s>' (boar), and the like, the meaning accepted by the <s>ārya</s> should be taken, from the <s>Vedic</s> context (<s>vākyaśeṣa</s>) — not the meaning accepted by the <s>mleccha</s>, because of contradiction with the <s>Vedic</s> context there. But for those words whose usage among the <s>āryas</s> is not observed and which are used only by <s>mlecchas</s> with a difference in meaning — such as '<s>pika</s>' (cuckoo), '<s>nema</s>', '<s>tāmarasa</s>' (lotus), and the like — though used in the <s>Veda</s>, their meaning should be determined from the <s>mleccha</s> convention alone, because of the acceptance of that [usage] by the experts and because it does not conflict with the <s>ārya</s> convention. This being established, the idle prattlings of those who are deficient in the study of <s>Nyāya</s> and <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, being more external [to the tradition], should be disregarded. Therefore it is well said: 'like a word deviating from [correct] usage.' And the grammatical explanation is not purposeless — thus [it is established]. He shows, prefaced by a question, the reason for the restriction of order in the <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest: 'How then is this? First...' Having restated and responded to the second [objection], he refutes [it]: 'As for what was said — "because of the non-acceptance of convention"' — He who, describing the understanding [of meaning] as operating through the force of meaning tracing back along the earth, says: 'it should not be criticized' — [i.e.,] he is not to be faulted. 'In a treatise, sentences are employed for the purpose of summarizing the meaning' — for in a treatise, the summary of meaning is accomplished somehow, as in 'the whole day was a debate' — but that does not mean it should be done the same way in [actual] debate, since in debate and the like, both the proponent and the opponent are being examined, and what has been examined [properly] belongs to the treatise. //11//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.12: Deficient [means:] lacking in any one of the members [of the syllogism]. //

etadapīti /
(557/1) siddhasādhyārthayoḥ siddhāntapratijñayormahān bheda ityarthaḥ // 12 //
children.translated_text: It has been shown that the five members — <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest — together constitute the proof. When deficient, the proof-status does not exist; in its absence, the provable is not established. For an effect that requires a complete set [of causes] does not arise from merely a part of that set — this is the meaning. He presents the view of others: 'but some' — 'Some say: a [syllogism] lacking the <s>pratijñā</s> is not a ground of defeat.' He refutes: 'but this is not correct.' Is [the claim that] a [syllogism] lacking the <s>pratijñā</s> is not a separate ground of defeat, or that it is not a ground of defeat at all? He states this: 'Is he defeated or not?' In the first alternative, he states the defect: 'if.' In the second alternative, he states the defect: 'but if there is no defeat' — The meaning is: it was stated that the <s>pratijñā</s> is a subsidiary (<s>aṅga</s>) of the proof. 'And as for what you say — "it is merely acceptance of the <s>siddhānta</s> of <s>Dignāga</s>"' — He refutes this: 'this too' — (557/1) The meaning is: there is a great difference between what is established and what is to be proved — between a <s>siddhānta</s> and a <s>pratijñā</s>. //12//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.13: Excessive [means having] more than the reason and the example. //

tadetanniyamābhyupagama iti bhāṣyam /

niṣpāditakriye karmaṇi aviśeṣābhidhāyinaḥ sādhanasya sādhananyāyātipātāt /
yatra tu prativādinaḥ pariṣado vā jijñāsā bhavati kati sādhanānisaṃbhavantyasminsādhya
iti tatra yāvanti sādhanāni tāvanti sarvāṇyeva vācyāni anyatarābhidhāne nigrahaprasaṅgāditi,
nādhikaṃ nigrahasthānamiti ya āhustanmatamupanyasyati /
tacca na dārḍhyāditi /
dūṣayati na dārḍhyārtheti /
yadi niścayo dārḍhyaṃ tadekasmādeva pramāṇādbhavati aniścāyakasyāpramāṇatvāt /
atha sphuṭhatvaṃ tadapi cenniścayaḥ sa dattottaraḥ /
atha sāmānyaviśeṣatadvatāṃ grahaṇaṃ na tadanumānasahasrairapi teṣāṃ sāmānyavaddravyamātraviṣayatvāt /
śaṅkate atha bravīṣi dve api jñāpake iti /
nāsmākamanadhigatārthagantṛtvaṃ pramāṇatvaṃ yenaikenādhigate pramāṇāntaramapramāṇaṃ syāt /
api tu gantṛmātraṃ pramāṇaṃ tacca dvitīyasyāpyaviśiṣṭamiti śaṅkārthaḥ /
nirākaroti satyaṃ dve api jñāpate iti /
children.translated_text: He refutes: 'It is true that both inform' —

children.text: puruṣo 'trāparādhyate yo jñātamarthamajijñāsitaṃ jñāpayati na tu pramāṇaṃ taddhi sāmarthyena mene pravartata eva /
children.translated_text: The person is at fault here — the one who informs another of a known meaning that was not inquired about; but the means of valid knowledge [is] not [at fault], for it operates merely by its own capacity.

children.text: yadi jijñāsāyāṃ sityāṃ pravartate pratipādayati jñeyaṃ nāsya kaścidaparādha iti /
children.translated_text: If, when an inquiry exists, [the second means of knowledge] operates and informs of what is to be known — there is no fault of it at all.

children.text: na hi dhānyeṣvalūneṣu dātramavraścanaṃ bhavati tasmādanapekṣitakāraṇādanavasthāprasaṅgācca puruṣasya nigraha iti sthitam // 13 //
children.translated_text: For when the grain has not been harvested, the sickle does not become a non-cutter. Therefore, because of [the excess being] without a required reason and because of the consequence of an infinite regress, it is established that the person's defeat [stands]. //13//

The <s>Bhāṣya</s> [reads]: 'This is indeed the acceptance of a restriction.' In that [context], the inquiry 'how then is this provable established?' — since the provable is established by a single proof alone, the statement of another proof is purposeless. Because of the transgression of the principle of proof by a proof that states what is not distinctive when the task has [already] been accomplished by [another] action. But where the opponent or the assembly has the inquiry 'how many proofs are possible for this provable?' — there, as many proofs as there are, all of them should be stated, because of the consequence of defeat in stating [only] one. [Thus] 'the excess is not a ground of defeat' — he presents this view. 'And that is not for the sake of strengthening' — He refutes: 'not for the sake of strengthening.' If certainty is the strengthening, that arises from a single means of valid knowledge alone, since what does not produce certainty is not a valid means of knowledge. But if clarity [is meant] — if that is certainty, then that [objection] has been answered. But if [it is] the apprehension of the universal, the particular, and the [substance] possessing them — that [cannot be achieved] even by a thousand inferences, since all of those have as their object only substance in general. He raises a doubt: 'But if you say that both are informers' — [We reply:] for us, being a means of valid knowledge does not consist in being a conveyer of what has not [yet] been ascertained, such that when ascertained by one [means of knowledge], another means would be a non-valid-means. Rather, a means of valid knowledge is merely a conveyer; and that [capacity] is undifferentiated even for the second [means] — this is the meaning of the doubt.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.14: Saying again, with respect to both word and meaning, what has been said — that is repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), except when it is a restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>). //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.15: Saying again with [different] words what has been arrived at from the meaning — that is repetition. //
