jalpavitaṇḍayorvakturnaipuṇyaṃ cintyate /

children.translated_text: And in the use of repetition, [the speaker] would be unskillful —

children.text: anapekṣitābhidhānātsādhanasya viṣayaḥ sādhyo 'rtho na siddhaḥ tasyāparijñanānnigṛhyate /
children.translated_text: because of stating what is not required — the domain of the proof is the meaning to be proved, which is not [yet] established; because of the non-comprehension of that, [the speaker] is defeated.
And futility (<s>vaiyarthya</s>) is purposelessness, or [it is] having a contradictory purpose — this is the intended [meaning].

children.text: tathā hi punaruktaprayoge tatprayojanānusaraṇasamākulacittaḥ prathamābhidhānādāpātataḥ pratītamapyarthamapratītamiva manyamāno na niścetumarhatīti tataśca pratipādanāya pravṛtto na pratipādayiteti viruddhaprayojanavattvavaiyarthyaṃ syādityupapannaṃ nigrahasthānamiti // 15 //
children.translated_text: For indeed, when a repetitious [statement] is employed, the person whose mind is agitated by pursuing the purpose of that [repeated statement], thinking that the meaning — even though understood at once from the first utterance — is as if not understood, is unable to ascertain [it]. And thereupon, having set out to communicate, he does not communicate — thus there would be futility because of having a contradictory purpose. Therefore, the ground of defeat is tenable. //15//

By these two <s>sūtras</s>, repetition is a single ground of defeat, [but] stated as threefold through the intention of [describing] sub-varieties — for the sake of elaboration. That very repetition is sometimes through verbal repetition, sometimes through synonyms, and sometimes through [what is arrived at from] the meaning. He raises an objection: 'not, because of non-harm' — He resolves: 'true' — In <s>jalpa</s> (disputation) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive criticism), the cleverness of the speaker is being assessed.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.16: Failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly, even when stated three times, is silence (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>). //

children.text:
vyācaṣṭe vijñātasya vākyārthasyeti /
nigrahasthānatve 'syopapattimāha /
apratyuccārayan kimāśrayaṃ pratiṣedhaṃ brūyāditi /
vārttikaṃ nedaṃ nigrahasthānamiti ke cit /
(555/9) uttareṇa
uttaraguṇadoṣanirūpaṇena prativādino mūḍhatvāmūḍhatvāvasthāpanāt /
etadvibhajate uttareṇa guṇadoṣavatetīti /
tasmātkiṃ punaruccāritenoccāraṇenāsti prayojanamiti śeṣaḥ /
asti hi kaściditi kva citpāṭhaḥ /
tatrāsti hīti nipātadvayaṃ vākyāvatāre draṣṭavyam /
puṃsāṃ vicitrasvabhāvatvāt kaściduttare samartho na pratyuccāraṇe nāsau saduttaparamabhidadhānaḥ
tāvatānanubhāṣaṇamātreṇa nigrahamarhati /
nanu yadyananubhāṣaṇaṃ na nigrahasthānaṃ tadā 'nubhāṣitumupakramya sarvamananubhāṣamāṇo na nigṛhyetetyata āha /
yastvārabhya na nirvāhayet saduttaraṃ tu brūyāt tasya syāt khalīkāramātrasamāmarthyakṛtaṃ na tu tattvavāditvavihatirityarthaḥ /
tamevaṃ bhadantākṣepaṃ samādhatte nottaraviṣayāparijñānāditi /
dūṣyaviṣayaṃ hi dūṣaṇam asati dūṣyābhidhāne na śakyaṃ vaktum /
na khalu pratijñāhetūdāharaṇopanayanigamanadoṣāstatsvarūpamanabhidhāya śakyā doṣatvenāvasthāpayitumityanuccārayanna doṣamabhidhātumarhatīti /
tadidamuktaṃ tadidaṃ vyāhatamucyate noccārayati uttaraṃ ca bravītīti /
syādetad na prativādinā sarvaṃ dūṣaṇīyam
anyatamāvayavadūṣaṇenaiva sādhanasya dūṣitatvena doṣāntarābhidhānavaiyarthyāt /
na khalu mṛto mṛtyunā rakṣito mārayituṃ śakyaḥ evaṃ dūṣitamapi dūṣayituṃ, tasmāt satyapi dūṣyabāhulye 'nyatamaṃ dūṣyaṃ tathā ca sarvānubhāṣaṇe sarvasyādūṣyatvād yaddūṣaṇīyaṃ tatpunaranuvādyamiti sarvānuvāde dviranuvādo 'dūṣyānuvādaśceti dūṣakanigrahasthānadvayaṃ tasmādanubhāṣaṇameva nigrahasthānamiti viparītamāpatitamityata
āha apratijñānācceti /
etadvibhajate na cedaṃ pratijñāyate /
pūrvamekagranthena sarvamuccārayitavyaṃ paścāduttaraṃ yaddūṣyaṃ tadanuvādenābhidheyaṃ yena dūṣyānuvādo dviranuvādaśca doṣau syātām api tu yathākathaṃ ciduttaraṃvaktavyam /
uttaravādaparasyottaramāśrayābhāve na yuktamiti tadāśrayamātramanuvaditavyaṃ tadantareṇāśakyābhidhānatvāduttarasyeti /
tasmādyuktaṃ tanmātrasyāpratyuccāraṇamananubhāṣaṇaṃ na sarvasyāpratyuccāraṇamananubhāṣaṇamityarthaḥ /
nanvapratibhāyā nigrahasthānatvavidhānenānanubhāṣaṇasyāpi viditaṃ tasya tadviśeṣatvāt /
na khalu nānubhāṣataityetāvataiva nigṛhyate api tvananubhāṣamāṇo dūṣyaṃ na budhyate abudhyamānaśca tatrottaraṃ na pratipadyate tato 'pratibhayā nigṛhyate /
tadevamananubhāṣaṇamapratibhāviśeṣa iti apratibhāyā vihitaṃ nigrahasthānatvaṃ tadviśeṣe 'pi vihitaṃ bhavati /
yathā gavi sāsnādimattvaṃ vihitaṃ śābaleye 'pi vihitaṃ bhavati na punastatra sāsnādimatvavidhānāya pṛthag yatnāntaramārabhante /
atra brūmaḥ, na tāvaduttarāpratipattisāmānyaviśeṣo 'nanubhāṣaṇaṃ puṃsāṃ sāmaryyavaicitryāt /
kaściddūnaṣyaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ ca vidannapi nānubhāṣituṃ pārayati bahuvacanakuṇṭhatvāt /
tasmādasatyāmapratibhāyāmananubhāṣaṇasambhavānnāpratibhāyā viśeṣo 'nanubhāṣaṇamiti /
kaściddūṣaṇaviṣayaṃ vedānubhāṣate ca uttarapratipattivikalastu syātso 'yamapratibhayā nigṛhyate nānanubhāṣaṇena tatra sāmarthyāt /
kaścitpunardūṣyameva na jānāti so 'jñānena nigṛhyate na cājñāne 'nanubhāṣaṇamavaśyaṃbhāvi dhāraṇāvator 'yānirūpaṇe vādyudīritākṣarasvarūpamātrapāṭhasambhavenānubhāṣaṇopapatteḥ /
apratibhā tvavaśyaṃ bhevad na hyasti sambhavo dūṣyaṃ na vedāsya dūṣaṇaṃ tu vedeti /
children.translated_text: But inability to respond necessarily occurs — for there is no possibility that one does not know what is to be refuted but does know the refutation of it.

children.text: tathāpi svarūpatastāvadbhedaḥ na hi yadeva dūṣaṇaviṣayamajñānamapratibhā tadeva dūṣyaviṣayamajñānaṃ tasmātsatyapyananubhāṣaṇāpratibhājñānānānāmuttarānabhidhānaphalatve tulye avāntarabhedavivakṣayā bhedenopanyāsaḥ /
children.translated_text: Even so, there is at least a difference in their intrinsic nature — for the ignorance regarding the subject of refutation that is inability to respond is not identical to the ignorance regarding what is to be refuted [itself]. Therefore, though silence, inability to respond, and ignorance are equal in having the result of non-statement of the response, they are presented separately with the intention of [showing] their intra-group distinction.
'That which has been stated three times' —
Even when stated three times, one who still does not understand — because of excessive dullness, he is not qualified for debate — this is the intent of the [phrase]. //16//

He explains: 'of the meaning of the statement that has been understood' —
He states the justification for its being a ground of defeat:
'One who does not repeat — on what basis would he state the refutation?'
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'Some [say] this is not a ground of defeat' —
(555/9) By the subsequent [statement] —
by the determination of the merits and faults of the response, the confusion or non-confusion of the respondent is established.
He analyzes this: 'by the subsequent [statement], which possesses merits and faults' —
Therefore — what purpose is there in the repeating or non-repeating? — this is the remainder.
'There is indeed someone' — in some readings [this is found].
Therein, 'there is indeed' — the two particles should be seen as introducing the sentence.
Because of the varied natures of people, someone is capable of responding but not of repeating — such a person, so long as he gives a good response,
should not be defeated merely by non-repetition.
But if non-repetition is not a ground of defeat, then one who begins to repeat but does not repeat anything [at all], while giving a good response, would not be defeated — therefore he says:
'But one who, having begun, does not carry through — yet gives a good response — for him, it would be mere mockery caused by [his] ability, but not the destruction of [his status as] a truth-speaker' — this is the meaning.
He resolves this very objection of the venerable [<s>Uddyotakara</s>]: 'Not, because of incomplete knowledge of the subject of the response' —
For a refutation has [its own] subject to be refuted; without stating what is to be refuted, [the refutation] cannot be stated.
Indeed, the faults of the thesis, reason, illustration, application, and conclusion cannot be established as faults without stating their own form — therefore one who does not repeat is not entitled to state the fault.
This is what was said: 'This is stated as contradictory — he does not repeat, yet he gives the response.'
One might say: the respondent need not refute everything;
by refuting just one member, the proof is [already] refuted, making the statement of other faults pointless.
Indeed, one who is dead cannot be protected from death to be killed [again]; similarly, what is [already] refuted cannot be refuted [again]. Therefore, even when there are many [things] to be refuted, [only] one [need be] refuted. And thus, if everything must be repeated, since not everything is to be refuted — for what is to be refuted is to be repeated — in repeating everything, [there would be] the two defeat-grounds of the refuter: repeating twice and repeating what need not be refuted. Therefore, repetition itself being the ground of defeat — the opposite has resulted — therefore
he says: 'because of non-undertaking' —
He analyzes this: 'this is not being undertaken.'
Previously, everything must be stated in one passage; afterwards, the response — whatever is to be refuted — should be stated by way of repetition, whereby the faults of refuting-what-need-not-be-refuted and repeating-twice would occur. Rather, the response is to be given in whatever manner [is appropriate].
For one intent on giving a response, when there is no basis for the response, it is not proper [to proceed] without it — therefore just the basis must be repeated, since the response cannot be stated without it.
Therefore, the non-repeating of just that much is silence (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>), not the non-repeating of everything — this is the meaning.
But one might say: by the prescription of inability-to-respond (<s>apratibhā</s>) as a ground of defeat, silence too is known [to be one], since it is a specific [form] of that.
For one is not defeated merely by not repeating; rather, one who does not repeat does not understand what is to be refuted, and not understanding, does not arrive at a response to it — so one is defeated by inability to respond.
Thus, since silence is a specific [form] of inability to respond, the ground-of-defeat character prescribed for inability to respond is prescribed for its specific [form] too.
Just as the property of possessing a dewlap prescribed for cows is prescribed for the piebald [cow] too — and one does not undertake a separate effort to prescribe dewlap-possessing for that [specific cow].
Here we say: first, silence is not [merely] a specific [form] of the general [category of] non-attainment of response — because of the diversity in people's capacities.
Someone, even while knowing what is to be refuted and the refutation, is unable to repeat, because of being tongue-tied in extensive speech.
Therefore, since silence is possible without inability to respond, silence is not a specific [form] of inability to respond.
Someone [else] knows the subject of the refutation and does repeat, but is deficient in arriving at the response — that person is defeated by inability to respond, not by silence — because of his capacity [to repeat] in that regard.
Someone else, again, does not even know what is to be refuted — that person is defeated by ignorance, not [by silence] — and in ignorance, silence does not necessarily follow, because for one with [good] memory, the possibility of repeating the mere letter-form uttered by the proponent enables repetition even [while not understanding the meaning].
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.17: And not understanding is ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>). //
He explains that: 'of [a statement] whose meaning has been understood by the assembly' —
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> applies here the general definition of a ground of defeat.
'From non-attainment [of the meaning], it is a ground of defeat.' //17//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.18: Non-attainment of the response is inability to respond (<s>apratibhā</s>). //

children.text: arthāntare hi nigrahasthāne prasaktānuprasaktaṃ tatsiddhyarthatāvyājenāvatārayatā na prakṛtāvajñānaṃ kriyate iha tvavajñānametāvatā bhedenopanyāsa
children.translated_text: For in the ground of defeat [called] 'shifting to another topic' (<s>arthāntara</s>), by introducing tangentially connected matters under the pretext of [their being] for the purpose of establishing [the main point], one does not show contempt for the topic at hand; but here [in <s>apratibhā</s>], contempt [is shown] — by this much there is the distinction, and [hence] the separate presentation.
Thus —

children.text: iyaṃ cāpratibhā samyaksādhanopanyāse draṣṭavyā sādhanābhāsopanyāse tu paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam // 18 //
children.translated_text: And this inability to respond should be observed [as a ground of defeat] when a correct proof is presented; but when a proof-semblance is presented, [the relevant ground of defeat is] overlooking-what-should-be-questioned (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>). //18//

He explains that:
'Of the opponent's position' —
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'by [engaging in] recitation of verses and the like, he shows contempt' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.19: Interruption of the debate because of the pretext of [attending to] business is evasion (<s>vikṣepa</s>). //

children.text:
sādhanasya dūṣaṇasya copanyāsamabhyupagamya tadavasthaḥ pratīyamāna eva prativādino dārḍhyaṃ sabhyānāṃ vā kaṭhoratvamavagamyākasmātkāryaṃ vyāsajyābhyupagatāṃ kathāṃ vyavacchinatti tatra vikṣepo nāma nigrahasthānam /
tadanenāpratibhayā tūṣṇīṃbhāvo 'pi saṃgṛhīto veditavyaḥ /
kāryavyāsaṅgasyābhyupagatakathāvicchedamātropalakṣaṇatvāt /
na cedamarthāntaraṃ tatra prakṛtameva sādhayāmīti vyājena prasaktānuprasaktāvatāreṇa kathāvicchedābhāvād
iha tu kathāvicchedāt /
na cāsya hetvābhāseṣvantarbhāvaḥ /
na hi vikṣepasyānyatamaliṅgadharmānuvidhānaṃ nāpi prakṛtasādhyasiddhaye prayogo yena hetvābhāsaḥ syāt /
na ca vādino vikṣepo hetvābhāsaḥ /
anantaraṃ kathāmamyupatyaiva hetumanabhidhāyāpasāraṇāt /
yadi cāyaṃ samyañcaṃ hetumabhidhāya tatsamarthanāsamartho 'pasaret kimetāvatā na nigṛhyeta hetvābhāsena vā nigṛhyeta kiṃ tu vyāsaṅgādeva /
anarthakāpārthakāmyāṃ tu bhede 'sya sphuṭa eva /
na hyatrāsamānasaṃketaḥ pratipādako yenānarthakaḥ syāt /
nāpīha padāni vākyāni vā paurvāparyeṇāsambandhāni yenāpārthakaḥ syāt /
na cāvajñānaṃ yenāpratibhā bhavet /
tasmādvikṣepaḥ pṛthaṅ nigrahasthānamiti siddham
// 19 //
children.translated_text:
Having accepted the presentation of the proof and refutation, remaining in the same state, and being perceived [as such] — perceiving the firmness of the respondent or the harshness of the assembly-members — suddenly inventing some business, he interrupts the accepted debate. Therein, evasion (<s>vikṣepa</s>) is the ground of defeat.
By this, silence caused by inability to respond too should be understood as included.
Because the pretext of business is merely indicative of any interruption of the accepted debate.
Nor is this [the same as] 'shifting to another topic' (<s>arthāntara</s>) — because there, under the pretext of 'I am proving the very topic at hand,' there is no interruption of the debate through the introduction of tangentially connected matters;
but here, there is interruption of the debate.
Nor does this fall under the semblances of reasons —
for evasion does not conform to any characteristic of a reason, nor is it employed for establishing the thesis in question, such that it would be a semblance of a reason.
Nor is the proponent's evasion a semblance of a reason —
because he departs immediately after accepting the debate, without even stating a reason.
And if this person, having stated a correct reason and being incapable of defending it, departs — would he not be defeated just by this much, or would he be defeated by a semblance of a reason? Rather, [he is defeated] precisely by the pretext [of business].
And regarding the meaningless (<s>anarthaka</s>) and incoherent (<s>apārthaka</s>), the difference from this [evasion] is clear —
for here there is no conventional expression of a different [community] such that it would be meaningless;
nor are the words or sentences here unconnected in sequence such that it would be incoherent;
nor is there contempt such that it would be inability to respond.
Therefore, evasion is a separate ground of defeat — this is established. //19//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.20: From the acceptance of a fault in one's own position, the consequence of a [similar] fault in the opponent's position is acceptance of the opponent's position (<s>matānujñā</s>). //

children.text:
vyācaṣṭe yaḥ pareṇa deśita doṣaṃ svapakṣe 'bhyupagamya /
kathaṃ jñāyate abhyupagamyataityata
āha /
anuddhṛtyeti /
anabhyupagame 'sābuddharediti bhāvaḥ /
vārtikaṃ kiṃ tu parasvenānatisṛṣṭenādattenetyarthaḥ /
(559/13) prasaṅgavidhānānna nigrahasthānamityanya
iti /
yadi puruṣatvāccoro 'haṃ tato bhavānapi coraḥ syāt /
na ca bhavata evamiṣṭaṃ tasmāttvayaivānaikāntikatvānnāyaṃ heturiti prasaṅgaviparyayaḥ tasmānnātmanaścoratvamanenābhyupagatamiti matānujñā nāsau nigrahasthānamityarthaḥ /
nirākaroti etattu na, kasmāt ata eva /
children.translated_text: He refutes: 'But this is not [so]; why? For this very reason' —

children.text: kutaḥ ? yata evāsau uttare kartavye prasaṅgaṃ karoti ata eva nigṛhyate /
children.translated_text: Why? Because this very person who employs <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) when he should give a response — for this very reason he is defeated.

children.text: yadi hi vādī prativādinaṃ brūyātsatyamahaṃ cora eveti tadā kimanaikāntikatvaṃ śaknuyātkartum /
children.translated_text: For if the proponent were to say to the respondent 'indeed, I am truly a thief' — then how could inconclusiveness be established?

children.text: tasmātpuruṣatvaṃ na coratvahetuḥ api tu parasvenādattena sambandha ityuttare kartavye yaduttarābhāsamāha tena jñāpayati nūnamayaṃ sabhyaguttaraṃ na jānāti samyaguttarājñānānnigṛhyate, taccottarāparijñānaṃ matānujñādvāpareṇodbhāvyamānaṃ matānujñetyucyate // 20 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, person-hood is not the reason for thief-hood; rather, the connection with what belongs to another, not given [to one] — when this should be stated as the response, the fact that he states a semblance of a response reveals that 'surely this person does not know the good response from the assembly.' He is defeated because of not knowing the correct response, and that non-knowledge of the response, being revealed through the medium of acceptance of the opponent's position (<s>matānujñā</s>) as demonstrated by the opponent, is called <s>matānujñā</s>. //20//

He explains: 'one who, having accepted the fault pointed out by the opponent in his own position' —
How is it known that he accepts [it]? — therefore he says:
'By not dispelling [it]' —
In non-acceptance, he would dispel [it] — this is the import.
The <s>Vārttika</s> [reads]: 'But by [taking what] belongs to another, not granted, not given' — this is the meaning.
(559/13) 'Because of the method of <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio), [it is] not a ground of defeat' — says another.
'If I am a thief because of being a person, then you too would be a thief.
And this is not what you wish. Therefore, by your own [reasoning], because of inconclusiveness, this is not a [valid] reason' — this is the reversal of the reductio. Therefore, one's own thief-hood is not accepted by this — so [this] acceptance of the opponent's position is not a ground of defeat — this is the meaning.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.21: Non-defeat of one who has incurred a ground of defeat is overlooking-what-should-be-questioned (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>). //

children.text:
vyācaṣṭe paryanuyojyo nāmeti /
nigrahasyopapattiḥ pramāṇataḥ siddhistayetyarthaḥ /
etattu na tāvadvādinodbhāvanīyaṃ na hyasau svasvasādhanāvadyamanunmatta udbhāvayati,
nāpi prativādinā na hyanunmatta ātmānamātmanā nigṛhṇāti /
api tu paryanuyojyaṃ jānānaḥ kasmādupekṣatetasmātsabhāpanitā vādiprativādibhyāmanuyuktayā vā pariṣadā tannigrahasthānamudbhāvanīyam /
atra ca tattvanirṇayāvasāne vāde dvayorapi nigrahātpariṣadeva vijayate jalpavitaṇḍayośca tattvānapekṣaṃ puruṣasāmarthyaparīkṣaṇapravṛttayoḥ prativādī nigṛhyate /
sādhanābhāsavādinā 'pi vādinā sphuratā prativādī stambhito yataḥ samyaksādhanopanyāso vihitaḥ /
prativādina
uttarāpratipattirapratibhā sādhanābhāsopanyāse ca uttarāpratipattiḥ paryanuyojyopekṣaṇamiti viśeṣaḥ /
vārtikaṃ nānyavacanādityeke /
yatra prativādī tūṣṇīṃbhavati tatra tūṣṇīmbhāvenaiva vādina uttarānarhatāṃ darśaya nnasya sādhanābhāsavāditāṃ sūcayati yatrāsya doṣodbhāvanaṃ samyagdoṣamanuktvā karoti tatrāpyasau duṣṭamuttaraṃ dadattatsādhanadoṣameva sūcayati /
upadiśanti hi vṛddhāḥ duṣṭe hi sādhane dṛṣṭottaraṃ deyamiti /
tasmādavacane 'nyavacane vā na paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ nigrahasthānamubhayathā 'pyanupekṣaṇādityarthaḥ /
dūṣayati tacca neti /
(560/1) sādhanasya hi samyañcaṃ doṣaṃ jānan tameva brūyāt /
so 'yaṃ prāptāvasaro 'bruvan vibruvan vā nūnaṃ na samyañjaṃ doṣa jānāti /
niścitapramāṇabhāvasya puruṣasyeṅgitādibhirabhiprāyaḥpa sūcyate na tvaniścitapramāṇabhāvasya /
yathā'huḥ /
śrutismṛtyatirekeṇa yuktajalpākabhāṣitam /
tadyathāśrati duṣṭaṃ ced duṣṭamevāvadhāryatām
// iti suṣṭhūktaṃ jānāno 'pyayaṃ kimarthamanyad bravītīti// 21 //
children.translated_text:
He explains: "what is to be questioned" —
The tenability of defeat — its establishment through the means of valid knowledge — this is the meaning.
But this is not to be raised by the proponent, for one who is not insane does not expose the fault in his own proof;
nor [is it to be raised] by the respondent, for one who is not insane does not defeat himself by himself.
Rather, one who knows what should be questioned — why does he overlook it? Therefore, it should be raised by the moderator of the assembly appointed [to judge] between the proponent and respondent, or by the assembly when asked.
And here, in a <s>vāda</s> (truth-seeking debate), at the conclusion of the determination of truth, because both are defeated, the assembly alone is victorious; but in <s>jalpa</s> (sophistic debate) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive debate), where [the disputants] are engaged in testing personal ability without regard for truth, the respondent is defeated.
Even when a proponent who employs fallacious proofs is brilliant, the respondent is still blocked — because the presentation of a correct proof has been prescribed.
For the respondent,
the failure to respond is <s>apratibhā</s> (inability to respond); but in the case of the presentation of a fallacious proof, the failure to respond [is called] overlooking what should be questioned (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>) — this is the distinction.
The <s>Vārttika</s>: "Some [say] not from stating something else."
Where the respondent remains silent, there, by his very silence, he indicates that the proponent's [proof] does not deserve a reply, [thereby] hinting that [the proponent] employs fallacious proofs. Where [the respondent] raises faults without stating the correct fault, there too, by giving a faulty reply, he hints at the very fault in the proof.
For the elders teach: 'When the proof is faulty, the seen [i.e., well-known] reply should be given.'
Therefore, whether by not speaking or by speaking something else, there is no overlooking of what should be questioned as a ground for defeat — because in either case there is no overlooking — this is the meaning.
He criticizes: "And that is not so" —
(560/1) For one who knows the correct fault in the proof should state just that.
This person, having the opportunity, either not speaking or speaking wrongly — surely does not know the correct fault.
The intention of a person who has ascertained the means of valid knowledge is indicated by gestures and the like, but not [the intention] of one who has not ascertained the means of valid knowledge.
As they say:
'What is spoken by a clever debater beyond <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>,
if that is faulty when heard, let it be ascertained as faulty indeed.'
// Even though he knows [the proof] is well-stated, why does he say something else? // //21//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.22: Imputing a ground of defeat where there is no ground of defeat is questioning what should not be questioned (<s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s>). //

children.text:
na cāyamapratibhāto na bhidyate /
sā hyunarāpratipattiriyaṃ tvanuttarasyaivottaratvena
(vi) pratipattiriti mahān viśeṣaḥ /
anenaiva sarvā jātayo nigrahasthānatvena saṃgṛhītā bhavanti /
na ca hetvābhāsānāmito na bhedaḥ
te hi vādino nigrahasthānamayaṃ tu prativādina
iti mahānviśeṣaḥ /
ata eva bhavatāmapi gāthā /
'asādhanāṅgaṃ vacanamadoṣodbhāvanaṃ tayoḥ /
nigrahasthānamanyattu na yuktamiti neṣyate iti /
apratibhāyā eva prasajyapratiṣedhātmikāyā asyā niranuyojyānuyogasya bhede darśayati bhāṣyakāraḥ /
nigrahasthānalakṣaṇasya mithyādhyavasāyā tsamāropādityarthaḥ /
sugamaṃ vārtikam
// 22 //
children.translated_text:
And this is not undifferentiated from <s>apratibhā</s> (inability to respond).
For that [apratibhā] is the failure to respond; but this [niranuyojyānuyoga] is the cognition of what is not a reply as being a reply — this is a great distinction.
By this alone, all the <s>jātis</s> (futile rejoinders) are comprehended as being grounds of defeat.
Nor is there no distinction of the fallacious reasons from this;
for those [fallacious reasons] are grounds of defeat for the proponent, but this [niranuyojyānuyoga is a ground of defeat] for the respondent — this is a great distinction.
Therefore, even your verse [states]:
'A statement that is not a component of proof, and the non-demonstration of defects in those [proofs] —
these are grounds of defeat; anything else is not considered proper.'
The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> shows the difference of this <s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s> from <s>apratibhā</s>, which has the character of a simple negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>):
"From the attribution of the defining characteristic of a ground of defeat through erroneous determination" — this is the meaning.
The <s>Vārttika</s> is easy to understand.
//22//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.23: Having accepted a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine), a discourse involving unrestricted [application] is <s>apasiddhānta</s> (self-contradictory doctrine). //

children.text:
abhyupetpayetyasya vyākhyānaṃ kasya cidarthasya tathābhāvaṃ pratijñāyeti /
pratijñātārthavipayaryāditi /
abhyupetārthaviparyayātsiddhāntaviparyayādityarthaḥ /
tadetadaniyamādityasya vyākhyānam /
tatra sāṃkhyīyaṃ siddhāntamāha /
yathā na saditi /
tasya paryāyāntareṇa kathanaṃ na sata itañ nāsidātmānamityasya paryāyāntareṇa vivaraṇaṃ nāsadutpadyata iti /
so 'yaṃ siddhāntaḥ sāṃkhyānāṃ tamabhyupetya tadviparyayātkathāprasaṅgamāha svapakṣaṃ vyavasthāpayati /
pakṣāvasthānaṃ darśayati /
ekā prakṛtirvyaktasyopalabhyamānasyārthajātasya yukteti pratijñā /
vikārāṇāmiti vyaktasyaivānuvādaḥ /
anvayadarśanāditi hetuḥ /
mṛdanvitānāmiti sādharmyodāharaṇaṃ tathā yaṃ 'vyaktabhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvito gṛhyate ityupanayaḥ /
nigamanamāha tasmātsamanvayadarśanādviśvavyaktasya kairityapekṣāyāmuttaraṃ sukhādibhiriti /
ekaprakṛtiḥ sarvo vikāra iti seyaṃ kathā /
siddhāntamabhyupettyaivamuktavān sāṃkhyo naiyāyikena paryanuyujyate /
dūṣaṇāya pṛcchyate /
atha prakṛtirvikāpara iti kathaṃ lakṣitavyamiti /
sa evaṃ naiyāyikena pṛṣṭaḥ sāṃkhya uttaramāha yasyāvasthitasya mṛdāderdharmāntaranivṛttau śarāvavināśe yaddharmāntaraṃ maṇimādi pravartate asadeva jāyate sā prakṛtirmṛdādi /
yaddharmāntaraṃ nivartate pravartate vā sa vikāra iti /
etāsminnudāharaṇe 'pasiddhāntaṃ yojayati /
soyaṃ pratijñātārthasya siddhāntārthasya vādī viparyayādaniyamātkathāṃ prasañjayati pratijñātaḥ siddhāntaḥ khalvanena nāsadāvirbhavatīti utpadyate na sattiro bhavatīti na vinaśyatīti /
tathā 'pi kasmādanena siddhānto bādhyate atha siddhāntenaiva kasmānna bādhyataityata āha /
sadasatośceti /
idaṃ hi laukikaṃ pramāṇasiddhaṃ siddhāntastvabhyupagamamātrasiddho 'prāmāṇikaḥ
tasmādanena siddhānto balavatā bādhyate /
tadetanmṛddharmāṇāmapi na syāditi /
na kevalaṃ prekṣāvatāṃ kartṝṇāmapi tu saddharmāṇāmapyutpādavināśau pravṛttyunaparamau dṛśyamānau na syātāmityarthaḥ /
evaṃ pratyavasthitaḥ sāṃkhyonaiyāyikena pṛṣṭo yadyasata ātmalābhaṃ sataścātmahānamabhyupa iti tato 'syāpasiddhānto bhavati /
atha nābhyupaiti pakṣo 'sya na siddhyati /
vikāro hyanena pakṣīkṛta ekaprakṛtitvena tatra vikārāṇāmanirūpaṇāt tadabhāve na pratijñārtho na ca hetvarthaḥ āśrayāsiddhatvāt /
nanvevaṃ pratijñātārthavirodhitvātsato nirodhasyāsataścotpādasya hetvābhāsa
eva nigrahasthānaṃ bhavet /
pratijñāvirodho vetyāśaṅkya vārtikakāra āha /
pratijñātārthavyatirekeṇeti /
na hyatraikaprakṛtayo vikārāḥ ekaprakṛtikatvādityayaṃ hetuḥ sādhyaviruddhena vyāpta udbhāvito yena viruddho bhavet /
nāpyekaprakṛtikatvaṃ vikārāṇāṃ śabdato viruddhaṃ samanvayena hetunā yena pratijñāvirodho bhavet /
vaibhavamātreṇa ca pratijñāhetvorvirodha
ityatroktaṃ vārtikakṛtā svasiddhāntaspaya gotvārdernityatvavirodhādvirodha

children.translated_text: — etc.

children.text: api ca tatra balavatā siddhāntenānaikāntikadeśanā bādhyate iha tu siddhānta eva bādhyate /
children.translated_text: Moreover, there [in the contradiction of thesis], the teaching of inconclusiveness is sublated by the stronger <s>siddhānta</s>; but here [in <s>apasiddhānta</s>], it is the <s>siddhānta</s> itself that is sublated.
Being weaker — thus there is no redundancy of the example either.

children.text: tasmādyatra pratijñārthena virodhaḥ tatra viruddho hetvābhāsaḥ pratijñāvirodho vā iha tu pratijñārthavyatirekeṇābhyupagamāntareṇa virodha iti puruṣasya pūrvāparaviruddhārthābhidhāyino 'sāmarthyānnigrahasthānaṃ jalpavitaṇḍayoriti siddham // 23 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, where there is contradiction with the thesis-object, there [the fault is] a contradictory fallacious reason or a contradiction of the thesis; but here, the contradiction is with an acceptance apart from the thesis-object — therefore, because of the incapacity of the person who asserts mutually contradictory meanings in his earlier and later [statements], this is the ground of defeat in <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> — this is established. //23//

The explanation of 'having accepted' is: 'having asserted the truth of some object.'
'Because of the reversal of the asserted object' —
Because of the reversal of the accepted object — because of the reversal of the <s>siddhānta</s> — this is the meaning.
This is the explanation of 'because of unrestricted [application].'
Therein, he states the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine:
'As, for instance, "nothing arises from non-being"' —
The paraphrase of this [in other words] — of 'nothing arises from non-being' — the elucidation in alternative phrasing is: 'non-being does not come into being.'
This is the <s>siddhānta</s> of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>. Having accepted that, he states the discourse that leads to its reversal. He establishes his own thesis.
He shows the thesis-position:
The thesis is: 'There is one <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) of the manifest — of the class of perceived objects.'
'Of the modifications' — is merely a restatement of the manifest.
'Because of the observation of uniformity' — is the reason.
'Of those pervaded by clay' — is the positive example through similarity. Similarly, 'that which is the manifest variety — pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion — is grasped' — this is the application (<s>upanaya</s>).
He states the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>): 'Therefore, because of the observation of uniformity in all manifest [things] — when the question arises "by which?" — the answer is "by pleasure and the like."'
'All modification has one <s>Prakṛti</s>' — this is the discourse.
Having accepted the <s>siddhānta</s>, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, having spoken thus, is questioned by the <s>Naiyāyika</s>.
He is asked for the purpose of refutation:
'Now, how is <s>Prakṛti</s> to be distinguished from modification?'
Thus questioned by the <s>Naiyāyika</s>, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> gives the answer: 'That which is established — such as clay and the like — when one property ceases — upon the destruction of the bowl — and another property arises — [such as] a gem and the like — what arises is nothing but non-being that comes into being — that is <s>Prakṛti</s>, [namely] clay and the like.
That property which ceases or arises — that is modification.'
He applies the <s>apasiddhānta</s> to this example:
This proponent, by the unrestricted [application], brings about a discourse that reverses his asserted object — the <s>siddhānta</s>-object. For the <s>siddhānta</s> accepted by him is: 'Non-being does not come into being' — [i.e.,] it does not originate; and 'Being does not cease' — [i.e.,] it does not perish.
Nevertheless, why is his <s>siddhānta</s> contradicted by this? Why is it not rather not contradicted by the <s>siddhānta</s> itself? — to this he says:
'Of being and non-being' —
For this — [the arising and perishing of being and non-being] — is worldly, established by means of valid knowledge; but the <s>siddhānta</s> is established merely by acceptance, not by means of valid knowledge.
Therefore, this <s>siddhānta</s> is contradicted by that which is stronger.
This very [point] — that 'the properties of clay too would not exist' —
The meaning is: not only of discerning agents, but of real properties too — the origination and perishing, [i.e.,] the arising and cessation that are observed — would not exist.
Thus counter-argued, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, when asked by the <s>Naiyāyika</s>: 'If you accept the self-acquisition of non-being and the self-loss of being' — then he incurs <s>apasiddhānta</s>.
If he does not accept [this], his thesis is not established.
For modification has been posited by him as having one <s>Prakṛti</s> — and therein, since the modifications are not analyzed, in their absence there is neither the thesis-meaning nor the reason-meaning, because of the unestablishedness of the substratum.
Now, if thus the contradiction with the asserted thesis-object [constitutes a] fallacious reason —
that would be a ground of defeat. Or it would be a contradiction of the thesis — anticipating this, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> says:
'Apart from the asserted thesis-object' —
For here, 'all modifications have one <s>Prakṛti</s>, because of having one <s>Prakṛti</s>' — this reason is not raised as pervaded by what contradicts the provable, such that it would be a contradictory [reason].
Nor is the having-one-<s>Prakṛti</s> of modifications contradicted verbally by the reason through [positive] uniformity, such that there would be a contradiction of the thesis.
And merely by implication, the contradiction of thesis and reason —
regarding this, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> has said in the [section on] 'the contradiction of [cow-ness] established in one's own <s>siddhānta</s> with eternality'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.24: And the fallacious reasons are as previously stated. //

children.text:
vyācaṣṭe hetvābhāmāśceti /
yadyanuktamapi kiṃ cidavaśiṣyate nigrahasthānaṃ taccakāreṇa samucceyam /
yathoktā iti sūtrāvayavanirākaraṇīyāmāśaṅkāmāha /
kiṃ punarlakṣaṇāntarayogāddhetvābhāsānigrahasthānatāmāpadyante yathā pramāṇāni prameyatvaṃ teṣāmeva pratyakṣādīnāmupalabdhisādhanatvena lakṣyamāṇānāṃ pramāṇatvaṃ pramāvyāpyatayā prameyatvaṃ lakṣaṇāntareṇa pramāṇāni prameyatvamāpadyanta iti śaṅkāyāḥ sambhavādata āha bhagavān sūtrakāraḥ
yathoktā iti /
sakalaśāstrārthamupasaṃharati /
ta ime pramāṇādaya uddiṣṭā lakṣitāḥ parīkṣitāśceti /
itiḥ śāstrapaparisamāptau /
vārtikakāraḥ saṃgṛhṇāti jātīnāṃ saprapañcānāmiti /

children.translated_text: "the definition of a ground of defeat" —

children.text: samāsena jātīnāmapi prativādinigrahasthāne 'sti niveśa iti sūcayati /
children.translated_text: He indicates in brief that the <s>jātis</s> too are included within the grounds of defeat for the respondent.
"And the conclusion of the treatise" —

children.text: ta ime pramāṇādaya uddiṣṭā ityanena kṛta ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: "These — the means of valid knowledge and the rest — have been enumerated" — by this, [the word] 'done' is meant — this is the meaning. //

He explains: 'and the fallacious reasons' —
If some ground of defeat remains unstated, it should be included by the [conjunction] 'and.'
'As previously stated' — he states the doubt that should be dispelled by this portion of the <s>sūtra</s>:
'Do the fallacious reasons perhaps acquire the status of grounds of defeat through having another defining characteristic?' — just as the means of valid knowledge [acquire] the status of objects of valid knowledge — for perception and the like, which are defined as means of valid knowledge by their nature as instruments of apprehension, [also acquire] the status of objects of valid knowledge (<s>prameyatva</s>) through another defining characteristic — because of the possibility of this doubt, the venerable <s>sūtrakāra</s> says:
'As previously stated.'
He concludes the meaning of the entire treatise:
'These — the means of valid knowledge and the rest — have been enumerated, defined, and examined.'
The [particle] 'iti' [marks] the completion of the treatise.
The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> summarizes: 'of the <s>jātis</s> together with their elaboration' —

Whatever <s>puṇya</s> (merit) has been obtained — from the rescue of the aged cows of <s>Uddyotakara</s>, mired in the mud of the difficult-to-cross swamp. //1//
Upon <s>Vṛṣaketu</s> (Śiva), the causeway across the ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>, the cause of the cessation of all suffering —
the entire fruit of this [work] is offered to Him; may the Lord be pleased. //2//
Fragrant with the blossoming of knowledge of reality, containing many hidden meanings,
this [commentary], whose fruit is the nectar of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), whose beautiful sprouts are well-spoken words,
whose great roots are the <s>Nyāya</s> [principles] consisting of perception, testimony, and scripture —
may this delightful creeper of the <s>Ṭīkā</s> (commentary) be the <s>Nandinī</s> (joy-giving cow) for the bee-like meritorious [scholars]. //3//
O cruel ones! This salutation is offered, this tribute is given;
my body [is here] — strike as you please.
I [only] entreat: do not defile the rivers of fame of others
with showers of dust made of false words. //4//
Thus, in the <s>Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Miśra Vācaspati</s>,
the fifth chapter is completed. //
And this treatise is completed. //
May there be auspiciousness! //
